chapters.title: The Festival of Aadi
paragraphs: We invite our readers to embark with us, for a short while, upon a journey in the boat of imagination, drifting upon the endless flood of time. Let us swiftly traverse centuries at the rate of a hundred years per second, and travel back to an era one thousand and fifty-eight years before today (written in 1950).

In the southern part of Thirumunaippadi, the land that lies between Thondai Nadu and Chola Nadu, two leagues west of the sacred Chidambaram temple, there stretches a vast lake, spreading out like a surging sea. This is the Veeranarayana Lake. It measures a league and a half from south to north, and half a league from east to west. Over the passage of time, its name has been shortened, and in these days it is known as the “Veeranarayanam Lake.”

Whoever beholds the Veeranarayana Lake during the months of Aadi and Avani, when the fresh floods pour in and the waters brim and overflow, cannot help but feel a surge of pride and wonder at the marvelous deeds accomplished by our ancient Tamil forebears. Did our ancestors act only for their own welfare and that of their contemporaries? Did they not also perform great works that would benefit the countless generations yet to come, who would be born and live in this beloved motherland, age after age?

On the eighteenth day of the month of Aadi, as evening approached, a young warrior rode his horse along the banks of the Veeranarayana Lake, which spread out before him like a restless sea. He belonged to the illustrious Vaanar clan, famed in the martial history of Tamilakam. His name was Vallavarayan Vandiyathevan. His horse, weary from a long journey, now walked at a slow, tired pace. Yet the young warrior was unconcerned about his steed’s fatigue; his heart was utterly captivated by the boundless beauty of the Veeranarayana Lake.

On the day of Aadi Perukku, the rivers of Chola Nadu traditionally overflow their banks, their waters touching both shores. The lakes that draw water from these rivers also fill to the brim, their waves lapping at the very crest of their banks. From the river known as Vadakaveri to devotees, and as Kollidam to the common folk, water flowed through the Vadavaru and poured into the Veeranarayana Lake, transforming it into a churning sea. Through the seventy-four sluices of the lake, the water gushed forth, spreading prosperity to the lands all around for many miles. With the waters of this lake... As far as the eye could see, the fields were alive with the bustle of ploughing, planting, and the fragrance of fresh earth. The men who tilled the land and the women who planted the young rice sang sweet songs here and there, their voices ringing with joy. Listening to these melodies, Vandiyathevan did not urge on his weary horse but let it proceed at a gentle pace.

Ever since he had ascended the bund of the great lake, he had been counting the canals, curious to know whether it was true that there were seventy-four channels feeding into this reservoir. As he journeyed for about a mile and a half along the massive embankment, he had already counted seventy canals.

Ah! What a magnificent lake this was! How great its length, how vast its breadth! Compared to this, all the lakes built by the Pallava emperors in Thondai Nadu seemed mere ponds. Was it not the son of Parantaka, the conqueror of Madurai, Prince Rajaditya, who conceived of this sea-like reservoir to harness the waters of the northern Kaveri that would otherwise flow wastefully into the ocean? Did he not dream of it and then bring it to reality? What a visionary he must have been! Who could match him in valor? Was it not he who, at the battle of Takkolam, led the charge atop an elephant, fought at the very front, and fell heroically, bearing the enemy’s spear in his chest? Was it not for this that he became known as “the lord who slept upon the elephant” and attained the heaven of heroes?

The kings of this Chola dynasty were truly wondrous! As great in virtue as in valor, as devout as they were righteous. The more Vandiyathevan thought of the fortune that had brought him into the friendship of such a royal house, the more his shoulders swelled with pride. The western wind, blowing fiercely, sent waves crashing against the banks of the Veera Narayana Lake, and his heart, too, surged with pride and elation.

Thus musing, Vandiyathevan reached the southern edge of the Veera Narayana Lake. There he saw the Vadavaru, which branched off from the northern Kaveri, flowing into the lake. For some distance from the embankment, the lake’s inner shore sloped gently. To prevent the banks from eroding when the floods arrived, karuvelam and vilva trees had been planted and nurtured along the slope. Thick bamboo grew along the water’s edge. From the southwest, the floodwaters of the Vadavaru, flanked by rows of trees on both sides, merged with the lake—a sight which, from a little distance, looked like a beautiful painting.
Vandiyathevan beheld yet more scenes that heightened the sweetness and exuberance of this enchanting spectacle.

Was it not the festival day of the eighteenth flood? From the neighboring villages, people arrived in throngs, pulling along palanquins fashioned from the green stems of young coconut palms. Men and women, children and even a few elders, all bedecked in new garments and adorned in myriad ornaments, streamed in together. The women’s hair was lavishly decorated with clusters of flowers—thazhamboo, sevandhi, jasmine, mullai, iruvatchi, champakam, and more.

Many families had come carrying pots of festive rice and delicacies. Some stood at the edge of the lake, setting their food upon areca palm leaves and eating by the water. A few bold souls waded a little distance into the water, reached the bank of the Vadavaru river, and ate their meal standing there. Some children, after finishing their meal, tossed the areca leaves into the mouth of the canal, and burst into applause and laughter as the leaves floated swiftly along the current, swept out of the lake.

Among the men, a few mischievous fellows slyly plucked the flowers from their lovers’ hair and, without their knowledge, set them afloat at the canal’s edge, delighting as they watched the blossoms drift across to the far side of the lake.

Vallavarayan lingered there for a while, taking in all these sights. He listened intently to the sweet voices of some women standing nearby, singing. They sang folk songs, flood songs, and performed dances—kummi, sindhu, and more.

“The Vadavaru swells and surges, Come and see, O dwellers of the hamlet! The floodwaters rush and race, Come, behold the spectacle, O friends! The Kaveri rolls and roars, Come and witness, O companions!”
Such flood songs flowed into Vandiyathevan’s ears like a flood of delight.

Others sang songs extolling the valor and glory of the kings of the Chola dynasty. Some women sang of the bravery of Vijayalaya Cholan, who had fought in thirty-three battles and adorned his body with ninety-six wounds as ornaments.

Another woman, in a melodious voice, praised the valor of his son, Aditya Cholan, and sang of how he had built sixty-four Shiva temples from the source of the Kaveri River to the place where it meets the sea.

Yet another woman, her voice brimming with enthusiasm, sang of the true fame of Aditya’s son, Parantaka Chola Maharaja, who had defeated the Pandyas, Pallavas, and Cheras, sent his armies to Lanka, and planted the flag of victory there.
As each woman sang, many people gathered around her to listen. From time to time, they expressed their joy by exclaiming, “Ah! Ah!” in delight.

Vandiyathevan, who was listening to their songs while still seated on his horse, caught the attention of an old woman. “Young man! It seems you have come from a great distance. You must be tired! Get down from your horse and have some gruel with us!” she called.

At once, several young maidens turned to look at our youthful traveler. They whispered secretly among themselves about his appearance and burst into peals of laughter. Embarrassment and delight tugged at Vandiyathevan’s heart in equal measure. For a moment, he wondered if he should dismount and accept the food the old woman offered. If he did, it was certain that the young women standing there would surround him, tease him, and laugh at his expense. But so what? Was it an easy thing to see so many beautiful women gathered in one place? Even if they laughed at him, that laughter would sound like celestial music to his ears. To Vandiyathevan’s youthful eyes, all the maidens standing by the lakeshore appeared as heavenly dancers, as divine nymphs!

But at that very moment, a scene unfolding in the southwestern direction, along the flow of the Vadavaru River, made him hesitate. Seven or eight large boats, their white sails unfurled, were gliding over the water like swans spreading their silver wings, driven swiftly by the upper wind.
All the people who had been engaged in various amusements on the lakeshore now turned eagerly to watch the approaching boats.
Among those boats, one sped ahead of the rest and reached the northern corner of the lakeshore first. In that boat were several tall, broad-shouldered warriors, holding sharp, gleaming spears.

Some among them leapt down onto the banks of the lake and, turning to the people gathered there, shouted, “Go! Move along!” They herded the crowd away, not allowing them to linger, so the people hastily gathered their vessels and belongings and began to climb up the bank in a hurry.

Vandiyathevan could not make sense of any of this. Who were these soldiers? Who were those coming in the boats with the canopies behind them? Where did they come from? Could they perhaps belong to the royal family?

Vallavarayan approached an elderly man standing on the bank, leaning on a staff. “Sir! Whose men are these soldiers? And those boats coming behind, looking like a flock of swans—who do they belong to? Why are these soldiers driving the people away? And why are the people fleeing?” he asked, piling question upon question.
“Young man! Don’t you know? Look there, in the middle of those boats, a flag is flying! Can you see what’s on it?” said the old man.
“It looks like a palmyra tree,” replied Vandiyathevan.
“It is a palmyra tree! Don’t you know the palmyra flag belongs to the Pazhuvettaraiyars?”
“Is the great warrior Pazhuvettaraiyar coming?” Vandiyathevan asked, startled.
“It must be so; who else would come bearing the palmyra flag raised high?” said the old man.

Vallavarayan’s eyes widened in boundless wonder as he gazed in the direction from which the boats approached. He had heard much about the Pazhuvettaraiyars. Who in the land had not? From Eelam in the south to Kalinga in the north, the names of the elder and younger Pazhuvettaraiyars were renowned. Their city, Pazhuvur, lay near Uraiyur, on the northern bank of the river Kaveri. Since the time of Vijayalaya Cholan, the Pazhuvettaraiyar clan had been famed for their valor. Their family had long maintained ties of alliance and exchange with the Chola royal house. Because of this, and owing to their ancient lineage and martial glory, the Pazhuvettaraiyars enjoyed all the privileges of royalty. They even possessed the right to bear their own flag.

Of the two Pazhuvettaraiyars now living, the elder had fought in twenty-four battles. In his time, he was famed throughout Chola country as a warrior without equal. Now, being over fifty years of age, he... He never went directly to the battlefields. Yet, he held some of the most exalted positions in the Chola kingdom. He was the Treasurer of the Chola Empire; the Keeper of the Granaries; both the royal treasury and the royal granaries were under his authority. He possessed the power to levy and collect taxes as required by the needs of the state. He had the right to command any minor king, district chief, or great landlord, saying, “This year, you must pay this much in tribute,” and to collect it. Therefore, after Emperor Sundara Chola himself, the most powerful man in the Chola Empire at this time was none other than Pazhuvettarayar.

A longing to see such a mighty hero, a man of boundless strength and authority, surged in Vandiyathevan’s heart. But at the same time, he remembered the confidential message that Prince Aditya Karikalan had entrusted to him in the new golden palace at Kanchi.

“Vandiyatheva! I know well that you are a pure-hearted warrior. Moreover, I trust that you are a man of good sense, and that is why I am entrusting you with this great responsibility. Of the two letters I give you, one must be delivered to my father, the Emperor, and the other to my younger sister, the Princess. I have heard many things about the high officials of the kingdom in Tanjore. Therefore, no one must know the message I am sending. No matter how important they are, no one should know that you are carrying a letter from me. You must not get into any quarrels along the way. It is not enough that you yourself avoid getting into fights; even if others try to drag you into a brawl, you must not get caught up in it. I know your valor well. You have proved it many times. So, even if you avoid a fight, it will not diminish your honor in the least. Most importantly, you must be extremely cautious with the Pazhuvettarayars and with my younger uncle, Madurantaka. They must not even know who you are! Under no circumstances must they learn why you have come!”

Thus spoke Aditya Karikalan, the crown prince of the Chola Empire and Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Armies. He had also repeatedly instructed Vandiyathevan on how he should conduct himself. Remembering all this, Vallavarayan suppressed his eagerness to meet Pazhuvettarayar. He spurred his horse and tried to ride faster. But no matter how much he urged it on, the tired horse moved only slowly. He resolved within himself that tonight he would stay at the Kadambur Samburayar’s palace, and in the morning, when he set out again, he would secure a better horse.

The sun blazed fiercely, as if determined to scorch the earth. The red-hot rays poured down relentlessly, making the very dust on the road shimmer and dance. The river, which once flowed in full spate, now lay shriveled, its bed cracked and parched, with only a few scattered pools of water reflecting the sky like broken mirrors.

On that sweltering Aadi festival day, not a soul could be seen on the long, winding road that ran along the banks of the Veeranarayana Lake. The trees that lined the path drooped in exhaustion, their leaves wilted and lifeless. Even the birds had retreated into the deepest shade, silent and still.

But suddenly, a lone horseman appeared in the distance, riding at a brisk pace. Dust rose in clouds beneath the horse’s hooves, swirling around the rider like a cloak. As he drew nearer, his features became clearer—a young man, tall and well-built, with sharp eyes that sparkled with intelligence and mischief. His clothes, though travel-stained, hinted at noble origins. A sword hung at his side, and a spear was slung across his back.
This was Vandiyathevan of the Vaanar clan, setting out on a journey that would change the fate of the Chola empire.

chapters.title: Azhwarkkadiyan Nambi
paragraphs: As Vandiyathevan guided his horse down from the bank of the lake and onto the southern path, his heart danced with joy, like a boat swaying upon the waves. The exuberance that had lain hidden deep within him now surged forth, overflowing. His inner sense whispered that the time was near when he would experience wonders unknown to any other in life. If simply approaching the Chola country filled him with such rapture, what would it be like once he crossed the Kollidam? What wealth of water and land would that Chola realm hold? What of its people and its women—how would they be? How many rivers, how many lakes, how many sparkling streams? What vision would the famed Ponni river—celebrated in poetry and epic—present to his eyes? How enchanting would be the banks lined with blossoming punnai, konnai, and kadamba trees, swaying in the breeze? How delightful the sight of waterlilies and kumudams beckoning from the streams, and red lotuses blooming in welcome? How beautiful the wondrous temples, adorned with exquisite carvings, that the Chola lineage—devotees of Shiva—had raised on both banks of the Kaveri?

Ah! Pazhaiyarai city! The capital of the Chola kings! The city that had reduced Poompuhar and Uraiyur to mere villages! What would its mansions and towers, its gopurams, its barracks, its bustling market streets, its Shiva temples, and the celestial shrines of Vishnu be like? Vandiyathevan had heard that in those temples, masters of music sang the sweet verses of the Thevaram and the sacred hymns of the Thiruvaimozhi, transporting listeners to ecstasy. Soon, he would have the fortune to hear them all. And was that all? In a few days, he would attain blessings he had never even dreamed of. He was to meet, face to face, the mighty Parantaka Sundara Chola Maharaja—peerless in valor and beauty, rival to Murugan and Manmatha themselves. Was that all? He would also behold the king’s precious daughter, the incomparable jewel among women, Princess Kundavai.

Yet, he hoped that no obstacle would arise along the way. But what if one did? He had a spear in his hand, a sword hanging at his side, armor upon his chest, and courage in his heart. However, the great commander, Prince Aditya, had set a stern restriction: before fulfilling the entrusted mission, he must not quarrel with anyone. That command... Fulfilling it was what proved most difficult. Somehow, after journeying this far, it felt as though the task was nearly accomplished. Only two more days of travel remained, after all. Until then, he would have to endure with patience.
With the thought that he must reach Kadambur before sunset, Vandiyathevan pressed on. Before long, he drew near the Veera Narayanapuram Vinnagara temple.
That day, the grand festival of Aadi Thirumanjanam was being celebrated, and so, great crowds had gathered in the groves of trees surrounding the temple.

Vendors had set up stalls here and there, selling jackfruit slices, bananas, sugarcane, and all manner of delicacies. Some were selling flowers for women to adorn their hair, lotus buds and other blossoms for divine worship. Others had heaped up coconuts, tender coconuts, eaglewood, sandalwood, betel leaves, jaggery, flattened rice, and puffed rice in great piles. Here and there, amusements and entertainments were taking place. Fortune-tellers, palmists skilled in the science of lines, soothsayers, and those who chanted mantras to cure snakebite—all these were present in abundance.

As Vandiyathevan made his way through the crowd, he noticed at one spot a large gathering standing together, and from within that throng, the sound of a heated argument being shouted in loud voices. Curiosity surged within him to know what debate was taking place. He could not suppress his eagerness. He reined in his horse at the roadside, dismounted, and, signaling to the horse to remain where it was, he plunged into the crowd.

He was surprised to see that only three people were engaged in the debate. Yet, though only three argued, many in the crowd from time to time cheered for the disputant whose side they favored. That was the reason for the commotion, Vandiyathevan realized. He then turned his attention to the subject of the debate.

Of the three disputants, one was a devout Vaishnavite, his body smeared with sandalwood paste in the Urdhva Pundra pattern, a tuft of hair tied at the crown of his head. In his hand, he held a short staff. His frame shone with the vigor of both strength and austerity.
Another was a Shaivite devotee, his body streaked all over with sacred ash.
The third man was clad in ochre robes, his head clean-shaven. Yet he was neither a Vaishnavite nor a Shaivite; it became apparent that he was an Advaita Vedantin, one who transcended both sects.

The Shaivite said, “Oh, Azhwarkadiyan Nambi! Answer me this! Did not Brahma strive to see the crown of Lord Shiva, and did not Thirumal (Vishnu) attempt to find His feet? Did not both fail, and at last surrender themselves at the feet of Shiva? If that is so, how can your Thirumal be considered a greater deity than Shiva?”

At this, Azhwarkadiyan Nambi swung his staff and replied, “Very well, I shall answer you, O valiant Shaivite, dust of the holy feet! Cease your prattle! Was it not your Shiva who granted boons to Ravana, the ten-headed king of Lanka? And did not all those boons turn to dust before the bow of our Thirumal’s avatar, Lord Rama? If that is so, how can your Shiva be considered a greater deity than our Thirumal?”

At this moment, the Advaita Sannyasi in ochre robes interjected, bowing his head and saying, “Why do you both argue in vain? No matter how long you debate whether Shiva or Vishnu is the greater god, the matter will never be resolved. Vedanta gives the answer to this question. As long as you remain on the lower path of devotion, you will quarrel over Shiva and Vishnu. Beyond devotion lies the path of knowledge. And beyond knowledge, there is something called realization. Once that state is attained, there is neither Shiva nor Vishnu. All the world is pervaded by Brahman. What does Sri Shankara Bhagavatpada say in his Brahmasutra Bhashya…”

At this, Azhwarkadiyan Nambi interrupted, “Enough, I say! Stop! Do you know what your Shankaracharya finally said, after writing commentaries on all those Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita, and the Brahmasutras?
‘Bhaja Govindam, Bhaja Govindam, Bhaja Govindam, Mudhamate!’
He repeated it thrice. It was seeing fools like you that made Shankaracharya exclaim, ‘Mudhamate!’—O foolish one!”
As soon as he said this, the crowd erupted with cries of “Aha!”, mocking laughter, and shouts of approval.

But the sanyasi did not remain silent. “Hey! Munkudumi Nambi! You were right to call me ‘foolish-minded,’ for you, standing there with a bare staff in your hand, are nothing but a staff-bearer yourself. Was it not my foolishness that brought me to speak with a staff-bearer like you?” he said.

“Oi, Swamigal! What I hold in my hand is not a mere staff. Know that, when the time demands, it holds the power to shatter your shaven skull!” retorted Azhwarkkadiyan, brandishing the short stick in his hand. At this, his supporters cried out, “Oh-ho!” in excitement.

Then the Advaita Swami said, “Enough, my friend! Let the stick remain in your hand. Even if you strike me with that staff, I shall not be angered. Nor will I come to fight you. The one who strikes is Brahman; the one who is struck is Brahman. If you hit me, it is as if you strike your own self!”

Azhwarkkadiyan Nambi declared, “Look, everyone! Brahman is about to strike the Supreme Brahman with a staff. I am about to beat myself with this stick!” So saying, he spun the staff and advanced towards the Swami.
Watching all this, Vallavaraiyan was, for a moment, tempted to intercept the staff from that tufted Nambi, snatch it away, and give him a sound thrashing with it himself.
But suddenly, the Swami was nowhere to be seen! He had slipped into the crowd and vanished. Witnessing this, the Vaishnava group shouted even louder.
Azhwarkkadiyan turned to the side of the Veerasaiva and said, “Hey, Patha Thooli Pattar! What do you say? Do you wish to continue the debate, or will you, like the Swami, take to your heels?”

“Me? Never! I will never run away like that Vedantin with the foul mouth. Did you mistake me for your Kannan? Was it not your Krishna who stole butter from the Gopis’ houses and was beaten with the churning stick?” said Patha Thooli Pattar, but before he could finish, Azhwarkkadiyan cut in.
“Why so? Have you forgotten how your Paramasivan carried mud for the madman and was beaten on the back?” he retorted, swinging his staff and stepping closer to the Veerasaiva.
Azhwarkkadiyan was a stout, well-built man. The Veerasaiva, Patha Thooli Pattar, was somewhat thin and frail.
The onlookers, who had been encouraging the two disputants with great enthusiasm, now themselves grew ready to join in the fray, their voices rising in a tumult.
A thought arose in Vallavaraiyan’s mind that this foolish quarrel must somehow be stopped.

Stepping a little forward from where he stood, he said, “Why are you two fighting, sirs? Don’t you have any other work? If you are so eager for a fight, why not go to Eelam? There, a great war is raging even now!”
Nambi turned sharply and looked at him. “Who is this fellow who comes here to preach justice?” he demanded.
Some among the crowd, however, were taken by Vandiyathevan’s valiant bearing and the handsome expressiveness of his face.
“You tell us, brother! Speak justice to these quarrelers! We are on your side!” they called out.

“I shall speak the justice as I know it,” said Vallavaraiyan. “It is not known that Lord Shiva and Narayana ever quarreled with each other. They have always lived in friendship and harmony. If that is so, why should this Nambi and this Pattar fight amongst themselves?”
At this, many in the crowd burst out laughing.
Then the Veerasaiva Pattar said, “This boy seems clever enough. But can a debate be settled by mere jesting? Let him answer this: Is Lord Shiva a greater god than Thirumal, or not?”
“Shiva is indeed a great god; Thirumal is also a great god—both are equal. Worship whomever you wish; why quarrel over it?” replied Vallavaraiyan.
“How can you say that? What proof is there to claim that Shiva and Vishnu are equal gods?” demanded Azhwarkkadiyan, his tone sharp.

“Proof, is it? I shall tell you! Just yesterday evening, I went to Vaikuntha. At the same time, Parama-Shiva also came there. Both sat on equal thrones. Their heights were exactly the same. To be sure, I measured both with my own hand, from head to foot, and found them equal…”
“You wretch! Are you making a mockery of us?” roared Azhwarkkadiyan.
The crowd roared, “Speak, brother! Speak!”

“When I measured them, both were of equal height. Not stopping with that, I went and asked Shiva and Vishnu themselves directly. Do you know what they said? ‘Hari and Shiva are one; those who do not know this, their mouths are filled with dust.’ That’s what they told me. And to seal their words, they gave me this handful of earth to throw into the mouths of those who quarrel about them!” So saying, Vallavaraiyan opened his right hand, which had been closed, and revealed a handful of earth. He tossed it away with a flourish.
Many in the crowd, fired up with enthusiasm, bent down, grabbed handfuls of earth from the ground, and began to hurl them at the heads of Nambi and the priest. Some tried to stop this unruly act.
“Hey! You scoundrels! Are you atheists?” cried Azhwarkkadiyan, spinning his staff as he pushed his way into the crowd.
It seemed as if a great commotion and a brawl would erupt right there.
Fortunately, at that very moment, a great stir arose a little distance away.

“Here comes the mighty warrior! The valiant hero who routed the army of Marapandiyan and uprooted them in battle! The victorious spear-bearer who fought in twenty-four wars and bears sixty-four glorious scars upon his body! The sole authority of Chola Nadu, the Lord of the Granary, the Deity who carries out the will of the gods, the great Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar is arriving! Make way! Make way!”—so rang out the herald’s thunderous voice.

Those who proclaimed this came first. Next came the drummers. Behind them marched men bearing palm banners. Then, several warriors strode in, holding spears with pride. Following them, upon a richly adorned elephant, sat a broad-shouldered, dark-complexioned figure of imposing presence.
The sight of that warrior seated atop the royal elephant was like a dark raincloud resting upon the peak of a great mountain.

All those in the crowd moved to either side of the road and stood watching. Vallavaraiyan too stepped aside and gazed at the procession. He guessed that the man upon the elephant must be none other than Pazhuvettaraiyar.

Behind the elephant came a palanquin, its sides veiled with silk curtains. Before Vallavaraiyan could wonder who might be inside, a hand, adorned with bangles and bracelets and glowing with a ruddy hue, emerged from within and gently parted the silk curtain. Like the full moon shining forth when the clouds part, a radiant woman’s face appeared within the palanquin.

Though Vallavarayan’s eyes were well-versed in delighting at the beauty of women, and though that woman’s face shone like a radiant full moon of gold, for some reason, no joy blossomed in his heart upon seeing her visage. Instead, an inexplicable fear and revulsion arose within him.

At that very moment, the woman’s eyes fixed intently upon Vallavarayan as he stood nearby. The next instant, a piercing, fearful cry—“Kreech!”—rang out in a woman’s voice, and immediately, the silken curtain of the palanquin was drawn shut as if to hide her face.

Vallavarayan glanced around him. His intuition told him that the woman had glimpsed something—or someone—close to him before letting out that shriek and closing the palanquin’s curtain. Therefore, he looked all about. He saw Azhwarkkadiyan leaning against a tamarind tree a little behind him. The face of that valiant Vaishnavite had twisted into an indescribable grimace, transforming into a fearsome visage. Vallavarayan felt a surge of bewilderment and disgust for which he could find no reason.

chapters.title: The Temple of the Lord of the Skies
paragraphs: Sometimes, great events arise from the smallest of incidents. Such a minor occurrence now befell Vandiyathevan. Was he not standing by the roadside, watching the retinue of the Periya Pazhuvettarayar pass by? His horse stood tethered a short distance from where he waited.
The eyes of a few men at the tail end of Pazhuvettarayar’s entourage fell upon that horse.
“Hey! Look at this mule!” exclaimed one of them.
“Don’t call it a mule, man! It’s a horse, I say!” retorted another.
“Let your scholarly debate continue; first, find out whether it’s a mule or a donkey!” quipped a third, a lover of jest.

“We can check that too!” said another, and with those words, one among them approached the horse. He tried to leap onto its back. But the clever beast instantly sensed that this was not its master. It stubbornly refused to allow this stranger to mount!

“This is a wicked horse, I tell you! It won’t let me get on its back! Only a true scion of royal blood may ride it, it seems. In that case, only the Mutharaiyar of Thanjavur, if he were to return, could mount it!” he said, his words laced with sarcasm, drawing laughter from the other soldiers.
For it had been a hundred years since the Mutharaiyar clan of Thanjavur was destroyed. Now, the tiger flag of the Cholas fluttered over Thanjavur.
“The horse may have its own opinions. But if you ask me, I’d say the living Tandavarayan is better than the long-dead Mutharaiyar of Thanjavur!” said another soldier.

“Tandavaraya! See if the horse refuses you as well! For all we know, it might be one of those false-legged horses brought for the Lord Perumal’s festival!” joked another, ever fond of mockery. “I’ll test that out as well,” said Thandavarayan, and as he prepared to mount his horse, he twisted its tail. The already irate horse immediately lashed out with its hind legs four times, then bolted away at a gallop.
“The horse is running! It’s a real horse, indeed!” shouted the warriors, raising a cheer of “Uy! Uy!” as they spurred the fleeing horse on even faster.

The horse plunged into the midst of the festival crowd. The people, in a flurry, scattered this way and that to avoid being trampled under its hooves. Even so, a few were struck and knocked down. The horse, losing its way, ran on in a frenzy.
All this happened before Vandiyathevan’s eyes in the blink of an eye. From the look on his face, Alwarkadiyan realized that it was Vandiyathevan’s horse.
“Did you see that, brother? The handiwork of those Paluvur henchmen! You came to show your valor to me, but it’s them you should have shown it to!” he said, pointing accusingly.

A surge of anger welled up in Vandiyathevan. Nevertheless, he clenched his teeth and maintained his composure. The Paluvur warriors were gathered in great numbers. There was no point in fighting so many at once. Nor were they waiting to pick a fight with him. Laughing at the horse’s wild run, they hurried on their way. Vandiyathevan set off in the direction the horse had gone. He knew it would run some distance and then stop on its own. So he was not worried about it.
But the thought that those arrogant followers of Pazhuvettaraiyar needed to be taught a lesson was firmly imprinted in his mind.

Beyond the tamarind grove, in a place where there was no crowd, the horse stood still, the very picture of dejection. As Vandiyathevan approached, the horse neighed plaintively, as if to say, “Why did you leave me and put me through this ordeal?” Its weariness was evident in its tone. Vandiyathevan patted its back to soothe it, then turned it around and led it back toward the road.
Many from the festival crowd, seeing him, called out, “Why did you bring this wild horse into the crowd, brother? Do you know how many people it kicked and knocked down?”
“What can this boy do? It’s the horse’s doing. Wasn’t it those rough Paluvettaraiyar men who caused all this?” a few others said in consolation.
Azhwarkkadiyan was still standing by the roadside, waiting. “What a nuisance this fellow is! It seems he won’t let me go!” thought Vandiyathevan, his face twisting in irritation.
“Brother! Which way are you headed?” asked Azhwarkkadiyan.
“Me? I’ll go a little west, then turn south, curve a bit east, and after that, head southwest!” replied Vandiyathevan.
“I didn’t ask all that. I asked where you’ll be staying tonight.”
“Why do you want to know that?”
“In case you’re staying at Kadambur Sambuvarayar’s palace, I have some business there…”
“Do you know magic or sorcery? How did you find out that I’m going to Kadambur palace?”
“What’s so miraculous about that? Today, guests are arriving there from many towns. The Pazhuvettarayar and his entourage are also going there.”
“Truly?” Vandiyathevan exclaimed in surprise.

“Truly! Don’t you know? The elephant, the horses, the palanquin, the parasol—all belong to Kadambur palace. They are going to escort Pazhuvettarayar. Wherever Pazhuvettarayar goes, all these honors must follow him.”

Vandiyathevan sank into silent thought. The chance to stay where Pazhuvettarayar was staying was not easily come by. Perhaps he might even get an opportunity to become acquainted with that great warrior. But the memory of his recent encounter with the rude retainers of Pazhuvettarayar still rankled within him.
“Brother! Will you do me a favor?” asked Azhwarkkadiyan in a pleading voice.
“What help could I possibly give you? I’m a stranger to this region.”
“I’ll only ask what you are able to do. Tonight, take me with you to Kadambur palace!”
“For what reason? Is some valiant Saivite coming there? Are you going to debate whether Shiva is the greater god or Vishnu, and settle the matter?”

“No, no, don’t think that picking quarrels is my only business. Tonight, a grand feast is to be held at Kadambur Palace. After the feast, there will be festivities—dancing, divine plays, and the Kuravai dance. I long to see the Kuravai dance!”
“Even so, how can I take you along?”
“If you say I am your servant, that will suffice.”
Vandiyathevan’s earlier suspicion grew stronger.

“For such tricks and deceptions, you must look for someone else. I do not need a servant like you, and even if I said so, no one would believe it. Moreover, from all that you have said, I now begin to doubt whether they will let even me inside the fort tonight.”
“In that case, just say you did not receive an invitation to Kadambur!”
“In a way, I do have an invitation. Sambuvarayar’s son, Kandhamaaran, is my close friend. Whenever I come this way, he has insisted many times that I must visit their palace.”
“Is that all? In that case, your task tonight will be somewhat difficult!”
Both of them walked on in silence for a while.
“Why do you still continue to follow me?” Vandiyathevan asked.
“I could ask you the same question—why are you following me? Aren’t you going this way?”
“It’s only because I don’t know the way. Nambi, where are you going? By any chance, are you heading to Kadambur?”
“No; you already said you cannot take me there. I am going to the Vinnagara temple.”
“To the sanctum of Veeranarayana Perumal, is it?”
“Yes.”
“I too wish to visit that temple and worship Perumal.”

“I wondered if perhaps you would not come to the Vishnu temple. It is a shrine one must see; a sanctum that must be visited. Here, Iswara Munigal, the priest, serves the Lord with great devotion—he is a true saint.”
“I have heard of him as well. What a crowd there is! Is there some special festival in the temple today?”

“Yes; today is the sacred star day of Andal. The auspicious star of Andal has coincided with the festival of Aadi Perukku; that is why there is such a grand celebration. Brother! Have you ever heard any of Andal’s hymns?”
“I have not.”
“Then do not listen! Do not listen to them, not even by accident!”
“Why such prejudice?”

“It is not prejudice; nor is it enmity. I say this for your own good. If you listen to the sweet hymns of Andal, you will throw away your sword and spear, fall in love with Krishna as I have, and set out on a pilgrimage to the heavenly city!”
“Do you know Andal’s hymns? Will you sing them?”

“I know a few; I also know some of the hymns of Nammazhwar, the one who rendered the Vedas in Tamil. I am going to sing them in the presence of the Lord. If you wish, listen! Look, here is the temple!”
Even as he spoke, they had indeed come close to the Veeranarayana Perumal temple.

Vijayalaya Chola’s grandson, the first Parantaka Chola, bore the title “Kopperakesari, Conqueror of Madurai and Eelam.” He was the one who laid the foundation for the great Chola Empire. He was famed in history for roofing the sacred Chidambaram temple with gold. Along with many honorifics such as Chola Chikamani and Sura Chikamani, he also bore the distinguished name of Veeranarayana.

During Parantaka’s reign, the Rashtrakuta kings of the northern twin provinces grew powerful. Parantaka anticipated that they might march their armies down from the region of Manyakheta. Therefore, he stationed his eldest son, the crown prince Rajaditya, with a large army in the land of Thirumunaippadi. The hundreds of thousands of soldiers belonging to that army, having no immediate battle to fight, were left idle— In those days, Rajaditya devised a plan. He wished to accomplish a great work for the benefit of the people, employing them in the task. Through the mighty river, known as Vadakaveri by devotees and as Kollidam by others, boundless floodwaters flowed, only to be wasted as they mingled with the sea. Rajaditya resolved to harness a portion of this water, and with the soldiers under his command, constructed a vast lake, as expansive as the ocean itself. He named it Veeranarayana Lake, after his beloved father. Upon its banks, he established the town of Veeranarayanapuram and there erected a temple to Vishnu. In those days, the term "Vinnagaram" was the Tamil rendering for Vishnugriham, the celestial abode of Vishnu. Was not Sriman Narayana said to recline upon the waters, his very form composed of water? Therefore, it was customary in those times to build a temple for Sri Narayana Murthi upon the banks of such lakes, to beseech his protection over the waters. In accordance with this tradition, Rajaditya caused a temple for Veeranarayana Perumal to be constructed in the Vinnagaram of Veeranarayanapuram, and installed the deity there.

It was to this very temple that Vandiyathevan and Azhwarkadiyan now came. Upon reaching the sanctum, Azhwarkadiyan began to sing. After rendering a few verses from Andal’s hymns, he sang some pasurams from the Tamil Veda of Nammazhwar:
“Poliga, poliga, poliga…”

Gone is the curse of mortal life! No more suffering, no more hell, No more fear of Yama in this world— Know this, the age of Kali will perish! Behold! The sea-hued Lord’s spirits Have descended upon the earth in abundance, Singing, dancing, whirling in ecstasy— We have seen them, seen them, seen them! We have seen what delights the eye! Devotees, all of you, come! Come, worship, worship, stand in awe! The spirits of Madhavan, He whose cool garland is wreathed with bees, Are singing, dancing, Spreading everywhere upon the earth!

As he sang in this manner, tears welled up in Azhwarkadiyan’s eyes and streamed down his cheeks in rivulets. Vandiyathevan listened intently to those songs. Though tears did not come to his own eyes, his heart melted and softened within him. His opinion of Azhwarkadiyan, which he had held until then, changed. “He is a true devotee!” he thought to himself.

Just as Vandiyathevan listened attentively, several others too heard those hymns with rapt attention. The temple elders listened; the chief priest, Iswarapattar, stood with tears brimming in his eyes. Beside him stood his young son, a boy whose breath still smelled of milk, listening as well.
Azhwarkadiyan, having sung ten verses, said:
“In the paddy fields of Kurugur, where the palms sway…” Kaari Maaran Sadagopan The ten of the thousand verses that resound with fame Will cleanse the heart of all impurity.”
Thus he finished reciting the paasuram.

The young boy, son of the temple priest who had been listening, whispered something to his father. The priest wiped away the tears that had welled in his eyes and asked, “Sir! It is said that Kurugoor Sadagopan, our Nammazhwar, composed a thousand hymns in total? Do you know all of them?”
“I have not had the fortune to learn them all, only a few sections are known to me,” replied Azhwarkkadiyan.
“Whatever you know, you must teach this child,” said Isvaramunigal.

In the days to come, this village is destined for great glory. The boy who listened to Nammazhwar’s hymns, his face radiant with the glow of youth and innocence, will grow up to become the first in the line of Vaishnava acharyas, bearing the revered name of Nathamunigal. He will journey to the sacred city of Kurugoor, the abode of the Azhwar, and there, he will seek out and collect all the thousand hymns composed by the one who “made the Vedas speak in Tamil.” His disciples will sing these hymns to music and spread them throughout the land.
In time, his own descendant, Aalavandhaar, will be born and will perform many wondrous deeds.

To pay homage to the holy places where these two great souls were born, the illustrious Sri Ramanuja himself will one day come. When he arrives, he will marvel at the Veeranarayana Lake and its seventy-four sluice gates. Just as the waters of the lake flow through those seventy-four channels to nourish the people, so too will it dawn in his heart that the flood of Narayana’s grace must flow to all living souls. To that end, he will establish seventy-four acharya seats.
Thus, seventy-four Vaishnava acharyas, bearing the title of “Simhasanadhipathi,” will come into being.
Let the detailed account of these great events be left to the chronicles of the Vaishnava Guru lineage. Let us, for now, turn our attention once more to Vandiyathevan.

After offering his worship to Perumal and stepping outside the temple, Vandiyathevan turned to Azhwarkadiyan and said, “Nambigaḷe! I had no idea you were such a devout soul, nor that you were a crown among scholars. If I have spoken anything out of turn, I beg your pardon.”
“I forgive you, Thambi! But now, will you do me a favor? Tell me!”
“Haven’t I already told you that I cannot grant the favor you asked? And didn’t you agree as well?”
“This is something else; a small matter. I will give you a little note. If you stay at Kadambur Palace, at the right moment, you must hand it to someone.”
“To whom?”
“To the lady who traveled behind the Pazhuvetaraiyar’s elephant, in the closed palanquin!”
“Nambigaḷe! What do you take me for? Am I the sort to get entangled in such errands? If anyone else besides you had dared to utter such words to me…”

“Thambi! No need to get agitated! If you cannot do it, then go on your way, O Maharaja! But if you had done me this favor, perhaps at some time, my help would have proved useful to you as well. No harm, go on your way!”
Vandiyathevan did not linger there for even a moment longer. He sprang onto his horse and, without delay, set off swiftly towards Kadambur.

chapters.title: The Kadambur Palace
paragraphs: The horse that had been resting for so long beneath Vallavaraiyan was now full of renewed vigor; within the span of a single naazhigai, it had reached the gates of Kadambur’s Sambuvaraiyar Palace. Among the great clan-chiefs of Chola Nadu in those days, Sengannan Sambuvaraiyar was one. The gateway to his palace resembled the entrance to a mighty city’s fortress. On either side of the entrance, tall walls rose and curved away like the ramparts of a citadel.

At the fortress gate, elephants, horses, and bulls stood tethered; men bustled about, tending to these beasts, feeding them, giving them water. Here and there, others held aloft flaming torches, casting light all around, while some poured oil into the lamps. The whole scene was a swirl of activity and commotion. Witnessing all this, a slight hesitation and unease crept into Vallavaraiyan’s heart. “Clearly, some great event is taking place here. And I have arrived at just such a moment,” he thought. Yet, mingled with his apprehension, a keen curiosity surged within him to discover what this occasion might be.
The fortress gates stood open, but within the entrance, several spear-bearing guards stood watch. To behold them was to see the very minions of Yama, the god of death.

Vallavaraiyan reasoned that if he hesitated, they would surely stop him; it was best to boldly ride his horse straight in. No sooner had he resolved this than he put it into action. But what a disappointment! As the horse approached the gate, two of the spear-bearing guards crossed their weapons, blocking his way. Four more came and seized the reins of his horse. One among them stared intently at Vandiyathevan, while another brought a torch close, raising it high so its light fell directly on his face.
Anger flared in Vallavaraiyan’s face. “Is this the custom of your town? To stop guests at the very threshold?” he demanded.
“Who are you, brother, to speak so boldly? What is your village?” asked the gatekeeper.

“You ask my name and village? Vanagapadi’s Thiruvallam is my home. In days past, your own warriors bore my ancestors’ names upon their chests with pride! My name is Vallavaraiyan Vandiyathevan! Do you know it now?” he declared. “To say all this, did you really have to bring even a carpenter along?” said one of the guards. The others laughed at this remark.

“Whoever you are, you cannot go inside any further! All the guests who were to arrive today have already come. The master’s orders are strict: no one else is to be admitted!” declared the chief of the guards.

Noticing that some argument was taking place, a few warriors standing a little distance away inside the fort came closer. One of them said, “Hey! Isn’t that the same donkey we chased away at the festival gathering?” Another replied, “Call it a mule, not a donkey.” A third added, “Look at the way that fellow sits so stiffly atop the donkey!”
These words reached Vallavarayan’s ears.

He thought to himself, “Why get into pointless trouble? Should I just turn back? Or should I show them the signet ring stamped with Prince Aditya Karikalan’s royal seal and go inside?” The prince was the commander of the northern army—after seeing his insignia, who from the northern Pennai to Kanyakumari could dare stop him? As he debated thus within himself, the mocking words of the Pazhuvettaraiyar’s men stung his ears. At once, he decided what he must do.
“Let go of the horse; I will turn back!” he said. The guards released the reins of the horse.

With both legs, Vandiyathevan pressed hard against the horse’s belly. At that very instant, he drew his sword from its scabbard. The blade flashed like lightning, spinning in his hand as if he were wielding the divine discus of Lord Vishnu himself. The horse leapt forward, charging into the fort. The warriors in its path fell away in sudden confusion. Spears clattered to the ground. The horse bounded straight at the Pazhuvur men who had mocked him. Taken completely by surprise by this lightning assault, the warriors scattered in all directions.

Meanwhile, other events unfolded. The gates of the fort slammed shut with a resounding clang. Shouts of “Catch him! Catch him!” rang out. Spears and swords clashed with a metallic ‘clang, clang’. Suddenly, the drum of alarm thundered—‘tatam!’ “Thadam!” thundered the sound.

Vandiyathevan suddenly found himself surrounded by soldiers on all sides. Twenty, thirty, perhaps more than fifty men closed in around his horse. Without hesitation, Vandiyathevan leapt from his mount and landed on the ground. Whirling the sword in his hand, he shouted, “Kandhamaaran! Kandhamaaran! Your men are trying to kill me!”
At his cry, the soldiers who had encircled him started in surprise, hesitated for a moment, and stepped back.

At that instant, from the upper balcony of the palace, a voice boomed like thunder, “What is this commotion? Stop at once!” Seven or eight men were standing at that spot, watching what was happening below.
“Master! Someone has broken through the guards and entered. He is shouting the young master’s name!” called one of the men below.

“Kandhamaaran! Go and see what this disturbance is about!” came the same thunderous voice from the upper floor. Vandiyathevan guessed that the owner of that commanding voice must be Sengannan Sambuvarya.
He and the soldiers surrounding him stood frozen for a moment.

“What is this uproar?” came a youthful voice. At the sound, those standing there parted to make way. A young man hurried through the opening, lightly spinning a dagger in his hand. For a moment, he gazed in astonishment at Vandiyathevan, who stood poised like Subramanya himself after slaying the demon Surapadman.
“Valava! My dearest friend! Is it truly you?” he cried, his voice trembling with emotion. Rushing forward, the youth embraced Vandiyathevan tightly.

“Kandhamaaran! You have invited me so many times, urging me to visit your home. And now, on my arrival, I am greeted with such a heroic welcome!” Vandiyathevan said, gesturing at the men who had surrounded him.
Turning to them, Kandhamaaran exclaimed, “Fools! Get away, all of you! Your brains are nothing but chaff in an empty husk!”

Kandhamaaran seized Vandiyathevan’s hand and, in a flurry, dragged him along. His feet barely touched the ground, bounding forward in excitement. His heart, too, leapt and danced. In the bloom of youth, what could be more exhilarating than finding a true friend with whom one’s soul is united? Yes, love exists, of course. But in love, for all its joys and thrills, there is even more sorrow and pain. In the rapture of youthful friendship, not even the shadow of grief falls—there is only pure, unalloyed delight.
As they hurried along, Vallavarayan asked, “Kandhamaaran! Why is there such a commotion here today? What is the reason for all this security?”

“I’ll tell you in detail later about the special occasion today. Remember, when you and I were camped on the banks of the Pennai river, you kept saying, ‘I must see Pazhuvetaraiyar; I must see Mazhavarayar; I want to meet this person; I want to meet that person’? Well, today you can see all those ‘this’ and ‘that’ and even the ‘wall’—everyone is here!” replied Kandhamaaran.

Then, Kandhamaaran led Vallavarayan up to the upper floor of the palace where the guests were seated. First, he brought him before his father, Sambuvarayar, and said, “Father! I’ve often spoken to you about my friend Vandiyathevan of the Vanar clan. This is he!” Vandiyathevan bowed respectfully to the elder. Sambuvarayar did not seem particularly pleased.
“Is that so? Is this the one who caused all that commotion at the palace gate below?” he asked.
“My friend was not the cause of the commotion; it was those fools we appointed to guard the gate!” Kandhamaaran replied.
“Even so, on a day like this, and that too after midnight, he need not have arrived in such a tumultuous manner!” said Sambuvarayar.

Kandhamaaran’s face fell; he did not wish to argue further with his father. He led Vandiyathevan away. Among the assembled guests, on a high seat in the center, sat Pazhuvetaraiyar, the chief guest. Kandhamaaran brought Vandiyathevan before him and said, “Uncle! This is my dearest friend, Vandiyathevan, scion of the Vanar dynasty. He and I served as border guards at the northern bank of the Pennai. All that time, he would constantly say, ‘I must see the valiant, heroic Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar!’” He would keep on asking, “Is it true that there are sixty-four battle scars on the body of Pazhuvetarayar?” I would reply, “One day, you can count them yourself.”

Pazhuvetarayar, his face tightening, said, “Is that so, young man? You won’t believe it unless you count for yourself? Do you have so much distrust? Or do you doubt whether any clan other than the Vanar clan could possess such valor?”
Both friends were startled. They had not expected him to twist their words, spoken in praise, into something so accusatory.

Vandiyathevan’s mind seethed with irritation. Yet, without showing it outwardly, he replied with humility, “Sir! The valorous fame of the Pazhuvetarayar clan has spread from Cape Kumari to the Himalayas. Who am I to doubt that?”
“Good answer; you’re a clever lad!” said Pazhuvetarayar.
Feeling they had escaped trouble for now, the two young men left the place.

At that moment, Sambuvarayar called his son close and whispered in his ear, “Quickly serve your friend some food and arrange for him to rest somewhere private! He must be exhausted after his long journey.” Maara Vel shook his head in annoyance and left.
Afterwards, Maara Vel led Vandiyathevan into the women’s quarters. There were many women there. Vandiyathevan paid his respects to Maara Vel’s mother.
He guessed that the shy young woman hiding behind her must be Kandhamaaran’s sister.
Vandiyathevan had imagined many things about this ‘little sister’ from the many times Maara Vel had mentioned her. Now, in some way, he felt disappointed.
Among that gathering of women, Vandiyathevan’s eyes searched restlessly, trying to discern who the lady might be who had arrived in the palanquin with Pazhuvetarayar.

chapters.title: The Kuravai Dance
paragraphs: The two friends emerged from the women’s quarters. From inside, a woman’s voice called out, “Kandanmaran! Kandanmaran!”

“My mother is calling me. Wait here for a moment! I’ll be back soon,” said Kandanmaran, and went inside. Vandiyathevan could hear a chorus of women’s voices asking questions in quick succession, and Kandanmaran stammering and stumbling as he replied. Then came the sound of laughter, a bright, ringing mirth that echoed from within.

Vandiyathevan felt a flush of embarrassment and a spark of anger at the thought that perhaps they were laughing at his expense. When Kandanmaran returned, he took Vandiyathevan by the hand and said, “Come! Let’s take a tour of our palace!” and led him away.

Kandanmaran showed Vandiyathevan the moonlit courtyards of Kadambur Palace, the halls for music and dance, the storerooms, the shining marble pavilions, the towering gopurams and domes, the stables for horses, and many other wonders.

In the midst of this, Vandiyathevan asked, “Kandanmaran! When you left me at the entrance to the women’s quarters and went inside again, there was such laughter and excitement in there. What was the reason? Were they so delighted to see your friend?”
“They were indeed happy to see you. My mother and the others seem to like you very much. But they weren’t laughing about you…”
“Then what was the cause of their laughter?”

“You know the great Pazhuvettaraiyar, don’t you? Even at his age, he’s just taken a young bride. He brought her here in a closed palanquin. But instead of sending her to the women’s quarters, he’s locked her away in his own lodge! One of the nursemaids managed to catch a glimpse of her through the lattice and came back describing her beauty. That’s what they were laughing about! Now there’s a debate—whether she’s a Sinhalese woman, a Kalinga woman, or from the Chera country! You know, of course, that Pazhuvettaraiyar’s ancestors came to Tamil Nadu from the land of the Cheras?” “I have heard about it, of course—why, you yourself have told me once before. Leave that aside, Kandhamara! How long has it been since the Pazhuvettaraiyar married this mysterious, beautiful woman?”

“It can’t be more than two years; ever since their wedding, it seems he hasn’t left her alone for even a moment! Wherever he goes, he takes his beloved lady along with him in the palanquin. People all over the land are beginning to talk and make fun of it. Vandiyathevan! When men of a certain age are overtaken by such infatuation for women, isn’t it always a little ridiculous to everyone?”

“That’s not the real reason at all. Shall I tell you the true cause, Kandhamara? Women are always a little prone to jealousy. Don’t think I’m speaking ill of the women in your house! The whole world of women is like this! The women of your family are dusky beauties. But Pazhuvettaraiyar’s beloved lady is fair as gold, with a rosy glow. That’s why they don’t like her! And so, they make up all sorts of stories about her…”
“Hey! What’s this wonder! How do you know about her complexion? Have you seen her, then? Where and how did you see her? If Pazhuvettaraiyar comes to know of this, your life will not be your own!…”

“Kandhamara! You know well that I am not one to be frightened by such things. Besides, I haven’t done anything improper. When Pazhuvettaraiyar’s entourage was passing through Veeranarayana Puram, I too stood at the roadside among the crowds and watched. Elephants, horses, palanquins, parasols—all those honors you sent, weren’t they? Is that true?”
“Yes, we sent them. So what?…”
“So what? Nothing at all. I only compared the welcome and honors you gave Pazhuvettaraiyar with the welcome you gave me—nothing more…!”

Kandhamaran laughed lightly and said, “We gave him the honors due to a lord who wields the power of fate. To you, we gave the welcome due to a pure warrior! Someday, by Murugan’s grace, if you become the son-in-law of this house, we’ll give you the proper bridegroom’s honors and welcome you accordingly!” Then he added, “But you were saying something else before; the conversation has wandered. Yes, you said Pazhuvettaraiyar’s beloved lady is fair and rosy—how do you know that?”

On the broad, dark-backed elephant of Kadambur palace, Pazhuvetaraiyar was approaching, like Yama, the god of death, riding upon his buffalo! All my attention was fixed upon him. There was a time when I, too, dreamt of becoming like him. Just then, following him, came a closed palanquin. While I was wondering who could be inside, a hand from within gently drew aside the curtain. Through the parted veil, a face was visible. The hand and the face were both of a radiant golden hue! That was all I saw! From what you have just told me, I surmise that the woman must be the object of Pazhuvetaraiyar’s desire.

“Vandiyatheva! You are a fortunate man. It is said that no man has ever laid eyes upon the young queen of Pazhuvur. Yet, for at least a moment, you have seen her hand and her face, have you not? From what you saw, can you guess from which land such a beauty might have been born?” asked Kandhamaaran.

“At that moment, I did not think about it. But now, reflecting upon it, she might be a maiden from Kashmir; or perhaps a princess from distant lands beyond the seas—Java, Kadaram, Yavana, or even Misra. Perhaps she could even be a woman from Arabia. In that country, it is said, women wear a veil from birth until death!”
At that moment, from somewhere nearby, the sound of musical instruments began to rise. Salli, karadi, parai, pullanguzhal, and udukkai all joined in a clamorous symphony.
“What is that sound?” Vandiyathevan asked.
“The Kuravai dance is about to begin! This is the opening fanfare! Do you wish to watch the Kuravai dance? Or would you rather eat quickly and lie down to sleep in peace?”

At that instant, Vandiyathevan remembered what Azhwarkkadiyan had said about the Kuravai dance. “I have never seen a Kuravai dance; I must see it,” he replied. The friends walked a few more steps, and as they turned a corner, the stage for the Kuravai dance came into view. Already, the audience was gathering before the stage.

In a spacious courtyard, spread with white sand, surrounded on all sides by the palace walls and the battlements of the fort, the stage for the Kuravai dance had been set up. On the stage were painted images—like a hen, like a peacock, like a swan... They had adorned the stage splendidly. The platform was beautified with roasted red rice grains, silver vessels, millet and rice mixed with turmeric, flowers of many hues, and strings of kunri beads. Along with the traditional oil lamps, torches burned brightly, striving to drive away the darkness. Yet, mingling with the fragrant smoke of incense, the smoke from the torches spread like a thick mist, veiling and dimming the light of the lamps. Musicians sat facing and flanking the stage, passionately playing their instruments. The mingled scents of flowers and incense, combined with the thunderous music, made Vandiyathevan’s head spin.

Once all the important guests had assembled, nine women dancers, skilled in the Kuravai dance, ascended the stage. Their bodies were tightly wrapped in costumes suited for the dance, adorned with ornaments that clung to their forms, anklets ringing on their feet. In their hair, they wore garlands of flowers beloved to Lord Murugan—kanne, kadamba, kanthal, kurinji, and sevvalari. With a long, intricately woven floral garland binding them together, they stood upon the stage, each linked to the next. Some gracefully held in their hands beautiful green parrots, carved from sandalwood and painted in vivid colors.

After bowing in greeting to the assembly, they began to sing and dance. They sang songs praising the glory of Murugan. They sang of his heroic deeds—how he slew the demon hosts of Surapadman and Gajamukha, and how his victorious spear dried up the ocean’s waters. They sang of the maidens of the celestial realms who, while performing penance to wed Murugan, saw that divine son of Shiva descend to the land of Tamil, where he wed the mountain huntress who stood guard in the millet fields of the wilds. They extolled the compassion and grace of Velavan.
Such singing and dancing, joined by the beat of the drum and the notes of the flute, sent the onlookers into a frenzy.
“Hunger, disease, and enmity—let them perish! May rain, prosperity, and wealth ever increase!”
With these blessings, the Kuravai dance came to an end. The women descended from the stage and departed.

Next, a man and a woman, called the ‘Devaralan’ and ‘Devaratti’, stepped onto the stage to perform the Velan dance. They wore garments of blood-red hue, and garlands of sevvalari flowers as red as fresh-spilled blood adorned their necks. They had adorned their foreheads with deep red kumkum. Their lips, reddened by chewing betel leaves and areca nut, glowed with the color of blood. Their eyes shone crimson, like ripe kovai fruit.

At first, the dance began calmly. They danced alone, sometimes joining hands. As time passed, the frenzy of the dance increased. On one side of the stage, the vel—the sacred spear—rested. The temple dancer, Devaratti, took it in her hand. Devaralan tried to snatch it from her; Devaratti resisted. In the end, Devaralan leapt with such force that the stage trembled, vaulted across with a great bound, and wrenched the spear from Devaratti’s grasp. Devaratti, feigning fear at the sight of the weapon, descended from the stage.

Then, Devaralan stood alone on the stage, spear in hand, and danced in wild ecstasy. The demon hosts—Sooran and the other asura hordes—were shattered and fell. Sooran’s severed head sprouted anew again and again. Each time it grew back, the fury of the spearman intensified. Sparks seemed to fly from his eyes. At last, Surapadman fell dead. Devaralan cast the spear to the ground.

Now, all the other instruments fell silent. Only the beat of the udukku drum could be heard. Near the stage, the priest, possessed by fervor, struck the drum with mounting excitement. Every atom of Devaralan’s body quivered and danced. “The trance has come!” whispered those in the assembly to one another.

After a while, the priest, caught up in the same frenzy, turned to the entranced Devaralan and pleaded, “Vela! Muruga! Devasenapati! Kantha! Slayer of Sooran! You must grant your divine prophecy to your devotees!”
“Listen, I will speak! Ask what you wish to know!” cried the one possessed by the trance.
“Will rain fall? Will the floods rise? Will the land prosper? Will our desires be fulfilled?” asked the priest.

“Rain will fall! The floods will rise! The land will prosper! Your wishes will be fulfilled! But—you have not offered worship to my mother! Durga demands sacrifice. Bhadrakali demands sacrifice; Chandikeswari, who slew Mahishasura, demands sacrifice!” the possessed one shouted, still dancing in a frenzy.
“What sacrifice is required?” asked the priest.
“If I tell you, will you give it?” demanded the wild dancer.
“We will give it; we will certainly give it!” replied the priest.
“She asks for royal blood; she asks for the blood of a thousand generations of kings!” Thus cried the frenzied man, his voice echoing in a dreadful, fearsome roar.
Before the dais sat the great lords—Pazhuvettarayar, Sambuvarayar, Mazhavarayar, and others—each turning to gaze at the other. Their bloodshot, wild eyes spoke in silent signals.

Sambuvarayar glanced at the priest and nodded his head in sign. The priest ceased his drumming. The possessed Devaralan collapsed onto the stage like a tree felled at its roots. The priestess rushed forward, lifted him up, and carried him away.
The assembly dispersed in silence; from far outside, somewhere in the distance, the howling of jackals could be heard.

Vandiyathevan, who had been swept up in the tumult of all he had seen and heard, turned toward the direction of the jackals’ cries. There, on the outer wall of the palace, a head could be seen. It was the head of Azhwarkadiyan! For a moment, Vandiyathevan was seized by a terrible sensation—as if Azhwarkadiyan’s head had been severed and placed atop the wall.

He blinked and looked again; the head was gone! Ashamed at having succumbed to such a wild fancy, he chided himself. Yet, many other unfamiliar emotions, never before experienced, now stirred and troubled his heart.

chapters.title: The Midnight Assembly
paragraphs: After the dance of the kuravai and the wild revelry, a grand feast was held for the assembled guests. Vallavarayan found no pleasure in the banquet. His body was weary; his mind, unsettled. Yet, his friend Kandhamaran, seated beside him, took great pride in pointing out the other guests, naming each one with a sense of importance.

Apart from the Pazhuvettaraiyars and the Sambuvaraiyars, there was Mazhavarayar, the lord of Mazhapadi; Perunilakizhar of Kunrathur; the Pallavarayar of the Three Crowns; the Dangling Kalingarayar; Vanangamudi Munaiyarayar; Devasenathipathi Poovarayar; the Fearless Singamutharaiyar; the Twin-Parasol Rajaliyar; the Perunila Velar of Kollimalai—these and others, Kandhamaran whispered into his friend’s ear, discreetly pointing them out so that none else would notice. These dignitaries were no ordinary men; nor was it easy to gather them all in one place.

Most of them were minor kings in their own right, or men who, by their valorous deeds, had earned the honor due to such rulers. In those days, the title of “Raja” or “King” had evolved into “Arai­yar,” a term of respect and authority.
Not only minor kings, but also those who were their equals in distinction, were addressed by the title “Araiyar.” It was customary to append the name of their region or town to this title.

In those days, to be called a minor king did not mean one inherited the title and lived in the comforts of a palace, indulging in luxury. Only those who stood at the forefront of the battlefield, ready to fight, and who could defend and preserve their royal rights through their own valor, could maintain their sovereignty. Thus, each of them bore the scars and fame of many a battle. Now, all these men ruled their respective domains under the supreme authority of Sundara Chola Chakravarthi of Pazhayarai. Some among them also held high offices in the Chola imperial government.

To see so many eminent dignitaries of the Chola Empire gathered in one place should have filled Vallavarayan with just pride. Yet, no such joy arose in his heart. “Why have so many people gathered here?”—this thought arose in his mind again and again. All sorts of vague doubts surged and tossed within him.

With such confusion in his heart, Vallavaraiyan went to the place that Kandhamaaran had specially arranged for him. Since many guests had arrived, all that Vallavaraiyan had been allotted in that vast palace was an open pavilion in a corner of the upper floor.
“You are very tired; so lie down and sleep peacefully. After I have attended to the other guests, I will come and sleep beside you,” Kandhamaaran had said, and then left.

No sooner had Vandiyathevan lain down than his eyes began to spin with drowsiness. Very soon, the goddess of sleep claimed him. But what use was that? The mind—ah, that mind!—even the goddess of sleep cannot keep it in check. Though the body lies motionless and the eyes are closed, the thoughts etched deep within the mind transform into dreams. In that dream world, countless events and experiences arise—meaningless, incongruent, and strange.

From somewhere far away, the sound of a jackal’s howl reached him. One jackal became ten, ten became a hundred, and together they howled in unison! Howling, they drew nearer and nearer to Vandiyathevan. In the pitch darkness, the eyes of those jackals glowed like tiny embers as they approached him. He turned to flee in the opposite direction. But there, too, ten, a hundred, a thousand hunting dogs rushed at him in a pack, barking ferociously. The eyes of those hounds shone like sparks of fire.

Caught between the jackals and the hunting dogs, Vandiyathevan trembled, wondering what his fate would be. Just then, he saw a temple ahead. He dashed towards it and slipped inside through the open door, bolting it behind him. Turning around, he saw that it was a Kali temple. From behind the statue of Kali, with her mouth agape in a terrifying snarl, a priest emerged. In his hand was a fearsome chopping sword.
“You have come? Come, then!” said the priest, advancing closer and closer and closer.
“What is the history of the royal lineage into which you were born? For how many years have your ancestors ruled? Speak the truth,” the priest demanded.
“The Vallavaraiyars of the Vanar clan ruled for three hundred years; in my father’s time, we lost the kingdom to the Vaidhumba kings,” replied Vandiyathevan.
“In that case, you are not a worthy sacrifice! Flee at once!” declared the priest.

Suddenly, in the place of Goddess Kali, Lord Kannan (Krishna) appeared. In Kannan’s presence, two women entered, garlands in their hands, singing the hymns of Andal and dancing. As Vallavaraiyan watched this scene in rapture, from behind him came the song, “We have seen, we have seen, we have seen, we have seen the beloved of our eyes!” He turned to look. The singer was none other than Azhwarkadiyan Nambi.
No! It was only Azhwarkadiyan’s head that was singing! That head alone was placed upon the sacrificial altar!
Unable to bear the sight, Vallavaraiyan turned away and bumped into a pillar. The dream shattered; his eyes opened. Yet, he was confronted by a scene that seemed to bind dream and reality together.

Directly opposite the place where he lay, above the encircling wall of Kadambur Palace, a head was visible. It was indeed the head of Azhwarkadiyan Nambi. This time, it was no dream, nor was it a mere illusion. For, no matter how long he looked, the head remained there. It was not just a head; it was clear that a body was attached behind it. For Azhwarkadiyan’s hands were gripping the edge of the wall.

Moreover, he was peering intently down into the inner courtyard of the wall. What was he observing so carefully?… Surely, there must be some secret plot afoot. Azhwarkadiyan could not have come there with good intentions. He must have come with some wicked purpose, to carry out some evil deed.

Was it not his duty, as Kandanmaran’s dearest friend, to prevent Azhwarkadiyan from committing such a misdeed? Could he simply lie there, doing nothing, while harm befell the household of those who had kindly offered him a meal?
Vallavaraiyan sprang up. He took the sword, still sheathed, that he had placed beside him, and fastened it at his waist. He walked toward the direction where Azhwarkadiyan’s head had been seen.

Was it not in a corner pavilion on the upper floor of the palace that Vallavaraiyan had been lying? Leaving that spot, he walked toward the wall. As he did, the decorative pavilion domes, platforms, vimana spires, and pillars that adorned the upper floor— He had to walk past, cross over, and circle around. After proceeding a short distance in this manner, Vallavarayan suddenly paused, startled by the sound of voices coming from somewhere nearby. Grasping a pillar, he stood concealed behind it and peered out cautiously. Below, in a narrow courtyard surrounded on three sides by tall walls, ten or twelve men were seated together. The high walls blocked out most of the moonlight. Yet, from an iron lamp fixed to one of the walls, a small flame cast a faint glow.

All those gathered there were the same dignitaries he had seen at the banquet earlier that night—minor chieftains and officials of the Chola Empire. Surely, they must have assembled at this midnight hour to discuss some matter of great importance. What were they doing, what were they speaking about? That was what Azhwarkadiyan was observing so keenly from atop the wall. There could be no doubt—Azhwarkadiyan was a sly and cunning fellow. From his vantage point, he could see those gathered below and hear their conversation clearly. But those below could not see Azhwarkadiyan at all. The palace and outer walls were constructed in such a way at that spot. Somehow, Azhwarkadiyan had discovered this place! A true trickster, without question. But all his trickery would not avail him against this scion of the Vanara clan, Vandiyathevan! If only he could catch hold of that disguised Vaishnavite and drag him down by the hand…

Yet, if he were to attempt such a thing, he would have to approach the wall in full view of those gathered below, risking drawing their attention. There could be danger in acting so rashly. He remembered what Sambuvarayar had said: “He had no business coming here tonight!” All these men had gathered here to deliberate on some vital matter. Clearly, they did not wish outsiders to know of their plans. If they were to spot him suddenly, would they not become suspicious of him? And before he could say anything about Azhwarkadiyan, that fellow would leap off the wall and escape. Then suspicion would fall solely on him. “What are you doing here when you should be asleep?”—what answer could he give to that? It would only serve to put Kandanmaran in a difficult position. Ah! There—Kandanmaran was seated on one side of the gathering. He, too, seemed to be participating in their council! If he questioned Kandanmaran in the morning, all would become clear.

At that moment, the closed palanquin placed beside the gathering caught Vandiyathevan’s attention. Ah! Was this not the very palanquin that had followed the Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar’s elephant? The palanquin in which the woman had traveled—the woman who, for a fleeting instant, had drawn aside the curtain and looked out—where in this palace might she be now? The old lord had not even sent her to the women’s quarters, it seemed. This is always the trouble when older men marry young women. Suspicion gnaws at their very life. Not for a moment can they bear to be parted from their young wives.

Perhaps, even now, the young wife of Pazhuvettaraiyar is inside this very palanquin. Who knows? Ah! Look at the fate of this warrior among warriors! At his age, he is ensnared by a young woman, made her slave, and suffers for it! And yet, she is no Rathi, nor Menaka, nor Rambha! Vandiyathevan could not forget the feeling of revulsion that had arisen in him when he saw her for that brief moment. What strange infatuation bound this valorous Pazhuvettaraiyar to such a woman, he could not fathom.

Stranger still was the madness of Alwarkadiyan. It seemed that he, too, was waiting atop the wall only because this palanquin was placed here! But what connection could there be between him and her? How could we know? She might be his sister, or perhaps his beloved. Pazhuvettaraiyar might have abducted her by force! He was capable of such deeds. Perhaps Alwarkadiyan wandered about like this, hoping for an opportunity to see and speak with her! But what did any of this matter to me? Better to keep silent, go, and sleep.
Just as the young man reached this decision, he heard his own name mentioned in the conversation below. Instantly, he began to listen more intently.

“That boy who came claiming to be your son’s friend—where is he sleeping? None of our conversation must reach his ears. Remember, he serves under the northern lord, Mathanda Nayakar. Until the time comes for our plan to be fulfilled, no one else must know of this. If there is even the slightest suspicion that boy has learned something, he must not be allowed to leave the fort. It would be best to deal with him at once…”
Dear reader, you can imagine how Vandiyathevan must have felt upon hearing this. Yet, he did not move from his place. He resolved to listen to their conversation to the very end.

Who is the Lord of the Northern Province? He is the eldest son of Emperor Sundara Chola. The crown prince, destined to ascend the Chola throne next. What objection could these men possibly have to serving him? What matter are they about to discuss that must remain hidden from him?
At that moment, Kandhamaaran’s words, spoken with concern for his friend, reached Vallavaraiyan’s ears.

“Vandiyathevan is lying peacefully asleep in the corner pavilion of the upper floor. He will not overhear a word of this gathering’s conversation. Nor is he the sort to meddle in matters that do not concern him. Even if he happens to learn something, it will not bring any harm to your plans; I will take responsibility for that!” said Kandhamaaran.

“I am glad to see you have such faith in him,” replied Pazhuvetarayar. “But none of us here knows him well, and that is why I cautioned you. What we are about to discuss concerns the rights to a vast empire. If, by carelessness, even a single word escapes these walls, it could bring about terrible disaster. Let this be remembered by all of you!”

chapters.title: Laughter and Fury
paragraphs: The moment Vandiyathevan heard the words of the Pazhuvettaraiyar regarding the royal succession, he immediately came to a decision.
