What are these men going to discuss about the right to the throne? Who are they to speak of such matters? Whatever is about to happen in this gathering, I must find out! I must remain seated right here. Nowhere else could I find a more convenient spot than this. Let Azhwarkkadiyan leave if he must—what concern is that of mine?

Already, Vandiyathevan had sensed that some mysterious event was about to unfold here tonight. The cryptic words of Azhwarkkadiyan, the brisk and secretive behavior of the guards at the fortress gate, the half-hearted welcome from Sambuvaraiyar, the frenzied and impassioned speech of the attendant—all these had aroused various suspicions in his mind. Now, by some stroke of fate, he had been granted this opportunity to dispel those doubts and uncover the truth; why should he let it slip away?

Ah! Even Kandhamaaran, whom he had considered his dearest friend, had not revealed the truth to him. After putting him to sleep, Kandhamaaran had come to attend this secret midnight gathering. Tomorrow, he would have to settle accounts with him.
Meanwhile, below, the Pazhuvettaraiyar had begun to speak. Vandiyathevan listened intently, giving his full attention.

“I have come here to inform you all of a matter of utmost importance. It is for this very reason that Sambuvaraiyar has convened this assembly. The health of Emperor Sundara Chola is in a most precarious state. I have inquired privately with the royal physicians. They have said, ‘There is no longer any hope; he will not live much longer.’ Therefore, we must now deliberate on the actions that must follow!”
With these words, the Pazhuvettaraiyar paused.
“What do the astrologers say?” asked one of those gathered.
“Why go to the astrologers? For several days now, a comet has been visible in the evening sky! Is that not sign enough?” said another.

Then the Pazhuvettaraiyar continued: “The astrologers have been consulted as well. They only postpone matters by a few days; that is all. Whatever the case, we must now consider who is next in line for the throne…”
“What is the use of thinking about it any further? The title of Crown Prince was firmly bestowed upon Aditya Karikalan two years ago!” said another deep voice.

“That is true, but before the title of Crown Prince was given, was the opinion of any of us ever sought? I wish to know. Each one of us gathered here belongs to an ancient clan that has, for over a hundred years and through four generations, toiled for the glory of the Chola kingdom. My grandfather’s father died in the battle of Thiruppurambiyam. My grandfather gave his life in the war at Velur. My father sacrificed his life at Thakkolam. In the same way, the ancestors of each of you have laid down their lives to uphold the greatness of this Chola land. In every one of our families, young children have perished on the battlefield. Even today, sons of our clans and households are fighting in the land of Eezham. Yet, when it came to deciding who should next ascend the throne, the Maharaja did not seek our counsel. Even Dasaratha, before crowning Rama, convened a council of ministers and deliberated. He sought the advice of ministers, chieftains, commanders of the army, and minor kings. But Sundara Chola Maharaja did not deem it necessary to consult anyone…”

“It is true that he did not seek our opinion. But to claim that he did not consult anyone at all is not correct, O Lord of Fate. The advice of the great princess Sembiyan Mahadevi and the young princess Kundavai Devi was indeed sought. Can the Pazhuvettaraiyar deny this?” said someone in a mocking tone, and a few in the gathering laughed.

“Ah! You laugh! I do not know how you find it in yourselves to laugh, but as I think of it, my stomach burns; my blood boils. Why should I continue to live, bearing this shame? Today, the soothsayer who came to the assembly said that Durga demands a sacrifice. He said, ‘A human sacrifice is needed from a royal lineage that has endured for a thousand years.’ Offer me as the sacrifice! My clan is more ancient than a thousand years. Each of you, with your sword, strike a blow upon my neck and offer me as the sacrifice. Mother Durga will be satisfied; my soul will find peace…”
Thus, with a voice trembling with the same frenzy as the soothsayer who had danced in the assembly, the Pazhuvettaraiyar spoke, and then fell silent.

For a short while, silence reigned. The sound of the western wind blowing with a “whirr,” and the mysterious rustle of the trees swaying outside the fortress wall in that wind, were all that could be heard.

“Pazhuvur Mahārāja must forgive the jesting words and the laughter that followed, which were spoken in ignorance. You are our unrivaled leader. All of us here are ready to carry out your commands. We walk the path you show us. I beg you, please forgive us!” said Sambuvaraiyar with emotion.

“I too lost my patience for a moment. For that, you must pardon me. Consider this: exactly one hundred years ago today, Vijayalaya Chola defeated the Mutharaiyars and seized Thanjavur. In the battle of Thirupurambiyam, he aided the Pallava army and annihilated the forces of the Madurai Pandyas. From that day onward, the Chola kingdom has grown and expanded day by day. Not even in the time of Karikala Valavan, who raised the banks of the Kaveri, did the Chola realm reach such greatness. Today, from the southern tip at Kanyakumari to the northern rivers Tungabhadra and Krishna, the Chola empire stretches wide. Pandya Nadu, Nanjil Nadu, the Chera land that had never bowed to anyone, Thondai Mandalam, Pāgi Nadu, Gangapadi, Nulambapadi, Vaithumba Nadu, Chitpuli Nadu, Perumpanappadi, and the land of Kodagu where the Ponni river is born—all these lands are now subject to the Chola empire and pay tribute. In all these lands, our Chola tiger flag flies high. Even Lanka to the south, and the twin regions and Vengi to the north, should have submitted to us by now. I need not explain the reasons why they have not; you all know them well!…”

“Yes, everyone knows. There are two reasons why Lanka, the twin regions, Vengi, and Kalinga have not submitted. One reason is the northern conqueror, Prince Aditya Karikalan; the other is his younger brother, Arulmozhi Varman, the commander of the southern forces…”

“I agree with the reason Malavaraiyar has given. For the past hundred years, the tradition in Chola Nadu for appointing commanders has been different. Only those who have fought in many battles and gained experience—heroes among heroes—were appointed as commanders and northern conquerors. But what has happened now? The eldest prince is the commander of the northern army; and what does he do? He has not marched against the twin regions or Vengi. He sits in Kanchipuram, building golden palaces. I ask you, heroes born of heroic clans, has any king in Tamilakam before this ever built a palace for his own residence—” Has anyone ever built a palace out of gold? Even Parantaka Chakravarthi, who conquered Madurai and Eezham and now resides in Kailasa, famed throughout the world, did not build a golden palace for himself. He only thatched the roof of the Chidambaram temple with gold. But now, Prince Aditya Karikalan is building a golden palace for himself in Kanchipuram! The palaces where the Pallava emperors lived and ruled for generations are, it seems, not grand enough for his status. He is building a palace adorned with gold. He is embedding gems and cat’s-eye stones into the very walls of that golden palace. Of all the treasures he has won by conquering the lands of Gangapadi, Nolambapadi, and Kudagu, not a single copper coin has he sent so far to the treasury in the capital city…”
“Is the golden palace finished?”

“Yes, it is finished, as I have learned from my secret spies. Along with this, letters have arrived from his beloved eldest son to Sundara Chola Maharaja. The prince has written that the Maharaja must come and stay for some time in the newly built golden palace.”
“Is the Maharaja going to Kanchi?” someone asked, their voice trembling with concern.

“You need not worry so much about that. I am here to see that nothing of the sort happens; my brother, the guardian of Tanjore Fort, is also there. Without the permission of Chinna Pazhuvettarayar, no one can enter the Tanjore Fort. Without my knowledge, no one can meet the Maharaja or deliver him any letter. I have already intercepted two or three such letters that came.”
“Long live the Pazhuvettarayars!” “Long live the Chanakya-like cunning of the Lord of Pazhuvur!” “Long live his valor!”—these cheers rang out.

“Listen further. Compared to the deeds of the crowned prince, the actions of Prince Arulmozhi, who has gone to wage war in Eezham, are even more astonishing. What do we know of the laws of war? What have our ancestors observed for hundreds of years? When our armies march upon foreign lands, they must procure their food from those very lands. The spoils seized in those lands must be used to pay the soldiers. The greater treasures must be sent to the royal treasury in the capital. But do you know what Prince Arulmozhi is doing? In Eezham, our war…” “They say that food must be sent from here by ships for all the warriors! For a whole year now, I myself have loaded food onto ships and sent it ten times…”
“Strange! Strange!” “This injustice cannot be tolerated!” “Never have we heard of such a thing!” voices rose from the gathering.

“Listen also to the reason Prince Arulmozhi Varman gives for this astonishing arrangement. If, in the lands we conquer, we procure food for our warriors, it seems we risk incurring the displeasure of the local people. Other than the conflict with the royal house of Eezham, we have no quarrel with the people of Eezham, it seems. Therefore, they must not be troubled in any way! After defeating the royal family, the prince says, we must rule with the wholehearted consent of the people. Thus, both money and food must be sent from here!”
At this moment, someone in the assembly said, “Never have we heard of such a war dharma, that in conquered lands we must not ask the people for anything, but instead fall at their feet and beg!”

“Listen also to the disaster this causes. Because of the actions of the two princes together, the treasury and the grain stores of the Thanjai palace are often greatly diminished. I am forced to impose and collect higher taxes from all of you. That is why I have been appointed as the chief officer! If I did not consider the greatness of the Chola land as paramount, I would have long ago abandoned this post.”
“Ah! That cannot be! Your holding this post is our greatest protection. Have you not spoken to the Maharaja about these irregularities?”

“How could I not! I have spoken many times. Each time, the reply is, ‘Ask the elder princess; ask the younger princess!’ As I said before, the Maharaja no longer has the strength to think for himself! In important matters, he does not seek our counsel. The words of his mother, Sembiyan Maadevi, are like the Vedas to him; next, he tells us to seek the advice of his beloved daughter, Princess Kundavai. I, whose hair has turned grey in royal service, along with the other ministers, must go and stand before that young girl—who has never traveled north of Kollidam or south of Kudamurutti—to seek her counsel! What a tale this is! Since the beginning of the Chola kingdom, have women ever—”

We have never heard of such a thing happening before! How long are we to endure such humiliation? Or, if all of you unanimously wish it so, I will relinquish this royal responsibility, abandon the burden of collecting taxes and filling the treasury, and retire to my own native land…”

“No! No! Pazhuvettarayar, you must not forsake us like that. The Chola Empire, which was established through the toil and the blood of thousands of your warriors over four generations, will be shattered to pieces in an instant,” declared Sambuvarayar.

“In that case, you must be the ones to advise me on what should be done in this situation. You must tell me what remedy there is for this state of affairs, which has become more disgraceful than the kingdom of Alli Rani, under the rule of this woman!” said the Lord of Pazhuvur.

chapters.title: Who is in the Palanquin?
paragraphs: For a while, those gathered there were engaged in heated discussion, voices rising and falling as they debated amongst themselves. So many voices mingled together that Vandiyathevan could not make out a single word clearly.

In a loud voice, Sambuvaraiyar said, “Should we not give a reply to what the Lord of Pazhuvur has asked? What is the use of talking in circles? The third watch of the night has already begun. Look, the moon has risen as well.”
“I have a doubt. Perhaps some others here share the same doubt as I do. If the Lord of Pazhuvur will not take offense, I wish to ask about it!” said the deep, gruff voice that had spoken earlier.
“It is Vanangamudiyar speaking now, isn’t it? Let him come forward into the light!” said Pazhuvetaraiyar.
“Yes, it is I. Here, I have stepped into the light.
“It is my custom to show all my anger only on the battlefield, and only to my enemies; never to my friends. So you may ask me anything you wish, without hesitation.”

“In that case, I will ask. The accusation that Pazhuvetaraiyar levels against Sundara Chola Maharaja—some people are now leveling that same accusation against Pazhuvetaraiyar himself! I do not believe it myself, but at a time like this, I wish to ask and clarify!” said Vanangamudiyar.
“What is it? How so? You must explain in detail.”
“It is known to all of us that two years ago, the Lord of Pazhuvur married a young woman…”

At this point, Sambuvaraiyar’s voice rang out, tinged with anger, “We object to Vanangamudiyar speaking about this matter. To question our great leader, our chief guest, in this untimely manner is most improper…”

“I must earnestly request Sambuvaraiyar to be patient. Let Vanangamudiyar ask whatever he wishes, freely. It is better to clear up what is in one’s mind than to let it fester. At the age of fifty-five—” It is true that I married a woman. I admit that freely. But I have never gone around proclaiming myself as the incarnation of Rama in this Kali Yuga. I have never claimed to be a man devoted to a single wife. I loved that woman; she loved me in return. According to the ancient customs of Tamil Nadu, we married for love. What fault is there in that?”
“There is no fault at all!” several voices rang out.
“I did not say that marrying was a mistake either. Who among us here is truly devoted to only one wife? But… but…”
“But what! Speak your mind without hesitation!”
“Some say that the young queen whom you married now has a say in all your affairs, that even in matters of state you seek her counsel. They say you take her with you wherever you go.”
At this, a ripple of laughter spread through the gathering.
Sambuvaraiyar sprang up and shouted, “Who laughed? Step forward at once and explain the reason for your laughter!” As he roared, he drew his sword from its sheath.
“It was I who laughed! Do not be alarmed, Sambuvaraiyar!” said Pazhuvettarayar.

Then he continued, “Vanangamudiyar! Is it a crime to take my wedded wife with me wherever I go? It is true that I have taken her with me to many places. But the claim that I consult her in matters of state is mere slander. That is something I have never done, not even once…”

“If that is so, then I beg you, Pazhuvoor Thevar, to clear up just one more doubt. Why is the palanquin, which ought to remain in the women’s quarters, here in this place where we are holding a confidential council? Is there someone inside the palanquin, or not? If not, then from where did those sounds—the thud we just heard, and the jingling of bangles—come?”
As Vanangamudiyar asked this, a strange silence fell over the assembly. Since the same thought and question had arisen in many minds, no one dared to speak against Vanangamudiyar at once.
Sambuvaraiyar’s lips moved in a mutter, but no words emerged from his mouth.

Tearing through that silence, Pazhuvettarayar spoke in a deep voice: “A proper question; I am bound to give an answer. Before this assembly disperses, I will resolve your doubt. Can you wait for just half a nazhikai more? You do have that much trust in me, do you not?”
“Yes, yes, we have complete faith in Pazhuvettarayar!” cried many voices in unison.

“No one should think that I have less devotion or respect for Pazhuvettarayar than the rest of you,” said Vanangamudi Munaiyarayar. “I asked, as he himself invited us to speak openly. Otherwise, I am ready to obey any command he gives. Even if he were to ask for my life at this very moment, I am prepared to give it!”

“I know Vanangamudi’s heart. I know the trust all of you have placed in me. Therefore, let us first decide the matter for which we have gathered today. May Sundara Chola Maharaja live long and rule this Chola Empire for many years to come. But if, by chance, something happens to him—if the words of the physicians come true, if the omens that have appeared these past days, like the comet, prove portentous—then we must determine who is next entitled to the throne of the Chola Empire.”
“We request that you express your opinion on that matter. There is no one in this assembly who would speak against your view.”

“That is not right. Each one of you should think carefully and express your own opinion. I wish to remind you of some old events. The great warrior, the great sage, the virtuous Kandaraditya Devar, passed away unexpectedly twenty-four years ago. At that time, his son, Madurantaka Devar, was but an infant of one year. Therefore, Kandaraditya’s younger brother, Arinjaya Devar, was to ascend the throne. This was conveyed to us by his own dharmapatni and chief queen, Chembiyan Mahadevi. Accordingly, we crowned Arinjaya Chola and seated him on the imperial throne. But by fate’s decree, Arinjaya Chola did not sit on the Chola throne for more than a year. Arinjaya Chola’s eldest son, Parantaka Sundara Chola, was then a youth of twenty. So, for the welfare of the kingdom, the ministers, feudatories, minor kings, city chiefs, and district lords all deliberated and crowned Parantaka Sundara Chola. No one need regret that decision. For, until two years ago, Sundara Chola Maharaja ruled the land without deviating from the path of righteousness, respecting us all and seeking our counsel in matters of state…” …carried the burden. Because of this, the Chola kingdom expanded and flourished even further. Now, however, Emperor Sundara Chola’s health has become a matter of grave concern. In this situation, who is next in line for the throne? Kandaraditha Devar’s royal son, Madurantaka, is now of age and capable of governing the kingdom. In wisdom, learning, character, and devotion, in every way, he is worthy of the crown. Just a year younger than him is Aditya Karikalan—son of Sundara Chola—who currently serves as the commander of the northern army, stationed at Kanchi.

Between these two, who has the rightful claim to the throne? What is the tradition of our lineage? What does the law of Manu decree? What is the ancient custom of Tamil Nadu? Is it just that the son of the elder, Madurantaka, should ascend the throne? Or is it proper that the grandson of the younger should inherit it? Each of you must speak your mind freely…”
“The son of the elder, Kandaraditha Devar—Madurantaka—is the rightful heir to the throne. That is justice, dharma, and tradition,” declared Sambuvaraiyar.
“That is my opinion as well,” “I too agree,” echoed each member of the assembly in turn.

“Your opinion is mine as well. The crown belongs to Madurantaka. But are we each prepared to strive to establish that right? Are we ready to fight, offering our bodies, wealth, and very souls for this cause? At this moment, are we prepared to swear an oath at the feet of Durga Devi, pledging ourselves to this?” asked Pazhuvetarayar, his voice ringing with a passion hitherto unseen.

For a moment, silence settled over the gathering. Then Sambuvaraiyar spoke: “We are indeed ready to swear such an oath before the goddess as witness. But before we do so, you must clarify one thing. What is Prince Madurantaka’s own wish? Is he willing to ascend the throne and accept the burden of rule? We have heard that Kandaraditha’s ascetic son has renounced worldly life and is wholly absorbed in devotion to Shiva. Many say he has no desire for the kingdom. We have also heard that his mother, Sembiyan Madevi, is entirely opposed to her son’s accession. We wish to know the truth of these matters from you.”

“A fair question, and asked at the right time. It is my duty to clarify this. I should have spoken of it earlier. Forgive me for my omission,” said Pazhuvetarayar, rising to his feet. “Sembiyan Madevi has turned her only son away from all desire for kingship and set him firmly on the path of Shaiva devotion…” It was a matter known throughout the land that efforts were being made to enthrone him. But the reason behind this, neither the kingdom nor the people knew. The sole cause was that the Periya Piratti feared that if it became known that Madurantakan desired the throne, his very life would be in danger…
“Ah!” “Is that so?” voices rose from the gathering.

“Yes; for a mother, the desire that her only son should ascend the throne is surely outweighed by the wish that he should remain alive. Madurantakan, who had always revered his mother’s word as the word of God, had turned his mind towards the path of renunciation. He had been wholly immersed in devotion to Shiva. But of late, his heart has slowly begun to change. The thought that this Chola empire is his by right, and that it is his duty to safeguard it, has taken root and grown strong in his mind. If he learns that you all support him, he is ready to come forward at the right time and declare it openly…”
“What proof is there for this?”
“I will now provide you with proof that will satisfy you all. If I do, are you all prepared to swear your allegiance?”
Many voices resounded, “We are! We are!”
“There is not the slightest doubt in anyone’s mind?”
“No! None at all!”

“In that case, here—I shall bring forth the proof. I will now dispel the doubts of Vanangamudi Munaiyarayar as well!” So saying, Pazhuvettarayar rose. With majestic strides, he walked to the closed palanquin that had been placed nearby.

“Prince! Please draw aside the curtain of the palanquin and step out. Bestow the sight of your face upon these brave warriors, who are ready to offer their bodies, wealth, and very souls for your sake!” he said in a voice filled with utmost reverence.
From the upper floor, hidden behind a pillar, Vandiyathevan, who had been listening with unrestrained curiosity without uttering a word, now looked down carefully.

A hand drew aside the curtain of the palanquin, just as before. It was a golden-hued hand. It was the same ruddy hand he had seen once before. But what he had earlier thought to be a bangle, he now realized was in fact a royal armlet worn by princes. In the next instant, that golden face, radiant as the full moon… It became clear. A handsome figure, resembling Manmatha himself, stepped out of the palanquin and stood there with a radiant smile.

Ah! This is Prince Madurantaka, son of Kandaraditya Devar! Was it not because he remained inside the palanquin that we made the mistake of assuming he must be a woman? Did Azhwarkkadiyan Nambi, like myself, make the same error and is he now craning his neck over the wall to see? Vandiyathevan looked to check. That spot was shrouded in the shade of a tree, cloaked in darkness, and nothing could be seen there.

Meanwhile, from below, fervent shouts arose: “Long live Madurantaka Devar! Long live the crowned prince! Victory to the spear! Victory to the brave spear!” Vandiyathevan saw that everyone in the crowd had risen, lifting their swords and spears high, and were shouting these slogans with great enthusiasm. Thinking that it might be dangerous to remain there any longer, he quickly returned to the place where he had been lying down and stretched himself out once more.

chapters.title: A Conversation on the Road
paragraphs: Vandiyathevan had spent all his life thus far in the arid lands north of the Palar river. He did not know how to swim in the river’s floodwaters. Once, when he was serving as a border guard on the northern bank of the Pennai, he descended into the river to bathe. He was caught in a great whirlpool. That treacherous, perilous vortex spun him round and round, tormenting him. At the same time, it pulled him downward. Soon, all of Vandiyathevan’s strength was drained by the swirling waters. “Now there is no escape; I must drown and die in this whirlpool!” he thought in despair. At that very moment, by some divine intervention, he was cast out of the river’s grasp. The floodwaters carried him to the shore and saved him!

That night, when Vandiyathevan lay down to sleep again, he felt the same sensation as when he had struggled in the river’s whirlpool. It seemed to him that he had fallen, against his will, into the swirling eddies of a great royal conspiracy. Would he be able to escape from this whirlpool of intrigue as he had from the river’s vortex? Would the gods save him once more?

The things he had learned that night from the midnight gathering in the Kadambur palace had left him utterly bewildered. Only a few years had passed since the external troubles that plagued the vast Chola Empire had been quelled. The young prince Aditya Karikalan was a mighty hero, an expert in the arts of war; in statecraft, a Chanakya. By using his intelligence and the full might of the Chola armies, he had utterly destroyed the power of the twin-kingdom Krishna ruler in the Thondai region. The external threat was, for the most part, eliminated. In this situation, internal strife and conspiracy had begun to rear their heads. What would be the outcome of this internal danger, more perilous than any external foe?

Were not the renowned warriors, ministers, leaders, and officers of the Chola land themselves involved in this dreadful undertaking? What kind of men were the Pazhuvettaraiyars and his brother? What was their power? Their influence? And the others who had gathered here today—how much fame, prestige, and valor did they possess? Was this the first such gathering? How many more times would the Pazhuvettaraiyar, carrying Madurantaka in a closed palanquin, orchestrate such schemes? Where could he have taken them? Ah! How advantageous it has been for him, in this treacherous endeavor, to have married a young woman in his old age!

Until now, Vandiyathevan had never harbored the slightest doubt in his mind that Prince Aditya Karikalan was the rightful heir to the Chola throne. Not even in his dreams had he imagined that a rival might arise. He had heard of Madurantakan, the son of Kandaradithar. He knew that, like his father, the son too was a wealthy devotee of Shiva. But he had never heard that Madurantakan had any claim to the kingdom, nor that he might compete for it. Such a thought had never occurred to him until now.

But what of justice and fairness? Who, in truth, is the rightful heir to the throne? Is it Aditya Karikalan? Or Madurantakan? The more he pondered, the more it seemed that there was justice on both sides. If a real contest were to arise, who among them would prevail? What would his own duty be? Ah! What castles in the air he had built in his mind since setting out from Kanchi on this journey! Had he not longed to act in a manner befitting the Crown Prince Aditya Karikalan and thereby attain great positions in the Chola Empire? Had he not even dreamed, in time, of regaining the ancient kingdom of his own Vanar clan? And now, the very staff he had grasped to achieve all this seemed as if it might snap in his hands…

With such thoughts swirling in his mind, Vandiyathevan, after lying down for the second time, tossed and turned for a long while, unable to sleep. At last, in the fourth watch of the night, as the east began to lighten, sleep finally claimed him.

Even when the sharp red rays of the rising sun fell upon him the next morning, Vandiyathevan had not yet awakened. Only when Kandhamaran came and shook him awake did he rouse himself, startled and disheveled.

“Did you sleep well last night?” Kandhamaran asked, in the manner of a host attending to his guest. Then, on his own, he added, “After all the other guests had gone to sleep, I came here and found you performing Kumbhakarna’s service most diligently!”

Suppressing the tumult of thoughts that surged within him, Vandiyathevan replied, “I remember lying down here after watching the Kuravai dance, and only now have I woken up. Ah! How late it has become! It seems the sun has been up for a whole watch already! I must leave at once. Kandhamara! Order your servants to ready my horse immediately!”
“It is beautiful! But are you already preparing to leave? What is the hurry? You must stay here at least ten days before you go,” said Kandhamaaran.

“No, my friend! In Thanjavur, my uncle is unwell. News has come that his survival itself is doubtful. Therefore, I must go and see him at once, I must leave immediately,” Vallavaraiyan replied in a single breath.
“If that is so, then at least on your return you must stay here for a few days without fail.”
“That can be decided then. For now, give me leave to depart!”
“Don’t be in such a rush! Have your morning meal and then set out. I will come with you up to the banks of the Kollidam river.”
“How can that be? So many important guests have come to your house—how can you leave them and—”

“There is no guest more important to me than you!” Kandhamaaran began, but then abruptly stopped himself. “The guests who have come are indeed distinguished, but my father is there to attend to them; the palace officials are there as well. Even last night, I did not get to speak with you for long. Only if I spend at least a little time in conversation with you along the way will my heart find peace. I must certainly come with you up to the Kollidam’s banks!” he insisted.
“I have no objection. As you wish, as is convenient for you,” said Vandiyathevan.

After one naazhigai’s time, the two friends mounted their horses and set out from the palace of the Sambuvaraiyar. The horses ambled along at a gentle pace. The journey was filled with delight. Even when the upper winds swept the road’s dust and showered it upon them, the friends paid it no mind. So absorbed were they in their talk of old memories.

After a while, Vandiyathevan said, “Kandhamaaran! Though I stayed only a single night at your house, it was of great benefit to me. But there was one disappointment. You had described your sister, the northern maiden by the riverbank, in such glowing terms! Yet I could not even get a proper look at her. When she peered out from behind your mother, I saw only a fraction of her face! Shyness and modesty are virtues for women, but your sister seems to possess them in excess.”
Kandhamaaran’s lips and mouth quivered as if to say something. But no words came forth.

“Even so, there is no harm done. Didn’t you say that when I return, I must stay at your house for a few days? We can talk about it then. By that time, perhaps your sister’s shyness will have faded a little, won’t it? Kandamaaran! What did you say your sister’s name was?”
“Manimekalai!”
“Ah! What a sweet name! If her beauty and character match her name…”
Kandamaaran interrupted, “My friend! I beg you one thing. Forget my sister; forget everything I told you about her; do not even mention her!”
“What is this, Kandamaaran! Such a sudden change of heart! Even last night, you were boasting about how I might become your brother-in-law and come to your house!”
“What I said then was true. But since then, the situation has changed. My parents have decided to marry my sister elsewhere; Manimekalai too has agreed to it!”

In his heart, Vandiyathevan said, “Long live Manimekalai!” He had no difficulty guessing to whom Manimekalai had been promised. Surely, it must be to the prince Mathuranthakan, who had emerged from that closed palanquin. The Pazhuvettarayars must be forging such alliances to strengthen Mathuranthakan’s faction. The Pazhuvettarayars are cunning and ruthless indeed!
“Ah! So you’ve planned to make a son-in-law out of one of those wealthy guests who came last night! Kandamaaran! I am neither surprised nor disappointed by this; in fact, I rather expected it…”
“You expected it? How so?”
“Who would give their daughter to a poor orphan like me? What woman would agree to marry a man with neither home nor village? Even if my ancestors once ruled kingdoms, what use is that now?”

“My friend! Enough, stop. Don’t belittle yourself or my family so much! What you say is not the reason. There is another, far more important reason. If you knew it, you would agree yourself. But I cannot reveal it now. When the time comes, you will know for yourself!”
“Kandamaaran! Why are you speaking in such riddles today?”

“Forgive me for that. It is such a great matter that I cannot even speak openly with you. Whatever happens, trust that nothing will ever come between our friendship. When the time comes for the truth to be revealed, I will come running and tell you first. Until then, have faith in me. Believe me, I will never abandon you, not for a single day!”

“Thank you very much for that promise. But I do not understand what situation could ever arise for you to abandon me! Besides, I am not one to survive by trusting another, Kandamaaran! I have always placed my trust in my sword and my spear!”
“The time may soon come when you will need to use that sword and spear. Then, the two of us will stand on the same side, fighting shoulder to shoulder; and your purpose too will be fulfilled…”
“What is this? Are you expecting a war to break out soon? Or do you intend to go to the war in Eezham?”

“To Eezham? If you heard about the beautiful war being waged in Eezham, you would be astonished! They say that rice and other provisions must be sent from Chola Nadu for our warriors in Eezham! What a disgrace! But that is not what I am talking about. Be patient, I will tell you when the time comes; please, do not force me to speak now!”
“Alright, alright! If you do not wish to say anything, then do not. You need not even open your mouth—look, there is the Kollidam!” said Vandiyathevan.
Indeed, in the distance, the floodwaters of the great Kollidam river could be seen. In a few moments, the friends reached the riverbank.

The mighty river surged with fresh, dancing currents, rolling over its banks. The far shore seemed a great distance away. The trees on the opposite bank looked like tiny shrubs. The vast, blood-red floodwaters, swirling and eddying in circular patterns, roaring and crashing, striving to break the banks, rushing onward with a thunderous “Ho!”—the sight left Vandiyathevan awestruck.

At the ferry landing, a boat stood ready. Two boatmen, long poles in hand, waited prepared. A man was already seated in the boat. At a glance, he appeared to be a great devotee of Shiva, a shining gem among Shaivites.
Seeing the men approaching the shore, one of the boatmen called out, “Sirs, are you coming to cross in the boat?”
“Yes; he is coming. Hold the boat for a moment!” Kandhamaaran replied. The two friends leapt down from their horses.
“I came without thinking—what shall I do with this horse? Can it be taken onto the boat?” Vandiyathevan asked.

“No need for that. Look, two men have come along with us. One of them will take your horse from here to Kadambur. The other will come with you in the boat and arrange for another horse for you on the opposite bank,” said Kandhamaaran.
“Ah! What foresight! Truly, you are a real friend!” exclaimed Vandiyathevan.
“You must have thought of the Kollidam as you would the Palar or Pennai rivers. You would never have imagined that it’s impossible to take a horse across here!”
“Yes, forgive me for thinking so carelessly about your Chola country’s river! My goodness, what a river this is! What a flood! It surges like the sea itself!”
The two friends embraced each other and took their leave.
Vandiyathevan walked along the riverbank and boarded the boat. One of the men who had come with Kandhamaaran also got in.
The boat was ready to depart. The boatmen began to push off with their poles.
Suddenly, from a little distance away, a voice called out, “Stop! Stop! Hold the boat!”
The boatmen hesitated, pausing with their poles.
The man who had shouted came running swiftly and soon reached the bank. At first glance, Vandiyathevan recognized who it was: it was none other than Azhwarkkadiyan Nambi.
As soon as the Shaivite in the boat realized the newcomer was a Vaishnavite, he said, “Let it go! Push off! I will not travel in the same boat with that heretic; let him come in the next one!”
But Vandiyathevan turned to the boatmen and said, “Wait a moment, let him come too! There is plenty of space in the boat! We can take him along with us!”
Vandiyathevan wished to learn more about the events of the previous night from Azhwarkadiyan.

chapters.title: The Astrologer of Kudanthai
paragraphs: Born and raised in the land of Kodagu, the river Ponni, having crossed the threshold of maidenhood, longed to reach her bridegroom, the Lord of the Ocean. She hurried forward, traversing forests and hills, leaping over rocks and ravines. As she drew closer and closer to the Ocean King, her heart brimmed with the thrill of soon beholding her beloved, and her whole being swelled with joy. A little further she went, and now she had two arms with which to embrace her lover. With both arms outstretched, she leapt and bounded forward. Yet, it seemed to her that two arms were not enough for the overflowing eagerness in her heart; her arms of desire multiplied—ten, twenty, a hundred! With all those eager arms outstretched, she approached the Lord of the Ocean.

What are the adornments bestowed by the nurses of Chola Nadu upon a bride who sets out to meet her beloved in this manner? Ah! How many beautiful green silks did they drape her in? In what wondrous ways did they crown her with colorful flowers? How lavishly did they sprinkle her with fragrant perfumes? Oh! How can one describe the marvel of the punna and kadamba trees, grown thickly on both banks, showering her with their jeweled blossoms? Can even the divine rain of flowers from the heavens compare to this?
O Ponni river! Is there any maiden who would not rejoice at the sight of you? Is there any young woman whose heart would not overflow upon seeing your bridal attire and ornaments?

Just as all the maidens of a village gather around the bride, so too is it only natural that the rivers—like women—come seeking you and join your flow. Of all the golden arms Ponni stretches out in longing to embrace her bridegroom, one is called Arisilaaru. To the south of the Kaveri, very near to her, flows the beautiful river Arisilaaru. Such a river can only be known to those who are told of it from a little distance away. The lovely green trees growing densely on both banks hide that river from view. From birth, Arisilaaru could be called a royal maiden who has never stepped out of her inner chambers. There is no comparison in this world for the beauty of that maiden river.

Well then, let us forget the thought of the inner chambers, and let our dear readers come with us as we draw near to Arisilaaru. Let them enter amidst the trees that have grown close together like a grove! Ah, what a marvelous sight is this! Is it not as if beauty is being adorned with more beauty, as if sweetness is being added to nectar? Who are these radiant women, seated in the swan-shaped, wondrously adorned, colorful boat? Among them, who is that luminous jewel of a lady, who sits as the central figure—like the full moon among the stars, like a queen born to rule all seven worlds, resplendent with grace and majesty? Who is this peerless woman? And who is the serene beauty seated beside her, holding a veena in her hands? Who are these celestial maidens, whose sweet voices blend with the river’s flood, their songs swelling and mingling with the surge of the waters?

One among them is Meenalocani; another, Neelalocani; one is she of the lotus face; another, she of the lotus-petal eyes. Ah, look at her who plucks the strings of the veena! One could gaze endlessly at the beauty of her slender fingers, like stalks of golden grass, dancing gracefully across the strings.

How can one describe the sweetness of the melody they play? Even the river’s flood seems to have stilled its own murmur, just to listen to their song. The parrots and cuckoos that dwell in the trees along the riverbank have fallen silent, their beaks unopened, plunged into a deep, listening stillness. Is it any wonder, then, that those fortunate enough to be born human, blessed with ears to hear, are transported with delight at this nectar-like music?
Let us listen to what these maidens in the boat are singing:

As the bees hum all around… Draped in a garment of shining gems, With dark, lotus-like eyes wide open, You walked forth in splendor! Hail, Kaveri! With dark, lotus-like eyes wide open, All your steps, I now perceive, Were to reveal your lord’s just scepter Was never bent—hail, Kaveri!

In groves where peacocks dance among flowers, Where cuckoos sing their sweet melodies, With fragrant garlands of arugam grass, You walked forth in splendor! Hail, Kaveri! With fragrant garlands of arugam grass, All your steps, I now perceive, Were to reveal your lord’s valor with the spear— I understand now, hail, Kaveri!

Have we not heard these nectarous Tamil verses somewhere before? Yes, these are the lines sung in the Silappathikaram. Yet, when these women sing them, they are adorned with a beauty and allure never seen before. These women seem to be the beloved companions of the Ponni river herself! That is why they sing with such rapturous emotion, their hearts brimming with ecstasy. Ah! How the song, the melody, the rhythm, and the feeling all blend and entwine, pouring from their voices like a flood of nectar! Is it song, is it music, is it melody, is it harmony? It is none of these. This is some magical art! A bewitching spell that drives both singers and listeners into a sweet madness!

The boat, gliding gently, comes to rest at a landing where the trees part to offer a narrow path. Two women alight; one among them possesses a majestic bearing worthy of being called queen of all seven worlds. The other, her fingers dancing over the strings of a veena, draws forth enchanting music. Though both are beautiful, there is a striking difference between their charms. One has the regal beauty of a blooming red lotus. The other, the gentle sweetness of the white kumudam flower. She was a maiden of beauty. One was the full moon; the other, the crescent at dawn. One was a dancing peacock; the other, a singing koel. One was Indrani, queen of the gods; the other, the beloved of Manmatha, god of love. One was the swift-flowing Ganga; the other, the meandering, gentle Kaveri.

Let us not keep our readers in suspense any longer, but reveal who these two women are. The majestic Ganga is none other than Kundavai, the cherished daughter of Sundara Chola, the radiant princess. She is the sister of Arulmozhi Varman, renowned in history as Rajaraja. The people revered her as the Young Princess, the Royal Maiden, the jewel of the Chola realm, the noble lady who laid the foundation for the Chola dynasty’s greatness. It was she who raised Rajendra, son of Rajaraja, shaping him into the bravest of warriors and the greatest of kings.

The other maiden, who now enjoyed Kundavai’s companionship, was a noblewoman from the Kodumbalur clan. In time, she would become the most fortunate woman in all of history. Today, she shone forth with modesty, sweetness, and serenity.

These two maidens alighted from the boat onto the riverbank. Kundavai turned to the other young women and said, “You all wait here. We shall return within an hour!” The maidens she addressed were princesses born in the palaces of many minor kings of divine Tamil Nadu. They had come to Pazhayarai, considering it a rare fortune to be companions to Kundavai Devi. Now, when the princess stepped ashore with only one among them, saying she would return soon, disappointment and envy flickered in their eyes.
On the bank, a horse-drawn chariot stood ready. “Vanathi! Get into the chariot!” Kundavai said to her companion. As soon as Vanathi climbed in, Kundavai joined her, and the chariot sped away.
“Sister! Where are we going? May I know?” Vanathi asked.
“Why not? We are going to the house of the astrologer at Kudanthai!” Kundavai replied.
“To the astrologer’s house? For what purpose, sister? What do you wish to ask?”
“What else? To ask about you, of course. For some months now, you seem to be lost in a daze, and you are growing thin. I want to ask when this spell will leave you and when your health will return!”
“Sister! You are truly virtuous; there is nothing wrong with my health. Let us not go just to ask about me. Let us turn back!”
“No, my dear, no! I am not going to ask about you; I am going to ask about myself.”
“What is there to ask about yourself? What do you hope to learn from the astrologer?”
“I want to ask whether I will ever get married, or if I am destined to remain a maiden all my life.”

“Akka! For that, will you go to the astrologer? Shouldn’t you ask your own heart? It is you who must decide! Won’t the kings of all the fifty-six kingdoms, from the Himalayas to Kanyakumari, come running to compete for your hand? Why, even princes from lands across the seas will come! Which brave royal youth is destined to win the fortune of holding your hand? Isn’t it you who must decide that?”

“Vanathi, even if what you say is true, there is still an obstacle. If I marry a prince from another land, wouldn’t I have to go to his country? I do not like to leave this Chola land, through which the Ponni river flows! I have sworn never to leave this land for any other…”
“That is no obstacle; whichever prince marries you will become your slave, lying at your feet. Even if you wish to stay here, he will remain here with you.”
“Ah! So you suggest that, like catching a mouse and tying it to your lap, we should keep a foreign prince here in our own land? Do you know what troubles that would bring?”
“Whatever happens, women are born to marry one day, aren’t they?”
“No scripture says so, Vanathi! Look at Avvaiyar! Did she not live for many years as an ever-chaste, immortal poetess?”
“Avvaiyar became old by the grace of God while she was still young. You have not become like that, have you?”

“Well then, if I ever do marry, I will only wed an orphaned warrior of Chola land. Such a man will never inherit a kingdom. He will not ask me to go with him to another country. He will remain here, in Chola land…”
“Akka! Then you will never leave this Chola land, will you?”
“Not for a single day will I leave. Even if they promised to make me queen of the heavens, I would not go.”
“Only today has my heart found peace.”
“What do you mean by that?”
“If you were to go to another country, I too would have to go with you. I cannot bear to be separated from you. At the same time, I have no heart to leave this fertile Chola land.”
“But if you get married, you will have to leave, won’t you?”
“I will never marry, Akka!”
“Oh, girl! What happened to all the advice you gave me?”
“How could I ever be like you?”

“You sly one! Do you think you can throw dust in my eyes? I know everything. You have no particular affection for the Chola land. The Chola country you long for, bearing sword and spear, has gone to wage war in Eezham, hasn’t it? Did you think I do not know your heart’s secrets?”
“Akka! Akka! Am I so foolish? Where is the sun, and where is the morning dewdrop? What use is it if the dewdrop yearns for the friendship of the sun?”
“The dewdrop is small, yes! The sun is great and radiant, true! Yet, does not the dewdrop sometimes capture that mighty sun within itself?”

With a voice full of excitement and eagerness, Vanathi asked, “Is that what you are saying? Are you saying even the dewdrop can reach the sun?” Then, suddenly, a shadow of sorrow crossed her face. “The dewdrop desires; it captures the sun. But what is the result? In a short while, it receives its just punishment. It dries up in the heat and vanishes without a trace!”

“That is not so, Vanathi! Seeing the longing of the dewdrop, the sun unites it with himself. The sun’s wish is that the dewdrop maiden, who desires him, should not be seen by any other man. When night falls, he releases her again. The vanished dewdrop returns and shines anew, does it not?”
“Akka! You say all this just to comfort me.”
“In that case, admit that there is a flaw in your heart. All these days you insisted, ‘There is nothing at all!’ That is why I am going to see the astrologer of Kudanthai.”
“If there is a flaw in my heart, what use is there in going to an astrologer to ask about it?” replied Vanathi with a deep sigh.

The house of the Kudanthai astrologer stood in a secluded spot at the edge of the town, near the Kali temple. Without entering the town proper, the chariot circled around and reached that house. Seeing how the charioteer drove the chariot there without any hesitation or delay, it seemed he must have brought the chariot to this place many times before.

At the threshold of the house, the astrologer and one of his disciples stood waiting in readiness. The astrologer welcomed the visitors with great reverence and devotion, and offered them his hospitality.
“Great Lady! Mother in whom Saraswati and Lakshmi have taken a single form! Welcome, welcome! What fortune for this poor man’s hut, that you have come seeking it once again!” he exclaimed.
“Astrologer! At this hour, surely no one else would come seeking you here, would they?” Kundavai asked.

“No one will come, Mother! These days, very few come in search of me. Only when hardships increase in the world do people flock to astrologers. Now, under the rule of your revered father, Sundara Chozhar, there is no such thing as hardship for the people. All live in happiness, enjoying every comfort and prosperity. Why would they come seeking me?” replied the astrologer.
“So, you are saying that I have come to you only because some trouble has befallen me!” said Kundavai.

“No, Great Lady! Not at all! Who would dare say that hardship has come to the princess of Pazhaiyarai, where wealth overflows like fresh butter? Since there is no hardship for the people of this world, only this poor astrologer has fallen into difficulty; there is no one to pay him heed. Therefore, you have come like the Goddess Ambika herself to relieve the troubles of this wretch. Mother! Please step inside the hut. It would be a grave discourtesy on my part to keep you waiting here at the entrance!” said the astrologer with gentle wit.
Turning to the charioteer, Kundavai said, “Take the chariot near the temple and leave it under the shade of the banyan tree!”
Then, guided by the astrologer, Kundavai and Vanathi entered the house.
The astrologer turned to his disciple and warned, “Son! Stand guard at the entrance and be vigilant; do not let anyone in, no matter who tries to slip past you!”

The astrologer’s chamber had been adorned in a manner befitting the reception of a royal princess. Upon the wall, in a niche, a painting of the goddess Ambikai shone resplendent. Two seats had been arranged for them. A brass lamp burned brightly, and decorative designs sparkled here and there. Around the room, palm-leaf manuscripts and wooden tablets inscribed with astrological charts were stacked in neat piles.
Once the two women had seated themselves upon the pedestals, the astrologer too took his place.
“Lady! Please be gracious enough to tell me the purpose of your visit,” he said.
“Jyotishar! Can you not discern that as well through your astrology?” Kundavai replied.
“So be it, my lady!” said the astrologer, closing his eyes and chanting some mantra softly for a while.

Then, opening his eyes and looking at her, he said, “Princess, you have come today chiefly to inquire about this maiden’s horoscope. Is that not what the grace of Goddess Parashakti reveals to me? Is it true?”

“Ah! Marvelous! What can I say of your powers? Yes, astrologer! I have come to ask about this girl. A year ago, she came to the palace at Pazhayarai. For eight months after her arrival, she was lively and full of cheer. Among all my companions, she was the one who laughed and played the most, always bright and merry. But for the past four months, something has changed. She often seems weary, as if in a daze; she has forgotten how to laugh. She claims there is nothing wrong with her health. If her parents come tomorrow and ask me, I do not know what answer to give them…”
“Lady! Is she not the cherished daughter of Kodumbalur’s noble house? Is her name not Vanathi?” asked the astrologer.
“Yes; you seem to know everything already!”

“I even have this royal maiden’s horoscope with me. I have kept it safe! Please wait a moment,” said the astrologer, and opening an old box beside him, he rummaged through it for a while. Then, from within, he took out a horoscope document… He took it and examined it carefully.

chapters.title: A Bold Entrance
paragraphs: The city that today finds its place even in the English dictionaries as ‘Kumbakonam’ was, in the time of our story, known as Kudanthai, and was also called Kudamooku. Apart from its sanctity as a holy place, Kudanthai was famed for its astrologers. Not far from Kudanthai, to the southwest, stood the Chola’s interim capital, Pazhaiyarai, resplendent with palace towers that seemed to touch the sky and majestic temple gopurams.

The astrologer of Kudanthai had in his possession the horoscopes of all the royal family members residing in the palaces of Pazhaiyarai. It was while leafing through these collected horoscopes that he discovered the horoscope of the Kodumbalur princess, Vanathi. After gazing intently at the horoscope for a while, the astrologer lifted his eyes to study Vanathi’s face. Then he looked back at the horoscope. Thus he kept alternating his gaze between the horoscope and Vanathi, but did not seem to find a way to open his mouth and speak.
“Well, astrologer! Are you going to say something or not?” asked Princess Kundavai.

“My lady! What am I to say? How am I to say it? Once before, by chance, I happened to look at this horoscope. I could not believe it myself; I doubted whether such a thing could even be possible, and so I put it aside. Now, when I compare this young woman’s face with the horoscope, I am left astounded!”
“Be astounded! Be astounded as much as you wish, and then, when you are done, say something definite!” Kundavai said.
“This is a most fortunate horoscope, my lady! I assure you, you will not think otherwise. In fact, it is even a step above your own horoscope. I have never seen a horoscope as lucky as this!”
Kundavai smiled; Vanathi, blushing with embarrassment, said, “Akka! He calls this wretched girl the luckiest in the world! This is how he always is, with his words!”

“My child! What did you say? If what I say is false, I will give up my profession altogether,” declared the astrologer. “No, astrologer! Please, do not do such things. Say something pleasant for the sake of the people gathered here. But you are only speaking in generalities—nothing specific! That is why she is suspicious!”

“Do you want me to be specific? Very well, I shall speak! Four months ago, an incident occurred that seemed like a bad omen. Something fell by accident; but in truth, it was not a bad omen at all. From that moment onward, all manner of fortune is destined to come to this young lady!”
“Vanathi! What did I tell you? Did you hear that?” said Kundavai Devi.
“It seems you have already instructed him beforehand!” said Vanathi.
“Did you hear that, astrologer? Listen to this girl’s words!”
“Let her speak, my lady! Let her say whatever she wishes now! Tomorrow, when the king weds the king…”
“Say it like that. If you speak of marriage to young women, won’t they listen with delight?…”
“That is exactly what I meant to say, my lady! One should not suddenly bring up talk of marriage, should one? If I do, people will say, ‘This old man has lost his wits!’”
“Where will her husband come from? When will he come? What are his marks? Can you tell all this from her horoscope, astrologer?”
“Ah! Why not? I can tell it all very well!” said the astrologer, and once again examined the horoscope.
Whether he truly examined it or only pretended to, we cannot say.

Then, raising his head, he said, “Young lady! This princess’s husband need not come from afar. He is quite near; yet, that hero of heroes is not now in this land. He has crossed the seas and gone away!”
At these words, Kundavai looked at Vanathi.
The joy that surged within Vanathi could not be contained, though she tried; it showed plainly on her face.
“After that? Who is he? What is his lineage? Is there any mark by which we might identify him?”
“There is, indeed, Amma! In the sacred hands of the fortunate man who will wed this maiden, the lines of the conch and discus will be clearly visible!”
Once again, Kundavai turned to look at Vanathi. Vanathi’s face had fallen, and she gazed down at the earth.
“If that is so, will there not be some distinguishing lines on her hands as well?” asked Princess Kundavai.
“Mother! Have you ever seen the soles of her feet?” inquired the astrologer.
“Why, astrologer! What words are these? Are you asking me to hold her feet in my hands?”

“No, no; I did not mean that. But in times to come, thousands upon thousands of royal women—queens, princesses, empresses—will perform penance, yearning for the fortune of touching the feet of this princess, Amma!”
“Sister! This old man is making fun of me. Is this why you summoned me here? Come, let us go!” said Vanathi, her anger rising in earnest.
“Why do you get so flustered, girl? Let him say what he will…”

“I am not saying anything of my own; I only repeat what is written in this horoscope. Poets may sing of ‘lotus feet’ as a form of praise, but in this maiden’s soles, you will surely find the lines of the red lotus petals. Ask her to show the inside of her feet; the marks will certainly be there.”
“That’s enough, astrologer! If you say anything more about her, she will drag me away by the hand and leave at once. Tell us a little about the husband she is destined to marry…”

“Ah! I shall tell you! The fortunate hero who will take her hand will be a warrior among warriors! He will stand at the forefront of a hundred battlefields and be crowned with victory garlands. He will be a king among kings; for countless years, he will sit upon the imperial throne, revered by thousands of rulers.”
“I do not believe what you say—how could such things come to pass?” asked Kundavai, her face a dance of curiosity, delight, doubt, and concern mingled together.
“I do not believe it either. He is speaking with something else in mind. He says these things only because he thinks it will make you happy!” said Vanathi.
“It does not matter if you do not believe me today; one day, you will believe. When that time comes, do not forget this poor astrologer…”
“Akka! Shall we go?” Vanathi asked again.
At the corners of her dark eyes, two tears trembled, threatening to fall.
“Let me say just one more thing. Listen to this before you leave. The warrior who is destined to wed this princess will face countless dangers and obstacles; there are many enemies…”
“Aiyyo!”

“But all those dangers and obstacles will, in the end, vanish; the enemies will meet utter destruction. The hero who wins this goddess will overcome every hindrance and ascend to the loftiest heights… There is a message even more important than this, Mother! I am an old man, so I will not hide what I know. One day, look at this girl’s stomach. If you do not see the lines of the banyan leaf there, I will renounce this profession of astrology…”
“What is so special about the lines of the banyan leaf, Astrologer?”

“Do you not know who reclines upon the banyan leaf? That Maha Vishnu himself! With his aspect, a child will be born in her womb. Her beloved may face many interruptions, obstacles, dangers, and calamities. But for the prince who is to be born from this maiden’s womb, there will be no such hindrance. Whatever he desires will come to pass; whatever he undertakes will be fulfilled; whatever he touches will turn to gold; wherever he sets foot will fall under his dominion; wherever his gaze falls, the tiger flag will fly. Mother! The armies led by her son will surge forth like the new floods of the Ponni river, flowing everywhere without impediment. Jayalakshmi herself will stand before him with folded hands, serving him. The fame of the land where he is born will spread across all three worlds. The glory of the clan into which he is born will endure as long as the world exists!”
As the astrologer spoke thus, as if possessed by a divine fervor, Kundavai Devi gazed intently at his face, drinking in every word he uttered.
“Akka!” came a plaintive voice, startling her into turning around.
“Something is happening to me!” Vanathi said in an even more plaintive voice; suddenly, she swooned and collapsed onto the floor.
“Jyotishar! Quickly, bring some water!” Kundavai called out, and then she lifted Vanathi and laid her gently on her lap.
The astrologer brought water; Kundavai took it and sprinkled it on Vanathi’s face.
“Do not worry, Amma! Nothing will happen…” said the astrologer.

“There’s nothing to worry about; this is usual for her. This has happened five or six times already! In a moment, she will open her eyes and rise, and as soon as she does, she’ll ask if this is the earth or Kailasa!” Kundavai said.

Then, in a softer voice, she continued, “Jyotishar! I actually came to you to ask something important. For some time now, people in the towns and villages have been talking about various things, haven’t they? For the past few days, a comet has appeared in the sky. Do these things have any real meaning? Is there any danger to the kingdom? Will there be any upheaval or confusion?”

“Please do not ask me about such matters, Amma! Countries, kingdoms, royal affairs—these have no horoscopes, and astrology cannot speak of them. In the discipline I have studied, such things do not appear. Perhaps sages, rishis, great souls, and yogis may see and declare such things through their wisdom. This poor man does not possess that power. In matters of state, days, stars, horoscopes, and astrology all lose their strength…”

“Jyotishar! You speak with great skill! Let us not look for the kingdom’s horoscope. But surely you can look at my father’s and my brothers’ horoscopes and tell me something? If you look at their horoscopes, it is almost as if you are looking at the kingdom’s fate, isn’t it?”
“I will look and tell you another day, Amma! In general, this is a time filled with confusion and dangers. Everyone must be a little cautious…”
“Jyotishar! Ever since my father, the Emperor, left Pazhayarai for Thanjavur, I have been filled with worry.”
“I told you before, Mother! The Maharaja is in grave danger. Your family too faces great perils. By the grace and power of Goddess Durga, all will be resolved.”
“Sister! Where are we now?” came Vanathi’s feeble voice.
Resting her head on Kundavai’s lap, Vanathi fluttered her eyelids like the wings of a bee and slowly opened her eyes.

“Beloved! We are still here on this earth! The Pushpaka Vimana has not yet arrived to take us to the heavenly realms. Come, let us climb into our flower-adorned chariot and return to the palace!” said Kundavai.
Vanathi sat up and asked, “Did I faint away?”
“You did not faint; you simply lay down on your sister’s lap and slept a little! I even sang you a lullaby—did it not reach your ears?”
“Do not be angry, sister! Without my knowing, my head began to spin.”
“Spinning, spinning—if this astrologer had told me such fortunes, my own head would have spun as well!”
“That is not the reason, sister! Did I really believe everything he said?”
“Whether you believed or not, the astrologer was frightened out of his wits! He has decided never again to take along a terrifying girl like you.”
“I told you then itself that I would not come to the astrologer! It was you who…”
“It is my fault indeed. Come, let us go. Can you walk a few steps to the door, or must I carry you on my hip?”
“No, no! I can walk just fine.”
“Please wait a moment, Mother! I will give you the goddess’s prasadam—take it with you,” said the astrologer, beginning to wrap up his palm-leaf manuscripts.
“Sir Astrologer! You told me all sorts of things, but you said nothing to my sister,” said Vanathi.
“Child! I have told the Young Princess everything—what more should I say?”
“The heroic warrior who is to marry my sister—”
“Asakaya Soorar,” Kundavai interjected.
“What doubt is there? A prince of great valor…”
“One who possesses all thirty-two auspicious marks; in wisdom, he is like Brihaspati; in learning, Saraswati herself; in beauty, Manmatha; in strength, Arjuna!”
“From where and when will that gentle prince, so worthy of the young princess, arrive?”
“He is coming, Mother! He is coming! Without fail, he will come—he will arrive very soon.”

“How will he come? Will he arrive on horseback? Riding in a chariot? Mounted on an elephant? Will he come on foot? Or will he leap down straight from the sky, breaking through the roof?” Kundavai asked, her voice laced with playful mockery.
“Akka! I hear the sound of horse’s hooves!” Vanathi exclaimed, a hint of excitement in her tone.
“What is strange is that you alone hear what no one else can!”
“No, I am not saying it for fun—listen, can’t you hear it?”
Indeed, at that very moment, the sound of a horse galloping swiftly down the street reached their ears.
“So what if you hear it? Is it possible that horses never pass through the streets of Kudanthai town?” said Kundavai.
“No; it seemed as if it was coming here!”
“Everything seems strange to you. Get up, let’s go!”
At that instant, a commotion was heard at the entrance of the house; voices could be made out.
“Is this the astrologer’s house?”
“Yes; who are you?”
“Is the astrologer here?”
“You must not go inside!”
“I must go in!”
“I won’t let you!”
“I must see the astrologer!”
"Come later."
"I can't come later; I am in great haste!"
"Hey! Hey! Stop! Stop!"
"Move aside! If you block me, I will kill you..."
"Sir! Sir! Please! Don't go inside!"

Such confused cries and shouts came closer and closer; suddenly, the door burst open with a loud bang. With tremendous commotion, a young man strode boldly into the room. Someone was trying to pull him back by his shoulders from behind. The youth, shaking off the grip, crossed the threshold and entered. Readers will have guessed who this young man is—our hero, Vandiyathevan himself!

The eyes of the three people inside the house turned simultaneously toward the valiant newcomer. Vandiyathevan, too, looked at those present. No; he looked at only one among them. Not even that; he did not see Princess Kundavai in her entirety. He saw only her golden face. Did he at least see her whole face? No, not even that! He saw the slightly parted coral-red lips, widened a little in surprise; he saw her wide eyes, brimming with majesty, astonishment, and a mischievous smile. He saw the eyelids and the dark brows; he saw the vermilion-tinted, dimpled cheeks. He saw the smooth, conch-like neck. He saw all these, each separately, yet all at once. Each feature imprinted itself upon his mind.

All this happened in the span of a few seconds. Immediately, he spun around to the astrologer's disciple and said, "Why didn't you tell me there were women inside? If you had told me, would I have come in like this?" Even as he spoke, he pushed the disciple aside and crossed the threshold again to leave. Yet, before stepping out, he turned once more to look at Kundavai Devi before departing.
"Ah! Father, doesn't it feel as if a storm has just swept through and subsided?" said Princess Kundavai.
"It hasn't subsided yet; listen!" said the Kodumbalur Princess.
At the entrance, Vandiyathevan and the astrologer's disciple were still arguing.
"Astrologer, who is he?" asked Kundavai.
“I do not know, Mother! He seems to be someone from Asalur. Looks like a big, rough fellow.”
Kundavai suddenly remembered something and burst into peals of laughter.
“Why are you laughing, Akka?”

“Why, you ask? We were just talking about whether the bridegroom destined for me would come riding a horse, or arrive on an elephant, or perhaps leap down through the roof! I laughed thinking of that!”
Now Vanathi too could not contain her laughter. The laughter of the two young women mingled and rose in waves. Even the commotion and noise outside was drowned by the sound of their mirth.
The astrologer, lost in silent contemplation, applied kumkum to the foreheads of both royal maidens. They received it and rose; they stepped outside the house. The astrologer followed them.

Standing a little apart at the threshold, Vandiyathevan, upon seeing the women, said in a loud voice, “Forgive me. This clever fellow did not tell me there were women inside. That is why I came in so hastily. Please pardon me for that!”

With a blooming face, eyes brimming with mischief and laughter, Kundavai glanced at Vandiyathevan for a moment. She did not utter a single word in reply. Taking Vanathi by the hand, she drew her away towards the banyan tree where their chariot stood waiting.

“It seems the women of Kudanthai city have no manners at all. If a man comes and speaks to them, should they not at least turn and give him a word in reply?” Vandiyathevan grumbled aloud. His words reached their ears.

The charioteer had already harnessed the horse and stood ready. As soon as the princesses climbed into the chariot, the charioteer mounted in front. The chariot sped swiftly towards the banks of the Arisil river. Vandiyathevan stood watching until the chariot disappeared from view.

chapters.title: Nandini
paragraphs: We must now tell how Vandiyathevan, whom we left on the banks of the Kollidam, after he was put into the boat, came to reach the house of the astrologer at Kudanthai, must we not?

The elder Saivite, who objected to Azhwarkkadiyan boarding the boat, after the boat had started moving, turned to Vandiyathevan and said, “Brother! I allowed him to board only because you requested it. But as long as he is in this boat, he must not utter that eight-lettered name. If he does, I will order him to be thrown into this Kollidam. The boatmen are my men!”
“Nambi Adigal! Did that fall upon your sacred ears?” Vandiyathevan asked.
“If he refrains from uttering the five-lettered name, then I too will not utter the eight-lettered holy name!” replied Azhwarkkadiyan.
“Who is he to forbid the utterance of the Panchakshara mantra, the very sacred syllables of Lord Shiva himself? Impossible! Impossible!
Even if I am bound with ropes and cast into the sea, My sole refuge is ‘Namashivaya’!”
Thus thundered the Saivite elder in a majestic roar.
“I sought, I searched, and at last I found— The name ‘Narayana’!”
Azhwarkkadiyan began to sing in a loud voice.
“Shiva! Shiva! Shiva!” cried the Saivites, pressing their fingers into their ears to block the sound.

When Azhwarkkadiyan stopped his song, the Saivites removed their fingers from their ears. Azhwarkkadiyan turned to Vandiyathevan and said, “Brother! Just listen to this valiant Saivite. See how much he suffers even to hear the name of Thirumal! The Kollidam river flows downstream only after washing the lotus feet of Perumal, who reclines at Srirangam. The water that has touched the Lord’s feet is holy water— “Isn’t that why Lord Shiva himself is said to be performing penance, immersed in those very waters at Thiruvanaikka?” Even as he uttered these words, the Saiva elder grew furious and sprang at Azhwarkkadiyan. As the two men grappled at the edge of the boat, it seemed as if the vessel would overturn at any moment. The boatmen and Vandiyathevan intervened, separating them.

“O paragons of devotion! It seems you both are eager to fall into the swirling flood of the Kollidam and attain salvation straightaway. But I still have unfinished business left in this world!” said Vandiyathevan.
One of the boatmen remarked, “Who knows if falling into the Kollidam will lead you to salvation! But you’ll certainly end up in a crocodile’s belly! Look there!”
At the spot he pointed to, a crocodile could be seen, its jaws gaping wide in a terrifying manner.
“I have no fear of crocodiles; where has the primordial Narayana, who saved Gajendra, gone now?” asked Azhwarkkadiyan.
“Where has he gone? Perhaps he’s hiding in the end of a gopi’s sari in Brindavan!” replied the Saiva.
“Or maybe, just as he granted a boon to Padmasura and then ran away in distress, perhaps Shiva has found himself in some new predicament, and Narayana has gone to save him from it,” said Nambi.
“It seems this Vaishnavan has forgotten how Vishnu’s pride was humbled during the destruction of Tripura!” retorted the Saiva elder.
“Swamigal! I truly do not understand why you are quarreling like this. Whoever has devotion to whichever deity, should they not worship that very god?” said Vandiyathevan.
Why did the Saiva elder and Azhwarkkadiyan quarrel in this manner? Why did a similar debate erupt at Veera Narayanapuram? It is fitting at this juncture to explain these matters to the reader.

For nearly six hundred years in ancient Tamil Nadu, the Buddhist and Jain religions held sway. Their influence brought many benefits to the Tamil land. Sculpture, painting, poetry, and epic literature all flourished. Later, the Alwars and Nayanmars arose. They poured forth divine Tamil hymns sweet as nectar, causing Vaishnavism and Saivism to thrive and spread. Their methods of propagation were exceedingly powerful. For their propaganda, they combined the art of sculpture with the art of music. The hymns of the Alvars and the Thevaram songs of the three Saiva saints were set to music resembling the celestial tunes of the gods, and many began to sing them. These musical hymns enchanted the hearts of listeners and instilled a fervor of devotion. The Vishnu temples praised by the Alvars and the Shiva temples celebrated by the three Saiva saints attained new glory and sanctity. Temples that had previously been built of brick and wood were renovated and reconstructed in stone. This work of temple restoration was carried out extensively by the Chola kings and members of the royal family from the time of Vijayalaya Chola.

At the same time, a remarkable event occurred in the land of Kerala. In a place called Kaladi, a great sage was born. In his youth, he renounced the world and became a sannyasi. He mastered all the scriptures in Sanskrit and reached their farthest shores. On the basis of the Vedas, the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita, and the Brahma Sutras, he planted the flag of Advaita Vedanta. With the help of his profound knowledge of Sanskrit, he traveled throughout the land of Bharat, conquering all directions, and established eight Advaita monasteries in various places. The sannyasis who supported his philosophy spread far and wide across the country.

Thus, in Tamil Nadu, at the time when our story takes place—about 980 years ago (from 1950, when this was written)—a great religious upheaval was underway. From this turmoil, some harmful elements also arose and spread. Fierce Vaishnavites and fierce Saivites sprang up here and there. Wherever they met, they clashed in disputes. The Advaitins too joined in these debates. Sometimes, these religious arguments escalated into physical brawls.

There is a remarkable story that illustrates the Saiva–Vaishnava conflicts of that era. A Vaishnavite from Srirangam was walking along the outer wall of the Thiruvanaikaval temple. Suddenly, a stone fell on his head. He was wounded, and blood began to flow. The Vaishnavite looked up in surprise. Seeing a crow perched on the gopuram, he realized that a stone from the old tower must have come loose and fallen. Instantly, his pain and injury were forgotten, and he was filled with delight. “O valiant Vaishnavite crow of Srirangam! Keep striking down the Shiva temple of Thiruvanaikaval!” he exclaimed.
In those days, such sectarian rivalry between Saivites and Vaishnavites was widespread. Understanding this will greatly help in following the story as it continues.
Once the boat reached the opposite shore, the great Saivite elder turned to Azhwarkkadiyan and, casting a final curse, declared, “You shall be destroyed!” Then he went on his way.

The warrior from Kadambur, who had accompanied Vandiyathevan, said he would go to the nearby town of Thiruppanandal to procure a horse and left. Azhwarkkadiyan and Vandiyathevan sat down beneath a royal tree on the riverbank. In the thick, expansive branches of that tree, hundreds of birds were chattering sweetly, filling the air with melodious noise.
Vandiyathevan and Nambi were both eager to extract some information from each other, each trying to grasp what the other knew. At first, they spoke in a roundabout fashion for a while.
“Why, brother! Didn’t you leave me behind and go without taking me to the Kadambur palace?” asked Azhwarkkadiyan.
“It was a great struggle for me to get there myself, Nambi!” replied Vandiyathevan.
“Is that so? Then how did you manage to go? Or did you perhaps not go at all?”

“I went, I went! Once I set my mind on something, do you think I would turn back? The gatekeepers tried to stop me. I gave my horse a slap and rode inside. All those who tried to block me tumbled to the ground. Before they could get up and surround me, my friend Kandhamaaran came running and led me in.”
“I thought it must have been something like that. You are a very brave man. Well, what happened next? Who all were there?”
“Many important people had come. I don’t know all their names. The Pazhuvettaraiyar was there. His young wife had also come. Oh, what can I say about that woman’s beauty?...”
“Did you see her yourself?”

“Yes, of course I did! My friend Kandhamaaran took me into the women’s quarters. I saw her there. Among all those women, the young queen of the Pazhuvettaraiyar shone with extraordinary beauty! Amidst the dark-complexioned maidens, her face glowed like the full moon. Rambha, Urvashi, Tilottama, Indrani, Chandraani—all of them pale in comparison to her!”
“My goodness! What a description you give! What happened next? Was there a Kuravai dance?”
“Yes, there was, and it was wonderful. At that moment, I thought of you.”
“They didn’t give it to me. What happened next?”
“The Velanattam took place. The Devaralan and Devaratti came up onto the stage and danced with great fervor.”
“Did the sannadham happen? Did they make any proclamations?”
“Ah! The sannadham man said things like, ‘What you wish for will come to pass; rain will fall; the land will yield its bounty…’”
“Was that all?”
“He said something else too, something about affairs of the kingdom. I didn’t pay much attention to that.”

“Oh dear! Was that all? You should have listened carefully, brother! You are a young man; you seem to possess great valor. Whenever anyone speaks about matters of the state, you must listen and remember.”
“What you say is true. Even I felt the same way this morning.”
“Why this morning?”

“This morning, Kandamaran and I were talking as we walked along the banks of the Kollidam. After I went to sleep last night, apparently the guests who had come to Kadambur palace gathered and discussed all sorts of matters concerning the kingdom.”
“What did they talk about?”
