Or have those Machahasta conspirators changed their plan and gone elsewhere? What a disappointment! If I am deceived tonight, I shall never forgive myself!… Ah! There, I see a faint light! What is it? The light disappears; now it appears again—there is no doubt. Look, someone is coming, holding a torch! No, two people are coming. My waiting has not been in vain!…”

The two newcomers crossed the battlefield and went a little further. In the midst of the dense forest, they stopped at a small clearing. One of them sat down; the one holding the torch looked around in every direction. There was no doubt he was expecting someone’s arrival.
After a short while, two more people arrived. They must have come here before; otherwise, how could they have found their way through this darkness, through the thick forest?

The first arrivals and the newcomers exchanged words. But none of it reached Azhwarkkadiyan’s ears. “Alas, after all this trouble, it seems there is to be no benefit! I cannot even make out who these people are…”
It seems so!’

Then, two more people arrived; those who had come earlier and those who came last spoke among themselves. One of the last arrivals carried a bag in his hand. He untied it and poured out its contents. In the flickering light, gold coins gleamed brilliantly.

The man who poured them out laughed like a madman and said, “Friends! With the Chola nation’s treasure, we are going to set fire to the Chola kingdom itself! Is this not a grand spectacle?” With that, he burst into laughter again.
“Ravidasan! Do not make such a noise; let us speak a little more softly,” said one of them.
“Ah! What does it matter if we speak like this here? Only foxes, wild dogs, owls, and bats will hear our words! Fortunately, they will not go and tell anyone!” said Ravidasan.
“Even so, it is better to speak softly, is it not?”

After that, they began to speak in hushed tones. To Azhwarkadiyan, it seemed pointless to sit atop the mandapam without being able to hear their conversation. He had to climb down from the mandapam and stand close to the gathering to eavesdrop. He would have to face whatever dangers might arise as a result—so thinking, Azhwarkadiyan tried to climb down from the mandapam. As his body brushed against the tree branches, a rustling sound was made.
Two of the men who had been talking leapt up at once and roared, “Who’s there?”

For a moment, Azhwarkadiyan’s heart stopped beating. There was no way but to escape without being caught by them. But even if he ran, the rustling in the forest would surely be heard! What if they came and caught him? At that tense moment, a bat spread its wings and, flapping them, let out a loud “Oom! Oom!” growl.

chapters.title: "The First Enemy!"
paragraphs: At that timely moment, Alwarkadiyan inwardly praised the owl for its help. For, the conspirators gathered in the heart of the forest, upon seeing the owl flapping its wings and hooting, assumed that the noise had come from it.
“Hey! This wretched owl has frightened us! Cut it down!” said one of them.

“No! Save your knives for more important tasks. Keep them sharp for wiping out our enemies, roots and all! The owl and the horned owl are not our foes; they are our friends! When ordinary men sleep, we keep our eyes open. Along with us, the owls and nightjars too remain awake!” declared Ravidasan.

Listening to his words, Thirumalaiyappan quietly stepped, one foot after another, and approached a great marudhu tree. The roots of that hundred-year-old tree spread in all directions. Between two of its main roots, there was a hollow in the ground; at the base of the tree, a fine cavity had formed. In such a hollow, blending with the tree itself, Alwarkadiyan stood.

“As long as the treasury of the Thanjavur kingdom remains, we will lack nothing for our needs. What we require is the courage of heart to complete what we have begun. Until the deed is done, we must have the strength to keep our secret hidden from the world! We must divide ourselves into two groups. One group must go to Lanka at once; the other must go to the Thondai region and wait for the right moment to accomplish our purpose. Both tasks must be completed at almost the same time. If, after finishing off one enemy, we give time, the other will become cautious! We must not give any such chance. Do you understand? Who among you are ready to go to Lanka?” asked Ravidasan.
“I will go!” “I shall go!” Several voices answered at once.
“Who will go can be decided next time we meet in Pandya country! Until then, there are still some arrangements to be made here,” said Ravidasan.

“Which route to Lanka would be best?” one of them asked. “We can go by way of Kodikkarai; it is a good route for crossing the sea. But the journey from here to Kodikkarai is difficult—enemies everywhere, spies at every turn. Therefore, it is best to go to Sethu, cross the sea there, and land near Mahodaya. Those who travel to Lanka must know how to row a boat, push a raft, and swim in the sea. Who here knows how to swim?”
“I know,” “I know too,” came several voices.

“First, we must meet King Mahindan of Lanka and speak with him before we proceed with our mission. So, at least one among those going to Eelam must know the Sinhala language. Ah! Our Soman Sambavan has not yet arrived? Has anyone seen him today?”
“Here I come!” came a voice from very close to Azhwarkadiyan.

Azhwarkadiyan pressed himself even closer to the tree, blending into it as if he were part of the wood. Alas! How troublesome it is that this wretched body has grown so large! Two more men now joined the gathering. Azhwarkadiyan peered out from behind the tree, revealing only a small part of his face. He recognized that these newcomers were the same men he had seen conversing under the peepul tree on the banks of the Kollidam.

As soon as the new arrivals appeared, Ravidasan said, “Welcome! Welcome! I feared something might have happened to you, or that you might not come at all. From where, and by what route, did you arrive?”
“We came along the Kollidam bank. On the way, a pack of jackals surrounded us. It took time to escape from them and reach here!” replied Soman Sambavan.
“There is some sense in fearing tigers and lions. But what can those who fear jackals ever accomplish?” said one of the men who had arrived earlier.

“Don’t say that, sir! The jackal is more cunning than the lion or tiger! Lions and tigers attack alone; one can fight and defend against them. But jackals come in packs, and thus, their strength is greater. Was it not because the jackals of Chola Nadu came in great numbers that our peerless king of kings was defeated and forced to give up his life? Would such a fate have befallen him otherwise?”
“We shall utterly destroy that jackal clan! We will annihilate them, root and branch!” cried Soman Sambavan, his voice brimming with arrogance.
“Here are the tools needed for that very purpose!” said Ravidasan, pointing to the heap of gold coins.
Soman Sambavan picked up a few of the coins and examined them. “Ah! A tiger on one side, and a palmyra tree on the other!” he remarked.
“Chola gold; the seal of Pazhuvetaraiyar. I have fulfilled my promise exactly as I said I would. Now, what news do you bring? Surely our Idumbankari must have brought some tidings?” asked Ravidasan.
“Yes, he has brought news; listen! He will tell you himself.”

Idumbankari began to speak: “As per your command, I have been working as a servant in the Samburayar palace. The fruits of that labor ripened only last night. Yesterday, a grand feast was held at the Samburayar palace. Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar, Vanangamudimudiyaraiyar, Mazhapadi Mazhuvaraiyar, and many others were present. There were performances of the Kuravai dance and the Velanattam. During the Velanattam, the oracle came and delivered his prophecy to the dancer Devaralan. What he said was in perfect alignment with our aims. Everyone believed that the veiled palanquin accompanying Pazhuvetaraiyar contained his young queen. Pazhuvetaraiyar declared that Sundara Chola Maharaja’s health was failing and that he would not live much longer. They all agreed that the next to ascend the throne should not be Aditya Karikalan, but rather Madurantaka Devar. However, some wondered whether Madurantaka Devar would consent to this. ‘I shall have him answer with his own mouth,’ said Pazhuvetaraiyar, and opened the curtain of the veiled palanquin. From within, Madurantaka Devar emerged! He declared that he was willing to accept the crown…”

“So, they are about to crown a man who has the courage to don a woman’s disguise! Let them crown him well; everything is unfolding just as we expected. Such confusion arising in the land of the Cholas is most favorable to our cause. Whatever happens, no one will ever suspect us, will they? Idumbankari! You have brought most important news. But how did you come to know all this? How did you get such an opportunity?” asked Ravidasan.
“When they convened their council at midnight, they stationed me as a guard to ensure that no one else approached. While keeping watch, I made use of both my ears and my eyes.”
“Did you discover anything by doing so?”
“I did. Everything that happened in that midnight gathering was being observed by another stranger from atop the fortress wall!”
“Ah! Who was he?”
“A Vaishnavite with a prominent tuft at the front…”
“Aha! Was it him? I thought as much! What did you do with him? Did you not hand him over to Sambuvaraiyar?”
“No. For a moment, I thought he might be one of ours. I wondered if you yourself had sent him.”
“You have made a grave mistake; he is not one of ours. He is sturdy as a log, and goes by the name Thirumalaiyappan, a quarrelsome fellow who calls himself ‘Azhwarkkadiyan’.”
“It was indeed he. I realized my blunder myself this afternoon; it became clear he was not our man.”
“How did you come to know that?”

“Last night, a close friend of Kandanmaran also came to Kadambur palace. It was evident that he had no connection with the Pazhuvettaraiyar faction. He lay down in a corner and slept peacefully. This morning, the young master brought his friend as far as the banks of the Kollidam. Knowing that he would be coming, I went ahead and waited for him; he asked me to come along as well. He turned back at the northern bank of the Kollidam. He instructed me to cross to the southern bank, procure a horse for the young man, and then return. I told him I would go to Kudanthai to visit my aunt and return, and thus I was able to come here without arousing any suspicion.
“Very well, very well! What else did you learn about that Veera Vaishnavite?”

“When the boat was about to depart on the Kollidam, that Veera Vaishnavite boarded it. From a few sharp words he exchanged with Kandanmaran’s friend, I became somewhat suspicious, wondering if he might be one of ours. Moreover, on the southern bank of the Kollidam, he waited for me…” …it seemed so. I made our secret sign to him. But he did not understand. From that, I decided he was not one of us…”

“What a grave mistake you have made! One should never reveal our sign to strangers, whether known or unknown. Friends! Listen to me; our mission lies in Kanchipuram! It lies in Lanka as well. In both these places, our most formidable enemies reside. Yet, more dangerous than either of them, our greatest and most cunning foe is that man who roams about under the false name of Azhwarkkadiyan, that very Thirumalaiyappan. He is the one who can utterly destroy us and our cause. He is the one who seeks to take away the goddess who is our matchless leader. Therefore, if any of you see him anywhere, under any circumstance, draw the weapon in your hand and plunge it into his chest at once. If you have no weapon, twist his neck with your bare hands and kill him. Or, by cunning, poison him. Or, push him into the flood and let him be devoured by crocodiles. Or, with some excuse, lure him to the top of a cliff and hurl him down. Just as you would show no mercy to a scorpion, a poisonous centipede, or a snake, show him none—kill him! If you can offer him as a sacrifice to Durga Devi or Kannagi Amman, all the better. In any case, as long as he lives, he will remain an obstacle to our purpose!…”
“Ravidasar! For you to urge us so insistently, he must be a great mischief-maker. Who is this man?”
“Who? He is a spy of terrifying skill!”
“Whose spy?”

“For a long time, I too was uncertain. I suspected he might be the spy of Sundara Chola, or perhaps of Aditya Karikalan; but I found that was not so. Now, I suspect he may be the spy of that old woman in Pazhayarai, the great mistress herself.”
“Ah! Is that so? Why would that Sembiyan Devi, who is immersed in Shaivite devotion and busies herself with temple renovations, need a spy?”

“All that is a lie. Just as this man with the forelock’s fierce Vaishnavism is but an outward disguise, so too is that old queen’s Shaivite piety. Is she not a demon who is a deadly enemy even to her own child? That is why, her very own—
“Even her own brother, Mazhavarayan, has quarreled with her and joined the side of Pazhuvetaraiyar?”
“Ravidasar! Is there anyone else like that front-tufted Vaishnavite?”

“There is an astrologer in Kudanthai. I have my suspicions about him as well. He pretends to tell fortunes to everyone who comes and goes, but in truth, he cunningly extracts all sorts of information from them. None of you should go to him; if you do, you will most certainly be deceived.”
“Whose spy do you think he is?”

“I have not yet been able to discover that. Perhaps he is now acting as a spy for the false prince who is currently in Lanka. But I am not overly concerned about the astrologer. He cannot cause any great harm. It is the Vaishnavite that I fear! Wherever you see him, he must be killed without mercy, like one would strike down a scorpion, a poisonous centipede, or a snake!”

Listening to all this from behind the marudhu tree, Azhwarkkadiyan trembled from head to toe; his whole body broke out in a cold sweat. He began to doubt whether he would escape alive from beneath that tree. As if all this were not enough, at that very moment, he felt the urge to sneeze. He tried his utmost to suppress it, but could not. Pressing a cloth tightly against his mouth, he sneezed—a muffled “nach!” At that moment, the wind had died down; even the rustling of the forest trees had ceased. Because of this, Thirumalaiyappan’s stifled sneeze was heard, faintly but clearly, by the conspirators conversing nearby.
“There’s some sound coming from behind that marudhu tree. Take the torch and see what it is,” said Ravidasan.

The man holding the torch approached the tree. As he drew nearer, the light grew brighter. Disaster! Now he was about to turn around the tree’s trunk. The moment he turned, the torchlight would fall directly upon him. What would happen then? If he escaped, it would be nothing short of a rebirth!

Thirumalaiyappan’s heart pounded furiously. He looked all around for a way to escape; he found none. He gazed upwards in desperation; there, hanging upside down from a branch that had broken away from the tree, was a giant bat, meditating in stillness! Suddenly, an idea struck him. Swiftly, he reached up, grabbed the bat, and held it ready in his hand. As the torchbearer rounded the tree, Thirumalaiyappan flung the bat straight at the man’s face. The torch fell to the ground, its light dimming.

The man who had been struck on the face by the bat’s wing muttered, “Ah! Ah! What! What is this?” He heard the sound of many people running towards him. Azhwarkadiyan, too, took to his heels; in the very next moment, he vanished into the dense forest.

The crowd gathered, shouting, “What happened? What is it?” The man with the club began to explain how a bat had attacked him. All this reached the ears of Thirumalaiyappan, who listened to the commotion for some distance as he hurried away.

chapters.title: The Curtain Ripples!
paragraphs: Can two minds operate within a single man at the same time? Yes, they can—this Vandiyathevan learned from his own experience that day.

He was traveling through one of the most fertile regions within the prosperous Chola land. It was the season when the rivers brimmed and surged with fresh, overflowing waters. Through canals, sluices, and tanks, water rushed and gurgled into the channels and fields. Everywhere he looked, the land was awash with water. How fitting it was to call the Chola country “Valanadu”—the Land of Plenty—and the Chola king “Valavan”—the Lord of Prosperity!

But no sooner had this thought crossed his mind than the dangers looming over the Chola land and its king came to his memory. In such a situation, what was his duty? Was it enough to simply deliver the scroll given by Prince Karikalan to the Emperor and consider his responsibility fulfilled? Why should he involve himself in the feverish turmoil and strife of this royal succession? What did it matter to him who ascended the Chola throne? After all, were these not the ancient enemies of his own lineage? Was it not the Cholas, the Gangas, and the Vaithumbas who had joined forces to utterly destroy the Vanagopadi kingdom?

Just because Aditya Karikalan was now gracious to him, would all those injustices be wiped away?… Tch! How could those old events be called injustices? Among kings, is it not natural to wage war against one another? Likewise, is it not natural for victory and defeat to alternate? What use is there in harboring resentment against those who have triumphed? When our ancestors were in power, did they not, too, strike terror into other kings? Did they not seek to destroy them utterly?
Ah! What is that song? There—it comes to mind!
“Making the army flourish, damming the red blood, In the thick mire trampled by elephants—Manabaran, The king of kings, the Vanan, snatched away And danced upon the crowns of the three great kings!”

Thus, even our forefathers committed cruel deeds on the battlefield. The fate of the vanquished in war is always misery. Can all kings be merciful and generous like Rama or Dharmaputra? If they were so, would they not have ended up wandering the forests… They struggled! Though they were men of valor, and though they had the company of warriors, they suffered greatly. In matters of state, there can be no room for mercy. Yet, if one were to look closely, it must be said that the Chola clan possessed a certain compassion. They even sought to make friends of their enemies whenever possible. For that purpose, they would arrange marriages between clans, setting aside their own lineage. Did not Arinjaya Cholan, the father of Sundara Cholan, marry the daughter of Vaidhumbarayan? Is it not because Sundara Cholan and his children are born of that famed beauty that they shine so radiantly in their own beauty? Ah! When one speaks of beauty, the thought immediately turns to that maiden of Kudanthai… the woman by the banks of the Arisil river. The memory does not come anew from somewhere else; it has always ripened within him, deep in his heart.

While Vandiyathevan’s outward mind was occupied with thoughts of the natural riches of Chola country and the political confusions swirling about, his inner mind was wholly absorbed in thoughts of that maiden. Now, both his inner and outer minds joined together, and he began to ponder her with single-minded intensity. Thereafter, no matter what beautiful object of nature he beheld, he found himself comparing it to some aspect of that maiden. The supple bamboo reminded him of her shoulders. The blue lilies clustered in the streams became a simile for her eyes. He wondered if the golden lotus flowers could truly rival the radiance of her golden-hued face. The humming of bees among the blossoms trembling on the riverside trees—could that be likened to the music of her voice? Poets may have taught such comparisons, but where, in truth, are such things to be found? Where is the beauty of that maiden? When he beheld her face, his very skin had tingled! Even now, recalling it, his heart trembled! Yet, seeing these flowers and bees, he felt no such thrill…

Shame! We have forgotten all the teachings of our elders! In this world, there is no greater illusion than the enchantment of women. He who wishes to succeed in life must never fall into the snare of women’s allure; if he does, he is lost! Is not the story of Kovalan a rare example of this very truth? And not only Kovalan—look at the present day! Is it not for this very reason that people mock the mighty Periya Pazhuvettarayar, the greatest of warriors and the most influential man in Chola land? But the people do not know the truth. They do not know whom Pazhuvettarayar brings in that closed palanquin! So they speak foolishly. Even so, that Madurantaka Devar need not degrade himself so! Fie! To sit hidden in a closed palanquin, passing from town to town, concealed in the place of Pazhuvettarayar’s queen—is this the glory of manhood? Is this how one must win a kingdom?

Could he truly protect and preserve the kingdom he had thus acquired? Must he rely on men like the Pazhuvettaraiyars and govern the realm only by submitting to their authority? In this matter, the actions of Emperor Sundara Chola were not particularly shrewd! He ought not to have granted so much power and influence to men like the Pazhuvettaraiyars. Especially when he had two such illustrious sons? And a daughter whose intelligence and ability astounded the entire land? That maiden—the one he had seen at the astrologer’s house, the one who had spoken with him on the riverbank—whose features did her face resemble? Could it truly be so? Madness! It could never be!—But why could it not be? If it were so, there would be no greater fool than himself! No one more unfortunate! From Lanka to the Vindhya mountains, the fame of which princess had spread so widely? And how had he behaved before her, like a wild, uncouth brute! No, it could not be! How could he dare show his face before her tomorrow, bearing the prince’s letter?

With such thoughts—thoughts that seemed to encompass both heaven and earth—Vandiyathevan walked along the banks of the Kaveri and reached Thiruvaiyaru. The wealth and beauty of that town captivated his heart. He learned that this indeed was Thiruvaiyaru. All he had heard about the glory of this wondrous holy place seemed, if anything, an understatement of the truth. The descriptions in the Thevaram hymns of Gnanasambandar could be seen here, alive and unchanged. In three hundred years, nothing seemed to have altered. Look at the trees on the banks of the Kaveri—how luxuriantly they have grown! The jackfruit trees bore enormous fruits, hanging in clusters. Nowhere else in the Thondai region could such sights be found. Ah! In such fertile places, monkeys seemed to appear from nowhere. How gracefully they leapt from branch to branch! What had Sambandar sung? The memory returned to him.

At the street corners of Thiruvaiyaru, women danced upon raised platforms. The sound of drums resounded, accompanying songs suited to the dance. Hearing that thunderous music, the monkeys, imagining it to be the roar of clouds, climbed to the highest branches of the tall trees and gazed skyward, wondering if rain would come! How apt it all seemed, even today! The monkeys climbed to the very tips of the tallest trees! And not only that—the sweet sounds of music and song drifted from within the town. The notes of the yaazh, kuzhal, muzhavu, thannumai, and other instruments mingled with the jingling of anklets. The dancers here were not the professional kuravai performers as in the Kadambur Sambuvaraiyar’s palace. Ah! What melodious and refined music was heard here!
The forest. The melodious jingling of anklets worn by skilled Bharatanatyam dancers. Listen— even the rhythmic tapping of the dance masters’ sticks joins in the music!
“When the women with bangled arms dance with their sticks, and the ones with radiant faces smile, when the girls play with their bows and silks, who is the young maiden that dances in Thiruvaiyaru!”

Ah! Sambandar Swamigal was a great devotee of Shiva; but even more so, he was a connoisseur! Even today, Thiruvaiyaru shines just as he described it in his verses! In such a town, one must spend at least a day, witnessing the wonders of dance and song, and only after beholding Lord Ayyarappar and the virtuous Lady Amman, the patroness of dharma, should one depart!

How marvelous! How many devotees are seated on the banks of the Kaveri, performing their rituals? How splendid they look, adorned in neat rows with sacred ash! At times, the sounds of dance and music are hushed, and the chant of “Namashivaya” can be heard! Why is that? Ah, someone is singing Sambandar’s Thevaram in a sweet, melodious voice! It is as if this Thiruvaiyaru was created by the Lord solely for the sake of music and art! In this town, I must surely stay at least one day and see it all before I leave! What is the use of hurrying to Thanjavur? Is it even possible to enter the fort? And even if I do, will I be granted an audience with the Maharaja? It is said that the two Pazhuvettaraiyars have all but imprisoned the Maharaja together… I must go to the northern bank of the Kaveri!

Just as Vandiyathevan reached this decision, an incident occurred. From the west, along the banks of the Kaveri, a palanquin approached. A few guards walked before and behind the palanquin. A suspicion arose in Vandiyathevan’s mind. He waited there until the palanquin drew near; and as he had guessed, on the outer curtain covering the palanquin, the emblem of the palm tree was painted. Ah! This is the palanquin coming from Kadambur! While I came by way of Kudanthai, they must have taken another route! But the Pazhuvettaraiyar is not to be seen! Perhaps he has stopped somewhere else along the way.

The palanquin turned towards the southern direction from Thanjavur. That was enough—Vandiyathevan abandoned his plan to stay at Thiruvaiyaru. He resolved to follow the palanquin. For what purpose he made this decision, even he could not have said at that moment. He was certain only of one thing: it was Prince Madurantaka who sat within the palanquin. The aversion he already felt towards him grew a little stronger. Still, if he followed the palanquin for a while, perhaps a good opportunity might arise. The bearers might set it down for some reason; the prince might step out. At that moment, he could make his acquaintance. That might help him gain entry into the Thanjavur fort and to see the Emperor. If he spoke a few fitting words and played his part well, it would suffice. If one could not wield tricks and stratagems, how could any task be accomplished—especially in matters of state?

Therefore, Vandiyathevan let the palanquin and its retinue go ahead and followed a little behind. But the opportunity he hoped for did not come. Between the Kaveri and Thanjavur, they had already crossed four more rivers. Even so, the palanquin was never set down; it continued on in a single breath. And now, in the distance, the walls and gates of Thanjavur fort began to appear. If the palanquin entered the fort, his plan would come to nothing. Before that happened, he must do something bold and daring. What was the worst that could happen? Would he lose his head? If that was his fate, so be it! What profit was there in turning back alive, having left his mission unfinished?

Underlying all this, Vandiyathevan also felt a growing anger towards Prince Madurantaka. His hand itched to tear aside the palanquin’s curtain and reveal to the world that inside was not a woman, but a mustachioed young man. His heart thudded with excitement.
As he was pondering intensely what to do, one of the attendants with the palanquin, noticing Vandiyathevan following a little behind, turned and scrutinized him.
“Who are you, sir? Why are you following us from Thiruvaiyaru?” he demanded.
“I am not following you, sir! I am going to Thanjavur! Is this not the road to Thanjavur?” replied Vandiyathevan.
“This road does go to Thanjavur, but only important people may use it; there is another road for others!” said the guard.
“Is that so? But I too am a very, very important man!” said Vandiyathevan.
Hearing this, the warrior smiled and asked, “Why are you going to Thanjai?”
“My uncle is in Thanjai; I heard he is ill, so I am going to see him,” replied Vandiyathevan.
“What does your uncle do in Thanjai? Does he work in the palace?”
“No, no; he is a timekeeper at the choultry!”
“Oh! Is that so! Well, you were ahead of us, weren’t you? Why are you following behind now?”
“My horse has grown weary, sir! That’s the reason! Otherwise, what satisfaction would I get from simply following behind you, staring at your backs?”

Conversing thus, Vandiyathevan had come right up to the side of the palanquin. At once, the clever scheme he had been devising in his mind became clear to him. He pressed his legs to urge his horse forward, pulled the reins, and drove the animal straight into the path of those carrying the rear pole of the palanquin. Alarmed, they turned around to look.
Immediately, Vandiyathevan shouted, “Maharaja! Maharaja! The palanquin bearers are attacking my horse! Alas! Alas!” The curtain covering the palanquin fluttered.

chapters.title: The Velakkara Army
paragraphs: First, the outer curtain of the palanquin—a cloth screen bearing the emblem of the palmyra palm—was drawn aside. Then, the inner silk curtain began to move. As before, Vandiyathevan glimpsed a golden-hued hand. Realizing it was no longer proper for him to remain mounted, he leapt from his horse in an instant.
He ran to the side of the palanquin, exclaiming, “Princess! Princess! The men carrying your palanquin—” and, as he spoke, he gazed at her in astonishment.
He looked again, closed and opened his eyes, and looked yet again; his eyes faltered! His voice stammered. Suddenly, his throat went dry.
“No, no! You… the Lady of Pazhuvoor! The Lady of Pazhuvoor… your men’s horse struck my palanquin!…” he babbled incoherently.

All this happened in the blink of an eye. The spear-bearing guards who marched before and behind the palanquin rushed forward and surrounded Vandiyathevan. He was aware that they had encircled him. Instinctively, his hand moved to his sword hilt. But his eyes could not tear themselves away from the moon-like face of the enchantress shining through the silk curtain.

Yes; contrary to his expectations, what Vandiyathevan saw in the palanquin now was the form of a real woman! But what a woman! Vandiyathevan had never imagined that such beauty, capable of driving men to madness, could exist in this world! Fortunately, at that very moment, a nerve in his brain twitched. A marvelous idea dawned in his mind. He decided to make use of it.

With a great effort, he cleared his throat, summoned the strength to his tongue, and said, “Forgive me! You are the younger queen of Pazhuvoor, are you not? It is to see you that I have come this far!”

A gentle smile blossomed on the honeyed face of the Lady of Pazhuvoor. The lotus bud of her lips, which had been tightly closed, parted slightly, revealing a glimpse of the string of white pearls within. The magnetism of that smile left our young hero utterly bewildered. The warriors who had come and stood near him seemed to be waiting for their mistress’s command. That queen, with her hand— At a mere gesture from her, they immediately withdrew and stood at a little distance. Two soldiers held onto the horse that had collided with the palanquin.
The queen inside the palanquin looked at Vandiyathevan. Two sharp spearheads seemed to pierce Vandiyathevan’s heart!
“Yes; I am indeed the younger queen of Pazhuvoor!” declared that lady.
What intoxicating essence could be mingled in her voice? Why should my head spin so upon hearing it?
“What did you say just now? You made some complaint, didn’t you? About the men carrying the palanquin?”

Could the softness of silk, the intoxication of wine, the sweetness of wild honey, and the brilliance of lightning in the monsoon sky all blend together in a woman’s voice?… Indeed, here they are, mingled so!
“Did you say that they brought the palanquin and rammed it into your horse?”…
The mocking smile that played upon the coral lips of the Pazhuvoor queen showed how much she relished the jest. This gave Vandiyathevan a little courage.
“Yes, Maharani! That is exactly what they did! My horse was startled!” he said.
“And you too seem to have been startled! Go to the priest at the Durga temple and ask him to wave neem leaves over you! Let your fear be dispelled!”
By now, all of Vandiyathevan’s fear had vanished; he even felt like laughing.
The expression on the Pazhuvoor queen’s face changed; the crescent of her smile turned into the flame of anger.
“Enough of jesting; speak the truth! Why did you bring your horse and collide with the palanquin?”
He must give a fitting reply to this. If he did not…?
Fortunately, that reply had already dawned in Vandiyathevan’s mind.

In a voice lowered deliberately, so that no one else might overhear—a voice intimate, meant only for secrets—he said, “Devi! Nandini Devi! Azhwarkkadiyan… he himself, Thirumalaiyappar… he asked me to meet you. It was for that purpose I devised this scheme; you must forgive me!”

As he spoke thus, Vandiyathevan keenly observed the face of the Queen of Pazhuvoor. He watched her with anxious curiosity, wondering what outcome his words might bring. It was like throwing a stone at a fruit-laden tree: would a ripe fruit fall? Or an unripe one? Would the stone rebound? Or would some unexpected thunderbolt descend? The dark brows of the Pazhuvoor Queen arched slightly. Surprise and doubt flickered in her eyes. In the next instant, that royal lady had reached a decision.
“Very well; it is not proper to speak here in the middle of the road. Tomorrow, come to my palace! There, we can discuss everything in detail,” she said.
Vandiyathevan’s heart brimmed with joy. It seemed his plan would succeed! Yet, there was no use in crossing three-quarters of a well; he must cross the remaining quarter too.
“Devi! Devi! They will not let me enter the fort! Nor will they let me into the palace! What am I to do?” he asked anxiously.
At once, the Pazhuvoor Queen opened a silk pouch that lay beside her in the palanquin, and from within it she took out an ivory ring.
“If you show this, they will let you into the fort; they will let you into my palace as well!” she said, handing it to him.

Vandiyathevan eagerly received it. For a moment, he gazed at the ivory ring engraved with the palmyra insignia. When he looked up again, intending to bow to the Queen, the curtains of the palanquin had already closed. Ah! When Rahu swallows the full moon, it does so little by little. But these curtains had devoured that radiant moon-face in a single instant!

“From now on, do not follow me! Danger may come; wait and come slowly!” came the silken voice from within the palanquin. Then the palanquin moved on; the guards marched before and behind it as before.

Vandiyathevan took hold of his horse’s reins and withdrew to the roadside. He noticed that the Pazhuvoor retainer who had spoken to him earlier turned back two or three times to look at him, and his eyes sent a message to his inner mind. Yes; while his outward mind was still enchanted by the allure of the Pazhuvoor Queen… …circled around that form again and again. Was all that he had seen and heard until now real? Or was it but a magical, enchanting dream? Could such a beauty, such a form of grace, truly exist in this world?

The Puranas speak of celestial maidens—Arambai, Urvashi, Menaka. It is said that their beauty disturbed even the austerities of sages who had renounced everything. But in this world… The rumors that the great Pazhuvetaraiyar lay enslaved at the feet of this enchantress might well be true. If so, there is nothing to be surprised about! Where is Pazhuvetaraiyar, aged, grey-haired, his body marked by the scars of many battles, his visage stern and formidable? And where is this young maiden, delicate and exquisitely beautiful? What deed would that old warrior not perform to win a single smile from her?…
After standing for a long while at the roadside, lost in such thoughts, Vandiyathevan mounted his horse and slowly guided it toward the fortress of Thanjai.

He reached the main gate of the fort as the sun was setting. The city began a short distance from the fortress itself. Streets lined with shops selling all manner of goods, neighborhoods bustling with people engaged in various trades, all clustered in layers around the fort. The streets teemed with passersby, buyers and sellers haggling over prices, carts drawn by oxen, chariots drawn by horses—everywhere was a lively commotion. Vandiyathevan longed to enter those streets, to see the people of the new capital of Chola Nadu and observe their way of life. But there was no time for such diversions now. He must first attend to the task that had brought him here; all sightseeing must wait until later.

With this resolve, Vandiyathevan approached the main entrance of Thanjai city. The massive gates of the fortress were closed at that hour. Guards stationed at the entrance were pushing the people back, instructing them to stand aside along the edges of the street. The crowd complied, stepping back. Yes, instead of going about their business, they stood waiting as if for a procession or a festival to pass by. Men, women, children, the elderly—all stood there, eager and expectant.

A stretch of open space lay before the fortress gate, guarded only by the sentries. Vandiyathevan was curious to know what was happening. While everyone else stood back, he alone approached the fortress gate—

He did not wish to go and clash with the guard. That could lead to pointless arguments and quarrels. Right now, his mission was of greater importance than displaying his valor; this was not the time to get entangled in needless fights.

Therefore, Vandiyathevan withdrew to the side of the street, at a spot from where he could keep an eye on the fortress gate. Nearby, a faint fragrance of flowers drifted through the air. He turned and saw a young man, adorned with the sacred ash and rudraksha beads—marks of a Shaivite devotee—standing there with a basket of flowers in each hand.
“Brother! Why are all these people standing aside on the edge of the street? Is some procession or festival about to pass this way?” Vandiyathevan asked.
“Aren’t you from around here, sir?” the youth replied.
“No, I am from Thondai Nadu.”
“That’s why you’re asking. You too should dismount from your horse and stand aside.”
Thinking it would be convenient to converse with the youth, Vandiyathevan dismounted from his horse.
“Brother! Why did you ask me to get down?” he inquired.
“The Velakkara army is about to come out of the fort after paying their respects to the king; that’s why all these people are standing aside.”
“To watch the spectacle, is it?”
“Yes.”
“What if I watch from horseback?”
“You may, but if the Velakkara soldiers see you, it could be dangerous.”
“What danger? Will they take away my horse?”
“They’ll take your horse—and you as well! They are a ruthless lot.”
“If they take both horse and rider, will they let us go afterward?”

“What else can they do but not let you go? In this city, the law is set by the Velakkara army. No one dares question them. Even the Pazhuvettaraiyars do not interfere in matters concerning the Velakkara forces.”

At that moment, a great tumult and commotion arose within the fortress. The sound of drums resounded, the blare of trumpets echoed, and the thunder of clarions mingled with the cheers of hundreds of voices, all reverberating together.

Vandiyathevan was well acquainted with the Velakkara warrior regiments. In ancient Tamil lands, especially in Chola country, this was an important institution. The ‘Velakkarars’ were, from time to time, the sworn protectors of the reigning monarchs. Yet, there was a difference between these men and ordinary bodyguards. The Velakkarars had taken a solemn oath: “We will lay down our lives, if need be, to protect the king’s life.” If, through their negligence or failure, any harm befell the king, they had vowed to offer their own heads as sacrifice at the shrine of Durga, severing them with their own hands.
For such warriors who had taken so severe an oath, was it not natural that they enjoyed certain privileges denied to others?

The doors of the fortress gate swung open with a resounding ‘padar, padar’. First, two horsemen rode in, each holding aloft a tall, fluttering banner in his right hand. The appearance of that banner was striking. Upon the red cloth, a tiger was depicted at the top, and beneath the tiger, a crown. Below the crown, an altar was shown, and upon the altar, a severed head and a large sacrificial sword. The sight of the banner was somewhat fearsome.
Behind the banner-bearing horsemen came a great bull, bearing two large drums upon its back. Two men stood beside it, beating the drums with thunderous rhythm.

Following the bull, about fifty warriors marched, beating small and large drums, and tambourines. After them, another fifty men came, blowing long, curved horns with a resounding ‘paam, paam, papaam’. Behind these came yet more warriors, perhaps a thousand in number. Most of them raised their voices in thunderous acclaim, chanting the following praises:

“Long live Paranthaka Chola, Emperor of the Earth!” “Long live! Long live!” “Long live Sundara Chola, our king!” “Long live! Long live!” “Long live the king of the Koli clan!” “Long live! Long live!” “Long live the lord of Thanjai!” “Long live! Long live!” “Long live the great one who felled Veerapandiyan in the forest!” “Long live! Long live!” “Long live Ko Rajakesari, conqueror of Madurai, Eelam, and the Thondai region!” “Long live! Long live!” “Long live the sacred lineage of Karikala Valavan for endless ages!” “Long live! Long live!” “Victory to Durga Mahakali, Parathpari, Parashakti!” “Victory! Victory!” “May the valiant tiger banner spread and triumph over all the world!” “Victory! Victory!” “Victory to the victorious spear!” “Victory to the heroic spear!”

The resounding cheers that arose from hundreds of powerful voices sent shivers down the spines of all who heard them. As the procession passed through the fortress gates, the echoes produced by those shouts joined in, amplifying the effect. Many among the crowds lining the streets joined in the acclamations.

In this manner—(readers may know that the god Murugan, the deity of Tamil Nadu, is also called ‘Velakkaran’; scholars believe this name was given to Murugan because he is the god who vowed to protect his devotees)—the Velakkara soldiers, as they began to emerge through the gates of Thanjai Fort and proceeded along the street, created an unbroken tumultuous uproar that lasted until they disappeared into the distance.

chapters.title: Amudhan’s Mother
paragraphs: The regiment of Velakkara warriors marched along the great bazaar street. At the tail end of the procession, a few soldiers indulged in some mischievous pranks. One of them entered a sweet shop, seized a basket brimming with adhirasam, and distributed the treats among his fellow soldiers. Then, when he upturned the now-empty basket onto the shopkeeper’s head, both the soldiers and the passersby burst into raucous laughter—“Ha ha ha ha!”

Another soldier snatched a basket of flowers from an old woman he encountered along the way. Scattering the blossoms in all directions, he cried out, “Let a shower of flowers rain down!” The soldiers leapt and laughed, trying to catch the falling petals, making merry with their antics. Yet another soldier stopped a passing bullock cart, unfastened the bull from its yoke, and chased it away. Startled, the bull charged into the crowd, scattering people left and right as it ran. Once again, laughter and chaos erupted everywhere!

Watching all this, Vandiyathevan thought, “Ah! These men play just as the Pazhuvettaraiyar’s warriors do. Their games become a nuisance to others. It’s fortunate I kept out of their sight. Otherwise, a quarrel might have broken out, and my mission would have been ruined.”

But one difference became clear to him. The townspeople did not seem to resent the Velakkara soldiers’ antics as much. Instead, they joined in the laughter and excitement, delighting in the commotion! Wondering about this, Vandiyathevan turned to look for the young man with the flower baskets, but he was nowhere to be seen. Amidst the crowd and confusion, the youth had vanished—perhaps he had gone off to attend to his own business.

Vandiyathevan learned that after the Velakkara regiment left the fort in the evening, no one else would be allowed inside. Only those with special privileges—the royal family, ministers, and commanders—could enter the fort at any hour, day or night. He also discovered that the Pazhuvettaraiyar family enjoyed this right. Thus, Vandiyathevan abandoned his plan to enter the fort that night.

He did not wish to risk showing the signet ring he carried. Better, he thought, to spend the night outside the fort, exploring the city and waiting for another opportunity. It would be best to enter the fort only after sunrise tomorrow. Even if I were to enter the fort at night as I am now, would it be possible to meet the king and deliver the letter? Surely, that is not an easy matter.

Vandiyathevan made his way slowly along the streets that circled the fort’s ramparts, taking in the sights as he went. His horse, having traveled a great distance that day, was thoroughly exhausted. He knew he must soon find a place to let it rest; otherwise, when necessity arose on the morrow, the horse would be of no use to him! He must quickly find a suitable place to stay. Thanjai, at that time, was a city newly burgeoning, swelling and spreading in all directions. It was evening; hundreds of street lamps had been lit and were beginning to cast their glow.

Every street was thronged with crowds shouting, “Jai, Jai!” People from outlying towns had come for various official matters and were moving about in all directions. Among them were those from the towns and villages of Chola Nadu, as well as visitors from lands newly annexed to the Chola Empire. From the banks of the Porunai River to the banks of the Palar, from the eastern seashore to the western coast, people from all these vast regions had come to the capital. Some had even arrived from north of the Vindhya mountains and from lands across the seas, appearing here and there in the city’s streets.

In shops selling appam, athirasam, and other sweets, people swarmed like bees, crowding to purchase the delicacies. Bananas and many other fruits were piled high in great mounds. As for the flower shops, there was no need to even mention them. Jasmine, mullai, thiruvathi, champaka—these flowers rose in heaps like floral hills. Around these hills of blossoms, women buzzed like bees, gathering in swarms.

As he passed near the flower shops, Vandiyathevan thought of the young flower seller he had met earlier. How convenient it would be if he could meet him again! He could ask him about a comfortable place to stay in this city, could he not? As he was thinking thus, he saw, a short distance away, that very youth approaching. Dismounting from his horse, Vandiyathevan went up to him.
“Young man! I don’t see any flower baskets with you. Where are all the flowers? Have you sold them all?” he asked.
“I did not bring flowers to sell. I brought them for the temple puja; I have given them, and now I am returning home.”
“To which temple are you offering these flowers?”
“Have you heard of the Thalikulaththar temple?”
“Oh! I have heard of the Thanjai Thalikulaththar. Is it that temple? Is it a large one?”

“No, it is a small temple. For some time now, the Durga Amman temple here in Thanjai has gained more renown. There, the worship, pongal offerings, sacrifices, and festivals are celebrated with great pomp. The royal family and the Pazhuvettaraiyars mostly visit the Durga Amman temple. The Thalikulaththar temple does not enjoy such fame; not many people come there for darshan…”
“You are performing this floral service? Do you receive any reward for it?”
“Our family receives a grant for this. Since my grandfather’s time, there has been a land endowment given by Emperor Kandaraditha. At present, my mother and I are carrying out this service.”
“Is the Thalikulaththar temple built of brick, or has it been reconstructed in black stone?” asked Vallavarayan.
He asked thus because, on his way, he had seen many brick temples undergoing renovation with black stone.

“At present, it is a brick temple; I have heard that the renovation in black stone will begin soon. The great elder princess of Pazhaiyarai wishes that the renovation should be carried out immediately, but…” The youth hesitated and stopped.
“But what?..”
“What is the use of repeating all the rumors one hears? I have heard it said: ‘In the day, speak looking around; at night, do not speak at all.’ This is a crossroads; people are all around us…”
“It is in places like this, amidst such crowds and noise, that secrets can be spoken most boldly. In this throng and clamor, no one will hear our words.”
“What secret is there to speak of?” asked the youth, looking at Vandiyathevan with a hint of suspicion.

Ah! This boy is clever! There is profit in befriending him; I can learn many things. But I must not arouse unnecessary suspicion in his mind—thus thought Vandiyathevan, and said, “Yes; what secret is there… “Is that so? Nothing at all. Let it be, brother! Tonight, I must find a place where I can sleep in peace. I have traveled a great distance and am utterly exhausted. Where can I stay? Could you guide me to a good inn and help me?” he asked.
“What scarcity of places is there to stay in this city? There are so many choultries; there are even royal lodges established for travelers from foreign lands. But, if you wish…”
“Brother! What is your name?” Vandiyathevan asked.
“Amudhan; Sendhan Amudhan.”
“Ah! What a lovely name! Just hearing it, my tongue is sweetened as if with nectar… You were about to say, if I wished, I could come and stay at your house, weren’t you?”
“Yes, but how did you know that?”
“I possess a little magic; that’s how I knew. Where is your house?”
“Our flower garden lies just beyond the city limits, within calling distance; our house is inside the garden,” said Amudhan.
“Aha! In that case, I shall certainly come to your house. I cannot spend this night amidst the bustle of this city. Moreover, I wish to meet the noble lady who bore such a virtuous son as you.”
“My mother is indeed a noble woman; but she is unfortunate…”
“Alas! Why do you say so?”
“Perhaps, your father…”
“My father passed away; but that is not all—my mother has been unfortunate since birth. You will understand when you see her. Come, let us go.”

After walking for half an hour, they reached the flower garden beyond the outskirts of the city. The sweet fragrance of the night-blooming flowers brought an exquisite, intoxicating pleasure to Vandiyathevan. The tumult and clamor of the city streets could scarcely be heard there. In the center of the flower garden stood a tiled house.

There it stood. Beside it were two huts. Two families who assisted with the garden work lived in those huts. Amudhan called one of them and instructed him to feed Vandiyathevan’s horse and tie it beneath the shade of a tree. Then he led Vandiyathevan inside the house.

The moment Vandiyathevan saw Amudhan’s mother, he understood the depth of her misfortune. It became clear that the old woman was mute and deaf, unable to speak or hear. Yet, Vandiyathevan saw that her face overflowed with compassion and love. The radiance of keen intelligence also shone from her features. Is it not one of the strange wonders of creation that those who are impaired in one faculty often possess exceptional sharpness of mind in other ways?

Amudhan made a few gestures, and the old woman understood that the visitor was a guest from a distant land. With her expressions alone, she conveyed her affection and welcome. Soon, the lady served food, spreading leaves before them. First came idiyappam and sweet coconut milk. Never in his life had Vandiyathevan tasted such delicious fare. He ate ten or twelve idiyappams and half a measure of coconut milk. Then came tamarind curry and chola maize paniyaram; he sampled those as well. Even after all this, his hunger was not sated; finally, he devoured a quarter measure of rice with half a measure of curd! Only then did he rise from his leaf.

While eating, he asked Amudhan about a few matters and learned some details. He inquired who, apart from Emperor Sundara Chola and his royal household, were currently residing within the Tanjore fort. The palaces and households of Periya Pazhuvettarayar and Chinna Pazhuvettarayar were there. Since the royal treasury and granaries were housed within the fort, the officials and accountants who managed them also resided there. Aniruddha Brahmarayar, the minister who was the Emperor’s most trusted confidant, and the chief of the sacred palm-leaf archives, also lived within the fort. Moreover, under the command of Chinna Pazhuvettarayar, the soldiers guarding the Tanjore fort and their families were stationed there. Gold and silver jewel merchants, gem traders, and goldsmiths had all been allotted places within the fort. Under Periya Pazhuvettarayar’s authority, hundreds of tax officials worked there. The temple of Durga Amman stood in one corner of the fort. The temple priests, attendants, and courtesans lived nearby.
After learning all this, Vandiyathevan asked, “Are all the ministers presently in the fort?”

“How is everyone doing? As usual, they are all coming and going, busy with various matters. Aniruddha Brahmarayar has not been in the city for some time now. I heard he has gone to the Chera country. Periya Pazhuvettarayar left four days ago. I heard he went to the midlands, north of the Kollidam.”
“Perhaps he has already returned? You might not know!”

“This evening, the palanquin of the young mistress of Pazhuvoor arrived. I myself saw it at the fortress gate; but Pazhuvettarayar did not come. Perhaps he has halted somewhere on the way and may return tomorrow.”
“Thambi! Prince Madurantaka Devar is still staying inside the fort, isn’t he?”
“Yes; next to Pazhuvettarayar’s palace is Madurantaka’s mansion. After all, he is the son-in-law, having married the younger Pazhuvettarayar’s daughter.”
“Oh! Is that so? I did not know this until now!”
“Very few people know. Because of the Emperor’s ill health, the marriage was not celebrated with much pomp.”
“Very well; so Madurantaka Devar is now inside the fort, isn’t he?”

“He should be inside the fort; but Madurantaka Devar rarely comes out. The people do not get to see him. I hear he spends most of his time absorbed in devotion to Shiva, engaged in yoga, meditation, and worship.”
“Yet, after all these years, he has now married?”

“Yes; that is somewhat surprising. They say that after the marriage, the groom’s mind has changed completely; but what is it to us? It is better not to talk about matters concerning such great people…”

Vandiyathevan was eager to learn more from Sendhan Amudhan, but he did not wish to arouse suspicion by asking too many questions. The friendship of such a simple-hearted youth would be of great help to him. It was his good fortune that he had found such a house to stay in at Thanjavur. Why should he ruin it all? Moreover, the fatigue of his long journey and the first night’s sleeplessness weighed upon him. Sleep began to overtake him as he closed his eyes. Sensing his condition, Sendhan Amudhan quickly prepared a bed for him.

In the final moments of his drowsy stupor, the face of the young mistress of Pazhuvoor appeared in Vandiyathevan’s mind. Ah! What beauty! What radiance! The instant he beheld that enchanting, bewitching form, he was utterly transfixed, bereft of all action, standing motionless, unable even to blink. That experience reminded him of another from his past.

Once, in his childhood, while traveling through a forest path, a snake suddenly reared up and danced before him. Its beauty was beyond compare! Its allure, irresistible! Vandiyathevan could not tear his gaze away from the serpent’s form; he could not even blink. He stood rooted, staring, as the snake continued its mesmerizing dance. As the snake swayed, his own body seemed to sway in rhythm—who knows what might have happened next? Suddenly, a mongoose leapt upon the snake. The two began a fierce battle. Seizing the opportunity, Vandiyathevan had taken to his heels and run away!

Tch, tch! What a comparison! How could he liken the bewitching, world-enchanting beauty of this celestial maiden to a dancing snake? Just a single glimpse of her milk-pure face would be enough to banish all hunger!… And tomorrow, he would see her again! What sweetness there was in her voice! She was indeed a rare beauty. But then, what of that other woman he had seen at the astrologer’s house in Kudanthai, and again on the banks of the Arisil river?… Her face, too, had a magnetic glow! Her beauty shone like a flame!… Though both faces were radiant with loveliness, how different they were! That one, majestic and noble; this one, enchanting and alluring!…
As his mind compared the faces of those two maidens, yet another woman intervened. The all-powerful, tyrannical queen of the night—Sleep herself—took complete possession of Vandiyathevan.

chapters.title: The Crow and the Cuckoo
paragraphs: Vandiyathevan slept through the night like a log and awoke only after the sun had risen in the morning. Even after opening his eyes, he lay there, reluctant to get up. The breeze from above blew briskly, and the branches and leaves of the trees and shrubs rubbed against each other, producing a soft, continuous ‘sho’ sound. In harmony with that natural music, the sweet voice of a young boy sang a Thevaram hymn of Sundaramurthi Swamigal in a melodious tune:
“O golden-hued one, who girds the tiger skin about your waist, O wearer of the radiant konrai blossoms upon your shining, ruddy locks!”

Hearing this, Vandiyathevan opened his eyes and looked around. Before him, in the flower garden, the konnai trees displayed their golden blossoms, swaying gently. Sendhan Amudhan, holding a basket in one hand and a sickle in the other, was plucking konrai flowers while singing, his voice rising with the morning. Having risen early, bathed, and smeared himself with sacred ash, Sendhan Amudhan resembled the devoted Markandeya himself. As he listened to the boy’s sweet and melodious voice, Vandiyathevan thought with a tinge of envy that his own mother had not given him such a gift. Why could he not, like Amudhan, tend a flower garden, serve Lord Shiva, and spend his days in bliss? Why must he wander from town to town, sword and spear in hand? Why must he always be prepared either to kill or be killed? Such thoughts arose in his mind.

But soon his mind changed. Could everyone in the world become a devotee of Shiva like Sendhan Amudhan? Thieves, robbers, tricksters, and those who found joy in tormenting the innocent would always exist. There must be a government to restrain such people and establish justice and dharma. To run a government, there must be kings and ministers. To protect them from danger, there must be guards and soldiers. And for kings, there must be messengers like himself to carry their letters… Yes! Today, he must see Emperor Sundara Chola at any cost. He must see the Emperor before Periya Pazhuvettarayar returned; otherwise, it might become impossible…

After bathing in the lotus pond beside the flower garden, Vallavarayan adorned himself with his finest clothes and ornaments, dressing with great care. Could he go to meet the Emperor in an ordinary manner? For this— Did he adorn himself simply out of habit, or was it because the thought of seeing the young mistress of Pazhuvoor once again lingered in his mind that day? We cannot say for certain.

After the morning meal, when Sendhan Amudhan set out with a basket of flowers for the midday pooja service, Vandiyathevan too departed, intending to seek an audience with the Emperor. The two of them walked together. Vallavarayan had already decided not to take his horse inside the fort. It was necessary to give the animal ample time to rest. Who could say—he might need to use it for a swift journey at any moment. In any case, it was best for the horse to remain here. As they made their way toward the fort gates, Vandiyathevan conversed with Amudhan, gleaning a few more details.
“Other than your mother, do you have any other close relatives?” Vallavarayan asked.

Amudhan replied, “Yes, I do. My mother has a brother and a sister, both born to the same mother. My aunt passed away some time ago; my uncle serves at the temple of Kuzhagar in Kodikkarai, tending to the flowers. At night, he also lights and guards the lamp at the lighthouse… He has a son and a daughter; the daughter…” He paused.
“What about the daughter?”
“Oh, nothing. There’s a peculiarity in our family. Some are born mute; others possess the sweetest voices and sing beautifully…”
“Your uncle’s daughter isn’t mute, is she?” asked Vandiyathevan.
“No, no!”
“Then say she sings well. Does she sing better than you?”

“Your question is amusing—it’s like asking, ‘Does the cuckoo sing better than the crow?’ When Poonguzhali sings, even the king of the ocean halts his roaring waves to listen in silence. The cows, goats, and even the wild beasts of the forest stand transfixed, forgetting themselves…”
“Is your uncle’s daughter’s name Poonguzhali? What a beautiful name!”
“Is it only the name that is beautiful?”
“She must be beautiful as well; otherwise, would you speak of her with such rapture?”
“The sky and the peacock must beg for alms of beauty from her. Even Rathi and Indrani would need to perform penance for many lifetimes to attain such loveliness as hers.”
Vallavaraiyan could see that Sendhan Amudhan’s heart was not wholly immersed in his devotion to Shiva.
“In that case, tell me who would be a suitable bride for you. Since she is your uncle’s daughter, she is your cousin, isn’t she? When is the wedding?” asked Vandiyathevan.

“Never shall I claim that anyone is suitable for me. In no way am I worthy of her. If, as in the olden days, a swayamvara were held for Poonguzhali, kings from fifty-six lands would come to compete for her hand! Just as gods descended from the heavens to wed Damayanti, so too would they come for her. But perhaps, in this Kali Yuga, such things do not happen…”
“In that case, even if she wished to marry you, would you refuse her?” asked Vandiyathevan.

“That would be something! If the Lord himself appeared before me and asked, ‘Will you come to Kailasa with this body like Sundaramurthi, or will you remain on earth with Poonguzhali?’ I would say, ‘I wish to live with Poonguzhali.’ But what use is it for me to say so?”

“Why do you say it is of no use? If you are willing, then the marriage is as good as done, isn’t it? Does everyone marry only after asking the woman’s consent? For example, Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar married after the age of sixty-five! Do you think that marriage took place only with the queen’s consent?”

“Anna! That is a matter for great people; why should we speak of it? More importantly, I must warn you. You are going inside the fort; do not speak of the Pazhuvettaraiyars within the fort. If you do, it will bring danger!”
“What is this, brother? You are frightening me all of a sudden!”
“I am only telling the truth. Truly, it is the two Pazhuvettaraiyars who rule the Chola empire now. There is no authority greater than theirs.”
“Not even the Emperor himself has more authority than they?”
“The Emperor lies ill. The people say that he does not cross the fortress built by the Pazhuvur lords. They also say that even the words of his own sons do not reach his ears.”
“Is that so? The Pazhuvettaraiyars must wield immense influence, then. Two years ago, they did not have such power, did they?”

“No; especially after the Emperor came to Thanjai, the authority of the Pazhuvettaraiyars has become boundless. There is no one who dares to speak to them harshly. I have heard that even Aniruddha Brahmarayar, out of frustration, left for the Pandya country.”
“Why did the Emperor come to Thanjavur from Pazhayarai? Do you know, brother?”

“I will tell you what I have heard. Three years ago, Veerapandiyan fell in battle. At that time, it is said that the Chola armies committed some atrocities in Pandya country; but such is the nature of war. Madurai came under the rule of the Cholas. However, some close confidants of Veerapandiyan swore to take revenge, to repay blood with blood, and began plotting. The Pazhuvettaraiyars brought the king to Thanjavur, saying that he could not be protected if he remained at Pazhayarai. The fortress here is strong; the guards are many. Besides, the physicians said that Thanjavur was better than Pazhayarai for the Emperor’s health.”
“Everyone talks about Sundara Chozhar’s health. But no one seems to know what his illness is.”
“How could they not know? The Emperor has been struck with paralysis; both his legs have lost all strength.”
“Alas! So he cannot walk at all?”

“He cannot walk; he cannot mount an elephant or a horse; he is confined to his bed. Only if he is carried in a palanquin from place to place can he move, and even then, it causes him great pain. Therefore, the Emperor never leaves the palace. They say that even his mind has not been as steady as before, of late.”
“Ah! What a tragedy!”
“One should not even call it a tragedy, elder brother! The Pazhuvettaraiyars would call that royal slander and punish you for it.”

Pazhuvettaraiyar! Pazhuvettaraiyar! — Wherever one goes, whomever one speaks to, the talk is always about the Pazhuvettaraiyars! So what if they are such mighty warriors? Their own treasury; the granaries, the defense of the city of Thanjai, even the network of spies — should the Emperor have entrusted all these into their hands? Was it not because so much authority was given to them that they have now begun to conspire against the Emperor? How far will their conspiracy succeed? We must do all we can to ensure it does not succeed. If the opportunity arises, I must also warn the Emperor!...

By then, the gates of the fort had come into view. Sendhan Amudhan, parting from his new friend, went towards the temple of Thalikulaththar. Vandiyathevan, meanwhile, approached the fort gates with a thousand castles of thought in his mind.

chapters.title: Within the Fort
paragraphs: The signet ring engraved with the palmyra emblem possessed a magical power, like the enchanted rings of legend. In the morning hours, milk and curd sellers, flower vendors, vegetable merchants, fruit sellers, and people of many other trades, along with accountants and officials, all thronged together, trying to enter the fort. At the fort’s main gate, the guards displayed their pompous authority by opening the wicket gate and letting them in one by one. But when our young hero showed the ring bearing the palmyra emblem, that alone caused a delay—then, with great respect, the guards opened one of the main gates for him; Vandiyathevan entered the fort.

Ah! Who could have guessed what hour it was when he set foot inside the fort of Thanjai? How many significant events followed from that moment! Was it not a turning point in the very history of the Chola Empire?

For a while after entering the fort, Vandiyathevan was lost in wonder. Kanchi had been the capital of the ancient Pallava dynasty. It had endured many enemy assaults. The palaces, halls, and other buildings there had grown old and dilapidated, with wild mushrooms blooming in the cracks. The buildings were adorned with beautiful sculptures, yet many parts lay in ruins and decay. Only a few palaces, rebuilt and restored after Aditya Karikalan’s arrival, shone here and there like flowers blossoming on a dry tree, accentuating the city’s desolate appearance.

But the sight of Thanjai was the very opposite. All the palaces were new; the halls were new. Amidst the whitewashed mansions, a few buildings constructed of red bricks baked in red earth gleamed like gems set among diamonds and pearls. Here and there, the palace gardens flourished with trees that drew nourishment from the rich red soil, standing tall and luxuriant. The thick foliage of punna, coconut, ashoka, arasu, banyan, jackfruit, and neem trees, with their many shades of emerald green, delighted the eye and filled the heart with joy. This was a city newly built by the wondrously powerful magician, Mayan. Entering this new city, a fresh exhilaration was born; the heart brimmed with pride, filled with a mysterious sense of elation. Vandiyathevan, who had observed the fort’s sentries and the restrictions on entering the fortress, had expected the inside to be rather deserted, with little movement of people. But, on the contrary, every street was crowded with throngs shouting “Jey! Jey!” Horses and horse-drawn chariots thundered past, making the ground tremble with their noise. The sound of bells from elephants, moving with a slow and majestic gait like black mountains in motion, echoed on all sides. The cries of vendors selling flowers, vegetables, fruits, milk, and curds assaulted the ears. Now and then, the sound of the town’s official time-telling bells mingled with the booming of drums. Sweet melodies from musical instruments blended with the honeyed songs sung by women. Everything was a grand festival, a tumult of celebration.

If this is not a city, what is? Surely, the capital of a vast empire that grows and spreads day by day must be like this! Vandiyathevan did not wish to reveal himself as a complete stranger to such a city. If he asked anyone for directions, they would look him up and down and carelessly ask, “Are you new to this town?” They might even mistake him for some rustic from a distant village, seeking the way to the palace. Therefore, he resolved to find the emperor’s palace without asking anyone for directions; after all, that should not be an impossible task…

Whichever way he looked, he saw mansions adorned with makara archways and fluttering flags. Battling fiercely with the swift upper winds, the flags flapped and snapped noisily. Tiger flags and palm flags were the most prominent. Towering above all other banners, a great tiger flag soared grandly, almost brushing the clouds. That must be the palace where the emperor resided, Vallavarayan guessed, and, pondering the task ahead, he walked in the direction where that flag flew.

The first task was to meet the emperor in person and deliver the letter. Along with that, he must also convey what Aditya Karikalan had instructed him to say by word of mouth. Without the permission of the Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar, it was impossible to see the emperor. How to obtain his permission? Divine favor had helped him enter the fort, but could he rely on divine guidance for everything? To see the emperor, he must devise his own strategy! What strategy would that be? O brain, descended through generations of the Vanar clan! Get to work now, let’s see! Let your imagination… Summon your imagination! It is not only poets and epic writers who require the power of imagination. Even those engaged in affairs of state, like yourself, must possess it. Come now, let us see your skill at work!
Vandiyathevan confirmed to himself that Periya Pazhuvettarayar had not yet returned to the fort.
As soon as he crossed the fort’s gateway and entered within, he approached a guard standing inside and asked, “Well, brother! Has Pazhuvettarayar come back?”
“Whom are you asking about, young man? The younger lord is in the palace.”
“As if I didn’t know that! I am asking about the elder lord, who had gone to Nadu Nadu.”

“Oh! The elder lord went to Nadu Nadu, did he? I did not know that. Yesterday evening, the young queen’s palanquin returned. The great king has not come yet; word is he may return tonight!” replied the guard.
This was good news indeed. Before Periya Pazhuvettarayar returned, Vandiyathevan must somehow see the Emperor and deliver the scroll. But how to do it…?
A plan dawned in Vandiyathevan’s mind. In that very instant, the worry vanished from his face; a mischievous smile and a gleam of excitement appeared.

He did not have to wander much to approach the Emperor’s palace. He followed the path marked by the great tiger banner. Soon, he reached the palace entrance. Ah! What a palace this was! Was it not like the palace of Indra in the celestial realms, or the palace of Vikramaditya in the city of Ujjayini? What marvels adorned the pillars of the entrance hall! The sculpted horses on each pillar seemed to leap forward, their forelegs raised, as if they would spring into life at any moment!

Many roads led to the palace from all four directions. At the end of each path stood two horsemen and several foot soldiers. Many among the people walking those streets, seeing the guards, turned back without approaching. Some came close, paused for a moment to peer at the palace entrance, gazed in awe at the tiger banner, and then departed. If anyone lingered too long or if a crowd seemed to be forming, the guards would signal with their hands for them to move along. Those who gathered and stood together spoke in hushed tones, whispering quietly to one another.

Vandiyathevan did not hesitate in the least, unlike the others. He strode forward swiftly and boldly, approaching the palace guards who stood along the path. Instantly, two horses blocked his way, standing face to face so closely that their muzzles nearly touched. The men mounted on the horses, as well as those standing on the ground, all leveled their spears, the tips meeting to form a barrier across his path.

Vandiyathevan extended his signet ring. That was all it took; at the sight of it, the pride and arrogance of those brave guards subsided at once. One after another, three of them examined the ring closely.

“All right; let him pass!” one of them said. Two spears were immediately withdrawn, clearing the way. Vandiyathevan walked on with confidence. Yet, what now? How many more such guards would there be? Where was Chinna Pazhuvettarayar? How could he find out? Whom should he ask? Without Chinna Pazhuvettarayar’s permission, it was impossible to see the Emperor. In this vast and sprawling palace, where was the ailing Emperor residing? How could he discover that?

Sensing a group approaching behind him, Vandiyathevan turned to look. Yes, a band of ten or fifteen people had come up and were standing near the guards. They wore rich silk garments of bright colors. Pearl necklaces, makara-shaped pendants, and earrings adorned them. Some had sacred ash smeared on their foreheads, others sandalwood paste, vermilion, or saffron dots! Ah! At first glance, did they not look like poets?… Yes, in the next instant, he realized it was indeed a troupe of poets.

One of the guards—he must have been their leader—said, “The Kaviraayars have arrived! Make way!” Then, turning to one of the soldiers, he added, “Chinna Pazhuvettarayar is in the Asthana Mandapam. Take them to him!”

“Poets! If you receive any gifts, return by this same path! If you do not, find another way out!” he added, and the others laughed at his words. Vandiyathevan, who had been standing by and listening to this exchange, thought to himself, “The fruit has slipped and fallen into the milk!” If he went along with these poets, he could reach the place where Chinna Pazhuvettarayar was. There would be no need to ask anyone for directions. After that, he had his own cleverness—and luck! Thinking thus, he joined the group of poets.

Vandiyathevan, who had been waiting for the right moment, now entered the fort through the gateway. The guards at the entrance did not stop him, as he had already shown the signet ring bearing the royal insignia. The bustling activity inside the fort was a sight to behold. Messengers hurried to and fro, soldiers marched in formation, and officials discussed matters in hushed tones. The air was thick with anticipation and tension.

Vandiyathevan’s heart beat faster as he made his way through the inner streets of the fort. He marveled at the grandeur of the Chola capital—the tall ramparts, the majestic towers, and the intricate carvings on the stone walls. The aroma of sandalwood and incense wafted from the temples, mingling with the clamor of the busy marketplace.

He remembered the words of Azhwarkadiyan, who had warned him to be cautious within these walls. Every face seemed to hide a secret; every shadow appeared to conceal a lurking danger. Yet, Vandiyathevan’s spirit was undaunted. He walked with confidence, his eyes keenly observing everything around him.
As he approached the palace gates, a group of palace guards stepped forward, barring his way. One of them, a tall man with a stern face, demanded, “Who are you? What business brings you here?”
Vandiyathevan drew himself up and replied, “I am a messenger from the Crown Prince, Aditya Karikalan. I bear a letter for Princess Kundavai Devi.”
The guard scrutinized him for a moment, then glanced at the signet ring on Vandiyathevan’s finger. Satisfied, he signaled to the others to let him pass.

Vandiyathevan entered the palace courtyard, his mind racing with thoughts of the tasks ahead. He wondered what kind of reception awaited him inside. Would Princess Kundavai grant him an audience? Would he be able to deliver the prince’s message without falling into the traps set by his enemies?

As he crossed the courtyard, he caught sight of a group of noblewomen walking along the colonnade. Their laughter rang out like silver bells, and their silken garments shimmered in the sunlight. Vandiyathevan’s heart skipped a beat as he wondered if one of them might be the illustrious Kundavai herself.
He pressed on, determined to fulfill his mission, no matter what dangers lay ahead within the formidable walls of the Chola fort.

chapters.title: “Danger! Danger!”
paragraphs: Vandiyathevan entered the royal audience hall even before the poets had arrived. He guessed that the majestic figure seated on the elevated throne must be none other than the Younger Pazhuvetarayar himself. Around him stood many, arms folded and mouths covered in respectful silence. One man stood with a pile of palm-leaf letters received that day. The accountant waited to present his accounts. The commanders of the guards stood expectantly, awaiting the daily orders of the Younger Pazhuvetarayar. Servants waited to carry out their assigned tasks. Behind the throne, a few attendants waved white fans. Another stood ready with a betel box in hand.

Even Vandiyathevan, who was second to none in boldness and pride, approached the Younger Pazhuvetarayar with a touch of restraint and humility. Compared to his elder brother, the younger lord appeared even more imposing in valor and majesty. As soon as he saw our hero, his stern face brightened with a welcoming smile.
“Who are you, young man? Where do you come from?” he asked.
Whenever he saw brave young men, the Younger Pazhuvetarayar’s stern visage would blossom. He had a great interest in recruiting valiant youths from all over the land into his guard.
“Commander! I have come from Kanchipuram! The prince sent me with a letter!” Vandiyathevan replied in a respectful tone.
At the mention of Kanchipuram, the Younger Pazhuvetarayar’s face hardened. “What? What did you say?” he asked again.
“I have come from Kanchipuram with a letter from the prince!”
“Where is it? Give it here!” Though he asked indifferently, there was a note of agitation in his voice.
