She sat with effortless grace, her legs dangling, her hands gripping the branch for balance. Her eyes sparkled with mischief as she gazed down at Vandiyathevan. For a moment, he wondered if she were some forest sprite or a vision conjured by his own imagination.
“Who are you?” he called out, unable to hide his astonishment. “Are you a goddess of these woods, or a mortal maiden?”
The girl laughed again, the sound echoing through the trees. “I am neither goddess nor ghost, sir. I am as human as you are. But tell me, what brings you to this lonely forest path?”
Vandiyathevan, regaining his composure, replied, “I am but a humble traveler, making my way through these woods. But I did not expect to find a maiden sitting atop a tree, laughing at passersby!”

“Ah, but you are mistaken,” she said, swinging herself lightly from the branch and landing gracefully on the ground before him. “It is not every day that I see such a dashing traveler wandering through these parts. Tell me your name, and perhaps I shall tell you mine.”
Vandiyathevan bowed with a flourish. “My name is Vandiyathevan of the Vaanar clan. And now, may I know the name of the maiden who so startled me from her perch?”
She smiled, her eyes twinkling with amusement. “All in good time, noble Vandiyathevan. For now, let us walk together. There is much to see in this forest, and many secrets to uncover.”

With that, she turned and began to walk along the path, her steps light and swift. Vandiyathevan, curiosity piqued, followed her, wondering what new adventure awaited him in the company of this mysterious maiden of the woods.

chapters.title: The Latha Mandapam
paragraphs: As the maiden hurried along the narrow path winding through the dense mango grove, Vandiyathevan followed swiftly behind her. It was no easy task to walk in that darkness without stumbling into the trees and shrubs. At one point, when he hesitated, nearly colliding with a tree, the maiden turned and asked, “Why have you stopped? Have you lost your way? You’re supposed to be the man whose eyes can pierce the darkness!”

In reply, Vandiyathevan pressed a finger to his lips and, just as she had done earlier, whispered, “Hush!” At that very moment, a sound drifted from beyond the wall—a noise that resembled the movement of people. After a pause, both resumed their walk. A little further on, Vallavarayan let out a soft chuckle. The maiden turned and asked, “What are you laughing at?”
“I am not laughing at what I see; I am laughing at what I heard!”
“Oh? And what is that?”
“Did you not hear the footsteps of those who were searching for me just now? I am amused at the thought of how they have been deceived!”
With a hint of fear, she asked, “Is someone searching for you? Why?”
“Otherwise, why would I have to sit here in the pitch darkness, bumping into the wall?”
At that moment, a breeze parted the branches, and a shaft of moonlight fell across Vandiyathevan’s face.
The young woman looked at him with a mixture of surprise and astonishment.
“What are you looking at?” he asked.
“I was just checking if it was really you!”
“If not me, who else could it be?”
“The last time you came, you had a big moustache!”
“You ask a good question! How else could someone like me, who climbs over walls and sneaks in, avoid changing his disguise from time to time?”
“But now you look so much younger than before!”
“Youth comes naturally when one’s spirits are high!”
"Why are you so enthusiastic all of a sudden?"
"When your Maharani’s grace is upon me, what lack can there be for enthusiasm?"
"Don’t mock me. Today, our mistress is only the Young Queen. One day, she will surely become the Maharani!"
"That is exactly what I am saying."
"Is this how you say it? You would even claim that it was by your magical powers she became Maharani! If someone asked for half the kingdom, you would not hesitate to ask!"
Vandiyathevan thus managed to learn, in some manner, what he wished to know. After that, he did not speak further. He walked on, deep in thought.

Whom was he about to meet? Could it be the younger queen of Pazhuvoor? Or perhaps the daughter of the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar, who had married Madurantaka Devar? That woman, thinking him a magician, was leading him away. Whoever this 'Young Queen' might be, how should he conduct himself when he met her? O heart! Do not lose your courage! As long as courage remains, victory will follow! At the right moment, some clever idea will surely arise! So far, in no predicament have we ever been defeated. And now—are we to be defeated by a mere woman?

They approached a grand palace. But they did not head towards the main entrance, nor did they near the back gate. Instead, they drew close to a Shringara Latha Mandapam—a bower entwined with flowering vines—stretching into the garden from one side of the palace. As they came nearer, Vandiyathevan saw that this Latha Mandapam seemed to connect two vast, magnificent mansions, like a bridge between them. The two buildings thus joined were, in some ways, quite different from each other.

The mansion on the right glowed with the brilliance of many lamps burning within. From inside, a variety of lively sounds drifted out. The building on the left, however, was not lit by even a single small lamp. In the moonlight, its tall outer walls loomed pale and high. But within that mansion, silence and darkness reigned.

The woman who had brought Vandiyathevan led him to the Latha Mandapam and, with a gesture, bade him wait there. He did as she instructed. Standing thus, he became aware of the fragrance of the flowers that filled the air around him. Ah! What a scent! What a scent! It rose to his nose like a vapor, making his head spin with its intoxicating sweetness!

As soon as that woman entered the Latha Mandapam, her voice and another sweet feminine voice could be heard. “Tell her to come at once! Do you hear me? She knows I have been waiting all this time, doesn’t she?” These words sent a wave of dizziness through him. That voice—it was the voice of the young queen of Pazhuvoor! There was no doubt! In the next moment, he would be standing before her. How was he going to handle that situation? Instead of the magician she expected, what would she think when she saw the man who had collided with her palanquin now standing before her? Would she be surprised? Would she be angry? Perhaps, would she be pleased? … Or would she, perhaps, show no emotion at all and conduct herself as if nothing had happened?
The maiden who had brought him there stood at the threshold of the Latha Mandapam and beckoned him in with a gesture.

Vandiyathevan reached the spot where she stood and looked into the inner chamber of the mandapam. In the span of a single heartbeat, the scene that appeared before him was imprinted upon his mind through his eyes. The golden lamp’s flame, shining from its pedestal, spread a golden radiance. They must have poured some rare scented oil into that lamp, for the smoke from the flame wafted a rich fragrance through the air. Upon a low couch, strewn with flowers of many colors and scents, a woman reclined gracefully, enthroned in elegance.

She was indeed the young queen of Pazhuvoor. In the daylight, when he had seen her in the palanquin, she had seemed beautiful. But now, in the glow of the golden lamp, it was as if the very goddess of beauty had taken form before him. The mingled fragrance of flowers, the scented smoke of the lamp, and the enchanting form of the queen of Pazhuvoor combined to intoxicate Vandiyathevan.

Vandiyatheva! Beware! Only once did you taste wine, and you knew how it clouded your senses! You swore never to touch it again! Remember that vow now! Do not lose your wits in this intoxication, which is more potent than any wine!

Nandini, the young queen of Pazhuvoor, looked at Vandiyathevan with her coral lips parted slightly, revealing a row of pearl-like teeth, her face filled with astonishment. For a moment, she seemed unable to speak, and this silence worked in Vandiyathevan’s favor.
With a light laugh, he said, “Lady! Your maid suddenly grew suspicious—whether I was a magician or not! Do you know how she asked? She said, ‘Are you really him?’” And with that, he laughed again.
Nandini smiled. Before Vandiyathevan’s eyes, a lightning flash seemed to spark! It poured out honey.

“She’s always like this—sudden doubts strike her out of nowhere! Vasuki! Why are you standing here like a tree? Go to your place! If you hear the sound of anyone’s footsteps, shut the door at once!” said Nandini.

“Yes, Amma!” replied Vasuki, and, after saying so, she walked along the inner path of the Latha Mandapam towards the Prakasa Palace, and sat down at the dimly lit entrance steps a little distance away.

Lowering her voice slightly, Nandini asked, “Does she suspect that you are not a magician? Silly girl! Of those who call themselves magicians, three-fourths are mere imposters. You are the true magician! What magic spell did you cast to come here at this hour?”
“Ammani! I did not come here by magic. I simply climbed up the ladder that was propped against the wall!” replied Vandiyathevan.
“That much I can see! I was asking what magic you used to deceive that girl.”
“I smiled in the moonlight. That was all! If that hadn’t worked, I thought of showing her the magic ring you gave me.”
“You’re keeping that ring safe, aren’t you? With that ring, you could have come here openly in broad daylight! Why did you sneak in like a thief along this blind path?”

“Ammani! Your brother-in-law, the Younger Pazhuvettarayar—his men are real thieves. First, they tried to steal my clothes and belongings. Then, they followed me everywhere, not letting me out of their sight for even a moment. It was a great ordeal to escape from them. After I got away, I wandered through alleys and byways, circling around the walls of your palace. When I saw the ladder propped against the wall, I thought you had remembered this poor soul and arranged it for me. I later realized that was a mistake. Forgive me.”
“There’s nothing that calls for forgiveness, is there?”
“How is that, Ammani?”
“You are not entirely wrong in what you guessed. Do you know why I wished to summon the sorcerer?”
“I do not know, Lady! I know nothing of sorcery; nor do I know astrology!”
“From the moment I saw you yesterday morning, you have remained in my thoughts. I wished to know why you had not yet come to see me. That is why I sent for the sorcerer.”
“That is truly astonishing.”
“What is?”
“What you have just said. From the moment I saw you yesterday, you too have remained in my thoughts!”
“Do you believe in the impressions of a previous birth?”
“What do you mean?”
“They say that if two people were friends or relatives in a previous birth, some bond will arise between them in this life as well. That is what I meant.”
“Until yesterday, I did not believe in such things. Only yesterday did I begin to believe.”

Though Vandiyathevan spoke thus, and it was clearly a lie, in his heart he was thinking of the girl he had seen at the Kudanthai astrologer’s house. But how could Nandini know anything about that? She believed he was speaking of her.
“But even so, you did not come to see me, did you? I heard that someone named Azhwarkkadiyan Nambi sent you with a message…”
“Yes, Lady, it was to deliver the message he gave me that I first wished to see you. But after seeing you once, I forgot all my earlier reasons.”
“Where did you meet Azhwarkkadiyan? What message did he send?”

“I met Azhwarkkadiyan Nambi near Veera Narayanapuram. With the power of his staff, he tried to prove that Vishnu is the greatest of all gods. At that moment, the retinue of Periya Pazhuvettarayar arrived. Your palanquin followed behind them. Perhaps to see what the commotion was, or for some other reason, your golden hand drew aside the palanquin’s curtain. At that very moment—” Knowing who you were, Azhwarkkadiyan wished to send you a message. As I too was staying that night at the Kadambur Sambuvaraiyar palace, he entrusted the message to me. However, I could not meet you at Kadambur. It was only near the Thanjavur fort, on the road, that I was able to encounter you. And that too, only because your palanquin collided with my horse!”

As Vandiyathevan narrated this, Nandini was gazing upwards, lost in thought. Therefore, it was impossible to discern anything from her expression. But when she heard the last part of Vandiyathevan’s words, she turned to look at him and offered a bewitching smile. “Yes; the palanquin I ride is indeed a most troublesome one!” she said.

chapters.title: The Sorcerer
paragraphs: In the distance, the thunderous roar of drums was heard. Trumpets blared. Human voices shouted in jubilation. The sounds of the fortress gates opening and closing, and the heavy footfalls of elephants and horses, echoed through the air.
Vandiyathevan realized that these sounds had caught Nandini’s attention. The nurse who stood guard started in alarm, came a little closer, and said, “Amma! It seems the lord has arrived.”
Nandini replied, “I know; you go back to your place!”

Then, turning to Vandiyathevan, she said, “The Commander is entering the fort. After inquiring about the Emperor’s health and meeting the commander of the garrison, he will come here. You must leave before he arrives. What is the message Alwarkadiyan brought?”
“Lady! That valiant Vaishnavite claimed you as his sister; is that true?” Vallavaraiyan asked.
“Why do you doubt that?”
“If someone said that a green parrot and a wild monkey were children of the same mother, would it be easy to believe?”
Nandini laughed and said, “In a way, what he said is true. We grew up in the same house, in the same family. He cherished me as a younger sister. Alas! I have caused him great disappointment!”
“In that case, it is well! The message Alwarkadiyan sent for you is that Lord Krishna is waiting for you. The multitudes of Vaishnavite devotees are also waiting to witness your wedding with Kannan!”

Nandini let out a deep sigh. “Ah! It seems he has not yet rid himself of that delusion! If you see him, tell him this from me. Tell him to forget me completely! Tell him I am in no way worthy to be a supreme devotee like Andal!”
“I do not agree with that, Amma!” “What is it that I did not accept?”

“It is only that you cannot become the Goddess herself that I did not accept. The Goddess had to worship, sing hymns, weep tears, string garlands of flowers and adorn herself with them before she could wed Krishna. But you need not undergo such hardships. All that is required is for Lord Krishna to lay eyes upon you. He would instantly forsake Rukmini, Satyabhama, Radha, and all the Gopikas, and seat you upon the throne where they once sat!”
“Sir! You are most skilled in flattery. I do not care for it in the least.”
“My lady! What do you mean by flattery?”
“To praise someone to their face—that is flattery.”
“In that case, please turn away and sit with your back to me.”
“For what purpose?”
“So that I may praise you without seeing your face, but only your back. There would be nothing wrong in that, would there?”
“You are exceedingly mischievous in your speech.”
“Is it not you who are flattering me now?”
“And are you not turning your face away and showing only your back?”
“Queen! Whether on the battlefield or before ladies, I have never turned my back. You may freely praise me as much as you wish!”
At this, Nandini laughed aloud, a clear, ringing sound.
“You are truly a magician; there is no doubt! It has been a long time since I laughed so openly!” she said.
“But, my lady! It is most dangerous to make you laugh! When the lotus smiled in the pond, the honeybee swooned and fell!” said Vandiyathevan.
“You are not only a magician, but seem to be a poet as well!”
“I do not fear flattery, nor will I falter at poetry.”
“Who made you thus?”
“Did you not just now call me a ‘poet’?”
“If that is so?”
“When I was a boy, some people used to call me ‘monkey-face!’ Only today, after so many years, have I heard it again from your coral-red lips.”
“They called you ‘monkey-face’? Who were those clever people?”
“None of them are alive now.”
“I did not call you that. I merely said you looked like someone who could sing poetry.”
“I do compose a little poetry; but only before my enemies. If they do not die by the arrow, let them die by the word!”
“Sir, O poet-warrior Veerasimha! You still haven’t told me your name!”
“My given name is Vandiyathevan; my title is Vallavaraiyan.”
“Are you of royal lineage?”
“I come from the ancient and renowned Vanathi Raja clan.”
“And your kingdom now?”
“The sky above; the earth below; at this moment, I am the sole emperor of the entire world!”
For a moment, Nandini gazed at Vallavaraiyan, her eyes lingering on him.
“Nothing is impossible. You could regain your ancestral kingdom.”
“How is that possible? Does anything return from the belly of a tiger? Can a kingdom that has merged into the Chola Empire ever be restored?”
“I can make it happen.”

“Lady! No, thank you! I have never desired to rule a kingdom. Whatever little longing I had vanished completely after seeing Sundara Chola today. Rather than becoming an emperor by depending on the hands of others, I would prefer to be a free man, uncertain even of where my next meal will come from.”
“My thoughts are the same!” said Nandini. Then, as if suddenly recalling something she had forgotten, she asked, “Why are the men of the Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar searching for you?”
“Just as your nursemaid’s daughter suspects me, so too has he begun to harbor doubts about me.”
“What sort of doubts?”
“How did the signet ring bearing the palmyra emblem come into my possession?”
A faint trace of fear appeared on Nandini’s face.
“Where is the ring?” she asked in a startled voice.
“Here it is, Lady! Would I so easily let go of it?” he said, taking out the ring and showing it to her.
“How did he come to know that you have it?” Nandini asked.

“For a long time, I have wished to see Sundara Chola Chakravarthi. To fulfill that desire, I made use of this signet ring. After I had seen him, the commander of the fort asked me how this ring came into my hands…”
“What did you say?” Nandini’s voice quivered with anxiety.
“I did not mention your name, Lady! I said that the Elder Pazhuvettaraiyar gave it to me. I told him it was given to me at the Kadambur palace…”
Nandini let out a deep sigh. The fear that had been on her face and in her voice faded away.
“Did he believe what you said?” she asked.

“It did not seem that he believed me entirely. That must be why he sent men to follow me. Perhaps, once his brother returns, he intends to bring me before him and learn the truth!” said Vandiyathevan.
Nandini smiled and said, “You need not fear the Elder Pazhuvettaraiyar. I will see to it that he does not devour you alive.”
“Lady! The whole world knows how great your influence is over the lord of this fort. But I have urgent business outside. That is why I seek your help to escape.”
“What is this urgent business you have?” “There are many things. For example, you must give your reply to Azhwarkkadiyan. What shall I tell him on your behalf?”
“Tell him to utterly forget that there ever was a woman named ‘Nandini’ who was his sister!”
“I can tell him that; but I doubt it will have any effect.”
“What do you mean?”
“Forgetting you, of course. Even I, who have seen you only twice by chance, find it impossible to forget you! How could someone who has spent his whole life with you ever forget?”
A victorious pride blossomed across Nandini’s face. Her spear-like eyes pierced through Vandiyathevan’s heart as she gazed at him.
“Why were you so eager to see the Emperor?” she asked.

“What wonder is there if I wished to see that world-renowned, handsome king? In this world, valiant monarchs desire that their valor and prowess should increase, that their kingdoms and fame should expand. They ask their subjects to pray for such things. But what prayers do the Buddhist monks offer in their monasteries for our Emperor?
‘…May the strength, beauty, and firmness of Sundara Chozhar shine and flourish above all in this world…’
That is how they pray. For a long time, I have yearned to see such a Manmatha of the Kali age…”
“Yes, the Emperor is very proud of his own beauty. But his royal daughter is even more arrogant…”
“Daughter? Whom do you mean?”
“The one in Pazhaiyarai, that proud and haughty princess—I mean the young princess Kundavai Devi.”
Vandiyatheva! You are indeed fortunate. The very opportunity you have been seeking has come and stood before you! Make good use of it!—Thus Vallavaraiyan spoke to himself.
All this while, Nandini had been reclining gracefully upon her bed. Suddenly, she sat upright.
“Sir! I have something to say. Will you agree to it?” she asked.
“Speak, Lady!” he replied.
“Let us make a pact between us. You must help me; I must help you. What do you say?”

“Lady! You are the queen of the most powerful chieftain in the Chola Empire. You possess the strength to accomplish whatever you desire. I, on the other hand, am a man without any influence. In what way could I possibly be of help to you?” he said.
Nandini fixed her sharp gaze upon him, trying to discern whether he spoke from his heart or merely from his lips.
Vandiyathevan stood firm, unperturbed by her scrutiny.
“I am in need of a confidant, someone to carry out secret tasks for me. If I secure you a position here in this palace, will you accept it?” she asked.
“I have already agreed to serve another noble lady in a similar manner. If she refuses me, then I shall come to you.”
“Who is this woman who dares to compete with me?”
“The very same young princess with whom you spoke so affectionately a short while ago—Princess Kundavai Devi herself.”
“Lies! Lies! Such a thing could never be! You are trying to make sport of me…”

“Queen! This letter has already been stolen and read by many. Therefore, there is no harm if you too see it!” So saying, Vandiyathevan produced the letter that Aditya Karikalan had given him for Kundavai and handed it to her.

Nandini took the letter by the lamp’s light and read it. When she finished, the lightning that flashed in her eyes reminded Vandiyathevan of the forked tongue of a cobra darting from its mouth; involuntarily, a shiver ran through his body.
With regal composure, Nandini looked at Vandiyathevan and asked, “Sir! Is it not your intention to escape alive from this fortress?” “Yes, madam! That is precisely why I have come seeking your help.”
“I can help you escape, but only on one condition.”
“Tell me your condition!”
“Whatever reply Kundavai gives to this letter, you must bring that reply back to me and show it. Do you agree?”
“You are setting a most dangerous condition!”
“Did you not boast just now that you are one who does not fear danger?”
“If I am to risk such danger, should there not be a worthy reward for it?...”

“A reward? You want a reward? You shall receive a reward beyond your wildest dreams. The very reward for which the great Periya Pazhuvettarayar, who now wields supreme power in the Chola Empire, has been performing penance for years—you shall receive such a reward!”
So saying, Nandini once again cast her enchanting spell over Vandiyathevan.
Alas! Vallavarayan’s head spun. “Heart! Hold fast to your courage! Do not lose your wits!” he told himself inwardly.
At that moment, as if to come to his aid, the harsh cry of an owl sounded from the nearby garden. Once, twice, thrice it called.
A shiver ran through Vandiyathevan’s body. Nandini turned toward the spot in the garden from where the owl’s cry had come and said, “The true sorcerer has arrived!”

Then, looking at Vandiyathevan, she said, “I have no further need of him. Yet, I will send him away with a word or two. Perhaps he may prove useful in helping you escape. For now, go over there, to that side, and hide yourself in the darkness!” She pointed in the exact opposite direction to where her nurse had gone earlier.

chapters.title: “Do You Remember?”
paragraphs: Nandini came and stood near the garden entrance of the Latha Mandapam and clapped her hands three times.
At that moment, it was impossible to say whether the lines on her face were those of fear or merely the dark shadows cast by the trees.
A little way into the garden, large trees and the vines that twined around them could be seen. Beyond that, it was a single mass of darkness.
Tearing through the gloom, pushing aside the creepers, a sorcerer emerged from behind a tree.
Nandini went and seated herself on her flower-strewn couch. Now, a calm had settled over her beautiful face.
The sorcerer entered the Latha Mandapam. The golden lamp’s flame cast its light upon his face.

A familiar face! Who was he? Yes! He was one of those men who had gathered at midnight near the Thirupurambiyam school barracks. The one who had poured out gold coins from his pouch with a clatter. This was Ravidasan, the man who had told the others, “Wherever you see Azhwarkadiyan, kill him at once!”
Even as he approached, anger was boiling on his face. When he saw Nandini, sitting serenely on her bed of flowers, his cat-like eyes flashed with a wild, furious fire.
He sat down on the plank that lay opposite the couch, fixed his gaze on Nandini, and began to chant, “Hoom Hreem Hram! Bhagavati! Shakti! Chandikeswari!…” reciting several mantras.
“That’s enough! Stop!” Nandini interrupted. “The old woman has fallen asleep on the threshold, it seems. Say what you must quickly! ‘He’ has come into the fort!”
“Wretched woman!” Ravidasan’s words hissed like a cobra.
“Whom do you mean?” Nandini asked, her voice still calm.
“You, ungrateful Nandini! The younger queen of Pazhuvoor! You!” Ravidasan pointed a finger at her.
Nandini remained silent. “Girl! It seems you have forgotten some events that you ought to remember. Let me remind you of them,” said Ravidasan.
“Why bring up old tales now?” asked Nandini.
“Do you ask why now? I will tell you. First, let me remind you, and then I shall explain,” replied Ravidasan.
As if she thought it useless to try and stop him, Nandini let out a deep sigh and turned away to face the other side.

“Queen! Listen! Three years ago, one night at midnight, on the banks of the Vaigai river, a funeral pyre was burning in the cremation ground. No last rites were performed there by priests according to the scriptures. They had gathered dried logs, twigs, and leaves from the forest to build that pyre. From behind a tree, they brought forth a body that had been hidden and placed it upon the pyre. Then they set it alight. The flames caught well on the forest wood and blazed fiercely. At that moment, from the shadows of the forest, some men dragged you forth. Your hands and feet were bound. A cloth was stuffed into your mouth. Today, you sit adorned with flowers and your hair neatly coiled, but then your tresses were loose and tangled, trailing on the ground. Those men intended to throw you alive into the flames that were devouring the pyre. ‘Let the fire burn a little stronger!’ said one of them. Leaving you there, those men each took a dreadful oath. You heard them. Though your mouth was gagged, your eyes were not covered; nor were your ears stopped. So you watched and listened to everything. After they had all finished swearing their oaths, they approached you. Until then you had been still, but now, with your bound hands, you tried to make some sign. You rolled your eyes, widened them, and strained your brows in effort. One of them said, ‘She wants to say something!’ Another replied, ‘It will be some old tale; throw her onto the pyre!’ Yet another said, ‘No! Before we burn her, let us hear what she wants to say! Remove the cloth from her mouth!’ Since he was their leader, they obeyed and took the cloth from your mouth. Do you remember what you said then, girl?” asked Ravidasan, and fell silent.

Nandini neither replied nor turned to look at him. Her face revealed the disgust and fear that filled her heart, and at the same time, the fierce resolve of a terrible determination. From her dark eyes... Tears brimmed in her eyes.

“Girl! You say you will not speak? No matter! I shall speak for you. You declared that, like those men, you too would take a vow of vengeance. You swore that you had even greater cause than they to seek retribution. You said you would use your beauty and your intellect for that very purpose. You promised to help them as much as you could. And once the vow was fulfilled, you declared you would end your own life. You swore it, you commanded it. Others did not believe you. But I believed. I believed, and I stopped you from throwing yourself into the flames. I saved your life—do you remember all this?” Ravidasan finished, his voice trembling.
Nandini turned slightly to look at him. “You ask if I remember? All of it is etched into my heart as if written by fire,” she replied.

“Later, one day, all of us were traveling along the wild paths by the endless banks of the Kaveri. Suddenly, we heard the sound of horsemen approaching from behind. We decided that each of us would hide separately in the forest until they passed. But you alone defied that decision and stood right there on the path. The horsemen seized you. Their leader, the great Paluvettaraiyar, was bewitched by you and fell into your snare. You married him. All those who were with me mocked me, saying I had been deceived. But I did not give up on you. Somehow, one day, I managed to catch you alone. I thought to stab you, the traitor, with my dagger and be done with it. But once again, you begged for your life. You said you were here only to fulfill our vow. You swore that, even from within this palace, you would do all you could to help us. Is all this true or not?” Ravidasan demanded, his voice quivering.
“It is all true; who said otherwise? Why do you keep repeating it? Now tell me why you have come!” Nandini retorted.

“No, girl! You do not remember. You have forgotten everything! You have drowned in the luxuries of the Paluvur palace and forgotten your vow! Savoring every delicacy, adorning yourself with fine clothes and jewels, sleeping on silk mattresses in the royal chamber, traveling in ivory palanquins—queen that you are! How could you possibly remember the past?”
“Shame! Shame! Who wants this bed, these silks, these jewels? Do you think I live for these petty pleasures? Never!”
“Or perhaps, seeing the handsome face of that youth who came along the way, you lost your senses! Maybe, in this newfound infatuation, you have forgotten your old desire for revenge—haven’t you?”
Nandini was startled for a moment. She quickly composed herself and said, “Lies! Utter lies!”
“If that is a lie, then why, even though I sent word in advance that I would come today, did you not send your nursemaid to the usual place?”
“I did send her. But someone else climbed up the ladder meant for you. That foolish woman thought it was you and brought him here. Is that my fault?”

“What does it matter whose fault it is? In another moment, my life would have been in danger. The fort guards, who were searching for that youth, nearly caught me. I had to hide in the pond in the forest near the palace, holding my breath until I nearly drowned. Only after they left did I escape, drenched and shivering…”
“You deserved it. That plunge washed away the sin of doubting me!”
“Woman! Swear to me—did you not lose your heart to the beauty of that youth?”

“Shame on you! What words are these! Who ever speaks of the beauty of men? Only in this shameless Chola land do they celebrate ‘the king is handsome’. For men, isn’t beauty nothing but the scars of battle on their bodies?”
“Well said; if you truly mean that, then why did that young wanderer come here?”
“I already told you, Vasuki brought him here by mistake, thinking he was you.”
“Then why did you give him your signet ring, which you have never given even to me?”
“I gave it to bring him here and speak with him. Now, I am going to take it back from him…”
“Why did you bring him here? What were you discussing with him for so long?”
“I was conversing with him only with an eye on a significant gain. Through him, we can secure a great advantage in achieving our purpose.”
“Wretched woman! In the end, have you shown your feminine cunning? To entrust our secret to some young man whose past and future are unknown—”
“Why are you agitated for nothing? I haven’t told him anything. On the contrary, I gleaned the secret from him.”
“What did you glean?”

“He is carrying a palm-leaf letter from Kanchipuram to Pazhayarai. He showed it to me—he’s taking it to the she-tiger of Pazhayarai. I was persuading him to bring back the reply she gives and deliver it to me. That’s when you arrived.”
“So there’s the palm-leaf; and the stylus as well. What use is all this to us?”

“That’s the limit of your intelligence! We have sworn to destroy the Tiger Clan from its very roots. But you’re counting only the male tigers. Have you forgotten that the clan thrives through the she-tiger as well? Not just that—do you know who truly rules this Chola kingdom now? Is it the old man, lying helpless and speechless on his sickbed? The princes in Kanchi and Lanka?”
“No! It is the lord of Thanjavur, the Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar, who has the fortune to have you as his queen. The whole world knows this!”

“That too is wrong! The world may think so; the old man too is deluded by that belief. You, too, have fallen for that deception. In truth, it is the she-tiger cub in Pazhayarai who rules this kingdom. Sitting within the palace, that proud woman pulls the strings and makes everyone dance to her tune! I will subdue her arrogance. For that, I intend to use this youth…”
On Ravidasan’s face appeared signs of both astonishment and respect.
“You are indeed a master strategist; there’s no doubt about that. But how can I be sure all this is true? How can I trust you?” he asked.

“I will hand over that youth to you myself. You take him, blindfolded, through the secret passage and lead him outside the fort! Wait near Pazhayarai! When Kundavai gives her reply on the palm-leaf, bring it back here with—”
“Bring him back here again! If he tries to escape, if he attempts to deceive you, kill him at once,” said Nandini.

“No! No! You both leave, somehow! Right now, the men of Chinna Pazhuvettarayar are searching for him inside the fort; soon, they will begin searching outside as well. If I go with him, I too will be in danger. Tell me about the task for which I have come!”
“You still haven’t revealed what that task is…”
“Arrangements have been made for people to go to Kanchi and Lanka. For those traveling to Lanka, the journey is especially perilous. They must conduct themselves with great cunning there…”
“What do you want me to do for that? Do you need more gold? Is there no limit to your greed for gold?”

“The gold is not for our personal use; it is only to accomplish the task we have undertaken. Then, for what other reason do you think we have kept you here? For those going to Lanka, Chozha country’s gold coins are of no use; it would be best if we had Lankan gold…”

“Why did you take so long to say this? I had already set it aside for you before you even asked,” said Nandini, bending down beneath the couch where she sat. She took out a pouch and handed it to Ravidasan. “This contains plenty of Lankan gold coins. Take it and go! It is almost time for him to arrive!” she said.

As Ravidasan took the pouch and prepared to leave, she said, “Wait a moment! At least take that young man outside the fort and let him go! After that, let him take whatever path he wishes! I do not wish to show him the way through the tunnel!” With these words, she stood up and looked toward the darkened palace.
Nothing was visible there. She signaled with her fingers; she clapped her hands softly; but nothing happened.

She and Ravidasan walked a short distance along the Latha Mandapam corridor. They approached the entrance to that grand, shadowy palace. But Vandiyathevan was nowhere to be seen! Nowhere around, in any direction, could they find him!

Vandiyathevan was startled. He turned around quickly. There, in the dim light of the corridor, he saw a figure standing, half-shrouded in darkness. For a moment, he could not recognize who it was. The voice, however, was unmistakable. It was the same voice that had spoken to him in the dark, on the banks of the Veeranarayana Lake, the same voice that had whispered secrets in the midnight silence.
“Do you remember?” the voice repeated.

Vandiyathevan’s heart pounded. He took a step forward, peering into the gloom. The figure stepped closer, and the faint light revealed the face of the enigmatic woman—Azhwarkadiyan’s companion, the mysterious one who seemed to appear and vanish at will.
“Yes, I remember,” Vandiyathevan replied, his voice steady despite his inner turmoil. “How could I forget? You saved my life that night.”
A faint smile played on the woman’s lips. “You have a sharp memory. But do you remember what I told you then?”
Vandiyathevan hesitated. Fragments of that night flashed through his mind—the hurried whispers, the warning, the sense of danger lurking in every shadow.
“You told me to be careful,” he said slowly. “You warned me that enemies were everywhere, that I should trust no one.”
“Good,” she said. “You have not forgotten. That advice is even more important now. The dangers have multiplied. The net is closing in.”
Vandiyathevan looked at her intently. “Who are you? Why do you help me?”
The woman’s eyes glinted in the darkness. “That is not important now. What matters is that you heed my warning. Do not let your guard down, even for a moment.”

She turned to go, her figure melting into the shadows. Vandiyathevan reached out, as if to stop her, but she was already gone. Only her words lingered in the air, a chilling reminder of the perils that surrounded him.
He stood there for a long time, lost in thought, the weight of her warning pressing heavily upon him.

chapters.title: When Lions Clashed!
paragraphs: The people of Thanjavur held a special affection for the brothers of Pazhuvoor. Was it not the Pazhuvettarayar clan that had bestowed new glory and influence upon that ancient city? A procession of elephants, horses, and camels was always a spectacle that delighted the townsfolk. Whether the great lord, Periya Pazhuvettarayar, was leaving Thanjai or returning to the fortress from outside, crowds would gather on either side of the streets to watch the pageantry; they would shout their praises, offer their blessings, and shower flowers and puffed rice in celebration.

Usually, when the elder brother returned from outside, the younger would come to the fortress gate to welcome him and lead him inside. The sight of the two brothers embracing each other was like the Nilagiri and Podhigai mountains coming together in a loving clasp. If both rode side by side on elephants or horses, one would need ten thousand eyes to truly behold that magnificent sight.

Some compared the Pazhuvoor brothers to Hiranya and Hiranyatchan. Others called them the “Sundopa Sundarars.” There were those who said they were brothers as noble as Rama and Bharata, and others who likened them to the heroic brothers Bhima and Arjuna.

But today, when Periya Pazhuvettarayar entered the Thanjai fortress, though his retinue made the customary proclamations, there was no festive cheer in the streets; the crowds were sparse. Chinna Pazhuvettarayar was not waiting at the fortress gate to receive his elder brother.

Yet the great lord paid no heed to this, and proceeded directly towards his younger brother’s palace. He thought, “The younger one must be engaged in some important matter.” A suspicion arose in his mind—perhaps the Emperor’s health had taken a grave turn, or… or perhaps the “great deed” itself had been accomplished.
Thus, moving more swiftly than usual, his retinue made their way to the palace of the fortress commander, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar.

On the threshold of the palace, the commander who had come to welcome his younger brother bore an expression of agitation and concern upon his face. After offering his respects to his brother, he embraced him warmly. The two of them entered the palace together and proceeded straight into the inner council chamber.
Once they were alone, the elder asked, “Brother! Kaalandhagan! What is the matter with you? Is there any special news? Is the Emperor well?”
Kaalandhakandar, the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar, replied, “The Emperor is as he always is. There is no improvement in his health, nor is there any decline.”
“Then why does your face look so troubled? Why did you not come to the fort gate? Even the town seems unusually subdued!” the elder inquired.
“Anna! A small incident has occurred. Nothing dangerous. I will tell you about it later. How did all your affairs go?” Kaalandhakandar asked.

“My mission was a complete success. All those who were summoned came to Kadambur. Everyone unanimously agreed that your son-in-law, Madurantakan, is the rightful heir to the throne. They approved it with shouts of victory. If justice is not served, they are all ready to take up arms and establish his right by force. Even Kolli Mazhavan and Vanangamudi Munaiyaraiyan have agreed—what obstacle remains to fulfill our purpose? Sambuvaraiyar is prepared to commit his fortress, his army, his wealth—everything. His son Kandhamaaran is fiercely determined. There is no need to worry about Nadu Nadu or Thirumunaippadi Nadu. The Chola country is always in our grasp. What else is there to consider? Thirukovalur Malayaman, Parthibendran of the Pallavas, and the Velan of Kodumbalur—these three alone might possibly oppose us. Of them, the lord of Kodumbalur is not here; he is in Lanka. What can the other two accomplish? We must speak to the Emperor at the earliest and settle the matter at once!” declared the elder Pazhuvettaraiyar.
“What you say about the chieftains is true; but what about the people? What if the people object?” asked Kaalandhakandar.

“Ah! Who is going to ask the people? Are kingdoms run by consulting the people? If the people dare to object, we must ensure that they never again interfere in such matters. But I do not think it will come to that. If it is the Emperor’s wish, they will submit without a word.

Moreover, it is fortunate that Arulmozhi Varman is in Lanka. Even so, the people might still try to display their blind devotion. The people do not hold as much affection for Aditya Karikalan. It would be easy to turn their loyalty toward Madurantakan. He already has a reputation as a ‘devotee of Shiva’ and a man of ‘upright character’. You know well enough that, compared to Sundara Chozhar’s two sons, your son-in-law’s face bears more of the marks of beauty. The foolish masses believe that ‘the beauty of the heart is reflected on the face’. It would be more surprising if they did not shout, ‘Long live Emperor Madurantaka!’ Whatever may happen, as long as I am here, what have you to fear…?”
“But what about the Velakkara army! How are we to manage them?”

“The Velakkara soldiers have sworn an oath of life-sacrifice only to Sundara Chozhar, not to his children. And even if they interfere, where is your own fortress guard? In the span of a single hour, could you not seize them all and throw them into the dungeons?”
“Anna! The main opposition will come from Pazhayarai. Who knows what that old woman and the princess will plot together? That is what we must watch most closely…”
“Thambi! Kalanthaka! Are you really telling me to fear two women? I have countermeasures for all their tricks and schemes. Do not worry!”
“The Emperor has ordered that both of them be summoned to Thanjavur…”

“Aditya Karikalan will not come. Perhaps Arulmozhi, obeying his father’s command, will set out and come. If he does, he must be stopped! Only after Madurantakan is crowned prince and seated on the throne with full authority should either of them be allowed to come. They must not arrive before that. Leave that to me! But you mentioned some minor incident that happened here—what was it?”
“A young man came from Kanchi. He brought a letter for the Emperor and another for Kundavai…”
“What did you do with him? You seized the letters and had him imprisoned, did you not?”
“No, Anna! He said he had seen you at Kadambur, and that he was told to deliver the letters directly to the Emperor. Is that true?”

“Aha! Sheer lies! A young man, uninvited to Kadambur—he came claiming to be Kandhamaaran’s friend. But he never once mentioned to me that he had brought a letter! The moment I saw his face, I was suspicious. Did you let yourself be deceived by him?”
“Yes, Anna! I was indeed deceived. I was fooled because he spoke your name!”
“You fool! What did you do after being deceived? Did you hand the letter over to the Emperor? Did you not even look at it?”
“I saw it. There was nothing in it. It simply asked that he come to the golden palace at Kanchi. After handing over the letter, that youth kept muttering something about ‘danger’…”
“At least then, did you suspect him and have him arrested?”
“I did suspect him; but I did not arrest him!”
“Then what did you do?”

“He said he wanted to see the city. I told him to go ahead, but sent two men to follow him. He tricked them and disappeared. I was just making arrangements to search for him. That’s why I couldn’t even come to the fort gates! I have already warned the people of the city…”

“Shame on you! Are you even a man? Did you let yourself be outwitted by a mere boy whose moustache hasn’t even sprouted? I named you Kaalandhakakandan, and now I must regret my foolishness. I made you commander of the fort? This is what I deserve! Aren’t you ashamed to admit that some reckless fellow deceived you by using my name?”
“It wasn’t just your name he used. He also showed your signet ring. Did you give it to him?”
“Absolutely not! Do you think I’m as gullible as you, to be so easily fooled?”

“It’s true he had the signet ring. He showed it to me as well. He showed it to the guards at the fort gate, and only then was he allowed inside. If you didn’t give it to him, there’s only one other place he could have gotten it from.”
“Whom are you talking about?”
“Can’t you guess? I mean the Young Queen herself…”
“Fie, fie! Beware! I will cut off your tongue!”

“Even if you cut off my tongue, understand this; even if you sever my head, do so. I am going to say now what I have long wished to say. You are keeping a venomous serpent in your house, thinking it beautiful and nurturing it. One day, it is bound to bite. It will destroy all of us! No! Cast her out and turn your attention to other matters!”

“Kalanthaka Kanda! There is something I too have long wished to tell you, and today I shall say it. About any other matter, you may freely express your opinion. If you dislike my actions, you may boldly criticize me. But if you ever utter a single word against the woman I have taken by the hand and wedded, if you ever speak ill of her, I swear by the very hand that raised you—I will kill you! I, who taught you to wield a sword, will snatch your own sword and cut you down! Beware!”

The furious war of words that erupted between those two brothers was like the dreadful clash of two lions. Their voices resounded like the roar of beasts. Though their conversation took place within the secret council chamber, to those waiting outside, their voices rang out like thunder, though the words were indistinct. All who heard trembled, wondering, “What disaster is this?”

chapters.title: Nandini’s Sulk
paragraphs: When Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar finally returned to his mansion, midnight had passed and the third watch of the night had begun. He dusted off the grime of the street, but within his heart, a storm raged fiercer than the swirling winds outside, raising clouds of confusion and turmoil. He felt a pang of regret for having rebuked his dear younger brother so harshly. There was no limit to the affection he bore for his sibling; it was only because of that deep love that he had spoken as he did. Yet, why should a man so full of suspicion unnecessarily speak ill of Nandini? Such is human nature, perhaps. It is the way of ordinary men to blame others for their own faults and thus escape censure. But why should his brother, of all people, stoop to such a base method? Instead of punishing the wily, thieving youth who had fallen into his hands, was it fitting for him to cast aspersions upon a woman—upon his own wife, no less? Was this in keeping with his valor and manliness? Let it be! After all, he had already repented and asked for forgiveness, had he not? Why should he dwell on it any further?

Still, could there be even a grain of truth in what his brother had said? Was it possible that, at this advanced age, he himself had fallen prey to a woman’s wiles? For the sake of a woman he had plucked from the wilderness, had he really been compelled to rebuke his own brother, his companion through a hundred battlefields, the one who had stood by his side as his strength, who had, time and again, risked his own life to save him from danger? What was so special about her? He knew nothing of her lineage. Her actions and words, at times, did give rise to suspicion. Shame! His brother’s words had sown such confusion even in his own heart! What injustice is this? How dearly she loves him, how respectfully she conducts herself! With what enthusiasm she involves herself in all his affairs! At times, she even offers him wise counsel. Had she not, with courage, married this old man of over sixty? Shouldn’t that count for something? If a swayamvara were held for this beauty, even Indra himself would descend from the heavens to win her hand! Which crowned king in this world would not desire to marry her? Ah! If this Sundara Chozhan were to lay eyes upon her, would that not be enough? How foolish, then, to harbor any suspicion about such a woman! How ridiculous for old men who have married young women to entertain baseless doubts! We have heard of people who, by their own actions, turn their lives into a living hell. We have seen such examples in the world. Should we, too, make ourselves the object of others’ ridicule in such a way?

Yet, it is necessary to learn certain details from her own lips. Why does she so often ask for the signet ring? For what purpose? Why does she frequently go alone and sit in the Latha Mandapam? What is the reason for that? We have heard that some magician comes to see her often—she herself has admitted it—why is that? What does she seek to learn from the magician? Whom does she wish to enchant with his spells?

With all this going on, for how much longer does she intend to keep me in this state of ‘married, yet a celibate’? She keeps talking about some vow, some penance, but never explains what vow, what penance! Is this not like the cunning women in stories who use clever tricks to evade and manipulate? I must not allow this to continue any longer! Tonight, I must speak to her about it and settle the matter once and for all!

When Pazhuvettarayar reached the entrance of his palace, the women of the household, the servants, and the nursemaids were waiting to welcome him. But, though his eyes searched all around, he did not see the young queen whom he most wished to see. Upon inquiry, he learned that she was still in the Latha Mandapam. In his mind arose the question, “What business does she have there even at this hour, past midnight?” Along with that, a suspicion and anger that she was neglecting him also took root. With a touch of irritation, he strode toward the Kodi Mandapam.

As he reached the entrance of the Kodi Mandapam, he saw Nandini and her companion approaching him. When she saw him, Nandini stopped, but instead of looking at him, she turned her gaze toward the darkness that had settled over the garden. The nursemaid stood a little distance away.
Even after Pazhuvettarayar came near her, Nandini did not turn to look at him. Instead of rebuking her as he had intended, he found himself needing to soothe her anger!
“Nandini! My precious one! Why are you angry? Why this indifference?” he asked, gently placing his iron-like hand upon her shoulder.
But Nandini, with her hand softer than a flower, pushed away his hand, which was as hard as a thunderbolt. Ah! Is it possible that such strength can reside in such softness and delicacy?

“My life! You touched me with your silken hand and pushed me away—ah, that itself is my fortune! From the peaks of Trikona Malai to the Vindhya mountains, not a single hero among the bravest of warriors could accomplish what you have done! That is my luck! Yet, should you not tell me the reason for your anger? My ears burn with longing to hear the honey-sweet music of your voice,” pleaded that great warrior, who had triumphed in a thousand battlefields.

“How many days has it been since you left me? Has it even been a full four days?” Nandini’s voice quivered with emotion. That trembling tone, which could melt the hearts of even the unyielding Pazhuvetaraiyar—who had withstood countless swords and spears—softened him like wax placed in fire.
“Is this the reason for such anger? Could you not bear a separation of four days? What would you do if I had to go to war? Would you not have to endure months apart?” he asked.
“If you go to the battlefield, do you think I would spend months apart from you? Change that thought. Like your shadow, I too will follow you to the field of war…”

“How beautiful that sounds! If I were to take you to the battlefield, it would be as if I myself were waging war! Beloved! This chest and these shoulders have withstood the sharpest arrows and the points of many spears. The world praises me for having sixty-four such wounds. But if a tiny thorn were to prick your soft, flower-like skin, my heart would shatter. What countless swords and spears could not accomplish, a small thorn at your foot would achieve. How could I ever take you to the field of battle? Even now, seeing you stand so long upon this hard stone floor pains me. Come, come and rest upon your bed of flowers! Let me gaze upon your radiant face. Do not think that only you suffered from our four days’ separation! Every moment without you was an age for me. Now, at least, let my thirst be quenched as I behold your golden face!” So saying, he took Nandini’s hand, led her, and seated her upon the couch.

Nandini wiped her eyes and looked up at Pazhuvetaraiyar. In the golden glow of the lamp, he saw the pearl-like smile blooming on her face. Ah! For that gentle smile, one could give away all three worlds! Since the three worlds are not within my grasp, I can offer her my body, my wealth, and my very soul! Yet she asks nothing of me!—thus thought that peerless warrior. The very intention to question or reproach her vanished completely! Whatever task Nandini set with her foot, he would bow his head and fulfill. He has come to a state where he is being led by the nose! Any kind of servitude is wretched indeed! But nothing else can make a man lose his wits like servitude to a woman!

“You were away in a distant town for four days, weren’t you? Why didn’t you come straight here as soon as you returned? Has your younger brother become more important to you than I am?” asked Nandini. Having asked, she glanced at him from the corner of her eyes with a feigned anger.

“It is not so, my beloved! My heart longed to come to you like an arrow shot from a bow. But that scatterbrained boy—Madhuranthakan—I had to linger at my brother’s house to make sure he returned safely through the underground passage…”

“Sir! I am interested in everything you undertake. I too wish for all your efforts to succeed. Yet, it pains me to think of you taking a young man in the closed palanquin meant for me. People in every city and town believe that wherever you go, you take me along with you…”

“Do you think that brings joy only to me? Not at all! But the task we have undertaken is a great one. I endure and do all this for the sake of accomplishing it. Besides, have you forgotten that it was you who suggested this idea? Was it not you who told me to take Madhuranthakan in your closed palanquin? Was it not you who devised the plan to send him alone through the underground passage both when leaving and returning to the fort?”
“I only did my duty. Is it not a wife’s duty to help her husband in his undertakings? I merely shared with you the strategy I knew. Because of that, you…”

“Is that all you did? This Madhuranthakan, who used to smear his body with sacred ash, wear a rudraksha garland, and chant Namashivaya, who went about temples and tanks proclaiming himself to be ‘Mother’s son’—we tried so much to kindle in him a desire to rule, but failed. Twice you spoke with him, and immediately he changed! Now, the royal ambition burning within him cannot be described. His imaginary kingdom now stretches from Lanka to the Himalayas! It has spread from the earth to the sky. He is more impatient than us. He is yearning to ascend the Chola throne. Nandini! That…” What magic spell you cast upon that child, I do not know!… Yes, indeed, you yourself are such a master of enchantments—why then do you summon another sorcerer? Why call for a magician when you are one yourself? People might begin to talk unnecessarily about it…”

“My lord! If anyone dares to speak unnecessarily about such matters, it is your duty to teach those wicked tongues a lesson by cutting them off. I have already told you why I wish to summon the magician. If you have forgotten, I will say it once more. It is to draw out the venom of that woman-snake in Pazhayarai. You are men of courage. On the battlefield, you stand face to face and fight with other men. You dismiss women as ‘mere girls’. You think it shameful to wage war against women. But a single woman can cause more harm than a hundred men. Only a snake knows the ways of another snake. You do not know the depths of Kundavai’s treachery; but I do. Perhaps you have forgotten how she humiliated both you and me together, but I cannot forget. In the midst of a hundred women, she looked at me and said, ‘That old man, at the very brink of death, has lost his wits, overcome by lust for a woman—where has your sense gone? Why did you go and marry that old man?’ Can I ever forget those words? ‘You shine like a celestial nymph—any prince would have longed for you, would have garlanded you and made you his queen. Yet, of all people, you went and married that old buffalo!’—can I ever forget how she mocked me so?”
Saying this, Nandini began to sob. Tears welled up in her eyes and streamed down her cheeks, soaking her bosom.

chapters.title: The World Turned!
paragraphs: Pazhuvettarayar was well aware that many people gossiped in various ways about his marriage at such an advanced age. He had even heard that among those who spoke disparagingly, Princess Kundavai was one of them. Yet, until now, no one had ever come to him and bluntly repeated what Kundavai had actually said. Now, hearing it from Nandini’s own lips, his heart became like the blazing furnace of a blacksmith’s forge. His breath came in hot, heavy gusts, as if mixed with fire.
Nandini’s tears only served as oil to make the fire in his heart leap higher and burn fiercer.

“My dear! Did that wretched, sinful woman truly say such things? Did she call me an old buffalo? Let it be; that woman… that woman… Watch what I shall do to her! Just as a buffalo tramples a lily creeper under its hoof, I shall crush her! And more… that woman… that woman…” Pazhuvettarayar stammered, unable to speak further in his rage. The terrifying expression that came over his face was indescribable.
Nandini tried to calm him. She took his iron-like hand in her own soft, flower-like palm, entwining her fingers with his.

“My lord! I know you cannot bear the humiliation that has befallen me. But a lion, mighty enough to split the skull of a great elephant and drink its blood, cannot simply pounce upon a mere cat. Kundavai is a female cat, but she is a great enchantress. With her magic and sorcery, she has everyone dancing to her will! She has the entire Chola kingdom under her sway! Her sorcery can only be overcome by a greater spell. If you do not wish it, tell me so. This very day, I will leave this palace…” she said, breaking down into sobs once more.
Pazhuvettarayar’s rage subsided; his infatuation grew stronger.

“No, no! Summon a thousand sorcerers if you wish. But you must not go! You are my very life! No, more than that—you are my life itself! What use is this body if life departs? Even now, your keeping me at a distance is killing me while I yet live! You know so many spells—will you not teach me just one?” he pleaded. “Natha! When you hold sword and spear in your hands, what need have you for spells? Leave those magical incantations to a foolish woman like me! Why do you, of all people, require magic and mantras?” said Nandini.

“Beloved! The moment your coral lips part and you call me ‘Natha’, my whole body shivers… When I gaze upon your golden face, my mind reels! It’s true that I carry sword and spear in my hands. I shall wield them on the battlefield, to strike down my enemies. But what use are those weapons here, in this flower-laden pavilion? Against the arrows of Manmatha, the god of love, I have no weapon at all. But you—do you not possess such power? You ask why I need magic! My body and soul are being consumed ceaselessly by a fire—only to quench that fire do I seek a mantra! If you know any spell for that, tell me! If not, grant me the fortune of touching your flower-soft skin! Somehow, save my life! My jewel-eyed one! It has been two and a half years since you and I were wed, as the world knows, according to the rites of the shastras. Yet, we have not begun our married life as is customary. You keep me at a distance, always speaking of vows and fasts. You torment and torture the husband whose hand you took in marriage! Or else, in some way, give me poison with your own hand and end my life…”

Nandini covered her ears and cried, “Ayyo! Do not utter such cruel words! If you speak so again, I shall do just as you say. I will drink poison and die. Then you can live on in peace, without sorrow!”
“No, no; I shall not speak so again. Forgive me! If you die by drinking poison, will I ever find peace of mind? I am half-mad now—then I would become wholly mad…”

“Natha! Why should you become mad? From the very day we joined hands in marriage, we became one body, one soul. Our lives have mingled; our hearts have merged; every beat of your heart echoes here in mine. Every thought that arises in your mind is reflected here in the mirror of my soul. When your brow furrows, my eyes grow dim. When your moustache quivers, my very entrails tremble. Now that we are life to each other, why think only of this body? This body is made of earth; one day it will burn to ash and return to dust…”

“Stop! Stop! My ears are burning from your cruel words!” cried Pazhuvetarayar. Without giving her a chance to speak further, he continued: “You say your body is made of earth? Lies! Lies! Do not utter such a great falsehood with your honeyed lips that exude the scent of nectar! Did you say your body was fashioned from clay? Never, not for a single day. There may be countless women in this world. Brahma may have created them from earth, from stone, or by mixing charcoal and ash. But do you know how Brahma created your divine form? He gathered flowers that had fallen from the mandara trees of Devaloka; he came to Tamilakam and plucked fresh red lotuses; he collected all these blossoms and placed them in a golden vessel filled with the nectar of the gods. When the nectar and the flowers had steeped together and become one wondrous mixture, he took it up. Into that mixture, he poured the rays of the full moon. He summoned the ancient bards of Tamilakam and bade them play the yāzh. He blended the music of that yāzh into the mixture. From that miraculous blend, Brahma fashioned your divine form…”

“My lord! You speak as if you stood beside Brahma himself and witnessed it! Am I the only one to whom you offer such descriptions? There are so many queenly women in your harem, born of royal lineages. For so many years you have lived with them as husband and wife. It is only two and a half years since you set eyes on me!…” Nandini began, but Pazhuvetarayar interrupted her. It seemed he wished to express, if only through words, the flood of emotion surging within him. He seemed to want to douse the burning fire of his longing with a shower of words.

“Nandini! You spoke of the women of my harem. I married them only for the sake of continuing the ancient lineage of the Pazhuvur kings. Some of them were barren and passed away. Others bore only daughters. ‘God’s grace goes only so far,’ I told myself, and found peace. For a long time, I had banished even the memory of women from my mind. Affairs of state alone absorbed my every thought. Nothing but the glory of the Chola kingdom found a place in this heart of mine. It was then that the final great war with the Pandyas broke out. Though there were many young commanders, I could not remain behind. Had I not gone to the battlefield, such a great victory would never have been won. After utterly destroying the Pandya army and planting the flag of triumph in Madurai, I went to Kongu country. From there, I returned along the endless banks of the Kaveri. It was on that journey, in a dense forest, that I saw you. At first, I could not believe you stood there. I closed my eyes and opened them again. Still, you were there. ‘She must be a forest goddess; nearby— Thinking you would vanish as soon as I approached, I drew near. Yet, even then, you did not disappear. Like the stories told in ancient legends, I thought, “She must be a celestial maiden or a gandharva woman, cursed from heaven and sent to earth; she cannot know the language of mortals!” With that thought, I asked, “Lady, who are you?” You replied in flawless Tamil, “I am an orphaned woman; I have sought refuge with you; please protect me.” As I brought you here in the palanquin, my mind was filled with countless thoughts. It seemed as if I had seen you somewhere, at some time, long ago. But no matter how much I tried to recall, I could not remember where. Suddenly, the veil of illusion that shrouded my mind was lifted; the truth dawned upon me. I realized that I had not seen you before in this life. But it became clear that I had known you in many previous births. Memories from those past lives surged within me.

You were born into this world as Ahalya; at that time, I was Indra. I abandoned my throne in the heavens and, braving a sage’s curse, came in search of you. Later, I was born as King Shantanu. While hunting along the banks of the Ganga, I saw you; you had taken the form of Ganga, appearing as a woman of this earth, and I loved you. In another age, I was born as Kovalan in the city of Kaveripoompattinam; you incarnated as Kannagi. Enchanted by the illusion that clouded my mind, I forgot you for a time. But then the veil of illusion was lifted. I realized your worth. I took you with me to the city of Madurai. On the way, I left you in a cowherd’s village and went to sell the anklet. Through treachery, I lost my life. As retribution for that, in this birth, after destroying the Pandya dynasty of Madurai, I saw you again as I was returning. I realized that you were the very Kannagi from whom I had been separated hundreds of years ago!…”

As Pazhuvettarayar recounted these tales of former births, Nandini was looking away, not meeting his gaze. Because of this, Pazhuvettarayar did not notice the shifting expressions that crossed her face at that moment. Had he noticed, it is doubtful whether he would have continued speaking.

When he paused for breath, Nandini turned to him and said, “My lord! The examples you have given are not quite appropriate. In fact, they seem rather inauspicious. If you wish, call yourself Manmatha and me Rathi!” she said, her face blooming once more with a smile.

Pazhuvettarayar’s face then shone with joy and pride. However wretched a man may be, who would not be elated to be called ‘Manmatha’—the god of love—by the woman he loves? Yet, he spoke as one who shunned self-importance:
“My beloved! It is indeed fitting to call you Rathi. But is it appropriate to call me ‘Manmathan’? You say so only out of your abundant love!” he said.

“My lord! To my eyes, you alone are Manmathan. For men, beauty lies in valor. The whole world proclaims that there is no warrior in this southern land to match your heroism. Next, what brings beauty to men of valor is compassion towards women. I myself am the witness to the compassion that dwells in you. Not knowing my town or lineage, you took in this poor, orphaned girl and gave her shelter. You showered upon me unparalleled love and support. Such as you, I will not keep waiting for long. The time for my vow and penance to end is drawing near…” she said.
“My jewel! Just tell me openly what vow, what penance it is! I will fulfill it as quickly as it can be done!” said the Lord of Pazhuvur.
“The descendants of this Sundara Chozhar, who thinks there is no Manmathan greater than himself, must not ascend the throne of Thanjai. The pride of that arrogant Kundavai must be humbled…”

“Nandini! You may consider both those tasks as already accomplished. Neither Aditya nor Arulmozhi Varman will gain the crown. All the leaders of this realm have agreed that the crown must go to Madurantakan…”
“‘All’ have agreed? Is that the truth?” Nandini pressed him sharply.
“Except for two or three, everyone else has agreed. Kodumbalur’s lord, Malayaman, and Parthibendran will never side with us. But they do not concern me…”
“Still, until the matter is fully accomplished, we must remain vigilant, must we not?”

“There is no doubt of that. I am taking every precaution. Only if others act foolishly will there be trouble. Even today, such a mishap has occurred. A youth who came from Kanchi deceived Kaalandhagan and met the Emperor, handing him a letter…”
“Ah! You never tire of praising your younger brother. Did I not say he lacks the necessary cleverness?”
“In this matter, he acted carelessly! They say that youth showed our palace signet ring!”
“Those who have been deceived always come up with some excuse like this! Did you not make any attempt to catch that youth who tricked you?”

“How could I not try? The hunt has already begun, both inside and outside the fort! They will surely catch him, one way or another. None of this will hinder our cause. Once the Emperor passes away, it is certain that Madurantakan will ascend the throne...”
“My lord! The time has come for me to reveal to you the true nature of my vow…”
“My dear! That is what I have been waiting to hear from you…”
“Madurantakan—that foolish boy—he is one who loses his wits at the sight of a woman. If he ascends the throne, my vow will not be fulfilled…”
“Then by what means will it be fulfilled? Tell me your wish! I am here to see it accomplished…”
“O King! When I was a child, a renowned astrologer read my horoscope. He said that until the age of eighteen, I would face many hardships…”
“What else did he say?”
“He said that after the age of eighteen, my fate would change. That I would attain a peerless, exalted position…”
“What he said is true! Tell me who that astrologer is! I will shower him with gold and honors.”
“My lord!”
“My beloved!”
“There is one more thing that astrologer foretold. Shall I tell you?”
“You must tell me! You must tell me everything!”

“He said that the man who takes my hand in marriage, who weds me, would one day wear the imperial crown and sit upon the throne of a great empire, where kings from fifty-six realms would come to bow before him and hail him as Emperor. Will you make that come true?”

The moment these words fell upon the ears of Pazhuvetarayar, Nandini, who sat before him, and the couch upon which she reclined, spun around. The Latha Mandapam spun. The pillars of that pavilion spun. The dark grove before him spun. The treetops, glimmering in the moonlight, spun. The stars in the sky spun. The mansions on either side spun. The whole world spun!

chapters.title: The Palace of Darkness
paragraphs: Let us now turn our attention to what became of the missing Vandiyathevan.

We saw him slip away and hide near the darkened palace, did we not? At first, he tried to listen in on what the sorcerer and Nandini were discussing. But not a word of their conversation reached his ears. Nor did he have much desire to eavesdrop and discover what they were saying. He now realized that, while speaking with Nandini, his senses had deserted him and a strange, intoxicating stupor had overtaken his mind. It would be best, he thought, if he could escape without encountering her again. Far more danger lurked in falling into the hands of this young queen than in being caught by the Pazhuvettaraiyars. In their presence, his wits worked sharply; the pain in his shoulder surged; his hand always rested on the dagger at his waist. He could rely on cunning or, if need be, on his blade. But before this enchantress, his mind grew clouded; his hand lost the strength to grasp his dagger. What fate might befall him if he went before her again? Enough—more than enough! She even keeps the company of a sorcerer! What sorcery might the two of them conjure together? How much hatred does she harbor toward Princess Kundavai? That hatred sparkles in her eyes like embers! Perhaps, on a sudden change of heart, she might even hand him over to the Pazhuvettaraiyars! Are not the fickle hearts and wavering minds of women renowned? Therefore, it would be best to escape without meeting her again. But how? He would have to find a way through the garden! He would have to climb the wall and jump down! What if those searching for him were waiting outside the wall?… Was there no other way? Where had the luck that had aided Vandiyathevan all these days gone? Think! Think! Use your wits! Use your eyes as well! Look all around you!

Here stands this palace, shrouded in darkness! Why is it so dark? What lies within? If he entered, where might another door lead him? Could he not go inside and have a look? Even if it did not help him now, it might prove useful another time. Who would know? But how to enter? What a massive, grand door! What a huge lock! My goodness! What strength! What solidity! Ah! What is this? There seems to be a small door within the main one! As soon as he placed his hand on it, the little door opened… How fortunate! If this is not luck, then what is? I must go inside and see!

Opening the small, cleverly concealed door within the large main entrance, Vandiyathevan slipped into the dark palace. The very first thought that struck him as he set foot inside was that even Nandini must not know he had entered this place. So, he quietly shut the little door behind him.

As soon as he closed it, the darkness within seemed to grow even denser, many times over. For the brief moment when the door was open, he had glimpsed a few massive pillars standing inside. Now, even those were invisible. Darkness—could such utter darkness even be imagined? Tch! Tch! It must be because he had come straight from the light; at first, it would always seem like this. In a short while, the heaviness of the darkness would lessen, and objects would begin to appear faintly to his eyes. How many times had he experienced this before, and yet, why this confusion at the sight of darkness now? Instead of simply standing still, perhaps he should try walking a little. He could feel his way forward with his hands. Where would that pillar he had just seen go, after all?

Stretching his arms out before him like a blind man, Vandiyathevan walked a short distance. As he had expected, his hand bumped into a pillar! Ah, what a massive pillar! A pillar of black stone! He could move around it and see where it led. Walking a little further, his hand found another pillar. Yet, still, nothing was visible to his eyes. Had he suddenly gone blind? What a mad thought! How could one go blind all at once? He decided to walk a little more. No more pillars met his hand! He felt as though he were descending into a hollow! Ah, here was a step! Thank goodness he hadn’t fallen! How long, and how far, could he go on like this, unable to see anything in this darkness?

For some reason, a sense of dread crept into Vandiyathevan’s heart. He did not have the courage to go further. He must turn back the way he had come! He must open the door and return to the Latha Mandapam! Better to meet Nandini again and act according to her plan, than to wander in this terrifying darkness. Whatever promise she might demand, he could give it for now, and later, when the time was right, he could reconsider! Thinking thus, Vandiyathevan turned back. But was he retracing his steps along the same path? How could he be sure? As he walked, nothing touched his hand! Where had those black stone pillars gone? Would he be unable to find the door again? Would he have to spend the whole night wandering in circles in this darkness? Oh God! What danger is this!

Ah! What is that sound? A sharp, rustling noise! Where is it coming from? It must be the sound of bats flapping their wings. In such darkness, it was only natural that bats would abound. No! That is not just the sound of bats’ wings! Footsteps! Someone is walking! Who is it that walks? Are they human?

Or… Vandiyathevan’s throat went dry! His tongue seemed stuck to his palate! Suddenly, it felt as if someone had struck him across the face. Summoning all his strength, Vandiyathevan threw a punch! His fist ached as though it had been severed. With his other hand, he reached out to feel—he realized, not only had he collided with a stone pillar in the darkness, but he had also struck it with his fist! If his hand had not throbbed so painfully, Vandiyathevan might have laughed at himself. Yet, the pain somewhat dispelled his fear—though not entirely. When he listened intently, the sound of footsteps grew louder and louder. At times, it seemed to recede; at others, it drew nearer!
Vandiyathevan stood rooted to the spot, listening keenly. At the same moment, his eyes strained toward the direction from which the sound came.

Ah! Light! There—a light! Gradually, it grew brighter and closer! Along with the light, there was smoke. Someone was approaching with a torch. Was it Nandini herself, coming in search of him? If so, that would be good. But what if it was someone else? In any case, it would be best to hide and observe for a while. There was no shortage of places to conceal himself here! The distant torch flame revealed that this was a vast hall. Massive pillars stood within. On those pillars, terrifying forms of demons were carved. A staircase rose from below, curving and turning as it ascended. Vandiyathevan realized that the torchlight was coming from the base of that staircase. Therefore, it could not be Nandini who was approaching. Was the “dungeon” he had heard about located beneath this dark palace? Perhaps someone was coming from there? Vandiyathevan had heard many fearful tales about the terrors of the dungeon, and the thought made sweat bead on every hair of his body. In the next instant, he slipped behind a large pillar. The ever-courageous Vandiyathevan’s arms and legs now trembled uncontrollably with fear!

Three figures ascended the staircase. All three were men. One held a torch. Another carried a spear. The one in the middle held nothing in his hands. As their faces became visible in the torchlight, Vandiyathevan’s fear vanished completely. In its place, a wonder many times greater arose. The man leading them was none other than his dear friend, Kandanmaran! The figure in the middle, at first, filled Vandiyathevan with a strange illusion.
