For a moment, he thought it was Nandini, the young queen of Pazhuvoor, herself. But in the next instant, the illusion faded. The person approaching was a man. In the Kadambur Sambuvarayar palace... He realized that the prince he had glimpsed briefly was none other than Madhuranthaka Devar.
Thirdly, the man who had come holding the torch was someone Vallavarayan had never seen before. He must be a guard of the entrance, or perhaps a servant.

Vandiyathevan’s mind worked at lightning speed. The mystery of why they were ascending that underground passage was soon clear to him. The younger Pazhuvoor queen had arrived on the very first day in her palanquin. The elder Pazhuvettaraiyar had returned to the Thanjai fort that very night. Both had come openly through the main gate. But Madhuranthaka Devar—no one must know when he left, nor when he returned. For that, they were using this secret tunnel. This, it seemed, was the very secret of this darkened palace! After Kandhamaaran had left him on the banks of the Kollidam, he must have joined the elder Pazhuvettaraiyar somewhere else. The Pazhuvettaraiyar was now using him for this clandestine task.

He had sent him as a companion to escort Madhuranthaka Devar through the tunnel. Ah! Now that he thought of it, he remembered: “I too have some business in Thanjavur. If I come there, I’ll see you!”—hadn’t Kandhamaaran said so?… Now, if he were to suddenly appear before Kandhamaaran here, what would happen?… The moment this thought arose, Vallavarayan dismissed it. If he encountered Kandhamaaran at this time, he might be forced to kill him because of the vow Kandhamaaran had taken—or else, he himself might be killed by Kandhamaaran. Why bring such a moral dilemma upon himself?

By then, the three had already climbed the stairs and gone above. The light began to fade as they moved away. For a moment, Vandiyathevan considered following them, but he immediately changed his mind. Surely, they were heading to the palace of the commander of the fort, Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar. What was the use in going there? It would be like escaping from a lion’s den only to offer up his head again! There was no point in returning to the Latha Mandapam where Nandini had been either. Perhaps the elder Pazhuvettaraiyar had already arrived there. That, too, would be dangerous. What else could he do?… Why not try descending the stairs through this passage and see where it led? With this thought, our young warrior began to descend the steps of the secret tunnel.

chapters.title: The Treasury Hall
paragraphs: In the dark tunnel, Vandiyathevan planted his foot firmly, walking carefully so as not to fall. The steps descended for a short distance. Then the path leveled out. Again, there were steps. Once more, a level floor. He stretched out both hands to feel for the walls, but his fingers touched nothing. So, this tunnel must be quite wide. After proceeding a little further, the steps now ascended. It seemed to curve as well. Oh, how much farther must I stumble and grope in this pitch darkness?

Ah! What is this? The darkness is lessening! A faint, very dim light is appearing! Where does this pale light come from? Is it the moonlight filtering through some opening in the roof? Or light entering through some lattice in the walls? Or is it the glow from a hidden lamp placed somewhere?
No, no! What a wonder is this? Is the scene unfolding before my eyes real, or is it an illusion conjured by a confused mind?

It was a vast hall. A treasury chamber carved out of solid stone. That is why the ceiling above was so low and flat, threatening to strike his head. The dim, silvery light filling that treasury was not coming from outside; neither through the roof nor through any lattice. Here and there, in clusters and in scattered heaps, the light shimmered across the hall. Ah! What are these objects that glimmer with such moonlight? In one corner, there were jeweled crowns—crowns encrusted with pearls, rubies, and diamonds. In another place, necklaces—strings of pearls, garlands of navaratna gems. And there, in that wide-mouthed casket—what is that? My God! All those are white pearls, like unopened jasmine buds! Round, plump, heavy pearls! And in that vessel, gold coins gleaming like the bright yellow sun. Here, stacked in heaps, were gold ingots. This must be the treasury chamber of the Thanjavur palace!
Is it any wonder that, adjoining the mansion of the Chief Pazhuvettaraiyar, there should be this secret, dark palace and within it, this treasury chamber?

Oh, what fortune! Have I truly entered the treasury hall? Surely, Lady Luck and the goddess of destiny themselves must have brought me here! What a marvelous, rare secret I have discovered—without any effort of my own! How to use this knowledge? Let that come later; for now, I feel no desire to leave this place! I feel as if I could wander here forever! If I stayed here, would hunger and thirst... I do not know! Sleep does not come near me, not even close! All the rewards of the victories won by the brave armies of Chola Nadu over the past hundred years are gathered here. The very navanidhi—the nine treasures—they speak of, all of it is here! The wealth stored here would put Kubera’s own treasury to shame. Why should I leave this behind and go elsewhere?

Vandiyathevan circled around the moonlit chamber. He touched the jeweled crowns lying in one corner. In another place, he picked up the radiant gem-studded necklaces and examined them in his hands. Putting those down, he moved to another side and plunged his hands into a bronze vessel filled with pearls, letting them flow through his fingers. In yet another vessel, he scooped up handfuls of gold coins and let them pour down in a shining cascade. In one corner, he noticed something spread across the floor, glittering with a strange brilliance. He went over to investigate. At first, he could not tell what it was; then, bending down and looking closely, he realized with a start—Oh God! It was a skeleton! The bones of a human body that, once upon a time, had flesh and blood, skin and hair, nose and face, eyes and ears!
Ah! The skeleton is moving! It is rising up, coming to life! It rattles just like the gold coins! It seems to be rising to deliver some message to me...

Every hair on Vallavarayan’s body stood on end. He thought he had gone mad. Nonsense! The skeleton had not risen! From within it, a large rat came scurrying out! It ran over his foot and darted away! Yes; now that he looked again, the skeleton still lay on the ground. But it was true that it was sending him a message. “Run away! Do not linger here! I too was once a man with flesh and blood like you. I came here and was trapped. Here I died and perished! Now I lie as a skeleton! Run away!”—thus it was warning him. If we escape from here at once, we may survive. Otherwise, the same fate that befell that man will be ours.

Vandiyathevan resolved to leave that moonlit chamber. But he could not find the way out. He could not discover the path by which he had entered. Wherever he went along the edge of the chamber, the demon called darkness opened its mouth wide. Looking down, it seemed like a bottomless abyss. The staircase he had climbed must be somewhere, but he could not find it. Vandiyathevan searched and searched, wandering about. As he wandered, he saw, at one spot along the wall, a heap of gold coins. Over that heap, something seemed to be woven like a net. Looking closely, he realized that a spider had spun its web over the pile. The spider’s web stirred his thoughts.

The elders have compared the desires for land, women, and gold to a spider’s web. The spider sits in wait, its web spread wide. From somewhere, a fly comes buzzing and gets caught in it. Then, little by little, the spider draws the fly in and devours it. These three desires are just the same. Man, losing his way, stumbles into these webs of desire and is ensnared; after that, there is no return! The nature of these three desires—land, women, and gold—we have experienced all in a single day. Nandini, the young queen of Pazhuvoor, tried to entrap us in her web. She tempted us with the desire for land, the hope of regaining the ancient Vanar dynasty’s kingdom. And finally, here, this terrible demon of greed for gold seeks to swallow us whole. We escaped the first two; now we must escape this third danger as well.

For what do we need all this trouble? Why do we need kingdoms? Why do we need wealth? Why do we need the company of women? The vast earth, which stretches beneath the sharp sky, is our palace! “Every town is our town; all people are our kin,” so have the ancient Tamil elders declared! Every place is our own. All people are our relatives. We must travel from town to town; delight in the rivers that swell with fresh floods, in the trees that burst forth with new leaves, in the many-colored birds, in the great sages, in the peacocks, in the mountains and their peaks, in the sky, the clouds, the sea, and the waves that rise upon the sea. We must eat wherever food is found for our hunger; sleep wherever sleep overtakes us! Ah! Is this not the true life of bliss? Why should we abandon such a simple, easily attainable life of joy and instead take up a life filled with troubles, intrigues, desires, and dangers? If only I could somehow get out of this treasury room now; then, I must leave this dark palace and the Thanjavur fort behind. Never again must I get caught in such troubles…

Ah! The sound of the door opening and closing!… Again, the sound of footsteps!… It seems there is no end to the wonders of this night! There is no limit to the marvels! No bounds to the terrors! This time, the footsteps were heard from a great distance. It seemed as if they were coming from both sides. Vandiyathevan listened intently, giving his full attention. He peered into the darkness that surrounded the treasury room, as if trying to pierce it with his gaze. After a while, just as he expected, he witnessed a rare sight.

It was like watching a play on stage from a seat far away—the scene on the stage appearing distant and indistinct. That was how the sight appeared to Vandiyathevan at that moment. The place where it happened was at a higher elevation than where he was, and seemed far away. From one side of the stage, a torch appeared—
They came. From another direction, pushing aside the heavy curtain, another torch approached.

Both torches drew nearer and nearer. In the light of one torch, two tall, dark figures became visible. In the glow of the other, two more figures appeared. Among these, one was tall and imposing; the other, a little shorter and slender in form. Both pairs of figures advanced toward each other. Vandiyathevan, his eyes wide with tension, watched intently, trying to discern who these figures were.

The two figures approaching from the left were Kandanmaran and the guard, who had escorted Madurantaka Thevar. The figures coming from the right were Periya Pazhuvettarayar and his young queen, Nandini Devi.
What would happen when these two groups met? Would something disastrous occur? Or would they simply step aside for each other and pass by cautiously?...
In that moment of suspense, Vandiyathevan even held his breath, watching with utmost attention.

The two groups met. From the way they hesitated and faltered, it seemed clear that the encounter had brought surprise and shock to both parties. Yet, nothing untoward happened. Pazhuvettarayar asked something of Kandanmaran. Kandanmaran replied. The question and answer did not reach Vandiyathevan’s ears. Then, Pazhuvettarayar gestured with his hand, pointing to the steps leading down to the underground passage. Kandanmaran bowed respectfully to him, then descended the steps. The guard who had come with the torch looked at Pazhuvettarayar, who made another sign. Without a word, the guard covered his mouth with one hand and bowed, then followed Kandanmaran down the steps.
Pazhuvettarayar and his young queen turned and walked to the left.

All these events, resembling a play of shadows and puppets, transpired within a few moments. Vandiyathevan noticed that everything had happened near the steps leading down to the underground passage. Ah! How fortunate that I did not linger anywhere along the way, but kept circling about in this treasure chamber! If I had been caught between those two groups, what would have become of me? Somehow, I have escaped so far. Now, how to find a way out? There is no doubt that Kandanmaran, having brought Madurantaka Thevar, is now returning through the underground passage. I must have strayed a little from that path and ended up in this treasure chamber. If I follow the way Kandanmaran goes now, I should be able to find the exit. Then, somehow, I must devise a plan.

One could escape by force if necessary. If it came to that, he could seek help from Kandhamaaran. If not, he could deal with both Kandhamaaran and the guard, and then make his escape. Therefore, for now, he could continue following Kandhamaaran.

At first, the torchlight seemed to be approaching the moon chamber. Vandiyathevan held his breath and stood still. Then, the light appeared to move away. In that brief moment, Vandiyathevan looked all around. He identified which staircase led into the moon chamber. He descended by that way, then climbed back up again. Without letting the torchlight out of his sight, yet not drawing too close, he walked softly, placing his feet carefully so that no sound would be heard. In that winding, twisting, turning, ascending, and descending tunnel, how impossible it would have been to find one’s way in the darkness unaided! Long live Kandhamaaran! What reward could he ever give for the help Kandhamaaran was now unknowingly rendering him?
Vandiyathevan never imagined that an opportunity to repay that favor would come so soon!

The tunnel had come to an end. Before him stood a great wall. No one would have guessed there was a door or entrance there. Yet, there must be! Surely, a secret passage must have a hidden door at its end.

The guard shifted the torch from his right hand to his left. With his right hand, he pressed a spot on the wall and did something—he twisted it, as one would turn a screw. A thin crack appeared in the wall, like a faint line. The crack widened, growing larger and larger, until it was wide enough for a person to pass through. The guard pointed to it with one hand. Kandhamaaran said something to him, then placed one foot into the opening in the wall. His other foot was still in the tunnel. At that moment, his entire back was exposed!

Ah! What is this? What is the guard doing? He is drawing a sharp, curved dagger from his waist! My God! He has plunged it deep into Kandhamaaran’s back! The wretch! The villain who would stab a man from behind!
Vandiyathevan sprang from his hiding place. He leapt forward in a single bound! Hearing the sound, the guard turned. The torchlight fell upon Vandiyathevan’s face, ablaze with fury.

Vandiyathevan followed the maidservant through the winding corridors of the palace. The night was deep and silent; the moonlight streamed through the latticed windows, casting intricate patterns on the marble floors. The only sound was the soft tinkling of the anklets worn by the servant, echoing faintly in the stillness.

They passed through several doors and finally reached a secluded chamber. The maid paused, turned, and gestured for Vandiyathevan to wait. She entered the room, leaving him standing outside, his heart pounding with anticipation and curiosity.

After a few moments, the maid returned and beckoned him inside. Vandiyathevan stepped into the chamber, his eyes quickly adjusting to the dim light. The room was bathed in a gentle silver glow from the moon, which filtered in through a high window. The air was cool and fragrant with the scent of jasmine.

At the far end of the chamber, seated on a low couch, was Princess Kundavai. She was dressed in simple yet elegant attire, her face radiant in the moonlight, her eyes shining with intelligence and resolve. For a moment, Vandiyathevan stood transfixed, unable to speak.
Kundavai broke the silence. “Vandiyatheva, you have come safely. I am glad.”
Vandiyathevan bowed respectfully. “Princess, your command brought me here. Even if a thousand dangers awaited, I would not have hesitated.”
A faint smile played on Kundavai’s lips. “I have heard much about your courage and wit. But tonight, I need your loyalty and discretion more than your bravery.”
“Princess, my life is at your service,” Vandiyathevan replied earnestly.
Kundavai gestured for him to be seated. “Sit down. There is much to discuss, and little time.”
Vandiyathevan obeyed, his mind racing with questions. What urgent matter could have prompted the princess to summon him at this hour, in such secrecy?

Kundavai’s gaze was steady. “You have seen with your own eyes the dangers that surround our family and the empire. Treachery lurks in every shadow. Even within these palace walls, we cannot be certain whom to trust.”
Vandiyathevan nodded. “I have witnessed it, Princess. The conspirators are bold and cunning.”
Kundavai leaned forward, her voice low. “You must carry a message for me. It is of utmost importance. It must reach my brother Arulmozhi Varman without delay.”
Vandiyathevan’s heart leapt at the mention of the prince’s name. “I will deliver it, Princess, even if it costs me my life.”
Kundavai’s eyes softened. “I do not wish for you to lose your life, Vandiyatheva. But I know you will not fail me. Listen carefully…”

She began to speak, her words measured and precise, outlining the message and the dangers that lay ahead. Vandiyathevan listened intently, committing every word to memory, determined to fulfill the trust placed in him by the noble princess.

The moonlight streamed in, illuminating the two figures—one a princess burdened with the fate of an empire, the other a brave messenger ready to risk everything for her cause. Outside, the silent palace slumbered, oblivious to the secrets being woven in the moonlit chamber.

chapters.title: Is There Beauty in Friendship?
paragraphs: Vandiyathevan’s first thought was that, somehow, he must save Kandhamaaran. But if he tried to save him first, he knew the same fate would befall him as well. Therefore, he must first subdue this cruel guard. With that resolve, he sprang forward and wrapped one arm tightly around the guard’s neck. With his other hand, he struck the lamp from the guard’s grasp. The lamp fell to the ground. Its flame shrank, smoke billowing up and thickening the darkness. Tightening his grip around the guard’s neck with all his strength, Vandiyathevan forced him down. The guard’s head struck the wall of the tunnel and he collapsed to the floor. Vandiyathevan picked up the lamp and bent over him. The guard lay as if dead. Still, acting with caution, Vandiyathevan took the man’s waistband and tied both his hands together, binding him securely.

All this he accomplished in a matter of seconds, then ran to Kandhamaaran. He saw him lying half inside the tunnel and half outside, the knife still embedded in his back. His spear lay fallen beside him. Vandiyathevan hurried outside, lifted Kandhamaaran onto his shoulder, and dragged him out; he also picked up the spear. At that moment, the door closed by itself. The wall, concealing its great secret, stood tall and silent in the darkness. Vandiyathevan realized that he had come out of the fort and into the open air, for the strong wind that struck him was no longer confined within stone.

Dense trees and the fort’s battlements hid the moon, so its light was faint and ghostly. Hoisting Kandhamaaran onto his shoulder, Vandiyathevan took up the spear in one hand and stepped forward. Suddenly, the earth crumbled beneath him and he felt himself slipping straight down. He quickly planted the spear into the ground and, with great effort, managed to steady himself. Looking down, he saw, in the shadows cast by the trees and the fort wall, the glimmer of flowing water. He could just make out the swift current, swirling and eddying as it rushed by. What luck! One wrong step and death would have been certain. The gods had saved him! That wretched, murderous guard—but what use was there in blaming him? He had only carried out his master’s orders! Surely, the plan had been to stab him at the threshold and then push him into the floodwaters below. If his foot had slipped just a little more, both he and Kandhamaaran would have fallen into the river’s depths. Even if he had somehow survived, Kandhamaaran’s fate would have been sealed!

At one spot, Vandiyathevan knew, the wall of Thanjai fort ran very close to the Vadavaru river. This must be the Vadavaru, he thought. Though there was not much floodwater in the Vadavaru at that time, there could still be a deep pit at the edge of the fort wall. Who could say? Vandiyathevan thrust his spear into the water to test its depth. The entire length of the spear sank beneath the surface, yet it did not touch the bottom! Ah! What cruel villains these are!… But this was not the time to dwell on such thoughts. He needed to find a way to escape himself and save Kandanmaran as well.

Staying close to the edge of the flood’s current, Vandiyathevan pressed his feet firmly, careful not to slip, and walked on. On his shoulder was Kandanmaran, and in his hand, his spear. Kandanmaran groaned and gasped two or three times; these sounds from his friend gave Vandiyathevan courage and determination. After proceeding thus for some distance, the fort wall veered away, and beyond it, a forest appeared along the riverbank. The ground below was thick with thorns, making each step painful and difficult.

Ah! What was this? A tree had fallen across the river! It must have been a tall, sturdy tree. The flood must have torn it up by the roots! Half of it lay stretched into the river. Clambering onto it, Vandiyathevan stumbled and staggered along. The tree swayed in the rush of the floodwaters; its branches and leaves thrashed and writhed in the current. The wind, too, was blowing with relentless force. When he reached the tip of the tree, he tested the depth with his spear. Fortunate indeed! Murugan had protected him. There was not much of a hollow here! Vandiyathevan climbed down from the tree into the river and crossed over. Here and there, he managed the dips and rises of the riverbed as best he could. He fought against the force of the flood and the fury of the wind with the strength of his own resolve. At times, his body shivered uncontrollably.

Kandanmaran, slung over his shoulder, sometimes threatened to slip and fall. Escaping all these dangers, Vandiyathevan finally reached the opposite bank. For a short distance, soaked to the waist, he staggered along, bearing the heavy, broad-shouldered body of Kandanmaran. Then, finding a spot beneath the shade of a tree where there was a little clearing, he gently laid Kandanmaran down. First, he wanted to tend to his own exhaustion. At the same time, he wished to ascertain whether there was still life in Kandanmaran’s body. What use was it to carry a lifeless corpse? Better, as the guard had suggested, to have left it in the floodwaters. No! No! There was life—he could feel the heavy breathing, the pulse racing, the chest heaving. What could he do now? Should he draw the knife from his back? If he did, blood would spurt out in torrents. That would surely mean death. The wound needed immediate treatment and bandaging. But this was not something he could do alone. Whom could he seek for help?… The memory of Sendhan Amudhan came to him. His garden and house were on the banks of the Vadavaru… It is here. It must be somewhere nearby. If only I can somehow carry Kandhamaaran to Sendhan Amudhan’s house, there will be a way for him to survive. Let me try, at least.
When Vandiyathevan tried once more to lift Kandhamaaran, he was surprised and delighted to see the man’s eyes open.
“Kandhamaaran! Do you know who I am?” he asked.

“I know, I know very well. You are Vallavaraiyan! How could I not recognize such a wonderful friend as you? How could I ever forget? Are you not the trusted companion who stabs from behind?” said Kandhamaaran.
These last words struck Vallavaraiyan like a lash.
“Alas! Was it I who stabbed you from behind…?” he began, but then something struck his memory and he stopped abruptly.

“You did not stab me… Your dagger merely brushed my back… Oh, you wretch! Was it not for your sake that I hurried through this underground passage? I rushed to reach you before the men of Pazhuvettaraiyar could catch you. I came running to protect you from any harm. I found you and swore to bring you safely to the guards of Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar’s fort. I came with the intention of doing you good, and yet you have betrayed me thus? Is this the beauty of friendship? How many times have we sworn, hand in hand, to help each other? You have let all that blow away like the wind! I even intended to warn you about a great change about to take place in the Chola kingdom! Alas! Whom can one trust in this world now?” So saying, Kandhamaaran closed his eyes again. Speaking so much and with such passion must have made him faint once more.

“Are there any humans left to trust? Or should one trust the Pazhuvettaraiyars?” muttered Vandiyathevan. Yet, tears welled up in his eyes. He thought it was just as well that he had not spoken what he intended to say.

Once more, he hoisted Kandhamaaran’s body onto his shoulder and began to walk. The fragrance of night-blooming flowers wafted thickly through the air. His guess that Sendhan Amudhan’s house must be nearby was not in vain. Soon, he reached the garden—but what a garden! How different it looked today from the first day he had seen it! At that moment, the garden resembled the Ashoka grove destroyed by Hanuman, or the Madhuvan ravaged by the vanaras. Ah! In search of him—

It seemed that the men of Pazhuvetarayar had been here. Those who came must have committed these outrages before they left! Alas! How much toil must Sendhan Amudhan and his dear mother have endured to nurture this garden? All of it has now been laid to waste!

His sympathy for the ruined garden vanished in an instant. The memory of his own perilous situation returned. What if the spies and the fortress guards were still lurking nearby?… He would have to deal with them if they appeared. Fortunately, there—his horse was still tied to the same tree!… Or perhaps they had left it there deliberately to trap him? Whatever the case, what could he do? He must entrust this man to the good people in this hut and then mount his horse and make his escape. The horse that leaves here must not stop until it reaches Pazhaiyarai.

Step by cautious step, he walked towards the hut’s entrance. He roused Sendhan Amudhan, who was lying on the verandah, with a gentle shake. As Amudhan awoke with a start, he quickly covered his mouth. Then, in a soft voice, he said:
“Brother! You must help me. I am caught in great trouble. This is my dear friend—Kandhamaaran, son of Kadambur Sambuvarayar. On my way here, someone stabbed him in the back. I brought him with me.”
“Wretches! They stabbed him in the back! What sort of vile cowards are these!” exclaimed Amudhan.

Then he continued, “I will look after him as best I can. Since evening, groups of soldiers have come searching for you and have left only after turning the garden to ruin. Let it be, as long as you escape safely. Luckily, they left your horse untouched. Mount it and leave at once!”
“That is my intention. But I must do something to save his life!”
“Do not worry about that. My mother is skilled in such matters. She knows well how to treat wounds!” So saying, Sendhan Amudhan lightly knocked twice on the door of the hut.
At once, the door opened. Sendhan Amudhan’s mother stood on the threshold.
Together, they lifted Kandanmaran and carried him inside, laying him down in the hall.

In the light of the hand-lamp, Sendhan Amudhan communicated with his mother through gestures. She seemed to understand him well. She looked closely at Kandanmaran, noticed the knife embedded in his back, and then went inside to fetch some betel leaves and an old piece of cloth. She looked up at both of them.
Sendhan Amudhan held Kandanmaran tightly. Vallavaraiyan Vandiyathevan, summoning all his strength, pulled out the knife that had been lodged in Kandanmaran’s back for so long.
Blood gushed out in a crimson stream. In his unconscious state, Kandanmaran let out a cry of pain.
Vandiyathevan quickly covered his mouth.
Sendhan Amudhan pressed down hard on the wound.
Amudhan’s mother placed the betel leaves on the wound and bound it with the old cloth.
Kandanmaran groaned again, struggling for breath.
From a distance, the hurried, pounding footsteps of people running could be heard.
“Go! Go! Quickly!” urged Amudhan.
Vandiyathevan picked up the blood-stained knife and spear. He started to leave, then hesitated and stood still.
“Brother! Do you trust me?” he asked.
“I trust in God. I have affection for you. Why do you ask?”

“I need your help. I do not know the way around here very well. I must reach Pazhaiyarai urgently. I have an important message to deliver to Princess Kundavai. Will you come and guide me for a short distance?”

At once, Sendhan Amudhan made some more gestures to his mother. She did not seem particularly surprised by any of this. She signaled for him to go and return safely, and indicated that she would take care of the wounded man.
Sendhan and Devan set out. Devan mounted his horse first, followed by Sendhan.
Vandiyathevan guided his horse slowly, so that its hoofbeats would not be heard. After traveling a short distance, he gave it a slap. The horse sprang forward and galloped away at full speed.
At that very moment, five or six soldiers arrived at the hut. They knocked on the door with a loud, insistent thudding.
Amudan’s mother opened the door and stood on the threshold.
“We heard some commotion here, didn’t we? What was that?” demanded one of the soldiers.
Amudan’s mother mumbled something incoherently.
“What’s the use of talking to this deaf-mute woman? Let’s go inside and see for ourselves!” said another.
“She’s standing here, blocking our way!”
“Where did that flower-selling boy go?”
“Push the mute aside and get inside, fellows!”

Senthan Amudan’s mother began to shout in her mute’s tongue even more loudly. When one of the soldiers tried to push her aside, she pushed him back and tried to bolt the door. Four or five of them grabbed the door and forced it open, making it impossible for her to close it.
With a louder wail of grief, Amudan’s mother suddenly let go of the door. Two or three of the men tumbled inside, rolling on the floor. The others trampled over them and burst into the hut.
“There’s someone here!” shouted one of them.
“Has he been caught?” asked another.
“He’s trying to escape! Grab him and tie him up!” yelled a third.
The mute woman wailed even louder.
“There’s blood everywhere!” one of them cried out.
The mute woman seized the oil lamp, pointed to the man lying on the floor, and cried, “Peh! Peh! Peh!”
“Hey! This looks like someone else altogether!”
“Peh! Peh!”
“Is this the same man who came here yesterday?”
“Pei! Pei!” (No! No!)
“Where is your son?”
“Pei! Pei!”
“Mute wretch! Be quiet for a moment! Hey! Look at this man carefully! Does anyone recognize him?”
“That’s not him!”
“It is him!”
“Absolutely not!”
“Pei! Pei!”
“Whoever he is, he’s a stranger! Lift him up! Let’s take him away!”
“Pei! Pei! Pei! Pei!” Amudhan’s mother wailed incessantly.
“Damn you! Be quiet!”
Four men together lifted Kandhamaaran.
“Pei! Pei! Pei! Pei!” Amudhan’s mother cried out without pause.
“Hey! I hear the sound of horses approaching!”
“Half of you carry him! The rest, run and see!”
“Everyone run! He won’t be able to go anywhere!”
They dropped Kandhamaaran to the ground and all of them ran.
“Pei! Pei! Pei! Pei!” Amudhan’s mother’s lament followed after them.

chapters.title: Pazhayarai
paragraphs: Before Vandiyathevan, having endured many hardships and escaped countless dangers, arrives at the city of Pazhayarai, let us invite our readers to accompany us on a visit to that ancient capital.

Let us stand on the southern bank of the Arisil River and gaze upon the city. Ah! Is this merely a city? Does it not gleam like an ornament hanging upon the beautiful forehead of Mother Tamil herself? Does it not shine like a forehead jewel set with green emeralds, red rubies, and blue sapphires?

Rivers, streams, tanks, and fields brim with fresh, sparkling water. In them bloom flowers of every hue. Coconut and punnai trees spread their cool, verdant shade. Amidst all this, here and there, the golden domes of towering mansions and the gilded stupas atop temple gopurams flash in the sunlight.

Oh, what a marvel! Within this great city of Pazhayarai, how many smaller towns nestle? Nandhipura Vinnagaram, Thiruchathimuttam, Pattiiswaram, Arichandrapuram, and their temples—all these are encompassed within Pazhayarai, the capital of the Cholas. In each of the four directions of Pazhayarai stand four Shiva temples: Vadathali, Keezhthali, Metrali, and Then-thali. The Aryapadai quarters, Pudupadai quarters, Manapadai quarters, and Pampapadai quarters—four neighborhoods where the warrior clans dwell—are also found here.

And at the very heart of all this stands the Chola Palace. But is it a single palace? Before the time of Vijayalaya Chola, it was but one mansion. Later, for each prince and princess, new palaces were built adjoining the old Chola palace. To behold this spectacle, a thousand eyes would not suffice; to describe it, the imagination of ten thousand poets would not be enough.
Two hundred years later, the great Sekkizhar would sing: “On streets where chariots thronged, shining with jewels, Glorious among the cities of the world—Pazhayarai.”

If he thus described it, imagine how splendid, how vibrant this city must have been in the days of Sundara Chola! Even so, when we first set foot in this ancient capital, we could not behold it in all its former grandeur and festive splendor.
We were not granted the fortune to witness the city in the days when Sundara Chola Chakravarthi sat enthroned in the Chola palace here, governing his vast empire.

After the Emperor fell ill and moved to the great city of Thanjavur, the stream of petty kings, royal envoys, chief ministers, and commanders who once came here from foreign lands ceased altogether. The throngs of attendants and retinues who customarily accompanied them dwindled as well.

Of the brave warriors who once filled the four military quarters, half now upheld the valor of the Tamils on the battlefields of Eelam. Among the rest, some were stationed on the northern frontiers, while others were in Madurai.
Thus, in the military quarters, one now saw mostly the elderly, women, and children.
The Velakkara soldiers who had lived in Mazhavarpaadi had departed with their families to Thanjai, leaving that part of the city deserted, its houses locked and forlorn.
The ministers, feudatories, and officials who managed the affairs of the state had all moved with their families to Thanjavur.

Yet, despite all this, the streets of Pazhaiyarai had not lost their crowds and their bustle. Now, the thoroughfares teemed mostly with temple architects, sculptors, Saivite devotees, Devaram chanters, palace servants, temple workers, and pilgrims who had come from distant towns to worship at the shrines and witness the temple festivals.

Today, the city seemed to be in the midst of some grand festival. Men, women, boys, and girls, all dressed in beautiful garments and ornaments, strolled through the streets. At every street corner, groups of people gathered. In the midst of these crowds, performers in various costumes sang and danced! Let us look a little closer. Ah! Are they not dressed as Krishna and the cowherds? In the center of one group, a Krishna stands holding aloft a mountain, while Indra, the king of the gods, comes and bows before him! In another group, Brahma, with his four faces, approaches Krishna... He bows down in worship! Ah! Now I understand. Today is Srijayanthi—the birthday of Kannan. That is the festival the people are celebrating with such exuberance. Here and there, the festival of breaking the hanging pot is taking place. They are pouring and splashing turmeric water everywhere.
Around the great temple of Perumal at Nandhipura Vinnagaram, these festival celebrations are being conducted with particular fervor. But what is this?
“Seen, seen, seen! I have seen the one dear to my eyes!”

Who is singing thus? That voice sounds familiar! Look, our old friend Azhwarkkadiyan Nambi stands revealed before us! He stands there singing. A crowd is gathering around him. Some listen with devotion and reverence. Others begin to clap in rhythm. We fear whose head might suffer damage from Azhwarkkadiyan’s staff.

At the entrance of the Vinnagara temple, there is a commotion. The chariots and palanquins that were parked by the roadside are approaching the temple gate. From within the temple, some noble ladies are coming out. These women must surely be of high birth.
Yes, yes! They are the queens and princesses who dwell in the palaces of Pazhaiyarai.

First among all comes Sembiyan Maadevi, whom the entire land reveres as the ‘Periya Piratti’. She is the daughter of the Malavarayar clan; the chief queen of Kandaradithar, the lord of divine wisdom. Though she appears in the garb of an aged widow, what radiance shines forth from her face! Behind her comes Queen Kalyani, the daughter of the Vaidhumba royal line, wife of Arinjaya Chozhar. Ah! How can one describe her beauty! Even in this advanced age, her face glows with such freshness! What must she have been like in her youth? Is it any wonder that her son, Sundara Chozhar, is famed for his handsome bearing?
Following her comes Paranthakan Devi, daughter of the Cheraman, another wife of Sundara Chozhar.
Further behind, like divine maidens descended straight from the heavens, come Princess Kundavai, Vanathi, and the other royal women we saw on the banks of the Arisil river.

From the time of Vijayalaya, the Chola dynasty had worshipped Shiva and Durga as their family deities. Yet, they bore no hatred towards Thirumal or the other faiths. It seemed that, on account of today being Krishna’s birthday, they had come to the Perumal temple.

As Periyapirati Sembiyan Maadevi was about to ascend her palanquin, the song of Azhwarkkadiyan reached her ears. It appeared that Azhwarkkadiyan had sung in a loud voice precisely for this reason. Sembiyan Maadevi had him summoned to her side.
Azhwarkkadiyan came and stood before her with humility and restraint.
“Thirumalai! We have not seen you these past few days. Have you been on pilgrimage?” she asked.
“Yes, Mother! I have been on pilgrimage. I visited many holy places—Tirupati, Kanchi, Veeranarayana Puram, and others. In every place I saw and heard many marvels!”
“Come to the palace tomorrow and tell us the wonders you saw and heard on your journey!”
“No, Amma! I must depart again tonight.”
“In that case, come this evening before you leave!”
“I shall come, Mother! Your wish is my good fortune!”
The palanquins and chariots all set out, hastening towards the palace.
Kundavai Piratti pointed out Azhwarkkadiyan and said something, at which the other young princesses laughed with a tinkling “kaleer.”

To understand the cause of their laughter, Azhwarkkadiyan glanced in that direction. Kundavai Piratti’s eyes spoke to him in a secret language. Azhwarkkadiyan bowed his head, signaling that he had understood her message.

Among the Chola palaces, the residence of Sembiyan Maadevi stood as the central jewel. In its audience hall, upon a throne wrought of gold and inlaid with nine precious gems, that venerable matriarch sat enthroned. Descended from a line of supreme devotees like Karaikkal Ammaiyar and Thilakavathiyar, that noblewoman wore only a white silk garment, adorned herself with sacred ash and a rudraksha garland, and bore no other ornaments. Amidst immeasurable wealth—surrounded by the eight treasures—she proved that one could live a life of renunciation even in the midst of abundance. Though she wore neither a jeweled crown nor other adornments upon her head, her majestic bearing and self-effulgent presence... Her very face revealed that she was born into royal lineage and had entered into the royal household as a queen. It is no wonder, then, that all the members of the Chola royal family, without exception, revered this great matriarch as a deity, praised and celebrated her, and conducted themselves without ever uttering a word against her wishes.

Yet, now, a blemish had appeared upon such unwavering reverence and devotion. The son of that queen, Prince Madurantaka, had, against his mother’s wishes and in defiance of her command, married into the clan of the Pazhuvettaraiyars. Moreover, rumors had begun to spread that he harbored aspirations for the Chola throne—news that, when it reached the ears of Sembiyan Maadevi, caused her no small measure of distress.

It was customary for the palace courtyard and the audience hall of Sembiyan Maadevi to be ever filled with gatherings of sculptors and groups of devotional singers, their voices resounding in praise. From distant lands, devotees of Shiva and Tamil poets would often come to receive her patronage and depart with gifts. The number of priests bringing offerings from Shiva’s worship was ever on the rise.

That day, sculptors and devotees had come from Thirumudukunram (Virudhachalam), Thengurangaduthurai, Thirumazhapadi, and other towns, seeking the queen’s assistance for the renovation of stonework in their temples. They had brought with them drawings and miniature models to show how and where they intended to build the temples in their respective villages.
After agreeing to provide assistance for the renovation of the first two temples, the elder princess asked, “Mazhapadi? Which Mazhapadi is this?”
“It is the very Mazhapadi where the great lord, whom Sundaramurthi Swamigal called by voice and received a song from, resides!” answered the man from that town.
“What is that incident?” asked the daughter of the Mazhavar chieftain, and the man from Mazhapadi recounted:

“When Sundaramurthi Swamigal was on pilgrimage to the sacred sites of the Chola land, he came upon a river that he needed to cross. He began to wade across to the other side. At that moment, a voice called out, ‘Sundaram! Have you forgotten me?’
Sundaramurthi was startled, but realized that it was the voice of the Lord who had claimed him as His own.
He turned to the disciples beside him and asked, ‘Is there a Shiva temple nearby?’”
“Yes, Swami! Hidden behind those blooming konnai trees lies the Shiva temple of Mazhapadi village!” replied the disciples.

Immediately, Sundaramurthi set out for that place. Beneath the shade of the konnai trees, heavy with golden blossoms, stood a small temple. Sundaramurthi entered, beheld the Lord, and his heart melted with devotion as he sang. He marveled at the compassion that had summoned him there, just as once before the Lord had halted him on his path. “Swami! Could I ever forget you? What question is this you ask? Whom else could I think of, if not you?” With these feelings, he composed:

O golden-hued Lord! You who wear the tiger skin as your garment, Upon your radiant, matted locks You adorn the shining konnai flowers— O King! O peerless gem! O precious jewel of Mazhapadi! O Mother! Whom else shall I think of, If not you?
Thus he sang. O Mother! Even now, that temple remains a small shrine, hidden amidst the konnai trees. That is why we beseech you to immediately begin its renovation.”
“So be it!” declared Sembiyan Madevi.
Azhwarkadiyan and another companion, who had arrived a short while earlier, listened intently to all that transpired.

chapters.title: All Her Doing!
paragraphs: A sculptor, descended from the great lineage of master artisans of Mamallapuram, now came forward. According to his own creative imagination, he had crafted a small model temple in a new style for constructing black granite sanctums. He now presented this model to the Queen.

The Queen was greatly astonished upon seeing it. Turning to the man standing near Azhwarkadiyan, she said, “Pattar! Have you seen how remarkable this temple design is? My heart overflows with desire to have temples built in this new style at all the important Shiva shrines in Tamil Nadu!”

“Mother! What obstacle stands in the way of your wish being fulfilled? At all the Shiva shrines graced by the hymns of the Tevaram, such sanctums can be constructed. At a mere glance, people will recognize from this temple design that it is a ‘Paadal Petra Sthalam’—a shrine celebrated in song!” said Isana Sivapattar.

“Yes, yes! We must collect all the hymns sung by Appar Peruman, Jnanasambandar, and Sundaramurthi. In every shrine sanctified by their feet and made divine by their songs, such sanctums with towering vimana gopurams should be constructed. These are my two heart’s desires. Yet, I often doubt whether they will ever be fulfilled. If only my lord had not gone west and joined the divine feet of the Lord before his time—if only he had lived a little longer—all my dreams would have been realized…”

“What is lacking now, Mother? Has not the Emperor himself issued an order that whatever you wish should be fulfilled as you desire? Both his sons, even before you voice your thoughts, have already guessed your wishes and are eager to see them accomplished. In such a situation…”

“Even so, my heart does not feel the same enthusiasm now. I hear all sorts of things. Some complain that the royal treasury is being emptied by the temple renovations I undertake. They ask, ‘Why so many temples for Shiva?’ I do not care about what others say. Even the prince in Kanchi…”
When the Periya Piratti spoke thus, Azhwarkadiyan stepped forward and said, “Mother! I am one among those who would ask such questions!”
The Maharani looked at him with some surprise. The others stared intently at Azhwarkadiyan, their faces expressing, “What madness is this?”

Azhwarkadiyan continued, his voice trembling with anger, “Mother! My heart boils within me! Is such injustice possible? Can you, who shine as the very incarnation of Dharma Devi, allow such unrighteousness?”
Standing beside Thirumalaiyappan, Isana Sivapattar said, “Maharani! My brother is always prone to such babbling. Suddenly, he is seized by a fit of madness. I beg you to kindly forgive him!”

In those days, Saivites and Vaishnavites had not split into separate castes. In the same family, there would be both ardent devotees of Shiva and fierce Vaishnavites. The same priest would serve in both Shiva and Vishnu temples. Isana Sivapattar was one of such broad-minded men. Thirumalaiyappan was his own younger brother. The two shared deep affection for each other. Therefore, Isana Sivapattar sought forgiveness from the Maharani for his brother’s impassioned words.
The Devi smiled and said, “Thirumalai! Speak a little more calmly! What injustice has occurred now?”

“Mother! How many temples, how many grand towers, how many halls are there for Shiva, who, as Bhikshatana, wanders with a skull in his hand, begging for alms? But for Vishnu, the Lord who protects and preserves the world, is there not even a single temple? Can we not at least renovate an old shrine for him?” Thirumalaiyappan cried out.

“Mother! For the Lord who dances the blissful cosmic dance to redeem the world, there must be halls and stages, golden courts, grand temples, and palatial mansions surrounded by walls. But for Thirumal, who sleeps without end, is not a small place enough? All he needs is a dark room without a lamp! Why does he need grand temples and halls?” said Isana Sivapattar.
“Brother! The Lord who sleeps without end is the very same who measured the worlds! The Lord who pushed Mahabali down to the netherworld!” said Azhwarkadiyan.
“That very Lord, who measured the worlds, dug and dug all the way to the netherworld to behold the lotus feet of our Lord Shiva, but could not find them!” retorted Isana Sivapattar.
“If your Sivan is so great,” said Azhwarkkadiyan, “then why does he need a temple at all? If he were to enter the temple, wouldn’t his head strike the roof and bring the whole place crashing down?”

Mazhavaryar’s daughter laughed at this and said, “Enough of your quarrel for now. Thirumalai, what do you say? Who said that we should not build temples for Perumal? Which town’s Vishnu temple do you wish to renovate? Shouldn’t you explain it properly?”

“Ammani! Your father-in-law is the renowned Paranthaka Chakaravarthi, whose fame fills the three worlds. I had gone to Veeranarayanapuram, the town that bears his name. There, Veeranarayana Perumal stands watchful day and night, never sleeping, never closing his eyes, guarding the vast Veeranarayana lake like a mighty ocean. But the brick walls of that great lord’s temple are crumbling and falling. If the temple collapses, the banks of the lake will break, and hundreds of villages will be laid waste. We must restore Veeranarayana Perumal’s temple and make it strong again!”
“So be it, we shall do it! Tell me the details. Let everyone else leave for now,” said the matriarch of the Chola clan.
Sensing her meaning, everyone, including Isana Sivapattar, withdrew from the room.

Immediately, Sembiyan Madevi lowered her voice and said, “Thirumalai, where all did you travel on your pilgrimage? What did you see? What did you hear? Tell me everything in detail. You have brought some important news, haven’t you? That’s why you interrupted the conversation, isn’t it?”

“Yes, mother! I have indeed brought important news. But I will wait for your command before I speak. Just now, you began to say something about the prince in Kanchi. That is why I interrupted. Of those who were here a moment ago, who can tell who is genuine and who is a spy? So many strange things are happening in the land. Who can say when and by whom treachery will occur?”

Periya Piratti let out a deep sigh. “It has come to this, that those of the same family, bound by blood, must suspect one another. Once, Aditya Karikalan had such faith in me! He loved and respected me a hundred times more than his own mother. Even he now doubts me! Thirumalai, my lord and I should leave this earth together— How wonderful it would have been if he had left! Why did he stop me from coming? Had he not already assigned me the tasks to be done here before he departed? What an unfortunate soul I am!” she lamented.

“Mother! Your husband was a great soul, aware of three-fourths of all things. In this age of Kali, he sat upon the Chola throne like King Janaka himself. The fact that he instructed you to remain here is a blessing for this land. The responsibility of preserving this Chola Empire, which has flourished and grown for a hundred years, from being destroyed by fraternal strife, rests upon you. Only you can accomplish this!”

“I do not think so. When my own son does not heed my words, how can I hope to control others? Let that be; you spoke of spies, did you not? Who could have sent spies here? Do you think Prince Aditya Karikalan would have sent them? Has he come to distrust me so much?” asked the lady, the foremost among devotees of Shiva.
“I heard it with both my ears, Mother! Otherwise, I would never have believed that Prince Karikalan could ever doubt you…”
“What did you hear, Thirumalai? What did you hear with your own ears?”
“I heard them speaking as they sat near a stone temple in Mamallapuram…”
“Who do you mean by ‘them’?”

“Prince Aditya Karikalan was one; Thirukovalur Malayaman was the second; Pallava Parthibendran was the third—these three were conversing together. I hid myself within the darkened stone temple and listened. Malayaman and Parthibendran spoke with great agitation. They said that both the Pazhuvettaraiyars, along with their son, Prince Madurantaka, had conspired and imprisoned the Emperor. Malayaman insisted that you too must be involved in this plot. The others agreed with him. Parthibendran declared that they must march upon Thanjavur with their army and rescue the Emperor. The other two concurred as well. But the Prince said that they should first attempt, one more time, to bring the Emperor to Kanchipuram without bloodshed. They decided to write a letter to the Emperor and send it with a messenger. I also discovered who that messenger was. He is no ordinary envoy, but a man of great skill and valor—a messenger who can also serve as a spy. I even spoke with him. When I tried to enter through the main gate, he tried to enter through the side entrance. He is not at all an ordinary man…” Without revealing it, he tried to glean many things from me. The astrologer of Kudanthai displayed his own sleight of hand to him. That too did not succeed. Later, I hear, he went to Thanjavur and delivered the palm-leaf letter to the Emperor…”
“What happened after that? What reply did the Emperor give him?”
“He said he would write a reply the next day, it seems. In the meantime, the Pazhuvettarayar brothers began to suspect him. Somehow, he managed to escape, breaking through all their guards!”
“If that is so, he must be very clever indeed; there is no doubt. What did you do then? After you left Kanchipuram?”
“I set out directly to come here. On the way, I stopped at Veeranarayanapuram to have darshan of Perumal. By the grace of Perumal, I happened to learn a great secret at the place where I stayed…”
“What is that? Yet another secret?”
“Yes, Mother! I learned that there was a grand feast at Kadambur Sambuvarayar’s palace that night. The elder Pazhuvettarayar attended that feast. The young queen’s palanquin arrived with him!”
“Tirumalai! All of this is her doing! The danger that has now befallen the Chola country is because of that woman! Were you able to meet and speak with her?”

“No, Amma! I could not! By your command, I raised that serpent of a woman as my own sister for so many years! I wandered far and wide, searching for rare hymns, learned them, and taught them to her! When I think of all that, my heart burns! After becoming the wife of the great Pazhuvettarayar, she refuses even to see me…”
“What use is it to grieve over that? Such are the ways of people in this world. What we imagine is one thing, what actually happens is another… What happened then at Kadambur?”

“Thinking that the one who arrived in the palanquin was Nandini, I went to Kadambur with the intention of meeting her somehow, or at least sending her a warning by letter. Daring great danger, I climbed over the outer wall of Kadambur palace and leapt inside; it was then that I discovered that astonishing, mysterious secret…”
“Thirumalai! This is always your way. You only stir up more and more curiosity, but you never reveal the news itself. What is this extraordinary, mysterious secret…?”

“Forgive me, Mother! I hesitate even to speak of it. It was not the Young Queen of Pazhuvoor who was in the closed palanquin. We have all believed that wherever the Lord of Pazhuvoor goes, he takes the Young Queen with him. That is a great mistake…”
“If not the Young Queen, then whom does the Lord of Pazhuvoor carry in the closed palanquin? Does that old man’s cunning know no bounds?”
“It was not a woman in the closed palanquin, Mother!”
“If not a woman, then? What man would hide himself and travel in such a palanquin?”
“Forgive me, Amma! The one who came hidden in the closed palanquin was none other than your own son, Prince Madurantaka!”
Sembiyan Maadevi stood stunned for a moment.
“Oh God! Is this the punishment for the sin I have committed?” she murmured to herself.
Then, Azhwarkadiyan recounted the secret meeting that had taken place at midnight in the Sambuvrayar mansion. Hearing this, the distress that overcame the queen was beyond words.

“Alas! My son! I tried to raise you as a treasure of Shiva’s wisdom! Is this the result? Must such disgrace befall the great Chola lineage because of you? Must such a great calamity come upon the Chola Empire through you?” she lamented.
Afterwards, she said, “Thirumalai! Come and see me again before you leave! In the meantime, I will speak with Kundavai and think of a way to avert this great disaster!”
“Mother! It would be best if you did not speak of this even to the Princess.”
“Why? Do you even suspect her?”
“Is it not natural, Amma? She is the beloved sister of Aditya Karikalan, after all.”

“So what of that…? Thirumalai! If you told me that the sun rises in the west and sets in the east, I would believe you. If you proved to me that Thirumal is a greater god than Shiva, I would believe that too. But if you accuse Kundavai of wrongdoing, I will never believe it. On the day she was born, the palace midwife brought the child—” She placed both her hands in mine. From that day onward, I myself raised her. I cherished her even more dearly than the son born of my own womb. She too, considering me as her own mother and father, has continued to show me love and respect to this very day…”
“Mother! May I ask you something? Did Princess Kundavai tell you about her visit to the astrologer of Kudanthai?”
“No; why do you ask?”
“Did she mention seeing a young man of the Vanar clan at the astrologer’s house, or meeting him again on the banks of the Arisil river?”
“No; what are these questions? Why do you ask such things? What is your intention?”
“It means the princess is keeping a secret from you. The youth I mentioned is none other than the messenger of Aditya Karikalan; it would not be wrong to call him a spy.”

“Thirumalai! Let all that be as it may. If Kundavai has not told me something, there must be a good reason for it. Rather than suspect her, I would sooner give up my very life!” declared the chief queen of Sivagnana Kandaraadithar.
“Oh no! Let nothing like that ever happen. May your trust prove true. The princess has asked me to come, perhaps to ask me something. I will let her know that you wish to see her,” he said.

chapters.title: The Spy Who Committed a Crime
paragraphs: Two thousand years ago, the Chola king Karikala Peruvazhuthan raised embankments on both sides of the Kaveri River. For a long time, those banks remained in good condition, keeping the Kaveri’s waters under control. Later, the strength of the Chola dynasty waned. The Pandyas, Pallavas, Kalabhras, and Vaanars rose in power. During this period, the Kaveri, left without a vigilant guardian, frequently breached its banks and broke through its confines. On some occasions, when the embankments broke on a large scale, the very course of the river would change, flowing in new directions. The old Kaveri would become the new Kaveri; if the river’s path changed entirely, the former riverbed would sometimes turn into fertile land, or at other times, become stagnant pools, surging and foaming like the sea.
To the south of the Chola palaces in Pazhaiyarai, adjoining the royal compounds, there was such a watercourse.

This channel, formed due to the altered course of the Kaveri, had been deliberately deepened and widened by the Chola kings, so that water always brimmed within it. For the palace, and especially for the inner quarters, this broad waterway served as a formidable line of defense. No one could easily approach by that route. Only those closely associated with the palace could come by boat.

The beautiful pleasure gardens of the palace women were laid out along the banks of this waterway. The ladies of the palace would stroll there at any hour, without fear. They would gather together, frolic like peacocks, sing like nightingales. Sometimes, they would descend into the channel to bathe. They would row boats and play upon the water.

Whenever a king of the Chola dynasty passed away and another ascended the throne, it was customary to build a new palace. The queens and children of the deceased monarch would reside in the old palace.

Among the palaces of Pazhaiyarai, next to the residence of Sembiyan Maadevi, the palace of Princess Kundavai stood out in beauty and grandeur. Was it not the palace where Sundara Chola himself had once resided? After he departed for Thanjavur, Kundavai became the mistress of that palace. Behind that palace, the garden bloomed in splendid beauty. Towering banyan trees stretched towards the sky; delicate, tiny flowering shrubs clustered below. Creepers wound themselves in and out, embracing the trees, and there were bowers woven from flowering vines.
It was the custom of Kundavai and her companions to spend most evenings in that very garden.
At times, they would all gather in one spot, sitting together, exchanging stories, and bursting into laughter.
At other times, they would split into pairs or groups of three, wandering off to share secrets in private.
For some days now, Kundavai and Vanathi had formed the habit of separating from the rest and conversing alone.
That day, the two of them sat together on a swing made of vines, tied to a great banyan branch, swaying gently as they spoke.
The cheerful laughter of the women, vying with the chattering of birds, could be heard now and then throughout the garden.
But Kundavai and Vanathi alone did not laugh. The laughter of the others did not particularly please them. Nor could it be said that they spoke much more than the others.
From one of the vine bowers, a young woman began to sing. Was it not Krishna’s birthday? The song she sang was, of course, about Krishna.
In the moonlight, the sound of the flute is heard. It torments a maiden who loves Krishna. She opens her lips and pours out her sorrow. From a branch above, a parrot offers her comfort.
Maiden: In the moonlight that brings me pain— Who is the flute-player here? Is it a virtue for my lordless, foolish heart To be tormented so?
Parrot:
May the heavens and the earth be filled with joy— O Lord, the music of the flute, Sweet as honeyed speech, Does it torment you, O maiden, With a pain unknown to this world?
Maiden: O flower! I will worship you— I will pluck the finest punnai blossoms and adorn you— In the hour when my soul is shattered— Is it to offer me solace that you have come?
Parrot: O beauty with the slender waist! By your love— I have come to speak of the sorrow of our Kannan— From the day he parted from you— Even the sweetest butter has turned bitter to him!

Kundavai, who had been listening intently to the latter part of the song, said as soon as it ended, “It is well that our Kannan has become the deity of this land of pure Tamil! If he spends his days eating butter, playing the flute, and idling with women, what will become of all other matters?”
She turned to Vanathi, who had remained silent, and asked, “Why this silence, girl? Have you too been enchanted by Kannan’s flute?”
“Akka! What did you say?” asked Vanathi.
“What did I say? Where had your attention wandered?”
“It did not wander anywhere. It was with you.”
“Ah, sly one! Why do you lie? Truly, your mind is not here at all! Shall I tell you where it is?”
“If you know, do tell!”
“I know it well. He has gone to the battlefield in Eezha Nadu. There, my younger brother—such an innocent soul—your mind is scheming how to bewitch him, what new spell to cast upon him!”

“There is some truth in what you say, Akka! My mind does wander often to Eezha Nadu. But I have never thought of casting any spell upon him. I only wonder how much hardship he must be enduring on the battlefield, how many wounds must mark his noble body, where he lies down to rest, what food he eats—such thoughts fill my mind. When I think of him suffering there, while I remain here, eating in comfort, dressed in fine clothes, sleeping on a soft bed, it pains me. If only I had wings, I would fly to Lanka this very instant…!”
“And what would you do if you flew there? Would you only bring him more trouble?”
“Never, not for a single day. Just as Subhadra drove Arjuna’s chariot, and Satyabhama drove Krishna’s, I too would drive his. I would shield my chest from the arrows aimed at him…”
“If you shielded him so, would he stand by and watch?”

“If that displeased him, I would wait in the camp. When he returned from the battlefield, I would tend his wounds, bind them with healing herbs. I would spread a bed of flowers for him. I would prepare delicious dishes and serve them to him. To ease his pain, I would play the veena and sing him to sleep…”
“These are all things that will never come to pass, Vanathi! The warriors of the Chola clan do not take women with them to the battlefield…”
“Why is that, Akka?”
“They do not fear wounds; what they fear more is women!”
“Why is that? What could women do to them?”

“Women would do nothing to them; but if women like you went to the battlefield, what if the enemy soldiers, captivated by your beauty, surrendered themselves? Then, would our Chola warriors have a chance to display their valor? The Chola clan does not desire the fame of winning victories through women.”
“Is that truly possible? Would enemy soldiers be so foolish—so easily bewitched by the beauty of women?”
“Why wouldn’t they, Vanathi? Do you remember, at the astrologer’s house in Kudanthai and on the banks of the Arisil river, we saw a young warrior—do you recall?”
“I do remember; but what of it?”
“Do you remember how, upon seeing us, he stood there as if intoxicated, utterly entranced?”

“That too I remember. But it’s wrong to say he was dazed by seeing all of us. It was only after seeing you that he stood there, lost in a trance. He didn’t even glance at those standing beside you, sister!”
“Vanathi! What a fine liar you are! Are you teasing me?”
“Not at all! Let me ask you something—will you answer truthfully?”
“Ask, and see!”
“Why did you suddenly remember that young warrior now?”
“You’ve become quite the talker! What’s wrong with remembering him?”
“Who said it was wrong? Did I say so? It’s only natural! Even I wonder what became of that young man after that.”
“Why should you be concerned about him?”
“Why shouldn’t I be? If we have seen someone, if their memory comes to us again and again, isn’t it only natural to wish to know what happened to them?”

“Very natural, indeed! But we mustn’t let our minds wander so. We must learn to control our thoughts… Listen, Vanathi, what is that sound of drums? What is that voice saying? Listen carefully—let’s see!”
Yes; from somewhere far off in the street, the sound of drums beating and, in between, the shouts of human voices could be heard. When they listened intently, this is what the voice was proclaiming:

“A spy from enemy lands has entered the Thanjavur fort, showing a false seal, and gathered intelligence before fleeing. He escaped after grievously wounding two men. He is a young man, of slender build…”

The Udaiyavan. A master of illusion and cunning, like Indrajit himself. His name: Vallavaraiyan Vandiyathevan. Those who grant him refuge shall be punished with death. Those who capture and hand him over shall be rewarded with a thousand gold coins. This is the stern command of the Commander of Tanjai Fort, Pazhuvetaraiyar Kaalandhakandar!”
As the human voice finished proclaiming thus, the drum thundered—“tham, tham, thadathadatham”—reverberating through the air.
For some reason, the body of Princess Kundavai trembled.
At that moment, a nursemaid entered and said, “Devi! The valiant Vaishnavite, known as Azhwarkkadiyan, has come to see you. He says it is an urgent matter!”
“I am coming at once!” said Kundavai, descending from the swing and making her way out.

chapters.title: The Murmuring of the People
paragraphs: From the presence of the venerable matriarch of the Chola clan, Azhwarkadiyan set out towards the palace of the Young Princess. The sights he beheld along the streets of Pazhayarai filled him with great enthusiasm. How joyously these people were celebrating the sacred day of Krishna’s birth! There could be no doubt that Vaishnavism was destined to take root and spread throughout this Chola land. True, there were many reasons for the growing influence of Saivism here. For a hundred years, the kings of the Chola dynasty had been building new Shiva temples across the realm. The hymns of the three great Saivite saints were being propagated through these temples. Grand temple festivals and processions were conducted with great pomp. Yet, for all this, the glory of Lord Thirumal had not diminished in the least. Krishna, the ninth and complete incarnation of Vishnu, had captured the hearts of the people.

The divine exploits performed by the Lord in Gokulam, Brindavan, and northern Madurai had taken up residence in their souls. Ah! How many groups of Bhagavathas! How many street plays! How many different costumes and disguises! Yes, there were more now than ever before. The crowds that gathered around these troupes, their excitement and noise, too, had grown greater than before. New drama troupes kept arriving from the villages surrounding Pazhayarai.

In one such troupe, Vasudeva, Devaki, Krishna, Balarama, and Kamsa appeared in costume. There was much singing, dancing, and dialogue among the performers in this group, so Azhwarkadiyan paused to watch. At that moment, a conversation was taking place between Krishna and Kamsa. The boy playing Krishna, in his childish voice, listed out the crimes committed by Kamsa and challenged, “Come, fight with me!” In reply, Kamsa, in a loud, thunderous voice, declared, “Hey, Krishna! Your tricks and illusions will not work on me any longer. I am going to kill you now. I will kill your brother Balarama too. I will kill your father Vasudeva as well. And look there—standing with his body smeared in sandal paste and marked with sacred symbols—that fierce Vaishnavite—I will kill him too!”

At this, everyone standing around turned to look at our Azhwarkadiyan and burst into laughter. Even those dressed as Krishna and Balarama turned their gaze upon him. Many in the crowd pressed closer, surrounding him, laughing boisterously and making fun of him. Thirumalai Nambi was seized by a tremendous anger. He spun the staff in his hand, wondering if he should try it out on someone in that crowd. Most of all, he longed to land a blow on that Kamsan’s head. But there was no use striking Kamsan’s head, for the man playing Kamsan had covered his own face and was wearing a fearsome false head made of wood, adorned with a grotesque moustache and sharp teeth, painted with vivid colors. All in all, Thirumalai decided it would not be wise to use his staff in such a large gathering, and so he slipped away from that place.

Even though Kamsan’s voice—loud and booming as it was—rang out above the crowd, to Azhwarkadiyan it sounded strangely familiar, as if he had heard it somewhere before. Pondering where he might have heard that voice, he walked along the street.

Suddenly, a change swept over the crowd’s enthusiasm. As time passed, the people’s excitement visibly waned. What was this? Why had this sudden change come over them? Why was the crowd dispersing so quickly? The blare of instruments and the sounds of singing and dancing had ceased! In their place, people gathered in small groups along the sides of the street, whispering secrets to each other. After speaking, why did they hurry away? Why were doors being slammed shut with such urgency?

Now the reason became clear. The drumbeats that had sent a chill even through Princess Kundavai’s body, and the proclamation about capturing the spy—these were the cause. The sound of those drums had utterly destroyed the festive spirit of the people who had gathered for the celebration. Those walking alone were eyed suspiciously by others as they passed! Every unfamiliar face was regarded with doubt. Even Azhwarkadiyan was met with wary, distrustful glances from some, who then hurried on their way.

Thirumalai guessed the reason behind this. Not only that, but he also had some idea, through intuition, of what the people were discussing in small groups along the roadside. A few words that reached his ears confirmed it. They were speaking about the tyrannical rule of the Pazhuvettaraiyars. It was only natural that both the people of Pazhayarai and the villagers from the surrounding areas harbored anger against the Pazhuvettaraiyars.
“Who can equal Sundara Chozhar of Pazhayarai In all this ancient land!”

So sang the poets in praise of the emperor, but had they not taken him away from Pazhayarai to Thanjavur? Was not the glory of Pazhayarai diminishing day by day since then? Today, this... If only the Emperor himself had remained in this city for the Krishna Jayanthi festival, how much more magnificent would the celebrations have been! Would not all the drama troupes, dressed in costumes depicting stories of Krishna, have paraded through the streets and finally gathered in the courtyard of the Emperor’s palace? Would not the Emperor have bestowed generous rewards upon the actors, singers, bards, dancers, and poets? Would not the crowds have swelled so much that it could be said the entire Chola land had assembled in Pazhayarai? Would not the trade in the shops have increased a hundredfold compared to now? When, at night, Venugopala Swami set out from the Nandipura Vinnagara temple and proceeded in procession through the streets, how much music and drumming, dance and song, stick games and mock sword fights would have resounded through the air?

All of this had vanished because of the Pazhuvettaraiyars. Besides this, another deep sorrow had taken root in the hearts of the people of Pazhayarai. Their beloved prince, Arulmozhi Varman, had crossed the seas and was waging war in the island of Lanka. Ten thousand soldiers from all four military quarters of Pazhayarai had gone to Eelam under the prince’s command. In that land of forests and mountains, they were fighting to uphold the honor and valor of Tamilakam. Did not Ilango of Kodumbalur lead an army to Lanka, stand at the forefront of battle, and lay down his life with a spear in his chest? Did not all the remaining Chola warriors fight to the very end and perish? It was to bring peace to the souls of those who had died, and to once more establish the victory of the tiger flag on that island, that Prince Arulmozhi had gone. Yet, it was said that these Pazhuvettaraiyars were refusing to send food, clothing, money, and weapons to our soldiers fighting under his command. What injustice was this? Could such a thing be? Had they not filled the granaries in the Thanjavur fort with paddy? For what purpose was all that? What of the wealth that had been accumulating in the palace treasuries for a hundred years? Of what use was grain and gold that could not aid our warriors at such a time? What were these Pazhuvettaraiyars planning to do with all of it? Were they planning to take it with them to the land of Yama when they died…?

Such were the murmurings that had been circulating among the people of Chola Nadu for some time, and Thirumalai Nambi was well aware of it. It was only natural that the people of Pazhayarai felt this anger more keenly. After all, the wives, children, and relatives of the ten thousand soldiers who had gone to the battlefield of Lanka were still living in this city, were they not?

Therefore, the people of Pazhaiyarai did not like the beating of drums and the public proclamation about the capture of the spy, as ordered by the Pazhuvettaraiyars. It became yet another reason for them to speak among themselves about the grievances they held against the Pazhuvettaraiyars.

A spy, they said! From which land could a spy have come here? From the tip of Kumari to the banks of the Northern Pennai, only the tiger flag flies! Which foreign king is so powerful as to send a spy here? If there is anyone whom these Pazhuvettaraiyars dislike, they simply accuse him of being a spy and settle their scores! Or else, they throw him into the underground dungeons!…

But what does it matter to us? The authority is in their hands! They can do whatever they please, just or unjust! Once someone is branded a spy, there is no need even to consult the village councils, is there…?

All these thoughts that simmered in the hearts of the people of Pazhaiyarai, all the mutterings that escaped their lips, all the quiet conversations they exchanged in hushed voices—Azhwarkkadiyan came to know of them through his keen ears and sharp intuition. He wondered where this growing discontent in the hearts of the people would ultimately lead, as he made his way to the palace of Princess Kundavai.

The Young Princess always delighted in discussing the affairs of the world with Azhwarkkadiyan. He would wander through the towns and villages, bringing news of happenings from far and near. The royal maiden was eager to hear all that he had to tell. She was also fond of listening to the hymns of the Alwars that he sought out and sang for her. Therefore, whenever Thirumalai Nambi came, she would greet him with enthusiasm and inquire after his well-being with a bright and welcoming face.

But today, Azhwarkkadiyan noticed a slight change in the princess’s expression and manner. Her face bore the look of someone whose mind was preoccupied elsewhere; there was an unusual agitation in her speech, a hint of confusion.
“Thirumalai! What news? Where have you come from?” Kundavai asked.
“There is no special news, my lady! As usual, I thought you had summoned me to inquire about the affairs of the world. Pardon me, I shall take my leave.”
“No, no! Stay a while longer! It was I who asked you to come…”
“Mother! I forgot to tell you! Just now, I was in the presence of the Periya Piratti. She asked me to tell you that she has some important news to convey, and requested you to come to her…”
“Very well; I was thinking of going there myself. But first, tell me—where all have you traveled during this journey?”
“I have journeyed from the southern tip of Kumari to the northern heights of Venkadam.”
“What are the people saying in the places you have visited?”
“They are speaking of the glory of the Chola royal clan. They say that before long, the Chola Empire will stretch northward to the river Ganga and up to the snowy Himalayas…”
“And then?”
“They praise the valor and prowess of the Pazhuvettaraiyars. They say that the reason the Chola Empire has reached such heights is because of the minor kings of Pazhuvur…”
“That’s enough. What else do they say?”
“They speak with affection about your two brothers. Above all, the love and support the people have for Prince Arulmozhi cannot be described in words.”
“There is nothing surprising in that! Is there any other talk?”
“They are wondering why the illustrious son of the Chola Emperor has not yet married. Many even asked me about it…”
“What did you reply?”
“I said that no prince worthy of marrying our Ilaiya Piratti has yet been born on this earth…”

“How charming! In that case, such a man must be born in the future! By the time he is born and reaches marriageable age, I will have become an old crone! Leave my affairs aside, Thirumalai! Is there any other gossip?”
“Why not? Many are astonished that the lord, who once declared he would renounce the world and become a Siva-gnana Yogi, has suddenly gotten married…”
“Your dear younger sister… You used to say she was destined to become a paragon of devotion, like Andal herself… How is she now?”
“What could she possibly lack, Mother! She rules as the absolute authority in the great Periya Pazhuvettarayar’s palace…”
“Is it only in Pazhuvettarayar’s palace? Haven’t I heard that she is, in truth, the absolute power behind this entire Chola kingdom?”

“Some do speak so, Mother! But let us leave her aside. On this auspicious day, why speak of her at all? Since you mentioned the name ‘Andal’, it brought something to my mind.
