I had gone to Srivilliputhur. I learned a few of Pattar Piran Vishnu Chittar’s songs. Listen to this, Mother! A song about the day Kannan was born:—

‘In Thirukottiyur, ringed by colorful mansions, On the day Kannan, Kesavan’s noble son, was born, Oil and sacred ash were flung in joyous rivalry, Kannan’s courtyard overflowed with celebration! Some ran, some fell, some rejoiced and clapped, Some searched, asking, “Where is our Lord?” While singers sang and drums thundered, Dancers swirled in Ayarpadi’s delight!’
Today, our city of Pazhaiyarai too is filled with such jubilation, Mother!”
“It is indeed filled with joy; but just a short while ago, a different kind of drum was beaten—what was that, Thirumalai?”
Azhwarkkadiyan had been waiting for this very question.
“Someone, it seems, was a spy! He escaped, they say! Whoever captures him will be rewarded, so they say! But what did I see of all that, Mother?”
“You know nothing? Not even the slightest suspicion of who it might be?”

“There is a doubt in my mind, but speaking of it is dangerous. As I walked along the street, some people even glanced at me suspiciously. What if someone were to seize me and throw me into an underground dungeon...?”
“To catch you, they would need to have horns growing from their heads! If you wish to share what’s on your mind, tell me! Do you think I would betray you?”
“Krishna! Krishna! It’s nothing like that. In Veeranarayana Puram, I saw a brave young man. He said he was going to Thanjavur. He didn’t say why. He asked me many questions...”
Kundavai, agitated, asked, “What did he look like?”
“He appeared to be born of a noble clan. His face was bright and handsome. He seemed to possess both courage and inner strength...”
“What did he ask you?”

“He asked about the Emperor’s health. Then, he inquired about the one next in line to the throne. He asked about the prince who has gone to Lanka. Later, I learned that he asked the same questions of the Kudanthai astrologer...”
“Ah! So he had gone to the astrologer’s house?”
“Now I remember. While you were at the astrologer’s house, he apparently barged in with much commotion... Fortunately, he did not recognize you...!”
“What I suspected has come true...”
“What did you suspect, Mother?”
“I thought that reckless youth would soon face some danger...”
“What you thought is correct. I suspect he is a spy. I believe the Pazhuvettarayars have announced a reward for his capture.”
“Thirumalai! Will you do me a favor?”
“Command me, Mother!”
“If you ever happen to see that young man...”
“Shall I seize him and bring him to you, so that you may reward me with a gift?”
“No, no! Bring him to me yourself! I have an important matter to discuss with him.”

Azhwarkadiyan stood gazing at Princess Kundavai for a moment, as if struck by wonder. Then he said, “That will not be necessary, my lady! There is no need for me to go in search of him and bring him here. He himself will come seeking you out!”

chapters.title: Eesan Sivapattar
paragraphs: Azhwarkkadiyan, after meeting the young prince, went to the house of his elder brother, Eesan Sivapattar. His house was very close to the Vadameyyattrali Sivan temple, at a distance of about half a katham from the palace. If one traveled from the Chola palace to the Vadameyyattrali temple, one could, in a way, observe the expanse of the city of Pazhaiyarai and its other unique features.

Azhwarkkadiyan noticed that the celebrations for Krishna Jayanthi had more or less subsided. As he walked through the residential quarters, he observed women gathered in the corners of their homes, speaking to each other with anger and agitation. All these women had, with great enthusiasm, adorned the necks of their husbands or sons with garlands of vanji flowers and sent them off to the Eelam war front. In the heroic battles waged by the Chola armies in all four directions, not a single house was spared from sending at least one warrior to attain the hero’s heaven. Now, these very women were murmuring and speaking in discontent. Thirumalaiyappan saw this and wondered anxiously what strange fate all this would lead to.

By the time he reached the Vadameyyattrali temple, it was quite dark. This was the temple sung by Appar Peruman. In the time of that great saint, Jain monks had brought artificial hills and placed them around the temple, carving out caves in those hills. In those man-made mountain caves, Digambara Jain monks sat in meditation. To remind us of this, there still exists a village near Pazhaiyarai called Muzhaiyur.

When Appar Peruman heard of the glory of Pazhaiyarai and came there, the Jain caves had completely hidden the Sivan temple. Appar, realizing this through his spiritual wisdom, was deeply grieved. He petitioned the minor king who, as a representative of the Pallavas, was then ruling the Chola land. The king demolished a portion of those artificial caves and cleared them away. Inside, a small Sivan temple was revealed. Appar, in ecstasy, sang his hymns.

Later, the temple was expanded and beautified by the Chola kings, and a hall of learning was constructed. Yet, even now, the temple was surrounded by those caves, forming a wall like a prakara. There was only one gopura entrance to enter the temple; there was no other... There was no entrance there. It would be easy to reach Isana Sivapattar’s house by entering the temple’s prakaram through the gopura entrance. Otherwise, one would have to take a long detour.

Thus, in order to reach his elder brother’s house by this shortcut, Thirumalai entered through the gopura entrance. Inside, he saw a few devotees standing near the sanctum. They appeared to be members of a troupe, dressed as Krishna and Balarama. “Aha! How did these people end up here?” he wondered, but before he could finish the thought, Isana Sivapattar hurriedly came out from within the temple. Just then, he grabbed Thirumalai, who had just entered through the gopura, by the hand and quickly pulled him outside.
“Anna! What is this?” asked Azhwarkadiyan.

“I’ll tell you, Thirumalai! From now on, let all our dealings remain outside the temple. You are a heretic, a blasphemer of Shiva; do not set foot inside this sacred abode of Shiva! Do you understand? I have tolerated much. But today, what you said in front of the great queen—I can no longer bear it. If you want, come to the house, fill your big belly, and leave! But do not set foot inside the temple! If you do, I will become Sandesvara Nayanar himself!”

So saying, Isana Sivapattar grabbed Thirumalai by the neck, gave him a forceful shove, and slammed the temple door shut. “Anna! Anna!…” Thirumalai began to say something, but Sivapattar did not listen for even a moment. He locked the temple door from the inside and left.

“Oh ho! So that’s how it is?” muttered Azhwarkadiyan to himself. He stood there for a while. Then, circling the temple—including the Jain shrines—two or three times, he walked around deliberately to the left, lest it be considered a clockwise pradakshina. He saw that all the entrances to the Jain shrines, which were built in a circular fashion, were tightly closed. Afterwards, he went to Isana Sivapattar’s house. Thirumalai, who was always ready with a jest, was especially dear to the priest’s wife. Speaking to her with even more humor than usual, he ate his fill of the Shiva temple’s prasadam, and then lay down on the raised platform at the entrance.

He recalled a sight he had seen on the first day, when he had come along the banks of the Kudamuruti river. He heard the sound of horses galloping rapidly towards him from the opposite direction, and quickly hid himself behind a dense bamboo thicket nearby.

The first horse came running as if in a wild frenzy. It was drenched, dripping wet; whether it was from sweat or from having plunged through the floodwaters of the river, it was impossible to tell. Upon that horse sat a small boy. He had been tied together with the horse. On the boy’s face, fear mingled with a certain determination could be seen.

A little behind, four or five more horses followed. Upon them rode warriors armed with spears. It seemed as if they would catch up very soon. One among them raised his spear above his head, aiming to hurl it at the horse in front. Another stopped him.

At that moment, the boy had to go beneath the thick bamboo thickets. A low-hanging bamboo branch caught in his hair. As the horse pulled forward, it was uncertain what would become of the boy. In that tense instant, those behind caught up and seized the horse.

They looked upon the boy tied to the horse with a mixture of surprise, shock, and anger. They questioned him about something. The boy stammered and replied. Alwarkadiyan could not catch the details in his ears. Only the repeated question, “Where is he? Where is he?” reached him. The young boy, sobbing and weeping, cried out, “He went with the river! He fell into the flood!” That too reached his ears. Afterwards, those warriors took the boy and the horse with them along the riverbank and disappeared.
At that moment, Thirumalaiyappan could not understand the meaning of this incident. Now, it seemed as if he was beginning to understand a little.

Meanwhile, the memory of that street drama troupe returned to him. Most of all, he recalled the one who had donned the role of Kamsan, hiding his own face behind a wooden puppet mask—the gait, the costume, the gestures, and the voice all came back to him. The voice, which he had heard before, now began to clarify in his mind as to whom it belonged.
Having completed the midnight worship, Isana Sivapattar returned home. On the threshold, he saw Alwarkadiyan lying down.
“Thirumalai! Thirumalai!” he called out in an angry voice.
Thirumalai pretended to be deep in sleep.

Fearing the door would be barred, the priest went inside. The sound of him quarreling with his wife reached Thirumalai’s ears in snatches. Thirumalai was quite certain that the quarrel was about himself. He understood.
The next morning, Isana Sivapattar came to Thirumalai and asked, “When are you setting out again to travel the country?”
“I will leave after your anger has subsided, anna!” he replied.
“Do not call me ‘anna’ anymore. From this day forth, I am no longer your elder brother; nor are you my younger brother. You are a mocker of Shiva; a vile one; a chandaalan…”

Pattar’s wife, feeling pity for Thirumalai, intervened, “Why do you curse him so harshly? What new thing has he said now that he hasn’t said all these days? It is you who have become excessively zealous in your devotion to Shiva!”

“You know nothing! Do you know what he said yesterday in the presence of the great Maharani? He asked, ‘What need is there for a temple for Parameshwaran, who smears himself with ash and roams the cremation ground?’ It felt as if hot oil was poured into my ears. The Maharani, it seems, did not sleep the whole night!”
“He will not speak like that again. I will advise him and set him right. If spoken to kindly, he listens!” she said.

“Enough of kind words; enough of harsh words as well. Let him go at once to Rameswaram. Just as Rama worshipped the Shiva Linga there to absolve his sins, let him too worship and return. That shall be his penance. Until he does so, I will not even look upon his face!” said Sivapattar.
Thirumalai’s lips trembled. He wanted to retort with interest. But he restrained himself, thinking that if he spoke, matters would only worsen.

At this moment, Pattar’s wife again interjected, “What of it? If you ask him to go to Rameswaram, he will go. We can go with him. All these years, we have not had a child. Who knows what sin we committed in a previous birth… Thirumalai! Shall we all go together to Rameswaram?” she asked.
Isana Sivapattar glared at both of them in anger and left.
After a little while, Isana Pattar returned and spoke to Thirumalai in a calm tone.
“Thambi! The elders have said, ‘Anger is sin, anger is chandaalam.’ I have given way to anger. You are not upset, are you?”
“There is absolutely nothing!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.

“In that case, stay right here! I will finish the midday puja and return. I need to discuss some important matters with you and seek your counsel. You’ll be here, won’t you? You won’t disappear anywhere, will you?” he asked.
“I am not going anywhere, anna! I have no intention of leaving you!” replied Azhwarkkadiyan.

The priest departed. Azhwarkkadiyan muttered to himself several times, “Is that so, indeed!” Then, without even telling his companion, he slipped away. He circled the temple at the northwestern edge, surrounded by rocky knolls, two or three times. Whenever he heard any sound, he immediately hid himself in the shadows.

His vigilance did not go unrewarded. The door of one of the Jain hermitages opened slowly. First, Isana Sivapattar stepped out, glancing in all directions. Behind him, another man emerged. Ah! Who is this? The face is unrecognizable. Judging by the build, he looks like someone dressed as Kamsan in a play! Who could it be? I must not let this mystery go unsolved. Oh! So this is the reason for all that anger, secrecy, and incantations!
The two who emerged from the hermitage walked ahead. Azhwarkkadiyan slipped into the shadows and followed them stealthily.

After a short walk, they reached the bank of the stream. This was the stream that flowed behind the Chola palace, spreading out and surging like the sea. But the landing was far to the west of the palace.
Dense trees lined the bank. Concealed behind one of them, Azhwarkkadiyan peered through the gap between two branches.
A boat rocked gently on the waves. It looked like one of the palace boats. The boatman stood waiting on the shore.
When he saw the priest and his companion, he pulled the boat closer to the bank.
Both men boarded the boat. As soon as it began to move, the man who had come with the priest turned back toward the shore.
His face was suddenly illuminated, clearly visible.
There was no surprise for Azhwarkkadiyan. The man he had been expecting was indeed this very one.
It was the same brave youth he had met at Veeranarayana Puram and again on the ferry across the Kollidam! There was no doubt that the one who had donned the guise of Kamsan was also him.
Where were they going now, boarding that boat? — That too must be discovered! He needed to confirm whether his suspicions were correct.

On a street lined with many Chola mansions that soared towards the sky, the last mansion stood locked and deserted. This was the residence of Aniruddha Brahmarayar, the chief minister of Sundara Chola. The chief minister Aniruddha had gone to Madurai to reorganize and strengthen the royal administration of the Pandya country. His family remained in Thanjavur. Therefore, his old mansion in Pazhayarai was locked up.

Azhwarkkadiyan arrived at this mansion. The guards, seeing him, approached with reverence and awe. He ordered them to open the door. The guards obeyed and opened the door. Then, at his command, they locked it again from the outside. Passing through the three courtyards of the mansion, he reached the rear garden. From that garden, a narrow path wound its way through dense trees and shrubs. Thirumalai entered this path and, after a short while, reached the garden of Princess Kundavai’s palace. He stood hidden in a secluded spot in a creeper-covered arbor, watching all around him. All the trouble he had taken was not in vain.
A scene worthy of being described by great poets like Kalidas was unfolding before him.
A boat came to rest on the bank of the stream. From it, Isana Bhattar and Vandiyathevan disembarked. Then they climbed up the steps leading from the water’s edge.
A little distance from the steps, in the garden, Princess Kundavai was seated on a marble dais.
As the newcomers ascended the steps and reached the upper level, Princess Kundavai rose to her feet.
Only then did Vandiyathevan gaze intently at the face of that royal maiden. He stood transfixed, gazing at her.
Between him and Princess Kundavai, a flowering creeper stretched out its tender hand, gently intervening.
On that flag, a beautiful silk butterfly—its wings adorned with many colors—came fluttering down and settled. Kundavai lowered her golden face slightly and gazed at the butterfly.
Vandiyathevan, meanwhile, stood without blinking, his eyes fixed upon the blossoming beauty of Kundavai’s face. The ripples in the stream subsided and grew still.
The birds ceased their melodious songs. The worlds, near and far, seemed to stand motionless.
Ages seemed to pass in that moment.

chapters.title: The Swirl of Water, the Swirl of Eyes
paragraphs: The first man created by God lived on the slopes of a mountain. For rain and wind, the mountain cave offered him shelter. The wild trees of the forest gave him the fruits he needed for food. The beasts of the jungle trembled at the sight of him. Like the birds of the sky, he lived freely, without want or worry. Yet, deep within his heart, there was some lack—an unknown longing that would not leave him. Some magnetic force seemed to draw him, to pull him towards something. His heart searched for a rare treasure, a joy he had never seen, felt, or known before. By day, he imagined it; by night, he dreamed of it. “Where shall I find that wondrous thing created just for me—the fruit of the wish-giving tree, the magnet that draws me? When shall I see it?”—thus his heart yearned and suffered.

At the same moment that He created the first man, God also created the first woman. She lived on the other side of the mountain’s slope. She had food for her hunger, spring water for her thirst, and a mountain cave for shelter. Outwardly, nothing seemed lacking. But within, a spark of fire burned her, a flame that would not die. Some force drew her, pulled her along. She did not know from where that force was pulling her, or in which direction it led.
Between the first man and the first woman, a great mountain stood tall, preventing them from meeting each other.

One day, in the heat of summer, by the law of nature, fire broke out in the forest and began to spread in all directions. The fire circled the mountain, racing swiftly. The man and the woman realized that if they entered the forest, they would be in danger, and so they climbed up the mountain. At the summit, they saw each other. Their eyes met and remained locked, unblinking. They forgot the forest fire. They forgot why they had climbed to the mountaintop. They forgot hunger and thirst entirely. By an inner knowledge, they understood that all the life they had lived so far was for this one meeting. They realized that this was the unknown force that had drawn them together. They understood that the lack in one could be filled and completed by the other. They knew with certainty that no power in the world could ever separate those who had thus come together. The divine creator, Brahmadeva, who beheld this wondrous scene, felt a profound and perfect satisfaction, realizing that the work he had begun was now proceeding in the finest manner!

At that moment, our Vallavarayan and Kundavai Devi resembled that primordial man and woman spoken of in ancient tales. Their innermost feelings told them that all their birth and growth upon this earth had been for this very instant—for this meeting. Yet, unlike those first man and woman, were they not children of civilization? Therefore, they could not forget the differences in their respective stations. They did not surrender themselves entirely to emotion, nor did they let their hearts run wild and unrestrained. For a moment, their eyes met and gazed deep into each other’s, and in the next instant, they turned their gaze aside to look at the flowers, trees, butterflies, and the stream nearby.
Only after Isana Sivapattar cleared his throat did the two remember that they had come together here for some important purpose.
“Is it true that you asked Isana Pattar to arrange a private meeting with me?” the young princess inquired, her voice sharpened and her tone commanding.
The sternness and authority in her voice made Vandiyathevan stand up straight.
“How can I answer your question unless I know who you are? I am beginning to suspect that Isana Pattar has brought me to the wrong person!” replied the young warrior.
“I, too, have the same suspicion. Whom did you wish to see?”

“I told Isana Sivapattar that I wished to see the shining jewel of the ancient Chola lineage, the beloved daughter of Sundara Chola, the younger sister of Aditya Karikalan, the cherished sister of Arulmozhi Varman, the young princess Kundavai Devi…”
Kundavai Devi smiled and said, “I am indeed the one who bears all those great titles, though I can barely withstand the weight of such honor!”
“In that case, the radiant lady I saw at the house of the Kudanthai astrologer and on the banks of the Arisil river was not you, was she?” asked Vallavarayan.
“Yes, yes! It was I who behaved so discourteously toward you in both those places. You could not have expected to meet that uncivilized maiden again so soon, could you?”
“It is not quite right to say we shall meet again, Devi!”
“Why not?”
“Only if we had parted could we speak of meeting again, could we not? But you have not left my thoughts for even a single moment…”
“I did not expect the people of Thondai Mandalam to speak with such subtle wit.”
“You would grant all greatness only to the land of Cholas, it seems. You will not bestow even a little honor upon other lands.”
“Yes, I confess I am guilty of that. Perhaps you do not like our Chola country!”
“How could I not? I like it very much indeed. But there are two great dangers in this Chola land. The mere thought of them fills me with fear…”
“The swords and spears of Chola warriors are indeed dangerous weapons! Foreigners must tread carefully here—especially those who come to work as spies…”
“Princess! Those are not the two dangers I meant. I too possess a sword and spear. I know well how to wield them…”

“Did I not witness the might of your spear that day on the banks of the Arisil river? How swiftly your spear struck the dead crocodile! With a single blow, you brought out all the cotton that was packed inside it!”

“Lady! I did not know that the noblewomen of Chola land were so brave as to die of fright at the sight of a dead crocodile. Nor did I know that Chola warriors are such pure heroes as to attack only dead crocodiles. I hurled my spear thinking it was alive. That was my mistake that day; or rather, the mistake of my spear…”

“The fault was that of the foolish crocodile! Did it not die before the valiant Vandiyathevan of the Vanar clan could come with his spear? It well deserves this disgrace! But what were the two other dangers you spoke of?”
“When new floods come to the rivers of this Chola land, the whirlpools that form are perilous! One should never trust them. They tossed and tormented me greatly!”
“How did you come to be caught in the midst of the flood? Looking at you, one would think you would not even set foot in water!”

“If a Vedalam’s life depended on it, would he not climb a drumstick tree, even if he swore he wouldn’t? For the sake of my mission to Chola Nadu, I ended up plunging into the river’s flood and getting trapped in its whirlpools! It happened because of the stubbornness of a reckless boy who accompanied me. Listen, Devi! That boy claimed he could not utter even the smallest lie. That is how all this trouble began…”
“Your words are rather enigmatic. It would be better if you explained a little more clearly.”

“I shall. I came as a messenger bearing your esteemed brother’s letter, but the commander of the Tanjore fort, the Younger Pazhuvettarayar, accused me of being a spy and sent men to arrest me. I did not wish to be imprisoned before completing my mission. So I summoned the boy from the house where I was staying in Tanjore to guide me, and set out with him…”
“In whose house did you stay in Tanjore city?”
“Outside the fort, I stayed at the house of a flower-seller woman. That lady is mute.”
“Oh! What is her name?”
“I do not know her name; but I do know her son’s name. He is called Sendhan Amudhan…”
“I thought as much; go on!”

“I mounted that boy on my horse and set out for this city of Pazhaiyarai. By then, some of Pazhuvettarayar’s men had already begun to close in on us. I did not wish to be caught by them before my task was done. When we reached the Kudamuruti river, I told the boy, ‘I will get down here, little brother! You take the horse and ride on to your mother. They will think you are me and continue to chase you. Once they catch you, they will be disappointed! If they ask where I am, tell them I fell into the river and was swept away!’ But that boy must be a descendant of Harishchandra himself. ‘How can I lie and say you drowned when you haven’t?’ he protested. To spare the boy from having to tell a lie, I tied him securely to the horse and plunged myself into the river. Oh, my! The rivers of Chola Nadu, especially near the banks, what whirlpools they hold! Caught in one of those, I…” I struggled greatly. In the end, I grasped hold of the root of a tree that was at the riverbank, and, clinging to it, I managed to pull myself ashore and escape with my life. Devi! Do you know what I saw, what I thought of, as I was caught in that whirlpool, spinning round and round, my senses reeling, breathless and tormented?”
“How could I possibly know? Perhaps you thought of Gajendra Moksha…”

“No, no; I saw some kaval fish caught in the same whirlpool, struggling just as I was. Those kaval fish reminded me of the eyes of the women of this Chola land. A man caught in the river’s whirlpool may somehow escape; but a man caught in the whirlpool of the eyes of Chola women can never escape, not in any lifetime! That is what I thought…”
“For some, there is a strange pride in blaming women thus; it is the custom of men to lay the fault for their own misdeeds upon women…”
“I too have adopted that custom. What wrong is there in it?” said Vandiyathevan.

At that moment, from within the palace, the sweet sound of flutes was heard. Following it came the tinkling of anklets and the deep resonance of drums. Then, the melodious voices of young women rose together in song. They sang the following shepherdess’ kuravai song from the epic Silappadikaram:

“If the Lord who made the fruit fall for the calf’s staff Should come into our midst today, Shall we not hear the sweet flute at his lips, friend? If the Lord who broke the kurundu branch in the wild Should come into our midst today, Shall we not hear the sweet flute at his lips, friend?”
Until the song ended, Kundavai and Vandiyathevan stood enraptured, lost in its sweetness. Again, with the blare of instruments, the sound of anklets signaled the start of the dance.
“It seems the kuravai dance is being performed in the palace! I saw a kuravai dance at Kadambur Palace. That was entirely different!” said Vallavaraiyan.
“Yes; my companions are practicing the Kuravai dance. Very soon, if they do not see me, they will begin searching for me. What is the purpose of your visit?” asked the young princess Kundavai Devi.

“This, here, is the purpose of my coming; a letter from your brother. Escaping countless dangers, from whirlpools of water—and whirlpools of eyes—I have protected it and brought it to you!” said Vallavarayan, taking out the letter and extending it to her.

chapters.title: Stranger Than Strange!
paragraphs: Princess Kundavai took the palm-leaf letter that Vandiyathevan extended to her and read it. Until then, her face, which had been drawn tight with furrowed brows, now blossomed and shone with radiance.
She looked up at Vallavaraiyan and asked, “You have delivered the letter. What do you intend to do next?”
“My duty is done once I have handed over the letter to you. Now, I must return to my town.”
“Your work is not finished; it has only just begun!”
“I do not understand what you mean, Devi!”
“Does not the prince write here that you are worthy of being entrusted with even the most secret of tasks? Will you not act accordingly?”
“I came here having agreed to that with the prince. But I beg you, do not entrust any important task to me. I earnestly request this of you.”
“I do not understand your request. Is it the way of the Vanar clan to withdraw after once giving their word?”
“To boast of ancient glory is not the Vanar tradition; nor is it our way to go back on our word after agreeing to something.”
“Then why this hesitation? Is it some aversion you bear towards women? Or is it that you do not like me?” asked the princess, a gentle smile playing on her lips.

Ah! What a question is this? Would the sea ever not desire the moon? If it did not, why would it stretch out its thousand arms of waves, leaping to clasp the full moon? Who would say the earth does not long for the blue sky? If it did not, why would it gaze all night with a thousand thousand starry eyes, brimming with yearning? Would the cloud not desire the lightning? If it did not, why would it split itself and fiercely embrace the lightning, pressing it to its breast? Is there such a thing as a bee not loving the flower? If so, why would it ceaselessly circle the flower, intoxicated, and fall upon it? Would anyone believe that the moth does not love the lamp? If so, why does it whirl around the lamp’s... Does it die when it falls into the light? Devi! You have asked a fine question! If I do not like you, then why does the glance from the corner of your eye leave me so bewildered? Why does the gentle smile that plays at the edge of your lips drive me to such a state of delirium?… All these thoughts arose in Vandiyathevan’s heart. Yet, he could not utter them aloud.

“Sir! You have not answered my question. Is the brave man born of the Vanar clan hesitant to carry out the bidding of a mere woman? When the prince gave you this letter, did he not tell you what was written in it?” the princess asked again.

“Devi! I set out fully understanding the prince’s wishes. But now it seems fortunate that I did not begin my journey at once. Along the way, I have made enemies at every turn. I have even turned a close friend into a foe. On all sides, enemies are searching for me. In such a situation, how can I promise to fulfill the task you entrust to me? That is why I hesitate. I would not wish for your mission to fail because of me,” said Vallavaraiyan.
“Who are these enemies? May I know?” Kundavai asked, her voice tinged with concern.

“The Pazhuvettaraiyars have sent men everywhere to hunt me down. Kandhamaran, who was once my dearest friend, now believes I tried to stab him in the back. A valiant Vaishnavite in disguise, known as Alwarkadiyan, is trailing me. The young queen of Pazhuvur, Nandini Devi, has set a sorcerer upon me. At any moment, I may fall into the hands of one or another—I do not know when or where…”

The memory of that night, when he escaped the flood only to encounter the sorcerer, flashed through Vandiyathevan’s mind. Fearing the dangers of traveling by day, he had spent his time hiding in bamboo groves and plantain orchards. At night, he walked along the riverbank. After journeying a great distance and growing weary, he reached an abandoned old mandapam in the third watch of the night. Outside, the moon shone as brightly as midday. Even inside the mandapam, the moonlight streamed in for some distance, illuminating the place. Passing through the lit area, Vandiyathevan lay down in the shadowed part. As sleep began to close around his eyes, the ominous hoot of an owl sounded very close by.

When he was speaking with the younger queen of Pazhuvoor in the Latha Mandapam, that same owl-like voice echoed in his memory, startling him to his feet. From the darkened part of the hall, two small points of light stared intently at him.

He thought to slip outside and took two steps forward. At that moment, he heard the sound of footsteps approaching from outside. Grasping a crumbling, jagged pillar, he hid himself behind it. The face of the one entering was faintly visible in the moonlight.

He realized it was the sorcerer who had come to see the queen of Pazhuvoor. The sorcerer walked straight toward the pillar. Vandiyathevan thought the man did not know he was hiding there and would pass by into the mandapam without noticing him. But as the sorcerer drew near, he crept forward like a cat, and suddenly, with a fearsome cry, seized Vandiyathevan’s throat with one hand and twisted it.
"Give it! Hand over that palmyra signet ring! If you refuse, I’ll wring your neck and kill you!" he shouted.

Vandiyathevan felt as if his neck would snap; his eyes seemed about to pop from their sockets. He struggled to breathe. Yet he steeled his mind. With one hand, he pressed against the old pillar, lifted one leg, and with all his strength, delivered a powerful kick. The sorcerer howled and fell to the ground. At that very moment, the ancient pillar collapsed. Stones tumbled down from the roof above with a clatter. A bat flapped its wings and flew out. Following it, Vandiyathevan too made his escape. He did not look back until he had run some distance. Only after he was certain that no one was pursuing him did he stop. Even now, the memory of that night made Vandiyathevan’s whole body shudder with fear.
Amidst those terrifying recollections, Kundavai’s voice fell upon his ears, bringing clarity to his mind: "Sir, how long has it been since you set out from Kanchi?"
"It has been one week and one day, Devi!" he replied.
"In such a short time, you have managed to earn so many enemies—truly, it is a wonder upon wonders. How did you accomplish such a marvelous feat?"
"That is a long story, Devi!"
“In that case, there is no harm. You may speak. Only after I have learned those details can I assign you the task I wish to entrust to you.”
So saying, the princess called Eesana Sivapattar close and asked, “What sort of man is the boatman?”
“Both his ears are quite deaf; even if thunder strikes, he will not hear it, my lady!”
“Very good. Let us board the boat and go a little way down the canal and return! Come! I wish to hear his story in full!” she said.

Vallavaraiyan was elated. Was it an easy fortune to travel in the same boat as the noble daughter of the Chola clan? Would one not have to perform penance for seven lifetimes to earn such a blessing? Once aboard the boat, he must stretch and embellish his tale as far as possible! He must not bring it to a swift conclusion! What was the hurry? Should he let slip so rare a fortune so easily?

Vandiyathevan was in no hurry, indeed. But as the boat glided along the canal and he began to recount all that had transpired at Kadambur Sambuvaraiyar’s palace, Kundavai’s impatience and excitement grew with every passing minute. “What happened next?” “And then?” she kept urging him on. Vandiyathevan, true to his resolve, spun out the story as much as he could. Yet, however long a tale may be, it must come to an end, must it not? By the time the story concluded, the boat too had returned to the landing at the edge of the canal.

When they disembarked and entered the flower garden, the sounds of musical instruments and anklets could still be heard from the palace, a sign that the Kuravai dance was still in progress. The following lines from the Silappathikaram were also heard:
“The great one, the mysterious one, throughout the wide world...”

He whose eyes, holy feet, hands, and divine lips are crimson as the spreading lotus, He who is dark as the raincloud—what use are eyes that have not beheld Him? What use are the eyes that merely blink and see the world, but not Him? He who crossed the deceit of Kamsa, whose heart was sunk in evil, He who was praised by a hundred sages and worshipped in all four directions, He who went as a messenger to the Pandavas, with the conch’s roar resounding, What use is a tongue that does not praise Him? What use is a tongue that does not utter, “Narayana!”?
Hearing this, Vallavarayan said, “Kamsa may have been the most deceitful of men! But yesterday, he did me a great favor!”
“What is this? How could Kamsan have helped you?” asked the young princess.
“It was Kamsan who helped me enter this city!” replied Vandiyathevan. Then he recounted the tale of that help.

Vandiyathevan had guessed that before he could reach Pazhaiyarai, the men of the Pazhuvettaraiyars would have already arrived. At every gate of the city, they would be waiting. If they suspected anything, they would seize him at once. How could he enter the city of Pazhaiyarai without falling into their hands? With this worry, Vandiyathevan stood for a while on the banks of the Arisil river, a short distance from the main gate of that great city. At that moment, a troupe of actors arrived. Among them were those dressed as Krishna, Balarama, and Kamsa. Only the one playing Kamsa wore a wooden mask. An idea struck Vandiyathevan. He struck up a conversation with the troupe. He claimed that the man playing Kamsa did not have enough skill in acting. The man in the Kamsa costume challenged him to a contest. Would Vallavarayan, who had faced so many perils, shrink from such a contest? “I can dance better than you. Shall I show you?” he said, and forcibly snatched the mask from the actor’s face and began to dance with it himself. The crowd, delighted by his energetic performance, applauded him. They said his dance was far more fitting for the role. The actor who had played Kamsa, angered, walked away. “Let him go; “I myself will come with you into the city and dance,” agreed Vandiyathevan. The troupe of performers, delighted, included him among them and set off together.

After all the dances and songs had ended in the streets of Pazhayarai, Vandiyathevan, as per the instructions given by Aditya Karikalan, went to the northern Isana temple and met with Isana Bhattar. The priest made him wait in the Jain cloister surrounding the temple, sent word ahead to Princess Kundavai, and then led him through the garden path.

Hearing all these details, the princess looked at Vandiyathevan with eyes blossoming in wonder and said, “The victorious goddess, the patron deity of triumph, has bestowed her full grace upon this Chola dynasty. That is why, in this time of distress, she has sent you to me as the goddess’s own aid!”
“My lady! I have not yet been given any task by you. The time to prove the full extent of my abilities has not yet come!” said Vallavarayan.
“Do not worry about that. I am about to entrust you with a task so fraught with danger that all the perils you have faced so far will seem like nothing in comparison!” she replied.

Vandiyathevan’s heart swelled and his body stood tall with pride. To fulfill the task set by this princess, he was ready to cross seven seas, to fight unarmed against a thousand lions, to climb to the summit of Mount Meru and pluck the stars from the sky with his own hands.
In the center of the palace gardens stood a spring pavilion made of crystal. Kundavai walked toward it. The priest and Vandiyathevan followed the princess.
From a bell tower within the pavilion, Kundavai took a small strip of palm leaf and a stylus with a golden handle. On the palm leaf, she wrote as follows:
“Ponniyin Selva! Upon seeing this letter, set out at once. The bearer will explain the details. You may trust him completely.”

Having written thus, she drew at the bottom a small symbol resembling a leaf of the sacred Aathi tree. Extending the palm leaf toward Vandiyathevan, she said, “Without the slightest delay, you must take this letter and go to Eezha Nadu. Give it to Prince Arulmozhi Varman and bring him back with you at once!”

Vandiyathevan was tossed and buffeted by waves of joy. One of the two dreams he had cherished for so long had now come true. He had met the young princess, the shining lamp of the Chola clan. And through her, his second dream too was about to be fulfilled. The fortune of meeting Prince Arulmozhi Varman was within his grasp.
“Devi! You are granting me the very task my heart desires. I shall take the letter and set out at once!” he exclaimed, stretching out his right hand to receive the scroll.

As Kundavai handed him the letter, her fingers—delicate as the petals of the blue lily—brushed against Vandiyathevan’s lucky hand. A shiver ran through his body; his heart felt as if it would burst. Thousands upon thousands of silk-winged butterflies fluttered before his eyes. Thousands upon thousands of cuckoos joined together in melodious song. Mountains of brilliantly colored flowers seemed to rain down upon him, scattering in every direction.
In that moment, Vandiyathevan lifted his head and looked at Princess Kundavai. His heart surged with things he longed to say. But what power did lifeless words have to express such feelings?

All that he wished to say, his eyes alone conveyed. At that instant, even Kalidasa could not have composed love poems to match the verses Vandiyathevan’s eyes wove, nor could the ancient Tamil poets who created the ‘Muttollāyiram’ have equaled them—what more can be said?
Outside the Vasantha Mandapam, somewhere in the distance, dry leaves and twigs rustled with a soft sound. Isana Sivapattar raised his voice in a resonant chant.
Vandiyathevan returned to the world of men!

chapters.title: Paranthakar’s Hospital
paragraphs: The next morning, as the Sun God rose and bathed the world in light, his crimson rays fell upon the golden domes of the palaces of Pazhaiyarai, making them gleam and shimmer. In front of Princess Kundavai’s palace, a grand elephant, adorned and caparisoned, stood waiting with an ambari mounted upon its back. Kundavai and Vanathi emerged from within the palace, ascended the steps of the portico, and mounted the elephant. The mighty beast set off, its tread shaking the earth, making its way toward the Paranthaka Chola Hospital, which stood amidst the soldiers’ quarters.

The mahout walked beside the elephant, restraining its pace and guiding it gently. Hearing the sound of the elephant’s bells, the townspeople hurried out from their homes to see what was happening. When they saw the two royal women, their faces blossomed with joy; they stood with folded hands and bowed in respect.

Passing through various streets, the elephant entered the part of the city where the soldiers’ quarters were located. The appearance of these streets was quite unique. Plump red roosters wandered about, searching for rivals to fight. Rams with twisted, curling horns stood here and there, looking around as if challenging anyone to battle. Fierce hunting dogs, whether with leather leashes or bejeweled ropes, were tied to the pillars at the thresholds of houses. Little children, holding bamboo sticks in their hands, played mock duels with one another, the sticks clashing with sharp ‘clack-clack’ and ‘thud-thud’ sounds.

On the walls of the verandas, various scenes were painted with saffron-colored chalk. Most depicted the divine exploits of Lord Muruga and the historical deeds of the Chola kings. Scenes of war were especially prominent. There were vivid images of Lord Muruga striking down the heads of the demon Surapadman as they sprouted anew, and of Goddess Durga slaying the buffalo demon Mahishasura—both rendered with terrifying intensity. The walls also portrayed, in lifelike detail, the wondrous feats of valor performed by Chola warriors in battlefields such as Thellaru, Thanjai, Kudamooku, Arisilaru, Thiruppurambayam, Vellur, Thakkolam, and Sevur.

As the elephant bearing the princesses entered these soldiers’ quarters, the entire street was thrown into a flurry of excitement. The roosters flapped their wings noisily and flew up to perch on rooftops, crowing loudly. The children shouted to one another, calling out in excitement… They ran. Knocking on the doors of their houses, they informed those inside of the news.

As the elephant made its way through the streets lined with soldiers’ homes, women, children, and elders stood at every threshold, joyfully hailing, “Long live the young princess Kundavai Devi!” “Long live the cherished daughter of Sundara Chozhar!” Some among them even began to follow the elephant. The crowd grew larger and larger. Through a chorus of varied blessings, they expressed their happiness as they went along.

It has already been mentioned that in those soldier’s quarters lived the wives, children, and parents of warriors who had gone to wage war in Lanka. For their welfare, Kundavai had established a hospital using the income from her own land grants. The Chola clan was renowned for their tradition of honoring their ancestors. Among Kundavai’s forebears, her grandfather’s father, the first Paranthaka Chakravarthi, was especially famous. To keep his name alive, Kundavai Devi had founded and managed this ‘Paranthakar Hospital.’ It was her custom to visit the hospital often, using that opportunity to inquire about the well-being of the families of the warriors.

As they neared the hospital, the elephant came to a halt. First folding its front legs, then its hind legs, it knelt down and settled on the ground. The two princesses descended from the elephant to the earth.
Once the elephant moved aside, the crowd—mainly women and children—pressed in, surrounding the princesses.
“The hospital has been useful to all of you, hasn’t it? The physicians come every day and give medicine to those in need, do they not?” the princess asked.
“Yes, Mother! Yes!” came the reply from many voices.
“For three months, I suffered from a cough. After taking medicine from the physician for a week, I was cured!” said one woman.

“Amma! My son climbed a tree and fell, breaking his leg. The physician set the bone and gave him medicine for fifteen days. He is well now. He runs and plays, and has even started climbing trees again!” said another woman.
“My mother’s eyesight had been failing for some time. For a month, she came to this infirmary to receive treatment. Now, her vision is clear once again!” said a young woman.
“Did you hear that, Vanathi? What remarkable people our ancestors of Tamilagam must have been! How did they discover which herb could cure which disease? It is a wonder!” exclaimed Princess Kundavai.
“They must have possessed the eye of wisdom to discover such miraculous medicines. How else could it be possible?” replied Vanathi.

“It is true—they discovered so many wondrous remedies. Yet, for those who suffer from maladies of the mind, like you, no medicine has been found! What can be done?” said Kundavai, her voice tinged with gentle teasing.
“Akka! I have no such affliction of the mind. Please, do not say such things with such compassion again and again! My friends never cease to tease me and torment my very soul!” protested Vanathi.

“You deserve it! My brother, who lived his life without a care in the world, now finds his heart troubled because of you. Every time someone comes from Lanka, he sends word asking after your health!” said the young princess with a mischievous smile.

At that moment, a cry arose: “Make way for the physician! Make way for the physician!” The guards parted the crowd that had gathered there. The aged chief physician of the infirmary approached and respectfully greeted the princesses.
“Physician! Did you not say that there are rare herbs in the forests near Kodikkarai? I sent a young warrior there to fetch them. Has he returned?” Kundavai inquired.

“Yes, my lady! That energetic young man has come. Isana Sivapattar brought him here. I am sending my own son along with him. My son will return from Kodikkarai soon. The warrior you sent says he will go as far as the island of Lanka…”
“Must we even bring herbs from Lanka?” asked Vanathi in surprise.

“Yes, my lady! When Hanuman brought the Sanjeevani mountain to save Lakshmana’s life, it is said he crossed the sea by way of Kodikkarai. Some herbs from the Sanjeevani mountain fell into the forests of Kodikkarai, and that is why rare herbs are still found there today. In Lanka, the Sanjeevani mountain itself—” Therefore, even now, rare herbs can be found there, can they not? If only I can obtain the herbs I am hoping for, I myself will certainly cure the Emperor’s illness…”
“By God’s grace, let it be so. Now, where are those two young men?”
“They are inside, Amma! They are waiting to bid you farewell and depart, prepared for their journey!”

At the chief physician’s summons, the two princes entered the infirmary. They walked through the corridors, observing those who had come to collect medicine and those waiting for treatment. Upon seeing Kundavai Piratti, everyone’s faces and hearts blossomed, and they praised the princess for establishing such a fine hospital for them.

In the chief physician’s chamber, two men awaited. Among them, our Vandiyathevan was dressed in a new manner, and the younger princess smiled upon seeing him. Vanathi, too, recognized the brave youth in some way. Leaning close to Kundavai’s ear, she whispered, “Akka! He looks like the one we saw at the Kudanthai astrologer’s house!”

“I thought so too. After seeing the astrologer, he has come to the physician. Like you, he seems to have some strange affliction of the mind!” Kundavai replied, then turned to Vandiyathevan and asked, “Well, sir! Are you the one who agreed to go to Lanka to fetch herbs for the Emperor’s health?”

Vandiyathevan’s eyes and eyelids spoke in some secret language of their own. With his lips, he replied, “Yes, Princess! I am the one going to Lanka. If by chance I see the prince there, shall I convey any message to him?”

“If you do see him, you must certainly deliver this message: The Princess Vanathi of Kodumbalur is not well. She often loses consciousness and faints. If he wishes to see the princess in her full senses, he must return at once,” said the younger princess.

“I shall deliver the message exactly as you say, Ammanni!” Vandiyathevan replied, turning to look at Vanathi. At Kundavai’s words, Vanathi’s sweet face, flushed with shyness, grew many times more beautiful and radiant. Struggling to master her embarrassment and confusion, Vanathi stammered, “Sir! There is no need for you to say such a thing—” “Don’t forget. I earnestly request you. Please inform them that Vanathi of Kodumbalur is living in comfort, eating well and dressed in fine clothes, under the care of the Young Princess,” she said.
“I will convey it exactly as you say, Ammani!” replied Vandiyathevan.
“How wonderful! Whatever I say, you promise to convey ‘exactly as it is.’ Now, you agree to convey what she says ‘exactly as it is’ too? Only one of these can be true, can it not?”

“What does it matter, Ammani! I will report both the plaintiff’s and the defendant’s words just as they are. Let the prince himself act as judge and decide which is true and which is not!” said Vandiyathevan.
“But do not simply swap what one says for what the other said and report it! You will earn great merit!” said Vanathi.
Kundavai, wishing to end this conversation, asked, “Vaidyar! Did you receive the letter from the palace’s chief minister to be given to them?”

“I did, Lady! There is a general letter stating, ‘As these people are bringing medicinal herbs for the Emperor’s treatment, all government officials along the way must render any assistance they require.’ There is also a special letter for the guards at the Kodikkarai lighthouse. I have handed both to them!” replied the physician.
“In that case, why the delay? You must depart at once, must you not?” said the Young Princess Kundavai.
“Yes, we must depart at once!” said Vandiyathevan.
But setting out immediately was not so simple.

They left the hospital and came outside. The howdah elephant stood waiting to carry the royal princesses. Two palace horses, pawing the ground impatiently, were ready to carry Vandiyathevan and his companion, flying like the wind.

Yet, doubts kept arising suddenly and unexpectedly in Vandiyathevan’s mind. Kundavai, too, kept thinking of new warnings to give. She cautioned them especially about the dangers they might encounter along the way.
The royal princesses mounted the howdah atop the elephant. After them, Vandiyathevan and his companion mounted their horses.
The elephant did not set off immediately. Kundavai, with a mere gesture, indicated that those undertaking a long journey should depart first.

Vandiyathevan, his heart reluctant, turned his horse with hesitation. Once more, his eyes brimming with yearning, he glanced back at the princess. Then, as if angered, he struck his horse with a sharp kick. The spirited animal, stung by his command, leapt forward and galloped away at full speed. The physician’s son, following after him, had to struggle to keep up.

After the elephant began to turn and proceed on its way, Kundavai sank into deep thought. What a strange nature this heart possesses! This heart that has rejected emperors among kings and heroes among warriors—why does it now show such concern for this young man, a mere traveler who has come by chance? Why does she worry so much that he should successfully complete the task he has undertaken and return safely?...
“Sister! What are you thinking about?” Vanathi’s voice brought Kundavai back to this world.
“Nothing, Vanathi! I was just thinking about that young man’s proud and haughty nature. I am beginning to wonder why we sent him with a message to my brother…”
“Yes, sister! He is a very mischievous fellow! Sometimes I even think he is a great thief…”
“What is this? Why do you call him a thief?”

“Ordinary thieves steal gold, silver, and other worthless things. But I fear this young man might steal away the very guardian deity of the Chola land itself. You won’t let that happen, will you?” said Vanathi.
“You little rogue! Did you think I am like you? Such a thing will never happen!” Kundavai replied.

As the elephant proceeded a short distance down the street, the royal maidens saw a crowd of women gathered at one spot. Ordering the elephant to stop, the young princess Kundavai asked, “Why are you all gathered here? Is there something you wish to say?”

One among those women stepped forward and asked, “Mother! We have received no news at all about our husbands who are in Lanka! We hear that the people of Thanjavur have forbidden us from sending rice to them. Amma, how can they fight without food in their stomachs?”

“For that, you need not worry,” replied the young princess. “From the port of Mamallapuram, the necessary grain is being sent to them. Whatever the people of Thanjavur may do, do you think your prince will simply stand by? Will he allow the great heroes of Chola Nadu to go hungry and lie in want?”

Had it been another occasion, Kundavai would have descended right there and offered further comfort to those women. But now, her mind was troubled by a different kind of unrest, and she longed for solitude. The elephant proceeded toward the palace.

chapters.title: Mamallapuram
paragraphs: We now wish to take our readers, who are already well acquainted with Mamallapuram, once more to that place.
It has been more than three hundred years since the time when Mahendra Pallava and Mamalla Narasimha transformed this port city into a dreamland through their wondrous works of sculpture.

The city’s appearance has somewhat faded. The change does not bring joy to our hearts. Tall mansions have crumbled and lie in ruins. There is no longer the bustling crowd in the streets and at the harbor as there once was. The thriving trade has diminished. There are no longer great warehouses. The streets are not piled high with mountains of goods for export and import.

Once, we saw how the sea had entered the land, forming a deep canal, creating a natural harbor where ships could safely anchor. Now, that canal has silted up with sand, its depth greatly reduced. Only small boats and canoes can now enter that shallow backwater. The larger ships and wooden vessels must anchor farther out at sea. Goods must be loaded onto boats and ferried out to those ships.

Yet, during the intervening years, Mamallapuram has acquired some new distinctions as well. Most notably, the beautiful stone temple shining on the seashore captivates both our eyes and our minds. It is not like the cave temples hewn into the hills during the time of Mahendra and Mamalla. This temple was built by bringing stones from the hills and assembling them. It gleams like a splendid jeweled crown placed upon the head of the King of the Ocean. Ah! How can one describe the beauty of that temple’s structure?

Besides this, in the center of the city stands the Vishnu temple of Vinnagara, where the Lord who measured the three worlds reclines. This Vinnagara was constructed by Parameswara Pallava, who cherished both Shaivism and Vaishnavism as the two eyes of his realm. Thirumangai Azhwar came to this temple, worshipped the reclining Perumal, and sang Tamil hymns that overflowed with waves of devotion. From his verses, we learn that even in his time, the Pallava empire flourished in glory, and Mamallapuram was a prosperous port city:

“With heaps of precious gems, With mighty tusked elephants, With piles of splendid navaratna stones, I have wandered everywhere, bearing these treasures, In ships that sail the Mallai sea, To the sacred reclining place at Mallai, To those whose minds are full of virtue, Go around them in worship, O my gentle heart!”

A hundred years after the time of Thirumangai Azhwar, the sun of the Pallava Empire had set. The glory of the great city of Kanchi, famed as ‘unmatched in learning’, had diminished. The commercial prosperity of ‘Mallai, where ships sail the sea’, had waned.

Yet, the wondrous sculptural arts of that immortal city, which bestowed everlasting fame upon the Tamil land, suffered no decline. The intricate and marvelous sculptures carved into the rocky walls, the temple towers and chariots hewn from the hills—these, even after three centuries, shone as fresh and resplendent as they did when first created. The crowds who came to marvel at these treasures of sculpture were greater than the throngs of merchants who arrived to trade their wares.

Along the streets of Mamallapuram, a beautiful chariot drawn by a pair of horses made its way. The horses’ ornaments, the exquisite craftsmanship of the chariot, the golden plates that adorned it, and the canopy that gleamed in the afternoon sun like a second sun—all these proclaimed that those within belonged to royal blood.

Yes; within the spacious interior of that golden chariot sat three members of the royal family. One among them was himself, the bravest of the brave, the eldest son of Sundara Chola—Aditya Karikalan. From a very young age, he had entered the battlefield and performed heroic deeds of valor. He slew the mighty Veerapandiyan in the final battle, earning the title “Kopperakesari who took the head of Veerapandiyan.”

No sooner had Veerapandiyan attained the warrior’s heaven and the Pandya country come under the Chola Empire than Sundara Chola fell ill. Aditya Karikalan was the next... To establish without a shadow of doubt that he was the rightful heir to the throne, Aditya Karikalan was invested with the title of Crown Prince. From that moment, he gained the privilege of inscribing his name on the royal edicts and issuing decrees in his own right, as recorded in the earliest inscriptions.

Subsequently, in order to liberate the Thondai Mandalam entirely from the dominance of Kannara Devan of the twin kingdoms, Aditya Karikalan set out on a northern campaign. There, too, he performed many valiant deeds on the battlefield. He drove the armies of the twin kingdoms north of the Vadapennai river. To continue his northern campaign, it became necessary to augment his military strength. Therefore, he came to Kanchipuram, where he began to assemble his forces and gather the weapons and equipment needed for the campaign.

At this juncture, the Pazhuvettarayar chieftains began to obstruct his efforts. They insisted that the northern campaign could only commence after the war in Lanka was concluded. Various other rumors began to drift through the air. It was said that the army sent to wage war in Lanka was not receiving the necessary food supplies from Chola Nadu. All these matters caused the valiant heart of Aditya Karikalan to burn with restlessness and agitation.

For about three hundred years before and after the time in which our story unfolds, the sacred womb of Mother Tamil gave birth to heroic sons who rivaled the great warriors of the epics. Heroes who matched Bhima, Arjuna, Bhishma, Drona, Ghatotkacha, and Abhimanyu were born in Tamilakam. They performed feats of valor that astonished the world. Every victory they achieved in battle added further strength to their shoulders. The elders, even in their advanced age, possessed the might to move mountains. The young men, though not yet of age, had the power to soar through the air, touch the vault of the heavens, and scatter the stars.
At that very time, two such warriors were seated beside Aditya Karikalan in the chariot he had mounted, sharing the same seat with him.
One of them was Thirukovalur Malayaman. The land he ruled, Malayamanadu, was commonly called ‘Maladu’ or ‘Miladu’ for short. Hence, he was known by the honorific title ‘Miladudaiyar.’

Vanamadevi, the second queen of Emperor Sundara Chola, was his beloved daughter. Thus, he was the maternal grandfather of Aditya Karikalan. Though advanced in age and endowed with profound wisdom, he resembled Bhishma, the grandsire of the Kauravas. Even though Aditya Karikalan held him in great reverence, the old man’s shrewd intellect sometimes tested the patience of the young prince.

Among those in the chariot, another was Parthibendran. He hailed from a collateral branch of the ancient Pallava lineage. He was a few years older than Aditya Karikalan. Deprived of royal rights, he sought to establish his valor and fame on the battlefield. He had joined Aditya Karikalan and, in the war against Veerapandiyan, had served as his right hand. Because of this, he became one of Aditya Karikalan’s closest confidants. From the day Veerapandiyan fell, the two had become inseparable friends.
As these three traveled in the chariot, they were discussing the alarming news that had arrived from Thanjavur.

“I can no longer bear, even for a moment, the arrogance of these Pazhuvettarayars. Day by day, they are exceeding all bounds. How much pride must they have to accuse the messenger I sent of being a spy? They have even announced a reward of a thousand gold coins for anyone who captures him! How can I tolerate all this? The sword in my scabbard has dulled in disgrace. Yet you preach patience to me!” said Aditya Karikalan.

“I am not preaching patience. But I did say at the time that Vandiyathevan should not be sent on such an important mission. I knew that hothead would ruin everything! Is it enough to simply know how to wield a sword or throw a spear? One sent on royal business must possess sharp intelligence…” said Parthibendran.

The affection Prince Karikalan showed Vandiyathevan was not to Parthibendran’s liking. He was always finding fault with him, always criticizing whatever he did. So, even on this occasion, he spoke in the same vein.

“Have you started your story again? If you don’t find something to say about Vandiyathevan, your day won’t pass. If he lacks intelligence, then who else possesses it? In one way or another, he fulfilled the command I gave him—to deliver the letter directly to the Emperor. That is why the Pazhuvettarayars are enraged. In this, what fault is there of Vandiyathevan?” asked Aditya Karikalan.
“He wouldn’t have stopped with the task you assigned him. He must have meddled in other unnecessary matters as well!” said Parthibendran.

“Be quiet for a moment! Grandfather! Why are you sitting there in silence? What is your opinion? What if we gather a great army, march to Thanjavur, rescue the Emperor, and bring him here to Kanchi? How long are we to simply watch while the Pazhuvettaraiyars keep the Emperor imprisoned as if he were their captive? How long are we to waste away our days in fear of the Pazhuvettaraiyars?” thundered Aditya Karikalan.
Thirukovalur Malayaman—Miladudaiyar—who had witnessed and experienced sixty-six battlefields in his lifetime, cleared his throat to reply. In the meantime, the waves of the sea became visible ahead.
“First, let us get down from this chariot, my boy! Let us go and sit in our usual place and talk. I am old now, am I not? It is not easy for me to speak while the chariot is in motion,” he said.

chapters.title: The Old Man’s Wedding
paragraphs: On the seashore of Mamallapuram, there are many small rocks scattered about. At times, the sea swells and its waves crash upon those rocks. At other times, the sea recedes, giving the rocks a chance to dry under the sun. Not even a single one of those small rocks was left untouched by the master sculptors of Mamallapuram. According to the nature of each stone, they imagined grand or delicate scenes and carved upon them imperishable sculptures.

It was to such a place, where two small rocks stood facing each other, that Aditya Karikalan and his two companions came. They alighted from their chariot and walked towards the rocks. Considering the two stones as twin thrones, Karikalan and Malayaman seated themselves upon them. Parthibendran stood a little apart from them. Waves frequently rolled in, wetting them up to their knees. Sometimes, the spray thrown up by the waves as they struck the rocks would shower upon them like a rain of pearls. A little distance away, boats moved in rows, slicing through the sea, laden with various goods. Men were unloading these goods from the boats and transferring them onto large wooden ships anchored nearby.
“My heart boils when I think that all the goods we have gathered for the twin-pronged invasion must be sent to Lanka!” said Parthibendran.

“What of it?” replied Aditya Karikalan. “The brave warriors conscripted from Chola land are in Lanka. They are winning victory after victory on the battlefield. They have captured Anuradhapura, where the kings of Lanka have ruled for a thousand years, and have planted the flag of triumph there. Should such warriors be left to starve and die?”

“Who said they should be left so?” asked Parthibendran. “Of course, food supplies must be sent. But they should be shipped from Nagapattinam port in Chola land, or from Sethukarai in Pandya country. What need is there to send them from this arid Thondai region? I only spoke thinking that this would hinder our own plans to march north with our army!”

“When I think of it, my heart too burns with rage. I cannot fathom what those wretched Pazhuvettaraiyars truly intend. How much longer are we to endure all this? Grandfather! Why do you sit there, lips sealed, saying nothing? Please, open your mouth and speak!” demanded Karikalan.

“My child! These waves of the sea never cease their roaring. Competing with the sea’s tumult, your friend Parthibendran too shouts at the top of his voice. Amidst all this, what am I to say? Age has rendered me feeble…” replied Malayaman, the Lord of Miladu.
“Parthibendra! Be silent for a while. Let Grandfather express his thoughts,” said Aditya Karikalan.

“There, I have shut my mouth. Poor Grandfather! In his advanced age, he has come all the way down from his mountain fortress, enduring so much hardship. How can I speak before him? This sea, however, has no sense at all! It rages on without pause! There is no one to restrain it. It seems our mountain king holds no fear for the lord of the ocean!” said Parthibendran.

“Brother! Parthibendra! There was indeed a time like that. At the mere mention of the name ‘Thirukovalur Malayaman,’ every king in this land would tremble. The Chalukyas of the twin provinces, the Vanakovarayar of Vallam, the Vaidhumba Rayars, the Gangas, and the Kongas—at the sound of the Malayaman name, they would cower like snakes hearing thunder, hiding in their holes. Even the lord of the ocean would keep himself subdued. But now, as this body has grown weak, all have begun to leap and prance. The Pazhuvettaraiyars, who came from the west only yesterday, now seek to cast aside me, a man of a clan a thousand years old! That shall never come to pass! Karikala! You said a moment ago that you do not know the true intent of the Pazhuvettaraiyars. I shall tell you what it is—listen! Their aim is to weaken you and your brother separately. In Lanka, your brother Arulmozhi must suffer defeat, and thus be shamed. Here, you must be made to grow angry with your brother. The two of you must quarrel. And this old man must be made to suffer at the sight! That is their secret purpose…”
So spoke Miladudaiyar with rising fury, when Karikalan interrupted him.

“They will never succeed in that aim, grandfather! No one can ever separate my brother and me. I would give my life for Arulmozhi. Time and again, I feel—should I board a ship and go to Lanka myself? Who knows what hardships he is enduring there! And here I am, living in comfort, eating well, wearing fine clothes, sleeping in the palace, letting the days slip by. My sword and spear are gathering rust. Every moment feels like an age to me. I cannot bear to stay here any longer. Grandfather! Tell me! Shall I board one of these ships loaded with goods and sail to Lanka as well?” asked Karikalan.

“Your Majesty! A splendid idea! You have spoken what I have been thinking for many days. Let us set out, come! There is no use in asking the old man for his opinion. If you ask him, his wisdom will only say, ‘No, wait!’ We can leave as soon as tomorrow. We can take half the Thondai Mandalam army with us. We’ll finish the war in Lanka one way or another, then come straight to Nagapattinam and land there. From there, we’ll go to Thanjavur and teach those Pazhuvettarayar a lesson…” Parthibendran said, pounding his fist in excitement.
“Karikala! Did you see? What did I say at first? Didn’t I tell you I would only speak if he kept his mouth shut?”
“Here, I’m shutting my mouth, grandfather! Say all that you wish to say!” Parthibendran said, clamping his mouth shut with his hand.

“Karikala! You are a hero among heroes. Not many as valiant as you have been born even in this land of valorous Tamils. In my eighty years, I have seen many great battlefields. But never have I seen another warrior who could plunge alone into the midst of the enemy and fight as you do. When the great battle of Sevur was fought, you were not even sixteen. At that age, the speed with which you rushed into the enemy ranks, the way your sword spun left and right, the swiftness with which enemy heads rolled—I have never seen anything like it. That scene still stands vivid before my eyes. Your friend Parthibendran is also a hero among heroes, just like you. But both of you are impulsive; quick to anger. Because of that, your power to think things through is diminished. Whatever must be done, you are seized by the urge to do the opposite…”
“Grandfather! How many times have you given us this same advice before…”
“I have done it. But you say it was of no use? Are you telling me to return to my town without another word?”
“No, no! Tell me now what needs to be done.”
“Your brother Arulmozhi must be brought here at once. You and your brother must not be separated at any cost…”
“Grandfather! What is this idea? If Arulmozhi comes here, what will happen to the war in Lanka?”

“The Lankan war has reached a certain stage now; Anuradhapura has been captured. Now it is the rainy season there. For the next four months, nothing can be done. The only task is to hold on to what has been won and guard it without losing ground. The other commanders will take care of that. At this moment, it is crucial for Arulmozhi to be here. Karikala! What is the use in hiding the truth any longer? A great danger has come upon the line of Vijayalaya Chola and the very foundation of the mighty Chola Empire. You, and all those who belong to you, must now stay together in one place and remain on the highest alert. We must gather all our strength in one place. No one can say what kind of danger may arise, or when…”

“Grandfather! Why do you try to frighten me like this? As long as I have a sword in my hand, what have I to fear? What sort of danger could come? I will stand alone and face it. I am not one to be afraid of any peril…”
“Child! Do you need to tell me what a courageous soul you are? Even so, sometimes we must remember the words of the great Thiruvalluvar:
‘To fear not when one ought to fear is folly; To fear what should be feared is the wise man’s part!’

Thus has that great sage spoken. On the battlefield, when standing face to face with the enemy, there must be no fear. One who is afraid in such a moment is a coward. If such a coward were born in my lineage, I would myself cut him down with these old, feeble hands of mine. But when it comes to conspiracies hatched in secret, to plots and unseen dangers, one must indeed be afraid. One must be cautious, and take every precaution suited to the situation. Those born in royal families, destined for the throne, must never be careless in such matters. If they are, it will bring ruin to the kingdom itself.”
“Grandfather! What secret dangers do you foresee? Only if you explain a little more can we be truly cautious…”

“I am about to tell you. A few days ago, at the Kadambur Sambuvarayar palace, a gathering took place at the hour of midnight. Periya Pazhuvetarayar was present at that assembly. Along with him were Thenavan Mazhavarayar, Kundrathur Kizhar, Vanangamudi Munaiyarayar, Anjaadha Singa Mutharaiyar, and Irattai Kudai Rajaaliyar—all of them were there, it seems. These are the names that reached my ears. Perhaps many others attended as well…”

“Let them have come; what of it? All of them must have watched dance and amusements till midnight, eaten until their bellies ached, drunk toddy until they were senseless, and then gone off to sleep. What does it matter to us? What could those old men with their beards and moustaches turned white possibly plot by gathering together?”
“If you hold such a fine opinion of old men, what is the use of my telling you anything? Am I not an old man myself? Among all of them, I am the most ancient of the lot!”
“Grandfather! Don’t be angry. Would I ever compare you with those useless old fellows? All right, tell me what happened next!”

“Again you call them useless old fellows! Do not forget that the chief among them only recently got married! And know this too—there is no more dangerous youth in the world than an old man who has married a young woman!”

At the mention of the old man’s marriage, a strange change came over Aditya Karikalan’s face. His eyes suddenly reddened and flared like a bloodthirsty demon seeking sacrifice. His lips quivered. His teeth ground together in fury.
Malayaman did not notice any of this. But Parthibendran did.
“What is the need to speak of that marriage now, sir? Tell us what happened next at Sambuvarayar’s palace,” urged the Pallava warrior.

“That is what I was coming to, but old age has caught up with me, hasn’t it? My mind falters and wanders elsewhere. Listen, Karikala! Parthibendra! You too, pay heed! That midnight assembly was not only a gathering of elders. Some young men were present as well. One was Sambuvarayar’s son, Kandhamaaran. Another…” He hesitated.
“Who, grandfather? Who was the other?” Karikalan pressed him eagerly.
“The son of your great uncle Kandaradithar, your paternal uncle—he is none other than Madurantaka Devar!”
At these words, both Aditya Karikalan and Parthibendran burst into hearty laughter.
“What is this laughter! What does it mean? Are you mocking me again?” asked Miladudaiyar.

“No, grandfather! No! It’s just that you called Madurantakan a ‘youth’—that’s why we laughed. Among all the elders, isn’t he the most shriveled old man? Isn’t he a ripened sage, a true elder of wisdom?” said Aditya Karikalan.

“Haven’t you heard that sometimes, old age gives way to youth again? In the same way, youth has returned to Madurantakan. Until a few days ago, he kept saying, ‘I will renounce the world; I will devote myself to the service of Shiva.’ But now, one after another, he is marrying—one, two, three marriages…”
“Let him marry. Let him marry as many times as he wishes; what does it matter?”
“My boy! Madurantakan’s marriages are not ordinary marriages. They are royal alliances. They are marriages woven into the secret intrigues of the Pazhuvettarayar clan!”

“Grandfather! Why do you still speak in riddles? Tell us plainly! What do the Pazhuvettarayars truly desire? What is the purpose behind their gatherings in every town? What are they planning to do with Madurantaka Devar?” asked Aditya Karikalan.

“It is nothing else. They have resolved to deny both you and your brother your claim to the throne, and to seat Madurantakan upon the Chola kingdom’s throne. It is for this reason that they keep your father confined in the Tanjore fort, as if he were a prisoner, in order to obtain his consent!” said Miladudaiyar.

chapters.title: The Fury of Malayaman
paragraphs: Just as he had gained wisdom, strength, and experience in equal measure, the words spoken at last by the ruler of Thirukovalur, Malayaman, did not cause Aditya Karikalan to faint and collapse! Yet, for a moment, he stood paralyzed, bereft of action. Parthibendran too was struck dumb, standing in silence. It seemed as if even the sea had stilled its roar. In the distance, even the “Eleyo!” cries of those unloading goods from boats onto the wooden ships had faded into silence at that moment.

Ashamed for having allowed himself to be so surprised, Aditya Karikalan swiftly raised his gaze to his grandfather’s face and said, “Grandfather! I too have heard that some people in the towns and villages speak thus. I thought it was nothing but a baseless rumor. But you speak with such certainty! Do you say this with full knowledge? Can such a thing truly happen?”

“Why can it not happen?” replied Malayaman Miladudaiyar. “Before your grandfather, it was your great-uncle Kandaraditha Devar who ruled the Chola land! His son has even more right to this kingdom than you, does he not?”

“Absolutely not! That utter fool, who cannot speak two words, who has never wielded a sword, who was born a man by accident when he should have been born a woman—does he have a right to this kingdom? Is it for him? For Aditya Karikalan, who, at twelve years of age, set foot on the battlefield, who is the lion that slew Veera Pandiyan, who knows not the meaning of defeat, the bravest of the brave—does he not have the right? Sir! Miladudaiyar! Has your wisdom faded with your advancing years?” Parthibendran burst out in anger.

Karikalan silenced him with a stern glance and said, “Grandfather! This kingdom means nothing to me. If I wished, with the help of my sword, I could establish ten such kingdoms. But where is the justice in this? If, from the beginning, it had been declared that the kingdom was for Madurantakan, I would never have stood in the way. Before the whole country, before the cities, before all the people, I was proclaimed heir and crowned as prince. How can it be changed now? Are you in agreement with this?”

“I do not agree, nor will I ever agree. If you consent and say you will give the kingdom to Madurantakan, first I will strike you down with this sword and make an end of you. Then, the woman who bore you for ten months—” “I will cut down your mother. Then, I, who fathered you, will also cut myself down with my own hand and die. As long as there is life in my body, I will not let this Chola kingdom slip away from you!” thundered the old man. As he roared, a flash of lightning seemed to blaze in his dimmed eyes. His entire body, weakened by emotion and agitation, trembled uncontrollably.
