Parthibendran cried out, “Say it again, Grandfather! Say it again!” and rushed forward to embrace Malayaman. Tears welled up in his eyes.

Karikalan, too, stood for a moment gazing out at the deep sea. Then, turning to his grandfather, he said, “Grandfather! If that is your resolve, why hesitate? Let us at once gather our forces and set out for Thanjavur. We will destroy the Pazhuvettaraiyars and all those allied with them—the Mazhavarayars, Sambhuvarayars, Mutharayars, Munaiyarayars—in a single stroke and seize the fort at Thanjavur. We will imprison Madurantakan and free the Emperor. If we have your blessings, what more do we need? If Parthibendran and I join together, who in this world could defeat us?” he declared with pride.

“It is true, you cannot be defeated in battle. But what will you do if cunning and treachery rise against you? As you approach Thanjavur with your army, rumors will spread that a son is coming to wage war against his own father! They will say that the Emperor, unable to bear such disgrace, has given up his life. There will be those among the people who believe such tales, will there not? In such a situation, what will you do, my child? Even your own heart will falter! Can you bear the shame of being called one who came to wage war against his own father?”
Aditya Karikalan covered his ears and cried, “Shiva, Shiva! I cannot bear to hear it!”
“That is why I said at the very beginning—great danger surrounds us!”
“What is the way out, Grandfather? What is the way?”

“First, we must send a trustworthy man to Lanka. We must send him to bring Arulmozhi back. He will not easily leave the battlefield or his loyal soldiers. We must send someone who has the power to change his mind and bring him back…”

Parthibendran stepped forward and said, “Sir! If you permit, I myself will go and bring him back!” “That is Karikalan’s wish; and yours as well. But the one who goes—like Vandiyathevan—should not meddle in matters that do not concern him…”
“Did you hear that? Didn’t I tell you so?” said Parthibendran.
“Grandfather, have you received any news about Vandiyathevan?” asked Aditya Karikalan.
“At first, I even suspected him—wondered if he too had joined our enemies. But later, that suspicion was dispelled.”
“Did you hear that, Parthibendra!” said Karikalan.
“Let him finish. Why are you so impatient? Sir! What suspicion did you have about Vandiyathevan?”
“On the day the assembly was held at the Samburayar palace, I learned that he too was present there. But later, I found out he was not involved in the conspiracy.”
“Grandfather! How did you come to know all this?”

“I did not receive an invitation to the feast at Kadambur palace. That itself aroused some suspicion in me. Later, I captured the elder of Kundrathur, who had attended the event and was returning to his village, and brought him to the prison in my mountain fortress. From him, I learned everything that had transpired there. Vandiyathevan is a friend of Samburayar’s son, Kandhamaaran…”
“Yes; both of them served in our army, did they not? They guarded the northern bank of the Pennai river together. I know that their friendship began there…”

“In any case, Vandiyathevan was present at the palace that day. I could not determine whether he was involved in the plot or not. Later, a clue presented itself. When I heard that inside the Tanjore fort, Vandiyathevan had stabbed Kandhamaaran in the back and escaped…”

“Grandfather! I will never believe that. Whatever else Vandiyathevan may have done or left undone, he is not one to stab a man in the back. Least of all, the back of a friend—he is not such a wretch…”
“What if that friend was involved in a conspiracy against his own lord? What if that friend had tried to draw Vandiyathevan into that plot as well?”
“Whatever else he may do, he would only fight face to face—never, not for a single day, would he stab a man in the back!”

“I marvel at the faith you have in your friend, my boy! Let the truth be what it may. What I know for certain is this: the Pazhuvettaraiyars have accused Vandiyathevan of stabbing Kandanmaran in the back, and are now hunting him down. Therefore, there must have been some kind of quarrel between Vandiyathevan and Kandanmaran. Doesn’t this prove, at least, that he has not joined in any conspiracy against you?”

“There is no need for so much evidence for that! If Vandiyathevan were ever to join our enemies, then this very earth would turn upside down. The surging sea would dry up. The sky would come crashing down. The sun would rise at night. The Chola dynasty would meet with utter destruction…” Aditya Karikalan exclaimed, his voice trembling with emotion.

“I agree with the prince,” said Malayaman. “Vandiyathevan would never betray us or join hands with our foes. I have only one complaint against him. If he sees a beautiful woman’s face, Vandiyathevan’s head will spin. His mind will be bewitched!”

Hearing this, Aditya Karikalan smiled. “That is precisely why I sent him to the princess after he delivered the letter to the Emperor. Once he sees the princess, how could he ever escape? He would have no choice but to become her slave, wouldn’t he?”

At once, Malayaman Miladudaiyar said, “Oh! Is that so? You sent Vandiyathevan with such instructions? And I knew nothing of it! Since leaving Thanjavur, has any word come from Vandiyathevan? Or any message from the princess?”
“I am waiting every moment in expectation. But so far, there has been no news…”
“Once Arulmozhi comes here, you must have your sister brought here as well. Then we need have no more worries. If we leave every decision to the princess and act as she says, all will be well!”
“Grandfather! In this matter, you are worse than Vandiyathevan!”

“Yes, Karikala! When your sister was just two years old, she took the sceptre in her hand. She ruled over me, your grandmother, your father and mother, all according to her own will. Even now, it is the same with me. She—”

“What I have decided is law for me. Karikala! Do not think it is any slight to you if I speak of your sister. For you, it is nothing but a matter of pride. There has never been, among men or women, anyone born with the wealth of wisdom possessed by the young princess Kundavai. You know well what kind of man our Prime Minister Aniruddha Brahmarayar is, do you not? Even he seeks counsel from the young princess—what more can I say?” spoke Miladudaiyar, his voice brimming with admiration.

Parthibendran, who harbored jealousy towards Vandiyathevan, interjected, “All that is true; who would deny it? But what if, before Vandiyathevan met the young princess, he had already lost his heart to another woman? For instance, what if he had beheld that enchantress, the young queen of Pazhuvoor…?” His last words were uttered in a lowered voice, so the elder did not catch them. But Aditya Karikalan heard them clearly. He turned sharply, his eyes flashing fire, and fixed Parthibendran with a piercing gaze. That look unsettled the Pallava warrior.

Malaimaan rose from the rock and said, “Parthibendra! Are you not leaving for Lanka tomorrow? You young men have much to discuss among yourselves. I am an old man; I shall slowly make my way to the palace. Speak of what you must and come at your leisure!” With that, he started to walk away.

After he had gone a little distance, Parthibendran turned to Aditya Karikalan and said, “My king! My lord! There is some deep anguish dwelling in your heart. Some pain gnaws at your soul. I know it is connected to the young queen of Pazhuvoor. Whenever the subject of Periya Pazhuvetarayar’s marriage arises, your whole countenance changes. Your eyes redden and blaze with fire. How long will you let this torment churn within you? You have called me ‘the very soul of your soul’ a thousand times. Should you not open your heart to such a friend? Should you not tell me what this pain is? Will you not give me a chance to find some remedy for it? How many days more can I remain silent, watching you suffer in silence?” he pleaded, his voice trembling with unrestrained concern.

Aditya Karikalan let out a long, heavy sigh. “Friend! The anguish in my heart is a pain that will never be healed. It is a sorrow that must die with me. There is no remedy for it. Yet, it is not that I cannot tell you. Tonight, I shall speak. For now, let us go with the elder to the palace. It is not right to let him go alone.” So saying, he rose from the rock.

The elderly Malayaman, the lord of Thirukovalur, was pacing back and forth like a caged lion in the audience hall of the Chola palace at Pazhayarai. His face, usually radiant with laughter and cheer, now burned with anger. His eyes, which had seen many a battlefield, flashed with a fierce light. His thick, white moustache bristled as he ground his teeth in rage.

He stopped abruptly and turned to the men assembled before him. “What is this?” he thundered. “What sort of kingdom is this? What sort of rule? In the old days, would such things have happened? Would enemies have dared to enter the capital and plot against the king? Would traitors have been allowed to roam free?”
The ministers and noblemen standing before him hung their heads in shame. None dared to meet his gaze.

“Is this the valor of the Cholas?” Malayaman continued, his voice rising. “Is this the famed courage of our ancestors? In my youth, if such a thing had happened, the traitors would have been dragged to the town square and beheaded before sunset! But now, you sit here, wringing your hands, afraid even to speak their names!”

He strode over to the throne where Sundara Chola sat, frail and weary, his face pale with illness. Malayaman’s expression softened for a moment as he looked at the king. “My son,” he said, “I do not speak these words to wound you. I know the pain you bear. But I cannot remain silent while our enemies grow bold and our people tremble in fear.”
Sundara Chola raised his hand weakly. “Father-in-law, I understand your anger. But what can we do? The times have changed. The world is not as it once was.”

Malayaman drew himself up to his full height. “Let the world change as it will! The honor of the Cholas must not change! If we allow this insult to pass, our enemies will only grow stronger. We must act, and act swiftly!”
He turned once more to the assembled nobles. “Who among you will stand with me? Who will defend the honor of our house? Who will root out these traitors and restore peace to the land?”
For a moment, there was silence. Then, slowly, one by one, the nobles stepped forward, their faces set with determination.
Malayaman’s eyes gleamed with pride. “That is how it should be!” he cried. “Let us show the world that the blood of the Cholas still runs strong!”

chapters.title: “More Poisonous Than Venom”
paragraphs: That night, in one of the ancient Pallava emperors’ palaces at Mamallapuram, those three illustrious heroes took their rest. After they had finished their evening meal, the Malaiyaman king, having heard that the tale of Aravan was being recited near the Five Chariots, went there to listen. Aditya Karikalan and Parthibendran ascended to the upper terrace of the palace.

From the terrace, Aditya Karikalan gazed for a while at the nightscape of Mamallapuram. Here and there, a few lamps flickered dimly, casting a faint glow. Silence reigned over most of the streets. In the temples, the midnight rituals had ended, and the outer doors were being shut. The roar of the sea sounded with a mournful note, echoing “Ooo…” By the Five Chariots, the ballad singer and his troupe were performing the tale of Aravan; the crowd gathered around them, listening intently, appeared as dark, shadowy forms in the lamplight.

“At this age, the old man has gone off to listen to stories! See that? Whatever else may be said, men of the old days were truly men! Who among us today possesses their strength of body and firmness of mind?” said Aditya Karikalan.

“My lord! Have you too begun to praise the greatness of the olden days? What feat did those men of the past accomplish that we have not matched in our own time? Even in stories and epics, I have not heard of anyone who, in his youth, performed deeds of valor on the battlefield as you have,” said Parthibendran.

“Parthiba! You are a man of true heart. I know well that you do not speak one thing while harboring another in your mind. Otherwise, you would not be my friend; I would suspect you to be a secret enemy. Yet, you flatter me so much! Nothing else can cast a man into the deepest pit of hell as surely as flattery!” said Aditya Karikalan.

“Sir! If one, with selfish intent, invents and utters false praise about another, that is flattery. If I were to go to Madurantakan, who is now a slave to the Pazhuvettarayars in Thanjavur, and say, ‘You are the bravest of the brave,’ that would be flattery. If ever you find me doing such a thing, kill me at once with the sword in your hand. In what I have said about you, not a word—” “Not many words, are there? In ancient times, what hero achieved such great deeds at so young an age? If one must name someone equal to you, perhaps your great-grandfather, Rajaditya—who sleeps atop his elephant—might be mentioned; but even he cannot be said to have surpassed you…”

“Stop, Parthiba, stop! Where is Rajaditya, and where am I? Who are we to even speak of Rajaditya, who, with a small force, stood against the vast, surging armies of the Rashtrakutas—raging like the great ocean—and destroyed them utterly, attaining the hero’s heaven? To compare ourselves to him? Leave aside the Chola lineage; even in your own Pallava clan, what great souls once lived! Will this land ever again see the likes of Mahendravarman or Mamallar? Where is Narasimhavarman, who, from the Tungabhadra in the south to the Narmada in the north, ruled under a single umbrella, defeated Pulikesi, destroyed Vatapi, and erected the pillar of victory? And where are you and I? In our time or in the ages to come, can anyone create a dream-city like this Mamallapuram? Ah! Just look around you, Parthiba, look well in all four directions! See there, the villu paatu is being performed—look closely! Were those who carved such wondrous chariots from living rock mere ordinary men? When I think of what a glorious spectacle Mamallapuram must have been three hundred and fifty years ago, my very body thrills! Do you not feel such emotion? Do your shoulders not swell with pride when you think of your ancestors?”

“Your Majesty! Just now you accused me of flattery, did you not? Sometimes you forget that I also point out your faults. This madness for sculpture, painting, and art has seized you as well! It was this very madness that rendered all my ancestors’ victories fruitless. After Mamallar went to Vatapi, erected the pillar of victory, and returned—what did he do? He sat carving stones and hollowing out rocks! And what was the result? In a short while, the Chalukyas rose again, flourishing. They returned with great armies to take revenge. They destroyed Kanchipuram and Uraiyur. They marched as far as Madurai. If Nedumara Pandiyan had not halted and defeated the Chalukya army at Nelveli, would not the whole of this southern land still be under Chalukya rule today?”

“No, Parthiba, no! We have never heard of any royal dynasty in this world that endured forever. Even the Ikshvaku line, in which Rama was born, came to an end. To overthrow the Chalukyas, the Rattamandalam kings arose.

It is the nature of kingdoms that sometimes they rise to great heights, and at other times they fall into decline. Some kingdoms, after flourishing in glory for a time, vanish without a trace. Look at my own ancestors! Karikala Valavan, Killivalavan, and other Chola kings—how illustrious and renowned they were! What do we know of them now? Only because a few poets sang their praises do we even know their names. Did those bards truly sing the truth, or did they, after indulging in strong drink, sing whatever came to their minds? We cannot say.

But Mahendra Pallava and Mamalla—did they not create this city of sculptures? For thousands of years, this city will proclaim their greatness to the world. What have you and I done to match their deeds? We have slain thousands on the battlefield; we have caused rivers of blood to flow. What else have we done to make our names endure in this world?”

Hearing these words, Parthibendran stood stunned for a moment, wondering if it was indeed Aditya Karikalan who spoke thus. After a deep sigh, he said, “My lord! If you yourself speak this way about war and valor, what is left for me to say? Your mind is not in its usual state today. That is why you speak so. My lord! Will you not tell me what sorrow weighs upon your heart? Will you not open your iron heart to me, even a little?”
“Parthiba! If I were to split open my heart, what do you think you would find within—who do you think would be there?”
“That is what I wish to know, Swami!”

“My mother and father would not be there. My beloved sister and brother would not be there. You and Vandiyathevan, my dearest friends, would not be there. There would be a woman, the very embodiment of deceit. There would be the younger queen of Pazhuvoor, the very form of sin. Nandini, more poisonous than venom itself, dwells within my heart and torments me; until this day, I have never spoken of this agony to anyone. It is to you alone that I have revealed it today!” So spoke Aditya Karikalan, and his words blazed like the tongues of fire.

“My lord! I had suspected as much. Whenever the name of the younger queen of Pazhuvoor is mentioned, your face darkens, your eyes redden, and an unspeakable anguish shows itself. But how did this unworthy infatuation take root in your heart? How did you, who...” Is it in the tradition to consider her as your mother? The Pazhuvettaraiyars have been long-standing allies of your lineage; he is a man of advanced years. Even if today he stands as our adversary, was it always so in the past? How much respect and honor did your father and grandfather show him? The woman who was married to such a man, with Agni as witness… however wicked she may be… could you even harbor such thoughts in your heart?”

“No, Parthiba, no! Do you think I do not know this? It is precisely because I know it that my heart is tormented so. After she married the Pazhuvettaraiyar, she found no place in my heart. But long before that, the poison of her allure had seeped into my soul. However much I tried to rid myself of it, I could not. I speak as though all the blame rests upon her. Who is truly at fault, only God knows. If you look at it, perhaps all the blame and sin should fall upon the God who created us. Or perhaps it is fate, which brought us together only to tear us apart, that must be accused!”
“Sire! Did you meet Nandini before she became the Queen of Pazhuvoor? Where, when, and how did you meet her?”
“That is a long story. Do you wish to hear it today?”

“I certainly wish to hear it. If I do not know the truth, my heart will not be at peace. You are asking me to go to Lanka tomorrow, are you not? I will not be able to fulfill my duty there properly. Only if I learn what has happened and offer you some comfort before I leave will my heart find some measure of peace!”

“My friend! Are you going to comfort me? In this life, there is no comfort for me. Whether there is any in the next birth is doubtful too. I will tell you for the sake of your peace of mind. You need not go to Lanka thinking that I have hidden something from you!”
So saying, Aditya Karikalan paused for a moment. Then, with a long, heavy sigh, he began to speak.

chapters.title: Nandini’s Lover
paragraphs: “The very first time I met Nandini was when I was twelve years old.

One day, in Pazhayarai, my younger sister, my little brother, and I were playing with a boat in the stream that ran behind our palace. When our game was over, we got out of the boat and walked back to the palace through the blossoming grove. On the way, we heard the voice of our great-grandmother, Sembiyan Maadevi. The three of us had been raised with great affection by our grandmother. Wanting to tell her about our boating adventure, we followed her voice and entered the kodivettu house. Besides our grandmother, there were three others in the room. Of the three, one was a little girl about our age. The other two, it was clear, were her parents. They were telling our grandmother something about that girl. As soon as we entered the kodivettu house, everyone turned to look at us. But all I could see were the wide, astonished eyes of that little girl fixed upon us. Even now, when I think back, that scene stands vivid before my mind’s eye…”

So saying, Karikalan gazed up at the sky, falling into silence. Whether he saw the face of that little girl within the drifting veils of thin clouds that wandered across the heavens at that moment, none could say.
“Sir! And then? Please continue!” Parthibendran urged, and Karikalan returned to this world and resumed his tale:

“It was my sister Kundavai who told our grandmother about our boating escapade. After hearing it, the queen mother said, ‘My dear ones! Did you see this girl? How bright and lovely she is! They have come from the Pandya country to stay at our Isana Sivapattar’s house. They will be here for a few days. This girl’s name is Nandini. Sometimes, include her in your games. She will be a good friend to you!’ But I could sense that my sister did not like this suggestion. As the three of us left for the palace, Kundavai said, ‘Anna! Did you see that girl standing there? How strange and ill-omened she looked! Why does her face resemble a clay doll’s? Grandmother wants me to play with her? If I look at her face, I can’t help but laugh! What am I to do?’” The moment I heard this, an important truth dawned upon me. That is, women are born with jealousy in their very nature. No matter how beautiful a woman may be, she cannot bear to see another woman who is beautiful.

“It is well known that among the women born in our clan, my sister is famed for her beauty. Even she could not tolerate the sight of another woman who was beautiful. Otherwise, why would she speak of that girl in such a manner? I did not let my sister off easily. Just to provoke her anger, I insisted that the other girl was indeed more beautiful. We often argued and quarreled about this. Our brother Arulmozhi, not knowing the reason behind these disputes, was left bewildered.

After some days, I set out with my father, who was leaving for the Pandya country’s war. We defeated the Pandya army and the forces sent by the king of Lanka to aid the Pandyas in several places. In the end, whether Veerapandiyan had fled and gone into hiding or died on the battlefield, we did not know at that time. After Veerapandiyan’s disappearance, the Lankan soldiers who had come to aid the Pandya army retreated and fled. Pursuing them, we reached the shores of Sethukarai. Except for the dead, the rest escaped by boarding ships.

My father wished to teach a lesson to the kings of Lanka, who frequently sent forces to trouble us by aiding the Pandyas. He decided to send a large army to Lanka under the command of the Kodumbalur Chinna Velar. It took some time to gather the necessary ships and equipment for this. Nevertheless, we stayed there, loaded the armies onto the ships, and sent them off. Only after we learned that our soldiers had safely landed at Mathottam did we return to Chola country.

By the time I returned to Pazhayarai, more than two years had passed. I had completely forgotten the priest’s daughter who had come from the Madurai side. When I returned to Pazhayarai, I saw that both my sister and that girl had grown so much that they were almost unrecognizable. I also saw that the two of them had become close friends. Nandini had not only grown up, but she now glittered with fine clothes and ornaments. I learned that this was my sister’s doing. Unlike before, Nandini now felt shy to see or speak with me. I tried hard to overcome this. I found a pleasure in talking and mingling with her that I had never found in anything else. I cannot express how much wonder this brought me at that young age. Like the fresh floodwaters swelling in the Kaveri, some new emotion surged and overflowed within my heart.

But I soon realized that none of those close to me liked this. From the time I returned, Kundavai began to show dislike towards that girl. One day— Our grandmother, the revered Mathevadigal, called me to her and said, “Nandini is the daughter of a temple priest; you are the son of the Emperor. Both of you have now come of age. Therefore, it is not proper for you to associate with Nandini.” She spoke with wisdom. Until then, I had worshipped my grandmother as a goddess, but at that moment, I felt anger towards her and a sense of insult in her words. Defying her wisdom, I sought out Nandini, found her, spoke with her, and became close to her.

But this did not last long. Suddenly, one day, it became known that Nandini and her parents had left for their native place in the Pandya country. At that time, sorrow welled up within me; anger overcame me. I kept my sorrow locked in my heart and showed my anger towards my sister. Fortunately, within a few days, I had to travel north. I set out with the Chola army that was marching to drive out the Rashtrakuta forces who had occupied Thirumunaippadi and the Thondai region.
It was then that you and I met; we became inseparable friends.

“With the help of the Malayaman king, you and I fought against the Rashtrakuta armies. We chased them north of the River Palar, defeated them, and captured the city of Kanchi. At that time, bad news arrived from Lanka. We learned that our army had been defeated there and that the Kodumbalur Chinna Velar had died. Upon hearing this, Veerapandiyan, who until then had been hiding in a rocky cave in the midst of the desert, emerged like a snake from its hole. Gathering an army once more, he seized Madurai and hoisted the fish flag.

You remember, do you not, the surge of heroic fervor that filled both our hearts when we heard all this? The two of us immediately set out for Pazhaiyarai. My father, the Emperor, had already begun to lose his health. The strength in his legs was waning. Yet, the Emperor was determined to set out for the battlefield in the Pandya country. I stopped him, saying it was not necessary. I vowed before my father that I would not return to Chola country without first defeating the Pandya army, recapturing Madurai, and bringing back the head of Veerapandiyan. You were with me then. Accepting my vow, my father sent us to the battlefield in Pandya Nadu.

He ordered that we should fight under the command of Kodumbalur Boothivikkirama Kesari, who had already taken charge of the army. We agreed and set forth. On the way, we met Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar. We came to know that he was dissatisfied because the Kodumbalur prince had been appointed as the army commander instead of himself.

“Upon witnessing our warlike fervor, the Commander-in-Chief Boothivikrama Kesari entrusted the responsibility of leading the battle to us. My friend! There is no fault in us taking pride in the incredible feats of valor you and I performed in that war. We defeated the Pandya army and captured Madurai. Yet, we were not satisfied with that alone. We wished to utterly destroy the Pandya forces, so that they could never rise again. We ordered our soldiers to pursue the fleeing warriors in all directions and annihilate them to the last man. With a strong force, we ourselves chased after the Pandya king. The high-flying fish banner showed us the direction in which the Pandya was fleeing. We followed that path and caught up with him. Around Veerapandiyan, his bodyguards stood protecting him like a fortress wall. The Pandya bodyguards were a step above even the Chola country’s Velakkara troops in valor. They had sworn never to retreat, and to protect their king even at the cost of their own lives. If, by any chance, they failed and danger befell the Pandya king, they had vowed to cut off their own heads and offer themselves in sacrifice. Such were the warriors who fulfilled their duty. We slew them all, leaving not a single one alive. The corpses of the dead piled up like mountains. Yet, amidst them, we could not find Veerapandiyan. We had been deceived by the fish banner. An elephant stood bearing the fish banner, but neither on it nor beside it was the Pandya king to be seen! Is not Veerapandiyan skilled in escaping and hiding from the battlefield? Suspecting that he might have fled again, we divided our forces and sent them in all directions.

“You all hurried along both banks of the Vaigai river. I too did not remain idle. I entered the Vaigai, walking southward along the sand. In some places, the hoofprints of a lone horse were imprinted in the sand. Along the horse’s path, I also saw stains of blood in the sand. I followed those traces. In the middle of the Vaigai river, I reached a grove that stood like an island. Within that grove was a temple of Thirumal. Nearby stood a couple of priests’ houses. The grove was filled with trees bearing flowers for the deity’s worship. A small lotus pond bloomed and swayed in the breeze. My friend! Perhaps you remember. I had pointed out that grove and given strict orders that none of our soldiers, under any circumstances, should enter it by mistake or otherwise. The reason was not merely that I wished no harm to befall the worship of the deity in that temple. It was because, in the house of the priest there, dwelled a queen who had captured my heart and reigned in my soul.”

“One day, when I entered that grove, I saw Nandini. Her appearance had changed somewhat since before. She had tied her hair in front like a crown, resembling the image of the goddess Andal, and had adorned it with a garland of flowers. She wore a garland around her neck as well. ‘What is this attire?’ I asked her. She told me that after parting from me, she had resolved never to marry any mortal, and, like Andal, to wed only Kannan. This struck me as sheer madness. How could a human woman marry a god? Still, I did not wish to argue about it then. ‘Let the war end; I will deal with this later,’ I thought. I asked if she needed any help. She replied, ‘Make sure none of your soldiers come here. Only my aged parents live here, and they are blind. I have a sturdy younger brother, but he is away on a pilgrimage to Tirupati!’ As she requested, I promised that none of our soldiers would come near, and I left. After that, I visited her two or three more times. The old longing I had for her grew tenfold and burned within me. Yet I maintained patience. I decided that I must first complete my mission—take Veerapandiyan’s head to Pazhaiyarai; then, as a reward, I would ask my father’s permission to marry Nandini.

“In this state of resolve, when I saw the hoofprints of a lone horse leading into that grove, I was seized with boundless surprise and anger. Going further, I saw the horse tied in the shade of dense trees. So, the fugitive must be hiding in one of those huts. I went to Nandini’s house and peered in through the window. My friend! The sight I beheld there is seared into my heart as if by a red-hot iron. On an old rope cot, Veerapandiyan lay stretched out. Nandini was giving him water to drink, quenching his thirst. Her face shone with a radiance I had never seen before. Two tears brimmed in her eyes. Overcome with rage, I kicked open the door and burst inside. Nandini, who had been dressing his wounds, stopped at once and came forward. She prostrated herself before me, then rose, palms pressed together, and pleaded, ‘Sir! For the sake of the love you once bore me, I beg you—do not harm him! Do not kill this wounded man with your own hands!’
“I stammered, ‘What is the connection between you and this man? Why do you beg for his life?’” “She said, ‘This is my beloved; this is my god; this is the merciful one who has agreed to marry me!’”

“The little pity I had felt for the wounded Veerapandiyan vanished from my heart. This wretch, this outcaste—how cunningly he has avenged himself upon me! Even if he had seized my entire kingdom, it would not have been such a crime; but did he not snatch away the princess who had taken up residence in the innermost chambers of my soul? How could I show mercy to him? It was impossible—utterly impossible!

“I pushed Nandini aside and strode past her. With a single sweep of my sword, I severed Veerapandiyan’s head from his body. When I think now of that savage, terrible act, shame burns within me. But at that moment, the frenzy of battle and the madness of rage possessed me utterly. In that wild fury, after slaying Veerapandiyan and as I crossed the threshold of that house, I turned once to look at Nandini. She too gazed at me without blinking. Never in this world have I seen a look like that. In that glance, the six passions—lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy—flared up as tongues of fire, burning fiercely. I have pondered countless times on the meaning of that look, but to this day, I do not know what it meant!

“By then, you and many others had come searching for me. Seeing Veerapandiyan’s headless body and his blood-soaked head, all of you raised cries of victory. But in my own heart, it felt as if the weight of the Vindhya mountains had been placed upon me!...”

chapters.title: The Happenings in the Women’s Quarters
paragraphs: Many centuries ago, when Mahendra Pallava Chakravarthi ruled in Kanchipuram, he made arrangements for the Mahabharata to be read throughout the land. Owing to the spread of Buddhist and Jain philosophies, the people of Tamil Nadu had become gentle and ascetic; to rekindle and spread the spirit of valor, he made these arrangements. He built Bharata Mandapams in many towns specifically for the recitation of the Mahabharata. The tradition he began continued unbroken in the Thondai region. At night, people would gather in the mandapams or in open spaces to listen to the stories of the Mahabharata. Many bards arose who could narrate the great epic and its sub-stories in song, verse, and prose, with stirring heroism.

When Arjuna went on his pilgrimage, he encountered Chitrangi, the princess of Manipur, in a forest near Manipur. The two fell in love. To Chitrangi was born a beloved son, Aravan. Being the son of Arjuna and a princess of the hill country, Aravan was a mighty warrior. When he learned that the great war of the Mahabharata was about to begin, he joined the Pandava army. Before the war commenced, it was said that a young hero possessing all auspicious qualities must be offered as a sacrifice for victory. At that moment, Aravan stepped forward and declared, “Here I am; offer me as the sacrificial victim!” As there was no greater warrior than Aravan among the Pandavas, and since he had volunteered, it was decided that he should be the one sacrificed.

The tale of the valiant Aravan, who gave his life for the victory of his side, captured the hearts of the Tamil people. Wherever temples were built for Draupadi Amman, shrines for Aravan were also constructed nearby, and festivals were held in his honor.

That night, near the Five Rathas of Mamallapuram, the story of Aravan seemed to have come to an end. “Long live Sundara Chola Chakravarthi, lord of the three worlds!” “Long live Kopparakesari Aditya Karikalan!”—such shouts arose from many voices and floated through the air. Those who had been listening to the story began to rise and disperse.
“The story is over. Malayaman will return in a little while,” said Karikalan. “The tale of Aravan has ended; but the story you were telling us is not yet finished, is it?” asked Parthiban.
“Look at the resolve of Malayaman at this age! He intends to stay awake until midnight, listening to stories!” said Karikalan.
“Is it such a wondrous thing to remain alive into old age? There are so many elders in the land. They too stay up at night, unable to sleep, listening to tales…”

“Would you compare Thirukovalur Miladudaiyar to such ordinary old men? How many battlefields has he witnessed? It is doubtful whether we will even be alive at his age. Even if we are, we will not possess his strength of will.”
“Sire! There is a reason why the men of olden times were so steadfast…”
“And what is that reason?”

“They did not get ensnared in the wiles of women. They did not lose their hearts to the daughter of a mere priest and spend their days pining for her. If ever their hearts did stray towards a woman, they would seize her by her hair, bring her to the harem, and then turn to other matters!”
“Parthiba! Nandini is not truly the daughter of a priest; there must be some secret about her birth…”

“What does it matter whose daughter Nandini is? Whether she is a priest’s daughter, a king’s daughter, or even an orphan—what difference does it make? Look at that other elder, Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar! He saw her somewhere along the way, immediately seized her, and locked her up in the harem, adding her to his wives…”
“Friend! When I think of it, I find it astonishing!”
“What do you find astonishing? That the old man fell into her snare?”
“No, no! What amazes me is how a woman who once claimed to love me, then loved Veerapandiyan and tried to save his life, could agree to marry this aged nobleman. That is what I find so astonishing.”

“That does not seem at all surprising to me, my lord! It is your own actions that strike me as truly astonishing! The Pandiyan, the mortal enemy of the Chola dynasty—though he became more cowardly than a coward, fleeing and hiding after his defeat, yet still called himself ‘Veerapandiyan’—when a woman who had sheltered him and begged for his life sought your mercy, you simply let her go unharmed! That, to me, is more wondrous than any marvel. You ought to have done one of two things: either struck her down there with your sword, or, if you did not wish for that, at least bound her hands and feet and brought her as a captive! Yet you did neither, but left her free and walked away!… Now I remember it clearly, O King! At the entrance of that hut, you brought and laid down Veerapandiyan’s body. We all, like men possessed, raised shouts of victory. Amidst those cries, a sound of weeping came from within the hut. ‘Who is that?’ I asked. ‘Some women from the priest’s family. They are already terrified and distraught. None of you should go inside!’ you said. In our frenzy of triumph, we paid it no heed. At once, we all took up Veerapandiyan’s head and set off; you came with us. But you did not join in our joy and celebration as much as the rest of us. You seemed subdued, lacking in enthusiasm. When I asked you the reason, you gave me some vague reply. I even remember now that I suspected you might have suffered some grievous wound!”
So spoke Parthibendran.

“There was no wound upon my body, Parthiba! But in my heart, a wound was struck that will never heal. The sight of her standing before Veerapandiyan’s deathbed, hands folded, begging me for his life, has never left my mind. My heart trembled, thinking, ‘Alas! I left her plea unanswered!’ If, by giving my own life, I could have restored Veerapandiyan to her, I would have done so without hesitation. Since that was impossible, I have been tormented by my own helplessness.

Parthiba! We think so highly of our own powers. We imagine there is nothing we cannot do, and pride ourselves on it. We hear it written in the ancient palm-leaf manuscripts, ‘Kings possess a portion of Maha Vishnu’s divinity,’ and we even come to believe it is true. But do we possess the power to recall a soul that has departed its mortal frame? Has anyone born in a royal house ever had such strength? We may take life, but to bestow it—no man born of woman has that power!…”

“It is far better that it did not happen so. If you had possessed that power, do you realize what a terrible mistake would have taken place? You would have given life to the Pandya once again. He would have gone and hidden himself in some mountain cave. The war in the Pandya country might still be raging even now! And all this because of a woman’s false tears!” said Parthibendran.
“Pallava! You are an unfortunate soul who despises womankind! You know nothing of what love is! That is why you speak in this manner!”

“Yes; I have never been ensnared by any woman’s eyes. But your intimate friend Vandiyathevan—he loses his senses and grins foolishly at the sight of any turmeric-anointed face. That is why you prefer him to me, isn’t it, my king?”
“Aha! So, at last you have come around to Vandiyathevan, haven’t you? I was wondering how you managed to forget him for so long!”

“Yes, if I were to speak the truth about him, it would only be bitter for you. Let us leave that topic aside. What happened afterwards, my king? Did you never meet Nandini again? Did you not ask her how she, who melted for Veerapandiyan, came to marry the elder Pazhuvettaraiyar?”

“On the night Veerapandiyan was slain, after the celebrations of victory, you all lay down and slept in the camp. But sleep would not come to me. Every nerve in my body ached with the desire to see her again. I longed to speak some words of consolation to her, to beg her forgiveness. At times, a surge of anger would rise in me, and I wished to pour it out upon her. I felt that unless I saw her, I would never find peace of mind, never be able to return to Chola country. So, in the middle of the night, without anyone’s knowledge, I left the camp, mounted my horse, and rode away. I reached the island in the middle of the Vaigai river. My heart was pounding, my whole body trembling, my legs unsteady—I dismounted and walked slowly towards the Perumal temple. There, I saw that all the huts had been burnt to ashes. An old man and an old woman were sitting beside the charred huts, weeping. As I drew closer, I realized they were the same people who had once brought Nandini to the palace gardens at Pazhayarai. The moment they saw me, their grief and fear multiplied manifold.

At first, they could not speak at all. Little by little, I encouraged them and questioned them. It seems their eldest daughter lived in a village on the other bank of the river. Having heard that she was due to give birth, they had gone to visit her. Nandini had refused to accompany them. That stubborn girl, accustomed to acting as she pleased, could not be persuaded, and so they had gone without her and returned alone. On their way back, they saw some ruffians attempting to tie up a woman’s hands and feet and force her into a burning pyre. Thinking that such atrocities were common during times of war, and fearing to go near, they hurried here. When they arrived, they found the huts burning. Nandini was nowhere to be seen.

After relating this, the priest and his wife cried out, “Prince! Where is our daughter? Where is our precious child?” I already knew that they were not Nandini’s real parents. Now it was absolutely certain. If they had truly been her parents, would they have left her alone like that? Therefore, I felt no pity or sympathy for them. But an unspeakable sorrow regarding Nandini’s fate welled up and filled my heart. To ease my burning anguish, I cursed them, saying, “Go search for your daughter’s ashes in the pyre and burn and die along with her!” Then I turned away and, before dawn broke, returned to the camp. You were all sleeping soundly. None of you knew that I had gone or returned…”

“Yes, Prince! We did not know. But it is astonishing to think that you have kept all this in your heart for so long. I never dreamed you would act so contrary to the bonds of friendship. Had I been in your place, I would not have hidden it from you,” said Parthiban.
“But you are not in my place, Parthiba! In this world, no one can ever be in my place. If you had been, who can say how you would have acted?” said Karikalan.
“Sire! Let us not debate now about what has already happened. What happened next? When did you see Nandini again? Was it after she became the Young Queen of Pazhuvur? Or before that?”

“If I had seen her before that, she would not have become the Queen of Pazhuvur. When the marriage of Pazhuvetaraiyar took place, neither you nor I were in town. You remember how we spoke of it with disgust when the news reached us? A few days after that, my investiture as Crown Prince took place.

There should not be any doubt as to who should inherit the next title—that is precisely why my father, my grandmother, and the other elders together made those arrangements. Perhaps they feared that someone might cast an evil eye or perform some dark ritual against Madurantakan? Not only did they tie the prince’s diadem upon me, but they also bestowed upon me the Parakesari title and granted me, in my own name, the right to issue stone inscriptions and royal edicts. “Henceforth, the full responsibility of ruling this Chola Empire is yours,” my beloved father declared, with all his heart and voice. The people of the land, the townsfolk, ministers, and commanders—all accepted this and raised a jubilant cheer. Amidst this tumultuous celebration, I had completely forgotten Nandini. Yet, within moments of the coronation ceremony, an event occurred that ensured I could never forget her again.

With the ancient Chola crown upon my head, the emperor led me into the women’s quarters. He brought me there to receive the blessings of my mother, my grandmother, and the other ladies of the palace. Following me came my brother, the chief minister, and the Pazhuvettaraiyars. Inside the women’s quarters, aged mothers stood together, as did my sister, her companions, and many other young maidens. All of them, adorned in splendid garments and glittering jewels, their faces blooming with happiness, stood eagerly awaiting our arrival. Yet, among all those faces, only one face did my eyes perceive—Nandini’s face. She, whom I had thought burned to ashes, was my heart’s goddess! How had she entered the inner sanctum of the palace? How did she stand there, among the queens, as the chief queen herself, resplendent in such magnificent attire and ornaments? What was that mysterious radiance upon her face? How had her beauty increased tenfold from what it once was? In those few moments, my heart built countless castles in the air! Was the day I crowned myself as heir to the Chola Empire truly to be the most fortunate day of my life? Was I to attain the queen who had captivated my soul, as my royal consort? Was some wondrous magic, some mystical power, about to make this happen?… As I was lost in such thoughts, my mother Vanamadevi stepped forward, two paces ahead, and blessed me, saying, “My child!” and kissed my forehead! At that very instant, an unexpected event occurred. My father cried out, “Ah!” and suddenly collapsed to the floor in a faint. Immediately, chaos broke out in that place. I and everyone else rushed to lift the emperor and seat him, focusing all our attention on reviving him. Except for my mother and my grandmother, Sembiyan Madevi, all the other women withdrew inside. My father soon regained consciousness.

“I took my sister Kundavai aside to a private place and asked her, ‘How did Nandini come there?’ Kundavai told me that Nandini had married Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar and now reigns as the younger queen of Pazhuvur. A sharp spear pierced my heart. My friend! I have been wounded many times on the battlefield. But the wound that Kundavai’s words gave me—‘Nandini is now the younger queen of Pazhuvur’—has not healed yet!” said Aditya Karikalan, pressing his chest with his hand. It was clear that the pain in his heart still lingered.

chapters.title: The Enchantress of Illusion
paragraphs: From the beginning, Parthiban had listened to Karikalan’s story without much sympathy. But now, his heart melted. He wiped away the tears that had welled up in his eyes.

“Sire! I never imagined, even in my dreams, that such suffering could befall someone because of love for a woman! None of us knew that you had such an experience on the day of the prince’s coronation. That is why we were surprised to see you so despondent. We tried to cheer you up with all sorts of jesting words. Now, I recall all those attempts to make you happy!” he said.

“Yes, you spoke in jest. You tried to encourage me. You spoke of the great deeds I would accomplish during my reign. That very day, you expanded the Chola Empire from Lanka to the Himalayas! Not only that, you even crossed the seas and conquered distant kingdoms. I still remember all those words. I also remember how much pain those words caused me.

Then, one day, Nandini sent an invitation for me to come to the fortress at Pazhuvoor. A battle raged within my heart—should I go, or should I not? In the end, I decided to go. I wanted to ask her about the doubts that had arisen in my mind regarding many matters. I wanted to know the truth of her birth. I even wondered if there was some connection between my father’s sudden fainting in the women’s quarters and his unexpected encounter with Nandini there. You may recall that although the Emperor soon recovered from his fainting spell that day, he never regained his former health.

I thought that by speaking with Nandini, some mystery that had eluded me until then might be revealed. I kept all this as a pretense, but in truth, the real reason I went was the magnetic force she exerted over me. I deceived myself with other excuses, but it was her attraction that drew me there. The Elder Pazhuvettaraiyar was not in town. No one in his palace would stop me; nor were there any who knew of the old friendship that existed between Nandini and me. They all thought that the prince, newly crowned, had come to the Pazhuvoor palace to receive the blessings of the queens.
I met Nandini in the Latha Mandapam within the palace gardens.

Parthiba! You must have heard tales of those who journey by sea, haven’t you? They say that in certain places in the ocean, there are currents of immense force and speed. If a ship is caught in those currents, it will be swept away in an instant, whirled and spun without hope. When I stood before Nandini, I felt as though I had met the fate of a ship caught in such a current. My body, my mind, my very heart—all seemed to be torn into a thousand fragments. The words that came from my mouth astonished even me! “Oh! What is this I am saying?” I wondered in one corner of my heart, while my lips uttered all manner of things without restraint.
Nandini expressed her happiness at my being crowned as prince.
“I have no happiness in it!” I said.
“Why?” she asked.

“What sort of question is that? How could I possibly feel joy? Was it not you who did this injustice?” I replied. She pretended not to understand what I meant. Thus, our conversation continued to grow more heated. I accused her of rejecting my love, of loving Veerapandiyan instead. I even spoke harshly about her marrying the elder Pazhuvettaraiyar.

“Prince! First, you killed my love; then, before my very eyes, you killed the one who loved me; it seems your heart will not be satisfied unless you kill me as well. You cannot bear that I am still alive. Very well, kill me too and fulfill your desire!” she said, drawing a small dagger from her waist and extending it to me.
“Why would I kill you? Is it not you who keeps me alive only to torment me?” I replied.

In the end, even now I blush to recall the words that escaped my lips. “Even now, nothing irreparable has happened. Say just one word! Promise me you will leave that old man and come away! For your sake, I will abandon this kingdom. Let us both board a ship, cross the seas, and go to a distant land!” I said.

Nandini laughed at that—an awful, chilling laugh. Even now, the thought of it makes my skin crawl. “After crossing the sea to a far-off land, what will we do there? Will we chop firewood to make a living? Or plant a banana grove and—” “To survive?” she asked. “Of course, you don’t like any of that! Raised in the house of a priest, and now you’ve become the queen of Pazhuvoor, haven’t you?” I replied.

“I have no intention of being satisfied with just this. My ambition is to sit upon the throne of the Chola Empire as Empress. If you so desire, tell me—kill both the Pazhuvettaraiyars, imprison Sundara Chola, ascend the throne as Emperor, and make me your chief queen! If that is your wish, say so!” she said.
“Oh! What terrible words you speak!” I exclaimed.

“Was it not a terrible deed to kill the wounded Pandya right before my eyes?” Nandini asked. At this, my anger began to boil over. I uttered all manner of mad, furious words, reviled her, and stormed out. Even then, she did not let me go.

“Prince! If ever you change your mind, come back to me. When your heart finds room to make me Empress, return to me!” she said. From that day, I parted from her and never saw her again!” said Aditya Karikalan.

Hearing all this, Parthibendran was seized with horror and amazement. “My lord! Can such a demoness truly exist in this world? It is for the best that you never met her again!” he said, letting out a deep sigh.

“It is true that I never went to see her again! But she has never left me. Pallava! Day and night, she circles around me, tormenting me. By day, she comes to me in memory; by night, she comes in my dreams. Sometimes, with an enchanting smile upon her face, she embraces me and comes to kiss me. At other times, with a sharp dagger in her hand, she comes to stab and kill me. Sometimes, with tears brimming in her eyes, she comes, sobbing and weeping. At other times, with her hair disheveled, she comes, scratching her cheeks with her fingernails, wailing and crying. Sometimes, like a madwoman, she comes, laughing hideously. At other times, with a calm face, she comes to comfort me. God! I cannot begin to describe how that sinner torments me. Do you remember what my grandfather said this evening? He gave all sorts of reasons why I should not go to Thanjai. The real reason I avoid going to Thanjai, and wish to summon my father to Kanchi, is Nandini…”
“My lord! Are you truly avoiding Thanjai out of fear of a mere woman? What could she possibly do? Are you afraid she might treacherously poison you and kill you?...”

“No, Parthiba, no! You still do not truly understand me. It is not because I fear that she will kill me. What I fear is that she will bend me to her will and make me act as she desires. If that enchantress were to command me again—‘Imprison your father!’ ‘Banish your sister from the land!’ ‘Kill this old man and place me upon the throne!’—I am afraid that I might indeed do all these things.
My friend! Either Nandini must die, or I must die, or both of us must perish. Otherwise, in this life, I shall never find peace of mind!” said Karikalan.

“Sire! What is this you say? Why should you die? Grant me permission! I will go beyond Lanka. I shall go straight to Thanjavur and kill her myself. Let the sin of slaying a woman fall upon me if it must…”

“If you do such a thing, I will consider you my mortal enemy. If Nandini must be killed, then it shall be by my own hand. After killing her, I shall kill myself as well! I cannot bear for anyone else to so much as harm the nail on her little finger!

My friend! Forget Nandini! Forget all that I have told you about her! As grandfather said, you must depart for Lanka tomorrow! Somehow persuade my brother Arulmozhi and bring him here! We shall keep him here. Let grandfather and grandson decide together what must be done.

We shall go to Lanka, board ships again, and with a great army, sail the southern seas. We shall plant the flag of victory in lands such as Java, Pushpaka, and Kadaram. Then we shall turn westward, and in the lands of Arabia, Persia, and Egypt, we shall establish the valor of the Tamils and the banner of the tiger. Parthiba! Do you know that in those lands, the restraint called chastity is not as it is in this country? It is said that kings, at their pleasure, summon any woman under their rule and add her to their harem!...” said Karikalan.
Before Parthiban could reply, Malayaman of Thirukovalur arrived there.

“There is no tale in this world as wondrous as the story of Aravan. Not in any of the lands you were just speaking of. But are you still awake, talking without rest? Parthibendra! You remember that you must depart for Lanka tomorrow, do you not?” he asked.
“That is exactly what we are talking about, without sleep!” replied Parthibendran.

Vandiyathevan’s mind was in turmoil. He could not comprehend whether what he had just witnessed was a dream or reality. The events that had unfolded before his eyes seemed to belong to another world, a realm of magic and illusion. The moonlight that filtered through the dense canopy above cast strange, shifting patterns on the forest floor, making the shadows dance like spirits.

He stood rooted to the spot, his breath caught in his throat. The sound of anklets tinkling softly reached his ears, and from behind a thicket, a figure emerged—graceful, ethereal, as if she had stepped out of a celestial painting. Her eyes shone with a mysterious light, and her lips were curved in a smile that was both alluring and enigmatic.

Vandiyathevan’s heart pounded. Was this woman real, or was she a phantom conjured by the night? He tried to speak, but his voice failed him. The woman advanced, her silken garments rustling softly, her ornaments glinting in the pale moonlight.
“Who are you?” Vandiyathevan finally managed to ask, his voice trembling with awe and uncertainty.

The woman laughed—a sound as sweet and clear as the song of a nightingale. “Do you not recognize me, brave warrior?” she asked, her tone teasing. “Have you forgotten the one who saved you from peril not long ago?”

Vandiyathevan searched his memory. The face was familiar, yet elusive, like a half-remembered dream. Suddenly, realization dawned upon him. “You! You are the one who appeared in the boat that night, on the Ponni river!”
The woman nodded, her eyes sparkling with mischief. “Yes, it was I. But tonight, I am not here to save you. I am here to test your courage.”
Vandiyathevan’s confusion deepened. “Test my courage? In what way?”

She stepped closer, her gaze locking with his. “The path you have chosen is fraught with danger. Treachery and deceit lurk at every turn. If you wish to fulfill your mission, you must be prepared to face not only your enemies, but also your own fears and doubts.”
As she spoke, her form seemed to shimmer and blur, as if she were dissolving into the mist. Vandiyathevan reached out instinctively, but his hand grasped only empty air.
“Wait!” he cried. “Who are you truly? Why do you help me?”

Her laughter echoed through the trees, growing fainter and fainter, until it was swallowed by the night. Vandiyathevan stood alone, the silence pressing in around him. The enchantress of illusion had vanished, leaving behind only questions and a lingering sense of wonder. Part Two – The Whirlwind

chapters.title: Poonguzhali
paragraphs: Evening had settled in, calm and radiant. The sea at the edge of Kodikkarai lay still, its waves subdued and resting. Fishing boats and rafts drifted gently toward the shore. Birds that had ventured out over the ocean in search of prey were now returning home. A stretch of white sand extended along the coastline, and beyond that, for a great distance, the forest spread thick and wild. The branches of the trees did not sway; not a leaf stirred. Silence reigned in every direction. The red-gold sun hastened downwards, toward the place where sea and sky merged. Clusters of clouds, trying to veil the sun’s crimson rays, caught his light and glowed with borrowed brilliance.

At the water’s edge, a small boat floated on the sea. The gentle ripples of the ocean rocked the boat as softly as a mother might rock a jeweled cradle for her child. In that boat sat a young woman. At the sight of her, we are reminded of the way Sendhan Amudhan once described his uncle’s daughter. Yes; this must be Poonguzhali. True to her name, a petal of the fragrant thazhampoo flower adorned her hair, shining with delicate beauty. Her long, dark tresses curled and cascaded down, adorning her well-shaped shoulders. She wore ornaments fashioned from the shells and conches that the waves had cast upon the shore. Yet, it was not these ornaments that lent her beauty; rather, it was her beauty that gave these ornaments their charm. When beauty itself takes form, what jewel can further enhance it?

Poonguzhali reclined gracefully in the boat and sang. It seemed as though the sea had stilled its waves just to listen to her song! As though the wind, too, had ceased to blow and crept softly, not to disturb her melody! Even the distant forest trees appeared to stand motionless, listening intently to her voice, not a leaf stirring. The sky and the earth seemed entranced by her song, pausing in silent wonder. Even the sun, it seemed, hesitated at the horizon, reluctant to plunge into the ocean and vanish, drawn by her melody.
Let us lend our ears for a moment to that song, sweet as honey, floating through the air:

“When the waves of the sea are stilled, Why does the ocean within me surge?” When Mother Earth herself lies in slumber, why does my heart alone throb restlessly? The birds that dwell in the forest have all sought their nests! The hunters and bowmen have returned homeward; The sky and the earth are sunk in deep silence— Yet why does a tempest rage within the heart of a doe-eyed maiden? While the ocean lies still and the breeze creeps softly, Why does a whirlwind stir within the soul of this dark-haired girl?

Who can say what sorrow has made its home in the heart of that young maiden? Who can tell what mingled bliss and anguish tremble in her melodious voice? Or perhaps, when the song was first composed, the poet mixed tears with the words—who knows? But when we hear her sing that song, why does our own heart swell and threaten to break?

Poonguzhali ceased her singing. She dipped the oar into the water four times. The boat drew near the shore. Poonguzhali leapt lightly from the boat and landed on the bank. She pulled the boat up onto the shore. There, several bundles of timber lay in a heap. She propped the boat against them so that it rested securely. Leaning against the tilted boat, she cast her gaze all around.

There! Atop the lighthouse, a fire had been kindled. The flames leapt high. All through the night, that beacon would burn, warning the ships at sea: “Do not come near!” At the edge of Kodi Karai, the sea is shallow. Only timber rafts and small boats can approach the shore in that place. If a ship or a barge draws near, it will run aground and sink into the sand. If it strikes the shore with force, the hull will split and shatter. Therefore, the lighthouse at Kodi Karai is of utmost importance to sailors.

On the other side, in the midst of a dense grove of stunted trees, a temple tower rose above the canopy. At its base, the Kodi Karai Kuzhagar temple stood. Nearly two hundred years ago, Saint Sundara Moorthi Nayanar had come to this very Kodi Karai. In the heart of the forest, he had visited the solitary shrine of Kuzhagar.

“Oh Lord! How is it that you dwell alone, without companion, in the midst of this wild coastal forest? Was there no other place for you? When there are so many holy sites where throngs of devotees gather to sing your praises, why did you come to this lonely Kodi Karai and endure such hardship?” Why does the temple stand alone in the midst of the forest? Why have these wretched eyes of mine been fated to witness such a sight!” she sang, her heart melting in sorrow.

“When the swift sea-wind comes rushing to the shore, Is it a fault if the hut stands alone by the sands? These wretched eyes have seen you, O Lord of Kodikkarai, Were you not always alone, with none to share your side?”

“To the south of the sacred, fragrant-encircled forest, Where many devotees once gathered in song, O Supreme One, Why did you, Lord of Kodikkarai, amidst blossoming groves, Dwell in solitude? O my Master, why?”

Even two hundred years after Sri Sundaramurthi Nayanar had come and worshipped here, the Lord of Kodikkarai remained in the same state. (And even a thousand years later, to this day, the Lord of Kodikkarai endures in that same solitude!) Around the temple, the forests had grown even denser. In those woods, from the hollows of the trees, owls and nightjars hooted and wailed. Only a few fearsome hunters, wild in appearance, had built scattered huts in the heart of the forest and lived there.

Yes, there was but one difference. When Sri Sundaramurthi Nayanar had visited, there was no lighthouse. Only a few years ago, during the reign of the first Parantaka, had it been built. Around the lighthouse, a few cottages had been constructed for those who worked there. The priest who performed the rituals at the temple of the Lord of Kodikkarai had also come to reside there.

Poonguzhali, leaning against her boat on the seashore, gazed in all directions. She looked at the lighthouse, wondering whether she should go that way. Then her eyes turned to the golden finial of the temple tower. At that moment, the sound of the drum being beaten in the temple reached her ears, and Poonguzhali made up her mind. What was the use of going home now? She could go to the temple! She could ask the priest to sing the Thevaram hymns for her. Afterwards, she could also receive the prasadam and take it home.

Having thus made up her mind, Poonguzhali began to walk in the direction of the temple. She walked along, dancing, singing, and leaping with joy. On the way, she spotted a herd of deer. The deer were crossing the sandy expanse, heading towards the forest. Among seven or eight large deer, a tiny fawn bounded and ran alongside them. The sight of the herd filled Poonguzhali with excitement. As if she were about to catch them, she too began to run and leap in pursuit. But no matter how swiftly she ran, could she ever compete with the deer? The herd easily outpaced Poonguzhali.

At one spot ahead, the deer suddenly lifted all four legs and leapt a great distance into the air, as if they were flying. Poonguzhali guessed that there must be a hidden mud pit there. All the grown deer cleared the pit in a single bound and landed safely on the other side. But the little fawn could not leap far enough. Its hind legs got caught at the edge of the muddy pit. Planting its forelegs on the bank, the fawn tried its best to climb up, but its hind legs sank deeper and deeper into the mire. The mother deer stood on the bank, watching her fawn's plight with anxious eyes, unable to offer any help.

In a single instant, Poonguzhali took in the whole scene and quickly discerned where the mud pit ended. She ran along the edge of the pit, crossed over at a firm spot, and approached the place where the fawn was struggling, trapped in the mud. At first, the mother deer was startled to see her. It seemed as if Poonguzhali understood the language of deer! She spoke softly in a gentle voice, and the mother deer, reassured, stood still. Poonguzhali knelt at the edge of the muddy pit, folded her legs, stretched out her arms, grabbed the fawn, and pulled it up with all her strength onto the bank.

For a few moments, the little fawn's body trembled all over. The mother deer stood close by, sniffed it, and seemed to offer words of comfort! That was all! In the very next instant, mother and fawn bounded away together once more.
“Pah! Such ungrateful creatures, these animal lives!” Poonguzhali muttered to herself. “But still, these deer are not any worse than humans!” she added, consoling herself.
Then, once again, she set off towards the Kuzhagar temple.

After crossing the sandy expanse, she had to make her way through a dense forest path, thick with trees and shrubs. She had to climb up hills and descend into hollows. That forest must surely be counted among nature’s marvels. There were no mountains or hills made of rock there—only a vast stretch of sand. Here and there, the sand had risen into mounds, and upon those mounds, shrubs and trees had sprouted, binding the earth together and transforming the landscape into veritable hills. Beside these hills, there were also deep hollows. To find one’s way through such a forest was no simple task. It might seem as though one had walked a great distance, yet one would find oneself returning again and again to the very spot from which one had set out!

Poonkuzhali entered that forest path and, walking swiftly, soon reached the vicinity of the temple. Outside the temple, as well as within the inner courtyard, trees such as konnai and paneer grew tall and blossomed, their flowers swaying in the breeze. Poonkuzhali entered the temple. The priest’s face brightened upon seeing her. It was a rare thing for anyone to come to that temple for darshan; thus, it was only natural for the priest to rejoice at the sight of a rare visitor.

He brought her a coconut shell filled with prasadam and offered it to her. “Child, will you wait a little while? I shall lock up the sanctum and come home with you!” he said. After nightfall, it was indeed a difficult thing to traverse that forest path. But with Poonkuzhali as a guide, there was no need for worry.

“I will wait, Ayya! I am in no hurry. Finish the temple duties at your leisure and then let us depart,” said Poonkuzhali, and went out to the temple courtyard. Grasping a tree branch, she leapt up onto the temple wall. In the corner of the wall stood a great statue of Lord Nandi. Leaning slightly against the statue, she stretched out her legs and lay down along the wall. With her teeth, she scraped at the coconut shell and began to eat.

As Poonkuzhali gazed at the strange darkness gathering on all sides, she heard the sound of horse’s hooves. She looked eagerly in the direction from which the sound came. The rhythm of the hooves awakened old memories within her, carrying her away into a world of dreams. From somewhere, an unknown sorrow welled up and filled her heart. Who could it be coming? Whoever it might be, what did it matter to her? Of late, many new people had been coming and going. They said they came on royal business; they said they were leaving on royal business. Even yesterday, two men had come. Just to look at them was repulsive. They had made her brother row them to Eezham, to Lanka. They had given plenty of money. May lightning strike their money! Who needs money? What use was money in this wild forest? Yet for her brother and his wife, money was everything. For what reason, she did not know! They saved and saved, burying it away.

The sound of horse hooves—there it is, drawing near. Not one horse; it seems as though two horses are approaching. Look, they are visible now. Slowly, they are climbing up the slope from the hollow below. The horses are weary, exhausted from a long journey. Upon each horse rides a man. The one who comes first is a youth, a man in the prime of his youth. He is handsome to behold; yet, he is gaunt and worn. There is a certain majesty upon his face. But where is the beauty and grandeur of that other face that dwells in the innermost chamber of her heart? Where is his face, and where is that other? If one were to look closely, would not his face resemble the flat, owl-like visage carved upon a wooden post?

Of the two who approached on horseback, the one who came first is our old friend, Vallavarayan Vandiyathevan. The one who follows is the physician’s son. Both have grown thin and weary by the time they have reached here from Pazhaiyarai. Yet, the moment Vandiyathevan’s eyes fell upon Poonguzhali, who was reclining with her legs stretched out atop the temple wall, his face brightened a little. When he realized that she was gazing intently at him, a natural enthusiasm welled up within him. He too halted his horse and looked at her face with eager curiosity. Had he known that she was comparing his face to that of an owl carved on a wooden post, he might not have been quite so elated. How convenient it is that no one can ever fully know the thoughts that dwell in another’s mind!

Poonguzhali realized that the man on horseback was gazing intently at her. She also became aware that she was sitting there, holding a coconut in her hand, scraping at it with her teeth and eating. Suddenly, from somewhere, a sense of shyness seized her. She leapt down from the temple wall onto the white sand below. She began to run along the edge of the wall.

Seeing this, Vandiyathevan too felt an urge to leap down from his horse. He wanted to jump down and chase after Poonguzhali, to catch up with her. And so, he ran after her in pursuit. Who can unravel the reasons and causes behind such meaningless actions? It must be said that it is the ancient, inherited nature of humankind, passed down through thousands and tens of thousands of years, that made Poonguzhali run, and that same nature that made Vandiyathevan chase after her.

chapters.title: The Quagmire
paragraphs: Across forest and hill, over stone and thorn, Vandiyathevan ran, pursuing that maiden. At one moment she appeared before his eyes; in the very next, she vanished. Just as he thought it would be impossible to catch her, she would again come into view. The tale of Rama chasing the illusory Maricha came to Vandiyathevan’s mind. Yet, this was no illusion, nor was she Maricha—only the speed of a deer was certainly present in her feet. Oh, how swiftly she ran! “Why am I chasing after her like this? Is this not sheer madness?” he wondered. But at once, he invented a reason for himself. As they drew closer to Kodikkarai, the image of the maiden described by Sendhan Amudhan kept recurring to him. Surely, this must be that very Poonguzhali. If he befriended her, it would be advantageous for the task at hand. Moreover, he could ask her the way to the lighthouse. From afar, as they approached, the summit of the lighthouse had been visible to them. But nearing it was not so easy. Once they entered the forest, the lighthouse could no longer be seen. They wandered in circles within the woods, unable to find the path. It was at this time that Vandiyathevan had glimpsed Poonguzhali atop the wall of the Kuzhagar temple. He thought to catch her and ask for directions, but she now fled like a magical deer, eluding his grasp. Should he simply give up and turn back? Yet, even in a race, to be defeated by a woman was not something his heart could accept…

Ah! There, the open plain had arrived. In the distance, the blue sea was visible. How beautiful was the sight of that vast, tranquil ocean, stretching out in serenity! There—the lighthouse could be seen, too. At its summit, the beacon now blazed forth, its crimson rays spreading in all directions, weaving wondrous magical patterns. Should he abandon the chase here and head straight for the lighthouse? No! No! In this open plain, catching her would be easy. Here, there was not so much sand; his feet did not sink. The earth was covered with sturdy grass. In some places, mud had dried and cracked. Here, he could run unhindered. He could easily catch that maiden! Moreover, was she not running toward the sea? However far she ran, in the end, she would have to stop at the shore! Perhaps this… Will that mysterious woman vanish, swallowed by the sea itself? Alas! Why did I not come on horseback? Had I arrived thus, in this open plain, I could have caught her in a single instant!

Look—she hesitates for a moment. Instead of running straight towards the sea, she turns to the right! She runs towards the forest visible at some distance to her right, perhaps to avoid being caught by me. If she enters the woods, it will be impossible to catch her! All this running would be in vain! Even Vandiyathevan’s legs had begun to falter at that moment...

But it seems she has changed her mind again! She appears to have abandoned her intention of entering the forest! Like a spinning top, she turns and runs back. Perhaps she now wishes to go to the foot of the lighthouse. With just a few leaps, I could catch her. If I seize her by the hand and say, “Girl! Why do you flee in fear at the sight of me? I have brought a message from your beloved!”—how astonished she would be! It is true that Sendhan Amudhan did not send any message through me. But what of it? I could invent something myself and say it...

Resolving thus in his mind, Vandiyathevan gathered all the remaining strength in his body and dashed forward. His intention was to catch her in four swift strides as she ran back towards him. Suddenly, he cried out, “Aiyo!” At first, he did not understand what had happened to him. Then, it began to dawn on him. Both his legs were sinking into the mud. At first, only his feet were caught. Then, the mud rose to his ankles, and soon it had climbed up to his knees!

Alas! How this place has deceived me! From above, it looked dry and firm, baked by the sun. But beneath, the mud was still wet. Vandiyathevan had heard tales of such ever-damp, treacherous mud-pits—where cattle, horses, even elephants, if they fell in, would slowly sink deeper and deeper, until at last they were swallowed whole and vanished without a trace! Is this one of those deadly pits? It seems so. I am already buried up to my knees! Will I keep sinking further? Soon, I may be buried up to my thighs! Will this mud, which swallows elephants and horses and belches them down, spare me? Aiyo! Is this to be my end? Are all the countless daydreams I have cherished to be buried here as well?

At this perilous moment, only if that strange woman comes and lends a hand to save me, is there hope. There is no other way to escape. With a great shout... Let’s see. Thinking thus, Vandiyathevan cried out, “Ayyo! I am done for! I am sinking in the mud and dying! Is there no one to lend a hand and save me?”

That desperate cry reached the ears of Poonguzhali. She, who had been running a short distance ahead, stopped in her tracks. For a moment, she hesitated. She saw and understood the perilous state Vandiyathevan was in.

The next instant, her eyes fell upon a boat lying half-buried in the sand and half in the muddy pit. When the pit had been filled with water and had formed a deep stream, that boat must have been in use. Now, with agile grace, she leapt into it. She seized the oar and rowed twice with force. Ah! What a wonder! The boat, instead of gliding over water like a swan, now skimmed swiftly over the mud! Floating thus, it reached the opposite bank of the muddy pit. Poonguzhali jumped onto the firm ground. Planting her feet firmly on the shore, she grasped Vandiyathevan’s hands and pulled him up onto the bank.
Oh my! How much strength there was in those slender hands! Compared to the iron hands of the commander of Thanjavur Fort, the young Pazhuvettaraiyar, hers seemed even stronger!
Once he reached the bank, Vandiyathevan burst out laughing. Only his legs trembled a little.
“It seems you think you have saved me and brought me to shore! Did you imagine that, if you hadn’t come, I wouldn’t have managed to get out myself?” he said.
“Then why did you cry out ‘Ayyo! Ayyo!’ like that?” Poonguzhali asked.
“It was only to stop you from running away!”
“In that case, I’ll throw you back into the pit. With your cleverness, get out on your own!” said Poonguzhali, pretending to push him back.
“Aiyayyo!” exclaimed Vandiyathevan, stepping away from her.
“Why are you shouting?”
“I’m not afraid for my life; it’s the mud I fear! Already, I’m covered in it up to my thighs!”
A smile blossomed on Poonguzhali’s face. She looked Vandiyathevan up and down.
“There’s the sea! Go, wash off the mud and clean yourself!” she said.
