“You must go a little ahead and show the way!” said Vandiyathevan. The two of them walked towards the seashore, skirting around the muddy hollow.
“As soon as you saw me, why did you fall down and run away like that? Did you think I was some terrible ghost or demon?” Vallavarayan asked.
“No; I didn’t think you were a ghost or demon. I thought you were an owl. Your face looks just like an owl’s face!” she said, and burst out laughing.
Vandiyathevan took great pride in his appearance. So, being called an owl-faced fellow made him quite angry.
“Compared to your monkey face, my owl face is far better!” he muttered.
“What did you say?”
“Nothing. I just asked why you ran away when you saw me.”
“Why did you chase after me like that?”
“I chased you to ask the way to the lighthouse…”
“There it is, you can see the light! Why would you need to ask me?”
“After entering the forest, I couldn’t see it anymore. That’s why! But why did you run away as soon as you saw me?”
“Boys are very troublesome. I don’t like boys at all!”
“Not even Sendhan Amudhan?” Vallavarayan asked, his voice a little softer.
“Whom did you mention?”
“I meant Sendhan Amudhan of Thanjavur.”
“What do you know about him?”
“I know he is your beloved.”
“What? What?”
“Your name is Poonguzhali, isn’t it?”
“My name is Poonguzhali. What did you say about Sendhan Amudhan? He is my…”
“I said he is your lover.”
Poonguzhali laughed like a koel. “Who told you that?” she asked.
“Who else could it be? Sendhan Amudhan himself told me.”
“Thanjavur is very far from here. That’s why he made up such stories and escaped!”
“If not…?”
“If he had said such things in front of me, I would have thrown him into that muddy pit over there.”
“What of it? There’s plenty of water in the sea to wash off the mud!”
“In that quicksand pit you fell into, cattle and horses have sunk and died. Even an elephant would be swallowed by it!”

A shiver ran through Vandiyathevan’s body. He recalled the feeling he had when the pit had slowly begun to drag him down. If this girl had not come and pulled him to safety, by now… The very thought made his whole body tremble.
“What else did Sendhan Amudhan say about me?” Poonguzhali asked.
“He said you are his uncle’s daughter. He said that even in the heavenly realms, there is no beauty to compare with you…”
“Has he been to the heavenly realms himself, then, to know that…?”
“He said you sing beautifully. That if you sing, even the sea will hush its roar to listen to your song! Is that true?”
“Find out for yourself! Look—the sea is here!”
The two of them stood together at the edge of the shore.

chapters.title: A Madman's Delusion
paragraphs: The stars in the sky were winking their eyes. The crescent moon was making its procession, like a silver boat floating upon the blue sea. The wind was fierce. The sea roared; the waves stretched out their arms, trying to pull those standing on the shore into its embrace.
“Why are you standing there? Quickly wash off the mud! We must go home at once. Otherwise, I won’t get any supper tonight. My sister-in-law will tip over the rice pot!” said Poonguzhali.
“Is the sea very deep here?” asked Vandiyathevan.

“I’ve never seen a coward like you. There’s no depth here for a long distance. Even if you walk far into the sea, the water will only reach your waist. That’s why the lighthouse must burn every night!”

Vandiyathevan hesitated, then stepped into the water. He washed off the mud, cleaned his hands and feet, and climbed back onto the shore. A little distance away, he saw the physician’s son riding his horse towards them. Vandiyathevan’s own horse was beside him.
“Oh no! My horse is about to step into the mud!” cried Vandiyathevan.
“It won’t. Horses are wiser than men!” said Poonguzhali.
“But there’s a man on one of the horses! He’s pulling my horse along with him!”
“That’s a bit dangerous! Run and warn him!”
“Stop! Stop!” shouted Vandiyathevan as he ran and managed to halt them.
Poonguzhali soon joined them. The three of them walked towards the lighthouse.
“You could ride your horse, you know,” said Poonguzhali.
“No; I’ll walk with you.” Poonguzhali went near the horse and gently stroked its face. The horse, as if delighted by her touch, shivered its body and neighed softly.
“It seems my horse has taken a liking to you! That is very good.”
“In what way is it good?”
“I must go to Lanka. I was thinking I could entrust this horse to you before I leave. Will you take care of it?”
“Oh! I will take care of it. All animals quickly become fond of me. Only humans dislike me at first sight.”
“Why do you say that? Sendhan Amudhan cares for you…”
“My affection too is only for animals; I do not like to see humans!”
“What have humans done to you?”
“Humans are wicked. Lies and deceit are their only business!”
“You mustn’t speak so of everyone. Sendhan Amudhan is a good man. Look, here comes the physician’s son—he is a very good man…”
“How about you?”
“I am a good man too. But I shouldn’t boast of my own virtues, should I?”
“Why have you both come here?”
“The Emperor is unwell, is he not? Some rare herbs are needed to cure his illness. It is said that such rare herbs are found in this forest. That is why the physician’s son and I have come…”
“Just now you said you must go to Lanka?”
“The herbs that cannot be found here must be brought from Lanka. Isn’t the Sanjeevani mountain, which Hanuman brought, still said to exist in Lanka?”
“Yes, it is there. That is why thousands of people are now dying of fever and poison in Lanka…”
“Is that so? I did not know that! Nor does the palace physician who sent us know that…”
“I have never seen anyone lie as much as young men do. Two days ago, two men came here. They too told some lie just like you. But at least their lie was a little more believable.”
“Who were they? What lie did they tell?”

“They claimed that some magician had sent them. They said they needed a tiger’s claw and an elephant’s tail hair to tie a protective charm for the Emperor, and that they were going to Lanka for that purpose. My brother took them in his boat and has gone to Lanka with them…”

“Oh! Oh! Is that so too?” exclaimed Vandiyathevan. The memory of Ravidasan, that fearsome sorcerer, flashed through his mind. He also remembered the terrifying experience he had endured that night in the ruined mandapam.

‘God! Why do I keep getting entangled in such affairs? I should be standing face to face with my enemy on the battlefield, fighting with valor and courage. Why have I become ensnared in these webs of trickery and sorcery?’

‘Who could those men who went to Lanka by boat before me be? How much can I trust this girl? Could she too be part of that treacherous group?… No, no! She is a woman without deceit or guile. It is best to win her friendship somehow.’
“Poonguzhali! I will tell you the truth. Earlier, I said I came to fetch herbs, but that was a lie! I am going to Lanka on a very important and secret mission. I wish to tell you about it.”
“No! Don’t you know that important secrets should never be told to women? Don’t tell me anything…”
“That’s what they say about ordinary women. If I share a secret with you, nothing bad will come of it.”
“How do you know I am not an ordinary woman? You haven’t even known me for an hour.”
“Poonguzhali! The moment I first saw you atop the wall of that temple, I was drawn to you. Let me ask you something. Will you answer me truthfully?”
“Ask and see!”
“Sendhan Amudhan is not your lover— is that true? Are you not going to marry him?”
“Why do you ask?”
“Sendhan Amudhan is my friend; I must not do anything against him. But if he is not your lover…”
“Speak! Why do you hesitate?”

“I was wondering if I might apply for that position myself. Poonguzhali! I do not like the way you speak so little of love. In this world, there is no force more divine than love. Appar, Sundarar, Sambandar—all sang of God as their beloved. Tholkappiyar, Valluvar, and the great Tamil poets have all sung of love. Kalidasa sang of love. In Brindavan, Kannan was ensnared by the love of the Gopis…”
“Sir! Let me say one thing. Listen well and take it to heart!”
“What is that?”
“I, too, find you likable. When I saw the men who came two days ago, I felt a strong dislike, but I did not feel that way towards you…”
“Oh! Oh! I must be a yogi, then!”
“But do not speak of love and such things!”
“Why? Why?”
“Sendhan Amudhan is not my lover. But I do have other lovers…”
“Oh my! Oh my! Other lovers? Who? How many?”
“In the middle of the night, I will leave my house. If you follow me, I will show them to you. You can see for yourself!”
So saying, Poonguzhali laughed out loud, “Ha ha ha!”
That laughter did something strange to Vandiyathevan’s heart.
“Poor girl, she must be a little mad! It is useless to expect any help for my mission from her. It is best not to tell her anything.”

They approached the house near the lighthouse. From within the house, an elderly man and an aged woman came outside. The old man stood astounded, having seen Poonguzhali, the two strangers, and their horses.
“Poonguzhali! Who are these people? Where did you find them?” he asked.
“I didn’t find them, Father! They found me!” replied Poonguzhali.
“It’s all the same. If I tell you, ‘Come home before nightfall,’ you never listen. The other day, you brought two people home. Today, you’ve brought two more. Why have they come here?”
“They’ve come to take herbs for the Emperor’s treatment, Father!”
“Is this true, sir? Is what this girl says the truth?” the old man asked, turning to Vandiyathevan.
“Yes, elder! Here is the letter!” said Vandiyathevan, and from the cloth tied around his waist, he took out a palm-leaf letter and handed it to the old man.
At that moment, another palm-leaf slipped and fell to the ground. He quickly bent down, picked it up, and secured it carefully.
“What a fool I am! Even after things go wrong once, I don’t learn my lesson!” he muttered to himself.

The old man took the letter and examined it carefully in the light of the lighthouse. His face brightened. Looking at his wife, he said, “The Young Princess has sent this letter. We must give them food. Go inside and tell your daughter-in-law! She’s about to overturn the rice pot in her haste!”

chapters.title: At Midnight
paragraphs: After the evening meal, Vandiyathevan met privately with the head of the lighthouse and explained that he needed to travel to Lanka without delay. The venerable man, known as Thyagavidanga Karaiyar, expressed his regret.

“In earlier times, there were many large and small boats along this shore. Now, all of them have gone to Sethukkarai. They have been sent to aid our army stationed in Lanka. I own two boats myself. Of those, my son left yesterday, taking two men with him. I do not know when he will return. What can be done?” he said.
“Who are those men? Your daughter mentioned that they seemed rather suspicious,” asked Vandiyathevan.

“Yes, I too did not like the look of them. I do not know who they are, nor do I know their purpose. They carried the palm insignia of the Pazhuvettarayar. Even so, I would not have sent my son with them. But my daughter-in-law is extremely greedy for money. When she heard them promise a bag full of gold, she insisted that her husband must go…”

“What is this, sir? Is it proper that your son should obey the words of a young girl with no experience of the world?” said Vandiyathevan. Then, hesitating a little, he added, “Forgive me, that is your family’s concern!”
“My boy, there is nothing wrong in your asking. My family is under a curse. My son…” The old man faltered.
At that moment, Vandiyathevan remembered what Sendhan Amudhan had told him about this family.
“Is your son unable to speak?” he asked.
“Yes; but how did you know?” the elder replied.

Vandiyathevan then told him about Sendhan Amudhan, his mother, and how he had stayed at their house. “Aha! So you are that man? News of you has already reached here before you arrived. They say you are being searched for all over the land?”
“That may be so; but I do not know anything about it.”
“Now I understand why you are so eager to go to Lanka.”
“Elder! What you are thinking is not correct. I am not going to Lanka merely to save my own life. I am carrying a very important letter to someone there. If you wish, you may see it.”
“That is not necessary. It is enough for me that the young princess has written about you. But at this moment, I am unable to give you the help you seek!”
“You mentioned there was another boat?”
“There is a boat. But there is no one to row it. If you and your friend are willing to row it yourselves, I will give it to you…”
“Neither of us knows how to row a boat. In fact, I am a little afraid of water. Especially the sea…”

“Even if you know how to row, those without experience cannot row a boat in the sea. Once you go a little distance, the shore will disappear. Then you will be left to wander, lost, not knowing which direction to go.”
“I am not taking the man who came with me. I must leave him here to gather herbs. You must help me by suggesting some other way.”
“There is a way. But it is not easily accomplished. You must try! If fortune is on your side…”
“What must I do? Elder, tell me and I will surely do it,” said Vandiyathevan.
“In this region, there is no one as skilled at rowing a boat as Poonguzhali. She has gone to Lanka many times. I will speak to her; you too must ask her!”
“Call her now; let us ask her and see.”

“No, let it be; she is extremely stubborn. If you ask her now and she says ‘No,’ then it will be impossible to change her mind later. Tomorrow, at an opportune moment, I will speak to her. You too, try to ask her when you find her alone!”

Thus saying, Thiyagavidanga Karaiyar turned and walked towards the lighthouse. Vandiyathevan lay down on the veranda of his house. The physician’s son who had come with him had already fallen asleep. Fatigue from his long journey weighed heavily on Vandiyathevan’s eyelids, and soon he too drifted into sleep.

Suddenly, his sleep was broken. He heard the sound of a door opening. With some effort, Vandiyathevan forced open his tired eyelids. He saw a figure stepping out from inside the house. He looked more closely. It was the figure of a woman. The light from the lighthouse fell upon her form. Ah! It was Poonguzhali! There was no doubt.

What was it she had said to him? “Follow me at midnight! I will show you my lovers!” At the time, he had thought it was merely a jest. But now, here she was, truly rising in the middle of the night and leaving! Where was she going? If she were going to meet her lover—or lovers—would she have told him so openly? Would she have said, ‘If you follow me, I will show you’? There must be some mysterious meaning behind this! Or perhaps… Whatever it was, why shouldn’t he follow her and see for himself? Tomorrow, he needed to persuade her to row the boat to Lanka. If he followed her now, it might help his cause. If she were to encounter any danger, and he were to save her, she might be more willing to agree to his request tomorrow.

Vandiyathevan rose silently, careful not to make a sound. He followed the path Poonguzhali had taken. He remembered well the experience he had suffered earlier that evening when he had fallen into the muddy pit. He did not wish to repeat that ordeal. Therefore, he was determined not to let Poonguzhali out of his sight.

For a short distance from the lighthouse, the land was open and clear. Thus, Poonguzhali’s figure was visible. There was no difficulty in following the path she took. He quickened his pace, thinking to catch up and confront her. But it was not possible. The faster he walked, the quicker her steps became. She did not seem to notice that he was following her.

Once past the open ground, the land became hilly and densely wooded. Instead of climbing directly over the hill, Poonguzhali skirted its base. She reached the end of the hill and the forest, and turned around the edge. Vandiyathevan hurried after her. As soon as he rounded that corner, he saw her walking a short distance ahead. “What luck!” he thought, his courage returning. But in the very next moment, she had vanished.

How could she have disappeared so suddenly? Was this some magic, some sorcery? Could there be a hollow or pit there? She had been walking at a brisk pace—where could Poonguzhali have stopped and vanished? Wondering thus, he hurried to that spot and stood, looking all around. She could not have gone in three of the directions; if she had, she could not have escaped his sight. He carefully pressed his foot on the ground to check for mud or quicksand, but found none. Therefore, she must have climbed up the mound and entered the forest.

Looking more closely, he noticed a narrow footpath winding up the thickly overgrown mound. Vandiyathevan climbed it. As he ascended, his heart pounded with anxiety. Not even the dim light from the lighthouse reached here. The crescent moon had already sunk beneath the sea. In the faint glow of the twinkling stars, he could barely see the path a short distance ahead. The thorny shrubs and stunted trees took on fearsome shapes. Their shadows turned into black demons. When the leaves rustled, the shadows swayed as well. Each movement sent a tremor through Vandiyathevan’s heart. In that dense darkness and shadow, who could say what danger lay in wait? Venomous creatures, ferocious beasts could be lurking, ready to pounce. Danger could come from above, from the sides, from behind. Alas! What is this? Have I come here only to be trapped? I don’t even have a weapon in hand!
What is that rustling sound? What is that dark figure visible atop the tree? In the gloom of that bush, two tiny points of light are gleaming—what could they be?
Vandiyathevan’s legs trembled without his knowing. Enough! Enough! What business have I here? Why did I come?—What foolishness! I must turn back at once and leave!
Just as he resolved to descend and turned to do so, a voice was heard. A voice that pierced his heart; a woman’s voice. A sound choked with sobs. Then, this song:
“When the waves of the sea are stilled
Why does the inner ocean surge? When Mother Earth herself is asleep, Why does my heart overflow?...

Vandiyathevan abandoned his plan to climb down from the mound. Instead, he ascended, drawn toward the direction from which the voice had come. Soon, the summit of the mound came into view. There she stood—Poonguzhali. It was she who had sung. She alone. Gazing up at the radiant stars in the sky, she sang. It seemed as if she imagined those very stars to be an audience of connoisseurs, gathered to listen to her song!

Among the stars, one was a comet. From it, a long, silvery tail stretched out like a fan, spreading across the heavens. Upon the summit of the mound, the silhouette of that maiden, her voice and her song, and the comet blazing in the sky—all these together cast a spell upon Vandiyathevan. His feet carried him, almost against his will, to the very top.

He stood directly before Poonguzhali. Far behind her, at what seemed a great distance, the red light of the lighthouse at Kalangarai flickered. Beyond that, the vast sea stretched out endlessly. A silver line of waves, curving and bending, marked the boundary of the ocean as if drawing its very limits.
“So, you have come? I thought you were sleeping on the veranda like Kumbhakarna…” she said.
“I woke up at the sound of the door opening. You walked away so lightly, without a backward glance! Oh my! How hard it was to chase after you!”
“Why did you follow me?”
“A good question! Wasn’t it you who asked me to come? Have you forgotten?”
“Why did I ask you to come? Do you remember?”
“How could I forget? You said you would show me your lovers! Where are your lovers? Show me, let me see them!”
“There, behind you—turn and look!” said Poonguzhali.

chapters.title: In the Midst of the Sea
paragraphs: Vandiyathevan turned around. From his stomach, his intestines seemed to rise up and block his chest. Then, climbing higher still, they choked his throat. A thousand flashes of lightning coursed through his body. The points of a hundred thousand ripe and hardened needles pierced him all over—such was the terrifying sight that unfolded before his eyes.

In the endless expanse of darkness, here and there, ten, twenty, a hundred balls of fire appeared. There was no smoke from them; there was no light; nor were they the flames that rise from burning wood below. They were mere lumps of fire. Somehow, they had risen from the earth and stood suspended. Suddenly, some of those fireballs vanished. New ones sprang up in their place.

A colossal demon, black as the night itself, like the Kabandha of legend—one without a head, with a mouth in its belly—stood there. But this demon had not one, but many mouths. He opened and closed those mouths again and again. When he opened them, tongues of fire leapt out from his belly through those mouths. When he closed them, the flames disappeared.

Witnessing this scene, Vandiyathevan felt as though blood was seeping out through every hair on his body. Never before had such terror seized him—not even in the subterranean chamber of Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar.

Behind him, he heard a laugh—“Ha ha ha!” He turned. It was Poonguzhali! At another time, that very laughter might have filled him with unspeakable dread. But now, it gave him courage. The presence of a living, breathing woman of flesh and blood beside him was like a staff to cling to in the midst of great peril.
“Did you see my lovers?” Poonguzhali asked.
“These fiery-mouthed demons are my lovers. It is to converse with them that I come here at midnight,” she said.

There was not the slightest doubt in Vandiyathevan’s mind now that this woman was quite mad. Was it possible to reach Lanka with her help?—so he wondered. Yet, from deep within, another thought struggled to surface. What was it? Something about these fiery-mouthed demons.

“Can your friend Sendhan Amudhan ever hope to compete with such lovers?” asked Poonguzhali, her voice echoing as though it came from the depths of a well. For, at that moment, Vandiyathevan’s mind was striving to recall something. Ah! At last, a great struggle—yes, now he remembered…

In lands where the earth is mixed with sulphur, water often stagnates for a long time, turning the ground into a marsh. In such places, at night, strange phenomena appear. When sulphur-laden gases rise from the earth and escape into the air, it sometimes looks as if tongues of fire are flickering above the ground. Sometimes these flames linger; sometimes they flare up briefly and vanish. People who do not understand this natural occurrence are frightened by it. They give it a terrifying name—‘the demon of the burning mouth’—and are seized by fear…

He had heard elders speak of such things; now it all came back to him. Then, within him, a battle raged between his reason and his fear. Reason triumphed. But there was no use explaining all this now to this girl, who was so gripped by her own delusions. Somehow, he had to speak kindly to her and persuade her to come away.
“Girl! Your lovers are not going anywhere; they will remain here. You can come and see them again tomorrow, can’t you? Let’s go home, come!” he said.
Poonguzhali did not reply; she began to sob uncontrollably.
“What a nuisance this is!” thought Vandiyathevan. He stood silent for a moment.
“Girl! Shall we go?” he asked again.
Her sobs did not cease.
Vandiyathevan grew impatient.
“Very well; do as you wish! I am feeling sleepy. I’m going,” he said, and began to descend.
At once, Poonguzhali stifled her sobs. She started down from the mound, and in a flash, she was ahead of Vandiyathevan, standing below.
Vandiyathevan hurried after her and caught hold of her.
Together, they began to walk towards the lighthouse.
‘Is it wise to trust this mad girl and get into the boat? To cross the sea with her? Yet, it seems there is no other way. Should I try to win her over with kind words, and make her a friend?’
“Look, a comet has appeared in the sky! What do you think about that?” asked Poonguzhali.
“I have no particular opinion. A comet appears; that is all,” replied Vandiyathevan.
“They say that when a comet appears in the sky, great calamities befall the earth!”
“Yes, that is what some people say.”
“What do you say?”
“I have never studied astrology. I only know what people say among themselves.”
They walked in silence for a while.
Then Poonguzhali asked, “They say the Emperor is unwell. Is that true?”
‘She is not as mad as she seems,’ thought Vandiyathevan. A little hope arose in him.

“I have seen it with my own eyes. The Emperor lies bedridden. He has no feeling in either leg. He cannot take even a single step. I have come to fetch a rare herb to cure him. Girl, will you help me?” he asked.
Without answering, Poonguzhali asked, “They say the Emperor will not live long, that he will die soon. Is that true?”
“If you do not help me now, it may well happen as they say. There is a rare life-restoring herb in Lanka. If we bring it, the Emperor may recover. Will you row the boat and take me to Lanka?”
“If the Emperor dies, who will ascend the throne next?” Poonguzhali’s question struck Vandiyathevan like a blow.
“Girl! What does it matter to you or me? Why should we worry about who ascends the throne?”
“Why shouldn’t we worry? Aren’t you and I subjects of this kingdom?”
‘This girl is not mad at all. I must deal with her cautiously. There must be some other reason behind her strange behavior.’
“Why are you silent? Who will ascend the throne next?” Poonguzhali asked again.
“The title of Crown Prince has been given to Aditya Karikalan. Rightfully, he should be the next to ascend.”
“Madurantakan—does he have no claim at all?”
“Didn’t he himself say he did not want the kingdom?”
“He said so before; but now they say he wants the throne.”
“Is it enough if he alone says so? Shouldn’t all the people accept it?”
“They say many important men are on his side.”
“That’s what I’ve heard too. I’m truly surprised that all this news has reached your ears.”
“What if Sundara Chozhar suddenly passes away?”
“The whole country will be thrown into great turmoil. That is why your help is needed now…”
“What help can I give?”
“I told you before. I must go in haste to Lanka to fetch the medicinal herb. For that, you must row the boat and take me there.”
“Why are you calling me? Aren’t you ashamed to ask a young woman to row a boat?”
“Your father says there is no one else. Even your brother left yesterday, didn’t he?”
“What if he left? You have two hands, and the man who came with you has two hands, doesn’t he?”
“We don’t know how to row a boat…”
“Is rowing a boat some kind of magical art? If you grip the oar and row, the boat moves, doesn’t it?”
“But you must know the direction, mustn’t you? If you lose your way in the middle of the sea…?”
“If you lose your way in the middle of the sea, then drown and die! What can I do about it?”

They had now come near the lighthouse. Vandiyathevan, too, wished to end the conversation there. He did not want to prolong the talk and further strengthen Poonguzhali’s refusal. Though she had replied with such firmness, her voice and the tone of her speech had kindled a small spark of hope within his heart.

After lying down for the second time, Vandiyathevan could not sleep for a long while. His mind was greatly disturbed by a thousand thoughts. Only at the beginning of the fourth watch did he finally fall asleep.

In his sleep, Vandiyathevan dreamed. He and Poonguzhali were seated facing each other in a small boat made of lashed logs. All around them was the sea; wherever he looked, there was only water. A gentle, sweet breeze blew; the boat seemed to float along with that wind. Poonguzhali’s face shone with exquisite beauty. Her curly hair danced across her forehead. The end of her saree fluttered in the breeze. Where were they going, for what purpose were they going—Vandiyathevan had forgotten all such things. It seemed as if he had journeyed all these days just to travel in a boat with Poonguzhali. Only one thing was lacking. What was it? What was it? Ah! Poonguzhali’s song! Had not Sendhan Amudhan mentioned it?
“Maiden! Will you not open your coral lips and sing a song?” asked Vandiyathevan.
“What did you say?” Poonguzhali asked with a smile. Ah! Was there anything in all the seven worlds to compare with that smile?
“I asked if you would open your sweet lips and sing a melody.”
“If I sing a song, what will you give me?”
“I will come close to you and on your beautiful cheek…”
Immediately, Poonguzhali took a sharp knife from her lap. She raised the hand holding the knife.
“Look here! If you come even a hair’s breadth beyond that log, I’ll stab you with this knife. The sea fish are very hungry!” she said.

The ship sailed on, cleaving the vast expanse of the ocean as if it were a mighty chariot racing across an endless plain. The waves rose and fell, sparkling in the sunlight, their crests crowned with foam like garlands upon the heads of jubilant maidens. The wind, wild and unrestrained, whipped the sails and filled them with its invisible strength, driving the vessel forward with a relentless force.

Upon the deck, Vandiyathevan stood gazing at the horizon, his heart swelling with wonder and anticipation. Never before had he witnessed such a sight—the boundless sea stretching in every direction, its blue depths concealing untold mysteries. The cries of seabirds echoed above, and the salty spray stung his face, awakening in him a sense of adventure he had never known.

Beside him stood the captain, a seasoned mariner whose skin had been darkened by years beneath the sun. His eyes, sharp and steady, scanned the skies and the shifting waters with practiced ease. “Young man,” he said, “do you see that cloud bank to the south? A storm may be brewing. The sea is not always as gentle as she appears now.”
Vandiyathevan smiled, undaunted. “Let the storm come, captain! I have crossed forests and rivers, faced wild beasts and fiercer men. What is the sea to me?”

The captain laughed, a deep, booming sound that mingled with the roar of the waves. “Brave words! But remember, the sea has swallowed men braver than you. Pray to your gods, and keep your wits about you.”

As the sun dipped lower, painting the sky with hues of crimson and gold, the ship pressed on. The sailors moved about their tasks with silent efficiency, their faces set and determined. The air grew heavier, and the wind shifted, carrying with it the scent of rain.
Suddenly, a shout rang out from the lookout perched high above the mast. “Storm ahead! Clouds rising from the south!”
The captain’s voice rang clear. “Reef the sails! Secure the cargo! All hands, prepare for rough waters!”

In an instant, the tranquil mood vanished. The crew sprang into action, their movements swift and sure. Vandiyathevan gripped the rail, his heart pounding with excitement and a touch of fear. The sky darkened, and the first drops of rain fell, cold and sharp as arrows.

The ship heaved and pitched as the waves grew taller, crashing against the hull with thunderous force. Lightning split the sky, illuminating the churning sea in ghostly flashes. The wind howled, tearing at the sails and rigging, while the captain shouted orders above the storm’s fury.

Vandiyathevan clung to the deck, his mind racing. Was this to be the end of his journey? Would the sea claim him before he could fulfill his mission? Yet even as the tempest raged, a strange exhilaration filled him. He was a warrior, born to face danger. Whatever fate awaited him, he would meet it unflinching, in the midst of the roaring sea.

chapters.title: The Hidden Mandapam
paragraphs: The next morning, the crimson rays of the rising sun gently roused Vandiyathevan from his slumber. Even after waking, it took him a few moments to regain full awareness. He could not immediately discern whether the light that fell upon him was the sunlight or the beam from the lighthouse. When he tried to recall which of the previous night’s experiences were real and which were dreams, he found himself utterly confused.

At home, only the elder’s wife and his daughter-in-law were present. They told him that the elder had gone to the Kuzhagar temple to offer flowers for the morning rituals. Vandiyathevan did not have the courage to ask them about Poonguzhali. After partaking of the breakfast they offered, he looked around the house, searching with his eyes. Poonguzhali was nowhere to be found.

He thought to go to the temple and see. There, he found her father, who was gathering flowers from the trees surrounding the temple for the puja. The old man said that sometimes Poonguzhali came to string the flowers into garlands, but she had not come today.
“She must be chasing deer somewhere in the forest. Or perhaps she is wandering along the seashore. Go and search for her if you wish!” he said.

“Brother! Be careful about one thing. She is a strange girl; do not say anything to her that might lead her astray. Don’t let the tales you’ve read in poetry tempt you into romantic mischief! She can turn into a fierce Kali in an instant. Then, your life will no longer be your own!” the elder warned him.

Remembering the dreamlike events of his first night, Vandiyathevan shivered with excitement. Then he set off into the forest to search for Poonguzhali. But where in that vast wilderness could he look? After a while, he grew weary of the search. He decided it was enough to simply leave the forest. Once outside, he headed towards the seashore. He wandered a long distance along the shore, but it was of no use. Poonguzhali was nowhere to be seen.

“She will surely return home for the midday meal. I can see her then!” he thought, and turned back. Suddenly, a new idea struck him. The sea was calm and gentle, its waves subdued. He felt a desire to bathe in those tranquil waters. He had already heard that the sea was not deep on this side, and Poonguzhali herself had mentioned it the previous evening. So, what was there to stop him from taking a dip? He decided to cast aside his fear of the sea. It was necessary to overcome this fear. There might come a time when he would have to travel by boat or ship. If he were afraid of the sea, how could he manage? He must rid himself of that fear.

He untied the cloth bundle and the dagger that were fastened around his waist, placed them on the shore, and stepped into the sea. Carefully, slowly, he set his feet, treading with caution. As he went further, the water never rose above his knees. When small waves came and struck him, the water reached his waist. No higher than that. “What a beautiful sea this is! There isn’t even enough water to drown and bathe!” he said to himself, and ventured further in.

‘Oh dear! Thinking there’s no depth, I’ve come quite far from the shore, haven’t I? What if suddenly the sea swells? What if the waves grow large and crash over me?’ This thought struck him, and he turned to look back at the shore.

‘It’s true—I have come a long way from the shore! But the sea won’t suddenly rise up like that!… Oh! Look, there’s Poonguzhali coming! I must get to the shore and catch her. I must seize her and ask her again with sweet words. It seems she’s coming this way only after seeing me! She’s walking straight toward where I am! She’s even making some sign at me…’

‘Oh! Oh! What’s this? She’s bending down on the shore—what is she looking at, what is she picking up? Isn’t that the cloth bundle I left around my waist? Girl! Don’t take that! That’s mine… But my words don’t reach her ears! The roar of these sea waves!’
‘Ah, now she’s heard my voice! She’s saying something to me, too! Poonguzhali! That’s mine! Don’t take it!…’
‘Look at that! Won’t you listen if I tell you? You take it in your hand as if it’s your own and walk away towards the hut—wait, wait!…’

Vandiyathevan began to run toward the shore! For a moment, Poonguzhali turned and looked at him. Then she, too, started running. But she ran toward the forest, in the direction opposite to the house and the lighthouse!
‘Ah! This girl is a mischievous one! Is she mischievous? Or merely mad? Somehow, I must get my half-cloth back from this madwoman…’

Twice he slipped and fell into the sea, swallowing a mouthful of salty water, before Vandiyathevan slowly made his way to the shore. Then he ran after that girl. The more he ran, the faster her pace became. Not far away, a herd of fifty or sixty deer darted past.

“How beautiful it is to see deer startled, leaping and bounding away! But look—this girl too is skipping and running! Her flight is no less graceful than that of the deer! The beauty of women who live so naturally and freely—what beauty it is!… But I must not say any of this to her. If I do, everything will be ruined! Didn’t the elder warn me?… Still, why is she running away so stubbornly? If she disappears into the forest, how will I ever find her again?… There, she’s already vanished into the woods. Now the task has become as difficult as finding a wall in the wilderness. There can be no fool in this world like me!… Will a garland snatched by a monkey ever return?”

Vandiyathevan too entered the forest after a short while. He wandered here and there. In his haste and excitement, he failed to part the bushes properly, and his whole body was scratched by thorns. He called out, “Poonguzhali! Poonguzhali!” Then he began to ask, “Tree! Have you seen Poonguzhali?” “Crow! Have you seen Poonguzhali?”
“What is this? I think I’m going mad!” he began to think, when suddenly something fell from above, from the tree!

Ah! It was his waistcloth, rolled up! With great eagerness, he picked it up and unrolled it. The palm-leaf, the gold coins—everything was safe! “Is your money safe?” a voice called from above. Vandiyathevan looked up in astonishment. Poonguzhali was sitting on a tree branch.
Dripping with sweat, Vandiyathevan, overcome by anger, said, “I’ve never seen such a madwoman as you!”
“I’ve never seen such an owl as you, oh my! What are you blabbering about?” said Poonguzhali.
“Why did you make me run around like this? If you wanted money—”
“Pah! Who here wants your money?”
“Then why did you run off with it?”
“If I hadn’t done as I did, you wouldn’t have come into the forest. You would have turned back to my house!”
“So what if I had?”
“Climb up this tree and see—you’ll understand!”
“What will I see?”
“You’ll see ten or fifteen horses! You’ll see swords and spears flashing!”

From the look on her face, it seemed she was telling the truth. Still, wanting to be certain, Vandiyathevan climbed up the tree. Before climbing, he tied the scroll securely around his waist. Who could say—perhaps she had dropped it from the tree earlier. Was she now plotting to snatch it back? Who could know her mind?

He climbed the tree and looked toward the lighthouse. “Yes, what Poonguzhali said is true.” There, ten or fifteen horses stood. Upon the horses sat warriors holding swords and spears, their weapons glinting in the light.
“Who could they be?… Surely, they must be the men of the Pazhuvettaraiyars, come to capture me! Who else could it be?”
Poonguzhali had saved him from great danger. But why? For what purpose?—Some questions still remained unanswered!
The two of them climbed down from the tree. “Poonguzhali, you have saved me from grave peril. I am deeply, deeply grateful to you!” said Vandiyathevan.
“Lies! Do men even know how to be grateful?” retorted Poonguzhali.
“Don’t think of me as just like all other men!”
“So, you’re not like everyone else; you’re a unique specimen, is that it?”
“Girl! May I ask you a question?”
“Ask as you please; whether I answer is up to me.”
“Why did you want to save me? What made you suddenly feel compassion for me?”
Poonguzhali fell silent. It was clear from her face that she was a little startled.
Then, after thinking for a moment, she said, “Whenever I see fools, I always feel a bit of pity for them.”
“Wonderful; but how did you know that these warriors had come searching for me?”

“Isn’t it obvious just by looking at you?—I guessed as much yesterday itself, that you were someone who had escaped and come here to hide. This morning, your friend, the physician’s son, confirmed it.”
“What nonsense did he babble?”

“As soon as he woke up this morning, he said he needed to go into the forest to search for herbs. I told him I would take him, and brought him here. He began to try and woo me. I said, ‘Your friend has already beaten you to it, hasn’t he?’…”
“What did you say?”

“Wait a moment; listen to the whole story! I told him that you had already started courting me. Only then did he reveal his suspicions about you. He said that, for various reasons along the way, he had begun to suspect you were fleeing in fear of royal punishment! ‘Don’t trust such a man and ruin yourself unjustly! Marry me instead!’ he pleaded. I replied, ‘Why are you in such a hurry? Shouldn’t we ask our elders?’ He said, ‘Let’s follow ancient Tamil custom and marry in secret!’ That’s what your charming friend said. How do you like the story?”
“You wretched scoundrel!” Vandiyathevan shouted.

“Amidst all this, we heard the sound of horses approaching. I told him to climb up the tree and look. When he stood atop the tree, the way his legs trembled and shook still makes me laugh whenever I remember it,” said Poonguzhali, and she laughed aloud.
“Enough of your games; what happened next?”

“He climbed down from the tree. ‘Did you see? What I said has come true. Royal guards have come to capture him!’ he said. ‘In that case, won’t they capture you too, since you came with him? You’d better run and hide somewhere!’ I told him. ‘That’s exactly what I must do,’ he replied. He left me and went away. And just as I expected, it happened…”
“What? What happened?”
“He told me he was going to run and hide, but instead, he walked straight in the direction where those horsemen were waiting—and let himself be caught by them…”
“Oh no! Poor fellow!”
“Don’t waste all your pity on him! Save a little for later!”
“Why do you say that?”

“Listen to the rest! You’ll understand for yourself. He went straight to them. They looked at him in astonishment. They stared and stared, then whispered secretly among themselves. ‘Who are you?’ he asked. ‘We are hunters! We’ve come here to hunt deer,’ one of them replied. ‘No, I know what you have come to hunt,’ he said. They were even more surprised and prodded him on. ‘You’ve come searching for Vandiyathevan. I’ll show you where he is. Will you let me go if I do?’ he asked. They agreed to this. He then led them towards our house…”
“Traitor! Wretch!…”
“After they left, I came looking for you. You were bathing in the sea…”
“Why didn’t you tell me all this right there? Why did you grab this bundle and run?”

“If I hadn’t, would you have run so fast? Perhaps you would have gone looking for those hunters, just to see them! Maybe you wouldn’t have believed a word I said. By the time I explained everything and got you to come with me, they might have spotted you…”
‘Ah! And we thought this girl was a fool,’ thought Vandiyathevan, feeling ashamed.
‘I must place my full trust in her. Without her help, I cannot cross the sea to Lanka. All this journey would be wasted. I might even fall back into the hands of the Pazhuvettarayars.’
“Girl! I cannot express how great a help you have been to me. You must help me with the rest as well…”
“What do you want me to do?” she asked.
“You have seen my friend’s character for yourself, haven’t you? You have realized there is no use in trusting him, haven’t you? You must be the one to row the boat and take me to Lanka!”
Poonkuzhali remained silent.

“Do you believe now that I am not one to do anything wrong? O maiden! I must go to Lanka at once for a matter of utmost importance. You must help me with this—this help is absolutely necessary for me…”

“What will you give me if I do it?” Poonkuzhali asked. For the first time, a sign of shyness appeared on her face. Her cheeks dimpled; the beauty of her face increased manyfold and shone with a radiant glow.

Vandiyathevan remembered that in the dream he had on the first night, she had asked him the very same question. The same words struggled to rise to his lips again. He bit his tongue with his teeth and stopped those words from escaping.

“O maiden! If you do this for me, I will never forget it as long as I live; I will be forever grateful. I do not know if there is anything I can do for you in return. If you ask me to do something, I will surely do it!”
Poonkuzhali fell into deep thought. She seemed to hesitate, as if unsure whether to say what she had in mind or not.
“If there is any return favor I can ask of you, shall I say it? Will you surely do it…?”
“Is that a promise?”
“A promise! A promise!”
“In that case, I will tell you when the time comes. You won’t forget then, will you?”
“I will never forget. I will wait for the day you ask your return favor.”
Poonkuzhali again fell into thought for a moment.
“Alright, come with me! I will take you to a place in this forest. You must stay there until evening today. You must remain fasting…”
“There’s no need to worry about that! This morning, your sister-in-law served me old rice. I ate more than usual just to provoke her heartburn. I won’t need any more food until night…”

“Who knows if you’ll even get food at night? I’ll try to bring you something in my hand. You must stay exactly where I tell you until it gets dark! After night falls, I’ll come back and make a sound. Have you ever heard the cuckoo sing ‘koo-koo, koo-koo’?”
“I’ve heard it well. Even if I hadn’t, I would recognize your voice.”
“As soon as you hear my call, you must come out from that place. Within an hour of nightfall, we must board the boat and leave.”
“I’ll wait for the cuckoo’s call.”

In the heart of the forest, Poonguzhali led Vandiyathevan to a spot where a mound of sand had been heaped. On the other side of the mound, the trees, shrubs, and vines grew even more thickly than elsewhere. Skillfully parting them with her hands, she descended into a hollow by the side of a tree. Vandiyathevan followed her down. There, the edge of an old mandapam could be seen. Looking more closely, two pillars of the shadowed mandapam became visible. Trees and vines concealed everything. From any direction, no one would know that a mandapam stood there.

“A leopard used to live in this mandapam. After it left, I made it my own. I keep it as my private dwelling. Whenever I wish to avoid people, I come here. There’s water in that pot. Stay here all day today! Even if you hear people’s voices all around, or the sound of galloping horses, or any other commotion, do not show yourself outside. Don’t climb up the mound to look!” said Poonguzhali.
“You want me to stay here even after nightfall? What if a wild animal, a tiger, or a leopard comes?…” asked Vandiyathevan.
“There are no tigers or leopards here now. If anything comes, it will be a jackal or a wild boar. Surely you’re not afraid of jackals or boars!”
“I’m not afraid. But what if something comes in the dark and falls on me? I don’t even have a spear in my hand—I left it at home.”

“Here! Take this weapon!” said Poonguzhali, handing him a weapon that lay in the mandapam. It was a strange weapon. On both sides, sharp, sword-like spikes gleamed. The spikes were harder than iron. Perhaps Indra’s own vajrayudha would look like this!
“What kind of weapon is this? What is it made of?” Vandiyathevan asked.
“This is the tail of a fish! When the leopard that lived in this mandapam leapt at me, I struck it with this and killed it!” replied Poonguzhali.

chapters.title: "Samudra Kumari"
paragraphs: That afternoon passed easily for Vandiyathevan. He spent more than half of it in sleep. All the time he was awake, his thoughts circled around the strange nature of Poonguzhali.
What a wondrous woman! What a sweet and simple name! But how stern is her character! Is it only sternness? No, there is a sweetness mingled within it as well!

How casually she spoke of the deed of slaying the leopard! And yet, at times, she behaves as if seized by a kind of madness—why is that? Surely, some bitter event must have occurred in this woman’s life! Or perhaps it was a sweet event? Either could have turned a woman into such a wild spirit! Or perhaps, with no cause at all, she was simply born with such a nature? But then, there is nothing unusual in the nature of her parents; they are gentle, peaceful souls!… Whatever her temperament, what is the reason for the special concern she has shown me? She has gone to such lengths to help me escape from the men of Pazhuvoor! She even said she would row me across to Lanka! Is there some deception in all this?… No, not for a moment. Yet, what caused the change in her heart? What favor does she expect from me? She said she would tell me later—what could it be?…

Thus Vandiyathevan’s mind wandered in thought. Meanwhile, just as Poonguzhali had foretold, there was frequent commotion all around him. The pounding of horses’ hooves, the shouts of men, the frightened cries of small forest creatures, the screeching of birds—all these together, at times, created a veritable battlefield of noise. Then, at other times, peace would descend and silence would reign.
Vandiyathevan realized that all this commotion was for the purpose of searching for and capturing him. The betrayal by the physician’s son also kept returning to his mind!

“Fool! He must have imagined that I had already fallen for Poonguzhali! Like the water in a small pond falling in love with the mighty Vaigai river! Like a mouse dreaming of marrying a lioness! But how cleverly this woman used his foolishness— She has done it! What kind of jealous fire has she kindled in his heart?… In the span of half an hour, she has turned him into a traitor! The power of womanhood is truly immense!

“Vandiyathevan! There is one thing you must admit! You thought yourself to be very clever! You were proud, believing that in cunning and wit, there was none to match you! But this wild, uncivilized forest girl has defeated you! What words can describe the trick she used to bring you, who were bathing in the sea, into this hidden mandapam? If she had not taken your waist-cloth and run away, what would have happened by now? You would have fallen into the hands of the Pazhuvur men! The mission would have been utterly ruined!… Yes, from now on, you must never be so careless again.”

In the western sea, the sun had set. On the shores of Kodikkarai, this was a wondrous sight. Until that point, the coastline running southward suddenly turned west at that tip. Thus, from the elevated ground at Kodikkarai, one could see the sea stretching out to the east, west, and south. In certain months, one could witness the sun and moon rising resplendently from the eastern sea. One could also see the sun turning the western sea to gold as it sank and disappeared. Vandiyathevan longed to climb atop the sand mound that covered the mandapam and watch the sun vanish into the sea. He suppressed the urge with effort.

Darkness gathered on all sides. The darkness that had already settled within the hidden mandapam grew many times blacker. Vandiyathevan could not remain there any longer; he stepped outside. He stood atop the sand mound that covered the mandapam. Far in the distance, the light from the lighthouse was visible. In the sky, diamonds glittered and shone. Strange sounds arose from the forest. The sounds heard in the wild during the day were very different from those heard at night. The nighttime sounds were filled with mystery, stirring both fear in the heart and a shiver in the body. Even if one saw a tiger face-to-face in the daytime, the mind would not be alarmed; there would be no fear. But at night, even if a tiny mouse scurried through a bush, the heart would skip a beat!

There—the call of the cuckoo; “Koo-koo! Koo-koo!” That voice echoed in Vandiyathevan’s ears like a divine melody. He walked toward the direction from which the sound came. There stood Poonguzhali. She gestured to him, “Come with me, without making a sound.” From there, it became clear that the seashore was very near.

On the seashore, a boat stood ready. Within it lay a rolled-up mat, a raft, and the ropes to bind them together. Two oars extended from the boat, and at the ends of those oars, a large wooden plank was fastened securely. Vandiyathevan moved to help launch the boat into the sea.
“You just stay still!” signaled Poonguzhali.
With practiced ease, she pushed the boat and set it afloat upon the sea. The boat entered the water without the slightest sound.
Vandiyathevan attempted to climb aboard. “Hush! Wait a moment! Once we’ve gone a little further, you can get in,” Poonguzhali whispered softly, pulling the boat along as she spoke.
Vandiyathevan, wanting to help, tried to push the boat as well. The boat came to a halt.
“It’s enough if you just come quietly!” said Poonguzhali.

After they had passed the place where the waves crashed against the shore, she said, “Now you can get into the boat.” She climbed in first, and Vandiyathevan leapt in after her. At that moment, the boat rocked violently. For an instant, it seemed as if Vandiyathevan would fall into the sea; but he managed to steady himself and sat down. Still, his heart pounded within his chest.
“Can we speak now, at least?” he asked.
“We can speak as much as you like—if your trembling has subsided!” Poonguzhali replied.
“Trembling? Who’s trembling? There’s nothing of the sort.”
“If there’s nothing, then that’s good!”
“Shouldn’t we tie the raft?”
“If we tie the raft, someone on the shore might spot us. They’ll come running and catch us.”
“If they come now, I’ll show them what I can do! You need not be afraid at all!” Vandiyathevan began to boast of his valor.

“Right now, the wind is against us. If we spread the raft, the boat will be driven back to the shore. After midnight, the wind may change. Then, if we spread the raft, it will be useful!” said Poonguzhali.
“Oh, you seem to know all about these things; that’s why your father asked me to bring you along.”
“My father? Whom are you talking about?”
“I’m talking about your father, of course. The guardian of the lighthouse at the sacred Thiyagavidanga shore.”
“He’s my father only when I’m on the shore. Once I set foot in the sea…”
“Does your father change then, too?”
“Yes. Here, the Lord of the Ocean is my father. My other name is Samudra Kumari—the Ocean’s Daughter. Hasn’t anyone told you?”
“No, they haven’t! What a strange name that is!”
“Don’t some people call the Emperor’s younger son ‘Ponniyin Selvan’—the Son of the Ponni? It’s just like that!”
At this, Vandiyathevan instinctively felt for the scroll tucked at his waist.
Noticing this, Poonguzhali asked, “Is it safe?”
“What are you asking about?”
“The thing you’ve kept in your waist scroll.”
A jolt of alarm ran through Vandiyathevan’s mind. A small doubt took root.
All the while, Poonguzhali continued rowing, her oar slicing through the water. The boat moved steadily onward.
“When will we reach the island of Lanka?” Vandiyathevan asked.
“If both of us row, and if the wind favors us, we’ll reach there by dawn!”
“I’ll row too; do you think I’d let you do it alone?”
Vandiyathevan grabbed the oar beside him and began to row. Ah! Rowing a boat was no easy task. It was hard, grueling work. The boat spun around with a ‘whirr’ and came to a complete stop.
“What’s this? When you row, the boat moves; but the moment I touch the oar, it stops!”
“Am I not the Princess of the Ocean? That’s why! If you simply remain quiet, that’s enough! Somehow or other, I will take you safely to Lanka; is that not so?”
Vandiyathevan felt a little embarrassed. He remained silent for a moment. As he looked around, his eyes fell upon the poles and planks that extended from the boat.
“What are these planks for?” he asked.
“To keep the boat from rocking too much.”
“Does the boat rock even more than this? Even now, it’s swaying as much as it pleases! I feel as if my head is spinning.”
“Is this what you call rocking? You should see it when the monsoon winds blow in Aippasi and Karthigai!”

From the shore, the sea had appeared calm, as smooth as a sheet of metal. But Vandiyathevan now realized that this was not so in reality. Wave after wave, though without foam, rose and fell ceaselessly. They rocked the boat as if it were a cradle.
“What happens to this plank when a strong wind blows?”

“It depends on how strong the wind is. If it’s just an ordinary gale, this plank will keep the boat from capsizing. But if a whirlwind strikes and the boat overturns, we must not let go of this plank; by holding onto it, we might save our lives.”
“Oh no! Can the boat really capsize in the wind?”
“If a whirlwind strikes, even the largest ships can be smashed to splinters. What chance does this little boat have?”
“What is a whirlwind?”

“Don’t you know even that? When winds from one direction and winds from another direction collide, a whirlwind is formed. Here, in the months of Thai and Maasi, the ‘Kondal wind’ blows. There’s no danger then. One can easily go to and return from Lanka, even by night. From Vaikasi onwards, the ‘Chozha wind’ blows. During the Chozha wind, it’s a bit difficult to go from here to Lanka. Now, it is the period between the Chozha wind and the monsoon wind. Sometimes, in the sea, the winds clash against each other. It’s as if the ocean is being churned, like curd being whisked— The wind churned the sea. Waves rose and crashed like mountains. Vast chasms appeared in the ocean. In those depths, the water swirled with a roaring sound. If the boat were to be caught in such a whirlpool, it would be the end.
A sudden terror seized Vandiyathevan’s heart. Along with it, a doubt sprang up.
“Oh no! I won’t go! Take me back to the shore and leave me there!” he shouted.
“What nonsense are you babbling? Be quiet! If you’re afraid, close your eyes. Otherwise, lie down and sleep!”
Vandiyathevan’s suspicion now became certain. “You are a great deceiver! You’re taking me out to sea to drown me. You think your task will be much easier if I fall asleep!”
“What madness is this?”
“There’s nothing wrong with me! Will you turn the boat around or not? If you don’t, I’ll jump into the sea!”
“Jump, by all means! But before you do, hand over the letter you’re supposed to deliver to Ponniyin Selvan!”
“Oh! How did you know about that letter?”

“I saw it when I untied the scroll at your waist. Would I have agreed to row you to Lanka without knowing who you are and why you’re going? This morning, while you sat atop the tree, I untied your waist scroll and read the letter…”
“Deceiver! I trusted you and came with you! Will you turn the boat or not?”
Vandiyathevan’s fear and rage multiplied many times over. “Turn the boat! Turn the boat!” he shouted.
“If I were the young princess Kundavai herself, I would never have entrusted such an important letter to a restless fellow like you!” said Poonguzhali.
“Oh! You even know who gave me the letter! There’s no doubt you are a traitor. Will you turn the boat, or shall I jump into the sea?”
“Jump! Jump, by all means!” said Poonguzhali.

Maddened, Vandiyathevan plunged with a splash into the sea. He had jumped in thinking that, as near the shore, the water would be shallow. He did not realize that the boat had already reached the deep part of the sea where it could not touch the bottom. Only after he had leapt into the water did he understand this. Once he realized it, he cried out and floundered.

By this time, Vandiyathevan had learned to swim to some extent. But the natural fear that arose in him upon seeing the water sapped the strength from his arms and legs. If it had been a river or a pond, he could have taken courage by looking at the nearby shore; but this was the vast sea. Wherever he looked, there was only endless water. The waves there were gentle, yet at one moment they lifted him up, and the next, they cast him down into a hollow. When he was lifted up, he could see the boat. “Oh!” he shouted. When he sank into the trough, the boat disappeared from view; all he could see were the dark watery walls surrounding him. Even the strength to cry “Oh!” deserted his tongue. The third time the sea wave lifted him up, it seemed the boat had gone even farther than before. The thought arose in his mind: “That’s it, I am going to drown and die in the sea!” Not only I, but my waistcloth and the palm-leaf letter tucked in it are going to drown as well! The face of Princess Kundavai appeared before his mind’s eye.
“It is for this that you have done all this?” she seemed to ask.

“Ah! What dreams I dreamt! What castles I built in my mind! Did I not imagine that the old Vanar dynasty would be restored, and that I would sit beside the young princess on the jeweled throne? All that has come to nothing! This wretched woman has ruined everything! She is not a woman, but a demoness in woman’s form! She belongs to the clan of the Pazhuvettaraiyars. No, she is allied with that enchantress, Nandini. Even if I drown and die in the sea, it is no great loss. If only this demon-woman would fall into my hands now, I would wring her neck… Fie, fie! What a thought! At the moment of death, let me think of something good! Let me remember God! Umapati! Parameswara! Lord of Palani! Lord who reclines on the ocean of milk!… Princess Kundavai! Forgive me. I am dying without completing the task you entrusted to me… There, I can see the boat. If only that woman would fall into my hands now!”

When Vandiyathevan had first jumped into the sea, Poonguzhali had remained indifferent. She thought he would flounder about for a bit and then swim over and grab hold of the boat. With the thought, “Let him struggle a little,” she increased the distance between the boat and him. Soon, she realized her mistake. “He does not know how to swim well; on top of that, he has become frightened; ‘Ah!’ ‘Oh!’ he is… Crying out was not for play; it was from true fear. If he went a little further, he would begin to swallow the salty water! He would drown and be lost. Afterwards, even his body could not be found. Alas! Had we not made a mistake? It seems this game is about to end in disaster! We should have kept our mouths shut until we reached the other shore. We should not have revealed that we knew his secret. But we were too hasty. Still, who could have known this brute would act this way? Who could have guessed he would be so terrified at the sight of water?

When Vandiyathevan next appeared atop the crest of a wave, Poonguzhali steered the boat toward him. In a moment, the boat drew close to him. “Come! Come! Climb aboard!” she called. But it seemed he did not hear her. Even if he did, he did not look like someone about to grab hold of the boat and climb in. It seemed as if he had lost both the power to hear and the power to see. Only the power to cry out remained. Raising one hand above the water, lifting his head, he let out a long, desperate “Oh!” Poonguzhali knew it was the cry of a man who, having lost all hope, was about to drown and die. When he raised his head, his face was visible for a moment in the pale, wan moonlight. It was the face of a man driven mad with terror! To think he would come and climb into the boat himself was foolish!... It was up to her to save him and pull him aboard! She had brought this trouble upon herself! “They say women’s wit comes last—how true that is!”

Immediately, Poonguzhali acted with great urgency. She took one end of the rope used to tie the coir mat in the boat and fastened it to the long pole that extended from the boat. The other end she tied around her own waist; then she plunged into the sea. With swift, practiced strokes, she swam toward him.
She drew close to Vandiyathevan, stopping at a distance where she could leap and grab him with her hand.
Vandiyathevan saw her too. In his face and eyes, a terrible, murderous frenzy danced.

Poonguzhali’s mind raced. She knew what those who could not swim, or who were about to drown from exhaustion, would do at the last moment. If someone came to save them, they would clutch desperately at the rescuer’s shoulder or neck. They could even drag the rescuer down, making it impossible for them to swim. The desperate desire for life would, at that moment, give them the strength of an elephant. The one who came to save— They would seize those who approached and try to push them under the water. It was impossible to escape from their fearsome, demonic grip; nor was it possible to swim away. The only fate was for both to be dragged together to the depths of the sea!

Poonguzhali, who knew all this very well, thought at lightning speed; she made a decision. She drew even closer to Vandiyathevan, who was floundering, pleading for his life. She came up beside his head. With one hand she continued to swim, while with the other she clenched her fist tightly and raised it high.

She struck Vandiyathevan’s face with all her might. The blow landed between his nose and forehead. The punch, delivered by her arm hardened and strengthened by rowing the boat, struck Vandiyathevan like the thunderbolt weapon of the gods. His head exploded into a thousand sparks. His eyes shattered into ten thousand fragments. Before each fragment of his eyes, a hundred thousand electric sparks flashed and flew. In every spark, the face of the Samudra Kumari appeared, laughing a ghostly “Ha ha ha ha!” The dreadful laughter of a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand demons thundered in his ears, deafening him. After that, he could no longer hear; he could no longer see! He had no memory! Endless darkness! Infinite silence!

chapters.title: The Haunted Island
paragraphs: Vanamadevi, oh, Vanamadevi! In the vastness of her wisdom, she seems to embody all of humankind. Men allow Paranjothi, the Supreme Light, to slip away from the sky of their hearts. Then, in the dark corridors of temples and in the sanctum sanctorum, they light a hundred thousand lamps to seek that very Paranjothi.

Vanamadevi, too, performs such a clever act every day! She lets the radiant Sun God slip away from her presence into the sea. Later, she is stricken with sorrow, lamenting that she cannot see her lord. Lighting a hundred thousand lamps, she searches for the Sun! Is it only a hundred thousand lamps she lights? She kindles countless, sleepless lights, and through the whole night, without rest, she keeps searching for the Sun!

When Vandiyathevan regained consciousness and opened his eyes, he saw before him the glow of thousands of flames. He wondered in amazement which temple could be so magnificently adorned with so many lamps. Then he realized they were not lamps at all, but stars shining in the sky. He understood that he was lying stretched out in a boat, and that a rope had been tied around his waist over a damp cloth. The cool, shimmering breeze caressed his body, filling him with boundless comfort and peace. The resonant hum rising from the tranquil sea brought a rare tranquility to his soul.
Amidst that sound, a song reached his ears. What was that song? Where, when, had he heard it before?

“When the ocean lies calm and still, And the breeze comes creeping soft, Why does the wind swirl and beat Within the chambers of my heart? When the waves of the sea are at rest, Why does the inner ocean surge?” Aha! That mysterious woman! Poonguzhali! He straightened himself and sat up, looking ahead.

Yes, it was her! She was rowing the boat! Singing that sorrowful song, she was rowing the boat! Just as a flash of lightning in the dark reveals many things in a single instant, the events of the previous night flashed vividly before Vandiyathevan’s mind. That is, he remembered only up to the point when Poonguzhali had dived into the sea and swum towards him as he struggled in the waves. After that, he could recall nothing. That woman must have rescued him and brought him aboard the boat. Only when the boat rocked, to keep him from falling back into the sea, she had tied a rope around his waist and fastened it to the crossbeam of the boat. She had wound the rope over his garment so that it would not chafe his skin. Vandiyathevan touched the knot tied around his waist. He found that his money and the letter were safe.

“Aha! What a grave mistake it was to suspect this woman! If she had harbored any evil intentions, was there any need for her to save me? How much effort she must have taken to haul my limp, unconscious body from the sea into the boat! How did she manage it all alone? What an extraordinary maiden she is!”

“Look, she’s up! Why? Has she noticed that I’m awake, and is she coming towards me? What is she going to do? No, no! She’s doing something else. Aha! She’s going to tie the mat to the raft! What a difficult task! And she’s doing it all by herself?”
“Poonguzhali! Poonguzhali!”
“Oh! So you’ve woken up?”
“Untie this rope! I’ll help you.”
“It’s help enough if you just stay quiet. If you want the rope untied, you can do it yourself. But don’t jump into the sea again!”
Vandiyathevan untied the rope that bound him. Poonguzhali lifted the mat and set it in place. She spread the sail and let it catch the wind! Now the boat moved joyfully; it sped along swiftly.
“Daughter of the sea!”
“Why?”
“I am thirsty!”
“You’ve drunk salt water, haven’t you? How else could you not feel thirsty?”
With these words, Samudrakumari approached Vandiyathevan, carrying a small water gourd.
“I even brought you some food. But when you jumped into the sea, that too fell in! Luckily, this water gourd escaped unharmed.”
As she spoke, she removed the stopper from the gourd and handed it to him. Vandiyathevan took it and drank the water.
Clearing his throat and steadying himself, he said, “I misjudged you; I am sorry for that.”
“That’s nothing to worry about. Who are you? Who am I? When dawn comes, we’ll part ways.”
“What time is it now?”
“Look at the sky and find out. See the Saptarishi constellation!” said Poonguzhali.

Vandiyathevan looked to the northern sky. When he had boarded the boat, the Saptarishis were in a different place; now, they had moved halfway across the arc. How wondrously the Arundhati star races alongside Vashishta! Only the Pole Star remained unmoved, steadfast in its place. For ages untold, at the place where the sky meets the corner of the sea, the Pole Star has stood fixed, guiding countless sailors and showing them their way.

The Pole Star! Who was it that used it as an example? Who said it, and about whom? The memory returned—Kudanthai the astrologer had spoken of it. He had likened the northern Pole Star to Prince Arulmozhi. Would I truly have the fortune to meet the prince? Would it be through this woman’s help?
Poonguzhali went back to her place and sat down.
“Did you find out the time? It’s halfway through the third watch. The wind has shifted. By dawn, we’ll reach Nagathivu,” she said.
“Nagathivu?” Vandiyathevan asked in surprise.
“Yes; there are many islands off the northern coast of Lanka. One of them is Nagathivu. If we land there, we won’t need to cross the sea again—we can reach the island of Lanka by land…”
"After you set me ashore, what will you do...?"
"Why are you worried about me?" asked Poonguzhali.
"You have done me such a great favor, haven't you? Should I not express my gratitude to you? You said you would ask me for some return of favor—what is it?" he asked.
"I have changed my mind about that. I will not ask you for anything. You are an ungrateful man."
Vandiyathevan realized there was a reason for her accusation. Once more, he felt the half-scroll tucked at his side and assured himself the palm-leaf letter was still there.
"Samudrakumari! I am ashamed when I think of how I suspected you the night before last. Forgive me for that!"
"Let it be; you forget it too! Think about what you must do next! After I set you ashore in Lanka, what will you do? How will you find where the prince is?"
"The god who helped me cross this sea will help me in that too!"
"You seem to have great faith in God. Do you think God takes an interest in the affairs of insignificant people like us?"
"I have not delved so deeply into philosophy. If I face any hardship or danger, I pray to God. God helps at the right time. Did not God send you to push the boat for me across this sea?"
"Don't be so arrogant. I did not come to row the boat for you. Nor did God send me in a dream to help you..."
"Then why did you save me yesterday? Why are you rowing the boat for me now?"
"Do not ask about that. That is my own affair."

Vandiyathevan sank into silent thought. In his proud heart, a notion arose. Perhaps, he thought, this girl had become enamored with him, captivated by his heroic beauty. Immediately, he cast aside that thought. He changed his mind. Her speech and actions left no room for such suspicions. There must be some other mysterious reason. He must pry open her lips and discover what it was.
“There is one thing I’m a little worried about…” he said.
“What is it? Even you feel anxious?”
“They say there are many forests and mountains in Lanka.”
“More than half of Lanka is indeed forest and mountain.”
“I’ve heard that wild animals are abundant there.”
“Herds of wild elephants roam about. Sometimes, the elephant herds even come out of the forests.”
“I’ve heard that the people in Lanka are savages.”
“That is a complete lie.”
“If you say so, then it must be true. Still, in such a wild region, I must search and find where Prince Arulmozhi Varman is hiding.”
“Didn’t you just say that it wouldn’t be difficult?”
“Yes, I did. At first, I thought, what difficulty could there be in finding where the sun is?”
“Why do you think differently now?”
“The sun might be hidden by clouds; or it might have sunk beneath the sea.”
“No cloud or sea can hide this sun. Any cloud that tries to conceal Ponni’s Son will only be illuminated; the sea itself will shine!”

How her enthusiasm overflows when she speaks of the Prince! Like so many subjects of Chola Nadu, this woman too regards him as a deity! What kind of enchanting power does Arulmozhi Varman possess?—pondering thus, he asked, “So you say it won’t be difficult to find the Prince in Lanka?”
“If you inquire where the Chola army is, you will know where the Prince is.”
“How is that? I heard that half the Chola army is spread across Lanka.”
“Yes; I too heard that the Chola forces are stationed all the way from Mathottam to Pulastiyanagar…”

“Then? In such a vast region, who knows where the Prince might be? It could take many days to search for him through the jungle paths. I must deliver this letter to him without delay. You have seen the letter yourself, haven’t you? You know how urgent it is.”
Samudrakumari remained silent, giving no reply.
“If we knew for certain where the Prince is, we could go straight to him without wandering in vain,” said Vandiyathevan.
“There is a way,” said Poonguzhali.
“I asked you because I believed there must be.”
“I told you this morning that I would drop you off at Nagath Theevu, didn’t I?”
“Yes!”
“Next to Nagath Theevu, there is another island called Boothath Theevu.”
“The very name of the island sounds frightening!”

“Don’t be afraid! In ancient times, the island was called Bodhath Theevu. When Lord Buddha came to Lanka by the aerial path, it is said that he first landed on that island. Seated beneath the royal tree there, he preached the Dharma. That’s how the name Bodhath Theevu came about.”
“Later, it must have become ‘Boothath Theevu’—the Island of Spirits.”
“Yes! Just hearing the name ‘Boothath Theevu’ has terrified many, just like you. After that, ordinary people stopped going there. Only those unafraid of spirits dare to set foot on that island.”
“In other words, the brave ones like you. Aren’t you the one who fears not even the demon of the whirlpool? Very well; what were you about to say about Boothath Theevu?”
“If you wait for just one naazhigai on the shore of Boothath Theevu, I will find out and tell you where Ponniyin Selvan is now in Lanka…”
“Whom will you inquire on Boothath Theevu…?”
“There is a spirit on the Island of the Spirits. I am going to investigate it…”
“Will you not show me that spirit as well?”
“That is not possible. You must not follow me into the island. If you swear to stay by the shore and watch over the boat, I will go, investigate, and return to tell you what I find.”
“Very well, let it be so!” agreed Vallavarayan.
The wind blew pleasantly. With the help of the palm-leaf sail, the boat sped swiftly, slicing through the sea. The deep, resonant roar of the ocean continued to fill their ears.
Vandiyathevan’s eyelids began to droop. Sleep crept over him as his eyes rolled, and he slipped gently from wakefulness into slumber.

chapters.title: "This is Lanka!"
paragraphs: When Vandiyathevan opened his eyes once more, the sight that greeted him on all sides filled him with wonder. In the east, at the edge of the sky, the sun was rising. There, the sea shimmered like molten gold, dazzling and radiant. The maiden of the dawn was adorned in a golden silk garment and shone resplendently.

In the direction the boat was heading, directly before him, an emerald isle glimmered, draped in a robe of blue sea. To the right, another stretch of green land appeared, much the same in hue. It was not clear whether this was an island entirely surrounded by the sea, or a vast expanse of land stretching out into the distance. Looking further, between these two emerald realms, many more islands appeared in the distance, each displaying a different shade of green, as if to demonstrate the endless variety of that color.

From the boat, if one looked all around, the seven colors of the rainbow and their seven thousand subtle blends shone forth. Altogether, the scene before his eyes did not seem real. It was as if a master artist, skilled in the art of painting, had sworn an oath—“Here, let me show you what paradise looks like!”—and had created this wondrous vision in color.
As Vandiyathevan, entranced by this vision, lost himself in awe, words fell upon his ears, awakening him: “This is not paradise; this is Lanka!”
“Yes! I truly wondered if this was paradise,” replied Vandiyathevan.
“This is not the land of heaven; but it is a land like heaven. For a long time, men in the form of demons have been striving to turn this paradise into hell,” said Poonguzhali.
“Whom do you call demons?” he asked.
“Those whose profession is war, like you.”
“Even Ponniyin Selvan?”
“Why do you ask me about him?”
“You said you would inquire about the prince.”

“I said I would find out where he might be. I never said I would tell you whether he is a man, a demon, or a god, did I?” The boat was drawing near the islands. Instead of the deep, resonant hum that echoed in the middle of the sea, the sound of the waves now changed to the gentle, continuous murmur as they broke upon the shore.

“What do you say? You can see it ahead, can’t you? That is Boothaththivu, and to the right lies Nagaththivu. Where shall we go? Shall I take you to Nagaththivu and leave you there? Or will you decide after making some inquiries?”
“No; let us go to Boothaththivu. Even if it takes a little longer, it is better to find out where the prince is before proceeding.”
“If that is your wish, so be it. But remember the promise you made me!”

The boat came to a stop at the shore of the small island. Telling Vandiyathevan to look after the boat, Poonguzhali stepped onto the emerald isle and disappeared into its depths. Vandiyathevan watched the direction in which she went. Soon, she vanished amidst the green trees.

Vandiyathevan first pondered how the island, once called Bodaththivu by the people, had become corrupted into Boothaththivu. Then he wondered what sort of ghost might now inhabit this island. After that, he marveled at the mystery hidden within the heart of this extraordinary woman.
