As Poonguzhali had promised, she returned within an hour. She climbed into the boat and beckoned Vandiyathevan to do the same. The boat now set off toward Nagaththivu.
“Were you able to find out what you needed?” Vallavarayan asked.

“The Chief Minister, Aniruddha Brahmarayar, has come to Maathottam to meet Ponniyin Selvan. The prince should have arrived at Maathottam yesterday. No one knows how long he will stay there. You can go there and find out,” Poonguzhali replied.
“How far is Maathottam from here?”

“It is about five or six katham away. The whole way is through forest. Don’t think it will be like the Kodikkarai woods. These are dense forests, with trees that reach the sky. In some places, it will be dark even at midday. There are herds of elephants and other dangerous beasts. You must be careful as you make your way.”
“If only there were a daring woman like you to guide me through the forest…” Vallavarayan sighed deeply.

“At that moment, what need is there for you! Hand me the palm-leaf letter! I will take it myself and deliver it… No, I cannot! I am speaking like a madwoman. I simply cannot do it. You promised the Young Princess, didn’t you? You must be the one to see it through!” she said.
“Very well, Poonguzhali! I will see it through. Even if someone else pleads with me, I will not hand it over. The help you have given me is more than enough!”

The boat was drawing near Nagadweepa. Poonguzhali’s hands were rowing the oar with their usual strength, but it was clear from her face that her mind was wandering somewhere far away, roaming in a world of dreams.
“Daughter of the Ocean!” called Vandiyathevan, and she started, returning to this world.
“Why did you call me?” she asked.
“You said you expected some return of favor from me, didn’t you? If you want to ask, now is the time. Look, the shore is drawing near.”
Poonguzhali did not answer at once; she seemed to be thinking. Seeing this, Vandiyathevan gathered his courage and spoke further.

“The help you have given me is immense. You have not only helped me, but you have rendered a great service to the Chola Empire itself. You have done a great favor to the royal clan of the Chola Emperor. If I do not do something in return, my heart will not be at peace,” he said.
“Are you saying all this truly? Or, like the other men in the world, are you speaking deceitfully?”
“I swear by the King of the Ocean, I speak the truth.”
“Is that like writing your oath upon water?”
“I swear by the voice of the heavens, by Mother Earth, by the guardians of the eight directions, by the Sun and Moon themselves.”
“I do not trust your oaths and vows. Do those who speak lies and practice deceit fear only oaths and vows? The moment I first saw you, I felt you were a good man, and so I will tell you…”
“The first thought is always the best. Do not change it.”

“After you meet Ponniyin Selvan and hand him the letter, after you have said all that needs to be said and spoken all that needs to be spoken, when you find him in a relaxed mood, ask him, ‘Do you remember the Samudra Kumari?’ If he says, ‘Yes, I remember,’ then tell him, ‘It was she who rowed the boat for me and brought me safely to Lanka!’”

“Poonguzhali! Are you aiming to soar so high? Can a little sparrow decide to fly to the heights where the king of the skies, Garuda, soars? Should I too begin to fly, thinking I can reach such heights? Is this good for you?” Thus thought Vandiyathevan to himself.
Aloud, he said, “Was this all you hesitated so much to say? I thought you were going to ask something grand! I will certainly tell the prince! Even if he doesn’t ask, I myself will tell him!”
“Oh no! If he doesn’t ask, you must not say anything on your own!”
“That won’t do; I will have to tell him.”
“What will you say?”

“I will tell him exactly what happened. ‘Prince! Son of Ponni! Do you remember the Samudra Kumari? If not, remember her now! She is the one who saved me from falling into the hands of the murderous men of the Pazhuvettaraiyars. She is the one who, all by herself, rowed the boat and brought me to Lanka. When I was floundering in the sea, it was she who rescued me and pulled me into the boat. If not for the help of the Samudra Kumari, I would not have come alive to see you. This letter would never have reached you!’ That’s what I’ll say—isn’t that right?”
“What you’ve said so far is right, but don’t add anything more! And don’t say that I told you to say all this!”
“Tut! Did you think I was a complete fool?”
“If the prince gives any reply, you must tell me exactly what he says. You must not exaggerate or leave anything out.”
“How will I see you again?”
“What difficulty is there in seeing me? I’ll be at Kodikkarai, or on this Poonthurai island, or somewhere in between, on the boat.”
“When I return to the mainland, if I come this way, shall I look for you on Poonthurai island?”

“For any reason, you must not come onto the island; if you do, it will end in disaster. See if the boat is still at the seashore! If it is, make some sign and call out! Yesterday, I called like a koel bird, didn’t I? Can you call out like that?”
“I can’t call like a koel? But I can make a sound like a peacock. Listen to this!”
Vandiyathevan covered his mouth with his hand and let out a harsh cry, imitating the call of a peacock.
Hearing that, Poonguzhali burst into sparkling laughter.
The boat approached the shore of Nagaththivu. Both of them got out of the boat.
Vandiyathevan climbed up onto the shore and took his leave. Poonguzhali turned the boat around.
Vandiyathevan looked back restlessly. “Will she say, ‘I’m coming with you’ and join me?”—the hope still lingered in his heart.
But Poonguzhali did not pay him any attention. Her face showed that she had already gone wandering into a dream world.

chapters.title: Aniruddha Brahmarayar
paragraphs: At the very beginning of this tale, we became closely acquainted with Alwarkadiyan Nambi, but for some time now, we have neglected to pay him any attention. For this, we beg forgiveness from our readers and, most importantly, from Nambi himself. Indeed, at this very moment, we must certainly seek Nambi’s pardon, for Alwarkadiyan is now in a state of great, great anger! His front tuft is flying in the wind that blows along the shores of Rameswaram. His staff is whirling above his head. Around him, many Adi Saivites and Veera Saivites have gathered, encircling him. Their commotion is so loud that we cannot help but feel a little anxious about what might become of Alwarkadiyan. Yet, the fierce Narasimha-like appearance of Nambi, and the speed with which his staff spins, dispel some of that worry.

Alwarkadiyan, who had overheard the conversation between Vandiyathevan and the Young Princess in Pazhayarai, set out that very day. With the swiftness of the wind and the speed of thought, he journeyed southward. Nowhere along the way did he involve himself in the usual Saivite-Vaishnavite quarrels. He restrained his mind, determined not to let any distraction interfere with his purpose, and even when arguments arose, he brushed them aside and continued on his way. He stayed for a short while in Madurai, where he inquired and learned the news he sought, and then departed for Rameswaram. On the very evening that Vandiyathevan, traveling in Poonguzhali’s boat, landed on the island of Lanka, Alwarkadiyan Nambi arrived at Rameswaram.

The moment he set foot on that sacred soil, the Vaishnavite fervor that had lain dormant in Alwarkadiyan’s heart for so many days surged forth, breaking all bounds. The Veera Saivite Pattars, who thronged everywhere on the island of Rameswaram, only added fuel to that fervor. The duties of these Pattars were to guide the pilgrims who came to that holy place, to lead them to bathe in the many sacred waters, to arrange for their worship of the deity in the temple, and to explain the special significance of each tirtha and each idol. Therefore, whenever new pilgrims arrived, many Pattars would immediately surround them. Thus, they now swarmed around Alwarkadiyan as well.

“Come, sir! Come, come! Bathe in the sixty-four sacred tirthas of this place and wash away the Vaishnavite heretical marks that stain your body! Is this not the holy place where even Rama was freed from the sin of Brahmahatya?” “You can even wash away the sins you have incurred by wearing those Vaishnavite heretic symbols!” said one of the priests with a sly smile.

Another interrupted, “There are sixty-four sacred tanks here—Rama Theertham, Lakshmana Theertham, Anjaneya Theertham, Sugreeva Theertham, and so on. Each person bathes in the appropriate tank to absolve his own faults. Come with me first to the Anjaneya Theertham! I will make the proper vow to cleanse you of the taint of those Vaishnavite marks!”

A third priest chimed in, “Oh, don’t listen to these fellows! I will take you straight to the very place where Rama, after slaying Ravana, fashioned a lingam out of the sand and worshipped Shiva to rid himself of the sin of Brahmahatya. I will take you there myself!”

At this, Azhwarkkadiyan’s eyes flashed with sparks of anger. He glared at them all and said, “Enough of your nonsensical talk! First, go and wash your own tongues in those sacred tanks you mentioned, and cleanse yourselves of your own sins!”

“Oh ho! Do you think we have incurred sin just by uttering the names of Rama and Lakshmana? Not so! The very name of this kshetra is Rameswaram; it is the place where Rama worshipped Shiva, the Lord of Lords, and freed himself from sin. Along with that, any taint associated with the name of Rama has also been washed away!” declared a zealous Saivite priest.
“Oh, you crown jewels of ignorance! Why do you keep babbling such nonsense? You haven’t even understood the true meaning of this holy place’s name!”
“Let’s see if you know—go on, tell us!”

“Because Shiva severed one of Brahma’s heads, he was afflicted with the sin of Brahmahatya. It was here, at this sacred spot, that Shiva, touched by the feet of Rama—who is none other than the full incarnation of Vishnu—came to rid himself of that sin. Since it is the place where Shiva was worshipped by Rama, it is called Rameswaram! Have you understood now, you peerless gems among fools?” thundered Azhwarkkadiyan.
“Who are you to call us peerless fools? Hey, stick-wielder! Have you grown horns on your head?” one of the priests shouted angrily.

“No, sir, priest! I have not grown horns on my head; it is only in my hand that I carry this staff! You asked who I am, did you not? I shall tell you. I am the servant of the servants of Nammazhwar, who was born in Thirukkurugur and rendered the Vedas into Tamil!” “The man who cracks skulls with his staff!” he said, raising his stick for all to see.
“O devotee of Alwarkadiyan! Why do you wear your kudumi at the front of your head? If you shaved that off as well, your skull would be the same inside and out!” mocked a Saivite.
“Priests! I had come to this sacred kshetra with the very intention of removing my kudumi before you. You have reminded me just in time!...”
“Hey! Go to the barber’s street and fetch a barber! Tell him to sharpen his razor well! We can have this fellow’s tuft uprooted, root and all!” said a priest.
“Why call a barber for this? We can do the service ourselves! Bring a good sharp knife!” said another Saivite.

“Wait a moment; there’s still one thing left to do. Once, my head was covered with thick hair. I took a vow that I would break a Saivite’s skull and then pluck a single hair from my head. According to that vow, three-quarters and a half of my hair is already gone. In this town, I intend to complete my vow and cast the last lock into the sea. Come, show me your skulls one by one and let’s see!” said Alwarkadiyan, brandishing his staff.
“Oh! How boldly this Vaishnavite speaks!” exclaimed one.
“Will you break all our skulls? Do you think you can?” challenged another.
“How else would I have lost three-quarters and a half of my hair?” retorted Alwarkadiyan, spinning his staff rapidly.
“Beat him! Catch him! Tie him up! Cut it off!” they all shouted, heads clamoring together, but none in the crowd dared approach Alwarkadiyan.

At that moment, a new commotion arose nearby and drew everyone’s attention. “The illustrious chief minister of the Tribhuvana Emperor Sundara Chola Parantaka, the most honorable Aniruddha Brahmarayar, is arriving! Move aside! Move aside!”

All were startled and turned toward the direction of the shout. Alwarkadiyan was the most astonished of all; he set his staff on the ground and looked on. The place where they had been quarreling was at the edge of the wall of the Rameswaram temple. A Bend. As soon as they turned that bend, an endless expanse of sea stretched out before them. The sight of that sea was a wondrous spectacle, the likes of which the eye had never beheld. Great ships, merchant vessels, small boats, rafts, catamarans, canoes, and barges could be seen in long rows, as far as the eye could reach. White sails, billowing in the wind from the swift-moving boats, covered much of the sea, the sky, and the many islands that appeared as scattered dots in the distance.

As described above, with guards leading and following, the renowned Chief Minister of the Chola Empire, Anbil Aniruddha Brahmarayar, was approaching with royal dignity in a boat. Walking along the temple wall on the shore, he noticed Satcharavai. In the midst of the crowd, standing with a staff like a perfect ascetic, was Azhwarkkadiyan. Aniruddha gestured with his hand and summoned him nearby. With reverence and awe, Azhwarkkadiyan folded his hands and stood by the seashore.
“Thirumalai! What is this street play?” asked Aniruddha.
“Guru! All this is the divine drama of that master of deception, Kannan! I do not know whether to believe what my eyes see or not. Is what I see a dream? Or is it all mere illusion?...”
“Thirumalai! I thought you were a staunch Vaishnavite. When did you become a Maya-vadi, calling the universe a mirage?”

“Guru! When you, born in the lineage of supreme Vaishnavites, have become a Saivite, why should I not become a follower of Maya? I shall change my name and become Sri Sankara Bhagavatpadachariyar’s Adiyarkkadiyan...”
“Enough! Enough! Who said that I have become a Saivite?”
“The marks on your holy body declare it!”
“Aha! Thirumalai! You are just as before, giving importance only to outward symbols! Does it matter if the sandal paste on the forehead is applied crosswise or upright?”
“Guru! I am an ignorant man; I do not know what is important and what is not. You alone must enlighten and guide me.”
“I will explain everything. Come to the place where I am staying! Look there! Do you see that small island in the sea? Come to the pavilion there.”
“Guru! Are these quarrelsome Saivites not going to let me pass?” said Azhwarkkadiyan, pointing at them with his hand.
Until then, the fierce Saivites had remained silent, but now they immediately stepped forward.
“Brahmadi Rajar! This Vaishnavite threatens to break our heads! He must be punished accordingly!” began one of them, and the others joined in, each raising their voices.
“I will punish him myself. You may leave,” said Aniruddhar.
This did not satisfy them. “Can’t we punish him ourselves? Let us shave off his front tuft, destroy all his ascetic symbols, and throw him into a well—” one of them started, piling on threats.
“What did you say?” Azhwarkkadiyan turned, his eyes blazing with fire.
At that moment, Aniruddha Brahmarayar said, “Pattarmani! He is a great ruffian. You cannot punish him. I will take care of it.”
Then, turning to the palace guards who had followed him in the boat, he said, “Eight of you, come ashore and bring him to our quarters!”
That was enough. In the next moment, eight soldiers leapt onto the bank and surrounded Azhwarkkadiyan.
The boat moved on.
Azhwarkkadiyan went, encircled by the soldiers.
The priests and others dispersed, talking among themselves about the Vaishnavite’s insolence in various ways.

chapters.title: The Chosen Commando Force
paragraphs: On one of the small islands near the great island of Rameswaram, in an ancient mandapam, Aniruddha Brahmarayar was seated in council. The tools and implements necessary for his ministerial duties surrounded him. Accountants, scribes skilled in writing on palm leaves, and inner circle guards were all stationed at their respective places, ready and attentive.

After Aniruddha had disembarked from the boat and settled himself in the mandapam for a short while, he issued an order to summon those who had come to meet him. Five men entered first. At a glance, they appeared to be wealthy merchants, prosperous and dignified. On a platter, they offered a necklace of nine precious gems as a gift. Aniruddha Brahmarayar accepted it and handed it to the accountant, saying, “Record this as a donation for the temple renovations of Sembiyan Mahadevi.”
Then, turning to the newcomers, he asked, “Who are you?”
(This merchant guild with its long, illustrious name conducted trade with overseas lands under the Chola Empire.)
“We have come as representatives of the Nanadesa Tisai Ayirathu Aindhu Nooruvar,” one of them replied.
“Excellent. Your trade in the Pandya country is flourishing, I trust?”
“It prospers more with each passing day!”
“What do the people of Pandya Nadu say?”

“They say the rule of the Chola dynasty is far superior to that of the Pandya lineage. Above all, they praise the valor and generosity of Prince Arulmozhi Varman. News of all that transpires in Lanka has spread among the people here…”
“How is your maritime trade with the southern countries faring now?”
“Under the reign of Emperor Sundara Chola, there is not the slightest hindrance. All the ships we sent last year have returned safely; not a single one was lost.”
“There has been no trouble from sea pirates?”

“Not in the past year. Ever since the Chola navy destroyed the pirates near the island of Manakkavaram, there has been no fear of plunder in the southern seas.” “Very well; what arrangements have you made regarding the palm-leaf letter we sent?”

“We have done as ordered. We have brought to this Rameswaram island a thousand sacks of rice, five or six sacks of millet, and a hundred sacks of pigeon peas to be sent to the Lankan army. Arrangements must be made to send them across to Lanka.”
“Can you load them onto your own ships and send them?”
“If you command, we will do it. We wish to know when the war in Lanka will end.”
“Ah! Who can say that? Doesn’t your merchant guild have an astrologer? Ask him and let me know as well!”
“Brahma Rajar! Even we cannot believe everything our astrologer says.”
“Oh? What does he say?”

“He says that wherever Prince Arulmozhi Varman goes, only victory follows. He says that under his rule, the Chola navy will cross the seas to distant lands and conquer them. He says the tiger flag will fly in many far-off countries.”
“In that case, your fortunes are cause for celebration!”
“Yes; he has also said that our maritime trade will flourish and prosper even more.”
“Very good. If the grace of Sriranganatha is upon us, it will all come to pass. Until the war in Lanka is over, you must continue to send rice and other supplies like this once a month. Go now.”
“We shall do so. We take our leave.”
After the representatives of the Five Hundred Guild had departed, a guard came and announced, “The commanders of the Terinja Kaikkola regiment are waiting and wish to see you.”
“Send them in!” said Prime Minister Aniruddha.
Three imposing men entered. On their faces and in their bearing, the goddess of valor herself seemed to reside. At a glance, it was clear they were men of indomitable courage and manliness.

(Today, those who toil at the handloom in Tamil Nadu, struggling for want of thread, once belonged to a class of warriors renowned during the era of the great Chola Empire. From among these brave men, the Chola emperors would select and form the “Aga Parivara Padai”—the Imperial Household Regiment. This specially chosen force was known as the “Therinja Kaikkolar Padai”—the Chosen Regiment of the Handpicked Warriors. It was customary to prefix the reigning emperor’s or king’s name to the regiment’s title.)
“Are you not the Sundara Chola Therinja Kaikkolar soldiers?” Aniruddhar asked.
“Yes, sir! But to claim that title now fills us with shame.”
“Why is that?”
“For six months, we have been idling here, eating the emperor’s rice and wasting our days in vain.”
“How many hands—how many warriors—are there in your regiment?”

“Our army is made up of three divisions. This man is the commander of the left division; this one, of the right; I am the commander of the central division. Each division has two thousand warriors. All of us do nothing but eat and sleep. It seems as if we might forget the very art of war.”
“What is your request?”
“We ask to be sent to Lanka. We wish to join the army under Prince Arulmozhi Varman, who is now the commander there, and fight in the war!”
“Very well; once I reach Thanjavur, I shall seek the emperor’s permission and inform you.”
“Brahmaraja! What if, before that, the Lankan war is already over…?”
“You need not fear that. It does not seem likely that the war in Lanka will end so soon.”
“Are the Lankan warriors so formidable? Send us there. Let us have a try—just one division!”

“One division? Why, you will have all three! If the three divisions of the Therinja Kaikkolar enter the battlefield, do I need to tell you what will become of the enemy? The central division will pierce through the heart of the enemy’s ranks, while the left and right divisions will strike from either flank, falling upon the foe like thunderbolts…”
“That is how we struck and utterly destroyed the Pandya army; we shattered the Cheras as well.”

“The Pandyas and the Cheras stood and faced you on the battlefield; that is why you attacked and routed them. Only when you see the enemy warriors with your own eyes can you fight them—whether they have one arm or three arms, it matters not.
“Have the warriors of Lanka in these times become like the asuras of Ravana’s age? Are they hiding in the clouds and waging war from there?”

“They have indeed vanished like sorcerers; but they do not fight. If only they would fight, we could discover their hiding places! Neither the King of Lanka, Mahindan, nor his army has been seen; no one knows where in the forests or mountains they have concealed themselves. For six months now, there has been no war in Lanka. What is the use of sending us there?”

“Great Minister! Just send us there and see! Let Mahindan and his warriors hide in the forests and mountains, or even in the clouds—wherever they may be, we will seize them by the hand and bring them before the prince’s feet. If we fail to do so, we will abandon the name ‘Therinja Kaikkolar Battalion’ and accept the title ‘The Velaalar’s Slave Army’!”

“No, no! There is no need for such vows now! Who in this Jambudvipa does not know the valor of the Therinja Kaikkolar battalion? Once we reach Thanjavur, I will speak to the Emperor and send you orders. Until then, be patient. For now, go to the Pandya country, subdue the remaining enemies, and restore peace!”

“Great Minister! There are no more enemies left to subdue in the Pandya land. The people are rejoicing that the war has ended. Each has returned to his own pursuits—farming, trade, crafts—and is leading a peaceful life. The Pandya royal line itself has been destroyed…”

“Do not think so! You believe that with Veera Pandiyan’s death, the Pandya dynasty has ended. That is a mistake. There are still those who claim rights to the Pandya throne! And there are those who plot on their behalf…!”
“Ah! Where are these conspirators? Reveal them to us!”

“When the time comes, you will know. The ancient jeweled crown of the Pandya clan, the gem-studded necklace given by Indra, and the diamond-encrusted royal sword—all these still remain somewhere in Lanka, hidden away in the mountains of Rohana…” ...have been kept safe. Until those are recovered, the Pandya war will not come to an end.”
“The ornaments must be recovered; and the day must come when Prince Arulmozhi Varman is seated upon the throne of Madurai, adorned with the Pandya’s jeweled crown and the royal sword!”
“Ah! What words are these you utter?”
“We speak only what dwells upon the tongues of the people and in the hearts of the warriors!”
“All that concerns great affairs of state; let us not discuss them. I am about to tell you something else, something important that will bring you joy...”
“We are listening attentively, O Great Minister!”

“Do not think that the war will end with the campaign in Lanka. After the Lankan war, Prince Arulmozhi Varman will set forth to conquer all four directions. He will load a thousand ships with warriors and sail across the southern seas. The mighty hero will conquer the lands of Manakkavaram, Mabappalam, Mayirudingam, Kadaram, Ilamuri, Srivijaya, Chavakam, and Putpagam. To the south, he will seize the ancient island of Munnirpazhantheevu and its sixteen thousand isles. To the west, Kerala, Kudamalai, and Kollam will come and submit at his feet. Then he will march northwards. He will set out to wage war upon the lands of Vengi, Kalingam, Irattapadi, Chakkarakkottam, Angam, Vangam, Kosalam, Vidhegam, Koorjaram, and Panchalam. Like the famed Karikala Valavan of legend, he will reach the Himalayas and plant the tiger banner upon its heights. O valiant commanders! Such are the plans our lord, the Sun of the Southern Lands, has made. For all in Tamilagam who possess valorous blood and diamond hearts, there will be work to do; there will be opportunities to establish your heroic prowess. Therefore, you and your chosen Kaikkolar troops must not lose patience!”
All three commanders cried out in unison, “Long live Sundara Chola Chakravarti! Long live Prince Arulmozhi Varman! Long live the Great Minister Aniruddha!”
Then, one among the commanders spoke: “Mahamandiri! We wish to make just one more humble request. You know well that our force is called the ‘Sundara Chola Chosen Kaikkolar Battalion.’”
“That is well known to me.”
“We have sworn, with blood-stained hands dyed red with the blood of our foes, to lay down our very lives in the service of Sundara Chola Chakravarti.”
“I knew that as well.”
“That is why, except for the Emperor, we will not join with anyone else; we will not heed the words of any other.”
“This is exactly what I expected from you!”
“Once, in the past, we were a part of the great army of the Pazhuvettaraiyars. No one should ever have any suspicion about us because of that…”
“Aha! What is this talk? Who has any suspicion?”
“Rumors about what is happening in Thanjavur are blowing in the wind.”
“If they come with the wind, let them go with the wind! You need not believe all that; you need not repeat it either.”
“The Kodumbalur Velalars might try to stir up suspicion about us…”
“They will not; and even if they do, no one will listen.”
“The human body is impermanent…”
“Therefore, true warriors do not fear for their lives.”
“Even the Tribhuvana Emperor, one day…”
“Must attain the holy feet of the Lord.”
“The Emperor’s health is not well…”
“A comet is shining in the sky!”
“If something were to happen to the Emperor, our soldiers wish to become the close retinue of Arulmozhivarman!”
“It is your duty to act according to the Emperor’s command!”
“It is your duty to convey the Emperor’s command to us. Please accept that responsibility. Or else, grant us permission to go to Thanjai and have audience with the Emperor ourselves…!”
“No; it is not proper for you to go to Thanjai; unnecessary confusion will arise. I myself will meet the Emperor and convey your wishes. You remain at peace!”

“The very moment we revealed it to you, the burden that weighed upon our hearts has been lifted! We take our leave now!” With these words, the three commanders of the Thirinja Kaikkola regiment withdrew from the chamber and departed.

Aniruddha Brahmarayar muttered to himself, “Ah! I wonder what strange power of attraction Ponniyin Selvan possesses! Even those who meet him but once seem to lose their wits and become utterly bewitched!”
Then, in a louder voice, he commanded, “Where is that obstinate Vaishnavite? Summon him here at once!”

chapters.title: The Guru and the Disciple
paragraphs: At this juncture, we wish to share with our readers an incident related to the study of Tamil Nadu’s history. In the Lalgudi taluk of the Tiruchirapalli district, there is a village named Anbil. Sanskrit scholars have translated this as “Premapuri.” (This chapter was written in 1951.) About forty-five years ago, a Vellalar from this village began to demolish his old house to rebuild it anew, and as he dug the foundation, a remarkable object was unearthed from beneath the earth. Several copper plates, pierced at the top and strung together with a ring, were discovered. Something had been inscribed on those plates. The plates were so heavy that it took two men to lift them. The Vellalar kept them for some time. Later, when Sri R.S.L. Lakshmana Chettiar came to the village to oversee the renovation of the temple, the Vellalar handed the plates over to him.

Sri Lakshmana Chettiar, suspecting that these plates might contain historical information, took them to the renowned scholar Mahamahopadhyaya Swaminatha Iyer. Upon examining the copper plates, Swaminatha Iyer realized that they contained highly significant details. He handed them over to Sri T.A. Gopinatha Rao, M.A., who was then engaged in the study of stone inscriptions. The moment Sri Gopinatha Rao saw the copper plates, he was as delighted as a man who had discovered a rare treasure. For, inscribed upon them were details of immense importance regarding the lineage of the Chola kings.

The plates contained the record of a land grant of ten velis, given in the fourth year of Emperor Sundara Chola’s reign to Anbil Aniruddha Brahmarayar, the “Manya Mantri” (Chief Minister) of Sundara Chola. The scribe of this land grant, Madhava Battar, had listed the genealogy of the Cholas up to Sundara Chola. He had also described the Vaishnavite lineage of Aniruddha Brahmarayar, mentioning the services rendered by his father, mother, grandfather, and great-grandfather at the temple of Sriranganatha. The genealogy found in the Anbil copper plates closely matched that found in the previously discovered Anaimangalam and Thiruvalangadu copper plates. This confirmed the historical authenticity of the details inscribed on the Anbil plates. Moreover, the Anbil plates contained some additional information not found in the other two sets, making them especially renowned in the field of Tamil historical research.

Therefore, keeping in mind that Aniruddha Brahmarayar is the illustrious minister of the Chola Empire, as celebrated in the chronicles of history, we request our dear readers to continue reading the story further.

Azhwarkkadiyan entered the mandapam where the chief minister, Aniruddha Brahmarayar, was seated. He circled him three times! Then, prostrating himself in full sashtanga namaskaram, he rose to his feet.
Chanting “Om Hraam Hreem Vashat” in a loud voice four times, he said, “Gurudeva, grant me leave!”
With a smile, Aniruddhar replied, “Thirumalai! What is this commotion? Why do you ask me for leave?”

“Having surrendered the Srivaishnava tradition I have followed, the name ‘Azhwarkkadiyan’, and the fortune of serving you, into this great ocean, I am about to join the heroic Shaiva Kalamukha sect. With a skull bowl in my hand, chanting the mighty mantra ‘Om Hraam Hreem Vashat’, I shall wander from town to town! I will grow matted locks upon my head, a long beard upon my face, and with this staff, I shall split open the skulls of any Srivaishnavas who cross my path…”
“Good heavens! Stop! Stop! Will my own skull meet the same fate?”
“Guru! Do you still adhere to the Srivaishnava tradition?”
“Thirumalai! What doubt do you have about that? Who do you think I am?”

“Who are you? That is precisely what I have begun to doubt. Are you not the grandson of Anbil Ananthalwan Swamigal, who considered service to Sri Ranganatha—He who lies in sacred sleep between two rivers, protecting all the worlds—as the sole purpose of life?”
“Yes, my child! I am he!”
“And are you not the very same Anbil Aniruddha Pattachariyar, who expounded the glory of the name Sriman Narayana to all the world?”
“Yes, I am! They bestowed upon me the holy name of that great man as well!”
“Are you not the very son of Narayana Pattachari, who enchanted countless devotees by singing the nectarous, sweet songs of the Alwars?”
“Yes, father; yes, indeed!”

“And are you not also the son of the jewel among women, who daily lit the eternal lamp in the golden temple of Sri Ranganatha, where the Lord reclines, and who served the pilgrims by offering rice on silver plates?”
“There is no doubt about it!”
“If that is so, then are my eyes deceiving me? Is what I see before me a lie? Are my ears too deceiving me, is what I heard false?”
“What are you saying, father? What has happened to make you doubt your own eyes and ears?”
“My ears heard that you went to the Siva temple in this town and performed abhishekam and archana and all the rituals.”
“That is true; your ears have not deceived you.”
“My eyes see the marks on your sacred body, the signs that you have been to the Siva temple. That too must be true!”
“That is also true!”

“In this Kali Yuga, was it not you, my guru, who taught me that Sriman Narayana alone is God, that the hymns of the Alwars are the true Vedas, and that chanting the name of Hari is the only path to salvation?”
“Yes; but what of it?”
“If you, my guru, say one thing and do another, what is left for me, your disciple, to do?”
“Tirumalai! Are you speaking of my visit to the Siva temple?”
“Guru! Which deity did you worship there?”
“What doubt is there? Narayana Murti, of course!”
“But have I not heard that within the Rameswaram temple, it is a lingam that is installed? Is that not why the fierce Saiva priests here surrounded me and raised such a commotion?”
“My child! Is it not true that we have taken pride in being the humble servant of the servant of our Sadagopan, who incarnated in the holy city?”
“What doubt is there in that?”
“Recall, for a moment, the divine utterance of Nammazhwar. If you have forgotten, let me remind you; listen:
‘You, who argue vehemently, O followers of the Lingam, O Jains and Buddhists, He stood as your very own deity as well!...’
When Sadagopan himself has declared thus, was it wrong that I beheld Narayana within the Sivalingam?”
“Ah! The grace-filled utterance of Sadagopan! What words! See how he has cast those who worship the Lingam alongside the Jains and Buddhists!”
“Oh father! I do not know when your perverse logic will leave you. Listen to what our Sadagopan has further sung:
‘As water, as earth, as fire, as air, as the vast sky, as the two radiant orbs, as Siva, as Brahma...’
He who is within is indeed the form of Sri Narayana, so has his sacred mouth declared. Listen further, Thirumalai! Listen, and cleanse the stains from your heart’s desire!
‘O Sage! O Four-faced One! O Three-eyed Lord!’
“My mischievous one, Sweet-voiced, lotus-eyed, black-gemmed treasure— My thief! Alone, my very life, you have come to rest upon my head…”
Did you hear, Thirumalai? Our Sadagopan called out, “Mukannappa!” and prayed that you would come and rest upon his head! Yet here you are, objecting to my visit to Shiva’s temple!…”
“Gurudeva! Forgive me; pardon my transgression! Because I did not know all the hymns of Nammazhwar, I wasted my time in pointless quarrels. I even doubted you. Now, you must grant me a boon.”
“If you tell me what boon you desire, I can consider granting it.”
“I wish to go to Thirukkurugur and remain there. I want to collect all the thousand hymns of our Sadagopan, and then travel from town to town, singing those songs…”
“Why has this desire come to you?”
“On my journey from Vadavengadam, I sang a few Azhwar hymns in the sanctum of Veera Narayana Perumal. The great man who serves there, Iswara Pattar, heard me and wept tears of joy…”
“Iswara Pattar is a great devotee; a good disciple.”

“One of his young sons stood beside him, listening. That child’s milk-sweet face shone like the full moon as he heard the Azhwar’s hymn. ‘Do you know the other songs too?’ the little one asked, his mouth still fragrant with the scent of milk. I was ashamed to say, ‘No, I do not know them.’ At that moment, I thought—why should I not dedicate this dog’s life to the service of the Azhwars? Today, that thought has become firm…”
“Thirumalai, has not the teacher of the Gita declared that each must follow his own dharma?”
“Yes, Guru!”

“Just as great souls are born to collect and spread the hymns of the Alwars, so too, incarnations will arise in this land to establish, through the medium of Sanskrit, the Vedic essence and philosophies found in the songs of the Alwars throughout the whole of Bharat. You and I have taken royal service as our own svadharma. Have you forgotten the vow we made to dedicate our body, wealth, and soul in the service of the Chola Emperor?”
“I have not forgotten, Guru! Yet, a doubt gnaws at my heart as to whether it is right. Especially, when I hear people speak about you in certain places…”
“What do they say?”

“Some say that you have abandoned the Vaishnava tradition because the Emperor granted you a fief of ten velis of land and even recorded it on a copperplate. They also claim you disregarded the duties of your caste by undertaking a sea voyage…”

“Pay no heed to the words of those envious people. They want our caste to remain like frogs in a well. It is true that the Emperor granted me a fief of ten velis of land. He did indeed record it on a copperplate. But you know well that I became a minister to the Emperor even before that, don’t you?”
Azhwarkkadiyan remained silent.

“Do you know when the Emperor and I first became friends? We both studied under the same teacher in our youth. We learned classical Tamil and Sanskrit. We studied mathematics, astronomy, logic, grammar—everything. In those days, no one even dreamed that Sundara Chola would ascend the throne. Neither he nor I ever thought about it. Who imagined that Rajaditya and Kandaraditya would pass away and Arinjaya Chola would come to the throne? Who thought that Arinjaya would meet with an untimely death and Sundara Chola would have to ascend the throne so soon? When Sundara Chola took the throne, he foresaw that many complications would arise. He said he would accept the crown only if I stood by his side to help him, otherwise he would refuse it. I pledged then to assist him in the affairs of the kingdom. I have been fulfilling that promise to this very day. Do you not know all this, Thirumalai?”
“I know, Gurudeva! But what use is it if only I know? The people do not know, do they? The gossips in the towns and villages do not know, do they?”

“You need not worry in the least about those who spread rumors. There were times when I myself was confused about leaving my ancestral priestly profession and entering royal service. But for the past two days, I have had no such confusion at all. Thirumalai! You know well that I did not come here to Rameswaram temple for the sake of worship, but rather that I came here only to go to Mathottam, do you not?”
“That is what I guessed, Gurudeva!”
“Your guess was correct. Even today, Mathottam on the banks of the river Paalavi is just as Sambandar and Sundaramurthi ecstatically described it in their songs.
‘In the groves of great blossoms where bees hum sweetly, Where the swan-like maidens dance, Mathottam blooms. Where devotees praise day after day, There stands the gracious Kedheeswara temple!’

So sang Sambandar. Could he have written of that Mathottam without seeing it with his own eyes? Some frog-in-the-well scholars claim that he merely glimpsed Mathottam from this very island of Rameswaram and wrote his verses. Do not heed the words of such people…”
“Swami! Did you go to that sacred place only to delight in the natural beauty of Mathottam?”
“No; I mentioned it only because I intended to send you there. I went to see Prince Arulmozhi Varman…”
“Did you see the prince, Gurudeva?” asked Azhwarkadiyan. Now, for the first time, a note of eagerness and excitement rang in his voice.

“Aha! So even you have become eager to know about the prince? Yes, Thirumalai! I saw the prince; I spoke with him. I learned firsthand how much truth there was in the astonishing news coming from Lanka. Listen, my friend! The king of Lanka, Mahinda, once possessed a mighty army. That army now exists no more! What happened to it— Do you know? Like frost melting and vanishing at the sight of the sun, it has disappeared! In Mahindan’s army, there were many warriors who had come from the Pandya and Chera countries. As soon as they learned that our prince was leading the forces, they all laid down their arms. As if they were one, all of them have joined our side! How can Mahindan wage war now? He has fled. He has gone into hiding in the mountain-encircled land of Rohana. So, at this moment, there are no enemies left there for our army to fight!”
“In that case, Gurudeva! Shouldn’t the prince return with our army? Why should he remain there any longer? And what is the point of all these disputes about sending grain to our soldiers?”

“We could indeed return, saying there are no more enemies. But the prince does not wish for that. Nor do I agree with it. If the prince and the army return, Mahindan will emerge from his mountain refuge. The war will begin again as before. What use is there in that? The king and people of Lanka must become our friends—or else, the rule of the tiger flag must be established there permanently. The prince is engaged in both these efforts. Do you know what our warriors are doing in Lanka now? In the old wars, the city of Anuradhapura was destroyed. The ancient Buddhist viharas, temples, and the sacred relic towers there all lie in ruins. At the prince’s command, our soldiers are now restoring all those ruined structures!”
“How fine it is! Perhaps the prince will abandon both Shaivism and Vaishnavism and join the Sakyamuni’s faith instead? Who knows? And would you approve of that as well?”

“Whether you and I approve or not, it is all the same! Even if we do not approve, it is all the same. People like us may quarrel, claiming our own faith is supreme. But a ruler who governs a land must support and protect all the religions his subjects follow. The prince has realized this truth on his own, without anyone’s prompting. And when the opportunity arises, he puts it into practice. Thirumalai, listen! I have heard it said that the conch and discus lines are marked on the palms of our prince, Arulmozhi Varman—you too must have heard it. But I have never asked him to show his hands. Whether or not those marks are truly there, I can say one thing for certain: If there is one man fit to rule this earth as a universal emperor, it is Prince Arulmozhi Varman. Some are born with such divine grace— They are being born. Just a while ago, some leaders of the merchant guilds and commanders of the mercenary forces were here, conversing—did you overhear any of that? Did you notice how generous our merchants—those who care only for coin—become when it concerns the prince?”

“A few days ago, atop the summit of the Podhigai Hills, I met a sage in deep penance; he was a great soul endowed with the eye of wisdom. Do you know what he told me? ‘When the time comes for the elephant, the cat too shall have its day. Now, the time has come for the South to rise. For a long time, in this sacred land of Bharata, the greatest emperors, the bravest of warriors, the wealthiest of sages, and the most illustrious poets have all been born in the North. But soon, a shadow will fall upon the North. From beyond the Himalayas, a fierce, barbaric race will descend and lay waste to the North. They will shatter temples and idols. Sanatana Dharma itself will face grave peril. In that hour, it is the South that will safeguard our dharma, our Vedic scriptures, our temples, and our worship. Emperors of unmatched valor will arise in this southern land and rule over all four directions. Great sages, scholars of the highest order, and the foremost of devotees will be born here!’ Thus spoke that Shiva-yogi of the Podhigai Hills. Now, Thirumalai, I find myself believing that the prophecy of that yogi will indeed come to pass!”

“Swami! You are building castles in the air. But over there, they are trying to shake the very foundations of the kingdom, O Guru Deva! If you had seen all that I have seen, if you had heard all that I have heard, you would not be so elated. You would be stricken with fear at the danger looming over this Chola Empire…”

“Thirumalai, yes, I had forgotten. My excessive enthusiasm has clouded my mind. I have yet to hear the news you gathered on your journey. Speak, I am listening. No matter how dreadful the tidings, do not hesitate—tell me everything!”

“Swami, do you command me to speak of them here? If the Lord of the Winds were to hear the news I bring, he would tremble; if the King of the Seas heard it, he would be struck dumb; if the birds heard it, they would lose the power of flight and fall to the earth; even the voices of the sky and Mother Earth herself would cry out in anguish. Would you have me speak such tidings aloud in this place?” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
“In that case, come! There is a subterranean cave on this island, where neither wind nor flame may enter. Come there and tell me everything in detail!” said Aniruddha Brahmarayar.

The sun had already set. Darkness was beginning to spread over the land. The forest, which had been alive with the chirping of birds and the rustling of animals during the day, now fell silent, as if it too was preparing to sleep. In the midst of that silence, two figures were making their way through the dense trees.

One of them was a tall, imposing man with a radiant face and a long beard. His forehead was smeared with sacred ash, and his eyes shone with an inner fire. The other was a young man, his features sharp and handsome, his gait energetic and eager. The elder was none other than the great ascetic, the revered guru of the Chola land, and the younger was his devoted disciple.
They walked in silence for a while, the only sound being the crunch of dry leaves beneath their feet. At last, the guru spoke.
“My child, do you know where we are headed?”
“Swami, I do not know. I only follow your footsteps,” replied the disciple with humility.
The guru smiled. “That is good. In life, too, one must learn to follow the path shown by the wise. But one must also learn to find one’s own way when the time comes.”
The disciple bowed his head in respect. “I shall remember your words, Swami.”

They continued walking. The forest grew darker, and the path became harder to see. But the guru walked on without hesitation, as if he could see even in the pitch darkness. The disciple followed, trusting completely in his master.

After some time, they reached a clearing. In the center stood a large banyan tree, its roots spreading out like the arms of a giant. The guru sat down beneath the tree and gestured for the disciple to sit beside him.

“My child,” the guru began, “the world is full of dangers and temptations. A man who wishes to walk the path of righteousness must be ever vigilant. The mind is like a wild horse—it must be tamed and controlled.”
The disciple listened intently, absorbing every word.
“Remember, my son, the greatest enemy is not outside, but within. Conquer your desires, and you will conquer the world.”
The disciple prostrated himself at the guru’s feet. “Bless me, Swami, that I may have the strength to follow your teachings.”

The guru placed his hand on the disciple’s head in blessing. The darkness of the forest seemed to recede, and a gentle breeze stirred the leaves above them. In that moment, under the shelter of the ancient banyan tree, the guru and his disciple sat in silent communion, their hearts united in the pursuit of truth.

chapters.title: "Ponniyin Selvan"
paragraphs: At the very moment when Vandiyathevan was disembarking at the tip of Nagathivu and making his way toward Maathottam—at the same hour when Aniruddha Brahmarayar and Azhwarkadiyan were engaged in heated debate over the state of the empire—Princess Kundavai and the Kodumbalur princess Vanathi were approaching the city of Thanjavur, riding atop an elephant fitted with an ambari.

For some time now, the young princess had refrained from visiting Thanjavur. There were many reasons for this. In Thanjavur, there were not yet enough palaces for the royal women to reside separately. All the women were expected to stay within the main palace of the Emperor. The other palaces had been seized by the Pazhuvettaraiyars and other high-ranking government officials of great power. In Pazhayarai, the royal women could live as they pleased. They could go out or return as they wished. But in Thanjavur, they would have to submit to the restrictions imposed by the Pazhuvettaraiyars. Within the fortress and the palace, it was not possible to come and go at will. Such constraints and compulsions were intolerable to the young princess.

Moreover, the arrogance of the young queen of Pazhuvur and her haughty behavior greatly displeased Princess Kundavai. Even the Emperor preferred that the royal women remain in Pazhayarai. For these reasons, Princess Kundavai had continued to reside in Pazhayarai. She had even restrained her longing to see her beloved ailing father and serve him.

But ever since Vandiyathevan had come and gone, a change had come over the young princess’s heart. While grave intrigues and conspiracies were unfolding in the realm of kingship, was it right for her to while away her time in Pazhayarai, sailing boats on the rivers and singing and dancing in the gardens? Her elder brother was in Thondai Nadu; her younger brother was in Eezham; in the absence of both, was it not her duty to pay heed to the affairs of the kingdom? Her brother, Aditya Karikalan, had asked her to keep him informed of the secret happenings in the capital through trusted messengers. How could she know what transpired in Thanjavur while living in Pazhayarai?

The news brought by Vandiyathevan was truly terrifying. Until now, the only thing that had displeased the young princess was that the Pazhuvettaraiyars were wielding authority beyond their station. But now, they had begun to plot for the very throne itself. Alas! Even that paragon of virtue, Madurantakan, had been ensnared in their web. They had brought under their sway many of the minor kings and high officials of the Chola land. Who could say what might happen at any moment? Who could predict the extent of their schemes, their treachery, their insatiable ambition? If it served their purpose, they would not hesitate even to threaten the life of Sundara Chola! How could one say with certainty that they would not? If anything were to befall the emperor while both his sons were away, would it not be easy for them to place Madurantakan upon the throne? For this, there was nothing they would not dare! Even if they lacked cunning, that demoness Nandini would instruct them. If they faltered, she would embolden them. Therefore, it would be best for me to remain near my father in Thanjavur. I can watch how far their plots and conspiracies go. And at the same time, I can ensure that no harm comes to my beloved father.

Why do they wish to see the saintly Madurantakan upon the throne? Is it for the sake of justice and righteousness? Not at all. If Madurantakan were crowned, they could use him as a puppet and conduct all affairs as they pleased. Then, whatever Nandini decreed would become law in the Chola empire! Others would have to live in fear of her authority. The other women of the palace would have to stand before her with folded hands. Disgusting! Can we allow such a state of affairs to come to pass? As long as I am alive, that will never happen. Let us see the extent of her cleverness!

Staying in Thanjavur would be difficult for me in many ways. My mother and father would ask, “Why have you come here, leaving the comfort of Pazhayarai?” I would lose all freedom. Someone might raise the topic of my marriage; I cannot bear to hear of it. Sometimes, I would have to see Nandini. I cannot tolerate her arrogance and the pride of her power. But is it right to consider all this at such a time? The kingdom is in grave danger. There is the fear that my father’s life may be in peril. In such a situation, is not Thanjai the place where I ought to be?

Besides all this, there was another, more important reason. It was the desire to know if there was any news of Vandiyathevan. The young princess had heard that Vandiyathevan had gone towards Kodikkarai, and that the Pazhuvettaraiyars had sent men to capture him.

Would that clever youth, so skilled in the arts of intrigue, allow himself to be caught by these men? Even if, by some chance, he were to be captured, surely they would bring him to Thanjavur. At such a time, is it not essential that I be there as well? The messenger sent by Aditya Karikalan cannot be dealt with so easily by them. If they wish to punish him, they must first accuse him of some crime. That is why they have already charged him with attempting to stab the son of Sambuvarayar in the back. There is no doubt that this is a lie. But the falsehood must be proven. Speaking with Kandanmaran and learning the truth from his own lips may be useful for that purpose...

While Kundavai’s mind wandered through such grand conspiracies and tangled affairs, her companion Vanathi, who had come with her atop the elephant, was thinking of but one thing—with a heart as pure as milk, as clear as crystal. That one thought was: When would Prince Arulmozhi Varman return from Lanka?
“Akka! You said you had sent a letter urging him to set out at once, didn’t you? When he comes, where will he arrive—at Pazhaiyarai, or at Thanjavur?” Vanathi asked.
Vanathi’s worry was what would happen if, while they were away in Thanjavur, the prince returned to Pazhaiyarai.
Kundavai Piratti, absorbed in other thoughts, turned to Vanathi and asked, “Whom are you asking about, girl? About Ponniyin Selvan?”

“Yes, Akka! About him. You have called the prince ‘Ponniyin Selvan’ several times now, but you have never explained why. Each time, you have put me off, saying you would tell me later. At least now, please tell me! The fortress of Thanjavur is still far away, and this elephant moves as slowly as a tortoise!” said Vanathi.
“If the elephant goes any faster, we won’t be able to stay on its back. Both the howdah and we would tumble to the ground! Child, do you know what happened at the battle of Thakkolam?”
“Akka! Please tell me how he came to be called ‘Ponniyin Selvan’!”
“You sly girl! It seems you will not forget that. Very well, I will tell you. Listen!” said Kundavai Piratti, and began her tale.

When Sundara Chola Chakravarthi first ascended the throne, his family life was filled with bliss. The Emperor would sit with his family in the royal barge and joyfully cruise along the Ponni River. At such times, the boat would be alive with merriment. The music of the veena and the songs of the bards would mingle, swelling to compete with the surging waters of the Kaveri. Now and then, someone would do something amusing, and immediately, peals of laughter would arise, blending with the rippling sounds of the Kaveri’s current.

Sometimes, the elders would converse among themselves with delight. On one side of the boat, the children would be playing boisterously. At times, everyone together would join in some playful diversion, losing themselves in happiness.

One day, as the Emperor, his queens, and the children were seated in the royal barge, enjoying a pleasant journey on the Kaveri, suddenly a voice cried out, “Where is the child? Where is the child Arulmozhi?” It was Kundavai’s voice. Arulmozhi was five years old then; Kundavai was seven. Arulmozhi, the darling of the palace, was dearer than life to all. But more than anyone, his sister Kundavai cherished him. It was Kundavai who first noticed that the child was missing from the boat. At once, she cried out as above. Everyone was thrown into confusion. They searched here and there in the boat. But where was there space to search in the royal barge? They looked all around, but the child was nowhere to be found. Kundavai and Aditya wailed. The queens lamented, the maids shrieked. Some of the boatmen jumped into the swirling Kaveri to search. Sundara Chola himself plunged in to search likewise.

But where to search? Who could say how far the river’s current had carried the child? Who knew when the child had fallen into the flood? With no aim or direction, those who had leapt into the Kaveri swam about in all directions, searching desperately. The child could not be found.

Meanwhile, some of the queens and maids in the boat fainted and collapsed. There was no one to tend to them. The others, overwhelmed with emotion, cried out in grief, their wailing rising above the roaring voice of the Kaveri. The birds dwelling in the trees along the riverbank, startled by the sound, fell silent in shock.

Suddenly, a wondrous sight appeared. A short distance from the boat, in the midst of the river’s current, it could be seen—a female figure, standing with the child held aloft in both hands. The form of that maiden was hidden in the water up to her waist. Only her golden face, her chest, and her upraised arms were visible above the surface. And even these were largely concealed by the child she held aloft. Everyone, including Sundara Chozhar, witnessed that scene. At once, he leapt into the water and swam swiftly in that direction. Stretching out his arms, he caught hold of the child. By then, the boat had also drawn near to him. The people in the boat took the child from Sundara Chozhar’s hands. They also grasped the Emperor’s hand and helped him aboard. No sooner had the Emperor climbed into the boat than he lost consciousness and collapsed. Everyone was preoccupied with tending to him and the child.

No one paid any attention to what became of the lady who had saved the child. No one bothered to notice her appearance, so as to later identify her. She did not come forward to claim, “It was I who saved the child!” and ask for a reward. Thus, it was unanimously decided that it must have been the goddess of the Kaveri river herself who had rescued Prince Arulmozhi. From that year onward, arrangements were made to offer worship to the Ponni river on that day annually. Until then, Arulmozhi Varman had been known as the cherished son of the palace; from that day forth, he became “Ponniyin Selvan”—the Son of Ponni. From then on, almost all the members of the royal family who knew of that incident called Arulmozhi Varman by the name “Ponniyin Selvan.”

chapters.title: Two Full Moons
paragraphs: That day, the city of Thanjavur was in a state of jubilant commotion. Was it any wonder that the people of the capital were so elated to hear that the princess, who had not visited the city for many years, had changed her mind and was coming to Thanjavur? There was not a soul in Chola Nadu who did not know of Princess Kundavai’s beauty, wisdom, and compassion. Nor was there anyone who did not, at least once a day, mention her name in connection with some rumor or another. The gossip that the princess would be present at the palace in Thanjavur for this year’s Navaratri festival had already spread, heightening the people’s anticipation. Therefore, as soon as it was known that she was arriving today, a veritable ocean of people gathered at the gates of Thanjavur fort, waiting in eager expectation. Like the waves of the sea rejoicing at the sight of the full moon rising, this human sea surged with excitement and clamorous joy.

At last, the full moon did rise. No—two moons rose at the same time. When Princess Kundavai arrived at the gates of Thanjavur fort with her retinue, the great doors swung open with a resounding clang. The palace attendants came out to welcome and escort her inside. At the head of these attendants stood the two Pazhuvettaraiyars. Not only that; behind them came a palanquin adorned with ivory and set with pearls. As its silk curtains parted, the radiant, moon-like face of the young queen of Pazhuvoor, Nandini Devi, was revealed.

Kundavai alighted from her elephant, and Nandini descended from her palanquin. Nandini hurried forward and greeted Kundavai with a smile and words of welcome. Kundavai acknowledged the greeting with a gentle smile of her own.

The enthusiasm of the crowd, who beheld together those two peerless beauties of Chola Nadu, overflowed its bounds. Nandini’s complexion was golden; Kundavai’s was the hue of the red lotus. Nandini’s golden face was round and full, like the full moon; Kundavai’s visage, sculpted as if by the hands of a master, was delicately elongated. Nandini’s dark eyes, rimmed with crimson, were wide and restless, like bees with outspread wings; Kundavai’s deep blue eyes were long and radiant, like the petals of the blue lotus. Nandini’s nose was flat and gleaming, as if carved from ivory; Kundavai’s nose was slightly long, like the bud of a paneer flower. Nandini’s lips, a little thick, glowed like coral cups brimming with nectar; Kundavai’s slender lips were like... The pomegranate bud shone, bursting forth in brilliance. Nandini had adorned her hair, coiled into a chignon and decorated like a garland of blossoming flowers. Kundavai’s tresses, on the other hand, were arranged like a jeweled crown, as if to declare, “She is the queen of beauty.”

It cannot be said that everyone there delighted in separately comparing and contrasting the beauty and adornment of those two peerless women. Yet, it was evident to all that both were unparalleled in their loveliness, and that in their appearance and ornamentation, they were distinctly different.

Until then, the townspeople had harbored a certain dissatisfaction and envy toward Nandini. Each person revered Princess Kundavai with devotion, as if she were their family deity. But now, when the young queen of Pazhuvoor herself came to the fort’s entrance to welcome the younger princess, it filled the people with immense joy.
While the crowd was thus immersed in happiness, the conversation that took place between Nandini and Kundavai crackled like lightning striking against lightning.
“Devi! Welcome, welcome! We thought you had completely forgotten us. Today we have learned that the compassion of the young princess knows no bounds,” said Nandini.
“How is that, Rani? Does being far away mean one has forgotten? Since you have not come to Pazhaiyarai, should I assume you have forgotten me?” replied Kundavai.

“Bees themselves come toward the honeyed blossom; no invitation is needed. Who would not come to beautiful Pazhaiyarai? But for you to come to this ill-fated Tanjai fort—does it not speak to the greatness of your compassion?”
“How can you say such a thing? Can one call the city of Tanjai an ill-fated place, when beauty itself is imprisoned here?” said the young princess.

“That is what I too have heard—that the Emperor has been imprisoned here. But now there is no more worry; you have come to set him free, have you not?” said Nandini, and in her eyes, a flash of lightning appeared and vanished.

“How beautiful! Not even the gods themselves could imprison Sundara Chola Chakravarthi. How could mere mortals do so? I was not speaking of that. I was speaking of Nandini Devi, the goddess of beauty…”
“Speak clearly, Devi! Say this so that he may hear it. The Lord of Pazhuvur keeps me as though I am a prisoner. If you could put in a word for me…”
“What use is my recommendation? Is it an ordinary prison that holds you? Is it not the prison of love? And moreover…”
“Yes, Devi! And if it is the old man’s prison of love, then there is no escape! They speak of some underground dungeons, do they not? At least those locked within them may one day emerge! But…”

“Yes, Queen! And if it is a shackle we have placed upon ourselves, if it is a prison we have sought out and entered, then liberation is indeed difficult!… Those who walk in the path of Sita, Kannagi, Nalayini, and Savitri will not even seek deliverance!… Look, what is that commotion over there?” said Princess Kundavai.

Indeed, from amidst the crowd of women gathered a short distance from the fortress gate, a great clamor was rising. Kundavai and Nandini drew near to the spot. At first, since many women were shouting at once, it was difficult to understand what was happening. Then, gradually, it became clear. The women wished to visit the younger princess at the palace more often, and so they were petitioning for the restrictions on entering the fortress during the nine days of Navaratri to be lifted.

“Queen! At least speak to your husband or your brother-in-law and ask them to grant these women’s request. Would he be afraid merely at the sight of these women? What harm could they possibly bring to the Chola empire? Are not the orders of the Pazhuvur brothers spread far and wide, to all four directions, even to the seashore?” said Kundavai.

“Why do you stop at the seashore? Their power and authority reach beyond the sea as well. Soon, you will see proof of that!” Nandini replied, her smile slicing through Kundavai’s heart. ‘What could be the hidden meaning behind this traitor’s words?’ she wondered.
Meanwhile, Nandini signaled to Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar, called him near, and conveyed to him both the women’s request and the younger princess’s wish.
“Who would dare contradict the word of the younger princess?” said Pazhuvetaraiyar.
Then, amidst the tumult and uproar of the crowd, they entered the fortress.

From that day onwards, for several days, the city of Thanjai and its surrounding regions overflowed with boundless excitement and jubilant commotion. The arrival of Kundavai Devi in Thanjai coincided with the Navaratri festival. The Pazhuvettaraiyar too fulfilled his promise. For those ten days, he allowed the people to enter and leave the fortress without any hindrance. The gates of the fort stood wide open at all hours. Within the fort’s palaces and in the outskirts of the city, countless grand festivities unfolded. Crowds of people gathered in great numbers to witness these spectacles. Amidst those throngs, time and again, two full moons seemed to rise together in the sky. At the sight of this, the sea of people surged and roared with delight.

Yet, while outwardly all was celebration and festive joy, within the hearts of those two full moons, volcanoes raged, spewing forth molten fire. Between the younger mistress of Pazhuvoor and the young princess of Pazhaiyarai, an unceasing battle was being waged. With words as arrows and glances as spears, those two beauties fought a fierce war. In that struggle, whenever the sharp swords of both sides clashed, sparks flew. When their polished spears struck one another, flames leapt forth. In the dark sky, when two lightning bolts slashed at each other, both trembled and quivered together. Two beautiful, ferocious tigresses entwined in combat, their claws drawing blood from one another. Two deadly, alluring serpents danced in rivalry, extending their slender, crimson tongues, each seeking to swallow the other whole.
In this astonishing contest, they were swept up in a frenzy of exhilaration; yet, within, their hearts writhed in pain and turmoil.

Amidst the exuberance of the city’s people, without joining in their joy, and without understanding the battle between these two radiant moons, there was a single soul in torment. Princess Vanathi of Kodumbalur now found no opportunity even to speak with the young princess. Though she accompanied her elder sister everywhere, her mind was not engaged in anything happening outside. She had created a world of solitude within herself and wandered only in that realm.

chapters.title: A Mournful Voice in the Night
paragraphs: In those days, the arts of music and dance flourished abundantly in the Chola land. Dance and drama grew together, hand in hand. The city of Thanjai especially gave rise to many distinguished artists of the dramatic arts. The devout Shaivite poet, Karuvur Thevar, who lived in those days, sang of Thanjai, encircled by ginger gardens, in his verses:
“Where peacocks with lightning-shaped brows Perform in the drama halls, In ginger-girt Thanjai, they learn their arts.”
(*Ginger refers to the fort walls encircling the city.)

Thus does one of his songs describe it. The presence of many drama halls in Thanjai city was a sign of the flourishing dramatic arts there. Of all these drama halls, the finest was within the emperor’s own palace. Artists who invented and staged new dramas lived in Thanjai. Previously, it was customary to adapt stories from the epics and puranas into plays. But for some time now, the dramatists of Thanjai had turned their attention to a new field and found success: they began to dramatize the lives of famous historical heroes. They even staged the heroic tales of those who lived just before their own time.

Where else could such heroes be found as those born in the Chola dynasty? Thus, they dramatized and performed the histories of Chola kings such as Karikala Valavan, Vijayalaya Chola, and Parantaka Deva.

During the Navaratri festival, for three days in the emperor’s palace, plays depicting the heroic histories of Chola kings were performed. Opposite the wondrously decorated drama hall, in the palace courtyard bathed in moonlight, thousands of people gathered to witness the plays. A special section, adorned with pearl-studded, painted pillars beneath a canopy of blue silk, was arranged for the royal women to sit. Beneath this, the queens, princesses, and their intimate companions sat and watched the performances. At such times, Nandini always came and sat close by Princess Kundavai. Though some of the other women disliked this, they kept their feelings to themselves and bore it in silence. Nothing else could be done. Who would dare to become the target of the wrath of Periya Pazhuvettarayar and the Young Queen of Pazhuvur? When even the Young Princess herself showed such respect and honor to that proud woman, what could others do?

Of the three plays about the kings of the Chola dynasty, the third—Parantaka Devar Natakam—shone the brightest. It was on that day, after witnessing the play, that a certain murmur began to stir and grow among the people.

Until then, among the line of Chola kings who had ruled the land, Sundara Chozhar’s grandfather, the illustrious Kopparakesari Parantaka, stood out for his valor and glory. He ruled for about forty-six years. During his reign, the Chola Empire expanded far and wide. His command extended from the land of Lanka to the banks of the Tungabhadra River. Many wars were fought; great victories were won. He earned the title “Kopparakesari Varman, Conqueror of Madurai and Lanka.” He covered the Chittrambalam at Thillai Chidambaram with gold and won eternal fame. In the final years of his life, a few defeats befell him and the empire shrank. But his heroic fame never diminished. In the north, at Thakkolam, a final great battle was fought against Kannaradevan, a king who had marched with a vast army like the ocean from the twin regions.

In this war, Parantaka’s eldest son, Rajaditya—the greatest of warriors ever seen in this land of Bharata—led the army. He routed Kannaradevan’s forces and, atop his elephant, gave up his life and ascended to the hero’s heaven. His arrow-pierced body was brought back to the city just as it was. It was taken to the palace. The Emperor Parantaka and his queens, placing the body of the great hero who had given his life to protect the nation among them, wept torrents of tears. From behind the curtain, a disembodied voice proclaimed: “Grieve not! Grieve not! Prince Rajaditya has not died; he lives, shining like a temple in the heart of every Chola subject!” With this final scene, the play ended.

The people delighted and marveled at this drama, filled with heroic deeds from the previous generation. The reason for the stir that arose among the audience was this: in the great wars of Parantaka Devar’s time, two minor kings had been his steadfast allies. One was the prince of Kodumbalur; the other, the chieftain of Pazhuvur. Both were bound to the Chola dynasty by ties of kinship—by giving and taking daughters in marriage. Both had aided Parantaka like two hands. It was impossible to say which was the right hand and which the left. Parantaka Chozhar cherished and honored them both, as he would his own two eyes. Of the two eyes... How can one truly say what is exalted and what is lowly? The great elder of the Pazhuvettaraiyar clan, who now wield authority, was once the supporter of Paranthaka. His name was Pazhuvettaraiyar Kandan Amudhanar. The father of the valiant Kodumbalur chieftain who lost his life in Eezham—who is, in fact, Vanathi’s grandfather—was the Kodumbalur petty king who aided Paranthaka Devar.

Those who staged the play about Paranthaka Devar had taken great care not to depict any difference in rank or status between these two minor kings. They had acted in such a way that the valor and fame of both would shine equally. They made it a point to show that Paranthaka Devar honored both these warriors with equal distinction.

Yet, it soon became apparent that the audience did not share such impartiality. Among them, some were revealed to be of the Kodumbalur faction, while others favored Pazhuvur. When the valorous deeds of the Kodumbalur chief were enacted on stage, a section of the audience erupted in cheers. When the Pazhuvur hero appeared, another group responded with their own shouts. At first, this rivalry was minor; but gradually, it grew in intensity. In the midst of the play, the audience’s cry of “Navalo! Naval!” rose up and echoed in all directions.
(*In those days, instead of the modern practice of shouting slogans to show enthusiasm and support, people would cry out “Navalo! Naval!” in the assembly.)

These competing cries in the hall delighted Princess Kundavai. Whenever the Kodumbalur faction’s cheer grew stronger, she would nudge the Kodumbalur princess beside her and say, “Did you see, Vanathi? Your side is winning now!” The guileless Vanathi would express her happiness at this. When the Pazhuvur faction’s cheer gained strength, the young princess would turn to Nandini and say, “Queen! Now your side is in the lead!” But this did not seem to excite Nandini, as her expression revealed. The very fact that such a rivalry had arisen, that the people were openly taking sides and shouting, that the young princess was encouraging it further, and that she was teasing both the little Vanathi and herself as equals—this only stoked the fire in Nandini’s heart many times over. More than once, she considered rising and leaving in anger. But she clenched her teeth and stayed, thinking that if she did so, it would only make the rivalry more dramatic and be seen as an admission of defeat.

Kundavai had been observing all this closely. She could discern Nandini’s state of mind from her facial expressions, as if gazing into a mirror. Yet, there was one thing that remained a mystery even to the young princess. When the play depicted the defeat of the Pandya king in battle, his seeking refuge with the king of Lanka, his fleeing to Chera country after leaving behind the jeweled crown and the gem-studded scepter without receiving any aid from the Lankan king—all these scenes filled the entire audience with boundless enthusiasm. Yet, at those very moments, only Nandini’s face reflected deep anguish. The reason for this puzzled the young princess. She thought to probe a little through conversation.

“It’s a pity the Emperor could not be with us to witness this wonderful play, isn’t it? He too achieved such feats in his time, just as our grandfather did. If only father’s health would improve…” she said.
“He will surely recover. Now that his beloved daughter has returned, and if the medicinal herbs from Lanka arrive soon, the Emperor will certainly regain his health,” replied Nandini.
“Are herbs coming from Lanka? What is that?” asked Kundavai.
“You ask as if you do not know! Didn’t the physician from Pazhaiyarai send someone to fetch herbs from Lanka? I heard that you yourself arranged for someone to go. Is that not true?”

Kundavai bit her lip with her teeth. Though her row of teeth was as lovely as a string of jasmine buds, biting her lips did cause her pain. Fortunately, at that moment, a great cheer of “Navalo! Navalo!” rose from the crowd, and the conversation was interrupted.

After blessing Sundara Chola with strength, beauty, long life, and a prosperous reign, the play came to an end. The audience dispersed, dancing with joy and excitement, and made their way home. The queens of the minor kings, along with their retinues, also departed. Afterwards, Empress Vanamadevi and the other palace women set out for the temple of Durga, the tutelary goddess of the Chola clan.

The daughter of Malayaman had undertaken many vows for the recovery of Sundara Chola’s health. She often visited the temple of Durga to offer her prayers. During the nine nights of Navaratri, special poojas were performed for the goddess Durga.

Sacrifices were offered, seeking the Emperor’s well-being. Each night, it was customary for the Maharani to go to the temple and return after the midnight worship. Many of the elder women of the palace would accompany the Maharani to the shrine.

It was not the custom to take young women to the sanctum of Durga. Sometimes, the goddess would descend upon the priests, causing them to dance in a wild, frenzied manner. They would recount tales of curses and their consequences. Fearing that young women might be frightened by such sights, they were not taken along. But who among them had the courage to tell the young princess, “You might be afraid!” and stop her? On all those nine days, Kundavai too went with the mothers to the Durga temple, offering prayers to the goddess. During these times, Vanathi was left alone in the palace.

On the night of the Parantaka Devar play, Vanathi’s heart was brimming with excitement. Watching the heroic deeds of her ancestors enacted upon the stage had filled her with pride. Along with this, memories of Lanka arose. Thoughts of her father, who had died in the war in Eelam, and of the prince who had gone to avenge his death, surfaced again and again. Sleep eluded her entirely. Her eyelids refused to close. If only the young princess would return from the temple and speak with her for a while about the night’s play, perhaps then sleep would come; but not before that.

Rather than simply tossing and turning in bed, she thought she might as well stroll for a while on the upper terrace of the palace. From the upper terrace, she could see the entire city of Thanjavur. She might even catch a glimpse of the Durga temple—so thinking, she rose from her bed and set out. Vanathi was new to that palace. Yet, finding the moonlit upper terrace was not so difficult. With long corridors, pillars on either side, and ever-burning lamps, what hardship could there be?

The corridors wound on and on. Many of the lamps that had shone brightly earlier in the night had now gone out. Some, shrouded in smoke, cast a dim, hazy light. Here and there, at the bends in the corridors, nursemaids lay sleeping or dozing. Not wishing to wake them and ask the way, Vanathi continued on by herself. It seemed as if those palace corridors had no end.
