Suddenly, a voice was heard. It rang out as a plaintive, sorrowful cry. Vanathi was seized with a chill; her body trembled. Her feet froze where she stood.
Again, that sorrowful voice:
“Is there no one to save me?”

Ah! Is this not the Emperor’s voice? What danger could it be? It is not clear. Is it the affliction of his body? Or could it be something else? All the elder women, including the Empress, have gone to the temple, haven’t they? Is the Emperor truly left alone, with no one by his side? Still, I must go and see.

With trembling legs, Vanathi took a few more hesitant steps forward. The voice seemed to come from below. At that spot, the corridor ended. When she bent down and looked, she saw a vast hall below. Ah! Is this not the Emperor’s bedchamber? Yes; there he is, the Emperor himself, lying down—lying all alone. And he is muttering something to himself; perhaps I can hear what he says.

“Accursed woman! It is true, indeed! I did kill you! Not by intent, but still, I am the cause of your death. What do you want me to do? It has been twenty-five years. Yet you still haunt me, refusing to leave! Is there no peace for your soul? Will you not grant me peace as well? Tell me what penance I must do! I will do it, whatever it is. Leave me!… Alas! Is there no one to free me from her torment? Everyone seeks medicine for my bodily illness! Is there no one to cure the sickness of my mind and save me?… Go! Go! Leave me! No, do not go! Stay! Tell me what I must do before you leave! Do not torture me with this silence! Open your mouth and say something before you go!”

These words struck Vanathi’s ears like red-hot iron. From the crown of her head to the soles of her feet, she trembled. Unconsciously, she bent down and peered below. She let her gaze wander around the hall as far as her eyes could see.

A short distance in front of the Emperor stood a figure. It was the form of a woman—half her figure was visible, the rest hidden in the shadow of a pillar and the swirl of incense smoke. As far as she could discern, that figure… Ah! Does it not resemble the Young Queen of Pazhuvoor? What is this—some dream? Some trick of the mind? No! It is real! There, behind that pillar, who stands in hiding? Is it not Periya Pazhuvettarayar? There is no doubt—it is them! Did the Emperor speak so because he saw the Young Queen of Pazhuvoor? “It is true that I killed you,” he cried—what could that mean?

Suddenly, it seemed as if a faintness was coming over Vanathi; her head began to spin. No, it was as if the very palace itself was beginning to whirl around her. No, no! She must not lose consciousness here. She must not, at any cost.

Clenching her teeth, Vanathi walked away from that place. But the path back seemed endless, as if it would never come to an end. The room where she had been resting appeared as though it would never welcome her again. She could walk no further; nor could she stand.
When Princess Kundavai returned from the temple, she saw Vanathi lying unconscious, like a lifeless log, on the walkway a short distance from her own chamber.

chapters.title: Sundara Chozhan’s Delusion
paragraphs: The next morning, Emperor Sundara Chozha summoned his beloved daughter to his presence. He ordered all attendants, nurses, and physicians to withdraw far from his chamber. Seating Kundavai beside him, he lovingly stroked her back. Kundavai sensed that her father was struggling to express what he wished to say.
“Father! Are you angry with me?” she asked.
Tears glimmered in Sundara Chozhar’s eyes.
“Why, my dear, should I be angry with you?” he replied.
“For coming to Thanjavur against your command, of course!”
“Yes; you should not have come here against my orders. This Thanjavur palace is not fit for young women to reside in. You yourself must have realized that after last night’s incident.”
“Which incident are you referring to, Father?”
“I am speaking of that woman from Kodumbalur fainting. How is she now?”
“She is perfectly well today, Father! Even in Pazhayarai, she often loses consciousness like this. She recovers completely after a short while.”
“Did you ask her, dear? Did she say she saw or heard anything unusual in the palace last night?”

After thinking for a moment, Kundavai replied, “Yes, Father! When we all went to the Durga temple, she tried to go alone to the upper floor. There, she said she heard someone weeping in great sorrow. That frightened her, she said.”
“I thought as much. Do you understand now, child? There are spirits haunting this palace. You must not stay here. You must leave at once!” declared Sundara Chozhar.

As he spoke, Kundavai noticed his body trembling and his eyes staring wildly into some distant void. “Father! If that is so, why should you alone remain here? Why should Mother stay here? Let us all go to Pazhayarai! Coming here has not even improved your health, has it?” she asked.
The Emperor, with a smile tinged in sorrow, replied, “Will my body ever recover now? I have no such hope left in me.”
“Why should you lose hope like that, Father? The physician at Pazhayarai says he can cure you.”
“I have heard that, trusting his words, you have even sent someone to Lanka to fetch herbs! My dear, that shows the depth of your affection for me.”
“Is it wrong for a daughter to love her father, Father?”

“There is nothing wrong in that. To have a daughter with such devotion is my good fortune. There is nothing wrong in sending someone to bring herbs from Lanka either. But even if the herbs come from Lanka, or from the island of Java, or even if nectar itself descends from the heavens, my body will not be cured in this lifetime…”
“Oh no! Please do not say such things!” the princess cried.

“You have come here against my orders, child! Yet, I am truly glad for it. I have long wished to open my heart and tell you the truth one day. Now the time has come. Listen! If it were a bodily ailment, medicines and herbs might cure it. But my illness is not of the body; what remedy is there for a troubled mind?”
“Father, what unsolvable sorrow could trouble you, the Emperor who rules the three worlds?”

“You too speak in the fanciful exaggerations of poets, child! I am not the Emperor who rules the three worlds; nor do I rule the whole earth. My kingdom is but a small corner of this world. Even the burden of this, I am unable to bear…”
“Why should you bear it, Father? Are there not those fit to shoulder the weight of the kingdom? You have two sons, both as brave as lion cubs, heroes among heroes. They can bear any burden…”

“My daughter! It is only when I think of that, my heart shudders within me. Both your brothers are unparalleled warriors. Just as I raised you as the apple of my eye, so too did I cherish them. Yet, I doubt whether entrusting this kingdom to them would truly be an act of goodness. Would you have me hand over to them, along with the realm, a great and terrible curse as well?”

“What curse could possibly afflict this kingdom? Sibi, who gave his own flesh for a dove, and Manu Needhi Cholan, who sacrificed his son for a calf—these are our ancestors. Karikala Valavan and Perunarkilli ruled this land. The valiant Vijayalaya Cholan, who bore ninety-six wounds upon his body, sat upon this very throne. Aditya Cholan, who built a hundred and eight temples along the banks of the Kaveri, and Parantaka, who gilded the temple at Chidambaram and made it the Golden Hall, expanded this realm. This is the righteous empire ruled by Kandaraditya, who realized that love is Shiva, and in whose reign love and divinity dwelled together. What curse could ever befall such a kingdom? Father! You are gripped by some illusion of the mind! If you were to leave this Tanjavur fort…”

“You do not know what would happen the very moment I leave this place! Do you think I remain in this prison that is the Tanjai fort, having left beautiful Pazhayarai, for my own happiness? Kundavai, it is only because I am here that this ancient Chola kingdom is preserved from utter ruin. Think of what happened last night while the play was being performed! I was watching everything from the terrace beneath the moonlight. I even considered stopping the play midway…”
“Father! What is this? The play was wonderful! My heart swelled with pride at the glory of the Chola clan! Why did you wish to stop it? What part of the performance displeased you?”

“The play itself was flawless, my child! I found no fault in it. I speak of the behavior of those who watched it. Did you not notice the rival cries raised by the Kodumbalur faction and the Pazhuvettaraiyar faction?”
“I noticed, Father!”

“Even while I am here, they dare to behave so! Imagine what would happen if I were not! The moment I leave Tanjavur, strife will erupt between the two factions. Just as the descendants of Krishna Paramatma destroyed each other, so too will these men perish, and with them, this great empire will be destroyed…”

“Father! You are the supreme emperor of this Chola Empire. The Pazhuvettaraiyars, the Kodumbalur Velirs—all of them are bound to obey your slightest command without question. If they act against your will, they are only inviting their own ruin. Why should you worry?”

“My daughter! For the past hundred years, both these noble houses have rendered unparalleled service to the Chola Empire. Without their support, could the Chola kingdom have grown so vast and powerful? If they are destroyed, will that not weaken the kingdom as well?”
“Father! If it is found that one faction among them is plotting treason against you…”
Sundara Cholar gazed at Kundavai in astonishment. “What are you saying, my child? Treason against me? Who is plotting such a thing?”
“Father! Some who pretend to be your loyal servants are secretly conspiring against you. They are scheming to deny your sons the throne and to crown another in their place…”
“For whom? For whom, my daughter? If not for your brothers, for whom are they plotting to give the crown?” the emperor asked, agitation in his voice.
In a soft voice, Kundavai replied, “For uncle Madurantakan, Father! While you have been lying ill, they have been committing this terrible act of treachery…”
At once, Sundara Cholar straightened up a little and said, “Ah! If only their efforts succeed, how wonderful it would be!”
Kundavai was taken aback.
“Father! What is this? Will you yourself become an enemy to your own children?”
“No; I am not an enemy to my children. I wish only for their well-being. This cursed, ill-fated kingdom is not what they need. If only Madurantakan would agree…”
“What is there for uncle to agree? He is more than willing. He is ready to accept the crown even tomorrow. Are you truly going to do this? Will you not even ask for my brother’s consent…?”
“Yes; it is Aditya Karikalan whom you must ask. But it is not enough to ask him alone. Your great-aunt must also give her consent…”
“If the crown is to be placed on her son’s head, would a mother refuse?”

“Why wouldn’t she? Even after all these years of being close to your great-aunt, have you not come to understand her? It was only because of Sembiyan Maadevi’s insistence that I ascended the throne that day. I also invested Aditya with the title of prince. Kundavai! Your great-aunt has much affection for you. Go to her, speak to her gently, and win her consent to crown Madurantakan!…”
Kundavai was struck dumb with astonishment and stood silent.

“Then go to Kanchi! There, speak to your elder brother Aditya Karikalan, and persuade him to say, ‘I do not want this kingdom, cursed as it is.’ Let us crown Madurantakan instead. Then, all of us will be freed from this curse and live in peace,” said the Emperor.
“Father! You keep speaking of a curse. What curse do you mean?” Kundavai asked.
“My child! Do you believe in what they call previous births? They say that sometimes memories of past lives come to us in this life—do you believe in that?”
“Father! Those are great mysteries. What do I know about such things?”

“They speak of the ten incarnations of Maha Vishnu! They say that before the final incarnation as Buddha, the Lord took many other forms. There are many beautiful stories about those incarnations, aren’t there?”
“I have heard them, Father!”
“If even the gods and incarnate beings have previous births, would ordinary humans alone be exempt?”
“Perhaps not, Father!”

“Sometimes, memories of my past life come to me, my child! I have never spoken of them to anyone until now. If I did, no one would believe me; no one would understand. They would say that along with my bodily illness, I have also fallen prey to delusions of the mind. Not content with summoning physicians to trouble me, they would begin to call in sorcerers as well…”
“Yes, Father! Even now, some are saying so. They claim your illness cannot be cured by medicine; that sorcerers must be summoned…”
“Did you hear that? You wouldn’t think such things, would you? You wouldn’t laugh at me for saying so, would you?” asked the Emperor.
“Must you even ask, Father? Do you think I do not know how much your heart is pained? Would I ever laugh at you?” replied Kundavai. Tears welled up in her eyes.
“I know, my daughter! That is why I speak to you of things I would tell no other. Listen, I will share with you some memories from my previous birth!” said Sundara Chozhar.
A beautiful island, encircled on all sides by the sea. Everywhere on that island, lush green trees grew in abundance. Where there were no trees, dense thickets flourished.

By the seashore, hidden in a thicket, a young man concealed himself. At a short distance, he watched intently as a ship sailed away, its sail spread wide upon the sea. He kept watching until it vanished from sight. Then, with a deep sigh, he said, “Father! We have survived!”

That young man was born of royal blood. Yet he had no claim to the throne; nor did he harbor any desire to rule. His father had three elder sons born before him. Therefore, the thought of ruling the kingdom never even visited his dreams; he had no longing for it. When the army set out across the sea to wage war in a foreign land, he too joined them. He was given command of a small battalion. In battle, his force was defeated. Countless men perished. All those under his command fell in the fight. That young man, too, performed many daring deeds, resolved to lay down his life in battle. Yet death did not come for him. Among the defeated, those who survived fled and reached the harbor. They prepared to return to their homeland. Only that young man did not wish to go back. Having lost every soldier under his command, he could not bear to return home. His clan was famed for its mighty heroes. He did not wish to bring disgrace upon that renown. So, as the ship sailed on, when a beautiful island appeared in the distance, the young man quietly slipped into the sea, unnoticed by any. He swam ashore to the island. He waited until the ship disappeared from sight. Then he climbed a tree, seated himself on a low branch, and gazed all around. The beauty of that island captivated his heart.

But on that island, it seemed as though there was no trace of human presence. At that moment, this did not strike him as a shortcoming. His spirits were soaring. Leaning against a tree branch, he sat and indulged in daydreams about the future.

Suddenly, a human voice—no, a woman’s voice—cried out. He turned to look. A young woman was running, screaming. Chasing her was a fearsome bear. Even as he watched, the bear drew closer and closer to the woman. The distance between them was rapidly shrinking. There was no time to think of any other plan. The youth leapt nimbly from the tree branch to the ground. Grabbing the spear that was stuck in the tree, he ran forward. The bear was nearly upon the woman, its terrifying claws about to seize her by the neck. At that critical moment, he aimed and hurled his spear. The spear struck the bear. With a thunderous roar that seemed to shake the seven worlds, the bear turned away. The woman was saved, but now the youth himself was in danger. The wounded bear charged at him. A fierce struggle ensued between the youth and the beast. In the end, it was the youth who emerged victorious.

The triumphant youth’s eyes immediately searched all around. At first, he did not even know what he was searching for. Then, in a flash, he realized. The woman he sought stood leaning against a coconut tree that bent and curved across the path. She rested against its trunk. Wonder shone in her eyes, and joy lit up her face. Her appearance and clothing revealed that she was a woman of the wild, unacquainted with the civilized ways of the world. Yet, her beauty was such that one might say there was no one in this world to compare with her. The sight of that woman standing there was like a painting wrought by an artist of unparalleled skill and power. Though she was truly a woman, the youth felt she could not possibly be a woman of this world.

He drew nearer. But, contrary to his expectation, she did not vanish like a phantom. Instead, quite unexpectedly, she turned and fled. He ran after her for a short distance, then stopped. He was too exhausted to pursue a woman who ran with the swiftness of a deer. Moreover, he thought, it was uncivilized to chase after a woman.

“She must be somewhere on this small island, must she not? Shall I leave without seeing her again?” he thought, and stopped. He walked along the seashore and lay down on the soft, clear sand to rest his weary body.

His expectation was not in vain. After a short while, the woman returned, bringing with her an elderly man. She brought along a man as well. It became clear that the man belonged to the ‘Karaiyar’ community, who lived along the seashore of Lanka and made their living by fishing. Through him, the young man learned an important truth: that woman had, at the right moment, saved his life.

While he was sitting on a tree branch, intently watching the sea, a bear had crept up behind him and stared at him closely. Then it began to climb the tree. The woman had witnessed all this. To distract the bear in another direction and to warn the young man, she had shouted in that peculiar manner. The bear, abandoning its climb, began to chase after her instead.

Is it even necessary to describe how the young man felt upon hearing this? He expressed his gratitude to the woman who had saved him. But she did not utter a single word in reply. For everything the young man said to her, it was the man who had come with her who answered. At first, this surprised the young man. But once he learned the truth, his surprise vanished. The woman was mute, unable to speak. He also discovered that she was deaf, unable to hear. Once he knew this, his affection for her multiplied many times over. The circumstances and the setting only helped that affection to grow and flourish. Her inability to hear or speak did not seem a flaw to the young man. Her eyes revealed wondrous truths and intimate secrets that could not be spoken by the mouth. What language in this world could match that language of the eyes? Likewise, to make up for her deafness, her sense of smell was endowed with extraordinary power. Even in the midst of the dense forest, she could, by her sense of smell alone, detect what wild animal was hiding far away. But what did all this matter? When two hearts have become one, why worry about the other senses?
To the young man, that island seemed nothing short of paradise. Days, months, and years passed in this way. He even forgot to keep count of how many days or years had gone by.

Suddenly, one day, an end came to the young man’s paradise. A ship came and anchored near the island. From it, many people came ashore in boats and on rafts. Curious to see who they were, the young man approached them. He learned that they had come searching for him. Many unexpected events had occurred in his homeland. His father’s two elder brothers had died. The remaining brother had no children. Thus, a great empire was waiting for him. A great turmoil arose in his heart. He could not bear to leave that beautiful island and the mute woman who had made it a paradise.

At that very moment, the longing to see his village and his kin pulled him powerfully in one direction. He knew that his homeland was surrounded on all sides by danger. The distant thunder of war drums reached his ears from far, far away. This helped him make his decision.

“I will return; I will fulfill my duty and then come back,” he promised that maiden a thousand times before he departed. The mute girl, born and raised in the forest, did not wish to come among the people who had arrived from the land. When the youth boarded the boat, she sat a little distance away, perched upon that old, bent coconut tree, watching him. To the youth, her two eyes seemed at that moment like twin oceans of tears.
Yet, hardening his heart like stone, he boarded the boat and made his way to the ship…

“Kundavai! That fisherfolk maiden stood there watching like that—the memory of that scene often appears before my mind’s eye. No matter how much I try, I cannot forget it. But there is another scene, even sadder, one that makes me tremble with grief whenever I think of it. Day and night, whether asleep or awake, it torments and pains me. Shall I tell you about that too?” asked Sundara Chozhar, looking at his beloved daughter.
With her throat choked by emotion and her voice trembling, Sundara Chozhar’s precious daughter replied, “Tell me, Father.”

chapters.title: Can the Dead Return?
paragraphs: Until now, Sundara Chozhar had spoken as though he were telling the story of some third person, someone else entirely. But now, he began to recount it as an episode from his own life:

“My dearest daughter! Today, I am about to tell you something that a father would not ordinarily share with his daughter. I am about to reveal to you a secret I have never confided to anyone else. In this whole world, only my friend Aniruddhan knows of it; even he does not know it in its entirety. He does not know the turmoil raging in my heart at this moment. But to you, I shall tell everything. Someone in our family must know the truth. I cannot tell your mother. For some time now, I have felt that I must tell you, and you alone. Today, the opportunity has come. You will not mock my condition; you will try to heal the wound in my heart; you will help me fulfill my wish! With this faith, I speak to you…

“From that island, I boarded a ship and set sail, reaching Kodikkarai. I learned that my grandfather, Paranthaka Chakravarthi, was staying here in the Tanjore palace at that time, and so I came straight here.

“When I arrived in Tanjore, Paranthaka Chakravarthi was awaiting death. His heart was heavy with sorrow. The great empire he had built over forty years was now falling into disarray. Rajaditya, who should have succeeded him, had fallen in the battle of Takkolam. My father, Arinjaya, who had been grievously wounded in that same battlefield, was hovering between life and death. The armies of Kannara Devan had seized the Thondai region and were advancing further. In the south, the Pandyas were rising up again. In Lanka, the Chola forces had been defeated and had returned. In many battlefields, the bravest of Chola warriors had laid down their lives. All these tidings came together to pierce the heart of the aged Paranthaka Chakravarthi, plunging him into a sea of sorrow.

“In this state, when he saw me, his face brightened. From the days of my childhood, my grandfather had cherished a deep affection for me. He kept me with him in the palace for many years, never letting me go anywhere. It was only after much insistence that I obtained his leave to go to Eezha Nadu. When he learned that I was not among those who had returned from there, his… My grandfather’s heart was broken. Not knowing whether I was alive or dead, he kept sending groups of men, one after another, to search for me.

“At last, one such group found me. When I finally reached Thanjai, a small measure of peace returned to his wounded heart. In the twilight of his life, as the Chola Empire was descending into decline, a hope somehow took root in his mind that it would rise to greatness again through me. The astrologers had fostered that hope within him. As if to fulfill their predictions, though he had four sons, I alone was his only grandson during his final days.

“When the Emperor was on his deathbed, he called me close, placed his hand on my head, and wept tears of longing. ‘My child! After me, your elder uncle Kandaradithar will ascend the throne. After him, this Chola kingdom will come to you. It is in your time that the Chola dynasty will regain its former glory,’ he said to me many times.
“He told me that upholding the greatness of the Chola land must be the purpose of my life, and he took a solemn promise from me to that effect…

“The love my grandfather bore for me was matched only by the devotion I felt for him. Therefore, I resolved to bear his command upon my head and fulfill it. Yet, peace eluded my heart. What would become of the noblewoman of the Karaiyar clan, who had saved me from the jaws of the bear on that island surrounded by the sea? Could a mute girl of humble birth ever sit as queen upon the Chola throne? Would palace life suit her? Would the people of the land and the city not laugh at me?… Such thoughts often arose and disturbed my mind. And that was not all—my elder father, Kandaradithar, had, only a short while before, taken a second wife. You know well that the fortunate woman he married was a princess of the Mazhavarayar clan. If the first wife bore no children, what certainty was there that the second would remain childless? If my uncle were to have a son, how would the kingdom come to me? I had heard whispers of such doubts circulating in the kingdom even then. But it seems my great-hearted elder father wished that no such suspicion should arise in anyone’s mind. After Paranthaka Chakaravarthi passed away, Kandaradithar’s coronation was held. At the same time, my uncle—the new emperor—arranged for my own coronation as Crown Prince…

“My beloved daughter! Today, the people of this land cherish your brother Arulmozhi with boundless affection; in those days, they had such love and pride for me. While the coronation was taking place within the palace, outside… Thousands of people waited eagerly. Everyone wished that the newly crowned Emperor and the Crown Prince would appear together before the people. Just as they desired, Periyappa and I came out onto the terrace of the palace’s upper storey. Below us was a veritable ocean of humanity. So many faces bloomed and shone with joy. The moment they saw us, the entire multitude erupted in jubilant cheers. So many thousands of people were rejoicing at my investiture as Crown Prince—when that is so, what sense is there in us worrying about a mute girl living on some unseen island in the heart of a forest? Is the happiness of this multitude more important? Or is the life of a single mute girl more important?…

Thinking thus, I gazed out, taking in each of those radiant faces turned up towards us. Among that crowd stood men and women, elders and youth, boys and girls. All appeared united in their joy. Yet suddenly, one face—a woman’s face, a face brimming with sorrow, eyes filled with tears looking at me with deep pity—caught my attention. In the midst of that vast crowd, I do not know how that one face drew my gaze and focus. After that, my eyes could not move away; my attention would not shift. That face seemed to grow larger and larger, as if it were coming closer to me. In the end, the entire throng disappeared, those standing near me vanished, the ceremonial gateway faded, the fort walls of Thanjai dissolved, sky and earth were gone—only that one face, like the cosmic form of Goddess Parameswari, appeared before my eyes. My head spun; my legs lost their strength; my senses failed me…

Later, I learned that I had fainted and collapsed, and those beside me had caught and supported me. Others thought I had simply become exhausted by the elaborate coronation ceremonies. They decided that it was enough for me to have appeared before the people and led me back inside the palace. When I regained my senses, I called my friend Aniruddha to me in private and told him what I had seen. I described the mute girl and ordered him to find her and bring her to me at any cost. Aniruddha searched every nook and corner of Thanjai city, but returned to say that no such mute girl could be found. He suggested it might have been a figment of my imagination. I grew angry with him and said, “If you cannot even do this favor for me, what sort of friend are you?” I told him to send men along the paths leading from the Thanjai fort towards the seashore and search there. Accordingly, people were sent in all directions. They searched all the way to the shore. Those who went to Kodikkarai heard that there was a mute girl living in the house of the lighthouse keeper there. They found her. It seems she appeared as though possessed by madness. All their efforts to communicate the matter to her through various gestures and signs were of no use. She flatly refused to come with them to Thanjavur. When they brought me this news, I was plunged into confusion, not knowing what to do next. For two days, I remained in that turmoil. Yet, I could not bring myself to forget her, however much I tried. Day and night, her memory haunted me. I could not sleep even for a moment at night.

Afterwards, I took Aniruddha with me and set out for Kodikkarai. I drove the horses as fast as they could possibly go. As I journeyed, my inner turmoil only grew. If I found that mute girl there, what was I to do with her? The thought of it left my mind in disarray. Should I take her to Thanjavur or Pazhaiyarai and declare, “She is my queen!”? When I imagined that, both my heart and body seemed to shrink away.

“My precious princess! In those days, I had gained an unwanted reputation for being unmatched in physical beauty. I never considered it a glory. Yet, others spoke of it ceaselessly. Though my grandfather’s name, ‘Paranthakan,’ was given to me, it was soon forgotten, and the name ‘Sundara Cholan’ became famous instead. I, who was thus praised by all, how could I bring a mute girl, ignorant of all civilization, into the palace? If not, what else could I do with her?—Tormented by such thoughts, I reached Kodikkarai. That Maharani made things easy for me. The news I learned there left me utterly stunned.

The day after our messengers had returned, that girl had climbed to the top of the lighthouse. It was a new moon night; the wind was blowing fiercely. The sea was surging, raging around the lighthouse. The girl stood for some time, gazing at the tumultuous waves. Since it was her habit to stand thus, no one paid much attention. Suddenly, above the roar of the sea, a sound—‘weel’—was heard. After that, she was nowhere to be seen! A couple of people saw a woman’s form plunge headlong from the top of the lighthouse into the sea. Boats were sent out, and they searched as much as they could, but it was of no use. The raging sea had swallowed that girl—this was the only conclusion to be drawn.

“When I heard this news, a pain like being stabbed with a spear pierced my heart, and a deep sorrow overcame me. Yet, after a while, a certain peace settled upon me. The question of what to do with her no longer remained. There was no need to torment my mind with such thoughts anymore!...

“With this strange agony, mingled with both sorrow and peace, I returned to Thanjai. I immersed myself in affairs of state. I went to the battlefields. I married your mother. I begot brave sons. I was blessed to have you as my daughter…

“Yet, my child! I have not been able to completely forget that unfortunate soul who perished. At times, that dreadful vision—one I have never seen with my own eyes—would appear in my dreams and torment me. The image of a woman’s form, plunging headfirst from the summit of the lighthouse into the surging sea, would haunt both my dreams and my waking thoughts. Whenever that terrifying vision appeared in my sleep, I would wake up in a panic, crying out. Those sleeping beside me would ask, ‘What is it? What happened?’ Your mother has asked me countless times. But I have never spoken the truth. Sometimes I would say, ‘It’s nothing.’ Or I would conjure up some horror from the battlefield as an excuse. In time, by the mercy of fate, that dreadful vision faded from my mind; she too faded from my memory. At least, I believed so until recently. But it seems the dead are more cruel than the living. My daughter! The spirit of Umai Nachiyar has not left me. For some time now, it has begun to appear again and torment me! My daughter! Do you believe that the dead can return…?”

Having spoken thus, Sundara Chozhar cast his gaze far into the distance, staring blankly. There was nothing in the direction he looked! Yet Kundavai saw his body tremble. An infinite compassion welled up in her for him. Tears brimmed in her eyes. Pressing her face against her father’s chest, she wept. It seemed that her embrace lessened his trembling.

Then, raising her head to look at her father, she said, “Appa! You have borne this terrible agony in your heart for so many years, suffering in silence. That is why your body has become so frail. But now you have told me everything, haven’t you? From now on, your health will surely improve.”
Sundara Chozhar heard her words, and in the sound of his laughter, pain and disbelief mingled together. He said:

“Kundavai! You do not believe. You do not believe the dead can return. But look—right there, beside that pillar, behind the oil lamp, the spirit of that unfortunate woman stood at midnight last night. I saw it with my own eyes. How can I not believe? If what I saw was mere illusion, then what about your friend— “Will you tell me? She fainted only because she saw something and asked about it! Bring her here, Kundavai! I will ask her myself and find out!” Sundara Chozhar said anxiously.

“Father! Vanathi is a timid girl! I do not know how she was born into the valiant Kodumbalur Velir clan. Even if she sees a pillar in the dark, she will scream, beat her chest, and faint. There is no use in asking her. She would not have seen anything; nor would she have heard anything.”

“Is that so? Let her be, then. Listen to what I have yet to say! For a long time, I too did not believe that the dead could return. I thought such visions were nothing but the vain delusions of my mind. Do you remember when we were all traveling by boat on the Kaveri river, and little Arulmozhi suddenly went missing? While we all stood there, stunned and distraught, a queenly woman lifted the child from the floodwaters of the Ponni and handed him to us. The moment the child was taken, she vanished. We have spoken of this many times; you cannot have forgotten. All of you concluded that it was Kaveri Amman herself who saved the child. But do you know what I saw? That fisherwoman—the mute one—she was the one who handed over the child. Do you remember that I fainted that day? Everyone thought I lost consciousness because of the danger that had befallen the child. But that was not the truth. After all these years, I am telling you now: I fainted because I felt that the woman who handed over the child was not of flesh and blood, but the spirit of that mute girl…

“Daughter! Do you remember the day your brother was crowned prince? After the coronation, Aditya Karikalan came to the women’s quarters to receive the blessings of the elders. I came in after him. In the midst of the women, I saw the spirit of that same mute girl staring at Karikalan with a terrible, piercing gaze. Once again, I lost my senses. Later, when I thought about it, I began to doubt that incident. Why should she look at Karikalan with such cruelty? Perhaps it was just another illusion of my mind. But, my child! Since I have come to Thanjai this time, all those doubts have vanished. In her lifetime, I could read her heart by looking at her face; by watching the movement of her lips, I could understand what she wished to say— “I will find out what it is! I have regained that power, Kundavai! Four or five times, in the dead of night, she has appeared before me and warned me.

‘You killed me! I forgive you for that. But do not sin again! Do not give the kingdom that belongs to one man to another!’—I understood her words. It was as clear to me as if she had spoken aloud with her own mouth. Daughter! You must help me to fulfill this. This cursed kingdom—this Chola throne—my sons do not need it! Let us give it to Madurantakan…”

At that moment, Kundavai interrupted, “Father! What are you saying? Why is there any need now to change something that the entire land and city have already accepted and settled? Even if you change it, will the world accept it?”

“What does it matter whether the world accepts it or not? My duty is to act according to what is right. From the time I was crowned as the prince, and later as emperor of this Chola kingdom, my heart has never been at peace. My conscience has tormented me. It was not right that I, the son of the younger queen, ascended the throne while the elder queen’s son was still alive. Today, I am reaping the fruits of that sin. Why should my sons also be subject to such a sin? Aditya does not want this kingdom; nor does Arulmozhi. Nor do they want the curse that comes with it. While I am still alive, Madurantakan must be crowned. After that, I will go and live in peace in the golden palace that Aditya built in Kanchi…”
“Father! Should not Periya Piratti agree to this?”

“Daughter! That is why I seek your help. By any means, persuade my elder aunt to come here. Ah! Why does that wise old lady, who knows so much, not understand this moral law? Why did she urge me to commit this sin? Or is it only because it concerns her own child that she is so angry? Why is she so obstinate in this matter, which goes against the very nature of a mother? When Madurantakan was intent on renouncing the world and becoming a sanyasi in his devotion to Shiva, there was reason for it. But now, when he himself desires to rule the kingdom, how can we crown another?”
“Father! He may desire to rule; but should he not also be worthy of it?”
“Why is he not qualified? How could the son born to the great Kandaradithar and the wise daughter of Mazhavarayar lack any qualification?”
“Let him have the qualifications; but shouldn’t the people of the kingdom also consent to it?”

“If you were to ask the people’s opinion, they would immediately crown your younger brother. Is that fair? Would Arulmozhi himself agree to that?… All that is pointless speculation, my daughter! Somehow, make sure your elder grandmother comes here at once! Write to her that I am battling with Yama himself; tell her that if she wishes to see me alive, she must set out immediately…”

“That is not necessary, Father! The Periya Piratti has long wished to oversee the renovation of the Thalikulathar temple in Thanjavur. I shall write to her, mentioning that, and ask her to come at this time. Until then, please be patient and do not distress yourself, Father!”

Thus speaking, Kundavai took leave of her father and returned to her quarters. On the way, she met her mother, Vanamadevi. “Mother! From now on, do not leave my father’s side even for a moment! Let others perform the rituals that need to be done!” she said.

The doubts that had been troubling Kundavai’s heart for some time now began to clear a little. In the darkness that had clouded her mind, a faint light began to appear. Her keen intelligence now fully realized that some dreadful web of sorcery and conspiracy was being spun against her father and brothers. Yet she could not discern the full nature of the plot, nor how and by whom it was being carried out. She understood that a great danger threatened the Chola empire and the rights her brothers held to that throne. She believed, too, that the responsibility to protect them from that peril now rested upon her, a woman.

chapters.title: Which Betrayal is the Worst?
paragraphs: Those who have studied the history of ancient Tamil Nadu know well that, in those days, many women stood at the forefront of social life. Queens born into royal families were held in the highest esteem. Women born into the Chola dynasty, as well as those who had married into it, possessed property rights of their own. Each of them owned, in her own name, villages, fertile and dry lands, and herds of cattle. It is important to note how these women made use of their possessions. Many used their wealth to sponsor various religious services in temples under their own names. Lighting sacred lamps, weaving garlands for the deity, providing food for wandering ascetics and devotees of Shiva—numerous royal women endowed such charitable acts, ensuring they were inscribed in stone or copperplate grants.

While it was common practice in those days for palace women to undertake temple services, Princess Kundavai, the beloved daughter of Sundara Chola, chose to use her wealth for a different kind of charity. Perhaps it was out of compassion for her ailing father, or for some other reason, but a fervent desire arose in her heart to establish charitable hospitals throughout the land. We have already seen that an infirmary had been founded at Pazhaiyarai in the name of Emperor Parantaka. In the same manner, Kundavai Devi had made arrangements to establish a hospital in Thanjavur, bearing her father's name. On this Vijayadasami day, preparations had been made to inaugurate the hospital and to issue the necessary grants and charters.

In Purampadi, outside the Thanjavur fort, in the Garuda Mandapam opposite the Perumal temple, the inaugural ceremony of the Sundara Chola Hospital took place. Since Lord Vishnu is the presiding deity, and Garuda is the one who brought the nectar of immortality, Kundavai chose the Garuda Mandapam adjacent to the Vishnu temple as the site for the hospital’s founding. For this grand occasion, the people of Thanjavur city and the surrounding villages had gathered in countless numbers. Men, women, and children, adorned in festive garments and ornaments, thronged the place in joyous celebration. The ministers of the Chola emperor’s council, high and low officials, sculptors who inscribed the stone edicts, Viswakarma artisans who wrote the copperplate grants, and numerous palace attendants had all assembled in great numbers. The air resounded with the beating of drums and the music of... The Velakkara soldiers advanced, their drums resounding so thunderously that all eight directions seemed to tremble. The guards of the Thanjai fort came, spinning their swords and spears, making a clamor of “tanar, tanar” as they marched. The two Pazhuvettarayar brothers arrived in majestic splendor, mounted atop their elephants. Prince Madurantaka Devar, astride a white horse, struggled awkwardly, unable to sit properly, and joined the procession in discomfort. Princess Kundavai, her companions, and several elderly women of the palace came in procession, seated in their palanquins. From another direction, the ivory palanquin bearing the palm insignia of the young queen of Pazhuvoor, Nandini, arrived.

In the area adorned with a blue silk canopy, arranged especially for the palace women, Kundavai Devi, the Queen of Pazhuvoor, and the other ladies took their seats. Then, at a signal from the elder Pazhuvettarayar, the festivities commenced. First, two Oduvamoorthis sang the Thevaram hymn, “Mandiramaavadhu Neeru.” Accompanied by the harmonious strains of the yāzh and the maddalam, their voices blended so sweetly that the people were utterly enraptured. A profound silence prevailed over the vast gathering.

But in the section where the palace women were seated, a soft conversation arose between two voices. The young queen of Pazhuvoor, Nandini, drew close to Kundavai and asked, “Devi! Once, did not Sambandar Peruman sing this very hymn, apply the sacred ash, and cure the Pandya king’s illness? Why does this song lack such power now? Not only has the hymn lost its power, but even the sacred ash seems to have lost its potency. In these times, nothing can be accomplished without medicine, herbs, physicians, and hospitals—why is that so?”

“Yes, Rani! In those days, dharma reigned supreme in the world. That is why the sacred ash, empowered by mantra, possessed such strength. Now, sin has overrun the world. Traitors who plot against the king have arisen in the land. Have we ever heard of such things before? That is why the power of mantra has waned, and medicine has become necessary!” replied the young princess, gazing intently at the face of the young queen of Pazhuvoor.
Nandini’s expression betrayed no change. “Is that so? Are there truly traitors plotting against the king in these times? Who are they?” she asked, her tone carefully measured.

“That, I do not know either. Some name one person; others, someone else. I think I shall remain here a few more days to discover the truth. How can one know the ways of the world while staying in Pazhaiyarai?” said Kundavai.

“You have made a wise decision. If you ask me, it would be best for you to stay here. Otherwise, the kingdom will be reduced to rubble. I too will help you as much as I can. There is a guest in our house. He might also be able to assist you!” she said.
“Who is this guest?” asked Kundavai.

“Kandanmaran, the son of Sambuvaraiyar of Kadambur. Have you seen him? He is tall as a coconut tree and always restless. He keeps rambling on, calling someone a ‘spy’ and a ‘traitor’ without end. Just now you spoke of treason against the throne, didn’t you? Can you tell me if there is a treachery greater than treason against the crown?”
“I can tell you very well. If a woman betrays the man whose hand she has taken in marriage, that is a treachery far worse than treason against the throne!”
Having said this, Kundavai Devi looked intently at Nandini’s face. But the change she expected did not occur. The same enchanting smile lingered on Nandini’s lips as before.

“What you say is quite true; but Kandanmaran will not agree. He says, ‘Of all betrayals, the worst is the betrayal of friendship.’ Not only did the one he considered his dearest friend turn into a spy, but he also stabbed him in the back and fled. Since then, Kandanmaran has been raving like this!”
“Who is he? Who committed such a despicable act?”
“Someone called Vandiyathevan! He belongs to the ancient Vanar clan that once ruled at Thiruvallam in Thondai Nadu. Have you heard of him?”
Kundavai bit her coral-red lips with her pearl-like teeth.
“It seems I have heard of him… What happened afterwards?”
“What else? After stabbing Kandanmaran in the back, his friend ran away. I hear that my brother-in-law has sent men to capture that spy and bring him back!”
“How can you be sure he is a spy?”
“Whether he is a spy or not, how would I know? I am only repeating what Sambuvaraiyar’s son says. If you wish, you can ask him directly and learn all the details.”
“Yes; I too must see the son of Sambuvaraiyar. I heard that his survival was nothing short of a rebirth. Has he been staying at the Pazhuvur palace ever since?”
“Yes; the morning after he was wounded, they brought him to our palace. The responsibility of treating his wounds fell upon me. Slowly, he began to recover; but the wound has not yet fully healed!”

“It is surprising that, even with your care, he has not completely recovered. Never mind, Queen! I will certainly come and see him. Was the Sambuvaraiyar clan established only yesterday or the day before? Is it not a lineage renowned for valor since the time of Paranthaka Chakaravarthi?”
“That is precisely why I said so. Even if it is only under the pretext of seeing Kandhan Maran, will you not grace our humble palace with your presence?” said Nandini.

By then, the Devaram hymn had ended, and the reading of the royal edict had begun. First, the letter from Sundara Chola Chakaravarthi was read aloud. “Since our beloved daughter, Princess Kundavai, has graciously agreed to donate the entire income from the village of Nallur Mangalam, which we had granted her as a tax-free endowment, to the Tanjai Purampadi hospital, we hereby declare all the fertile lands of that village to be free of taxes,” the emperor had stated in that palm-leaf edict. After the chief priest read it out, he handed it to Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar, who received it with both hands, pressed it to his eyes, and then gave it to the accountant, instructing him to record it in the accounts.

Next, the copper-plate grant of Princess Kundavai was read. It was inscribed on black stone that the aforementioned tax-free lands of the village would be enjoyed by the farmers with all rights, and that every year, two hundred kalams of paddy, as well as fifty measures of fresh cow’s milk, five measures of goat’s milk, and one hundred tender coconuts were to be sent daily for the patients receiving treatment at the Thanjavur Sundara Chola hospital. The name of the donor and the names of the officials who had supervised the inscription were also meticulously carved on the stone.

After reading the copper-plate grant, it was handed over to the leaders of Nallur Mangalam village, who had come for this ceremony. The village leaders received the inscribed stone with reverence and placed it on the elephant standing nearby.

At that moment, a resounding cheer of “Long live Maduraikonda Koiraajakesari Sundara Chola Chakaravarthi!” arose from thousands of voices, echoing in all directions. Competing with that thunderous acclaim, the booming of a hundred temple drums filled the sky. Then, in due order, “Long live the young princess Kundavai Devi!”

“Long live Aditya Karikalan, the bravest of the brave, who beheaded Veerapandiyan!” “Long live Prince Arulmozhivarman, conqueror of Eezham!” “Long live Madurantaka Devar, ascetic son of Sivagnana Kandaradithar!”
Such cries and counter-cries arose from the crowd.

At last, when the shouts of “Long live the Treasurer, Chief of the Granary, Lord of Destiny, the great Pazhuvettarayar!” and “Long live Kaalandhakandar, Commander of the Tanjore Fort, the younger Pazhuvettarayar!” rang out, the volume of the cheers diminished greatly. Except for the warriors of Pazhuvur, few among the assembled people joined in those acclamations.

At that moment, Princess Kundavai tried in vain to catch a glimpse of the face of the younger queen of Pazhuvur. Especially when the cheers for Aditya Karikalan resounded, had she seen Nandini’s face then, even the iron-hearted young princess would have been deeply shaken—of that, there could be no doubt.

chapters.title: "The Spy is Caught!"
paragraphs: The events of that day had left Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar seething with irritation. Had it not become an occasion for the people to openly display the trust they held in the Emperor and his family? “People! Mere people! Mindless sheep and cattle! If four men take one path, four thousand will follow behind them! How many among them know to use their own judgment?” he muttered to himself again and again, trying to contain his anger.

“It seems the Emperor will ruin the empire before he departs for heaven! ‘Waive the taxes for this town!’ ‘Make that village a tax-free settlement!’—he keeps issuing such orders! Soon, there won’t be a single village left to pay taxes. Yet, for the battlefield, money for expenses and grain for food must continue to be sent. From where are we to send them?” he lamented, his voice rising in anguish, so much so that even his servants grew a little fearful.
“Anna! What is the use of making such a commotion? We must wait for the right time and act then!” Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar had to counsel him to patience.

When he learned that Kundavai was coming to the palace, the elder’s irritation knew no bounds. He went to Nandini and asked, “What is this I hear? Why should that wretch come here? Did you invite her? Have you forgotten all the insults she heaped upon you?”
“I do not forget the good someone has done me, nor do I forget the harm another has caused me. Do you not yet know this nature of mine?” replied Nandini.
“Then why is she coming here?”
“It is her wish—she is coming! She comes with the pride of being the Emperor’s daughter!”
“Why did you invite her?”

“I did not invite her; she invited herself. She said, ‘Is not the son of Sambuvaraiyar staying in your house? I wish to see him!’ Could I say, ‘Do not come’? The day will come when I can say so. Until then, I must bear all insults in silence.”
“I cannot bear it any longer. I cannot remain in this palace when she arrives. I cannot even stay in this city. There is some business to attend to in Mazhapadi. I shall go and return.”

“Do as you wish, my lord! I was about to suggest it myself. Leave that venomous serpent to me. I know well how to draw out her poison. When you return, if you happen to hear some astonishing news, do not be surprised…”
“What sort of astonishing news?”
“You may hear that Princess Kundavai is to wed Kandanmaran, or that Aditya Karikalan is to marry Kandanmaran’s sister…”
“Heavens! What are you saying? If such things come to pass, what will become of all our plans?”

“Just because there is talk, does it mean the deed will be done? You go about telling your friends that Madurantaka Devar will be crowned next, do you not? Do you truly believe that will happen? Are we to endure all this hardship only to see the timid, bashful Madurantakan crowned king?” said Nandini, fixing her dark, piercing eyes upon Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar. Unable to withstand the force of that gaze, the old warrior bowed his head, took her hand, pressed it to his eyes, and said, “My beloved! The day is not far when you will ascend the throne of the Chola Empire as its Empress!”

From the moment Kandanmaran learned that Princess Kundavai herself was coming to see him, he had been in a state of restless agitation. Was not the whole land aware of Kundavai’s wisdom, beauty, and other noble qualities? What a great honor it was that such a princess was coming to visit him! For this, he would gladly have suffered many more wounds and lain ill for even longer. Ah! Would it not have been far more glorious if he had received such wounds upon his chest in the battlefield and lain stricken there? If, at that moment, Princess Kundavai had come to see him, what an honor it would have been! Instead, now he must recount to her, as to so many others, the tale of a friend’s treachery.

From time to time, the memory of his secret involvement in plots against the royal family of that noble princess pricked his conscience and troubled him. Kandanmaran was an upright youth, unversed in cunning schemes and devious intrigues.

Even though Nandini’s enchanting beauty had intoxicated him, he had built a fortress around his heart with the thought that she was another man’s wife. But Princess Kundavai was unmarried. How should he conduct himself with her? How should he speak? Could he speak sweetly while harboring deceit in his heart? Or would he, overcome by her beauty, falter in his resolve and abandon his oath? He must never allow even a single day for such a thing to happen… Ah! Why should the princess come here to see him? Let her come! Let her come! He could speak harshly and send her away, so that she would never return.

But the moment Kandanmaran saw Princess Kundavai, all these resolutions melted away and vanished without a trace. Her enchanting form, the radiance of her face, her nobility, her restraint, and the sweetness brimming in her compassionate words made Kandanmaran lose all self-control. His imagination surged and overflowed. He acted as if he did not wish to boast of his own greatness, yet at the same time, he spoke of his heroic deeds as though compelled by her insistence. He displayed his shoulders and chest, and the wounds he had received on the battlefield, as if reluctant to show them, yet unable to resist.

“That treacherous friend Vandiyathevan—if he had stabbed me in the chest and killed me, I would not have minded. But it pains me that he stabbed me in the back and fled. That is why I am compelled to speak of his betrayal. Otherwise, would it not be a disgrace to have turned my back in battle? If he had wounded my shoulder or chest, I would have forgiven him!” Kandanmaran spoke with such emotion that Kundavai found it utterly convincing. Doubt crept into her mind—could Vandiyathevan have truly done such a thing? Had she been deceived about him? When she asked for a detailed account of what had happened, Kandanmaran narrated the events. That day, his imagination soared to such heights that even Nandini would have been astonished.

“Look, Devi! He deceived me the very day he stayed at Kadambur. He did not tell me what business took him to Thanjavur. He came here and, showing some false token, gained entry. He even went and saw the Emperor. He claimed to have brought a letter from Aditya Karikalan. Was that all? He even involved your name, saying he had brought a letter for you as well. That made the commander of the fort suspicious. He suspected that Vandiyathevan might be a spy and ordered him to be kept under guard. Somehow, he managed to escape. In that, I must admit, his cleverness is admirable. When I heard these things, I could not believe that my friend had become the enemy’s spy. There are some twists in his character. He must have done something reckless…” I believed. “Somehow, I will find him and bring him back. You must forgive him,” I said, making this condition with the commander of the fort before I set out. In the dead of night, I walked along the banks of the Vadavāru that encircled the fort. I did not wish to take anyone with me and thus humiliate my friend. If he had escaped from the fort, surely he must have left by climbing over the walls, must he not? Even if he had already gotten out, he would have hidden somewhere in the nearby woods. So I went along the Vadavāru’s edge.

In the dim moonlight, I saw a man climbing down the sheer wall of the fort. I immediately went and stood there. As soon as he landed, I said, “Friend! What is this you are doing?” That wretch at once struck me in the chest. What could his blow do to my chest, which even elephants could not crush? Still, I could not bear that he, whom I had sought with good intentions, struck me. I too struck back. The two of us wrestled fiercely. In half a nāzhigai, he lost his strength and became subdued. I said to him, “Tell me truthfully why you have come! I will forgive you and help you as you wish!”

He said, “I am tired, let me sit somewhere and I will tell you.” I agreed and led him away, guiding the way ahead. Suddenly, that sinner stabbed me in the back with a knife. The blade went in half a span deep. My head spun; I fell to the ground. That traitor to friendship escaped and ran away! When I regained consciousness and opened my eyes, I found myself in the house of a mute woman…”
Hearing Kandanmaran’s tale, Nandini laughed inwardly. She could not decide how much of it Kundavai Devi would believe.
“How did you end up in the mute woman’s house? Who brought you there?” she asked.

“That is the mystery I cannot unravel. That mute woman knows nothing. Even if she does, she cannot speak. She has a son, it seems. But from that day, he too has vanished. No one knows how he disappeared so mysteriously. If he returns, perhaps I can ask him. Otherwise, I must wait until the Pazhuvur warriors capture my friend…”
“Do you think he will be caught?” she asked.

“How can he escape without being caught? He cannot fly away with wings, can he? That is why I am waiting here, to see him. Otherwise, I would have gone to my village. I still have hope that I can obtain forgiveness for him from the lords of Pazhuvur.”
“Sir! Your magnanimity is true greatness!” said the young princess.
In her heart, she thought, “Vandiyathevan must not be caught—even if he is a traitor, so be it!”
At that moment, an old palace nurse came running in, shouting, “Amma! The spy has been caught! They are bringing him here!”
On the faces of both Nandini and Kundavai, anguish and distress could be seen; but Nandini quickly masked her feelings. Kundavai, however, could not do so.

chapters.title: Two Tigresses
paragraphs: The moment the nurse came running in with the news that the spy had been captured, bound, and was being brought through the streets, the hearts of all three present were seized with agitation. Kundavai’s heart fluttered the most.
“Devi! Shall we go and see what that mischievous spy looks like?” asked Nandini.
With hesitation, Kundavai replied, “What is it to us, about him?”
“In that case, very well!” Nandini said carelessly.
“I’ll go and take a look,” Kandanmaran said, stumbling as he tried to rise.
“No need; you can’t walk yet, you’ll fall!” Nandini said.
As if she had changed her mind, Kundavai said, “Since he is your dear friend, shouldn’t we too see what he looks like? Won’t we be able to see from the upper terrace of the palace?”
“We’ll see very well; come with me!” said Nandini, rising and walking ahead.
“Devi! If he is indeed my friend, I must speak to my uncle and arrange to meet him!” said Kandanmaran.
“How are we to know if he is truly your friend?” Nandini asked.
“In that case, I will come along too, no matter what!” Kandanmaran declared, stumbling after them.

The three of them went to the front façade of the palace’s upper terrace. At a short distance, seven or eight horses were approaching. On them rode warriors armed with spears. In their midst, a man walked, his hands tied behind his back with rope. The two ends of the rope were held by horsemen on either side. A little behind the soldiers, a crowd had gathered to watch the spectacle.
From the palace terrace, those watching could not at first see the face of the man walking between the horses.

Until the procession drew near, silence reigned on that upper terrace of the palace. Kundavai’s heart was a tumult of longing and anxiety, her tear-brimming eyes fixed upon the approaching procession.
Nandini, meanwhile, kept glancing down the street, then immediately turning to watch Kundavai’s face.
Kandanmaran broke the silence that had settled over them.
“No; that is not Vandiyathevan!” he declared.
Kundavai’s face blossomed with relief.
At that moment, the strange procession had reached the base of the palace balcony.
The man being led, bound with ropes and surrounded by horsemen, looked up in bewilderment. Kundavai recognized him as the physician’s son.
Suppressing her joy, Kundavai said, “What madness is this? Why are they dragging him here? Is he not the son of the Pazhaiyarai physician?”
The man who had looked up seemed about to speak, his mouth opening as if to say something. But before he could utter a word, the rope binding him was tugged forward, pulling him along.
“Oh! Is that so? My brother-in-law’s men are always like this. They let the real culprit go and bring in someone else to trouble us!” said Nandini.
Meanwhile, Kandanmaran said, “Would Vandiyathevan be caught so easily by these people? My friend is a great Indrajit! The man who fooled even me—would he fall into their hands?”
“Still you call him your friend!” Nandini remarked.
“He may have turned traitor, but my affection for him has not changed,” replied Kandanmaran.

“Perhaps these men have already killed your handsome friend. I heard that two spies were pursued by these soldiers all the way to Kodikkarai,” Nandini said, and then turned her gaze upon Kundavai’s face.

The word “might have killed” made Kundavai’s heart flutter, and Nandini noticed it. Ah, arrogant woman! Now I have found a fine weapon to take revenge on you! If I do not use it at the right moment, I am not the Young Queen of Pazhuvoor! Wait! Just wait!

Kundavai transformed her inner turmoil into anger and said, “Spies! Mere foolishness! As time passes, these old men seem to lose their wits! They suspect everyone they see! Was it not I who sent this physician’s son to Kodikkarai to fetch herbs? Why have they arrested him? I shall go at once and ask your husband myself!”
“Oh! So he is the one you sent? Devi, you spoke of suspicion—now I too have a doubt. Did you send him alone to fetch the herbs? Or did you send another along with him?” asked Nandini.
“I sent another with him. Of the two, I told one to go to the island of Lanka.”
“Aha! Now I understand everything! It has happened just as I suspected!”
“I understand nothing. What did you suspect? What has happened?”
“There is no more doubt now; it is certain, Devi! The man you sent with him—was he someone you already knew? Or a new person?”
Kundavai hesitated a little. “A new person? An old one? He was the one who brought a letter from Kanchipuram; he came from my brother.”
“That’s him! That’s the one!”
“Who is the one?”
“He is the spy! Here too, he claimed to have brought a letter from the Emperor…”
“For what reason did they suspect him to be a spy?”

“How would I know about that? That’s men’s business! But it seems that spy behaved suspiciously enough. Otherwise, why should he escape secretly in the middle of the night? Why should he stab this good man in the back before running away?”
“I do not believe that he was the one who stabbed this man in the back. If he had stabbed him, why would he have carried him back and left him at that mute woman’s house?”

“You speak as if you had witnessed it yourself, Devi! It seems you have a strange compassion for that spy. He must possess some magical power. Even he here still calls him his friend, does he not? But what does it matter? A lost life cannot be brought back. If these warriors had killed him…”

Sweat beaded on Kundavai’s brow. Her eyes reddened. Her throat tightened, and her heart pounded violently within her chest. “That could never have happened! It will never happen, not for a single day,” she told herself inwardly.
“If, as he says, that spy is such a cunning fellow…” she began.
“Yes, Princess! Vandiyathevan would never allow himself to be caught by these men, not for a single day!” said Kandhamaaran.
“If not today, then another day he will be caught!” said Nandini.
Kundavai clenched her teeth and said, “Who knows what tomorrow may bring?”

Then, with rising anger, she continued, “Even if the Emperor is bedridden with illness, let him be! The whole kingdom has been turned upside down! What right do these men have to detain those whom I sent to fetch medicine? I shall go and ask my father about this myself.”

“Devi! Why trouble the Emperor, who is already weakened by illness, with this matter? Why not ask my husband instead? Perhaps he is unaware of your wishes. If you inform him, he will act accordingly. Who in this Chola kingdom would dare to act against the wishes of the Younger Princess?” said Nandini.

In the battle that took place that day between those two tigresses, it was Nandini who emerged victorious. Many wounds were inflicted upon Kundavai’s heart. The princess had to make a great effort to conceal them from the world.

chapters.title: The Underground Prison
paragraphs: There is nothing in this world as mysterious and unfathomable as life itself. Who can say how happiness arrives, or how sorrow descends? For ages, the sky has shone, unblemished and serene. Then, all of a sudden, dark clouds gather; every direction is shrouded in darkness, thunder roars, lightning flashes, and rain pours down in torrents. Sometimes, it seems as if wind itself has vanished from the world. Even the leaves of the trees stand motionless. Then, from somewhere, a whirlwind arises and sweeps through with fury. In its wake, mighty trees are uprooted and topple to the ground. The lush green groves that just moments before stretched skyward in tranquil beauty are now transformed into a devastated forest, as if Hanuman himself had laid waste to Ashokavana.

Such a whirlwind was now raging through Kundavai’s life. Until recently, she had not known the meaning of worry. Life had been an unbroken festival of joy. Love and affection, dance and song, poetry and painting, jewels and adornments, pleasure gardens and graceful boats—these were what she believed life to be, as her days passed in delight. Her father, her mothers, her elder brother, her younger brother, ministers, teachers, nurses, and friends—all regarded the young princess as the very apple of their eye. Sorrow was something she knew only as a creation of poetry and drama, a thing of imagination.

But when suffering finally came to this fortunate one, it struck her again and again without respite. Her father’s condition was a cause for grave concern. The kingdom itself was beset by great trials. Her brothers were far away in distant lands. Astrologers and soothsayers spoke in riddles, foretelling some great calamity about to befall the Chola dynasty. Secret conspiracies were brewing in the land. The people were plunged into an unnamed, pervasive fear.

Born into a lineage of warriors with hearts of diamond, Kundavai possessed the courage to face all this with valor. She had a steadfast faith that, with her sharp intellect, she could overcome any danger threatening her family or her kingdom. Yet, a small incident in her life—an unexpected encounter—had softened her diamond heart and shaken her courage. When Kundavai met Vandiyathevan, the lotus of her heart, which until then had remained a closed bud, blossomed open. But what misfortune! At that very moment, a black beetle crept into the heart of that flower and, stinging it with its venom, caused its delicate petals to fall! Alas! What agony! How much pain did the thought that the valiant scion of the Vanara clan might be imprisoned somewhere bring her? How cruelly did the dreadful words that he might have been killed rend her heart? How hard she had to struggle to keep such torment from showing on her face! Though she had parents, kin, siblings, and dearest friends—so many loved ones—why did her heart flutter so for someone who was a mere traveler passing by, someone she had met only two or three times by chance? Why should her heart beat so wildly for him?

There was no time now to ponder all this, to weigh cause and effect, or to reach any conclusion. Without waiting for an auspicious hour, without heeding omens or portents, what needed to be investigated must be investigated at once, and what needed to be done must be done without delay…

And so, that very afternoon, the young princess sent word that she would visit the palace of the Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar and departed. The women of that palace welcomed the princess with eager hearts, showering her with affection and attending to her every need. After conversing amiably with them for a while, the princess made her way to the picture gallery. There, the Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar awaited her arrival and, upon greeting her, began to explain the paintings that adorned the gallery walls. Kundavai listened and observed with polite attention.
When they reached the last painting, Kundavai turned to Kalantaka Kandar and said, “Sir! The Pazhuvettaraiyars, through generations, have rendered incomparable service to the Chola dynasty!”
“Lady! That is our good fortune,” replied Kalantaka Kandar.
“There is no doubt that this Chola Empire alone is worthy recompense for all that service…”
“Mother! What is the meaning of these words?”
“Still, can you not wait until the emperor’s life comes to its natural end and he attains the seat of Kailasa? Is there such need to hurry in seizing the powers of the empire?”
These words struck Kalantaka Kandar’s heart like sharp arrows, as his face betrayed. Beads of sweat broke out on his brow. His moustache quivered; his hands and feet trembled.
Kaalandhaka Kandhar wiped the sweat from his brow and looked at Kundavai.
“Lady! Why this much fury? Are you truly intending to send me to the realm of Yama just by your words...?” he asked.
“Sir! You know well that I do not possess such power. Even Yama himself would fear to approach Kaalandhakar; how could a foolish girl like me accomplish such a thing?”
“Princess! Rather than uttering such cruel words, you might as well pour molten lead into my ears! What wrong have I committed that the goddess should show me such mercilessness?”
“Who am I to speak of your faults? It is you who must tell me what wrong I have done. Was it a mistake on my part to send someone to fetch herbs to cure my father’s illness?”
“No, Princess, that could never be a mistake.”
“Do you know that I sent the son of the Pazhayarai physician to Kodikkarai to bring back those herbs?”
“I know, Princess!”
“Today, I saw your horsemen dragging that physician’s son through the streets, bound with rope. Was it not you who gave the order? Did you arrange this knowing that it was I who sent him?”
“Yes, Princess! But perhaps you sent him without knowing that he was a spy?”
“The son of the Pazhayarai physician? A spy? Do you expect me to believe such a tale?”
“Lady! If he himself confessed, should we not believe it?”
The princess was startled for a moment. “He himself confessed? How is that? What did he confess to?” she asked.
“He confessed that another man who came with him was a spy. He admitted that this other man did not truly set out in search of herbs, but instead carried a letter to someone in Lanka...”
“He is a great fool; he must have babbled something. I am the one who sent that other man with him as well. You know that, do you not?”
“I know, Mother! But I also know that man has deceived you. That youth named Vandiyathevan is, in truth, a spy…”
“That is not so at all! He is the one who brought the letter written by my brother from Kanchipuram.”
“Princess! He brought letters from both the Emperor and the Prince—so what? Spies must always find some means or other to carry out their work, must they not?”
“Sir! What proof do you have that Vandiyathevan is a spy?”
“If he were not a spy, why would he avoid the royal highway and take a secret path? Why would he go to the Kudanthai astrologer and inquire about the Emperor’s horoscope?”
“I too have asked the Kudanthai astrologer about the Emperor’s horoscope. What of it?”

“It is different when you, the Emperor’s own daughter, ask; but it is another matter entirely when some unrelated traveler inquires. Only if he were a spy for an enemy kingdom would he be so curious.”
“That is merely your suspicion. Do you have any other reason?”

“He could have openly sought my permission and entered the Tanjore fort. Why did he not do so? Why did he show the signet ring of Pazhuvoor and enter instead? Why did he lie, saying the great Pazhuvettaraiyar gave it to him?”
“Who, then, gave him the signet ring?”
“That is not yet known. It must be found out.”
“And what have your men done, failing to discover that?”
“Dear lady, my men are not magicians. Only by catching the spy and questioning him can we learn how the signet ring came into his possession.”
“What certainty is there that he will tell the truth?”

“There are ways to make him speak the truth. Mother! There is always the underground prison. The spy knows of this as well. That is why, once again, he vanished and escaped from the fort under cover of night.”
—Sambuvaraiyar
“He stabbed my son in the back and ran away!”
“What proof is there that he was the one who stabbed him?”
“Kandanmaran himself said so.”
“That is not enough! I say that he did not stab Kandanmaran!”
“Mother! Did you see it with your own eyes?”
“I did not. But I can tell by looking at a man’s face whether he is guilty or not.”
“That wretched spy is fortunate indeed. Somehow, he has managed to win your good opinion. Why has that fortune not come to me?”
“Sir! Why do you keep calling him a spy?”

“Mother! If he is not a spy, why did he enter Pazhaiyarai in disguise, wearing a mask with the actors? Why did he travel to the port of Kodikkarai in disguise? If he is not a spy, why did he hide in Kodikkarai all day as soon as he saw my men? Why did he board a boat at night and go to the island of Lanka?”
“Oh! Did he escape by boat as well? Could your men not catch him?”
“Yes, mother! That magician of a spy tricked my men and escaped. These fools let him go and instead caught the physician’s son and brought him here…”
“Sir! Let the spy go, whatever happens. I sent the physician’s son myself. I am certain he is innocent. He must be released at once.”
“Lady! Even if he is not a spy, he has been an accomplice to the spy. He must have deceived my men with some fabricated stories. He helped the spy to hide and to escape by boat…”
“Whatever it may be, the physician’s son must be set free.”

“I am not willing to take that responsibility. Dangers surround the land on all sides. Enemies are waiting to invade. The sworn avengers of Veera Pandiyan have vowed to destroy the Chola dynasty. Conspiracies are taking place everywhere…”
“Sir! If everyone who plots conspiracies is to be thrown into prison, there would be no room left in the cells!”
“As long as there is space, we can keep putting them in, can’t we?”
“At least leave some space for the true conspirators. Sir! Release the physician’s son at once!”
“I cannot take that responsibility upon myself, Lady!”
“If an order comes from the Emperor, will you obey it? Or will you ignore even that?”

“Princess, for this matter, the Emperor’s command is not necessary. The whole world knows that whatever the Young Princess desires is as good as a Vedic command to the Emperor. Here, I hand over the key to the underground prison to you. Go yourself and open the door to set him free. If you wish to release anyone else, feel free to do so. For any profit or loss that may result, the responsibility will be yours!…”

So saying, Kaalandhakandar took out a large key and handed it to her. Kundavai, suppressing the anger that surged within her, said, “Very well, sir! I accept full responsibility for any profit or loss!” and took the key.
“If any great harm befalls this Chola Empire, it will be because of two women,” said the Commander of the Thanjavur Fort.
“I am one; who is the other woman?”
“The younger queen of Pazhuvoor, Nandini Devi!”
Kundavai smiled and said, “You are equating me with the all-powerful authority of the Chola Empire? If this reaches the ears of the great Pazhuvetaraiyar, he will brand you a traitor to the nation!”
“That would be for the best! I am waiting for that,” said the younger Pazhuvetaraiyar.

chapters.title: Sendhan Amudhan in Captivity
paragraphs: Within the walls of Thanjai Fort, the royal mint where gold coins were cast was itself built like a small fortress. The outer security of the mint was as formidable as that at the main gates of Thanjai Fort. That evening, when Kundavai Devi and Vanathi went to visit the mint, the goldsmiths were just finishing their work and preparing to leave. The gatekeepers were ready to search the goldsmiths before letting them out. The goldsmiths gathered near the entrance.

At that moment, the royal chariot arrived and halted at the mint’s gate. Kundavai and Vanathi alighted. At the sight of them, both the guards and the goldsmiths forgot themselves and cried out, “Long live the young princess!” The head of the mint hurried forward and welcomed the royal maidens with great enthusiasm. He led them inside and showed them the blazing fire-pit where gold was melted, the molds used for minting coins, and the newly struck coins themselves.

That day’s freshly minted gold coins lay in heaps on one side. The gleam of that pure gold dazzled the eyes. On one side of each coin was stamped the seal of a tiger, and on the other, the seal of a ship.

“Do you see, Vanathi? For countless ages, gold from all corners of the world has flowed into this Chola land. It came by land, it came by sea.
