Until now, the responsibility of carrying all that gold has fallen upon the women of Chola Nadu. They bore it as ornaments, adorning themselves, unable to sleep for the weight they carried. But in recent times, that burden upon the women of Chola Nadu has begun to lessen. Our Lord of Tanjore, Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar, has arranged for dazzling gold coins like these to be minted!” said Kundavai.
“Akka! What convenience does this bring?” Vanathi asked.

“What convenience? Oh, you know nothing, girl! When gold is made into coins like this, it is easy to measure its value without having to weigh it each time. It is convenient for the people to pay taxes to the government. Merchants, when trading with foreigners, need not struggle to barter goods for goods. They can buy goods with gold coins; they can sell goods and receive gold coins in return. That is why the traders of Chola Nadu praise our Lord Pazhuvettaraiyar… Let me tell you one more thing. Listen!” Kundavai lowered her voice as she spoke. She said, “For those who plot against the Emperor and his family, these coins offer great convenience. Even the most virtuous men can be turned into traitors through these gold coins, can they not?”

The words Kundavai spoke last fell lightly upon the ears of the chief officer of the mint who stood nearby. That officer replied, “Yes, my lady! We hear of such dreadful rumors in these times. That is why, for some days now, the security around this mint has been greatly increased. The number of those coming to and going from the underground prison beneath has also grown!”
“There are those who come; but are there also those who leave?” Kundavai asked.
“Why not? That too happens. This very morning, someone was brought in. Barely an hour ago, he was taken away again!” said the officer.
“Who could that be?” Kundavai wondered, a trace of surprise in her voice.

They passed through the various work areas within the mint, then proceeded toward the back. There, in the rear wall, was a small door. They opened it and went through. The place they entered was dimly lit, the ceiling low. From all sides came a rumbling sound that would make the hair on one’s neck stand on end. A servant stood holding a torch. By its light, as they looked around, they saw many cages, and within them, tigers imprisoned. Some were royal Bengal tigers, some leopards. Some lay sprawled; others paced back and forth within their cages. In the dim light of that place, their eyes glowed like embers.
Kundavai gripped Vanathi’s hand tightly and said, “Dear girl! Are you frightened? Don’t faint and fall down here!”
Vanathi laughed softly and replied, “Why should I fear the tiger, sister? Is not the tiger the guardian of our clan?”
“At times, even the guardians may join hands with the enemy, may they not? Then the danger is all the greater.”
“No, sister! Human guards may perhaps betray us. But these tigers would never do such a thing!”
“One cannot say. These tigers have devoured many a traitor to the realm. Their blood must surely run in the veins of these beasts, must it not?”
“Just now, Vanathi had declared, ‘I have no fear,’ yet now her body trembled slightly.
‘Akka! What are you saying? Would they really throw living people to these tigers as prey?’ she asked.

‘They would not do such a thing. Did I not tell you that beneath this golden hall lies an underground prison? There is only one way in and out of it. That passage lies here, in this Tiger Hall. If anyone tries to escape from the prison, they must come into this hall. Then, they will become prey for the tigers!’
‘Shiva, Shiva! What cruelty is this?’

‘Such is the nature of a kingdom! There is mercy; there is cruelty too. Vanathi! There may come a time when even I am locked away in that underground prison. If you had heard what the Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar said to me today…’

‘That would be a fine thing, Akka! There is no one in all the fourteen worlds who has the power to imprison you. If anyone even tried, would not the earth split open and swallow up this very city of Thanjai? I have no fear for you. It is our old friend, the physician’s son from Pazhaiyarai, whom I worry about. That gentle boy—surely he would not have tried to escape, would he?’
‘A gentle boy, yes! But who can say when and how people might change?’
The tigers’ roars grew even louder.
Looking at the guard, Kundavai said, ‘The tigers seem to be very angry!’
‘No, my lady! They are welcoming the emperor’s noble daughter with their roars!’ the guard replied with a touch of humor.
‘A fine welcome indeed!’ said Kundavai.
‘And the time to feed the tigers draws near. They are roaring in anticipation of their meal!’
‘In that case, let us leave quickly. Where is the entrance to the prison?’

They had now reached one corner of the hall. The guards moved aside one of the tiger cages. There, set into the floor, was a door. Two men bent down and opened it outward. Inside, a flight of steps was revealed. One by one, they descended the steps.

Darkness deepened. From the two torches held by the servants, a smoke-laden, dim light flickered forth. Along the narrow paths that crisscrossed and wound through the place, they were forced to walk in single file. If, outside, the fearsome roar of tigers could make one’s hair stand on end, here, the wretched, sorrowful voices of men rising from all sides made the heart tremble and the body shudder.
Yet, amidst those pitiful voices—what a wonder!—a sweet voice was heard, singing!
“O golden-hued one! You who wear the tiger skin as a garment, You who adorn your shining red locks with the radiant konrai flowers!”

The cells in that subterranean prison were not arranged in a straight line. They twisted and turned, some jutting forward, others receding. At each cell door, the guard would raise his torch high. In some cells, a single man was confined. In others, there were two. In certain cells, the prisoners were chained to iron rings fixed in the wall. In some, they were left unbound, free to move as they wished. As soon as the faces of those within each cell became visible, Princess Kundavai would shake her head, and the group would move on.
At one point, Vanathi asked, “What cruelty is this? For what reason are these people imprisoned so? Is there no trial or inquiry?”

To this, Kundavai replied, “For ordinary crimes, there are inquiries and trials. But those who plot against the state, foreign spies, and those who aid spies—such as these are kept here. Once the truth we seek is obtained from them, they are released! But from some, no truth is ever revealed. How can they tell us anything if there is nothing to tell? Their suffering is indeed great!”
By then, the song—“O golden-hued one!”—had drawn very near. When they reached that cell and raised the torch, they saw a young boy inside. It was a boy we already know—Sendhan Amudhan.
His innocent, milk-fresh, youthful face drew the attention of the princesses.
Looking at him, Kundavai asked, “Was it you who was singing?” “Yes, Mother!” he replied.
“You seem to be in high spirits!”
“What reason do I have to lack enthusiasm, Amma? The Lord who pervades all is here with me as well!”
“You speak like a great sage! Who are you, my son? What were you doing outside?”

“I am neither a great sage nor a minor one, Amma! While I was outside, I was stringing a garland of flowers and offering it to the Lord. Here, I weave a garland of verses and find contentment in my heart!”
“It seems you are not only a sage, but a poet as well. Is this the only song you know? Or do you know many more?”
“A few more songs come to me, but ever since I arrived here, I have been singing only this one.”
“Why?”
“When I came here, I passed by the treasury. I saw heaps of fresh gold coins, the like of which I had never seen before. That sight reminded me of the golden-hued form of the Lord…”
“Fortunate are you! Many people, upon seeing gold, are seized by all manner of desires. But your thoughts turned to the divine form of the Lord. Do you have any family or relatives, my son?”
“Only my mother remains. She lives outside the Tanjavur fort, near the lotus pond.”
“What is that mother’s name?”
“Vaani Amma.”
“I shall tell that mother of yours that you are here, brimming with joy.”
“It is of no use, Amma! My mother cannot hear, nor can she speak…”
“Oh! Is your name Sendhan Amudhan?” the young princess asked in surprise.
“Yes, Amma! How is it that you know the name of this poor soul?”
“For what crime have they brought you here and imprisoned you?”
“Until yesterday, I did not even know what crime I had committed. Only today have I come to understand.”
“What is it that you have realized?”
“That I have been arrested and imprisoned for the crime of helping a spy.”
“What is this? Which spy did you help?”

“One day, at the gates of Thanjai fort, I met a traveler who had come from outside. He said he needed a place to stay for the night. I brought him to my house. But never, even in my dreams, did I suspect that he was a spy…”
“Do you know his name?”
“He said his name was Vallavaraiyan Vandiyathevan. He also claimed to belong to the ancient Vanar clan…”
Kundavai and Vanathi looked at each other. Their hearts spoke in silent accord.
Vanathi turned to Sendhan Amudhan and said, “Tell us everything in detail, father!”
Sendhan Amudhan recounted it all as it happened—from the moment he met Vandiyathevan at the fort gates, to the point when the men of Pazhuvur spotted him by the riverbank and arrested him.
“Why did you go to such lengths to help a stranger, someone you knew nothing about?” Vanathi asked.

“Mother! There are some people whom, the moment we see them, we feel drawn to them. We feel as though we could even give our lives for their sake. How can I explain why? And then, there are others whom, at first sight, we feel we could kill. Today, they kept a man locked up with me for a while. The anger I felt toward him was boundless. Fortunately, just a short while ago, the men of the younger queen of Pazhuvur came and released him, taking him away…”
“Is that so?” Kundavai bit her rosy lips with her pearly teeth. Her brows knit together. A heavy sigh of anger escaped her.
“Do you know who that man was, the one who was released in such haste?” she asked.
“How could I not know? He is the son of the physician from Pazhayarai!”
“What is it, father? Did he say something improper? You said you were so angry that you wanted to kill him?”
“My uncle’s daughter, Poonguzhali, lives at Kodikkarai. He spoke ill of her, used words unfit to utter. That is why I was so furious with him. But since he brought some good news, I let it go.”
“What is that good news, father?”
“It was with my friend Vandiyathevan that he went to Kodikkarai. There, this wretch tried to betray my friend and hand him over to the men of Pazhuvur. But he failed…”
“He failed? Then did that spy escape?” Vanathi and Kundavai asked in unison, their voices eager. It was to learn this, after all, that they had come into this underground prison!
“Yes, dear ones! My friend escaped. Poonguzhali took him at night in her boat and sailed to the island of Lanka. Those who went searching for him were deceived. This traitor too was fooled!”
The two women looked at each other. The joy that brimmed in their hearts blossomed on their faces.
Kundavai looked at Sendhan Amudhan and said, “Father! You are so happy that a spy escaped? Then it is only right that you are kept in prison!”
“Mother! If that is a crime worthy of prison, then both of you should be put in the cell next to mine!” he replied.
The two women laughed. In that dark, subterranean prison, just as Sendhan Amudhan’s song had been wondrous, so too was the rare sound of their laughter.

“You are a mischievous fellow; a true rogue. If you stay here, you’ll spoil the others with your songs. I must speak to the commander and have you released, so I can attend to other matters,” said Kundavai.

“Mother! Please don’t do that! There is a man in the next cell. Every day, a hundred times, he begs me, ‘Teach me a song! If you teach me, I’ll tell you where in Lanka the Pandya dynasty’s crown and garland are hidden…’” “He says, ‘I have hidden it away, I will reveal it.’ Until I learn that secret, please let him remain here!” said Sendhan Amudhan.

“Poor fellow! So, you say you’ll stay here until you too lose your mind like him? Then what will become of your mother, Vanjiammai?” said the Young Princess, and with that, she departed from there. The others followed her.
Within half an hour, some attendants came and released Sendhan Amudhan from the underground prison and escorted him to the gates of the Thanjai fort.

chapters.title: Nandhini’s Missive
paragraphs: That evening, Nandini sat upon the Hamsathoolika couch in the Latha Mandapam, composing a letter. She had written only a few lines. As she wrote, her body trembled at times, like a tender creeper shivering in the swirling wind. She let out deep sighs often. Though her attendant stood nearby, fanning her with a peacock-feather fan in that cool hour, beads of sweat gathered like pearls upon her crystal-smooth brow. The letter she wrote was as follows:

“Prince! With much hesitation and fear, I have dared to write this letter. Many kinds of news about the state of the kingdom have reached my ears. You seem to pay no heed to any of it. Though your father, weakened by illness, has sent for you many times, you have not come to Thanjavur. The thought that I might be the cause of this torments me. If I could meet you just once, I could dispel all doubts. Will your noble heart grant me this? If you do not wish to come to Thanjavur, we may meet at the Kadambur Sambuvarayar palace. I now occupy the place of your grandmother. What objection could there be to our meeting and speaking? The brave young man who brings you this letter, the son of Sambuvarayar, is someone you may trust completely and to whom you may send any message. Thus writes, with misfortune as her companion since birth, the hapless Nandini.”
Indeed, after much hesitation and deep thought, Nandini finished writing the above letter. Then, turning to the attendant fanning her, she said, “Go! Bring the young prince of Kadambur here at once!”
The attendant went and brought Kandanmaran, then stepped aside and stood at a distance.
Kandanmaran’s eyes were shy to meet Nandini’s gaze. He stood looking somewhere off into the garden.
“Sir! Please be seated,” said Nandini. The tremor in her voice made Kandanmaran look directly at her face.
Nandini continued, “It is no wonder that the eyes which beheld Kundavai Devi cannot bear to look at me!” She smiled as she spoke.
Those words tore through Kandanmaran’s heart. Her smile made his head spin. Stumbling and faltering, he exclaimed, “A thousand Kundavais would not equal one Nandini Devi!”
“Yet, if the Young Princess so much as lifts her finger, you would ascend to the heavens and bring back Indra’s very throne. But if I plead with you in sorrow, you would not even deign to sit down!”
At once, Kandanmaran seated himself on the dais opposite and declared, “If you command it, I will ascend to Brahmaloka and bring back Brahma’s very head!”

Nandini trembled at her core. Without looking at Kandanmaran, she turned her gaze elsewhere and said, “Even after what Parameshvara did, Brahma still has four heads left. Even if you bring back one more, Brahma will survive!”

“Devi! Ask me for anything else you desire. But do not praise Kundavai Devi in my presence. When I think of how she spoke kindly to that traitor-friend Vandiyathevan, my blood boils!” said Kandanmaran.
“Still, it is true that your imagination was boundless this morning! How fancifully you spoke of the duel between you and your friend!” Nandini’s words brought a slight embarrassment to Kandanmaran.
“I had to say something about how I met him, didn’t I? That he stabbed me in the back is at least the truth!” he replied.
“Sir! Would it not be wise for you to recall everything that happened that night, once again?” asked Nandini.
“Do you too doubt my words?”

“I do not doubt you. Yet, there are some things you seem to have forgotten. One day, Vandiyathevan will surely be captured and brought here. When that time comes, the accusation you level against him must taste of truth, must it not?”
“I have no particular interest in that. In fact, I still wish to forgive him.”

“I commend your magnanimity. Still, it is best that we ascertain the truth between us. Recall once more everything that happened that night. When you came through the moonlit chamber, you met both Pazhuvetarayar and me on the way. Do you remember that?”
“I remember it well. As long as there is life in my body, I can never forget it.”
“Then you must also remember what you said at that time, do you not?”
“I do not recall what I said. When I saw you, I lost all sense of myself.”
“But I remember very well what you said. ‘Sir! I have heard so much about your daughter’s beauty. But none of that could do justice to what I see before me,’—that is what you said!...”
“Oh dear! Did I really say that? No wonder her face turned so red! Even now, she does not seem to like me much when she sees me…”
Nandini laughed and said, “It does not matter if she does not like you; what matters is that you like her, is it not? That is enough!”
“Devi! I speak the truth. What is the use of hiding it from you? I do not like her either,” said Kandanmaran.
“That too does not matter! I like her; that alone is enough. How much penance I must have performed to obtain such a husband?” she said.
Hearing this, Kandanmaran’s heart was thrown into confusion. He sat silent, not knowing what to say.
“Let that be. After you saw us in the moonlit chamber, what did you do?” Nandini asked.

“The guard who brought the lamp led the way. I followed, my mind still filled with thoughts of you. The guard opened a secret door in the wall and moved on. I entered through it. Immediately, someone stabbed me in the back—that is all I remember. Vandiyathevan must have somehow known that I would come there and waited outside for me.”
“No, sir! Your guess is quite wrong. He was not waiting outside.”
“So, you too have joined his side?”
“Why should I join his side? What profit is there for me? Or what profit is there for him? Now I am certain that things must have happened just as they did.”
“Tell me, Devi! Tell me how it happened!”
“Vandiyathevan is not waiting outside!…”
“Then who was waiting?”
“There was no one else; didn’t I just say that Vandiyathevan is not waiting outside? He is waiting inside that very treasury chamber!”
“What? What? How is that possible, Devi!”

“That day, he vanished suddenly, as if by magic. How could he have disappeared? Think about it yourself! Somehow, he slipped into the treasury chamber and uncovered all its secrets. Afterwards, he followed behind you. When you opened the door, he pushed you from behind and slipped out himself. Perhaps, later, his conscience pricked him. He must have taken you and left you at that mute woman’s house!…”

“Devi! Things must have happened exactly as you say; there is no doubt. All these days, this never occurred to my mind; nor did it occur to anyone else! If someone were to ask who in this Chola land possesses the keenest intellect, I would say it is you. In this world, there are those who are blessed with wisdom; there are those who are blessed with beauty. It is rare to find both united in one person in all of Brahma’s creation. In you, I see both beauty and wisdom combined!” Kandanmaran exclaimed in rapture.
“Sir! Are these words you just spoke truly from your heart? Or are they the empty flatteries men utter to women everywhere in the world?”
“It is not flattery; I swear, I spoke only what is in my heart.”
“If that is so, will you trust me completely? Will you do me a favor?”
“If it is within my power, I am ready to do anything.”
“For my sake, you must go to Kanchi.”
“Even if you ask me to go to Kashi, I will go.”

“There is no need to go so far. I will give you a message for Prince Aditya Karikalan who is in Kanchi. You must deliver it to him. After delivering it, you must invite him to be a guest at your Kadambur palace…”
“Devi! What are these words you speak? Are you unaware of the arrangements being made for the kingdom by your husband, my father, and many other prominent men of Chola Nadu?”

“I know them very well—and I know even more than that. Sir, your family, my family, and many other great families are now standing at the very threshold of grave danger. Do you know who is the cause of this?”
“Tell me, Devi!”
“The very woman who came here as a guest this afternoon—she is the culprit!”
“Oh no! Do you mean the Young Princess?”

“I speak of that serpent-woman. Only a serpent can recognize another serpent’s trail. Nandini alone can fathom Kundavai’s schemes. It is she who has sent your friend Vandiyathevan to Lanka. Do you know why? The tale of fetching medicinal herbs is a great lie! She is not tormented by any desire to save Sundara Cholar’s life. After him, she does not wish for Madurantakan to ascend the throne. Nor does she want Aditya Karikalan to become king. Her only wish is that her beloved younger brother, Arulmozhi Varman, should ascend the throne. If Arulmozhi Varman becomes king, she can play her games as she pleases. Then, the Empress of the Chola Empire will be none other than Kundavai Devi! And do you know who the Emperor will be? Your friend, Vandiyathevan!”
“Ah! Is that so? This must be stopped at any cost. I must inform my father and the Pazhuvettaraiyars at once…”
“There is no use telling them. They will not believe you. Kundavai’s cunning must be countered with greater cunning. If you help me, we can succeed!”
“Command me, Devi!”

“Here is this letter. You must take it with utmost care and deliver it to Aditya Karikalan in Kanchi. Will you do it?” she said, extending the rolled palm-leaf letter and the small tube in which to carry it.
Kandanmaran, lost in a delirium of infatuation, instead of taking the letter and the tube, seized Nandini’s hand and stammered, “For your sake, I will do anything!”

At that moment, a sudden, hurried sound was heard. The Pazhuvettaraiyar was coming swiftly along the path from the palace to the Latha Mandapam. The old nurse, startled by the unexpected arrival, quickly moved aside. There, in the mandapam… Suspended from the ceiling, swinging in a corner, there was a large parrot tethered by a chain. In his haste, without realizing it, Pazhuvetarayar grabbed the parrot with his hand. The storm that raged in his mind surged through his arm. The parrot’s wings fluttered frantically. Unable to withstand the cruel grip of Pazhuvetarayar, the parrot screeched shrilly.

chapters.title: Wax in the Fire
paragraphs: The shrill ‘kreech’ of the parrot, mingled with the nursemaid’s frightened cry, startled both Nandini and Kandanmaran. Kandanmaran turned to see who had come, and when he realized it was Pazhuvettarayar approaching, his heart was thrown into confusion. A sudden fear seized him: had the lord overheard him say, “I too do not like Pazhuvettarayar,” just moments ago? Even more terrifying was the thought that Pazhuvettarayar might suspect something improper between himself and Nandini. That notion sent a chill through his heart. Is it not said that the ways of men who marry in their old age are peculiar? Perhaps that is why he is coming with such anger now. What he would do upon arrival, Kandanmaran could not guess. He must be prepared for anything.

All these thoughts crashed like waves through Kandanmaran’s mind in the span of a single moment. Yet, that day, he was to witness a great marvel—something entirely contrary to what he had feared. As Pazhuvettarayar drew near, Nandini’s face blossomed with a smile. She looked at him with her dark eyes and said, “My lord! I was afraid you might be delayed in returning. How fortunate that you have come back so soon!”

At the sight of her face and the sound of her voice, all of Pazhuvettarayar’s anger melted away, like wax placed in the fire. He let out a sheepish laugh and said, “Yes, the business I went for is finished; I have returned.”
Then, turning to Kandanmaran, he asked, “What is this boy doing here? Has he come to compose and recite some love poetry for you?” He laughed at his own jest.

Kandanmaran’s face flushed red. But Nandini laughed even more than Pazhuvettarayar and replied, “He knows nothing of love, nor of poetry. He only knows how to get into fights and end up wounded. Fortunately, his wound has healed. He was just saying he wanted to return to his village!”

“What shall we say about the valor of the youth of these days? In twenty-four battles, I have received sixty-four wounds. Yet never once did I take to my bed. But for his wound to heal, he has had to—” “It has been a long time. But all my wounds are on my chest, shoulders, head, and face. This boy, however, was wounded on his back, wasn’t he? That’s why it has taken so long. It is only fair!” he said, and let out a mocking laugh.
Kandanmaran sprang up in anger. “Sir! You stand in my father’s place. That is the only reason I tolerate your mockery!” he said.
“If not, what would you have done, boy?” asked Pazhuvetarayar, placing his hand on the dagger at his waist.

At this moment, Nandini intervened. “My lord! He does not bear wounds only on his back. You know well that he has wounds upon his heart as well! The thought that the one he considered his friend stabbed him in the back and fled has left a deep wound in his heart. Though the wound on his back may heal, the pain in his heart has not. We should not speak as though rubbing salt into that wound, should we? Do you not remember what happened that night, the very night he was wounded?” As she spoke, Nandini looked at Pazhuvetarayar with a gaze that seemed to carry a hidden meaning. Pazhuvetarayar’s expression changed at once!

“Yes, what you say is true! Poor boy, he is innocent. His father is my dearest friend. I should not take to heart the words he spoke in ignorance. Let this matter rest. Nandini! I came now to tell you something important. It is something he too should know. In Lanka, at Mahodaya, they have caught a man on suspicion of being a spy. He is said to have a letter for Prince Arulmozhi Varman. From certain signs, I believe he may be our Kandanmaran’s handsome friend. He must be a clever rogue. He slipped through our men’s hands and escaped to Lanka!”
Neither of the others noticed the fleeting change that came over Nandini’s face at that moment.
“What! He escaped? He went to Lanka?” Kandanmaran exclaimed in disappointment.
“My lord! It is no surprise to me that he escaped. How many times have I told you that your brother is unfit to guard this fortress? Would not the men he sends be the same?” said Nandini.

“In the past, when you spoke like this, I did not think much of it. But now, even I am beginning to feel the same way. Listen to one more strange thing! The spy who was caught in the mango grove was found to possess one of our Pazhuvur signet rings. He refuses to say how it came into his hands…”
Nandini let out a soft sigh and said, “What is this, a comedy? How did the palm signet ring come into his possession? What does your brother say about this?”

“Him? If you hear what he says, you’ll burst out laughing! Kalandhagan claims that the palm signet ring must have gone to the spy from you!” said Pazhuvetaraiyar, and then he laughed thunderously. The laughter seemed to shake the very pillars of the Latha Mandapam. The trees in the palace gardens shivered and trembled as if in response.
Nandini, joining in his laughter, said, “My brother-in-law—there is no one in all the fourteen worlds with a mind as sharp as his!”

“Do you know what else your brother-in-law says? It’s even more amusing! Just thinking about it makes me laugh! He says that when you arrived at the gates of Tanjore fort in your palanquin, that Indrajit met and spoke with you. Later, that magician even entered the palace. Therefore, you must have been the one to give him the Pazhuvur signet ring! If not, then perhaps that sorcerer who visits you so often must have taken it from you and given it to the spy! To cover up his own foolishness, he spins such wild tales and babbles nonsense!” said Pazhuvetaraiyar, baring his long teeth as he laughed again, “Ha ha ha ha!”

“It was a great mistake for me to ever doubt my brother-in-law’s sharpness of mind. His intellect is truly a blazing fire! There is no doubt about it! But what astonishes me is that you listened to all this and remained silent!” said Nandini. Her expression changed once more; now, scorn and derision flashed across her face. Sparks seemed to fly from her eyes.

The mighty Pazhuvetaraiyar, who had faced countless spear-thrusts on the battlefield with pride and courage, now faltered, unable to withstand even the slightest anger from Nandini. A sudden weakness appeared in his manner and speech.
“Devi! Do you think I just listened to all that quietly? I spoke to him very harshly about his incompetence and made him weep. Had you seen it, you would have felt pity for him!” he said.

Listening to all this, Kandanmaran’s plight became most miserable. He felt a certain fear towards Nandini, and towards Periya Pazhuvettarayar, a mix of pity and contempt. He wished to escape from being entangled in the marital affairs of these conspirators and leave that place at once. Clearing his throat, he said, “Sir!…”
Nandini interrupted, “While speaking of my brother-in-law’s cleverness, we have forgotten him. He says he wishes to return to his village—should we not let him go?”
“Of course, let him go. His father must have been worrying all these days about his staying here!”
“I wish to send a letter with him. May I?”
“A letter? To whom?”
“To the prince in Kanchi!”
Pazhuvettarayar looked at Nandini and Kandanmaran with suspicious eyes. “A letter to the prince? You wish to write it? For what purpose?” he asked.

“The young princess wrote a letter to her brother and sent it through his friend. Why should not the younger queen of Pazhuvoor write a letter to her brother? Why should I not send it with him?” said Nandini.
“The letter his friend carried—was it really written by the young princess Kundavai? How do you know of this matter?” Pazhuvettarayar asked.

“Why else do you think the magician comes to see me so often? I learned of it through his magic. My brother-in-law is so skilled at knowing people’s secrets! The men who found the palm-leaf seal with him did not say the letter was from Kundavai, did they? See!”
“Our men did not say anything about the seal; Anbil Brahmarayar has returned from Rameswaram. The news he brought…”
“Did that Brahmin say anything to you about Kundavai Devi’s letter?”
“No.”

“My lord! Think of the warnings I have given you. Did I not say that everyone in this kingdom is trying to deceive you? Do you now realize that this is true? I do not believe only what the magician says. From Kodikkarai—” I summoned the physician’s son, who had been kept under guard, and questioned him as well. He confirmed it. He said that the young princess had sent a letter to her brother!” said Nandini.

To Pazhuvetaraiyar, it felt as if he had been blindfolded and abandoned in a dense forest. He looked at Kandanmaran with disgust. He did not like discussing such matters in the presence of that young boy.

Sensing his displeasure, Nandini said, “We have our own story to discuss. Why should his journey be delayed because of it!” With that, she turned to Kandanmaran and said, “Sir! You must take this letter directly to the Prince at Kanchi and deliver it to him. If he gives a reply, you must send it back with utmost caution. And do not forget to invite the Prince to your Kadambur palace!”
“What should I tell my father? Can I say this is the wish of the Lord of Pazhuvur?” Kandanmaran asked hesitantly.
“You may say so without hesitation. My wish is the wish of the Lord of Pazhuvur. My lord! Is that not so?” said Nandini.
“Yes, yes!” Pazhuvetaraiyar nodded. He understood nothing. His head was spinning. He could not bring himself to speak against Nandini.

After Kandanmaran left, Nandini fixed her magnetic gaze upon Pazhuvetaraiyar and, in a voice as sweet as a parrot’s, said, “My lord, it seems your trust in me has diminished! It appears my brother-in-law’s evil influence has prevailed over you!”

“Never, Nandini! Even if I lose faith in the spear I hold in my hand, or the sword at my waist, I will never lose faith in you. Even if I lose faith in the warrior’s heaven, I will not lose faith in your word!” he replied.
“If that is true, then why did you question me so much in front of that young boy? I felt humiliated!” said Nandini, and tears began to well up in her eyes.
Pazhuvetaraiyar was shaken. “No, my dear! Please, do not punish me so!” he said, wiping away the tears that brimmed in Nandini’s eyes and trying to comfort her.
“Still, some of your actions are beyond my understanding. Do I not have the right to ask what, why, and for what purpose?” he asked.
“You have the right to ask; I too have the right to answer. Who said you do not? I only said you should not ask in the presence of strangers. Now, ask whatever you wish!” she said.
“Why are you sending a message to Aditya Karikalan? Why are you inviting him to the Kadambur palace? Is he not the foremost enemy to the fulfillment of our plans?” asked Pazhuvetarayar.

“No, no! Aditya Karikalan is not our foremost enemy. That serpent-woman of Pazhayarai is our first and greatest foe. Why did I summon her to our palace? For the very same reason, I now ask Aditya Karikalan to come to Kadambur. My lord! Recall what I have often told you before. Did I not say that the young princess Kundavai harbors some secret design within her heart? I have now discovered what that is. She has resolved, setting aside all others, to place her younger brother Arulmozhi Varman upon the throne of Thanjavur. We must counter her schemes with our own, and prevent her purpose from being fulfilled. Now do you see the reason why I sent the message to Kanchi?” asked Nandini, her gaze piercing Pazhuvetarayar’s heart and unsettling his mind.
Even though he did not fully understand, the valiant elder stammered, “Yes, I see it!”

“My lord! It is only because of the heroic deeds performed by you and your forefathers that this Chola empire has grown so vast and mighty. Until the day I see you seated upon the golden throne of Thanjai, these sinful eyes of mine shall know no sleep, neither by night nor by day! But if ever, before that day comes, you should harbor the slightest doubt about me, then with your own sword, strike me down with a single blow and end my life!” declared Nandini.
“My beloved! Do not torment me with such cruel words!” said Periya Pazhuvetarayar.

chapters.title: The City of Mahathotta
paragraphs: It has been a long time since we last parted ways with our protagonist, Vandiyathevan. We have lingered in Thanjai for many days. Though it was only a few days, it felt like an eternity. In those few days, Vandiyathevan had journeyed along the Eelam coastline and reached the great city of Maathottam, which stood on the banks of the Paalavi river.

That city, situated on the Eelam coast beyond the Rameswaram sea, was, just as it had been in the times of Thirugnana Sambandar and Sundaramurthi, still surrounded by lush groves of verdant trees, presenting a delightful sight to the eye. Mango, jackfruit, coconut, areca, plantain, and sugarcane flourished in abundance along that shore. Monkeys swung from the branches of those trees. Bees hummed their melodies; green parrots chattered in childish tones.

Upon the ramparts of the city’s fort, the waves of the sea crashed and roared with a ceaseless sound. From the great wooden ships to the smallest boats, vessels crowded the harbor of Maathottam. Goods unloaded from them lay heaped in mountainous piles. Though all these were as they had been in the days of Sambandar and Sundarar, there were some changes to be seen. The streets of Maathottam no longer thronged with devotees making their way to the Kedheeswarar temple. In places where once devotees sang the praises of the Lord in ecstasy, now only warriors could be seen. Men armed with swords and shields, spears and lances, wandered everywhere.

For more than a hundred years, that city had served as a center of war. Armies from Tamil Nadu, coming for the Eelam wars, most often landed there. Returning armies too boarded their ships from that place. The city had changed hands many times. At times it belonged to the kings of Lanka, at others to the Pandya rulers. Since the reign of Paranthaka Chakravarthi, it had remained under Chola dominion.

At the gate of such a war-torn city’s fortress, one day, Vandiyathevan stood. He wished to enter the city. He said he wanted to see the Chola commander. The guards refused to let him in. At this, he employed the same ruse he had used earlier at Kadambur. He tried to force his way in by pushing past the guards. The guards seized him and brought him before the commander of the fort. Vandiyathevan told the commander that he bore an important letter for Prince Arulmozhi... He said that he had just arrived, and that only the Chola Commander-in-Chief could give details about it. They examined him. They found with him a letter for ‘Ponniyin Selvan’ and the palm insignia of Pazhuvoor.

At that time, Kodumbalur Periya Velar, Boothi Vikrama Kesari, was the Commander-in-Chief of the Lankan campaign. They went and informed him. Boothi Vikrama Kesari was then speaking with the Prime Minister, Aniruddha Brahmarayar. He was preparing to travel with him as far as Rameswaram. Therefore, he said he would return and inquire into the matter, and until then, ordered that the warrior be kept under guard.

Afterwards, Vandiyathevan was taken away and locked in a room of a ruined palace. Guards were posted at the door. Vandiyathevan, exhausted from his long journey, was actually pleased at being imprisoned. At least now he could rest for a day or two without any wandering! On the first day, he enjoyed such rest. But on the second day, a disturbance arose.

From the next room, strange and peculiar sounds began to be heard. Someone was scolding and threatening another. His words of bravado were astonishing. “Here! Take this!” “Tch, tch!” “Go, go!” “Don’t come near!” “If you come close, I’ll kill you!” “I’ll smash you to pieces!” “Beware!” “Your life is not your own!” “I’ll send you to the land of Yama!” “With one kick, your life will be gone!”—thus, someone in the next room was raging on. It was unclear at whom he was hurling these threats. Only one voice could be heard; there was no reply. Perhaps he was a mad warrior, thought Vandiyathevan. If so, wouldn’t he keep him awake all night? Even the hope of sleeping peacefully was now disturbed!

“Won’t you listen if I tell you? Won’t you just go away? All right, all right! Watch what I do to you!” After these words, something suddenly came flying into Vandiyathevan’s room. Lying down, Vandiyathevan leapt up in alarm. He looked closely to see what had fallen. Instantly, laughter bubbled up within him. He laughed out loud, for it became clear that what had come flying so swiftly from the next room was a cat!
“Oh ho! So you know how to laugh, do you? Laugh! Laugh! But don’t you dare come here again!” said the voice from the next room.

There was no doubt that he was some kind of madman. Otherwise, would he argue so much with a cat? Or would he truly believe that a cat could laugh like a human? Yet, what was even more astonishing was that the voice which had spoken so much seemed somehow familiar to him. It felt like a voice he had heard somewhere, sometime before. But whose voice was it? Where had he heard it?—No matter how much he racked his brain, he could not remember!

Let it be as it may, let whoever it is be, thought Vandiyathevan, and lay down. He closed his eyes and tried to sleep, but sleep would not come. After a while, he felt something soft and slippery brush against the soles of his feet. When he opened his eyes, he saw the cat lying there. Oh, Lord! How could he sleep with this creature at his feet? He kicked it away. The cat moved off. He closed his eyes again; once more, something soft brushed against his hand. Opening his eyes, he saw the cat had come back to lie beside him, purring affectionately!
Again, he pushed it away with his hand. The cat went farther off. He closed his eyes once more. This time, the cat came and lay near his head, and began to stroke his forehead with its tail.

That brave man, who could withstand sword and spear without fear, could not bear the sensation of the cat’s tail brushing against him. He got up, caught the cat by its neck, and lifted it. There was a spot on the wall between his room and the next, where the plaster had crumbled and left a hole. Through that opening, he flung the cat into the next room.

For a while, there was a great commotion in the next room. The shouts of a human voice mingled with the angry yowling of the cat. After a moment, a voice cried, “Go! Get lost!” The cat’s “meow, meow” faded away into the distance and then ceased. Silence reigned.

Vandiyathevan drifted into sleep. In a half-dreaming state, he had a dream—a very pleasant dream. The young princess Kundavai came and sat beside him, gently caressing his forehead. Ah! What a difference between the touch of the cat’s tail and the princess’s delicate fingers!
Suddenly, he woke with a start. He was disappointed that the dream had vanished. From the next room, someone knocked on the wall—it must be that madman again.
“Who is there? Who threw the cat in here?”
Vandiyathevan did not reply. He remained silent. Ah! What is this? That sound, like a cat giving birth, again? No, no! Someone is trying to climb the wall on the other side!
Vandiyathevan did not get up. He lay there, listening intently, his ears alert. But, ever cautious, his hand was already gripping the hilt of his dagger.
From the top of the wall, two hands appeared first, clutching the edge. Then a turban came into view. Beneath the turban, a face rose up and peered down.
Ah! Is that not Azhwarkadiyan? The headgear makes him look a little different! But there is no doubt—it is Azhwarkadiyan.
Why and how has he come here? He must have known I was here! Has he come to help me? Or to cause trouble?
Vandiyathevan sat up and called, “Oh, valiant Vaishnavite! Welcome! Welcome! Come to the holy land of Thirukkedhiswaram, a place of Shiva’s grace! Welcome, welcome!”
“Brother! Is it you? I thought so! Who else could sit so quietly, without making a sound, like a pressed-down Pillaiyar idol?” said Azhwarkadiyan, leaping down into the room.

chapters.title: The Bloodthirsty Blade
paragraphs: Vandiyathevan’s mind was in turmoil, wondering how that valiant Vaishnavite had arrived there and for what purpose. Yet, he did not let any of this show outwardly.

“What a marvel to speak of! Just a moment ago, I was thinking about you. I look up, and there you are, leaping over the wall. They say, ‘When the giving god bestows, he even pierces the roof to deliver it’—how true that is!” he said.
“Dear boy! You were thinking about me just now? Why should you think about this mere mortal? Even if you had thought of Lord Rama himself, it would have been worthwhile…”

“Your lips deserve only sugar, Swami. First, I did think of Lord Rama. As I came this way, I saw the towering spires of Rameswaram on the far side of the sea. I thought of how Rama worshipped Shiva there to absolve the sin of slaying Ravana…”
“Stop, my boy! Stop!”

“I cannot stop, Swami! Truly, I cannot stop. My legs are weary from walking and standing without rest. Have mercy and sit down with me. After that, shall I tell you whether I thought of Rama? The moment I thought of him, the image of his great devotee Hanuman came to mind. And as soon as I thought of Hanuman, I remembered you. And lo! There you were, appearing before me. Did you leap over the wall alone, or did you, like Hanuman, leap across the very sea to come here?”

“Brother, where is Hanuman, the crown jewel of devotees, and where am I? Hanuman came to Lanka and laid waste to Akshaya Kumara and other demons. I, on the other hand, cannot even chase away a mere cat. Look here! See how a cat has scratched my legs and left them bleeding!” said Azhwarkkadiyan, pointing to the wounds on his legs.
“Alas! Did it come to this? But what was the reason for your battle with a mere cat…?”
“I did not go looking for a fight. It was the cat that picked a quarrel with me…” “How is that possible, Swamiji!”

“I came here searching for you. I deceived the guards at the gate and climbed over the outer wall, leaping down into the courtyard. At the very spot where I placed my foot, that cat had deliberately stretched out its tail. My foot only brushed its tail lightly. Even so, that wicked cat began to attack me with its claws. Brother! Listen to what I say! One may fight with a tiger, one may even fight with an elephant, but never, ever fight with a cat!”
“Swamiji! That secret is now clear to me…”
“What secret?”

“That cat came here to my room. It brushed my forehead with its tail. It played with me, purring affectionately. It did not scratch me with its claws. It attacked and scratched only you! What could be the reason? It must be a fierce Shaivite cat that cannot stand the sight of Vaishnavites!…”
“Oh ho! Is that so? How did such a thought not occur to me? If I had known it was a fierce Shaivite cat, I would have given it four sacred blows with my staff!”

“It is good that you did not have your staff in hand. Because, ever since I entered this holy place, even my own body has begun to boil with Shaivite blood. The dagger in my belt cries out, ‘I want fierce Vaishnavite blood!’ I have restrained it only in gratitude for the great help you have done me!”
“My boy! I have not done you any help at all!”
“Vaishnavite! Did you not tell me about your sister, the younger queen of Pazhuvoor?”
“Yes, I told you.”
“When the younger queen of Pazhuvoor was traveling in a closed palanquin near Kadambur, the curtain was drawn aside, and at that moment you pointed her out to me, did you not?”
“Yes, yes, I did. What of it?”

“I shall tell you. That same palanquin, as it was passing near the Thanjai fort, I saw it again. The palanquin bearers deliberately came and struck against my horse. To seek justice, I drew aside the palanquin’s curtain and looked inside…”
“Who was inside?”
“The younger queen of Pazhuvoor is none other than Nandini Devi herself!”
“Oh ho! You are a fortunate man. No matter how much I tried, I could never catch a glimpse of Nandini. But you have managed it!”
“When fortune comes, it arrives of its own accord!”
“And then?”
“I mentioned your name. I told the Devi that you had sent me with an important message…”
“Even if I tried, I could never match you. Nowhere in this universe have I seen anyone who can lie so shamelessly as you do…”
“Vaishnavite! My ancestors had a great fondness for poets. They themselves composed many poems…”
“So what?”
“The blood of that poetic lineage runs in my veins as well. That’s why, at times, my imagination overflows. Common folk like you might call it lying…”
“Very well; what happened next?”
“Amazed by my imagination, Nandini Devi gave me the Pazhuvoor signet ring. She told me to come and see her at the palace.”
“Did you go?”
“Of course, how could I not? I went at once. Nandini Devi, who learned of my valorous exploits from my own lips, entrusted me with an important task.”
“What task was that?”

“It seems that in Lanka, the Pandya dynasty’s crown of Madurai and the Indra-mala are hidden. The royal family of Lanka has concealed them in the hill country. She sent me, saying, ‘Somehow, find those jewels and bring them back!’ I set out, not knowing how difficult this task would be…”

“They say the jewels in the great Pazhuvettaraiyar’s treasury weigh a thousand donkey-loads. Even all that is not enough for the younger queen, it seems. Well, what did she promise to give you if you brought them back?”
“He promised to wrest the guardianship of the Thanjai fort from the hands of the Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar and grant it to me.”
“Thambi! Thambi! If the guardianship of the Thanjai fort comes to you, then I can enter the fortress without any hindrance, can I not?”

“That would indeed be a fine thing. But how could I ever gain the guardianship of the Thanjai fort? Look at me—I came to this town and have ended up trapped like this!” said Vandiyathevan in a voice heavy with sorrow.
“Why did you get caught? Do you know why they have imprisoned you?” asked Azhwarkadiyan.
“I brought with me the signet ring given by the Lady of Pazhuvoor. I thought it would hold sway here as well. That was my mistake, was it not?”

“It was a mistake, Thambi, a grave mistake! Do you not know that the Commander here is the great Velar of Kodumbalur? There is a deep enmity between the houses of Pazhuvoor and Kodumbalur—were you unaware of that?”
“I came here in ignorance, and so I was caught. I do not know what to do…”
“Thambi! You need not worry!”
“How can I not worry…”
“I have come here precisely to set you free…”
“Oh!”
“There was a time when I sought your help; you refused me. Yet, I have come to help you. Rise and come with me! This very moment, we can escape from this prison!”
“Vaishnavar! You must leave here at once!”
“Why, my friend?”
“The knife in my belt has begun to wail more and more. It is crying out for the blood of a ‘valiant Vaishnavan.’”
“Let it cry out if it wishes! There is enough blood in my body. If your knife needs it, let it take a little and be done. Now, get up and come with me!”
“No, I cannot come!”
“What is the reason?”
“My eyes are growing heavy with sleep. For so many nights, I have not slept at all. Tonight, I have resolved to sleep well. That is why I even threw the cat out.”

“Thambi! What is this you are saying? Is this how you intend to fulfill the task you promised to Princess Kundavai Devi? Did you not agree that you would travel day and night, without rest, until you delivered this letter into the hands of ‘Ponniyin Selvan’?” So saying, Azhwarkkadiyan took the palm-leaf letter from his lap and handed it to Vandiyathevan.
Vandiyathevan received it eagerly. Until now, he had suspected that Azhwarkkadiyan was trying to trick and deceive him. Now, that suspicion vanished.
“How did this letter come into your possession?” he asked.
“It was Commander Vikramakesari who gave it to me. He also told me to return this Pazhuvoor palm insignia. He said you may depart on your journey whenever you wish.”
“Vaishnavar! My heartfelt thanks to you.”
“Keep all your gratitude stored up. You can give it to me when the time comes.”
“Sir! Do you know where the prince is at present?”
“No one knows that. He has gone from Anuradhapura into the hill country. We must search and find him. The Commander has ordered me to guide you on your way. If you wish, I shall come with you.”
Once again, a slight doubt arose in Vandiyathevan’s mind.
“Swamigal! Before we depart, may I see the Commander?” he asked.
“Of course, you must see him. Only after meeting him should we begin our journey. Can we leave without informing the Commander about Vanathi Devi?” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
Hearing this, Vandiyathevan was astonished, wondering if this brave Vaishnavite truly possessed some magical powers.

The silence of the night was shattered by the sudden clash of swords. The moonlight, filtering through the thick canopy of the forest, glinted off the blades as they flashed and met in deadly combat. Vandiyathevan’s heart pounded in his chest as he realized the gravity of the situation—this was no mere skirmish, but a fight for life itself.

The assassin who had crept upon him with feline stealth now stood revealed, his eyes burning with murderous intent. Vandiyathevan’s own sword was already drawn, and he met the first furious onslaught with all the skill and agility he could muster. Sparks flew as steel met steel. The assassin’s blade darted and twisted, seeking a gap in Vandiyathevan’s defense, but the young warrior parried every thrust, his mind racing, his senses heightened by the danger.

For a moment, the two men circled each other, breathing heavily. The silence of the forest seemed to press in on them, broken only by the distant hoot of an owl and the rustle of leaves underfoot. Then, with a guttural cry, the assassin lunged again, his sword slashing through the air with deadly precision. Vandiyathevan sidestepped, feeling the cold wind of the blade as it missed him by a hair’s breadth.

But the assassin was relentless. Again and again, he attacked, his movements swift and merciless. Vandiyathevan’s arm began to ache from the effort of blocking the blows. He knew he could not keep this up forever. Desperation lent him strength. With a sudden burst of energy, he feinted to the left, then brought his sword down in a powerful arc. The assassin staggered back, blood welling from a gash on his arm.

The scent of blood seemed to drive the attacker into a frenzy. With a savage roar, he rushed at Vandiyathevan, his sword raised high. But Vandiyathevan was ready. He sidestepped once more, and with a swift, decisive thrust, drove his blade into the assassin’s side.

A gasp escaped the man’s lips. He dropped his sword and fell to his knees, clutching at the wound. Vandiyathevan stood over him, breathing hard, his own sword stained with blood. The assassin looked up at him, hatred and pain mingling in his gaze.
“Who sent you?” Vandiyathevan demanded, his voice cold and steady.
The man’s lips twisted in a grimace. Blood bubbled from his mouth as he tried to speak. At last, with a final, shuddering breath, he collapsed to the ground, lifeless.

Vandiyathevan stood for a moment, staring down at the fallen man. The forest was silent once more, but the memory of the fight lingered in the air—the sword’s thirst for blood had been quenched, but at what cost?

chapters.title: The Forest Path
paragraphs: Kodumbalur’s Periya Velar, the Commander-in-Chief Boothi Vikrama Kesari, was a man seasoned by age and experience; a veteran who had braved many battlefields and earned his scars. He was bound to the Chola dynasty by deep friendship and kinship. His younger brother, the Chinna Velar of Kodumbalur, had attained a hero’s heaven on the battlefield of Lanka a few years earlier. The army that had accompanied him had also suffered defeat and was forced to return. Boothi Vikrama Kesari was deeply aggrieved by this stain upon their honor and was determined to erase it, to restore the valorous reputation of Kodumbalur. That was why, despite his advancing years, he had come to Lanka to lead the army himself.

We have already seen how the machinations of the Pazhuvettaraiyars had hindered the proper conduct of the Lankan war. The long-standing rivalry and enmity between those two minor royal houses had now grown even more intense because of these events. Therefore, it was inevitable that Vandiyathevan, who had been apprehended with the Pazhuvur signet, would face difficulties with the Periya Velar, the Commander-in-Chief.

Fortunately, Aniruddha Brahmarayar had occasion to mention this matter to him. Having learned the truth about Vandiyathevan from Alwarkadiyan, Aniruddha had immediately sent him to Commander Boothi Vikrama Kesari to reveal the facts.

The Commander-in-Chief, Boothi Vikrama Kesari, scrutinized the young warrior of the Vanar clan from head to toe and must have formed a favorable impression of him. In a kindly tone, he asked, “Young man! Were you properly looked after here? Did you have a place to stay, and was your food adequate?”

“Yes, Commander! They took care of me without any shortcoming. There were always five or six attendants at the door, ready to carry out any order. Accommodation was plentiful. For dinner, they even sent me a cat. Just as I was about to eat it, I saw this brave Vaishnavite and became angry. The cat, scratched by his nails, ran away!” replied Vandiyathevan.
The Commander laughed. “Oh ho! This boy seems to be quite a jester! Thirumalai, is what he says true?”

“Commander! His ancestors were poets. So, he has a vivid imagination. But apart from that, what he says is true. When I went to see him, a cat did scratch my hands and legs!” said Alwarkadiyan. Looking at the bloodied wounds on his body, Commander-in-Chief Boothi Vikrama Kesari burst into laughter again and again.
“A mere cat has caused you all this trouble! Fortunate indeed! At least you had this brave man as your guide on the forest path…”
“Commander! I do not need a guide. My walking stick is sufficient for me. It was only because I left it behind to go see him that I landed in this predicament…”

“In that case, you be his guide! Before you set out, make sure he is given a proper meal, and only then depart! Young man! At present, food is rather scarce in Lanka. All the tanks and lakes here have had their banks breached by Mahindan’s soldiers. Because of that, agriculture is not proceeding as it should. There are not enough people to farm, either. The people of this land themselves are starving. How can our soldiers get food? Even from our own country, enough rice is not being sent…”

“Commander! I am well aware of this. When the Young Princess traveled through the valiant barracks of Pazhaiyarai, I heard the women complaining to her. ‘In Lanka, our husbands and sons are starving!’ they lamented…”
“Oh! So the complaints have reached there as well? Good, good! And what reply did the Young Princess give them?”
“The Commander-in-Chief Periya Velar is in Lanka; as long as he is there, he will not let our soldiers die of hunger. She told them not to worry and comforted them thus…”
“Ah! Did the Young Princess say so? In this world, many royal families have produced maidens of great renown. But there is no one to equal our Young Princess…”
“There is one other princess who might be mentioned next, Commander!”
“And who is that, young man?”
“The Princess Vanathi Devi of Kodumbalur!”
“Ah! This boy is truly incorrigible. His imagination might even enchant me. Young man! Did you see the light of our lineage in Pazhaiyarai?”

“I saw them, sir! How could I not, when the young princess and her companion are never apart? The two of them mounted the elephant together, just as the lamp cannot part from its light, the flower from its fragrance, or the body from its shadow—so too Vanathi Devi will never leave the young princess…”
“Ah! This boy is very clever! Thirumalai! Take him to our treasury, give him whatever garments and ornaments he desires, and bring him back!”
“Sir! Let everything remain in the treasury for now. When I return, I will collect what I need and take them with me.”
“Brother! About our household’s women, about Vanathi—did the young princess send me any message?”
“Commander! I do not wish to lie to you.”
“Never lie to anyone, at any time, brother!”
“In the matter of this Veera Vaishnavar, please grant me an exception, Commander; if I tell him the truth, my head will surely burst…”
“No, no!… It seems the young princess has not sent me any message!”
“She did not send you a message. But…”
“But what?”
“She has sent it to the one who ought to receive it. She has instructed me to convey certain matters about Vanathi Devi directly to the prince…”
“I have never seen a sharper lad than you!” exclaimed the Commander-in-Chief, Periya Velar, embracing Vandiyathevan to his chest. Then he said, “Enough of wasting time; set out at once!”
“Sir! Must this Veera Vaishnavar accompany me? Can I not go alone, without him?”
“What objection do you have to his coming?”

“I have no objection. But the dagger at my waist is a true Veerasaiva blade. For a long time, it has been thirsting for ‘Veera Vaishnava blood.’ If, against my will, it leaps out, he will be in grave danger, I fear.”

“In that case, leave that dagger here and take another one with you! If Thirumalai does not go with you, you will not be able to find the prince. No one knows where he is. Moreover, he too brings an important message to deliver to the prince. Therefore, it is best that the two of you go together! Do not quarrel with each other along the way and ruin the task!”
Having said this, the Periya Velar once again drew Vandiyathevan close and whispered secretly in his ear.
“Brother! He will not cause any hindrance to your mission. Even so, be cautious! Find out what message he delivers to the prince and come back to tell me!”
At first, Vandiyathevan had thought that Alwarkadiyan was being sent as a spy to follow him. Now, he felt that he himself was the spy. This situation pleased Vandiyathevan greatly.

That very night, Vandiyathevan and Alwarkadiyan, accompanied by two soldiers, set out on their journey. For two days, they traveled eastward. At first, the surroundings were rural, with a fair amount of people coming and going. Gradually, the landscape turned wilder. At first, it was a forest thick with small trees. Then, it transformed into dense woodlands where towering trees reached for the sky. Here and there, they saw lakes, but their banks had collapsed in many places. Water had flowed away in all directions, leaving the lakes dry. The fields lay uncultivated. In one place, a vast stretch of land was covered with stagnant water. It seemed that the banks of the Paalavi river had been breached, causing its waters to spill out and form these stagnant pools.

As they traveled, they took in all these sights. Alwarkadiyan explained to Vandiyathevan the devastation that the long war had brought upon this region. He often spoke of the cruelty of war. The two of them frequently debated this subject.

After two days, their direction changed. Having traveled east, they now turned south. The land grew denser as they went. The open plains gave way to rocks and small hills. Still... In the distance, great mountain ranges appeared, their peaks caressing the sky. The forests took on an increasingly fearsome aspect. Along with the sweet calls of birds, strange and terrifying sounds of unknown creatures mingled and rose.
Talk turned to the dangers that might arise from wild beasts in such jungle paths. Azhwarkkadiyan spoke of the presence of animals like jackals, leopards, bears, and elephants in those woods.
“If a pack of jackals comes upon us, wouldn’t that be dangerous?” Vandiyathevan asked, recalling the terrifying dream he had seen at the Kadambur palace.
“More dangerous than a pack of jackals is the howl of a lone jackal,” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
“How is that, Swami?”

“In these forests, jackals and leopards sometimes hunt together. The leopard will lie in wait here and there, while the jackal runs about searching for prey. If it spots a man, or a gentle animal like a deer, it will let out a single, piercing howl. At once, the leopard will leap forth and kill the prey. The jackal that serves as the leopard’s scout in this way is called an ‘Oori’…”
As they conversed thus, a sound like the roaring of the sea was heard from a short distance away.
“Have we come so far from the seashore? What is that sound?” Vandiyathevan asked.
“There must be a lake or a pond nearby. It sounds as if a herd of elephants is coming to drink water there!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
“Oh no! What if we get caught in the midst of an elephant herd…!”
“There is nothing to fear from that. Elephants that come in a herd will do us no harm. If we stand aside quietly, they will pass by without even glancing at us!”
Meanwhile, one of the soldiers accompanying them climbed up a tree and looked in all directions.
“Sir! Sir! A lone elephant is coming! A rogue elephant! It is breaking trees and wreaking havoc as it comes!” he shouted.
“Aiyo! What a calamity this is! How will we escape?” cried Azhwarkkadiyan in terror, glancing anxiously in all directions.
“You said there’s no need to fear a herd of elephants. Why, then, are you so afraid of a lone elephant?” asked Vandiyathevan.
“My lord! A single rogue elephant is equal to a thousand ordinary elephants. No one can stand before its fury and madness…”
“We three have spears in our hands. You have a stout staff as well!”
“Even a thousand spears cannot withstand a mad elephant. Look there! Do you see that steep hill? If we climb up, perhaps we might escape. Run!”

So saying, Azhwarkkadiyan dashed toward the hill. The others followed close behind. But after running a short distance, they saw before them a deep, precipitous ravine. The ravine lay between the spot where they stood and the hill a little further away. They halted at the edge of the chasm. The elephant was charging toward them at great speed. Perhaps the sight of humans had only increased its frenzy. As it raised its trunk and trumpeted, the sound was so thunderous that it seemed the very heavens would shatter. All four men clapped their hands over their ears and scattered in panic.

The elephant drew nearer and nearer, ever closer. It seemed to have fixed its sights on Azhwarkkadiyan, charging straight toward where he stood. A couple more steps and Azhwarkkadiyan would be forced to tumble into the abyss below. There was no easy way to run sideways either—the thickets and vines were too dense. Was escape even possible?
Vandiyathevan gripped his spear. But he felt that not even Indra’s thunderbolt could halt the charge of that maddened beast at this moment. His hand, clutching the spear, weakened and trembled.

At that instant, Azhwarkkadiyan’s actions struck Vandiyathevan as almost comical. Brandishing his staff, he shouted, “Stop! Stop right there! If you come any closer, you are lost! I’ll kill you, dig a pit, and bury you! Beware!”

Vandiyathevan did not immediately set out on the path shown by the Vaishnavite ascetic. He stood there for a while, gazing at the spot where the ascetic had disappeared into the darkness. The forest was silent, save for the occasional chirping of crickets and the distant hoot of an owl. The moonlight, filtered through the thick canopy of trees, cast strange, shifting shadows on the ground.

A gentle breeze rustled the leaves, carrying with it the fragrance of wild jasmine. Vandiyathevan’s heart was filled with a strange mixture of excitement and anxiety. The events of the night—his encounter with the mysterious woman in the palanquin, the sudden appearance of the Vaishnavite, and the cryptic words exchanged—played over and over in his mind.

He tightened his sword-belt and, after a moment’s hesitation, began to walk along the narrow path that wound through the dense undergrowth. The path was barely visible, overgrown with creepers and thorny bushes. Every now and then, he had to push aside low-hanging branches or step over fallen logs.

As he walked, the sounds of the forest seemed to grow louder—the rustle of small animals in the underbrush, the flutter of wings as birds settled down for the night, the distant roar of a tiger. Vandiyathevan’s keen eyes scanned the darkness, alert for any sign of danger.

After some time, the path began to slope downward. The air grew cooler, and the trees stood closer together, their trunks like silent sentinels in the moonlight. Vandiyathevan pressed on, his mind racing with thoughts of the messages he carried, the people he had met, and the dangers that lay ahead.

Suddenly, he heard a soft sound behind him—a twig snapping underfoot. He spun around, hand on his sword, but saw nothing but shadows. For a moment, he stood still, listening intently. The forest seemed to hold its breath.
Convinced that it was only a small animal, he continued on his way. But he could not shake the feeling that he was being watched, that unseen eyes were following his every move.

At last, the path emerged into a small clearing. In the center stood a massive banyan tree, its roots twisting and turning like the coils of a serpent. Vandiyathevan paused beneath its branches, taking a moment to catch his breath.

He looked up at the sky, now bright with stars, and wondered what fate awaited him on this perilous journey. The forest path stretched ahead, dark and mysterious, beckoning him onward into the unknown.

chapters.title: The Royal Road
paragraphs: Would a maddened elephant, roused to fury, ever pause for the waving staff or the shouts of Azhwarkkadiyan? Lifting its trunk high, it crashed through the shrubs and creepers that blocked its path, advancing ever closer. In the next instant, there could be no doubt what fate awaited Azhwarkkadiyan! The two soldiers who had come to his aid stood rooted to the spot, crying out, “Hai!” in alarm. Vandiyathevan, retrieving the spear that had slipped from his grasp and fallen to the ground, resolved to make one last desperate attempt.

At that very moment, Azhwarkkadiyan hurled his staff at the charging elephant. In the blink of an eye, Azhwarkkadiyan vanished from sight. His turban, caught by the wind, flew off and landed on a tree branch. Before Vandiyathevan could even wonder what had become of him, an even more momentous event occurred. The elephant, which had charged past the spot where Azhwarkkadiyan had disappeared, suddenly bent its forelegs and collapsed forward as if kneeling. A terrible, reverberating roar echoed through the forest. In the next moment, the massive form of the elephant was gone. It had rolled and tumbled into a deep chasm, sending up a cloud of dust and debris that billowed over the area.
It took Vandiyathevan a few moments to comprehend what had happened.

There had been a great pit behind Azhwarkkadiyan. When he threw his staff, the force of the motion made him lose his balance and fall backward into the pit. The maddened elephant, charging at him, had also set its forelegs into the chasm. Try as it might, it could not recover. The very weight of its mountainous body became its enemy, dragging it down into the abyss! In the same instant, both the crazed elephant and the man who had faced it—Azhwarkkadiyan—met the same fate, vanishing into the pit together!

As this realization struck Vandiyathevan, a shiver ran through his body. A deep sorrow welled up in his heart. All the suspicions he had once harbored against the Srivaishnavan had faded during their journey together, replaced by a sense of affection. Was this the end that awaited such a companion? The thought that he must now accomplish the task he had undertaken, without the help and guidance of Azhwarkkadiyan, filled him with anxiety.

Vandiyathevan approached the edge of the pit where both the Vaishnavan and the elephant had disappeared, and peered down into its depths. At first, there was nothing but a cloud of dust—nothing could be seen at all. As the dust slowly settled, the path the elephant had taken became clear: shrubs and creepers, rocks and stones, all lay crushed and scattered in its wake.

“What’s this, brother! Are you just going to stand there and watch the spectacle? Won’t you lend a hand?” The moment Vandiyathevan heard this voice, he was startled as if someone had given him a sudden jolt. Reeling with surprise, he turned toward the direction of the voice. Clinging to the exposed root of a tree at the edge of a steep rock face, right along the path where the elephant had fallen, hung Azhwarkkadian.
Can one even describe Vandiyathevan’s delight at this sight? At once, his playful spirit returned.
“Oh-ho! O Vaishnavite! After granting salvation only to Gajendra, have you decided to remain suspended in Trishanku’s heaven?” he called out, clapping his hands to summon the soldiers.

He quickly unwound the cloth girdle from around his waist and had two of the soldiers grip one end tightly. Dropping the other end down, Azhwarkkadian let go of the tree root and seized the cloth. The three of them, pulling together with all their might, slowly and carefully hauled the Vaishnavite up to safety.
For a while, Azhwarkkadian lay stretched out, gasping for breath, as if bereft of all awareness. The others stood around him, offering words of comfort.
Suddenly, he sat up and said, “Let’s move! We must reach Rajapattai before it gets completely dark. Where’s my head-cloth? Where’s my staff?”
“There’s no need to hurry. Rest a little longer, and then we’ll set out,” said Vandiyathevan.

Just then, the cry of a jackal echoed through the air. From another direction, a second jackal began its plaintive song. Soon, a hundred, two hundred jackals joined in a chorus. From the wooded hills above, down into the valley below, the sounds of furtive movement could be heard in many places. There was no need to say that the stealthy rustlings in the undergrowth were caused by leopards slipping through the brush. Over the valley, eagles and kites began to circle.

“The death of an elephant is no ordinary matter. From far and wide, beasts and birds that feed on flesh will soon arrive to feast upon the body of the great Gajendra. We too may become prey for them. Let us depart at once!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
Vandiyathevan did not object to his words now. The four of them hastened along the forest path as swiftly as they could. By the time dusk fell, they reached the royal highway.

The royal highway was abuzz with people coming and going, with carts and vehicles of every kind. Vandiyathevan was astonished to see people mounting elephants as if it were the most natural thing in the world. He wondered again and again, “Was it just one such beast that caused so much terror along the forest path?”
“Where does this royal highway lead? Where are we now? Where are we headed?” he asked.
“We have joined the royal highway that runs from Anuradhapura to Simhagiri. Tamballai is less than half a league away. We can reach there by nightfall,” replied Azhwarkkadiyan.
“Could we not have traveled comfortably along the royal highway? Why did we take the forest route?”

“Had we come all the way along the royal highway, we would have been stopped and questioned at a hundred places. In Anuradhapura, they would have detained us completely. I have learned that the person we seek has gone towards Simhagiri. That is why I chose the shortcut. Even now, will we find him, or not? Let us hope he has not gone elsewhere!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.

On either side of the royal highway stood numerous houses, villages, market streets, and the workshops of smiths and carpenters. The people who lived and worked there appeared, for the most part, to be Sinhalese. Across the royal highway, Chola warriors marched back and forth. Yet the Sinhalese who dwelt on both sides went about their trades fearlessly, without hindrance.
“To whom does this region now belong?” Vandiyathevan asked.
“The Chola army holds sway up to Tamballai. Beyond that, the Simhagiri hill and fortress remain under Mahindan’s control.”
“The people who live in these parts?”

“Mostly Sinhalese. Ever since ‘Ponniyin Selvan’ came here, the course of the war itself has changed. Now, only the Chola warriors and Mahindan’s soldiers fight each other—meaning, only when they meet on the battlefield. Otherwise, the common folk can live without fear. For the Buddhist monks, it’s a time of great celebration. Our prince has ordered that all the ruined Buddhist viharas in Anuradhapura be restored and rebuilt! Have you heard the story? Why wouldn’t the Buddhist monks rejoice? When I meet the prince, I’m going to tell him, ‘I do not like what you are doing, not in the least!’”
“Who is this prince to do things you don’t like? Has he grown horns on his head?” asked Vallavarayan.

“He hasn’t grown horns, my friend! That’s the truth! Yet, he possesses some mysterious power. No matter who criticizes him behind his back, the moment they stand before him, they become dazed and fall silent. No one has the strength to oppose the prince face to face. Such a power—the power to make the prince act according to one’s will—belongs to only one person…”
“Yes, yes! Who doesn’t know of the wondrous power of the valiant Vaishnavite Azhvarkadiyan? If he could defeat a raging mad elephant with just a staff, what is the prince to him!”

“You haven’t understood what I meant, brother! Where is Ponniyin Selvan, and where is this poor Vaishnavan? I might face a mad elephant with a staff; I might face tigers, bears, and lions with my bare hands. But when I stand face to face with Ponniyin Selvan, all my courage vanishes. My heart melts. My throat tightens. To get even a single word out of my mouth becomes a Herculean task…”
“Then who is the one who holds sway over him?”
“That’s something the whole world knows; don’t you? I’m talking about the young princess. The word of Kundavai Devi is as sacred to him as the Vedas!”
“Oh! You mean the young princess of Pazhayarai? I thought you were talking about your sister, the young queen of Pazhuvoor!”
“Nandini too possesses a rare power. But her power is of a different kind.”
“How so? What is the difference?”

“If a man is destined to fall into hell, Kundavai Devi possesses the power to halt his descent, lead him by the hand, and deliver him safely to heaven; that is one kind of strength. But do you know what Nandini would do? Her power must be said to surpass even that. She would convince him that hell itself is heaven, make him believe it, and induce him to leap joyfully into hell itself!”

A shiver ran through Vandiyathevan’s body. How astutely this valiant Vaishnavite has measured and weighed Nandini’s character and her fearsome, bewitching power! Can it truly be that she is his sister? Vandiyathevan was so lost in this thought that he did not ask anything further. They walked on in silence for a while.

That silence was broken by the sound of horses’ hooves. The noise came from ahead of them. In a few moments, four horses came galloping at full speed, kicking up clouds of dust like a whirlwind. In the blink of an eye, the horses swept past our travelers on foot. Yet, in that brief instant, Vandiyathevan managed to catch a glimpse of one of the riders’ faces and recognize him! Ah! Is it not Parthibendra Varman? The close confidant of Prince Aditya in Kanchi? The one who does not particularly favor us? Where has he come from, and where is he going? Why has he come to Lanka? When did he arrive?…

The horses that had passed the travelers soon came to a halt at a commanding voice that rang out, “Halt!” The horses stopped and then turned toward them. The one who appeared to be their leader rode forward, the others following behind. The man who came forward was, just as Vallavarayan had suspected, none other than Parthibendra Pallavan, whom they had met earlier at Mamallapuram.

After scrutinizing Vandiyathevan closely, he exclaimed, “What is this, my friend? How did you end up here? They said you had vanished suddenly from Thanjavur! I thought the Pazhuvettarayars must have finished you off!”
“Do you think the Pazhuvettarayars could dispose of me so easily? Am I not a scion of the ancient Vanar clan?”
“Yes, yes! When it comes to saving your own skin and escaping from danger, there is truly no one to match you…”

“Sir! When it is necessary to save my life, I know how to protect it. When the time comes to give up my life, I know how to do that as well. If I must die, I would rather die fighting against a descendant of the ancient Pallava clan like yourself, than perish at the mere hands of the Pazhuvettaraiyars!” Saying this, Vandiyathevan drew his sword from its sheath.
“Shame! Are you asking me to fight with you? And that too in this far-off land! No, brother, no! I have urgent matters to attend to! What of the task the prince entrusted to you?”
“I have completed it, sir! The letter he ordered me to deliver to the Emperor, I have handed over to him. The letter meant for the young princess, I have given to her as well!”
“Then why have you come here?”
“I have long harbored a desire to see Lanka. For that reason, I set out with this Vaishnavite…”
“Ah! I feel as though I have seen this man somewhere before!”
