This is the very throne upon which Dushtagamani the Emperor, Devanampiya Tissa, and Mahasena sat and were crowned. This is the crown that adorned their heads. This is the scepter they held in their hands. Such an ancient throne—one that has created kings for a thousand years—now awaits you. Is it your wish to ascend it, to wear this jeweled crown and hold this scepter?”

Vandiyathevan, who had been listening intently to all this, was seized by a great agitation. He wondered what would happen if, at that very moment, the prince were lifted and seated upon the throne. Yet, there was no change whatsoever in the prince’s expression. In the same calm voice as before, he replied, “Athiyatchaka! How can that be possible? King Mahinda, who ascended this throne and was crowned, is still alive, is he not? Though his whereabouts are unknown…”
He paused, leaving the sentence unfinished.

“Prince! It is the decree of the gods that the royal lineage of Lanka must change; it is destined to happen. In this dynasty, founded by King Vijaya who came from the land of Bengal where the Ganga flows, many great kings have arisen; they upheld dharma and ruled justly. But in later times, this lineage committed many heinous deeds and fell under the curse of the gods. In this dynasty, a father killed his son; a son killed his father; a younger brother killed his elder; an elder killed his younger; a mother killed her daughter; a daughter-in-law killed her mother-in-law. The gods have decreed that those born into such a sinful line are unworthy to uphold the dharma of the Buddha. At last, King Mahinda, who was crowned, has lost his claim to the throne of Lanka. Now, as the royal lineage is to change, the right to choose the first ruler of the new dynasty belongs to this Sangha. The members of this Sangha wish to choose you. If you consent, the coronation ceremony can be held tonight itself…”

For a moment, a silence as deep as that of the earth’s core or the ocean’s depths settled upon the hall. Vandiyathevan’s excitement had reached its peak. At that moment, Ponniyin Selvan rose from his seat and bowed in reverence to the assembly of Buddhist monks. Vandiyathevan’s joy knew no bounds. He was so eager that he wished the prince would ascend the throne at once and crown himself with the jeweled diadem.

The prince spoke: “Great ones! I bow to you. I honor and revere your magnanimity in placing boundless love and trust in this young man and offering him this ancient throne. Yet, the task you now place before me is beyond my strength. I was born and raised in the land of Cholas. The food grown in that soil, the water from its rivers, have shaped this body. I have come here under the command of my father, Emperor Sundara Chola. Without knowing his will, I cannot do anything…”
A monk interrupted: “Prince! Do you not know that your father, Sundara Chola, is today as if imprisoned, deprived of his freedom?”

“Yes; my father is ill and bedridden. He has lost the use of his legs. Yet, by his name, by the authority I have received from him, I am bound to obey the commands of those who rule the Chola land. If I accept this throne without their order, I would be a traitor to my country and to my king…”
“If that is your wish, we are prepared to send a delegation to Thanjavur. Your father is deeply devoted to the Buddhist dharma. He will not refuse our request.”
“The people of this land exist. Without their consent, who has the right to divide the kingdom?”
“The people of this land would consider it a rare blessing to have you as their king…”

“Let everyone agree; let them rejoice. Yet, in this world, there is no one’s wish I value more than my elder sister’s. My mother gave me birth; the Ponni river saved my life. But it was my sister who nurtured my intellect and opened my inner eyes. Even so, above her wish, there is a command from a voice within my heart that I hold supreme. Noble ones! The voice within does not tell me to accept the great fortune you so graciously offer this young man! I beg you, please forgive this youth!…”
Once again, silence settled over that great assembly for a while. Vandiyathevan could hear the furious pounding of his own pulse echoing in his ears.

After a moment, the chief of the Bhikshu Sangha spoke: “Prince! Your reply does not surprise me; in fact, I expected it. This is why you are the most worthy among all to ascend the throne of Lanka. For those of us who understand the subtlety of dharma, there is no doubt about this. Yet, we do not wish to compel you. We grant you time to consider. A year from now, on a day like this, we will send for you again. Then, come and declare your final decision!… Only one thing must remain in your memory. In this ancient Anuradhapura, many Buddhist viharas have been destroyed by the cruelty of war. But this Maha Bodhi Vihara alone has remained untouched. This is because it is built deep beneath the earth. The path to this place is known only to the leaders of the Buddhist Sangha presently gathered here. No one can come here without one of us to guide them. The kings of Lanka are summoned here only once in their lives, to be crowned by the Buddhist Sangha. Such is the sanctity and secrecy of this vihara. You must not speak to anyone outside about your coming here, your departure, or anything that happened here. Your friends must not speak of it either. If you do, you will incur the most severe divine curse!”

“Athiyatchaka! There is no need for an oath; I have already promised that I would not reveal this to anyone outside, and only after giving that word did I bring my friends here. I shall never break the promise I have given,” said Ponniyin Selvan.

Half an hour later, Prince Arulmozhi Varman, Azhwarkadiyan, and Vandiyathevan were walking along the moonlit streets of Anuradhapura. While they were inside the vihara, Vandiyathevan had kept his mouth tightly shut, but now, as they walked outside, he let loose all the thoughts he had restrained.

“Chola Nadu! It is indeed a land blessed with water and fertile soil. But it cannot compare to this Lanka. You have just kicked away the throne of such a secretive and wondrous island! What folly is this? And what can one say of the wisdom of those monks who came to offer you the jeweled crown? And as for me, I stood there like a pillar! Could they not have given it to me instead?” Thus did he grumble and mutter to himself.
The prince tried to console him. “Did I not tell you that Dushthagamanu’s son, Sali, gave up the kingdom of Lanka for the love of a woman named Asokamala? Did that not reach your ears?”
“I heard it all. But then, which woman do you love? Who is the woman who stands in the way of you ascending the throne?” asked Vandiyathevan.
“It is not one woman, but two. Truth and righteousness—Satyam and Dharmam—are the two women I love. For their sake, I refused the jeweled crown of Lanka.”
“Prince, to look at you, you seem so young. But your words are those of an old man.”
“Who among us knows who is truly old, whose time is nearly at an end?” As they spoke thus, they were passing near an old mansion at the edge of the street.
From the opposite side of the road, the sound of someone clapping their hands was heard. At the spot where the sound came from, a figure was standing.
“Come this way!” said the prince, and, turning toward the figure, he crossed the street.

The others continued on their way. As they were halfway across the street, a loud crashing noise sounded from behind; they turned to look. The front façade of the upper story of the house they were passing had collapsed and was falling down!
Had they not turned back to cross the street at that very moment, it would have fallen directly upon their heads and killed them!

In the difference of a single moment, three lives were spared. And what lives they were! How true were the words spoken by Ponniyin Selvan: “Who among us knows when our time will come?” As Vandiyathevan stood in the middle of the street, pondering this, the other two had already gone ahead.
When Vandiyathevan approached them again, the figure standing there was clearly visible in the moonlight. For a moment, he doubted his own eyes—should he believe what he saw before him, or not?
“What madness is this? How can this be possible?”
“How could Nandini, whom I saw in the palace of the Pazhuvettaraiyar at Thanjai, have come here to this street in Anuradhapura? Why would she be standing here in the dead of night?”
The next instant, that figure vanished like a phantom. Only the other two remained standing.

chapters.title: Is Merit Valued?
paragraphs: Vandiyathevan strode swiftly toward the spot where the prince and ‘Nandini’ stood.

But before he could reach them, a doubt crept into his mind. Is this truly Nandini? She wears none of the garments or ornaments befitting the Lady of Pazhuvoor! She is clad in the simplest attire, almost like a mendicant woman. The face resembles Nandini’s, yet there is some difference. What is it?

As Vandiyathevan approached the place where they had stood, the woman moved away and vanished into the shadows cast by the houses along the street. In a flurry, Vandiyathevan tried to follow her, but the prince caught his hand and stopped him.
“Sir! Who is that lady? She seemed familiar!” he exclaimed.

At that moment, Azhwarkadiyan arrived and said, “That lady must be the guardian goddess of the Chola land. Look there! Had we not moved from that spot in time, we would now be at the feet of Lord Buddha himself!”

They looked where Thirumalai pointed. The upper part of a building had collapsed, forming a mound like a small hill. Even a young elephant would have been crushed and unable to escape from beneath that heap. What chance would three mere men have had?
“It was at the right moment that our clan’s goddess appeared and beckoned us away,” said Ponniyin Selvan.
“Prince! Who was that lady?” Vandiyathevan asked in astonishment.
“Who did you think she was? Why did you try so hard to follow her?” the prince asked in return.
“This Vaishnavite said she was the guardian goddess of the Cholas; but to me, she seemed like the goddess who has brought ruin upon the Chola clan.”
“If that is so… whom do you think she is?”

“Perhaps it is only my delusion, but I thought she was Nandini Devi, the young wife of Pazhuvettaraiyar. Did she not seem so to either of you?” asked Vandiyathevan. “I did not see clearly. Still, it must have been a trick of your imagination. How could the Lady of Pazhuvoor have come here?” said Azhwarkadiyan.

“What he says is not entirely a figment of imagination. There is some illusion of the eyes mixed in as well. Even I have, at times, felt there was an astonishing resemblance in that face… Come! Let us walk and talk!” said the prince.
Instead of walking in the shadows cast by the houses along the street, the three of them now began to walk in the middle of the road, bathed in moonlight.
After a short distance, Azhwarkadiyan asked, “Prince! What did that lady say when she beckoned you with her hand?”
“She said that two enemies have come searching for me. She warned that they are waiting for the right moment to kill me.”
“Alas! Could it be that she was speaking about us?” Vandiyathevan asked, startled.

Ponniyin Selvan laughed and replied, “No, she did not specifically say it was you. Even if it were, there is no need to worry. That goddess has declared my life to be a charmed one! Many times before, she has saved me!”
“Sir! I know who those two enemies are. They are the ones who came searching for you along with Parthibendra Pallavan. I saw two figures in the ruined palace. It must be them!” said Thirumalai.
“Sir! Vaishnavite! Why did you not say this earlier? You go on ahead. I will go and investigate that ruined house and return!” said Vandiyathevan, turning to leave.

The prince caught his hand and stopped him again. “There is no need to hurry. It would not be possible to find them in that deserted house. We can look into it later. Until I give further orders, you must stay with me, do you understand? Who knows what dangers may be lurking in the corners and shadows of this ruined city? O brave lion among warriors! Was it not because I trust you that I have not called anyone else for my protection? If you leave me alone in the middle of the street like this, what am I to do?” he said.
Those words intoxicated Vandiyathevan. His voice quivered as he said, “Sir! From this moment, I shall not leave your side, not even for a single instant!”
Azhwarkkadiyan replied, “Nor shall I leave you. You are the shield for the prince; I am the shield for you.”

After a short while, the three of them reached the inner quarters of the ruined palace of Mahasen Chakravarthi. In a spacious chamber, beds had been spread out for all three on ancient cots from days gone by. They lay down to rest. Through the slatted windows in one wall, the moonlight crept in, peering curiously into the room.

“Many hundreds of years ago, in this very palace, in this very spot, the emperors and princes of Lanka, along with their royal consorts, must have lain down to sleep. Even then, the rays of the moon would have reached in through these same slats, peeking inside. Now, these moonbeams must feel disappointed to find only ordinary men like us lying here, mustn’t they, Vandiyathevan?” said Arulmozhi Varman.
“Sir! Say whatever you wish about yourself and this Vaishnavite here. But please, do not call me an ordinary man!” protested Vallavaraiyan.
“Ah, I forgot; forgive me. Are you not a young prince born of the ancient line of the Vallathar rulers?”
“Yes, sir, yes! If you heard a poem composed about one of my ancestors, this valiant Vaishnavite would die writhing in envy!”

“Let him die, then! Thirumalai is a true lover of Tamil. Like Nandivarman of the Pallava clan, he would not hesitate to give his life for the sake of Tamil poetry. So, recite the poem; let us hear it.”
With some hesitation, Vallavaraiyan recited the following verse:
“My helmet is my palanquin

“My armor, my banner, My elephant, my horse— They are mine, they are mine, They cry—O poet! O king of kings, O Vaanan, Who bestows gifts in order, You have given the poets What the kings brought you!”
Hearing this, Ponniyin Selvan said, “Thirumalai, you have become a Tamil poet yourself! Tell me, what is the meaning of this song?”

“Sir! It seems you are testing me. Very well, I shall explain: At the palace gates of the great king Vaanan, many minor kings waited for royal audience. They did not easily gain an audience, for the poets—the bards—had already entered the palace. The emperor, delighted by their songs, bestowed gifts upon them and sent them away. He gave them parasols adorned with the royal emblem, ivory palanquins, pearl-studded armor, jeweled banners, elephants, horses, and many other kinds of gifts. The minor kings waiting at the entrance, seeing these gifts, were consumed with envy and lamented, ‘Alas! Is that not my parasol? Is that not my palanquin? Is that not my elephant? Is that not my horse? These wretched poets are carrying them away!’ The emperor was giving as rewards to the poets the very gifts that the minor kings had brought to him as tributes. Prince! Is that not the meaning of the song?”

“How could there be any error in what you say! Ah, what a marvelous song! What a delightful imagination! No one knows who composed this great poem! O jewel of the Vaanar clan! Vandiyathevan! Whether your ancestors’ kingdom was great or small, it does not matter. They have received such a song—what greater honor could they want? You, born in their lineage, are indeed worthy to rest in this palace! Why only the bed of the Mahasenar? If the very bed on which the mighty emperor Dushthagamanu once slept were available now, you could sleep upon it. You are truly worthy of it!”

“Yes, sir! Yes! I am indeed worthy of anything. But in these days, who gives any value to worthiness? Did those bhikshus offer me the crown of this Lanka kingdom? Did they offer it to you, who would have refused it? Do you know how angry I was at that moment? I even thought of snatching the crown and placing it on my own head! But I stayed quiet, thinking this valiant Vaishnavar would come forward to claim it!”

Hearing this, Arulmozhi Varman burst into hearty laughter. The sound of his laughter filled Vandiyathevan’s heart with joy. Outwardly, he feigned more anger and said, “Is everything solved just by laughing? What is the atonement for the mistake you made?”
“Sir! Jewel of the Vanara clan! I swore upon truth and dharma, did I not? Do you not consider those good enough reasons for refusing the throne?”
“I already had some doubts about truth and dharma. Now I have decided never to look upon their faces again, never to have anything to do with them.”
“Oh, is that so? Why? What made you decide so? Why are you angry with them?”

“I am not angry. Did you not say that you are in love with those maidens named Truth and Dharma? Did you not say you renounced the Lanka kingdom for their sake? I do not even think in my heart about women loved by others!”
Ponniyin Selvan laughed aloud again. “I have never seen a jester like you!” he said.

“Yes, sir! It is amusing to you. But my stomach burns. If you did not want the throne of Lanka, I was standing right there, was it not your duty to point to me and say, ‘Give it to him!’?” said Vandiyathevan.

After Arulmozhi Varman finished laughing, he said, “Vandiyathevar! Is accepting a kingdom such an easy matter? Especially, it is not proper to accept it when offered by Buddhist bhikshus. Later, it will lead to great disasters. Religious leaders must confine themselves to religious matters. If religious leaders interfere in royal affairs, it will bring ruin to both religion and the kingdom. Moreover, the Buddhist bhikshus who came to offer me the throne today are not the leaders of all Buddhists in this land. They are the leaders of a single sect. Just as there are many sanghas like theirs…” “There are two factions. If we hand over the kingdom to these people, we must rule according to their wishes. The other two factions will immediately become our enemies!” he said.
“Does the Prince of Vallam now understand the situation here?” asked Azhwarkkadiyan.
“I understand, I understand! Just as there are fools who quarrel over whether Vishnu or Shiva is greater, there are such people here too!” replied Vandiyathevan.
“Please don’t start a quarrel here. It is already very late at night. Listen, you can hear the sound of people dispersing from the Perahara procession. Now we can get some sleep,” said the Prince.
“I cannot sleep. Only if I find out who that lady was—she who clapped her hands in the middle of the street and called us, and saved us from being entombed alive—only then will sleep come to me.”
“I do not yet know who she is either. But if you wish, I can tell you what I know about her. If you want to hear, come and sit beside me!” said the Prince.

chapters.title: Kaveri Amman
paragraphs: Vandiyathevan and Azhwarkadiyan rose eagerly and sat down on the floor beside the prince’s cot. The prince began to speak as follows:

“When I was a small boy, there was an occasion when I was traveling with my parents in a boat on the Kaveri river. My elder brother and my sister were also in the boat at that time. They were engaged in conversation about something or other. I alone was watching the swirling flow of the Kaveri’s waters, and how, now and then, some kadamba flowers would get caught in those eddies and spin around. Seeing those tiny flowers trapped and struggling in the whirls caused me pain. Sometimes, I would lean over the side of the boat and rescue the struggling kadamba flowers from the water’s grip. On one such occasion, as I was reaching out, I lost my balance and fell into the river. Since I fell headfirst, I was completely disoriented and floundered helplessly!

“I still remember the sensation of my head striking the sandy bottom of the Kaveri. Then I recall the swift current pushing and dragging me along. From somewhere far away, I seemed to hear the shouts and cries of many people. I began to suffocate. I thought, ‘Well, the Kaveri river is going to carry me away and cast me into the sea.’ The thought struck me of how much pain my parents, my sister, and my brother would feel if they could not find me. At that moment, it felt as if someone scooped me up with both arms and embraced me. In the next instant, I surfaced above the water. Water was streaming from my head, eyes, nose, and mouth. Yet, I could clearly see the hands that had lifted and saved me. Then I saw the face of the one to whom those hands belonged. Though it was only for a few moments, that face became imprinted in my mind. It seemed as though I had seen that face somewhere before. But I could not tell who it was.

“After that, those hands handed me over to someone else. In the next moment, I was back in the boat. My mother, father, sister, and brother all surrounded me. Their sorrow, their concern, their love, and their support completely absorbed my attention. Only after a little while did the question arise—who was it that had lifted me out of the water and saved me? They asked one another; they asked me as well. I looked all around. That divine face was nowhere to be seen. So, unable to answer their question, I remained silent. In the end, everyone agreed that it must have been Kaveri Amman herself who saved me. They resolved that I must have been saved. From the day I survived falling into the river, every year they arranged for a special puja to Kaveri Amman. Yet, only my mind remained unsatisfied. Whether it was truly Kaveri Amman who saved me, or some other mortal woman, the face of that savior had been etched into my heart, and a longing to behold that divine visage once more took root within me. Whenever I went near the banks of the Kaveri, I would look around with the hope, “Will that goddess suddenly rise from the waters and appear before me?” As the days passed, the thought grew stronger in me that she might have been a mortal woman after all. Therefore, whenever I attended any festival, it became my habit to closely observe the faces of all the elderly women gathered there, searching with keen interest. After some time, I realized that such searching was not a good habit. As the years went by, I gradually lost the desire to see that divine face again.

“About a year ago, I came here as the commander of our southern forces. Even before that, Senapathi Boothi Vikrama Kesari had captured many regions of Lanka. This Anuradhapura had changed hands several times, and at that time, it was again under the control of Mahindan’s forces. Our soldiers had laid siege to the city. While the siege was ongoing, I wished to travel and learn about various parts of Lanka. The Senapathi sent a thousand chosen warriors with me. We traveled to all the regions under our army’s control, leaving no forest, hill, or river unexplored, and I became well acquainted with the nature of each region. You must know that, surrounding the island of Lanka, there are many small islets in the sea. I visited those islands as well.

During these travels, once, to the north of this city, we camped in the midst of a forest, several leagues away. Near our camp was a place called ‘Yaanai Iravu’—the Elephant Crossing. There, the eastern and western seas of Lanka come very close and join through a narrow canal. Through that crossing, herds of elephants sometimes travel to the northern parts of Lanka. That is how the place got its name, ‘Yaanai Iravu.’ While we were camped there, a strange incident occurred. At night, near the camp, a wailing voice was heard. At first, it was unclear whether it was the voice of a human, a bird, or a beast; but it carried a sorrow so deep that it sent shivers through those who heard it.

At first, the soldiers stationed at the edge of the camp heard it. They ignored it. Later, the sound was heard in several places around the encampment. Some came and told me about it. I paid it no mind. ‘Are you afraid of ghosts and spirits? If so, return home and rest in your mother’s lap—’ “Sleep without fear!” I said. This seemed to anger them.

They resolved to find out whether that wailing voice was human, animal, or some spirit. They ran towards the direction from which the cry had come and looked around. As they drew near, the figure responsible for the voice began to run. It appeared to be a woman’s form. But they could not catch her. Even after that, the wailing did not cease; it continued to be heard at intervals.

“At first, I paid it no particular attention. But soon, my soldiers had no other topic of conversation. In truth, some of them became almost delirious with fear. Because of this, I decided to unravel the mystery. One night, following the direction of the cry, I set out with a few of my men. From behind a thicket, a woman’s figure emerged. For a moment, she stood there, startled, looking at us. Then she began to run again. A voice within me said that if we all pursued her together, we would never be able to catch her. So I told the others to stop and wait, and I alone continued the chase.

“At one point, the figure turned and looked back. Seeing that I was coming alone, she waited as if to welcome me. Now, even I felt a shiver of fear. For a moment, I hesitated. Then, gathering my courage, I went forward and approached the womanly form. The moonlight fell clearly upon her face. A divine smile blossomed there. In that instant, memory returned to me. This was Kaveri Amman herself! The divine maiden who had saved me from being swept away by the flood! For a while, I gazed at her face, as if in a trance. Then I cried out, ‘Mother! Who are you? When did you come here? Why have you come? I have been searching for you for so long! If you wished to see me, why not come directly to me? Why do you circle around this camp? Why do you wail so?’

“That maiden gave no reply. No matter how many times I asked, it was of no use. After a little while, her eyes began to brim with tears. Those tears tore at my heart. It seemed as if she was trying to say something. But no words came out. Only an inarticulate sound emerged from her throat. Then, suddenly, I understood. She was mute, unable to speak. Never before had I felt such anguish as I did at that moment. Not knowing what to do, I stood there, helpless.

“That woman suddenly embraced me and kissed my forehead. Her tears fell upon my head. Immediately, in the very next moment, she let go of me and ran away. She did not look back. I did not try to follow her.

“When I returned to the camp, my anxious soldiers crowded around me and asked—‘She—’” It was neither a ghost nor a demon; merely an ordinary woman! Some great sorrow in her life had driven her to a state of mental delusion. I sternly commanded, “If she comes again, do not follow her or trouble her further.”

All the next day, the thought kept recurring to me—should I take the horse and leave that place at once? Yet, I could not come to a decision. Deep within, there lingered a hope that perhaps that woman might return. Lost in such thoughts, the day passed; night arrived. My expectations were not in vain. Near the thicket, that plaintive voice was heard again. I told the other soldiers not to follow me, and set off alone towards the place from where the voice came.
The same mysterious woman greeted me with a smile, just as she had on the first day. For a while, she gazed intently at me. She tried to say something, but I could not understand.

Then she took my hand and led me away. I felt not the slightest hesitation in following her. As we walked through the forest path, she gently pushed aside the thorny branches so they would not touch me—this gesture stirred my heart. After a short distance, a hut came into view. Inside, a small earthen lamp flickered. In that light, I saw an old man lying down. I realized he was ill. His whole body trembled as if from an unbearable cold. At times, his body would jerk and shudder. His teeth were clenched tight. His eyes, red and burning like embers, glared fiercely. He was muttering incoherent words…

Do you remember? Today, in the subterranean cave, at the Maha Bodhi Vihara, we saw a bhikshu shivering, did we not? They said the gods had possessed him, did they not? At that moment, I remembered the old man I had seen in the forest hut. I wondered—was it truly the gods who had possessed that bhikshu, or was it the dreadful fever of chills that had seized him? I did not bring it up. Why should I? Why should I destroy the faith of those devotees? By granting permission for this Perahara festival to be held this year, I feel I have committed a grave mistake. If this ancient city, already more than half in ruins, is now struck by the fever of chills, what will become of it? The remaining people too will be forced to flee…

Thus speaking, Arulmozhi Varma sank into deep thought. After waiting a moment, Vandiyathevan pressed him, “Ayya! Let the matter of this city be for now. What happened next in the hut? Please tell me!”

“Nothing happened in the hut; it seemed that the lady thought I should not remain there for long. At once, she seized my hand and drew me outside. Then, through a few gestures, she conveyed what she wished to say. My heart understood what she meant to communicate. ‘You must not stay in this region. If you remain here, you will be struck by this fever of chills. Take the elephant and leave this place at once!’—this was what she told me through her signs, and made me understand. I realized that it was only out of her boundless affection for me that she gave this warning. I took it as a divine caution, and that very night ordered the elephant to be moved from there. My soldiers who were with me were also delighted by this. They were relieved at the thought that they would no longer have to hear that dreadful howling voice…”

chapters.title: When Paintings Speak
paragraphs: The prince abruptly halted his tale and asked, “Did either of you hear the sound of footsteps?”
His two companions, who had been listening with rapt attention, replied that they had heard nothing.
After a moment’s pause, Azhwarkkadiyan said, “The place where we are sitting now feels warmer than before!”
“There’s even a faint smell of smoke!” said Vandiyathevan.
“Sir! There’s no danger in this place, is there?” Azhwarkkadiyan asked anxiously.
“If there were any danger, Kaveri Amman herself would surely come and warn us. Do not worry!” said the prince, and continued his story.

“We left that place at once, spurring our horses forward. Even so, ten of our soldiers were struck down with fever. Ah, that fever is a terrible thing. It can turn even the bravest warrior into a coward. Men who would not flinch from wounds in battle, after three days of fever, would lose heart and begin to say, ‘I must return home.’ I believed it was Durga Parameswari, the guardian goddess of the Cholas, who came in the form of that mute woman and made us leave that place. Even after that, the goddess did not abandon me. Wherever I went, she continued to follow me. Wild beasts, mountain serpents, hidden enemies—she protected me from all such dangers. She would appear suddenly, and vanish just as suddenly. In a few days, I gained the power to converse with that goddess through expressions and gestures. Most of the time, whatever she thought in her heart, my own heart would come to know. Not only that; even without seeing her with my eyes, I would sense where she was nearby. Even now… Well, enough. You both go at once and lie down in your beds. Even if sleep does not come, pretend to sleep! Quickly!” said the prince. In this manner, the two of them lay down to sleep. They tried to close their eyes. But the eagerness that possessed them refused to let their eyelids shut.

As they watched, a figure appeared near the moonlit balcony. It was the same woman they had seen earlier, standing opposite the ruined mansion on the street. A very soft “hush” sound came from her. Arulmozhi Varman rose and went to the edge of the balcony. The figure standing outside made some sign. The prince pointed towards his companions who were lying in the room. In the language of gestures, some reply was given to that as well.

Immediately, Arulmozhi Varman told his two friends to follow him and left the mansion. The three of them walked silently along the path the old woman took. On either side, trees grew thick, shrouding the path in darkness. After they had walked a considerable distance, suddenly, in the moonlight, they beheld a wondrous sight. Huge black elephants stood in rows, guarding a magnificent stupa. At the sight, Vandiyathevan felt as if his breath had stopped. But the old woman, without the slightest hesitation, walked towards the group of elephants. Only when Alwarkadiyan, leaning close to Vandiyathevan, whispered, “Did you see how lifelike those elephant statues are?” did Vandiyathevan’s astonishment subside. Yet his sense of wonder did not leave him.

The elephant statues stood close together, as if supporting the mountain-like stupa. Each one had two long tusks. Among the hundreds of elephants standing in such a row, only one had a broken tusk. The old woman went near that elephant. She removed a large black stone lying at its feet. Beneath it, a staircase was revealed. She descended by that way, and the others followed her. After going a short distance along a narrow passage, they came upon a mandapam. In it, two large oil lamps were burning.

The old woman took one of the lamps and held it in her hand. With a gesture, she indicated that only the prince should come with her. At first, the other two were a little concerned about this. But when they saw that the old woman was merely showing the prince the paintings on the walls of the mandapam, their worry lessened somewhat.

The pictures that the prince saw on the walls of that hall appeared to be a series of paintings narrating, in sequence, the events of some story. Much like the manner in which the previous incarnations of Lord Buddha are depicted in the Buddhist viharas, these paintings too were arranged. But these did not portray the incarnations of Buddha. Instead, they depicted the story of a mortal woman. The features of the woman in those paintings closely resembled the face of the old woman now holding the lamp and showing him the way. Thus, the prince easily understood that this mute woman had painted her own life story upon these walls.

The first painting showed a young woman standing alone on an island surrounded by the sea, while her father returned from fishing, riding a raft. Next, the woman was shown walking through the forest. Upon the branch of a tree, a young man sat—he looked like a royal prince. A bear was climbing up that very tree. The prince, unaware, was looking off in another direction. The woman screamed and ran. The bear chased after her. The young man leapt down from the tree and hurled his spear at the bear. A fierce battle ensued between the bear and the youth. The woman, leaning against a coconut tree, watched the fight between the bear and the young man. At last, the bear fell dead. The youth approached the woman and expressed his gratitude to her. But she, without replying, wept silently. Afterwards, she ran and brought her father. The fisherman explained to the youth that his daughter was mute and could not speak. The prince was saddened at first, but soon his sorrow faded, and he befriended her. He plucked wildflowers from the forest, wove them into a garland, and placed it around her neck. The two wandered hand in hand through the woods.

One day, a great ship approached the island. Many warriors disembarked from it. They found the royal prince and paid him their respects. They entreated him to return with them to the ship. The prince comforted the woman, bade her farewell, and boarded the vessel. After he left, the woman was overcome with grief and wept bitterly. Her father saw her sorrow. He placed her in a boat and crossed the sea. They reached a lighthouse on the shore and disembarked. There, a family welcomed the father and daughter. All together, they boarded a bullock cart and set out on a journey. They arrived at a city within the fortress walls. On the upper terrace of the palace, the royal prince stood, a crown upon his head. Many, adorned in splendid garments and ornaments, surrounded him. Seeing this, the young woman's heart was troubled. She ran away at once, reached the seashore, climbed to the top of the lighthouse, and leapt down. The waves bore her up. In a boat... A man who came lifted her up, placed her in a boat, and saved her. Thinking she was possessed by a spirit, he took her to a temple. The temple priest applied sacred ash to her and struck her with neem leaves.

One day, a great queen came to that temple to have darshan of the deity. The priest told the queen about this woman. The queen was pregnant. She learned that this woman too was with child, just like herself. She had her brought in a palanquin to the palace.

In the palace garden, that woman gave birth to two children. The queen came and declared that she would raise one of the children as her own. At first, the fisherwoman refused. Then, after thinking it over, she decided that both children should be raised in the palace. Leaving the children behind, she slipped away in the dead of night, telling no one.

For a long time, she wandered in the forests. Yet, the desire to see her children would often overcome her. She would come to the riverbank and hide behind the trees. The king, queen, and children would come by boat. She would watch from afar and then leave.

Once, one of the children accidentally fell from the boat. No one noticed. She plunged into the water and rescued the child. At once, she disappeared again, diving into the floodwaters of the river, reaching the opposite bank, and vanishing into the forest.

All these events were depicted on that wall as vivid paintings, drawn with ochre lines, as if they were living images. Prince Arulmozhi gazed at these paintings with boundless curiosity and wonder. When he reached the last painting, the prince pointed to it and, by gesture, indicated, "The boy who was saved from the river is me; the one who saved me is you!"
The old woman embraced the prince tightly and kissed his forehead.

Afterwards, she led the prince to another corner of the hall. There, she showed him some other paintings. These did not depict events from her own life. Through these paintings and her gestures, she warned the prince of dangers that might befall him.

Vandiyathevan and Alwarkadiyan, standing at the edge of the hall, had witnessed all this. Vandiyathevan often compared Nandini’s face with that of this mute woman; many thoughts arose in his mind, many doubts took shape. But he felt this was not the time to speak of them, so he remained silent.

They all emerged from the secret chamber guarded by elephant statues. The old woman led them onward. She climbed towards the summit of the stupa. Others marveled at her physical strength. Vandiyathevan was extremely weary. Yet, without showing it outwardly, he climbed as well.
When they had ascended halfway up the stupa, they paused and looked around. In one corner of the city, the flames of a fire were leaping high, burning fiercely.
“Ah! The ancient palace of Mahasena Chakravarthi is ablaze!” said the prince.
“The very place where we lay down to rest?”
“That’s the one!”
“If we had been sleeping there now…?”
“We too might have become food for the god of fire!”
“How can you say from this distance that it is the palace where we slept?”
“The paintings I saw inside the hall spoke to me.”
“We didn’t hear anything!”
“There’s nothing surprising in that. Paintings speak in a language of their own. Only those who know that language can understand their speech.”
“What else did those paintings reveal to you?”
“They told me many secrets about my family. They also urged me to leave this island of Lanka at once!…”
“Long live the language of the paintings! Vaishnavar! My side has won!” exclaimed Vandiyathevan.

“Prince! The paintings did not stop there. Did they not also say, ‘As long as you are in Lanka, do not sleep beneath a roof. Do not walk along the edges of houses. Do not go beneath trees’?” said Azhwarkadiyan.
“You have spoken truly! How did you know?”
“You know the language of paintings. I know the language of gesture. While your family deity was conversing with you, I was observing the deity’s expressive gestures!” said Azhwarkadiyan.
“Happiness! There is still a yāma left in the night. Let us climb to the top of this stupa, lie down and sleep for a while, and set out at dawn,” said Arulmozhi Varman.

At sunrise the next day, the sharp rays of the sun struck Vandiyathevan and woke him from his sleep. The true events of the first night had not been enough; in his dreams, conspirators, arsonists, mutes, the deaf, tree-climbing bears, ghosts and demons, Buddhist monks, and jeweled crowns all came together in a whirlwind of confusion to torment him. But in the sunlight, all those things faded away like illusions in a dream. The confusion and fear vanished.

Vandiyathevan saw that the prince and Azhwarkadiyan had already risen and were preparing for the journey. He too hurriedly made himself ready. The three of them descended from the summit of the stupa. Walking through the central streets, they made their way towards the Mahāmegavana. In the center of that ancient grove stood the sacred Bodhi tree, more than a thousand and five hundred years old.
Monks and lay devotees alike were circumambulating the Bodhi tree, showering it with flowers and offering their worship. Prince Arulmozhi Varman also paid his respects to the Bodhi tree.
“Kingdoms and the kings who ruled them may vanish from this world. But Dharma will endure forever—this Bodhi tree stands as living proof of that!” the prince said, turning to the other two.
As he spoke, he looked around. In one corner, three horses stood ready for the journey, each held by a man standing beside it.
As the prince approached, the three men greeted him with beaming faces and respectful bows. The prince spoke to them, asking questions and learning what he needed.

Turning to Vandiyathevan, he said, “It was the Mahāsēna palace where we slept last night that burned! These men were afraid we had perished in the fire. Now, seeing us alive, their joy knows no bounds!”
“It may be true that the thousand-and-five-hundred-year-old Bodhi tree still stands. But Dharma has been dead and gone for many a day!” said Vandiyathevan.
“Never say such a thing again! As long as I draw breath, how can Dharma die?” declared Azhwarkadiyan.

The three of them mounted their horses and set off. They exited through the northern gate of Anuradhapura city. Since the festival crowds were still streaming in all directions from the city, shouting “Jai Jai,” no one paid them any attention.

To the northeast of Anuradhapura, at a short distance, there was a small town called Mahindalai. “It was here that Prince Mahinda, son of Emperor Ashoka, first set foot and began to preach the Buddhist faith! What a fortunate soul he was! He did not go about bearing arms, leading armies to conquer lands. He never had the need to hide and wander in fear of murderers!” said Arulmozhi Varman.
“That was all that was destined for him!” replied Vandiyathevan.
The prince laughed. “You must never leave my side. When you are near, any hardship turns into happiness!” said the prince.
“In the same way, any happiness might turn into hardship!” said Azhwarkadiyan.

At that moment, a cloud of dust appeared on the road ahead of them. The sound of several horses galloping at full speed could be heard. In a short while, a small cavalry troop came into view. The spearheads held by the horsemen gleamed brightly in the morning sun.
“Sir! Draw your sword from its sheath!” warned Vandiyathevan.

chapters.title: “Here Comes War!”
paragraphs: As soon as Vandiyathevan said, “Draw your sword from its sheath!” the prince cried out, “Here, I have drawn it!” and unsheathed his sword with a flourish. At that very moment, Vandiyathevan too drew his sword from its scabbard. These were no ordinary blades—they were grand, monstrous swords. The men who had come with their horses and halted near the sacred Bodhi tree at Anuradhapura had handed over these very swords before departing.

The prince leapt down from his horse and said sternly, “Come, get down! I can no longer endure your endless speeches! We must settle this here and now, with our own hands, before we leave!” Vandiyathevan was taken aback. He could not tell if this was mere sport or deadly earnest. Yet, since the prince had already dismounted, he too was compelled to follow suit.

“What is this, sir! Why do you hesitate? Did you not try to humiliate me last night? Did you not say that your grandfather’s palace courtyard was guarded by my ancestors? Did you not claim that poets watched as their umbrellas and palanquins were snatched away, and bore it in silence? The more I think of it, the less I can bear it. One of us must settle this matter here and now before we move on!” So saying, the prince gripped the hilt of his sword with both hands and, spinning it, advanced towards Vandiyathevan.

Yes, as we have said, this was no ordinary sword. No matter how strong a man might be, it was a great feat to hold it upright with one hand. Only by gripping it with both hands could one swing it and strike at an enemy.

When the prince thus spun the sword with both hands, he no longer appeared as the delicate, pampered royal youth raised amidst palace luxuries. He seemed instead like the ancient heroes—like Bhima, Arjuna, and Abhimanyu. In his very form, he resembled the battle-scarred Vijayalaya Chola, who bore ninety-six wounds, and the valiant Rajaditya Deva, who fell atop his elephant. He stood there, a living reminder that he was descended from such a heroic lineage, radiating martial splendor and grandeur.

Vandiyathevan too gripped his sword with both hands and began to swing it. At first, confusion and hesitation held sway in his mind. But as the moments passed, his resolve hardened. The frenzy of valor surged within him. Though his opponent was the prince, worthy of his respect and loyalty... He forgot. He even forgot why this fight had begun. Before his eyes, only the enemy’s whirling dagger remained. His entire attention was fixed on a single thought: how to escape being struck by that blade, how to knock it aside and wound his opponent in return.

The speed at which the daggers spun, the force with which they clashed—clang! clang!—against one another, began at a measured tempo, passed through a moderate pace, and now surged into a furious tempo. At first, even Azhwarkkadiyan could not comprehend the prince’s intention. Yet, he was certain there must be some purpose behind it. Perhaps it was a strategy to halt the approaching riders, to discover who they were, and to decide what action should be taken accordingly. Therefore, he let both warriors’ horses stand crosswise in the middle of the road, seized their reins, and waited.

The mounted warriors who had been approaching from the opposite direction now drew near. When Azhwarkkadiyan saw the tiger banner fluttering among them, his anxiety vanished. They are our men—but who could they be?
The heralds at the front of the party announced the answer with resounding voices.

“Victorious is the commander of the Lankan forces who routed Mahinda’s armies in the war of Eelam, the mighty Kodumbalur Periya Velar, Bhoothi Vikrama Kesari Maharaja, who took the head of the valiant Pandiyan at the battle of Vaigai! Hurrah!” thundered a voice like rolling thunder.

“Victorious is the scion of the Pallava clan—the peerless hero who took the head of the valiant Pandiyan at the battle of Vaigai, the conqueror of the Vengi army at the battle of Vadapennai, Parakrama Bhoopathi, Parthibendra Varman! Hurrah!” echoed another thunderous voice.

Behind these heralds rode about thirty horsemen. At their center, mounted on splendid white steeds, sat the imposing commander Periya Velar and Parthibendran. Following the cavalry, a great elephant advanced, bearing a howdah.

A little distance further back, the infantry could be seen, their ranks blurred by a cloud of dust. The horsemen in the vanguard, delayed by the obstruction in their path, appeared visibly displeased.
“Who is that?” “Move aside!” “Clear the way!” came several voices.
Afterwards, the secretive murmurs of the crowd—those “kasamusa kasamusa” whispers—and exclamations of astonishment, “Oh ho!” and “Ah ha!” arose.
The warriors leapt down from their horses. They surrounded those who had fought with knives, standing guard.
Both Boothi Vikrama Kesari and Parthibendran had also dismounted from their horses and set foot on the ground. They came forward to stand at the forefront of the warriors.

Parthibendran was bristling with agitation. He turned to Vikrama Kesari and said, “Did you see? Was I right or not about Vallaththaan? What a blustering braggart! He has begun to display his tricks right before the prince himself. Are we to stand by and watch this in silence?…” As he spoke, he raised the knife in his hand.
Boothi Vikrama Kesari caught his hand and restrained him. “Wait a moment, let us see! What a marvelous knife-fight! It has been so many days since I witnessed such a thing,” he said.
The foot soldiers—about three hundred of them—who had come up from behind, now joined the gathering. They formed a circle and began to watch the spectacle.

Meanwhile, a woman descended from the howdah atop the elephant. She slipped between the horses and the warriors, coming to stand at the very front of the watching circle. The excitement that had taken hold of her face at that moment is beyond description. As the knives flashed and darted here and there, her eyes too darted in every direction. When the fighters leapt this way and that, her slender waist, without her knowing, swayed in rhythm with their movements. After a while, she took from her hair the blue lotus flower, still attached to its stem. She began to twirl it this way and that. The stem of the flower spun in her hand in time with the rhythm of the circling knives. There is no need for us to tell the readers who this woman is. Yes; surely they could not have forgotten Poonguzhali? For a while, the warriors fought in such a way that the prince’s face was visible directly opposite hers. Gradually, as they moved, they circled halfway around. At last, Vandiyathevan’s face came to stand opposite Poonguzhali’s. From time to time, Vandiyathevan’s eyes swept over the swelling crowd of warriors around him. In that moment, he too saw Poonguzhali.

Suddenly, his attention wavered for a split second, startled by the sight of that woman. That single moment was enough for the prince. Like Indra’s thunderbolt striking, the prince’s knife came down upon Vandiyathevan’s blade. The Vanar clan warrior faltered. The knife slipped from his grasp and fell to the ground with a clang.

The tumult raised by those gathered all around resembled the roar of a stormy sea. Rising above that clamor, the exuberant laughter of a young woman rang out, clear and bright. Vandiyathevan tried to retrieve the sword he had dropped to the ground. But before he could, the prince leapt forward and embraced him.
“You did not lose to my sword. You fought with a skill equal to sword for sword. But you were vanquished by a maiden’s glance! There is no shame in that. It happens to everyone!” he said.
Vandiyathevan began to offer some reply in his own defense, but by then, Commander-in-Chief Boothi Vikrama Kesari and Parthibendran had come near them.
“Prince! It was I who sent this youth to you! Did he behave improperly in any way? For a moment, we were all quite bewildered!” said the commander.
“Yes, General! I could not bear his taunting. ‘They say there is war in Lanka, but where is the war? Where is the war?’ he kept asking, and pierced me with his words. So I showed him—‘Here is war!’”
As the prince said this, all those around broke into renewed cheers and laughter.
The commander came up to Vandiyathevan and patted him on the back.

“My boy! It’s been many days since I’ve seen such a sword fight! You are the right companion for the prince! At times, he is seized by such sudden impulses! Is he not born in the line of Paranthaka Chakravarti, famed as Kunjara Mallan? Those who cannot stand face to face with him in combat cannot remain his friends for long!” he said.

Meanwhile, the prince approached Parthibendra Pallavan and said, “Sir! I heard that you have come seeking me. I hurried here just to meet you. Is my elder brother well in Kanchi? How is my grandfather?”

“Both your brother and grandfather have sent you very important news. It has been four or five days since I arrived in Lanka to find you. There is not a moment to lose now…” Parthibendran began to say, but the prince interrupted him.
“If it were not a matter of great importance, would you yourself have come? There is no need to delay even a moment longer. You must convey the message right now!”

At that moment, the recently arrived Commander-in-Chief, Periya Velar, said, “It is impossible to speak amidst so many people in the middle of the road. Look, there is an abandoned mandapam over there! Let us go there! Fortunately, there is no shortage of ruined mandapams in this Lanka!”
Everyone proceeded towards the ruined mandapam, which stood a short distance away, across the road.

chapters.title: The Council of Ministers
paragraphs: As they walked, Vandiyathevan drew close to Azhwarkkadian and said, “What is this, why does the prince behave so? That day he suddenly started a wrestling match; today he jumped into a knife fight. Couldn’t he at least announce before starting a fight? The prince’s friendship seems to be quite dangerous!”
The prince, overhearing this, had already come near them.
“Yes, sir! My friendship is indeed very dangerous. Didn’t you realize that last night itself? If you wish to avoid danger, you must keep at least ten leagues away from wherever I am!” he said.
“Prince, that’s not what I meant. I am ready to face any danger that comes from being near you. But you—why do you act so suddenly, without warning…”

At this, the valiant Vaishnavite interjected, “Don’t you understand, brother? The prince used this tactic to find out who was approaching and to act accordingly! Whoever they might be, if they see a knife fight, they’ll at least pause to watch, won’t they?”

The prince said, “Thirumalai’s words are true. There’s also something peculiar in my horoscope. Whoever becomes my friend is sure to attract the envy and enmity of others. That’s why, if I desire someone’s friendship, it is my habit to quarrel with them often. Only those who don’t mind this can remain my friends!”

“In that case, fine! From now on, I won’t wait for you to start a fight—I’ll begin it myself. Prince! I, who brought you news, forgot to tell you something important. I wish to tell it now! I must tell it. If you don’t wish to hear it, pick up your knife again!” said Vandiyathevan.
“No need! Tell me the news, I am listening.”

“In the crowd that surrounded us, there was a woman standing with a lotus stem in her hand. Didn’t you even say that I was defeated by her glance? Do you know who that woman is?” “I do not know; I did not see her clearly. I have no habit of observing her either.”

“Prince! She is the one who sent you a message; I forgot to tell you. How shall I explain? Ever since I met you, I have been busy fighting alongside you and escaping from having a house collapse on my head! So, I never found the right moment to tell you. When I suddenly saw that girl, I remembered that I had not conveyed her message. I was a bit startled at that moment. Just then, you struck my sword away…”
“Let it be; who is that girl? Why should she send me a message?”
“Sir! She is Poonguzhali.”
“A beautiful name. But I have never heard of it.”
“Sir! Do you remember the name ‘Samudra Kumari’?”
“Samudra Kumari—Samudra Kumari—I do not recall such a name! I do not even remember seeing her!”

“Please, try to remember a little. If you do not remember, that girl’s heart will break. At Kodikkarai, you were about to board a boat to reach the ship. At that time, a girl came alone, rowing her boat from the sea to the shore. You watched her in surprise. She, too, came nearer to find out who you all were. You asked the lighthouse keeper, ‘Who is this girl?’ He replied, ‘She is my daughter.’ Immediately you said, ‘Oh! She is your daughter? I thought she was Samudra Kumari!’ That girl has not forgotten those words; she has kept them in her memory. It was only with that girl’s help that I was able to cross the sea and come to Lanka…”

“Now that you mention it, I vaguely recall something. But what business does the Samudra Kumari of Kodikkarai have here, near Anuradhapura? Why has she come with these people? Did she perhaps come searching for you?…”
“No; never. She has no reason to come looking for me. If she has come searching for anyone, it must be you. Why, I do not know!”

As he continued speaking thus, Vandiyathevan glanced at Poonguzhali, who was approaching from a short distance away, walking beside the Commander-in-Chief. She walked with her head bowed. Yet, he realized that all her attention and thoughts were fixed upon the prince. He also noticed that, every now and then, her sidelong glance would seek out the prince. At that moment, she must have sensed by some inner feeling that they were speaking about her. Otherwise, what need was there for her to walk with her head so persistently bowed? Ah! Were not her eyes the kind that never rested, never ceased their restless wandering, never once looking in the direction they had just seen?

They reached a mandapam where only the carved black stone pillars stood, without a roof above. All around, tall trees had grown, casting a measure of shade upon the mandapam. In the center of the mandapam was a raised platform. There, the prince, the Commander-in-Chief, and Parthibendran seated themselves. Vandiyathevan and Azhwarkadiyan stood a little apart.

On the other side, behind the concealment of a pillar, Poonguzhali stood. From there, she could see both the prince and Vandiyathevan. Around the roofless mandapam, soldiers stood in two lines, as if forming a battle array. A little farther away, the horses and the elephant were tethered.
The prince turned to Parthibendran and said, “What message have my brother and grandfather sent? I am eager to hear it!”
“Prince! The Chola kingdom is in great peril. This you must already know…”
“Yes, sir! The Emperor has been ailing for a long time…”

“That is not the only danger; a far greater peril threatens the very empire itself. Those in high positions of authority have turned traitorous. They have begun to plot against the Emperor, the Crown Prince, and yourself. They have resolved to deny your brother the throne, and instead to crown Madurantakan, that Shiva-devotee who wears the guise of a holy man, the so-called ‘Uthiratcha Poonai’. The Pazhuvettarayars, the Sambuvarayars, the bearers of the twin royal umbrellas, the Mazhavarayars of Mazhappadi, and many other traitors like them have joined in this conspiracy. But we need not be overly concerned about their efforts. The northern and southern armies are under our control. Thirukovalur Miladudaiyar and the great Velar of Kodumbalur are on our side…” …are at your side. With their help, and with the support of the army, the traitors’ conspiracy can be crushed to dust in a single instant. But we must not give the enemy too much time. The traitors’ schemes must be nipped in the bud and cast away. In light of this situation, your brother and your grandmother have sent me to bring you immediately to Kanchi. At this critical juncture, it is imperative that you and your brother are not separated, and that you both remain in the same place—this is your grandmother’s firm conviction.

Moreover, I wish to share what is in your brother’s heart. He has no desire to rule the kingdom from a single place. His heart yearns to board ships and sail to the lands beyond the seas, to conquer those realms and let the Chola tiger flag fly high over them all. Ever since the Pazhuvettaraiyars blocked the northern campaign, his thirst for war has increased tenfold. Therefore, once you come to Kanchi, we shall march upon Thanjavur, destroy all the conspirators, and seat you upon the Chola throne, crown you king, and then—”

All this while, the prince had listened attentively and respectfully. Now, covering his ears with his hands, he said, “Enough! Do not utter such dreadful words. There is a vast gulf between the Chola throne and myself!”

“If you do not like it, I will say no more; but that is your brother’s wish, his desire. It is for you brothers to discuss and decide among yourselves. But in the matter of destroying the traitors, it is essential that you both stand united. Come at once to Kanchi. Let us wipe out the Pazhuvettaraiyars and the Sambhuvaraiyars, root and branch. Let us send that Shiva-devotee in disguise, Madurantaka, straight to the abode of Shiva. Afterwards, you and your brother may deliberate and decide as you see fit!” said Parthibendran.
“Sir! Is it for us alone to make such decisions? My father—the Emperor—should we not learn his wishes? Perhaps you already know? Has my brother received any secret message from our father…?”

“Prince! At this juncture, it is necessary to speak the truth. There is no use in concealing it. At this moment, it is impossible to know your father’s wishes. The Emperor is no longer a free man. He is a prisoner of the Pazhuvettaraiyars. Without their permission, no one can see the Emperor; nor can anyone speak to him. How then can we know his wishes? Your brother made great efforts to summon your father to Kanchi for this very reason.
He built a golden palace in Kanchipuram. He sent an invitation, requesting that the Emperor should come, conquer, and perform the housewarming ceremony. But there was no reply from the Emperor...
“Is it not well known that my father is ill and unable to travel?”

“Prince! Should your father—the Emperor of the Three Worlds—walk all the way to Kanchipuram? Are there no elephants or horses? Are there no chariots or carriages? Are there not golden chariots and pearl-laden palanquins? Would not thousands and tens of thousands of crowned vassal kings compete to carry him on their shoulders? That is not the reason; the reason is the treachery of the Pazhuvettaraiyars. The Tanjore palace has now become the Emperor’s prison... Prince! If you wish to save your father’s life, set out at once and come!”
It was clear that these words had deeply disturbed the Prince’s heart. For the first time, a shadow of worry appeared on his usually cheerful face.
The Prince fell into deep thought for a while, then raised his eyes to look at the Commander.

“Commander! What is your opinion? A few days ago, the Prime Minister Aniruddha Brahmarayar came here. He is a man worthy of my father’s trust and intimate affection. He advised me to stay in Lanka for some time. You too agreed with him. When I asked, ‘There is no battle here, why should I remain?’ you gave me a satisfactory answer. The Prime Minister has sent the same advice again through this Vaishnavite standing here. You know how much respect I have for my elder sister, the Young Princess. I would never cross a boundary she set. I came here only because she asked me to bring her to Lanka. The Young Princess has sent a letter through this brave scion of the Vanar clan. In some ways, my sister’s message matches what Parthibendran said. But she has written, urging me to set out at once and come to Pazhayarai. My brother, on the other hand, has sent word through him, asking me to come to Kanchipuram. Commander! What is your opinion?” he asked.

“Prince! Until this morning, I too was of the opinion that you should remain on this island of Lanka. Even last night, I debated this at length with him. Though he argued for a long time, I did not agree. But early this morning, that woman standing there came and told me some news. Hearing it changed my mind. Now I think it is absolutely necessary for you to go to Kanchipuram at once!” said the Commander of Lanka.
Standing behind the pillar, Poonguzhali was watching him out of the corner of her eye. The prince turned his gaze upon her.

“I have heard that Abhimanyu was slain by enemies attacking him from all sides. It seems I too am about to be struck down—not by enemies, but by tidings coming at me from every direction!” the prince said.
“What news has that girl brought?” he asked.
“Let her speak for herself!” said the Periya Velar.

Poonguzhali hesitated, then slowly walked forward. She came and stood before the prince. She glanced all around her—looked at the Commander-in-Chief, looked at Parthibendran; then she looked at Vandiyathevan and Azhwarkadiyan, who stood a little distance away. Only the prince’s face she could not bring herself to meet.
“Speak, girl, quickly!” commanded the Commander-in-Chief.
Poonguzhali tried to say something, but no words came.
“Ah! It seems as if the whole world has been struck dumb,” said Arulmozhi Varman.

At that, Poonguzhali lifted her eyelids and, for the briefest instant, looked at the prince. In that moment, tears welled up in her eyes and began to flow. At once, she turned and fled from there, running off into the distance, vanishing among the thickly grown trees.
Everyone stood watching her in astonishment. Vandiyathevan stepped forward.
“Sir! She ran away like this once before too. I’ll go after her and bring her back!” he said.
“Do so! But in the meantime, let the Commander-in-Chief tell us what news she brought,” said the prince.

To this, the Commander-in-Chief replied, “It can be told in just two words. Prince! The Pazhuvettarayars have sent two large ships, filled with soldiers, to capture and bring you back. The ships have entered the Thondaiman river canal and are lying in wait at a hidden spot!”

chapters.title: “Look There!”
paragraphs: As soon as he heard the news brought by Commander-in-Chief Bhoothi Vikramakesari, a smile blossomed on the prince’s face.
“At last, it seems an end has come to the turmoil within my heart,” he murmured in a gentle voice, as if speaking to himself.

Parthibendran sprang up, boiling with anger. “Commander! What did you say? Is this true? Why did you not tell me until now? Only now do I understand why you dragged this madwoman along with us! I ask again: is it true that the Pazhuvettaraiyars have sent ships to capture the prince and bring him back as a prisoner?” he demanded.
“Yes, my lord! If we are to believe what this woman claims to have seen with her own eyes and heard with her own ears, then it is true!”

“Aha! Then the words of that elder, the lord of Thirukovalur, Miladudaiyar, have proven true. He alone truly understood the Pazhuvettaraiyars! Commander! Even after learning such news, why do you remain idle? The scion of Paranthaka the Emperor, the beloved son of Sundara Chozhar, the prince cherished by all the towns and cities, the jewel whom all the people of Tamil Nadu hold as precious as their own eyes, Arulmozhi Varman, born with Aditya Karikalan—have these wretched Pazhuvettaraiyars truly dared to send men to capture him? What more is there to consider? Let us at once set out with our armies, destroy those who have come to imprison the prince, and raise their graves here on this very island of Lanka!… Afterwards, we shall proceed with our plans as we have devised! Come, let us go! Why do you still hesitate?” Parthibendran thundered, sparks flying from his words.

Commander Bhoothi Vikramakesari looked at him and said, “Parthibendra, it was precisely because I knew you would be so impetuous that I did not tell you the news this woman brought. This is a matter that requires careful thought. There is no use in haste!”

“Is there need for thought? What is there to consider? Why should we hesitate? Prince! You tell us. What is left to ponder? If you had any doubts before, surely now there is no room for hesitation? Should we not utterly destroy the Pazhuvettaraiyars?” At that moment, the prince calmly asked, without the slightest agitation, “Shall we not also learn what is in the mind of the Commander-in-Chief? Sir! What is it that you think we should be pondering?”

“To imprison you… Even to utter these words, my tongue hesitates… Yet, it must be said. If those who have come to imprison you have arrived bearing the Emperor’s own command, what are we to do then? Even then, should we fight against them?”
Hearing this, Parthibendran laughed aloud and said, “How splendid, your words! Is the Emperor in any position to issue commands of his own? Is he not himself held captive by the Pazhuvettarayars?”

At this juncture, Vandiyathevan interjected, “What the Pallava Commander says is entirely true. I have seen it with my own eyes. The Pazhuvettarayars are keeping the Emperor as though he were a prisoner. Without their permission, no one can see the Emperor, nor speak with him. When I dared utter a single word, the treatment they gave me… Ah! Even now, my wrist aches from the grip of the Younger Pazhuvettarayar’s iron hand!” he said, rubbing his wrist.
“Is that so, Vallavaraiya! I thought you were something else entirely. Tell the prince and the Commander-in-Chief once more, and make it clear!” said Parthibendran.

The prince replied, “No need; he has already said all that needs to be said!” Then, turning to Vandiyathevan, he said, “Sir! Did you not say you would go and bring that woman here? Why do you still stand here? We can hear the message she brings directly from her own lips! She seems a little touched in the head. Somehow, speak kindly and bring her here!”

“I shall go, Prince! I will bring her. But I cannot bear the thought of you being imprisoned by the Pazhuvettarayars. As long as life remains in my body, that shall never happen!” So saying, Vandiyathevan departed.
“Commander-in-Chief, you have yet to share your opinion,” Arulmozhi Varman asked.

“This is my view. You must not meet the men sent by the Pazhuvettarayars. Board the ship Parthibendran has brought and depart for Kanchi at once. I will go to Thanjavur. There, I will meet the Emperor in person and learn the true state of affairs…”

“To go to Thanjavur now is like placing your head into the lion’s jaws. If you go, you will not return. You will be thrown straight into the underground dungeons there. You will not even be able to see the Emperor…”
“What words are these? Who in Chola Nadu has the power to imprison me? Who has the courage to prevent me from meeting the Emperor? Moreover, the Prime Minister Aniruddha Brahmarayar is there…”
“Brahmarayar is there, yes. But what use is that? Even he cannot see the Emperor. Look, here stands his disciple—let us ask him what he has to say.”

The Commander-in-Chief turned to Azhwarkkadian. “Ah, I had forgotten that this Vaishnavite is standing here. Thirumalai! Why are you standing so silent? Have you, like the Prince just now, become mute?”

“Commander! God has given us two ears, but only one mouth. Therefore, my guru has instructed me: ‘Use your ears well; keep your speaking to a minimum.’ Especially, he has told me to strictly observe this vow in places where great affairs of state are being discussed.”
“You fulfill your guru’s words well. But now, since we are asking you, speak. What is your opinion?”
“About what matter do you seek my opinion, Commander?”
“About the matter we have been discussing all this while. What should the Prince do now? Should he remain in Lanka? Or should he go to Kanchi?”
“Shall I tell you my true opinion? If the Prince permits, I will speak.”
Arulmozhi Varman, who had been sunk in thought, looked up at Azhwarkkadian and said reassuringly, “Speak, Thirumalai, speak freely and from your heart!”
“In this island of Lanka, whichever is the most secure and strictly guarded prison, that must be found, and the Prince must be locked inside it! Strong guards must be posted outside!”
“What nonsense is this?” exclaimed the Commander.
“Is this the time for jesting?” asked Parthibendran.

“I am neither raving nor jesting. I have merely spoken what is in my heart. Last night, the prince was making his way through the streets of Anuradhapura. As he passed, the front façade of a house collapsed upon his head. Later, we were resting in another house. By good fortune, we rose and left for some errand. Barely moments after, that house caught fire and was consumed by flames. If you wish to know whether these things are true or not, ask the prince himself!”
Both men turned to the prince. The expression on his face confirmed Alwarkadiyan’s account.
“Ask yourselves for whose sake these dangers have arisen. Would anyone set a house ablaze merely to kill me or Vandiyathevan?”
Parthibendran immediately sprang up and exclaimed, “It is clear that someone tried to kill the prince! This only strengthens the necessity for the prince to come with me to Kanchipuram!”
“That must not be! Rather than sending the prince with you, it would be better to hand him over to the Pazhuvettaraiyars themselves,” retorted Alwarkadiyan.
“Vaishnavite! What did you say?” Parthibendran cried, drawing his sword.
The Commander-in-Chief restrained him, saying, “Thirumalai! Why do you speak so? Do you not know that Parthibendra Pallavan is a steadfast pillar of the Chola dynasty?”
“I know, Commander. I know! But is friendship alone sufficient?”
“I know that Parthibendran would lay down his very life for the sake of friendship, Thirumalai!”

“That may be so. But let me ask a question. And I ask that you demand an answer from him. The evening before last, as we were approaching Thamballai, we saw two men accompanying him! Ask him who those men are, and where they are now.”

Parthibendra Pallavan was taken aback. With some hesitation, he replied, “I met them at Trikonamalai. They brought me, claiming they would show me where the prince was. In Anuradhapura, they suddenly vanished. Why do you ask, Vaishnavite? Do you know anything about them?”

“I know! I am certain that those two are among those who have sworn to utterly destroy the Chola dynasty. I suspect it was they who tried to kill the prince yesterday at Anuradhapura… Ah! Look there,” said Azhwarkadiyan, pointing with his finger.

The place he indicated was a little distance away from the mandapam. Amidst the thickly clustered trees, a beautiful young woman and a handsome youth stood conversing together. It was easy to guess that they were none other than Vandiyathevan and Poonguzhali.
As they continued their conversation, Vandiyathevan suddenly spun a small dagger and flung it. The dagger landed in a nearby bush. A voice cried out, “Whee!”

chapters.title: Poonguzhali’s Knife
paragraphs: From the ruined mandapam, Vandiyathevan went in search of Poonguzhali. He found her leaning against a tree, her body trembling ever so slightly with suppressed sobs.
Softening his voice as much as he could, he called out, “Poonguzhali!”
Startled by the sound, Poonguzhali turned around abruptly.
“Oh, it’s you?” she said, and turned away again.
“It’s me! Why are you so angry with me?” he asked.
“I have no anger towards you whatsoever.”
“Then why are you so agitated?”
“I simply cannot stand the sight of men.”
“Not even the prince?”
Poonguzhali turned and looked at Vandiyathevan, her eyes blazing with fire.
“Especially him! I dislike him the most!” she declared.
“What fault has he committed?”
“He doesn’t even remember me. He won’t even look at my face.”
“He remembers you very well. When I mentioned you, he said, ‘Oh! Don’t I know the princess of the sea?’”
“You’re lying.”
“Come and ask him yourself.”
“If he remembers me, why hasn’t he spoken a single word to me?”
“He did speak; you’re the one who ran away without replying.”
“I never did such a thing. Isn’t it natural to ask, ‘Who is it? What is it?’ when you see someone you know? What you say is a lie! He never even looked at my face.”
"Poonguzhali! There is a reason for that."
"What reason?"
"The prince is going through a very difficult time right now."
"Who said so?"
"All the astrologers have said it. The astrologer from Kudanthai told me himself."
"What did he say to you?"

"He said that for a few days, hardship upon hardship will keep coming to the prince. He said that everyone close to him will also face troubles. The prince knows this too. That’s why he doesn’t want anyone to be friendly with him. He wants the misfortunes destined for him to fall on him alone."
"Then why are you still friendly with him?"
"Didn’t you see just now? He’s trying to quarrel with me and drive me away as well. For no reason, he picked a fight with me on the road. The quarrel stopped only because you arrived."
"Even if he drives you away, won’t you leave him?"
"I will not. I will share and experience all the hardships that come to him."
"Do you like him that much?"
"Yes; I like him very, very much."
"Why do you like him?"
"I don’t know how to explain it. The moment I saw him, affection for him blossomed in my heart."
"It’s the same for me!" said Poonguzhali. Immediately, she bit her lip, regretting that she had revealed her heart so openly.
"I know you have affection for the prince. That’s why I came to take you with me. Come with me!"
"I will not come!" Poonguzhali said firmly and resolutely.
"If you refuse, I will forcibly drag you with me."
“If you come any closer, beware—here is a knife!” said Poonguzhali, drawing the knife that was tucked into her waist and showing it to him.
“Poor girl! Why have you come to stab and kill me? Is it because I reminded the prince about you?”
“You are lying; you did not say a word about me to him!”
“So be it, let it go. Didn’t you say that two ships have come to take the prince away? Go and tell him that, then disappear however you wish!”
“I have already told all the details to the Commander-in-Chief.”
“The prince wishes to hear it directly from you.”
“If I stand before him, I will become mute.”
“The prince is very fond of dumb women!”
“Shame on you! You are mocking me!” exclaimed Poonguzhali, raising her knife.
“Then, are you not coming with me?”
“No!”
“Very well, I am leaving!” said Vandiyathevan, taking two steps forward. Suddenly, he spun around, snatched the knife from Poonguzhali’s hand, and flung it away!
The thrown knife spun and spun, flying far into a dense thicket. From the spot where the knife landed, a sound rang out—“Weel!”
It was impossible to tell whether it was a human voice, or the cry of some animal or bird.

Poonguzhali, who had glared at Vandiyathevan in fierce anger when he snatched her knife, now turned her gaze with curiosity toward the place where the sound had come from. Then, both of them looked at each other in astonishment.

Slowly, they walked toward the thicket where the knife had fallen and peered through the bushes. Fresh blood was splattered on the leaves and the ground. But there was no sign of a human; nor of any animal. Poonguzhali’s knife was also nowhere to be seen!

“Did you see now, Poonguzhali! Do you realize at last the truth of what I told you? The prince is surrounded by dangers on all sides. At any moment, from any place, danger could strike—no one can predict when or how. By chance, I snatched your knife and threw it away. That revealed that someone was hiding here. Think for yourself—why would anyone be lurking here? Only to seize an opportunity to harm the prince! Do you remember, on the very first day I came to Kodikkarai, your brother ferried two men across, and you told me you felt suspicious about them? Recall that!
