In times like these, can those who care for the prince afford to leave his side?”
With these words, Vandiyathevan spoke breathlessly and fell silent.
“What if he himself asks me to go?” Poonguzhali asked.
“Even if he asks us to go, we must not!”
Poonguzhali thought for a moment and then said, “Shouldn’t we find out who was hiding here?”

“That is not something we can do. In this dense forest, how could we search and find them? If we delay any longer, the prince will truly be angry. Everyone will leave us behind! Come with me, without another word.”
“All right, I’m coming!” Poonguzhali replied.
The two of them walked toward the pavilion where the others were gathered.
As soon as Vandiyathevan and Poonguzhali approached, those in the pavilion questioned them about the incident.
“Why did you throw the knife? We heard a ‘whizz’—what was that sound?” they asked.
“It seemed as if some animal—a leopard or a jackal—was hiding in the bushes. So I snatched her knife and threw it. We went closer to look, but found nothing,” Vandiyathevan replied.
“If that’s so, let it be; but now, ask this girl what you need to ask!” said the Commander.
Since her arrival, Poonguzhali had been looking only at the prince. At that moment, the prince too looked up at her.

“Tch, tch! Why does this heart beat so restlessly? Something seems to be stuck in my throat—what is it? Why do tears well up in my eyes? Foolish girl! Where has all your courage gone? You, whose spirit did not waver even before the raging sea and the mighty storm—why does your heart falter now? You, whose eyes dared to look into the fierce, blazing gaze of the savage tiger—why do your eyes grow dim now? Girl! Do not once again earn yourself the title of madwoman! Look up at the Prince! Answer his questions boldly! What could he possibly do to you? Is he not renowned throughout the world for his compassion and kindness? What could the Prince do to a foolish girl like you…?”
“Samudrakumari! Do you remember me?” he asked, his voice echoing in her ears like a sound rising from the depths of the ocean.

chapters.title: “I Am the Culprit!”
paragraphs: “Samudra Kumari! Do you remember me…?”

“Ponniyin Selva! What kind of question is this! At whom are you asking, ‘Do you remember?’ After mingling and growing close for thousands and thousands of years, is it fitting to ask, ‘Do you remember?’ Or is it that you yourself have forgotten? How many ages have you climbed into my little boat? In the sea, in that endless ocean, amidst the boundless surging waves, have you forgotten all those joyous journeys we took together in my small boat? When suddenly, darkness surrounded us on all sides, did you forget how we stood side by side, holding each other’s hands for a long time, giving each other courage? When the terrifying storm winds blew, when the mountainous waves struck our boat, lifting us to the sky in one moment and plunging us into the abyss the next, in those days of wild turmoil, did you forget how we stood together, supporting each other, and braved that terrible storm and triumphed over it? Do you not remember the time when we soared and soared, flying through the vast sky? Did you forget how you leapt up to the stars, plucked them, and adorned my hair with them as ornaments? Did you also forget how you brought the full moon close to my face and said, ‘Here, look at your golden face in this silver mirror!’?

And another time, when you dived into the deep sea; my heart trembled in fear; but after a while, you emerged with pearls and corals in both hands, strung them into garlands, and placed them around my neck! Even if you have forgotten, how could I ever forget? O King! In the twilight hours, on the blue-hued banks of the lakes, where the branches, heavy with clusters of flowers, bent down to form a decorated canopy, on mats of fresh green grass, how many, how many, countless days did we spend gazing into each other’s faces—can all that ever be forgotten? In those moments, a hundred pairs of cuckoos sat on the branches and sang their melodies, thousands and tens of thousands of bees circled around humming, and millions of butterflies, beating their many-colored wings, danced in delight—could I ever forget any of that? In how many births could I forget? Yet you looked at me and asked, ‘Do you remember?’—is it right to ask so? I remember, my lord, I remember it all so well!…”
Her foolish, innocent heart leapt and fluttered, longing to say all this.
But from her coral lips came only two softly murmured words: “I remember!”

“Ah! Samudrakumari, you have opened your mouth and spoken! In this wondrous island of Lanka, in how many pillared halls of the palaces are there statues of beautiful divine maidens carved upon the columns! For a moment, I thought you too might be such a sculpted form. Fortunately, you have opened your mouth and spoken. Say a few more words! How much I have longed to hear your sweet voice. They say you told our Commander a few things. That two large ships had come and were anchored in a hidden spot on the Thondaiman river, and that many warriors had arrived in them. Is that true, Samudrakumari? Did you see those ships with your own eyes?” the prince asked.
“Yes, my lord, I saw them with my own eyes!” answered Poonguzhali.

“Ah! Now I can hear your voice a little. My ears are rejoicing. Good; after seeing the ships, you took your boat along a narrow canal. You hid yourself in the dense forest, lying low in a secret place, waiting for the ships to pass. At that time, some of the warriors who had disembarked from the ships came there. They stood and spoke near the place where you were lying. You did not wish to listen to their conversation. Yet, against your will, their words fell upon your ears. You happened to hear them. Are these the things you told our Commander?”
“I told what happened, just as it happened.”

“Upon hearing their conversation, you felt you must immediately warn the Commander about it. As soon as the warriors left, you set out. You hurried, searching for the place where the Commander was! How did you come, Samudrakumari?”
“I came halfway by boat; then I walked through the forest path.”
“With what intention did you set out, child?”

“I thought the Commander would be at Mathottam city, so I set out to go there. On the way, I learned he was at Mahindalai. Before I could speak to the Commander, so many people stood in my way and stopped me! How many stood in my path?” said Poonguzhali, turning toward the Commander. In her gaze, there flashed a lightning bolt, like the one that appears before the thunder of summer storms.

“Is it such an easy matter to meet the Commander-in-Chief? Here stands my friend—if you heard of the troubles he endured in his attempt to see the Commander-in-Chief, you would be astonished. It is good that you stubbornly persisted and managed to see the Commander, O maiden with the lovely tresses! Will you repeat to me what you told him? When you listened from behind the tree, what were those soldiers discussing?”
“My lord! I feel embarrassed to say it aloud.”
“Be generous of heart and tell me once more, for my sake!”
“They were talking about having come here to arrest and take you away.”
“Did they mention on whose orders they had come?”
“I do not believe what they said, my lord! I thought it must be a plot by the Pazhuvettarayars.”
“You may share your opinion later. For now, just tell me what they said, Samudrakumari.”
“They said it was by the Emperor’s command.”
“Very well; did they give any reason for this?”

“They did. They said you had conspired with the Buddhist monks in this land to have yourself crowned as King of Lanka… When I heard those wretches speak thus, I was filled with anger and wanted to kill them right there.”
“You tried to do a noble deed! But do you not know that it is forbidden to hinder the Emperor’s messengers in any way…? Well then, do you remember if they spoke of anything else important?”

“They said the Commander-in-Chief must not know the reason for their coming, and that if he found out, he might try to help you escape. Therefore, they said they must find out where you were staying, deliver the order to you in person, and take you away immediately…”

“So that is why you set out at once in search of the Commander-in-Chief. You have done me a great service, Samudrakumari! Stay a little apart now. I must discuss an important matter with these gentlemen. But first—” “Don’t run too far away. Don’t make me send Vandiyathevan after you again to catch and bring you back!”
The Princess of the Ocean moved slightly and stood near a pillar. She positioned herself where she could see the prince’s face.
Two bees, having plunged into a pot of honey, were now struggling for breath. Slowly, they managed to reach the edge, and then began to relish the taste of the honey, delighting in its sweetness.

Poonkuzhali’s eyes were now in a similar state of bliss. They drank deeply of the honey that was the prince’s handsome face, savoring its beauty. But her heart, stubborn and restless, refused to remain confined within her chest. It longed to burst free, to soar into the sky and fill the heavens with its overflowing joy.

The prince turned to the Commander-in-Chief, Boothi Vikrama Kesari, and said, “Sir! For generations, your clan has been a friend to my family. You are my father’s dearest companion. I have always respected you as I would my own father. You, too, have cherished me as your own son. Therefore, at this moment, you must help me fulfill my duty. You must not stand in my way!”

Before the Commander-in-Chief could reply, the prince turned to Parthibendran and said, “Sir! I appeal to you as well. You are my beloved brother’s closest friend. I revere my brother’s word as if it were divine. Therefore, I am bound to honor your words, too. I earnestly beg you—do not say anything that would prevent me from fulfilling my duty!”
The Commander-in-Chief and Parthibendran looked at each other. Through that glance, they conveyed their shared anxiety.

The Commander-in-Chief turned to the prince and said, “Prince! I do not understand what you are saying. I have spent my whole life on the battlefield. I am not one to decipher riddles. You say you are about to perform your duty. What do you mean by that? What duty, and in what manner do you intend to perform it?”
“At this moment, I have only one duty. I must carry out my father’s command. My father has sent men with orders to arrest and bring me back. They are searching for me—”
“Why should I wait for them to come and seize me? I myself will go to where they are and surrender. That is my duty now…”
“That is something absolutely impossible! As long as there is life in my body, I will never allow it—I will stop it at any cost!” declared Parthibendran.
The Commander-in-Chief looked at him and said, “Do not be agitated; be patient!” Then he turned to the prince and spoke:

“Sir! You spoke of your duty. I too have a duty. I beg you to kindly listen to it. Of the great clan of the Kodumbalur Velalars, I am the only male alive today. All the others have given their lives in the service of the Chola Empire. Most of them fell on the battlefield. One day, I too shall die thus—who can say when? Therefore, I ask you to listen to my words with patience. You, who were raised with such care in the palace halls, were last year appointed by the Emperor as the commander of the southern armies. At that time, he called me aside and said: ‘The prince leaving me is like my very soul departing from my body. Yet, for my own desire, I cannot keep him confined within the palace. He must go forth; he must win fame as a hero like his elder brother. But if any danger befalls his life, in that very instant, my own life will depart. It is your responsibility to protect him from all harm…’ Thus did the Emperor command me.

Would the same Emperor who spoke thus last year now order that you be taken prisoner and brought before him? What have you done to warrant such a command? How absurd is the accusation that you plotted to seize the throne of Lanka! Can anyone believe such a slander?…”
The prince, who had listened patiently so far to the words of the great Velalar of Kodumbalur, now interrupted.
“Perhaps others cannot believe it—who knows? But I can believe it!” he said.
“What are you saying, Prince?”
“I say that it is true—I did plot to seize the throne of Lanka.”

Vandiyathevan now stepped forward and exclaimed, “What is this, my lord! Only a moment ago you were speaking of truth and righteousness, and now you utter such a great falsehood! Commander! Do not believe his words. Last night, the Buddhist monks—" The members of the great assembly offered him the throne and crown of Lanka, but he refused them. “I am a witness to this, as is this Vaishnavan standing here!” he said.

Ponniyin Selvan smiled and replied, “Vandiyathevan! Let me ask you a question. Do conspirators ever plot their schemes in the presence of witnesses? Is it not possible that I refused the throne and crown of Lanka precisely because you two were standing by my side?”
Vandiyathevan was taken aback! He could not find any words to counter this.

The prince continued, “Valiant scion of the Vanar clan! If you still have doubts, you may ask that Vaishnavan standing there. Inquire what instructions the Prime Minister Aniruddha Brahmarayar gave him before sending him to me. Did he say, ‘The Buddhist monks will offer you the throne of Lanka; refuse it in the presence of witnesses’? Find out for yourself whether such a message was sent or not!”
Hearing this, everyone present stood astounded.

The prince turned to the Commander-in-Chief and said, “Sir! Listen to this. It is true that I once harbored a great desire to conquer and rule Lanka. The one who planted this ambition in my heart was my elder sister. ‘Brother! You were born to rule a kingdom. The lines of the conch and discus are etched on your palm. There is no place for you here. Therefore, go to Lanka! Seize the throne of Lanka!’—thus, the young princess would often say such things and nurture this desire in my heart. Therefore, I am indeed a culprit; there is reason for the Emperor to order my arrest and bring me back…”

“Wait a moment, Prince! If such a thought arose in your mind, it is the good fortune of this island of Lanka. Neither you nor your elder sister, the young princess, are responsible for it. It is Sundara Chola Chakravarti who is responsible. He has told me many times that he wished to see you seated on the throne of Lanka. It was the Emperor himself who first spoke of this to Princess Kundavai. Your sister only conveyed your father’s wishes to you. Therefore, you are not at fault…”

“Commander! If that is so, why should I hesitate to go to my father? I will tell him everything that happened, just as it happened. Let these two here bear witness for me. Then, whatever command the Emperor gives, it is my duty to obey…”

Parthibendran now spoke in a voice that crackled like fire: “Commander, we are merely exchanging empty words. There is no use in hiding the truth any longer. We must tell the prince everything. Will you speak, or shall I?”

“I will speak; have patience!” said the Commander. He glanced around and then addressed the prince: “Prince! My intention was that your pure heart should not be sullied. But that intention has proved futile. I am compelled to tell you of a poisonous matter. You already know that the elder Pazhuvettarayar, at this advanced age, has married a woman named Nandini. She is a sorceress. She is versed in terrible magical arts and spells. With their aid, she has brought the great Pazhuvettarayar under her feet. Whatever task she commands with her foot, he bears on his head and fulfills. That great man, born of an ancient clan and famed for many heroic deeds, has, by the decree of fate, fallen into such misfortune.”
“Commander! This is not news to me. Is this not the very thing that is spoken of throughout the Chola land, in every town and city?” said the prince.

“Until now, the power of that enchantress Nandini was exerted only over the Pazhuvettarayar brothers. But now, Prince, forgive me! She has begun to cast her spell over the Emperor himself. That is why such an order—an order to arrest and bring you—has been issued by the Emperor!...”

“Commander! Beware! Do not speak disrespectfully of the Emperor. As long as my father draws breath, whatever command he gives, at whatever time, in whatever circumstance, that command is as sacred as the word of God...”

“We do not deny that, Prince! It is not only the Emperor’s freedom, but even his very life, that we fear may be in danger. Until yesterday, I myself did not know the full truth about Nandini. Only last night did I learn it through Parthibendran. It is necessary that you, too, know this dreadful matter.”

“Three years ago, was there not a final battle near Madurai with Veera Pandiyan? At that time, your brother Karikalan, Parthibendran here, and I acted together, consulting each other on every matter. The Pandiyan’s armies were utterly destroyed. Veera Pandiyan, as he once did before, tried to escape by fleeing into the desert. For that, the place—”

We three resolved that, no matter what, we must capture him and not let him escape. This time, we swore an oath that we would not return to Thanjavur without bringing back the head of Veera Pandiyan. Therefore, trusting no one else, we ourselves followed him. At last, we discovered that he was hiding in a hut beside a temple. Leaving us to guard outside the hut, your elder brother Karikalan alone entered within. He killed Veera Pandiyan and brought out his severed head. We too, believing our task accomplished, returned in triumph. But we did not know that, within that hut, a small drama had unfolded.

A woman who had given shelter to Veera Pandiyan stood in Karikalan’s way and pleaded for her lover’s life. Karikalan pushed her aside with a kick, then cut off Veera Pandiyan’s head and brought it out. Prince! The woman who thus tried to save the mortal enemy of the Chola dynasty was none other than Nandini! She is the same woman who later married a seventy-year-old elder and came to Thanjavur to shine as the ‘Young Queen of Pazhuvoor’! Can we not guess why, and with what purpose, she has come? She has come to avenge Veera Pandiyan, to exact retribution for his death. She has come to utterly destroy the Chola dynasty, to uproot it from its very foundation.

It is difficult for anyone who goes near her to escape from the snare of her enchantment. There stands Vandiyathevan, who can testify to this. And there stands the Vaishnavite, who can bear witness to the terrible oath sworn by the group determined to annihilate the Chola clan. All the money they need is given by Nandini herself. Prince! Alas, it seems even our Emperor has fallen into the net of that wicked woman. It appears that the Emperor himself is contemplating crowning Madurantaka Deva. Therefore, this is not the time for you to go to Thanjai, thinking it is the Emperor’s command…”

“Commander! The news you have revealed has filled me with great astonishment. Yet, the decision I have made remains unchanged. When such terrible dangers surround my father, the only place for me is at his side. What need have I for the kingdom of Lanka? Or even for this very life? There is no need for further deliberation. Let no one attempt to stop me!” declared the Prince with resolute grandeur.
Then, his gaze turned to Poonguzhali, who was leaning against a pillar some distance away, watching him intently without blinking.
“Daughter of the Ocean! Come here, a little closer!” he called.
Poonguzhali approached him.
“Girl! Through the message you brought, you have done me a great service. There is yet another favor I need from you. Will you do it?” he asked.

‘Oh dear! What is this? Is he asking help from this poor boatwoman? I came here seeking the fortune of serving him, and now he is pleading for my help! I came to beg a boon from God; but here, God himself is stretching out his sacred hands and asking me for alms!’ Thinking thus in her heart, Poonguzhali replied, “Prince! I am waiting to fulfill any command you give!”

“Daughter of the ocean! Did you not say that two ships are waiting near the mouth of the Thondaiman river, searching for me? I must reach that place as quickly as possible. Will you guide me there and take me with you?”
“Girl! Say ‘No’!” thundered a voice. Poonguzhali realized it was the voice of the Commander-in-Chief.

All this while, she had been wandering in some dream world, but only now did she become aware of her perilous situation. With the hope of rescuing the prince from some danger, she had come running in haste—yet now, the prince was asking her to lead him straight into the jaws of that very danger!

“Girl! Say ‘No’!”—the meaning of the Commander’s command was now clear to her. From all sides, a thousand voices echoed the same order. The trees roared it; the pillars of the mandapam cried it aloud; the birds shrieked it from the branches above.

But within the heart of that foolish girl, a gentle voice whispered. ‘Poonguzhali! Here is your fortune! If you guide the prince, you can spend two days with him. You can be near him. When he does not look at you, you can look at him. The breeze that touches him will also touch you. His voice will often fall upon your ears. Ah, girl! A little of that unattainable dream you have cherished will come true. What does it matter what happens after that? Poonguzhali! Consent!’ Thus did that soft voice speak in the ear of her heart.
“Daughter of the ocean! Why do you hesitate? Will you not do me this favor? Must I find my own way?” The prince’s words gave her heart the resolve it needed.
“Prince! I will come to guide you!” she said.

At that moment, the voice of Commander Boothi Vikrama Kesari thundered forth, echoing with a deep resonance akin to the ominous rumble that rises from the bowels of the earth before an earthquake. Stepping a pace forward, he declared:

“Prince! I shall not stand in the way of your wishes. Yet, I ask that you lend your ear to one request of mine. Until the moment I hand you over to those who have come to arrest you, it is my duty to protect you. Your companions have just now spoken of the attempts made on your life last night. Those assassins have not yet been caught. We do not even know who they are. Forgive me for speaking my mind, but I harbor some suspicion regarding this woman. Is it not possible that she too is in league with those murderers? Might not the tale of ships coming to take you captive be nothing but her own invention? Why should it not be so? Just a short while ago, when your friend Vandiyathevan snatched away her dagger and threw it aside, did we not hear a cry as it struck someone? Whose voice was that? Let this woman freely lead the way. Let her ride ahead of us on our elephant. But until I see with my own eyes the ships on the banks of the Thondaiman river, I shall not leave your side! That is my duty!”
The prince, listening to this speech with a smile blooming on his face, replied, “So be it! I too shall not stand in the way of your duty!”

chapters.title: The Elephant Was Terrified!
paragraphs: Once the above decision had been reached, Commander-in-Chief Boothi Vikramakesari took Parthibendran aside and spoke with him privately for some time. Afterwards, he issued a few separate orders to the soldiers who had accompanied him.

Parthibendran then took leave of the prince. “Sir! I am returning empty-handed, my mission unfulfilled. For this, Karikalan will be greatly angered with me. But what can I do? You are adamant in your refusal; I am not to blame. All those present here are witnesses to this!” he declared.
The prince asked, “Is it necessary for you to leave in such haste? Could you not at least accompany the Commander-in-Chief as far as Thondaimanaru before departing?”

“I will not be a party to that treachery. The ship I came on is anchored at Trincomalee. I must go there, board the ship, and proceed to Kanchi as soon as possible. I must report all that has transpired to Karikalan!” Parthibendran replied.
Then, turning to Vandiyathevan, he asked, “Vallavaraiyan! Will you not come with me to Kanchi?”
Vandiyathevan hesitated for a moment and then replied, “No; I wish to go with the prince.”
“Very well; you will regret not coming with me!” Parthibendran said, and departed. In accordance with the Commander-in-Chief’s orders, several other soldiers left with him.
Vandiyathevan turned to Azhwarkadiyan and asked, “What did that Pallavan mean by his words? Why did he say I would regret not going with him? Do you know anything about it?”
“They have certainly conspired together! We shall soon learn the details of their plot. In truth, the root cause of the predicament we now face is this very Kodumbalur Elder!” he replied.
“How so? What could the Commander-in-Chief have done?”
“It is all his doing. You know, do you not, that a woman from his family is being raised in Pazhayarai?” “Of course I know—are you speaking of Vanathi Devi?”

“Yes; the Commander-in-Chief desires to have that maiden wed to the Prince, crown him as King of Lanka, and place the island’s diadem upon his head through the hands of devout gurus. It was he who sent those pious teachers to offer the Lankan crown. Did you think he kept his efforts secret? Not at all. The news has already reached Thanjavur. That is why Prime Minister Aniruddha came to Lanka; he sent me to the Prince as well. Vandiyathevan! Whatever may happen, we must safeguard our own lives. We may be called upon in Thanjavur to bear witness that the Prince refused the throne of Lanka!”

By now, the Commander-in-Chief’s business was concluded. Except for four of the soldiers who had accompanied him, the rest dispersed in different directions. At last, the Prince’s party set out. The Prince, the Commander-in-Chief, Vandiyathevan, Alwarkadiyan, and the aforementioned four soldiers mounted noble steeds and rode northward. Following them, Poonguzhali’s elephant strode majestically, trumpeting “jam jam” with every step. Apart from Poonguzhali, only the mahout sat atop the elephant.

For a short distance, they traveled along the royal road. But the journey was not easy, for the road was crowded everywhere. Somehow, word had spread among the people that the Prince was passing that way. In those days, the northern part of Lanka was inhabited mostly by Tamils. Here and there, groups of people stood together, shouting, “Long live Prince Arulmozhi Varman! Long live the Commander-in-Chief, the Kodumbalur Velar!” In some places, the crowds surrounded the horses and followed behind. The throng grew larger and larger, making it impossible for the horses to move swiftly.

After discussing the matter with the Commander-in-Chief, the Prince decided to leave the royal road and take a forest path. Gradually, they managed to slip away from the crowds and entered the woods. But the natural obstacles of the forest made rapid travel impossible. After a short distance, they came upon a lotus pond. As they reached its bank, they saw a large crowd standing on the opposite shore. At the sight of the travelers, a great tumult of drums, cymbals, horns, and other instruments erupted from the midst of the assembly.

“Wait a moment; let me go and see who they are!” said the Commander, urging his horse forward and riding ahead. After a short while, he returned and said, “It seems the people of the nearby villages have somehow come to know that the Prince is passing this way. They have come only to pay their respects to the Prince!”

The people drew near. They gathered around the Prince, gazing at him with irrepressible curiosity. They raised various shouts of victory and words of blessing. Among them, the cry, “Long live Arulmozhi Varman, King of Eezham!” was the most prominent.
A smile blossomed on the Prince’s face. He called near a man who seemed to be the leader of the crowd. “Why are these people proclaiming me as the King of Eezham?” he asked.

With great humility, the man replied, “O King, for many long years this land of Eezham has suffered without a stable government. It is our plea that Ponniyin Selvan should become the ruler of Eezham. That is the wish of all the people living in this land. Tamils, Sinhalese, Saivites, Buddhists, ascetics, householders—all desire the same.”

The people had arranged a feast for the Prince and his companions. It was impossible to refuse their hospitality. After partaking in the feast, much time had passed before they could take their leave and set out again.
While the Prince was being honored with these courtesies, Vandiyathevan and Azhwarkadiyan found an opportunity to speak privately.
“Brother! Did you see? Don’t you realize all this is the Commander’s scheme? He must have sent word ahead in haste and arranged all these honors!” said Azhwarkadiyan.

“It does seem to be the Commander’s arrangement. But what is the purpose of this scheme? Does he think that, hearing the wishes of the people on this island, the Prince—who refused the throne just yesterday—will now suddenly desire it?” asked Vandiyathevan.
“That may be one intention. But more important than that is to delay our journey!” said Azhwarkadiyan.
“What benefit does the Commander expect from delaying our journey?”
“That I do not know either; but surely, we will find out soon enough? Look at the Prince’s face! Isn’t it clear that he does not like any of this?”

Vandiyathevan looked at the prince’s face. Even when he spoke words of anger, that face would bloom and shine with a radiant charm. But now, a shadow of scorn and bitterness had spread across it. His brows were furrowed. His eyes revealed a deep, consuming thought.

At that same moment, Poonguzhali sat alone on the opposite bank of the lotus pond, lost in her own thoughts. Contrary to her expectations, this journey brought her no joy. She had hoped that, during the voyage, she would have the chance to be alone with the prince. She had imagined that he would converse with her intimately. She had longed to express, if only a little, the emotions surging within her heart. But it seemed there was never an opportunity for any of that. The prince was always surrounded by a crowd.

“Will I be left with nothing but the blame of having delivered him into the hands of his enemies? Why should such a disgrace fall upon me? Why shouldn’t I just run away from here, without anyone knowing? At least I would escape the wrath of the Commander-in-Chief!”

“Bah! What can the Commander-in-Chief’s anger do to me? What can anyone’s anger do to me? I am not afraid of any of that. But why must all my hopes be dashed to dust? How long must this fire in my heart continue to consume me? For what purpose does this life persist in this body? Could not a sudden bolt of lightning strike me down and end it all? How many thousands of times have I wished for that—yet it has never come to pass. This life will not leave me on its own. Only if I do something myself will it end…”

“Ah! What is this? Am I dreaming? No, it is not a dream! There, beside that ruined mandapam, the very dagger that the prince’s friend snatched from me has come and fallen near me! Who could have thrown it? Surely, it must have been thrown by one of his enemies! Surely, it was meant to kill me. What ill fortune! Why did it not fall upon me, but just a little to the side?—But perhaps that too is for the best. Let this dagger remain in my hand. After I have fulfilled the promise I made to him, after I have delivered him into the hands of those traitors, I shall stab myself with this dagger and die before his very eyes. No, no! Why should I wound his heart so? After he boards the ship and sails away, I can take a boat, row into the middle of the sea, and there plunge the dagger into myself and die. My beloved dagger, you have returned to me, have you not? Salutations to those who sent you back.”

“Perhaps the dagger was meant to be thrown at the prince himself? Yes; even the Commander-in-Chief said that many dangers might await him on this journey… Should I not have such an opportunity? If a dagger aimed at him—” Should it not fall upon my heart? And if it does, might there not come a time when I must give up my life for him? If such a moment should arrive, at the very instant when I shed my blood and surrender my life…’
A strange vision arose in Poonguzhali’s mind. A dagger had pierced her chest. Blood was pouring forth from the wound. The prince came running.

“Alas! Are you giving up your life for my sake?” he asked. Poonguzhali’s heart swelled, and blood spurted more fiercely from her breast. The prince gathered her into his arms and laid her across his lap. The blood streaming from her chest soaked his body and garments. Poonguzhali burst into laughter.
“Prince! At least now, do you understand what lies within my heart?” she asked.
“Wretched girl! Did I not know this already? Is this why you would give up your life?” the prince cried out. Poonguzhali was overcome with joy. She laughed aloud, her voice ringing out…
“Hey, madwoman!” came a voice, and Poonguzhali looked up. Vandiyathevan stood before her.
“The prince is already angry; he says the journey is delayed. Don’t cause any more delay. Get up quickly and come!” said Vandiyathevan.
Still laughing, Poonguzhali rose and ran to mount the elephant. She hugged the dagger to her chest and caressed it.

After they had traveled a little further along the forest path, an unexpected event occurred. From the dense woods on their right, with a sharp ‘whizz,’ an arrow flew out. There was no doubt it had been aimed at the prince. But even swifter than the arrow, the prince pulled the reins and turned his horse. The arrow sped so close to him that it struck the headgear of Azhwarkkadiyan, who was riding just behind, and stuck there. Azhwarkkadiyan rubbed his head and looked around in astonishment.
Commander-in-chief Boothi Vikramakesari was startled. Everyone stood frozen in shock.
As for Poonguzhali, she was disappointed that the arrow had not struck her and ended her life.

After a moment, when the shock had subsided, the commander said, “Prince! Do you see now? If we had sent you alone, unprotected, what a disaster it would have been!” With that, he ordered the guards to send soldiers into the woods to search.
They searched for a while and returned, saying, “No one was found.”
The Commander began to make arrangements for the journey. “We must place the prince in the center and surround him on all four sides,” he said, and started to organize the formation.
At that moment, the prince said, “Commander! I have a request.”
“What is this word? Please command me!” replied the Commander.
“I wish to reach Thanjai alive. I want to prove to my father that I am innocent…”
“Your father would never doubt you, Prince!”

“Not just my father; I want to prove it so that all the people will accept it. After accomplishing that, I will have no concern for my life. But until then, I do not wish to lay down my life on the way.”
“Sir! If any danger should befall your life, that very instant this Kodumbalur sword will be plunged into my own chest.”
“That would be of no use. Chola Nadu would suffer a great loss.”
“What greater loss could there be for Chola Nadu than losing you? If I were the cause for any harm to come to you, would this wretch of Kodumbalur keep his life even for a moment after that?”
“In that case, it is all the more important that I protect my own life.”
“There is nothing in this world more important than that.”
“I have an idea for that.”
“Tell me, sir!”
“As long as we travel on horseback, dangers like the one that just occurred with the arrow will keep arising.”
“Are you suggesting we go on foot? Or…”
“You know well that I am fluent in the language of elephants. You are aware that elephants will obey my commands, are you not?”
“Yes, sir! I know that, disguised as a mahout, you have traveled through most of this island of Lanka.”
“So, what I am saying is, for a little while longer, I shall become the mahout again. Let the man who is now guiding the elephant ride my horse and follow us for some distance.”
Hearing this, the Commander-in-Chief seemed somewhat perturbed. He looked around anxiously, as if wondering whether anyone would object to the prince’s suggestion. But everyone remained silent.
“Sir! Does the mahout know how to ride a horse?”
“If he doesn’t, let him walk back.”
“That woman seems to be very modest. What if she refuses to sit on the elephant beside you, saying it is not proper?”
“Let her jump down and walk along.”
“As you wish, Prince!”

Immediately, the prince dismounted from his horse. He went near the elephant. Poonguzhali’s dark eyes grew wide with curiosity and wonder as she watched him. He helped the mahout down and then leapt up onto the elephant, seating himself on its neck. The interrupted journey resumed once more.

Poonguzhali was filled with delight. From the elephant’s back, she felt as if she was leaping onto the clouds. She wandered through the sky. She gazed at heaven itself and, in some manner, understood that this was the indescribable bliss spoken of in legends. ‘Ah! What is this, a celestial grove? How sweet is this happiness! No, even the gardens of the gods cannot match this joy. Is it not the prince himself who is speaking to me?’
“Daughter of the ocean! Do you find it unpleasant to be alone with me on this elephant?”
“By the merit of the penance I have performed over seven births, I have attained this fortune, my lord!”
“If suddenly this elephant goes mad and starts running, will you be afraid?”
“As long as you are by my side, even if the sky falls, I will not be afraid, sir!”
“Where did you leave your boat, Poonguzhali?”
“Near the funeral ghat, my lord!”
“On this bank, or the other?”
“There was a separate spot to anchor the boat on the opposite bank. I left the boat there and came.”
“How did you cross the elephant ghat?”
“When I came, the sea was at low tide. So, for the most part, I walked across. I swam a little as well.”
“Now, if this elephant enters the sea, will you be afraid?”
“Even if I am thrown into the sea itself, I have no worries. Am I not the daughter of the ocean? Was it not you who gave me that name?”
“When we reach the place where your boat is, we shall board it. You must row the boat for us. You can row with both of us aboard, can you not?”

“These hands have held the oar since I was ten years old, my lord! They are not as soft as the hands of palace women, softer than flowers. Did not your friend Vandiyathevan tell you how I rowed him across?”
“He did! But today, you must row even faster than that. We must reach the mouth of the Thondaiman river as quickly as possible.”

“Prince! Why do you command me to do such a cruel thing? I came running to help you escape capture, and now you ask me to take you to those who have come to imprison you. Why do you inflict such cruelty upon this poor girl?”
“Poonguzhali! You know my father—the Emperor—is ill, do you not?”
“I know, sir! I also know that people have been talking about the comet that has appeared in the sky these past few days.”
“At any moment, my father’s life might come to an end, is it not so?”
Poonguzhali was silent.
“If, by chance, he must leave this world, is it right that he should go with the thought that I plotted against him and tried to seize the throne?”
“The Emperor would never believe such a thing of you, not for a single day. This is the plot of the Pazhuvettaraiyars!”
“Even so, I wish to prove that I am innocent, even to the Pazhuvettaraiyars…”
“For what reason, sir?”
“Truly, I have no desire to rule a kingdom, Poonguzhali!”
“Then what is it that you desire?”

“My heart longs to board a boat and journey endlessly upon the boundless sea! I have heard that, beyond the oceans, there are countless lands like the lost Eelam. I yearn to travel to those distant countries. I wish to see their people, to speak with them!”
“How strange! How strange!”
“What is strange?”
“I am astonished that the very longing that dwells in my heart also lives in yours. When you set out on such a voyage across the seas, will you take me with you?”
“First, I must fulfill the duty that lies before me now. Will you help me with that?”
“As you wish!”
“On either side of the seat where you are sitting, there are ropes hanging down, are there not? Take them and tie yourself tightly.”
“For what purpose, Prince?”
“The elephant is about to run amok—be careful, Poonguzhali!”

Saying this, the prince stroked the elephant’s forehead with his hand and whispered something into its ear. Suddenly, the elephant’s pace quickened. The prince bent down again and murmured something more into its ear. That was enough—the walk turned into a gallop. Raising its trunk, the beast let out a terrifying trumpet and began to charge forward. Trees in the forest, battered by the storm’s fury, now suffered under the elephant’s rampage. Branches and boughs snapped and crashed to the ground. The earth trembled; all eight directions quaked in fear. Flocks of birds, startled from the treetops, beat their wings in panic and flew away, shrieking in terror. Wild beasts, hidden deep in the jungle, burst out and scattered in all directions.
“Alas! The elephant seems to have gone mad! What disaster is this!” cried Commander Boothi Vikramakesari.

So far, even Poonguzhali’s heart was seized with fear at what the prince had said. Signs of terror appeared on her face. Poonguzhali felt as though she had been caught in a vast, terrifying, colossal whirlpool of the sea. The prince too was caught in the same whirlpool, spinning round and round. The elephant likewise spun in dizzying circles. Poonguzhali squeezed her eyes shut. Like a dark cloud driven by the storm wind, the elephant kept moving forward. At last, the elephant reached the place known as Iravuththurai—the Elephant’s Landing.

There, the southern and northern seas of Lanka met and merged. That narrow stretch of water where the two seas joined was called Iravu, the Elephant’s Landing. It was at this shore, where the northern and central parts of Lanka converged, that the elephant descended. It plunged into the water as if a mountain hurled by Hanuman had fallen into the sea.

chapters.title: The Prison Ship
paragraphs: In the blink of an eye, the seaport known as ‘Yaanai Iravu’ slipped away behind them.

Then, the forest trees seemed to rush backward. Birds in the sky flew away in retreat. Streams, ponds, village outskirts, temples, mandapams—all darted past and vanished behind. A herd of deer tried to race alongside the elephant for a short distance. The deer, too, fell behind in defeat. Only the elephant pressed on, ever forward, ever ahead. How far, how long—Poonguzhali could not tell. Yet she marveled: was this elephant still traveling within the land of Eezham? Surely, by now, it must have crossed the island three times over! No, no! This elephant had not left the land of Lanka. It was traversing the very earth itself—journeying from the southern tip of the world to its northern crown! Riding upon its back, I too am circumnavigating the globe. Am I alone? The prince is with me!

At first, when the elephant began its wild, frenzied run, Poonguzhali had felt a twinge of fear. Along with fear, there was an anxious uncertainty, not knowing what might happen next. Two or three times, the prince turned to look back at her and smiled. After that, her fear and hesitation melted away. An unbounded exhilaration seized her.

For a while, she rode upon the back of that mighty elephant across this earth. Suddenly, it seemed as if she had ascended to the heavens. In the celestial realms, she was seated upon Indra’s own Airavata. Airavata paraded along the skyways. Kalpaka trees showered her with fragrant blossoms. Gandharvas followed behind, playing sweet harmonies upon their divine instruments. Apsara maidens danced as they came. On either side of the heavenly avenue, star-lamps blazed with radiant, dazzling light! Thus, countless ages seemed to pass!

Now, Airavata’s speed was slackening. Suddenly, it had returned to earth. They were once more amidst the forests of Lanka. The mahout bent forward and tapped the elephant’s forehead. He whispered something into its ear. Wait! Was he not the mahout, but Indra himself?—No, was he not the prince?

The elephant came to a gentle halt upon the bank of a pond, surrounded on all sides by trees. Poonguzhali, with a trace of anxiety, looked to see if a crowd had gathered on the opposite bank to welcome and attend to the prince. No! She glanced back to check if a line of horses was following them—no, not that either! She looked at the pond; the blooming alli flowers and the red lotuses floated towards her, entwined with their vines. They surrounded her on all sides. Those flowers caressed her cheeks, her shoulders, her whole body, embracing her in delight. Then, the relentless vines tightened around her, squeezing her so that she struggled for breath. Her body shook, as if it had been turned upside down and thrown from the grip of those flowered creepers to the earth.
The elephant bent its massive forelegs and knelt. Then, folding its hind legs as well, it lay down on the ground. The prince leapt down from the elephant’s neck.
“Poonguzhali! Don’t you wish to get down from the elephant?” he asked.
Poonguzhali shivered, coming back to her senses. “Ayya! Is it not hard to descend from heaven to earth?” she muttered as she dismounted.
The elephant rose again and broke off a large branch from a tree on the pond’s edge, stuffing it into its vast mouth.
Arulmozhi walked to the bank of the pond and sat down. He beckoned the hesitant Poonguzhali to come and sit beside him.

In the clear water, Poonguzhali’s face was reflected. From the rush of the elephant’s ride and the turmoil of emotions she had just experienced, her face was flushed, glowing red, rivaling the hue of the lotus flower.
Gazing at her reflection in the water, the prince said, “Daughter of the ocean! I like you very much!”
Once again, the alli flowers and red lotuses drifted over and kissed Poonguzhali’s entire body. “Do you know why I like you?” the prince asked.
Before Poonguzhali’s eyes, the sky and earth, the pond, its flowers, and the trees on the bank all spun and whirled around.
“Everyone I know wishes for me to act according to their desires. Only you, you alone, agreed happily to act according to my wishes! I will never forget this favor, O daughter of the ocean!”

Poonguzhali’s body had become a veena. Every nerve of hers was a string of that veena. Her golden-hued fingers plucked those strings and brought forth music sweeter than that of the celestial musicians.

“Senathipathi and Parthibendran conspired together to hinder my journey! Senathipathi created many obstacles along our path. He sent messengers ahead of us in haste, instructing the villagers to prepare receptions for us. Parthibendran hurried to Trincomalee. His intention is to board a ship there and reach the mouth of the Thondaiman river before us. Ah! They thought I was ignorant of their schemes! With your help, I have foiled their plot…”
Suddenly, Poonguzhali remembered what she had done. It was as if the messengers of Yama were dragging her alive into the fires of hell.
“Sir! All of them tried to help you escape without falling into the hands of your enemies. But I, wretched woman that I am, am leading you into captivity!” she cried, and began to sob.
“Oh dear! What is this? I had such a good opinion of you. And now you have become like them?”

“I did not commit this crime by my own will. I was bewitched and driven mad by your words and desires. Now my mind is clear. I am leaving…” So saying, Poonguzhali sprang to her feet. The prince lightly touched her hand to stop her from running away.

At that moment, the maidens of the celestial world had no other task. They mixed the moonlight with sandal paste and sprinkled it upon Poonguzhali. She lost all her strength, her will deserted her, and she sat down again. Covering her face with both hands, she began to sob uncontrollably.
“Daughter of the sea! I wished to tell you something important. But if you are going to cry like this, there is no point. We must leave at once.”
Poonguzhali wiped her tears and looked up at him.
“That’s better. Listen! You said all of them are trying to save me from being captured, didn’t you? That is true. Do you know why?”
“It is because of the love they bear for you. Only I am the traitor!…”

“Wait, wait! Everyone claims to love me! Do you know why? Some astrologers and palmists have foretold that one day I will become an emperor. That is why each and every one of them is eager to lift me onto the throne and place a crown upon my head. Such greedy souls!”
“Sir! Even if they desire so, what is wrong in that? Are you not worthy to be emperor not just of this world, but of all three worlds?”

“Aha! You too speak just like them! Girl, in this world, there is no prison more confining than a palace; no sacrificial altar more dreadful than a throne; no punishment more severe than wearing a crown. If I were to say this to others, they would never agree; I thought at least you would understand.”
Poonkuzhali’s eyelids fluttered like the wings of a silk moth. With her wide, eager eyes, she gazed at the young prince.
“Princess of the sea! Tell me truly! If you were asked to sit on a throne for the rest of your life, would you do it?” the prince asked.
Poonkuzhali pondered for a moment. Then, with clarity, she replied, “I would not!”
“See? Then why do you wish to condemn me alone to such a punishment?”
“Are you not born of royal blood?”

“What of being born in a royal clan? By good fortune, the gods have spared me from such a punishment. My elder brother is there to rule the kingdom; and my great-uncle’s son is also there. He too desires to rule…”
“Aha! So even your ears have heard of that?” asked Poonkuzhali.
“What a story! Did you think I did not know? So, the throne of Thanjavur will not be left wanting for someone to sit upon it. Besides, I have no desire to bear the crown or to rule the kingdom!”
“Then what is it that you desire?” asked Poonkuzhali.

“Listen, I will tell you! Just now, did we not travel seated upon this great elephant? In the same way, I long to wander through forests and wildernesses, roaming like the wild wind. I yearn to board ships and cross the seas…”

A desire to climb to the peaks of lofty mountains. I have heard that, beyond the seas, there are countless islands like this Lanka, and vast continents like Bharata-kanda. I long to travel to all those lands and witness the wonders they hold!”

Poonguzhali listened with her mouth open, as though she would swallow every word the prince uttered. Her curiosity overflowed its bounds, and she asked, “Ayya! When you travel to all those places, will you take me with you?”
“All that I spoke of are but my desires. Who can say if they will ever be fulfilled?” replied the prince.
Poonguzhali descended from her world of dreams to the earth below. “Ayya! If that is so, why must you go to Thanjavur now?” she asked.

“That is what I began to tell you. But you changed the course of our conversation and led it elsewhere. Samudra Kumari! On this island of Lanka, there is a mute woman who cannot speak, wandering here and there like one possessed by visions. Do you know her?” asked Prince Arulmozhi.
With unconcealed astonishment, Poonguzhali replied, “I do, Prince! Why do you ask?”
“I shall tell you the reason later. How do you know that woman? What do you know of her?” he asked.
“Ayya! I lost my birth mother when I was a child. Afterwards, it was that old woman who gave me a mother’s love. She is my teacher; my goddess. What more do you wish to know about her?”
“Does that old woman have a permanent dwelling? Or is she always wandering about?”
“As one approaches Lanka from Kodikkarai, there is an island called Boothathivu. On that island is a rocky cave. That is where she usually stays. It was there that I first saw you.”
“You saw me there?”

“Yes! That old woman has drawn some beautiful paintings on the walls of that rocky cave. In those paintings, I saw your likeness too! That is why, when I later saw you in person at Kodikkarai, I was so astonished.”
“Oh! Now everything is clear to me. Even what was once obscure has become plain.
Samudra Kumari! Do you know about the relationship between that old woman and myself?”
“I guessed there must be some connection. But I do not know exactly what it is!”
“Poonguzhali! That old woman is my great-aunt. By right, she is the noble lady who should be seated upon the throne of Thanjavur!...”
“Heavens! Is that so?”

“But the writing of fate was otherwise—who can change it? Sometimes I have felt that there is a secret sorrow gnawing at my father’s heart, tormenting him. Only now have I discovered the truth of it. My father believes that my great-aunt has died. He thinks she passed away because of him. But she did not die—she is alive! I must go and tell him this. If I do, the burning anguish in his heart will be soothed! The torment that is consuming him will be relieved. You know that the Emperor’s health is not well, don’t you? Human life is fleeting—none can say what may happen or when. For some days now, a comet has appeared in the sky. People are speaking of it in many ways. It seems the Emperor’s mind too has been disturbed by it. In such a situation, before anything untoward happens, I must reveal to him what I have discovered. Samudra Kumari! That is why I am so eager to go to Thanjai at once. Now you understand how important the help you are giving me is, don’t you?”
Poonguzhali, who had been listening to the prince’s words with keen interest, let out a deep sigh. “Oh God! Why did you place so much sorrow alongside joy in human life?” she murmured.

Then, turning to the prince, she said, “Sir! If this foolish girl can be of any help to you, it must be the merit of my past birth. But why do you need my help for this? If you had told the Commander-in-Chief and the others, would they not have sent you to Thanjai?”

“No, I did not wish to tell anyone. To those who are so intent on placing me upon the throne, this matter would not seem important. Nor do I wish to reveal my father’s innermost secrets to them. Even if I did, they would not understand. I have another favor to ask of you, Samudra Kumari! That is why I came here especially—”

I halted the elephant. Astrologers who once promised me the imperial crown and the throne of the empire also foretold that many dangers—many calamities—would befall me in my life. If, during this journey, something of that sort were to happen to me… If I am unable to meet my father… then you must go to the Emperor. Somehow, you must find a way to meet him and tell him that my Periyamma is still alive. If he wishes, you must bring that old lady to him. Will you do all this, Poonguzhali?”
“No harm will ever befall you; danger will flee from your presence in fear; you will certainly reach Thanjavur safely….”
“But if something does happen to me, you will do as I have asked, won’t you?”
“I will certainly do it, my prince!”
“To whom else can I entrust this important task? Tell me yourself, let us see.”

“The task that needs to be entrusted to me has already been given. With that, my usefulness is over, is it not? May I take my leave now?” said Poonguzhali. Her voice was tinged with the dampness of tears.

“Ah! How can that be? We have not yet reached the mouth of the Thondaiman River! We have not yet seen the Chola warships! How can you take leave before that? Don’t be angry! Bear with my company for a little while longer, gritting your teeth if you must. Climb onto the elephant once more and come with me a little further! Once you spot the ship with the tiger flag flying in the distance, you may leave me and go your way!” said the prince.

Without a word in reply, Poonguzhali walked towards where the elephant stood. The prince followed her. Obeying his command, the elephant knelt down. Both of them climbed onto its back. This time, the prince did not urge the elephant forward as before. Yet, it moved swiftly.
“Daughter of the ocean! I have told you about the things I like most, haven’t I? Should you not tell me what you like?” asked Arulmozhi Varman.
“I am very fond of Yama, who comes riding on his buffalo vehicle. I love to stand atop a rocky peak at midnight and watch the goblins of the burning gorges, losing all sense of time….”
“What a strange and wondrous girl you are!”

“Call me a madwoman, as your friend says. I will not be offended by it. In fact, I enjoy riding a small boat into the heart of the stormy sea. When the wind howls and the waves rise, my excitement knows no bounds. At such times, the boat climbs the crest of a wave, reaching up as if to touch the heavens; the next moment, it plunges with a crash into the abyss below. There is nothing else I love more than this. Just a while ago, when that elephant came charging in a frenzy, even then I felt the same thrill!”

“Ah, Poonguzhali! If Lord Muruga himself had come seeking your smile, he would have been utterly defeated! He once sent the elephant-faced Ganesha to frighten the tribal maiden Valli, but such tricks would never work with you!” said the prince.
As they approached the mouth of the Thondaiman river, Poonguzhali suddenly cried out, “Ah! What is this?”
“What? What is it?” asked the prince eagerly.

“The ships with the tiger flag are not where I saw them before! What will you think of me now? Just as the Commander-in-Chief suspected me, I have deceived you and brought you here under false pretenses!” she exclaimed.
“I would never think that, not for a moment. Poonguzhali! You have shown no sign of lying or deceiving me…”

“Why not, my prince? Could it not be for the sake of love? Suppose a foolish girl, infatuated with Ponniyin Selvan—whom the world praises as the equal of Manmatha in beauty and Arjuna in valor—did something like this, could it not happen?”
“Girl! If the Commander-in-Chief were here at this moment, perhaps he might suspect such a thing. But in your heart and in mine, there is no room for such mad thoughts.”
“Sir! In the palace at Pazhayarai, there is a princess of noble warrior lineage named Vanathi Devi—would you say the same about her?”

“Yes, yes! I have not forgotten. That Commander-in-Chief and my sister are both trying to tie that girl to my neck. Perhaps, driven by the desire to see me seated on the Chola throne, that foolish girl too harbors such ambitions. But I am not responsible for that, Poonguzhali! Let that be! Where were the ships when you saw them?” asked the prince.
“There! It was right at that very spot!” said Poonguzhali. “I remember it very well!”
“So what? It could have moved a little this way or that. Let’s go along the shore and see for ourselves!” said the Prince.
“If the ships have left, so much the better. Why should we go searching for them now?” asked Poonguzhali.
“Ah! You may think so. But for me, nothing could be more disappointing!” replied the Prince.

Three hundred years ago, the Lankan prince Manavarman had come to Kanchipuram seeking refuge. To restore his kingdom to him, Emperor Mamalla sent a great army. The troops he dispatched landed right here in this region. At that time, the Thondaiman River was but a small stream at this spot. To make it convenient for the ships to anchor and for the soldiers to disembark, they cut and deepened the stream, making it wider. Later, that stream became known as Thondaimanaru. Near its mouth, the river wound its way, twisting and turning. On both banks, thick trees grew. Because of this, it was easy for ships to remain hidden from those looking out from the sea.

It was at such a place, where the river entered the land and water pooled deeply, that Poonguzhali had seen the ships that had come to capture the Prince. Now, at the spot where she had first seen them, those ships were nowhere to be found. The rafts, the masts, and the flags were all missing. As they drew closer to the place, a strange sight appeared before them. One ship had left the floodwaters and gone far inland, where it now lay sunk deep in the mud. Its rafts and masts were broken and scattered. There was no sign of any people aboard.

Poonguzhali recognized at once that this was one of the ships she had seen two days before. To her astonishment, she realized that one of the very ships that had come to capture the Prince now lay imprisoned in the mud!

chapters.title: A Heart Overflowing
paragraphs: The prince whispered a charm into the elephant’s ear; the elephant knelt down. Both of them hastily dismounted from its back. They went to examine the wooden ship that lay half-buried in the sand near the shore. The fate of that vessel was pitiable to behold. The planks were shattered and strewn about in utter disarray. They wondered if perhaps someone might be inside the wrecked ship or nearby. The prince clapped his hands to make a sound. Poonkuzhali cupped her hands to her mouth and called out. There was no response.

Both of them waded into the water, grasped the edge of the ship, and climbed aboard. The bottom planks had split open, and water and sand had poured in abundantly. Any hope that they might push it into the water and set sail was dashed. It was impossible to move that ship from there. Even to drag it ashore, a single elephant would not suffice; it would require many elephants and many men. To repair it, shipwrights would have to labor for months.
Amidst the broken planks, the prince found the tiger flag ensnared. It was clear that this sight caused him deep anguish.
“Poonkuzhali! Is this one of the ships you saw?” he asked.
“It seems so. The other ship appears to have sunk completely and disappeared!” replied Poonkuzhali, a note of excitement in her voice.
“Why are you so elated?” the prince asked.
“Should I not be glad if the ships that came to capture you have sunk and vanished?” said Poonkuzhali.

“It is wrong for you to rejoice, O Princess of the Sea! Something calamitous has occurred here. It pains me to see the ship bearing the tiger flag in such a state. I do not even know how this happened. What became of the warriors and sailors aboard? The thought troubles my heart even more. Are you saying the other ship must have sunk?”

“I only say it might have sunk. If it has, that would be for the best.” “There is nothing good about this, not at all. Such a day should never have dawned. After seeing the fate of this ship, perhaps another vessel has sailed away to where the waters are deeper. I do not understand why this ship had to come so close to the shore. The sailors of Chola Nadu come from a lineage that has been accustomed to the sea for thousands of years. Why would they make such a mistake? Surely, those who were on board must have escaped. Perhaps they boarded the other ship and left! Come! Let us go and see!”
“Where shall we look, Prince? The sun has set and darkness is gathering on all sides!” said Poonguzhali.
“Daughter of the Ocean! Where did you leave your boat?”

“My boat is almost in the middle of this river, is it not? Since we came on the elephant—and you were the one guiding it—we have arrived so quickly. Had we come by boat, we would have reached here only at midnight.”

“Very well! Before it gets completely dark, let us walk along the riverbank and see. The trees here block the view of the sea. Perhaps they have anchored another ship a little farther out in the sea, haven’t they?”

Leaving the elephant where it was, the two of them walked along the riverbank towards the sea. Very soon, they reached the seashore. The sea lay in perfect tranquility. There was not the slightest sign of a wave. As far as the eye could see, it appeared as a vast sheet of green. The green of the sea and the pale blue of the sky mingled together far off in the distance.

There was no sign of a ship or a boat. A couple of birds flew from the sea towards the shore. That was all! After standing there for a while, looking around in all directions, the Prince said, “Very well! Let us go to the sunken ship!”
They turned and began to walk back the way they had come.
“Poonguzhali! I will never forget the help you have given me. But here, we must part ways,” said the Prince.

Poonguzhali remained silent. “Did you hear what I said? I have decided to wait at the sunken ship itself. Commander-in-Chief and the others will surely come searching for this place. I will consult with them and decide what to do next. But you have no more work here. Find your boat and leave. Remember what I told you about my father…”
Poonkuzhali hesitated and stood still, leaning against a tree nearby. She grasped one of its low-hanging branches.
“What is it, Samudrakumari? What troubles you?”
“Nothing, Prince! I am taking my leave of you here. Please, go on your way!”
“Are you angry, Poonkuzhali?”
“Angry? What right does this fool have to be angry with you? I have not grown so proud as that.”
“Then why have you suddenly stopped here?”
“It is not anger, sir! Only weariness! It has been two days since I last slept. Let me lie down here for a while, and then I will search for my boat and be on my way.”

It was the day after the full moon. At that hour, the moon was rising over the eastern sea. A few pale rays fell upon Poonkuzhali’s face. The prince looked at her face. He saw the exhaustion and fatigue that had settled there. He saw her eyes, heavy with sleep, her lids closing of their own accord. It is natural for the red lotus to close when the moon rises. But one could not say that Poonkuzhali’s lotus-like face merely closed; it had withered and drooped in utter weariness.
“Girl! You say it has been two days since you slept? How many days since you last ate?” he asked.
“It has been more than two days since I ate. While I was with you, I did not even feel hunger.”

“How can I describe my foolishness? Today, all of us feasted until we could eat no more. I even forgot to ask, ‘Did you eat?’ Come, Poonkuzhali! Come with me to that sunken ship! I remember seeing grains scattered there. Let us gather those grains and cook a meal together tonight. After you have eaten, you may go your way…”
“Sir! If I eat, I will fall asleep right there. Even now, my head is spinning.”
“So what of it? You go and lie down peacefully in that sunken ship and sleep! The elephant and I will keep watch from the shore. At daybreak, you can go in search of your boat!”

So saying, the Prince took Poonguzhali by the hand, as if to support her, and led her along. He saw that her steps were indeed faltering. When he thought of the boundless love of this woman, he wondered if there was anything in all the seven worlds to equal it, and tears welled up in his eyes.

When they returned to the sunken ship, they were startled to see smoke rising from behind it. Could it be that those who belonged to that ship had gone somewhere and now returned? If they suddenly appeared before them, anything could happen. So, they proceeded quietly, making no sound. Even after they drew near, no voices or conversation could be heard. There was no way to tell who was hiding there, or how many there were. Only the fragrant aroma of roasting yams drifted on the air.

Knowing Poonguzhali’s condition well by now, the Prince decided that the first order of business was to satisfy her hunger. So, thinking to let come what may, he circled the ship and peered beyond. There, he saw that it was a woman preparing to cook, having kindled a fire. In the next moment, he realized who that woman was. The old lady did not seem surprised to see them; rather, she appeared as if she had been expecting them. Without a word, she welcomed them. In a short while, she had prepared a meal.
To the Prince, the simple meal of hot rice and roasted yam given by that old woman seemed tastier than all the royal feasts he had enjoyed in the palace at Pazhayarai.

After eating, the three of them went to the deck of the ship. By now, the moon had risen high. From the deck, they could see the place where the sea and the Thondaimanaru River merged, and beyond that, the vast expanse of ocean. In the twilight of early evening, the sea had looked like a sheet of green copper; now, bathed in the golden beams of the moon, it gleamed like a plate of gold.

Though they were surrounded by water in the open, moonlit night, sweat broke out on their bodies from the stifling heat. Not a breath of wind stirred. The Prince had remarked on this to Poonguzhali, and somehow the old woman had understood. She pointed to a grey halo encircling the moon in the sky.
“When there is a ring around the moon, it is a sign that storm and rain will come,” Poonguzhali explained.
“Let the storm come when it will; for now, a little breeze is enough!” said the prince. Then he expressed his wonder at how that old woman could have arrived there so quickly.
“For my aunt, this is no great feat; she has accomplished things far more astonishing than this!” replied Poonguzhali.
“And the love she has for you knows no bounds. What cannot be achieved by the power of love?” she added.

Somehow, the old woman seemed to understand this conversation as well. She turned Poonguzhali’s face and pointed in a certain direction. There, they saw the elephant on which they had arrived standing still. Beside it stood a majestic, tall horse of noble breed, and both of them were amazed.
“Did she come here riding this horse? Does she know how to ride a horse?” the prince asked in astonishment.

“There is nothing my aunt does not know. She can ride a horse, ride an elephant, and even row a boat. Sometimes I wonder if she travels through the air itself, so swiftly does she appear from one place to another. It always amazes me how she manages it.”
At that moment, the prince was absorbed in another wonder. The majestic appearance of the horse grazing by the shore filled him with awe.
“Is this not one of the finest horses bred in Arabia? How did it come here? How did this old woman come to possess it?” he murmured to himself.

Poonguzhali used sign language to ask the mute queen about this. (Yes, from now on, shall we not call that old woman the ‘Mute Queen’?) The Mute Queen indicated that the horse had come ashore from the sea near the ‘Elephant Quay,’ and, upon reaching land, had stood there bewildered and frightened. She had then calmed it with gentle affection, tamed it, and ridden it here.
Hearing this, the prince’s amazement only grew.
As they continued speaking, the prince noticed Poonguzhali’s eyelids drooping. “You said you were sleepy before. Go and lie down!” he said.

No sooner had he spoken than Poonguzhali moved a little away and lay down. She picked up a ship’s blanket lying nearby and covered herself with it. Within a short while of lying down, she fell asleep. From the rhythm of her breathing, it was clear that she had drifted into slumber.
Yet, even in her sleep, her lips murmured a song in a soft voice.
“When the waves of the sea are still, Why does the ocean within surge so?”

Ah! This was the very song Vandiyathevan had been humming repeatedly yesterday! It seemed he had learned it from her. The prince thought that, at another time, when the Samudrakumari was awake, he must ask her to sing the entire song for him. Instantly, his attention turned to the mute queen. Ah! At times, everyone’s inner ocean surges! The heart swells with emotion! Yet, what comparison could be found for the storm of feeling within this old woman, who could never open her lips and express her emotions? How many desires and attachments, how many joys, how many sorrows, how much anger and pain—she had locked them all within her heart! For how many years she had kept them suppressed!

The mute queen shifted her place and came to sit beside the prince. She gently stroked his hair with affection. With her strong, diamond-studded hands, she softly touched both his cheeks as though caressing a flower. For a moment, the prince did not know what to do. Then, he touched her feet and pressed them to his eyes. She took his hands and held them to her face. Soon, the prince’s hands were dampened by the tears that welled up in the queen’s eyes.

With gestures, the mute queen told the prince to lie down and sleep as well. She assured him that she would keep watch and that he could sleep without worry. The prince felt that sleep would not come to him. Yet, to satisfy her, he lay down. For a long time, his inner ocean continued to churn restlessly. Later, a cool breeze drifted in from outside. As his body cooled, his heart too calmed; sleep came lightly to him.

But even in sleep, the prince’s mind found no peace. He saw many strange dreams. He rode a fine Arabian horse and journeyed through the sky. He passed through clouds and entered the celestial realms. There, Indra himself took him upon Airavata and led him on. Indra bade him sit upon his jeweled throne. “Oh! I do not want this. I wish to seat my great mother, the mute queen, upon this throne,” said the prince.

Devendran laughed and said, “Let her come here first, then we shall see.” Devendran handed the divine nectar to the prince and bade him drink. The prince tasted it and remarked, “Oh! This is not quite as good as the water of the Kaveri, is it?”

Devendran led the prince into the inner chambers. There, many celestial women were gathered. Indrani, upon seeing the prince, said, “Among these women, you may wed the one who is the most beautiful.” The prince looked around and replied, “None of these can compare to the beauty of Poonguzhali.”
Suddenly, Indrani transformed into the younger princess. “Arulmozhi! Have you forgotten my Vanathi?” she asked.

The prince exclaimed, “Akka! Akka! For how many more days are you going to keep me as your captive? The prison of your love is worse than the dungeons of the Pazhuvettaraiyars! Set me free! Otherwise, like Uttara Kumaran, the son of King Virata, keep me confined within the palace itself. I shall while away my days in music and dance.”

The young princess Kundavai placed her finger, as delicate as the stem of a kanthal flower, upon her coral-red lips and gazed at him in astonishment. “Arulmozhi! Why have you changed so? Who has corrupted your mind? Yes, my brother, love is indeed a kind of bondage. You must submit to it,” she said.
“No, Akka, no! What you say is wrong. There is a love that does not enslave. Shall I show it to you? Watch as I call her!… Poonguzhali! Poonguzhali! Come here!” he called out.

At the break of dawn, Poonguzhali awoke to the sound of a horse’s hooves. She saw the mute queen mounting a horse and setting off. Poonguzhali sprang up and ran to stop her. But before she could descend from the ship and reach the shore, the horse had already sped away.

The early morning was exceedingly beautiful. Poonguzhali’s heart brimmed with a joy she had never known before. Standing there, she gazed at the upper deck of the ship. The prince was still asleep. Poonguzhali walked along the riverbank, listening to the sweet songs of the birds. Upon the bent branch of a tree sat a large, demonic-looking parrot. Seeing Poonguzhali, it showed no fear. It stared at her as if to ask, “Where have you come from?”
“Parrot, my friend! In a little while, the prince will leave from here. After that, you alone will be my companion. Will you not speak with me?” Poonguzhali asked.

At that moment, she heard a voice calling, “Poonguzhali! Poonguzhali!” At first, she thought it was the parrot speaking. No; she realized the voice was coming from the ship. The prince was calling her. Knowing this, she ran swiftly. But when she climbed up to the deck and looked— The prince was still asleep. As Poonguzhali approached him, his lips once again murmured, “Poonguzhali!” The girl, her body tingling with delight, went near the prince and touched his forehead to wake him.
The prince awoke, shaking off sleep and dreams. In the eastern sky, the sun was rising. Poonguzhali’s face shone like a blooming red lotus.
“You called me—why?” she asked.
“Did I call your name? Perhaps I spoke something in my sleep. Last night, you sang even as you slept! Can’t I speak in my sleep too?” he replied.

The prince sprang to his feet. “Oh! Have I slept so long? Where is Periyamma?” he asked, looking all around. The sea maiden told him that the old woman had mounted her horse and left early in the morning.

“She did a good thing! Samudrakumari, you seem to have recovered from your fatigue. You may take your leave now. I must stay here until my friends arrive. Until then, I’ll go and inspect this ship,” he said.

Poonguzhali pointed and said, “There! Look there!” The prince looked in the direction she indicated. Far out at sea, a large wooden ship was visible. Near the shore, a small boat was approaching. There were five or six people in the boat.
“Ah! Now all the secrets will be revealed!” said the prince.

He feared that the boat might reach the shore without noticing their presence. So, without delay, he climbed down from the sunken ship and walked along the riverbank toward the seashore. Poonguzhali followed him. The elephant too ambled behind them.
They reached the shore and stood there. The large ship was moving farther and farther away from them. The boat was drawing nearer and nearer.
At first, Poonguzhali lingered behind, but curiosity soon brought her to the front.
Amidst the prince’s worries, Poonguzhali’s eagerness brought him cheer. A faint smile played on his lips.

He had many reasons for concern. He felt that he ought to have been on the ship that was now sailing away into the distance, leaving him behind. That was not all; in the boat that was nearing them, it seemed that one person was missing. Someone who should have been there was absent. Yes; there was the Commander-in-Chief— Thirumalaiyappar was present. Along with him stood the warriors; the boatmen were there as well. But that young man of the Vanar clan was nowhere to be seen. Where was Vallavaraiyan? Where was that spirited youth, that tireless hero, that fearless-hearted warrior, the secret messenger sent by the Young Princess?… Though only two days had passed in his company, to the Prince he had already become like a friend of many years. His qualities had so captivated the Prince's heart. Not seeing him in the boat, the Prince felt a pang, as though he had lost a rare fortune that had come to him by chance.
As the boat drew nearer and reached the shore, the Commander-in-Chief and the others leapt out onto the bank. Commander-in-Chief Boothi Vikramakesari ran up and embraced the Prince.

“My lord! You have done a noble deed; but how could you throw us into such confusion!… How does a mad elephant become calm? See how gentle this fierce elephant now stands!… Prince! When did you arrive here? Did you see the ships of the Pazhuvettaraiyars? Where are they?” The great Velar of Kodumbalur showered him with questions.
“Commander! I will tell you our story later. Where is Vandiyathevan? Tell me!” he asked.
“That impetuous lad is going on that ship over there!” said the Commander, pointing to a vessel moving away in the distance.
“Why? Why? Whose ship is that? Why is Vandiyathevan on it?” the Prince asked.
“My lord! My mind is in utter confusion. Ask this Vaishnavite! He knows your affairs, and also the nature of that youth!” he replied.
The Prince turned to Azhwarkadiyan and said, “Thirumalai! Why is Vandiyathevan going on that ship? If you know, tell me quickly!”

chapters.title: The Demon’s Laughter
paragraphs: After the prince and Poonguzhali mounted the elephant and departed, it is our duty, dear listeners, to recount what befell those who remained behind.
