When the Commander-in-Chief shouted, “The elephant has gone mad!” the others at first believed him without question. They tried to spur their horses to follow the elephant at full speed. But that proved impossible. As soon as the elephant reached the riverbank, their journey was brought to an abrupt halt. As usual, Vandiyathevan’s horse was the first to leap down into the muddy shore, only to become stuck in the mire. With great difficulty, they managed to pull it free, but the horse was no longer fit for travel.

Commander-in-Chief Boothi Vikrama Kesari struck his forehead in frustration, not knowing what to do next. “Never in my life have I made such a blunder. Why are you all standing idle? What can we do? How can we save the prince? If anyone has an idea, speak up!” he cried.
At that moment, Azhwarkadiyan stepped forward and said, “Commander! I have a thought; may I speak?”
“Are you waiting for an auspicious moment to speak? Out with it, quickly!” snapped the Commander.
“The prince’s elephant has not truly gone mad…”
“What nonsense are you babbling? Then who has gone mad? You?”

“No one has gone mad. The prince has begun to suspect that you are deliberately delaying the journey. That is why he spurred the elephant to leave us behind and sped away. We all know that the prince is a master of every secret art of handling elephants!”
The Commander realized this might indeed be true, and his heart found some peace.

“Very well; let it be so. But we must still reach the mouth of the Thondaimaan River. We must find out what is happening there, mustn’t we?” “We must go. We should follow the edge of the seashore and, if we find a boat somewhere, cross over in it. Otherwise, we will have to wait until Parthibendran Pallavan’s ship arrives.”
“Vaishnavar! You are a cunning man. It seems you have told the prince something of this sort.”
“Commander! Since this journey began, I have not spoken a word to the prince.”

After this, they proceeded eastward along the edge of the lagoon. Readers may already have some idea of the nature of the northern part of the island of Lanka. In those days, the northern tip of Lanka was known as Nagadweepa. The sea, jutting in from both sides, separated that region from the rest of the island. The narrowest point where one could cross from one part to the other was called the ‘Yaanai Iravu’ ferry. Sometimes, the water at this crossing would be shallow, making it easy to wade across. At other times, crossing was not so simple; one had to use boats. (The name ‘Yaanai Iravu’—the Elephant Crossing—came from the herds of elephants that would descend into the water and cross at this spot. It is also said that, in ancient times, elephants were loaded onto ships at this place and sent to foreign lands.)

At that time, almost all the boats along the Lankan coast had gone to Mathottam and Trincomalee. Even so, thinking that perhaps one or two boats might have been left behind by chance, the Commander and his companions kept searching as they went. At last, they found a small fishing boat belonging to a fisherman. Only the boatman was aboard. When he learned that his passengers included the Commander of Chozha Nadu, he agreed to take them.

They boarded the boat and crossed the sea channel. But then, how were they to reach the mouth of the Thondaiman River? Traveling through the forest would not be easy, nor quick. So, they decided to use the same boat and proceed along the southern seashore to reach the confluence of the Thondaiman River.
Until midnight, the boatman rowed along the coast. After that, he was exhausted. The others offered to help, but it was of no use.

“From here on, we must often change direction. There are many bends and rocky outcrops. If we hit a rock, the boat will shatter to pieces. We can only continue after daybreak,” he said. The Commander and his companions, too, were weary. So, they disembarked and lay down to rest in a grove by the shore.
Vandiyathevan did not like this one bit. He quarreled with Azhwarkadiyan.
“All this misfortune has come upon us because of you!” he exclaimed.
“What has come now because of me?” asked Azhwarkadiyan.

“You never speak your mind openly. Ever since Kadambur, I have been watching you. You speak as if you are telling everything, but you always keep half the matter secret. You knew the reason why the prince mounted the elephant, didn’t you? If you had told me that beforehand, wouldn’t I too have climbed onto that elephant? After all the trouble I went through to find the prince, now have I let him slip through my fingers? What shall I say to the young princess when I go to Pazhaiyarai?” said Vandiyathevan.
“Your duty ended when you handed over the letter. What more is there?” said Azhwarkadiyan.
“That is not so. Only after I bring the prince safely to the young princess will my duty be fulfilled. But it seems you yourself are standing in the way of that!”
“No, my friend, no! I am not standing in your way. Tomorrow itself, I will take leave of the Commander-in-Chief and go my own way.”
“Perhaps you think your task is done, that you have handed over the prince. I have always had some doubts about you. Now they are confirmed.”
In this manner, after quarreling for a while, they both fell asleep. So exhausted were they that they slept like men who had been knocked out.

At dawn, as the first light broke and the sound of oars reached their ears, Azhwarkadiyan was the first to wake. The sight before him startled him. A wooden raft, made of woven reeds, was floating a little distance out at sea. It was clear that it was ready to set out on a journey. From the shore, a boat was heading toward that raft. Besides the boatman, there were three people in it. It did not take Azhwarkadiyan long to recognize that this was the very same boat that had ferried them the previous evening.

He quickly guessed where that raft had suddenly come from. The sea had crept inland right beside the spot where they had lain down. Trees partly concealed that place. In that very cove— That marakkalam (wooden ship) must have been anchored there; it should have set sail at dawn.

Whose ship was that? Where had it come from? Where was it headed? Why was the boat rowing towards the ship? Who were those aboard? All these questions flashed through Azhwarkadiyan’s mind like lightning and vanished.
“Senathipathi! Senathipathi! Wake up!” he shouted.
The Senathipathi, Vandiyathevan, and the other two warriors all started awake in alarm.

The first thing that caught their eyes was the swift wooden ship standing in the sea. The Senathipathi exclaimed, “Oh! That is a Chola ship. It must have been sent by the Pazhuvettaraiyars! Perhaps the prince is leaving on it? Alas! We have fallen asleep! What a blunder we have committed!”
Then he said, “Where is the boat? Let’s see if we can catch up to the ship!”
Even as he spoke, he saw the boat already moving away. “Ah! There it goes—isn’t that the boat we came in? Who are those boarding it? Hey, boatman! Stop, stop!” he pleaded.
Whether the boatman heard him or not, it was unclear. He did not stop the boat; instead, he rowed it away at speed.

Vandiyathevan watched and listened to all this. The Senathipathi’s words—“The prince is leaving on that ship!”—entered his ears and became etched in his mind. After that, there was no room for any other thought. Was there any doubt about what he must do? Was there any need for his legs to wait for a command? Not at all! In the very next instant, he leapt into the sea. Pushing aside the waves, he swam with great speed. Fortunately, the water near the shore was not deep, so he was able to cover a great distance quickly. He reached close to the boat. Suddenly, the depth of the water increased, and he began to struggle. “Alas! I am about to drown! Save me!” he shouted.
He heard someone laughing from the boat. Then he heard voices speaking. The boat stopped; the boatman bent down and offered his hand. Vandiyathevan climbed aboard and sat down. The boat moved on.

Vandiyathevan examined those in the boat. One of them was clearly not from Tamil Nadu; he looked like an Arab. Wondering how he had come there, Vandiyathevan looked at the other two. Their faces were half-covered with turbans, but it was clear they were Tamils. Not only that— Faces he had seen before appeared before his eyes. Where, where had he seen them?—Ah! Now he remembered! Were these not the same men who had returned from Parthibendran Pallavan’s camp? Was it not Azhwarkkadiyan who had said that these were the men who had come to kill the prince? Oh! Had he not seen one of them elsewhere as well? Was this not the sorcerer Ravidasan? Was he not the one who had come to see the Lady of Pazhuvoor, howling like an owl? Yes, yes—now it was clear: knowing that the prince was on the ship, they were planning to board it! Ah! Was this then a danger lying in wait along the prince’s path? How fortunate it was that I rushed here and managed to catch this boat!

The boat was moving forward, drawing closer to the ship. The men in the boat maintained a heavy silence. Vandiyathevan could not bear the silence; he wished to break it, to draw them into conversation.
“Where are you going?” he asked.
“Don’t you know? We’re going to that ship over there!” replied the sorcerer. His voice, muffled by his half-closed mouth, sounded like the voice of a ghost.
“Where is the ship going?” Vandiyathevan asked.
“That will be known only after we board the ship,” said Ravidasan.
Once again, silence settled over the boat. Outside, the roar of the sea surrounded them. Now, the sorcerer Ravidasan broke the silence. “Where are you going, boy?” he asked.
“I too am going to the ship,” replied Vandiyathevan.
“And after you board the ship, where will you go?”
“That, too, I will know only after I have boarded the ship!” Vandiyathevan answered, turning the lesson back upon them.

The boat reached the side of the ship. From above, a ladder was lowered down. One by one, they climbed up. Before the ladder was pulled up, Vandiyathevan clung to it as well. On the deck above, some conversation was taking place in a language he could not understand. Vandiyathevan hurried up the ladder and leapt onto the deck. As soon as he landed, he cried out, “Where is the prince?” and looked around anxiously.
The sight that met his eyes shook even his iron heart. All around him stood men of Arab lands, their appearances fierce and terrifying.
They stood still. Each one of them appeared like a demon. All of them stared at him, unblinking. No one answered his question.

A feeling welled up in Vandiyathevan’s heart: “We have made a grave mistake.” This could not be a Chola ship; it was impossible. The men aboard were not Tamil sailors. These were Arabs who brought great horses for sale.

It was unthinkable that the prince would be on this ship. In their haste, they had boarded the wrong vessel. How to escape now? He bent over the edge of the deck and looked down at the sea. The boat was still moving away. “Boatman! Stop!” he shouted, preparing to leap into the water.
At that moment, a hand as hard as a thunderbolt seized his throat from behind—one pull, one shove. Vandiyathevan was flung to the center of the ship’s deck.
A fierce rage seized him. He sprang up and landed a blow on the jaw of the man who had pushed him. That six-foot-tall Arab, along with the man standing behind him, crashed to the floor.

A terrifying roar sounded behind Vandiyathevan. He turned just in time; otherwise, a knife would have plunged into his back. As he spun, he struck the knife aside. With a metallic clang, it fell to the deck, bounced away, and disappeared into the sea.

The next instant, several men surrounded Vandiyathevan and seized him. They spoke in a language he could not understand. Their leader barked an order in an authoritative voice. At once, they brought out ropes and bound Vandiyathevan’s hands and feet. His arms were tied tightly to his body. Then, four men lifted him and carried him below deck. All the while, Vandiyathevan struggled, kicking and writhing, trying to break free. But his efforts were in vain. They carried him to the hold of the ship and threw him down onto a pile of wooden crates. They tied him to one of the crates and left him there, ascending back to the upper deck.
The ship rocked and swayed. Vandiyathevan realized that the voyage had begun. As the ship rolled, the wooden crates tumbled over him. His hands were bound, and he could not push them away.
“If I escape with my life this time, I will never again act in haste. Like Azhwarkadiyan, I must think deeply before doing anything,” Vandiyathevan resolved in his heart.

At that moment, a laughter like that of a ghost echoed nearby. With great difficulty, Vandiyathevan turned his face slightly to look. There he saw the sorcerer Ravidasan standing. The cloth that had until now covered half of the sorcerer’s face had been removed.
“Ah! I came searching for the tiger of the Chola clan; the tiger was not caught. But you, the fox of the Vanar clan, have fallen into the trap! Until now, fortune favored you!” he said.

Of the events described above, those present had seen only up to the point when Vandiyathevan boarded the boat and left. What happened inside the ship was unknown even to the boatman who rowed it away. He immediately turned back and reached the shore.

The Commander-in-Chief and others boarded the boat. They had come to the decision that it was no longer possible to pursue and capture that ship. Therefore, they resolved to go and see the confluence of the Thondaiman River. Perhaps another ship might be there. Perhaps the prince might still be in it. Somehow, some news might be obtained.
They questioned the boatman. He knew nothing.

“I was lying down asleep in the boat. Early in the morning, someone came and woke me. They said if I took them to the ship, I would be paid well. They told me I could return before you woke up, so I went. I know nothing else,” he said.
Of all the events recounted above, Azhwarkadiyan told the prince everything he knew, leaving nothing out.

Then he said, “Prince! When Vandiyathevan jumped into the sea and swam away, at first I thought I too should follow him. But I have always had a little hesitation about the sea; I do not know how to swim well. Moreover, I had some doubts about that ship that was sailing away. It did not seem possible for you to board it. And I wondered if that ship could even belong to the Chola country. I mentioned this to the Commander-in-Chief as well. We both decided to come here and see for ourselves. Only after seeing you did our minds find peace!” he said.

Listening carefully to everything Azhwarkadiyan said, Arulmozhi Varman replied, “But my mind does not find peace, Thirumalai! Vandiyathevan is going on that ship. If the Pazhuvettarayars capture him and imprison him in the underground dungeon—” “They will cast me aside!” he said.

At that moment, the Commander-in-Chief spoke: “Prince! Why should we tolerate the authority of those cruel men? Only give your consent. Before the next full moon, I shall put an end to the power of the Pazhuvettaraiyars, lock them up in that underground prison, and then attend to other matters.”
“Sir! Do not even dream that I would act, even by a hair’s breadth, against my father’s wishes!” the prince replied.

At that moment, the sound of a horse galloping swiftly was heard, and everyone turned to look. The horse stopped a short distance away. When they saw that the rider, who had come mounted without bridle or saddle, was a woman, all were astonished.

chapters.title: The Death of ‘Kalapathi’
paragraphs: The prince immediately recognized the lady who had arrived on horseback. He hurried toward the spot where the horse had stopped. Poonguzhali followed him. The others, hesitating and uncertain, trailed behind at some distance.
The mute queen had already dismounted from her horse. She glanced anxiously at the group approaching from behind, then turned to Poonguzhali and conveyed something in the language of signs.
“Periyamma has seen something wondrous in the forest. She is calling us to come to that place!” Poonguzhali said.
The prince decided at once to go. He asked if the others could accompany them. The mute queen, after a moment’s thought, nodded her head in assent.

As they walked, everyone spoke in wonder about the horse she had ridden. How had this elderly lady come by such a magnificent, high-bred horse from Arabia? No armies had landed in this region recently; no wars had been fought. In that case, how could this horse have come into the possession of this woman?

We have seen a Chola ship run aground and half-buried near the mouth of the Thondaiman river. From there, the coast of Lanka curved and twisted away to the southeast. The sea often carved small and large lagoons into the land. It was from one such bay that the ship Vandiyathevan and the others had seen that morning had emerged and sailed out to sea.

Now, the mute queen led them toward the southeast, plunging into the dense forest. As they went, the prince’s curiosity grew—surely some significant event must have occurred; otherwise, this old woman would not have summoned them so far.
Suddenly, that very event appeared before their eyes!

There was a clearing in the forest. A water body came into view. On its bank lay several human corpses. The stench of death mingled with the dried scent of human blood. Even those seasoned by the experience of many battlefields— Lifeless human bodies and dried blood were not new experiences for these men. Yet, the thought that something extraordinary, mysterious, and terrifying had occurred here stirred both curiosity and revulsion in everyone’s hearts.
Upon closer inspection, it became clear that all the bodies lying there belonged to Tamil sailors.
“Hurry! Quickly—see if anyone is still alive!” the prince shouted.
Those who had come with him began to examine each body, one by one.

The mute queen once again gestured to the prince, beckoning him with her hand. She led him a little distance away from where the bodies lay, to the foot of a tree. There, a ghastly figure was sprawled on the ground. Though it was a man, it was hard to believe so at first glance. His body was covered in wounds. Blood from the gashes on his head had streamed down his face, making him look utterly terrifying. Every moment, he seemed to await death, yet upon seeing the prince, a faint sign of life flickered across his face. He tried to open his mouth and speak, but as his mouth too was filled with blood, his appearance became even more horrific.
The prince hurried to his side and sat down. “Quickly, bring water!” he shouted.

The man said, “No need, my prince! Just a moment ago, this lady gave me water. Had she not come at that time, my life would have already left me. Sir, I have already suffered here the consequences of coming to betray you. In the next world, God will not punish me again for this.”

The prince, recognizing his voice, looked closely at his face. “Ah! Kalapathi! (In those days, just as the commander of an army was called ‘Thalapathi,’ the captain of a ship was called ‘Kalapathi.’) What are you saying? How did all this happen? You came here to betray me? I cannot believe that!” he exclaimed.

“Sir, it is your noble nature that makes you say so. On the orders of the Pazhuvettaraiyars, I came to capture you and take you away. Here is the command!” he said, and from his lap, the dying Kalapathi took out a palm-leaf letter and handed it over.
The prince glanced over the letter in a second.
“What treachery is there in this? Weren’t you only carrying out the Emperor’s command? I learned of it and hurried here myself. How did such disasters occur in the meantime? Speak quickly,” he said.
“I must speak quickly indeed—otherwise, I may never get the chance to speak at all!” replied Kalapathi. Then, stumbling often over his words, he recounted the following tale.

Having received the Emperor’s order, Kalapathi set sail from Nagapattinam with two ships. He did not like this task, but he could not disobey the Emperor’s command, so he departed. Before he left, the Pazhuvettaraiyars had given him strict instructions. Upon reaching Lanka, he was to anchor the ships at a secluded spot and first ascertain the whereabouts of the Prince. Then, he was to meet the Prince in person and deliver the Emperor’s scroll. Under no circumstances was this news to reach the Commander-in-Chief, Kodumbalur Velar, before the Prince received the command. After handing over the order to the Prince, if the Prince agreed to come, well and good; if not, he was to be taken by force, even if it meant imprisoning him… So saying, the Pazhuvettaraiyars sent some of their trusted men along with Kalapathi.

Kalapathi set out with a heavy heart. Many of the sailors on his ship did not know the true purpose of their voyage to Lanka. This only increased his inner turmoil. He hesitated, unsure how to explain it to them. After anchoring the ships at the mouth of the Thondaiman River, Kalapathi, along with a few sailors, went to the port of Kangesan. He went there to inquire about the Prince’s whereabouts. At Kangesan port, he learned that the Prince was traveling in the interior of southern Lanka, and so he returned.

Before Kalapathi could return, the sailors had already learned the truth. After all, some of the Pazhuvettaraiyars’ secret men were among them, and the matter had been discussed. As soon as Kalapathi came back, the sailors gathered together and confronted him. “Have we come here to imprison Ponniyin Selvan and take him away?” they demanded. Kalapathi told them the truth. “We are servants of the kingdom. We must carry out the Emperor’s command,” he said.
“We cannot do this. This is not the Emperor’s command! It is the order of the Pazhuvettaraiyars,” they replied.
“Then what do you intend to do?” Kalapathi asked.
“We are going to Madhottam to join the prince.”
“The prince is not at Madhottam!”
“If he is not there, then we shall seek refuge with the Commander-in-Chief, the Velar of Kodumbalur.”

No matter how much they tried to persuade him, it was of no use with Kalapathi. Only about ten people, including some of the confidential men of the Pazhuvettaraiyars, agreed to stay with Kalapathi. What could ten men do against two hundred?
“Very well; in that case, leave at once! Face whatever comes after that as you will! As far as I am able, I shall do my duty!” declared Kalapathi.

Many of the sailors thought to take one of the two ships and sail to Madhottam. Some others objected to this plan. So, they disembarked from the ship and set out by land. In their haste to depart, they did not anchor the ship on which they had been. The ship drifted, struck the shore, broke apart, and was buried in the sand.

After this, Kalapathi did not wish to remain there with the other ship. At Kangesan port, he had heard some news: a few days earlier, an Arab ship had wrecked and sunk near Mullai Island, and some of the fierce Arab survivors were said to be roaming that area. Therefore, he did not want to leave the other ship anchored near the one already wrecked and buried. He took the sound ship away from there and sailed it to a cove where the sea entered deep into the land, and anchored it securely.

Then, Kalapathi disembarked with his sailors and consulted with them about what should be done next. He told them that he would go alone to deliver the message to the prince, and that until then, the others should guard the ship safely. The sailors expressed their worries to Kalapathi. While he was still encouraging them and giving them courage, suddenly, with hair-raising, terrifying screams, a group of men surrounded and attacked them. It was clear they were Arabs. The Tamil sailors had not expected such an attack at that moment. They were not prepared for battle, nor did they have knives in hand. Even so, they fought bravely. They fought—and all of them lost their lives.

“Prince! I alone escaped with mortal wounds, fleeing and hiding to save my life—only so that I might tell someone what had happened. Until now, I have clung to life for that one purpose. Prince! At last, fortune has granted me the chance to see you in person and speak to you directly. I have already suffered the consequences for ever having thought to betray you. Son of Ponni! Forgive me!” said Kalapathi.

“Kalapathi, who has fulfilled his duty! Why should I forgive you? If there is a warrior’s heaven for those who lay down their lives on the battlefield, you too shall surely reach it! There is no doubt!” said the prince, and gently stroked the brow of Kalapathi, which was burning like fire.

From Kalapathi’s eyes, tears now welled up and mingled with the blood that streamed down his face. With great effort, he lifted his hands, clasped the prince’s palm, and pressed it to his eyes. The prince’s hand was moistened by Kalapathi’s tears. Tears glimmered in the prince’s own eyes as well.
After a few moments, Kalapathi’s life departed from his body.

chapters.title: The Hunt for the Ship
paragraphs: They gathered the body of Kalapathi along with those of the other dead sailors, stacked them with dry wooden logs, and performed the cremation. As the fire was lit and began to blaze, Commander-in-Chief Boothi Vikrama Kesari noticed tears welling up on the prince’s face.
“My lord! Are you weeping for the death of these sinners? The gods themselves have meted out fitting punishment to these traitors who came to imprison you. Why should you grieve?” he asked.
“Commander, these men are not traitors; nor do I mourn for their deaths. I grieve that such an evil time has come upon the Chola land,” the prince replied.
“Evil times arrived along with the Pazhuvettaraiyars. Nothing new has happened now!”

“Something new has indeed happened. If the ship’s sailors have begun to disobey Kalapathi’s orders, what greater calamity could befall the kingdom than this? Commander, this is but a small sign! I fear that, just like this, divisions may arise everywhere in the Chola realm! If that happens, this great empire founded by Vijayalaya Chola will be torn asunder! Should such a disaster occur because of me? I have heard the tale of the Mahabharata. When Duryodhana was born, the epic says that jackals and wolves howled ominously. Surely, when I was born too, jackals and dogs must have howled in terror!” said the prince.
“My lord! When you were born into this world, every auspicious omen that could possibly arise did so. The astrologers who cast your horoscope—”

“That is enough, Commander! Enough! My ears have grown weary of hearing such talk. Let my horoscope be as it may. The time has come for us to part ways. Commander, I ask this of you: If any of the sailors who disobeyed Kalapathi’s orders from these ships come to you, you must not take them in. You must immediately imprison them and send them to Thanjai.”

“Prince! We have only heard what Kalapathi said. We have not heard the sailors’ side. How can we judge by listening to only one side? Is that just or righteous? Come with me. Those sailors—” “Decide after you have heard what they have to say…”
“Sir! That is not possible. Do as you see fit. I cannot delay here even for a moment longer. I must leave at once. Where is the boatman?” he asked.
“Where do you wish to go, Prince? Why do you need the boatman?”

“Is it necessary for you to ask about that? I must go to the ship that is to carry Vandiyathevan. Has not that peerless warrior, for my sake, boarded the Arab vessel and fallen into grave danger? Can I abandon him? As if the sins I have already committed are not enough, should I add betrayal of friendship to them as well…?”

“Sir! You have never knowingly committed any sin. Even if you say so, the world would not accept it. Vandiyathevan is but a reckless fellow, one who acts without a trace of forethought. How can you be responsible for the danger he has brought upon himself? Where is the betrayal of friendship in this? Prince! I do not like that you celebrate as your friend a youth who has come running from somewhere, out of nowhere. Are not friends supposed to be equals?”

“Commander! I do not wish to waste time in idle talk. Even if he is not my friend, is there not such a thing as gratitude? Have not the great ones, from the sage Valluvar onwards, all spoken of it? ‘The Cholas are famed for never forgetting a favor’—I will not let that praise be tarnished because of me. This very instant I will set out and seek that ship…”
“How will you set out? Where will you search, Prince?”
“I will board the boat you came in and set out…”
“Can you hunt a tiger with a rabbit? Can you pursue a ship sailing the deep sea with this little boat and catch it? And if you do catch it, what will you do then?”

“I will go in the boat; if the boat breaks, I will cling to a plank and swim after it. Even if the ship carrying Vandiyathevan sails beyond the seven seas, I will pursue it and catch it. And if, after catching it, I cannot save my friend, at least I will give up my life along with his… Where is the boatman?”

As he spoke thus, the prince turned and looked all around. He noticed that Poonguzhali was standing to one side, speaking with the boatman. The mute old woman stood nearby. The prince hurried toward where they were standing.
Recently, when she had gone, Poonguzhali’s eyes brimmed with tears as she spoke angrily with the boatman. It was clear that some heated exchange was taking place.
“Ah! What is this? Another conspiracy?” exclaimed the Prince.
Suddenly, the boatman fell at the Prince’s feet. “Prince! Without knowing, I have committed a grave mistake. I did it out of greed for money; please forgive me!” he cried.
“What is this?... Poonguzhali! It seems as if all of you together are trying to drive me mad. Can you at least tell me what is going on?”

“Prince! I was ashamed to say it all this time, but I can hide it no longer. He is my brother. It was he who brought those two wretches, who came to kill you, from Kodikkarai in his boat. He has been waiting here all this time according to their instructions. This morning, he took them back in his boat and put them aboard the ship we saw. Your friend, too, has boarded that ship…” she said.
“Lord! Kill me with your own hands! I did not know they were such evil men. Had I known, I would never have done it. Please, kill me with your own hands!” pleaded the boatman.

“My boy! At this moment, your life is of no value to me. Come, let us go! Take me in your boat and put me aboard that same ship. That is the only way you can atone for the harm you have done me. Come, let us go!” said the Prince.
As they walked along the seashore, the boatman dragged the boat lying on the shore into the water. The Prince gazed intently at the sea.
“Look, the ship is still visible! We can catch up with it!” he said.
The Commander-in-Chief, too, peered keenly at the distant ship.
“Prince! It is like the fruit slipping and falling into the milk!” he said.
“What? What? Even from you, a good word at last!”
“The ship we see is not the one you think, carrying Vandiyathevan away. That is Parthibendran’s ship. It is coming from the direction of Trikonamalai. It is heading towards us. Don’t you see?”

“Yes, yes! In that case, things have turned out very well. Parthibendran is coming with some other purpose. Still, he is arriving at a good time. We can hunt the leopard with the lion’s help!... But until that ship comes here, I—”
“I will not wait any longer. I will row a little way out in the boat and meet them…”
“Prince! To come with you in the boat…”
“Sir, none of you need come with me. If you remain here, I will consider it a great help… Thirumalai! I am telling you as well. Even you hesitated at the thought of the sea, didn’t you?”

“Yes, my lord! I too intended to stay behind. My orders are to look after you as long as you are on the island of Lanka. The Prime Minister is in Madurai. I must go to him and report all that has happened here…”

“Do as you must! Poonguzhali! You too must stay here. Do not worry about your brother. I will take care of him. Didn’t you say you left the boat you came in somewhere? Take that and continue on your way. I will never forget the help you have given me… Come now! Wipe away your tears! What will people think if they see you like this?”

Saying this, the prince went to the mute queen and bent to touch her feet in reverence. The old woman stopped him, placed her hand on his head, and blessed him. The next moment, the prince leapt into the boat waiting, ready on the sea. Those on the shore stood watching the boat.

The prince too, from the departing boat, kept looking at them. Though he looked at everyone in general, his eyes lingered only on Poonguzhali’s tear-streaked face. Strange! Strange indeed! As the boat moved farther and farther away, shouldn’t the figures on the shore appear smaller and smaller? The shapes of the others did grow smaller. But Poonguzhali’s face alone seemed to grow larger and larger, drawing ever closer to the prince.

A shiver ran through the prince’s body. He turned his eyes away. A scene from the dream he had on the first night flashed before his mind’s eye. The young princess Kundavai’s words rang clear in his ears, rising above the roar of the sea waves: “Brother! Do not forget that Vanathi waits here for you!”

chapters.title: “Rescuers in Danger”
paragraphs: The astonishment that seized Parthibendran upon seeing the prince in the boat is beyond words. It was as if the very deity he had gone to worship had suddenly appeared before him, not only granting him darshan but also saying, “Ask for whatever boon you desire!” Yet, what could be the reason for the prince’s solitary arrival in this boat? What had become of the ships of the Pazhuvettaraiyars?… Not recognizing this as his own ship, could the prince perhaps have thought that this was the vessel sent to capture him?

Soon enough, it became clear that he had not come with such mistaken suspicions. As soon as the prince boarded the ship from the boat, he did not wait for Parthibendran to ask but briefly recounted the events that had transpired.
“Vandiyathevan is on the ship that fell into the hands of the Arabs. We must somehow rescue him,” he said.
The news brought by the prince filled Parthibendran with immense excitement.

“Everything has turned out well. If only that reckless youth had not acted with such haste, it would have been even better. Still, we must not let him fall into the hands of foreigners. That ship cannot have gone far; we can surely pursue and capture it,” he said. Then, calling Kalapathi, he explained the situation.

“What is there to worry about? If the wind continues to favor us like this, we can catch up by evening! Where can that ship go, escaping us? It must head to Kodikkarai and then follow the coastline, mustn’t it?” said Kalapathi.

But the will of the Wind God was otherwise. Gradually, the speed of the wind began to diminish. By midday, the wind had ceased altogether. The sea was utterly calm, without even the semblance of a wave. An indescribable sultriness enveloped everything. The Sun God blazed in the sky like a torch, pouring fire upon the sea! If one touched the seawater, it would not burn; yet, to the eye, it did not appear as a sea of water, but rather as a boiling, steaming sea of oil. Where the sun’s rays struck directly, it looked like a molten sea of fire.

The ship did not move; all the sails had been unfurled from the masts. What was the use? Just as the sound of the waves had ceased, so too had the flapping of the sails against the masts. The sails and the masts stood still, crossing— There was not even the faintest creak that arises when the planks of a ship shift. There was no sound of the vessel slicing through the sea. In truth, that silence inflicted an unbearable agony.
Added to this was the prince’s deep anguish over Vandiyathevan.
“The wind has died, and the ship has come to a complete standstill! How long will this last? When will the wind rise again? Won’t that ship escape and get away?” he asked anxiously.
Parthibendran looked at the lord of the navy.

At that moment, Kalapathi said, “The wind cannot remain utterly still for long. Somewhere, a cyclone is brewing. Soon, it will either strike us or pass us by. Whether the cyclone hits us or not, the sea is certain to rage before long. See how calm it is now? Before this night is over, we shall witness waves rising and crashing like mountains, we shall see mountains themselves, and we shall see the very depths of the netherworld!”
“If the cyclone strikes the ship, it will be dangerous, won’t it?”
“Dangerous? It would be no ordinary danger! Only if God protects us will we survive!”
“In that case, it will be difficult for us to catch that ship.”
“Prince! The sea and the wind do not show partiality. The predicament we are in now is the same as that ship’s. At this very moment, it too will be standing still…”
“If, by chance, it has gone near the shore…” the prince asked.
“If it has gone near the shore, those aboard could disembark and escape to land! But the ship itself would be gone!” said Kalapathi.

“No matter how great the danger, as long as those we care for are by our side, there is no cause for worry!” said the prince. Again and again, before his mind’s eye, appeared Vandiyathevan’s face, brimming with enthusiasm, and Poonguzhali’s face, with her frightened gaze. Where would they be at this moment? What would they be doing? What would they be thinking?

Truly, in this perilous situation, let us now turn to Vandiyathevan, whom we left behind. In the hold of the great wooden ship that had come to abduct the prince, amidst a jumble of goods, wooden planks, and bundles… Knots and in the dark room where he was confined, he lay bound to a wooden post. For a long while, he felt as though he were possessed by delirium. The thought that he had landed himself in such a predicament through his own rashness tormented him. What was this ship? Whose ship was it? How was it that some rough Arabs and the sorcerer Ravidasan were together on it? Where was this vessel headed? What would they do to him? He tried to reason it out, but nothing made sense.

All the dreams he had cherished about his future now seemed to be nothing but dreams indeed! Had he not escaped from even greater dangers than this before? Would it be that he could not find a way out of this one? At times, such doubts assailed him. Let us see; as long as there is life in the body, as long as wit and the power of counsel remain, there is no need to lose hope entirely.

With this hope rekindled, he looked around. At first, his eyes could see nothing in the darkness. Gradually, things began to take shape. He saw that, quite close to him, a variety of weapons were heaped together. Though his body was tightly bound, his hands were not tied. If he loosened the rope around his wrists, he could reach out and take one of the knives lying there; he could cut the ropes binding his body and legs. But then, what next? The door to this room was shut. How could he get out? Even if he did, could he fight so many Arabs, the sorcerer, and his companion all at once? Suppose he fought and killed them all—what then? Could he steer the ship by himself? He knew nothing at all about ships!

No; he must not act rashly again. He must wait and see. The very fact that they had only bound him and not tried to kill him at once gave him some hope, did it not? Let them do what they would—he could wait and see.

But as time passed, Vandiyathevan’s patience was sorely tested. The room was so stifling, it was as though he were being roasted in an oven. Sweat poured from his body. Never in his wildest dreams had he imagined that a sea voyage could be so suffocating. He remembered that night when he had traveled in the boat with Poonguzhali. How cool the breeze had been then! How pleasant it had felt to his body! What a difference between then and now! People spoke of being thrown into a lime kiln—was this not the same?

Suddenly, he sensed a change. Yes, the ship had stopped moving. It seemed to be standing still, motionless. The stifling heat grew even more intense. Thirst parched his tongue and throat. What now? He could not endure much longer.

He reached out for the knife, intending to cut his bonds and escape to see what lay outside. Would they really have kept no drinking water at all on the ship? Vandiyathevan looked around. In one corner, a few coconuts lay scattered. Ah! Why should I cry for ghee when there is butter? With those coconuts, he could quench both his hunger and thirst. Vandiyathevan loosened the ropes around his hands as much as he could. He stretched out his hand to reach the knife. At that very moment, he heard footsteps. The sound of a door opening followed. He quickly drew back his outstretched hand.
The sorcerer Ravidasan, who had come and gone once before, entered with his companion. Both of them stood on either side of Vandiyathevan.
“How is the sea voyage, my boy? Are you comfortable?” asked Ravidasan.
Vandiyathevan, barely able to speak, managed to say, “Thirst is killing me; a little water!”
“Ah! We are thirsty too. Those wretches didn’t keep any water on the ship, did they?” said Ravidasan.
“Kali is thirstier than all of us. She thirsts for blood!” said the other man.

Vandiyathevan turned and looked at him closely. “Don’t you remember me, brother? Have you forgotten? After the Kuravai dance at Kadambur palace, Devaralan came and performed his mad ritual. He raved, ‘Goddess Kali demands a sacrifice; she asks for royal blood of a thousand years!’ Do you remember?”
“Ah! Now I remember! You are that Devaralan!” muttered Vandiyathevan.

“Yes, it is I! We came to Lanka to offer a thousand-year-old prince as a sacrifice to Kali. That did not succeed. We tried to send that brave Vaishnavite to Vaikunta, but that too failed. At least you have fallen into our hands. I am very pleased. For now, Kali must be satisfied with the blood of a petty chieftain’s line!” said Devaralan.
“If that is so, why do you delay?” asked Vandiyathevan.

“Can we offer the sacrifice of a brave youth like you wherever we find you? Only after reaching shore, in the presence of all the priests, with a grand festival, should the sacrifice be made. Most importantly, the priestess must be present!”
“Who is the priestess?”
“Don’t you know who she is? It’s none other than the younger queen of Pazhuvur.”
Vandiyathevan paused for a moment in thought, then said, “If you truly have such intentions, then give me a little water at once. Otherwise, I shall die of thirst right here!”
“There’s no water, brother!”
“So you’ve become a sorceress now?”
“Well said! I have cast a spell, look! See how the ship is now standing still, unmoving? Before night falls, a whirlwind will strike. Rain will come too!”
“What use is rain to me? You’ll be up on the upper deck! And I’ll be here…”
“You can come up to the upper deck too. Stretch out your tongue and drink the rainwater to quench your thirst. If only you would listen to what we say…”
“What are you saying?”
“We say that those Arab fiends must be sacrificed to the Lord of the Sea.”
“Why?”
“They want to take this ship to the land of Kalinga. We want to land at least at Kodikkarai or Nagapattinam…”
“There are six of them, and they are fierce brutes!”
“Three of them are asleep; the other three are dozing and nodding off. If the three of us finish off the three who are sleeping, then three of us can handle the other three, can’t we?”
Vandiyathevan remained silent.
“Well, brother, what do you say? If you agree to our plan, we’ll untie your bonds.”
The prince’s face appeared before Vandiyathevan’s mind’s eye. No; he would never approve of this. He would never consent to killing men in their sleep.
“I cannot do it; to attack and kill those who are sleeping is base and dishonorable.”
“Fool! It was when the sailors of Chola Nadu were asleep that these Arabs attacked and killed them.”
“If others commit a base act, why should I do the same?”

“Fine; as you wish!” said Ravidasan. From the pile of weapons nearby, he picked up a sharp, broad-bladed knife. Devaralan, for his part, took up a small club, like a pestle, with an iron tip at its end.

The two of them left the room. But they did not bolt the door from outside after closing it. As soon as they were gone, Vandiyathevan stretched out his hand, seized a knife, and cut through the ropes that bound him. He sprang to his feet, went to the corner, picked up a coconut, and broke it open. He drank the tender water to quench his thirst. He gathered the remaining coconuts into a sack and tied it shut. Then, he took up a fine sword, worthy of battle, in his hand. He stood ready, prepared to dash outside at any moment.

After a short while, there came a sound—‘thud’, ‘thud’—twice in succession. He understood that two bodies had been thrown into the sea. Immediately, a terrible uproar, the clash of arms, the sound of knives striking—everything came from the upper deck.

With the knife gripped in his hand, Vandiyathevan rushed out. Ravidasan, Devaralan, and the four Arabs were locked in fierce combat. The situation had reached a critical point for those who were pressed together in the melee. With a loud shout, Vandiyathevan charged forward. One of the Arabs turned to attack him. Vandiyathevan’s knife struck the Arab’s blade, sending it flying into the sea; at the same time, he inflicted a gash on the Arab’s face. Blood streamed down the Arab’s terrifying visage as he raised his fist and lunged at Vandiyathevan’s chest. Vandiyathevan sidestepped slightly. The Arab fell heavily to the deck. By the force of his fall, a loose crossbeam of the deck shifted and crashed down upon his head.
Vandiyathevan engaged another Arab in a brief but fierce struggle and managed to hurl him into the sea.

Ravidasan and Devaralan were not men skilled in the arts of war. Thus, it was difficult for them to fight the remaining two Arabs in single combat. They were growing exhausted as time passed. At that moment, hearing the splash of something falling into the sea, the two Arabs turned to see what had become of their companions. Seizing the opportunity, Ravidasan and Devaralan dispatched them swiftly.
When all was done, the three victors sat down to rest. “Father! You came at just the right moment! How did you get here?” asked Ravidasan.
“It seems as though you have cast some spell,” said Vandiyathevan. “The bonds that held me came undone by themselves, and this dagger found its way into my hand!”
“What of your thirst?” asked Devaralan.
“A coconut appeared above my head. It broke open on its own and poured a little tender water into my mouth!”
“Oh ho! You are a sly one indeed!” exclaimed Devaralan. Both of them burst into laughter.
“Brother! We were testing you. We deliberately loosened your bonds. We left the weapons nearby, and placed the coconuts where you could see them!” said Ravidasan.
Vandiyathevan could not discern whether these words were truth or falsehood. He remained silent for a moment.

“Think carefully, young man! Do you wish to live? Do you wish to survive, reach the shore, and see the faces of your kin and loved ones again? Do you wish to live with wealth, pleasure, rank, and honor? If you desire all this, speak! Join us! All these boons can be yours!” said Ravidasan.
“You killed men while they slept, did you not?” asked Vandiyathevan.
“We managed to kill only two. The other awoke. Had you joined us earlier, it would have been even easier.”
“To kill those who sleep—under what dharma does that fall? How could your hearts allow you to do such a thing?”
“If you are frightened by a mustard seed, how will you swallow great gourds? If you are to join us—”
“You keep saying ‘join us, join us.’ Who are you?”
Ravidasan looked at Devaralan and said, “There is no need for secrecy with him anymore. One, he must join us. Or else, he must be sacrificed to the sea. Therefore, we can tell him everything!”
“Tell him all, and tell it well!” said Devaralan.
“Listen, brother! We are the loyal protectors of the valiant Pandya king, those who have sworn an oath to guard him…”
“You could not do it! Aditya Karikalan was victorious…”

“How did he win? He won because of the foolishness of a woman. She placed too much faith in the power of her wiles. She believed she could make that Chola royal serpent dance to her tune. The serpent did dance for her, but in the midst of it, it revealed the strength of its venomous fangs. Our king’s head rolled in the dust. They carried it all the way to Thanjavur. They placed the head in a palanquin and paraded it through the streets. Ah! Thanjavur! Thanjavur! Watch closely, brother, and see what fate awaits that city!”

As Ravidasan spoke these words, his wide red eyes grew even wider and seemed to spit fire. His body trembled. The sound of his teeth grinding together echoed menacingly, sharp and terrible. Devaralan’s appearance too became equally fearsome.
“What is done is done. What will you do now? Can you bring the dead Veerapandiyan back to life?”

“I cannot bring Veerapandiyan back to life. Even my mantras do not possess such power. But we will destroy the one who killed him, and all those who are allied with him, root and branch. We will wipe out the Chola serpent’s brood, even the youngest of their children. Will you join us? Speak!”
“After you have destroyed the Chola dynasty—what then? What will you do next?”
“We will crown whomever our Maharani commands us to…”
“Who is the Maharani?”
“Do you not know, brother? The one now acting as the young mistress of Pazhuvoor!”
“Then, for Madurantakan…”
“He too is but a serpent’s hatchling, is he not?”
“Pazhuvettarayar?…”
“Ah! Do you think we intend to make that old man our king? We use his influence and his wealth for our own ends…”
“Your Maharani is staying in his house, is she not?”
“You have understood well! You are a clever one!”
“You said a woman was the cause of Veerapandiyan’s death?”

“It was the Queen of Pazhuvoor herself! She swore that she would save the wounded Veerapandiyan who lay stricken on the battlefield. But she did not fulfill that vow. Instead, she betrayed him. Believing her to be a traitor, we wished to burn her alive. Yet, because she too took an oath with us to avenge wrong with wrong, we spared her life. To this day, she continues to keep her word. Oh! Without her help, we could not have accomplished even this much.”
“You have not yet accomplished anything, have you?”
“Wait a little, my friend! Just watch and see!” said Ravidasan.
“He has learned all this from us. But he has not given us any answer to our question,” said Devaralan.
“Young man! What do you say? Will you join us? Who knows? Perhaps fortune will smile upon you. You yourself might one day ascend the lion throne of southern Tamilakam. What do you say?”

Had this been some time ago, Vandiyathevan would have exclaimed, “Ah! I will join you!” But three days spent in the company of the prince had wrought a great change in his heart. The taste for falsehoods, cunning tricks, and opportunistic schemes had left him. Wishing to change the subject, he asked, “How did you capture this ship? How did you befriend those Arabs whom you just now sent to the land of Yama?”

“It is all due to my magical powers, my friend! At Trincomalee, we bought horses from these very men. Using those horses, we followed you, coming and going in your wake. We saw the prince disembark and run along the ‘Elephant Death’ wharf. Determined to arrive here before him, we took a shortcut and reached this place. When we arrived, we found that our old friends had already seized this ship. The vessel they had come in was wrecked near Mullai Island. Hiding here, they captured this ship. They asked us if we would join them to guide the way along the coast. It was as if a ripe fruit had fallen into a bowl of milk.”
“How so?”

“We overheard that young serpent of the Chola clan conversing with the Chola commander-in-chief. We learned that, one way or another, he would return to Chola Nadu. Not only that, brother! In Lanka, there is a mute woman, a spirit, who protects Arulmozhi Varman by countering our spells with her own. But she will not come to Chola Nadu…”
That night, Vandiyathevan pondered over all that had transpired in Anuradhapura.
Ravidasan suddenly burst into laughter.
“What is that laughter? What amused you?” asked Vandiyathevan.

“It’s nothing, brother! I was just thinking about the nature of these Arabs, and it made me laugh. Aren’t they such rough men? For them, killing a man is as easy as slicing a plantain. But when it comes to horses, their affection knows no bounds. In their country, they never ride horses without iron shoes nailed to their hooves. They say we make our horses run barefoot. So, to them, we are merciless, uncivilized brutes, a danger even to humanity! Selling horses to us is a sin!… Do you know what happened this morning?…”
“Tell me!”

“We had all boarded the ship. The sails were unfurled, and the vessel had set off. Just then, the sound of a horse’s hooves was heard on the shore. That was enough for them to suspect that it might be one of their horses that had escaped from the wrecked ship at Mullai Island and made its way to shore. One of them said he would get down from the ship and check. They sent us along with him…”
“And then?”
“They didn’t catch the horse. Brother! But they caught you! See how well it turned out! How convenient it was for us to finish our business with these horse-lovers.”
“All that is fine; but this boy still hasn’t answered our question,” Devaralan reminded them.
“I will tell you, sir! I will tell you. I have pledged myself to serve the Chola dynasty. Never, not even for a day, will I join with you…”
“Are you part of the Velakkara army? Have you sworn an oath?”
“Nothing of that sort.”
“Then why hesitate? You are a warrior. Shouldn’t you join whichever side offers the greatest advantage?”

Vandiyathevan did not reveal to them the reason that bound him to the Chola dynasty with a force stronger than any oath. He did not speak of the glance from the Young Princess, nor of the chapter as lovely as a cluster of jasmine… Does one need any reason other than a smile, or more than that, to give one’s life for the Chola clan? And then, there is the unparalleled friendship of the prince! Once a man has become his friend, can he ever turn away from him?
“Whatever may be, I will never join your band of murderers!” declared Vandiyathevan.
“In that case, prepare to offer your life as a sacrifice to the King of the Seas!” said Ravidasan.

chapters.title: The Whirlwind
paragraphs: The wind did not stir; the sea did not move; the ship did not advance. Vandiyathevan sat silently for a while, gazing at the ocean, which now resembled a tranquil lake, calm and unruffled by a single wave. Only within his heart did mighty waves rise and crash.
Suddenly, he stretched both arms toward the sea and cried out, “Om Hreem Hraam Vashat!” In the next instant, he drew a dagger from his waist and spun it twice in the air in a circular motion.

“Yes! Yes! The Lord of the Ocean demands a sacrifice! He asks for a double offering! He commands that the lives of two fiends who slay sleeping men be given to him as sacrifice! Only then will he allow this wooden vessel to proceed further. Where are you? Let the two of you come forward and stretch out your necks at once! Quickly!” he thundered.
Ravidasan stared at Vandiyathevan in astonishment. Then, with a laugh that echoed like a ghostly cackle, he said, “Ha! Ha! Ha!”
“Brother! What sort of game is this?” he asked.

“Elders! This is no game; it is fate!” replied Vandiyathevan. “Just now, when I was bound and lying below, I dozed off for a moment. In that sleep, I had a dream. A blue-hued figure, like a spirit that united the sea and the sky, stood before me. It spoke something I did not understand then; but now I do! The Lord of the Ocean demands the life-sacrifice of two Kali devotees skilled in magic and sorcery. If it is not given, he will not let this ship move forward. The sacrifice of six wild Arabs did not satisfy him. Come! Quickly!” So saying, Vandiyathevan raised the dagger in his hand toward the sky.
Ravidasan and Devaralan looked at each other’s faces.
Ravidasan said, “Brother! I have never seen a trickster like you when it comes to spinning tales!”

Vandiyathevan replied, “Oh! You do not believe what I say? Do you think I am making up stories? O Lord of the Ocean, answer these fools yourself!” he cried. It seemed as though the voice he had called out with had reached the ears of the King of the Ocean himself. And it appeared as if the Ocean King wished to reply!

At that moment, a wondrous sight appeared upon the sea. As far as the eye could see, in all four directions, the ocean shivered with a strange thrill. Thousands upon thousands of tiny, delicate waves rose and fell. This lasted but a moment. In the next instant, all those waves transformed into fine droplets of silvery foam. Across the vast expanse of the sea, those white beads of foam leaped and played. What would it look like if, upon a wide green meadow, countless millions of thumbai flowers rolled and tumbled in a gentle breeze? Just so did the sea appear at that moment!

Yes; a light, gentle breeze—sweet and cool—embraced the ship for a moment and then passed on. A shiver ran through the vessel. Vandiyathevan’s body, parched by the heat, too, was refreshed by a pleasant chill.
Ravidasan and Devaralan burst into laughter. “Ha! Ha! Ha!”
“Brother! The King of the Ocean has already answered your question! It seems we must prepare ourselves to be sacrificed!” said Ravidasan.
Vandiyathevan’s heart was troubled. The sudden thrill that had swept across the sea, and the immediate change that followed, had left him bewildered.

Ah! What was this? Where had those thousands upon thousands of tiny waves and millions of white foam droplets gone? Had they vanished like a mirage? The sea had become calm again, appearing like a green, polished slab! Had the vision he had just witnessed truly occurred? Or was it merely an illusion? Perhaps it was the magic of this sorcerer, Ravidasan!
“Look there! Brother! The sky too approves what the sea has spoken!” said Ravidasan, pointing to the southwest.

In the direction he pointed—at the corner where the green sea and the blue sky met—a small, dark cloud fragment had risen a hand’s breadth above the horizon. The tip of that dark cloud glowed with a blood-red hue.

On ordinary days, Vandiyathevan would never have noticed such a sight. What wonder is there in seeing a cloud bank at the meeting point of sea and sky? None at all! Yet even that small vision, at that moment, disturbed our hero’s mind a little.
In the next instant, Vandiyathevan regained his composure. “We must not fall into the snare of this sorcerer,” he resolved firmly within himself.
He glanced sharply, first at Ravidasan, then at Devaralan, and exclaimed, “If that is so, why delay? Come on!” With those words, he tossed aside his dagger.
“Sir! Before we become a sacrifice, we wish to pray to our family deity. Grant us half a nazhigai’s time!” pleaded Ravidasan.
“Very well! Say your prayers and come at once. Do not attempt any of your tricks or sorcery on me. Even if you try, it will not work!” declared Vandiyathevan.
“We are coming right away. See, we are leaving our weapons here!” said Ravidasan.
So saying, both of them laid their weapons down and moved to the other side of the boat.

That half a nazhigai—those few moments—were necessary for Vandiyathevan as well. The strange sights in the sea and sky had stirred a nameless confusion in his heart, making his body feel somewhat weakened. If necessary, he had resolved to finish off those two murderers with a single sweep of his blade. But he doubted whether, at that moment, he possessed the strength in his arm to do so.
Therefore, he needed a little time to steady his mind and summon his full strength.

His attention was drawn once more, almost involuntarily, to the southwestern corner. The mass of clouds that had earlier appeared a mere cubit high now towered to its full height. The blood-red hue at its summit had faded somewhat. The cloud mass seemed to be rising higher and higher.

The wind, which had fallen still after its first gusts, began to blow once more, slowly at first. The sea, too, showed signs of unrest. Small waves began to dance. The cloud mass continued to climb higher in the sky. The wind’s force seemed to be increasing. The ship began to sway gently.

Amidst the whistling of the wind and the murmuring of the waves—what was that sound? It was as if something had fallen into the sea! Vandiyathevan turned around. Ravidasan and Devaralan were nowhere to be seen. There was nothing surprising in that—they must be on the other side of the ship. The mats and the raised deck at the center of the boat must be hiding them from view.

Ah! What is this? Isn’t that the sound of oars pushing a boat? Vandiyathevan immediately ran to the other side of the ship. The sight that met his eyes truly startled him. He had not expected this in the least. He had thought they had gone to confer together, to find some compromise with him. But instead, they had untied the small boat that was fastened to the other side of the ship, lowered it into the sea, and were already climbing into it! They had begun to row away with swift strokes!
When Ravidasan saw Vandiyathevan, he laughed. “Brother! Do you see now that we have no wish to become a sacrifice for the King of the Sea?”

In a single moment, Vandiyathevan realized his situation. They were leaving him alone on that great wooden ship and departing. He knew nothing of the art of steering a ship. He did not know where in the sea the ship was anchored, nor in which direction he should go to reach land. In such a helpless, abandoned state, they were leaving him behind.
“You wretches! Couldn’t you at least take me with you?” he cried.
“Brother! Can we leave the King of the Sea without a single offering?” Ravidasan replied, as the boat drifted farther and farther from the ship.

‘Should I jump into the sea and try to catch up with the boat?’ Vandiyathevan wondered for a moment. But he immediately abandoned that thought. He did not know how to swim well. He did not have the courage to leap from the ship. Even if he did jump and somehow managed to reach the boat, what would those murderers do to him? They had already revealed their secrets to him! They knew now that he would never join them. As he tried to catch the boat, they might strike him dead with their oars. And even if he managed to reach the boat, how could he fight them while struggling in the water?

‘Let them go! Let those fiends vanish! Better to be alone on this great ship than to be in a small boat with those murderous villains! Haven’t I escaped from many dangers before by the grace of God? Surely, God will show me a way out of this peril as well! Let those sinners go…

But is it right to let them escape alive? Where will they land? What other conspiracies and dreadful deeds will they commit? God exists—what can I do? Somehow… It would be enough if I could join the prince again, even in another life! Still, he should not have abandoned me like this! He could have taken me along with Poonguzhali on the elephant. If I get the chance to meet him again, I must surely quarrel with him. “Is this the famed friendship of your ancient Chola lineage?” I must ask him so. But will such an opportunity ever come?… Am I ever going to see the prince again?… Why shouldn’t I? The Commander-in-Chief and Azhwarkadiyan saw me getting caught in this predicament. Would they remain idle without doing anything? If they had met the prince, surely they would have told him everything, wouldn’t they?

As Vandiyathevan stood lost in such thoughts, he noticed that the boat had gone far out into the sea. How did the boat travel so swiftly? Not only the boat, but even the ship he was on was gently rocking and moving. That was why such a great distance had come between the ship and the boat so quickly! Vandiyathevan also saw the waves in the sea growing larger and larger. Was that all? What was this? In the bright daylight, suddenly one side was turning dark!

Vandiyathevan looked towards the southwest. The cloud that had earlier appeared only as a small mass had now grown vast and magnificent, spreading out and covering most of the western sky. More clouds were gathering, swirling, and rapidly rising in the sky. Even as he watched, they covered the sun, which had already sunk halfway down the western horizon. Then the west and south grew even darker. The black clouds in the sky reflected on the sea, turning the water into the color of jet-black ink. It was impossible to tell where the sea ended and the sky began; both had merged into a single, impenetrable darkness.
The masses of clouds rolled and tumbled, coming to hover right above Vandiyathevan’s head. Then they began to descend toward the lower sky as well.

Vandiyathevan looked in the direction the boat had gone. The boat was nowhere to be seen. It seemed to have gone beyond the limits of his sight! The gentle whistling of the wind had turned into a great, roaring howl.

Along with that, the sound of the waves, growing larger by the minute, joined in. The mats spread out on the ship flapped and snapped noisily. The masts and planks rubbed against each other, opening and closing like a thousand creaking doors. It made a sound. Vandiyathevan gazed in wonder at the woven mats. From their position, he realized that the ship was not moving in a straight direction, but was spinning round and round.

“They kept mentioning the ‘whirlwind’!” he thought. “It seems that very whirlwind is about to strike!” Vandiyathevan’s mind grasped that, when the whirlwind hits, the mats must be spun and tied around to secure them. But how could he do that alone? Wasn’t it a task for ten men working together? If not ten, at least four would be needed. What could one man do by himself? One had to simply resign oneself to fate—let the ship meet whatever end was destined for it!

Soon enough, he understood what fate awaited the ship. After tossing and turning for a while, it would inevitably sink into the sea! Even if it didn’t sink, it might break apart into pieces before that! Whatever happened to the ship, there was no doubt about his own fate.
Death in the middle of the ocean! That astrologer at Kumbakonam hadn’t uttered a word about this. Ha! Astrologer, indeed! If he ever met him again…
Madness! What chance was there of ever seeing him again?

Suddenly, something hard fell on Vandiyathevan’s shoulder. All at once, small, round stones began to rain down across the ship. How those stones sparkled like crystal! How could such things fall from the sky?

A few more stones fell on his head, back, and shoulders. At first, there was pain where they struck; then, a chill. Looking at the stones that had fallen on the deck, he saw—ah!—they were melting away! Yes, they were melting and disappearing! This was a hailstorm; until that moment, Vandiyathevan had never seen nor experienced such a thing. A strange excitement arose in his heart—at least, before dying, he had witnessed this wonder.

Sitting on the ship’s deck, he touched the melting hailstones and delighted in their feel. Ah, what a thrill! Touching them was like touching fire, yet it didn’t burn the skin as fire would. The heat quickly turned to coldness. The hailstorm, which had come so unexpectedly, stopped just as suddenly. It hadn’t lasted even half a nazhigai.

Then, an ordinary rain began to fall. Vandiyathevan watched as the rainwater struck the ship, scattered, and ran off into the sea. He marveled at the craftsmanship of the Chola country’s shipwrights. No matter how much it rained, no matter how great the waves that crashed and sent seawater onto the ship, the vessel was constructed so that the water would always flow back into the sea. Unless the lower part of the ship broke and let in the ocean, it could not be sunk!

This realization gave him a little courage. Immediately, another thought struck him. If the door to the cabin in which he had been tied was left open, water might enter through it. He ran to check. As he had feared, the door was open, banging in the wind. He quickly shut it tight and bolted it.

If the wind and rain above became unbearable, he could always retreat into that cabin and lock himself in. After that, he could leave his fate to the will of God and rest in peace. Thinking of how secure this ship was, Vandiyathevan felt a pang of pity for those two fools who had left it for a mere boat. Yet, that boat too was of a curious design. No matter how fierce the wind or how heavy the rain, it could not easily be sunk. Even if the boat broke and capsized, there was a log tied alongside it. Clinging to that, those murderous villains could escape and reach the shore! Most likely, they would soon land near Kodikkarai.

From Kodikkarai, Vandiyathevan’s thoughts leapt to Pazhaiyarai. How would the Emperor’s daughter learn of his fate? Who would tell her that, in his attempt to fulfill the task she had entrusted to him, he had drowned in the middle of the sea? Would the ocean tell her? Would the wind carry the news?—Oh God! Should I not have died before meeting that princess? Should I not have attained a heroic death on the battlefield? Is it not like being shown the heavenly earth only to be hurled at once into the deepest hell?
The wind’s fury kept increasing. The sea grew ever more tumultuous. The ship’s sails thrashed about, making a terrifying noise like ghosts and demons.
The darkness deepened and thickened. How could there be a darkness blacker than night itself? Yet it seemed such a thing was possible.
Suddenly, a flash of lightning split the sky, leaping from one corner to another. The darkness that followed was even blacker than before.
Lightning was followed by a peal of thunder; the ship trembled; the sea trembled; the very directions trembled.

Another bolt of lightning tore through the darkness of the lower sky. It stretched further and further, spreading beyond the ship and its mast, casting myriad patterns of light across the heavens, turning both sky and sea into a realm of radiance—then, in the next instant, vanished without a trace. The thunder continued to roll. Oh, heavens! There could be no doubt now that the very spheres of the universe were shattering and collapsing. More lightning; more thunder. “The sky has not yet split open—what a wonder this is!”—whether Vandiyathevan thought this or not, at that very moment, the sky exploded and split asunder. Through the fissure thus created, a deluge of cataclysmic rain poured down.
Yes; it could hardly be called rain. It was as if an ocean had been churning in the vault of the sky, and now, through this sudden rift, it was pouring down in torrents.

The waves of the sea danced in a frenzy. In the flashes of lightning, mountain-like crests could be seen as far as the eye could reach. The howling of the wind reached its peak. It was as if the god of wind had plucked those mountain peaks and was tossing them playfully across the sky. Some of those watery mountains crashed against Vandiyathevan’s ship.

From above, the flood of rain pounded down in relentless torrents; from all sides, mountainous waves came battering and crashing. The cyclone’s assault upon the spread-out matsails was beyond description. Even so, the wondrous wooden vessel, crafted by the carpenters of Chola Nadu, continued to spin and whirl, enduring all this.

But how long could it keep spinning? How long could the ship withstand the onslaught of these mighty elements?—It could not; in this moment, or the next, the ship was bound to sink. Along with it, Vandiyathevan too would be swallowed by the sea!

Yet, this thought did not bring him despair now. He considered that such a death, if it were to come, would be a marvelous one. Like the leaping waves, his heart too began to dance in exultation. The roaring of the wind, the crashing of the waves, the booming of the thunder—all these mingled with Vandiyathevan’s own voice. “Ha! Ha! Ha!” he laughed aloud.

He had tied himself carefully to the base of the matsail, so that he could witness all these scenes well. When the ship spun, the matsail spun; Vandiyathevan spun as well. For how long did the ship, the matsail, and Vandiyathevan continue to spin thus? He did not know how long it lasted. It could have been many ages, or perhaps only a few seconds.
At that moment, Vandiyathevan attained an immortal state, transcending all sense of time and place.

The force of the wind seemed to lessen a little. The deluge of rain had ceased. Only a light drizzle persisted. The lightning and thunder appeared to have stopped. The darkness of the sea seemed as thick as a wall. Just a short while ago, Vandiyathevan had been unable to bear the flashes of lightning and had closed his eyes tightly. He had pressed his hands over his ears to block out the deafening roar of the thunder. Now, he opened his eyes; he removed his hands and freed his ears.

“Ah! Have I truly escaped from such a great whirlwind disaster? Did God save me? Am I going to see the young prince of Pazhaiyarai again in this lifetime? Will I meet the prince and converse with him again?...”

“No, I must not hurry to conclusions. Who knows where this ship is now? How can I say for certain that it will reach the shore safely? Even if the ship survives, what guarantee is there that I will reach the shore alive?”
“How many more dangers might still await me...?”

As this question arose in Vandiyathevan’s mind, as if in answer, a bolt of lightning tore across the sky. Its brilliance was such that it seemed to bring a hundred suns before his eyes. In darkness, at least, one can see a little; but in that terrifying brightness, he could see nothing at all. Vandiyathevan feared that the lightning had snatched away his very sight. Even as this anxiety flared, danger struck his ears as well. Vandiyathevan had heard countless peals of thunder before; he had heard many even today. But this was unlike any thunder he had ever known—was it even thunder? It was as if Indra’s thunderbolt itself had entered through his ear and struck inside his skull.
For a while, Vandiyathevan could not open his eyes; in his ears, a ringing “Oyy” sound persisted.

With his eyes still closed, he sensed that some new light was spreading above his head. Amidst the ringing in his ears, he heard another strange sound. It was like the crackling noise that comes when a forest catches fire, when the trees are ablaze.
Vandiyathevan opened his eyes. He saw that the mast of the ship he was on was ablaze.
Ah! Now he understood! Now it was clear why that lightning had flashed so brilliantly, why that thunder had roared so deafeningly.

Lightning had struck either directly upon the ship or very close by! That was why the mast had caught fire! Of the five elements, two had already tried to destroy that Chola vessel. Water and wind had failed. Now, to accomplish what Varuna and Vayu could not, Agni himself had appeared!

chapters.title: The Broken Boat
paragraphs: When Vandiyathevan saw that lightning had struck and set fire to the top of the catamaran, he became certain that there was no longer any escape for that wooden craft. Therefore, he too could not hope to escape with his life. Yet, even at that moment, Vandiyathevan felt not the slightest distress. Instead, his heart brimmed with enthusiasm, and he laughed aloud. He untied the rope that bound him to the catamaran. Was it not better to sink quietly to the bottom of the sea in the cool water, rather than to burn alive in the middle of the ocean?

Vandiyathevan did not wish to waste even the few moments left in his life. In the glow of the burning boat, he looked all around, eager to savor the wild beauty of the raging sea. Was it not fitting to take a good look at the very place where his body would soon find its watery grave? Do they not say that those who die such untimely deaths will have their souls wander forever around the place where they perished? Would his spirit, too, hover above these waters? Would it float in the wind? Would it roam upon the waves? When the whirlwinds blew, would his soul also circle restlessly?

“Ah! Perhaps, one day, the Princess of the Cholas will sail upon this sea in a royal ship. The sailors will point and say, ‘Here is the spot where Vandiyathevan sank with his boat!’ If tears should well up in her spear-bright eyes and fall like pearls upon her moonlike face, if, as a spirit, I could be near to witness that sight—would I be able to wipe away her tears?”

The boat climbed to the crest of a giant wave. In the light cast by the burning catamaran, the surroundings were visible for a great distance. The sea, dark as polished onyx, gleamed wherever the fire’s glow touched it, shining like molten gold. Even as Vandiyathevan was marveling at the wonder of this beauty, something else caught his eye and drew his attention.
A short distance away, he saw a wooden boat. Upon it, the tiger flag fluttered in the wind.
“God! There seems to be no limit to Your miracles! The one coming in that boat must surely be Prince Arulmozhi himself. He is coming in search of me,” his inner voice declared.

The very same whirlwind that had ensnared and tossed about the ship Vandiyathevan was aboard, now caught Parthibendran’s vessel as well. But on this ship were sailors who understood the nature of such storms and were masters in the art of navigation. The mats spread across the decks were swiftly rolled up and secured. They steered the ship with expert hands, adjusting the helm so that the full force of the wind did not strike the vessel head-on.

One moment, the ship would tilt so steeply that it seemed certain to capsize; the next, it would right itself and stand firm. No matter how many times the mountain-like waves battered the ship, not a single plank or timber came loose. The Sea King himself seemed to toss the vessel about as if it were a mere plaything, hurling it up and down for his amusement. The whirlwind spun the ship around and around, like a top, sending it careening across the waves. Torrential rain poured from the heavens, pressing down upon the ship as if to crush it into the sea. Yet, the vessel—built by the master carpenters of Chola Nadu, steered by the renowned mariners of Tamilakam—remained unbroken, impervious to the combined assault of sea, rain, and wind.

“I have seen storms and tempests far more terrible than this,” declared Kalapathi. “I have survived them. There is no need for fear!” But even as he spoke these words to reassure Parthibendran, he confided another, deeper fear to the prince.

Black clouds gathered and blanketed the sky, plunging all directions into darkness. As if that were not enough, a monsoon rain lashed down. The waves that rose in the sea encircled the ship in ranks, like mountain ranges, hiding everything from view. In such a state, even if the ship they sought came very near, it would be impossible to see it. That other ship, too, must be spinning and staggering in the storm, just as they were. If the two vessels collided, both would be shattered to splinters. The fate of those aboard would be utter ruin.
“Therefore, the greater danger is not the storm itself, but the fact that we are blind to all that surrounds us,” said the captain of the ship.

This was a truth the prince already knew. Thus, amidst the howling wind and driving rain, he stood at the edge of the deck, his sharp eyes scanning all directions.
