Each time the lightning flashed, his gaze darted swiftly, searching every corner of the storm-tossed sea. The turmoil within his heart was beyond words. The messenger sent by his beloved sister was now in the hands of brutal Arabians and murderous sorcerers. As if that were not enough, this cyclone had now descended upon them. What if they failed to find the ship carrying that valiant youth?

Even if we find him, is it possible to see him alive? What if, as Kalapathi fears, our ship collides with the one he has boarded and both sink into the sea? That would be a spectacle indeed! But then, who will deliver the message that must be conveyed to my father? It is impossible to reveal that family secret to Parthibendran. If I do, that Pallavan will only laugh at it; he will never grasp its importance. Until now, the prince has never failed in anything he set out to do. Will he now face defeat? No, never. The King of the Ocean will never stand by and watch harm or failure befall Ponniyin Selvan!

Piercing through the darkness and rain, the prince kept scanning all directions. At that moment, he too heard that dreadful cry. The flash of lightning forced him to close his eyes for a moment. When he opened them again, he saw another light, not from the lightning. A short distance away, a ship was tossing wildly upon the waves, as if haunted by spirits! At the top of its mast, a fire was blazing! In the glow of that fire, the prince saw a man standing upon the mast! My God! Could such a miracle truly happen? That man was none other than the brave youth, Vandiyathevan! Why was he standing there alone? What had become of the others? There was no time now to ponder these questions. In a single instant, the prince decided what must be done.

Many others aboard the ship saw the same scene as the prince. “There!” they cried out in unison, their shout rising above even the terrifying roar of the wind. The prince hurried to the boat lashed to the side of the ship, and turning to the sailors nearby, asked in a loud voice, “Who among you will come with me?”
The sailors, guessing what he intended to do, were struck with astonishment. Yet many of them stepped forward eagerly, vying to be chosen.
Parthibendran and Kalapathi rushed forward to stop him.

“Prince! What are you doing? How can a boat be rowed in this raging sea? How can anyone be saved from a burning ship? Still, let us try. But you must not go. There are plenty of us here who can undertake this task,” said Parthibendran.

“Beware! I will never forgive anyone who tries to stop me at this moment,” declared the prince, his voice ringing with royal authority. At the same time, he untied the boat. “Two of you will suffice; come with me!”
He spoke thus.

The boat was lowered into the sea. The prince and the two men he had indicated leapt into it. In the next instant, the boat moved away from the ship. It danced wildly atop the waves. The prince and the other two rowed with all their might. Little by little, the boat drew closer to the burning ship. By now, the fire had descended from the masthead halfway down the mainmast. But Vandiyathevan still stood there. In the light of the flames, he gazed at the ship; he also saw the boat that had been lowered and was approaching. In that moment of wonder, he forgot himself. It did not even occur to him that he ought to do something.

“Jump! Jump into the sea!” shouted the prince. The words did not reach his ears. He stood there, motionless, like a lifeless lotus. It was over; if he delayed even a little longer, the fire would reach the ship’s lower decks; the ship would sink. After that, saving him would be impossible.

The prince made up his mind in an instant about what had to be done. For such emergencies, another end of a long rope had been tied to the lifeboat. He now wound that end tightly around his own waist. He warned the two sailors, then leapt into the sea. The waves that had played with the boat until then now began to play with the prince. One moment they lifted him up to the sky; the next, they hurled him into the depths. Yet the prince, without losing his sense of direction or purpose, sped towards the burning ship.

A great, a very great wave came! Had it crashed down upon the prince, it might have dragged him to the bottom of the sea! But it was a friendly wave; it had come to serve the prince. It lifted him high on its crest and hurled him onto the deck of the burning ship.

Vandiyathevan, who had already begun to untie his bonds, saw the prince and cried out, “Ah!” He bent down, ready to help him up. The prince seized him by the neck and tied the rope tightly around him. Into his ear, he said, “Hold on to me! Don’t let go!” No sooner had he spoken than both of them were once again afloat in the sea, battered by the waves.

The sailors stopped rowing and began to pull the rope in. The prince, clutching Vandiyathevan like a lizard gripping its prey, drew closer to the boat. To catch hold of the boat and climb aboard was no easy task. Every moment that Vandiyathevan, struggling with the waves and supporting the prince, tried to get into the boat felt like an age.

Here, it seemed as if the boat would come within their grasp; the next moment, it might drift away to an unreachable distance. At the last instant, a great wave lent its aid. Rising high beside the boat, that mighty wave lifted them up as well. With the help of the sailors, they leapt into the boat.
“Row! Row fast!” commanded the Prince.

For the burning ship was nearing the moment when it would sink into the sea. In the turmoil that would arise as it went under, the boat might capsize. Not only that; if the ship sank and the fire was extinguished, it might become impossible for them to catch up with another ship.

Ah! There—the ship had begun to sink. What a terrifying yet beautiful sight it was, to see the blazing timbers, burning with tongues of flame, submerge into the sea! But they could not witness it for long. Just as the Prince had anticipated, a great commotion arose in the sea. Waves towered sky-high.

The boat somehow managed to withstand the waves. But once the burning ship had sunk, in the surrounding darkness, they lost all sense of where the other ship was. They could not tell direction or distance. Was the boat drawing nearer to the ship, or drifting farther away? There was no way to know. Danger lurked on both sides.

If, in the darkness, they unknowingly approached the ship and collided with it, the boat would be smashed to pieces. If they drifted away—what then? In the midst of the open sea, in that pitch-black darkness, what could that tiny boat possibly do? O King of the Ocean! You must protect the precious son of the Ponni River, whom your beloved Ponni has bestowed!
The marvels of Lord Vayu, the Wind God, are truly wondrous. That great cyclone which had come with such sudden fury, departed just as swiftly. In its wake, it left the sea in utter turmoil.

The cyclone had passed, true; but the agitation it had caused in the sea would not subside so easily. It would last for a whole night and day, perhaps even longer. The force of that turbulence would travel far, covering the vast sandy stretches of the Kodikkarai coast with surging waves. Giant breakers would crash and batter the shores of Nagapattinam. The unrest would spread as far as Kankesanthurai and Trincomalee. Even Mathottam and Rameswaram would not be spared a taste of its fury.

The boat in which the prince and his companions were seated was being tossed and swallowed by the waves, drifting endlessly. After a while, even the rowing had ceased. What use was there in rowing when neither direction nor destination could be discerned, when it was impossible to tell where the ship was? The wind had died down; the rain had stopped; the thunder and lightning had ceased. Yet, the arrogance of the waves had not diminished in the slightest.

The boat continued to struggle amidst those waves. An entirely unexpected danger was drawing nearer and nearer. Now, it had arrived! The burning ship was sinking, was it not? At that moment, a raft that had not been completely consumed by the flames broke away from the wreck. Floating upon the sea, it drifted closer and closer to the boat. Because of the darkness, no one noticed it until it was almost upon them.

The moment they saw it, the prince shouted, “Row! Row with all your might!” But before he could close his mouth, the raft struck the bottom of the boat. With the force of the collision, the boat split apart with a loud crack. First, it broke into two pieces. Then, it shattered into small planks and fragments.
“Friend! Do not be afraid! That raft is safer than this boat. Leap and hold on to it!” said the prince.

chapters.title: The Song of Abaya
paragraphs: Part Two – The Whirlwind

Until Prince Arulmozhi reached Parthibendran’s ship, those who stood at the mouth of the Thondaiman river watched him intently. As soon as the prince boarded the ship, the boat that had ferried him returned.
The face of Commander-in-Chief Boothi Vikramakesari betrayed his elation.

“The Lord is on our side; there is no doubt about it. Will the conch and discus marks upon the prince’s sacred form ever be tarnished? Parthibendran will safely escort him to Kanchi. We, too, must set out towards Thanjai with our armies!” Thus, as if speaking to himself, the Kodumbalur Velar declared aloud.

Immediately, he turned to Alwarkadiyan, who stood beside him. “Vaishnavite! Are you still standing here? There is no harm in that. What is there that the Prime Minister’s secret spy does not know? Well, what are you going to do? Will you come with me to the flower garden?”
“No, sir! There is yet another task the Prime Minister has assigned to me, which I must fulfill…”
“What is that, my boy?”
Alwarkadiyan glanced toward the spot a little distance away, where the mute queen and Poonguzhali stood.
“Is it something concerning those women?” asked the Commander-in-Chief.
“It concerns one of them; the Prime Minister has ordered that if I happen to see such a mute woman in Lanka, I must somehow bring her to Thanjavur.”

“He has given you a fine task. He might as well have asked you to catch one of the storm winds that rage across the Lankan seas and bring it back. It would be just as easy to capture that mute woman and bring her here. No one knows who she is. She seems to have great affection for our prince. Do you know anything about her?” “She is mute, and also deaf from birth—I know that. I also know that taking her along would be harder than trapping a storm wind in a cage and carrying it away. Still, as my master has commanded, I shall make an attempt.”
“Even this boat-girl seems to be friendly with her. Look at how the two of them are conversing with gestures! Call that girl here! I must give her a warning…”
Azhwarkkadiyan went over to the women and conveyed the Commander’s summons to Poonguzhali.
Poonguzhali left the mute queen and approached the Commander.

“Listen, girl! You are very clever! You came at the right time and brought important news. You have rendered a great service to the Chola dynasty. I shall never forget this. At the right time, I will reward you suitably,” he said.
Poonguzhali replied humbly, “My respects, sir! I do not need any reward.”

“Who lets you go without a reward? Let all this confusion subside a little. Afterwards… afterwards, I shall find you a husband in the Chola army, a hero among heroes. It will not do if your husband is an ordinary fellow—he must be a Bhimasena! Otherwise, wouldn’t you just twirl him around your little finger?” said the Commander, smiling.

Poonguzhali stood looking at the ground. Anger surged within her, but she did not wish to show it at that moment. What was the use of quarreling with this rough old man? She tried to suppress her anger.

“But remember one thing—do not think that just because you have done some service for the prince, you can celebrate your closeness to him! Be content with casting your nets in the sea and catching fish! Do not aspire to cast your net and catch the prince! Beware, girl! If you go near him again, danger will come to you!” said the Commander. His voice was harsh then. Each of his words fell upon Poonguzhali’s ears like drops of boiling ghee.

Poonguzhali longed to reply to the old man with words as sharp as his. But she could not speak—her throat was choked. The drops of boiling ghee that fell in her ears seemed to flow out as hot tears from her eyes. Tears welled up and burned her eyes.

Without lifting her bowed head, Poonguzhali turned away. She walked in the direction opposite the seashore. Her steps began slowly, but gradually her pace quickened. For a moment, she glanced sideways toward where the Mute Queen sat. She saw that near the queen stood Azhwarkkadiyan, seemingly trying to communicate something to her. The thought struck Poonguzhali that she should not remain where people were gathered. She could not bear to hear the sound of human voices. Ah! How cruel human beings are! Why do they utter such harsh words? How wonderful it would be if everyone were mute!

After walking a short distance into the forest, she reached the bank of the Thondaiman river. She walked along the bank, heading inland. She made her way toward the spot where she had left her boat. Yes, she must reach that boat quickly. She must get in and row away. She must go alone, out to sea. She must reach the open ocean, where no human voice could ever reach her ears. She would lay down the oar and let it rest. The boat would drift, tossed by the waves, and she would drift with it. She would go on endlessly, across the boundless sea. Only then would her troubled heart find peace. Only then would the pain caused by the Commander’s words be soothed. Her anger would subside, and comfort would come.
What did that wretched old man say! “Be content with casting your net and catching fish in the sea! Do not cast your net for the prince!” he had said.

As if I am casting my net for the prince! Disgusting! See the way that old man’s mind works!… Yes; the fish that live in the sea are far better creatures than the men who walk the land. They do not speak such cruel words. How blissfully they spend their days, swimming and floating in the deep sea! What sorrow do they know? What grief? Ah! Could I not have been born as a fish in the sea? If I had been born so, I could have swum forever in the deep, never caught in the world’s sorrows, hatreds, desires, attachments, angers, and torments. Then, there would be no one to separate me from the prince, no one to deceive or speak ill of us… No, no! Even that is not certain. Even there, these wicked humans would come, casting their nets to catch and take us away! Even if they took only one of two fish, they would take it! Murderers!…

The anger that surged in Poonguzhali’s heart lent her feet an unmeasured swiftness. By the time the sun reached its zenith, she had arrived at the spot where she had left her boat. Fortunate indeed! The boat was still there, tied up just as she had left it. That boat was her dearest companion, her very soul. It was her sanctuary. In this cruel world, beset by sorrow and betrayal, it was that narrow canoe which gave her peace and joy. It was a great relief that no one had taken it away.

“Let whatever may happen, happen now. Let that old Commander guard the Prince. Let the woman of the Kodumbalur house tie herself to his neck if she wishes. What does it matter to me? I have my boat; I have my oar; there is strength in my arms; and the vast sea lies before me. O King of the Ocean! Even if everyone else abandons your precious daughter, you will not forsake her, will you?
You will not let the words uttered by the Prince’s sacred lips—‘Daughter of the Sea’—become a lie, will you?”

Poonguzhali climbed into her boat. She rowed towards the sea. With the river’s current aiding her, she soon reached the mouth of the Thondaiman River. Then she steered the boat into the sea. Before long, she realized that a cyclone was about to break. She knew well the signs that heralded a storm. On the first night, a pale ash-colored halo had circled the moon. All day today, the sky had been overcast. Not a leaf stirred on the trees. There, in the southwestern corner, dark clouds had begun to gather. A cyclone was certain to strike soon. The sea’s turbulence would be a wondrous sight. She must not get caught in the open sea. It would be wise to go and stay on Bootha Theevu. If she stayed there, she could watch and delight in the wild spectacle of the sea during the storm. After the winds had blown themselves out, and the sea’s fury had subsided a little, she could row her boat across to the Kodikkarai shore. What was the hurry now? By this time, that ship would most likely have reached Kodikkarai. It was fortunate that it had not been caught in the storm. The Prince would have safely landed there by now. Or perhaps, he might even have reached Mamallapuram. What did it matter where he had gone? He would not be caught in the cyclone; that much was enough to satisfy her.

Poonguzhali did not know that, before the cyclone began, the wind had died down completely, and that, though the ships had unfurled their sails, they could not move on the sea. So she assumed that by now the ship would have reached the other shore.

The words of the Commander—“Do not cast a net for the Prince!”—kept recurring in her mind, tormenting her. Therefore, she decided not to go to Kodikkarai immediately. She resolved to remain on Poonkuzhali Island, to watch the wild revelry of the whirling winds, and only after that, to set out at her leisure.

From the mouth of the Thondaiman River, Poonkuzhali Island was not far. Within an hour of her departure, she reached it. Poonkuzhali’s arrival on the island coincided perfectly with the onset of the storm.

She drew the boat up onto the shore, overturned it, and tied it securely. Then, she made her way to a small Buddhist stupa on the island. For a while, she sheltered in the cave chamber at its base, safe from the wind and rain. But she could not remain there long. The desire to witness the tumultuous divine play of Lord Vayu overwhelmed her. Emerging from the cave, she climbed the steps and reached the summit of the stupa.

At that moment, the scene around her matched the turmoil in her own heart. Hundreds of coconut palms, grown tall and proud on Poonkuzhali Island, danced wildly, as if demon hordes were circling the Destroyer at the end of the world. The sea waves, at times, rose higher than the palms, appearing for a moment like the snowy peaks of the Himalayas, only to shatter the next instant into a hundred million foaming droplets. The sound of the swirling, battering wind, the thunderous roar of the waves, and the intermittent peals of thunder all merged, making it seem as if the very directions of the world were collapsing and crumbling.

Lightning split the sky, flashing and darting, sometimes branching and streaking across, only to vanish. For a fleeting second, the tempestuous sea and the frenzied trees were illuminated, then plunged once more into impenetrable darkness.

Poonkuzhali stood there for a long time, watching all this tumult and chaos. Her body swayed like the trees in the wind. Her hair came undone and streamed in the gale. The rain drenched her. The thunder split her ears. The lightning dazzled her eyes. She paid no heed to any of it. For a long while, she stood there in the wind and rain. Her heart was wild and tumultuous. She felt as though all the wondrous commotion around her was happening solely for her delight, and she experienced it with pride.

From time to time, thoughts of Prince Arulmozhi came to her. She imagined that, by now, he would have reached Kodikkarai and found shelter in a safe place. Perhaps he was staying at her parents’ house; or perhaps he had gone to Nagapattinam and was resting in the royal palace there. Or perhaps, at that very moment, he was at sea—

Could he still be on the ship? And if so, what of it? What harm could any storm do to that great wooden vessel he had boarded? Surely, many would be gathered around him, shielding him from harm. Would he spare a thought for her? Would he, even for a moment, wonder, “Where might that foolish Poonguzhali be at this hour?” Never would he do so. He would think of Vandiyathevan, whom her sister had sent. Perhaps he might even think of the Kodumbalur princess. But where would there be room in his memory for this poor fisher maiden of the Karaiyar clan?

Long into the night, Poonguzhali endured the raging tumult of the cyclone, and at last, she retreated to the cave at the foot of the stupa and drifted into sleep. Yet even in sleep, peace eluded her. Dreams, strange and vivid, haunted her rest. Once, she dreamt she was casting a net from a boat upon the sea, and the prince himself was caught in it. Another time, she dreamt that she and the prince had become fish, swimming side by side through the ocean’s depths. Each time a dream ended, she awoke with a start and thought, “What madness is this?” She tried to clear her mind and return to sleep.

When dawn broke and she awoke fully, the fury of the cyclone had somewhat abated. There was no thunder, no lightning; even the rain had ceased. She rose and went to the seashore. Unlike the night before, the waves were no longer crashing so violently upon the shore. Yet the sea still churned with unrest. All around were signs of the havoc the cyclone had wrought upon the island the previous night. Trees, uprooted and flung to the ground, lay scattered; tall trees, their crowns bent low, stood in mournful disarray.

As Poonguzhali gazed upon these scenes, she noticed, a little way out at sea, something floating—a raft, it seemed. Tossed back and forth by the waves near the shore, it was at last cast up onto the beach. Only then did Poonguzhali notice that a man was lashed to the raft. She ran to him. The man, bound to the raft, was barely alive. She untied him and revived him. He was a fisherman from a coastal village in Eezham. He said he had been caught in the cyclone while out fishing. The sea, he said, had claimed his companion, and that he himself had survived was nothing short of a rebirth. He had yet another important piece of news to share.

“On the night before last, the cyclone raged fiercely for a while and then seemed to pause. Darkness enveloped us on all sides. Suddenly, a great bolt of lightning struck. In that flash, I saw two ships. One of them had caught fire and began to burn. For a few moments, I watched that terrifying scene—”

“We saw it. There was a hurried movement of people on board. Then, the burning ship sank into the sea. Another boat disappeared into the darkness!” stammered the man, his words tumbling out in confusion.

The moment she heard this, Poonguzhali wondered if the ship that carried the prince was one among them. But she quickly reassured herself that it could not be. Countless ships came and went upon the sea—why should she worry about this one? Yet, perhaps some who had been on the burning ship had fallen into the water. Like this raft-fisherman, perhaps someone else was clinging to whatever they could find, struggling to stay afloat. Why shouldn’t she help them? Why not row out, rescue those who were floundering, and bring them to shore? After all, what else was this life for?

No sooner had this thought arisen—if it had even fully formed—than Poonguzhali untied her boat, pushed it into the sea, and climbed aboard. She summoned the full strength of her iron arms and pulled at the oars. It was a hard task to get past the waves that crashed upon the shore, but once she had crossed them, it was no longer so difficult. As always, her hands worked the oars with practiced ease. The boat danced over the waves, gliding gently forward.

A thrill of excitement welled up in Poonguzhali’s heart. The old song she often sang in her boat took on a new form of its own accord. Overcoming the roar of the waves, her majestic, melodious voice carried the song across the four winds:

“In the tossing of the wave-filled sea, Why does my inner ocean brim with joy? As earth’s daughter struggles and heaves, Why does my heart leap in delight? When thunder crashes in all eight directions, And the world explodes in that moment, Like a master of the dance, Why does my soul begin its dance?”

Clinging to the floating wooden log, the prince and Vandiyathevan were tossed and tumbled by the surging waves, drifting upon the vast sea. Though it was but a single night that they thus floated upon the waters, to Vandiyathevan it seemed as though countless ages had passed. He had lost hope almost at once; all faith that they might survive and reach the shore had utterly deserted him.

Each time a wave lifted him to its crest and then hurled him down, he thought, “This is the end, I am dead now.” Yet, each time, he was astonished to find life and consciousness still within him. Again and again, he looked at the prince and lamented, “Because of my reckless haste, I have dragged you too into this peril.”
The prince offered him comfort and tried to instill courage. “There have been those who have survived, floating like this upon the sea for three or even four days,” he would say, repeating it often.
“How long has it been since we fell into the sea?” Vandiyathevan asked.
“Not even a single night has passed yet,” replied the prince.
“Impossible! Impossible! It must have been many days,” said Vandiyathevan.
After a while, another torment befell him. His throat grew parched, and a terrible thirst seized him. Though he floated surrounded by water, there was none fit to drink. This was a cruel torture.
He told the prince of his suffering.
“Bear it a little longer! Dawn will break soon! We shall drift ashore somewhere,” said the prince.
Vandiyathevan tried to endure a little longer, but could not. “Ayya! I cannot bear this torment any longer. Untie me from the log! Let me sink and die in the sea!” he cried.

The prince tried once more to encourage him, but it was of no use. Madness seized Vandiyathevan. He tried to untie himself from the log. The prince saw this, drew near, and struck him twice, sharply, upon the head. Vandiyathevan lost consciousness.

When he regained his senses, he saw that dawn had broken and light filled the world. The roar of the waves had subsided somewhat. The sun must have risen somewhere, but he could not see where. The prince... He looked at him with affection and said, “Friend! The shore must be somewhere nearby. Just a moment ago, I saw the top of a coconut tree. Be patient for a little while longer!”
“Prince! Leave me behind! You must escape and save yourself somehow!” said Vandiyathevan.

“No! Do not be afraid! I will not abandon you like that! Ah! What is that? It sounds like someone singing!” exclaimed the Prince. Yes; at that moment, the song sung by Poonguzhali from her boat reached their ears.
“In the tumult of the surging sea, Why does only the ocean within rejoice?”

This song echoed in their ears like a hymn of deliverance. Even Vandiyathevan, who had been drained of strength and spirit, who had nearly lost his very life, felt new life and vigor awaken within him at the sound of that song.
“Prince! That is Poonguzhali’s voice! She is rowing the boat towards us. We are saved!” he exclaimed.

In a short while, the boat appeared before their eyes. It drew closer and closer, until it was right beside them. Poonguzhali stood motionless, doubting whether what she saw was truly happening. The Prince untied the bonds that held Vandiyathevan. First, he leapt into the boat himself. Then he helped Vandiyathevan aboard. Poonguzhali, still clutching the oar in her hand, stood like a statue, frozen in disbelief.
Part Three – The Sword of Slaughter

chapters.title: On the Shores of Kodi
paragraphs: The whirlwind that had swept across the sea entered the Chola land’s coastline and continued its furious journey. Just as the saying goes, “Where the stone-grinder’s son has passed, the forests and hills are reduced to dust,” so too, everywhere the whirlwind had gone, it left behind countless scenes of terrible destruction. From Kodikkarai to Kaveripoompattinam, along the Chola country’s seashores, one could clearly see the handiwork of Lord Vayu’s playful wrath. Numerous trees lay uprooted, their branches snapped and scattered. The roofs of houses had been lifted clean away by the storm and flung far and wide, shattered to bits. Huts stood as nothing but stunted walls. Everywhere in the region of Kodikkarai, the land looked like a flooded wilderness. It seemed as if the sea itself had risen and invaded the earth.

Yet, the stretch of white sand that lay between the land and the sea belied that notion. Only in those places where the sand had been mixed with clay did water now collect in abundance. In such places, if man or beast were to step in, it would be their living grave! Even elephants would be swallowed up by those pits of quicksand, which would then belch them out with a gulp!

Two days after the whirlwind had struck, Periya Pazhuvettarayar and his retinue arrived at Kodikkarai. The palanquin followed behind them. But this time, it was the young queen Nandini Devi herself who traveled in that palanquin. “There is no longer any need to secretly take Prince Madurantaka away. Besides, if I take the young queen with me now, won’t the palanquin be available again when the need arises to take Madurantaka away?” So Nandini had said, and Pazhuvettarayar had readily agreed with enthusiasm. For that elderly lord, who was immersed in the intoxication of desire, it was only natural to wish to take that celestial beauty along with him.
Before the whirlwind, they had already reached Nagapattinam. There, the officer in charge first fulfilled his official duties.

At that time, Nagapattinam was one of the major port cities of Tamil Nadu. From foreign lands, all manner of goods arrived at that harbor in great wooden ships. Thousands of small boats would ferry those goods to the shore. From the shore, other goods would be loaded and taken back to the ships. There were many officials appointed to levy and collect tolls and taxes for all these things. Was it not the right and duty of the Chola Nadu’s Chief Administrator, the great Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar, to oversee whether they were performing their duties properly?

After completing that work, Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar visited the renowned Chudamani Buddhist Vihara in Nagapattinam. The bhikshus received him with due respect and attended to him. The Chief Administrator inquired whether the vihara needed anything, or if the bhikshus lacked anything. The bhikshus replied that they wanted for nothing, and expressed their gratitude to Sundara Chola.

A few days earlier, two bhikshus from this vihara had come to Thanjavur to see the Emperor. On behalf of the Buddhist Sangha, they had conveyed their wishes for Sundara Chola’s swift recovery from illness. At that time, they had also expressed their appreciation for the services rendered by Prince Arulmozhi Varman to the Buddhist faith in Lanka. They said that the prince had issued orders to restore ruined Buddhist viharas, and that these were being carried out, bringing immense joy to the Maha Sangha of Buddhist bhikshus in Lanka.

“O Emperor! We have also heard another joyous piece of news. It seems that a large section of the bhikshus in Lanka wish to offer their ancient throne to your younger prince, and crown him as the King of Lanka! They are discussing this among themselves! What greater proof could there be of our prince’s greatness than this?” they said.
As he listened to this, a rare thought dawned in the heart of Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar. After the bhikshus had left, he shared it with Emperor Sundara Chola.

“O Lord who rules the three worlds! Your authority is established and spreads in all eight directions. There is no one in this vast earth who does not obey your command. Yet, only your two beloved sons seem exempt from this. There are some who hold high positions in the Chola Empire who are poisoning their minds with ill counsel. Aditya Karikalan refuses to come here as you wish, and instead sends you a palm-leaf letter asking you to come to Kanchi. The one who is misleading him thus is none other than your father-in-law, Thirukovalur Malayaman. Likewise, you have repeatedly sent word for your younger son to return from Lanka. I too have sent men until they are weary. But that treacherous Periya Velar of Kodumbalur is ensuring that our men do not meet the prince, and that our letters do not reach him. Otherwise, your beloved— “Will the prince delay so long in coming, even after knowing your wishes?” asked Pazhuvetarayar. “In this situation, a thought occurs to me. If you permit, I will share it.”

With the Emperor’s consent, the nobleman revealed his idea. “Let us send an order accusing the prince of plotting to seize the throne of Lanka and crown himself, and command that he be arrested and brought here. Such an order cannot be stopped by Boothi Vikramakesari. Moreover, if we somehow ensure that the order reaches the prince directly, he will be compelled to come!”

Hearing this, Sundara Chozhar smiled. It was indeed a strange idea; yet, why not try it? The longing to see Ponni’s beloved son surged in the Emperor’s heart. He felt that his final days were drawing near. Therefore, he wished to express his heart’s desire regarding the kingdom to his dearly beloved younger son. If Arulmozhi learned of his father’s wish to grant the throne of Thanjavur to Madurantakan, he would accept it without a word of protest. Later, through him, it would be easier to change the mind of Aditya Karikalan as well.

Thinking thus, the Emperor approved the nobleman’s suggestion. It was on this basis that the order was sent to arrest and bring Arulmozhivarman. A strict command was also given to the captain of the ship that no harm whatsoever should befall the prince.

After the two ships set out for Eelam with the aforementioned order, Periya Pazhuvetarayar was troubled by some anxiety. He realized that if anything happened to the prince, he would bear great blame. Therefore, he wished to go in person to the port of Nagapattinam, to receive the prince properly and bring him to Thanjavur under his own responsibility.

There were other reasons for this plan as well. Before the prince came to Thanjai and met the Emperor, neither Sembiyanmadevi nor Kundavai should be allowed to see him. Both women wielded great influence over the prince and harbored a deep dislike for Pazhuvetarayar. They might say something to sway the prince’s mind. Before the right time arrived—before Sundara Chozhar’s death—something untoward might happen and ruin all plans.

Furthermore, since the attack from behind by the tunnel guard in the treasury chamber, the nobleman’s mind had been plagued by strange suspicions. Could someone be hiding in the treasury hall? If so, that— Who could it be? Could it be that valiant scion of the Vanar clan, who escaped without being caught by the guards of the Tanjore fort? If so, he might know even more secrets, might he not?

As Chinna Pazhuvettarayar had said, could the sorcerer who often came to see Nandini have any connection to this matter? That, too, must be found out. The news that it was none other than the young princess Kundavai Devi who had sent Vandiyathevan with a palm-leaf letter to Prince Arulmozhi Varman had also disturbed the mind of the chief. What message could she have sent through Vandiyathevan? Could it be that the woman serpent had caught wind of the plans that he and the likes of Sambuvarayar had made regarding the Chola throne? Might she have written and sent something about that?

Whatever the case, it would be best if he himself were the first to meet the prince when he landed on the Chola shore. Since he had already given orders to arrest Vandiyathevan along with the prince, he must also see that man first. He must find out what Vandiyathevan knew, and how much he knew.

Thinking thus, Periya Pazhuvettarayar resolved to go to Nagai Pattinam and wait there. Nandini Devi had even more reasons than he did. She was eager to see Vandiyathevan again and to find out what message Kundavai had sent with him. She was also keen to know how far the mission of the sorcerer Ravidasan had succeeded. Therefore, she too declared that she would go to Nagai Pattinam. Would one refuse the wages for eating sugarcane? The old man immediately agreed. He began to indulge in daydreams of a joyous voyage with Nandini in a pleasure boat along the seashore. He hoped that, through this, the burning desire that consumed his heart and body might find some relief.

It was while Pazhuvettarayar and Nandini were at Nagai Pattinam that the cyclone struck. Nandini experienced the fierce play of the wind to the fullest. She delighted in watching the waves rise and crash to the height of coconut trees along the shore. But Pazhuvettarayar’s fantasy of a blissful pleasure cruise with Nandini on the sea was not to be fulfilled.

After the cyclone had unleashed its fury and passed, Pazhuvettarayar made inquiries to find out whether any damage had been done to the ships and boats at sea. Since everyone along the shore had been forewarned about the coming storm and had been cautious, it was learned that there was not much damage. But out in the open sea, between Eezham and— Between Kodikkarai and the open sea, some fishermen who had gone out to catch fish on their catamarans reported that two ships had been seen struggling in the waves, and that one of them had caught fire and sunk. This news caused great anxiety to the Pazhuvettaraiyar. Could it be that those two ships were the ones bringing the prince as a captive? If so, what could have become of the prince? If anything had happened to the prince, would not a great blame fall upon himself? Had not Arulmozhi Varman won the boundless love of the people of Chola Nadu? What could he say to the people about this? What explanation could he give to the Emperor? An overwhelming desire arose within him to learn the truth for certain. If he went to Kodikkarai, perhaps he could find out more. There might be those there who had seen the sunken ship closely. Perhaps some who had escaped from the wreck might have reached the shore.
Yes; he must go to Kodikkarai at once!

When he expressed this thought to Nandini, she readily agreed with enthusiasm. “I have never seen Kodikkarai before. I have heard that region is very beautiful. In this circumstance, I can see it as well,” said Nandini.

There were two ways to reach Kodikkarai from Nagapattinam. One could travel by boat along the canal that ran beside the seashore, or one could go by road. Since the Pazhuvettaraiyar’s retinue was large, they chose to go by road. Moreover, Nandini did not prefer the canal route. One reason was that if they traveled by boat, the Pazhuvettaraiyar might begin to recount his tales of love, which Nandini dreaded. Not only that, if they went by road, they could question the catamaran fishermen and boatmen who had come ashore along the coast as they traveled, could they not?

However, their inquiries along the way yielded no new information. A few more people said only that, during the time when a strong cyclone struck the open sea, they had seen a ship catch fire and burn. When they reached Kodikkarai, the keeper of the lighthouse, Thyaga Vidangar, said that he would vacate his humble house for the Pazhuvettaraiyar and his wife. He pleaded with them to accept it.
There was no other mansion or palace to stay in at Kodikkarai. Yet, Nandini refused the offer. She said she preferred to stay in a tent pitched near the lighthouse.

So, tents were set up accordingly. At a little distance, tents were also erected for the Pazhuvur retinue. As soon as the tents were finished, a large ship was seen out at sea. It came as close to the shore as it possibly could and then stopped.

At the sight of this, the agitation of the Pazhuvettaraiyar grew intense. The planks of the ship were shattered and scattered, making it clear that it must have been caught in a whirlpool. Who were those aboard? Could it possibly have been the prince? There was no wonder that the tiger flag was nowhere to be seen; in the storm, it might well have been torn away and cast aside.

To learn the fate of the ship, Pazhuvettaraiyar immediately dispatched a boat from there. It seemed that those on the ship had been waiting for such a boat. At once, two men descended from the ship into the boat. One among them was Parthibendran Pallavan.

Had not Prince Arulmozhi himself left the ship in a boat to save Vandiyathevan, and not returned? Because of this, Parthibendran was plunged into boundless anxiety. After the wind had calmed and dawn had broken, he searched for the prince by steering the ship here and there. Of those who had left the ship with the prince in the boat, only one was found alive. He recounted how, after Arulmozhi had valiantly saved Vandiyathevan, disaster had struck the boat. This only multiplied Parthibendran’s grief a hundredfold. Yet, a faint hope lingered in his heart—could it be that the prince had reached safety at Kodikkarai?

Thus, he resolved to go to Kodikkarai and make inquiries. For this purpose, he brought the ship there and anchored it. After descending into a boat and starting towards the shore, he learned that the great Pazhuvettaraiyar had arrived there with his young queen. This knowledge filled him with intense irritation.

He recalled what Aditya Karikalan had said about the young queen of Pazhuvoor, Nandini. The words of that mighty hero, who had been bewitched and driven to madness by that enchanting woman, echoed in his mind. A restless curiosity to see what manner of woman could so captivate such a valiant heart stirred in a corner of his soul. That desire soon began to grow and take root. A new anxiety arose—what if he should leave without ever setting eyes upon her?
But that anxiety did not last long. As soon as he stepped ashore from the boat, Parthibendran was summoned directly to the tent of Pazhuvettaraiyar.

At the entrance of the tent stood Pazhuvettaraiyar himself, exuding an air of majesty. Parthibendran thought how wrong it was to call this heroic warrior, with his commanding presence, a mere “elder.” In strength of body and firmness of mind, he appeared more lion-like than many young men Parthibendran had ever seen.

Even as he was lost in these thoughts, a maiden emerged from within the tent. Like a flash of lightning gleaming from behind the clouds, she shone with a dazzling radiance that could blind the eye, her golden-hued beauty arresting all attention. She stood before the Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar like a graceful flowering vine entwined upon the sturdy trunk of a tall, mature teak tree.

Beholding that enchantress, who could bewitch the very world, Parthibendran stood transfixed in amazement. Casting her spear-like gaze upon him, she asked, “My lord! Who is this valiant warrior? I have not seen him until now, have I?”
Her parrot-sweet words intoxicated Parthibendran, as if he had drunk honeyed wine from a golden goblet.

chapters.title: The Ensnaring Net
paragraphs: Those who marry a young woman after reaching an advanced age always dwell in the illusory world of suspicion. For them, a natural aversion arises whenever they see strangers. For Pazhuvettarayar, there was even greater reason for such aversion. He did not at all like that Nandini had come and stood before him and begun to speak. At the same time, he could not bring himself to rebuke Nandini either.

Therefore, in reply to Nandini’s question, he said, “Queen! There are countless people in this world whom we do not know. It is not possible for us to have seen and known everyone, is it? So, there is no loss to us because of that!”

Hearing this, Parthibendran said, “Sir! There is no loss to the Chola kingdom’s treasurer’s queen for not knowing me; the loss is mine alone. Therefore, let me introduce myself, Lady! They call me Parthibendra Pallavan!”
“Oh! Is that so? I have heard your name before!” said Nandini.

“Parthibendra! Why did you mention only your name and leave out your honors? When did you become so modest and humble? Nandini! He is not just Parthibendran. He is the Parthibendra Pallavan who conquered Vengi and Kalinga and took the head of Veerapandiyan!” said Pazhuvettarayar in a mocking tone.

For a moment, Nandini’s face darkened like a storm-laden sky. Two flashes of lightning seemed to dart from her eyes, shining and vanishing instantly. The next moment, she laughed aloud, her voice ringing like silver bells.
“Sir! How many people have claimed the proud title of ‘the one who took Veerapandiyan’s head!’ Is there any count for that?” she asked.
“Lady! The commander said so out of his fondness for me. In truth, I am not worthy of that honor. The glory of taking Veerapandiyan’s head belongs to Aditya Karikalan alone!”

“Why do you say so, my boy? Shouldn’t you also claim a share in the pride of striking a dead snake?” Pazhuvettarayar asked in a mocking tone, and let out a short, sharp laugh. “No, my lord! No! Aditya Karikalan did not slay a dead serpent. When he raised his sword, Veerapandiyan was very much alive, a serpent with all its venom. To save his life, a maiden as enchanting as Mohini of the celestial realms appeared before him, joined her hands, and pleaded. Had I been the one holding the sword, I would have instantly cast it away. Veerapandiyan would have escaped with his life!” Thus replied Parthibendran to Pazhuvetaraiyar. Yet, his eyes were fixed keenly upon Nandini’s face.

Nandini sensed that the conversation was treading into dangerous waters. Turning to Pazhuvetaraiyar, she said, “My lord! Why recall that old tale now? Should we not inquire about the purpose of his visit?”
At once, Pazhuvetaraiyar said, “Yes, my boy! Enough of old stories! Tell us your tale! When did you leave Kanchi? Where are you bound? What brings you here?”
Parthibendran, whose mind had been clouded by the sight of Nandini, now remembered the purpose of his coming.

“Sir! Forgive me! I have been speaking of all manner of things. I have come bearing news of utmost importance. News so dire it could plunge the entire Chola land into a sea of sorrow— The prince Arulmozhi Varman, who set sail with me from Lanka, leapt into the sea when the storm struck our ship. His fate remains unknown. I have come to see if, by chance, he has found refuge here!”
Before he could finish, Pazhuvetaraiyar cried out, “Ah! What did you say?” and collapsed to the ground like a great tree uprooted by a whirlwind.
Parthibendran rushed forward to support him, but Nandini stepped between them and gently pushed away his outstretched hand. She seated herself beside Pazhuvetaraiyar, lifting his head onto her lap.
“Water! Water!” she cried.

A maidservant hurried in from the tent with water. Several warriors, the lighthouse guards, and members of his household came running. With great composure, Nandini motioned for them all to stand back. She sprinkled water on Pazhuvetaraiyar’s face and called to him in a tender voice, “My lord! My lord!” In a few moments, the old man’s eyes fluttered open. At once, his senses returned, and he sat up with a start.

“Nandini! Was what I just heard true? What did this Pallavan say? Did he not say that Ponniyin Selvan has been taken by the sea? When that valiant prince was but a small child, these very hands lifted him up and carried him on my shoulders with joy. Yet it was with these same hands that I set my seal upon the order to have him captured and brought here. Alas! What will the Chola land think of me?” cried Pazhuvettaraiyar, striking his forehead. Never before had Nandini seen that diamond-studded warrior so shaken and distraught; indeed, no one had ever witnessed such a sight.
“My lord! Do not be agitated! He has not yet told us the whole story, has he? Would it not be better to hear everything and then decide what must be done?” said Nandini.

“Yes, you are right. Parthibendran! Speak quickly! You said Ponniyin Selvan drowned in the sea and died, did you not? Is that true? Or are you, with some ill intent, spinning a tale? Do not play with a hungry tiger! Beware!” thundered the old lord, his eyes blazing with fire.

“Sir! Forgive me! I did not say that the prince is dead. Even I cannot believe that such a terrible loss could befall this Tamil land. I only said that, when the storm reached its fiercest, he jumped from my ship into the sea. By the grace of God, perhaps he survived. Perhaps he has come ashore somewhere along this coast. It is with that hope that I have come here to search…”
“He jumped into the sea during the storm! For what reason? Why did he jump? Why was he on your ship? What were you doing when he leapt?” demanded the lord of Pazhuvoor, his voice trembling.
Nandini interjected, “My lord! Let him tell us in detail, starting from why he went to Lanka!”
“Yes! Tell us everything as it happened! If you do not speak the truth, you will not escape with your life! I will…” Pazhuvettaraiyar ground his teeth in anger.

“Your Majesty! I am not accustomed to speaking anything but the truth. Even if I wished to lie, my tongue would not permit it. Listen! News reached Kanchi that you, Kadambur Sambuvaraiyar, and many others were plotting treason against the Chola dynasty.”
“Lies! Lies! Utter lies!”

“Let the news be false! That is what I wish for. I only conveyed the message that had reached Kanchipuram. Based on that, Thirukovalur Malayaman and Aditya Karikalan sent me to Eezham. They sent me with the command to bring Arulmozhi Varman back with me…”
Thus began Parthibendran, and from the moment he had arrived in Lanka, he recounted everything that had happened, describing in detail all that he knew.

When the tale ended, Pazhuvettaraiyar cried out, “Oh God! A great calamity has befallen the Chola land! And it is because of this sinner! Was it not I who gave the order to capture the prince and bring him here? Was it not I who sent the ships?”

“Sire! You are not at fault; even if you had not issued those orders, would not the prince have boarded this man’s ship and set out for Kanchipuram? Do not torment yourself in vain. Above all our actions, there is the hand of fate. Furthermore…” At this point, Nandini abruptly stopped speaking aloud and whispered something into Pazhuvettaraiyar’s ear. His face brightened a little.
“Yes—yes! That had not occurred to me!” he exclaimed.

Then, turning to Parthibendran, he said, “Pallava! I am going to inspect your ship myself. Until I return, you must remain here! Do not attempt to escape. If you try to run, I have already ordered my warriors to hurl their spears and kill you on the spot. Beware! Do not die with a wound in your back! Remember your lineage, your warrior ancestry!”
“Salutations, sir! I have no thought of fleeing. If I had such a thought, none of your warriors could stop me. Nor do I intend to die with a wound in my back!” replied the Pallavan.

“Sire! You need not worry about him. I will watch over him myself. If he tries to escape, this very dagger will plunge into his chest! Go in peace and inspect the ship. Question the sailors as well, and see if all he has said is true,” said Nandini, drawing a small dagger from her waist as she spoke.
“Queen! Why should you take on this responsibility? Go inside the tent! Or go to the house of Thyagavidangar. Our warriors will watch over him. Or else, I will take him with me to the ship…”
“I will not come, sir! If I come with you, you will only continue to suspect me. You will think the boatmen are bearing witness on my behalf. I shall not leave this place. You may go without worry!”
“Natha! Until you return from the ship, I too shall remain right here. I will watch over you from here!” said Nandini.
Then, leaning close to Pazhuvetarayar’s ear, she whispered, “Who knows if he has come here to spy on us? And the news about the prince—no one must know of it until you return.”
Pazhuvetarayar nodded and boarded the boat. The boat set off toward the wooden ship.

Nandini watched the boat as it moved away for some distance. At the same time, she sensed that Parthibendran was watching her intently, without so much as blinking. Suddenly, she turned toward him. She expected Parthibendran to lower his head in embarrassment. But would a bee turn away after beholding a honeyed blossom?
Nandini drew her sharp little dagger and brandished it once more. “Beware! Do not try to escape!”
“Devi! Would I be frightened by the sight of your dagger? Would I try to flee? How can a fish caught in a net escape? I am ensnared in the net you have cast…”
“What is this, sir, you say? Are you calling me a fisherwoman? If these words reach the ears of the lord of Pazhuvur…”
“I do not worry about that, Devi! But I was not speaking of the fisherman’s net. I speak of the enchanting net cast by your spear-like eyes…”
“Shame! What boldness you have! Even if I were a fisherwoman, it would not be a disgrace. But do you call me a courtesan who casts a net of desire for men?”

“Forgive me! I did not utter such a slander. Do you need to cast your net deliberately? Does the spider weave its web to catch flies? It spins its web simply to dwell within it. The flies come and fall into it of their own accord…”
“Are you calling me a spider? Am I so fearsome?”

“Mistake! Mistake! I should have spoken of the lamp. The lamp does not burn for the sake of the moths. The lamp burns, casting its light all around, making itself a radiant flame! The foolish moths, thinking it a fruit, rush toward it and perish in its fire…”
“A gentle breeze, a mere puff, is enough to extinguish the lamp. Even a breath from the mouth can put it out. Such is the strength of the lamp!”

“The lamp may be snuffed out; but who can extinguish the full moon? The full moon does not rise for the sake of the lord of the ocean. The moon rises according to the law of nature, spreading its cool, silvery light for the joy of both sky and earth. But look at the foolish sea! Why should the ocean churn and surge at the sight of the full moon? Why should it pine and yearn for a fruit it can never reach?”
“I have heard much about the poetic taste and imagination of the Pallava kings. Only now do I realize that all those tales are true.”
“Until yesterday, I did not believe what I had read and heard in the epics and legends; only today has faith dawned in me.”
“What are you speaking of?”

“I have heard that some, who bear the form of a woman, possess the power to place both heaven and earth beneath their feet. The asuras who churned the milky ocean and obtained the nectar were deceived by Mohini at the very moment they were to drink it. The Sundopa Sundaras fought and died for the sake of a woman. Viswamitra’s penance was broken by Menaka. Kovalan was ensnared in the web of Madhavi’s charms. Dasaratha sent Rama to the forest for Kaikeyi’s sake. Because of the queen of Egypt, the mighty Roman Empire began to fall…”
“Enough, sir! Enough! Why are you reciting all these examples?”
“Do you not understand, Devi? Do you truly not know for whom I am giving these examples?”
“If you mean me as the example, you could do no greater wrong.”
“There is no wrong in it. Their power was not greater than yours.”
“Your own words stand against you.”
“How so, Devi?”
“I sent the Lord of Pazhuvur to the ship on purpose, just so I could ask you about something.”
“Understanding your intention, I too chose not to go with him and remained here.”
“You told me, did you not, that a woman tried to save Veerapandiyan, and that Aditya Karikalan paid no heed to her attempt?”
“Yes, I said so.”
“Do you know who that foolish girl was, who tried to save him?”
“It was none other than the young queen Nandini Devi, who now shines as the jewel of the Pazhuvur palace.”
“If I possessed the power you described of me just now, would I not have saved the life of the man I wished to protect? Why was I unable to do so?”
“Aditya Karikalan, blinded by bloodlust at that moment, did not fulfill your wish. But I know well what kind of torment he has endured for the three years since.”
“How do you know, sir? Did he tell you himself?”

“For three years, he has suffered in silence, bearing the burden in his heart. I only knew that some deep sorrow gnawed at his soul. Ten days ago, on the very first day I set out for Lanka, he finally opened his heart to me and spoke…”
“And then? What did he say?”
“From that moment, the desire to see the young queen of Pazhuvur took root in my own heart as well!”
“Do you remember that I asked you whether, had you been in Aditya Karikalan’s place, you would have spared Veerapandiyan’s life at my request?”
“I remember it well.”
“Is that the truth?”
“By my oath, Devi! You may put me to the test.”
“Sir! There is a doubt in my mind. May I speak of it?”
“Whatever you say in your golden voice, my ears find delight; my heart overflows with joy.”
“I suspect you speak thus only to test me. You speak of the web of enchantment I weave, while you yourself try to cast a net over me. You are attempting to discover the secrets of my heart.”

Parthibendran was startled. When he first began to speak, it was indeed with such an intention. But later, he had forgotten it. The conversation, which had begun with guile, had truly swept him away into a sea of fascination. He now felt ashamed of his original intent. Without betraying this outwardly, he said, “Devi! If ever I try to test you in such a manner and act as a spy, may lightning strike my head!”
“Oh! Please do not say such things,” Nandini cried out.
“Why, Devi! Why?”
“Another man came from your great prince, what was his name?...”
“Vandiyathevan?”
“Yes, that’s him! He tried very cunningly to spy on me and gather information. From what you say, it seems as if lightning has already struck his head!”
“Unfortunately, lightning did not strike his head! Did it not strike the ship he was on instead? Because of that, the danger that befell him also afflicted the younger prince, did it not?”
“Alas! I feel such pity when I think of the young princess of Pazhayarai. The two people she loved most in this world perished at the same time! What misfortune!”
“Devi! Who are these two people?”
“The very two you mentioned! Does not the young princess have a special affection for her younger brother?”
“That is known to the whole world. And the other who was dear to her heart…?”
“Why, the messenger sent by your great prince.”
“You mean Vandiyathevan?”
“Him, indeed!”
“Tch, tch! The powerful Princess of Pazhayarai, who commands the very fate of the Chola Empire, has fallen for that youth—so petty, so vain, so boastful…”

“Yes; she has become enamored of that young man. That is why she gave him a letter and sent him to Lanka, to save him from the punishment of the Pazhuvettaraiyars. Poor old man! He torments himself, thinking he is the cause of the prince’s misfortune, but in truth, it is the Princess who is to blame. If she had not sent him away with that letter…”
“True, true! None of these calamities would have come to pass.”
“When my husband returns from the ship, you must tell him this truth. If you do, you will earn my gratitude!”
“Lady, is this the only way to earn your gratitude? Are there not other tasks you could entrust to me?”
“Sir! There are a hundred ways to earn the gratitude of a foolish woman.”

“Then name another two or three. Aditya Karikalan once had such an opportunity, but he let it slip through his fingers. Now, day and night, he is tormented by regret. I will never make such a mistake!”
“Is this truly so, sir? Would you do anything a woman asks, just to fulfill her wish?”

“That depends on the woman, Devi! Until yesterday, I would have laughed at any woman’s request. I would have done nothing for any woman I had met. But today, it is not so! Try me now. If I had a hundred lives, I would sacrifice them all to fulfill your desire. If a thousand kingdoms were mine, I would give them up for your wish. If you asked me to lose both this world and the next, I would be ready. If you commanded me to forgive my fiercest enemies, I would forgive them. If you ordered me to bring the heads of my dearest friends and lay them at your feet, I would do so and not think twice…”

As Parthibendran spoke thus, like one possessed, his whole body trembled from head to toe. The words tumbled from his lips; his lips quivered; his teeth clenched; his hair stood on end; the sound of his breathing was like the roar of a blacksmith’s bellows.

This transformation in Parthibendran will astonish the readers. Indeed! If, on the very first day, someone had told him, “You will become like this,” he would not have believed it. Even when he looked back upon it later, it was something that could amaze even himself. But this is not merely a marvel concerning Parthibendran alone; it is a mystery about human nature itself.

Despite countless scholars having studied it through the ages, we have not yet fully understood the secrets of the human body’s structure. Then how can we ever hope to comprehend the mysteries of the human heart? Those who have spent their entire lives wallowing in blame and sin suddenly, one day, become ascetic monks; they are swept away in the ecstasy of devotion, singing and dancing; they become recipients of divine grace; they perform unparalleled services for human society.
Conversely, those who have led pure and spotless lives for many years suddenly, one day, stumble and fall! And when they fall, they plunge into the very depths of the netherworld.

Nandini, who had been listening to Parthibendran’s impassioned words, said, “Enough, sir! Enough! Please stop! I will never, at any time, urge you to commit such a terrible deed. I am only going to tell you of something that will bring happiness suitable to both you and me.”

chapters.title: The Owl’s Cry
paragraphs: Nandini gazed out toward the sea. The boat in which Pazhuvettarayar had departed was drawing closer to Parthibendran’s ship.
Nandini let out a deep sigh. That sigh struck Parthibendran’s heart like a storm.

“Devi! Speak to me. Tell me what I must do. There is no need to distinguish between what is good for you and what is good for me. Whatever pleases you—that alone pleases me!” declared the Pallava warrior.

Strange thoughts arose in his mind at that moment. There could be no doubt: this woman was trapped with that cruel old man, suffering like a caged parrot. Why should she not be freed from that wild beast? Let her but express her wish! He could have the old man imprisoned on that very ship and taken away to some distant, unknown land! Scoundrel! How could he bring himself to marry a woman so young, fit to be his daughter or granddaughter…?
Nandini was still watching the boat and the ship. She saw Pazhuvettarayar boarding the ship from the boat.
“Thank goodness! He has boarded safely! No matter how great a warrior he is, he has grown old, after all. I was worried he might stumble while climbing from the boat to the ship,” she said.

The Pallava was disappointed! ‘Why does she show such concern for that old man? What if he had fallen into the sea and died? It would be a blessing for the country; she would be free! Why does she care so much for him?’

“Only today did I realize how much affection the elder has for the Chola dynasty. The moment he heard the prince was in danger, how he rushed away in agitation! Sir! The prince may have escaped, might he not? It isn’t certain that he must have perished, is it?” said Nandini.
“It is not certain; but for someone who leapt into the sea in such a whirlpool, survival is impossible! What can we do against the course of fate?” replied the Pallava.
“There is no fate behind this; it is only the insatiable greed of that old Pazhuvoor demoness that is to blame.

Do you know, sir? Kundavai Devi has immense faith in astrology and palmistry. She examined her younger brother’s horoscope and palm lines and became convinced that he would one day rule over the three worlds as an emperor. Alas! Poor soul! When she learns of the calamity that has befallen her beloved brother, how much anguish she will endure! At that time, it seems I must be by her side to offer comfort!”
In Nandini’s voice, as she spoke thus, there rang a note of excitement. For a moment, the Pallavan was taken aback. Then he decided that it must be his ears that were deceiving him.
“Queen, why should you be the one to comfort her? Is this not the misfortune brought about by her own boundless ambition? For that, she must indeed suffer…”

“How can you say so, sir? If a single tear were to well up in her eyes, there are thousands upon thousands in Chola Nadu whose hearts would tremble. She is the emperor’s cherished daughter, a beauty without equal in all the three worlds!”
“I too once thought so! That is, before I saw you!”
“And after seeing me, what do you think?”
“Kundavai Devi’s beauty cannot compare even to the beauty of your little toe.”
“That is what you say now. But tomorrow, if you see her, you will forget that I even exist in this world!”
“Never, not for a single day. Devi! I am only asking that you put me to the test. Tell me, this very moment, what your command is.”

“I have no right to command. Sir, I only make a humble request. After I married Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar, some have spread slander that divisions and confusion have arisen in Chola Nadu. I wish to prove that this is a lie. For that, I seek your help.”

Parthibendran felt a tinge of disappointment. He had thought that Nandini would send him on some difficult task for her sake. He was eager to accomplish it and win her delight. But now she was speaking of matters of the realm!
“Speak, O Queen! Whatever your wish may be, tell me!” he said.

“Sir! The one who prevented peace from settling upon the Chola land was the Young Princess. Because of her pride, she incited the minor kings and great officials of Chola Nadu to anger. She longed to see Prince Arulmozhi enthroned upon the Chola throne at any cost. For that reason, she obstructed any reconciliation. Now, that cause has vanished. Henceforth, it will be easy to bring about a settlement. Listen, sir! You yourself said it! The ministers and other great officials wish to crown Madurantaka after Sundara Chola. Even the Emperor has consented to this.”
“Is that so, Devi?”

“Yes, sir! Otherwise, would he have ordered the Prince to be captured and brought here as a prisoner? Yet, in my opinion, that is not right. There is still room for a peaceful settlement. Why not divide the kingdom—grant the realm north of the River Vellaru to Aditya Karikalan forever, and the southern part to Madurantaka? Did not your ancestors, the mighty Pallava emperors, find contentment only in ruling the Thondai Mandalam? Did not the ancient Chola kings rest satisfied with the land between the two Vellar rivers?”
“Devi, why do you tell me all this? What does it matter to me how the empire is divided? What concern is it of mine who rules which kingdom?”
“Sir! I thought you were a true friend, loyal to Aditya Karikalan.”

“I have spent my life so far being loyal to others, fighting for others’ glory, laboring for others’ benefit. From now on, I wish to live for myself. Queen! Listen to me! Many times I have pondered why I was born into this world, for what purpose I am alive. My ancestors, the Pallava emperors, ruled vast empires. They created dreamlike worlds such as Mamallapuram. I have wondered if I was born to restore their greatness in my time. But my heart did not delight in that. I felt no thrill in building empires. I found satisfaction only in laboring for the glory of the Chola clan. I rejoiced in the friendship of Aditya Karikalan. I thought to spend my days thus. Only today have my eyes been opened; only a short while ago did I understand why I was born. Listen! The roar of those ocean waves echoes the voice within my soul, crying ‘Yes, yes’ in agreement. See, all the birds in the forest are calling out, ‘So be it, so be it.’ Devi! As for dividing the Chola Empire— “Do not ask me such things. Speak of something else! Tell me to bring priceless corals from the coral islands beyond the seas. Tell me to fetch pearls from the depths of the ocean. Tell me to climb to the summit of Mount Meru and bring back the life-restoring Sanjeevani herb. Ask me to soar above the clouds, pluck the stars from the sky, string them into a necklace, and place it around your neck. Command me to bring the full moon itself, to fashion it into a mirror for you to behold your own face!”
“That is enough, sir, enough! Already that Princess of Pazhayarai calls me ‘madwoman.’ Please do not truly drive me mad!” said Nandini.
Parthibendran felt a tinge of embarrassment. “It is I who am mad; forgive me. Please tell me your wish first!” he said.

“All across Chola Nadu—throughout the land of the Tamils—I wish to rid myself of the ill repute that has befallen me. That is why I seek your help. People say that by marrying this old man, I have brought ruin upon the Chola dynasty. They claim it was I who incited Madurantaka Deva to covet the throne. They say it was I who turned the minor kings of Chola Nadu to his side. I do not wish to die bearing this infamy…”
“Why do you speak of dying? Is it only to torment me?”
“Pallava Prince! Do you know the science of palmistry? Do you have faith in it?” Nandini asked, abruptly changing the subject.
Parthibendran did not answer directly. “Where? Show me your hand!” he said.
Nandini extended her right hand. Parthibendran gazed at it intently for a moment and said, “Remarkable lines. It is rare to see such palms! Please show me your other hand as well.”
Nandini extended her other hand. The Pallava studied it too and asked, “Devi! Has anyone ever looked at the wondrous lines on your palms and said anything before?”
“Yes! The younger princess of Pazhayarai once looked at my hand and said…”
“What did she say?”
“She said, ‘I will die young.’”
“That is true!” said Parthibendran.
“Sir! Do you say so as well?”

“But it appears she has only half-learned the science. It is true that one line on this palm indicates a short life; but another line crosses that mark and foretells rebirth. After that rebirth, it says, there will be the fortune of journeying across the seas to many lands, and a life of happiness longer than even the greatest of kings could attain. All this, it seems, will come to pass through the true love of a young man she meets by chance on the seashore. The lines declare, with utmost clarity, that to fulfill even her smallest wish, he would offer up his very life…”
As he spoke thus, Parthibendran suddenly seized both of Nandini’s outstretched hands and gazed into her eyes.
Nandini pulled her hands away and said, “Fie, fie! What is this you have done?”
“Forgive me! I forgot these were your hands. I thought they were two blooming red lotuses,” he replied.
“If Pazhuvetaraiyar had seen this, he would have had you impaled on the tip of a spear!”
“Devi! I am troubled that all I have to offer you is this one life…”
“Would you give even that so lightly? Keep it safe, to help this orphaned woman!”
“Tell me what I must do!”
“The Chola Empire must be protected from ruin by the strife of rival heirs. I need your help for that.”
“How?”
“Bring your friend Karikalan to Kadambur, to the house of Sambuvaraiyar. Sambuvaraiyar has a daughter. If she is wed to Aditya Karikalan, my heart’s desire will be fulfilled.”
“Is it for such a trifling matter that you have built up so much suspense? I will certainly bring Aditya Karikalan to Kadambur. And then?”

“If Aditya Karikalan marries the daughter of Sambuvaraiyar, half the rebellion will be quelled. If the Chola Empire is divided, giving the southern part to Madurantakan and the northern part to Karikalan, the unrest will be completely resolved.”
“And after that?...”
“The ill-repute that clings to me will vanish. Then, I shall fulfill my own destiny. I will cast myself into the midst of the sea and surrender my life…”
“I will follow you and save you. Our next birth together will begin. We will cross the seas and travel to distant lands. There, I will establish a great kingdom for you.”
“Sir! Let us not speak such words. I am a woman born in the tradition of the chaste wives of southern Tamil Nadu. The dharma-patni of Pazhuvetaraiyar…”
“Devi! Tell me the truth. Why did you marry this old man? Was it out of love for him? Or was it because of his force?”
Nandini let out a deep sigh. Her eyes turned upward. For a moment, it seemed as if she had sunk into some old, sorrowful memory.
“Alas! Do not blame the old man. I married him of my own will.”
“Why? For what reason? What did you see in him?”
“I saw nothing in him. I married him out of desire for palace life and power.”
“I cannot believe it!”

“It is hard to believe, but it is the truth. From a very young age, someone constantly mocked me, calling me poor and orphaned. She always said I had no right even to play with the royal children. Unable to bear that humiliation, I committed this folly.”
“Devi! Who is that woman who insulted you so?”
“Do you not know? Can you not guess?”
“The younger princess, Kundavai, is it not?”
“Yes.”
“One day, I will teach her a lesson.”
“God himself has already punished her! Her beloved younger brother and her dearest lover have both departed along the same path. Now, when I think of her plight, I feel nothing but pity.”
“This punishment is far from enough for that arrogant woman.”
“If you help me with the matter I requested of you a short while ago, her punishment will be complete. Her desire to rule the Chola Empire as its sole sovereign will be dashed to dust.”
“I shall fulfill your wish. What reward will you give me?”
“I will give you anything you ask. As long as it does not violate the traditions of Tamil womanhood, whatever you desire, I shall grant…”

“Queen, they say a new religion has arisen in the western lands. It has spread across Arabia, Baghdad, Persia, and other countries. According to the tenets of that faith, married couples may separate if they wish. There is even a ceremony for it. Women, too, may remarry.”
“Yes, I have heard such things myself.”
“Let us go to those distant lands. Let us embrace that faith…”
“Sometimes, even I dream such daydreams. But is it something that could ever come to pass?”

“Devi! Why should it not? It certainly can. If only you consent, it shall happen. I will board a ship with you, cross the seas, and set foot in faraway lands. With the strength of this sword in my hand, I will establish a great kingdom. I will seat you upon a throne adorned with nine kinds of precious gems! I will crown you with a diadem so dazzling that all who see it will be blinded by its brilliance. For this alone was I born; for this alone have I survived so many battlefields without perishing…”
“Sir! Look, my husband is returning. The boat is nearing the shore. Compose yourself; we can speak of other matters later…”
“When, later, Devi?”
“Come with us to Thanjavur! If you do not receive an invitation as a guest, then come as a prisoner at least!”
“Your invitation alone is enough for me,” said Parthibendran.
The boat on which Pazhuvettarayar had arrived touched the shore. The elder disembarked from the boat and came forward, his very form seeming to embody wrath itself.

Nandini and Parthibendran rose to their feet. In the glance Pazhuvettarayar cast upon them, sparks of fire seemed to fly. Alas! The mere thought that they had been sitting together and conversing for so long filled the elder with rage. Yet, there was no way to express it. Thus, the anger within him boiled and surged all the more.
“My lord! Did you thoroughly inspect the ship? Did you question the sailors well? Is everything this man said true?” Nandini asked, her voice tinged with a gentle coaxing.
That voice soothed the lord of Pazhuvur a little.

“Yes, Queen! It is clear that all he said is true. The ascetic son of the Chola land, the treasured prince of the Chola dynasty—the very apple of Tamil Nadu’s eye—has gone!” he said, then turned to the Pallavan and thundered, “And the one responsible for it stands here—this murderous, villainous wretch!”

“Sir! I am not the cause of it; do not lay the blame upon me! The reason the prince was taken by the sea is the enchantress demoness in woman’s form, who manipulates the entire Chola realm!” replied Parthibendran.
Now the elder’s anger overflowed its bounds like a flood. He thought Parthibendran spoke thus about Nandini.
“Wretch! What did you say?” he cried, and swiftly bent to seize the spear lying on the ground. He raised it, aiming at Parthibendran.
Nandini caught his hand and restrained him. “My lord! What is this? Shall your victorious spear, which has slain so many enemies, be stained with the blood of this guest?” she said.
“Queen! Is he a guest? Did you not hear what he just said about you?” the elder demanded, his voice trembling and words faltering with rage.
“Did he speak about me? Find out exactly what he said. If so, I shall avenge myself with the dagger in my own hand. I will not trouble you!” said Nandini.

“Sir! Am I mad, to speak thus of the young queen of Pazhuvur? Was I not speaking of the enchantress demoness in Pazhayarai? Did not the young princess Kundavai give a secret letter to that youth Vandiyathevan for the prince—” She sent him. Was it not to save that reckless youth that, despite all my attempts to stop him, the prince plunged into the raging sea? That is why I said Kundavai was responsible for the prince’s death,” said Parthibendran.

Pazhuvetaraiyar felt a slight shame at his own hasty judgment. Without showing it outwardly, he said, “Don’t try to cover it up with empty words! You too are responsible for the prince’s untimely death. How could you have agreed to let him leave the ship and get into the boat at such a time, when a cyclone was raging? Get out of my sight! Do not stand before me!”

Nandini interjected, “My lord! Would it not be best to take him to Thanjavur as well? Is it not better that he himself reports what happened directly to the Emperor? Otherwise, those who are already waiting to accuse us will add this to their list. They will shamelessly claim that we drowned the prince in the sea ourselves!”

“Let them say what they will! I am not one to fear such things. I will have the tongue cut out of anyone who dares to utter such words. Still, it is indeed useful for him to come with us. Parthibendra! Why are you glancing about restlessly? Are you looking for a way to escape?” So saying, he signaled to the soldiers standing a short distance away.
Four men rushed forward.
“Tie him up!” he commanded.

The four soldiers closed in on Parthibendran. Until they drew near, he remained still. Then, in the blink of an eye, he displayed his skill. All four soldiers were sent sprawling in four different directions.

“Sir! If it is your wish to have me bound, do not send others. I am willing to submit myself to the hand of the great Pazhuvetaraiyar, the peerless hero who has received sixty-four wounds in thirty-six battles. I will not allow anyone else to come near me!” he declared.

A faint smile appeared on Pazhuvetaraiyar’s face. “You are indeed a hero born of the valiant Pallava clan, there is no doubt. If you agree to come with us to Thanjavur willingly, there is no need to bind you,” he said.
“That is my wish; I want to see the Emperor in person and tell him exactly what happened. I do not want false blame to fall upon my name,” replied Parthibendran.
“In that case, let us depart at once,” said Pazhuvetaraiyar.
At that moment, from the forest a short distance away from where they stood, the hooting of an owl was heard.
