There are, in total, twenty-one copper plate leaves. Each measures fourteen inches in length and five inches in width, all bound together by a large copper ring.

These copper plates, in recent times, crossed the seas by ship and reached Europe, to Holland… They are kept in the museum of the city called Leiden in that country. Therefore, some historians refer to these copper plates as the "Leiden Charter."

From the time of Vijayalaya Chola, the Chola kings were immersed in devotion to Shiva. Aditya Chola, Parantaka Chola, and Kandaraditya were all deeply attached to Shaivism. They commissioned the construction and renovation of many Shiva temples. However, they did not despise other religions. The subjects living in their kingdom, regardless of their faith, were treated with impartiality, and their religions were protected without bias. Sundara Chola Chakravartin went several steps further than his forefathers. He granted special privileges to Buddhist monasteries. Because of this, all the Buddhists living in the Chola empire at that time were filled with great enthusiasm. In Lanka, Arulmozhi Varman made arrangements to restore the ruined Buddhist viharas, which further increased their fervor.

With all this being the case, what was the reason for the confusion that occurred today at the renowned Choodamani Vihara? Why were the monks running here and there in agitation, unable to remain calm? What was the cause of the commotion and the clamor in the entrance hall of the Choodamani Vihara?—Well, let us follow Sendhan Amudhan and see for ourselves.

We have already said that Sendhan Amudhan and the other two had rowed their boat through the canal and reached the inner part of the Choodamani Vihara. Finding no one there, Sendhan Amudhan wandered about, searching for the way, and finally reached the entrance of the vihara. There stood the Chaitya, the temple of Lord Buddha, where the public came to worship. Many devotees had come that morning, carrying trays filled with lotus flowers, champaka blossoms, and other offerings for worship. But it seemed as if they had forgotten the purpose for which they had come. On the steps leading up to the chaitya, Buddhist monks stood in a row. Sendhan Amudhan saw that a man standing below was speaking to them. He also noticed tears brimming in the eyes of some of the monks. Among the devotees standing below, instead of the usual cries of "Sadhu! Sadhu!" many were lamenting, exclaiming, "Aha!", "Adaada!", "Aiyo!"

After drawing nearer and listening for a while, the matter became clear. The man speaking to the monks was one of the sailors from Parthibendran's ship. The ship had arrived at Nagapattinam the previous night. As soon as the sailors landed, the news spread that the prince had been lost to the sea. When a few people were told, the news spread throughout the city. To ascertain whether this news was true, the chief monk of the Soodamani Viharam summoned one of those boatmen early that morning. The man recounted what he knew: “When the whirlwind struck, the prince leapt into the sea and never returned,” he said in a sorrowful voice.

At that moment, the gathering was filled with the sounds of weeping and wailing. Tears streamed in torrents from the eyes of the chief monk. Without raising his bowed head, he climbed the steps, passed through the vestibule, and entered the viharam. The other monks followed him. No one noticed that Senthan Amudhan, too, had joined them.

The chief monk turned to the others and spoke: “Is this the compassion of Lord Buddha? How many castles I built in my mind! Only recently, I traveled to Thanjavur to meet the Emperor. At that time, I spoke of the wondrous deeds of Arulmozhi Varman in Lanka. The young princess Kundavai Devi listened to it all. Later, she called me aside and said she wished to establish a hospital attached to this viharam, and that she would provide whatever was needed. Was that all? She also asked, ‘Acharya! You must have heard the many rumors circulating in the land. Perhaps the prince may have to stay as a guest in the Soodamani Viharam for some days. Can you keep him safe?’ I replied, ‘Devi! If we are blessed with such an honor, we will guard him as we would our own eyes.’ What use was it! Has the prince drowned in the sea? All the noble hopes of this land have drowned with him! The Chola Empire itself is submerged. How did the Lord of the Ocean dare to commit such a great atrocity? Is there none to question that cruel one?”

All the other monks silently wept. When the chief monk finished speaking, a deep silence settled over the place for a while. Senthan Amudhan realized this was his moment, and he tried to approach the Acharya through the assembly of monks. Immediately, several of them stopped him. “Who is this? How did he come here?” they asked each other.
“Sir, my name is Senthan Amudhan! I am from Thanjai. I have something to tell your leader!” he said.
“Speak, speak!” many urged.
Seeing his hesitation, the Acharya said, “There is no secret here that these men should not know; speak.”
“Sir! I have brought a patient with me!”
“Who is this patient? What illness? Where have you left them?”
“I have left them in the central courtyard of the vihara…”
“How did you come here?”
“I brought the patient by boat, through the canal. He is shivering with a cold fever—if you could please come at once…”
“Heavens! Shivering fever—an infectious disease! Why have you brought such a patient here? And at such a time, too…”
“Acharya! Until now, I believed that Ashoka the Great was a patron of the Buddhist faith. But now, I see it is not so…”
“Why do you say that?”
“I saw an Ashoka pillar near Kanchi. On it, it is written that tending to the sick is the foremost dharma. Yet here you are, driving them away!” said Amudhan.
The Acharya Bhikshu turned to the others and said, “Please wait a moment; I will go and see, and then return to tell you,” and with that, he called, “Come, my boy,” and led Amudhan away.

In the central courtyard of the vihara, near the canal, the Bhikshu was startled to see a young man and a young woman. “What is this you have dared to do? Women are not even allowed within this vihara! There is a separate monastery built for the bhikshunis, is there not?”
As he drew closer and looked intently at the young man to see who he was, it would not suffice to say the Bhikshu was taken aback! For a moment, astonishment and delight rendered him speechless.
To dispel his doubts, Sendhan Amudhan asked, “Is this Prince Arulmozhi Varman?”

The words reached the prince’s ears. “No, Acharya, no. I am not a prince or anything of the sort. This girl and this child are conspiring to drive me mad. I am a boatman. Just a short while ago, I asked this girl, ‘Girl! Will you marry me? Let us both get into the boat and travel to distant lands.’ She began to babble all sorts of nonsense. I—”

(Chapter 10 – The Chudamani Vihara) Born to rule! Yet this girl, a poor fisherwoman by birth, says she will not marry me. If only I am happy, that is enough for her, she says. In the days to come, she claims she will rejoice in hearing of my great victories. What kind of tale is this? Is it I who am deluded, or she?”

Senthan Amudhan whispered something into the ear of the chief monk. Even before that, the monk had realized that the prince was speaking in a delirium brought on by the fever’s intensity. He also remembered that Princess Kundavai had requested him to shelter the prince.

Turning to the other monks, he said, “This young man has been struck by a poisonous fever. If we send him outside, thousands more may be afflicted. In Lanka, countless thousands have died from this fever. Therefore, I will take this youth to my own chamber and tend to him myself. If, in the grip of the fever, he should babble anything, you must pay it no mind!”
Immediately, the chief monk came close to the prince, and with one arm, he gently lifted him up. Senthan Amudhan supported the prince from the other side. Together, they all ascended the stairs.

‘There, in just a few more moments, they will have climbed the entire staircase. They will open the door and enter within. Then the door will be shut. Once it is shut, it is truly shut. After that, I will not be able to see him again.’

Everything happened just as Poonguzhali had expected. As soon as they reached the top of the stairs, the door opened. The chief monk said something to Senthan Amudhan, leaving him outside. Then, through the open door, the others entered.
The door closed with a resounding thud. It was as though the door to Poonguzhali’s own heart had been shut.

“Now, in this lifetime, there is no certainty that I will see the prince again. Will I be blessed with such fortune, at least in my next birth?” With such thoughts swirling in her mind, Poonguzhali stood there, watching as the prince disappeared from her sight.

chapters.title: The Smithy
paragraphs: Vandiyathevan spurred his horse onward. He was making his way toward Pazhayarai, using it as his guiding mark. Since he still remembered, at least vaguely, the path he had taken from Pazhayarai, he did not bother to ask anyone for directions; instead, he simply followed his sense of direction. At first, he traveled a short distance along a forest path. He realized that his horse was suffering greatly because of this. Vallavarayan himself was also quite exhausted. It had been many days since he had been able to rest and sleep soundly, even for a short while. Except for occasionally nodding off and falling asleep in the saddle, he had not had the comfort of lying down and sleeping in peace anywhere. Once he reached Pazhayarai and delivered his message to the princess, his responsibility would be over; then he could sleep peacefully. He could sleep for a long time—indeed, he planned to make up for all the lost days and sleep for days on end.

He imagined the joy he would feel when he stood before Princess Kundavai and said, “I have accomplished the task you entrusted to me.” He thought of how the goddess’s face would blossom and glow upon hearing those words. That thought sent a thrill through his body.

Another thought came to him. Since leaving Kanchipuram, how many lies and half-truths had he spoken? He had done so only out of necessity. Yet, when he thought about it all, his heart and body felt weighed down. After spending some time with Prince Arulmozhi Varman, his very outlook had changed. He had once believed that those involved in royal affairs must be well-versed in the stratagems of Chanakya. He had even harbored the hope that, through such royal intrigues, he might one day reclaim the kingdom his ancestors had lost. But now, all those thoughts had changed. After witnessing the prince’s integrity and steadfastness, he had developed a distaste for lies and deception. He recalled the lie he had told the magician last night, claiming he intended to protect the prince. What if something untoward happened because of that? The thought made his heart tremble. What if someone else had overheard? What if someone went and told Princess Kundavai? Surely, the young princess would not believe it! Still, how great a danger it could be! From now on, I must abandon the habit of inventing and embellishing stories that never happened. I must speak the truth; if hardship comes because of it, I must face it. Let those like that valiant Vaishnavite and those like Ravidasan do the work of spies. Why should I burden myself with such troubles? Let victory come to me by the strength of my sword alone. That is enough; even if I lose my life for it, so be it. It is time to cast aside all these tricks and stratagems.

Immersed in such thoughts, Vandiyathevan did not notice for a while that his horse’s pace had slowed. In fact, as he rode on, lost in contemplation, he had even dozed off a little. When the horse suddenly stumbled and bent down at one spot, he started awake. He realized that the horse was struggling, unable to set one of its forelegs firmly on the ground. He immediately dismounted, patted the horse reassuringly, and lifted the injured foreleg to examine it. He found that a small, sharp stone had become lodged in the underside of the hoof. With deft fingers, he removed and flung it away. Fortunately, there was no serious wound. Once again, he patted and encouraged the horse, then mounted its back with renewed vigor.

He recalled the conversation he had overheard among the Arabs on the ship: “The Tamils are cruel people; they lack intelligence! They make their horses run barefoot, without fitting iron shoes to their hooves. How long can such horses survive?”

Thinking of this, Vandiyathevan spurred his horse onward. When warriors go to battle, they wear armor on their chests. Fitting iron shoes to a horse’s hooves is indeed a remarkable thing. Yet, he had heard that in some foreign lands, such things were done. He resolved that, at the very first smithy he encountered, he must inquire about this. If possible, he would have iron shoes fitted to his horse’s hooves. Otherwise, it would be difficult for this horse to reach Pazhaiyarai. If it collapsed on the way, he would have to procure another horse. But how? He would have to steal one from someone! Fie! The very thought made Vandiyathevan blush with shame.

Leaving the forest path, Vandiyathevan guided his horse in what he guessed was the right direction, and soon reached the royal highway. Let come what may; from now on, he must travel along the main road. No one who knew him would be in this area. The retinue of the Pazhuvettaraiyars would be coming behind him. The sorcerer too would be following. Therefore, there was no danger. Moreover, if he stayed on the royal road, he was sure to find a smithy somewhere. There, he could see if iron shoes could be fitted to his horse’s hooves.

Vandiyathevan’s expectations were not in vain. After traveling a short distance, a village appeared before him. It seemed as though some sort of commotion had arisen in the village. On one side, the streets and houses were adorned with festoons and decorations. Perhaps, having heard that Periya Pazhuvettarayar was to pass this way, the villagers had thus embellished their town. It was certain that, before Pazhuvettarayar and his retinue arrived, he himself would be far away.

On the other side, the villagers—women, men, elders, boys, and girls—stood here and there in groups, conversing anxiously among themselves. Vandiyathevan could not guess what the matter might be. Some among them, noticing the horseman approaching, came near as if intending to stop him. But Vandiyathevan, unwilling to become entangled in needless quarrels, spurred his horse and rode on without giving them a chance.
Once he had passed through the village, he saw a blacksmith’s forge by the roadside. He felt no desire to ride further past it. Stopping his horse, he entered the forge.

Inside, he saw a blacksmith at work. A young boy was blowing the bellows. At the very moment Vandiyathevan entered, he thought he glimpsed another man slipping away through the back. But he paid no attention to this. His eyes and mind were wholly captivated by the sword in the blacksmith’s hand. It was an extraordinary sword. The blacksmith seemed to be engraving it with intricate designs. One part of the blade gleamed with the brilliance of silver, while another part, freshly drawn from the fire, shone with a golden, fiery glow.
“Now, this is what a sword should be!” Vandiyathevan thought to himself in wonder.

chapters.title: “Throw it into the Fire!”
paragraphs: The blacksmith was absorbed in his work for a while. Only after Vandiyathevan had knocked two or three times did he look up.

“Who are you, son? What do you want? Do you need a sword, a spear, or something of the sort? These days, there’s hardly any need for swords and spears, is there? Where do you intend to go with a sword?” asked the blacksmith.
“What is this, sir, that you say? You are working on a sword with your own hands, and yet you claim there is no need for swords?” said Vandiyathevan.

“This is just some rare job that’s come my way; someone brought in this old sword to be reforged. A few years ago, when the wars in Pandya country and the northern regions were raging, this workshop would be piled high with swords and spears, like mountains. Even when the Lanka war first began, there was brisk demand for weapons. Now, no one asks for swords or spears. People only come to sell their old swords and spears to me. Perhaps you too have come for that?”

“No, no! For a while yet, I still need my sword. Once I finish the task I have undertaken, then I’ll take up a cymbal in my hand, sing the Thevaram hymns, and set out on a pilgrimage to Shiva’s holy shrines. If you wish, I’ll bring my weapons to you then and hand them over.”
“Then, why have you come looking for me now?”
“I left my horse up on the mound. I have a long way yet to travel. I hear that horseshoes of iron are fitted to horses’ hooves to protect them. Can you do that?”
“Yes, that’s the custom in Arabia. Here too, some people have started fitting iron shoes to horses’ hooves. I have a little experience with that work myself.”
“Will you shoe my horse?”

“That will take quite some time. I must finish the work at hand before I can take up your task.” Vandiyathevan pondered; he too was weary. His horse was exhausted as well. He decided to wait a while, and then proceed, fitting armor to the horse’s hooves as they went.
“I’ll wait until you finish your work, but after that, you’ll do mine at once, won’t you?”
“What’s the trouble in that? Of course, I will!”
For a short while, Vandiyathevan watched the sword that the blacksmith was heating and hammering.
“This sword has an unusual workmanship, doesn’t it? It looks like a royal blade. Whose sword is this?” he asked.
“My lord! A little distance from here flows a river called the Arichandra.”
“I’ve heard of it too. But what of it?”
“It is my habit to go to the Arichandra river and bathe my head in its waters often.”
“A very good practice. The journey itself is a merit.”
“Therefore, as much as possible, I have resolved always to speak the truth, never to utter a lie.”
“What objection is there to that? Who asked you to lie? I didn’t, did I?”
“If you hadn’t asked me anything about this sword, I could have kept my vow and not lied!”
“Oh! Is that how it is?” thought Vandiyathevan to himself. “Well, I haven’t asked anything. You need not break your vow. Just finish your work quickly and then take up mine and do it for me!”
The blacksmith silently focused on his task.

Vandiyathevan gazed at the sword for a while. Near its hilt, at the base, he noticed a fish engraved. He was astonished. Why was there a fish? Did it have any significance? Or was it merely ornamental?

The blacksmith once again placed the fish-shaped object into the fire, heating it until it glowed, and then struck it with his hammer. It seemed his intention was to obliterate the fish shape so that it could no longer be recognized. Vandiyathevan wondered what purpose this act could serve.

As he pondered, his eyes began to grow heavy. For many days, the goddess of sleep, Nithradevi, whom he had managed to keep at bay, now cast her enchanting net over him with renewed strength. Vandiyathevan could not escape her grasp. After sitting for a while, he slumped over and fell asleep. Soon, he lay down beside the blacksmith’s furnace and drifted into a deep slumber.
In his sleep, Vallavaraiyan was tormented by dreadful dreams. One dream was about the dagger. Someone came and asked the blacksmith to return the dagger. The blacksmith handed it over.
“What payment do you want?” the man asked.
“I want no payment. Let it be my offering to the Young Queen of Pazhuvoor,” replied the blacksmith.
“Be careful! No one must know of this matter. Above all, never utter the name of the Young Queen of Pazhuvoor! Do you know what we will do if you do?”
“Why would I, sir, ever mention the name of the Queen of Pazhuvoor? I will not tell a soul.”
“Look, there’s a young man lying here! You’re speaking so loudly!”
“He is in a deep sleep. Even thunder would not wake him.”
“If we ever suspect that he has found out, throw him into the fire of this forge and be done with him!”
At the end of this conversation, Vandiyathevan dreamed that the blacksmith and the owner of the dagger dragged him and were about to throw him into the furnace. Then the dream changed.
Vandiyathevan was now being led to hell by the messengers of Yama. Yama, the Lord of Death, inquired about Vandiyathevan’s deeds on earth.
“He is an expert in lying. There is no measure to the number of lies he has told,” said Chitragupta, consulting the scroll in his hand.
“No, no! I told those lies only in service of the royal family. I lied only to accomplish the tasks I undertook.”
“A lie is a lie, no matter the reason. Cast him into the great fiery pit of hell!” commanded Yama. Instantly, from the depths of hell, a hundred thousand voices wailed in terror.

The messengers of Yama came and took him away. They prepared to cast him into a great blazing fire that burned with a terrifying, leaping flame. When he looked at those messengers of Yama, their faces resembled those of the Pazhuvettarayar brothers. As he stood there, startled by this, Princess Kundavai arrived at the scene.
“To fulfill my command, he spoke a lie. Therefore, instead of him, cast me into the fire!” she declared.

At that moment, Nandini Devi too somehow appeared there. “Throw both of them into the fire together!” said that virtuous lady. The messengers of Yama seized both of them and were about to hurl them into the flames. “No, please, don’t!” cried Vandiyathevan, struggling and shouting; he opened his eyes, sat up, and realized he had been dreaming. The thought that it was only a dream brought him some comfort. Yet, because it had all seemed so real, his body continued to tremble.
“Shame! From now on, whatever the reason, I must never tell a lie,” he resolved to himself.
“Did I sleep for a long time?” he asked, turning to the blacksmith.

“Not that long, only two watches have passed. My lord! Are you descended from the lineage of Kumbhakarna? To sleep like this in broad daylight! How will you manage to sleep at night?” the blacksmith replied.
“Heavens! Have I really slept for two watches? Is the armor for the horse’s hoof finished?”
“It is yet to be done. But what use is it for a sleepyhead like you? You’ll end up losing the horse itself! Perhaps you’ll even lose yourself!”
Vandiyathevan was jolted wide awake. A doubt arose in his mind. He got up and ran to the entrance and looked outside. The horse was nowhere to be seen where he had tied it!
“Alas! Where is the horse?” he cried out, his hand instinctively reaching for the hilt of his sword.
“Do not fear! Your horse is safe. Go and look in the backyard!”

Vandiyathevan went to the backyard and saw his horse standing in a thatched shed, enclosed on three sides. The blacksmith’s apprentice was feeding it grass at the entrance. At the sight of Vandiyathevan, the horse shivered with delight and neighed.
“Sir! Please come here and take a look at your horse. I need to measure its hooves!” said the boy.
Vandiyathevan went over to his horse, gently stroking it as he stood by its side. The boy took the measure of the horse’s hoof.
“Who brought it here and tied it up?” Vandiyathevan asked.
“I did,” replied the boy.
“For what reason?”
“Father told me to tie it.”
“And why did he ask you to do that?”
“Just a short while ago, Periya Pazhuvettarayar and his retinue passed through this village. If they had seen your horse at the entrance, they would surely have taken it away.”

A memory flashed in Vandiyathevan’s mind—a memory of Thiru Narayanapuram. He felt ashamed recalling the mistake he had made. In his heart, he felt gratitude towards the blacksmith and his son. Once the boy had finished measuring the horse’s hoof, the two of them went into the smithy.
The blacksmith picked up a piece of iron and began to shape it, bending it to match the curve of the hoof.
“You have saved my horse! For that, I am deeply grateful,” said Vallavarayan.
“Is it not my duty to protect the belongings of those who come seeking my help?” replied the blacksmith. “That is my responsibility.”
“How long has it been since Pazhuvettarayar’s retinue passed this way?”
“It’s been more than two nazhigais. With all that commotion, you were still sleeping soundly—when I think of that, I am amazed.”
“I did fall asleep. But you have wasted so much time because of me! At least after they left, you could have started the work right away?”
“How could I begin? After hearing the news they brought, who would have the heart to work? I am forcing myself to do this for your sake. Where are you coming from, young man?”
Wondering what news they might have brought, Vandiyathevan said, “I have come from Lanka.”
The blacksmith scrutinized his face up and down. Then, lowering his voice, he asked, “When you were in Lanka, did you see Prince Arulmozhi Varman?”
Vandiyathevan, who had only moments ago resolved to speak the truth, replied, “I saw him.”
“When did you last see him?”
“I saw him this morning.”
The blacksmith looked at Vandiyathevan with irritation.
“Are you playing games, boy?”
“No, sir! I am telling the truth.”
“It seems you might even tell me where the prince is right now.”
“Oh! If you ask, I’ll tell you!”
“Let’s see then—where is the prince?”
“He is at Nagapattinam, in the Choodamani Vihara!”
“Good heavens! I have seen many liars in my time. But never have I seen anyone who could spin such tales as you do.”
Vandiyathevan laughed inwardly. Everyone is ever ready to believe a well-crafted lie. But when told the truth, they refuse to accept it. Such must be the peculiarity of my fate!
“Boy! When did you leave Lanka?”
“Four days ago!”
“That’s why you don’t know the news.”
“What news, sir?”
“The news that the Prince of Ponni has been taken by the sea!”
Vandiyathevan feigned shock and distress with great effort.
“Oh no, is that so! Who said this?”

“Since yesterday, this has been the talk everywhere around here. Today, when the Pazhuvettaraiyar passed this way, the village elders questioned him. Pazhuvettaraiyar confirmed that the news was true. Yet, thunder has not struck the head of that wretched sinner!”
“Why do you blame that old man?”

“It is because of him that all this has happened. The villagers say he plotted something and pushed the prince into the sea to drown. Because of this, all the honors and arrangements that had been made for him have been stopped.”
“Do the people of this village love the prince so much?”

“Do you even need to ask? The whole village is now in tears and mourning. And not just this village—soon, the entire land of Chola will be wailing and cursing the Pazhuvettaraiyars. The Emperor is already ill. Who knows what suffering he will endure when he hears this news? Who knows what other calamities may yet occur? For the past few days, a comet has been seen in the sky. Shouldn’t something happen to fulfill its omen?”

Vandiyathevan wondered what further disasters might take place. It was fortunate that the blacksmith had not believed what he had said. Even if he did not lie anymore, there was no need for him to reveal the truth about the prince. Surely, the young princess had asked him to remain in the Choodamani Vihara for some important reason! After meeting and speaking with the princess, he must act according to her counsel.
“Brother! What are you thinking about?” asked the blacksmith.
“I too was caught in the whirlwinds of the open sea. I was just thinking of how, by the grace of God, I escaped and survived, and I was offering thanks to the divine.”
“Is there really such a thing as divine grace?”
“Elder, why do you say that?”
“If there were such a thing as divine grace, would the Pazhuvettaraiyars’ atrocities still continue? Would Ponniyin Selvan have drowned in the sea?”
“Elder! The Pazhuvettaraiyars are in power. Can we speak of them like this? What if someone overhears? Please be a little careful.”
“You are the one who must be more careful than I. At least when I speak, I am awake. But you— you babble in your sleep!”
“Oh dear! What did I babble?”

“You called the Pazhuvettaraiyars messengers of Yama. You called the young queen of Pazhuvur a female ghost. What you said may well be true. But what would become of you if anyone other than me had overheard? It was just when you were raving like that that the Pazhuvettaraiyars’ retinue passed along this very road. I was terribly frightened.”
“What did you do?”
“I went to the entrance, stood guard, and bolted the door to this kitchen. Before that, I took your horse and tied it up in the backyard.”
“Did I babble anything else in my sleep?”
“There was no shortage of babbling.”
“Oh no! What else did I say?”

“You urged the prince to come to Pazhayarai. He replied that he would be imprisoned by the orders of the Pazhuvettaraiyars if he did. You said all sorts of other things too. Brother! You even spoke indiscreetly about the young princess of Pazhayarai. Be careful, my boy! Be careful!”

Vandiyathevan hung his head in embarrassment. He was terrified that he might have spoken something improper about the young princess. If he were to sleep again, it must be in a locked room, alone. Or else, he must sleep in a forest where no man passes, or in a desert, or in a mountain cave.
“Brother! How did you get caught in the whirlpool? How did you escape?”
“The ship I boarded was struck by lightning and sank in the sea. I clung to a broken raft and floated for a long time. Later, with the help of a boatwoman, I managed to escape and reach the shore.”
“Perhaps the prince too might have escaped in the same way, might he not?”
“If it is the will of God, he might have survived.”
“Where did you stay last night?”
“On the shore at Kodikkarai. The Pazhuvettaraiyars’ retinue was gathered there in great numbers. So I lay down and slept for a while in the Kuzhagar temple. I set out before dawn.”
“That is why, it seems, you do not know the news about the prince.”
“My thanks for informing me, sir! I must reach Pazhaiyarai as soon as possible, and I must go without falling into the hands of the retinue of the Pazhuvettarayar. Which route would be best?”
“The Pazhuvettarayar is traveling along the royal road to Thanjavur. If you go along the banks of the Mullai river, you can reach Pazhaiyarai.”
“It would be good if you could shoe my horse a little quickly.”
“Here you go!” said the blacksmith. He began to hammer the curved, heated iron with his hammer.
“This is for Periya Pazhuvettarayar! This is for Chinna Pazhuvettarayar! This blow is for Sambuvarayar! And this, for Mazhavarayar!” he said, striking with each name.
From this, Vandiyathevan understood, in some measure, how much anger the people of the land bore towards those petty kings.
The shoeing of the horse was finished. Vandiyathevan tried to pay the blacksmith for his work. The blacksmith refused to accept it.
“I did it because you are a good lad. Not for money,” he said.
Vandiyathevan thanked the blacksmith once more, took his leave, and set out.
As he was about to depart, the blacksmith asked, “Thambi! Why are you going to Pazhaiyarai?”
“Sir! If you do not ask me about that, I will not be forced to tell a lie,” replied Vallavarayan.
The blacksmith laughed and said, “Ah! You are quickly becoming a clever fellow! Be this careful even in your sleep!” With those words, he bade him farewell and sent him on his way.

By the time Vandiyathevan resumed his journey, the sun had already set. In a short while, dusk faded and darkness gathered all around. By then, Vallavarayan had reached the banks of the Mullai river. From there, he had only to follow the riverbank. There was not even any need to ask the way.

It was the hour of early darkness. Yet, in the sky, a billion stars shone like radiant flames. Along the banks of the Mullai River, there were not many trees—only small, scattered thickets. Because of this, the starlight provided enough illumination to find one’s way.
As if competing with the glittering stars above, thousands upon thousands of fireflies circled and played around the riverbank shrubs.

Vandiyathevan’s heart brimmed with excitement. There were many reasons for this. While the entire land was sunk in anxiety over the prince, he alone knew the news that the prince was safe. He had come to understand, at least in part, how dearly the people of Chola Nadu loved their prince. He felt a thrill recalling how he had once again managed to outwit the sorcerer Ravidasan. But above all, the thought that he would soon see Princess Kundavai filled him with boundless elation.

Was he going merely to see her? No—he was going to accomplish the task entrusted to him by the young princess, and then see her! Thinking of all the obstacles that had arisen in that mission, and how he had faced and overcome each one, he was filled with pride. By tomorrow evening, at this very hour, there could be no doubt that he would have met the princess. Ah! Even the thought of that meeting sent a shiver through him.

The sky aglow with starlight, the earth alive with darting fireflies, the murmuring flood of the Mullai River, and the gentle, cool breeze—all these filled Vandiyathevan with rapture. At that moment, both sky and earth seemed to him to be suffused with pure bliss. An old love song came to his mind. This was the perfect place to sing it aloud with abandon. There was not a soul in sight; even the birds had retreated to their nests. What was there to stop him from singing? Here is the song he sang. There is no need to say whom he held in his heart as he sang, is there?
“All the lights of the sky…”

“Oh, dear! When I see you, My body shivers, oh! There I stand, lost in a daze! Is it honey, your voice? Or is it the breeze, your words? Your eyes, like blooming lotuses—when I see them, Do they intoxicate me with their fragrance?”
Whether Vandiyathevan finished singing thus or not, in the distance, as if to compete with him, jackals began to howl.
At that very moment, the sound of human laughter rang out, clear and bright.
Vandiyathevan, startled, looked all around. His hand instinctively went to his sword.
From the deep shadow of a punnai tree, a figure emerged.
“Brother, your song is splendid! But the jackals’ chorus is even more splendid!” said Devaralan, and burst into laughter again.

chapters.title: The Poisoned Arrow
paragraphs: At that place, at that moment, the sight of Devaralan made Vandiyathevan’s heart tremble slightly. Memories of Devaralan’s frenzied antics in the Kadambur palace, and the words he had uttered then, came rushing back. He also recalled the messages spoken by Ravidasan and Devaralan during that turbulent night when the storm raged in the midst of the sea. How much of it was truth, and how much mere imagination? It was hard to discern. Yet, there was no doubt that these men were involved in some mysterious and dreadful conspiracy.

To find himself, at such a time, in this desolate place, caught in the company of one of them—was it not dangerous? For a moment, Vandiyathevan wondered if he should spur his horse and escape from there at once. With that thought, he looked all around. In the distance, a glow of fire was visible. It must be a cremation ground.

‘Some mortal body is being consumed by flames. When there was life in that body, how many desires and attachments must have tossed it about? How many pleasures and pains must it have experienced? In half an hour, all that will remain is a handful of ash! That is the fate that awaits every soul born into this world—be it the king of kings or the poorest beggar, all must one day become fuel for the fire and be reduced to a handful of ash!’

But the chill that gripped him vanished as suddenly as it had come. Why should he flee in fear of this master of disguises and deception? Surely, this man had come here to say something. Why not listen to what he had to say? Perhaps, when he had entered the blacksmith’s forge, it was this man who had slipped away to the back and hidden himself! That wondrous sword, too, might belong to him. Wasn’t there a fish engraved near the hilt? If he engaged this man in conversation, perhaps some new information might be revealed.
So Vallavarayan guided his horse at a slow pace. The horse, still fresh from its recent acquisition, seemed to struggle a little with the walk. He did not feel like urging it to gallop.
“How is it, sir, that you have suddenly sprung up here out of nowhere?” asked Vallavarayan.

“Shouldn’t I be the one asking that question? We left you tied to a raft in the middle of the sea. How did you manage to escape?” replied Devaralan. “You thought you alone knew the secrets of incantations? I know a little myself!”
“I am glad that you have come to believe in the power of mantras. By the strength of my own magic, I knew you would be coming here alone. That is why I came ahead and waited for you.”
“Why did you wait for me? What business do you have with me?”
“Think for yourself! Or, discover it with your magical powers!”

“You have already told me your secrets in the middle of the sea. I do not know how much of it was truth and how much was mere imagination. Still, I have decided to forget those secrets. I will not tell anyone…”
“I am not worried about that either. The moment you even think of revealing those secrets to anyone, your tongue will be cut off. You will become mute!”

Vandiyathevan shuddered. Memories of the mute women he had encountered in Thanjai and Lanka came rushing back. He walked silently for a short distance. Why does this wretch keep following me? How can I escape from him? If only there were a muddy pit here as there was in Kodikkarai, how useful that would be! Or should I push him into the river and make my escape? No, that would be pointless. There isn’t enough water in the river. If there is no other way, there is always the sword at my side. I may have to use it.
“Thambi, I know what you are thinking. But it will not succeed. Do not waste your efforts in vain!”
Vandiyathevan wished to change the subject. He needed a little more time to find a way to escape. Until then, he must keep the conversation going.
“Where is your companion, Ravidasan?”
Devaralan let out a ghostly laugh. “Shouldn’t you be the one to know that? Where is Ravidasan?” he asked.
Vandiyathevan was startled. He should not have brought up Ravidasan; it was a mistake. Has this man seen Ravidasan and is now testing me? Or—
“Why are you sitting there quietly, my friend? Won’t you tell me where Ravidasan is? Let it be, then! Where is that boatwoman, Poonguzhali? At least tell me that!”
Vandiyathevan started as if he had stepped on a snake. He hesitated even to speak further.

“You won’t say anything about her either, will you? Let it be, then. Perhaps you have a good reason to want to protect her. Brother! Just now you sang a love song, didn’t you? Were you thinking of her when you sang it?”
“No, I swear I wasn’t!” Vallavarayan replied, flustered.
“Why are you so agitated? Why such anger?”
“All right, all right! There’s no time now to talk about all that. Why are you holding on to my horse’s bridle? Let go! I must go, I have urgent business.”
“You haven’t even asked why I came here.”
“How can I, unless you tell me?”
“There is a strange power on the banks of this Mullai river. Whatever a person desires here, it will be granted to them at once.”
“I don’t desire anything.”
“That’s a lie! The one you were thinking of when you sang your love song—she wishes to see you! If you wish, you may meet her.”
“When?”
“Tonight itself.”
“What is this tale?”

“It’s no tale, brother! Look there!” said Devaralan, pointing ahead. A little distance away on the path they had come, something appeared dimly in the dusk. Vandiyathevan peered intently. It was a palanquin—a closed palanquin, he realized.

Aha! That palanquin! Where have I seen it before? Why, isn’t that the palanquin of the young mistress of Pazhuvoor? Could it be that Nandini herself is inside? He could not suppress his curiosity to find out.
He rode his horse up to the palanquin and halted beside it. The palanquin was painted with palm motifs, and its curtains were drawn. The curtain seemed to be moving slightly.
Immediately, Vandiyathevan leapt down from his horse.

At that very instant, a strange sound emerged from Devaralan’s throat. From the thickets nearby, seven or eight men sprang forth with a rush, pouncing upon Vandiyathevan. They seized him so firmly that he could not even struggle. They bound his hands and feet with cloth. One of them tied a cloth over his eyes, while another forcefully took away his sword. Then, they lifted Vandiyathevan and threw him into the palanquin. Some of them at once hoisted the palanquin and hurried away. The rest went ahead and behind. Devaralan led the way. One man took charge of the horse and walked alongside.

All this happened in a flash. To say it took “the blink of an eye” would not be an exaggeration. Vandiyathevan was stunned by the sudden attack from so many at once. He had not expected such an assault. Until he was thrown into the palanquin and it began to move, he could not think at all, nor could he comprehend what was happening.

But once the palanquin started moving, his mind gradually cleared. The cloth over his eyes slipped off easily. With his bound hands, he pushed aside the curtain of the palanquin and looked out. He realized that the palanquin was being carried away from the riverbank, heading somewhere across.

It would not be so difficult to untie the bonds on his hands and feet and regain his freedom. Jumping out of the palanquin would also be easy. The horse was following behind. It would not be impossible for him to throw off those seven or eight men, leap onto the horse, and escape. He considered whether he should attempt it. But something held him back.

Within the palanquin, an extraordinary fragrance lingered. At first, it filled him with excitement. He could not easily tear himself away from its allure. Where was this palanquin taking him? There were reasons to suspect it would bring him to Nandini. A faint desire to see her stirred at the depths of his heart. Gradually, that desire grew into a burning curiosity. Many objections arose within him, but his longing overcame them all and took on a life of its own.

What could she possibly do to me? Why has she summoned me? Let me see for myself. If there is anything to be learned, let me learn it. Would he not be able to counter intrigue with intrigue? Would he ever again have the chance to see her? That was uncertain. The necessity of going to Thanjavur— That will not happen anymore. Going there is dangerous. It would be far easier to meet her somewhere along the way. Could he not see her just one more time…?
Yes, yes! There was yet another urgent reason to see Nandini. That mute queen he had seen in Lanka! Was it true that she resembled Nandini? Should he not find out for certain?

As Vandiyathevan pondered thus, his head began to spin. He felt as though sleep was overtaking him. No, no! This was not sleep! Had he not already slept enough during the day? This was some kind of stupor. The fragrance that filled this palanquin was causing this dizziness. Alas! What a terrible danger this was! He must leap out of the palanquin at once.

Vandiyathevan tried to loosen the strap binding his hands; he could not. His arms would not move at all. He tried to sit up; that too was impossible. He tried to kick his legs; his legs refused to obey. That was all! His eyelids closed; his consciousness faded swiftly, and the stupor took complete hold of him.

When Vandiyathevan regained his senses and opened his eyes, old memories came rushing back—he tried to leap out of the palanquin. But wonder of wonders! He was no longer in the palanquin! He was in a spacious chamber. The room was aglow with the light of many lamps. Here too, some fragrance hung in the air! But it was not the same as before; it seemed like the scent of burning incense; what he had experienced earlier was a fragrance that dulled the mind, but this one seemed to sharpen it. He sat up on the couch where he had been lying! He looked all around. A door stood open. Vandiyathevan gazed eagerly.

Through the open doorway, Nandini entered. He watched her without blinking. There were many reasons for his astonishment and wonder. Her indescribable beauty was one reason. The unexpectedness of meeting her in this manner was another. And then, the thought of how much this young woman resembled the old woman he had seen in Lanka was yet another. Did their forms truly resemble each other? Or was it that the old woman, adorned in regal garments and jewels, now appeared thus transformed?
In a sweet, tinkling voice, Nandini said, “Sir! You are a very good man!”
“Greetings!” replied Vandiyathevan.
“Is it the way of good men to leave without saying a word? You left from the Thanjavur palace without so much as a farewell, did you not?”
Vandiyathevan laughed.
“I helped you enter the fortress of Thanjai. I took the palmyra signet ring from my own finger and gave it to you. Shouldn’t you have at least returned it to me before you left?”
Vandiyathevan stood in embarrassed silence.

“Well? Even now, you can return it, can’t you? Its purpose must be over by now, isn’t it? You have no intention of coming to the Thanjai fort again, do you?” said Nandini, extending her beautiful, flower-like hand.
“Devi! That signet ring has been seized by the Lankan commander, Bhoothi Vikrama Kesari. Therefore, I am unable to return it. You must forgive me,” said Vandiyathevan.
“So, you gave the ring I entrusted to you into the hands of my lifelong enemy? Truly, you are a man of great gratitude.”
“I did not give it willingly. They took it from me by force.”
“A heroic scion of the Vanathi Rayar clan, submitting to force and letting such a thing happen? I find it hard to believe!”
“Dear lady! Even my presence here at this moment is due to force, is it not? Your people...”

“Tell me the truth, sir! Think carefully and answer! Did you come here only because of force? Was there no desire in your heart? After being placed in the palanquin, did you not have a chance to jump down and escape?” The questions Nandini asked pierced Vandiyathevan’s heart like sharp arrows.
“Yes? I came because I wished to,” he replied.
“For what reason did you come?”
“For what reason did you have me brought here?”
“To ask you to return my signet ring.”
“Is that all?”
“There is another reason. That night, did you not enter the treasury chamber under my husband’s protection?”
Vandiyathevan was startled.
“Did you think I did not know? How delightful! If I had not known, would you have been able to escape that night?”
“Devi…”

“Yes! I know, and Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar knows as well. Pazhuvettaraiyar ordered the guard of the underground passage to kill you right there. As soon as he left, I changed that order. That is why you survived. Your handsome friend fell into danger because of you. Otherwise, your bones would now be lying beside the heaps of pearls in that treasure vault!”

Vandiyathevan was plunged into a sea of astonishment. He could not believe that everything she said was true. But if it were not true, how did she know he had been hiding there that night? At least for the sake of courtesy, he felt it necessary to express his gratitude, and so he began, “Ammani…!”
“Enough! Why try to utter what is not in your heart? Do not attempt to thank me!”
“No, Devi…”

“Do you know why I told you about saving your life that night? Not because I seek your gratitude. I told you only to warn you not to try using that underground passage again. It is now heavily guarded. Do you understand?”
“I have no intention of going that way again.”

“Why would you? You are not one to remember those who have helped you, are you? Because of you, your friend fell into danger. I had him brought to my palace, had him treated and cured, and then sent him away. Is that not enough for you? Or, like betrayal of trust, were you born with the habit of betraying friendship as well?”
Each of Nandini’s words pierced Vandiyathevan’s heart like a poisoned arrow. He trembled and remained silent.
“You sent the physician’s son, who came with you to Kodikkarai, in your place to be captured; did you ever inquire what became of him?”
“I intended to ask you.”
“I will tell you; but what happened to the prince Arulmozhi Varman, who departed from Lanka with you? If you tell me that, I will speak of the physician’s son.”
A shudder ran through Vandiyathevan’s body. He wondered if this woman had put him through all this torment just to learn about the prince. He resolved not to be deceived.
“Queen! Do not ask me about that alone,” he said.
“Yes! That alone must not be asked! Even if I ask, I know no answer will come from you. How is your beloved? May I at least hear about her?”
Sparks flashed in Vandiyathevan’s eyes. “Whom are you speaking of? Beware!” he said.

“Ah! I am ever cautious. Do not imagine I speak of the queen of Pazhayarai. She would not so much as glance at you. She would value you no more than the dust at her feet. I ask about the boat-girl who took you to Lanka and brought you back—Poonguzhali. Is she not your beloved?”
“No, not at all! She herself showed me her lovers. In the dead of night, in the marshes of Kodikkarai, she showed me the ghostly spirits that rise. She said they were her lovers.”

“She is fortunate! For her lovers have taken forms of light. They appear before her, shining. But my lovers are shapes of darkness! Their forms cannot be known. Have you ever lain down at midnight in a ruined, darkened hall? Have you seen bats and owls beating their wings, flitting about as formless shadows in those dark halls? Such shapes ceaselessly fly within the hall of my heart. They beat their wings. They strike my breast. They brush my cheeks with their feathers as they pass! Where do these shapes of darkness come from? Where do they go? Why do they circle round and round me? Alas! Do you know?”
Having spoken thus, Nandini looked around with wild, frenzied eyes.
Even Vandiyathevan’s diamond-hard heart was shaken. On one side, pity; on the other, an inexplicable fear took root in his mind.
“Devi! Please, do not! Calm yourself a little!” he said.
“And who are you to ask me to calm myself?” Nandini retorted.
“I am but a poor youth descended from the Vanar clan. And who are you, Devi?”
“You ask who I am? That, even I do not know. I am still striving to discover it. Who am I? Am I a mere woman of this earth? Or—are you wondering if I am a ghost, a spirit, a demon?”
“No, no! Might you not be a divine maiden, fallen from the celestial realms? Perhaps by some curse of the gods…”

“Yes! Some divine curse does indeed rest upon me. Only, I do not know what it is. I know not who I am, nor for what purpose I was born. Until now, the gods have given me but a single sign. Look here!” So saying, Nandini picked up the sword that lay beside her and held it out. The newly polished, keen-edged blade flashed dazzlingly in the lamplight, blinding the eyes.

Vandiyathevan looked at the sword. The moment he saw it, he recognized it as the very sword he had seen in the blacksmith’s workshop. Until now, the venomous darts of Nandini’s words had left him trembling. But now, at the sight of this weapon forged of iron, his heart grew steady. For swords, spears, and such arms were familiar to him—companions since his birth. He had no fear of them. Even if Nandini were to wield that sword against him, he would not be afraid!

“Devi! I see it! I see the sword. A blade wrought with exquisite skill! A sword fit for royalty. A weapon worthy of the hands of the bravest of warriors. How did such a blade come into your delicate, beautiful hand? What is the sign the gods have given you through it?” he asked.

chapters.title: The Flying Horse
paragraphs: Nandini took up that radiant sword and, with longing, pressed it to her bosom. Then, bringing it close to her face, she kissed it with her crimson lips. For a moment, it was as if a lotus blossom of fire was kissing another lotus. In the next instant, it seemed as though a blood-red armored cloud was trying to block the full moon. Nandini’s face now resembled the fierce and beautiful visage of Kali, the goddess to whom the Kapalikas offer blood sacrifices. But when she set the sword down beside her as before, her face regained its former enchanting allure.

“Yes, this sword is the omen the gods have given me. But I do not yet know the meaning of that omen. I frequently send this sword to the blacksmith’s forge, to have it cleansed, tempered, and sharpened. I guard it as a tigress would protect her cub. Before the cub comes of age, it must not fall prey to the wild buffaloes with their long horns, must it? Just as the Arabs cherish their horses with tender love, so do I safeguard this sword. As Vanamadevi serves the ailing Emperor Sundara Chola, so do I serve this sword. The gods have not yet revealed to me what I am to do with it. Is it their command that these hands, accustomed to weaving garlands, must one day drive this sword into the venomous heart of some wretch? Or is it the divine will that I must turn this blade upon my own breast, letting my blood gush forth and smear these limbs adorned with silks and jewels, and thus meet my end? I do not yet know. The deity who gave me this sword will, when the time comes, reveal that too. Since I do not know when that moment will arrive, I remain ever prepared, day and night, at any hour.

Yes, it is well known throughout the land that the young queen of Pazhuvur, famed for her beauty, delights in fine garments and ornaments. All sixty nazhigais of day and night, I adorn myself, beautifying this body. Alas! Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar, for his sake and for the sake of his honor, rejoices in the thought that I am always resplendent, ever adorned! He does not know of the fire that burns unceasingly in my heart!” Vallavarayan, who had been listening to all this as if in a trance, regained his self-possession and asked, “Lady! Where is Periya Pazhuvetarayar?”
“Why? Are you afraid to meet that old man?” asked Nandini.
“No, Lady! I am not afraid to see you—why should I fear Pazhuvetarayar?” replied Vandiyathevan.

“Ah! That is the reason I like you. For some reason, everyone seems to be afraid of me. Even the mighty Periya Pazhuvetarayar, a warrior among warriors, who has fought in countless battles and bears sixty-four scars upon his body, trembles when he sees me. Chinna Pazhuvetarayar—Kalanthaka Kandar, who could strike terror even into Death itself—shudders when he comes near me. Even Madurantaka Devar, who aspires to rule this Chola kingdom as a sole emperor, approaches me with fear and reverence. Sundara Chola Chakravarthi himself, who stands at the threshold of Yama’s world, trembles if I come near him. Every time he sees me, he falls into a swoon. And today, Parthibendra Pallavan came, did he not? I have heard much of his fearless heart and his valor. I know well that he is the dearest friend of Aditya Karikalan. Yet, within half an hour of coming near me, see how subdued and docile he became! He forgot even his urgent duty to go to Aditya Karikalan, and follows me instead. He is ready to fulfill, with his head, any task I set with my foot. Yet, when he comes close to me, he trembles. When I see that, I am reminded of something from my childhood. When I was a little girl, I was always fascinated by fire. I would go near it, longing to touch the flame. I would stretch out my finger, eager to touch it, but courage would fail me. I would snatch my finger back in an instant. I have done this so many times. When I see Parthibendran approach me and then shrink away in fear, that old memory comes to me. And it is not just the Pallavan. The very prince for whom you carry a letter from Kanchipuram—Aditya Karikalan—is the same. Since our childhood, he has had an immeasurable longing for me, and along with it, a fear. How much my life has changed because of that! Sir, when you meet your master again, will you give him a message from me? Tell him, ‘I have forgotten all that has passed. Now, I am the Queen of Pazhuvur, bound to him by the ties of marriage. He need not fear to see me. I will not bite and swallow him whole!’ Will you say this for me?”

“Devi! It is not certain that I will return alive and see Aditya Karikalan again. If I do see him, there are so many messages I have to convey. But I cannot promise that I will deliver your message. Please forgive me!”

“Yes! Of all the people I have met, you alone are truly courageous. You speak without hiding what is in your heart. That is why I like you. Brave warrior of the Vanar clan! I do not meet many people. Unlike the young princess of Pazhayarai, I do not travel in chariots. If I must go anywhere, I go in a closed palanquin. If I need to accomplish something through someone, I see only those people. Most of them are cowards. They do not dare to speak what is in their hearts. But you—whatever arises in your mind, you say it without concealment…”
“I have learned, Queen, that there is no use in hiding anything! There is no secret in any man’s heart that your eyes cannot pierce and discover!”

“That may be true. But I have not yet been able to discover what lies in your heart. Let that be. You asked about the Pazhuvettaraiyars. My husband and Parthibendran, along with their retinues, have gone to a nearby village. There, the Kannagi dance and Velanattam are being performed. They have gone to see if they can learn anything from the madman about the young prince. Fools! Instead of questioning the one they ought to, they have gone to a soothsayer. It will be a long time before they return. That is why I had you brought here. Sir! I ask you again—surely you know the truth about the prince, don’t you? Won’t you tell it to me?”

“No, Devi! I cannot tell you! From this day forth, I have resolved never to fabricate anything for any purpose, and to speak only the truth. Therefore, I cannot speak about the prince. Just a moment ago, I forgot my resolve. Forgive me!” So saying, Vandiyathevan untied the knot at his waist and took out the palmyra signet ring hidden within.

“Ammani! Here is the palmyra signet ring you gave me. It is true that the men of Bhuthivikrama Kesari in Lanka took it from me by force. But the Commander returned it to me. Here, I return it to you…” “I shall return it to you; but you must accept it and bless me!” Saying this, he extended the signet ring.

Nandini looked at it intently and recognized that it was indeed the ring she had given him. “Sir! It is not my custom to take back what I have once given. I asked for it only to test your honesty. You have passed the test. You have not forced me to put you through a trial by my own people. You may keep the ring as a token of my remembrance!” she said.
“Lady! Please consider carefully. If I keep this, I might have to use it again when necessity arises…”

“There is no need to worry about that. You may use it however you wish. Now, I am going to have you blindfolded once more and carried in the palanquin. You will be left exactly where you were picked up…”
“What if I refuse?”
“From this ruined palace and from within this fortress, you cannot find your way out on your own. No matter how many times you try, you will only end up where you started.”
“Devi! This fortress? This ruined palace?…”

“Yes; once, this Chola land was long under the rule of the Pallavas. In those days, the Pallava emperors built this fortress and this palace. Later, Chola Nadu came under the Pandya kings. At times, the Pandya kings resided in this very palace. In the time of Vijayalaya Chola, a great battle was fought here. The fortress was shattered and collapsed. Half the palace was destroyed as well. We are now in the part that escaped destruction. Some call this the Pallavarayan Fort, while others call it the Pandiyarayan Fort. There is truth in both names. But only those who know the way well can enter and leave this place! What do you say? Shall I call my people to take you away? Or will you find your own way out…”

“No, Devi! I have no time to find my own way. Let those who brought me here take me back. But… before I leave… was there no other reason you summoned me? Is there no other help I can offer you? If there is anything, please tell me!”
“Very well; since you ask, I shall tell you. I want a flying horse. If you can, procure one and bring it to me.”
“What? Did you say a flying horse?”
“Yes; a flying horse, indeed!”
“Are you speaking of an Arabian steed that runs so fast it seems to fly?”

“No, no! I could never mount such a horse. I am not speaking of a horse that runs with its hooves on the earth. I speak of a horse that spreads its wings like a bird and soars through the sky. I have heard tales that such wondrous horses exist somewhere in this world. It is such a winged, flying horse that I desire!”
“For what purpose? To fly to the heavenly realms?”
“Do I appear to you as someone destined for heaven? I am not one who has earned such merit. I am a woman who has committed many grievous sins.”
“Are only the virtuous found in heaven? Sins are committed there as well. To seek atonement, they come down to this earth. Once their task is done, they return to heaven.”

“No, I have no wish to go to heaven. In the land of the Pandyas, there is a desert. In the midst of it stand some bald rocks—rocks upon which not a blade of grass or a sprig of garlic will grow. Some of those rocks have caves. Once, Digambara Jain monks dwelled in those caves and performed penance. Now, snakes and foxes inhabit them. More than the celestial city of Amaravati, it is those barren rocks in the Pandya desert that are dearest to me.”
“Devi! Your desire is indeed a wondrous one.”

“If I had a flying horse, I would go to that desert. Then, I would fly from there to the island of Lanka. In Lanka, they say, there are mountains that touch the sky, and forests so dense with towering trees that even those mountains are hidden from view. Just as herds of buffalo roam the Chola lands, herds of elephants wander the forests of Lanka; I would see them all. Further, in the heart of this world, there are mountains whose peaks have been shrouded in ice since the day the earth was born. At sunrise, they shine like silver hills. I long to mount a flying horse and behold those snowy summits. Beyond that, there are deserts a thousand times vaster than the Pandya wilderness, stretching as endless fields of white sand.”

In the daytime, it is said, it appears as though one is standing amidst a blazing fire. I wish to visit all those places. If you travel even further, the cold is so intense that the sea itself freezes solid, and both men and beasts can walk across it. I long to mount a flying horse and see those lands…”

“Devi! I cannot bring you such a flying horse. But there is an easier way to reach some of the places you mentioned. If you board a good boat, you can reach Lanka in half a day. If you travel by ship…”

“Sir! That is not an unknown way to me. But I am afraid when I see the sea. I fear boarding a ship. Even when I cross a river in a boat, if the boat sways, I am afraid. So your suggestion is of no use to me. You may go if you wish!” said Nandini, rising to her feet.
“Devi! Have you nothing else to say to me?”
“No! But it seems as though you wish to say something.”
“I wish to ask you a question. You must answer me just this one thing. Some days ago, did you not go to Lanka? Did you not stand alone in the dark shadows of the streets of Anuradhapura?”
“Not at all. I have never, even for a moment, gone beyond the palace and the guards of Pazhuvetaraiyar. Why do you harbor such a suspicion?”

“Lady! I saw you in Lanka a few days ago. You speak of ‘flying horses’ and such—perhaps you truly possess such a horse and rode it there. But you were not adorned as you are now, with fine garments and jewels. You wore only a simple sari, no ornaments, your hair let loose, standing there. Was that woman not you?”
“No, it was not I, sir! Did that woman you speak of open her mouth and speak?”
“No, she spoke only with gestures. But you are familiar with sorcerers. Perhaps, by some magical power, your subtle form traveled there?”
“What if neither I nor my subtle body went there?...”
“Then she must have been someone who greatly resembled you in form, but was unable to speak.”
Nandini’s gaze drifted far away, to some distant place. She let out a long, heavy sigh.
“Sir! Just a short while ago, did you not say you wished to help me in some way?”
“I did!”
“Was that truly your sincere word?”
“Without a doubt.”
“If so, then listen to this. If ever, at any time, you happen to see that woman again, somehow catch her and bring her to me. If that is not possible, at least take me to her!” said Nandini.

Half an hour later, Vandiyathevan once again stood on the banks of the Mullai river. His horse stood beside him. Those who had brought him there had vanished in an instant. Even Devaralan was nowhere to be seen.

Guiding his horse slowly along the banks of the Mullai, Vandiyathevan traveled through the night. In the third quarter of the night, the comet had reached its full brilliance and stretched across a vast expanse of the sky. Again and again, he wondered whether that comet, which had sown fear in the hearts of the people, truly foretold some impending disaster, or whether it was all mere superstition. The memory of Nandini kept returning to him. Her words were deeply etched in his mind. The revulsion he had felt upon first seeing her in the Thanjai palace had now faded. Instead, a certain sympathy had arisen in him, born from the thought that she was a woman battered by terrible sorrows. Yet, since her true intentions, the deed she wished to accomplish, and the real story of her life all remained shrouded in mystery, there was also a lingering anger within him. She seemed to possess, along with her peerless beauty, a strange and uncanny power. Therefore, it would be best not to have any further dealings with her. If only she had taken back the ring with the palmyra insignia, how much better it would have been. She had refused to take it! He could throw it into the river; but his heart would not permit it. In these perilous times, it might yet prove useful; why should he throw it away?

Once he had gone to Pazhayarai and delivered the message to the young princess, then he could throw it away. After that, he must never again become entangled in such troublesome affairs. In the fourth quarter of the night, in the eastern direction—
Silver dawn broke. Vandiyathevan had heard that one should not travel facing Venus. He halted his horse, tied it to a tree, and lay down upon the ground to snatch a little sleep.

chapters.title: The Kalamukhas
paragraphs: The crimson rays of the rising sun struck Vandiyathevan’s face with a sharp sting and woke him from his slumber. Even after his sleep had cleared, he did not feel like getting up; he opened his eyes and looked around. At a short distance, two ascetics of fearsome appearance were approaching. From their matted hair twisted atop their heads, the trident in one hand, and the fire-pot in the other, Vandiyathevan realized that these two were Kalamuka Veera Saivars.

He thought to himself, “Alwarkadiyan is not here to engage in a debate with these fellows.” He decided that until these Kalamuka ascetics passed by, he would keep his eyes closed and pretend to be asleep.
When he sensed that they had come and were standing beside him, he did not open his eyes. Even when one of them came close and thundered, he did not look.
“Shivoham! The boy is a true Kumbhakarna,” said one.
“Shivoham! If only we had a youth like him, how useful it would be!” said the other ascetic.
“Shivoham! You say that, but look at his face—there is no radiance. He is of no use to us. Very soon, a great danger is going to befall him!” declared the first Veera Saivar.

Pretending to sleep further became a struggle for Vandiyathevan; he felt as if he could not even breathe. Yet, if he were to open his eyes now, his act would be exposed. Moreover, he would miss hearing anything else they might say. Perhaps they would even reveal what great danger was about to come upon him…
But his hope was not fulfilled.
“Shivoham! Each one’s fate is his own! Come, let us go,” said one Veera Saivar, and both of them moved away from there.

Giving them time to walk some distance, Vandiyathevan rose. The words, “Very soon, a great danger is going to befall him!” echoed in his ears. The Kalamukas were descended from the ancient Kapalikas. Unlike the Kapalikas, they did not perform human sacrifices. In all other respects, however, they followed the customs and practices of the Kapalikas. Many believed that by sitting in cremation grounds and performing terrifying austerities, they had acquired the power to foresee future events. The common people thought they possessed the ability to pronounce curses as well. Therefore, many were always ready to render the Kalamuka Saivites whatever services they desired, so as not to incur their wrath. Several minor chieftains had even endowed lands to provide regular offerings of food to the Kalamukas in the temples. Until then, only the kings of the Chola dynasty had refrained from showing any support to the Kalamukas.

Vandiyathevan, who was aware of all these details, consoled himself, “Let them rave as they please; what new danger could possibly befall me that has not already come my way?” Yet, the desire to know the future did not entirely leave his mind.

When Vandiyathevan stood up and looked around, he saw those Kalamukas walking towards an old mandapam a little distance away. Near the mandapam was an artificial hillock, in which there was a cave, its mouth gaping open in the likeness of a lion’s face. In ancient times, such caves had been constructed by the Digambara Jain monks, but now the Kalamukas had taken possession of them.

Vandiyathevan felt a strong urge to go and converse with them for a while. Leaving his horse where it was tied, he walked towards the artificial hill. As he neared the mandapam, he could faintly hear the Kalamukas speaking on the other side of the cave.
“That boy did not pretend to sleep. He must have truly been asleep,” said one.
“How can you be so sure?” asked another.
“In all my life, I have never seen a man who, after hearing the words ‘danger is approaching,’ did not wish to know more about it.”
“The boy seems to be a brave soul. It would be good to have him join us. What do you say?”
“What need have we for such youths? In a few days, the very one who is about to ascend the throne of the Chola country will join the Kalamukas himself…”
“Whom do you mean?”
“Who else do you mean? I am speaking of Madurantaka Devan! Do you not know even this?”
“How can that be? What about the other two?”
“One is said to have drowned and died in the sea. The other’s time is drawing to a close…”
Vandiyathevan had no desire to listen any further to the conversation of those Kalamukha ascetics. Nor did he wish to engage in any talk with them.

He longed to reach Pazhaiyarai swiftly, deliver his message to the princess, and then depart for Kanchipuram. Above all, was he not most indebted to Aditya Karikalan? It was true that countless dangers surrounded him. Even Parthibendran had fallen into the enchantment of the Pazhuvoor queen. Aditya Karikalan, who was ever quick to leap into action, could at any moment fall prey to some unforeseen peril. To go to him and stand guard by his side was Vandiyathevan’s foremost duty. To waste time along the way would be a grave crime. He must leave this very instant.

Without a sound, Vandiyathevan turned and mounted his horse. He spurred the animal forward at speed. As he passed by the cave of the Kalamukhas, he saw them staring at him intently. One face seemed strangely familiar, as though he had seen it before. But he had no desire to stop and look; he pressed on.

On the way, he passed through several villages crowded with people. It was clear that the news of the prince’s drowning in the sea had not yet spread there. The villagers were calmly absorbed in their daily tasks. That was well and good. He must reach Pazhaiyarai before the news of the prince did. He must reveal the truth to the young princess. If some other rumor reached Kundavai Devi’s ears, who could say what calamity might ensue? The young princess might hesitate to believe, but that Kodumbalur princess—she would give up her very life!… This thought filled Vandiyathevan with great agitation. But his urgency was lost on his horse. The animal, whose hooves had been newly shod, could not even run at its usual speed and stumbled along.
At last, in the late afternoon, with two hours left before sunset, the great walls of Pazhaiyarai fort came into view.
There, at the fort’s entrance, he could see the temple of Durga. Countless thoughts flashed through his mind like lightning—how was he to enter the fort? Yet none of them seemed likely to succeed.

The palmyra signet ring would be of no use here. For, the guards at the fort had already been warned that anyone arriving with that ring was to be watched. Now, if they saw the ring, they would imprison him without further inquiry. They would send him straight to the Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar. Vandiyathevan had no desire whatsoever to be caught in such a manner before he could meet the young princess, Kundavai Devi.

Lost in thought, he slowed his horse as he approached the fort gates. At that moment, he saw a procession approaching from another direction. Warriors bearing spears, men adorned with honors, horsemen—amidst all these, a golden chariot shaped like a lotus blossom. Ah! Who was seated in that chariot? Was it not Prince Madurantaka Devar? The very same prince he had seen at Kadambur palace and in the treasure vault at Thanjavur! Instantly, a plan for entering the fort sprang to Vandiyathevan’s mind and filled him with excitement.

“If the word ‘danger’ falls upon someone’s ears, I have never seen a man who does not wish to know more about it.” These words, spoken by one of the Kalamukhas, were etched in his memory. Was it not he himself who had kindled that curiosity? Now, he must employ that Kalamukha’s trick here. Spurring his weary horse, Vandiyathevan made straight for the golden chariot shaped like a lotus flower. None among Madurantaka Devar’s retinue expected anyone to act in such a manner. Therefore, before any could move to stop him, his horse had reached the very side of the chariot.

At that moment, Vandiyathevan stood up on his horse and gazed intently at Madurantaka seated in the chariot. Then, in a loud voice, he cried, “Oh! Danger!” Immediately, he leapt from his horse and tumbled to the ground. The horse ran a few paces further and came to a halt.

All this happened in a matter of seconds. Some of Madurantaka Devar’s attendants, seeing his horse charging toward the chariot, hastily drew their swords. Some aimed their spears, ready to hurl them. But seeing him fall from his horse and lie on the ground, their alarm subsided. Then, seeing him sprawled on the earth, they all burst into laughter; even Madurantaka joined in. Meanwhile, the chariot had come to a stop. At a signal from the prince, two soldiers approached Vandiyathevan to lift him up. But before they could help, he sat up on his own. Springing to his feet without any assistance, he stood there, fixing his gaze on Prince Madurantaka as though nothing had happened.

“Bring him here, close to me!” commanded the prince. The two guards took hold of Vandiyathevan’s arms and led him to stand beside the chariot. Still, Vandiyathevan’s eyes remained fixed upon the face of Madurantaka.
“Who are you, boy?” asked the prince.
“I… I am myself! Oh Emperor! Do you not recognize me?” stammered Vandiyathevan.
“What nonsense are you babbling?.. Hey! You all, step back a little,” said Madurantaka, turning to the other guards. The soldiers withdrew a few paces.
“Who do you think I am?” Madurantaka asked again.
“Forgive me, Prince! I spoke in error. You are still… still…” Vandiyathevan faltered, stumbling over his words.
“Have you ever seen me before?” Madurantaka pressed.
“I have seen… No; I have not seen…”
“Have you seen me or not? Speak the truth!”
“Since yesterday, I have resolved to speak only the truth. That is why I cannot say for certain!”
“Oh ho! From yesterday you have become a truth-teller? What a jest!” Madurantaka laughed. “But why can you not say for certain?” he asked again.
“In these times, what can one say for certain? One man looks just like another. The one who was in a closed palanquin one day is in a chariot the next…”
“What did you say?” Madurantaka asked, his voice suddenly sharp with surprise.
“I said, because one man resembles another, I cannot say for certain!”
“Whom do I resemble?”
“I have seen you twice. Or perhaps I have seen someone who looks like you. I was uncertain whether you were the one I saw. That is why… just now…”
“Is that why you mounted your horse and gazed at me so intently?”
“Yes, sir!”
“What have you understood?”
“I have understood that you may be the one I saw, or perhaps not.”
It was clear from both the expression on Madurantaka’s face and the tone of his voice that anger was beginning to rise within him. “You are an utter rogue. You….”
“Prince, please do not be angry. I will tell you where I saw you, or someone like you. Then you may decide for yourself.”
“In that case, speak—quickly!”

“A great fortress, surrounded on all sides by tall walls. Many brave warriors had gathered there. It was midnight, and in the dim, smoke-filled light of a large oil lamp hanging on the wall, they were speaking heatedly among themselves. By the wall stood a palanquin. The leader of those warriors was being questioned again and again by the others. He grew angry. Rising swiftly, he went and stood beside the palanquin. He drew aside the silk curtain that covered it. From within the palanquin, a handsome man emerged. The moment they saw him, all the warriors gathered there shouted, ‘Long live! Long live!’ Some cried, ‘Long live the Crown Prince!’ I also remember them shouting, ‘Victory to the Emperor!’ Sir, the face of the man who emerged from the palanquin was just like yours. If I have said anything amiss, I beg your pardon.”
All this while, Madurantaka Devar had listened without interruption. Now, beads of sweat began to form on his brow. A shadow of fear spread across his face.
“From yesterday, you have been telling the truth! Were you present among that gathering of warriors?” he asked.
“No, sir! I swear I was not!”
“Then how do you speak as if you saw it all with your own eyes?”

“I myself am not certain whether what I saw truly happened, or whether I saw it in a dream. Listen to another vision. A dark underground chamber, with a tunnel winding down and up again. Along that path, three people were making their way. One walked in front, holding a torch. Another followed behind, keeping watch. In the middle, a handsome man—a prince, beautiful as Manmatha himself—came…” ...was standing there. As the light of the torch spread into the corners and recesses of that underground chamber, it seemed as if gold, gems, and cat’s-eye stones were glittering everywhere. It looked as though this was the secret treasury where the emperors of emperors stored their hidden riches. On the pillars, fearsome forms of demons were carved.
Of the three people making their way through such a subterranean passage, the man in the middle had a face that resembled his own. Whether that was true or not, you must be the judge...
Prince Madurantaka interrupted, “Enough, stop!” There was a note of fear in his voice.
