Vandiyathevan fell silent.
“Are you a soothsayer?”
“No, my lord! That is not my profession. But I will tell you what has happened; and I will also tell you what is about to happen.”
After thinking for a moment, Madurantaka asked, “When you were on horseback, you shouted something—what was that?”
“I cried out ‘Danger!’”
“Danger for whom?”
“For you, of course!”
“What danger?”

“Many dangers surround you. But just as many great honors await you as well. I must tell you about them at leisure. Even my dagger has been taken away by your soldiers, hasn’t it? If you take me with you into the fort...”
“Very well; come with me! We can speak at leisure.”

Madurantaka beckoned to the leader of the soldiers who had come with him, calling him closer. Pointing to Vandiyathevan, he ordered that he be brought into the fort along with them. That command did not seem to please the leader of the soldiers very much. Nevertheless, obeying the order, he took Vandiyathevan with him.
After a short while, the gates of Pazhaiyarai fort swung open. Madurantaka Thevar, his attendants, and Vandiyathevan entered the fort.

The Chozha Empire was renowned for its temples, its learned scholars, and its valorous warriors. But in the shadows of its grandeur, there lurked strange sects and secretive groups, whose ways were unknown to the common folk. Among these, the Kalamukhas were the most feared.

The Kalamukhas wore their hair matted, smeared their bodies with ash, and painted their faces with black marks. They roamed the land in groups, chanting mantras and performing rituals that sent shivers down the spines of those who witnessed them. Some said they possessed magical powers, others whispered that they could summon spirits and command the dead.

On that moonless night, Vandiyathevan found himself in the midst of a dense forest, the path ahead swallowed by darkness. The only sounds were the rustling of leaves and the distant howl of a jackal. He tightened his grip on his sword, every sense alert.

Suddenly, from the thicket ahead, a procession of shadowy figures emerged. Their faces were smeared with black, their eyes gleaming with a strange light. They carried tridents and skull-topped staffs, their bodies adorned with garlands of bones. The air was thick with the scent of burning incense and something else—something metallic and sharp.

Vandiyathevan’s heart pounded. He had heard tales of the Kalamukhas, but never had he expected to encounter them in the flesh. He pressed himself against the trunk of a tree, hoping the darkness would conceal him.

The procession halted. The leader, a tall figure with a mane of wild hair, raised his staff and began to chant in a guttural voice. The others echoed his words, their voices rising and falling like the wind through the trees. The ritual grew in intensity, the air crackling with unseen energy.
Vandiyathevan watched, transfixed and terrified. What unearthly rites were these? What secrets did these men guard in the heart of the forest?
He dared not move, scarcely dared to breathe. The Kalamukhas continued their ritual, oblivious to the silent watcher in the shadows.

chapters.title: Madhurandhaka Devar
paragraphs: We first encountered Madurantaka Devar, an important character in this tale, at the very beginning of the story in the Kadambur palace. We saw him once more when he made his way to the palace at midnight through the underground passage of the Pazhuvettaraiyar’s mansion. Yet, on those occasions, we did not properly introduce this renowned prince to our readers—the very one who would later ascend the throne of Thanjavur as Parakesari Uttama Chozhar. We wish now to remedy that omission.

Before we speak of Madurantaka himself, it is necessary to remind our readers a little of his lineage. Before Sundara Chozha Chakravarthi, the Chozha kingdom had long been ruled by his great father, Kandaraditya Chozhar. He and his virtuous consort, Chembiyan Maadevi, daughter of the Malavarayar clan, were both paragons of devotion to Lord Shiva. Their lives were wholly absorbed in the renovation and service of Shiva temples.

Kandaraditya cherished the wish to collect and compile the scattered Thevaram hymns found throughout Tamil Nadu. That wish was not fulfilled during his lifetime, though he did manage to gather some of the hymns. He himself composed several hymns in the style of the Thevaram, and among them, the hymn he sang in praise of Chidambaram is still preserved today in the collection known as Thiruvisaippa.
In a hymn he composed, Kandaraditya refers to his illustrious father, Parantaka Chakravarthi, and the golden roof he installed at the temple of Thillai (Chidambaram):

“The valiant king of the north, who conquered the southern lands And Lanka as well, The red-sceptred Chozhan, the king of kings, Chembiyan, adorned in gold, In the jeweled Thillai temple, where ankleted women sing and dance, Our Lord, who wears the crescent moon…” In that hymn, he alludes to the fact that his father conquered both the Pandya country and Eelam. In the final verse of the decad, not only does he mention his own name, but he also refers to the Chola capital of his time, Thanjai.

“Adoring the golden Annamalai of Thillai, He, the lord of the fertile groves, the king of Kozhi, The sovereign of Thanjai, Kandaradithan, whose words are like nectar— Those who master his rare Tamil garland Shall attain eternal fame and supreme bliss in the world beyond!”

Kandaradithar had no faith in expanding the empire through war. Having witnessed the sufferings that wars brought upon mankind, he strove, as much as possible, to avoid conflict and sought only peace. As a result, during his reign, the Chola empire shrank considerably.

In his later years, Kandaradithar married the daughter of the Mazhavarayar. Their son, Madurantakan, was but a small child at the time of Kandaradithar’s passing. Enemies were rising on all sides of the kingdom. At the same time, Kandaradithar’s younger brother, Arinjayan, was grievously wounded in battle and awaited death.

Arinjayan’s son, Sundara Cholan, by then had crossed into manhood, had beaten the drums of victory in many wars, and had earned a name as a great hero. Therefore, Kandaradithar decided that Sundara Cholan alone was worthy of the throne after him, and announced this to the people. To prevent any disputes over the succession, he declared that only the descendants of Sundara Cholan would be heirs to the throne.

He had also told his wife that their son, Madurantakan, should be raised as a devotee of Shiva and engaged in service to the Lord. All these were matters well known to the land in those days. Sembiyan Maadevi fulfilled the promise she had given her husband. From a young age, she instilled in Madurantakan a deep devotion to Shiva and a spirit of renunciation toward worldly life.

Until about the age of twenty, Madurantakan regarded his mother’s word as sacred scripture. He had no interest whatsoever in affairs of state; not even the thought that the Chola throne was his by right arose in his mind. But two years ago, after marrying the daughter of the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar, his heart began to change. The desire that had first appeared as a faint spark was fanned into a flame by the young queen of Pazhuvoor, Nandini. The small ember soon became a raging forest fire. Various... For various reasons, we have seen that many of the minor kings and great officials of Chola Nadu attempted to plot in support of Madurantaka. They were waiting for the moment when Sundara Chola would close his eyes, so they could raise Madurantaka to the throne. But Madurantaka himself did not wish to wait that long. He began to think that Sundara Chola had no right to the throne, and that the Chola Empire should have come to him by right. Moreover, was not Sundara Chola now bedridden with illness, unable to attend to the affairs of the kingdom? Then why should he not immediately ascend the throne of Thanjavur and take up the burden of rule?

Now, it was the responsibility of the Pazhuvettaraiyars to restrain this royal madness that had seized Madurantaka. They did not wish to act in haste and ruin the matter. Both sons of Sundara Chola were heroes among heroes. By their valorous deeds and other noble qualities, they had won a place in the hearts of the people. Two great chieftains—Kodumbalur Velar and Thirukovalur Malayaman—stood in support of Sundara Chola’s sons. Even within the army, a large portion of the soldiers favored the sons of Sundara Chola. Therefore, the Pazhuvettaraiyars resolved to wait patiently as long as the Emperor lived.

In the meantime, they came to know that the Emperor’s mind had changed somewhat. If Sundara Chola himself declared that, after him, the crown should go to Prince Madurantaka, there would be no trouble at all. The only ones who could stand in the way were the Younger Princess and Sembiyan Madevi. The intrigues of the Younger Princess could be overcome by counter-intrigues. But if Sembiyan Madevi, who was revered throughout the Tamil land as a divine being, stood in opposition, it would not be easy to overcome that obstacle. It was widely known that this great lady did not wish her own son to ascend the throne. How would the people accept it if the son ascended the throne against his mother’s wishes? There were only two ways: either that lady must follow her husband to the abode of Kailasa, or her mind must be changed. Who else but her own child could possess the power to change a mother’s heart? Therefore, the Pazhuvettaraiyars repeatedly urged Madurantaka Devar to speak to his mother and persuade her to change her mind.

But in this matter alone, Madurantaka showed no enthusiasm. The desire to rule the kingdom raged like a fever within him. Yet, he hesitated to speak to his mother about it. Indeed, he did not even wish to meet and speak with that venerable lady.

At this time, Sembiyan Maadevi had sent word to Thanjavur. She had informed them that she was planning to fulfill one of her husband’s most cherished wishes, and that, on this occasion, her son must be present with her. Accordingly, the Younger Pazhuvettarayar instructed Madurantaka to go to Pazhayarai. He also advised him to use this opportunity to argue with his mother about his rightful claim to the throne of Thanjavur and to try to change her mind.

chapters.title: Thirunaraiyur Nambi
paragraphs: Madhurantaka Devar, accompanied by his retinue and Vandiyathevan, entered the city of Pazhaiyarai. Their procession wound its way through the quarters where the warriors dwelled: the Arya Padai Veedu, the Pambai Padai Veedu, the Puthu Padai Veedu, the Mana Padai Veedu, and others. Then they passed through the bazaar streets, the neighborhoods where the common folk lived, the temples, and the sacred streets that encircled those temples. Here and there, a few people stood at their doorways and watched. But Vandiyathevan noticed there was no sign of excitement among the people.

The first time he had entered this city, it had been immersed in festivity. Now, the streets were deserted, almost as if Pazhaiyarai had become a forsaken city. It was glaringly obvious that the people of Pazhaiyarai did not place much faith in Madhurantaka Devar. In one sense, this was convenient for Vandiyathevan. If anyone who recognized his face happened to see him, there was little chance for trouble to arise.

As they neared the ancient palace street of the Chola kings, they saw another grand procession approaching from the opposite direction. At the center of that procession was an open palanquin. Though it was not clear who sat within, it was evident that he was a devotee of Shiva, and a young man at that. The crowd around the palanquin was dense, both before and behind. Some, holding cymbals in their hands, created a sweet jangling sound and sang as they walked alongside the palanquin.

From time to time, shouts of “Thiruchitrambalam!” and “Hara Hara Mahadeva!” rang out, mingled with cries of “Long live Thirunaraiyur Nambi!” and “Long live the blessed one of the mischievous Pillaiyar!”—the cheers soared up to the heavens.
Madhurantaka watched that procession with eyes full of envy. He turned to a soldier beside him and asked something. “Yes; the one in the palanquin is Thirunaraiyur Nambi!” came the reply.

“Still, what a display! In this town, not a soul pays heed to us! Yet, see how the people throng and make such a commotion around this Nambi?” said Madhurantaka Devar. That procession passed not far from where they stood. Among those who had come near the palanquin, Vandiyathevan recognized one as the Veera Saivite who had once quarreled with Azhwarkadiyan while crossing the Kollidam river by boat.

Madhurantaka Thevar and his attendants reached the palace street and arrived at the mansion of Sembiyan Madevi. At the palace entrance, the Periya Piratti herself stood waiting. It seemed she was prepared to welcome someone. Madhurantakan alighted from his chariot and approached his mother, bowing before her. The mother blessed the bowing Madhurantakan, placing her hand upon his head.
“My son! You have arrived at an auspicious moment! Thirunaraiyur Nambi is on his way. If necessary, refresh yourself quickly and come to the assembly hall without delay!” she said.

Vandiyathevan noticed the glow fade from Madhurantakan’s face. Poor man! He must have thought that the Periya Piratti was waiting at the palace entrance to welcome him. What a disappointment! When he realized that she was actually waiting to receive the Saivite devotee who followed in the palanquin procession, how natural it must be for Madhurantakan—who harbored hopes of ascending the Chola throne the very next day—to feel such bitter disillusionment!

They all proceeded to the quarters reserved for Madhurantakan in the palace. Madhurantakan took his time with changing his attire and other such matters. He did not seem particularly eager to go to the assembly hall. Messengers came one after another from his mother. At last, Madhurantakan set out. As he left, he asked, “Where is that soothsayer?”

Vandiyathevan, who was impatiently waiting to accompany him to the assembly hall, replied, “Here I am, ready.” Taking Vandiyathevan and a few others with him, Madhurantakan proceeded to the assembly hall.

The assembly had already gathered in the hall. On one side sat Sembiyan Madevi, Kundavai Piratti, and several other palace women. At the center of the assembly, on a raised dais, sat a young man. He was of youthful age, adorned with sacred ash and rudraksha beads, his handsome face radiant with grace. Several palm-leaf manuscripts lay before him; he held one in his hand as well. Beside him stood an elder, also adorned with sacred ash and rudraksha, who appeared deeply absorbed. The hall was filled with people. Vandiyathevan recognized that the young man was the one who had arrived in the palanquin, and that the man standing beside him was the same person he had seen before on the Kollidam ferry.
Though Vandiyathevan’s eyes wandered here and there about the assembly hall, in the end, they came to rest near the Periya Piratti.

Kundavai’s radiant face was the first to greet him. At their initial meeting, the Princess’s eyes showed a flicker of surprise. But after that, it seemed as if her gaze never once turned in his direction again. Vandiyathevan even began to wonder if perhaps she did not recognize him at all.

As Madurantakan entered the assembly hall, all except the women rose to pay their respects. Once Madurantakan had taken his seat upon the dais, the others too sat down in their respective places. Sembiyan Maadevi turned to Madurantakan and said,

“Prince! This young devotee hails from Thirunaraiyur. He has received the full grace of the famed Pillaiyar of that town. He has obtained certain Thevaram hymns that have not been found by anyone else until now. In a former age, a queen of our Chola dynasty became the Maharani of Pandima Nadu. At her invitation, the great child-saint Jnanasambandar journeyed to the mighty city of Madurai. There, he triumphed over the Jains in a battle of debate. Some of the hymns sung by Sambandar in Madurai at that time have come into this young man’s possession. In those hymns, Sambandar sings of our Chola queen as well. When I hear those songs, my whole body thrills with ecstasy. If your father had been here to listen, how happy he would have been! At least you must listen!”

Madurantakan replied, “I will listen, Mother! Let the hymn begin.” Yet, his face did not blossom with joy. His mind seemed to be wandering elsewhere. He did not like the idea of seating a simple boy, adorned only with sacred ash and rudraksha beads, upon a grand dais and making such a fuss over him. He sat there patiently only to satisfy his mother.

The devotee of Thirunaraiyur, blessed by the grace of the Pillaiyar, began to read from the palm-leaf manuscript in his hand. He first sang the hymns that Jnanasambandar had composed upon beholding the great city of Madurai, marveling, “Is this not the city where the illustrious Mangaiyarkkarasi, the queen of Shiva-bhakti, resides?”
“Mangaiyarkkarasi, the consort of the lord of valor…” When these songs were sung—

“O Pandima Devi, lotus-eyed, adorned with bracelets of gems, The radiant queen of Pandya’s line, Served with devotion, praised by all the land, By the Lord of blazing flame, the Master of Spirits, Who bestowed the Vedas and their truths, And dwells with Angayarkanni, cool and gentle, In Alavai—such is this!”

“And as long as the earth endures, so too shall endure The jeweled-crowned Chola’s daughter, She of melodious speech, Pandima Devi, Serving with devotion, praised by all, While those above in the heavens, and those below, In ways beyond measure, The Lord with Uma, in bliss, Dwells in Alavai—such is this!”

—tears of joy, like pearls, welled up and fell from the eyes of Sembiyan Maadevi. To have been born into the clan that gave birth to such a queen among women, to have lived as a Maharani herself—she thought again and again of the merit from her previous births that had granted her such fortune, and her heart brimmed with happiness.

But for Madurantakan, only one line from the songs lingered in his mind: “As long as the earth endures, so too shall endure the jeweled-crowned Chola.” The thought that the ancient and illustrious Chola crown, which ought to grace his own head, was now adorned by another—this filled him with anger.

Sambandar goes to see the Queen of Women. Pandima Devi looks upon the boy and laments, “Alas! Where is this young child, and where are those Jain monks, fierce as Brahma-rakshasas? How can this child possibly engage in debate with them and emerge victorious?”
Understanding her anxiety, Sambandar turns to Pandima Devi and speaks.

“To the women whose eyes are like those of the deer, O Great Queen of the Valuthi clan, listen! Do not think of this child, who speaks with the innocence of a babe, with pity or tenderness! In the many places, from the great hill of the elephant onward, where countless sorrows gather, I am not one among the lowly, for here stands the Lord of Alavay himself!”

When Thirunaaraiyur Nambiyandar Nambi sang this hymn, Sembiyan Maadevi, imagining herself as the Queen of Women, and the singer Nambi as none other than Jnana Sambandar himself, forgot all worldly thoughts and was filled with joy.

But Madurantaka Devar thought to himself, “Yes, I am but a young child! Yet, I shall not fear Thirukovalur Malayaman, nor Kodumbalur Boothi Vikrama Kesari, nor the sons of Sundara Chozhar who have won their support. Just as Sambandar had the grace of the Lord of Alavay, so too do I have the aid of the Pazhuvettaraiyars!”

Not a word of the song entered Vandiyathevan’s ears. His eyes and thoughts were wholly absorbed in Kundavai Devi. Did the young princess not recognize him at all? Or, having recognized him, was she deliberately ignoring him? Or was she angry that he had not come to her at once after completing the task she had entrusted to him? Thus his mind was filled with such questions. Along with this, he wondered how he might meet the princess in private, and how he could deliver his message to her when he did.

When the songs had ended, Sembiyan Maadevi looked at the elder who had come with Nambiyandar and said, “Sir, when I see this young boy, it seems as if Jnana Sambandar himself has been reborn. Take him with you and travel throughout the land of Tamil. Gather the divine Thevaram hymns that you find in each place. The hymns of Appar, those of Sambandar, and the songs of Sundaramurthi must each be collected separately. In every Shiva temple, these hymns must be sung daily. This was my husband’s wish. I long to see it fulfilled within my lifetime. Go from town to town—” “I shall make arrangements to provide you with all the necessary palanquins, attendants, and accompanying paraphernalia for your journey. I shall seek the Emperor’s permission and send word to my son himself!” he said.
The tumultuous shouts that then arose in that assembly sounded most unpleasant to the ears of Madurantaka.

chapters.title: The Soothsayer
paragraphs: As the assembly that had gathered to welcome Nambi Andar Nambi was dispersing, the Great Queen turned to her beloved son and said, “My son! I will accompany these guests up to the palace gates and see them off. In the meantime, go to your chambers, refresh yourself, and return. I must speak to you about something important!”

“So be it, Mother,” replied Madurantakan, and set off. He made his way to the part of the palace where he resided. Within him, anger and jealousy flared up like a blazing fire. What extravagant honors for some wandering ascetic and his retinue! It seemed as if his own mother was bringing shame upon the royal family’s dignity! No wonder the Pazhuvettaraiyars so often voiced their complaints about her. Anyone who arrived, smeared with sacred ash and adorned with rudraksha beads, was enough to win the Great Queen’s favor! All it took was a hymn or two sung in praise, or talk of temple renovations, tanks, and holy works, and she would be satisfied. For such people, she would lavish gifts, emptying the royal treasury itself!

As if that were not enough, there was Princess Kundavai, ever at her side. If anything remained after the temple renovations, she would spend it on establishing hospitals. If such things were allowed to continue, how would his own ambitions ever be fulfilled? How could he ascend the Chola throne and, sending forth Chola armies in all four directions, conquer the whole earth and rule under a single parasol?

And now, once again, the Great Queen wished to speak some secret to her son! Who knew what secret she intended to reveal? Perhaps she would begin discoursing on Ashtanga Yoga, on yama and niyama, on the art of meditation. Perhaps she would instruct him on how to focus the gaze upon the tip of the nose, to raise the kundalini upwards, and thus master all sixty-four arts without ever having to learn them! Or perhaps she would begin explaining the inner meaning of Nataraja’s blissful dance, what his matted locks symbolized, what the crescent moon he wore represented. With such endless talk, she had already brought him to the point where the world mocked him as half-mad. There must be no more room for such conversations. Even if she insisted on speaking, he must not listen… Let it be! Before the queen calls for me again, I must speak to that soothsayer. How did he come to know of those two mysterious matters, which no one else could possibly have known? Is it not astonishing to think of it? He must possess some extraordinary power. If he could recount past events as if he had witnessed them, could he also foretell what is yet to come? I must ask him myself.

As they were leaving the assembly, Madurantakan noticed the soothsayer standing there hesitantly, glancing about uncertainly. With a gesture, he commanded the man to follow him. Vandiyathevan’s eyes were eager to catch a glimpse of the princess’s face, to convey a message through the language of the eyes. But the princess, without so much as a backward glance, had already departed with the great queen.

What is this? Has the princess forgotten me altogether? It must be so. Every day, she sees thousands upon thousands of faces. How could she possibly remember the face of someone she has seen once—twice at most? I am the fool; day and night, through countless strange incidents and dangers, I have thought only of the princess’s radiant face. Why should the princess think of me? The bee, loving honey, circles the flower again and again. But what concern does the flower have for the bee? The flower smiles up at the sun. Who is the Sun God who makes Kundavai’s face bloom so beautifully?

Yet, could she really be so indifferent, even to the message for which she sent me? Perhaps someone else has already come before me and delivered the news? How could that be? No, no! Her face clearly showed she was troubled by some deep worry. Surely, it must be that she did not recognize me. If the messenger who took the secret letter to Lanka were to return as one of Madurantaka’s attendants and enter the assembly, how could she possibly recognize him? Ah! When I tell her of the tricks I used to enter that city and meet her, how astonished she will be! But how to meet her? How to send word to her?…
“Nimittakara! What deep thoughts are you lost in?” Madurantakan’s voice startled Vandiyathevan. By then, they had reached Madurantaka Devar’s private chamber within the palace.

In those days, there were many astrologers, soothsayers, palmists who foretold by reading lines, and omen-readers who spoke of the future. Astrologers would cast horoscopes, calculate the movements of planets and stars, and thus predict destinies. Soothsayers would interpret the words spoken by those who came to them, the precise moment when the question was asked, or ask the seeker to choose a number between one and one hundred and eight, and then pronounce general auspicious or inauspicious predictions. The science of palmistry, as it existed then, endures even today.

Omen-readers were those who, like ancient sages endowed with wisdom and inner vision, possessed the power to see with the mind’s eye. By focusing their minds, aided by their inner sight, they would look upon the events of past, present, and future as if they were happening before their very eyes, and then reveal them. Some would close their outer eyes and sit in meditation before speaking; others would fix their gaze upon the flame of a lamp, concentrate their minds, and declare the events that had occurred or were yet to occur, as seen within that flickering light. There were even some who, upon merely beholding the face of the person before them, would have the entire history—past and future—of that individual appear in their mind. Apart from these extraordinary individuals endowed with such miraculous powers, there were also ordinary omen-readers who would interpret the meaning of external occurrences—such as whether a crow flew to the left or right, or where it landed—to predict good or bad fortune.

Vandiyathevan was startled when Madurantaka addressed him as “Nimiththakkaran!”—omen-reader. He had no idea what further questions the prince might ask him. He would have to answer them all with cleverness and presence of mind. Oh God! How could he escape from here, from this man? How could he manage to meet the princess alone and speak with her?

“There is no other thought in my mind, my lord! Rather than being an omen-reader, I was just thinking how much better it would have been if I had learned four Thevaram hymns like that boy we saw in the assembly! How much honor and respect I too would have received!” he said.
“Who said you shouldn’t! You too can learn to sing the Thevaram hymns!” said the prince.
“But, my prince, it will happen only as it is written for each person! What is the use of yearning in vain?”
“What do you think of that boy who sang the hymn? His fortune…”

“A most exalted fortune. A union of Shiva Yoga and Raja Yoga. Kings and queens themselves will pay homage to that child. His name will shine alongside the names of great saints, and will endure in this world for a long, long time.”
Vallavarayan spoke thus, almost carelessly, as if it were a mere trifle. But his words stirred a great excitement in the heart of Madurantaka.
“Tell me, what of my own fortune? Let us see how it fares!”
“Your fortune, too, is a blend of Shiva Yoga and Raja Yoga, just like his. Yet, it is even greater!”
“Dear fellow! Tell me in detail, let me hear it.”

Vallavarayan asked for a moment to think about what he should say. So he replied, “Can such things be rushed? If you want me to tell you in detail, a lamp must be lit, incense burned, and you must sit behind the lamp. Then, as the events of the future unfold before me, I shall tell you what I see.”

Madurantaka, in a flurry of excitement, ordered a lamp to be brought and lit, and incense to be burned. Two mats were laid out, one before and one behind the lamp. After Madurantaka seated himself on one mat, Vandiyathevan sat on the other, facing him.

He closed his eyes and for a while seemed to sink deep into meditation. His lips moved, muttering some mysterious mantras. Then, with a sudden shake of his body, he acted as if possessed by a trance. His body trembled like that of a madman seized by frenzy.

Afterwards, he opened his eyes wide. He fixed his gaze upon the flame of the lamp before him. After staring for a while, he turned to Madurantaka and said, “Sir! If I have spoken carelessly about you, forgive me. Your fortune is no ordinary one. There is no connection between the fortune of that child who sat in the assembly singing songs, and your own. That child’s fortune is a Raja Yoga granted by the favor of kings; but what I see in this lamp about your fortune—ah! It astonishes even me!”
“What do you see? Tell me! Tell me!” exclaimed Madurantaka.

“Ah! How can I describe it? I cannot find words to express it! As far as the eye can see, kings adorned with jeweled crowns stand assembled in ranks. Ministers, chieftains, and officers stand in orderly rows. Beyond them, like an endless sea, waves of soldiers surge and stand, their spears and swords flashing, their breastplates gleaming, dazzling the eye. Upon the terraces of distant mansions, crowds of people stand and cheer. On every rampart and battlement of the fort, throngs upon throngs of people are gathered. They… they… are shouting all sorts of slogans!”
“Tell me, tell me! What are the people shouting?”

“Prince! Amidst the roar of thousands, it is hard to hear clearly. But it seems they are shouting, ‘Long live the scion of the Chola clan! Long live the Emperor of the Three Worlds! Long live the King of Kings!’ and such cries.”
“What then?”
“The people are pressing forward in great crowds. Soldiers armed with spears and swords are holding them back. For a while, there is nothing but confusion and uproar.”
“Alright, alright! Why has the crowd gathered? Tell me that!”

“That is what I am about to see now. In the midst of the crowd, the tiger banner soars high into the sky. Beneath it, the fish flag, the bow flag, the palmyra flag, the lion flag, the bull flag, and the boar flag flutter at lower heights. In the center of a grand assembly hall, resplendent as Maya’s palace, a golden throne inlaid with nine precious gems has been placed. Nearby, on a pedestal, rests a jeweled crown, dazzling with the brilliance of a million suns, studded with diamonds and cat’s-eyes. Above the throne, a white royal umbrella, cool and lustrous as the moon’s gentle light, is spread wide and droops gracefully. Women as beautiful as celestial maidens stand waiting, holding white chamara fans in their hands. Rows of golden pots filled with sacred water brought from many holy rivers are arranged in order. Prince! Everything is ready for the coronation!…”
“For whose coronation? Tell me that, father,” said Madurantaka.

“That too will soon be known. The main entrance of the assembly hall is opening. Accompanied by various auspicious music, some people are entering. An elderly man of majestic and heroic bearing enters. Another, who appears to be his brother, follows. Behind them comes a royal prince, handsome as Manmatha himself—look, he is coming!”
“Who is that? Who is it?” Vandiyathevan glanced once more at Madhurantakan, then turned his gaze back to the lamp.

“Sir! He looks just like you! What do I mean, just like you? It is you! Two men who came before are leading you towards the throne. The cry of ‘Jaya Vijayeebhava!’ rises like the roar of the ocean. Hundreds upon hundreds of hands shower you with flowers, jewels, and golden grains. Look, you are nearing the lion throne! Ah! What is this? Like an ill omen, someone comes in your way. A woman, with her head held high, strides across and stands between you and the throne. She bars your path, saying, ‘No!’ You push that woman aside!… Alas! What is this, at such an auspicious moment, this smoke comes and shrouds everything? I can see nothing….”
“Look! Look closely! What happens next?”
“Prince! Forgive me! A thick cloud of smoke has come and hidden everything!...”
“Look, man, look! At least see who that woman is! Have you seen her before?”

“Prince! That lady too has vanished, you have vanished as well. The assembly, the throne, the crown—all have disappeared. There must be people with magical powers in this palace! It seems they have deliberately cast a spell to stop me. Alas! My face burns as if it is on fire!...”
Saying this, Vandiyathevan covered his face with his hands. He remained thus for a while, then opened his eyes and looked around.

The nerves in Madhurantaka Devar’s body were twitching all over. Anger boiled on his face. His eyes glowed like burning embers. Vandiyathevan felt a little afraid. He wondered if he had stirred the prince’s passion and desire too much.
“Look again! Look carefully and tell me!” commanded Madhurantakan.
“Prince! There is no use! Once a vision disappears, it does not return at once. Only after a few days will it come again. I will gaze at the lamp, and if any other vision appears, I will tell you.”
“Speak, speak! Whatever vision you see, tell me!”
“The people are in utter confusion. They are filled with sorrow and anger. A messenger has come and is telling them some news. He claims that someone from the royal family has drowned in the sea.”

“Oh no! How tragic! The people are about to attack that messenger. Prince! If anything like that should happen, you must not go among the people at such a moment! Even if you must, go with utmost caution!”
“Didn’t he say whose name it was who drowned in the sea?”
“In the shouting and confusion, I could not catch the name. That scene has faded away.”

“Now, before my eyes, I see a terrifying group wearing garlands of skulls around their necks. They look like Kapalikas and Kalamukas. One among them is holding a dreadful axe in his hand. In front of him is a sacrificial altar. Prince! Here too, a royal prince is approaching. The Kalamukas are surrounding him and dancing wildly. Alas! Whatever happens, you must never go into the midst of such a crowd!…”

At these words, sweat broke out on Madurantaka’s face; his body trembled. Vandiyathevan noticed this carefully. Then, “Prince! I can see nothing more now, forgive me. My head is spinning; my eyes are darkening. Someone is casting a spell to block my vision. Another time, in another place, I will look and tell you more!” he said, clutching his head with his hands.

At that moment, a palace attendant arrived and announced that the great queen, Sembiyan Maadevi, had summoned the prince. Madurantaka, deciding to pour out all the anger boiling within him upon his mother, set out at once.
“Sir! I cannot bear this headache. I will go outside the palace and take a short walk around the city and return!” said Vandiyathevan, obtaining permission from him.

For Pinagapani, the son of the Pazhayarai physician, a new flavor had entered life. Until a few days ago, he had been content learning the science of medicine from his father. But during the journey to Kodikkarai, Vandiyathevan had told him many things about the outside world. And that was not all. It is natural for those newly ensnared in the web of love to feel the urge to speak of it to someone. The physician’s son, a first-class fool— Having thus come to know of it, Vandiyathevan began to speak to him about the dangers of falling in love with women. He spoke of the joys and sorrows he was experiencing as the result of loving a woman. At first, the physician’s son, Pinagapani, did not much relish these conversations. Little by little, his mind began to change. He felt a vague jealousy and anger toward Vandiyathevan. He asked the name and village of the maiden who had captivated Vandiyathevan’s heart. Vandiyathevan refused to tell him. This only increased Pinagapani’s anger. Before they reached Kodikkarai, the physician’s son had already begun to consider Vandiyathevan his enemy.

The fire he had buried in his heart began to blaze when he saw Poonguzhali. Not only did Poonguzhali reject him, she also mocked him. When he realized that she respected Vandiyathevan more than himself, Pinagapani’s madness reached its peak. He even resolved to betray Vandiyathevan to the soldiers who were following him.

Unable to capture Vandiyathevan, the men of Pazhuvettaraiyar seized Pinagapani instead and took him to Thanjavur. For a short while, he was forced to stay in the underground prison. All this only served to increase the anger he already bore toward Vandiyathevan.

Before Princess Kundavai could go to the underground prison to see him and arrange for his release, he had already been set free. The one who secured his release was none other than the younger queen of Pazhuvur, Nandini. Nandini was filled with anger and suspicion that Vandiyathevan had escaped from the Thanjai palace without her knowledge. When she learned that he had gone to Pazhayarai and then escaped to Eelam, her suspicions deepened. She guessed that, no matter what, he would one day return to Pazhayarai and attempt to see Princess Kundavai. She resolved that she needed a trustworthy person in Pazhayarai to find him at that time and send her word.
After speaking with the physician’s son, Pinagapani, she decided he was the right person for the job. She entrusted him with that great responsibility.

“The man who betrayed you and escaped will soon return to Pazhayarai one day. You must keep a close watch, observe where he goes and what he does, and immediately send me word. If you do this, I will reward you handsomely,” she said.

Afterwards, the younger Pazhuvettarayar summoned Pinagapani and gave him instructions regarding Vandiyathevan. “If you capture that royal traitor when he returns and hand him over, I will induct you into our network of spies and make you a high-ranking officer,” he promised, tempting him with prospects of power.

From that moment, Pinagapani lost all interest in his medical profession. He wandered ceaselessly through the streets of Pazhaiyarai, building castles in the air. Now and then, sudden suspicions would seize him. He would rush up to passersby, scrutinizing their faces closely. “Not him!” he would mutter to himself and move on. Observing this, many began to think that the physician’s son had fallen prey to madness.

Yet Pinagapani did not abandon his efforts. When Madurantaka Thevar and his retinue entered Pazhaiyarai, Pinagapani did not pay them much attention. He did not expect Vandiyathevan to be among them. Instead, he circled around the large crowd that surrounded Thirunaraiyur Nambi’s palanquin, watching carefully. At that moment, he noticed Madurantaka’s entourage moving at a short distance. When one of the riders near Madurantaka turned and looked back, Pinagapani’s suspicion was aroused. But as the group quickly entered the palace, he could not confirm his doubts.

chapters.title: The Saviour of the Faith
paragraphs: During the grand reception accorded to Nambiyandar Nambi, Pinagapani could not enter the assembly hall. He stood amidst the crowd gathered beyond the threshold, peering inside. We have already seen that Vandiyathevan’s attention was elsewhere. But Pinagapani’s eyes were fixed solely upon Vandiyathevan’s face. There was yet another who, though he saw all this, pretended not to notice—our old friend, Azhwarkadiyan.

After having unsettled Prince Madurantaka’s mind with his ominous predictions, Vandiyathevan emerged from the palace. There, a little distance away, the physician’s son, who had been waiting, approached him and asked, “Sir! Who are you?”
Vandiyathevan was startled to see Pinagapani. Without betraying his surprise, he replied, “What did you ask?”
“I asked who you are,” said Pinagapani.

“Who am I, you ask? Which ‘me’ do you mean? Do you refer to this body composed of the five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and ether? Or do you mean the soul, which is the basis of life? Or do you seek the Supreme Soul, which is the foundation of the soul itself? Sir, what kind of question is this? Neither you exist, nor I. All is filled with the Divine! The world is but an illusion; the truth of the soul, the Lord, and the bond—learn these from great men like Tirunaraiyur Nambi!” So saying, Vandiyathevan leapt onto his horse waiting at the palace gate. After riding swiftly for a while, he realized that the physician’s son was not following him, and so he slowed his pace and continued on leisurely.

But was the physician’s son one to be so easily deceived? His suspicions were now confirmed. He went straight to the city’s chief of police and reported the matter. Taking with him two guards sent by the officer, he began to search the town. Just as he had expected, he encountered Vandiyathevan at a crossroads.
“This is the spy! Arrest him!” he shouted.

“What’s this, man? Have you lost your mind?” exclaimed Vallavaraiyan. “Whom do you call mad? This body? The life within it? The soul? The Supreme Soul? Or the cow, the lord, or the bondage?” said Pinagapani, the physician’s son.
“From the way you’re raving now, it’s clear that you’re the madman!” retorted Vandiyathevan.
“I am not mad; I am the physician who accompanied you all the way to Kodikkarai! Guards! This is the spy who escaped from the Tanjavur fort and fled to Lanka! Seize him at once!”
The guards closed in on Vallavaraiyan. “Be careful! Don’t act rashly, just because you heard his words! I am the soothsayer who came with Prince Madurantaka Devar!” declared Vandiyathevan.
“No, no! He is a great liar. Arrest him at once!” shouted the physician’s son.
By now, a large crowd had gathered around them. Some in the crowd spoke in support of Vandiyathevan; others sided with the physician’s son.
“He doesn’t look like a soothsayer,” said one.
“Nor does he look like a spy,” said another.
“Can a soothsayer be so young?”
“Why not? Would a spy ride openly through the streets on horseback?”
“Why would a soothsayer carry a sword?”
“If he is a spy, whose spy is he? Why has he come to Pazhaiyarai to snoop around?”
Meanwhile, Pinagapani kept shouting, “Arrest him! Arrest him at once! This is an order from the Pazhuvettaraiyars!”
At the mention of the Pazhuvettaraiyars’ name, many in the crowd began to feel sympathy for Vandiyathevan. They wondered if there was any way to help him escape.
Just then, Azhwarkkadiyan joined the edge of the crowd.
“Is the soothsayer who came with the prince here?” he shouted.
“No; he is a spy!” Pinagapani yelled back.
“What nonsense is this? If you are truly the soothsayer who came with Prince Madurantaka Devar, come with me! The princess has sent for you!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
Vandiyathevan’s heart leapt with excitement. “I am that soothsayer! Here I come!” he declared.
“Don’t go! Don’t let the spy escape!” shouted Pinagapani, the physician’s son, from behind.
Azhwarkkadiyan said, “Prove that you are the soothsayer! Only then can you come with me!” At the same time, he signaled with his eyes.
“In what manner do you want me to prove it?” Vandiyathevan asked hurriedly.
“Look there—aren’t two horses approaching at great speed? It seems those who ride them are bringing some urgent news. If that is true, tell me what message they bear!”

Vandiyathevan scrutinized the riders approaching on horseback and replied, “Ah, I will tell you! A member of the royal family has met with a water-related accident! They bring tidings of that tragedy!”
Even before he could close his mouth after speaking, the horses had drawn near the crowd. Since the people did not make way, the horses came to a halt.
“You seem to be messengers—what news do you bring?” Azhwarkkadiyan asked.

“Yes, we are messengers! We bring grievous news. It is said that Prince Arulmozhi’s ship was caught in a whirlpool. The prince, in an attempt to save someone, leapt into the sea and has disappeared beneath the waves!”

As soon as one of the riders uttered these words, cries of “Ayyo! Aiyago!” rose from the crowd, their tones so sorrowful they seemed to rend the heart. No one knew from where such a multitude had gathered, nor could anyone say how they had assembled so quickly. Men and women, the old and the young, boys and girls—all surrounded the messengers in a great throng. Many bombarded them with questions; many wept and wailed.

It was already known to many in the city that the Pazhuvettarayars did not favor Arulmozhi. Rumors had reached their ears that the Pazhuvettarayars had sent men into Eezham to capture the prince and bring him back. Therefore, many in the crowd began at first to mutter about the Pazhuvettarayars. Soon, they began to curse them aloud.

“The Pazhuvettarayars must have deliberately drowned the prince in the sea—” “They must!”—so they spoke among themselves. The sound of their voices, their lamentations, and their curses against the Pazhuvettarayars all rose together like the mighty roar of the ocean.

In the midst of this crowd, the Thanjavur messengers found themselves trapped, unable to make their way up to the palace. Though they tried to push through the throng, their efforts were in vain. “How?” “Where?” “When?” “Is it certain?”—the people bombarded the messengers with questions, blocking their path and preventing them from moving forward.

Alwarkadiyan, seeing the guards who had come with the physician’s son, called out, “Why are you standing idle? Clear the crowd and escort the messengers to the palace!” The guards, too, were shaken by the news they had just heard. Now, gathering themselves, they stepped forward and tried to make way for the messengers. Gradually, the messengers began to advance toward the palace. The crowd, however, would not let them go, following close behind. More and more people joined, and the gathering swelled ever larger.

In that vast throng, where every heart was united in sorrow for Prince Arulmozhi and every voice was raised in lament, there was but one soul who cried out, “Alas! This is all a plot! A scheme to let the spy escape!” The physician’s son shouted thus, but no one paid him any heed. His cries fell on deaf ears. Like a great river in flood sweeping away a tiny twig, the immense crowd carried the physician’s son along with it, pushing ever forward.

As soon as the crowd began to gather, Vandiyathevan had dismounted from his horse. When the crowd started to move, Alwarkadiyan came up beside him and seized his hand. “Leave the horse! You can find it later. Come with me at once!” he whispered in Vandiyathevan’s ear.
“Ah, you have come to me as a savior in the nick of time! If not, who knows what would have become of me!” exclaimed Vallavarayan.
“This seems to be your fate, doesn’t it? To land yourself in trouble, and for someone to come and rescue you from it!” said Alwarkadiyan, with a touch of mockery.

The two of them stepped aside to the edge of the street, so the crowd would not sweep them away. After the crowd had passed, Alwarkadiyan took Vandiyathevan’s hand and led him in another direction, away from the palaces. They entered the locked mansion with the tall gateway that we have seen once before on the street. Passing through, they entered the garden in the backyard and walked along the winding paths bordered by creepers. After a short while, a blue-colored stream came into view. Upon its waters floated a small boat. In that boat sat a woman. The moment Vandiyathevan saw her, his heart leapt and danced with joy.

chapters.title: Mother and Son
paragraphs: Upon the word of the attendant who came to say that his mother had summoned him, Madurantakan went to see Sembiyan Maadevi. The fame of that venerable old lady, renowned for her deep devotion to Shiva, had spread throughout the land. Once, Madurantakan too had possessed boundless devotion towards his mother. Now, that devotion had transformed into a furious resentment. In all the tales he had heard, never had a mother been known to betray her own son and side with the heirs of another! Must such a mother befall him? The more he thought of it, the more the love in his heart turned to hatred, which, over time, had grown and flared within him.
Yet, upon seeing the mother’s face, suffused with an extraordinary peace, some of his anger abated. Following old custom, he bowed to her and stood up.
“May the wealth of your Shiva-bhakti ever increase and flourish!” blessed the queen, bidding him to be seated. That blessing pierced Madurantakan’s heart like an arrow.
“Madurantaka! Is my daughter-in-law well? Are all well in your father-in-law’s house and in the household of the Danadhikari?” the mother asked.
“All are well enough. Why should you be concerned about that?” the prince muttered.
“Before you left Thanjavur, did you see the Emperor? How is his health these days?” the queen asked.
“I saw him and took my leave before departing. The Emperor’s body grows weaker by the day. More than physical pain, it is mental anguish that torments him,” Madurantakan replied.
“What is this, child? What could have happened to cause the Emperor such mental distress?”
“Those who have committed wrongs—those who have acted unjustly, who seize and enjoy the possessions of others—it is natural for them to feel mental anguish, is it not?”
“What are you saying? What crime or injustice has the Emperor committed?”

“What else is there? Is it not enough that he has sat on the throne that should rightfully be mine for all these years? Is that not a crime? Is it not injustice?” “My child! How did this poison find its way into your heart, which was once as pure as milk? Who has corrupted you with evil counsel?” asked the mother in a voice filled with compassion.
“No one has corrupted me with evil counsel. Why do you consider your son so naive? Do you think I have no understanding of my own?”

“No matter how wise one is, the mind can be led astray by bad influence. Even stone can be dissolved if the right solvent is used, can it not? Was not Kaikeyi’s mind ruined by the evil counsel of the hunchback?”
“I too know that women’s minds can be corrupted in such a manner!”
“Madurandhaka! Whom are you referring to?”
“Mother! Tell me, for what reason have you called me here?”
“Just a while ago, you seemed happy at the celebration, did you not?”
“I was. You had a young boy, who was passing by, brought here in a palanquin. You seated him on the throne and honored him. He must be filled with pride beyond measure…”
“Oh! Do not speak so disrespectfully, my child. Though the guest who came was young in age, he is a great sage who has attained the fullness of spiritual wisdom…”
“Let him be a sage if he is. If I belittle him, will his greatness be diminished? I do not object to the royal honors you bestowed upon that sage. Just tell me why you have called me here!”

Sembiyan Madevi let out a long, deep sigh. Then she spoke: “The change that has come over your nature astonishes me. I never dreamed that two years’ stay in the Pazhuvettaraiyar palace would change you so much. Be that as it may, I must fulfill my duty. I must strive, as far as I am able, to keep the promise I gave your father, my son! Before I tell you the reason I have called you here, I must tell you my story—the history of how I married your father. Listen patiently for a while!”
Madurandhaka, as a sign that he was prepared to listen patiently, knelt down, braced his hands firmly on the pedestal, and sat attentively.

“You have visited my birthplace, Mazhapadi, once or twice when you were a child; you have also seen the temple of Lord Shiva in that town. I have heard the elders say that it is one of the sixty-four shrines built by King Kochchengat Chozha. Your grandfather, my father, was a prominent landholder in Mazhapadi. Our lineage is ancient. Once upon a time, the Mazhavarayars were influential minor kings. During the wars in the time of Vijayalaya Chozha, they sided with the Pandyas. Because of this, after the Chozhas triumphed, the power of the Mazhavarayars waned. When I was a little girl, I did not care about any of this. My heart was drawn only to the Nataraja in the temple at Mazhapadi.

A venerable elder once told me a story from the history of Mazhapadi when I was a child. Sundaramurthi Swamigal, along with his disciples, was traveling near our village. The temple at Mazhapadi was then surrounded by flourishing, thickly clustered konnai trees, their golden blossoms swaying and hiding the shrine from view. Thus, Sundarar passed by without noticing the temple. Suddenly, he heard a voice call out, ‘Sundara, have you forgotten me?’ Sundarar looked around and asked, ‘Did any of you say something?’ The disciples replied, ‘No, we heard nothing.’ Sundarar then wondered if there might be a hidden temple nearby. Searching among the konnai trees, he discovered the concealed shrine of Mazhapadi, hurried inside, and standing before the Lord’s sanctum, sang the hymn beginning, ‘O One with the golden-hued body!’
From the moment I heard this tale, O King! O radiant gem! O precious jewel of Mazhapadi! O Mother, but for you, Whom else shall I think of!

These lines became etched in my heart. I would often go to the temple, stand before the image of Nataraja, and recite those verses without ceasing. As days passed, the Lord of Mazhapadi took up residence in my soul. I built castles in my mind, dreaming that I would one day wed Lord Shiva himself. I imagined myself as Uma, as Parvati, as Dakshayani. Just as they had performed penance to win Shiva as their consort, I too would close my eyes and meditate in devotion. If anyone spoke of arranging my marriage, I would feel only aversion. Thus passed my childhood. When I reached maidenhood, my devotion to Lord Shiva grew even deeper than before. My family and the people of the town... They began to call me ‘Pichi’—the mad one. I paid no heed to any of it. Except for the hours spent eating and sleeping at home, I spent all my remaining time at the temple. I would pluck flowers for the puja, string them into garlands of various kinds, and delight in adorning Lord Nataraja with them! For long stretches, I would sit with my eyes closed, immersed in deep meditation.

One day, as I sat thus, eyes shut, mind wholly absorbed in contemplation of the Lord, a sudden burst of laughter and noise startled me. I opened my eyes. Before me stood five or six people. Of them, my gaze and thoughts were drawn to the one who stood foremost. In that instant, I believed that the very Lord Shiva I had been meditating upon had come to claim me, accompanied by his retinue. I rose, bowed my head, and stood in reverence. Tears streamed in torrents from my eyes. Surely, he must have noticed.
“Who is this girl? Why does she weep so?” a voice asked.

To this, my father replied, “She is my daughter. Like a fruit ripened while still on the branch, she has been seized by Shiva-bhakti at such a tender age. Without pause, she comes to the temple, sits with her eyes closed in meditation, sings hymns, and weeps thus!”

As these words reached my ears, I looked up once more. Then I realized—the man before me was not Lord Shiva, but a prince of royal lineage. The shame was unbearable. I fled from there, running all the way home. But the one who had claimed me did not let me go. He came to our house with my father.
My son! That man was none other than my husband, your noble father, Kandaraditya Devar!”
Having spoken thus, the great Maharani paused. Old memories brought fresh tears to her eyes. Wiping them away, she continued:

“Afterwards, I learned more about your father. Not long before, he had ascended the throne of Chola Nadu. Since then, he had journeyed to many sacred Shiva shrines, visiting and worshipping at temples. At that time, he was about forty years of age. The queen he had married in his youth had passed away. He had no intention of marrying again. He had taken a vow never to wed a second time. But when his pure heart beheld this foolish girl, it was stirred. In my father’s presence, he sought my consent. I, in my ecstasy, believed that Lord Shiva himself had come in human form to claim me. I was eager to marry him— I gave my full consent. Our marriage took place soon after. As a result, your grandfather regained the influence he had lost, and once again earned the title of ‘Mazhavaraayar’…”

“My son! After your father and I were married, we spoke openly with each other and came to a decision. We resolved to dedicate our lives to the service of Lord Shiva, and that neither of us would desire offspring. There was a significant reason for this. Child! Never, even in my dreams, did I imagine I would have to tell you all this. Yet, since such a necessity has arisen, I am telling you now. Listen carefully, and pay close attention!”
So saying, Sembiyan Maadevi let out another deep sigh. Madurantakan, with even greater attention than before, began to listen intently.

chapters.title: “Are You a Mother Too?”
paragraphs: The noblewoman, Chembiyan Devi, who shone as if the very embodiment of devotion to Shiva had taken form, continued to speak:

“My son! When your father, Kandaraditha Devar, ascended the throne, the Chola kingdom was plunged into a time of great distress. You are well aware of the glory of your grandfather, Parantaka Chakravarthi. During his reign, the Chola empire stretched southward to the land of Eelam and northward to the banks of the Krishna river. Yet, in his final days, many calamities befell both the kingdom and the royal family.

Like the main host of Ravana’s army, the forces of the twin Mandalams marched upon us. The eldest son of Parantaka Chakravarthi, your great father, Rajaditha Devar—peerless among warriors—set out to confront the mighty armies of the twin Mandalams. In the north, at a place called Thakkolam, a war as fierce as that of Kurukshetra was fought. Hundreds of thousands of warriors perished. Rivers of blood flowed in torrents. The armies of the twin Mandalams were scattered and fled, but in that battle, Rajaditha Devar fell. Your uncle, Arinjaya Devar, too, fought in that war and was grievously wounded. But at that time, nothing was known of his fate.

Arinjaya Devar’s eldest son, Sundara Cholar—a mere child—had gone to war in Eelam. There was no news of him either. In those troubled times, the only one of royal blood who remained near Parantaka Chakravarthi in the Tanjore palace was your father. But your father, even from his youth, had shunned affairs of state and devoted his heart to Lord Shiva. He had no liking for war. He lamented, ‘Why should people perish in battle for the land-hunger of kings?’ He argued this with his father and brothers. He spent his days in the company of great spiritual men, in pilgrimages to holy places, and in temple worship. He did not even wish to touch weapons like swords or spears. He had no training in the arts of war or battle strategies. He believed that kingship was filled with lies, deceit, trickery, disguises, counterplots, and sins like murder.
‘What difference is there between a thief stealing another’s property and a king conquering another’s land?’ he would ask.

My son! By the decree of fate, it came to pass that your father, with such convictions, had to bear the burden of this Chola land. Parantaka Chakravarthi, worn down by the many disasters that befell the kingdom and by the death of Rajaditha, grieved himself to death…” At the expected hour, your father was summoned and told, “You must bear the burden of the kingdom.” Your father, not wishing to further wound your grandfather’s heart as he lay on his deathbed, agreed. The fortunate Veeranarayani Devi, who had married your father before me, had already attained Shiva’s feet by then. As for me, I had not even seen your father at that time. Thus, after your father’s time, your grandfather became anxious about what would become of the Chola empire. By a stroke of fortune, at that very time, those who had gone to Eezham in search of your younger uncle’s son discovered Sundara Chola living on an island there, and brought him back.

Parantaka Chakravarthi cherished Sundara Chola beyond measure. From his childhood, he had cradled him on his lap, sung lullabies, and raised him with affection. Many elders had foretold that through Sundara Chola, the Chola dynasty would attain great glory.

For these reasons, your grandfather’s love for Sundara Chola was boundless. Therefore, when your father ascended the throne, your grandfather had decreed that the title of crown prince should be bestowed upon Sundara Chola, and that only his descendants should henceforth rule the Chola land. Having declared this, he departed to Shiva’s abode. Your father told me all these details. He was determined to fulfill the wish that Parantaka Chakravarthi had expressed on his deathbed. He resolved that neither Sundara Chola nor his descendants should face any obstacle in ascending the throne.

Your father had no desire to rule the kingdom; he had no attachment to royal affairs. He was a man of great virtue. His heart, at all times and in all seasons, dwelled upon the twin lotus feet of Lord Nataraja. Therefore, he entrusted all matters of state to his younger brother Arinjaya and to Arinjaya’s son, Sundara Chola. He himself was engaged in the service of Lord Shiva. As I have told you before, he had no intention of marrying again. But I was the one who came into his life and changed his resolve. Because he knew me to be a ‘madwoman’ devoted to Shiva, he grew fond of me and married me. I am fortunate to have gained him as my husband. I must have performed penance for countless births to attain him. You, who have him as your father, are also blessed. In this world, only a rare few have beheld the Lord with their own eyes and rejoiced. Lord Shiva, mounted on his bull, appeared before your father, granted him a vision, and took him from this earthly realm. Just as I now see you with my mortal eyes, your father beheld the Supreme Shiva. To fulfill the wishes of such a virtuous soul, you and I are both bound by duty...!”
When his mother finished speaking thus, the son who had been listening began to tremble. His body shuddered; his heart seethed with turmoil.
“How can this be, Mother! My father never revealed anything to me, did he? What duty am I bound to? In what way am I bound by duty?” asked Madurantakan.

“My son! Listen! When your father attained the lotus feet of Lord Shiva, you were but a small child. Therefore, he could not disclose anything to you. But he told me before he departed. When we were newly wed, we had resolved not to desire children. Yet, in my foolishness, I could not uphold that resolve. The devotion I had for Lord Shiva in my maidenhood transformed into love for your father. In time, my heart yearned for a child to cradle in my arms, to hold to my breast, to lull to sleep upon my lap and praise with endearments. Whenever I saw a child in another woman’s arms or lap, my whole body would tremble; my heart would burn with longing. I prayed to the Lord who had claimed me in my childhood. The Lord, too, granted this foolish woman’s plea. He gave you to me. On one side, having you filled my heart and body with joy; on the other, I feared I had incurred your father’s wrath. That great man did not grow angry with me. But he placed upon me alone the responsibility of fulfilling his vow.”

“My son! I promised your father that I would raise you to be a paragon of Shaivite devotion, untouched by worldly attachments. Until some time ago, I was proud, thinking I had fulfilled that promise.”

“But, my beloved son! My precious jewel, the apple of my eye! Of late, I have been hearing certain things. Every time I hear such talk, my heart is wounded. If all that I have heard is false, will you not assure me and heal the wound in my heart?” pleaded his mother, Sembiyan Maadevi.
“Mother! Your mysterious words wound my heart as well. What have you heard? What do you expect of me? What assurance do you seek from me?” Madurantakan retorted.

“My child! It seems you have lost the power to understand what lies in my heart! You insist I speak plainly; very well, I shall. I hear that your mind, once a river of Shaivite devotion, has now fallen into the muddy pit of worldly desire. I hear that you long to ascend the Chola throne—” “I have heard it said. I hear that our enemies have corrupted your sacred heart in such a manner. If you tell me that what I have heard is untrue, my mind will find peace!” said the old woman.
Until then, Madurantakan had been seated on his stool; now he rose to his feet. Seeing his agitation, his mother too stood up.

“No enemy has corrupted my mind. Are those who wish to see me ascend the throne my enemies? Are those who are ready to give their very lives for my sake my enemies? Never. In truth, who is my life’s enemy? It is you, the very woman who gave me birth!” Madurantakan cried.

Overcome by anger, he forgot all respect in that moment; he forgot the advice of the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar, who had urged him to speak gently and win over his mother’s heart, and instead poured forth a torrent of reproach.

“Yes, you are my life’s foe; there is no other. Are you even a mother? Are you even a woman? In this world, mothers endure countless hardships for the sake of their children’s rights. I have heard it in tales and epics, I have seen it in life. But you, whose nature is contrary to that of a true mother—are you a woman of mankind, or a demoness in a woman’s form? What treachery have I done to you? Why do you commit this great betrayal against me? By every law of justice, the kingdom that should rightfully be mine, you snatch away and give to another—what pleasure do you find in this? You say it is my father’s wish. You claim you made a promise to him. Where is the proof for all this? I do not believe it. You say someone has misled me. Not at all! It is you who have been misled by someone, it is your mind that has been corrupted. They have turned a mother into an enemy of her son. I will never relinquish my rightful Chola throne. Not even if you command me. Not even if my father, who has attained Siva’s feet, were to return and command me, would I obey. This Chola empire is mine; this ancient throne is my due; the jeweled crown once worn by Karikala Peruvallathan is my inheritance; I will attain them, whatever it takes. This Rudraksha garland you placed around my neck—I wore it all these days out of respect for you as my mother. But now, having made me a laughingstock before the land and people, having turned me into a coward, I cast off this Rudraksha garland at this very moment; you may keep it for yourself!”

Thus, raving like a madman, Madurantakan tried in haste to remove the Rudraksha garland from his neck. Unable to unfasten it, he tried to tear it off; but though his neck reddened, the garland remained.

Madurantakan was a man of striking beauty. One could even say he was more handsome than the sons of Sundara Chozhar. Upon his face shone a captivating, feminine charm that the others did not possess. But now, that gentle countenance was distorted by anger and agitation. Unable to bear the sight, Sembiyan Madevi closed her eyes.

After his loud outburst had subsided, she opened her eyes and looked at him. With not the slightest change in the calmness of her voice, she said, “My son! Be calm for a moment. Even if I am a deceitful demoness, at least incline your ear to my words and listen!”
Hearing that voice, Madurantakan calmed down a little. “I am listening well; I have not refused to listen, have I?” he said.

“You spoke of a mother’s nature. Even if she is a wicked demoness, a mother would never betray her own child. Even the most ferocious beasts strive to protect their young from other wild beasts. In the same way, I too am trying to protect you. There is another reason, apart from what I have already said, for my telling you not to desire the throne. The longing for the kingdom will bring danger to your very life. Is it wrong for a mother who bore and raised her son to wish that he should live? If you covet the throne, you will become an enemy to Sundara Chozhar’s sons. Both Aditya Karikalan and Arulmozhi Varman are warriors among warriors. You, on the other hand, are unskilled in the use of arms. The entire Chola army stands with Sundara Chozhar’s sons. The commanders too are on their side. In the neighboring countries, they have friends as well. Who are your supporters? On whom will you rely to wage war against them? My son! For the past few days, you must have noticed a comet blazing in the sky. The world knows that when a comet appears, it is an omen of danger to royal families. I am anxious only that such a calamity should not befall you. Child! Is it wrong for me to wish that my only son should live? Is that the treachery I commit against you?”
These words soothed Madurantakan’s anger a little. His heart softened.

“Mother! Forgive me! If you had told me earlier that this was your concern, I would have allayed your fears in a moment! I am not so friendless and helpless as you think. In the Chola Empire, many powerful minor kings and high officials are on my side. The Pazhuvettarayars are in my camp. Sambuvaryar of Kadambur is with me. Your own brother, my uncle, Mazhavarayar, is firmly on my side.
He is with me. Moreover, Neelathangaraiyar, the bearer of the twin royal umbrellas, and the great elder of Kundrathur, all support me with full strength. They have sworn oaths to stand by me…”

“My son! I have no faith in the oaths these men take. Once, they swore loyalty to Sundara Chola Chakravarthi and his descendants, promising to act with truth and fidelity. Perhaps they will act with loyalty towards you as well. But do you not know how meager their armies are? The northern forces are under the command of Aditya Karikalan. The southern army is led by the Velar of Kodumbalur…”
“Mother! The minor chieftains who support my cause can, at any moment, muster and bring ten thousand warriors to my side.”

“Let the armies be set aside for now. What about the people? Do you not know how much affection the people of Chola Nadu have for Sundara Chola’s sons? You saw it yourself today. If Arulmozhi Varman or Aditya Karikalan had come to this old city of Pazhayarai today, how the people would have gathered and welcomed them! Once, the people of this town too held you in affection. But ever since you allied yourself with the Pazhuvettaraiyars, the people have begun to hate you…”

“Mother! I am not the least concerned about the people’s affection. What use is the people’s love? The people are meant to be ruled; whoever sits upon the throne and governs, to them the people must offer their devotion!”

“My son! Those who taught you have not even imparted to you the first principles of political justice. No king can long rule without the affection of the people. Nor is there any virtue in ruling thus!”

As the venerable matriarch was speaking thus, a great commotion arose at the entrance of the palace. The cries of heralds, the voices of curses, shouts of anger, and the tumult of questioning voices rose from thousands of throats, blending into a mighty roar like the terrible sound of the ocean whipped by a fierce storm.

“My son! Some great calamity is approaching the Chola Empire. This is the first sign of it. I shall go outside the palace and find out what has happened. Until I return, you remain here!” said the mother.

Vandiyathevan was astounded. He stood rooted to the spot, unable to utter a word. The woman before him had asked the question with such deep emotion that it seemed to shake the very core of his heart.
“Are you a mother too?” she repeated, her voice trembling.

Vandiyathevan looked at her closely. The moonlight streaming through the window fell upon her face, illuminating her features. There was a strange beauty in her sorrowful eyes, a profound grief that seemed to have no end.
He hesitated for a moment, then replied softly, “No, Lady. I am not a mother. I am but a humble warrior, a servant of the Chola dynasty.”

The woman let out a long sigh. “Ah! Then you cannot understand the pain of a mother’s heart. You cannot know the agony of separation, the fear that gnaws at the soul when a child is far away, lost to sight and touch.”
Vandiyathevan’s heart ached at her words. He wondered who she was, what sorrow weighed so heavily upon her.

She continued, her voice barely above a whisper, “They say a mother’s love is boundless. They say a mother’s prayers can reach across oceans and mountains. But what use are prayers when fate is so cruel?”
Vandiyathevan could not bear her anguish. “Lady, do not grieve so. If you tell me your sorrow, perhaps I can help you. I am ready to risk my life for those in need.”
She turned away from him, gazing out into the night. “No one can help me. My son is lost to me. I do not even know if he lives or if he has perished in the dark waters of the Ponni.”
Vandiyathevan felt a chill run through him. The pain in her voice was unbearable.
“Who is your son, Lady?” he asked gently.
She did not answer. Instead, she began to weep silently, her shoulders shaking with the force of her grief.
Vandiyathevan stood helplessly, not knowing what to say or do. The silence in the room grew heavy, broken only by the sound of her quiet sobs.
After a while, she wiped her tears and turned to him. “Forgive me, stranger. My sorrow has made me forget myself. You are a guest in this house, and I have burdened you with my woes.”
“Do not say so, Lady,” Vandiyathevan replied. “It is an honor to share your grief. If there is anything I can do, please command me.”
She looked at him with gratitude. “You are kind. But some wounds cannot be healed by kindness. Only time can lessen the pain.”
Vandiyathevan bowed his head in respect. The woman’s sorrow had touched him deeply. He resolved to do whatever he could to help her, no matter the cost.
The night grew darker. The wind outside howled mournfully, as if echoing the pain within the walls of that lonely house.

chapters.title: “What is That Sound?”
paragraphs: As he neared the stream, Vandiyathevan clearly recognized that the young princess seated in the boat was none other than Kundavai herself. Since Azhwarkkadiyan was standing nearby, Vandiyathevan hesitated and paused.

“Why are you standing there, my friend?” said Azhwarkkadiyan. “The young princess has been waiting for you a long time. As soon as you board the boat, first tell her the good news: ‘The prince has arrived; he is safe.’ Don’t waste time recounting your heroic exploits! I am leaving now. Today, in Pazhayarai, we have unleashed the demon of chaos. Let me see if I can catch it and lock it up again. How many troubles your reckless adventures have caused!” With these words, Azhwarkkadiyan hurried away the way he had come.

Vandiyathevan was filled with wonder. How does he know all these details? He never asked me a single thing! Is it all guesswork? Or does he truly know everything? Among the Andis, there are two kinds: those who are Andis by lineage, and those who become Andis out of necessity; it seems there are two kinds among spies as well. I became a spy out of urgency; that’s why I keep landing in trouble. This Vaishnavan seems to be a hereditary spy; that’s why he does his work calmly and without any fuss. But for whom is he working? Is everything he told me about himself true?

Thinking thus, Vandiyathevan reached the bank of the stream and looked at the princess’s face in the boat. He forgot Azhwarkkadiyan. He forgot the mission he had just completed. He forgot the world—he even forgot himself.

Ah! This maiden’s face has never left his thoughts, not even for a moment. In dreams and in waking, in storm and on mountain, in forest and in the midst of the sea, it has always been with him. Yet what a wonder! When seen in person, why does the beauty of this face seem even greater? Why does his throat feel choked? Why does his heart beat so wildly?

Without conscious thought, Vandiyathevan stepped into the water, waded a few paces, and climbed into the boat. The princess signaled to the boatman, and the boat began to move. Vandiyathevan’s heart, too, began to sway. “Nimithakkara! Do you tell omens only for princes? Will you tell them for me as well? How do you divine omens? Do you look at the planets and stars in the sky? Or do you watch the crows and sparrows? Do you read the lines of the palm?… It seems you tell omens by reading faces. Otherwise, why do you keep staring fixedly at my face? If you behave so, no woman of noble birth will ever come to you to ask for omens!” said the young princess, her words ringing in Vandiyathevan’s ears like the sweet chime of anklets.
“My lady! I was not looking at your face to tell your fortune. I was only trying to recall where I had seen such a face before, as if I had glimpsed it somewhere, some time ago…”

“I know, I know! I know you are a master of forgetfulness. Let me remind you. Nearly forty days ago, you saw me for the first time at the house of the Kudanthai astrologer. Then, on that very day, you saw me again on the banks of the Arasalar river.”

“My lady! Please, stop! I cannot believe your words. Was it only forty days ago that I saw you for the first time? Was it not forty thousand years ago? Have I not seen you a hundred thousand times in a hundred different births? Did I not see you at the foot of a hill? Did I not see you atop a mountain peak? Did I not see you by the edge of a spring? Did I not save you when you came running, chased by a fierce tiger in the heart of a dense forest? Did I not hurl my spear and kill that tiger? At that time, I was a hunter roaming the woods! I caught beautiful parrots with multicolored wings in my net and brought them to you. You took those birds from me, released them to fly into the sky, and laughed with delight. Once, I was a fisherman. I traveled to distant lakes and rivers, caught silver fish, golden fish, emerald fish, and brought them to you. You took them from me and released them again into the flowing water, watching them dart away with joy. I journeyed to faraway seas, dived into the ocean’s depths, gathered pearls and corals, and brought them to you. You measured them in your hands, then called the little boys and girls of the village and poured the pearls and corals into their tiny palms. From the ilandhai tree that had grown for three hundred years, I waited for the fruit that ripens once every thirty years, plucked it, and offered it to you. You gave it to the naganavai bird you had raised, and watched with delight as it pecked and ate the fruit.
