I went to the celestial realm and brought you the mandara flowers that bloom there, and scattered them before you. ‘The beauty and fragrance of the jasmine that blooms on our garden fence far surpass these…’ “Would it suffice?” you asked. I brought you the incomparable ruby necklace worn by Devendran himself. “Would I, a woman of virtue, touch the garland worn by Indra the Immoral?” you replied. I journeyed to Kailasa, and after performing penance before Goddess Parvati, I brought back the anklet she wears at her divine feet. I promised to adorn your feet with it. “Oh no! How could the golden anklet of the Mother of the Universe touch my feet? What a sacrilege! Take it back and return it at once!” you cried.

I went to the battlefield, conquered the kings of sixty-four lands, gathered all their jeweled crowns, and laid them as an offering before you. You kicked those crowns away with your feet. I worried, “Alas! Would not your tender, flower-like feet be hurt?” Princess, are all these things true or not? Or is it only true that I first saw you forty days ago?” said Vandiyathevan. Even so, it seemed he had not finished speaking.

“Devi! Another memory comes to me. Once, we boarded a silver boat, grasped the golden-handled ivory oars, and journeyed through the celestial sea, parting the silvery waves beneath the moonlight…” he began.
“Oh dear! This omen-seeker seems to have gone completely mad. I must turn the boat around and take him back to shore!” said the princess.

“No, Devi, no! Just a short while ago, until this boat reached the shore, my mind was perfectly clear. Otherwise, would I have found a way to enter this city of Pazhayarai? Would I have convinced Madhurandhaka Devar that I was an omen-seeker and gained entry to the palace? Would I have so easily escaped from the physician’s son? Only when I boarded this boat and beheld your face did my mind become intoxicated, as if I had drunk wine!” said Vandiyathevan.

“Sir, in that case, you must not look at my face. Look at the clear waters of this stream. Look at the blue sky, the trees that rise up to the heavens along the banks, the palace towers, the crystal steps at the bathing ghats, the blooming white lotuses and red water lilies in this stream, or at least glance at this deaf boatman’s face. While you do so, tell me what happened to your mission—was it fruitful or not? Did you bring the prince? Is he well? Where did you leave him, and with whom? First, tell me all this. Then, recount everything that happened from the moment you left here!” said the princess.

To this, Vandiyathevan replied, “Devi! If I had not accomplished the task I promised you, would I have dared to return and show my face before you? I have brought the prince back from Lanka. I overcame a thousand obstacles that arose along the way and brought him here. But I cannot say the prince is well. When I parted from him, he was suffering from a severe fever. Yet, I entrusted him to safe hands. I left the prince in the care of the boatwoman Poonguzhali and the flower-seller’s boy, Sendhan Amudhan. If it were required a hundred thousand times to save the prince, they are people who would gladly give their lives for him!”

At that moment, from afar, there arose a terrible, tumultuous sound—a clamor like the unified roar of countless voices. Both the young princess and Vandiyathevan looked anxiously and fearfully toward the direction from which the noise came.
“What is that uproar? Does it not sound like the furious outcry of an enraged crowd?”
“Yes; that is exactly how it seems!” said Vandiyathevan.

chapters.title: Vanathi
paragraphs: If poets were asked to describe the beauty of the Princess of Kodumbalur, they would compare that maiden’s loveliness to the charm of twilight. When the day fades and dusk descends, a gentle melancholy settles upon the heart; yet, along with it, a serene delight also arises. After the sun’s final rays have waned and disappeared, the darkness of night gathers all around. To dispel the weariness that this brings to the mind, it is enough to gaze at the sky—how much joy is bestowed by the countless radiant lamps that Queen of the Heavens kindles in the blink of an eye! Unlike the blazing brilliance of the sun, they do not dazzle the eyes; one may gaze upon them and delight in their beauty. And if the moon has risen, nothing more need be said. The world is filled with the pearly glow of the full moon; heart and body are both suffused with its light. It is true that, at dusk, the lotuses close their petals. Yet, as if to rival the stars, jasmine buds burst open and bloom, and their fragrance intoxicates both earth and sky.

It is true that, once the sun has set, the joyous songs of birds fall silent. But listen! How sweet now are the deep notes of the temple’s bell and the melodious strains of the nadaswaram! From the tops of the palace towers, slender fingers pluck the veena and the yāzh, conjuring forth songs of exquisite delight!

In the beauty of Princess Vanathi of Kodumbalur, the hues of sorrow and the polish of joy were blended so subtly that they could not be distinguished. Her nature, too, was twofold, in keeping with her beauty. At times, she would appear as gentle and sorrowful as Chandramathi or Savitri, whose hearts were steeped in grief. At other times, she would shine as a living statue of joy, like an apsara or an urvashi, reveling in love and song in the celestial realms. Sometimes, she seemed the very image of Kannagi, mourning the loss of her beloved husband. At other times, she appeared like Valli, her heart entwined in longing for Lord Murugan. And again, she would glow with bliss, as if she were Deivayanai herself, garlanding Karthikeya while all the heavens rejoiced and danced in celebration.

For several days together, not even the faintest smile could be seen on Vanathi’s face. On other days, she would laugh without pause, her laughter scattering into the air in a million tiny droplets, mingling with the wind and filling the whole world… Such rapture, such ecstasy!

One might guess that the reason for Vanathi’s dual nature lay in the time and circumstances of her birth and upbringing. While she was yet in her mother’s womb, the young Velar of Kodumbalur was engaged in fierce wars. News of victory and defeat alternated, arriving one after another. These tidings brought joy and sorrow in turn to her mother’s heart. Not long after Vanathi was born, her mother passed away. Thereafter, her father raised Vanathi with the utmost care, cherishing her as the apple of his eye. But even this did not last long.

Vanathi’s father, a warrior among warriors, could not bear to remain seated in the palace, even for the sake of his beloved daughter. After Veerapandiyan had fled and hidden himself, her father pursued the supporting forces from Eezham, chasing them all the way to Lanka. There, on the battlefield, he gave up his life, earning in history the title “The Young Velar Who Fell in Eezham.”

After this, Vanathi’s life was for a time filled only with sorrow. Only those girls who have lost their mothers and been raised by their fathers can truly understand the depth of such grief. Though she was pampered and cared for in the palace of Kodumbalur, no one could ever fill the place her father had held in her heart. Many tried to comfort her in various ways. “Do not grieve, child! Your father will come into your womb and be born again as a heroic son; he will perform wondrous deeds of valor that will astonish the world,” said one.

These words sank deep into Vanathi’s heart and took root. To ease the sorrow and despondency caused by her father’s loss, she tried to immerse herself in thoughts of this imagined son. In this, she found some measure of success.

She would lose herself for days in a fantasy realm, imagining what sort of prince would be born to her, how he would walk, what heroic deeds he would accomplish. Through the eyes of her imagination, she saw that warrior son journeying to distant lands and winning great wars. She saw him returning swiftly, laying all the spoils of his victories at her feet. She saw him crowned, seated upon a heroic throne. She saw kings of kings coming to pay him tribute and bow before him. At the sight of his noble face, she saw crowds surge and roar like the ocean beneath the full moon. She saw him, with hundreds of ships filled with warriors, crossing the seas and planting the flag of victory in far-off lands. She heard him often come to her and say, “Mother! Is it not you who are the reason for all this greatness I have attained?”

Sometimes, that innocent, ignorant girl would touch and gently caress her own tender belly. She would wonder if, by some miracle, her imagined son had already come to dwell within her womb. In ancient Tamil Nadu, all men and women had heard the stories of the Mahabharata. They had heard of how Kunti Devi bore her children. Likewise, Vanathi would often marvel, wondering which deity might come to grant her the boon of a child. At such times, she never thought about marrying anyone. Only after she came of age, and gained some understanding of the world, did she realize that she must marry a husband, and that only through him could she attain the joy of motherhood. Even then, she did not indulge in much fantasy about her future husband.

After she went to the palace at Pazhayarai, there was a change in her life and in her disposition. The proud yet affectionate love of Kundavai Devi brought her comfort and delight. Kundavai’s refined manners, her elegant attire, her clever speech—all these transported Vanathi into a world she had never known before. The envy of the other royal maidens who had come to the Pazhayarai palace, just like her, awakened a new curiosity in her life. Her inner self told her that there must be some special grace within her, for others to be so envious. At the same time, her naturally sweet and generous nature prompted her to behave kindly with everyone. Yet, amidst all this, Vanathi never ceased to dream blissfully of the brave son she hoped to bear.

It was during this time that she had the chance to see Ponniyin Selvan. As a result, all the castles she had built in her mind crumbled to dust. She had learned that only after attaining a husband could she hope to bear a son. Until then, she had harbored a careless indifference—no matter who her husband might be, or what kind of man he was, it did not matter. But what could she do about this wayward heart of hers? Had it not gone and surrendered itself to the very prince who was the pride and joy of the Chola people? Was he not the illustrious one whom the kings of all the fifty-six kingdoms would beg and plead to marry their daughters? Would such a man ever even glance her way? Could she even dare to dream of the fortune of marrying him? Now that her foolish heart had turned toward the prince, how could she possibly marry anyone else? Thus, all the castles she had built in her mind about the heroic son she would bear had to be shattered and scattered. The more she thought of all this, the more her heart felt as if it would burst. Once again, she became her old, sorrowful self. Perceiving her state of mind, the young princess showed her special affection and support, and did her best to encourage Vanathi as much as she could. Her heart assured her that there was nothing wrong or impossible about her desires. The words spoken by the Kudanthai astrologer about the son she would bear fanned the embers of longing within her, nurturing her secret hopes. Her inner kingdom of dreams continued to expand. Melancholy and excitement alternated within her with ever-increasing speed. Just as she could not bear the pain of yearning, so too was she unable to contain the surges of joy that sometimes swept over her. When both these emotions became too much to endure, she would fall into a swoon; this natural, blessed oblivion was the medicine that preserved her life.

During her visit to Thanjavur, the play she had witnessed about Emperor Paranthaka, the terrifying voice she had heard that night, and the dreadful vision she had seen—all these had deepened her confusion. That day, she had come to understand the depth of the unending enmity between the Kodumbalur clan and the petty kings of Pazhuvur. She had also realized the extent of the influence wielded by the Pazhuvur lords in Chola Nadu at that time. Would the Pazhuvettaraiyars ever consent to her heart’s desire regarding Prince Arulmozhi? Even if they agreed, would the women of their household remain silent? Would the young queen of Pazhuvur give her assent? The world knew of her power and influence. Whenever Vanathi thought of Nandini, the image of a beautiful, venomous serpent came to her mind. She had learned of Nandini’s enmity towards the young princess; would that hatred not extend to herself as well? Why, even Ponniyin Selvan himself might not be immune to the touch of that poisonous snake! Had not a figure resembling Nandini appeared before the ailing emperor at midnight? Was it truly Nandini? What was the reason for the emperor’s terrified cries that night? Why did the young princess refuse to speak to her about any of this? Yes, the young princess’s heart had changed. She no longer spoke to her with the same cheerful intimacy as before. Often, she would leave Vanathi’s side and seek solitude. Some great sorrow seemed to weigh upon her. Was it perhaps a worry concerning Ponniyin Selvan? Was that why she avoided speaking of him?

Even today, the young princess had suddenly disappeared. In her absence, what torments did these women inflict upon Vanathi? What endless chatter did they indulge in? They knew nothing of sorrow or anxiety. Whatever happened, their boisterous merriment never diminished. Vanathi could never bear their teasing words. Especially during these past two or three days, as she had been drowning in a sea of sorrow, their idle talk grated harshly upon her ears. Wondering where the young princess might have gone, Vanathi set out in search of her. In the palace of the senior queen... She learned that some sort of assembly was in session and that he had gone there. So she went to the palace. Before Vanathi could arrive, the assembly had already dispersed. She heard that the great Maharani and her precious son, Madhurantakan, were engaged in a private conversation. For some reason, this news brought Vanathi even more anxiety. She left there once again. At the palace entrance, she heard the loud commotion of a crowd. She did not know what had happened. Her eagerness to see the Young Princess was overwhelming. She questioned each of the palace maids one by one. One maid said that just a short while ago, the Young Princess had been speaking privately with Alwarkadiyan, the valiant Vaishnavite, and then had gone towards the palace garden’s stream.

These days, when the Young Princess sought solitude, she did not wish to be disturbed by anyone. Therefore, Vanathi hesitated, wondering whether or not she should go in search of the Young Princess by the stream. At that moment, a maiden named Varini came running swiftly.
“Ponniyin Selvan has drowned in the sea!” she cried, delivering the dreadful news before bursting into tears. The other women, upon hearing this, began to wail in anguish.
At first, Vanathi felt no emotion at all. She simply stood there as the other women stared at her.
“You wretched girl! It is your misfortune that caused the prince to drown in the sea!”—it seemed as if all those eyes were striking her with those words.
Vanathi could bear it no longer. She could not remain there. She ran towards the stream in the palace garden.

As she ran towards the stream, Vanathi’s heart too was racing. The meaning of the words “The prince has drowned in the sea” became clear to her. Overcoming the shock that arose from it, another thought surfaced. For the past few days, whenever she looked at water, the prince’s face had been reflected in it. Whenever she stood on the bank and gazed, his face would appear vividly in the water. But if she tried to reach out and touch it, it would vanish. Now Vanathi understood the reason for this.

When the prince was drowning in the sea, he must have been thinking of me; he must have been calling out to me. Unaware of this, I, the wretch, stood idly on the shore, watching! Ah! What a terrible mistake I have made! There is no use in thinking of what is past. What must I do now?

Foolish girl! Is there anything left to ponder about what must be done now? What is there to think about? The stream beside the palace gardens merges with the royal river. The royal river flows on to join the sea. Beneath the sea, the prince awaits. He is waiting for me. In a wondrous palace beneath the sea, made of pearls and coral, he is waiting for me. What other task do I have in this world but to go and meet him? For whom else should I remain here?

Thus, as Vanathi resolved, a certain peace arose within her; her agitation subsided; her sorrow vanished; her worries were gone. She walked straight to the bank of the stream. She descended the steps made of crystal stone and stood there, looking all around. In the distance, she saw a boat approaching. The one in the boat was none other than the young princess herself. Who was the man with her? He seemed to be the youth she had first met at the house of the Kudanthai astrologer, the one who had carried a palm-leaf letter to Lanka. It must be he who has brought news about the prince! That must be why the young princess is taking him aside, questioning him, and learning the details. She has left me behind, thinking I would be distressed if I knew. If she arrives, I will not be able to act as I wish. She will try to console me, to comfort me, and will surely prevent me from going to join the prince.

Yet, is it right to leave without telling her, without bidding her farewell one last time? She, who has shown such affection to this orphaned girl without father or mother! Should I not at least utter a word of gratitude to her? No! I cannot wait even a moment longer! Look, I see his face in the water. There, his whole form shines forth. He is calling me; he smiles and beckons. “All obstacles to our union have vanished, come!” he calls. Why delay any longer?
Ah! Why does my head spin so? Is this a faintness, a swoon? No matter—so long as I do not fall on the bank, but into the waters of this stream!

Vanathi’s heart’s desire was fulfilled. She fell into the water. Her fevered body was soothed, her heart cooled. Down, down, down she went. How far, how long she traveled, she could not say. It might have been but a few seconds; it might have been many long ages.

Yes, she had reached that wondrous world beneath the sea. This must be the realm of the Nagas! Ah, what beautiful palaces! How many endless tiers of soft beds, rising so high that their summits could not be seen! How cool and enchanting is the light here! Perhaps the rays of light, passing through the water, have themselves become cool! From where does this light come? It seems to shine from the very walls of the palace!

It seems to be approaching! Yes. There is no wonder in that! Is it not natural for magnificent mansions, fashioned from gold and pearls, diamonds and sapphires, and crowned with the hoods of serpents and nagas, to radiate a cool, gentle light?

Look there—who are those coming in a crowd? How magnetic their bodies appear! What brilliance shines upon their faces! Do they not all seem like the men and women of the celestial realms? Have we, perchance, arrived in Nagalokam? Or have we entered Devalokam itself?

Then, like a dream within a dream, certain events unfolded with astonishing speed. They led Vanathi into a gem-studded hall adorned with exquisite decorations. In the center of the hall stood Ponniyin Selvan, his golden face aglow with a radiant smile, welcoming Vanathi. As divine drums resounded, bells and flowers rained down, and auspicious shouts filled the air, the prince and Vanathi exchanged garlands and were wed. Overwhelmed by the excess of joy, Vanathi fainted and fell. After lying unconscious for a long while, two hands gently lifted her up. At first, Vanathi thought those hands belonged to Ponniyin Selvan himself. She imagined he was the one who had lifted her, embraced her, and laid her upon his lap to revive her from her swoon. But when a bangle clinked upon her wrist, a slight doubt arose. “Vanathi! Vanathi! What have you done!” came a woman’s voice.
With great effort, Vanathi managed to open her eyelids a little. Kundavai’s face appeared before her eyes.
“Akka! Akka! Were you at my wedding? I did not see you there,” Vanathi murmured.

chapters.title: Memory Returned
paragraphs: Once again, Vanathi slipped into unconsciousness. Her eyes closed. Little by little, her awareness began to return. She realized that her marriage to the prince, in the realm of the Nagas or the Devas, had been nothing but a dream. She recalled the sorrowful news she had heard about the prince, how she had run to the riverbank in her grief, how her head had spun and she had fallen into the water. These memories brought her immeasurable disappointment; a sharp pain stabbed her heart like a spear. She tried to open her eyes, but could not.

Who could have lifted her from the water and brought her to the shore? It must have been the young princess. The woman approaching in the boat a short distance away must be Kundavai Devi. Why should she have saved her? Would it not have been better to let her drown and disappear forever? As soon as she could open her eyes and speak, she must quarrel with the young princess: “Why did you save me?” Was this all the affection she had for her beloved younger brother?
There—the young princess is speaking. What is she saying? To whom is she speaking? Let her listen.

“She is raving in her delirium! It is a great thing that she survived at all! What if our boat had been a little farther away? What if we had not seen her fall into the stream? Just the thought of it makes my heart tremble!”
“If we had not seen her, in one way it would have been for the best. The princess of Kodumbalur, whose life you have saved, would have been spared much sorrow in her life…”

‘Ah! Who is this speaking with such compassion for me? Yes, it is that young man—the brave youth I saw at the Kudanthai astrologer’s house and at the royal ferry! He must have brought the news of the prince’s drowning in the sea. What else are they going to talk about? Even if I cannot open my eyes, I can still hear well enough!’
“How can you speak so heartlessly? Are the hearts of men always made of stone?” said the young princess’s voice.
“What did I say now that makes you judge me as stone-hearted?” “If only this girl had died, you said—that wasn’t enough for you? Do you know how much hardship I have endured to raise her?”
“Did you hear the words she was raving?”
“What fell upon your ears?”
“Something about marrying the prince, I thought I heard…”
“Yes, even in her delirium, her lips kept murmuring so. Her desire for the prince has taken deep root in her heart.”
“That desire is not good for this girl! Only suffering and disappointment will come of it.”
“Why do you say that? Who else is more suited to the prince than this girl? Are you not aware of the ancient, valiant lineage of Kodumbalur from which she descends?”
“I know it well. But what I think is one thing; what you say is another. What does it matter how noble her birth is? The longing in her heart will never be fulfilled…”
“It will certainly be fulfilled. That longing is not hers alone—it is my heart’s desire; it is the decision I have made.”
“Even if it is your decision, it will not come to pass in this matter.”
“Why do you say that again? Did you not just say that the prince is safe at the Chudamani Vihara in Nagapattinam?”

‘Ah! What joyous news is this? The prince is safe? He is at the Chudamani Vihara in Nagapattinam? Were these ears given to me just to hear this news? How fortunate it is that I did not drown myself in the stream and die! I already owed the young princess a debt of gratitude in so many ways—now, this too is added.’
‘But alas! What is this news she now speaks? It is like pouring hot oil into my ears!’
“Lady! It is true that the prince is safe. But what certainty is there that this girl’s desire will be fulfilled because of it? I do not believe the prince will marry this girl…”
“You may think whatever you wish. In this world, is there a man who can cross the fortress I have built, or go against my word and still succeed? That man is my brother, Arulmozhi Varman!”
“Princess! I too am one such man…”
“Then what is lacking for me? What obstacle stands in the way of my wish being fulfilled? Will even the Pazhuvettarayar nobles dare to interfere in this matter?”

“I do not know that. But I know that you have boundless affection for the prince. In all other matters, he will heed your words. He has no desire whatsoever to rule the kingdom. Before my very eyes, he refused the crown of Lanka. Yet, if you were to insist, he would even consent to rule the realm. But to marry this maiden…”
“Are you saying he would not consent? What fault has he found in my dear friend that he would reject her? What fault do you see in her?”

“Lady! I see no fault in this maiden; even if I did, I would not believe it. Of all the maids who serve the younger princess in the palace, even the humblest servant girl seems to me a divine maiden. The baby monkey that lives in the princess’s garden appears to my eyes more splendid than Indra’s own Airavata. The prince too has found no fault in this maiden. But perhaps his heart has turned toward another woman…”
‘Alas! What cruel words! Why does this youth thus drive a blade into my wounded heart?’
“Brave warrior of the Vanar clan! I do not understand what you are saying. Why do you cast such slander upon my brother?”
“It is no slander, Lady! I speak only the truth—what I have seen with my own eyes and heard with my own ears.”
“Speak further! I am now prepared to hear even the most difficult matter.”

“I spoke of the boatwoman, Poonguzhali, did I not? She is the one who took me to Lanka. She is the one who saved both the prince and me from the sea. She is the one who ferried the prince to the Choodamani Vihara. I would never have entrusted the prince to Sendhan Amudhan alone; it was only because I trusted Poonguzhali that I did so. If that maiden had a thousand lives, she would offer them all to the prince…”

“So what of it? A boatman’s daughter is still a boatman’s daughter, is she not? Can she ever dream of wedding a man born to rule the world? Can the little sparrow that hops and flutters on the ground ever hope to gaze upon the mighty Garuda soaring high and circling the sky?”
“Why not? The sparrow too can lift its eyes and behold the Garuda; and the Garuda, in turn, may bend its gaze and long for the sparrow.”

“If such a thought has arisen in my brother’s heart, it is my duty to drive it away. It must not be! I have saved Arulmozhi Varman from countless dangers. I shall save him from the enchantment of this boat-girl as well…”

“Is being a boat-girl such a great fault? Are lineage and clan so very important? Does not the same red blood flow in the veins of the boat-girl? Does her heart not beat just as fiercely as that of a princess born in a palace? If you look closely, even the love of princesses may be tainted with ambition for the throne and other desires. But the love of that boatman’s daughter is pure, unblemished, and sacred. The prince believes so too. Why should others come between them and obstruct their path? Now, take my own case. If only I could split open my heart and show you what lies within…”

“No, no. Let what is in your heart remain safe and untouched. That is best. Love, desire, passion—these are well and good for ordinary mortals. But for those born to rule a kingdom, it is different. They must wed within royal blood. They must not let their hearts go astray. If they do, it will bring endless troubles. There is an example of this in our own family. In my father’s youth—when he had no thought of ever ascending the throne—he too… with a girl raised in the forests…! But why should I tell you all this now? Look, this girl is regaining consciousness; her eyelids are fluttering. Is there nothing else to speak of? Did you not say that you faced many dangers in Eezham? Tell me of those.”

“Yes, Princess! On the day the prince refused the throne and the jeweled crown of Lanka, as we were walking through the streets of Anuradhapura, suddenly the front portion of a building collapsed. Had we tarried there a moment longer, it would have fallen upon our heads. We would have been entombed alive. At that moment, a lady appeared suddenly. She signaled and called the prince…”
“I do not know who she is. But she seemed to be someone familiar to the prince… Do not fall prey to needless suspicion, Lady! That woman is of mature age…”
“How old would she be?”
“She could well be the prince’s mother. Moreover, she is deaf in her ears, and mute as well!”
“What? What did you say? Please, say it again!”
“A woman both deaf and mute by birth… She must be over forty-five years old…”
“Sir! Did you see such an old woman in Eezham? Tell me more about her. Do you know anything of her birth or upbringing? Where was she born?”
“She was born on an island in the sea, near Eezham…”
Princess Kundavai, overcome with boundless agitation, exclaimed, “Sir! Tell me more! What does she look like?”
“Lady! I saw a marvel in her appearance. I hesitate even to speak of it.”
“Do not hesitate! Speak quickly.”

“She looked exactly like a woman I have seen in Chola country; only older in years. She wore no ornaments or fine clothes, her hair was loose and unadorned. But otherwise, the same face! The same features. Truly, for a moment, I was utterly deceived.”
“Sir, who is the woman here who resembles her so?”
“Princess! Can you not guess and find out for yourself?”
“Me? Is it Vanathi? Or my mother, who is in the palace at Thanjavur?”
“It is none of those you mention.”
“Is it Nandini, the younger queen of Pazhuvoor?”
“Yes, it is Nandini!”
“Heavens! Then what I suspected is true.” “What did you suspect?”

“I once despised her, thinking she was more venomous than a poisonous serpent. Yet, I doubted—could she truly be my own sister? From your words, I now know it is true. The cruelty of fate is the greatest cruelty of all. Now I understand how complicated it is for a prince of royal blood to wed a woman of unknown lineage and clan.”

“Lady! I am not one whose lineage and ancestry are unknown. For three hundred years, my forefathers have ruled the land of pure Tamil. They have imprisoned the Cheras, Cholas, and Pandyas. Though today I possess no kingdom, I still have my sword in hand; there is strength in my shoulders; there is courage in my heart…”
“Sir! Spare me your boasts for now. There are many urgent matters to attend to. I still need your help. Will you grant it?”
“If I had a thousand lives, I would gladly give them all to you.”
“You seem as if you are truly the brother of that boat-girl, Poonguzhali. Very well; let us leave that conversation for another time. Look, this young woman is about to open her eyes…”

Yes; by now, Vanathi had regained full consciousness. Strength had returned to her body. Many thoughts sprang up in her mind. She resolved that she must live—at least until she could prove to the prince that her love was greater than that of the boat-girl. At that moment, the vision and the wailing she had witnessed one night in the emperor’s bedchamber at the Thanjavur palace came back to her memory! The meaning of those sights and sounds began to dawn on her.
As Vanathi opened her eyes, the young princess asked affectionately, “My dear! How are you feeling now?”
“There is nothing wrong with me, Akka. I only feel troubled because I have caused you so much worry,” Vanathi replied.

At that moment, Azhwarkkadiyan entered and said, “I too have come to cause trouble. Devi! There is a great crowd and confusion at the palace gates! The people are in a rage over the news that the prince has drowned in the sea. If you do not come at once and calm them, disaster may ensue.”

The Pandya brothers, who had been standing like stone statues until then, suddenly sprang to life. Their eyes, which had been fixed on the floor, now blazed with a strange fire. The eldest among them, Ravidasan, stepped forward and said, “O noble one, you have spoken words that have pierced our hearts like arrows. You have reminded us of the days when the Pandya throne shone like the midday sun, and the Pandya crown sparkled like the full moon. You have rekindled the embers of our sorrow and our rage.”

The second, Parameswaran, clenched his fists and said, “Yes, the memory has returned! The memory of the day when the Chola tiger pounced upon the Pandya lion and tore it to pieces. The memory of the day when the blood of our king, Veerapandiyan, flowed into the earth of the battlefield. The memory of the day when the Chola sword drank the life of our lord!”

The third, Soman Sambavan, ground his teeth and hissed, “We swore that day, upon the blood-soaked soil, that we would not rest until we had avenged our king. We swore that the Chola dynasty would pay for its crimes. We swore that the tears of the Pandya queen would be wiped only by the blood of the Cholas!”

Ravidasan’s voice trembled with emotion as he continued, “But fate has not favored us. The Cholas have grown stronger with each passing day. Their power has spread like wildfire. Their banners fly over lands that once belonged to the Pandyas. Their ships sail the seas that once bore the Pandya insignia. Our hearts burn with helplessness.”

Parameswaran said, “But now, a ray of hope has appeared. The gods have sent us a messenger. The time for vengeance is near. The day is not far when the Pandya lion will roar again, and the Chola tiger will cower in fear!”
Soman Sambavan added, “Let us not waste another moment. Let us act now, before the fire in our hearts is extinguished. Let us fulfill the oath we took on that fateful day!”

The three brothers turned to the nobleman who had addressed them earlier. Their faces were alight with a fierce determination. Ravidasan said, “You have awakened our memories. You have rekindled our resolve. Tell us, noble one, what must we do? Lead us, and we shall follow you to the ends of the earth!”
The nobleman smiled, a cold, calculating smile. “The time has come,” he said. “The hour of vengeance is at hand. The Chola dynasty will tremble before the wrath of the Pandyas. Let us begin!”

chapters.title: The Prime Minister Arrives!
paragraphs: The streets of Pazhaiyarai that day were in a state of commotion the likes of which had never been seen before. Crowds upon crowds of people streamed towards the part of the city where the royal palaces stood. Men and women, the old and the young, youths and children, all moved in groups, making their way together. Among them were Shaivites and Vaishnavites; Buddhists and Jains mingled in the throng. Here and there, a few fierce Kalāmukha ascetics, known for their severe vows, could also be seen amidst the crowd.

Many among the people wept and wailed as they went. Some cursed the Pazhuvettaraiyars loudly as they walked. Here and there, some youths could be seen carrying sticks in their hands. From time to time, they would strike each other’s sticks, making a sharp clacking sound as they walked. Whenever the sound of the sticks echoed, some would mutter, “Strike like that on the heads of the Pazhuvettaraiyars!” while others shouted it aloud. Among those who shouted, the Kalāmukhas were the most prominent.

The façades of the principal royal palaces in Pazhaiyarai were shaped like crescent moons. All the palaces together shared a vast open courtyard in front, known as the Nilā Muttam—the Moon Courtyard. On special occasions, this courtyard was spacious enough to hold tens of thousands of people. Surrounding the courtyard on the outside was a high enclosing wall. That wall had three gates. At each gate, a few palace guards stood watch.

The surging crowds now began to gather near all three gates of the Moon Courtyard. With every passing moment, the crowd grew denser. Only the two messengers who had brought the news, along with the town servants who had escorted them, were allowed inside by the palace guards. All others were stopped and held back.

But it was not possible to restrain them for long. From somewhere within the crowd, voices began to rise, calling out, “Go inside! Go inside!” Those at the back pushed those in front. Was it not like the waves of the sea, each one pushing the next, until at last a great wave crashes upon the shore? So it was with this human sea. Those in front, pressed by those behind, surged forward, pushing aside the guards at the gates and pouring into the courtyard.

That was all it took! Just as a small breach on the banks of the Kaveri quickly widens, letting the floodwaters rush through with a roar—so too did the crowd now flood into the palace grounds. The people surged into the moonlit courtyard with a thunderous commotion. In a short while, the courtyard was filled to the brim. Thousands had gathered there.

As the crowd broke past the guards and poured into the moonlit courtyard, the uproar they caused reached the ears of Sembiyan Maadevi, who was conversing with Madurantakan. She immediately ceased her debate with the prince and moved to the front balcony of the palace’s upper floor. The moment the multitude beheld the divine visage of that venerable matriarch, her serene countenance, and her folded hands raised in benediction, the tumult of that oceanic crowd subsided. For a few moments, silence reigned there.
“Mother! Where is our prince? Where is Ponniyin Selvan? Where is Arulmozhi Varman, the apple of your eye?” voices rose from the crowd.
That was enough; the uproar in that sea of people swelled many times over.

Sembiyan Maadevi stood bewildered, as if she understood nothing. She knew only this: some danger had befallen Ponniyin Selvan, who had stolen the hearts of the people of Pazhaiyarai. But what was that danger? How had it come about? Had the Pazhuvettaraiyars committed some terrible deed, bringing an indelible stain upon the Chola dynasty and upon Madurantakan?

At that moment, the messengers from Thanjavur forced their way through the crowd and came forward. One of the attendants who had brought them announced, “Perumatti! They have come from Thanjavur bearing important news!”
Sembiyan Maadevi gestured for the crowd to be calm and turned to the messengers. “What news have you brought?” she asked.

“Mother! We are the unfortunate bearers of grievous tidings. By the Emperor’s command, Prince Arulmozhi Varman was sailing from Lanka to Kodikkarai; on the way, the ship was caught in a cyclone. The vessel that accompanied him broke apart and sank. To save those aboard, the prince leapt into the sea. He has not been found since. Arrangements have been made to search the sea and the shores. The Emperor and the daughter of Malayaman, upon hearing this news, are plunged in deep sorrow. The Emperor has sent word through us, asking that you, Lord Madurandakan, and the young princess depart at once for Thanjavur!”

Thus, the words spoken by the messengers reached the ears of Sembiyan Maadevi. At the same moment, they fell upon the ears of the gathered crowd as well. Tears welled up in torrents from Sembiyan Maadevi’s eyes. Witnessing this, the people cried out all the more, “Oh!” in anguish.
One among those standing at the front of the assembly called out, “Mother! You must not go to Thanjai; nor should the young princess go to Thanjai! The Emperor must be made to come here!”
Another shouted, “It is a lie that Ponniyin Selvan drowned in the sea; it is the Pazhuvettaraiyars who must have killed him!”
Yet another voice declared, “Madhurantakan too should not go to Thanjai. He must remain here!”
Voices cried out, “Where is the young princess? We wish to see her!”
Sembiyan Maadevi turned to one of the attendants beside her and instructed her to summon the princess.

At that very moment, Azhwarkadiyan, who had mingled with the crowd below, quietly slipped away. Taking his usual shortcut, he swiftly made his way to the house with the flag, where Kundavai Devi was tending to Vanathi, who was just regaining consciousness. He relayed to her the last words the young princess had spoken to Vandiyathevan, and informed her of the tumult unfolding in the palace courtyard.

Entrusting the task of reviving Vanathi to her handmaidens, the young princess hastily set out. As Kundavai Devi approached Sembiyan Maadevi on the upper terrace of the palace, she noticed tears streaming from the old queen’s eyes. The sight brought tears to Kundavai’s own eyes as well. Witnessing this, the assembled people were plunged deeper into a sea of sorrow.
“Ponniyin Selvan did not drown in the sea. The Pazhuvettaraiyars have killed him. They must pay for their crime!”
“The Emperor is being held captive by the Pazhuvettaraiyars. He must be freed and brought here. If the princess commands, we are ready to set out this very instant!”
Thus did those in the crowd address the young princess.

Kundavai’s mind was seized by intense thought. The truth that the prince was alive could not be revealed at this moment. Yet, she must pacify the people and send them away reassured. A way occurred to her.

Wiping away the tears that brimmed in her eyes, the princess looked at those standing in the front row of the crowd. By then, Azhwarkkadiyan and Vandiyathevan had come and stood there. The young princess signaled to Azhwarkkadiyan to come up. He immediately ascended to the upper level. Kundavai spoke something to him in a soft voice.
Azhwarkkadiyan gestured to the people to be silent. In a voice that thundered like the roar of clouds, he proclaimed:

“The young princess cannot believe that Ponniyin Selvan has died. Just as once Mother Kaveri saved the prince by carrying him in her arms, she believes that now the King of the Ocean too has protected him. The soothsayer was consulted, and he too says the same. The princess will make the necessary arrangements to search for and find the prince. She requests all of you to return home in peace!”
No sooner had these words been spoken than a great sigh of relief, like a long exhalation, arose from the crowd.
“Where is the soothsayer? We too wish to hear this good news from his own mouth,” called out someone.

Seeing his chance, Vandiyathevan leapt and climbed up to the upper terrace. Azhwarkkadiyan stood nearby and said, “It is true that a great danger befell the prince. But his life is in no peril; he will soon be found!”
“How do you know this?” came a voice.
“I am the soothsayer; I have read the planets and the stars and learned the truth; I have read the omens and understood.”
“Lies! What you say is false! You are not the soothsayer! You are a spy!” the same voice accused.
Vandiyathevan looked closely at the man who spoke and recognized him as the physician’s son.
“Madman! Are you calling me a spy? If I am a spy, whose spy am I?” he retorted.
“The spy of the Pazhuvettaraiyars,” the physician’s son retorted sharply.
“What did you say?” Vandiyathevan roared.

Vandiyathevan stood on the upper balcony, twelve feet above the moonlit courtyard where the people had gathered below. Without a second thought, he leapt from the balcony straight at the physician’s son. A fierce struggle broke out between the two. Is there not, at all times and for all people, a certain delight in watching a fight? The crowd formed a wide circle around the spot where Vandiyathevan and the physician’s son wrestled, watching the spectacle with eager eyes. Those on the upper balcony gazed down anxiously at the scene. Most of the crowd, not knowing what had sparked the conflict, began to shout and clamor even louder than before.
At that moment, from near the entrance, the sound of conch shells and trumpets was heard.
“The Prime Minister Aniruddha Brahmarayar is arriving! Make way!” came a commanding cry.
In that great throng, a path opened up of its own accord for the Prime Minister.

chapters.title: Aniruddha’s Prayer
paragraphs: The palanquin bearing the Prime Minister, Aniruddha Brahmarayar, made its way through the gathered crowd in the moonlit courtyard. The people parted to either side, making way for him, and as he passed, they offered their respects. Many voiced their worries about the prince. The Prime Minister’s face, too, was clouded with concern. Yet, raising both hands, he gestured to the people, offering them comfort and blessings as he went.

When the palanquin reached the entrance of the palace, it was set down. The Prime Minister stepped out and first looked up. Seeing the Periya Rani and the princess standing above, he offered them his salutations. Then he turned his gaze to the spot where the recent skirmish had taken place. All this while, Vandiyathevan and Pinagapani, oblivious to the events around them, had continued their quarrel. Alwarkadiyan slipped in between them and whispered something in the Prime Minister’s ear. Turning to his attendants, the Prime Minister commanded, “Arrest these ruffians who are causing a disturbance in the palace courtyard at once!” Alwarkadiyan, along with the attendants, pushed through the crowd. The attendants seized the two combatants and bound their hands with rope. At a signal from Alwarkadiyan, Vandiyathevan offered no resistance as he was taken into custody.

Aniruddhar ascended to the upper floor. Standing there, he addressed the crowd: “I know your worries and your anger. The Emperor and the Queens are as deeply grieved as you. Do not do anything that will add to their sorrow. Arrangements have already been made to search for the prince. All of you, please return to your homes in peace.”
“We want to see the Emperor! The Emperor must return to Pazhaiyarai!” someone in the crowd called out.
“What is the fate of our brave men in Lanka?” another asked.

“The Emperor is safe in the Tanjore palace. The Velakkara guards are watching over him day and night. I myself will bring the Emperor to this city as soon as possible. Do not worry about our men in Lanka; the war there has ended in complete victory for us. Our soldiers will soon return and—” “The Chera forces are coming!” announced the Prime Minister, and at once a great wave of excitement and jubilant shouts swept through the crowd. The people offered their praises to Sundara Chozhar and Anbil Aniruddhar, then began to disperse.
The Prime Minister turned to the Great Queen and said, “Devi, I must speak with you about matters of utmost importance! Shall we proceed inside the palace?”
He glanced at the Princess and added, “Amma! I will come to you later.” With that, Kundavai set off toward her own chambers.

At that moment, her mind was beset by many worries. If there was anyone in the Chola Empire whom Kundavai feared, it was the Prime Minister Aniruddhar. He was a man with the eyes of a hawk. Not only could he see with his outward gaze, but he seemed to pierce right through the hearts of those before him, reading their innermost thoughts. How much did he know—how much did he not know? What could she reveal to him, and what must she conceal? The young princess was plagued by confusion. That he had ordered both the valiant scion of the Vanar clan and Pinagapani to be imprisoned had kindled anger in her heart. Yet she could not show it openly. Nor could she plead on Vandiyathevan’s behalf before that vast assembly. “He said he would come to me later? Let him come; I will see what I can do!” she resolved inwardly, hurrying toward her private quarters.

Sembiyan Maadevi was a figure revered by all in the Chola Empire, inspiring awe, devotion, and respect. Prime Minister Aniruddha Brahmarayar was no exception. Yet, at this moment, the venerable queen seemed to carry herself with a certain fear. She did not take her seat until Aniruddhar was seated.
“Ayya! For some time now, thunderbolt after thunderbolt has been striking my head. Have you brought more such tidings? Or are you come to offer words of comfort?” she asked.
“Ammani! Forgive me! I cannot answer your question just yet. It depends on how you receive the news I bring,” he replied, a master of subtlety.

“Ayya, is the news about Ponniyin Selvan true? I cannot bring myself to believe it! What hopes we have cherished for Arulmozhi Varman! How many times have we spoken of him as one born to rule the world beneath a single parasol’s shade?...”
“Perumatti! What you told me about the astrologers’ predictions is indeed true. I have never spoken against you; nor have I spoken in agreement!”
“Let that be. Tell me now—Is it certain that the Prince of Ponni has been abducted by the King of the Seas?”
“Who can say with certainty, Mother! But it is certain that such news has spread throughout the land and all the cities.”
“If it turns out to be true, what will be the fate of this Chola country? What kinds of calamities will befall us?”
“It seems the calamities will not wait until the truth is known…”
“Yes, yes! Even a rumor is enough to bring disaster. Never before have I seen the people of Pazhayarai gather in such anger and enter the palace in such numbers…”

“Do not think this has happened only in Pazhayarai; the city of Thanjavur has been in utter turmoil since yesterday. The Velakkara soldiers have deserted the Emperor’s palace. Crowds of people have surged into the fort, surrounding the mansions of the Pazhuvettarayars. It became necessary to unleash the temple elephants upon the crowds to disperse them…”
“Alas! What a calamity! What a terrible piece of news!”
“It is fortunate that Madurantakan has come to Pazhayarai. Otherwise, that dreadful blame would have fallen upon him as well…”
“Sir! You would be astonished if you knew how much Madurantakan has changed.”
“I would not be astonished, Mother! I have known of these matters for some time now.”
“Even knowing, you made no attempt to change his mind. At least now, offer some advice and help us.”
“Amma! I do not think there is any need to change Madurantakan’s mind. I have come here to speak in support of his cause…”
“If that is so? I do not understand, sir!”

“Lady! Madurantakan believes that this Chola throne is rightfully his. He desires to rule this kingdom after the Emperor. It is a just wish, a longing that has taken deep root in his heart. To try and prevent it will not bring any good to the Chola realm. It is only proper to fulfill it…”
“Oh no! What words are these? Have even you dared to betray the Chola Emperor? What a calamitous age is this?”

“Periyamatti! Not even in my dreams have I thought of betraying the Emperor. I have come here under his command. I am only conveying what he asked you to consider: after his time, Madurantakan wishes to ascend the throne. The Pazhuvettarayar clan is plotting for this. But now, the Emperor himself wishes to crown Madurantakan and step down from the throne. He has sent me to obtain your consent for this…”

“The Emperor may wish so. But my consent will never be given for such a thing. I will not agree to anything that goes against my husband’s wishes. O First Minister, who has seen the shores of the ocean of learning! Even if the Emperor himself commands, how could you come to me with such an unjust proposal? Have you completely forgotten that there are truths about the right to the Chola throne known only to you and me…?”
“Lady! I have forgotten nothing. There are truths known to me that you do not know. That is why I have come to you as the Emperor’s envoy…”
“Sir! The world knows your intelligence and your skill in statecraft. Do not try to display them to me, a woman…”
“Periyamatti! I have not come to argue with you. Nor have I come to display my cleverness. I have come to plead and pray that you save this Chola land from great peril.”
“Offer your prayers to the crescent-crowned Lord, or to your chosen deity, Vishnu Murti…”
“Yes, Mother! If you do not show your magnanimity, then only the Lord of the Hall and the Lord of the Stage can save this land.”
“What danger has come upon this land, then? How can it be prevented by stopping Madurantakan from ascending the throne?”

“Listen, noble lady! Today, this city’s people have risen in unrest; within two or three days, from Kanchipuram to Rameswaram, the people everywhere will be inflamed with anger and rise up as well. It will not end there. I have learned that from Lanka, Boothi Vikramakesari has already begun gathering his forces and set out. When the news reaches Aditya Karikalan, he too will not remain patient. He will march towards Thanjavur with the northern army. The Pazhuvettarayar chieftains and other minor kings have already begun mustering their troops. A terrible war of succession, like the battle between the Kauravas and the Pandavas, will erupt in this land. All your kith and kin will be destroyed. Are you going to stand by and watch all this happen…?”
“Sir! O first among ministers, wise and subtle-minded! I have no kith or kin. You must have heard of the great soul, Shankara, who was born in the mountain lands to the west. That sage has declared:
‘Mother is Parvati Devi, Father is Lord Maheshwara, My kin are the devotees of Shiva…’
My mother is Parvati Devi. My father is Parameshwara; my kin are the devotees of Shiva—there are no other bonds for me in this world…”
“Lady! I remind you of the fourth line in that same verse of Shankara:
‘Swadesho bhuvanatrayam’— He himself has said so. The land of our birth is for us the three worlds. Will you stand by and watch your own country destroyed by civil war?”

“My own land is indeed dearer to me than the three worlds. But is this narrow stretch of Chola land truly our own country? Never. The land stretching north to the Kailasa mountains is my country. If there is no place for me in Chola land, I will go to the sacred city of Kashi; I will go to Kashmir and Kailasa. I have long cherished the thought of such a pilgrimage—help me to set out on it…”

“Mother! I accept that our homeland stretches from the southern Trikona hills to the northern Imothgiri. This vast, sacred land of Bharata is now facing a great peril. The Patanis, Turks, Mughals, and Arabs—these foreign races are rising up in waves, setting out to conquer new lands. Just as, a thousand years ago, the Yavanas and Hunas invaded with their armies, now these followers of a new faith are marching in battalions upon our country. Their religion is a strange one—they believe it is virtuous to destroy temples and break idols.

Oh Lady! There are no great emperors left in the North now to stop them. I have dreamed that the warriors of Chola Nadu will march as far as the Ganga, even beyond to the Himalayas, and establish a mighty Bharata empire, halting the hordes who destroy our temples. Help me make that dream a reality. Consent to crown Madurantaka, and help prevent a succession dispute in Chola Nadu!”
Hearing this, Sembiyan Maadevi fell into deep thought for a while. Then she said,

“Sir! You have spoken of matters that this foolish woman cannot comprehend, and you have left me troubled. If such a danger were truly to befall this sacred land of Bharata, it is for the Lord of All to see and avert it. What can a helpless woman like me do? I will never forget what my husband told me before he departed this world. I will never act against his wishes!”
“In that case, I must now reveal to you a truth you have not known until this moment!” said Aniruddha.
At that moment, Madurantaka entered the room in a flurry and asked, “Mother! What is this I hear? Has Arulmozhi been claimed by the sea?”
“Great Lady! Please comfort your beloved son. What I wished to say, I shall tell you at another time,” said the Prime Minister, and took his leave.
As he crossed the threshold, Madurantaka said, loud enough for Aniruddha to hear, “There he goes—he is my chief enemy. Even while I am here, he comes to poison your mind against me, does he not?”

chapters.title: Kundavai’s Astonishment
paragraphs: Prime Minister Aniruddha Brahmarayar arrived at Kundavai’s palace. The princess, upon seeing him, rose to her feet and offered her salutations.
“May you be blessed with a long life, united with a husband who excels in both valor and virtue!” Aniruddha Brahmarayar bestowed his blessing.
“Sir! Is this the time for such a blessing?” the princess asked.
“I merely uttered the blessing that came to this old man’s mind. What other boon do you seek, dear child?”
“We are all anxious about my beloved father’s health. The entire land is plunged in worry over Arulmozhi Varman…”
“But I see no trace of such worry on your radiant face, dear one!”
“I am born of a line of warriors. Do you expect me to weep and wail at the mention of danger, like everyone else?”
“Never would I ask such a thing. I only say so that you may offer comfort to those like me, who lack your courage.”
“Acharyar! Is it I who must comfort you? You possess a diamond heart, unshaken even if the world itself were to turn upside down!”

“Yet you have managed to unsettle even me, child! Women of the inner palace ought to spend their days in joy, with song and dance. Instead, you have involved yourself in affairs of state—see what calamity has come of it!”
“Oh! What blame is this? In what matter of state have I interfered? What disaster have I caused?”

“I had advised that Ponniyin Selvan remain in Lanka for a while longer. But you sent a letter to your brother, urging him to return at once. Who would heed the words of this old man over your wishes? Do you see now the misfortune that has come to pass? The people of Chola Nadu—” The sea has taken away the prince who was the very apple of our eye. Just a short while ago, you saw the crowds gathered at the palace gates, raising a great commotion. Such unrest is spreading across the land today. Mother, are you not the cause of this turmoil?”
“Why do you say that Arulmozhi Varman set out from Lanka after reading my letter? Do you not know that the Pazhuvettaraiyars sent two shiploads of soldiers to capture the prince and bring him back?”

“I know, Amma! I know! Even so, if that is the case, we can hold the Pazhuvettaraiyars responsible for the fate that has now befallen Ponniyin Selvan. Both the ships they sent have been destroyed. If they say the prince set out because of your letter, who can deny it?”
“Sir! How do you know that I sent a letter? How do the Pazhuvettaraiyars know?”

“You have asked a good question, Amma! Is it only we who know? The whole world knows. The messenger you sent was first captured by our soldiers in Lanka. So, everyone there knows. Through the physician’s son who accompanied him as far as Kodikkarai, everyone in this land knows as well. The secret deed you performed has become so widely known! That is why our elders have said that women should not interfere in matters of state.”

Kundavai stood stunned for a moment. She did not know what reply to give. The Prime Minister had thoroughly cornered her. There was truth in his words. The moment this thought crossed her mind, anger arose in her towards the Vanar clan warrior. Daring deeds—he was certainly capable of those. But to expose the whole affair and ruin everything? He must be sternly reprimanded. As soon as she thought this, she remembered that, on the Prime Minister’s orders, he had been imprisoned. What trouble he brings upon himself, and upon me as well! Could he not have kept quiet for a while? If the physician’s son had babbled something, did he have to leap down from the upper floor and start a fight over it?
“Sir! I have a request. Please grant it with your generous heart.”
“Devi! Command me! In this kingdom, who would dare contradict your word?”

“When you arrived at the palace gates, two men were fighting. You ordered them to be imprisoned.” “What they have done is a grave crime. To begin a fight in the palace, right before the eyes of the queen—what a disgrace! And at such a time? When a great crowd was seething with excitement! If the people, ignorant of the cause, had joined in the brawl, do you realize what disaster might have occurred? Like a tiny spark setting an entire forest ablaze, the whole land and city could have been plunged into riot and chaos!”
“Yes, sir! What they did is indeed a great crime. Yet, I beg you, I implore you to pardon and release one among them.”
“Who is that fortunate soul, worthy of the princess’s grace?”
“He is the envoy I sent to the island of Lanka.”
“It is as if a ripe fruit has slipped and fallen into milk!”
“Why do you say so?”
“I myself wished to capture that envoy. Here he has come and fallen into our hands so easily.”
“For what reason? Of what crime is he accused?”
“Mother! He stands accused of a terrible crime.”
“What is it?”
“It is said that he is the one who pushed Ponniyin Selvan into the sea and drowned him.”
“What monstrous words! Who dares to accuse him so?”
“Many are casting such accusations. Parthibendran, who brought the prince by ship, says so; the Pazhuvettarayars claim it might be so; and I too have my suspicions.”
“Acharya! Beware! Do you suspect that I sent a murderer, that I dispatched him to kill my own brother?”
“Never, mother! You sent him, believing him to be a trustworthy envoy. But could it not have been a mistake? Could he not be a spy for our enemies?”
“Impossible. Aditya Karikalan himself sent him to assist me. He wrote that I could trust him completely…”

“Could not Aditya Karikalan too have been deceived, Princess? Could he not have been replaced along the way? When I came here, the accusation of ‘spy’ fell upon my ears. The one standing below accused the one above. What is that, Mother?”

“The one above is the messenger sent by my brother. Vallavarayan Vandiyathevan, descended from the clan of the Vanars. The one below is Pinagapani, the physician’s son. The physician’s son accused Vandiyathevan of being a spy for the Pazhuvettarayars. What do you make of that?”
“Why couldn’t it be true, Mother?”
“It could never be true, not for a single day. He escaped from the custody of the Pazhuvettarayars. They made every possible effort, sending many men, to recapture him…”
“Then how did the Pazhuvur signet ring come into his possession, Mother?”
“That deceitful demoness—Maya Mohini—the venomous serpent—please forgive me—the young queen of Pazhuvur herself gave him that ring.”

“I am glad you know this. If I had told you, you would not have believed me. It is true that this valiant warrior from Vallam is not a spy for the Pazhuvettarayars. But could he not be a spy for the Queen of Pazhuvur?”
“How could that be?”

“I will tell you how. Vandiyathevan—the secret messenger you sent to Lanka—met the Queen of Pazhuvur in her palanquin outside the gates of Tanjore fort. It was then that he received the signet ring. Later, within the fort, in the inner chambers of the Pazhuvur palace, he met her again. The young queen of Pazhuvur hid him in the treasury room and sent him out. She knew he was going to bring a letter to you. When he returned from Lanka, the two of them met and spoke at midnight in the ruined Pandya palace on the banks of the Arichandra River. Even after all this, the Pazhuvur signet ring remains with Vandiyathevan. What do you think of all this, Mother? Do you still have complete faith in your messenger?”
Kundavai’s heart was now truly plunged into confusion.

Kundavai Devi was standing on the terrace of the palace, gazing at the distant horizon. The gentle breeze from the Kaveri river played with the loose strands of her hair. The sun was setting, casting a golden glow over the lush gardens and the tall, majestic towers of Pazhayarai. The princess’s mind, however, was not at peace; it was filled with a thousand questions and a thousand anxieties.

She had just received news that Vandiyathevan had arrived in Pazhayarai. The words of her loyal companion, Vanathi, still echoed in her ears: “Akka, the brave youth from the Vaanar clan has come! He is waiting to see you.”

Kundavai’s heart beat faster. She had heard much about Vandiyathevan’s wit, courage, and charm. She had also heard about the dangers he had faced on his journey, and the perils that still surrounded the Chola dynasty. What message did he bring? What secrets did he carry? Would his arrival bring relief to her troubled mind, or would it add to her worries?
She turned to Vanathi, who stood nearby with a look of excitement and nervousness. “Vanathi, did you see him? How does he look? Did he seem tired from his journey?”

Vanathi smiled shyly. “He is as handsome and spirited as the stories say, Akka. There is a sparkle in his eyes—one can see that he is not easily frightened by danger. But he seemed eager, as if he could not wait to meet you.”
Kundavai tried to hide her own eagerness. She composed herself and said, “Let him come. But make sure no one else is present. I must speak to him alone.”

Vanathi bowed and left. Kundavai’s mind raced. What would she ask Vandiyathevan first? Should she inquire about her father, the Emperor Sundara Chola, whose health was failing? Or about her beloved younger brother, Arulmozhi Varman, who was far away in Lanka, surrounded by enemies? Or about the swirling conspiracies that threatened the very foundation of the Chola empire?
As she pondered, the sound of footsteps approached. Kundavai’s heart leapt. She turned, her eyes shining with anticipation and anxiety.
Vandiyathevan entered, his face flushed from the journey, his eyes bright with intelligence and courage. He bowed deeply before the princess.

Kundavai regarded him for a moment, her gaze steady and searching. Then, in a voice that was both gentle and commanding, she said, “Welcome, brave warrior. You have come at a time when the Chola dynasty needs friends more than ever. Tell me, what news do you bring?”

chapters.title: Spy for a Spy
paragraphs: Looking at the silent young princess, Prime Minister Aniruddha asked, “Mother! Why do you remain silent? Do you still trust Vandiyathevan?”
“Sir! Jewel among ministers! What can I say? If you continue speaking like this for a while longer, you will make me start doubting myself!” replied the princess.

“Such are the times, dear child! Deciding whom to trust and whom not to trust is not so easy these days. Enemies surround us on all sides; mysterious conspiracies are unfolding everywhere!” said Prime Minister Aniruddha.
“Even so, it seems there is no mystery you do not know, no intrigue hidden from you. How did you learn so many details about the messenger I sent?” asked Kundavai Devi.

“My dear! I am one with a thousand eyes and two thousand ears. They are spread across the land. My men are present even in the fortress of Pazhuvoor. Among the bodyguards of the younger queen of Pazhuvoor, there is one who sends me news. There are many who, like Azhwarkadiyan, roam from town to town and bring me tidings. I believe that in the neighboring lands, nothing can happen without my knowledge. Yet, who knows? There may be those who can deceive even me. Mysteries unknown to me may yet unfold!”

As the Prime Minister spoke thus, Kundavai wondered if this formidable man also knew that Ponniyin Selvan was now at the Choodamani Vihara. With great effort, she suppressed that thought and did not let it show.
“Sir! All that you say may be true; but I cannot believe that valiant scion of the Vanar clan could be the spy of the Pazhuvoor queen. Please, have mercy and set him free!” she pleaded.

“Think carefully, dear child! That woman Nandini possesses some sort of magical power! Shiva-devotee Madurantakan fell into her snare and began to covet the throne. Kandhamaran, son of Sambuvarayar, took her letter and…” He has gone to meet Aditya Karikalan. Parthibendran, who was once the sworn enemy of the Pazhuvettaraiyars, has now become a slave to the Lady of Pazhuvoor. He has come forward to propose dividing the Chola kingdom into two—giving one part to Madurantakan and the other to Aditya Karikalan, thus settling the matter with a compromise…”
“What is this outrage! To even think of dividing the kingdom? This great empire, which our ancestors toiled so hard to unite and expand!”

“You would not wish to see the kingdom divided; nor would I, Mother! Had this idea been suggested ten days ago, Parthibendran himself would have risen in furious opposition. But now, he stands as the chief proponent of this arrangement…”
“What a marvel this is! What sort of magical power does that Lady of Pazhuvoor possess?”
“Princess! That is what I wished to ask you. Yet you are the one asking me. No matter; but tell me, on what grounds are you so certain that only Vandiyathevan will not fall under her spell?”

“Sir! If you ask the reason, I cannot explain it. They say the heart is its own witness. In my heart, I am absolutely certain that the valiant scion of the Vanar clan would never commit such treachery.”
“If that is so, let us put it to the test, Amma!”
“What sort of test?”
“We must immediately send a messenger to Kanchi. We must send an urgent letter to someone whom Aditya Karikalan trusts implicitly.”
“About what matter?”

“Just now, you called Nandini a venomous serpent and then apologized for it. In truth, she is a thousand times more dangerous than any serpent. She has plotted to utterly destroy the Chola dynasty, to uproot it and wipe it from the face of the earth.”
“Heavens! How dreadful!” exclaimed Kundavai, as her inner sea churned with countless waves of thought.

“She has incited the Sambuvarayars to invite your brother Aditya Karikalan to Kadambur palace. She is speaking of marrying the daughter of the Sambuvarayar and the daughter of the Pazhuvettaraiyar to Karikalan. The matter of dividing the kingdom and settling the dispute is also to be decided there.

“She is leaving, it seems. All these are open words. But what purpose she truly harbors in her heart—no one knows. Even I, who pride myself on knowing all, have not been able to discern her true intent.”
“What should we do about that, sir?”

“We must, by any means, prevent Aditya Karikalan from going to Kadambur Palace. For that, you and I must send a message to Vandiyathevan. If, against our wishes, Karikalan insists on leaving for Kadambur, Vandiyathevan must accompany him. Like an inseparable shadow, he must follow your brother and guard him. He must not allow any opportunity for Karikalan to meet Nandini alone…”

Kundavai let out a deep sigh; she realized how grave was the matter the Prime Minister was speaking of. She could not tell whether he spoke with full knowledge of all the details, or only from a standpoint of statecraft.
“Sir! Why do you consider it so important to prevent their meeting?” she asked.

“Dear lady! Some of Veerapandiyan’s loyal followers have sworn to destroy the Chola dynasty, root and branch. Fresh gold coins from Periya Pazhuvettarayar’s treasury are finding their way to them. Need I say more than this?”
“No need,” murmured Kundavai. The thought of the prince lying in the Chudamani Vihara with Surya flashed through her mind. Was not Ponniyin Selvan too surrounded by dangers?

“Sir! In these times, when peril after peril descends upon Chola Nadu, it is indeed our fortune that you are the Prime Minister! What arrangements have you made regarding my younger brother?” she asked.

“I have ordered that in every Shiva temple and Vishnu temple throughout Chola Nadu, prayers and special rituals be performed for the prince’s well-being. Likewise, prayers will be offered in the Buddhist viharas and Jain monasteries. At the Chudamani Vihara in Nagapattinam, the Buddhist monks are about to conduct a special mandala of prayers. What else would you have me do?” When the subject of the Chudamani Vihara was brought up, Kundavai watched the face of the Prime Minister closely to see if any change came over his expression. She could discern nothing.

“Sir! The mention of the Chudamani Vihara brings something to my mind. It seems that Periya Pazhuvettarayar harbors some anger towards the Chudamani Vihara. Ever since the news arrived from Lanka that the monks there were planning to crown the prince, his anger has only intensified. If the prince were to disappear, they would surely place the blame on the monks of the Chudamani Vihara. It is your responsibility to ensure their safety and protection,” she said.
“I shall do so at once, Amma! If necessary, I will send a small battalion to guard the Chudamani Vihara, bearing the Emperor’s command. What do you say about sending Vandiyathevan to Kanchi?”
“Sir! For such an important mission, wouldn’t it be better to send someone else?”

“If you alone have faith in him, I wish to send him. I have heard of his brave and daring deeds. For a task such as this, we must send a fearless and tireless hero. Why, just today as I was coming to the palace courtyard, I saw with my own eyes what he did to that physician! If I had not intervened and stopped him, the physician’s son would have gone to treat Yama himself…”
Hearing this, the young princess was filled with satisfaction. Yet, with a slight hesitation, she said, “Is bravery alone enough? He is rather impulsive, isn’t he? How quickly he began a fight!”
“If you wish, I can send my disciple Thirumalai along with him. Azhwarkkadiyan is renowned for his calm and thoughtful nature!” said Aniruddha.
Within herself, the young princess wondered, “Does even God know what lies within this man’s heart? It seems he wishes to send a spy to accompany a spy!”

chapters.title: Vanathi’s Change
paragraphs: When Kundavai set out to release Vandiyathevan from captivity and send him once more on his journey, Vanathi came to meet her. She stood before the young princess, bowing in respect.
“My dear! I left you behind. There is still some important business left. I will finish it and return. Stay in the garden for a while! But do not go near the stream,” said Kundavai.
“Akka! I will not trouble you any longer. I wish to return to Kodumbalur. Please grant me permission!” said Vanathi.
“What is this, are you too striking a blow upon my head? Why are you angry with me? What sudden affection has blossomed for your ancestral home?”

“If I were angry with you, there would be no one more ungrateful than I. Nor has any new affection for my birthplace arisen in me. What is my ancestral home to me, who have neither mother nor father? Once, my mother prayed that she might offer worship at the Kali temple near our village. Before she could fulfill that vow, she closed her eyes forever. You know how I am often seized by fainting spells? Perhaps it is because that vow was left unfulfilled.”
“For that, you need not travel so far; I will send word and have that vow fulfilled myself.”

“That is not all, Akka! My elder uncle is returning from Lanka. He will not come past Thanjai to Pazhaiyarai. When he arrives, I wish to be at Kodumbalur. I long to hear directly from him all that happened in Lanka!”
“Why are you so eager to know what happened in Lanka?”
“How can you ask that? Have you forgotten that my father attained a hero’s heaven in the war in Lanka…?”
“I have not forgotten. That stain has now been washed away…”
“I do not feel it is entirely cleansed. Before the war ended, Periya Velar is hastening back.”
“Are you going to ask him to go to Lanka again and wage war? Is that why you say you must go to Kodumbalur?”
“Who am I to speak of such great matters? I only wish to ask and learn about what has happened…”
“Aha! Now I understand your mind. You wish to ask your great father about the heroic deeds performed by Ponniyin Selvan in the Lankan war, do you not?”
“Is that a fault, Akka?”
“It is not a fault, but at a time like this, you say you will leave me alone and go away—that is the greater fault!”
“Akka! Am I the one leaving you alone? How many friends you have, how many wait to know your mind and carry out your wishes…”
“Have you too begun to speak like this, Vanathi? It seems your heart has been disturbed by the news about my brother. Do not worry yourself too much about that news…”
“What worry can I have for your brother that you do not already possess, Akka!”
“Tell me the truth! Did you fall into the stream on purpose? Or did you faint and fall?”
“Why would I wish to fall on purpose? I fainted and fell. You and that valiant warrior of the Vanar clan saved me.”
“You do not seem grateful for having been saved!”
“Not only in this birth; in seven births to come, I shall remain grateful.”

“You speak as if this birth has already ended! Listen to me, Vanathi! Do not trouble your heart in vain! I do not believe any harm has befallen Arulmozhi Varman. What I told the people gathered in the palace courtyard just now, I say to you as well. Once, Mother Kaveri saved my brother. In the same way, the Lord of the Ocean must have saved him now. Soon, we will hear good news.”
“On what basis do you speak with such certainty and courage, Akka?”
“Something within my heart tells me so. If anything had truly happened to my beloved younger brother, my innermost self would have known it. I would not be speaking so calmly now…”
“I do not have such faith in what the mind says, Akka! Nor do I trust the inner mind! Not even the outer mind!”
“How is it that you alone can speak so decisively?”
“For the past few days, a strange delusion has been haunting both my inner and outer mind. It appeared in my sleep, in my dreams. Even while awake, at times, that same delusion would arise.”
“What is it, Vanathi?”
“In the water, your brother’s face would appear again and again. It was as if he were calling out to me. Even in my dreams, this strange vision would often recur.”
“Why do you call it a delusion? The news we have received and your own feelings seem to coincide, do they not?”

“If you hear the rest, you will realize just how mad a delusion it is. Did I not faint and fall into the stream? At that time, I truly believed I had gone to Nagaloka. There, a wedding celebration was taking place…”
“Whose wedding was it?”
“I do not wish to say, Akka! In short, I have no faith in what arises in my mind or in my dreams. From now on, I have resolved to believe only what I see with my eyes and hear with my ears…”

“Vanathi! What you say is entirely wrong. Sometimes, what you see with your eyes and hear with your ears can be false. What arises within the heart is what is truly real. I could tell you countless examples of this from stories and epics…”
“Then tell me another time, Akka! For now, please let me go!” said Vanathi.
Princess Kundavai was filled with astonishment. She wondered how such courage and sudden resolve had arisen in this girl.

“Vanathi! What is this haste? Even if you absolutely must return to your hometown, can you not wait a few more days before you depart? The whole country is in turmoil right now. Should I not ensure that you are sent off with proper protection?”
“What do I have to fear, Akka! The palanquin bearers and the four guards who brought me from Kodumbalur have been idling here all this time without any work. They will simply take me back with them…”
“How wonderful! Do you think I would send you off just like that?”

“I beg you, Akka! I truly have nothing to fear. No one in this land would dare harm Vanathi of Kodumbalur. Besides, who does not know that I am the beloved companion of the Young Princess? I ask only one thing—grant me permission for just this. Before I leave, I wish to visit the house of that Kudanthai astrologer once more and ask him a few questions. May I do so?”
“I too wish to visit him, but you seem to be in such a hurry…”
“No, Akka! This time, I wish to see him alone and have my fortune told…”
Kundavai placed her finger on her nose in surprise.
