The princess could not comprehend how, in a single day, in the span of one jamam, this woman had become so stubborn. She realized that she could not stop Vanathi’s journey.

“Very well, Vanathi! Let it be as you wish. Make whatever preparations you need for your journey. In the meantime, I shall go and arrange for the release of that valiant young prince of the Vanar clan who is imprisoned here,” she said.

chapters.title: Two Prisons
paragraphs: As soon as she parted from Vanathi, the young princess made her way straight to the Pazhayarai prison. She left her guards outside and went alone to the place where Vandiyathevan was confined. He was locked in a solitary cell. Staring up at the ceiling of his prison, he was singing a themmaangu folk tune with great enthusiasm.
“The stars in the sky Saw you, my dear, My body shivers with delight – I stand entranced, lost in wonder!”
Only after Kundavai came near and cleared her throat did he turn to look at her. At once, he stood up and said, “Welcome! Welcome, Princess! Please, be seated upon the throne!”
“Upon which throne shall I sit?” asked the princess.
“This is your palace. Here, your rule and your command prevail. The throne here—whichever you wish—please, sit as you desire,” said Vallavaraiyan.
“Sir! When your ancestors ruled the three worlds by their decree, perhaps the Vallam palace looked just like this! In our city, this place is called a prison,” said the princess.
“Lady! In our land, there is now neither palace nor prison. Kings from many countries joined together and razed both palace and prison to the ground, a hundred years ago…”
“Why? Why? What angered them so much against the Vallam palace and its prison?”
“All because of a poet’s mischief!”
“Oh! How so?”

“In the days when my ancestors ruled as emperors of the southern lands, from time to time, officials would capture kings who failed to pay tribute and bring them here. On either side of the palace courtyard, they would imprison those kings…” There were prisons. The petty kings, hoping that the Emperor would one day take pity on them and summon them, would wait patiently, thinking they could beg forgiveness and return to their lands. The chance to see the Emperor was not easily granted to them. While they watched and waited, poets and bards would proceed to the Emperor’s royal hall. In the presence of the Emperor, they would recite their verses, receive gifts, and depart. At such times, the petty kings waiting in prison would exclaim in wonder, “Ah! Look at the fortune of these poets! See the gifts they carry away!”

“One king would say, ‘Alas! Is not that poet taking away my white parasol of victory?’ Another would lament, ‘Oh dear! That bard is leaving seated in my palanquin!’ Yet another would cry, ‘Oh no! He is taking away my royal elephant!’ Still another petty king would say with a smile, ‘That is my horse! One day, surely, my horse will throw down this poet!’
After all the poets had come and gone, yet another poet arrived. He overheard the conversation of the petty kings in prison. Listening to them, he went before the Emperor and sang this song:
‘My poem is my palanquin, My shield, my banner, My elephant, my steed— So say they! Let the kings behold The bard who, by the grace Of the great king Vaanan, Wins the prize in order!’

Thus, the song sung by that poet spread far and wide throughout the land of Tamil. The people rejoiced, singing and listening to it often. Because of this, danger befell our kingdom. All the kings joined forces, marched upon our city, and destroyed our palace, our fortress, our prisons—everything…”
“But even if they destroyed everything, they could not erase the poet’s song, could they? Yours is a clan that has earned such fortune! Its fame shall endure forever!”
“I am the one who has now arisen to destroy the heroic fame of the Vanar clan…”
“Ah! You yourself admit that truth, do you not?”

“What else can I do but agree? Among all forms of servitude, the bondage of a woman is the most cruel. Because I heeded a woman’s word, I brought disgrace upon the honor of my ancestors. I was forced to flee, to hide, to wander in secrecy for the sake of my life. I thought I could quench all my anger by killing that physician’s son. But even that was thwarted by an unexpected obstacle…”
“Sir! Why do you harbor such anger against the physician’s son, Pinagapani?”

“There is reason enough for my wrath. You entrusted a good man to me and sent him along to Kodikkarai. That fellow nearly ruined my entire mission. And if that were not enough, just now in the streets of this town, he tried to have me seized by the Pazhuvettaraiyars, accusing me of being a spy for their enemies. When I escaped from there, he charged me in front of thousands in the palace courtyard, declaring me ‘the spy of the Lady of Pazhuvur’…”
“Prince of Vallam! But is that not the truth?”
“What is not the truth?”
“I mean, is it not true what Pinagapani accused you of—that you are the spy of Lady Nandini Devi of Pazhuvur? Will you tell me the truth?”
“I have taken a vow, Devi, never to speak the truth!”
“Ah! What vow is this? Did you make such a vow after meeting the Lady of Pazhuvur on the banks of the Arichandra River?”

“No, no! I made that decision even before that. As long as I kept speaking falsehoods, everyone believed me. But at one point, I slipped and said, ‘The Prince is safe in Nagapattinam.’ No one believed it; everyone who heard it laughed…”
“What a grave mistake you made! It is fortunate that they did not believe your words! Imagine the disaster if they had!”
“Such mistakes will never happen again…”
“Thank you greatly for your promise!”
“What promise did I make?”
“That from now on, you will carry out my commands without any further mistakes…”
“Oh God! I never promised any such thing. Enough! Release me from this prison! I will go my own way…”
“In that case, you shall not be released! You must remain here in this prison,” she said.
Vandiyathevan laughed aloud, a bright, ringing sound.
“Why do you laugh? Do you find my words amusing?”
“No, Devi! If you do not release me from this prison, is it impossible for me to escape on my own?”

The princess fixed her blossoming eyes on Vandiyathevan for a moment, then said, “Sir, you are a clever man; especially, you are most clever at escaping from prisons. For one who escaped from the treasure vault of the Pazhuvettaraiyars, is this such a great challenge?”
“In that case, why don’t you open the door yourself and set me free?”
“I myself could open this prison and let you go. Or you may escape on your own. But there is another prison from which you cannot escape…”
“Are you speaking of the underground dungeon of the Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar?”
“No; even that would not be impossible for you. You would defeat even the tigers guarding the gates of the subterranean prison and make your escape…”
“Then, which prison do you mean?”
“I speak of the prison that is my heart.”

“Devi! I am a wanderer without home or kin. All the pride of my lineage is but an old tale, a poet’s fancy. But you—you are the cherished daughter of an emperor who rules the three worlds beneath a single parasol…”
“Who knows? Even the glory of this Chola dynasty may one day become an old tale.”
“Yet, today, you are unrivaled in this land, possessed of authority. Neither the Emperor, nor the Pazhuvettaraiyars, nor the Prime Minister would dare act against your wishes…”
“If all this were true, how is it that you alone are able to defy my authority?”
“The authority of the state is one thing. But were you not speaking of the authority of the heart?”
“What is wrong in that?”
“The difference in status between the two of us—that alone is the fault…”
“Haven’t you heard the old saying, ‘Is there a bolt that can bar love?’”
“Doesn’t that proverb apply even to Ponniyin Selvan and the boat-girl Poonguzhali?”
“Yes! It does apply! I thought my brother was born to rule the world. That is why I wished for their hearts to beat as one…”

“I too came here, eager, after hearing so much about the prince. I longed to travel with him to the ends of the earth, to earn fame and glory by performing heroic deeds on the battlefield at his side…”
“But now, that desire has faded, hasn’t it?”
“Yes; Ponniyin Selvan prefers a peaceful life to royal power. Rather than wielding a sword on the battlefield, he yearns more for the work of carrying stones for temple construction…”

“Madurantakan, on the other hand, is fiercely intent on ruling the kingdom. The goat turns into a tiger; the tiger becomes a goat. The legend of the Lord of Alavai tells how he turned a fox into a deer and a deer into a fox. In the same way…”
“Devi, by your grace, I too have become a fox. I must now hide and scheme, weave plots and lies, and escape from enemies by any means. Princess! I can no longer do this work! Grant me leave…”
“Alas! Vanathi, whom I considered my soul’s dearest friend, is about to abandon me. And now, do you too wish to leave me?”

“Devi! I know nothing of the matter between the Kodumbalur princess and yourself. But how could I ever leave you? Great kings perform penance to win your jeweled golden hand. I am but a humble messenger…”

At that moment, the Young Princess extended her sacred hand. With a hesitation—wondering if this was dream or waking—Vandiyathevan clasped that flower-soft hand in both of his, and pressed it to his eyes. His heart and body were filled with rapture.

“O warrior of the Vanar clan! I am descended from the ancient Tamil kings, who held chastity as the most precious jewel of their lineage. In the great city of our dynasty, there have been women who ascended the funeral pyre with their husbands. They believed the fire that consumed their lord’s body to be as cool as the moonlight, and so they leapt into the flames!”
“I have heard of such tales, Devi!”
“This hand of mine, which has clasped yours, shall never touch the hand of another man, not for as long as I live…”
Vallavarayan stood speechless, his actions stilled, gazing at Kundavai’s tear-filled eyes, his own mind lost in a daze.
“Sir! If, because of your reckless deeds, any danger should befall your life, have you thought, even for a moment, what will become of me?”
“Devi! Can this fortunate soul, who has found a place in the throne of your heart, ever become a coward who fears for his own life?”
“Cowardice is one thing, caution is another, sir! Even the Prime Minister Aniruddha has no doubts about your valor.”
“Then, what is it that makes him suspicious…?”
“He suspects that you may be a spy for the Queen of Pazhuvoor…”
“If that is so, I am ready to give him the same reply I gave to Pinagapani, the physician’s son. Open the doors of the prison! Tell me where that man is!”

“The physician’s son has at least some experience in swordplay. Aniruddha knows only the art of words, not the art of war. The sharpness of his intellect is his weapon; he has never relied on the sharpness of a blade…”
“In that case, let my sword’s edge be tested for the first time against him!”
“Sir! In this land, next to the Emperor, the Prime Minister Aniruddha is the most respected man. Even the mighty Pazhuvettaraiyars hesitate to oppose him openly…”
“The Pazhuvettaraiyars have guilty hearts. They are afraid; why should I be afraid?”
“From my childhood, he has been my father’s closest friend. Any disrespect shown to the Prime Minister is as if shown to the Emperor himself, and to me as well.”
“In that case, at least tell me some way by which I might gain his trust.”
“The Prime Minister wishes to send someone he trusts deeply to Kanchi. I have assured him that you or Nambi could be sent.”
“Devi! Please do not send me to Kanchi! Some voice within my heart keeps repeating, ‘Do not go to Kanchi!’”
“Perhaps that is the voice of the Younger Queen of Pazhuvoor, is it not?”
“Not at all! Would I ever heed the voice of that venomous serpent, contrary to your own words?”
“Sir! Never speak of the Younger Queen of Pazhuvoor in such a manner again, at any time!”
“What is this? Why this sudden change?”
“Yes; my heart has changed completely regarding her. Ever since I heard the news you brought from Lanka.”
“Then, must I henceforth behave toward the Younger Queen of Pazhuvoor with reverence and awe?”
“Yes!”
“Even if she were to hand me the sacrificial sword she worships with such devotion, and say, ‘Bring me the head of so-and-so!’—must I obey and bring it to her?”
Kundavai Devi’s body trembled. When she replied, her voice, too, was unsteady.
“It is right to behave toward the Queen of Pazhuvoor with respect. But there is no need to heed her words. She herself may not know what sort of deeds she is involved in, is it not possible?”
“That is exactly what she said as well. ‘I do not even know why I worship this dagger,’ she said.”
Hearing this, the princess, in an even more trembling voice, said, “May the gods themselves protect this ancient Chola dynasty.”
“Let the gods use this wretch as their instrument to protect it,” said Vandiyathevan.
“Sir! That is what I too believe. Once you return from Kanchi, you must go to Lanka again. Somehow, you must bring that mute woman here…”
“Bringing her here would be like trying to trap a whirlwind in a pot. Someone said so once—yes, it was that brave Vaishnavan. Perhaps he himself has brought her already.”
“No; he could not accomplish that task. Only you can make it happen.”
“If that is so, then do not send me to Kanchi, Devi!”
“Why?”

“My master is there. If he asks, I will have to tell him everything. If he learns of the conspiracies plotted by the Pazhuvettarayar and the other petty kings, he will rise in anger at once. If he hears that the Emperor is being held almost as a prisoner, he will immediately take up arms and march forth. And if news of Ponniyin Selvan has reached his ears, he might have already set out by now…”
“That is precisely why I wish to send you. Somehow, you must prevent him from leaving Kanchi.”
“What if he has already departed before I reach Kanchi?”
“Wherever he is on the way, go and join him there. Above all else, there is one task you must absolutely accomplish…”
“Tell me!”
“News has come that Periya Pazhuvettarayar has set out for Kadambur Palace with the younger queen…”
“Is it truly the younger queen who is going? Or is it someone else in her palanquin…?”
“No; it is the younger queen herself. My uncle is still here, is he not!”
“For what purpose are they going?”
“They have invited Aditya Karikalan to come to Kadambur as well. The talk of a marriage alliance is the apparent reason. There is also talk of dividing the kingdom in two and making peace.”
“My lord would never consent to that, not even for a single day.”
“I am not troubled by that now.”
“Then what is it that troubles you, Devi?”

“A nameless fear has taken root in my heart. My chest pounds with dread. In half-sleep, formless terrors surround me. Even in deep slumber, I am haunted by terrible dreams, and when I awaken, my body trembles for a long time afterward.”
“In such a state, why do you ask me to leave you? No matter what danger may befall you, I would give my life to protect you—”

“Ayya! My fear is not for myself. It is for my brother; it is for the Queen of Pazhuvoor. My heart is troubled by what might happen if they were to meet. You must prevent them from meeting alone at any cost…”
“Devi! If she truly intends to do something, who could possibly stop her?”
“Ayya! You must help protect my brother as if you were a suit of iron armor around him. If necessary, you must tell him who Nandini truly is…”
“But he must believe it, must he not?”
“It is your responsibility to make him believe. I do not know how you will do it. If you can somehow prevent them from meeting, it would be a great relief.”
“Devi! I will do all that is within my power. If I fail, do not blame me,” said Vandiyathevan.
“Ayya! Whether you fail or succeed, in this lifetime you shall never be released from the prison of my heart!” said the young princess.

chapters.title: The Green Silk
paragraphs: The next morning, Vandiyathevan was riding along the banks of the Arisil River toward the city of Kudanthai, carrying a palm-leaf letter from the Chief Minister Aniruddhar. He did not urge his horse to gallop, but let it amble gently, taking in the delightful sights that unfolded on either side of the path. In the early days of the month of Aippasi, the land of Chola was resplendent in all its glory. Nature herself, as if a queen, wore a robe of green silk and shone with the beauty of youthful maidenhood. How many shades of green adorned that silken garment! The paddy fields, ripe and ready for harvest, were of one hue; the young crops, transplanted some weeks earlier, were of another; and the newly planted, tender golden-green shoots glowed with yet another shade! The leaves that flourished on the banyan trees were one kind of green; the trembling foliage of the peepal trees, another; the lotus leaves, thick and sprawling in the ponds, held a magical green; the banana leaves dazzled with their own verdant brilliance; the coconut saplings bore a pale, ivory-tinged green; the earth itself was carpeted with fresh grass; the streams shimmered with the green of clear water; and the frogs leaping here and there in the water added their own shade to the tapestry.

To highlight the beauty of this green silk robe, blue lilies, white lotuses, red lotuses, and the crimson blooms of the Sengazhuneer flower sparkled here and there, like stars embroidered upon it. Vandiyathevan drank in all this beauty with his eyes as he journeyed on. He was keenly aware of the difference between the scenes he now beheld and those he had witnessed when he had traveled this way in the month of Aadi. Then, the river had been in spate, surging and foaming with fresh floods. Now, the force and fury of the current had subsided; the water had lost its reddish tinge, become clear as crystal, and flowed along in cheerful procession. The roar of the new flood, the tumult of the wind striking the branches, and the cacophony of thousands of birds had then sounded like the revelry of a grand festival. Today, in the cool, gentle breeze, the rustling of leaves, the gurgle of water in the canals, the varied croaks of frogs awaiting the rain, and the humming of countless insects all blended together to form a plaintive symphony, as if Nature’s queen herself was singing a sorrowful song.

Within Vandiyathevan’s heart, too, a strange, indefinable sadness had taken root. He searched and searched for the cause, but could not discern it. In truth, there was every reason for him to be filled with boundless joy— There were reasons. All the dreams he had spun when he traveled this way two months ago—every one of them had come true. Even things he had never dared to hope for, not even in his dreams, had come to pass. He had had audience with Sundara Chola Chakravarthi! He had seen the great cities—Thanjavur, Pazhaiyarai, Mathottam, Anuradhapuram, and more. He had gained the friendship of Ponniyin Selvan, the very jewel of Chola Nadu; he had earned the privilege of aiding that valiant prince. To merely set eyes once upon the goddess of beauty of Tamilakam, the radiant lamp of the Chola clan, Princess Kundavai—how many lifetimes of penance would one have to perform for that? And yet, to win the pure affection of her noble heart—what a rare and precious fortune that was! When he thought of this, his heart swelled with pride.

But mingled with that proud elation, a certain unease followed close behind. Was he truly worthy of such great fortune? Would it last? How many obstacles might arise before what was within his grasp could truly become his own?

“Ah! What dearth of obstacles is there in this world? The world itself is a maze of hindrances! Sorcerers like Ravidasan, enchantresses like Nandini, conspirators like the Pazhuvettaraiyars, treacherous friends like Kandamaran and Parthibendran, madcap women like Poonguzhali and Vanathi, fierce Vaishnavite spies, fearsome Kalamukha Saivites, ghouls with gaping jaws, and bottomless pits of quicksand—what is this world but a place teeming with such perils? O God, somehow I have escaped each of the dangers mentioned above so far! But now, Prime Minister Aniruddha Brahmarayar has sent me on a mission fraught with even greater peril than all these! On one side, the impetuous Aditya Karikalan, quick to anger; on the other, the sorceress with mysterious powers who manipulates the great Pazhuvettaraiyar like a puppet! I am to stand in the way of their designs and emerge victorious! Is such a thing even possible? Who knows what the Brahmarayar truly has in mind? Perhaps his real aim is to separate me from the princess. Both he and the princess said that Azhwarkkadiyan would join me. But I have not seen him yet!

That valiant Vaishnavite—whatever sort of man he may be, he has never done me any harm so far; in fact, he has helped me many times. If he were with me, he would keep up a lively conversation, and the journey would never grow tedious. Where now can he join me? How much longer must I rein in this horse and proceed at a slow pace for his sake?...”

“Aha! There, a cluster of trees! Those roots lying in the river’s flood, like crocodiles! It was here that the episode of throwing the spear at the wooden crocodile took place! It was here that Varini, Tharagai, Sendhiru, and Mandakini laughed aloud at our heroic deed! It was here that the young princess, out of affection for us, scolded those women! Let us pause here for a moment and look.”

Vandiyathevan dismounted from his horse and walked to the edge of the riverbank. For a while, he stood gazing at the clear stream swirling around the roots of the trees… Aha! In that swirl, a face appears! Whose face is it? Need it even be said? It is the blissful golden face of Princess Kundavai!
“I have seen, I have seen, I have seen— I have seen what is dearest to my eyes!”
Startled by the song, Vandiyathevan looked up in surprise. He saw that atop a lofty branch of a tall tree sat Alwarkadiyan!
“Oh! Brave Vaishnavite! Am I so pleasing to your divine eyes? I see you quite well now. Come down here!” called Vandiyathevan.
The Vaishnavite—climbing down from the tree—replied, “I was not speaking of you, sir! With your sword at your waist and spear in your hand, you appear rather fearsome to my eyes!”
“Then, whom were you speaking of, Vaishnavite?”
“When the Supreme Lord, Thirumal, took the Vamana avatar and lifted his foot to measure the heavens, at that moment, to the eyes of your Lord Shiva—”
“Vaishnavite! Enough! Cease this belittling of Shiva. Otherwise, you will find yourself in great danger!”
“What danger, sir? When the discus of the Lord who slew the crocodile and saved the elephant is with me, who can do anything to me?”
“I have given you fair warning. After that, do as you please.”
“Tell me, brother, what danger will befall me?”
“Did not the people of Pazhayarai, in their agitation, come up to the palace gates? At that time, I overheard some Kalamukhas talking among themselves.”
“What were they talking about?”

“They said that the ever-increasing Veera Vaishnavas in Chola Nadu should be sacrificed to Mahakali, that their skulls should be heaped up in a pile, and that they should dance the blissful tandava upon them!”
Azhwarkkadiyan touched his own skull and said, “This seems quite sturdy! Surely strong enough to withstand the Kalamukha’s tandava!”

“From what I have heard, it seems true—today, everywhere I go, Kalamukhas are wandering about carrying skulls and tridents. Why don’t you change this front-tufted disguise of yours and declare yourself a devotee of Shiva—?”
“That cannot be, my friend, that cannot be!”
“Why not?”
“I cannot utter that name you just spoke. If you ask me to say ‘Vishnuve!’ and change my disguise, I might do it… Look there!”

On the road by the riverbank, a palanquin was passing by. Inside, it was clear that a lady was seated, but who she was could not be discerned. She must surely be a woman of royal lineage—who could it be? Besides the palanquin bearers, an elderly nurse walked alongside. Could it be the royal princess herself? No, that could not be.
“Vaishnavar! Do you know who is in that palanquin?” Vandiyathevan asked.

“Brother! Listen to me. Do not meddle in matters that do not concern you! You have already suffered enough troubles because of such interference, have you not? Many people travel along the road; what is it to you? Mount your horse and be on your way!” he replied.

“Oh! Is that so? It seems the Veera Vaishnavar has now become a great renunciant. Have you forgotten what happened at Veeranarayana Puram? Was it not you who asked me to deliver a letter to the woman traveling in a closed palanquin there?”
“All that is old history! Why bring it up now?”
“Let it be, then. You said you would join me along the way. It was for your sake that I have been riding my horse so slowly all this while. At least now, are you coming with me or not?”
“You are going on horseback! I am traveling on foot. How could we possibly journey together? You go on to the banks of the Kollidam. I will come and join you there tomorrow morning.”

Vandiyathevan became certain that Azhwarkkadiyan was engaged in some other secret task and would not accompany him. “Very well, as you wish!” he said, and sprang onto his horse. He looked toward the direction he needed to go.
At the foot of the northeastern sky, he saw dark clouds gathering.
“Vaishnavite! Will it rain today?” he asked.

“My dear fellow! How would I know astrology? Hasn’t the month of Aippasi begun? If it rains, let it rain. In any case, hurry your horse along! Find some choultry or inn to stay the night!” replied Azhwarkkadiyan.

Vandiyathevan spurred his horse as advised. The words “How would I know astrology?” spoken by Azhwarkkadiyan lingered in his mind. From there, his thoughts turned to the astrologer of Kudanthai. The astrologer’s house was on his way—what harm would there be in stopping by to see him? Among those who aspire to ascend the Chola throne, to whom will fortune favor? Did not the Kudanthai astrologer say that Ponniyin Selvan was equal to the pole star? Yet he himself refuses to set his heart on ruling the kingdom! How easily he renounced the throne and jeweled crown of Lanka! The astrologer’s prediction that many continents lay ahead for him had come true to some extent. Would his prophecy that Arulmozhi would shine with great glory in the future also come to pass? How could that possibly happen? And what of my own dreams—how far will they be fulfilled? Will the kingdom lost in my ancestors’ time ever be restored? The mission I have now set out upon—how far will it succeed? Is it possible to accomplish anything by standing between Aditya Karikalan and Nandini? Thus far, I have narrowly escaped Nandini’s snares two or three times! Will I be able to do so again?

At the thought of the young queen of Pazhuvoor, a shudder ran through Vandiyathevan’s heart. It was true that she had spoken to him with great affection and respect! Yet she— He could not fathom her heart. It seemed to him that, for some important reason, she was deliberately keeping him at a distance. That must be why she had shown such patience with Vandiyathevan. What could that reason be?

Just a short while ago, Vandiyathevan’s horse had overtaken the palanquin traveling along that very path. This time, he did not wish for his horse to collide with the palanquin, nor did the palanquin seem eager to cross his path. Yet, as his horse passed by, the curtain of the palanquin parted slightly. He caught a glimpse of the woman seated within—it was none other than Vanathi, the princess of Kodumbalur. For a moment, he considered stopping his horse, but then changed his mind and rode on. He remembered what the young princess had said about Vanathi. Why was the princess of Kodumbalur traveling alone at such a perilous time, surrounded on all sides by danger? She did not even seem to have proper protection.

Moreover, he noticed another strange thing. Not far away, two fearsome-looking Kalamukha Saivites were watching Vanathi’s palanquin intently. Why were they observing her so closely? Who were these two men? Were they not the same ones who had come and spoken to him as he lay resting on the banks of the Arichandra River?

It was true that Vandiyathevan did not feel much sympathy for Vanathi. He believed that Vanathi wished to usurp the place in Ponniyin Selvan’s heart that rightfully belonged to Poonguzhali. For this reason, he harbored some resentment toward her. Yet, he could not forget that the young princess held Vanathi in boundless affection. If any harm befell Vanathi, the young princess would be plunged into immeasurable sorrow. But why should any harm befall her? “Do not meddle in matters that do not concern you; mind your own business and move on!”—the wisdom spoken by Azhwarkadiyan was indeed sound. Even so, the image of the two Kalamukhas lurking in hiding, watching Vanathi’s palanquin, kept returning to his mind.

Ah, here was the astrologer of Kudanthai’s house! He could ask him about everything… Oh! All this while, that thought had not even occurred to him! It seemed Vanathi Devi too was coming to the astrologer’s house. The fruit has slipped and fallen into the milk. Before Vanathi arrives, he could attend to his own business. With this thought, Vandiyathevan stopped his horse at the astrologer’s doorstep and entered the small house.

chapters.title: Brahma’s Head
paragraphs: When Vandiyathevan entered the house of the Kudanthai astrologer for the second time, a strange and wondrous joy welled up within him. It was within that small house that he had first laid eyes upon the young princess Kundavai. He had stood transfixed, gazing at her lotus-like face and her large, dark eyes widened in astonishment. It was there that her honey-sweet, melodious voice had first fallen upon his ears. All these memories surged and crashed within his heart. Because of them, his ears tingled with sweetness; his heart overflowed with delight; his entire body thrilled with bliss!
The astrologer was just then preparing for his evening prayers. Upon seeing Vandiyathevan, he exclaimed, “Come, my boy, come! Aren’t you the valiant scion of the Vanar clan?”
“Yes, astrologer! Even if your predictions sometimes run ahead or behind, your memory is truly remarkable!” replied Vandiyathevan.

“My boy, to study the science of astrology, memory is absolutely essential. Planets, stars, planetary periods, sub-periods, yogas—there are a hundred thousand possible combinations. One must keep all of them in mind and calculate the year, month, day, hour, minute, even a hundredth part of a second—only then can one make a pronouncement. But let that be; you said my predictions sometimes run ahead or behind—what do you mean by that? Did what I foretold for you not come to pass?”
“Isn’t there a way for you to find that out through your astrology itself?”
“There is, there is! I can discover it through astrology—or even by intuition. Surely, what I told you must have come to pass. Otherwise, would you have returned to this hut?”
“Yes, yes. Your prediction did indeed come true.”
“Say it plainly, then! In what way did it come true, my boy?”

“What you told me happened exactly as you said. ‘If the task you set out for is destined to happen, it will happen; if not, it will not’—that’s what you said, and that’s exactly what happened. Even to say ‘it happened’ is a stretch. The moment it saw me, it turned and ran away!”
“My boy! You are quite the jester!” “It is true, I am a jester! And, in addition, a bit of a hothead!”
“When you enter this hut, you must leave your anger tied up outside.”

“I tried to do just that. But your disciple was not at the doorstep. If I left my bundle of anger on the porch, what if someone took it away? So I brought it inside with me. Where is your disciple, astrologer? I still remember how, last time, he tried to stop me at the door!”
“Today is the new moon day of Aippasi, is it not? For that reason, he must have gone to the banks of the Kollidam.”
“What connection is there between the new moon and the Kollidam riverbank?”
“Today, on the banks of the Kollidam, the great assembly of the Kalamukhas is taking place. My disciple belongs to the Kalamukha sect.”
“Astrologer! I am thinking of abandoning the Saiva faith altogether.”
“Abandon it, and…”
“Your friend Alwarkadiyan Nambi is still around, is he not?”
“You must be speaking of Thirumalai!”
“Yes; I am considering receiving initiation from him, covering my body with the sacred marks, and becoming a fierce Vaishnavite.”
“Why so?”
“I have seen some of these Kalamukha Saivites. Even on the way here, I encountered a few. After seeing them and the skulls they carry, I feel inclined to give up Saivism.”
“Brother! You, who have seen so many battlefields, are you frightened by the sight of skulls?”
“It is not fear; it is disgust. What connection is there between killing enemies on the battlefield and wearing garlands made of skulls?”
“Did not your master, Aditya Karikalan, cut off the head of Veera Pandiyan and parade it through the streets?”

“He did so because of some vow he had taken. He suffered greatly for it afterwards. Even he did not wear the skull as a garland around his neck; nor did he carry it about in his hand! Why do the Kalamukhas do such things?”

“They do it so that they never forget the impermanence of life. You and I smear ourselves with sacred ash, don’t we? Is that all there is to it? This human body is not permanent. One day, it will turn to ash. We wear the sacred ash so that we never forget this truth!”
“It is true that the human body is impermanent; it will burn to ash, or return to dust. But Lord Shiva’s divine body is not like that! Why does Parameshwaran hold a skull in his hand?”

“Brother! The skull in Shiva’s hand signifies arrogance. It shows that when arrogance is conquered, a state of bliss is attained. Isn’t it with the skull in his hand that Shiva performs his blissful dance?”
“How does a skull symbolize arrogance? I do not understand.”

“There are many things you do not yet know, brother! But for now, understand only this: the skull represents arrogance. Once, Brahma and Vishnu became proud. Each claimed, ‘I am the greatest; I alone am the greatest,’ and they quarreled. Shiva appeared between them. He said, ‘Let one of you find my head, and the other my feet. Whoever returns first after seeing them will be the greater among you.’ Mahavishnu took the form of a boar and burrowed into the earth to find Shiva’s feet. Brahma took the form of a swan and soared into the sky to find Shiva’s head. Vishnu returned and admitted honestly that he could not find Shiva’s feet. Brahma returned and falsely claimed that he had seen Shiva’s head! At that moment, Shiva plucked off one of Brahma’s five heads and punished him. Because Brahma quarreled out of arrogance and lied, his head became the symbol of arrogance…”
Vandiyathevan laughed aloud, as if struck by some sudden thought.
“What makes you laugh like this, brother?”
“I am not laughing at anything I see. Something came to mind, and that made me laugh.”
“What is it? There are no secrets here, are there?”
“What is the secret? If I am to be punished like Brahma was, then at the very least, I should have ten thousand heads for the punishment to be fitting! That is why I laughed.”
“You must have told that many lies!”

“Yes, astrologer! That seems to be my fate, written in my horoscope. After I met Ponniyin Selvan, I resolved to speak only the truth. Once, I even told a very important truth. Those who heard it laughed; not a single soul believed me!”
“Yes, my boy! The times have become so twisted. These days, people don’t even believe lies—how will they ever believe the truth?”

“Your astrology’s fate is the same, I suppose! Astrologer, do you remember what you said about Prince Arulmozhi Varman? Didn’t you say that Ponniyin Selvan is like the steadfast pole star, shining in the northern sky?”
“I did say so; what of it?”
“Haven’t you heard any news about him?”
“How could I not have heard? The whole country, every city and town, is abuzz with nothing else!”
“Have you heard that the pole star has sunk into the sea?”

“The pole star does not sink into the sea. But even that unwavering star can sometimes be veiled by clouds, can it not? Even tonight, clouds are gathering in the north. No matter how hard you try, you will not be able to see the pole star tonight. Does that mean the star has vanished?”
“Is that so? Do you know any true news about Ponniyin Selvan?”
“How would I know? The rumor is that you were the last to leap into the sea with him. If anyone knows, shouldn’t it be you? I thought I might ask you.”
Wishing to change the subject, Vandiyathevan asked, “Astrologer! How fares the comet these days?”

“It is growing exceedingly long in the late hours of the night. From now on, the length must decrease. If any misfortune is to befall due to the comet, it must happen very soon. Oh God! Who knows what fate awaits whom in the royal family!” said the astrologer.

Vandiyathevan’s mind darted swiftly from one thought to another. Sundara Chola, lying stricken by the cruel wind of fate in Thanjavur; Ponniyin Selvan, shivering with fever in Nagapattinam; Aditya Karikalan, on his way to meet Nandini at Kadambur palace; Madurantaka, who coveted the throne and had become the object of the people’s wrath; and Nandini herself, who caressed a murderous sword in her hand—all these figures paraded through his mind one after another.
“Let all that be, astrologer! What concern is the fate of the royal family to us? Tell me—how will the task I am about to undertake end?” he asked.
“I must tell you now what I told you before, my son! Many dangers will come your way; but to overcome them all, unexpected help will arrive!” replied the astrologer.

Vandiyathevan wondered whether what was now approaching the doorway was danger or help. For at that moment, along with the voices of men, women’s voices were also heard at the entrance. Both of them turned towards the door.
In the next moment, Vanathi Devi and her companion entered.
Vandiyathevan rose and stood respectfully. “Devi! Forgive me! Had I known you were coming here, I would not have come myself!…” he said.

chapters.title: The Aid Vanathi Sought
paragraphs: “Sir, why are you so angry with me? What wrong have I done to you?” The plaintive voice of the Kodumbalur princess melted Vandiyathevan’s heart. He wondered, in truth, what reason he had to be angry with this girl. For a moment, Poonkuzhali’s face flashed before his mind’s eye and vanished. What justice was there in being angry with this maiden for the sake of another?
“Lady! Forgive me. I did not mean to say anything of the sort. I only said I would wait outside until you finished speaking with the astrologer. I am in no hurry. Even now…”
“There is no need for you to leave. I am glad to know you are not in a hurry. In truth, I did not come here to see the astrologer. I have lost all faith in his predictions…”
“Devi! Your will is my fortune! One day, you will realize that my predictions are not false. When that day comes, you will praise this poor man!” said the astrologer.

“We shall see about that then!” said Vanathi, turning to Vandiyathevan. “Sir! I came here only to see you. I saw you riding by on horseback along the way. I thought you would stop and inquire. But you passed by indifferently! I was not greatly surprised by it. Why should you care so much for this orphaned girl?”
Vandiyathevan felt as if tears would spring to his eyes.

“Devi, what words are these? Who would call you an orphan? You are the cherished daughter of Parantaka Chinna Velar of Kodumbalur, the foster child of the southern commander Boothi Vikrama Kesari, the intimate companion of the young princess of Pazhayarai—who would dare call such as you an orphan? I merely passed by because I thought it would be disrespectful to stop and question you on the road. That is all. If there is anything I can do for you…”
“Yes, sir! There is indeed something you must do. I came into this house only to ask you for an important favor…”

“Tell me; if it is within my power…” “Is it possible that there is something even you cannot accomplish? I have heard, at least in part, of all that befell you during your journey to Lanka. Can you first promise that you will grant the help I seek?”
With hesitation, Vandiyathevan replied, “Devi! It would be better if you told me what kind of help you seek.”

“Yes; I must not obtain a promise from you by deceiving you. Therefore, I will tell you the matter plainly. The astrologer may also hear it; there is no harm in that. I have resolved to embrace the Buddhist faith and become a bhikshuni—a Buddhist nun…”
“What? What did you say?”
“What are these words?”
“That must not be!”
“The world will not tolerate it!”
“An impossible deed!”

Thus, the astrologer and Vandiyathevan, taking turns, exclaimed in shock. Listening to all this, Vanathi said, “Yes; I have decided to become a Buddhist nun. Why do you object so much to it? What is wrong in it? Have not many women in ancient Tamil lands embraced renunciation? Did not Manimekalai, the daughter of Madhavi, pursue the ascetic path and attain divinity? Do we not even today venerate her as ‘Manimekalai Devi’? I do not harbor such lofty ambitions. I only tried to end this useless life of mine. I failed in that attempt. It seems the will of God is that I must live on for some more time. I wish to spend that time in a Buddhist monastery, serving the cause of compassion. Surely, you will not hesitate to help me in this?”
A small doubt arose in Vandiyathevan’s mind. It startled him.

“Devi! Though your decision is not just, I have no right to question it. The elders of your family should advise you on such matters. I have heard that your noble father, Commander-in-Chief Boothi Vikrama Kesari, is soon to return…”
“Sir! I am not going to wait for anyone; nor will I heed anyone’s counsel. I have made my decision, once and for all. I seek your help…”
“How can I be of assistance in this matter, Devi?”

“I shall tell you. I have set out to go to the Choodamani Vihara in Nagapattinam. I left with the intention of meeting the Buddhist monks there and receiving initiation. I ask only that you accompany me as far as Nagapattinam. That is the help I seek from you!”

Vandiyathevan was taken aback. The princess of Kodumbalur was no simple maiden. It seemed she had overheard the conversation between himself and the younger princess, at least in part. Now she was trying to learn the whole truth from him. She had set out for the Choodamani Vihara in Nagapattinam, but her true purpose was to meet the prince there! He could not be a party to this, not even for a single day.
“Ammani! You must forgive me. The help you seek is beyond my power.”
“What is this wonder? The hero who went to Eezhanaadu and accomplished so many marvels now finds it impossible to escort this orphaned girl to Nagapattinam?”

“Devi! Nothing is impossible. But at this moment, I cannot undertake it. The Prime Minister and the younger princess have both commanded me to go to Kanchipuram at once. I am carrying their written orders. That is why I said I could not do it. If it were another occasion…”

“Yes, yes! If you do not wish to help, there are a thousand reasons you could give. It does not matter. I had already set out with the intention of traveling alone. Only, when I saw groups of Kalamukhas along the way, a little fear did arise. But there is a God whose duty it is to protect all living beings. I entrust my burden to Him and set forth. What can anyone do to a foolish woman who has resolved to renounce the world and become a sannyasini? I shall go. Farewell, Astrologer!” With these words, Vanathi set off.

Following her, the astrologer called out, “Devi! Devi! Darkness has already fallen! It is the night of the new moon. Clouds are gathering in the northeast. Why not stay in this poor man’s hut for the night and leave in the morning?”

“No, Astrologer! Forgive me. I intend to spend the night in Thiruvarur. This man has refused to accompany me. Will I not find someone in Thiruvarur? And even if I do not, I am not worried for my life. Who would benefit from that…?”
These were the last words that fell upon the ears of the astrologer and Vandiyathevan.
Vanathi climbed into the palanquin waiting at the entrance, and it began to move away. Until the palanquin disappeared from sight, Vandiyathevan and the astrologer stood watching it.

Afterwards, Vandiyathevan said, “Until some time ago, the Princess of Kodumbalur was known to be exceedingly timid. The other companions of the young princess used to tease her for this. They once floated a toy crocodile in the river to frighten her; even I was fooled by it. Now, all of a sudden, how has this girl gained such courage? What marvel is this, that she has set out to travel alone? And how did the young princess consent to it?”

“That amazes me as well. The last time this girl came to this hut, she suddenly fainted and fell; she spoke hesitantly, in a feeble voice. I am left wondering if this is the same Princess of Kodumbalur. Today, how boldly and resolutely she spoke!”
“What do you think could be the reason for such a sudden change of heart?” he asked.
“Some important news must have caused a great shock in her mind.”
“What important news could there be?”
“Why? Is not the news that Ponniyin Selvan has been taken by the sea enough? There was talk that this girl might even marry the prince!”

As the astrologer spoke thus, Vandiyathevan pondered, ‘Was it the news that Ponniyin Selvan was taken by the sea, or the news that he survived and is at Nagapattinam, or the news I told about Poonguzhali— which of these could have given her such a shock?’
“Yes, astrologer! The Kodumbalur lineage has been, for generations, staunch Saivites! How could this girl suddenly develop an attachment to the Buddhist faith?” he asked.
“It could be a residue from a previous birth,” said the astrologer.
“Will she set out for the Chudamani Vihara at Nagapattinam?”
“That is what astonishes me too!”
“Can you not look into your astrological scriptures and say?”
“Thambi! How can one know this through the science of astrology? This belongs to the science of espionage.”
“Is there truly a science called espionage?”
“Why not? Have you not heard of the Thirukkural by the poet Poyyamozhi Pulavar?”
“I do recall hearing that such a work exists.”
“In that book, there is a chapter titled ‘Espionage’. It contains ten verses.”
“Is that so? Recite a couple of good verses from it!”
“All the verses are excellent. Listen to this: ‘The spy is he who, without revealing himself, investigates All, both those who act and those who do not wish to act.’”
Valluvar says that a king must use spies to investigate those who serve under him, his own kinsmen, and likewise his enemies.
Listen to this as well: ‘Assuming the guise of ascetics, feigning death, Whatever the hardship, the spy never reveals secrets nor tires in his work.’”

Valluvar says that the spy is one who dons the disguise of a renunciant, pretends to be dead, and, no matter how much his enemies torment him, never reveals a secret and never tires of his duty. He also says that the work of one spy must be checked by another spy.
‘Even the information brought by one spy Must be verified by another spy.’
“Are you saying you have never heard these verses?”

Vandiyathevan was filled with wonder. He resolved that, when he found the time, he must read the Thirukkural before attending to any other task. What a genius the man must have been, to write about such matters of statecraft a thousand years ago!
After exchanging a few more words, Vandiyathevan set off. He did not heed the astrologer’s suggestion, “Why not stay here tonight and leave in the morning?”
“I will come another time; then, I shall be your guest,” he replied.
“When you return here another time, you shall see that my predictions have come true!” said the astrologer.
“Sir, O Astrologer! You haven’t made any predictions at all! If you had, wouldn’t they have had a chance to come true?” Vandiyathevan said, laughing as he mounted his horse and rode away.

From the astrologer’s house, there was only a single path for a short distance. He had to take the same road along which the palanquin had gone. After a while, the road forked in two. One path led northwards to the banks of the Kollidam river. The other, southeast, led towards Thiruvarur. Far ahead on the Thiruvarur road, Vandiyathevan could see the palanquin proceeding. For a moment, his heart wavered.

He had come to refuse the help sought by the Princess of Kodumbalur! If she truly needed help… if some danger befell her on the way—when that news reached him later, would he ever be able to forgive himself? Would he not have to regret for a long time his refusal to accompany her? Yet, what could he do? The orders from the Prime Minister and the Younger Princess were most strict. He could not involve himself in other matters now. He had already suffered enough from meddling in unrelated affairs before. Azhwarkkadiyan had also warned him. Moreover, the thought of escorting Princess Vanathi to the Chudamani Vihara at Nagapattinam was something he could not even dream of…

Thus resolving, Vandiyathevan turned his horse onto the path leading to the banks of the Kollidam. At that very moment, a faint, fearful cry—a woman’s voice, very soft—seemed to reach his ears. Startled, he turned to look back but could not see the palanquin. Perhaps it had turned at the bend in the road. Still, he decided he must go and see for himself. After all, it would not cause any real delay. His horse leapt forward.

Very soon, he reached the bend in the road. The sight that met his eyes there was enough to stop Vandiyathevan’s heart. A woman was tied to a tree at the roadside. A cloth was stuffed in her mouth. In the darkness, he could not at first tell who it was. He went closer and saw—it was Vanathi. It was clear now that the one walking with the palanquin was the maidservant. She was groaning softly, struggling to untie her bonds. Vandiyathevan leapt down from his horse, first removing the cloth that gagged her mouth, then quickly untying her restraints. He noted inwardly that she had not been bound very tightly.
“Girl, what happened? Tell me quickly! Where is the palanquin? Where is your mistress?” he asked anxiously.

The maidservant stammered and babbled her reply. As the palanquin turned the bend in the road, suddenly seven or eight men had leapt out from behind the nearby trees. Some of them carried clubs and spears in their hands. Two of them struck the maidservant on the head and threw her down. They gagged her mouth with a cloth. Meanwhile, the others said something in a terrifying voice to the palanquin bearers, who immediately abandoned the path and ran off with the palanquin along a side track… The rest followed after them. She had not heard Vanathi Devi’s voice at all. Having explained this much, the maidservant pointed out the side path along which the palanquin had gone.

“Girl! Go to the house of the astrologer in Kudanthai! I will try to find your mistress,” said Vandiyathevan, even as he sprang onto his horse. The horse turned off the royal road and galloped down the side path. Without regard for mound or hollow, forest or thicket, it sped along at a furious pace.

chapters.title: The Lamp Has Gone Out!
paragraphs: Part Three – The Sword of Slaughter

The night before the new moon, darkness had fully descended. Black clouds, rising from the northern horizon, had now spread across the entire sky, veiling it completely. Not a single star twinkled in the heavens. Only the fireflies flitting over trees and bushes lent a faint glimmer. By their feeble light, Vandiyathevan guided his horse onward. Where was he going, for what purpose, and would any good come of it? None of these questions had clear answers. Danger had befallen the beloved companion of Princess Kundavai. It was his duty to try and save her. Beyond that, there was God!

Even after riding for a full naazhigai, he could not find the palanquin. A doubt crept into Vandiyathevan’s mind—had he embarked on a madman’s errand? He reined in his horse. At that moment, a sound reached him from a little distance away. He listened intently. It was the sound of hoofbeats. Yes, a horse! Was it only one horse, or several? Perhaps these were the horsemen escorting the palanquin. He would have to proceed with caution—he must not be caught in the midst of a large group. That would be of no help to Vanathi Devi; his own mission would also be ruined…

Slowly, pausing often, he dismounted and led his horse on foot. Soon, he was able to ascertain that only a single horse was ahead. After a short while, the horse ahead seemed to be climbing a sloping embankment. Vandiyathevan wished to remain hidden, so as not to be discovered following. He looked around carefully. Nearby stood a ruined mandapam, its walls collapsed in places. He led his horse close and stopped behind a crumbling wall. Fixing his gaze on the embankment, he strained his eyes in the darkness to watch the horse ahead.
“Who is there?” A voice startled Vandiyathevan.
It sounded like the voice of someone he knew well.
“Maharaja! It is I, your humble servant!” came another voice in reply.

Within a minute, a lamp flickered to life at the spot where the voices had been heard. From behind a tree, a man emerged holding a lamp in his hand. In its glow, the horse became visible. Someone was seated upon it. It was now certain that the rider was none other than Madurantaka.

As the man standing on the ground seized the torch, the horse upon which the prince was mounted grew terrified. Rearing up on its forelegs, it spun around once. Then, with a sudden leap, it sprang forward and began to gallop away.

The spot where the horse had been standing was the bank of a wide canal. From that raised embankment, the horse leapt straight into the floodwaters of the canal. The man who had grabbed the torch shouted, "Maharaja! Maharaja!" as he plunged into the canal after the horse. But as he jumped, he slipped and fell. The torch was swallowed by the swirling waters.

In the next instant, a darkness far deeper than before enveloped everything. At that very moment, a light drizzle began to fall. Amidst the sounds of trees swaying in the wind, the patter of the rain, and the harsh croaking of frogs, the shouts of men and the pounding of horses’ hooves mingled in confusion.

Vandiyathevan knew well that Prince Madurantaka was not a man famed for his courage. His heart trembled at the thought of what danger might befall Madurantaka, perched atop the terrified horse. The horse might continue to bolt, carrying him away in panic. Or it might have thrown him into the canal’s floodwaters. Or perhaps, after carrying him a short distance, it might have tossed him elsewhere and run off.

Could the man who had come with the torch manage to follow the horse and save the prince? But he himself had already stumbled and fallen into the canal’s flood. What was to be done now? Should he go in search of Vanathi, or rush to Madurantaka’s aid? For a moment, this struggle raged within him.

He had no idea where Vanathi Devi had gone. But Madurantaka was in danger right before his eyes. It would be easy to help him; there was no risk in finding and rescuing him. Afterwards, there would still be time to search for Vanathi! Oh God! Had he not just resolved, only moments ago, never to interfere in matters that did not concern him? And now, what was he doing?

From behind the shelter of the mandapam wall, Vandiyathevan led his horse outside. Guided by instinct through the darkness and the drizzle, he made his way towards the spot where the prince’s horse had entered the canal. He too descended into the canal, looking carefully all around, but saw nothing. From somewhere far off came indistinct cries: “Aa-aa-aa!” “Oo-oo-oo!” “Ee-ee-ee!” “Tatapata tatapata!” “Kadaka kadakada!”—strange, unrecognizable sounds.
He climbed up onto the bank of the canal and peered beyond the raised embankment.

All around, as far as the eye could see, there were paddy fields. It was impossible to ride a horse through the muddy slush or the green crops of the fields. He would have to keep to the edge of the bank and search for a way forward.

But even along the canal’s edge, thick shrubs and thorny bushes grew in tangled profusion. Threading his way through a narrow, single-file path between them, he led his horse onward. Above, the rain fell; below, the ground was slick with slippery mud; on one side, the canal; on the other, the paddy fields; all around, thorny thickets. The horse moved slowly, step by cautious step. Time itself seemed to crawl—each minute stretched into an age! The drizzle thickened into a steady rain. The darkness deepened, growing ever more impenetrable. Vandiyathevan’s mind sank into troubled thought.

Why had Prince Madurantaka come alone on horseback? Where was he headed? Who was the man who had come to meet him? Was there any connection between this and the men who had seized Vanathi? What might Vanathi’s fate be at this moment? Why must I entangle myself in these troubles and lose sleep? Should I not simply attend to my own mission? I could seek out the royal highway, find my way to Kanchi, and continue on my path! But how could that be possible in this rainy, pitch-black night? And how could I decide that none of these matters concerned me?

Had it not been by paying heed to something that did not concern me at the Kadambur Sambuvarayar palace that I later gained so much advantage? And yet, wandering along the canal’s edge in this darkness tonight would bring no such benefit. The only result would be getting thoroughly drenched! If my horse were to slip and fall and break its leg, my journey would come to an abrupt end.

No, I must turn back and return to that ruined mandapam. Only after the rain lets up can I set out again. Suddenly, a flash of lightning—by its brief glare, he glimpsed, some distance ahead, on a mound in the field, what seemed to be a horse standing still. Now that I have come this far, let me go a little further and see what that is! If I can lend a helping hand to Prince Madurantaka at a moment of danger, it may prove useful in many ways in the future.

Vandiyathevan led his horse down from the canal bank onto the narrow ridge between the fields. He urged it toward the mound where he thought he had seen a horse. As he drew near, the mound loomed like a great black demon in the darkness. Another flash of lightning—and for a moment, he saw a horse standing atop the mound.

Vandiyathevan noticed that there was no rider upon the horse. Thunder rumbled! Perhaps frightened by the thunder and lightning, the horse once again became wild with fear and began to bolt. There was no use in following it any further.

Somewhere nearby, perhaps Madurantaka Devar, having fallen from his horse, might be lying. Therefore, Vandiyathevan called out several times. His thunderous voice, “Who is there? Who is there?” rose above the relentless roar of the rain, “Jhim jhim, rim rim.” But from all directions, only the echo replied, “Who is there? Who is there?”

The rain grew heavier. The gale blew fiercely. Driven by the force of the wind, the sheets of rain lashed sideways. The horse shivered all over its body. Vandiyathevan too, struck by the rain, began to tremble from the cold.

There was no use in standing there any longer. Vandiyathevan turned his horse back the way he had come, regretting his own lack of judgment. Hereafter, he resolved, he must not involve himself in such reckless deeds. He must remember that he had a mission, and that he himself must see it through…

Guided by its own instinct, the horse found its way and halted near the ruined mandapam, letting out a loud neigh. Only then did Vandiyathevan return from his world of thoughts to the world before him. He dismounted. His clothes were drenched and dripping. He must dry them. That night, he and his horse would have to shelter in the ruined mandapam—he looked around to see if there was any part of it that was safe from the rain.

What would it be like to have fire touch your feet in the midst of pouring rain in an open field? That was how Vandiyathevan felt as he suddenly leapt back. The reason was nothing else—not a ghost, not a demon—but the voice of a tiny child!
“Amma! Amma!”
How could one say there were no ghosts or demons? At such an hour, in that ruined mandapam, how could a child’s voice be heard?
How could one say with certainty that it was not the voice of a ghost or a demon? Nonsense! There are no ghosts! No demons! Ghosts and demons are the imaginings of frightened, deluded minds!
“Amma! Amma! Oom! Oom!” This was truly the voice of a human child! The terrified wail of a child separated from its mother!
The sound was coming from the shadowed part of the collapsed mandapam. Was it only a child? Was there no one else?
“Amma! Amma! Oom! Oom!”
Vandiyathevan approached the spot from where the voice came and asked, “Who is there?”
“Who is there?” echoed the child’s voice.
“It is I! Who are you? What are you doing in the dark? Come outside!”
“It’s raining outside!”
“The rain has stopped; come out!”
“Where is my mother?”
“Your mother has gone to fetch you some milk.”
“No; you are lying!”
“Will you come outside, or shall I come in?”
“If you come in, I have a knife in my hand! I’ll stab you!”
“Oh ho! What a brave warrior you are! Come outside and stab me then!”
“Who are you? You’re not a tiger, are you?”
“I am not a tiger; I am a horse!” said Vandiyathevan.
“You are lying; does a horse speak?”
“If I were a tiger, would I speak?”
“If I come outside, there might be a tiger. My mother said it might leap on me.”
“I am not a tiger; I won’t leap at you either. Come out without fear!”

“Fear? Why should I be afraid?” Saying this, a tiny little child emerged from the dark mandapam. By now, the rain had completely ceased. The clouds had parted a little, and the stars were visible. In the starlight, Vandiyathevan looked at the child. He seemed to be about four years old. Even in that faint light, Vandiyathevan could tell he was a striking child. He wore a small silk cloth around his waist and a necklace of gems around his neck.
A child must belong to a noble lineage. Who is the mother who left her child here all alone? Why did she come here? Why did she abandon the child and leave?
Meanwhile, the child gazed intently at Vandiyathevan and said, “You are not a horse; you look like a man.”
“There, look! There’s a horse too!” said Vandiyathevan.
The child looked at the horse.
“Oh! Did you bring it for me? Didn’t they say a palanquin would come?”

The boy’s reply stirred a multitude of conflicting thoughts in Vandiyathevan’s mind. Who was this child? Why was he here alone? Was it not astonishing that such a small boy showed no fear at all? Who had promised to send a palanquin for him? Why had it not arrived? Who was the mother who had left him behind? Where had she gone?
“Child! Why did your mother leave you and go away?” he asked.
“My mother didn’t leave me; I am the one who left her!” said the boy.
“Why did you leave her?”
“A horse came running. I said I wanted to catch it and ride on it, but my mother said no. Without her knowing, I ran to catch the horse. Is this the same horse?”
“No; this is a different horse. Then, how did you come here?”
“I couldn’t catch the horse. I couldn’t find my mother either. The rain started pouring down, so I came into this mandapam.”
“Aren’t you afraid to be alone in the dark?”
“What is fear? Every day is like this for me!”
“Are you not even afraid of tigers?”
“My mother is afraid, not me. I am a fish; I will swallow the tiger whole!”
“Hey! Will a fish swallow a tiger?”
“I am not an ordinary little fish! I am a great makara fish—a leviathan! I will swallow tigers, lions, elephants, and everything else…”
All sorts of thoughts began to arise in Vandiyathevan’s mind. A fish that could swallow a tiger—was that not a wondrous creature indeed! Who could have taught such things to this child?
“What is that sound over there?” the boy asked.

Vandiyathevan looked. In the distance, a group of people was approaching. Some among them carried flaming torches. In their midst, a palanquin was visible. All of them were rushing forward in a flurry. It seemed there was a young girl among them as well. Confused voices rose—“There!” “Here!” “Look!” “Over here!”
One of the group spotted the ruined mandapam and pointed it out. That was enough! All of them dashed toward the mandapam at a run.
“There they come, the palanquin is coming. I don’t like riding in the palanquin. Will you take me on your horse?” the boy asked.

The child’s face, his appearance, his speech—all of it captivated Vandiyathevan’s heart. He felt an urge to gather the boy up and hold him close. Yet, at the same time, some inexplicable hesitation arose within him.
“I have urgent business elsewhere,” Vandiyathevan said.
“Where are you going?”
“To Kanchi!”
“Kanchi! That’s where my most important enemy is!”

Vandiyathevan was taken aback. He thought even standing near this child might be troublesome. But there was no time to mount his horse and escape. The group was already very close. If he ran, it would arouse suspicion. And besides, a curiosity to see what would happen next gripped Vandiyathevan. So he quietly stepped aside and stood in the shadows by the crumbling wall.
“Here I am!” the boy called out, stepping forward.

The first of the newcomers was a young girl. She was breathless from running, but without a thought for it, she leapt forward, scooped up the child, held him close, and cried, “Pandya, is this what you have done?”
The next to approach her was Ravidasan. He came and stood beside the boy.
“Emperor! You have frightened us so much!” he said.
The boy laughed. “That is how I will frighten you. I asked for a horse, but you have brought a palanquin!” he replied.
Soman Sambavan, Idumbankari, Devaralan, and the others whom we have seen before now surrounded the boy.
“Emperor! What is a single horse? We will bring a thousand horses, ten thousand horses for you. But for today, please get into this palanquin!” said Soman Sambavan.
“I will not; I will only ride on that horse,” said the boy, pointing to the horse standing behind the wall.
Only then did they notice the horse—and Vandiyathevan, who stood beside it.
On Ravidasan’s face, surprise, shock, and anger flared up all at once. He stepped forward two paces and asked, “You wretch! How did you come here?”
Vandiyathevan retorted, “You fiend! How did you get here from Kodikkarai?”
Ravidasan laughed, “Ha ha ha! Did you really think I was a demon?” he asked.
“Some become demons after they die. You are a living demon!” said Vandiyathevan.
Meanwhile, the boy said, “Do not quarrel with him! I like him very much. He was my companion in the darkness. He said he would kill the tiger if it came. Let him come with us too.”
Ravidasan went near the boy and said, “Emperor! Certainly, we can take him along. But for today, please get into the palanquin!” he insisted.
The boy walked towards the palanquin as he was told.
Ravidasan once again approached Vandiyathevan and asked, “What are you going to do now?”
“Shouldn’t you be the one to tell me?”
"Come with us! You already know much of our secret. Now you will know even more. We cannot leave you behind and go. Come!"
"What if I refuse to come with you…?"
"That is impossible. I know you are a great warrior. Still, we are twenty in number. You cannot escape from us."
"You mean to say I cannot escape alive, is that it?"
"You are a young man. You have not tasted any of the pleasures of this world. Why should you throw away your life in vain?"
"Who would ever give up their life for nothing? You ask me to come with you—where are you taking me? Where are you all going?"
"If you ask so, I will tell you. To the younger queen of Pazhuvur!"
"Ah! I thought as much. Where is the younger queen now?"
"By now, the younger queen must have reached Thiruppurambayam. Will you come, or not?"
"I too must go that way. I was just wondering that there was no one to guide me. It is fortunate that you have come! Let us go, lead the way!" said Vandiyathevan.
By then, the boy had climbed into the palanquin, and it began to move. Around it, holding torches aloft and raising various cries, Ravidasan’s band marched. Vandiyathevan followed them.
A multitude of thoughts surged within him.
What had become of Vanathi? He did not know. What had happened to Madurantakan? That too was unknown. What would become of himself tonight? That was also uncertain.

There was no doubt that tonight he was about to learn, face to face, of a conspiracy far greater than the one he had uncovered at Kadambur Palace. Until then, it was useful. But what would happen after that? Would they let him escape with his life? Would they force him to join them? If he refused, would they sacrifice him? Perhaps, once again, by the mercy of Nandini…

Vandiyathevan pondered how, the moment Ravidasan mentioned the name of the younger queen of Pazhuvur, he had agreed to go with them. It surprised even himself. Perhaps this is what the elders call 'maya'—illusion—or 'moha'—fascination. How dangerous she is—

He already knew that she was involved in conspiracies. Yet, a desire arose in his heart to seize any opportunity to meet her. It surged up within him, uncontrollable, overpowering his restraint. Before he could even think it over, his lips had already uttered, “I will come…” But what other choice did he have? As Ravidasan had said, it was impossible to fight so many people alone. If only he could buy himself a little time, perhaps some means of escape would present itself. At the very least, he might learn more clearly about this band of conspirators and their true intentions.

“You are going to Kanchipuram? That is where my greatest enemy is!”—the words spoken in the innocent prattle of that small child kept echoing in Vandiyathevan’s mind. Who was that boy? Why did these people call him “Chakravarthi”—Emperor? And whom did that child mean by “greatest enemy”? Answers to these questions began to form in his mind, each one more terrifying than the last. The more he thought about it, the greater his fear grew. Oh God! When would all this come to an end? “Very soon,” a voice within him replied.

That strange procession continued on its way. It passed over fields, canals, bunds, and meadows, never pausing for a single moment. At last, crossing the swollen, rushing waters of the Manni river, it reached the border of Thiruppurambiyam. It entered the dense forest that encircled the ancient palm grove.

chapters.title: “The Time Has Come!”
paragraphs: We have already seen the ruined, overgrown temple of the Pallipadai, built a hundred years ago, now swallowed by the forest. It was here that Azhwarkkadiyan once hid himself and learned, to some extent, of the conspiracy plotted by Ravidasan and his companions. Now, Vandiyathevan and the others had arrived at that very same place.
They led Vandiyathevan and his horse to the side wall of the desolate Pallipadai.

“Sir! Remain here for a while. We will call you when the time comes. Do not dream of escaping! Except for those who know this place well, no one can enter or leave this forest. If you try to get out, you will surely lose your life!” said Ravidasan.
“If I try to find my way out, you’ll kill me with your sorcery, won’t you, magician?” Vandiyathevan replied with a laugh.
“Laugh, laugh! Yes, laugh as much as you want!” said Ravidasan, laughing as well.

At that moment, somewhere far away, a jackal began to howl. Hearing it, a wildcat nearby let out a low growl. Vandiyathevan shivered—not from the cold, but from something else. In the heart of that dense forest, even the wind seemed afraid to enter; why? It did not appear that much rain had fallen there. Only in a few places on the ground were there droplets of rain, making the earth damp. Because there was no breeze, the air felt stifling. By the time he had reached this place, Vandiyathevan’s half-dried garment had become dry again. Only the cloth bundle he had tied around himself was still damp; he untied it, spread it out, and laid it on a nearby rock to dry. Sitting on one corner of that rock, Vandiyathevan leaned against the wall of the Pallipadai. Only one man stood guard near him.

A little distance away, in a clearing at the center of the forest, the others sat in a circle. From inside the Pallipadai, someone brought out an old throne and placed it there. On it, they seated the boy whom they called ‘Chakravarthi’—the Emperor. Of the many oil lamps, only two were left burning; the rest were extinguished. As the lamps were put out, smoke rose and spread in all directions, shrouding the place. “The queen has not arrived yet?” asked one.
“Shouldn’t she come at the right time? I told her to come only at the second watch. Until then, someone sing the garland of glory of the Pandya clan!” said Soman Sambavan.
Idumbankari picked up a drum and tapped it lightly. Devaralan began to sing a song.

Vandiyathevan, from where he was seated, watched all this; he listened as well. He knew that the ‘Valudhi clan’ referred to the Pandya dynasty. The song echoed in his ears as a mournful lament. The sound of the drum and the sorrowful melody stirred a deep emotion within him. A few words from the song reached his ears. From those, the memory of the great war that had taken place there a hundred years ago came to his mind.

Yes; it was here that Varaguna Pandiyan and Aparajita Pallavan fought a fierce battle for three days. The Ganga king Prithiveepathi came to aid the Pallava. Like the hundreds of thousands of warriors who perished in that war, that mighty hero too fell and died. The temple built in his memory had now become the meeting place for conspirators.

After the Ganga king’s death, the Pallava forces began to scatter and flee. The victory of the Pandya army seemed certain. At that moment, the Chola forces came to the aid of the Pallavas. Leading that army, bearing ninety-six wounds on his body, came Vijayalaya Cholan. That heroic old man, who had already lost both his legs, was carried by four men. Wielding two long swords in his hands, he plunged into the Pandya ranks. Spinning both swords like wheels, he advanced. Wherever he went, the lifeless bodies of Pandya warriors piled up like mountains on either side.

The scattered Pallava soldiers began to return. Jan jan jan janar!—ten thousand swords flashed in the golden rays of the setting sun! Tan tan tan tanar!—ten thousand spears darted from the other side, gleaming as they flew! Swords and spears clashed! Thousands upon thousands of heads rolled in all directions. Thousands upon thousands of lifeless bodies fell! Ee ee ee ee!—horses neighed as they fell dead! Plee lee lee lee!—elephants trumpeted as they collapsed and died! In the flood of blood, the corpses of men and beasts floated. Twenty thousand vultures circled above, darkening and obscuring the sky!

Thirty thousand jackals howled and came running, encircling the battlefield! “Aiyo! O, O, O!”—fifty thousand wailing voices rose up as one! “Don’t let them escape! Catch them! Pursue! Strike! Stab!”—a hundred thousand voices thundered thus. Ten thousand victory drums boomed, “Adham! Adham! Adham!...” Twenty thousand conch shells of triumph resounded, “Boom! Boom! Boom!” Sixty thousand demons laughed, “Ha! Ha! Ha! Ha!”

Vandiyathevan started awake in fright. He opened his eyes wide and looked all around. Leaning against the wall of the barracks, he realized he had dozed off for a short while. He tried to recall the terrifying dream he had seen in that half-sleep. Was it truly a dream? No! Surely, the description of the battlefield that Devaralan had sung, in rhythm with the beat of the drum, must have conjured such visions before his mind’s eye.

At that moment, Devaralan was singing about how the Pallavas and Gangas had been defeated and driven away by the Pandya army. The laughter of those listening, filled with mirth, must have sounded like the laughter of thousands of fiends, startling Vandiyathevan awake. Suddenly, the drumbeat ceased. Devaralan too stopped his song at once.

A little distance away, a torchlight appeared. It came closer and closer. Following the torch, a palanquin approached. The bearers set it down. The curtains of the palanquin parted. From within, a woman stepped out. Yes; it was the Queen of Pazhuvur, Nandini. But whereas on previous occasions Vandiyathevan had seen her adorned in all her ornaments, radiant as a bewitching enchantress, now she appeared as the fierce goddess Ugra Durga, her hair unbound and wild. Seeing her thus, a chill ran through Vandiyathevan’s heart; his body trembled.

As soon as Nandini alighted from the palanquin, she looked at the boy seated on the throne. Fixing her gaze upon him, she walked towards him. The boy too looked only at her. All the others watched the two of them. The woman who had run into the ruined hall searching for the boy—the one he had called “Amma”—stood behind the throne. When Nandini came near, she stretched out both her hands. The boy looked from her to the woman standing behind him, and back again.
“Are you my mother? Not she?” he asked.
“Yes, my dear child!”

“Why does she call herself my mother?” “She is the mother who raised you!” “Why didn’t you raise me? Why didn’t you keep me with you? Why did she hide me away in some mountain cave?” “Kanmani! It was to fulfill your father’s wish. It was to take revenge upon those who killed your father!” “Yes, I know that!” said the boy, rising and approaching Nandini. Nandini embraced him with both her arms and kissed his forehead. The boy too held her tightly, clinging to her as if to prevent her from leaving him again! Yet, this scene did not last long. Nandini gently but firmly freed herself from his tender grasp. She seated the boy upon the throne. Once more, she walked to the palanquin. From within it, she took out the sword we have seen before. She signaled to the men who had carried the palanquin. They lifted it and carried it a short distance away, sitting down out of sight. Nandini returned to the throne and laid the sword across its seat. The boy gazed at it with irrepressible curiosity and asked, “May I take it in my hand?” “Wait a moment, my darling!” said Nandini. Then, she looked searchingly at Ravidasan and the others in turn. “Except for those who have taken the oath, there is no one else here, is there?” she asked. “No, Devi!” replied Soman Sambavan. Nandini turned to Ravidasan. “Senadhipathi!…” she began. Ravidasan laughed. “Today you are able to laugh. Who knows how you will be on this day next month!” “Devi! We have waited so long for that auspicious day to arrive.”

“Sir! We are but a few. Our Emperor is a mere child. The Chola kingdom is vast, the Chola army’s strength is immeasurable. If we had acted in haste, the entire affair would have been ruined at its very root. Because we have been patient, now the time for the fulfillment of our mission draws near. Ravidasar! Do you have anything to say? Do any others here wish to speak?”
Ravidasan looked around, surveying the faces of those present, one by one. All appeared to be observing a vow of silence.
“Devi! We have nothing to say. It is you who must speak. You said the time for the fulfillment of our vow is at hand. Tell us, where, how, and through whom it is to be accomplished.”
“Very well; it is for that very purpose I have come here. That is why I summoned all of you without fail. I have even had our Emperor brought here,” said Nandini.
