Everyone, including the young boy seated on the throne, fixed their gaze upon Nandini’s face. She continued:

“Some among you were impatient. Some doubted whether I had forgotten the vow we took. Let there be no such doubt. Of all of you, I have the greatest reason to remember it. No, I have not forgotten. For the past three years, day and night, ceaselessly, I have thought of nothing else. Except for the opportune moments and cunning strategies to exact our revenge as per our vow, I have considered nothing else. Wherever I went, whatever I did, whomever I spoke to, my only thought was whether it would serve our purpose. Now, the opportune moments have converged. The minor kings and great officials of Chola Nadu have split into two factions. The Pazhuvettarayar, Sambhuvarayar, and their ilk have resolved to crown Madurantakan. Kodumbalur Boothi Vikrama Kesari and Thirukovalur Malayaman are opposed to this. I hear that Boothi Vikrama Kesari is marching towards Thanjavur with the southern army. I also know that Malayaman of Thirukovalur is gathering his forces. War may break out between the two sides at any moment.
“Devi! We hear that you are making great efforts to prevent such a war. We have learned that peace talks are to be held at the palace of Kadambur Sambhuvarayar.”
“Yes; it was I who made that arrangement. But can you not guess for what reason?”
“I cannot, Queen! Even the great sages have said that it is impossible for anyone—even Lord Sarveshwara himself—to fathom the depths of a woman’s heart. How then could we hope to do so?”

“That is indeed beyond your powers. I shall tell you—listen and understand. If civil strife were to break out in the Chola kingdom before our vow is fulfilled, who can say what the consequences might be? Sundara Chola is still alive; Anbil Brahmarayan is still present; if they intervene, they will suppress both factions. Or, even if one party is defeated and the other grows stronger, our purpose will become impossible to achieve. That is why I have now begun these peace negotiations. We must accomplish our aim before open conflict erupts. Once our goal is fulfilled, the quarrels among the minor rulers of the Chola realm will have no end. The fighting will continue until one side is utterly destroyed. Do you see now… the reason for initiating these peace talks?”

At these words, signs of astonishment and excitement appeared on the faces of all those gathered there. They whispered to one another in low voices, marveling at the subtle intelligence of the younger Pazhuvur Queen. Even Ravidasan could not help but be amazed.

“Devi! We are astonished by your extraordinary foresight. We understand the true purpose behind the peace negotiations. But you say the day for fulfilling the vow is near. Who will carry it out? How? When?” he asked.

“I have devised this strategy for that as well. Under the guise of these peace talks, an invitation has been sent to our chief enemy to come to Kadambur Sambuvarayar’s palace; he will certainly come there. Our vow must be fulfilled there. O loyal followers of Veerapandiyan Chakravarti! The hour for your vengeance is at hand. Is today not Saturday? Before the next Saturday dawns, our vow will be accomplished!”

All twenty people present exclaimed “Aha!” in unison. Some leapt up in excitement. The man holding the drum struck it twice in his enthusiasm. The owls sleeping on the tree branches awoke and hooted, flitting to other branches. The bats flapped their wings and fled with a rustle. Vandiyathevan’s horse shivered with a thrill through its body.

Vandiyathevan too looked up. All he could discern was that Nandini was speaking to those around her about something that stirred a flutter of excitement. Her words, however, did not reach his ears. Ravidasan, meanwhile, calmed and subdued the enthusiasm of the others.

“Devi! Your final words have filled us with boundless exhilaration. We rejoice that the time to avenge ourselves upon our greatest enemy has drawn so near! But, to whom shall fall the fortune of fulfilling this vengeance?” he asked.

“It is only natural that there should be competition among us for that honor. To ensure that it is decided in a manner that leaves no one with resentment, I have summoned here the sacred prince, son of Veerapandiyan. Here too is Veerapandiyan’s dagger. Whomever among us this little child, touching his father’s dagger, hands it to—that person shall carry out the vengeance. The rest must stand ready to assist as needed. If the chosen one fails, the others may step forward to complete the deed. I shall remain within Kadambur Palace. Idumbankari will be stationed as one of the palace guards. We will help the one entrusted with the task to enter the palace. Are all these arrangements agreeable?”
The conspirators looked at one another with keen interest. To all, the plan seemed acceptable.

Ravidasan spoke: “What you have said is indeed a fair arrangement. We all agree to it. But one more thing: whoever is chosen to carry out the vengeance, the others must pledge to obey his word without fail. Until the prince comes of age, the one who avenges shall be regarded as law by all the rest.”
At these words, a smile blossomed on Nandini’s face.
“You include me in this as well, do you?” she asked.
“Yes, Devi! There can be no exceptions!” replied Ravidasan.
“Excellent. Now, what Ravidasan has proposed—do all of you agree?” Nandini asked, turning to the others.
They looked at one another; hesitation kept them from replying. To some, the arrangement seemed unacceptable.
Soman Sambavan spoke up, “How is that just? How can we subject the Devi, who has given us every assistance, to the same common rule?”

“Do not worry about me. The sole reason I still live is to avenge the cruel murder of Veerapandiyan Chakravarthi. Whoever it is that fulfills that vengeance, I am forever willing to be their slave!” said Nandini.

Then, turning to the young boy who had been listening to these conversations, half-understanding and half-bewildered, Nandini Devi said, “My dear child! This heroic sword belongs to your father. With your tender hand, take it and give it to whoever among those present here you like the most!”

Ravidasan stepped forward a little and said, “Chakravarthi, look at all of us carefully! Whoever among us you think is the bravest and most courageous, hand over this Pandya clan’s heroic sword to him!”

The young emperor, seated upon the throne, looked all around him. Everyone gazed at the emperor’s face with restless eagerness and excitement. The eyes of each one silently pleaded, “Give it to me! Give it to me!”
Only Ravidasan’s face and eyes, with an air of authority, commanded and threatened, “Give it to me!”
After glancing back and forth at everyone two or three times, the boy took the sword in his hand. He tried to lift it, but could barely manage.

The excitement in the room reached its peak. The boy suddenly turned, gleaming, towards Nandini. “Mother! I like you more than anyone else here. Until I grow up, you must rule the kingdom for me,” he said, and handed the sword to her.

chapters.title: A Figure in the Darkness
paragraphs: Nandini took the sword that the boy, who was called the Emperor, handed to her. She pressed it to her chest and embraced it. Then she lifted the boy himself, and, drawing him close, hugged him tightly to her bosom. Tears streamed down from her eyes in torrents.
For a while, the others stood transfixed, watching this scene in astonishment.
Ravidasan was the first to recover from his shock and spoke.
“Devi! The Emperor has not fully understood our request. Without comprehending, he has given you the sword. Let me explain it to him again, more clearly—”

Nandini stopped him; her voice trembled as she spoke. “No, sir, no! The Emperor gave me the sword fully understanding what it means. Do not be disturbed by my tears. I weep not from sorrow, but from overwhelming joy at having received the fortune of avenging the murder of Veerapandiyan, the Emperor!”
“Devi! Think about it! While we, the band of desperate warriors, are still alive—” Soman Sambavan began, but Nandini cut him off.

“There is nothing to think about. That responsibility is mine alone. You will not be without your own tasks. Half of you must safely escort the Emperor to the Panchapandava Hills. The rest of you, come to Kadambur. Those who can enter the Samburayar palace, come inside; the others, wait outside, ready and alert. Wait with swift horses. Once the deed is done, if possible, all of us must escape alive, must we not?” said Nandini.
Ravidasan stepped forward. “Ammani! I forgot to mention something; grant me leave to say it now.”
“Speak, sir! Speak quickly! Pazhuvetarayar has gone to the grand assembly of the Kalamukhas on the banks of the Kollidam. I must reach the palace before he returns!” said Nandini.
“You said our chief enemy, Aditya Karikalan, would come to Kadambur Samburayar’s palace, did you not? That is not entirely certain,” he said. “For what reason do you say so?”

“I say it for a fitting reason. A message is being sent to Aditya Karikalan, forbidding him from coming to Kadambur Palace under any circumstances. The Young Princess of Pazhayarai and Prime Minister Aniruddha have both sent such word…”
“Did you think I was unaware of this?”
“Even knowing it, do you still expect him to come to Kadambur?”

“Yes; I certainly expect it. The nature of Aditya Karikalan is unknown to that Pazhayarai she-serpent; unknown to the demon of love; and even you, skilled in the arts of magical sorcery, do not know it. If anyone forbids Aditya Karikalan from doing something, that is the very thing he will surely do. I know this; I know it for certain. Aditya Karikalan is not a gullible child like Arulmozhi Varman. He is not a fearful fool like Madurantaka. Precisely because his sister and the Prime Minister have sent word forbidding him from coming to Kadambur, Aditya Karikalan will most assuredly come here!”
Thus spoke Nandini.
“Devi! You must not place your full trust in that either. The message they sent will not reach Kanchipuram!” said Ravidasan.
“What are you saying, sir! Speak more clearly!” said Nandini, her voice now tinged with agitation.
“Devi! Do you know through whom the message to Aditya Karikalan was sent?” asked Ravidasan.
“Certainly not; but I can guess.”

“Good! There is no need for guessing. We have already captured him. He was present in the mandapam where the Emperor sheltered from the rain. All our secrets are known to him. If we let him go alive, we are inviting our own destruction. Idumbankari! Bring that spy here!” commanded Ravidasan.

Idumbankari went toward the temple of the Pallipadai. Two others went with him. Nandini began to gaze intently in that direction. The sharpness that had been on her face all this while was now replaced by a bewitching smile.

Idumbankari and two others approached Vandiyathevan. The valiant youth, exhausted and half-asleep where he sat, was suddenly set upon by them. For a moment, Vandiyathevan considered wrestling with them. But then he changed his mind. Let me see what they intend to do, he thought, and remained still. With a thick rope, they bound his hands together and tied them to his body. Then, two of them seized him by the shoulders and led him forward, bringing him to stand before Nandini.
Vandiyathevan looked at Nandini and smiled. There was no change visible now on Nandini’s face; tranquility reigned upon it.
“Sir! Once again…” she began.
“Yes, Devi, once again I have come! But this time, I did not come of my own accord!” he said, glancing at those around him.
The boy standing near Nandini asked, “Mother! It was he who saved me from being swallowed by a demon in the dark. Why have you had him tied up?”
Vandiyathevan looked at the boy and said, “Child! Be quiet! When elders are speaking, you must not interrupt. If you do, a tiger will swallow you up!”
“I will swallow the tiger!” declared the boy.
“Can a fish swallow a tiger?” Vandiyathevan asked.
From the faces of those around him came a terrible, rumbling growl. Even Vandiyathevan was startled for a moment by that dreadful sound.
Ravidasan spoke in a loud voice, “Devi, did you hear? We cannot let him escape alive any longer. Twice before, for your sake, we let him go with his life. Now, we can no longer do so.”

“Mage! What a grand lie you tell!” retorted Vandiyathevan. “Was it you who let me go alive? Was it not I who escaped from you? Devi! Please look closely and tell me—is this man truly Ravidasan, or is he Ravidasan’s demon?”
Ravidasan laughed menacingly. “Yes! I am a demon! Tonight, I shall drink your blood,” he said.
Once again, from the throats of those present, a terrible growling voice arose.
Meanwhile, the boy exclaimed, “Mother! He has a fine horse. Tell him to give it to me!”
“Child! Come with me! I will seat you upon my horse and take you along,” said Vandiyathevan.
Ravidasan glared fiercely at Vandiyathevan and barked, “Hey! Keep your mouth shut!” Then, turning to Nandini, he said, “Devi! Please give your orders quickly!”
Nandini asked calmly, “How did he come here? When did he arrive?”

“This spy tried to take him away from the pavilion where the Emperor had taken shelter from the rain. We arrived just in time to stop them and seize him. Had we been a moment late, disaster would have struck,” said Ravidasan.
“Sir! Is what they say true?” Nandini asked.
“Devi, you know best whether those who serve you are capable of telling the truth. How could I know?” replied Vandiyathevan.

The smile that had appeared on Nandini’s face vanished like a flash of lightning. She looked at Ravidasan and said, “Sir! All of you please step aside for a while. I wish to question him privately about certain matters.”

“Devi! Time is passing, danger is drawing near. At such a moment—” Ravidasan began, but before he could finish, Nandini said in a stern voice, “Recall the agreement we made just now. Leave at once without another word. Take the Emperor with you as well!” Then, bending to the boy’s ear, she whispered, “Prince! Go with them for a while. I will get you the horse from him.”

Without another word, Ravidasan and the others hurried away, taking the boy with them. Nandini gazed at Vandiyathevan through the faint lamplight and said, “Sir! It seems there is some bond between you and me.”
“Lady! That bond is a most wicked one; it is tight and unyielding. It has bound my body and hands together!” replied Vandiyathevan.
“Enough of your playful talk. Did you come here of your own will? Or was it by chance?”
“I did not come here by my own will! Nor did I arrive here by accident. It was your people who forcibly brought me here. Otherwise, by now, I would have reached the banks of the Kollidam.”
“You speak as if it was such a hardship for you to see me. It seems you are so eager to leave my presence.”

“It is not seeing you that pains me; in truth, it is having to leave you that grieves me. If only you would grant me permission—on one side, you are beset by that old, withered Pazhuvetarayar, and on the other, by these fearsome sorcerers. Just say the word. I will free you from all of them and take you away…”
“Where will you take me?”
“I will take you to your mother, who wanders like an orphan in the forests of Lanka,” said Vandiyathevan.
Nandini let out a long sigh, tinged with disappointment.

“Do you wish for me, too, to wander as an orphan? Perhaps such a time may come. If it does, I will surely seek your help to take me to my mother. But before that, my wish must be fulfilled. Will you help me achieve it?”
“Lady! If I knew what your wish was, then I could speak of helping you,” said Vandiyathevan.
“Those who truly care do not speak so. Without even knowing what the wish is, they come forward to help fulfill it.”

“Those who care, at the right time, will warn and strive to save you from danger, my lady. These murderers have ensnared you in some plot and placed you in great peril. They are about to use you for their own ends…”
“You are mistaken! It is I who am trying to use them for my purpose! You will come to know this for certain.”
“They have deceived you, like a little child taken from the wilds…”
“Do you know why the child is needed?”
“To place him upon the Pandya throne and crown him…” he replied.

“Once again, you are mistaken. Not merely to seat him on the Pandya throne; but to enthrone him upon the seat of the Chola Empire, which stretches from the Tungabhadra to Lanka, and to crown him there!”

“Oh heavens! With whose help do you intend to accomplish this grand deed? With the aid of those standing around you—this pack of jackals? Do you think you can defeat the mighty Chola army, a vast force of two million valiant warriors, with the help of these ten or twenty jackals who hide in the shadows by day and emerge at night?”
“I do not rely on them alone. I trust the sword in my hand. With its help, I shall fulfill the desire in my heart.”
“Lady! You will never use that sword, not even for a single day. You lack the strength in your hand—and in your heart—for such a deed!”
“Why do you say so?”
“I merely spoke what arose in my mind.”
“I can prove, right here and now, that what you say is utterly wrong!”
“In that case, I am indeed fortunate. Should I not prepare myself to die, struck down by your sacred hand?” said Vandiyathevan, bending his neck and gazing at the floor as if ready to be struck.
“Is it to be struck down by my sacred hand that you desire? Do you not wish to be crowned instead?” asked Nandini.
Vandiyathevan looked up and asked, “How many people will you crown with the crown you possess?”
“That is my will. In the end, I shall crown the one for whom my heart yearns.”
“Then what will become of this little child?”
“Whether he is crowned or not—that too is my will.”
“Devi, crown whomever you wish. I do not desire it.”
“Why?”
“Many have spoken about the beauty of the curls upon my head. I do not wish to ruin that beauty by placing a crown upon it.”

“You will never abandon your jesting words. Very well, sir! When the news came that Ponniyin Selvan had fallen into the sea and died, what did the Young Princess do? Was she greatly saddened?” Nandini suddenly changed the subject and asked.
Vandiyathevan, startled for a moment, replied, “How could she not be? Are all women heartless?”
“That woman from Kodumbalur—did she not try to end her life by throwing herself into the stream? Is that true? Who saved her?” she asked.
At once, Vandiyathevan remembered the danger that had befallen Vanathi. He was lost in thought, wondering what her fate had been, and did not answer the question.
Nandini’s voice grew harsh as she said, “Fine; I know you will not say anything about all that. Are you going to try to prevent Aditya Karikalan from coming to Kadambur Palace?”
“I will try to prevent it,” said Vandiyathevan.
“I say you will not succeed.”
“I did not claim that I would succeed. Devi! I only said I would try. If the prince has set his mind on something, it is not easy to change it!”
“You seem to know Aditya Karikalan’s nature very well.”
“You know it even better than I do.”
“Very well; no matter how much I say, you will not join my side. You will remain on the side of my enemy. Is that not so?”
“Lady! Who is your enemy?”
“Who is my enemy? The Princess of Pazhayarai! Who else?”
“That is your imagination, Devi! I wish to tell you a truth—a most important truth…”

“Enough, enough! If you begin to speak of truth, it will be as false as water strained through a sieve. Do you think I do not know? Keep your truth to yourself!” Nandini declared with fury, clapping her hands together. At once, Ravidasan and the others began to approach.

Vandiyathevan realized he had not made proper use of the opportunity that had come his way. This sorceress is about to order them to kill me. O God! What a death! Could I not have died a heroic death on the battlefield, fighting my enemies? Was this what was written on my forehead?
Ravidasan and his group came near and surrounded him. Like a pack of wolves closing in on their prey, they growled menacingly.
“Queen! No matter what you say, I know this man will never come to our side. You must leave at once. We will offer him as a sacrifice at this sacred place and then depart,” said Ravidasan.
“Sorcerer! Beware! That is not my wish. None of you are to do anything to him. If any of you so much as touch him, I myself will cut you down with this dagger and avenge it!” Nandini thundered.
Ravidasan and the others stood stunned.
“I still have much to accomplish through him. Do you understand? I am leaving now; you must leave as well. Let him go whichever way he chooses. No one is to hinder him!” Nandini commanded.
“Devi! One request! We will wait upon your command. But he has a horse. Is it wise to let him go first? Please consider it and tell us,” said Ravidasan.
“Very well; tie him to that pillar of the ruined temple. It will take him some time to untie himself and leave. By then, you will have crossed this forest,” she replied.

Vandiyathevan was tied to the pillar of the ruined temple. A short distance away, his horse was tethered to a tree. Nandini mounted her palanquin and departed. Two men carried the throne away. Ravidasan’s group took the boy and hurried off. The light from their torches gradually faded and disappeared with them. Darkness, thick and impenetrable, closed in around Vandiyathevan.

The scenes he had witnessed a little while ago, the events that had transpired, all now seemed like a dream. In the darkness, monstrous bats flapped their wide wings with a rapid, rustling sound. Mute owls hooted. Foxes howled in a dreadful chorus, their cries echoing through the night. Vandiyathevan felt as if those howling foxes were drawing closer and closer to him. Strange, unknown shapes prowled through the forest.

He remembered the dream he had seen in the Kadambur palace. He shuddered, imagining a thousand foxes surrounding him, ready to tear him apart and devour him. In panic, he tried to untie his bonds. But the knots did not seem to loosen easily.

If only there were some light, it would be easier to undo the knots. But there was not the faintest sign of light there. Not even a flash of lightning; not even the glow of a firefly. Even if the clouds had parted in the sky and the stars had appeared, their light could not penetrate the depths of that forest.

Ah! What was that sound? Countless creatures roamed the forest; what wonder in that? No, this sounded like a human footstep! A horse neighed softly. It shifted its feet restlessly, as if in distress. Was a tiger or a leopard approaching? Vandiyathevan hurried to untie his bonds; it was no use.

There! A figure. In that pitch-black darkness, a shadowy form. Was it human? Or... what else could it be? It came closer and closer. Vandiyathevan gathered all his courage. He summoned all the strength in his body to his legs. He kicked out with all his might! With a “veel” sound, the figure leapt backward. After retreating a short distance, there was a “danar” sound, as if it had collided with the wall of the pit!

After that, the figure stood there for a while. It seemed to lean against the wall of the pit. Though he could not make out its features in the darkness, Vandiyathevan felt as if the figure was staring intently at him.

He tried even more desperately to untie his bonds. Those sorcerous fiends had tied the knots so tightly! Never mind; the next time he saw that Ravidasan, he would have a thing or two to say! The figure shifted its position. It seemed to move into the pit. After a short while, he heard the sound of stones clattering inside the pit temple—‘dan’, ‘dan’—several times.

There was light at the temple entrance. Look—there, that figure is coming out of the temple, holding a trident in hand. It is walking towards him. It is the form of a fearsome Kaalaamukha Veera Saivite. A terrifying figure, adorned with a long beard, matted locks, and a garland of skulls around his neck. He came near Vandiyathevan, lifted the lamp, and stood still, staring intently at him.

chapters.title: The Disguise Revealed
paragraphs: At that moment, seeing the fearsome-looking Kalamukha Saivite in that place, Vandiyathevan was startled for a second. But then, his natural courage chased away his fear. “Where have I seen this man before? Where?” he wondered. Yes, yes; when he was lying under the tree by the banks of the Arichandra River, didn’t two men come and look at him closely before leaving? One of them was this very man! Was that all? Was it only that one time he had seen this face? Hadn’t he seen those sharp, piercing eyes somewhere else?
Meanwhile, the Kalamukha Saivite stared intently at him and burst out laughing, “Ha! Ha! Ha!” That voice—it sounded like a voice he had heard many times before.
“Ah, so it’s you! Was it for your sake that I struggled so much to come here at this midnight hour?” said the Kalamukha Saivite. It seemed as if he had deliberately changed his voice while speaking.
“Then, for whom did you come?” asked Vandiyathevan.
“I came searching for the prince!” replied the Kalamukhan.
“Which prince?”
“What does it matter to you? Why do you ask?”
“I too am a prince; that’s why I asked.”
“Look at the features of a prince’s face…!”
“What is lacking in my features, sir? If I wore a beard and moustache, matted locks, and a garland of bones like you, would my face not look princely?”
“Try wearing them! Then you’ll know.”
“How many days does it take for a beard, moustache, and matted locks to grow?”
“What’s the big deal? They can grow in a single day. If you wish, even in a single hour…”
“I thought it would be like that too…”
“What did you think?” “Nothing at all. Just untie these bonds that hold me. I will join your faction myself.”
“That’s enough, that’s enough! There are already spies like you in our midst. That’s why our great assembly ended the way it did today.”
“How did it end?”
“We were waiting for the prince to come to the great assembly; as soon as he ascended the throne, he was to promise to accept our great guru as the royal preceptor! But the prince never came.”
“Untie my bonds; I will tell you why the prince did not come.”
“Which prince?”
“Who else? Madurantaka, son of Kandaradithar!”
“So my guess was right!”
“What did you guess?”
“I guessed that you are a spy, that’s all.”
“What made you suspect that?”

“When I came searching for the prince, I saw some people leaving this forest. I know who they are. They must have tied you up because they suspected you to be a spy. But I do not understand why they left you alive.”
“I will tell you that; just untie me!”
“No need for you to say anything. I cannot untie you either. If you agree to do as I say…”
“What is it that you want me to do?”
“You must promise not to meddle in matters that do not concern you, and do a hundred and eight sit-ups as penance!”
“Is that so? Is that the news?” said Vandiyathevan.
All the while this conversation was going on, his hands had not been idle. Slowly, he had been loosening the knots that bound him.
“When he said, ‘We must perform the ritual of the Hundred and Eight Mango Groves,’ all the bindings came undone.

Vandiyathevan sprang forward and pushed the Kalamugan down. The torch that the Kalamugan was holding fell to the ground beside him; though it did not go out completely, it flickered, casting a faint light.

Vandiyathevan climbed atop the fallen Kalamugan, sat on his chest, grabbed his beard, and shook it. The beard came away in Vandiyathevan’s hand. At that very moment, the Kalamugan threw Vandiyathevan off and sprang to his feet.

Vandiyathevan snatched up the torch, which was burning low on the ground. The Kalamugan, now bereft of beard and matted locks, revealed a face that was unmistakably that of a devout Vaishnavite, a true Alvar’s disciple. For a moment, the two men looked at each other and burst into laughter.
“Vaishnavar! You told me not to meddle in matters that do not concern me, did you not? But what have you done yourself?” Vandiyathevan asked.
“I did not get myself into danger as you did, my friend! If I had not come just now…”
“Do you think it was you who undid my bonds?”
“Even if you had managed to loosen your own bonds, you could not have escaped this forest without my help. The jackals would have made a meal of you.”
“Let the jackals be. If you had seen the magician who was here just a while ago with his pack of jackals… Escaping from them was the real feat!”
“I know those magicians as well. Was it only the magicians who came? Did anyone else come?”
“A small fish came too. A most extraordinary fish, one that longs to swallow a tiger!”
“Ah! Tell me! Tell me! Who all came? What happened? Tell me everything in detail!”
“Why did you don this disguise? Where did you go this evening? What happened at the place you went?—If you tell me all that, I will tell you what happened here!”

“I do not have much more to say. Earlier tonight, I learned that the great assembly of the Kalamukhas would gather on the banks of the Kollidam. It was to see what would transpire there that I donned this disguise and went. After witnessing it, I thought I would come and meet you at the Kollidam ferry landing. The great assembly did indeed convene; Periya Pazhuvetarayar was present. The chief guru of the Kalamukhas was there as well. But the one they were all eagerly expecting, the most important of all, did not arrive!”
“They were expecting Prince Madurantaka, weren’t they?”
“Yes; but how did you know that?”
“If Madurantaka ascended the throne of Thanjavur, the burden of the kingdom would surely be carried with grace!”
“Why do you say so?”
“He could not even control a wild horse! How then could he hope to control and rule over minor kings like Pazhuvetarayar, the rebellious Kalamukha Saivites, and the quarrelsome Vaishnavite warriors?”
Azhwarkkadiyan laughed and asked, “Did you see Madurantaka on your way here? Do you know what happened to him?”

Vandiyathevan recounted how he had followed Madurantaka, how the prince’s horse had bolted in fright at the sudden sight of the torch, how he had searched for him for some distance, and how, in the end, he had found only the horse at Kalathumettu.

Then he said, “Alas! Poor man! Who knows where the horse might have thrown him? He could even be in mortal danger. That must be why he did not come to your great assembly; shall we go back and search for him?”
“How charming! But what is that to us? Let us mind our own business. Come! Let’s set out at once! Before dawn breaks, we must be at the Kollidam river ferry,” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
“But what if Madurantaka has fallen into a canal or a paddy field and lies there dead? Even then, would you say it is no concern of ours?”
“Nothing of the sort would have happened. Aniruddhar would have made arrangements for his safety beforehand.”
“Prime Minister Aniruddhar? What would he know of all this?”
“Aha! Why do you ask such a question? In this kingdom, nothing can happen anywhere without the knowledge of Anbil Aniruddhar.”
“Oh! Then does he know about the conspiracy that took place at Kadambur Palace?”
“Let me remind you of something. During the festival at Veera Narayanapuram, we both stood beneath a tree and watched the palanquin of the Pazhuvur Rani pass by, did we not?”
“Yes; I still remember the agitation you felt when the curtain of the palanquin was drawn aside. You asked me, ‘Can you deliver a letter to the Pazhuvur Rani?’”

“You replied, ‘Ugh! What kind of task is that?’ You thought I wished to send a love letter. But I only wanted to warn Madurantakan, as per the orders of the Prime Minister, not to be misled by the words of conspirators.”
“Did you know then that it was Madurantakan inside the palanquin?”

“At first, I suspected. When the curtain was drawn aside, the secret was revealed. You are quite stubborn. No matter how much I tried, you refused to admit that it was not the Pazhuvur Rani but Madurantakan inside the palanquin, did you not?”
“Are you the only one who is stubborn? Even this evening, you refused to tell me where you were going.”
“If I had told you, you would have insisted on interfering in that matter as well. See how much trouble you have already landed yourself in! At least from now on…”
“Does the Prime Minister know about the Kalamukha gathering and that Madurantakan intended to go there?”

“Would he have sent me without knowing? At the same time, he made arrangements to ensure that Madurantakan did not reach there. You mentioned that someone snatched away the torch—he too must have been Aniruddhar’s man. He must have deliberately frightened the horse into running wild. Surely someone would have rescued the prince who fell to the ground. By now, most likely, he is traveling towards Thanjavur in a chariot or palanquin. Come! Let us also go our way.”
“Vaishnavar! I cannot come.”

“What is this? What has become of the task you agreed to undertake? I hear that Aditya Karikalan has already left Kanchipuram. Only if we travel with the swiftness of the wind and the mind can we catch up…”
“Why don’t you deliver the letter meant for Aditya Karikalan yourself? He will not come disguised as a woman like Madurantaka; nor will he travel hidden in the night…”
“What are you going to do?”
“In truth, I did not set out this evening following Madurantaka. I began to follow someone else, and by chance encountered Madurantaka on the way.”
“I shall make a prediction. The one you started to follow must be a woman.”
“You wily Vaishnavite! One day I shall crack your skull and then attend to other matters.”
“That is a task beyond you. I have already pawned my skull to a Kalamukan. If it is lost, so be it. Tell me, whom did you start following from Kudanthai? Who is that woman?”

“The Princess of Kodumbalur had come to the astrologer’s house in Kudanthai. She left alone in her palanquin. In truth, I did not set out following that whimsical girl. Her palanquin happened to travel a short distance along the road I had to take. Suddenly, a group of men attacked the palanquin. They tied up the nurse who accompanied her to a tree and took only Vanathi away. Vaishnavite! I cannot come with you without knowing what has become of that girl.”
“Why are you so concerned about that woman?”

“How can you ask that? Is she not the daughter of the valiant commander of Eezham, the scion of the noble Velar? Is she not the beloved companion of the young princess of Pazhayarai? Moreover, was there not talk of marrying Vanathi Devi to Ponniyin Selvan?”
“Ah! But Ponniyin Selvan has drowned in the sea and perished, has he not? Why worry about his marriage now?”
“What certainty is there that he is dead? It is only a supposition, is it not?”
“If that is so, do you think he might still be alive?”
“Vaishnavar! If your intention is to pry open my mouth and extract some secret from me, you may as well forget it!”
“All right! All right! I know well that you are a stubborn fellow. But you need not worry about Vanathi Devi. You know very well that the Young Princess values her more than her own life, don’t you?”
“That is precisely why I am anxious. Perhaps this danger that has befallen Vanathi Devi is still unknown to the Young Princess?”
“If not today, she will surely come to know of it tomorrow.”
“What use is that? If the Kalamukas offer that maiden as a sacrifice tonight…”
“Are you saying that the Kalamukas have attacked and abducted Vanathi?”
“That is what I suspect. Vanathi’s companion told me the same.”

“If that is true, you need not worry in the least. The Kodumbalur clan are themselves adherents of the Kalamuka sect. If they learn that Vanathi Devi is a Kodumbalur maiden, the Kalamukas will treat her with royal honors!”
“Oh! I did not know that!”
“That is why the Kalamukas are opposed to Madurantaka Devar…”
“What does it matter if these skull-bearing ascetics are against him?”

“You do not know. The greatest families of this land belong to the Kalamuka sect. Many in the army are of their kind. That is why the Pazhuvettarayars made these arrangements today. They tried to secure the support of the Kalamukas for Madurantaka. But due to a mishap with a horse, the plan failed. Now, are you coming with me, or shall I go on alone?”
Vandiyathevan, with a reluctant sigh, stood up and took hold of his horse.
Finding a path through the dense forest just wide enough for a man to pass, they made their way out.
“Look there!” said Azhwarkkadiyan, pointing to the sky.

More than ever before, Vandiyathevan saw that the tail of the comet stretched long, spanning almost half the sky. A cold, wintry breeze was blowing. Vandiyathevan’s body shivered. In the distance, a village dog howled in a plaintive, sorrowful tone.

chapters.title: What Befell Vanathi
paragraphs: As the sun set and darkness gathered from all four directions, Vanathi was traveling by palanquin along the road from Kudanthai to Thiruvarur. Her heart was troubled. She longed to go to the Chudamani Vihara in Nagapattinam, to serve the prince who lay there stricken with fever. But how could that be possible? Would the Buddhist monks allow her into their monastery? Would she be able to see the prince there? Even if she saw him, would she be permitted to tend to him? The very thought of all this left her overwhelmed.

Yet, when she considered that she would have to journey alone to Nagapattinam, a certain courage arose within her. She tried to banish her fears and strengthen her resolve. After all, what great deed in this world is ever accomplished easily? How much hardship does each person endure to achieve their chosen task? How much courage must that boatwoman have possessed to row her craft alone across the sea? In the midst of storm and rain, amidst waves as high as mountains, she had braved the waters and saved the prince—what a heart of steel she must have had! How foolish it was of her, Vanathi thought, to be afraid of this small journey of hers.

If she could not enter the Chudamani Vihara immediately, it was no great loss. It would suffice if she could at least learn news of the prince from those nearby. Even if she could not see the prince, it would be enough if she could see that boatwoman. Yes, that was the way—if only she could find out who she was, perhaps through her she might be able to see the prince. The love she bore for him must serve some purpose. After that, she could even give up her life without regret. Or else, she could join the Buddhist order and become a nun…

To ask the bearers when she might reach Nagapattinam the next day, Vanathi drew aside the curtain of the palanquin and looked outside. Behind the tall trees lining the roadside, she thought she saw some figures lurking in the shadows. She peered more closely. It became clear that those hiding there were Veera Saiva Kalamukhas.

This did not trouble Vanathi in the least. During her childhood in the Kodumbalur palace, Kalamukhas had often come and gone. They would speak with her great-uncle and receive whatever they needed before leaving. Once, the chief guru of the Kalamukhas himself had come to Kodumbalur. He had been honored with all due offerings and worship. Her great-uncle, Bhoothi Vikrama… Kesari has endowed several temples with grants for feeding the Kalamukhas. Therefore, the Kalamukhas would never do him any harm. If anything, they might even come to his aid. Vanathi was well aware that today the great assembly of the Kalamukhas was to be held. That was why, when she traveled from Pazhaiyarai to Kudanthai that day, she happened to see groups of Kalamukhas along the road. Yet, why were these men hiding behind the trees? What if they mistook her for someone else and tried to harm her…?

While she was pondering thus, those who had been concealed suddenly rushed out with a clatter. They surrounded the palanquin. Even then, she did not feel fear. She resolved to reveal her identity to them. But before she could decide how to speak, she saw two of them seize the maid who had accompanied her in the palanquin and tie her to a tree. Instantly, an involuntary cry of terror escaped Vanathi’s lips.

One of the Kalamukhas who had surrounded the palanquin brandished a trident before her face and said, “Girl, do not scream! If you remain silent, we will not harm you. Otherwise, we will pierce you through with this trident and kill you.”

Vanathi gathered her courage and, striving to speak with dignity, declared, “Do you know who I am? I am the daughter of the Kodumbalur Velar. If you lay a finger on me, you will be utterly destroyed.” Though her heart was brave, her voice trembled as she spoke.
The Kalamukha replied, “We know everything. It is for you that we have been waiting. Now, keep quiet for a while! Otherwise…” He again extended the trident menacingly.

At that very moment, the sound of a whip cracking—“swish, swish”—and cries of “Aiyo!” were heard. Vanathi realized that those who were being beaten and crying out were the palanquin bearers. Some of the Kalamukhas must have struck them with their whips! Angered by this, Vanathi thought to get down from the palanquin. But she found no opportunity, for the bearers, still carrying the palanquin, began to run. The Kalamukhas ran alongside, surrounding the palanquin as they went. As they ran, they shouted fiercely.

Vanathi then understood that there was no use in her crying out. It was impossible to leap from the moving palanquin. Even if she did, she would only land amidst these terrifying men. Where were they taking her? For what purpose? These questions flickered through her mind from time to time.

After about half a naazhigai had passed, they halted near an old Durga temple, hidden amidst the trees. By now, darkness had settled thickly all around. One of them entered the temple, took the lamp that was burning inside, and brought it out, holding it up before Vanathi’s face. One of the Kalamukhas stared intently at her and said, “Girl! Tell us what we want to know, and we will let you go unharmed. Or else, wherever you wish to go, we will escort you there safely.”
A suspicion that had never before arisen in Vanathi’s mind now took shape. “What do I know? What are you going to ask me?” she replied.
“Girl! You set out on this solitary journey to meet someone in secret, didn’t you? Who is he? For whom did you set out?”

Vanathi’s suspicion was confirmed. In that instant, a great transformation came over her heart. The timid deer who had trembled at every little sound was now transformed into a lioness who feared nothing in this world.
“What does it matter to you whom I set out to meet? Who are you to question me about it? I cannot tell you!” Vanathi declared.
The Kalamukhan laughed. “You need not tell us; we already know. You set out to meet Prince Arulmozhi Varman! Tell us where he is hiding, and we will let you go unharmed,” he said.
“You may do whatever you wish. You will not learn anything from me,” Vanathi replied, her voice firm and resolute.
“Are you telling us we may do whatever we wish to you? If you knew what we intend to do, you would not dare to speak so boldly!”
“What are you going to do? Tell me that as well, if you dare!”
“First, we will burn one of your beautiful, flower-like hands in the flame of this lamp. Then we will burn your other hand. After that, we will set fire to your dark hair with this lamp…”
“Go ahead and do as you please. Here is my hand! Bring the lamp closer!” said Vanathi.
The intrigues and conspiracies that had been unfolding in the kingdom were all known to Vanathi.

“These villains must be agents of conspirators. They are trying to discover the whereabouts of the Prince. Surely, their intention is to do him harm. If, for the sake of the Prince and his safety, I am fated to endure such cruelties, what greater fortune could there be for me?” Thus thought Vanathi, the princess of Kodumbalur. It was this very thought that gave her such courage of heart.
“Girl! Think carefully before you answer! Do not be stubborn for no reason. You will regret it later! For the rest of your life, you will remain a blind cripple!” threatened the Kalamugan.
“Burn me to ashes, piece by piece; cut my flesh into shreds. Even so, you will not learn a single secret from me,” she replied.
“In that case, we must proceed with our work! Disciple! Bring that firebrand here!” commanded Kalamugan.

At that moment, Vanathi’s attention was drawn to a commotion in the distance. She saw a long procession approaching their spot—elephants, horses, foot soldiers, palanquins, and more. By the grace of the gods, she thought, unexpected help was on its way.
“Look out! See there!” she pointed, drawing their attention. Kalamugan laughed again.
“Do you know who is coming?” he asked.
“It looks like Prime Minister Aniruddha himself. If I cry out now, he and his men will hear me. Beware! Leave me and run away while you still can! Otherwise…” Vanathi threatened.
“Yes, girl! It is indeed Prime Minister Anbil Aniruddha who is coming. It was on his orders that we seized you and brought you here,” Kalamugan revealed.
Now, once again, terror seized Vanathi. Unbidden, a cry of fear escaped her lips. To suppress it, she tried to cover her own mouth with her hand.

chapters.title: Gajendra Moksha
paragraphs: All this while, Vanathi had remained inside the palanquin. Now, the bearers lowered it to the ground. Vanathi stepped out and stood, gazing at the approaching procession. The Kalamukhas too stood in silence, their eyes fixed in the same direction. Only the croaking of frogs in the waterlogged fields and the rustling of tree branches in the monsoon wind could be heard.

The thought of running away never even occurred to Vanathi. She knew well that such a thing was impossible. Perhaps, with some cleverness, she might escape these Kalamukhas, but to flee from Aniruddhar, the beloved minister, was a feat unthinkable even in dreams. His intelligence, his mastery of royal intrigue, his cunning—these were renowned throughout the land. Moreover, it was well known that he wielded great influence with the Emperor. In Pazhayarai, the palace women might gossip about other officials and minor kings of the Chola Empire, but never about Aniruddhar. Even if they spoke in the innermost chambers of the women’s quarters, they feared that their words would reach his ears. Everyone knew that, whatever else the Emperor might tolerate, he would never brook a word of slander against his chief minister, who was both his confidant and the guardian of his honor.

All this Vanathi knew well. She was also aware of the high regard Princess Kundavai held for him. Therefore, she expected that from him she would receive help and protection. But when the Kalamukhas spoke otherwise, her confidence was shaken. Why would he have ordered this orphaned girl to be seized? Perhaps these men were lying! Perhaps it was the Pazhuvettarayars who were coming. Or it might be Madurantakan and his retinue… Whoever it was, one thing was certain: she must not reveal to anyone the news she knew about the prince. Whatever befell her, so be it! Even if it cost her life, so be it!… This thought restored Vanathi’s shaken resolve. Let them come, whoever they may be. She would prove that she was born of the valiant lineage of the Kodumbalur Velirs. She would show that she was the intimate friend of Princess Kundavai.

From the procession, a single palanquin separated itself and came forward. The other elephants, horses, and attendants all remained a little behind. As the palanquin in front drew near Vanathi, it was set down upon the earth. From within it, the Prime Minister Aniruddha Brahmarayar stepped out and stood before her.

At his signal, the palanquin-bearers and the Kalamukha guards moved aside and withdrew. Aniruddha gazed intently at Vanathi from head to toe and exclaimed, “What marvel is this! Am I dreaming, or is this real? Is it not the Princess of Kodumbalur who stands before me? Are you not Vanathi, the beloved daughter of the valiant Parantakan’s younger Velar, who attained the warrior’s heaven in the war at Eezham?”

“Yes, sir! And am I not dreaming either? Is it not Aniruddha Brahmarayar, revered by all the people of the Chola Empire, who stands before me? Is it not the Prime Minister who enjoys the intimate confidence of the Emperor?” replied Vanathi.
“Child! I am glad that you know who I am. That will make my task easier, and you will not have to endure much trouble.”
“Ah! You need not worry about that. If I were to suffer at the hands of a minister of your stature, I would not mind it at all. I would not even consider it suffering.”
“Your words please me even more. I have no intention of causing you much distress. I wish only to ask you a few questions. If you answer them, that will suffice, and then…”
“Sir! Before you question me, I too have a few questions to ask you…”

“Ask, my child! Ask without hesitation. I am like a father to you. I consider you as my own daughter. Only a few days ago, I met your great father, the Commander-in-Chief Boothivikrama Kesari, at Mathottam. He asked me to care for you as if you were my own daughter. I promised him I would…”
“My respects, father! When I lost my father in childhood, the Emperor himself once promised to be a father to me; now, you too have appeared as a father. What more could I want?”
“Ask me what you wish to know, child, and quickly! The sky is darkening, and it looks as if rain is about to fall.”

“Father! Was it by your own orders that your men intercepted your dear daughter, who was traveling by palanquin along the road, and forcibly brought her here from those fearsome Kalamukhas? Was it you who commanded that this helpless maiden’s hand be held to the lamp’s flame and burned? These dreadful men laid such accusations upon you. I did not believe them…”
“My child! What they said is true. It was I who gave them those orders. If that is a crime, then I alone am responsible…”

“O First Minister of Chola Nadu, renowned throughout the three worlds! Your words astonish me. You said, ‘If it is a crime…’ You are learned in all the Dharma Shastras and the treatises of justice. You are the one entrusted with upholding the laws and regulations of the Chola Empire; even if the Emperor himself acts unjustly, you have the authority to censure him and ensure justice is done. If you do not know whether an act is a crime or not, who else would? Is it not a crime to forcibly waylay a defenseless woman traveling along the road and bring her to a secluded place? Is it not a crime to threaten her with torture? If you do not know whether these are crimes, to whom will you turn for an answer? I had heard that in the realm of Sundara Chola, travelers on the road need fear nothing. I had also heard that those who trouble women are punished most severely. Is it not astonishing that you should now doubt whether this is a crime or not?”

Prime Minister Aniruddha was flustered. Twice he tried to interrupt, but it was of no use. Now, raising his voice, he said, “Child! Have patience! Do not display the full extent of your eloquence just yet! There is a reason for my doubt about whether this is a crime or not. It depends on the answer you give to my question. I heard that a woman privy to a grave state secret was traveling on the Nagapattinam road. I ordered my men to intercept her. They must have acted thinking they were fulfilling my command. Perhaps they made a mistake. Instead of the woman involved in state conspiracy, they may have seized you—who had merely visited the Kudanthai astrologer and were returning. Daughter! Tell me: was it truly your intention to return from Kudanthai to Pazhayarai? Did the palanquin bearers mistakenly take you toward the Nagapattinam road? Or were you setting out for Nagapattinam with the intention of meeting, in secret, someone plotting against the state? If you can prove that it was not so— “What they have done is a crime; and I too have a share in it! What do you say, girl? I will ask you more plainly. Did you not set out for Nagai Pattinam to secretly meet Prince Arulmozhi Varman?”

The princess was now thrown into utter confusion. For a moment, she was seized with such anger that she wished she could burn the Prime Minister Aniruddha to ashes. But she realized there was no use in displaying her fury. That simple girl, who until then had known neither guile nor deceit, suddenly found within herself a newfound strength for deep thought and cunning. Therefore, instead of answering the Prime Minister’s question directly, she said, “Sir! What are you saying? Are you accusing Prince Arulmozhi Varman of conspiring against the kingdom? Is it not a crime for you to speak thus of the beloved son of the Emperor? Is it not a conspiracy against the Chola dynasty itself? Ah! I must at once go and tell Princess Kundavai about this!”
“Well said, child! If you answer my question, then there is no need for you to remain here even a moment longer. I myself will see you safely to the Young Princess…”
“And if I do not answer your question…?”
“There is no such thing as not answering, child! It is not so easy to escape from this old man. You must answer my question,” said the minister.

“Sir! Aniruddha Brahmarayar, Prime Minister endowed with all powers! You will learn nothing about the prince from this poor, powerless maiden. Even if these Yamadutas, who threatened me a moment ago, were to thrust my hand into the fire and burn it, I will not speak a word.”

“Daughter of the valiant Velir clan of Kodumbalur! I admire your firmness of mind. But you say you will not reveal a single detail about the prince—yet that is not entirely true. You have already let slip a few things. If you reveal just one more detail, no great harm will come of it. My task too will become easier…”

Once again, Vanathi was startled. Her heart clenched with fear at the thought, ‘Did I let something slip by mistake?’ Her whole body trembled. But then she thought, ‘No, I have not said anything; this old man is only trying to trick me,’ and she gathered a little courage. “Sir! The Vedas, Chapter 39 – Gajendra Moksha…” “Can falsehood ever pass your lips? Would the Prime Minister of Sundara Chola ever fabricate a tale? Did I say anything at all about the prince? Yet you claim I did!” she said.

“Think carefully, my child! Consider well! If you believe that it is impossible to reveal information about something without directly speaking of it, you are gravely mistaken. I am referring to the details you conveyed without uttering a word; listen! The whole world is abuzz with the rumor that Prince Arulmozhi Varman has drowned in the sea and died. The citizens and officials alike are plunged into a sea of sorrow. You, too, have heard this news. Yet, you insisted that you would not say a word about the prince. What does that imply? It means you know that the prince is not dead. When I said you were going to Nagapattinam to see him, you did not deny it. You did not retort, ‘How can I see a prince who has died?’ Nor did you say, ‘I am not going to Nagapattinam, I am going elsewhere.’ Therefore, you have admitted that the prince is alive in Nagapattinam, and that you are going to see him. Now, there are only two details left for you to reveal! You must tell me where exactly the prince is in Nagapattinam; and you must tell me how you came to know this information. If you tell me these two things, then you need not spend another moment here conversing with this old man. You may go wherever you wish.”

Vanathi’s heart was now utterly shaken. She realized that the Prime Minister spoke the truth, and that, in her ignorance, she had betrayed the prince. Was there any atonement for the crime she had committed? None! Nothing remained but to give up her life.
“Sir! You said you were my great father’s close friend. You claimed me as your own daughter. I beg you for one thing. I do not wish to go to Nagapattinam; nor do I wish to go to Pazhaiyarai…”
“You must wish to go to Kodumbalur, perhaps. That is only natural. I shall have you taken there at once.”
“No, sir! I do not wish to go to Kodumbalur either… I wish to leave this world and go to the next. Please, instruct your men to offer me as a sacrifice on that altar yonder! I am ready!” she cried.
“Mother! I promised to fulfill whatever your wish may be. Therefore, if you truly desire to depart for the next world, I will send you there. But before that, you must answer my questions!”
“Sir! Please do not torment me in vain. I will not answer any of your questions. If what you said just now—that you consider me as your own daughter—is true…”

“Daughter! There is no doubt about it. I consider you as my own daughter. Perhaps you do not know how dear your family is to me! Your elder father and I have been friends for forty years. But in matters of the state, there is no room for friendship or kinship. One cannot see even a birth father as a father, nor a beloved maiden as a beloved maiden. Why? Look at the Emperor himself! Because his own son conspired against the state, did he not order that he be captured and brought back in chains?”
“Sir! Are you speaking thus about Ponniyin Selvan? What treason did he commit against the state?”

“Oh! It seems you do not know. Ponniyin Selvan left, saying he was going to wage war in Lanka. There, our brave armies defeated the Lankan forces. Seizing that opportunity, Prince Arulmozhi tried to claim the throne of Lanka for himself. Is this not treason against the state? As soon as he learned of this, the Emperor sent orders to have his royal son arrested and brought back. The prince, defying that order, spread the false news that he had drowned himself in the sea. Then he came ashore and is now hiding somewhere. Since you are unaware of these details, it seems you refuse to reveal his whereabouts. If you attempt to hide such an enemy of the state, that too is a grave crime. Therefore, tell me, child!” said the Prime Minister.

All the anger Vanathi had suppressed until now surged forth uncontrollably. She could not bear the accusations the Prime Minister hurled at Ponniyin Selvan. That gentle maiden now took on the guise of a warrior as she spoke:

“Sir! Nothing you have said is true. You have slandered the prince without cause. When our armies were faltering in Lanka, it was only because the prince went there that they gained courage and fought. It is a truth known to the world that Ponniyin Selvan is the reason for our victory in Lanka. His—” The people of Lanka, seeing his valor and other noble qualities, grew fond of him. In place of their king, who had turned his back on battle and hidden himself, they wished to make the young prince their ruler. The Buddhist monks offered the throne of Lanka to Ponniyin Selvan. But Ponniyin Selvan refused the throne, declaring he did not desire it. About such a man of integrity, you have spoken so much slander! As soon as the prince learned it was his father’s command, he surrendered himself and set out straight for Thanjai. He did not leap into the sea out of his own will. He plunged in only to save the life of his dear friend. He has not plotted against the Emperor. I do not know what misfortune my ears have committed to be forced to hear all these monstrous accusations!”

Aniruddha Brahmarayar smiled lightly and said, “Child! Do you know what people will think, hearing you speak so passionately in defense of Arulmozhi Varman? They will think the two of you are lovers!”

“Sir! Only half of what you say is true. It is true that I have given him my heart. I do not wish to hide that from you. But there is no reason for him to give a place in his heart to this orphaned girl. A koel bird may fall in love with the moon shining in the sky. But the moon will never even know that a koel bird exists.”
“Ah! Until now, I did not know that my dear friend’s daughter was such a fine connoisseur of poetry. Are you not the intimate companion of the young princess Kundavai?” said the Prime Minister.
“Enough, enough! I do not wish to hear your praise. Let me go my way. Otherwise, call your guards and order them to take me away.”

“Child! Have patience! You seem to know many details about Ponniyin Selvan. Surely, you must also know where he is now. Just tell me that. I will send you at once to your great father. He is returning from Lanka. By now, he must have reached Madurai…”

“Sir! A man as full of deceit as you could never be my great father’s friend. I have no kith or kin. I have only told you what everyone knows about the prince. You will learn nothing more from me. Do not waste time…”
“We must not delay. It looks like a heavy rain is about to fall…”
“Is it only rain that will come? Wherever people like you are present, thunder, lightning, and even deluge will follow!”

As if to affirm Vanathi’s words, at that very moment, a long streak of lightning flashed across the sky, darting from one end of the heavens to the other, gleaming fiercely before vanishing. When the lightning faded and darkness enveloped them again, a tremendous peal of thunder shook the very firmament.
“Girl! Will you not tell me where Prince Arulmozhi Varman is?”
“I will not tell!”
“My suspicions are proving true. You have set out to carry some secret message to the place where the prince is hiding—is this true or not?”
“Sir! It is useless; I cannot answer any more of your questions.”
“If that is so, then there is no other way but to mete out to you the severe punishment reserved for those who plot treason against the kingdom.”
“I am ready to accept the punishment, sir! If you wish to lay my head upon the sacrificial altar, do as you will.”
“Shame! You are the daughter of the Kodumbalur Velir! Can I give you such a paltry punishment? Look there, at that elephant!”

Vanathi looked in the direction he pointed. There stood an elephant, as massive as a mountain, its form as dark as if it had been sculpted from black stone and smeared with black ink. Its darkness was set off by two long, curved white tusks that gleamed in the night.

“Girl! You have heard of Gajendra Moksha, have you not? Hearing the elephant’s cry for help, Lord Thirumal rushed forth, slew the crocodile, and sent Gajendra to salvation. But in contrast, this Gajendra has sent countless souls to that very world of salvation where Thirumal dwells. Did you not say you wished to leave this world for another? In the blink of an eye, this elephant will fulfill your wish. If it wraps you in its trunk and hurls you away, you will fall straight into the world of salvation!”
Having spoken thus, Prime Minister Aniruddhar laughed. That laughter sent a shiver down Vanathi’s spine. She thought, “This minister is no mere man, but a demon in human form.”

“Princess! I ask you one last time—will you reveal the whereabouts of Ponniyin Selvan? Or will you attain salvation through the trunk of this Gajendran?” As these words fell upon her ears, Vanathi regained her composure.
“Sir! Do you wish for Gajendran to come to me? Or shall I go to Gajendran myself?” she asked boldly.

Aniruddhar signaled with his hand. At the same time, he spoke something in a tongue that Vanathi could not comprehend. The elephant began to walk, shaking the earth with its steps. It came near Vanathi. With its long trunk, softer than any flower, it encircled her delicate form. It lifted her from the ground.

In those few moments, waves of countless thoughts surged and vanished within Vanathi’s heart. She marveled at her own courage in that fearful hour. “The young princess Kundavai Devi always calls me timid, cowardly—how astonished she would be if she could see my bravery now! One day, she is bound to learn of this incident; she will know that I gave up my life resolutely for Ponniyin Selvan. She will surely tell the prince himself. And then, what will the prince think of me? Will he not realize that the daughter of Kodumbalur Velar is braver than that boatwoman?”

The elephant’s trunk slowly rose higher. Along with it, Vanathi was lifted up. “Yes, yes! What that Brahmarakshasa said is true. This Gajendran is about to send me straight to salvation! In the next moment, it will fling me away! Who knows how far I will be thrown? But by the time I fall, I will have lost consciousness. My life will have left me by then!”

Now, Vanathi was above the elephant’s head. She closed her eyes. The elephant twirled its trunk, ready to hurl Vanathi away. At that instant, by the grace of God, Vanathi lost all awareness of herself.

chapters.title: Anaimangalam
paragraphs: One of our heroines, Vanathi, has developed the habit of fainting often, hasn’t she? We must beg our readers to bear with it just this once. For the time when her malady will leave her is drawing near.

When Vanathi regained a little consciousness, at first it felt as though she were swinging gently. Then she imagined she was journeying through the sky. The sound of the rain, “rim rim,” “jim jim,” reached her ears. The cold wind blew “koob koob” against her body, sending shivers through her. All right, she thought, we are traveling through the clouds to the celestial realms. Darkness surrounded her on all sides, and now and then, flashes of lightning would blaze and vanish.

She faintly remembered the Prime Minister’s last words about Gajendra Moksha, and how the elephant had lifted her up, curling its trunk around her. Everything had happened just as Prime Minister Aniruddha had described. ‘My life in this mortal world is over; now I am on my way to salvation. In the world of liberation, I shall see the gods and goddesses.’
‘But among all the gods, I will not see the one who is the deity of my heart. What is the use of going to a heaven where my heart finds no joy?’

Oh dear! What is this swaying motion! My body is being lifted and carried like this! But the place where my head rests is soft and comfortable. It feels like a mother’s lap. No—more than that, it feels like the lap of the beloved younger princess, who loves me even more than my own mother!… Ah! What must Kundavai Devi be doing now in Pazhayarai? Would news of me have reached her by now?

‘It is true that I am traveling through the clouds to the world of liberation. But what vehicle am I traveling in? Is this the Pushpaka Vimana of the celestial world? Or is it Indra’s Airavata, the divine elephant? Oh! The very thought of an elephant brings a little fear! The elephant, with its swaying, curling trunk!—How much strength lies in that swaying trunk!—But what does it matter now? What is there to fear or worry about anymore?’

‘But why is the place where my head rests so soft, like silk? Because it is dark all around, I cannot see anything. Perhaps I can feel with my hand. Truly, it feels just like a silken drape. It is a little damp as well.’
‘Ah! What is this? Who is touching my cheeks? Is it not a hand as soft as jasmine petals that touches me?’
“Vanathi! Vanathi!”
“Akka! Is it you?”
“It is I. Who else could it be?”
“Are you coming with me to the world of salvation?”
“What hurry do you have to go to the world of salvation already? Have you grown weary of this world so soon?”
“Then, where are we going?”
“Have you even forgotten that? Don’t you know we are going to Anaimangalam?”
“What place is that? Please tell me once more!”
“Enough! We are going to Anaimangalam! We are riding on the back of an elephant!”
“Oh no! An elephant?”
“Silly girl! Why is your body trembling? Have you started to fear just at the mention of an elephant?”
“Akka! Did I fall asleep just now?”
“Yes, yes! In the luxury of traveling atop the elephant in the howdah, you fell into a blissful sleep!”
“There is no bliss in it, Akka! I saw terrifying dreams!”
“I thought as much! You were rambling all sorts of things!”
“What did I ramble, Akka?”

“You spoke of the Kalamukhas! Of sacrifice! Of Gajendra Moksha! Of the elephant’s trunk! Then you called the Prime Minister Aniruddha a ‘sinner, a revenger.’ That Brahmarayar must be pleased! If he had heard all the things you shouted about him in your sleep, he would not have slept for many days!”
“Sister, did all that truly happen in a dream?”
“Was it truly a dream? Or a false one? How would I know? I don’t even know what you dreamt.”

“The Kalamukhas seized me and took me away. The Prime Minister questioned me about the prince’s secret. I refused to tell him. At once, he summoned an elephant and ordered it to seize me with its trunk and hurl me to my death. Even then, I did not falter; I stood firm and courageous. Akka! At that moment, I remembered you. You were not there to witness my bravery.”
“Well, at least in your dream you behaved so bravely! That alone is cause for happiness!”
After a brief silence, Vanathi said, “I still can’t believe it!”
“What is it you cannot believe?”
“I cannot believe that all I saw was a dream.”
“Sometimes dreams are like that. They seem as real as waking life. Even I have had such dreams many times.”
“What kind of dreams have you had? Tell me, please?”
“Why? My brother often appears in my dreams. How many months has it been since he left for Lanka? Yet, whenever I close my eyes at night, he stands before me, just as he is…”
“You are fortunate, Akka!”
“You should praise my fortune. Since the news came that he leapt into the sea, you cannot imagine how my heart has been trembling.”
“Then that too is a dreadful dream, isn’t it? Only the news of his plunging into the sea is real, is it not?”

“If only that too had been a bad dream, how much better it would have been! But that alone is real, Vanathi! Someone who saw the prince leap into the sea with their own eyes came and told us! How can we not believe it?”
“You mean the valiant scion of the Vanar clan, don’t you? Didn’t he say something else about the prince? Didn’t he mention the boat-girl, and the Chudamani Vihara at Nagapattinam?”

“All that must have been your dream. Yes, you raved in your sleep about the boat-girl Poonguzhali, and about the Chudamani Vihara at Nagapattinam! You even muttered that you would become a Buddhist nun! Why, child, do you have such hatred for this worldly life? Why do you wish to become a Buddhist nun?”

“Sister! Do you not know my heart? After hearing that the sea had claimed him, what life is left for me in this world! Sometimes I wish that the elephant I saw in my dream had really lifted me with its trunk and dashed me to death!”
“Oh, wretched girl! If you too were to go, what would become of me?”
“Your fate is different, sister! You…”
“Yes, yes! You care for Arulmozhi more than you do for me, don’t you?”
“Sister! I never said anything like that. I am not as strong-hearted as you. After he… after he is gone…”

“Shame on you! What words are you uttering? Why should you say he is dead? Are you certain? The Pazhuvettaraiyars, the Lady of Pazhuvur, and that fool Madurantakan will shout such things. But why should you or I say so? Why should we even think it?”
“Then what do you say? After he leapt into the sea in that whirlwind… what else could have happened? If he had survived, wouldn’t he have returned by now?”
“Oh, foolish girl! Just because he jumped into the sea, does it mean the sea has claimed him?”
“If he had come ashore, would he have remained hidden all these days?”

“Do you know my father’s story? When he was young, he was missing for many months. They searched for him and finally brought him back and crowned him prince. My grandfather, Arinjaya Chozhar, vanished completely after the battle of Thakkolam. Only after many years did we learn where he was. I…” “I will tell you, Vanathi! Listen. Once, Mother Kaveri saved my younger brother and brought him safely to the shore. In the same way, the Lord of the Ocean would have brought Ponniyin Selvan to land. Between our coastline and the island of Lanka, there are countless small islands. Arulmozhi could be hiding on one of those islands, couldn’t he? I set out on this journey, bringing you along, precisely to spur them on to search for him thoroughly. It seems as if you have forgotten all this. But it is not your fault. Ever since the news about the prince arrived, your mind has been utterly distracted. Only now have you begun to speak with some clarity!”
Vanathi was silent for a moment, then asked, “Akka! Which town did you say we are going to?”
“Anaimangalam.”
“Where is that?”

“It is on the seashore, near Nagapattinam. The Chudamani Vihara you babbled about in your dream is not far from Anaimangalam. Even if you were to become a Buddhist nun, it would be convenient for you. But there is no need to hurry to become a Manimekalai. Let us decide after we receive definite news about Ponniyin Selvan!” said Kundavai, and laughed softly.
“Akka! Why are you laughing? How can you find it in your heart to laugh at a time like this? Do you have such faith that the prince is still alive?”

“If I did not have faith, would I be like this, Vanathi? The horoscopes I have consulted have never failed me. The conch and discus lines on my brother’s palm have never proved false. So far, everything has happened just as foretold.”
“What has happened as foretold? I know nothing of it!” said Vanathi.

“How would you know? You are always wandering about in a daze! It was foretold that Arulmozhi would face many dangers in his youth. So it has come to pass. The rest too must surely follow, mustn’t it?”
“What do you mean, the rest?”
“I have told you so many times already. You have heard it before—why do you ask me to repeat it again? Be quiet and sleep! We can see what the morning brings.”
Vanathi once again fell into deep thought for a while, then asked, “Are we going to travel all night on the elephant, Akka? Why?”

“Have you forgotten even that? If we travel during the day, people from every village along the way will surround us. ‘Where is Ponniyin Selvan?’ ‘Where is the blessed son of the Chola land?’ they will ask. They will accuse the Pazhuvettarayars, curse the young queen of Pazhuvur, and even speak ill of the Emperor himself. Why should we listen to all that? The Pazhuvettarayars will say that I am the one who has incited the people like this—they will surely say so! Why invite such trouble? That is why we set out at night. I told you all this before we left Pazhayarai; yet you ask again. Some strange delusion is playing tricks on your mind! Perhaps we should ask the Buddhist monks at the Chudamani Vihara to find a cure for your delusions! Anyway, let it be; now you sleep! I too feel sleepy. Tonight, we must sleep sitting atop this swaying hill,” said the young princess.

Vanathi resolved not to speak another word and fell silent. Her heart was in utter confusion. She recalled, one by one, all that had happened that day. Everything seemed to her like real events. ‘I have no delusion; it is Akka who is trying to make me believe I am mad,’ she thought at times. She tried to remember what happened after the elephant lifted her with its trunk. Nothing came to mind. What could have happened? At that perilous moment, Akka must have come at the right time and saved her. At the sight of Akka, even the Prime Minister must have been shaken. But is it so easy to rescue someone from the grip of an elephant’s trunk?… Could it have happened like this?… Is this the same elephant that lifted her with its trunk? There was a howdah above. Even in the darkness, she could see it faintly. The young princess might have been in that very howdah. Instead of hurling her far away, perhaps the elephant had dropped her into the howdah. Vanathi had often seen elephants trained to do such things. Could the Prime Minister and the young princess have plotted this together? For what reason? Only to prevent her from traveling alone. Perhaps the young princess did this to test her courage. Had she not once left a toy crocodile near her to test her?… Whatever it may be, it was a great mistake to set out alone today. How peaceful it feels now, resting her head on Akka’s lap. How much courage and encouragement Akka’s words give! Ponniyin Selvan is safe somewhere, of that she is sure… There was no doubt. Perhaps, at the end of this journey, would she meet him?...
As this thought crossed her mind, an immeasurable excitement surged within Vanathi. An energy, the very opposite of her earlier despondency, now took hold of her.

The elephant strode majestically onward. The howdah atop it swayed and rocked gently. Guards marched ahead and behind. The rain had dwindled to a light drizzle, and soon even that ceased. The clouds in the sky scattered and dissolved. The stars peered out, twinkling.

Vanathi gazed up through the roof of the howdah at the stars visible in the sky. She wondered in amazement whether there could be any connection between the stars that wandered the heavens and the lives of people dwelling on earth. Was there any truth in what astrologers said about the compatibility between the star under which Ponniyin Selvan was born and her own birth star? Was it true, as her elder sister and the astrologers claimed, that the son to be born from her womb would one day rule the three worlds? People spoke of the comet’s appearance as a sign of impending calamity—how much truth could there be in that? What sort of calamity might occur? Was Ponniyin Selvan’s plunge into the sea that very calamity? Would he return, as her sister so confidently believed? If so, what other disaster could possibly happen?...

After pondering such thoughts for a long while, Vanathi slowly drifted into sleep. When she opened her eyes, dawn had broken. Birds sang their morning songs. The young princess, too, had awakened. Pushing aside the silk curtain of the howdah, she looked out and said, “Here we are—Aanaimangalam! We have reached the very entrance of the Chola palace!”

Both princesses descended from the elephant. They entered the palace. The palace attendants, who had been waiting in readiness, led the two princesses through every part of the mansion, showing them all its wonders. At last, they came to the southern wing of the palace and stood on the threshold of a decorated courtyard, gazing at the canal that mingled with the sea.
“Akka! You said you were making arrangements to search for the prince. What have you done?” asked the Kodumbalur princess.
“Yes, Vanathi! The arrangements to search for him have already begun. Look there—a boat is coming! Perhaps those arriving in it will bring us some news!” said Kundavai.
Vanathi turned around and looked back. Through the gaps between the branches, she could see a small boat approaching in the distance. There were two people in it.
“Akka! Who is coming in that boat?” Vanathi asked.
“The one rowing the boat is Sendhan Amudhan. The same man whom we freed from the underground prison of Thanjavur that day. The one sitting is Poonguzhali!”
A shiver ran through Vanathi’s body. “Akka! I do not wish to see that woman. I am going inside!” she said.
“Why are you so afraid to see her, dear? Do you think she will swallow you whole? I am here, I will take care of it. Don’t be afraid, just stay calm!” said Kundavai. The boat was drawing nearer.

How did Vanathi escape from the elephant’s trunk? Of the two guesses she had made, the second was correct. The elephant did not hurl her away with its trunk. Instead, it gently lifted her and placed her near the howdah. There, hidden behind a screen and waiting, Kundavai caught her in her arms and laid her on her lap.
Afterwards, the Prime Minister too got into his palanquin. “Devi, shall I take my leave? May your journey be pleasant. May its end be auspicious as well!” he said.
“Sir, I am deeply grateful for your help!” said the young princess.
“You called the princess of Kodumbalur a coward? I have never seen a girl with such courage as hers.”
“She used to be timid before. Only recently has she gained such bravery,” said Kundavai.
“It is all your training. That girl must think I am a terrible demon; let her think so if she wishes. Many people think of me in many ways. I do not worry about all that. Farewell, Amma!”
