With these words, the Prime Minister’s palanquin and his four guards set off towards the west, while the elephant, horses, and the rest of the retinue went east.

Shortly after the Prime Minister’s palanquin had departed, it began to rain. Undeterred by the downpour, the men carrying the palanquin and the soldiers guarding it continued on their way. When the rain lessened to a drizzle, the palanquin suddenly came to a halt.
“Why have you stopped?” asked the Prime Minister.
“Swami, it looked as if someone was lying beneath that tree!” replied one of the guards who had gone ahead.
The Prime Minister fixed his gaze in the direction the man pointed. A sudden flash of lightning illuminated the scene.
“Yes, it does seem like someone is lying there. I will get down and see,” said the Prime Minister.
He descended from the palanquin and approached. As he drew near, he heard the groaning of the man lying under the tree.
“Who is here?” called out Aniruddhar.
In response, a feeble voice replied, “It sounds like the Prime Minister!”
“Yes, it is I,” answered the Prime Minister.
“Who is lying here?”
“Sir! Don’t you recognize me? I am Madurantakan!”
“Prince! What is this state? How did you come here? What has happened?” exclaimed the Prime Minister in alarm, as he hurried to lift Madurantakan to his feet.

chapters.title: Madhurantakan’s Gratitude
paragraphs: The moment the Prime Minister’s hand touched Madurantakan, he cried out in pain.
“Aiyo! Father! I am finished! Do not touch me. My legs! Gone! Gone!”
Aniruddhar stopped trying to lift him and asked anxiously, “Prince! What has happened to you? What has happened to your legs?”
“My legs are completely broken; I cannot walk, I cannot even stand!”
The Prime Minister turned around and commanded his men, “Hey! Bring the palanquin here at once!”

Then he asked, “Sir! How did this accident happen? Why are you lying here alone in the rain? Where are the attendants who accompanied you? How could they dare to leave you like this? No punishment would be too great for them!”

“Prime Minister! Do not punish anyone! No one is at fault. In the evening, I myself mounted my horse and set out alone. I was riding along the riverbank. Suddenly, a heavy rain began. A great flash of lightning struck, followed by a thunderclap. The horse panicked and bolted. I got caught on a branch of this tree and fell down. The horse ran off somewhere. I do not know whether my leg broke in the fall or got twisted. I cannot get up or stand. Fortunately, you happened to come by at this very moment!”

“It must be the merit earned by your father, the great Kandaradithar, that brought me here at this time! Grit your teeth and bear it for a little while. I will have you placed in the palanquin. I will learn the rest of the details after we reach my house in Nathankovil,” said Aniruddhar.

When the palanquin was brought near and set down, the Prime Minister gently lifted the prince and laid him inside. He instructed the bearers to carry the palanquin slowly and steadily, without any jostling. He himself walked alongside the palanquin as it moved forward.

After a short while, they arrived at Sundara Chola Vinnagaram, known in common parlance as Nathan Koil. Near the grand Perumal temple of that town stood the mansion of the Prime Minister, Aniruddhar. The prince, Madurantakan, was carried inside and laid upon a bed within. When a lamp was brought and the injury examined, it was found that his leg was not broken, but merely sprained. The prince’s fear abated somewhat. Both of them partook of the prasadam brought from the Perumal temple.

Afterwards, the Prime Minister said, “Prince! Now, rest peacefully for the night. At dawn, you may act as you see fit. I am going to Thanjavur. If you wish to come with me, I will ensure your safe arrival there.”

“Sir! You have done me much harm in the past. Today, you have made amends for all of it. I shall never forget the help you have rendered me this day. I shall always be grateful to you. If, by chance, I am ever destined to ascend the throne of this Chola Empire, I will keep you as my Prime Minister!” said Madurantakan.

Aniruddhar, feigning astonishment, replied, “Prince! I am duty-bound to the Chola dynasty. It is my obligation to advise and assist all those who belong to this lineage. Therefore, there is no need for you to thank me personally. However, you mentioned that I have done you some harm—this, I do not understand. I do not recall ever having intentionally wronged you. If you would kindly explain, I shall atone for it in whatever way possible!”

“Sir Aniruddhar! The whole world knows you are a great trickster, a wise man, and an expert in statecraft. But do not display your cunning with me. Do not think I am unaware of the gravity of the harm you have done me. Even so, in light of the help you have given me today, I am willing to forget all that. Tell me in what manner I may express my gratitude to you. If there is any way I can repay you, let me know.”

Aniruddhar smiled and said, “Yes, Prince! There is indeed a way for you to show your gratitude. This old man has a boon to ask of you. Hereafter, do not set out alone on horseback like this. Travel in a chariot, surrounded by attendants before and behind. Better yet, travel in a palanquin, for the times are—” “It is a dangerous situation. For many reasons, the people are agitated and restless. You saw it yourself today in Pazhaiyarai! Therefore, it is better to travel in a closed palanquin rather than an open one. If it is the palanquin of the younger queen of Pazhuvoor, it would be even more advantageous. No one would ever suspect a thing!” he said.

Madurantakan was taken aback. Once again, signs of fear appeared on his face. After a moment’s pause, he composed himself and said, “Prime Minister! What words are these that you speak! What do you mean by asking me to travel in the closed palanquin of the younger queen of Pazhuvoor? Is it your intention to humiliate me?...”

“Prince! I do not know why you consider it humiliating to travel in the queen’s palanquin. Since when have you had such thoughts? Was it not your custom, until recently, to travel often in that very manner? Surely, you must have come to this noble decision only after returning from Kadambur Sambuvarayar’s palace…”
Madurantakan grew even more alarmed. The pallor of terror spread across his face. “Prime Minister! To Kadambur palace, I… I…” he stammered, beginning to say something.

“Prince! Did you not go to Kadambur palace on the eighteenth day of the month of Aadi, on the day of the great flood, along with the noble Periya Pazhuvetarayar? That is what I refer to. At that time, you went and returned in the younger queen’s palanquin. I must confess, I did not much like it. Palanquin travel is suited to old men like me. Young men such as yourself ought to ride elephants or horses. But for riding horses, one must have proper training. When your health permits, I myself will arrange for it…”

“Dear Aniruddha! Beware! You continue to utter words that humiliate me. Just because this unfortunate incident has occurred today, you have decided that I do not know how to ride a horse. Because I once traveled in a palanquin, you now say that I always travel in the closed palanquin of the Pazhuvoor queen. I have borne it, thinking of your age and the help you have rendered me today…”

“Prince! Your patience gives me great joy. ‘He who endures shall rule the earth’—so goes the ancient saying. What does the great poet of Tamilakam declare? ‘Like the earth that bears those who dig it…’ “Enduring the insults of others is the greatest virtue.”

The earth endures those who dig into her. Does she merely endure? No—she even aids those who dig, by offering them pure water. This quality of the earth should be possessed by those who wish to rule her. If an old man like me utters something inappropriate, it is only fitting that you, who desire to rule the land, endure it.”

“Sir! What are you saying? Are you accusing me of wishing to rule this Chola Empire?” asked Madurantakan. His lips trembled; his brows knit together. Signs appeared that his fear was turning into anger and agitation.

But the Prime Minister, without the slightest agitation, replied, “Prince! Why do you say I am accusing you? If you wish to rule this Chola Empire, how is that a crime? You are born in the illustrious line of the heroic Vijayalaya Chola. You are the noble son of the great Sivanana Kandaradithar. You have every right to ascend the Chola throne. How can it be a crime to desire it? Even if someone says it is a crime and advises you to engage in secret conspiracies for that purpose, do not believe them. Prince! Listen for a moment to the words of this old man. Your parents’ wishes were of one kind. You too, in accordance with that, immersed yourself in devotion to Shiva. Now your mind has changed. No one has the right to blame you for that. You may openly claim your right. You may express your desire directly to the Emperor. There is no need to seek the support of the Kalamukha sect in the darkness of Amavasya night by going alone to the banks of the Kollidam. Nor is there any need to gather in the Samburayar palace at midnight like a band of thieves to plot conspiracies. Consider those who give you such advice to be your greatest enemies!”

Madurantakan was thrown into deep confusion. He was astonished beyond measure at how much the Prime Minister knew. At the same time, fear grew on one side, and, because of that fear, anger swelled on the other.
“Sir, how do you know all this? Which traitor, pretending to be my friend, has been coming to you and revealing everything?” he asked.
“There is no use in your trying to find that out. Across this vast kingdom, I have eyes everywhere! And ears as well! Nothing can happen in this land without my knowledge…”
“In that case, does the Emperor know all these things too?” asked Madurantakan.
“No; he does not know. Many secrets that my eyes and ears have brought to me are locked within my heart. Unless necessity and urgency demand it, they shall never come out…”

“Yes, yes; countless dreadful secrets are buried within your heart. If only those came to light, would not this Chola Empire itself tremble in its core?” said Madurantakan. Now, in his voice, there was a note of cunning and deceit that had not been there before.

The Chief Minister, noticing this, yet pretending not to, replied, “The Emperor is my close friend. But even so, there are secrets in my heart that he does not know. Sundara Chola is afflicted with a cruel illness. For many reasons, his heart is already wounded. I do not wish to hurt him further by telling him of the conspiracies of the petty kings. There is no necessity for it. Prince! As far as your affairs are concerned, you may trust that I shall never speak of them to the Emperor.”
“Sir! O Aniruddha, full of affection! What is the reason for this sudden surge of fondness towards this fool Madurantakan?” asked Madurantakan, and let out a mocking laugh.

“Prince! It is not that I have suddenly grown fond of you. I have always cherished affection for you, just as I do for the sons of Sundara Chola. Only, until now, there has not been an opportunity to show it…”
“Today, that opportunity has come! Because I fell from my horse and broke my leg. But had it been a few days earlier, you would have strangled me to death beneath that very tree…”
“Narayana! Narayana! What words are these, Prince!”

“Sir! Do not think that I know nothing. Do not imagine me to be an innocent who will believe whatever is told to him. You began to plot against me from the very moment I was in my mother’s womb. On this earth—” “You had made arrangements to kill me as soon as I was born… Ah, I see the signs of astonishment on your face. Are you surprised at how I came to know all this? Do not imagine that you alone are privy to the terrible secrets of this Chola land!”

Aniruddha’s face now truly presented a remarkable sight. For a fleeting moment, a shadow passed across it and vanished. At last, with a smile tinged with regret and sorrow, the Prime Minister said, “Yes, Prince! It is true that I was once so arrogant. Today, that pride has been shattered. If, as you say, arrangements had been made to kill you at birth, how did you survive? If you reveal that secret as well, I shall consider myself fulfilled!”

“It seems you wish to test how much I truly know! Very well; I shall tell you. Those you had arranged to commit infanticide, in their haste, took the newborn away without even checking whether it was a boy or a girl. When they realized it was a girl, they returned to inform you. You told them to let the child live, to entrust her to a temple priest to be raised. Half a nazhikai after that girl was born, I was born. You had not anticipated that. My horoscope, too, was favorable. That is how I survived. Even after you learned that your plan had failed, you devised many schemes to prevent me from ascending the throne. You arranged for me to be raised as a devotee of Shiva—a madman, in other words. But you failed in that as well. I did not become as completely mad as you wished. Sir! O Prime Minister! Why do you sit there stunned and silent? Is it not your turn now to deny all this in one breath?”
The Prime Minister truly sat there, stunned. At length, mustering the strength to speak, he said, “Prince! When you know so many details, what is the use in my trying to deny them?”

“Yes, there is no use! I also know the reason why you have suddenly become affectionate towards me. You do not like Aditya Karikalan. You wished to place Arulmozhi Varman on the Chola throne. Now that the sea has taken him, you have turned your affection towards me! Still, let me say this: I am willing to forget all the wrongs you have done to me in the past. I shall also thank you for the help you have given me today. If, from this day forth, you declare yourself to be on my side, then when I ascend the throne, I wish to retain you as my Prime Minister!” said Madurantakan.
“Prince! Your words fill me with delight!” said Anbil Aniruddha Brahmarayar.

chapters.title: The Forest is Cleared
paragraphs: In the Chudamani Vihara of Nagapattinam, Ponniyin Selvan lay upon a wooden cot in the room adjacent to that of the venerable Acharya Bikshu. For three days, he had been gripped by a fierce fever; for the most part, he had been bereft of consciousness. During these days, the monks had watched over him with utmost care and vigilance. They administered medicine at regular intervals. Frequently, they poured water into his mouth and tended to him with great caution.

Now and then, whenever a flicker of awareness returned, he tried to contemplate his surroundings. His attention was drawn to a mural painted on the wall opposite him. In that painting, gods, gandharvas, and yakshas could be seen. Some among them held various musical instruments. Some bore white chowries and silver-tipped parasols. Others carried trays filled with flowers of many hues in their hands. The scene was rendered with such vividness that the forms of the gods seemed to possess life itself.

Often, after gazing at these images, Ponniyin Selvan fancied that he had indeed arrived in the realm of the celestials. He imagined that these divine yaksha and kinnara beings had come to welcome him. He wondered how he had come to reach the heavenly world. It seemed to him that he must have journeyed to the celestial realm along a stream bordered on both sides by dense thazhampu thickets, their golden blossoms in full bloom. When the memory of that stream arose, he fancied he could even smell the fragrance of the thazhampu flowers. He vaguely recalled being ferried along that stream in a boat, accompanied by a divine prince and princess. The prince seemed to be a devotee of Shiva, for he often sang sweet Thevaram hymns. What of the princess? She did not sing. She spoke only a few words now and then, but even those sounded like divine music. With eyes brimming with affection and longing, she often gazed at him. Where were those two now?

In the heavenly realm, it seemed, not only gods, yakshas, and kinnaras, but even Buddhist monks held a place of importance! Perhaps they were the guardians of the nectar vessel of the divine world! Frequently, a Buddhist monk would approach him, pour a little nectar into his mouth, and then depart. In the realm of the gods, among other... No matter how many comforts there are, thirst alone grows ever greater. Couldn’t this Buddhist monk pour just a little more nectar into my mouth before leaving? Why such poverty of spirit even in the celestial realms! Perhaps one should not drink too much nectar all at once! Is this truly nectar? Or could it be some kind of intoxicating liquor?—Nonsense, would monks even touch wine with their hands? Would they bring it to my lips and pour it themselves? If not, then why does this dizziness overtake me? Why does my memory fade so quickly after drinking this nectar?

For three days, thus, Ponniyin Selvan drifted between the world of the gods and a void of forgetfulness, his consciousness wavering between the two. On the morning of the fourth day, he awoke as if rising from a deep sleep, his mind fully restored. His body was weak, but his mind was clear. He realized that the figures before him on the wall were only painted images. Those devas, yakshas, and kinnaras were not standing there to welcome him; they were painted to greet Lord Buddha on his visit to the celestial realms. On another wall, he saw a painting of Lord Buddha ascending through the cloud-filled sky. He understood that he was lying in a Buddhist vihara. As he pondered which vihara and where, the events that had unfolded since he began his journey from Lanka returned to him one by one. He remembered, up to the point where he and Vandiyathevan had been tossed about in the surging sea, their arms growing weary. After that, all was confusion.

At that moment, a Buddhist monk entered the room, as usual, carrying a bowl of nectar in his hand. As the prince approached, the monk gazed intently at him. The prince reached out, took the bowl, and examined its contents. He confirmed that it was not the nectar of the gods. He realized it was medicine, or perhaps milk mixed with medicine. Looking at the monk, he asked, “Swami! What is this place? Who are you? How many days have I been lying here like this?”
The monk gave no reply, but turned and left the room. In the next room, the prince heard him say, “Acharyar! The fever has cleared well. His memory has fully returned!”

After a short while, an elderly monk entered the room where Ponniyin Selvan lay. Coming to the bedside, he too gazed intently at the prince. Then, with a gentle smile, he said, “Ponniyin Selva! The place where you are now is Nagai Pattinam…” Chudamani Viharam. You arrived here three days ago, suffering from a severe bout of typhoid fever. We have been given the privilege of serving you. We are indeed fortunate!” he said.

“I too am fortunate. I have long desired to visit this Chudamani Viharam. Once, long ago, when I was passing by this city’s harbor, I saw it from the outside. By divine will, it has now come to pass that I have come and stayed here. Swami, do you know how I came to be here? Can you tell me?” asked Arulmozhi Varman.
“Prince! First, please take the medicine in your hand. I will tell you all that I know,” said the Bhikshu.
The prince took the medicine and said, “Sir! This is not medicine; it is nectar. You have taken such care and arranged for my treatment. But I am not going to thank you for it.”

The Acharya Bhikshu smiled and said, “Prince, there is no need for you to thank me. Lord Buddha has declared that treating the sick is the highest dharma. The Buddha’s dharma commands us to treat even suffering animals. There is nothing special in treating you. We are deeply indebted to the Chola dynasty. Your father, Sundara Chola Chakravarthi, and your noble sister, the young princess, have given great support to the Buddha’s dharma. We know well how you arranged for the renovation and construction of Buddhist viharas in Anuradhapura, Lanka. In that case, we do not expect gratitude from you for this small service…”

“Acharya! I did not speak of gratitude in that sense. I know how severe a fever must have afflicted me. I have seen the fate of those stricken by this fever in Lanka. Rightfully, I should have departed for the world of the gods by now. There, the devas, yakshas, and kinnaras might have welcomed and served me, would they not? Today, I would truly be drinking nectar among the gods and goddesses, immersed in bliss, would I not? But you have ruined that! You have brought me back from the very threshold of the celestial world to this world of suffering and sorrow. Therefore, I do not consider that you have done me a favor. That is why I said I would not thank you!”
The face of the Acharya Bhikshu blossomed with the fullness of joy.

“Ponniyin Selva! When the time comes for you to ascend to the celestial world, Indra himself and the other gods will arrive in their heavenly chariots, the divine drums resounding, a shower of flowers raining down as they come to escort you. But that time is still far away. Here, in this mortal world, there are countless great deeds you must accomplish! Only after fulfilling those should you think of journeying to the heavens,” he said.

Until then, Ponniyin Selvan had been lying down, but now he sat up straight. An extraordinary radiance shone on his noble face. From his wide, beautiful eyes, beams of light flashed like lightning, filling the entire room with a luminous glow.

“Acharyare! What you say is true. In this world, there are certain tasks I long to achieve. I wish to accomplish many great works. I have seen this Choodamani Vihara from the outside once. I have also seen the stupas and viharas at Anuradhapura. I am going to rebuild this Choodamani Vihara to be as grand as the Abhayagiri Vihara in Anuradhapura. I will install statues here, like the great Buddha statues I saw there. I will also restore and rebuild the Shiva temples in this Chola land in the same manner. When I see the stupas and viharas in Lanka and then think of the temples here in Chola country, my body and soul feel diminished. I am going to construct a magnificent temple in Thanjavur, with a towering gopuram that reaches the sky. I will have a fitting statue of Mahadeva made and installed there. Acharyare! In this noble Chola land, the Buddhist stupas and the gopurams of the Shiva temples will compete with each other, striving to touch the clouds. Generations born in this divine Tamil land, thousands of years from now, will stand in awe before them…”

Thus, speaking with fervor, the prince, weakened by his illness, slumped back onto the bed. At once, the Acharya Bhikshu caught his shoulders and gently laid him down, making sure his head did not strike the cot. Stroking his forehead with his hand, he said, “Prince! In due course, you will accomplish all the great deeds you have envisioned. But first, your body must recover its full strength. Be calm for now!”

chapters.title: The Nandi Mandapam
paragraphs: The next afternoon, the Periya Bikshu came once again to see Ponniyin Selvan.

The prince was burning with eagerness to ask him many questions. His attempts to learn anything by questioning the Chinna Bikshu had not succeeded. “Ayya! The Guru Devar will reveal everything,” was the only reply he received, again and again.
As soon as the Guru Devar arrived, he asked, “Prince! How is your health now?”

“Ayya, my body is troubling me greatly. It keeps saying, ‘Why are you lying here idly? Get up and run! Mount a horse! Dive into the river and swim! Wrestle with an elephant! Don’t just lie here doing nothing!’ My stomach too is unusually lively. All the food the Chinna Bikshu brought and gave me was not enough. Acharyare! I can hardly believe that for so many days I was lost in a feverish delirium. Your medicine has worked wonders!” said Ponniyin Selvan.

“Ayya! One should not trust the body’s words too much. When the fever clears, it will be like this; you may feel a little reckless, but if the fever returns a second time, it could endanger your very life!”
“Gurudevar! I am not all that afraid about any danger to my life…”

“You may not be worried; that is well and good! But do you know how much the crores of people in this Chola land have been worrying these past four or five days? The towns and cities are in utter turmoil. From tiny children to the aged, all are shedding tears…”

“Ayya! I do not understand what you are saying. Why should the people be so distressed? Is it because they thought I might not recover from this fever? When they know you are treating me at the Choodamani Vihara, why should they be anxious?”

“Prince! The people do not know about your fever, nor that you are here at the Choodamani Vihara. If the people of this city knew, would there be such peace in this monastery? Wouldn’t they have broken down the walls and rushed in, all of them, to see you…?” “Did they not care? If you had heard the wailing and lamentation that arose in this city when the news came that you had drowned in the sea that morning… Why, even within this very vihara, was there a single soul who did not weep and cry aloud that day?”

Ponniyin Selvan sat up on his bed and asked, “Gurudeva! What is this you are saying? I do not understand a thing. News came that I had drowned in the sea? When did this happen? Who brought such dreadful tidings? And for what reason?”

“No one knows who brought it! One morning, that news had spread throughout the city. People were saying that the ship which brought you from Lanka to Kodikkarai was caught in a whirlpool and sank. Along the shores of Kodikkarai, the officer Pazhuvettarayar searched for you in every way, but even your body could not be found, and so the news spread in alarm that you must have perished in the sea. Hearing this, even I stood at the entrance of this vihara, grieving. At that moment, another bhikshu came and informed me that a patient had been brought by boat and was waiting in the canal behind the vihara. When I went at once to see, I found that the patient in the boat was you. After that, we have been treating you for three days. Only yesterday did you regain your memory.”
“Acharyare! Who was it that brought me here in the boat? Can you tell me?”
“A young man and a young woman brought you, rowing the boat.”
“Yes, yes; even I remember it now as if from a dream. Do you know who that young man and woman are? Was the young man Vandiyathevan of the Vanar clan?”
“No, my lord! He said his name was Sendhan Amudhan. He seemed to be a great devotee of Shiva. I did not learn the young woman’s name. She was strong in body and mind…”
“I think I can guess who she is. The boat-girl Poonguzhali; the daughter of Thyaga Vidangar. Did they not tell you why they brought me here?”
“No, Prince! I did not ask them about that.”
“Did you not inform anyone that I am safe here?”
“No, my lord! Those who brought you here asked that it not be told to anyone. Considering your condition, I too thought it best to remain silent.”

“Acharyare! There has been some conspiracy here. My father, the Emperor of the Three-Crowned Cholas, had ordered that I be brought back as a prisoner. In obedience to that command, I set out from Lanka. But in the meantime, various incidents have occurred. It seems this plot has been staged to accuse me of acting against the Emperor’s orders. They have even spun a tale that I drowned and died in the sea. Gurudeva! By giving me refuge in this Choodamani Vihara, you have already committed an act of royal treason. To keep me here any longer would be a grave offense. Please, send me to Thanjavur at once…”

“Prince! If I am to receive royal punishment for having given you shelter, I would welcome it with joy. Even if, for that reason, this ancient Choodamani Vihara is to be razed to the ground and reduced to dust, it matters not…”
“I am gladdened by your affection, Gurudeva! Yet, how did you accept me here without questioning those who brought me?”

“What need was there to question? What greater duty could there be for a bhikshu like myself than to receive you, who arrived in such distress, and tend to your wounds? Moreover, your noble elder sister, Kundavai Devi, had already informed me in advance that you might come here and stay for a few days.”
“Oh! Is that so? Did the young princess send word thus? When was this?”
“A few days before your arrival. Even Senthan Amudhan, who brought you here, said it was ‘the wish of the young princess.’”
“Gurudeva! Did the two who brought me here leave immediately? Can they be found? I must see them, for there are certain matters I wish to know.”
“Sir! Do not be anxious. Both of them are still in this city. Each day, they come to inquire about your health and then depart. For some reason, they have not yet come today…”

At that moment, a young bhikshu entered and made a sign to the Gurudeva. The Acharya bhikshu said, “I am coming, sir!” and left the room. When he returned after a short while, he saw that Prince Arulmozhi’s agitation had only increased.

“Acharyare! I cannot remain here even for another moment. I do not wish to bear the blame of having come here and hidden myself, defying the Emperor’s command. Nor do I wish any harm to befall this ancient Choodamani Vihara because of me,” said the prince.

The elder Bhikshu, his face blossoming with a gentle smile, replied, “Truly, I too can no longer bear such a great responsibility. I do not wish to keep you here against your will, not even for a moment. You may depart this very instant. A boat is ready and waiting in the canal!”
“To where am I to go?”
“That is for you to decide. The two who brought you here have come with the boat to take you away.”
The prince hesitated for a moment. Seeing the mysterious smile shining on the Acharya Bhikshu’s face, he wondered, “Could there be some new intrigue in this?”
“Have both of them returned? Did they not say for what purpose?”
“They did. About a naazhigai’s distance from this vihara, on the banks of the canal, there is a Nandi Mandapam. Two ladies are waiting there to see you.”
The prince hastily got down from the cot. “Acharyare! Please take me to the boat at once! So much time has already been lost,” he said.

The Bhikshu supported the prince with his hand and accompanied him to the canal bank. Yet, in the prince’s gait, there was no sign of the exhaustion that had weighed him down for more than four days in the harsh forest. Seeing Ponniyin Selvan striding forth with such majesty, the faces of Sendhan Amudhan and Poonguzhali blossomed with joy.

As Arulmozhi Varman boarded the boat and sat down, the Bhikshu looked at him and said, “Sir! If ever we have the opportunity to serve you, all the Bhikshus of this Choodamani Vihara would consider it a great fortune. It would be well if you could return here, stay for a week, and regain your strength!”
“Gurudeva! I too feel that I shall return. Otherwise, I would not have departed so hastily, without even bidding farewell to the other Bhikshus!” said the prince.
As soon as the boat began to move, Sendhan and Poonguzhali glanced at each other in turn. The prince spoke:

“When you brought me along this canal, I thought you were divine beings from the heavenly realms, come to lead me to paradise. But you have deceived me. You have taken me instead to a monastery of ascetics! So be it; let it be so. Ever since I was exhausted from swimming in the sea and lost consciousness, I must ask you both about everything that has happened. But first, tell me—who are those waiting for me at the Nandi Mandapam?”

Though Arulmozhi Varman addressed them both, it was not Poonguzhali who replied. It was Sendhan Amudhan who answered. He informed the prince that Princess Kundavai and the Kodumbalur princess had come to Anaimangalam and were now waiting for him at the Nandi Mandapam.
“Ah! Why has the younger princess brought along that girl who faints at the slightest thing?” asked the prince.

Sendhan Amudhan replied, “Sir, among the women of Tamil Nadu, a strange fever is spreading. They say they are abandoning the sacred Saiva faith and turning to Buddhism, intending to become bhikshunis.”
“Who is saying such things?”
“The Kodumbalur princess is said to be speaking thus. And this young princess here is saying the same!”

“Only two of them, Amudha! That will not bring any harm to the Saiva faith! In Lanka, I have seen many monasteries where bhikshunis lead lives of renunciation. If they wish, I myself will take them and leave them there!” said Ponniyin Selvan, and Sendhan Amudhan laughed.

Then, from the time the prince and Vandiyathevan came ashore from the sea, Sendhan Amudhan recounted all that had happened, as much as he knew. Ponniyin Selvan listened eagerly, matching the tale with his own memories.
“There, the Nandi Mandapam!” Poonguzhali said, pointing. The prince turned to look in the direction she indicated.

chapters.title: Nandi Grows!
paragraphs: At the place where the boat was now gliding, the banks of the canal rose high on either side. At the spot Poonguzhali pointed out, a bathing ghat pavilion could be seen on the edge of the canal. At the spot where the steps ended and the mandapam began, two Nandi statues stood on either side. Those statues of Nandi, crafted with exquisite workmanship and vibrant life, can be admired even today. It was because of the prominence of these sculptures that the pavilion had come to be known as the “Nandi Mandapam.” Once a year, during the spring festival, it was customary for the presiding deities of Thirunagikkaronam—Kayarogana Swami and Neelayadakshi Amman—to visit this pavilion and be ceremoniously seated in state. At that time, crowds of people would gather here in throngs. After witnessing the festival, they would partake in a moonlit feast before returning home. Since the pavilion stood a little distance from the city, on ordinary days, few people visited this place.

The boat drew near the mandapam. After seeing the two women standing there, the prince’s gaze and attention turned to nothing else. As the boat approached, the young princess Kundavai descended the steps and came down to the lower landing. Vanathi, meanwhile, stood in the pavilion itself, half-hidden and half-revealed behind a pillar.
The boat came to a halt near the bathing steps. To help the prince disembark, Sendhan Amudhan from the boat and the young princess from the steps both extended their hands.
Sendhan Amudhan and Poonguzhali then rowed the boat back a little distance and moored it there.
“Thambi! How thin you have become!” said Kundavai, her mellow voice trembling with tears.

Ponniyin Selvan replied, “Let my body be thin, Akka! But why does your face look so wan? Isn’t it your custom that your face blossoms like a lotus upon seeing me? Why today does a cloud seem to veil the moon of your face? Why are your eyes filled with sorrow? Ah! Many things must have happened to wound your heart and cause you pain. Otherwise, you would not have sent me such an urgent message!” “Yes, my brother! There are so many urgent matters I must tell you; so much I must hear from you. O generous one who refused the golden throne of Lanka! Sit for a moment upon this black stone throne!” she said.
As Ponniyin Selvan sat, he touched his sister’s feet and pressed them to his eyes. Kundavai placed her hand upon his head and kissed his crown. Tears welled up once more in her eyes.

After they both sat down, Kundavai said, “Brother! I should not have summoned you here today. The head of the Chudamani Vihara sent word that your health was fully restored. That is not true; the fever has worn you down. But I could not bear to remain without seeing you. Since coming to Anaimangalam, every moment has passed like an age!”

“Sister! Do not worry about having me come here. Had you not sent the boat, I would have already set out for Pazhaiyarai. Even in the grip of that terrible fever, it was your letter that troubled my mind. Whom did you send that letter with? I have never seen a man as valiant as that Vandiyathevan of the Vanar clan. I tested him in so many ways; he passed them all. Where is he now, sister?”

The cloud that had veiled the moon of Kundavai’s face parted a little. Her coral lips parted in a smile, revealing a row of pearl-like teeth. “Brother! Why worry about him now? There are so many other matters at hand!” she said.
“Why do you speak so, sister? Did he behave in a way that displeased you?”
“No, no! Why should I be displeased? He promised to bring you here, and he has fulfilled that promise…!”

“I am amazed when I think of the clever tricks and cunning stratagems he employed for that. Where is he, sister? When I learned you had come here, I thought surely Vandiyathevan would have come with you. Has not this princess, who faints at the slightest provocation, come as well?”

“You do not know how courageous she has become, brother! Yesterday, the Prime Minister’s elephant lifted her with its trunk and tossed her. It threw her right into my lap in the howdah above. But she does not know it! If only you had seen how brave she was at that moment…”
“Enough, stop praising your friend! Tell me about my companion!”
“What is there to say about him? The task he came for is done. He has already returned to his master, Aditya Karikalan.”
“In that case, he has broken his word. Didn’t he say he would not go to Kanchi, that he would remain here in Chola country?”

“How is that possible? What could he do, staying in Chola country? Even the fate of those who are here is uncertain for tomorrow. If you are so fond of him, you could inform the Emperor and have him restore to your friend the small kingdom once ruled by his ancestors!”
“What would that great hero do with a small kingdom, Akka?”
“He would do what all the other petty kings are doing! You refused the Lankan throne; do you think he too would say no if offered?”
The prince smiled gently. “Akka! I refused the Lanka throne with witnesses present. Even so, my father has ordered that I be brought back under guard, accusing me of treason…”
“Thambi! If you had accepted the throne, there would have been no order to arrest you! You would have been a free king! Who could have imprisoned you then?”
“Should I have acted in such a way, against my father’s wishes?”

“Ponniyin Selva! If you had accepted the Lankan throne, father would have been delighted! He would have divided the remaining Chola empire between your elder brother and Madurantakan, and found peace of mind. Even now, that is what they are trying to do. Thambi! There is an effort to split the kingdom—one realm north of the Kollidam, another to the south. Father believes that if you come, you will help him in this. Since you did not come when he sent word before, he has now ordered you to be brought back under guard. The Emperor knows well that you have refused the Lankan throne.”
“I will never help in dividing the kingdom. There is no greater crime than that. Better to give the entire empire to uncle Madurantakan.”
“In that case, it seems you and the Prime Minister share the same opinion!”
“Yes; the Prime Minister thinks so too. He came to Lanka for the very purpose of discussing this matter with me. Akka! Shall I tell you the real reason why I refused the throne of Lanka?”
“To whom else would you tell it, if not to me, my brother!”

“Yes; there is truly no one else to whom I can reveal my innermost thoughts. Before I went to Lanka, I had grand notions about that land. Only after going there did I realize how small a country it truly is. If one sets out on horseback or atop an elephant, one can travel from the western shore to the eastern coast of that island within a single day.”
“Is Chozha Nadu so much larger than that, brother? Can one not cross this land too in a single day on horseback?”

“Chozha Nadu is small as well; so, even if someone were to offer me the crown of Chozha Nadu, I would refuse it. They have divided this divine Tamil land into Chozha Nadu, Pandya Nadu, and Chera Nadu! What a great crime they have committed. That is why, though heroes of unmatched valor have been born in this land, our country has never flourished. In the North, look at Chandragupta, Ashoka, Samudra Gupta, Vikramaditya, Harshavardhana! Such great emperors arose and ruled over mighty empires. Has anyone in Tamil Nadu ever established and ruled such a vast empire? In the Pallava dynasty of Kanchi, there were Mahendra Chakravarthi and Mamalla. But even that line declined in the end. Akka, if I were to rule a kingdom, I would not rule over such a small, petty realm. I would rule a kingdom that stretches from Lanka to the Ganga. From the Maldives to the island of Java, in distant lands, the Tiger Banner would fly, and I would sit upon the throne of the mighty Chozha Empire! … You must think I am mad!”

“No, Arulvarma! I am delighted to know that you too, like me, build castles in the air and dream fanciful dreams. If you are mad, then I am an even greater madwoman than you. I know that our grandfather, Paranthaka Chakravarthi, cherished such dreams. In his time, they were not fully realized. But in my lifetime, I am going to witness it. I will not die until I have seen the Chozha Empire spread from Lanka to the Ganga, from the Maldives to Java. Once, I believed that this dream would be fulfilled by our elder brother, Aditya Karikalan. That… Hope has now left me. Aditya Karikalan is a great warrior; but he does not possess the strength to master his own mind. Therefore, he will not be able to accomplish great deeds. Yet, I still cherish the desire that my dream will be fulfilled through you. Perhaps, even that may not come to pass. Still, I shall not lose heart. If it cannot be achieved by you, I am certain it will be realized by the child born to you. I will take your son from the very day of his birth and raise him myself. I will make him a hero the likes of whom the world has never seen. I will not let his mind be ensnared by petty desires; I will shape him into a lion among men, capable of wondrous feats.”

“Akka! It is certain that you are a greater madwoman than I am. I have not even thought of marriage, and here you are, already speaking of the child I am yet to have. If any of your beloved companions whom you dote on have such dreams—if any of them hope to marry me and wear the royal crown, to sit upon the throne—tell them plainly that such a wish will never be fulfilled! Let them know this for certain!” said Ponniyin Selvan. As he spoke, his gaze, for a fleeting moment, turned toward Vanathi, who stood behind a pillar of the mandapam. The next instant, he looked away and fixed his eyes on the statue of Nandi that stood before the steps.

“Akka! Let me tell you something. Though Lanka is but a small kingdom now, the kings who ruled it in ancient times were men of greatness—noble souls with grand visions. They conceived vast plans and accomplished mighty deeds. With bricks, they built Buddhist stupas that touched the clouds like mountains. They constructed Buddhist viharas with a thousand, even two thousand chambers. They raised mandapams supported by ten thousand pillars. To reveal the greatness of the Buddha to all who beheld him, they erected Buddha statues as tall as coconut trees. Akka! Look at the Nandi statue before us! How small and insignificant it appears! Is it possible that Nandi, the mighty mount of Mahadeva, whose beginning and end cannot be known, should be so diminutive? In Kailasa, the retinue of Parameshvara—the hosts of spirits—are many. It is Nandideva who stands guard at the gates of Kailasa, preventing those spirits from disturbing the Lord. If he is so small, how can he restrain the hosts of spirits? Look, Akka! Before my very eyes, this Nandi is growing. Growing, growing, ever growing larger. He has become immense, his form so vast that it touches the roof of this mandapam. The roof is gone now. Nandi Bhagavan stands, towering into the sky. The hosts of spirits are approaching! They stand before Nandi Bhagavan in awe and reverence, seeking his permission to behold Shiva. If Nandi Bhagavan is so great, what must the temple be like where Lord Shiva himself resides? Dakshina Meru, they say—

“Should we not build a temple tower that seems to measure the very sky? Should there not be proper enclosures and walls befitting such a temple? The temples that now stand in Chola Nadu are only fit for sages like Agastya to worship in. They are not worthy of Lord Shiva himself. I desire neither kingdom nor riches. Whoever ascends the Chola throne, I will only ask to be appointed as the overseer of temple renovations…”

“Brother! It seems we must compete to see which of us is the greater madman. At this very moment, the Chola land is surrounded by grave danger. Threats loom from within and without, from enemies who pretend to be friends. For some time now, I have been haunted by a terrifying dream. A sharp, gleaming sword flashes before my mind’s eye. It is about to fall upon someone. I do not know upon whom. I do not know whether it will claim the life of someone from the Chola clan, or whether it is the sword that will split this Chola kingdom in two and bring it to ruin. You and I must think and strive together to prevent such a calamity from befalling our land!” said the young princess.
“Yes, Akka! From what Vallavaraiyar has described, I too sense the same. Do you know from whom the greatest danger to the Chola clan will arise?” asked the prince.
“You speak of the younger mistress of Pazhuvoor, Nandini, do you not, brother?”
“Yes, Akka! And you know who she really is, do you not?”
“I have learned that too from what Vandiyathevan has told me. That is why I came to see you with such urgency!” said Kundavai.

chapters.title: Danger for Vanathi
paragraphs: “Akka! Do you remember when I nearly drowned in the Kaveri floods at the age of five? Do you recall how Mother Kaveri saved me, lifted me up, placed me in a boat, and then vanished?” asked Arulmozhi Varman.
“What sort of question is that, thambi! How could I ever forget? Isn’t that very incident the reason you are called ‘Ponniyin Selvan’?” replied Kundavai.
“I saw the very Mother Kaveri who saved me in Lanka, akka!… What is this, you are silent? Are you not surprised?”
“I am not surprised, thambi. But I am filled with curiosity. Tell me everything about her!”

“I cannot tell it all in a single day, in one sitting. Let me tell you only the most important part. It was not only from the Kaveri flood that she saved me; in Lanka, she has saved my life many times. But saving my life is not the greatest thing, akka! Many people, by chance, save the lives of others. But the love she has for me—no world in all these fourteen realms can equal it… In fact, even the love you have for me, I must place only next to hers!”

“You need not hesitate to say that. My love for you is not so lofty; it is tinged with self-interest. I speak the truth, thambi! The greatness of this Chola Empire is what matters most to me. My affection for you is because you are of use to that cause. If ever I thought you would become an obstacle to that aim, my love could even turn to hatred. But the love of that mute and deaf woman is not like that. For over twenty years, the love that overflowed in her heart for our father she has now poured entirely upon you. No, not even the fourteen worlds can equal that!”
“How do you know this, akka?”
“What are you referring to, thambi?”

“That she is our Periya Thaayar—our elder mother?” “From what Father said, and from what Vandiyathevan told me, I have tried to guess, my brother! Does she think of you as her own son? Or as the son of the concubine?”
“Such a distinction has never arisen in my mind; nor do I see even a trace of it in hers. Why do you speak as if there is such a difference?”
“Brother, our mother sits upon the throne where that mute woman ought to have been seated. Even knowing this, if she still shows you such affection, is that not something remarkable?”

“She must surely know that I was not born of her womb. Can the difference in age go unnoticed? She cannot speak; she cannot express what is in her heart. Whatever I could understand from the signs and drawings she made, I have understood. Let her love for me be as it is; but when I think of the love she must have had for our father, my heart melts at once. Akka! Was our father like me at my age?”

“No, brother, no! At your age, our father shone with a beauty that could defeat Manmatha himself. Our Chola clan is famed for its valor, but not for its beauty. Our grandfather, Arinjaya Devar, married Kalyani, who was born into the Vaidhumba royal line, famed for their incomparable beauty. When Arinjaya married Kalyani, she was a celestial enchantress, with skin like new gold and a face like the full moon. Even now, after all these years, you have seen for yourself how beautiful our grandmother Kalyani still is. Because of that, our father too was endowed with such beauty. He earned the title ‘Sundara Chozhar’—the Handsome Chola. We, on the other hand, are born of our mother. The lineage of Thirukovalur Malayaman despises beauty; they consider beauty an enemy to valor…”
“I do not know what connection there may be between beauty and valor. But I do know that there is no connection between beauty and love. Otherwise…”
“Otherwise, why does this girl Vanathi gaze at you from behind the pillar without blinking? And look there—why does Sendhan Amudhan in that boat stare at Poonguzhali, utterly entranced?”

The prince smiled and said, “Akka! You have wandered far from where we began! I was speaking of the affection my elder mother has for me. Let that be; in this world, it is rare indeed for one person to be the exact image of another—” “Is it possible, Akka?”

“Why wouldn’t it be possible? If they were twins, that would explain it. Or sometimes, a mother and daughter can look exactly alike at a certain age. Beyond that, in this vast creation of Brahma, it happens on rare occasions that two people who have no connection whatsoever resemble each other exactly.”

“Could what Vandiyathevan says be true—that the younger queen of Pazhuvoor and our Periyamma whom I saw in Lanka look exactly alike? I saw Nandini only when she was a little girl. After she became the younger queen of Pazhuvoor, I haven’t seen her properly. What do you think?”
“I have seen the queen of Pazhuvoor, but I have never seen our Periyamma. Still, what Vandiyathevan says must be true. I learned it from the history our father told me, Thambi!”
“Father himself told you? What did he say? When did he tell you?”

“A few days ago, Vanathi and I went to Thanjavur. At that time, he told us about an incident from his youth. He spoke of how he was once left alone on an island near Lanka, and of the affection shown to him by a mute woman on that island. He told us how the men sent by Paranthaka found him there and brought him back. On the day he was crowned prince, he saw her in the crowd standing at the palace gates. The next moment, she had vanished. He sent even the chief minister Aniruddha to search for her and bring her back. But Aniruddha returned and said that the woman had leapt from the top of the lighthouse into the sea and died. I learned that this incident has tormented our father’s heart for twenty-four years, bringing him pain day and night. He believes she died. He thinks that, because of him—because of his fault—her heart was wounded and she gave up her life. Thambi! Let all our dreams of the Chola Empire stand aside for now. There is a duty you and I must fulfill for our father. You must somehow bring that lady from Lanka to Thanjavur. You must prove to our father, face to face, that she is not dead—that she is alive. Otherwise, our father will never find peace in this life, nor will he have rest in the next!”

“Akka! Recently, I have gone to the very threshold of death two or three times and returned. Do you know what thought kept coming to my mind each time? That I might die before bringing Periyamma to father…” Loneliness. Akka! Even the mere thought of that lady makes my heart ache. If only I had a mouth, I could pour out the burdens and sorrows within me and find solace. If only I had ears, I could listen to the comforting words of others and ease my grief. But imagine the plight of one who has neither speech nor hearing! All the love, longing, pain, suffering, anger, and thirst that churn within must be locked away inside the heart. And must I even speak of the state of mind of one who, like our elder sister, has lost all hope? Is it any wonder that she wanders like a madwoman through the forests of Lanka? The more I think of all this, the more it feels as though my heart will burst. I am seized by the desire to somehow bring her back and unite her with our father. But, Akka, do you think our father would wish for that?”
“Whether father wishes it or not, it is our duty, my brother! At night, our father cries out, believing that the spirit of the departed comes to torment him. That is why his body does not recover.”
“How do you know this, Akka? Did father tell you this as well?”
“Father told me; and so did my friend Vanathi.”
“Vanathi told you? What connection does she have to all this, Akka? Did you tell her about it?”

“No, no! I am only repeating what she herself witnessed one day in the palace at Thanjai. Still, you are a most mischievous fellow, my brother! You have forgotten the very manners of the Chola clan! Not a word have you spoken to the Princess of Kodumbalur! You have not even asked if she is well! Is this the respect you show to the daughter of the valiant Chinna Velar? How admirable!”
“Akka! Why should I worry about Vanathi’s well-being when you are here to care for her? What need is there for me to ask if she is well?”
“Very well, now keep your mouth shut for a while! Vanathi! Come here! The prince wishes to see you!” said Kundavai.

Vanathi came near. Without looking at the prince, she stood there and said in a voice as soft as silk, “Akka! Why do you make up such stories? Your brother does not wish to see me. His gaze is fixed only on that boat in the stream over there. It seems he is eager to leave at once!” She spoke thus, perhaps thinking of Poonguzhali who was in the boat!
The prince laughed and said, “Akka! Your friend can speak after all; I was afraid she might be another mute like those in our family!”
“Akka! When I look at him, I feel unable to speak. I am afraid I myself have become mute,” said Vanathi.

“That is very good. There is a man in Kodikkarai—Poonguzhali’s brother. He speaks with others in a halting, awkward manner. But when he sees his wife, he becomes utterly mute. Because of this, his family has come to regard him as a mute,” said the prince.

“This Kodumbalur girl is a little like that. Before, if you asked her to sit quietly for a while without speaking, she simply could not do it. Once she started talking, she would never stop. But ever since you first went to Lanka, her chatter has diminished. She sits alone, lost in thought. Let that be, Vanathi! Now, tell the prince in detail everything that happened that night in the Thanjavur palace,” said Kundavai.

“Let the Princess of Kodumbalur sit and narrate, Akka! If her great father saw her standing for so long, his heart would melt. Every time the Commander of the Southern Armies sees me, he asks about her. But you never send him any news. So, I am left struggling for answers,” said the prince.
“I did send a detailed message about her to the brave warrior of the Vanar clan. Did he not tell you anything?”
“Oh, he must have told him, Akka! But nothing ever reaches his ears. He forgets everything!” said Vanathi.

“That is true as well. After reading your letter, my mind has not turned to anything else. Since coming to this forest, even my hearing has dulled a little. Tell your friend to speak up!” said Arulmozhi.

Then, Vanathi recounted how, after Kundavai went to the Durga temple in the Thanjavur palace, she herself wandered alone on the upper terrace, how she heard the emperor’s voice of alarm, how she hurried to the spot and peered down, and what she saw there. Whenever Vanathi happened to glance at the prince’s face, she would lose herself and fall silent. The young princess had to prompt her, again and again, to continue speaking.

The prince, who had been listening to everything with keen interest, finally turned to his sister and said, “Akka! It seems your friend has left out an important incident! After witnessing and hearing all this, shouldn’t she have fainted and fallen down?”
Kundavai laughed; Vanathi stood with her head bowed in shyness.

Looking at her with eyes brimming with affection, Kundavai said, “Vanathi! Go walk along the riverbank for a while, or else go to where our attendants are waiting. Arulmozhi will be here for a few more days; you can meet him again!”
“All right, Akka! I’ll go for a stroll and return!” Saying this, Vanathi skipped away with a sudden burst of cheerfulness, the source of which she herself could not understand.
Arulmozhi watched her go, her face blooming and her eyes wide, and when she had disappeared from view, he turned to his sister.

“Akka! I understand the reason for our father’s lament. But what do you think about the vision he saw? What could have been the apparition that appeared before him? Was it merely a figment of his imagination? If so, how did your friend come to have the same delusion?”

“What father saw was no illusion; what Vanathi saw was no magical apparition. What happened before father was a midnight drama. The chief actress in that play was the younger queen of Pazhuvoor, Nandini. I guessed as much at the time and have since confirmed it from the details you and Vandiyathevan have given…!”
“What was the reason for that drama? Why would the Queen of Pazhuvoor do such a thing, Akka?”

“Nandini harbors doubts about her own birth. She knows that the Emperor, upon seeing her once, lost consciousness. Since then, she has never appeared before him. She must have staged such a drama, hoping to uncover some truth…”
“Would she have found out, Akka?”

“That I do not know! Even Brahma, who created her, could not fathom the depths of Nandini’s heart. When I think of the suffering that Pazhuvettarayar endures because of her, I feel pity for him. Thambi! Just now we were speaking of beauty, weren’t we? Among women, if there is one who can be called beautiful, it is Nandini. None of us could ever hope to gather even the dust at her feet.”

Men who come before Nandini become her slaves in an instant. Pazhuvetarayar, Madurantakan, Thirumalaiyappan, Kandanmaran, and finally Parthibendran! Even the Prime Minister Aniruddhar, fearing her beauty, never goes near her. Aditya Karikalan, for that very reason, does not come to Thanjavur. Brother! There is only one man who has faced Nandini’s beauty without fear, who has not succumbed or been defeated by her…
“You mean the brave scion of the Vanar clan?”
“Yes! Him! That is why I have sent him to Kanchi, to Aditya Karikalan.”
“For what purpose?”

“The Queen of Pazhuvur has sent word to our elder brother, inviting him to come to Kadambur Sambuvarayar’s palace. I have sent him to prevent their meeting. Even if they do meet, I have sent him to ensure that no disaster befalls. Karikalan does not know that Nandini is our sister. I do not know if Nandini has recognized our kinship either.”
“Is it certain that she is our sister, Akka?”

“What doubt is there in that, brother? From the moment I learned it, I have changed my heart completely. When we were children, I hated Nandini, I despised her. I was jealous of her beauty. I even plotted that you and Karikalan should not speak with her. Even after she went to Pandya Nadu, my envy and hatred for her remained unchanged. After she married the elder of Pazhuvur and returned, I humiliated her and insulted her many times. I have resolved to atone for all that…”
“How, Akka? What kind of atonement?”
“The next time I meet her, I will fall at her feet and beg her to forgive all my wrongs. Whatever punishment she gives, I will accept…”

“I will not allow that. You have done no wrong. You have no need to ask forgiveness from anyone. In all these fourteen worlds, there is no one who can punish you. You did not envy Nandini, the young queen of Pazhuvur. It was she who envied you. It was she who hated you…”

“Brother! You said your heart aches when you think of our great-aunt wandering like a madwoman in Lanka. But when I think of all the hardships Nandini has endured—she, who should have lived in the palace amidst every luxury—my heart feels as if it will break. Because of some mistake made by someone, long ago, our elder sister, born before me, was forced to marry this old man, Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar…”

“Sister! Do you know anything about how all this happened? Why does Father believe our great-aunt is dead? Why did Nandini, like an orphan, grow up in some stranger’s house and end up in this situation…?”

“I have thought about all this, day and night. But I have not yet been able to find out the truth. Of those who know these secrets, there are two people known to us. Our grandmother, Sembiyan Maadevi, surely knows something. And I believe Prime Minister Aniruddha must know everything. But from neither of them can we learn anything. Aniruddha’s disciple, Azhwarkadiyan, must know at least a part of the truth. He is cleverer than his master! But he will never open his mouth. Brother! There is no urgency now to uncover all that. What matters most now is to prevent Nandini from bringing disaster and disgrace upon our clan. Vandiyathevan said, ‘The Queen of Pazhuvur is worshipping with a sword, bright as lightning, bearing the fish emblem.’ Ever since I heard that, my heart has been pounding with fear. I worry that, not knowing she was born into the Chola clan, the Queen of Pazhuvur might do something terrible.”
“What if we told the Queen of Pazhuvur everything?”
“Even if we did, I do not know what good would come of it. She might only grow angrier with us. But we must do our duty, whatever happens!”

“It is right that you sent Vandiyathevan for that purpose. But should we not inform Father as well? Why should he suffer mental anguish on top of his physical pain? Can we not leave for Thanjavur at once?”
“That is not possible, brother! In two days, I will leave for Thanjavur. But you must remain here at the Choodamani Vihara for some more time.”
“Why do you say that? Are you asking me to stay hidden here, defying Father’s orders?”

“Yes! If you come to Thanjai now, the entire land will be thrown into chaos. The people are furious with both Madurantakan and the Pazhuvettaraiyars. Even the Emperor himself has become the target of their anger for ordering your arrest and capture. If they see you now, the flood of their emotions will surge and overflow. Who knows what consequences might follow? The people might raise a clamor demanding that you be crowned at once. They might even lay siege to the Thanjai fort and the palace. Your father’s heart, already wounded, will be hurt even more. Brother! I wrote to you, urging you to return, because I feared danger threatened the kingdom. For the same reason, I now think it would be best if you turned back and returned to Lanka…”

“Akka! That is something I could never do. I will not go back without seeing our father. If you think it is best for me to come to Thanjai in secret, I will do so. But I must see the Emperor. I must tell him who the Kaveri Amman was who saved me.”
“I will find the right moment and tell him all that myself. Must you settle everything by coming in person?”
“If I tell him myself, face to face, father will have complete faith! My own heart will find solace. I will also obtain his permission to bring Periyammai along…”

“Arulvarma! I do not wish to stand in the way of your desire. But stay at the Choodamani Vihara for just one more week. I will go to Thanjai ahead of you. I will inform father that you have arrived and send word to you. Brother! I did not come here seeking you out merely to see you; I came to ask a boon of you. If you grant me this, I will trouble you no more. Men are destined to face danger. My only wish is that you should be famed as a peerless hero of valor and courage. But before you once again risk yourself in peril, you must fulfill my request…”
“Why such a preamble, Akka! Have I ever refused anything you asked?”

“You never have; it is with that trust I ask you now. Aditya Karikalan has not married; nor does it seem likely that he will. The glory of Sundara Chola’s line must shine through you. In this matter, you must fulfill my wish…”
“If I agree to fulfill your wish, you will consent to let me marry the woman I love, won’t you?”
“Why do you ask like this? For twenty years, our wishes have never differed. Why do you seek my consent only in this matter?”
“Akka, there is a reason for it. The woman I marry must support me in realizing the dreams I see in broad daylight, must she not?”
“Thambi! Do you wish to fulfill your daytime dreams with the support of a woman?” asked Kundavai.
At that moment, a distressed cry echoed: “Ayyo! Ayyo! Akka! Akka!” It was Vanathi’s voice.

chapters.title: Vanathi Laughed
paragraphs: Part Three – The Sword of Slaughter

While the prince and Princess Kundavai sat conversing in the Nandi Mandapam— while Vanathi stood by the pillar, listening— an important conversation was taking place in the boat waiting in the canal, between Poonguzhali and Sendhan Amudhan.
“Amudha! I am going to ask you something. Will you answer me truthfully?” asked Poonguzhali.
“Poonguzhali, nothing but the truth ever passes my lips! That is why, these past few days, I have not seen or spoken to anyone,” replied Amudhan.
“For some people, truth never comes to their lips. That Vandiyathevan, who took the letter to the prince and went to Lanka—he is such a person.”
“Even so, he is a very good man. He has never lied to harm anyone.”
“He said something about you. I want to know if it is true or false…”
“He has no reason to say anything untrue about me. Still, tell me what he said!”
“He said you spoke very highly of me.”
“That is entirely true.”
“He said you have affection for me, that you wish to marry me…”
“Did he truly say that?”
“Yes, Amudha!”
“I must thank him for that.”
“For what?”
“I would never have had the courage to open my heart to you myself; I could not have found such boldness. He spoke on my behalf to you, did he not? For that, I must thank him.”
“If that is so, then what he said is true?”
“It is true, Poonguzhali! There is no doubt about it.”
“Why did you come to desire me, Amudha?”
“Can anyone ever explain the reason for love?”
“I will think and tell you. Could there be no reason at all?”
“No one in this world has ever discovered or explained why or how love arises, Poonguzhali!”
“Don’t people desire each other upon seeing beauty?”

“Yes, people do desire beauty; they may even feel infatuation. But that cannot be called true love, nor does it last. Just now, you spoke of Vandiyathevan—he became fond of me the moment he saw me. I was ready to give my life for him. Did he become attached to me because of my beauty?”
“But your friend described my beauty at great length, didn’t he?”
“He did praise your beauty. But he did not desire you. He praised the beauty of the Pazhuvoor queen a hundred times more, but he did not love her.”
“I know the reason for that.”
“What is it?”
“That warrior’s heart has already gone to the young princess who is speaking with the prince over there. That is the reason.”
“Doesn’t this show that there is no connection between beauty and love?”
“How does it happen, then? Are you saying I am more beautiful than the young princess?”

“What doubt is there in that, Poonguzhali! Compared to the junior princess of Pazhaiyarai, compared to the princess of Kodumbalur standing behind that pillar, you are many times more beautiful. Even the beauty of the junior queen of Pazhuvoor, whom many praise as the incarnation of Mohini, cannot equal yours. Such divine beauty is my enemy. That is why the love that surges and overflows in my heart—” “I cannot even reveal it to you. You, who possess a beauty coveted by the gods of the heavens and the emperors of the earth—how could I ever hope to keep you near me? The fear that I might lose you has taken up residence in my heart!”
Poonkuzhali fell into a brief silence, lost in thought. Then she asked, “Amudha! What if I told you that I have no desire for you? What would you do?”
“I would wait patiently for a few days. I would see if your heart changes.”
“How could it change?”

“The human heart is a strange thing. Sometimes, even the innermost corners of our hearts are unknown to us. Because of outward circumstances, the mind may be plunged into delusion. When that delusion is dispelled, the true heart will be revealed…”
“So you would wait and see. But if, even after that, there is no change in my heart…?”
“I would try to rid myself of the desire I have for you…”
“Is that possible…?”
“If I try, it is possible; if I turn my mind towards God, it is possible. Our elders controlled their hearts only by devoting themselves to the Lord…”
“Amudha! I do not believe that the love you have for me is true love.”
“Why do you say that? What is the sign of true love?”
“If you truly loved me, the moment I rejected you, you would feel you must kill me. If you saw me loving someone else instead of you, you would be seized with a rage to kill him as well…”
“Poonkuzhali! What I spoke of is a divine, sattvic kind of love. What you describe belongs to the asuric nature; one might even call it demonic…”

“I do not know of the divine; nor do I know of the demonic. I only know human nature. Love should bring happiness. If instead it brings suffering, why should one endure it? If we love someone, and they betray us by not loving us in return, why should we tolerate it? Is not revenge the true nature of man?”

“No, Poonguzhali! Revenge is not the nature of humankind; it is the nature of demons. If our love for someone is true, then their happiness should bring us happiness as well. Even if their rejection pains us at first, if we bear it with patience and respond only with kindness, the joy that will come to us later will be tenfold greater…”

“What you speak of is not human nature; it is not something humans are capable of. Once, a physician’s son came with Vandiyathevan. The moment he saw me, desire arose in him. When he realized that his wish would not be fulfilled, thinking that I stood in the way of his desire, he tried to betray Vandiyathevan to the men of Pazhuvetaraiyar. He would have even tried to kill me.”
“If that is so, he does not belong to the race of men; he belongs to the cruel clan of asuras.”

“Look, there stands the princess of Kodumbalur. She has surrendered her heart to Ponniyin Selvan. If Ponniyin Selvan does not accept her, what will she do? Surely, she will try to poison and kill Ponniyin Selvan. If she learns that some other woman has captured his heart, she will try to kill her as well.”
“Never have I thought so, Poonguzhali; gentle Vanathi, whose soul is pure, would never attempt such a thing.”
“Perhaps; but if it were I, that is exactly what I would try to do.”
“I shall pray that God forgives and protects you…”
“Why should God forgive me! It is I who must forgive God!”
“Even for your blasphemy, God will forgive you!”
“Amudha! You are a noble soul, born with the nature of my great aunt…”
“What is this? Suddenly you speak of something new?”
“Is it not being said among our family that my great aunt has passed away?”
“Whom do you mean? The eldest sister, born to both my mother and your father?”
“Yes! She has not truly died.”
“I too have heard such rumors, whispered in secrecy.”
“She is still wandering about the island of Lanka like a madwoman…”
“Who can do anything against the curse of the family?”
“It is not only the family curse that has made her wander like a madwoman today. It was the betrayal of trust by a man of the Chola clan that caused it.”
“What? What do you mean?”
“In her youth, my aunt lived on an island near Lanka. A Chola prince pretended to love her, and she believed him. Later, when that prince was crowned as a royal heir, he abandoned her…”
“How do you know all this, Poonguzhali?”

“I learned it through the sign language of my mute aunt. Listen, I will tell you something more! Some time ago, a few men from Pandya Nadu came here. They sought my help to take revenge on the royal clan that had betrayed my aunt. At that time, when I had just learned of my aunt’s story, my blood boiled within me. I decided to join them. It was then that I came to know the true nature of my elder aunt’s heart. She had never forgiven the man who betrayed her, but many times she had saved the child born to him through another wife. After that, I gave up the thought of joining the men from Pandya Nadu. As you say, my aunt’s love is truly divine. But I will not be like her.”
“Then what will you do?”
“If any prince deceives and wrongs me, I will take revenge for revenge’s sake. I will kill him; I will kill the woman who stole his heart from me. Then I will stab myself with a dagger and die!”
“Heavens! What terrible words you speak!”
“Amudha! For two years you have not known the turmoil in my heart. That is why you preach such gentle advice to me!”
“What burning rage has come to you that your aunt never had!”
“That is her story; this is mine!”
“Your story? Is it true, Poonguzhali? Speak carefully!”
“Yes, Amudha! If you were to take a little blood from my body and a little from that Vanathi’s body and compare them, would there be any difference?”
“There would be no difference at all.”
“In what way is she superior to me? In intelligence, in beauty, in strength?”

“In none of these is she greater than you. You grew up by the restless sea; she grew up in the palace. You can kill wild beasts with your bare hands! In the fiercest storms, you can steer a boat across the ocean! You save those who flounder and drown at sea! Vanathi would be terrified just to see the waves of the ocean! She would scream in fear at the sight of a house cat! If she hears any bad news, she would faint and fall!”
“If that is so, why does the Young Princess look down on me? Why does she cherish and praise Vanathi?”

“Poonguzhali! You are falsely accusing the Young Princess. Vanathi has been her companion for many years. You have only just now come to the attention of the Young Princess. Did she not show you much gratitude for bringing the Prince safely here from the sea?”

“Yes! Who here needs the gratitude of that palace lady? Let her keep it for herself. Amudha! If you must take the Prince back to the Buddhist Vihara by boat, you take him alone! If I come, I might even overturn the boat on purpose…”
“You would never do such a thing, Poonguzhali! What fault has the Prince committed, that you would capsize the boat he is in?”
“Amudha! I am mad. My mind is not under my control. If I remember the treachery her father did to my aunt’s husband, I might overturn the boat just for that. You take the boat yourself!”
“So be it; I will take the Prince and return. What will you do?”

“I will follow Vanathi and hurl a stone at her head!” So saying, Poonguzhali bent down and picked up a large clod of earth lying on the canal bank. At that very moment, from the dense grove of coconut palms along the canal, a majestic royal bull emerged. Seeing it, Poonguzhali, intending to vent her anger on her rival, flung the clod straight at the bull.
The clod struck the royal bull squarely on its forehead. The beast shuddered once, its whole body quivering. It turned and stared intently in the direction from which the stone had come.
“Oh, Poonguzhali! What are you doing? How can you throw a stone at a poor animal?” cried Amudhan.
“So what if I did?”
“It’s a dumb creature! It cannot even defend itself!”
“In my family, there was once a dumb, mute girl. What about those who wounded her heart? She could not defend herself, and so a prince deceived her and ruined her life!”
“What has this bull done for the injustice someone did to your aunt?”

“This bull is not some helpless creature. It has sharp horns. If someone tries to attack it, it can toss them aside. But what can a poor, deaf, mute girl do? If any prince dares behave with me as he did with her, I will not let him go so easily!”
“You won’t let him go easily! You’ll throw a stone at a bull! And that too, from a boat in the canal, where the bull cannot reach you to gore you!”
“If it cannot gore me, let it go and gore someone else!”
“So you’re venting your anger at someone else on this poor bull, aren’t you?”

The bull, of course, could not understand their conversation. But, as if following Poonguzhali’s words, it did almost exactly as she had said. Unable to vent its anger on Poonguzhali, who was safe in the boat on the canal, it turned, leapt, and bounded away. At that moment, Vanathi was walking alone toward the palanquin on the other side of the coconut grove, her heart leaping with joy.

She was filled with excitement at first, seeing Rishabarajan leaping and bounding towards her. But when Rishabarajan lowered his head, stretched out his horns, raised his tail, and advanced in her direction, fear overtook her. There was no choice but to turn and run towards the canal bank. Very soon, she reached the canal bank, quite close to the Nandi Mandapam. She could not go any further, for from the bank, the canal plunged down in a steep, precipitous drop. She turned, thinking she could walk along the bank towards the Nandi Mandapam. At that moment, the bull had come very close to her. There was no other way but to move backward, risking a fall into the canal. That was when she cried out, “Aiyo! Aiyo! Akka! Akka!” Vanathi’s desperate cry reached the ears of Ponniyin Selvan and Kundavai.

Startled, Ponniyin Selvan and Kundavai looked in the direction from which Vanathi’s cry had come. On the high bank of the canal, a short distance from the Nandi Mandapam where they stood, Vanathi appeared. Her back was to the canal; she seemed to be facing some terrifying object. In the next instant, it became clear what had frightened her so—Rishabarajan appeared before her, letting out a majestic “Amma!” If Vanathi took even one more step backward, she would have to fall into the canal. There was no other way for her but to retreat.

Arulmozhi Varman grasped the situation in a flash. Instantly, he leapt from the steps of the Nandi Mandapam into the canal and dashed forward like lightning. The timing was just right: as Vanathi was about to fall from the canal bank, Arulmozhi Varman reached her below. Before she could plunge headfirst into the canal water, he caught her with both hands and supported her.

For a moment, Kundavai’s heart fluttered with anxiety, realizing the danger Vanathi faced. The next instant, seeing Arulmozhi Varman catch and support her, she was overwhelmed with joy. Carrying Vanathi, who now hung limp in his strong arms—arms that had wielded spear and sword, arms as powerful as the thunderbolt—Arulmozhi Varman brought her to Kundavai’s side.
“Akka! Here, take your friend! How this girl was born into the valiant Kodumbalur Velir clan, I cannot fathom!” he said.
“Thambi! What have you done? How can you touch an unmarried maiden with your own hands?” Kundavai exclaimed.

“Oh God! Was that a crime? Then, do you mean to say she should have fallen headfirst into the water and drowned? Thank goodness! She doesn’t know that I caught and held her. She fainted even as she was falling! Here, take her!” said Arulmozhi Varma.
