Vanathi burst into laughter. Still laughing, she slipped free from his hands and leapt onto the bank.
“You little trickster! Were you fully conscious all along?” asked Kundavai.
“Ask her, Akka, why she closed her eyes and pretended to faint!” said Ponniyin Selvan.
“I didn’t pretend at all, Akka! The moment he touched me, I was overcome with shyness. Unable to bear the embarrassment, I closed my eyes!”
“How was I to know that? I thought fainting and falling was becoming a habit for your friend,” said Kundavai.
“Hereafter, I won’t faint and fall again. Even if I do, I won’t do it where he is present. Akka! Let him never forget the help I gave him today!” declared Vanathi.
“What? What? She helped me? How amusing!” said Arulmozhi Varma.
Kundavai, a little surprised, turned to Vanathi and asked, “What are you saying, girl? Are you claiming that my brother should never forget the help you gave him?”
“Not at all, Akka! I am the one who truly helped your brother. For that, he must always be grateful to me!”
“So, I should thank her for saving her from falling into the canal? Akka, does your friend have some strange affliction of the mind?” asked Ponniyin Selvan.

“My mind is perfectly sound! It is he who is confused. Let me explain: you once told me that, as a child, he fell into the Kaveri and was saved by a woman. Then, again, he fell into the sea and was rescued by a boatwoman. It seems being saved by women has become a habit for him. That disgrace—” “I helped her to hide. Didn’t I give her the fame of having saved a girl who was about to fall into the canal? Shouldn’t she thank me for that?”
Saying this, Vanathi laughed. Hearing her, Kundavai too laughed. Ponniyin Selvan tried to suppress his laughter, but could not; he burst out with a loud “Ho ho!”
The sound of their laughter, as the three of them laughed together, echoed through the Nandi Mandapam and traveled all the way up to the sky’s edge.

Even those in the boat heard the sound of that laughter. “Amudha! Did you hear those three madcaps laughing?” said Poonguzhali, and she too laughed. Amudhan joined her in laughter. The birds that dwelled in the southern groves chirped and chattered as if laughing along with them.
All this while, the majestic bull that stood on the bank of the canal let out a deep bellow, as if it too laughed, and then walked away.
The waves of the sea laughed grandly. The cool breeze that came from the ocean joined in, laughing softly in a gentle voice.
Part Four – The Crown Jewel

chapters.title: On the Banks of the Kedilam
paragraphs: Among the many rivers that enriched the land of Thirumunaippadi with their bountiful waters, the Kedilam was one. On its banks stood the sacred Thiruvathigai Veeratthaanam, where the Lord who claimed Appar as his own had manifested. Not far from this river was Thirunavalur, the abode of the Lord who drew Sundaramurthi into his fold. Between these two holy shrines, in those days, ran the royal highway that connected Thondai Nadu to Nadu Nadu and Chola Nadu.

The ferry crossing at the Kedilam river on this royal road was always bustling with activity. The calls and songs of birds in the riverside trees, the rustle of their wings, filled the air. Travelers, having unyoked their bullocks from the carts, would sit by the bank to eat their packed rice. As they ate, the crows would swoop down and snatch away the rice balls tossed playfully into the air. Watching these antics, the children would clap their hands and shout in excitement, exclaiming “Aahu!” in wonder, laughing and cheering in delight.

At the beginning of the month of Aippasi, the Kedilam was in spate, its floodwaters higher than usual. At midday, the noise of travelers who had stopped to eat their meals was louder than ever. Suddenly, a great commotion arose a little distance away on the road—a tumult so loud that it drowned out all other sounds and made the travelers look up in surprise. Some climbed up the bank to see what was happening. At first, they saw only a cloud of dust. Then, shapes emerged—elephants, horses, palanquins, attendants bearing parasols and royal insignia. As the procession drew nearer, the shouts of the heralds rang out clearly.

“Here comes the warrior who entered the battlefield at the age of twelve, the bravest of the brave, the slayer of Veerapandiyan, Kopparakesari, the lion who haunts the dreams of the lords of the twin realms, the ruler of Thondai Mandalam, the lord who shines in the northern direction, the son of Sundara Chola Chakravarthi, master of the three worlds—Aditya Karikala Chola Maharaja approaches! Make way!”

At this thunderous proclamation, which echoed in all directions, everyone at the Kedilam ferry hurried up the bank. Eager to catch a glimpse of such a mighty hero, they cleared a path in the middle and stood respectfully on either side. The heralds, the conch-blowers, and the standard-bearers came first and reached the riverbank. Behind the retinue, three horses approached side by side, and astride each horse sat a young warrior. Even from a distance, the people began to point them out and whisper among themselves, trying to guess their identities.
"The one riding the horse in the middle—that is Aditya Karikalan! Can’t you tell just by looking at the golden crown? See how it gleams in the sunlight!" said one.

"You call that a crown? You should see the jeweled diadem that Karikala Valavan used to wear! If he were to bear that upon his head, it would dazzle the eyes like the radiance of a million suns!" said another.

"That is not Karikala Valavan’s crown, brother! They just call it so by tradition. The jeweled diadem made during the reign of Parantaka Chakravartin is now worn by Sundara Chola. For how many more days, who can say?" remarked a third.
"They have been counting the days of Sundara Chola’s life for some time now. It seems he will live forever!" said the first speaker.
"Let it be so. As long as he lives, the land and its cities will remain free of turmoil."

"That cannot be said for certain; ever since the news came that Ponniyin Selvan was lost to the sea, the Chola country has been in a state of great unrest. Those who come from there say that at any moment, war may break out."
"Who is going to fight whom? And for what reason?"

"They say a clash will erupt between the Pazhuvettaraiyars and the Kodumbalur Velalars. To prevent such a thing, the minor kings are gathering at Kadambur Sambuvarayar’s palace. Aditya Karikalan is said to be going there as well."
"The horses are drawing near; do not speak so loudly!" warned one, then asked, "Have you seen how haggard Prince Aditya Karikalan’s face has become?"

"How could his face not be worn with sorrow? Aditya Karikalan’s very soul is bound to his younger brother. If there is no word of such a brother, would not the elder be grieved? And their father is bedridden, unable to move!"

“All this is the way of the world, my brother! These are not the reasons for the prince’s troubled countenance. Karikalan longs to march his armies against the kings of the twin realms; it is only because that desire remains unfulfilled that he is so worried!”
“Why has it not been fulfilled? Who is stopping him from leading his army?”
“Who else? The Pazhuvettaraiyars themselves! They refuse to provide the weapons and supplies needed for the campaign!”
“They keep inventing all sorts of excuses. None of you know the real reason,” said one among them.
“Oh, you who knows everything! Then you tell us the true reason!” challenged another.

“They say Aditya Karikalan was once in love with a woman from the Pandya country. While the prince was away at war in the north, the elder Pazhuvettaraiyar married that woman. Now she reigns as the young queen of Pazhuvoor, wielding supreme power throughout Chola land. It is said that from then on, Aditya Karikalan’s heart has been in turmoil!”
“That may well be; it may well be! Haven’t the elders always said that a woman is the cause behind every quarrel in this world?”

“Which elders, brother, have said such a thing? Utter madness! If the prince loved a woman, would she go and marry an old man of sixty? Do those who say such things think their listeners have no sense?”
“If that is so, why has Aditya Karikalan not yet married? You tell us, then!”
“Quiet, all of you! Look, they are approaching. The one walking at the prince’s right must be Parthibendra Pallavan. Who is that on his left? Is it Vandiyathevan of the Vanar clan?”
“No, no! That is Kandhamaaran, son of Sambuvaraiyar of Kadambur. Sambuvaraiyar must have sent his own son to bring the prince, fearing he might not come if only a message were sent.”
“From this, it is clear that something of great importance is afoot.”

“That important matter might well be political in nature. As long as Aditya Karikalan remains unmarried, the minor kings will continually try to ensnare him in their nets. After all, the woman who first marries him will have the fortune to ascend the throne of the Chola Empire, will she not?”

Thus, on the banks of the Kedila river, the crowd that had gathered to watch the spectacle spoke among themselves in various ways. The three horses came and halted near the water’s edge. The chariot that followed behind the horses stopped a little further away, beneath the shade of a royal tree. In that chariot sat an elderly warrior, about eighty years of age—Thirukovalur Malayaman.
Aditya Karikalan, still mounted on his horse at the water’s edge, turned and looked at him.

chapters.title: Grandfather and Grandson
paragraphs: When the elder who followed behind in the chariot made a sign, Aditya Karikalan turned his horse and rode up to where the old man sat enthroned in his chariot.

“My child! Karikala! Here, I wish to take leave of you and proceed to Thirukovalur. But before I depart, I must speak to you about some important matters. Dismount from your horse and come to the platform beneath that royal tree!” he said.
“So be it, Grandfather!” replied Aditya Karikalan, leaping down from his horse.
The elder too alighted from his chariot. Both of them walked to the platform beneath the royal tree.
At that moment, Parthibendran turned to Kandanmaran and said, “It’s a good thing this old man stopped here. I was afraid he might keep following us, refusing to let go.”
“If he had continued, I was thinking of pushing him into the floodwaters of the river and giving him a good dunking!” said Kandanmaran. Both laughed heartily at their own jest.
Turning to Aditya Karikalan, the lord of the hill country, Thirukovalur Malayaman, began to speak:

“Adithya! Today, it is twenty-four years since you were born! You were born in my palace at Thirukovalur! The celebrations that took place then are as vivid in my memory as if they happened yesterday. Members of your clan, my own kinsmen, and many minor kings from Chola Nadu and Thondai Nadu had gathered. Along with them, thirty thousand warriors assembled. Words cannot describe the grandeur of the feast given to them all. Not even during your father’s coronation were there such banquets and festivities. All the wealth my ancestors had amassed and stored in my treasury for a hundred years was spent in those three days of celebration!”

“At that time, your great-grandfather, Emperor Parantaka himself, came to Thirukovalur. Your elder grandfather Kandaradithar, and your father Sundara Chola, were there too. The moment they heard the news of a male child’s birth—” There was no limit to the joy that filled everyone’s hearts. They rejoiced, exclaiming, “You have been born to bring glory to the Chola dynasty!” Until then, your grandfather’s elder brothers had no heirs. Arinjaya, too, had only your father as his son. In his youth, your father shone with a beauty rivaling that of Manmatha himself. Nowhere in the Chola clan, nor among the lineages of the petty kings of Tamilagam, had anyone ever seen a child of such beauty before. This very beauty brought your father certain troubles as well. He was the darling of the entire family. The women of the palace delighted in dressing him in women’s attire, exclaiming in wonder, “If only he had been born a girl!” and spoke of it with endless joy.

From Lanka to the Vindhya mountains, kings and chieftains performed penance, hoping to wed their daughters to your father. Not only was he as handsome as Arjuna or Manmatha, but he was also the rightful heir to the Chola throne—this thought made them all the more eager. In the end, it was I who was blessed to have your father as my son-in-law.”

“In our lineage, whether man or woman, we are not famed for physical beauty. For our sons, the number of battle scars upon their bodies is the measure of their handsomeness. For the women of our clan, chastity and virtue are their beauty and their adornment. When it was decided that my daughter would wed your father, all of Malayamanadu was thrown into a tumult. The petty kings of Tamilagam were consumed with envy; but I paid it no heed. The marriage of your parents was celebrated in Thanjai with such grandeur that it astonished the three worlds. Yet, even greater than those festivities was the celebration that took place in Thirukovalur at the time of your birth. There was much debate and excitement over what name should be given to you. Some wished to name you after the illustrious Karikala Valavan, a famed ancestor of your line. I and a few others insisted that you should bear the name of your elder paternal uncle, Rajaditya. In the end, both names were joined, and you were christened ‘Aditya Karikalan.’”

“Look there, Aditya! The temple tower of Thirunavalur is visible. That is the birthplace of Nambi Arurar, Sundaramurthi Adigal. It was there, twenty-five years ago, that your elder uncle, Rajaditya Chola, had his encampment. I have heard tales of countless heroes in stories and epics. I have seen many warriors in this valiant land of Tamilakam. But never have I seen, nor heard of, a hero like Rajaditya. Anyone who witnessed him in battle would say the same.”

“He was preparing here to gather a mighty army and march upon the northern lands. His resolve was firm: to defeat Kannaradeva, the king of the twin realms, and to raze to the ground his capital city, Maniyakedam. Just as, in ages past, the great emperor Mamalla of the Pallava dynasty had destroyed the city of Vatapi, Rajaditya believed that only by utterly annihilating Maniyakedam would the arrogance of the twin kingdoms be subdued, and that he too would earn fame like Mamalla. But is it an easy task to assemble such a vast army? They say Mamalla took seven years to gather his forces. Rajaditya declared he would not require so long; three or four years would suffice. He chose this land between the rivers Kedilam and South Pennai as the most suitable region for mustering the army and training the assembled troops for war.”

“Aditha! In those days, you did not get to witness the lands between these two rivers. Those who beheld those sights can never forget them as long as they live. In Thirunavalur, Rajaditya stayed with thirty thousand soldiers. On the banks of the Pennai, at Mudiyur, the local chieftain Vellan Kumaran camped with twenty thousand warriors. Your grandfather Arinjaya was with me at Thirukovalur. Together, Arinjaya and I prepared fifty thousand soldiers. In addition, the great Velan of Kodumbalur, the Pazhuvettaraiyar who has now risen as a Saturnine force over Chola Nadu, the Sambuvarayar of Kadambur, Munaiyadaraiyar, the chieftain of this very Thirumunaippadi land, Mazhavarayar of Mazhanadu, Kunrathur Kilavan, Vaidhumbarayan, and many others were encamped with their own battalions between these two rivers. The elephant corps, the cavalry, and the three regiments of the renowned Kaikkolars had all pitched their camps here. Among these assembled forces, practice battles were frequently held. When elephants clashed with elephants, it felt as though an earthquake had struck. The thunderous sound of cavalry formations charging forward with spear-wielding warriors was like the tumult of a doomsday ocean. When the archers practiced shooting arrows, the sky itself would be obscured by the ceaseless hail of shafts. And when thousands upon thousands of soldiers, roaring ‘Navalo Naval’ in unison, surged forth to attack the enemy, it seemed as if the end of the world was at hand. Crowds upon crowds of people would gather to witness these spectacles.”

“The people of this Thirumunaippadi and Nadu Nadu are not only good-hearted but also exceedingly brave. During the time the army was assembled here, their agriculture suffered great hardships. Yet they did not mind these troubles. It was to express his gratitude to such people that Rajaditya, in both these lands…” He caused many lakes to be dug. He arranged for a new canal to be cut from the Kollidam, bringing water to fill the great lake at Veera Narayanapuram. Adiththa! It was Kadambur Sambuvaraiyar who reaped immense benefit from the fertility of that lake. When I compare the humility with which he once stood in submission before Rajadhitya, to the pride and arrogance he displays now in his wealth, I am filled with great astonishment!”

Aditha Karikalan interrupted, “Grandfather! Why do you worry about Sambuvaraiyar’s arrogance? Tell me about the battle at Thakkolam. When did the mighty army gathered here on the banks of the Kedila set out from this place? Despite all those preparations, and though my great uncle was such a valiant hero, why did our forces suffer defeat at Thakkolam? Weren’t you yourself a participant in that war? Surely you must have seen and known everything firsthand?”
“Yes, I too was present on that battlefield. It is about that very thing I am going to tell you.”

“Rajadhitya was gathering various kinds of troops here and training them to wage war in distant lands, was he not? For certain reasons, he could not set out at the time he had intended. News arrived that war had flared up once again in Lanka. To bring that to a successful conclusion, more troops had to be sent. The Emperor did not wish for the principal warriors and commanders of Chola Nadu to travel far to the north while there was an enemy still in the south. He kept saying, ‘Let us set out after we receive word that the war in Lanka is over.’ Rajadhitya, unable to go against his father’s word, waited patiently.

But the enemies were not willing to wait in the same way. At that very time, Kannaradevan, the Emperor of the Twin Realms, gathered a vast army to invade Chola Nadu. With that mighty force, he set out towards the south. The king of Ganga Nadu, Boothuga, joined Kannaradevan with his own great army. Like the northern and southern seas joining as one, the armies of the Twin Realms and Boothuga of Ganga Nadu merged into a single, vast ocean and advanced. In that ocean, there were thousands of elephants like whales, and tens of thousands of horses like makara fish. That surging sea of warriors, swelling like the seven seas in the time of the great deluge, seemed as if it would sweep over and submerge the southern land utterly. Our spies, who raced ahead with the speed of the wind and the swiftness of thought to gather information about that army, brought us this news.”

**Chapter 2 – Grandfather and Grandson** “But even this, in a way, is for the best,” said Paranthaka Chakravarthi. “Rather than sending our armies on long marches, making them fight the enemy’s forces in foreign lands, weary and exhausted from travel, it is better to draw the enemy’s armies close to our own country, surround them on all sides, and destroy them. That, the emperor said, is the right way of war. Only after learning that the enemy forces had advanced as far as Vadavengadam did he grant permission for the march.”

“Whether permission was given or not, Rajaditya set out. Three hundred thousand infantry soldiers, fifty thousand cavalry, ten thousand war elephants, two thousand chariots, three hundred and twenty commanders, and thirty-three minor kings joined together in that great army. I too had the fortune to go as one among them. But I also had the misfortune to be one of the few who survived and returned.”
“After three days’ march, at a place called Thakkolam, two katham north of Kanchipuram, our forces and the enemy’s met on the battlefield!”

“Aditha! We have heard in the Puranas about the battle between Indra and Vritrasura. We know of the war between Rama and Ravana, and the battle of the Pandavas and Kauravas. But those who witnessed the terrible battle at Thakkolam would say all those wars were nothing in comparison. The enemy’s forces were nearly twice as large as ours. It is said there were five hundred thousand soldiers and thirty thousand war elephants in their army. But what of it? There was no commander in that army like your great grandfather Rajaditya. That is why it seemed as if the goddesses of Valor and Victory stood by our side.”

“The battle raged for ten days. It became impossible to count the number of fallen warriors on either side. Elephants lay dead on the field like dark mountains. Though both sides suffered heavy losses, the enemy’s ranks weakened more quickly. The reason for this became clear to them. Wherever Rajaditya’s elephant went, with the tiger banner flying proudly, Jayalakshmi followed. Whenever there was a sign of faltering in our ranks, Rajaditya’s elephant would appear there. At the sight of that elephant and the heroic man seated upon it, our soldiers would regain their courage, their strength tripled, and they would attack the enemy with renewed vigor. For ten days the enemy observed all this, and then they hatched a most treacherous plot. Only later did we realize it was a plot. The one who devised and carried it out was the Ganga king, Boothuga. Suddenly, that traitor raised the flag of truce on his elephant, lifted both hands above his head, and crying, ‘Saranam! Saranam!’…” He came. At that moment, Rajadhitya himself was nearby. Only after seeing the howdah of his elephant, over which the tiger flag fluttered, must the Bhoothugan have acted as he did. The mighty Rajadhitya, upon witnessing an enemy king approach uttering the words “surrender,” felt his heart soften. He wished to know whether the emperor of the twin realms was seeking peace by halting the war, or if Bhoothugan alone had separated from him to join their side. Therefore, he sounded the conch and signaled the bodyguards who stood around him to step aside. He beckoned for the elephant upon which Bhoothugan rode to come near his own. Bhoothugan approached Rajadhitya with folded hands. Rajadhitya noticed the tears welling in his eyes, and his heart grew even softer.
At that moment, the words of the great Tamil poet did not come to Rajadhitya’s mind:
“Even the enemy’s sword is sheathed When hands are joined in prayer, And tears of repentance flow.”

Seeing those tears, he was moved. Drawing Bhoothugan even closer, he asked, “What news?” The reply Bhoothugan gave filled Rajadhitya with disgust. Bhoothugan confessed that, realizing defeat was certain for the armies of the twin realms, he had advised Kanna Devan to surrender, but as Kanna Devan refused, he had resolved to separate himself and surrender alone. Hearing this, Rajadhitya rebuked him harshly.

He declared that such a vile traitor could never be accepted into his ranks, and ordered him to turn back. Even as he was saying this, in the blink of an eye, Bhoothugan committed that dreadful act of treachery. He drew from his hidden place a bow and an arrow, strung the bow, nocked the arrow, and shot it. The cruel, poison-tipped arrow struck Rajadhitya in the chest at an unguarded moment, and he fell. No one around had expected such treachery, so for a moment, the warriors standing nearby could not comprehend what had happened. All they heard was Rajadhitya commanding Bhoothugan to turn back. Immediately, Bhoothugan spurred his elephant and fled!

When the news spread that Rajadhitya had died atop his elephant, it was as if a thunderbolt had struck each and every one of our soldiers. Overwhelmed by that immense sorrow, they forgot the very war itself. The minor kings, commanders, and soldiers alike lost all sense of action and began to lament. In such a state, is it any wonder that the enemy gained the upper hand? At that time, our army was compelled to retreat. Is it not always easy to pursue those who are fleeing? I too was one among those who fled! The enemy forces had advanced even up to the banks of this Kedila river. Only after reaching here did we regain our senses and turn to make a stand. We halted the enemy’s advance. From Thirukovalur, I took my family and settled them safely in my fortress in the western hill country. It was in those mountain slopes that I gathered my troops. From time to time, I launched attacks on the enemy who had reached as far as the Kedila river. Yet, those invaders who came then did not leave this region for many years. They lingered here and there, causing endless trouble. Kanchi city remained under their control. Only after you defeated Veerapandiyan three years ago and came this way, did you reclaim the city of Kanchi…”

Aditya Karikalan interrupted again, “Grandfather! I already know all this! But no matter how many times I hear about the battle of Thakkolam and the story of Rajaditya, I never tire of it. Why did you remind me of Rajaditya now? Tell me that!”

“My child! Your great uncle Rajaditya longed to expand the Chola Empire from Lanka to the Ganges. He died before that dream could be fulfilled. The whole land and all the cities speak of my grandson Aditya Karikalan as a hero equal to him. All over Tamilakam, people say you will accomplish what he could not. But I reminded you of his story so that, unlike Rajaditya, you will not fall prey to treachery…

“Grandfather! My great uncle lost his life on the battlefield through the enemy’s treachery. Why do you remind me of that now? Am I going to war? Am I venturing among enemies who might deceive me? Am I not going to meet my father’s closest friends? In what way, and for what reason, would they betray me?” asked Aditya Karikalan.

“Listen, Karikala! Did not the great Thiruvalluvar say that even in the folded hands and tears of an enemy, there may be hidden weapons? He also said that hidden enmity is more dangerous than open hostility.
‘Fear not the sword-like foe, but beware The foe who comes with honeyed words to share.’

There is no need to fear enemies who stand before you openly, like a drawn sword. It is those who act as friends, but are truly foes, whom you must fear—so it is said. Child! Now you are about to go among enemies who pretend to be your allies. Even though I tried to stop you, you would not listen. They have called you, claiming that some dispute over the kingdom has arisen and that you are to resolve it. I have also heard that they intend to tie the daughter of Sambuvaraiyan around your neck in marriage. But what their true purpose is, neither you nor I can know.

There are many kings in this land of Bharata waiting to give you their daughters in marriage. It is not necessary that it must be this Sambuvaraiyan’s daughter. I have heard that they plan to divide the kingdom, giving half to you and half to Madurantakan, and thus make peace. What trick or plot may be hidden in this, I do not know. Whatever may come, I shall at once go to Thirukovalur, gather all my guards, and camp on the banks of the Vellaru. While you are in the Sambuvaraiyar palace, if you sense anything suspicious, send word to me immediately!…”
At that moment, Malayaman noticed that Aditya Karikalan’s attention was not on him, but had turned elsewhere.
“Grandfather! Look there!” said Aditya Karikalan, his voice troubled.
Hearing these words, the valiant old man turned and looked in that direction.

chapters.title: The Hawk and the Dove
paragraphs: In the direction Aditya Karikalan had pointed, there stood a mandapam on the riverbank. It was a pavilion built of stonework. Some righteous soul must have constructed it long ago for travelers to rest in, sheltering them from sun and rain. That mandapam had endured many years of scorching heat and pounding rain, now bearing the marks of age and decay. At the corners of the mandapam, there were sculpted figures carved in stone. What those figures represented, the elder Malayaman could not tell.
“Did you see, Grandfather?” asked Aditya Karikalan.
“My child! You mean that mandapam, don’t you? I see nothing else there. The pavilion stands empty; I see no one inside,” he replied.

“Grandfather! Only now do I truly realize that you have grown old. Your eyesight has grown dim with age. Look there! A great royal eagle! How enormous it is! How wide its wingspan! What cruelty! What cruelty! It has caught a tiny dove in its talons; can’t you see? The eagle’s sharp claws have torn the dove, and its blood is spilling—don’t you see? Oh, what a marvel! Now look at that other dove, Grandfather! It is circling near that fearsome eagle! How it pleads with the eagle! The dove caught in the eagle’s claws must be its mate! It is begging for its beloved’s life! Grandfather! Is that dove pleading, or is it preparing to fight the eagle? From the way it beats its wings, it seems ready for battle. By the gods! What courage that female dove has! She is going to fight the monstrous fiend to save her lover’s life! Grandfather! Do you think the eagle’s heart will be moved? Never! Never! Not once will it show mercy! It has grown fat and strong by killing and devouring countless doves like these! Wicked eagle! Here, I shall put an end to you!”
So saying, Aditya Karikalan picked up a clod of earth lying nearby and hurled it at the mandapam. The clod struck one corner of the pavilion and fell to the ground.

“Monster! May you get what you deserve!” cried Aditya Karikalan, and then laughed thunderously, the sound echoing like rolling thunder. The elder already harbored some doubts about his grandson’s independent spirit. Now, those doubts grew even stronger.
“Grandfather! Why are you staring at me like that? Go and take a look near the mandapam,” said Karikalan.

As he was told, Malayaman walked closer to the mandapam and examined the spot where Karikalan’s stone had fallen. There, a sculpture was revealed. In that sculpture, a royal eagle was depicted clutching a dove in its talons, as if pecking at it and lifting it up, while another dove seemed poised to leap at the eagle—so lifelike was the artistry.
Malayaman returned and said, “Child! It’s true that I’ve grown old! My eyesight is not as sharp as it once was. Only after going near and looking closely did I realize what fine sculpture it is!”

“Fine sculpture? Call it a marvel, Grandfather! Some sculptor from the age of Mahendravarman or Mamallar—the emperors of sculpture—must have created this. When I first saw it, it seemed so real, as if it were actually happening before my eyes!” exclaimed Karikalan.

“Adithya! The marvel is not only in that stone! It is in your eyes as well; it is within your mind, too. So many travelers pass this way every day. Three-fourths of them probably never even notice this sculptural wonder. Many others, even if they see it, pass by as if they have not. Only a few, like you, are so astonished by a single sculpture!...”
“I am not astonished, Grandfather! I am angry. I feel such rage that I want to smash that sculpture to pieces right now. I cannot even stand to hear people praise and admire such a cruel work!”

“Karikala! What is this strange talk? When did your diamond heart become so tender? It is the nature of the royal eagle to kill and eat the dove. If the lion king starts to pity the goat, it is no longer a lion; it becomes a goat itself. Those who wish to sit upon the throne and rule must destroy their enemies and traitors. Those born to rule the world under a single umbrella must vanquish their rival kings. If the royal eagle does not kill the dove, can it remain a royal eagle? Why does this trouble you so much?” asked Malayaman.

“Grandfather! All that you say is true, but after seeing that dove’s desperate struggle, should not Rajaraja have felt compassion? Should he not have been moved by pity for the girl and granted her request for release? Sir, tell me yourself—if, at the moment you were about to kill an enemy, his beloved came and pleaded for his life, what would you do? Would your heart not be moved then?” asked Karikalan.

“If such a woman were to come between me and my enemy, I would kick her aside with my left foot and slay my foe. Karikala, there is no doubt about that. The poet Valluvar has said that enemies may hide weapons even in their folded hands, and that even in their tears, weapons may be concealed. The tears of women are more dangerous than those of men, for women’s tears have a greater power to soften the heart. One who allows his heart to be softened thus can never accomplish great deeds in this world—he will become the most wretched among women themselves!”
“Grandfather! What is this? Why do you speak so disparagingly of women? Does not speaking ill of women also diminish my own mother?”

“My child, listen! There is nothing in this world to equal the love I bore your mother. Six children were born to me. They grew up to be warriors like Bhima and Arjuna. I sacrificed them all on the field of battle. When news came of their deaths, I did not grieve. But when I gave your mother away in marriage, though I knew she was to ascend the imperial throne, I cannot describe the pain my heart felt. Yet did I show that pain openly? Did I reveal it to her? No, I did not. Do you know what I told your mother when I called her alone on the eve of her wedding? Listen, Karikala! ‘Daughter! You are about to wed a king who will rule the land. Do not let pride enter your heart for this. The greater the glory of the husband you marry, the greater will be your suffering. The servant women in your palace may be happier than you. Prepare yourself for sorrow and hardship. If you bear no children, your husband will surely take other wives. Do not grieve over that. If you do have children, raise them as brave sons. If news comes that they have died on the battlefield, not a single tear must you shed. If your husband is happy, you too must be happy. If your husband is sorrowful, strive to bring him joy. If your husband falls ill, serve him with devotion. If your husband dies, ascend the funeral pyre with him! Even if blood pours from your heart, not a single tear must fall from your eyes! In the lineage of Malayaman—’” “This is the tradition of women!”—thus I once spoke to your mother, giving her wisdom.

Just as I advised, your mother has lived by those words to this very day; she has upheld them unfailingly. Karikala! She raised you and your brother to be unparalleled warriors. After your father fell ill, she herself has tended to him day and night, performing every service with her own hands. Whenever I think of having such a daughter as yours, my shoulders swell with pride!” said Malayaman.

“Grandfather! The pride I feel whenever I think of my mother knows no bounds. But let me ask you one thing—please tell me! Suppose a cruel enemy of my father comes, brandishing a knife, intent on killing him. What would my mother do then? Would she stand before him, weeping, and beg the enemy to spare her husband’s life? Especially if that enemy were someone known to her…”

“My child! Your mother would never beg for mercy from such an enemy. The daughter of Malayaman would never, under any circumstance, bring shame upon the clan she was born into, nor upon the family she married into. She would consider her husband’s enemy as her own mortal foe. She would never fold her hands in supplication before the enemy; she would not shed tears. If her husband’s life were taken, she would immediately fall upon his body and surrender her own life as well! Or else, she would harden her heart to stone and remain alive only for one purpose—to exact vengeance upon the enemy!”
Hearing this, Aditya Karikalan let out a long, deep sigh. “Grandfather! May I take my leave now?” he asked.
“Is it truly necessary that you must go?”
“What doubt can there be about that, grandfather? I have already come more than halfway!”

“Yes, you have come more than halfway. At first, I too said you should not go; but later, I told you to proceed. After hearing the news about your younger brother, I decided it was best that you go. I do not believe that Arulmozhi Varman is dead…”
“Nor do I believe it…”

“In his youth, there was a time when your father’s whereabouts were unknown for a while. In the same way, Arulmozhi must be hiding on some island. I am certain he will return after a few days! Yet, I know that this news has caused turmoil throughout the Chola land. Your parents too must be deeply troubled. At such a time, it is necessary for you to be at their side, to offer them comfort. And when you go, rather than going as an enemy of the Pazhuvettarayars,
It is best to go with friendship. That is why I agreed for you to accept the invitation of Sambuvarayar. He did not invite me deliberately; if he had, I too would have come.
“Grandfather! Are you so afraid on my behalf? Do you think I am so helpless?” asked Karikalan.

“No, my boy! No! Do I not know what a peerless warrior you are? I would trust you to go alone into the midst of ten thousand armed enemies. But I am afraid only to send you alone before a woman who could move your heart with her tears.”

“I have not heard, Grandfather, that Sambuvarayar’s daughter is so skilled in enchantments! Kandhamaran has told me she is a girl too timid even to appear before men. And I would never act in haste or do anything without the consent of my mother and father. I am well aware, too, that two girls born in your ancient clan remain yet unmarried…”

“Adithya, I have no such thoughts. It is true that my elder son’s two daughters have reached marriageable age. But I have not the slightest intention of binding them to you. Already, many of the minor kings of Chola Nadu harbor envy and enmity toward me. If this too were to be added, nothing more need be said. On the contrary, if you were to marry Sambuvarayar’s daughter, I would be somewhat satisfied. My age has advanced; my body has grown weak. At times, even my spirit falters. Sometimes I wonder if I shall never see my beloved grandson again, if this is the last time I shall look upon you. Hereafter, I can be of no help to you. You must have new friends, those who will care for your welfare. Therefore, if you marry Sambuvarayar’s daughter, I would truly be happy.”

“Grandfather! Not even for your happiness can I do that. I am not going to Sambuvarayar’s palace as a guest out of desire for his friendship, nor to marry his daughter. You may rest easy on that account.”

“Then why are you going, my child? Can you not tell me the truth? Now and then, a few words from the conversation between your two friends reached my ears. Periya Pazhuvettarayar is over sixty years old—” “He did marry, didn’t he? They say that enchantress, that Mohini demoness, has sent you a palm-leaf letter, and that is why you agreed to come to Kadambur. Is that true?”
“Yes, grandfather! It is true!” replied Aditya Karikalan.

“Heavens! What times are these? Karikala! Listen to what I say. The Chola clan into which you were born is a lineage that has flourished with unbroken glory for two thousand years. Some of your ancestors were emperors who ruled the world under a single umbrella. At other times, they were petty kings who ruled only over Uraiyur and its surroundings. Some, like Rama himself, observed the vow of monogamy. Others married many women and begot many heroic sons. Some were devotees of Shiva, some of Vishnu; some declared, ‘There are no gods or spirits.’ But none of them ever brought disgrace upon themselves by their conduct. None coveted another man’s wife. My child! If you wish, marry as many maidens as you desire. Your grandfather’s father—the famed Parantaka Chakravarti—married seven women; you may do the same. But never, ever lay eyes upon that sorceress who has married Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar!”
“Forgive me, grandfather! I will never commit such a crime. I will not bring shame upon the Chola clan or the Malayaman lineage!”
“If that is so, then why do you go at her summons, child?”
“I will tell you the truth before I go. Once, I did her a great wrong. I am going to ask her forgiveness for that,” said Karikalan.
“What words are these? You, seeking forgiveness from a woman? My ears cannot bear to hear such a thing!” exclaimed Malayaman.

Aditya Karikalan hung his head for a moment. Then, steadying his heart, he recounted the old tale to his grandfather. He spoke in detail of how he had sought out Veerapandiyan, discovered his hiding place, how Nandini had intervened and begged for his life, how he, ignoring her pleas, slew him in a fit of rage, and how, from that moment, his mind had known no peace.

“That memory torments me without end, grandfather! Only if I see her once and ask her forgiveness will my heart find peace. She, too, seems ready to forget the past. With turmoil in the kingdom—” “She is also attentive in watching over me without playing around. That is precisely why she has summoned me. Once I have completed the task I am going for, I will return to Kanchi very soon, Grandfather! Upon my return, I will board a ship and set out to find and bring back my younger brother,” said Aditya Karikalan.

The elder Malayaman let out a deep sigh and said, “Many things that were unclear to me until now have become clear. Many matters that were shrouded in mystery until today now make sense. It is certain that no one can overcome fate!”

chapters.title: The Ayyanar Temple
paragraphs: While the old man and his grandson conversed on the banks of the Kedila River, at that very moment, in the village of Thirukanaattumulloor on the northern bank of the Kollidam, two old friends—Azhwarkkadiyan and Vandiyathevan—were engaged in a most peculiar affair. In those days, the northern Kaveri, known as the Kollidam, was considered as sacred a river as the southern Kaveri. During the month of Thula, it was customary for Lord Shiva, enshrined in the temple at Kanaattumulloor, to ascend his bull mount and proceed to the Kollidam’s bank, bestowing his presence and blessings upon the devotees who had come to bathe in the holy waters. Every day at noon, the festival would reach its peak. Worshippers from the surrounding villages would gather in great numbers. Though the Vishnu temple in that village was small, even from there, the Lord would ascend his Garuda vehicle and proceed to the Kollidam’s bank.

Thus, amidst the throng that had assembled on the northern Kaveri for the sacred Thula bath, Azhwarkkadiyan planted a staff of the naaval tree into the earth and began to shout, “Naaval, O Naaval! Naaval, O Naaval! I have come to this Naaval island to wage a debate and prove that the Vaishnava faith is the supreme faith. Let the Saivites, the Saktas, the Advaitins, the Kapalikas, the Kalamukhas, the Buddhists, the Jains—let anyone who wishes come forth to debate! If they win, I shall hoist them upon my shoulders and parade them around the village. But if they lose, they must leave behind everything but their loincloths and depart from here! Naaval, O Naaval!” he cried.

Before him, rudraksha garlands, makara-shaped beads, water pots, earrings, silk garments, and gold coins were heaped in piles. It was clear from these trophies that he had debated many and emerged victorious. Beside him, leaning against a kadamba tree, stood Vandiyathevan, a knife he had fashioned in his hand. Now, all that remained on him was a single cloth around his waist and the knife in his hand. From his appearance, it seemed he had used that knife to frighten away those who had tried to use force against Azhwarkkadiyan. This was further confirmed by the words he spoke, watching a group of Saivites approaching in a noisy crowd.

“Beware! Let those who wish to debate do so fairly. But if anyone dares to lay a hand on this Vaishnavan, they will answer to this sword!” he declared, twirling the blade twice for emphasis. The Saivites, who had approached in anger, now calmed themselves. One among them said, “O Vaishnavite! Do not be proud, thinking you have won the debate today! Go to Thirunaraiyur! There, Nambiyandar Nambi resides, who will defeat you in debate and send you running away in disgrace!”
Alwarkadiyan replied, “Tell your Thirunaraiyur Nambi to come and debate with Anantha Battar of Thirunarayanapuram! If I happen to be there, I shall be present as well!”

Though he repeatedly called out, “Is there anyone else for debate? Is there anyone else?” no one came forward to challenge him anew. So, Alwarkadiyan took up the branch of the neem tree, and planted the victory flag emblazoned with the conch and discus. Some of the Vaishnavites who had been standing nearby, watching everything, immediately came forward, lifted him onto their shoulders, and began to sing and dance:
“Narayana is our God! We shall all sing His praise!”
Afterwards, they entreated him, “Valiant Vaishnavite! You must come to our house and bless us by partaking of our meal!”

“So be it!” Alwarkadiyan declared grandly, and taking Vandiyathevan along with him, he went to their home. The two of them feasted heartily on tamarind rice, Thirukannamudu, and curd rice, until their stomachs were full. Of the prizes Alwarkadiyan had won in the debate, he gave Vandiyathevan a single yellow silk cloth suitable to be worn as an upper garment, and handed over the rest to the Sri Vaishnavites, receiving in return gold coins equal to their value. He explained that, since he had to travel north as far as Haridwar to establish the greatness of the Vaishnava faith, he was in need of gold coins. The Sri Vaishnavites, delighted, gave him even more gold coins than the value of the items. Having thus obtained the money, Alwarkadiyan and Vandiyathevan set out towards Kadambur in the afternoon.

At that time, the river Kollidam was in spate, so they could not bring along the horses they had ridden. The boat they took to cross the river was overcrowded with people, and as it reached the bank, it capsized. Like the others, Vandiyathevan too fell into the floodwaters and had to swim to the shore.

At that moment, the waistcloth Vandiyathevan had managed to keep safe through so many perilous adventures, along with the signet rings and the palm-leaf letter given by the Princess, were all swept away in the river’s flood. The gold coins he had were lost as well. It was to gather money for buying new horses that they had employed the aforementioned strategy. The plan succeeded, and they managed to obtain a little money.

But it was also known that in those remote village regions, horses could not be bought for any price. Perhaps, at the weekly market in Kadambur village, horses might be brought for sale; otherwise, one would have to go to Thiruppathiripuliyur to purchase them.

A debate arose among the friends about whether or not to go to Kadambur. They discussed the pros and cons of the matter. There was a chance they might hear some news about Aditya Karikalan’s arrival at Kadambur. Would it not be good if they could find out whether he had already set out from Kanchi, and by which route he was coming? But at the same time, they must not be seen by anyone they knew in Kadambur. If they happened to meet Kandhamaaran, it could become dangerous. And if the retainers of the Pazhuvettaraiyars had already arrived, that too would be troublesome!
“Vaishnavite! You are the one who knows how to climb over walls at night, aren’t you? Why not bring out two horses from the stables of the Sambuvaraiyar?” said Vandiyathevan.
“I can climb over walls, but shouldn’t the horses also know how to climb and jump over walls?” replied the Vaishnavite.

“If the Pazhuvur retainers are there, we can just take two horses by force. Didn’t they once chase away my horse in Kadambur? I must repay them for that insult!” said the valiant scion of the Vanar clan.

They spoke at length about their meeting in Kadambur some months ago, and the extraordinary events that had taken place that night, as they made their way along the road. By the time the sun was setting, they reached Kadambur. As they had expected, the place was bustling with activity. The palace and the fortress gates were adorned with flags, festoons, and garlands, shining in all their glory. At the fortress gate and along the surrounding walls, the guards had been strengthened more than ever before. Was it any wonder, with the crown prince Aditya Karikalan expected to arrive? At the same time, the chief dignitary, Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar, was also coming with the queen. The retainers of both parties would be arriving. For several days, the town would be in a state of grand commotion.

The two friends listened as the people of Kadambur’s main street discussed all this. From their conversation, it was clear that neither party had yet arrived. It was also learned that Sambuvaraiyar’s son, Kandhamaaran, had set out for Kanchi to escort Aditya Karikalan. Amidst all this excited talk, some people spoke of the “prince who was taken by the sea”—Arulmozhi Varman… They spoke in hushed, subdued voices. From the way they conversed, it was clear that many were displeased with the feasting and festivities being arranged here, even as such a great tragedy had just occurred.

Azhwarkkadiyan and Vandiyathevan listened as if they were not paying attention at all, and passed through the village. They did not wish to spend the night anywhere within the settlement. Surely, somewhere beyond the village, there would be an abandoned mandapam or a choultry where they could rest? If not, it would be better to go on to Veeranarayana Puram and spend the night there. In the vast hundred-pillared hall of the great Perumal temple, they could lie down and sleep in peace. After the events of the previous night, a good night’s rest was absolutely necessary for them.
Once they had crossed Kadambur and gone a little way along the road, they saw a dense bamboo grove, and within it, an Ayyanar temple.
“Vaishnavite! I cannot walk any further. Let us sleep in this temple tonight. It is a good place to stay out of sight,” said Vandiyathevan.
“My friend, what you say is not wise. How can we be sure that no one else like us will come to such a place?” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
“If those who come are mounted on horses, that would be all the better,” replied Vandiyathevan.
“No horse could make its way into this bamboo thicket. Even for men, it is a difficult task to get through!”
“There must be a narrow footpath somewhere. At the very least, the temple priest must have a way to come and go, must he not?”

Circling around the thick, tangled bamboo bushes, the two of them finally discovered a narrow footpath. It was a struggle to walk along it without having their bodies scratched by thorns. After proceeding a short distance in this manner, they found a small clearing. There stood a modest Ayyanar temple. Opposite the temple was a sacrificial altar, and beside it, rows of elephants and horses fashioned from clay and baked in the village kiln. It was customary for devotees, when making vows to Ayyanar, to bring such clay horses and elephants and place them here.
Upon seeing them, Vandiyathevan remarked, “We worry so much about horses—why not ask Ayyanar and take two of these for ourselves?”
“Don’t you know the old proverb, ‘One should not trust a clay horse to cross a river’?” said Azhwarkkadiyan.

“O Vaishnavite! Our Ayyanar is a most powerful deity. He grants boons the moment they are asked. He is not like your Vishnu, who lets his devotees suffer and sleeps through the broad daylight!” retorted Vandiyathevan.
“If that is so, then say that your Ayyanar will even bring these clay horses to life! That’s wonderful—money saved!”
“If there is true devotion, even clay horses will come alive! After all, what are our bodies but the same? Was it not Brahma who fashioned bodies from clay and breathed life into them?”

“Well said, brother! We tend to forget that these bodies are made of earth. To remind us of this often, Vaishnavite acharyas have commanded that we mix sacred clay and smear it on our foreheads and bodies!”

Vandiyathevan hushed him with a sharp “Hush!” and seized Azhwarkkadiyan’s hand, pointing ahead with his other hand. The sun had set some time ago. In the dim light that lingered in the small clearing surrounded by the dark bamboo grove, the vehicles of Ayyanar seemed to come alive and move. An elephant and a horse shifted their positions and moved aside. Vandiyathevan stood for a moment, stunned, unable to decide whether to believe the miracle he saw with his own eyes. Yet, he did not wish to miss the chance to immediately impress upon Azhwarkkadiyan the wondrous power of Ayyanar. “Vaishnavite! Did you see—?” he began, but before he could finish, Azhwarkkadiyan gripped his hand tightly, pressed a finger to his lips in a sign to keep silent, and drew Vandiyathevan with him behind the bamboo thicket, where they hid themselves well.

Had not the horse and the elephant moved aside and left a gap? In that space, only a human head was visible. That head turned this way and that, scanning all directions. The sight of a lone head appearing beside Ayyanar’s sacrificial altar and turning about to peer all around was a most terrifying sight. Vandiyathevan, who had witnessed many horrors, felt his skin prickle; but realizing that Azhwarkkadiyan’s hand, which held him, was steady and unshaken, Vandiyathevan regained his composure.

As they watched, that head slowly rose up above the surface. The figure became visible up to a man’s chest. Then, the man emerged fully, standing upright. At the spot where he appeared, a small fissure yawned open—dark, encircled by shadow, gaping like the mouth of some fearsome underworld cavern.

After peering intently for a moment, they realized who the man was. It was Idumbankari, who, while serving as an attendant at Kadambur Palace, had also been a member of Ravidasan’s conspiratorial band.

Both men recognized him at the same instant, and exchanged glances, signaling their astonishment to each other without words. Idumbankari left the opening as it was, glanced around once more to make sure he was unobserved, and then walked toward the Aiyanar temple. He opened the temple doors and went inside. After a short while, a faint, flickering light could be seen from within the temple. They understood that a lamp had been lit inside.
“Thambi! What do you make of this?” whispered Adiyan in a hushed voice.
“I think Aiyanar is a powerful deity; didn’t you see the horse come to life?” replied Vandiyathevan.
“That may be so! But what about the man who just arrived—what do you think of him?”
“He seems to be the temple priest. Shall we go in and have darshan of the deity as well?”
“Wait a bit! Let’s see if anyone else comes for darshan.”
“Do you think anyone else will come?”
“Then why is he lighting the lamp?”
“What’s so strange about a priest lighting a lamp in the temple?”
“Thambi! Don’t you know who he is?”
“I know very well—he’s the same Idumbankari who brought me a horse on the southern bank of the Kollidam! I’m thinking I might ask him for a horse again now…”
“That’s a good idea.”
“Did you not like it?”
“Idumbankari is not merely the man who bought you the horse; he belongs to Ravidasan’s group.”
“If that is so, another good idea comes to mind.”
“What? What is it?”
“While Idumbankari is engaged in Ayyanar’s service, I think I can find out where he came from, and how he appeared here.”
“How can that be done?”
“Can I not enter through the same doorway from which he came out?”
“You can, but there are dangers in that…”
“What deed is there without danger?”
“Then, as you wish?”
“Vaishnavar! You stay here and watch what happens…”
“What difficulty is there in that? I will stay and keep watch. Do you have any idea where the tunnel leads?”
“I do, Swami, I do! I wish to find out if it is correct.”
“Why do you need to know that?”
“Who knows? It may be useful at some point.”
At that moment, voices of conversation were heard a little distance away.
“There is no time to delay, Vaishnavar! You will stay here until I return, won’t you? Or will you do as Sugriva did to Vali?”
“As long as there is life in me, I will remain here. But what certainty is there that you will return?”
“If life remains, I too shall return…”

Saying this, Vandiyathevan darted towards the spot where the doorway was visible. He slipped inside, and in the next instant, vanished into the darkness of that pit. It seemed as if the mouth of the cave had swallowed him whole.

Idumbankari, who had gone into the temple, came out and looked around. His eyes fell upon the open doorway. At once, he went to that spot and twisted the trident weapon that had been planted beside the sacrificial altar.

The elephant and the horse, which had moved away, now drew near once more. The entrance that had been closed was nowhere to be seen—it had vanished without a trace! Having accomplished this task, Idumbankari returned again to the threshold of the temple. At that very moment, Ravidasan, Soman Sambavan, and the others arrived from another direction. Azhwarkkadiyan concealed himself even more carefully behind the bamboo grove.
Ravidasan seated himself upon the steps at the temple entrance; the others sat on the ground before him.
“Comrades! The time to fulfill the vow we have taken is drawing near!” declared Ravidasan.
“For six months now, we have been saying ‘It is drawing near, it is drawing near,’” said one of the men.

“There is nothing wrong in that; for six months, that day has indeed been approaching. Now, it is but a matter of days, easily counted on our fingers. News has come that Aditya Karikalan has left Kanchipuram. The lord of Thirukovalur tried to stop him, but his efforts have failed!”
“What certainty is there that no one else will try to stop him along the way?”
“Aditya Karikalan is not one to turn back once he has set his foot forward. Whoever tries to stop him now, he will not heed them…”
“If the message his sister sent reaches him…”
“How could it possibly reach him? The youth who carried the message—we bound him and left him in the forest, did we not?”
“Very well! Yet I saw him this morning on the northern bank of the Kollidam. Another of our enemies was with him.”
“Who is that?”
“The one disguised as a false Vaishnava!”
“In that case, we must be all the more vigilant. We must try to prevent them from meeting Aditya Karikalan.”

“This is like letting go of the stalk and catching at the tail. We could have finished off the one who fell into our hands right then and there. I do not know why the Queen ordered that he be spared…”

“Comrades! At that time, I too did not understand it. Only later did I come to know; I admit that the Queen outwitted even me. It was with a very important purpose that the Queen ordered Vandiyathevan to be spared alive. There is no need for you to know that reason now. Do not worry about Vandiyathevan. But if you come across that Vaishnavite, do not hesitate in the least—take his life at once and then attend to other matters…” said Ravidasan.

chapters.title: The Dreadful Moonlit Room
paragraphs: Vandiyathevan stepped into the pillared doorway and descended a few steps. Then the ground leveled out; a faint, very faint light could be seen. He walked on for ten or fifteen feet. There was a sound, like the turning of a cartwheel. Suddenly, darkness collapsed upon him, engulfing him completely. He remembered, not for the first time, his many resolutions not to meddle in affairs that did not concern him.

“What was the task I set out for? How important it is! And yet, leaving that aside, here I am, entering this subterranean tunnel. Where could it possibly lead? What dangers might be lurking here? What a foolish thing I have done! When will my impulsive nature ever leave me?”

These thoughts slowed his steps. He considered turning back and retraced his path, but his feet struck the steps. Yet, he could not see the entrance above; he groped about, but it was useless. Someone must have closed the door from above. Sweat broke out all over Vandiyathevan’s body. In a panic, he tried to open the sealed entrance. At that moment, from somewhere far, far away, he thought he heard voices—different voices, speaking. Perhaps it was the voices of people at the Ayyanar temple entrance, from where he had entered the pillared doorway. Had Idumbankari not lit the lamp in expectation of someone’s arrival? Perhaps they had come. If this were true, it would be a grave mistake to try and open the pillared doorway and emerge at this moment. Who knew how long they would sit there talking? If they were Idumbankari’s companions—Ravidasan and the other conspirators—they might well talk for a long time. Why had they gathered here? What were they discussing? What plot were they hatching?

That Veeravaishnavan would surely be keeping watch on all this. Rather than standing here, breathless and sweating, it would be better to go a little further ahead and see what lay beyond. Having dared to descend, let me see where this tunnel leads—would that not be better?

Resolving thus, Vandiyathevan placed his hesitant foot forward and began to walk on. Though the ground was level, it was rough and uneven. The tunnel must have been carved out of solid rock. He had a suspicion in his mind about where this underground passage might lead. Most likely… It must end within the Kadambur Sambuvaraiyar palace. But where exactly within that palace does it lead? Perhaps it ends in the treasury chamber, or perhaps within the women’s quarters where the royal ladies reside. Vandiyathevan already knew that such secret tunnels existed in the palaces of kings and minor chieftains. In times of great danger, when escape from the palace became necessary, these hidden paths would be used. Since it was often essential to evacuate the palace women, such passages typically ended in the women’s quarters. And since it might be necessary to carry away important treasures, these tunnels often led to the treasury as well. Where does this passage end? Since Idumbankari had entered and exited by this way, it was most likely that it ended in the treasury. Just as the conspirators, through the young queen, planned to loot Periya Pazhuvetarayar’s treasures without his knowledge, perhaps they had also plotted to rob Sambuvaraiyar’s treasury! But why would they undertake such a deed at a time when Aditya Karikalan and other distinguished guests were about to arrive? Could there be some other purpose behind their actions?

Vandiyathevan remembered what he had seen and heard in the Thiruppurambiyam forest camp. The long sword with the fish emblem, which he had seen with the Pazhuvur queen, flashed before his mind’s eye for a moment. A chill ran through his body. Perhaps these people harbored intentions even more terrifying than mere theft of treasure. If only he could find out for certain where this passage led, it might help him prevent their evil designs from succeeding.

He had only been walking for a few minutes along the underground passage, but because of the darkness, it felt much longer. The lack of air made him short of breath, and sweat poured from his body. When he considered the distance from the Ayyanar temple to the Kadambur palace, he was at first daunted. But then he reconsidered. Since he had come by winding streets and forest paths from the palace’s main entrance, it had seemed a long way. But if one came directly from the rear of the palace, the Ayyanar temple would not be so far. It would be only as far as an arrow shot from a bow. If that were true, he must be nearing the outer wall of the palace by now...

Yes, just so. Suddenly, from somewhere above, a cool breeze struck Vandiyathevan. He had been on the verge of fainting from heat and exhaustion, but that breeze revived him. He looked up in surprise; high above—

In the far distance, a faint light could be seen. Voices, too, reached his ears. It must be one of the turrets built here and there atop the fortress wall, where soldiers stood guard. There must be some arrangement for air to flow through the tunnel at that spot. But Vandiyathevan also realized that, while air could pass through, there was no way for a person to climb up or down there.

The thought that he had now entered the Kadambur palace, and the cool breeze that swept down upon him from above, revived him and filled him with new enthusiasm. The place where the tunnel ended must be close by now. Would it be a treasure vault? Like Periya Pazhuvetarayar, would Sambuvarayar too have amassed piles of pearls, corals, gems, diamonds, and gold coins? Would there, as he had seen before, be a skeleton lying amidst those heaps of wealth? Would spiders have spun webs over the gold coins?

As he pondered these things, something struck Vandiyathevan’s foot, startling him. Then, realizing it was a step, he regained his courage. Yes; once he climbed those steps, he was sure to see the treasure chamber.

If not, it might be the women’s quarters. If so, he would be in grave danger! Ah! Kandanmaran’s sister, Manimekalai! That dark-skinned beauty would be there! When he remembered that, at one time, he had considered marrying her, Vandiyathevan smiled. There was no one there to see and rejoice at that smile! What if, at a time when the women of the inner palace were in disarray, he suddenly appeared among them! The thought made him laugh.

But in the very next moment, his blood froze, his heart stopped, and his eyes widened in terror at the sight before him. He had climbed the steps, hadn’t he? As soon as he set foot on the top step and realized there were no more steps to climb, he looked around to understand where he had arrived. Hundreds and hundreds of fiery eyes were fixed upon him. All those eyes belonged to fearsome wild beasts! In the first wave of terror, he tried to turn back the way he had come. But there was no way behind him. As soon as he set foot on the top step, he heard a sound behind him. The tunnel seemed to have closed itself! But what was this dreadful horror? So many wild beasts were waiting here for him!

Tigers, leopards, lions, bears, wild buffaloes, wolves, foxes, rhinoceroses! There—two elephants! All of them seemed poised to leap upon him! Why hadn’t they attacked yet? Look, such a magnificent... A vulture! Oh no! That monstrous owl! That man-eating bat! Am I dreaming what I see? Or… what is this? There lies a crocodile here! Its jaws are gaping wide, displaying its fearsome teeth! Isn’t a crocodile supposed to be in water? But this is dry ground, isn’t it? How did this crocodile come to be among wild beasts of the forest…?

“Amma! I have survived!” cried Vandiyathevan aloud. He realized that all the beasts surrounding him were not living creatures. He remembered Kandhamaaran saying that the lords of the Sambuvaraya clan were fond of hunting. He also recalled that in that lineage’s palace, there was a hunting hall where the skins of some animals they had hunted were stuffed with cotton and straw and arranged to look like living beasts. Now, Vandiyathevan understood that he had entered that very hunting hall. Even so, it took him a little while to recover from the bodily tremor caused by his initial fear.

Then, he went near each animal, touched it, shook it, even stamped on it. He confirmed without doubt that these animals were not alive. Afterwards, he pondered what to do next. The way he had come in had closed by itself. Should he try to find it again and leave by the same route? Or should he try to discover which part of the Kadambur palace this terrifying hall was located in? Or should he attempt to find if there was a way from here into any other room? He began to search the walls for any sign of a door. There was no obvious door to be seen. He went around, touching and tapping the walls, but it was of no use. As time passed, Vandiyathevan’s anger grew. “Why did I get myself entangled in this unnecessary affair?” he fumed.
As he circled along the edge of the walls, at one spot he saw the face of an elephant, with trunk and tusks, fixed flush against the wall.

“Cursed elephant! Was it not you who moved aside and led me into this prison?” he scolded the elephant. The elephant did not reply; even a living elephant would not speak, so what could this lifeless form, stuffed with straw and cotton, do? It stood there, not even moving its trunk.
“I’m asking you—are you going to keep silent?” Vandiyathevan said, and as he spoke, he grasped the elephant’s tusks and gave them a twist. In the next instant, the magic happened.

When he twisted the tusk, the ear of the elephant, which was pressed against the wall, moved. Not only did it move, it folded back and shifted aside. There, in the wall, a large opening became visible.
With unrestrained astonishment, Vandiyathevan leaned forward, stretching his face close to that opening to peer inside.

In the spot he looked, the face of a woman appeared. It was the face of a young woman; the face of a beautiful, dark-skinned maiden. The large eyes in that face were wide open, staring in surprise! Astonishment! Near that woman’s face, Vandiyathevan also saw his own reflection. Just as a lover brings his face close to his beloved’s for a kiss, so close were Vandiyathevan’s face and the maiden’s face at that moment.

The eyes of the maiden, already wide with surprise, now widened even more, expressing an indescribable wonder. Along with astonishment, a hint of fear flickered in her gaze. For a moment, the maiden’s face remained thus, staring. In the next instant, she pursed her rosy red lips and cried out, “Koo…!”

Suddenly, a chill of fright seized Vandiyathevan. In that shock, he withdrew his hands from the elephant’s tusk. In the very next moment, the elephant stood as an ordinary elephant, and the wall as an ordinary wall. The opening had vanished, and so had the maiden. The piercing “Koo” of the maiden, which had rung like the buzzing of bees in his ears, was no longer heard. It took Vandiyathevan a while to calm the pounding of his heart. He sank into deep thought about the vision he had just witnessed.

chapters.title: Manimekalai
paragraphs: Manimekalai, the cherished daughter of Sambuvaraiyar, was a girl brimming with exuberance. Her father, mother, and her brother Kandanmaran had, from her childhood, raised her with love and care. Within the palace of Sambuvaraiyar, she reigned as a queen of command. Whatever she decreed became law within those halls. Until a few months ago, Manimekalai’s life had been one of dance, song, and joyous play. But four or five months ago, for the first time, an obstacle arose in her path. The elders of the house began to insist that she must do something against her own wishes. No matter how much Manimekalai tried to teach them the lesson that “obstinacy is of no use,” it seemed to have no effect on the elders.

For the past two or three years, whenever Kandanmaran returned home from the battlefield, he would speak to her about his friend Vallavaraiyan Vandiyathevan. He would lavishly praise his friend’s valor and skill, his cleverness and wit. He would marvel, saying, “In beauty, he is Manmatha himself; in valor, Arjuna; in cunning, Lord Krishna.” “He is the right husband for you. He is the one who can curb your mischief and keep you in check,” he would say.
Manimekalai longed to hear these tales again and again. Yet, at the same time, she would openly quarrel with Kandanmaran, flaring up at him and picking fights.
“You keep saying all this for nothing! One day, bring him here yourself! I’ll see for myself what his prowess is,” she would say.
“Very well, very well!” Kandanmaran would reply, feigning annoyance.

In her own way, Manimekalai had seen Vallavaraiyan Vandiyathevan with the eyes of imagination, befriended him in her mind’s world, laughed and played with him, quarreled and made peace—thus passing her days in such sweet daydreams. At times, she would speak with delight to her closest companions about her brother’s friend, the valiant scion of the Vanar clan. But four months ago, an unexpected obstacle disrupted these pleasant dreams.

Kandanmaran began to speak in a different tone. “Forget that orphaned boy, who has neither home, nor gate, nor rank, nor status!” he said. He revealed his desire to see her seated upon the throne of Thanjavur. Then, one day... He stated the matter plainly. He said that, already, Madhurantakan—who had married the daughter of the younger Pazhuvettarayar—was to marry this girl as well. Madhurantakan, with great pride, declared that he would be the next emperor. If she married Madhurantakan, Manimekalai would shine as empress of the three worlds, he said, and the child born of her womb might one day inherit the empire. Her parents, too, agreed to all this.

But Manimekalai did not like any of this talk. Her heart, having heard so much about Vandiyathevan, had become attached to him. Not only that, she knew that Madhurantakan was a man without valor, one who had never even seen a battlefield, who until yesterday had smeared his body with sacred ash, worn rudraksha beads, and declared his intention to become a saint. As if that were not enough, he was already married. The women of the Thanjavur palace were extremely arrogant; thinking themselves the only ones with true refinement, they looked down upon women from other regions. Thinking of all this, Manimekalai was filled with irritation. Whether it was the throne of Thanjavur or even the throne of Indra in the heavens, she insisted that she could never marry Madhurantakan.

Later, when another piece of news came to light, her resolve only strengthened. When the elder Pazhuvettarayar came to Kadambur, it was said that the young queen Nandini had come with him. But she did not enter the women's quarters, nor did she meet the women of the Kadambur palace. At first, this caused surprise. The palace women spoke of it mockingly and with scorn. Slowly, the truth began to emerge. It was learned that the young queen had not come in the closed palanquin; it was Madhurantakan who had come. Manimekalai's disgust grew even greater. “Ugh! Am I to accept as my husband a man who, out of fear, comes disguised as a woman in a closed palanquin? Never, not for a single day!” Manimekalai resolved.

At the very time Madhurantakan came to the palace in the closed palanquin, Kandamaran’s friend Vandiyathevan also arrived. He was in the women’s quarters only for a short while. At that moment, an overwhelming shyness seized Manimekalai from somewhere. She stood behind the other women. She could not look directly, face to face, at Vandiyathevan. Yet, from behind the others, she caught a half-glimpse of his weary, smiling face, and it became etched in her heart. His voice, and a few words he spoke, remained fixed in her memory.

Thus, once again, Manimekalai began an endless debate with her brother Kandanmaran. Even if Lord Shiva himself, the three-eyed god, were to come and command her, she declared, she could never marry Madurantakan. Though she had only seen Vandiyathevan for a brief moment, she made it clear that her heart had already gone to him.

This roused an immeasurable anger in Kandanmaran. At first, he tried to persuade her with kind words, but it was of no use. Then he said, “Vandiyathevan is not my friend; he is my mortal enemy. He tried to stab me in the back and kill me. If you intend to marry him, I will kill both you and him together!” He showed her the knife wound on his back, and told her how he had survived only through the devoted care of the younger queen of Pazhuvoor.
“If you have even a grain of trust in me, forget Vandiyathevan!” he demanded.

After hearing this, Manimekalai’s mind truly changed. She was very fond of Kandanmaran. To marry the enemy who had tried to kill her own brother was indeed impossible. So she tried to forget Vandiyathevan. Yet, it was not an easy task. Again and again, at unexpected moments, his smiling face would appear before her mind’s eye. He came to her in her daydreams, he came to her in her dreams at night!

Because of all this, for several months, Manimekalai had lost her natural cheerfulness. Sorrow and weariness weighed her down. The elders thought it was because she had reached the age of marriage. Her friends teased her about it. Her companions tried to cheer her up with playful games, but nothing worked.

But in the last few days, Manimekalai had begun to regain a little of her old spirit. She felt some relief when she learned that her parents and her brother Kandanmaran had abandoned the idea of marrying her to Madurantakan. She overheard them speaking, half in jest, about giving Manimekalai in marriage to Aditya Karikalan, the emperor’s eldest son and the crowned prince.

There was no one in all of Tamil Nadu, man or woman, who had not heard of the valor and heroic deeds of Aditya Karikalan. Everyone knew that, for some reason, he had refused to marry. To become his wife—was that not a fortune one could not even dream of? Across this vast land of Bharata, how many royal maidens were performing penance, longing for such a blessing! Thinking of all this, Manimekalai found herself once more filled with hope.

The news that Aditya Karikalan would be arriving from Kanchipuram and Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar from Thanjavur as guests to the Kadambur palace once again filled her with the old excitement. This time, the Pazhuvetaraiyar was bringing his young queen along. Nandini Devi was the one who had saved her brother’s life. Manimekalai had heard much from Kandanmaran about Nandini’s beauty, character, and intelligence. Kandanmaran had also said that it was the young queen of Pazhuvur who was the cause of these new marriage talks. He had insisted that while the queen was staying at Kadambur palace, Manimekalai must ensure she was treated with utmost hospitality. Manimekalai’s heart was mature enough for such a responsibility. She longed to befriend the queen of Pazhuvur and, by acquiring her manners, to surpass even the women of the Thanjavur palace in refinement.

Thus, for a week, Manimekalai was immersed in a single-minded enthusiasm, bustling about the palace, overseeing all arrangements for the guests. She paid particular attention to the section of the palace reserved for the young queen of Pazhuvur, ensuring every comfort was provided. Had not her brother instructed her so? Therefore, she drove the palace servants relentlessly. She even harried her own companions. In the room where the queen would stay, she insisted that every single item be moved and rearranged thirty times over.

She also frequently visited the rooms where Prince Aditya Karikalan and his companions would be staying. Someone called Parthibendran was said to be coming with him. What sort of man was he? Who could say how people might change in these times? Vandiyathevan, who had once been her brother’s friend, now belonged to Aditya Karikalan’s retinue! If only he had not turned into such a traitor to friendship, he too would have come and joined them now, wouldn’t he? Yes! No matter how much Manimekalai busied herself with other matters, she could not entirely banish the memory of that traitor from her heart.

It was said that the queen of Pazhuvur would arrive that very night. Therefore, Manimekalai was making a final inspection of Nandini’s room. At that moment, she came before the mirror that had been fixed to the wall for the queen’s use. She gazed at her own reflection for a while, calmly and steadily.
