“Oh, foolish girl! When you had already given your heart away to someone so completely, why didn’t you tell your brother about it? Why did he try to entice you with Madurantakan? Why did he make vain efforts to bring Karikalan here? Why did he summon me here unnecessarily?”
“Akka! My brother Kandanmaran does not like him…”
“How wonderful! Is your brother going to marry you off himself? But wasn’t it Kandanmaran who first told you about Vandiyathevan? Wasn’t it your brother who brought him here?”

“Yes, it was Kandanmaran who told me about him. He even brought him to the women’s quarters one day. But later, his mind changed; there was a reason for that too. In Thanjavur, he says that Vandiyathevan stabbed him with a dagger, Akka! Didn’t my brother lie wounded in your palace? Wasn’t it only because of your loving care that he survived and recovered?”
“Your brother exaggerates what I did. Let that be. Now, what will you do? The one who has captured your heart has now become your brother’s enemy!”
“But do you know what he says?”
“Who do you mean by ‘he’?”

“Him! The very person whose name you just spoke! He swears that he never stabbed Kandanmaran. He says someone else stabbed him and left him by the wall of Thanjavur fort, and that he himself found and saved him…” “He says so.”
“When did he tell you this?”
“Just yesterday…”
“Yesterday, did you see that Vandiyathevan in person? Didn’t you say you saw his very form and appearance?”

“That’s what troubles me, Akka. I don’t know whether it was truly him I saw yesterday, or just his apparition. When I think of all that happened yesterday, it all feels like a dream. Akka! Sometimes, people say that when someone dies, their spirit comes and speaks to the living—is that true?”

As Manimekalai asked this question, her voice trembled with boundless fear. Nandini’s body too shuddered; staring somewhere at the distant ceiling, she replied, “Yes, it’s true! The spirits of those who die untimely deaths wander among the living. If someone has been beheaded, sometimes only the head will appear. Sometimes, the body alone comes. And sometimes, both come separately and ask, ‘Have you avenged me?’”
Then, turning to Manimekalai, she raised her voice, “Girl! Why do you ask such questions? Are you afraid that something has happened to your beloved? Who has sown this doubt in your mind?”
“There’s a madman in this palace. I sent for him, but last night, someone beat him and sent him away. Instead, his wife, Devaratti, came—she was the one who told me!”
“Fie! Don’t believe such nonsense!”
“I too find it hard to believe. If it was only a spirit, you wouldn’t be able to touch it, right, Akka?”
“You cannot touch a spirit; nor can you touch an apparition. Why do you ask? Did you touch the one who has stolen your heart yesterday?”
“That’s what confuses me. It feels as if I did touch him; but when I think of certain other things, I begin to doubt.”
“Tell me everything that happened yesterday, in detail, girl! I will clear your doubts!”

“Let it be, Akka! If I ramble on out of order, please ask questions and find out!” said Manimekalai. Then she continued, “Yesterday, I was here at almost the same time. Just as my brother had instructed, I came to see whether the maids had provided you with every comfort you needed. For a moment, I was looking at my own face in that mirror over there!”
“You must have been admiring your own beauty…”
“Nothing of the sort, Akka! Don’t I know my own face and its features?”
“What flaw could there be in your face? Even Rathi, Indrani, Menaka, and Urvashi would be envious of you!”
“They would not be worthy to gather the dust of your feet, Akka!”
“All right, all right! Go on! You were looking at your face in the mirror…”
“Suddenly, another face appeared in the mirror; it was close to mine.”
“That must have been your lover’s face!”
“Yes; it startled me…”
“Why should that startle you? Didn’t you say you often see his face in your dreams?”
“There was a slight difference between that and this. In dreams, he appears a little distance away, facing me. Even in visions, it’s the same. But here— it feels awkward to say it…”
“No harm, speak up, you sly girl!”

“It was as if he was coming from behind to kiss my cheek. I was startled and turned around— but there was no one. Then, even in the mirror, that face was gone. I began to suspect something. You remember the secret door to the hunting hall next to this room that I showed you? Yesterday, the mirror was placed directly opposite that door. So I wondered if someone might have opened that door and peeped in from the hunting hall. But then I thought, how could that be? How could a stranger enter the hunting hall? Still, to clear my doubt, I opened the door and went into the hunting hall…”
Nandini had already begun to ask, her voice rising with excitement. “Was that thief hiding in the hunting pavilion? Did he get caught?”
“Sister, why do you call him a ‘thief’?”
“Do I mean a real thief? I spoke of the thief who stole your heart, girl! Was he in the hunting pavilion?”

“That’s the strange part! He wasn’t there. Instead, our palace servant, Idumbankari, was cleaning that room. His face looks just like the dark guardian statue at the entrance of the Ayyanar temple. I asked him, ‘Did anyone else come here?’ He insisted, ‘No, no one came…’”
“Do you think he was lying?”
“I don’t know, but it seemed to me that someone else was hiding in that pavilion. I thought, ‘Let the thief reveal himself,’ and came back to this room…”
“Did the thief reveal himself?”

“Listen! I came into this room and kept my ears open, wondering if I could hear any voices from the hunting pavilion. I did hear voices! And then, the sound of something falling with a crash. While I was thinking what to do, this door moved. I hid the lamp and waited. There’s a small round inner door in this very door. Someone tried to open it and come in. I heard a voice cry, ‘Mercy, mercy! Save me!’ The voice and the figure seemed to be his, so I helped him into this room and then lit the lamp. It was indeed him!”
“Manimekalai! What a wonder this is! Isn’t it just like the tale of Vikramaditya?”

“There’s more! For four months, I had seen him only in my dreams, and now, seeing him in person, my heart overflowed; my body trembled. But I spoke to him with feigned anger. I asked, ‘How could you sneak into the women’s quarters like a thief?’ He said that someone was chasing him, trying to kill him. I mocked him, saying, ‘Running in fear for your life, you coward!’ He tried to calm me, saying he had no weapon with him. Then I brought up how he stabbed my brother in the back. He swore it was not true, sister!”
“And you believed him, didn’t you?”
“At that moment, it all seemed believable. But when I think back on everything that happened afterward, I no longer know what to believe and what not to believe…”
“What other wonders happened after that?”

“Even as I was speaking with him, I kept one ear alert, listening for any sounds from the next room. I could hear the footsteps and voices of several people moving about. So, I thought it must be true that someone was following him, intending to kill him. Listen, Akka! At that moment, this foolish heart of mine resolved that I must somehow save him. I wanted to find out who those people were that had come to kill him. Was Idumbankari involved in all this? If so, was he on his side, or was he with those who had come to kill him? I wanted to know that as well.

The thought that so many people knew about the secret passage leading into the hunting pavilion filled me with dread. And when I remembered that you were going to stay here, my worry only grew. I thought of calling for my father, but I did not have the courage. If my father saw that he had come into the women’s quarters, his very life would be in danger. So, I told him to stay here for a while, and then, to find out who was in the hunting pavilion, I opened the door and went out.

Inside, five or six men were standing, pressed against the walls in the corners. When they saw me, they seemed stunned. Seeing them like that made me feel a little afraid as well. I tried to shake off that fear and summon up my anger, and I opened my mouth to ask who they were. Just then, my friend Chandramathi came running in through another door, calling out, ‘Amma! Amma!’ The thought that he was here struck me at once. I was afraid Chandramathi would see him and start screaming.

I decided I could look at the people in the hunting pavilion later, and turned back. Blocking Chandramathi’s way, I brought her into this room. But when I looked, he was nowhere to be seen; he had vanished as if by magic. I asked Chandramathi, ‘Did you see anyone here?’ She said she hadn’t seen anyone. I searched a little more, and then went back to the hunting pavilion. The people I had seen just a moment before were all gone. Only Idumbankari was there, cleaning the room as before.

‘Who were those people who were here just now? Where are they now?’ I asked. Idumbankari insisted, ‘No one has come here, Amma!’ I could not believe his words. And my friend Chandramathi began to tease me. ‘Akka! Today you seem to be suffering from some strange delusion! You’re seeing people in places where there’s no one at all!’ she said. Then you…” She said that everyone was approaching the fortress gate. She also mentioned that her father had immediately sent for her to come and welcome them. At once, I set out for the palace entrance. In order to reach there quickly, I walked as Chandramathi had come, crossed two steps, climbed up the machu path, and walked along the upper corridor. At that moment, I witnessed yet another marvel. That valiant warrior of the Vanar clan was crossing the moonlit courtyard, moving along the edge of the fort wall. I saw him place a bamboo pole against the wall, climb up, and leap over the ramparts. That is how it appeared to my eyes. Even now, I am not certain whether all this truly happened, or whether it was merely a figment of my imagination…”

Nandini was lost in thought. Before her mind’s eye appeared the two faces she had seen the previous evening among the dense trees, a short distance from the entrance of that mansion. She also knew that horsemen had been dispatched to capture them. Could it be that they had already been caught? If they had been caught, would they be brought here?…
“Akka! What do you think?” asked Manimekalai, interrupting Nandini’s reverie.
“What do I think? Are you asking what I think? I think you are completely possessed by a delusion,” said Nandini.
“Are you mocking me like Chandramathi?”

“I am not mocking you, dear! Even you, who saw and spoke to him directly, are unsure whether it was real, a dream, or an illusion! How can I say for certain? Is there any other secret way out of this room?”
“As far as I know, there is no other secret way, Akka!”
“Perhaps he too went the way you and Chandramathi came, and climbed up by the machu path?”
“There were many maidservants along that way, Akka! It would have been impossible to go unnoticed by them.”
“It is indeed strange… Haven’t you told your father about all this?”
“No, Akka! I feel too shy and afraid to tell my father. What if everything that happened here was true…”
“Yes, it is better not to speak of all this to men. Even if you tell them, they will not understand…”
“I am still wondering whether I should tell my brother or not…”
“If you tell him, it will certainly end in chaos. Right now, your brother is determined to somehow arrange your marriage with Karikalan!”
“Akka! You must be the one to help me. Kandamaran trusts you very much. If you speak to him, he will listen…”

“Oh, you clever girl! The very purpose for which I came here—you are asking for my help against it? You are a sly one! Even if you give up the idea of marrying Karikalan, what do you know about the other man? What certainty is there that he loves you?”
“I am not worried about that, Akka! Whether he loves me or not…”

“Such is the fate of women! No matter how men behave, women are destined to give up their very lives for them! Well, let us see how your fortune unfolds. If anything happens again like yesterday, you will tell me, won’t you?”
“To whom else can I speak if not to you, Akka! Last night I had a dream—I wish to tell you about that too…”
“As if your daydreams were not enough, you had another dream at night? What was it? Did he come again in your dream and deceive you before leaving?”
“No, no! This is something else. It frightens me even to think of it. They say a dream seen at dawn will come true—is that real, Akka?”
“Tell me your dream, let me hear it! If it is something else… did you dream of someone else?”

“It was about him! It seemed as if someone was coming to stab him with a knife. He had no weapon in his hand. But on the ground, a knife lay gleaming. I leapt forward, seized it, and rushed ahead with the thought that I must strike first the one who was coming to stab him. As I drew near, I saw the attacker’s face. It was my brother Kandamaran!… ‘Oh!’” I woke up with a cry. My whole body was drenched and dripping with sweat. For a long time, my hands and legs kept trembling. The dream had felt so real. “Will it come true, Akka?”

“Oh, silly girl! Your mind is truly muddled. What really happened seems like an illusion to you, and what you saw in your dream feels real! What a wonderful friend I have found! If I am mad, then you have gone a step beyond me!” said Nandini.
At that moment, Chandramathi entered. “They are coming! They have crossed the Veeranarayana Lake!” she announced.

chapters.title: Royal Homage
paragraphs: That evening, the front entrance of Kadambur Sambuvaraiyar’s palace witnessed a spectacle of wonders never before seen. As far as the eye could see, crowds upon crowds of people pressed together in a dense throng. Men and women, boys and girls, the elderly and the young—every age and kind were present in that gathering.

Old men and women, unable to stand firmly on their own, leaned on their staffs for support. Unmindful of being jostled and pushed by others, they swayed and struggled, driven only by their eagerness to behold the heroic visage of Aditya Karikalan. Children, heedless of being squeezed in the midst of the crowd, pushed and shoved, striving to reach the front. Young women, casting aside their natural shyness, struggled and fought their way forward through the mass of unfamiliar men, determined to catch a glimpse of the prince.

The young men, for their part, paid not the slightest attention to these maidens, not even sparing them a sidelong glance. Their sole concern was to secure a vantage point from which they could clearly see the prince. Many of them had climbed up the trees that lined the palace’s front and sides. Still others tried to scale the outer walls of the palace, only to be pulled down and pushed away by the palace guards.

Young mothers, with green infants perched on their hips, endured many hardships in that crowd, yet remained steadfast. When their children cried, the mothers soothed them, saying, “My dear! Don’t cry! The greatest of all heroes in valiant Tamilakam, the one who slew Veerapandiyan—Aditya Karikala Chozhar—is about to arrive! If you are blessed to see him, one day you too will become a hero like him!” In this manner, lovers spoke to their beloveds, mothers to their children, all speaking of Aditya Karikalan.

Thus, the heroic fame of Aditya Karikalan had spread far and wide throughout the land in those days. Who could remain indifferent to seeing the prince who, at the age of twelve, had entered the battlefield, sword in hand, and felled many foes; who, at the battle of Sevur, had routed the Pandya army, forcing Veerapandiyan to flee into the desert and hide in a rocky cave; who, at nineteen, had shattered the Pandya rescue force, tracked down Veerapandiyan’s hiding place, and returned with his severed head? Who would not yearn to see such a prince?

For the past three or four years, countless rumors had circulated about this heroic prince. Some said that after Aditya Karikalan’s coronation as Crown Prince, a rift had arisen between Sundara Chola the Emperor and his son, and that the Emperor did not wish for Aditya Karikalan to ascend the throne after him. Others claimed that, just as once in the past a Pallava prince had established an independent kingdom in Kanchi and founded the great Pallava dynasty, so too did Aditya Karikalan desire to establish a separate rule in Kanchi. Some said that the Emperor showed more affection and partiality towards his younger son, Arulmozhi Varman, and that this was the cause of Aditya Karikalan’s anger. Yet others denied all this outright, insisting that never had there been such loving and loyal brothers as Karikalan and Arulmozhi. Many spoke in various ways about the fact that the prince was still unmarried. Some said that Karikalan had refused to marry any princess of royal blood, and that his intention to wed the daughter of a temple priest and place her upon the throne was the true reason for the estrangement between father and son. Some whispered that Aditya Karikalan suffered from delusions, that sorcerers from the Pandya country had bewitched him with their black magic, and that this was why the minor kings did not wish for him to ascend the Chola throne after the Emperor.

Whatever the truth, the people’s eagerness to see that great warrior knew no bounds. From the moment the news spread that Prince Karikalan was to visit the Kadambur palace, a great excitement swept through the surrounding regions. Once it became known that he would arrive that very evening, people from every village within a radius of several miles had gathered there. To call that crowd a human ocean would not have been an exaggeration. The voices rising from the thousands upon thousands of people merged into an indistinct roar, like the tumult of the sea. In front of the palace gates, the royal guards stood ready, clearing a path for the arrival of the prince and his retinue. When the crowd pressed forward and those at the front were pushed aside, blocking the way, the guards would push them back, and they would retreat—just as the waves surge against the shore and then recede.
Suddenly, a man perched atop a tree shouted, “There they come!”

“Where? Where?” cried a thousand voices. A horse came galloping at great speed. Without the slightest regard for the crowd, it plunged straight through. The people pressed tightly to either side, making way so as not to be trampled under the horse’s hooves.
“It’s Ilanjambuvanarayan!” someone shouted.

Yes, the newcomer was— It was Kandhamaaran! Without answering the questions hurled at him by those in the crowd, Kandhamaaran swiftly urged his horse forward, stopped it near the fortress gate, and leapt down. He bowed respectfully to the Sambuvrayars and the Pazhuvettarayars who stood there.

“The prince is coming; but his mind is not in a calm state. He is seized by sudden fits of anger. I came ahead to warn you. We must receive him with all due royal honors. Whatever rash words he may utter, it is best not to respond!” he said. Having spoken thus, he did not linger there but looked up intently. From the upper storey atop the gateway tower, he could see the palace women waiting. Without delay, he entered through the fortress gate and, taking the side staircase, ascended to the upper floor.

Upon reaching the women’s quarters, Kandhamaaran’s eyes, disregarding all others, sought out and found the place where Nandini Devi sat. Approaching her, he said, “Devi! I have fulfilled your wish. I have brought the prince; there, he is on his way. But he is like a maddened elephant. I do not know how we are going to manage him!”
“Sir! Why worry about that? To subdue and control a maddened elephant, your sister’s two eyes are like twin goads!” replied Nandini.
Manimekalai exclaimed, “Akka! What kind of talk is this!”
Kandhamaaran said, “Manimekalai! There is nothing wrong in what the Queen of Pazhuvoor says! Shouldn’t one perform penance to win as husband a hero among heroes like Aditya Karikalan?”
Before Manimekalai could reply, Nandini interjected, “Sir! Is anyone else coming with the prince?”
“Yes, yes! Parthibendra Pallavan and Vandiyathevan are coming with him...”
Nandini looked particularly at Manimekalai and asked, “Which Vandiyathevan? The one you called your friend—is it he?”

“Yes, the very same bosom friend who tried to stab me from behind. He came from somewhere, somehow, and joined us on the banks of the river. Only for the prince’s sake did I tolerate him; otherwise, I would have made him food for my dagger right there!” he said.
Manimekalai’s face shrank and her brows knit together. “Anna! If it is true that he stabbed you in the back, why should you allow him to enter this palace?” she asked.
“My dear! You keep quiet! All that is men’s business. Yesterday they’ll quarrel and fight; today they’ll embrace and roll together!” said Nandini.

Kandhamaaran smiled and replied, “Nothing of that sort has happened. We must look at the prince’s face and see. Oh! You’ve brought baskets and baskets of flowers and kept them here! The shower of blossoms you pour from here will surely cool the prince’s anger and bring him peace! Look, they have arrived! I shall go down!” Saying this, he hurriedly descended the wooden steps.

From the upper verandah of the front entrance, as far as the eye could see, amidst the vast sea of people, a swirling eddy was forming at one spot, much like a whirlpool in water stirred by a gust of wind. At the center of that swirl, like a boat caught in the current, three horses and the warriors mounted upon them would appear now and then. The next moment, they would be hidden by the surging waves of the human sea. That eddy kept advancing, drawing ever closer to the front entrance of the fortress. At last, it reached the very gates.

Upon the three horses that reached the fortress gates sat Aditya Karikalan, Parthibendran, and Vandiyathevan. The elephants, horses, and the rest of the retinue following them had been halted far behind, blocked by the immense crowd. The horses halted at the palace entrance, and a great uproar arose. The blare of twenty drums, two hundred conches, three hundred trumpets, and five hundred cymbals burst forth; the thunderous sound of that welcome, rising from all those instruments, subdued even the mighty roar of the crowd. The music resounded for a while, then suddenly ceased.
In the silence that followed, the herald, standing on a platform next to the upper verandah, cried out in a voice like thunder:

“Born in the Solar Dynasty, descendant of Manu, in whose line the great king Sibi, who gave his own flesh for a dove, was born; after Sibi came Raja Kesari, his son Parakesari, the just Manu Needhi Cholan, who sacrificed his own son to uphold justice for a cow; Karikala Peruvazhuthan, who stamped the tiger emblem upon the Himalayas; Nalangilli, Nedungkilli, Perunarkilli who died at Kulamuttram, Killivalavan who died at Kurappalli, Killi Valavan who built seventy-two Shiva temples, the great Chola king Koperun Cholan, in whose line came the valiant Vijayalaya Cholan of Pazhaiyarai, who bore ninety-six wounds; his son Aditya Cholan, who built eighty-two Shiva temples along the banks of the Kaveri from Sasyamalai to Puhar; his son Parantaka Chola Chakravarthi, who conquered Madurai and Eelam and built the golden hall at Chidambaram; his son, the conqueror of the twin regions of the Kannara…” Having vanquished the enemy armies and fallen at Aattrur as the bravest among warriors, Arinjaya Thevar— His son, who rules from Eelam to Sittpuli Nadu beneath a single royal umbrella, the lord of Pazhaiyaarai, Parantaka Sundara Chozha Chakravarthi— His eldest prince, the noble scion, lord of the northern lands, Yuvaraja Chakravarthi, the conqueror of the Pandya chief Veerapandiyan—Aditya Karikalan Chozha, has arrived victorious! Baraak! Baraak!” As the herald finished his proclamation, it was as though the storm had ceased, the thunder and rain subsiding into silence.

Immediately, another herald standing nearby cried out, “The lord of Kolli Hills, the mighty archer who with a single shaft felled lion, bear, deer, and boar alike—Valvil Ori— From his lineage, generation upon generation, has arisen the king of kings, the majestic, valorous, and awe-inspiring Sambuvaraiyan— Eternal ally of the Chozha dynasty, guardian of the heroic Narayana Lake, commander of five thousand valiant warriors— He welcomes, with heart and soul, the noble prince Aditya Karikalan Chozha to grace his humble palace! May the arrival of the scion of the Chozha line be an auspicious one!”

When he finished his thunderous proclamation, a shower of flowers rained down from the upper balcony. Aditya Karikalan and Vandiyathevan looked up in astonishment. Amidst the many beautiful faces of the women gathered there, Vandiyathevan saw only the face of Manimekalai, radiant with a blossoming smile. Vandiyathevan, too, smiled for a brief moment. At once, as though realizing the impropriety of his action, he turned his gaze away.

At that very instant, the sternness on Aditya Karikalan’s face grew even sharper as he looked upward; he leapt down from his horse. The other two also dismounted. By then, the blare of trumpets and drums had begun anew. The tumultuous roar of the crowd, which had briefly subsided, now surged forth again. The guests and those assembled to welcome them entered through the fortress gates. Immediately, the doors of the fortress were shut with a resounding clang—padar, padar.

Aditya Karikalan turned and asked, “Why are the gates being shut in such haste? Are they planning to imprison me here as they have my father in Tanjore fort? What will become of the retinues that accompanied me?”
The two elders stood stunned for a few moments.

Pazhuvettaraiyar was the first to recover and replied, “Prince! The hearts of the countless millions in this Chozha empire, filled with love, have imprisoned both you and your father; to imprison you alone—” “For what purpose?” he asked.

“Sire! If the great crowd of people who have come for your darshan were to enter this small hut, what would happen? While they stand outside, the groves nearby have already become like a honey grove ravaged by monkeys. Once the crowd disperses, we shall bring in the attendants who have come with you. Until then, there are enough servants here to attend to your needs…” said Sambuvaraiyar.
At that moment, the noise of the crowd outside the fort gate seemed to grow louder. Karikalan turned to Kandhamaaran and asked, “Where is the way to the upper terrace from the front entrance?”
Kandhamaaran pointed out the place where the staircase was, and Karikalan strode briskly in that direction. Kandhamaaran, Vandiyathevan, and Parthibendran followed him.

Sambuvaraiyar turned to Pazhuvetaraiyar and said, “What is this? Have we bought a madman off the street as if we were buying a slave? I’m not sure his mind is sound. We have involved ourselves in this affair, listening to the words of these youngsters!”
“What great harm can come of it? If the matter is to happen, let it happen; if not, let it be,” said Pazhuvetaraiyar.

“I am not speaking of the affair itself. While he is in our house, nothing untoward should occur, should it? The omens are not right. He is like a crazed elephant. Did you not see the sharpness in his face and the venom on his tongue?”

“We must grit our teeth and be patient for a few days. That Pallava, Parthibendran, will help keep him in check. But there is another mischievous youth who has come along—I do not like him. I even suspect he is a spy. Was he not here the other day when we held the gathering? Was it not he whom I saw yesterday evening, standing outside the fort, hidden behind a tree?”
“Is he not my son’s friend? Therefore, I have no fear about him. But why are they now hurrying to the women’s quarters? Shall we go as well?”

At this moment, Parthibendran, who had gone as far as the fish-shaped gate, returned and approached the place where the two great minor kings were conversing. The last words spoken by Sambuvaraiyar fell upon his ears.
“My lord! Whatever other doubts you may have regarding the prince, you need not harbor any suspicion when it comes to women. He does not even cast his eyes upon them,” he said.
With a smile, Pazhuvettaraiyar replied, “If that is so, how will the purpose for which we have summoned him here be fulfilled?”
“That depends on the fortune of Sambuvaraiyar’s daughter and the fate of the Chola Empire,” was the answer.

“Parthibendra! Let Manimekalai’s fortune rest on one side! But tell me, why does the prince approach with such a stern and troubled face? Why does he speak so harshly? It seems to me that it would suffice if you could somehow pacify him and take him away from here peacefully,” said Sambuvaraiyar.

“Until we reached the banks of the Vellaru, the prince was cheerful and in high spirits. Then this Vandiyathevan and a certain Vaishnavite joined us. They must have said something. Since then, the prince’s mood has changed…”
“We too thought as much. What can we do now? That troublesome youth has come along with you, hasn’t he?”
“Please be patient; I have arranged everything. I too have a score to settle with that fellow. I shall find the right time and deal with it,” said Parthibendran.
When Karikalan and the other two ascended to the upper verandah at the main entrance, the women there were just turning to descend the steps.

Karikalan looked at Kandanmaran and said, “My friend! Is it right to make these ladies wait here for our sake? That is a grave mistake. Should we not go to where they are and pay our respects?” So saying, he bowed to the women and stepped aside to let them pass. As each one descended, he asked Kandanmaran who they were and learned their names. When he saw Nandini, he exclaimed, “Oh! Is this not the younger mistress of Pazhuvur? Have they truly come? I am most delighted!” Nandini passed by him without a word, her sharp gaze fixed upon him. The intensity of that look made Karikalan’s body tremble slightly. In the next moment, he composed himself and, turning to Manimekalai who followed behind… He looked and said, “Ah! This must be your younger sister, Manimekalai. She looks like a celestial maiden painted in a divine portrait. We must soon find her a worthy bridegroom and arrange her marriage!”
Manimekalai, her cheeks flushed with shyness, glanced at Vandiyathevan from the corner of her eye and hurriedly descended the stairs.

After all the women had left, Karikalan went to the front of the upper balcony and stood there. At the gates, the crowd that had just begun to disperse erupted once more in a great uproar. The people turned and began to approach the entrance of the fort once again.

Karikalan noticed the herald standing alone on a platform that jutted out from the upper floor. He signaled for him to come closer. When the herald approached, Karikalan instructed him to announce a few matters to the assembled crowd.

The herald turned, blew the conch several times, and then, with a gesture, requested the people to remain silent. After repeating some of Aditya Karikalan’s titles and omitting a few, he proclaimed, “This illustrious prince of the Chola dynasty will reside in the Kadambur palace for a week or ten days. He will visit all the surrounding villages. During those visits, he will meet the people of each village in person, listen to their grievances, and understand their needs!”

That was enough! The cheers that had arisen so far from the crowd were now drowned by a thunderous roar, so loud that it seemed to silence all previous noise. Jubilant voices, cries of praise, and the sound of applause mingled and rose, spreading far and wide, so that even the roar of the water rushing from the Veera Narayana lake through the seventy-four sluices seemed to be subdued.

Sambuvarayar, Pazhuvetarayar, Parthibendran, and the others remained standing where they were. As Aditya Karikalan approached them, he said, “Parthibendra! Why are you still standing here? Have you begun to conspire with these elders?”
The two elders looked startled and turned to Karikalan’s face. A smile was playing upon his lips.

Sambuvarayar recovered himself and said, “Prince! Just now you speak of prison; now you speak of conspiracy. I assure you, as long as you are a guest in this humble abode, not a hair on your head will be harmed. Before any such thing could happen, the life would have left my body!”

“Sir! Did you think I was afraid that some harm would befall me? Even when I was surrounded by a hundred thousand enemies in Pandya country, I did not fear for my safety. Why then should I be afraid when I am among my dear friends? But, please, do not call this palace of yours a mere hut; ah! Look at the height of these surrounding fortress walls! How thick and strong they are! Are they not even greater than the ramparts of the Thanjavur fort? Against which enemies have you built such formidable fortifications?” asked Karikalan.
“Prince! We have no enemies of our own. The enemies of the Chola dynasty are our enemies; the friends of the Chola dynasty are our friends as well.”

“Your assurance gives me great happiness. Please convey this to your son Kandanmaran. My friend, the prince of the Vanar clan, is being considered an enemy by Kandanmaran. Is this not a grave mistake?” said Aditya Karikalan. At these words, Kandanmaran bowed his head in shame.

chapters.title: “The Worry of Malayaman”
paragraphs: In the moonlit courtyard between the palace and the fortress wall, guided by Kandanmaran, Karikalan walked, glancing all around as he went. The other four followed close behind.
When they reached the spot where a stage and pavilion had been set up for the Kuravai dance, Karikalan halted.
“Oh! What is this? What is about to happen here?” he asked.
“Prince! If it pleases you, we thought to have a Kuravai dance performed here…”

“Ah! Excellent! Arrange for the Kuravai dance; arrange for the Villu Paatu as well. Stage the play of Karikal Valavan, the play of Vijayalaya Chozhar—stage them all! We shall spend our days hunting in the forests, and our nights in song and dance.

Sambuvaraiyar! Do you know what my grandfather Malayaman told me before I left? He warned me, ‘Do not sleep at night while you are in the palace of Kadambur Sambuvaraiyar!’ Do you know what I replied to my grandfather? ‘Grandfather! I do not sleep by day; nor do I sleep by night. It has been three years since I last slept. Therefore, you need not fear that my enemies will harm me while I sleep. Only if someone dares to harm me while I am awake, can they do so. Is there any man bold enough for that?’ Thus, I gave courage to Malayaman before I left!” Karikalan finished, and laughed aloud, his laughter ringing out.
Sambuvaraiyar, his voice trembling with anger, said, “Sir! Whether you sleep or stay awake… no one would dare to harm you while you are in this palace!”

“Yes, yes! Who could possibly harm me within the palace of Kadambur Sambuvaraiyar? Or who could cross these massive fortress walls from outside? Not even Yama himself could enter. Would not even Yama fear Kadambur Sambuvaraiyar? I told you about that old man of Thirukovalur and his needless worries. Is it not just old age? For some, courage wanes as the years advance. But look at my Pazhuvur grandfather! See how briskly he walks! Could anyone believe he is past sixty?” Karikalan said, with a slight, mocking smile. Pazhuvetaraiyar, thinking that he must give some reply to this, cleared his throat. The sound echoed like a lion’s roar.

“Behold! How true it is when people say, ‘If the great Pazhuvetaraiyar clears his throat, the whole world trembles!’ Kandhamaaran! Vandiyathevan! Parthibendran! Think for a moment—will you all be as sturdy as the old lord of Pazhuvur when you reach his age? Perhaps you may clear your throats like him, but at his age, you will not bring a new bride into the women’s quarters! Grandfather! It seems you have brought the young queen along with you! I saw her on the front verandah balcony! How did the young queen travel? In a closed palanquin? In a chariot? Or in a cart?”
Pazhuvetaraiyar interrupted at that moment and said with pride, “I brought her on an elephant, seated in a howdah, for all the towns and villages to see!”

“That is how it should be done, grandfather! Always do it so from now on! Never bring her in a closed palanquin. That only gives rise to all sorts of tasteless rumors. Listen to this amusing tale: it is said that sometimes my uncle, Madurantakan, secretly climbs into the young queen’s closed palanquin and travels from town to town! Such a rumor has spread throughout the land!” Karikalan said, and laughed thunderously.
But none of the others present laughed. In each of their hearts, a different kind of turmoil arose.
Vandiyathevan thought to himself, “Alas! What a grave mistake I have made! I have told everything to this madman! It seems he will reveal everything openly, without holding anything back!”

Within the heart of the great Pazhuvetaraiyar, fire and smoke swirled and boiled like the depths of a volcano. He cleared his throat again, like the terrifying rumble that comes before fire and smoke burst forth from a volcanic mouth.

Before he could speak, Parthibendran stepped forward and said, “Prince! I have only known the young queen of Pazhuvur for a short time. Even in that brief period, I have come to know what a goddess of chastity she is. If anyone dares to utter a slander against the queen of Pazhuvur, I will make him fall to my sword that very instant! This is my vow!”
Kandhamaaran took a step back and said, “There is no need for me to draw my dagger; if anyone slanders the Young Queen of Pazhuvoor, I will strangle him with my bare hands—this I swear!”
Hearing this, Vandiyathevan stepped forward and declared, “So will I! If anyone speaks ill of the Lady of Pazhuvoor, I will burn him to ashes with my very gaze!”

“Ahahaha! Hold on, friends! It seems you are about to start a fight with me! Did you see, grandfather? How fiercely these men are ready to defend the honor of Tamil womanhood! But no one has uttered a slander against the Young Queen of Pazhuvoor. If anyone did, I would not stand by and listen in silence. Before these mighty warriors could arrive, I would not leave such a slanderer alive! The complaints are only about the closed palanquin of the Lady of Pazhuvoor! They say that the cowardly Madurantakan travels from town to town in secret, hidden within the Lady’s closed palanquin! When a grown man journeys with curtains drawn on either side of a palanquin, and if the Young Queen herself travels in such a manner, will it not lead to certain calamities?”
“Prince! Why should Madurantaka Devar, grandson of Paranthaka Chakravarti and son of Kandaraditya, travel in a closed palanquin? I do not understand at all,” said Parthibendra Pallavan.
“The reason is an amusing one! They say Madurantakan goes from town to town in a closed palanquin, gathering support for his cause!”
“For what purpose is he gathering support?”

“For what, you ask? So that after my father, he may ascend the Chola throne! How do you like that tale? A few months ago, they say he even came to this very Kadambur palace in secret, traveling in a closed palanquin. In the dead of night, a secret council was held here. Parthibendra! Was it not the Elder of Thirukovalur who told us all this when you were with me? Did he not say that, driven by his eagerness to ascend the throne, Madurantakan might even hasten my father’s journey to heaven? Do you not remember all that?”
“I do remember, Prince! Even then, I did not believe it; and now, I do not believe it in the least. After going to Thanjavur and meeting your father in person…”

“What about you alone? Even I did not believe it. If I had believed, would I have come as a guest to this Kadambur palace?” said Karikalan, and once more he laughed, as if recalling some private thought.
Kadambur Sambuvaraiyar cleared his throat and said, “Prince! You know well that there has been a long-standing enmity between the clan of Thirukovalur Malayaman and our own!”

“How could I not know? Haven’t the poets of the Sangam age sung about that feud? In the battle, Malayaman Thirumudikkari killed Kolli Malai Valvil Ori. Since you are descended from Valvil Ori’s line, you still nurture that old enmity…”

“Prince! The blood feud for Valvil Ori’s death was avenged at once. Adhiyaman Neduman Anji, who was Valvil Ori’s kinsman, marched his army against Thirukovalur, destroyed that town, and razed Malayaman’s fortress on Mullur hill to the ground…”

“Sambuvaraiyar! Adhiyaman did not accomplish all that alone. It was only with the help of my ancestor, Cholan Killi Valavan, that Adhiyaman triumphed over Malayaman. But what is the point of recalling those ancient tales now?”
“Even if we forget, Malayaman does not. He keeps finding fault with us for something or other…”
“Didn’t I tell you? The old man has grown aged. His mind is faltering. Sometimes I even worry that he might gather a great army and come here, just to ensure that no harm befalls me while I am here…”
“Prince! If you have any such doubts…” Sambuvaraiyar faltered.

“Doubts? I have none at all. Our ties with Malayaman go back only two generations. But our bond with the Pazhuvettaraiyars has lasted six generations. The lord of Pazhuvur himself is here. Would I be mad to think he would ever act against the Chola clan?” said Karikalan, and laughed with a madman’s mirth.
Pazhuvettaraiyar, in a deep and dignified voice, said, “Prince! I will never do anything against the Chola clan—this I swear. Nor will I ever act against dharma or justice—this I swear doubly.”

“Yes, yes! There is indeed such a thing as dharma and justice. I have come here precisely to speak with you and learn more about it. When the hours for hunting and for watching performances have passed, perhaps we can spend a little time discussing matters of dharma and justice as well! Sambhuvarayar, in this magnificent palace, what arrangements have you made for myself and my companions to stay?” asked Karikalan.

“My lord! For you and the Lord of Pazhuvur, we have reserved the entire guest wing at the rear of the palace. As for the other minor kings who may arrive, I will keep them with me in the front quarters…”
“Oh! Are more minor kings expected to arrive?”
“Yes, Prince! All the local chieftains from the surrounding regions are eager to meet you here. Many of them will surely come.”

“Let them come, let them all come! That is very good. We can finally settle the matters that require careful thought and decision. Let Madurantakan’s conspiracies remain on one side for now. I myself wish to join you in plotting a conspiracy! And there could be no place more fitting for it than this palace!” said Karikalan.

chapters.title: Poonguzhali’s Desire
paragraphs: From Nagapattinam to Kodikkarai, Poonguzhali’s boat glided along the canal. With her in the boat was Sendhan Amudhan. The boat was drawing near to Kodikkarai. On the banks of the canal, golden screw-pine flowers spread their petals wide, filling the air everywhere with their fragrance. Upon one of those flowers, a green parrot flew down and perched. As it settled, the screw-pine blossom swayed as if it were on a swing, and the parrot swayed along with it. Then, with its coral-red beak, the parrot pecked at the golden petal.
As the boat approached, the parrot screeched “kikki, kikki!” and flew away.
“If I am to be born again, let it be as a green parrot!” said Poonguzhali.
“You wish for such a thing! Who knows how much sorrow and hardship it faces?” said Sendhan Amudhan.
“No matter what sorrow or hardship there may be, isn’t it free to fly as it pleases in the boundless sky? What greater joy could there be than that?” said Poonguzhali.
“But some people catch those wandering parrots and shut them up in cages!” said Sendhan Amudhan.

“Yes, yes! Princesses living in palaces lock green parrots in cages! Cruel ogresses! They imprison the parrots and then dote on them and play with them. If I were a maid in one of those palaces, I would poison the caged parrots and kill them. I would even give poison to the princesses who cage the parrots…”
“If anyone heard you now, they would call you a cruel ogress too!”
“Let them say so! I would rather be an ogress than a princess.”

“Why do you bear such anger towards princesses, Poonguzhali? If you think about it, shouldn’t we pity them too? Like the caged parrots, they too are shut up within palace walls, spending their days in captivity.” If they somehow managed to escape and step outside, what a multitude of guards! What secrecy! What vigilance! Could they, like you, climb into a boat and wander alone through streams and seas? Could they roam the forests as freely as a deer leaping at its whim?”
“Who is asking them to stay confined? Did I ever say so? If they wished, couldn’t they too wander the forests at their will?”

“Mere desire is not enough; it depends on one’s birth and upbringing. You, like a parrot, wish to soar in the sky—do you think that is possible? You were born and raised by the seashore. That is why you are able to live so independently. Those born and raised in palaces cannot do so. Listen to another strange thing. Some parrots, after being caged and fed by the hands of princesses, even if the cage is opened later, do not wish to fly away. They flutter a short distance, circle around, screech ‘kreech, kreech,’ and return to the cage. I have seen this myself in the palaces of Thanjai and Pazhaiyarai…”
“I would never consent to be caged, not for a single day. If I were a parrot, I tell you, I would bite the hand of the princess who tried to feed me through the bars…”
“You would not wish to be a caged parrot. Nor would you wish to be a princess confined within a palace, would you?”
“Never! Rather than that, I would choose to die by poison!”
“That is right; in that case, you should not wish to marry a prince who lives in a palace, should you?”

In the lower sky, dark clouds had gathered. Now and then, lightning flashed, illuminating the heavens. The distant rumble of thunder could be faintly heard. As Sendhan Amudhan finished speaking, flashes of lightning seemed to dart from Poonguzhali’s eyes as well.
“Who told you that I wish to marry a prince?” she asked angrily.
“No one told me; I said it myself. If you have no such desire in your heart, then it is well. Forget what I said!” replied Sendhan Amudhan.

For a while, silence reigned in that boat. Only the sound of Sendhan Amudhan’s oar pushing the boat, the croaking of dry frogs, the cries of sea birds, the roar of the ocean waves, and, from time to time, the distant rumble of thunder from the southern skies could be heard.

Sendhan Amudhan cleared his throat, steeled his heart, and said, “Poonguzhali! You said that Vandiyathevan revealed my innermost feelings to you, did you not? It would be good if you shared your thoughts about that. Look, the beacon of Kodikkarai’s shore is already visible. Soon, I may not get another chance to speak with you alone. Tomorrow, I too must depart. It has been many days since I left my mother alone in Thanjai!”
“Why should Vandiyathevan go as a messenger for you? Do you not have a tongue of your own? I will ask what I wish to know directly!” said Poonguzhali.
“Very well! I will ask: Will you marry me?” asked Sendhan Amudhan.
“For what reason do you ask me to marry you?” asked Poonguzhali.
“Because I have a deep, secret longing for you; that is why!”
“If you have a secret longing, must it be resolved only through marriage?”
“Not necessarily; but that is how the world usually resolves such things…”
“If I marry you, what will you give me? Can you provide the palace life I desire, with fine clothes and jewels, elephants and horses, palanquins and maidservants?”

“I cannot; but I can give you a life of peace, greater than all those things. Listen, Poonguzhali! My hut stands in the midst of a beautiful flower garden on the outskirts of Thanjai. Only my mother and I live there. If you come to live with us, your life will be transformed. My mother will cherish you with love, support you, and protect you. At dawn, we will rise and together weave the flowers that sway on the creepers and trees around our home into garlands of wondrous design. I will take those garlands to the temples of Thanjai’s Thalikulathar and Durga Parameswari and offer them. Meanwhile, you can bathe in the lotus pond of our garden and help my mother with the household chores. In the evenings, the three of us will carry water from the lotus pond to water the flower plants. And as dusk falls, I will teach you the sweetest divine Tamil hymns, more delicious than nectar.”

If you were to sing those songs in your sweet voice, your tongue would taste honeyed from singing them, and my ears would be delighted from hearing them. If we wished, we could go to the temples, have darshan of the Lord, sing those divine hymns, and return. The devotees who come to the temple would also rejoice to hear them. Poonguzhali! What life could be sweeter or more joyful than this? Think about it and tell me!” Thus spoke Sendhan Amudhan.
Poonguzhali listened to all that he said and burst into laughter, her voice ringing like silver bells.

“Amudha! You have spoken of the life you consider sweet! But do you know what kind of life I desire? I long to ascend to the heavens and marry Indra, the king of the gods. I wish to ride with Indra upon Airavata, journeying amidst the cloud realms in the sky. I yearn to seize the thunderbolt from Indra’s hand and hurl it upon the masses of clouds. When struck by the thunderbolt, I want to see a thousand, ten thousand lightning bolts burst forth from those dark clouds, splitting the sky into a hundred threads.

Now, whenever thunder falls from the sky, it strikes somewhere in the sea or the forest, does it not? I would not waste the thunder so. I would cast it upon the palaces where kings and queens, princes and princesses dwell, and watch with delight as those palaces crumble and fall to dust. If, by chance, Indra is unwilling to marry me, I will go to Vayu, the god of wind. Even if he already has many wives, I will tell him there is no harm in marrying me too. That is all; after that, in this world, there will always be storms and whirlwinds and fierce gales raging. Great trees will be uprooted and fall upon mansions, destroying them. The wooden ships that sail the sea will be shattered to splinters by the storm winds. Those who travel in those ships will be cast into the raging sea and struggle for their lives. If there are princes and princesses among them, let them sink to the ocean’s depths for all I care; I will save only the others, if possible.
If even Vayu refuses to marry me, then I will go to Agni, the god of fire. And then, do you wish to hear what will happen? The whole world will be set ablaze and burn to ashes...!”

“Poonguzhali, enough! Stop! You are speaking all this out of some bitterness in your heart; you are not speaking with a clear mind. It was my mistake to bring up marriage talk with you without understanding your state of mind. Forgive me for that! May God himself remove the bitterness from your heart and grant you peace. For that, I will pray day and night!” he said.

Poonkuzhali, who had been sitting, suddenly stood up. She peered intently towards the side of a tree on the bank of the stream. Sendhan Amudhan too turned his gaze in that direction. Amidst the branches of the tree, the face of a woman became visible. For a moment, Sendhan Amudhan was startled, seeing in the features of the woman standing there a resemblance to his own mother. But then he realized that she was not his mother. He surmised that she must be the aunt whom Poonkuzhali had mentioned, the one who lived on the island of Bootha Theevu.
Poonkuzhali leaped from the boat, landed on the bank of the stream, and hurriedly ran towards the woman.

chapters.title: The Arrow Struck!
paragraphs: From behind a tree on the bank of the stream, half-hidden and half-exposed, Poonguzhali saw the mute queen. The unexpected sight of her, at such an unexpected place and time, startled Poonguzhali. She knew well that the mute queen did not like to see strangers. “Sendhan Amudhan is in the boat—if my aunt sees him, will she perhaps run away?” That very thought had barely crossed her mind when her aunt indeed began to run.
Poonguzhali swiftly leapt from the boat onto the bank and climbed the mound to look around. She noticed her aunt disappearing into the dense forest a little distance away.
Meanwhile, Sendhan Amudhan too jumped onto the bank, climbed the mound, and reached the spot where Poonguzhali stood.
“Poonguzhali! Poonguzhali! Who was it that stood here just now?” he asked.
“Don’t you know, Amudha?”
“I can’t say for certain! Perhaps…”
“Yes, it was my aunt! The very same aunt whom you thought was dead—your mother’s elder sister!”
“Yes; she did seem to have a little of my mother’s manner.”

“Don’t just say anything that comes to mind! There’s no resemblance in appearance between the younger and elder aunts; nor in their natures. Where is the cow that’s tied up at home, and where is the lioness who roams the wild as she pleases?”
“All right, let it be so. But why did the lioness run away as soon as she saw you?”
Poonguzhali laughed and said, “She ran away after seeing you, not me. She has no fondness for seeing strangers.”
“I am not a stranger, am I?”
“My aunt doesn’t know that, does she? If she knew, she wouldn’t run away after seeing you. But before she comes to know, she hesitates a great deal.”
“Poonguzhali! What are you going to do now?”
“I’m going to search for my aunt and bring her back.” “May I come too?”
“For what purpose?”
“To see Periyamma in person and get to know her, that’s all.”
“Why do you need to know Periyamma?”

Senthan Amudhan, having learned a little about his Periyamma’s past from Poonguzhali, was eager to see her. Along with that, he also hoped that Periyamma might help change Poonguzhali’s mind away from her current loyalties.
“There are so many reasons; but is a reason needed to want to know Periyamma?” he replied.

Poonguzhali thought for a moment and said, “Alright, come! Let’s go. If I take you along, it might be a little harder to catch Periyamma. Still, who can stop us? We can tie the boat up here and leave it!”
As she said, they tied the boat securely, hiding it beneath a thicket of screw pine, and set off together toward the Kodikkarai forest.
As they walked, Senthan Amudhan asked, “Poonguzhali! Didn’t you say Periyamma lives either on the island of Lanka or on the island of Puthu?”
“Yes, sometimes she stays in Lanka, sometimes on Puthu island.”
“Does she come here often?”
“No; she comes only rarely. If I don’t go to see her for a long time, she’ll come here.”
“Has she come now just to see you?”
“This time, it seems she has come for some other purpose.”
“What other purpose?”

“She might have come to find out whether her adopted son drowned in the sea or managed to survive and reach the shore. She would have heard that after the prince boarded the ship, a cyclone struck at sea, wouldn’t she?”
“Is Arulmozhi Varman her adopted son? Then who is Periyamma’s own son?”
“That is what I do not know. But one day—if not today, then another day—I will uncover that secret and find out.”
“Is her own son still alive, or has he passed away?”
“Yes, he might have died—who can say for sure?” said Poonguzhali.
After a brief pause, she asked, “Amudha! You have seen your aunt, haven’t you? You once said her facial expressions resembled your mother’s. Did anyone else’s face come to mind?”
“It feels as if I remember something, but it’s not clear. It’s as though a veil of clouds has hidden it from me.”
“Have you often seen the younger queen of Pazhuvoor?”

“I have seen her a few times, yes! Now that you mention it, I realize whose face it is. It’s the very likeness of Nandini Devi’s features! How strange! How could such a resemblance have come about? Poonguzhali, how did you notice that similarity?”
“I have often seen my aunt. And only a few days ago, I saw the younger queen of Pazhuvoor here on this very Kodikkarai shore. The resemblance in their faces struck me at once.”
“What could be the reason for it?”
“That too, I will find out one day. Today, when I saw my aunt, I thought of asking her about it.”
“But your aunt is mute, isn’t she? How will you speak with her?”
“Don’t you speak with your mother, Amudha?”
“I speak with her through gestures—it’s been my habit since birth. But if it is to convey something new, it is difficult!”
“My elder aunt and I also communicate through gestures. If there is something we cannot express with gestures, we draw pictures to explain.”
“How hard it must be for both sisters in the same family to be born mute! How much sorrow it must have caused their parents!”

“That’s not all. When they were little, the elder and younger sisters would constantly quarrel with each other. Because of that, grandfather took only the elder aunt with him and went to live on the haunted island. Grandfather had such a deep affection for the elder aunt that—” She had cherished great desires. It seems that some astrologer had foretold she would become a queen as soon as she bore a child. That is why, when it became known that the child was mute, her sorrow was all the greater…”
Conversing thus, they entered the forest. For a long time they wandered, yet could not find the mute queen.
“Amudha! It is only because you are with me that I cannot find aunt. She hides herself deliberately when she sees you.”
“That is my fate. Nothing I wish for ever comes to pass. Shall I leave, then?”
“How will you go? I must be the one to lead you out of this forest.”

At that moment, a strange sound echoed from within the woods. It did not seem to be a human voice, nor did it resemble the call of any animal. That sound was heard two or three times. In the direction from which it came, a few deer bounded away in fright.
Poonkuzhali paused and pondered for a moment. “Amudha! Follow me silently!” she said.
The two of them walked quietly toward the direction of the sound. After a short while, they beheld a wondrous sight.

The mute queen was leaning against the base of a tree. In her hand she held a few tender shoots. Around her stood seven or eight beautiful deer, vying with one another to nibble at the shoots she offered. Upon her shoulder sat a small fawn, gazing at her face with its tiny, lovely eyes.

Beholding this rare scene, Poonkuzhali and Amudhan stood motionless for a while. It was the fawn on the queen’s shoulder that first noticed them. As soon as it saw them, it leapt down from her shoulder. The other deer, too, turned to look at the newcomers. All the deer stood poised, ready to bound away if the two approached any closer. Then the mute queen also looked at them. From her throat came another strange sound.

At that sound, all the deer sprang away and vanished into the forest. “Aunt knows only the language of animals, not that of humans,” said Poonkuzhali, making a gesture toward the mute queen as she spoke.
This time, the mute queen did not run; she looked at Poonguzhali and made a sign in response.
As Poonguzhali approached, the mute queen embraced her tightly and kissed her on the forehead.
Senthan Amudhan stood a little distance away, watching.
Aunt and niece conversed for a while in the silent language of gestures. Then, Poonguzhali beckoned Amudhan to come closer.

The mute queen examined him intently, looking him up and down several times, then placed her hand upon his head in a gesture of blessing and held it there for a moment. After that, she removed her hand from his head, took Poonguzhali by the hand, and led her away.
The three of them came to the bank of the stream. There, the mute queen sat down and signaled to Poonguzhali to go and return.
“Come, Amudha! Let’s go home. Aunt says she won’t come. We’ll have to bring her food here,” said Poonguzhali.
The two of them set off towards the lighthouse.
“Poonguzhali, what do you say to me?” Amudhan asked.

“I had thought of coming with you to Thanjai. But now, that’s not possible; aunt wants to see her beloved foster child. So, I must make another journey to Nagapattinam. If you come with me, aunt will immediately run away and hide. Then I won’t be able to learn the things I need to know from her.”
Senthan Amudhan sighed deeply. “That’s all I had hoped for, then. In that case, let me bid you farewell right now!”
“No, no! Come home, eat, and take leave from your uncle and the others before you go! Otherwise, everyone will quarrel with me!”
On the way, at another spot, they saw a man and a woman standing in the cover of a bush, speaking together.
“Aha! That looks like sister-in-law Rakkammal. Their secret conversation isn’t over yet. Who has come now? Are those the Pandya spies? Or someone else?” Poonguzhali murmured to herself.
Raakkammaal emerged from the cover of the bushes. At the sight of Poonguzhali, she started slightly, but quickly concealed her surprise and hurried towards them.
“Poonguzhali! Where have you been lost all these days? Your father and brother were terribly worried about you!” she exclaimed.
“Why should they worry? Is this the first time I’ve left home?” replied Poonguzhali.
“But this time you took your aunt’s son along with you, didn’t you? They were anxious you might both get married somewhere without telling anyone!”
“Anni! How many times have I told you not to speak such nonsense to me? If you talk like this again...?”

“No, no, girl! No! What does it matter to me if you marry your aunt’s son? Or if you marry a royal prince? Your elder aunt has come from Lanka and is searching for you. Have you seen her yet?” Raakkammaal asked.
“No, I haven’t seen her yet,” said Poonguzhali.

Before returning home, when she found a moment to speak privately with Sendhan Amudhan, she said, “Amudha! Be careful! Anni is in league with the conspirators from Pandya country. She’ll try to trick you into talking—don’t answer her questions!”
“I’ll remain mute for the little while I’m here,” replied Sendhan Amudhan.

That afternoon, Poonguzhali once again rowed her boat towards Nagapattinam. The mute queen sat enthroned in the boat. Whenever Poonguzhali was near the mute queen, she would always find peace of mind. Their hearts, attuned to the same emotions, brought each other a certain tranquility. But this time, Poonguzhali’s mind found no such peace.

Again and again, she remembered how, just a few days ago, she had carried the Prince of Ponni, unconscious, through these very waters. The thought that all her struggles had been only to unite that royal prince with another royal princess brought a sharp pang to her heart.
When she thought of how she had sent Sendhan Amudhan away, almost as if she had pushed him out with a brusque “Go to the town,” her heart was filled with regret.
Aside from these thoughts, her father, Thyaga Vidangakaraiyar’s warning kept returning to her mind throughout the day.

“My child! It would be good if you restrained your comings and goings a little. All sorts of new people are arriving here. We do not know why they come. Plots and conspiracies are afoot in the kingdom. Do not let yourself become entangled in them! Our family has always been bound in loyalty to the Chola royal house! Never forget this!” her father had said.

When she combined her father’s warning with her sister-in-law’s secretive actions, a fear that she had never known before took hold of Poonguzhali. ‘Perhaps these new people have come here searching for her? By following her, are they trying to discover the whereabouts of Ponniyin Selvan? If, through her, that secret were to be revealed, what a terrible crime it would be…’

As Poonguzhali’s mind grew more and more agitated, rustling sounds began to be heard along the wooded banks of the stream. At that moment, not a breath of wind was stirring; it was as if all eight directions had conspired together to capture and hold the wind captive. In such stillness, what could be causing the rustling in the riverside woods? For the mute queen, this disturbance meant nothing. She could not hear, so the rustling sounds did not reach her ears. Nor could Poonguzhali ask her what she thought about it.

But the mute queen possessed other heightened senses. With the help of her sixth sense, she could perceive things that could not be seen with the eye or heard with the ear. Was it not possible that she might sense a danger approaching, one that Poonguzhali herself did not know?
What was this? The queen too kept glancing anxiously at the riverbank. Was some real danger drawing near?…
The reason for the queen’s frequent glances at the riverbank soon became clear. It served to dispel Poonguzhali’s anxiety.

At one spot, five or six deer, half-hidden among the riverbank thickets, stood peering at the boat! No—they were not looking at the boat! They were looking at the mute queen! Ah! There are no creatures in this world as beautiful as deer!
Why did the God who created deer also create human beings? Who can say?
Cruel humans! Are there not those who hunt and kill such beautiful creatures?
Peering at the deer, marveling at their beauty, Poonguzhali’s hands ceased rowing; the boat came to a halt.
From the throat of the Mute Queen arose a strange sound. It was not like the voice heard that morning. This one was laced with fear and warning.

Hearing it, the deer too were startled, and began to flee in terror. At that very instant, from some hidden place, an arrow whistled forth and struck one of the deer. The wounded animal let out a sorrowful cry. The Mute Queen leapt from the boat onto the shore and ran towards the injured deer.

At the very moment she reached the deer’s side, there was a rustling sound in the surrounding thickets. In the next few seconds, seven or eight men emerged and surrounded her. Many among them carried spears and weapons.
A short distance away, Rakammal, who had guided them there, was also visible.
The Mute Queen tried to escape; she could not. Realizing that escape was impossible, she stood still.
Two men approached and bound her hands tightly with rope.
All this happened in just a few moments, while Poonguzhali watched.
When she saw the Mute Queen’s hands being tied, Poonguzhali sprang from the boat, shouting, and ran towards them, oar raised in her hand.

Five or six of those who stood around the Mute Queen rushed towards Poonguzhali. They seized her, dragged her back to the boat, threw her inside, and bound her tightly with rope. Then they turned away; the Mute Queen, who was brought along with them cautiously, vanished with them in a matter of moments.

chapters.title: Laughter and Fire
paragraphs: Poonkuzhali hurriedly tried to untie the knots that bound her to the boat. It was not such an easy task. The wretched fiends! They had tied the ropes haphazardly, knot upon knot. Poonkuzhali’s small knife lay beneath the boat. If she could free even one hand, she could grab the knife and cut through the bindings. But the villains had tied her wrists tightly together behind her back. Poonkuzhali struggled mightily, bending down to grip the knife’s handle with her teeth. Holding it between her teeth, she managed to cut the rope at one spot. The bonds on her hands loosened a little. With great effort, she freed one hand from the binding. After that, cutting the remaining ropes became somewhat easier.

It took nearly a quarter of an hour to completely free herself from the knots. At that moment, footsteps sounded on the riverbank. Then, a shadow appeared. It seemed that one of those who had tied her up was returning! Or perhaps they had left someone behind to make sure she did not escape after untying the knots! As soon as she saw him, Poonkuzhali resolved to throw the knife at him and kill him. She gripped the knife, ready for action. But what a disappointment!
“Poonkuzhali! Poonkuzhali!” came the voice of Sendhan Amudhan.
The next instant, Amudhan’s frightened, frantic face peered over the edge of the riverbank.
Poonkuzhali tucked the knife into her waist. Amudhan had seen her.
“Poonkuzhali! Are you alive?” he cried, leaping down and running toward her.
“My being alive must be a hardship for you! If you want, kill me with your own hands and go! But where are you going to get the courage for that?” said Poonkuzhali.

“Shiva! Shiva! What cruel words you speak! Why would I want to kill you? It is you who kill me with your words!” replied Amudhan. “Then, why couldn’t you have come a little earlier? Do you know how much I struggled to untie those knots and free myself?” Saying this, Poonguzhali tried to rise to her feet. But her legs were still hopelessly entangled in the ropes, and as she stumbled and nearly fell, Amudhan cried out in alarm and rushed to catch her, steadying her before she could hit the ground.
“Oh dear! Did those wretches really tie you up like this and leave you here? Your whole body is bruised and swollen!” he exclaimed.
“Now you’re showing so much concern! Why didn’t you come a little earlier?”
“Why do you keep asking the same thing? How was I to know you were in such danger? You were the one who told me to go away, and so I left…”
“Then why did you come back? Was it just so you could cremate my body if I had died?”

“Lord Shiva kept the poison in his throat; you, it seems, keep it on your tongue. I came running back as soon as your sister-in-law told me you might be in danger. And see what a fine reward I’ve received for my trouble!”
By this time, Poonguzhali had climbed out of the boat and onto the riverbank.
“I was about to throw this knife at you. You escaped; but with this very knife, I’ll first stab my sister-in-law to death before I do anything else. Where is that wretch?”
“Why are you leaving me and going after your sister-in-law? Why such anger against her? Is it a crime that she told me something about you?”
“She’s the one who betrayed my aunt. You yourself saw her secretly talking to someone in the thicket, didn’t you?” Poonguzhali demanded.

“You’re mistaken! Whatever secret your sister-in-law was discussing with whomever, I don’t know. But I’m sure she didn’t betray your aunt. The men who kidnapped your aunt also tied your sister-in-law to a tree. They even struck her on the head and wounded her before leaving.”

“What is this nonsense! I can’t believe it. She must have deceived you! Fine, then—tell me why you came back, where you saw my sister-in-law—tell me everything in detail!” Poonguzhali demanded, her voice trembling with agitation.

Senthan Amudhan thus recounted everything in detail. He was traveling along the road to Thanjavur. He was proceeding with hesitation, his heart heavy at having to part from Poonguzhali. At that moment, shouts and cries were heard from the nearby forest. The sound of several people hurrying along reached his ears as well. Senthan Amudhan concealed himself behind a tree at the roadside. Seven or eight armed warriors, spears in hand, came striding swiftly along the forest path and entered the royal highway. In their midst, it seemed, was a young woman.

When there was a slight gap between the people, the woman in the center appeared to resemble Poonguzhali’s aunt. But she could not possibly be her aunt, Senthan Amudhan thought; it must be a trick of his mind.

Even after that group of warriors had passed, the anguished cries of a young woman continued to echo from within the forest. At first, Senthan Amudhan thought, “Why should I get involved in trouble? Can I not simply go my own way?” Yet his heart would not allow it. He decided to see who was crying out, and if he could help in any way, he would. He went in the direction of the cries. There he found Raakkammaal, tied to a tree. Blood was streaming from her head, her face a ghastly sight. Senthan Amudhan was afraid to approach, but steeling his heart, he went forward and untied her bonds. As he loosened the knots, he asked, “Who committed this atrocity? Why did they do it? Who were the people who just went up the road? It seemed there was a young woman among them—who was she?”

“Yes, brother, they have tied up your aunt and dragged her away. I tried to stop them; that’s why they beat me and left me tied up like this. Your cousin and your aunt were traveling in a boat. It was from the boat that they dragged your aunt away, bound. I do not know what has become of Poonguzhali—run and see!” she said. Senthan Amudhan, startled, set off in search of Poonguzhali. At that moment, Raakkammaal called out, “Wait a moment, brother! Poonguzhali and that mute devil—did they board the boat together? Do you know where they were headed? Why did they leave you behind? Where were you going alone?” she asked.

The way she called the mute man a “devil” displeased Senthan Amudhan. “I’ll tell you everything later,” he replied, and ran toward the canal. He hurried on, anxious that those men might have beaten Poonguzhali, or perhaps even killed her. When he saw that Poonguzhali was alive and bore no wounds, he was greatly relieved…
After recounting these details, Sendhan Amudhan asked, “Poonguzhali! Now what do you say? Was it not wrong of you to be angry with your sister-in-law?”
“Listening to what you say, it does seem so. Where did you leave her? Let us go and see, come!” replied Poonguzhali.
“What certainty is there that she will still be there?”
“If she is not there, she will be somewhere nearby. If not, she will come searching for us. Amudha! Did not my sister-in-law ask where my aunt and I set out in the boat?”
“Yes, she asked.”
“You did not answer her, did you? Are you sure?”
“I am sure. When she called me ‘mute devil,’ I was so disgusted that I left without replying.”

“Hereafter, do not tell her, even if she asks kindly! Why does she want to know where we are going? There must be some reason for it, must there not? Amudha! We cannot say for certain that there is no connection between those who took my aunt away and my sister-in-law. Through her, they might have gathered information, and once their work was done, they could have tied her up and left her behind. Even if that is not the case, my sister-in-law must have followed us with some ill intent. So, be careful with her! Do not trust her completely and end up in trouble!”
“Poonguzhali! You have said that your brother becomes mute in your sister-in-law’s presence, have you not? In the same way, I too shall remain silent; you speak all that needs to be said…”
Hearing this, Poonguzhali laughed. “Your laughter is nectar to my ears. It is as sweet as the hymns of Thirunavukkarasar,” said Amudhan.
“I laughed by mistake; do not be deceived by it! In my heart, fire is boiling, flames are burning in my chest.”
“To quench the thirst of the heart, there is no better remedy than the flood of God’s grace!” said Sendhan Amudhan.

Vandiyathevan was startled. For a moment, he stood frozen, unable to decide whether what he had just heard was a dream or reality. The sound of laughter that had echoed from behind the curtains was not the laughter of a single person; it was as if several young women were laughing together, their voices blending and rising like the tinkling of silver bells. The laughter was not mocking, nor was it derisive—it was sweet, melodious, and enchanting.

But what did it mean? Why had they laughed at that moment? Was it because of something he had said? Or was it because of something that had happened elsewhere? Or was it simply the laughter of young women, blooming like flowers in the garden, with no particular reason?

Vandiyathevan’s mind was filled with questions. He glanced at the closed curtain, behind which the laughter had arisen. The curtain, made of fine silk, fluttered slightly in the evening breeze. Beyond it, the golden glow of lamps flickered, casting strange shadows on the walls. The fragrance of sandalwood and jasmine drifted through the air.
He took a step forward, then hesitated. Should he call out? Should he wait? Should he leave? His heart pounded with anticipation and curiosity.

At that moment, the curtain parted slightly. A slender hand, adorned with bangles, beckoned him forward. Vandiyathevan, gathering his courage, stepped closer. The laughter had subsided, but a faint smile lingered in the air, as if the very atmosphere was amused.
He bowed respectfully and said, “Princess, may I enter?”
A gentle voice replied from behind the curtain, “Come in, brave warrior. We have been waiting for you.”

Vandiyathevan pushed aside the curtain and entered the chamber. Inside, the scene was dazzling. The princess Kundavai was seated on a raised platform, surrounded by her companions. Their faces glowed with youth and beauty, their eyes sparkled with mischief. Lamps burned in every corner, their flames dancing like living things.
Kundavai looked at Vandiyathevan and smiled. “You seem surprised, sir. Did our laughter startle you?”
Vandiyathevan replied, “Princess, your laughter is sweeter than music. But I do not know if it was meant for me or for someone else.”
Kundavai’s eyes twinkled. “Perhaps it was for you. Perhaps it was for ourselves. Who can say? In this world, laughter and fire are alike—they arise suddenly, without warning, and spread everywhere.”
Her words were enigmatic, but her tone was light. The other young women giggled softly.

Vandiyathevan looked around the chamber. The walls were adorned with murals depicting scenes from ancient legends. The air was warm and fragrant. He felt as if he had entered another world—a world of beauty, grace, and mystery.
Kundavai gestured for him to sit. “Please, be seated. Tell us of your journey. What news do you bring from Kanchi?”

Vandiyathevan sat down, his mind still swirling with questions. He began to speak, but his thoughts kept returning to the laughter that had greeted him—the laughter that was both a welcome and a warning, both a delight and a danger.

chapters.title: The Physician’s Son Again
paragraphs: For a while, Poonguzhali and her cousin walked in silence along the forest path.
Poonguzhali let out a long sigh. “Amudha! I feel as though there is some bond between us from a previous birth.”
“Who cares about past lives right now? If you have any good news about this life, tell me that!” said Sendhan Amudhan.

“They say that the ties of previous births continue into this one, don’t they? It must be true; when I parted from you at midday, I thought I would never see you again. Yet within two hours, I have met you once more…”
“There’s no need to be upset about that; once we cross this forest path and reach the Thanjavur road, I’ll go my way, and you can go as you please…”

“I’m not going to leave you alone like that. After I meet my elder brother, I’m coming with you to Thanjavur. I’m going to seek a remedy for the suffering that has befallen my aunt. I will go to the presence of the Chola Emperor and make my appeal…”
“Poonguzhali, do you think it’s so easy to reach the Emperor’s presence? People like us can’t even enter the Thanjavur fort!”
“Why not? If the gates are not opened, I’ll break them down! If that’s not possible, I’ll climb over the walls and jump inside…”
“What will you do about the guards standing at the palace entrance?”
“When they hear the commotion I make, they’ll be so frightened that they’ll take me straight to the Emperor…”

“You can’t scare away someone like Chinna Pazhuvettarayar so easily. People in Thanjavur say that not even Yama, the god of death, can approach the Emperor without his permission.
