I’ve even heard some say that’s the only reason the Emperor is still alive.” “If I cannot see the Emperor, I will go to the Pazhuvettarayars themselves and ask whether there is any remedy for this outrage or not! If they do not provide a fitting remedy, I will go to the Prime Minister Brahmarayar. If that too proves fruitless, I will go to the queens in Pazhayarai and lodge my complaint. Until I find out what has become of my aunt, I will not stay in one place. Until justice is done for the wrong done to her, I will not sleep day or night. Didn’t my sister-in-law call my aunt a ‘mute demon’? I too shall become a demon and roam the towns and villages of this land. I will wander everywhere, crying out, ‘Justice! Justice!’... Amudha, will you come with me?”

“I will certainly come, Poonguzhali! If you wish it, I will come. But why do you let your mind be so troubled? You are thinking far ahead, going to distant places! Isn’t the first and most important task to find your aunt and save her? Shouldn’t we rescue her from those wicked men who took her away? Shouldn’t we tell your father, your brother, and the others...?”

“Amudha! My aunt possesses divine power. No one can do her any harm. Just as Damayanti burned the hunter with a glance, she too can burn with her eyes. So I am not so worried about her. But in this Chola Empire, such a great injustice is being done in broad daylight! They say that from the time of Parantaka Chola, this land has been ruled by dharma. In the land ruled by King Kandaraditya, the great devotee of Shiva, they boast that even cows and tigers drank water together at the same pond. Under the rule of Sundara Chola, they proclaim that any young girl in Chola Nadu can travel at any time, day or night, without fear. Yet in such a famed kingdom, if a helpless old woman—a deaf and mute, innocent lady—can be seized by evildoers in broad daylight, what kind of outrage is this? I am not so worried about my aunt alone. What happened to her today could happen to me tomorrow, could it not? Could it not happen to many other young women in this land?”

Senthan Amudhan now drew closer and said, “Yes; such danger does exist in this country now. Since Sundara Chola has fallen ill and taken to his bed, dharma has been turned upside down in Chola Nadu. Law and order have vanished. Danger lurks everywhere for young women. Therefore, it is best for all young women to get married as soon as possible!”
Poonguzhali burst into laughter.
“Amudha! If a maiden were to marry you, would you be able to protect her? Do you know how to wield a sword and fight in battle?” she asked.

“I have only learned to pluck flowers and string garlands, and to sing hymns in praise of the Lord. I have not learned to take up a sword and wage war. But what of that? Did you not teach me to grip the oar and row a boat? In the same way, I can learn to wield a sword and fight. When Madhurantaka Devar aspires to ascend the throne and rule the kingdom, is it such an impossible thing for me to learn the art of sword-fighting?” said Sendhan Amudhan.

By then, they had reached the base of the tree where Poonguzhali had tied her sister-in-law. But the woman was nowhere to be seen. Sendhan Amudhan pointed out to Poonguzhali the drops of blood that had dripped from the wound on her head and stained the ground.
“They have struck her hard; it is certain that she did not betray us to those who took away Aunt. But we must somehow find out for whom else she was spying!” said Poonguzhali.

“Daughter of my uncle! Listen to me! Everything that is happening here is shrouded in mysterious causes. Secrets within secrets, whirlpools within whirlpools. All of them seem to be entangled with the affairs of the kingdom and the royal clan. Why should you and I worry about these things? Why should we bring trouble upon ourselves?”

“Amudha! What if it is a matter of great state importance? What if it is shrouded in the deepest mystery? Can I remain unconcerned and idle when it involves my aunt? Can you remain indifferent about your own grandaunt’s fate?”

“I am only telling you what is in my heart, Poonguzhali! Did I not say that among the seven or eight people I saw, there was also a woman? Did I not say that she could be my grandaunt? From the way she walked, it did not seem as if she was being forced to go. She appeared to go willingly, as if it were her own wish…”

“That is possible, Amudha! It may well be so; that is her very nature! Perhaps she went of her own accord just to find out where they were taking her. If she did not wish to go, she would have escaped even from the midst of a thousand men. Not even the fort’s dungeons or the deepest underground prisons could— “It cannot be kept safe. That is why I said I was not overly worried about the danger that befell my aunt. My chief aim is to seek justice for the wrong done to her. That injustice was not committed today; it was a terrible wrong done twenty-five years ago! Until justice is served for that, I will not know peace!” said Poonguzhali.
“Heavens! Into what an impossible task you have let your mind wander?” sighed Sendhan Amudhan, releasing a long breath.

Voices could be heard a short distance away; one of them sounded like a woman’s. Amudhan and Poonguzhali saw the speakers at the Thanjavur royal road junction. When Poonguzhali recognized the man conversing with Anni Raakkammal as the son of the Pazhayarai physician, a look of distaste crossed her face.

As soon as Raakkammal saw Poonguzhali, she exclaimed, “Ah, girl! You have come back alive? I was so afraid they might have killed you. Look here! See what a great wound I have on my head from trying to save your aunt? I was just asking the physician’s son if he had any medicine for my wound.”
“If the daughter of the Karaiyar clan has any wounds, I will treat them and heal her too,” said the physician’s son.
Without replying to him, Poonguzhali asked, “Anni! Do you know which way they took my aunt?”
“I didn’t see, but this physician’s son says they went along the Thanjavur road...”
“Anni! Amudhan and I are going to follow them. Tell my father! Come, Amudha!” said Poonguzhali, immediately setting off from there.

At that moment, the physician’s son called out, “Poonguzhali! Wait a moment! You cannot follow them on foot. Not far from here, they have mounted waiting horses and gone. I have a horse; I will ride with the speed of the wind and the swiftness of the mind, find out where they have gone, and let you know. In return, you must do me a favor. When you and your aunt set out in the boat, where were you planning to go? Just tell me that much!”

Poonguzhali replied, “Anni! We do not need his help! We are going. Just inform my father!” The physician’s son was not yet done. “Ah! Behold the pride of the Karaiyar’s daughter! She claims she has no need of my help! Girl, why do you bear such anger toward me? Was it I who stood in the way when you wished to wed the royal prince? Was it I who deceived you, tricked you, and took you away in a boat? Was it not that Vandiyathevan of the Vanar clan who cast your beloved prince into the heart of the sea and killed him? What use is it to be angry with me?” So saying, he let out a false, mocking laugh—“Ha! Ha! Ha!”

Sparks flew from Poonkuzhali’s eyes as she shot him a fierce glance, then seized Amudhan’s hand and pulled him away, up the road. After they had gone some distance, she said, “Amudha! The first life your knife must claim, once you have learned the art of war, should be this wretched physician’s son. Let him be the first sacrifice to your blade.”

Day and night, Poonkuzhali and Sendhan Amudhan journeyed on toward Thanjavur. Along the way, they inquired about a group of seven or eight horsemen escorting a lady. For half the journey, they managed to gather some information, but after that, nothing more could be learned. Nevertheless, they resolved to search all the way to Thanjavur.

For Sendhan Amudhan, this journey was filled with excitement. One reason was the joy of conversing with Poonkuzhali as they traveled; another was the practice he gained with his new knife. Near Kodikkarai, in a smithy known to Poonkuzhali, he had purchased a blade. As they went, he would often whirl it about, imagining an enemy approaching and engaging him in combat, slashing the air in wild strokes. From time to time, Poonkuzhali would instruct him: “Hold the knife like this. Spin it that way.” Thus, she taught him as they traveled, making the journey lively for them both.

But when the fortress of Thanjavur finally appeared before their eyes, Poonkuzhali was seized by anxiety about how to accomplish the task that had brought her there. Sendhan Amudhan shared in her worry. Entering the fortress itself was a daunting challenge. How could Poonkuzhali carry out all that she had planned? Sendhan Amudhan’s mind turned to Vandiyathevan’s bold and clever exploits. Did he possess even a tenth of that man’s resourcefulness? Or, perhaps, would Vandiyathevan himself appear at this very moment…?

Sendan Amudhan began to wonder how Vandiyathevan would act in such a situation. At that moment, a closed palanquin appeared on the road. The sun had set in the west, and darkness was gathering all around. On the curtain of the closed palanquin, palm tree designs could be seen.

“Aha! Does it not look just like the palanquin of the younger queen of Pazhuvoor? How convenient it would be if I could meet the queen of Pazhuvoor outside the fort itself and obtain the signet ring from her!” thought Amudhan.

He shared this idea with Poonguzhali. She too agreed that it was a good plan. But how could they see the queen who was inside the closed palanquin? There were guards walking behind the palanquin as well. If they tried to approach the palanquin, wouldn’t the guards stop them?
“Amudha! Do not worry! The Thanjavur fort is still half a league away. Surely, before then, we will get some opportunity!” said Poonguzhali.
Unexpectedly, that opportunity presented itself to them.

chapters.title: The Fortune of the Palanquin
paragraphs: That year, the monsoon did not begin at its usual time. Twice, it seemed as though the rains would start, but each time, after a brief drizzle, they ceased abruptly. The flow of water in the Kaveri river and its tributaries gradually dwindled. The newly planted paddy fields began to wither for lack of irrigation. “It’s all a calamity brought on by the malefic star!” the people began to murmur among themselves.

“It seems as though misfortune is visiting the land in every way,” “Confusion in the affairs of the kingdom,” “No news of the prince,” “And now, even the skies seem poised to betray us”—such were the words that Senthan Amudhan and Poonguzhali heard all along their journey.

The absence of rain, however, was something of a convenience for their travels. That day, the sun had blazed fiercely since morning. By afternoon, the heat was almost unbearable. Even as they walked beneath the cool shade of trees lining the royal road, sweat poured from their bodies.
“Does this feel like the month of Aippasi at all? Isn’t it more like the scorching month of Vaikasi?” they said to each other as they went along.

A short while after the palanquin from the palace of the Pazhuvettaraiyars had passed them by, a sudden cool breeze began to blow. The leaves of the roadside trees rustled and whispered in the wind. To the northeast, the sky darkened. At the horizon, dense, dark clouds began to gather. In a matter of moments, those masses of cloud, like a herd of maddened elephants, collided and surged upward in the sky.

The gentle breeze turned into a strong wind; in that wind, small drops of rain came hissing down. Soon, a light drizzle began, and within half an hour, with a roaring sound, a heavy downpour commenced. The trees along the roadside suffered terribly in the wind and rain. Branches snapped and fell with a crackling sound. The birds that had sought shelter in those trees now shrieked and scattered in all directions. The travelers on the road, too, fled helter-skelter.

Some ran to escape the rain and wind. Others ran, fearing that tree branches might fall upon their heads and bring death. Still others, frightened by the thunder that roared like the bursting of the heavens, fled in panic. In the grip of the rain, within a short while, daylight faded and night drew near. The thought of entering the Thanjavur fort that very night was abandoned by both Sendhan Amudhan and Poonguzhali.
They decided that it would suffice if they could reach Sendhan Amudhan’s garden hut that night. In the monsoon darkness, they encouraged each other and walked on cautiously.

“Poonguzhali! You have witnessed so many storms and heavy rains in the midst of the open sea! You are one who has sailed a boat amidst waves as tall as mountains! Why are you so afraid of this rain?” asked Sendhan Amudhan.
“No matter how fierce the storm or how heavy the rain in the open sea, trees do not break and fall upon your head, do they? If anything falls, it is only lightning that strikes,” replied Poonguzhali.

Even as Poonguzhali spoke thus and closed her mouth, a little distance ahead of them, they heard the sharp crack and crash of a tree breaking and falling. Sendhan Amudhan gripped Poonguzhali’s hand tightly and stopped moving forward.
“There is no use hurrying on now. There are some mandapams along the roadside here; let us stay in one of them for a while and proceed after the rain’s fury has lessened,” said Sendhan Amudhan.
“That is a good idea. But how will we find the mandapam in this darkness?” asked Poonguzhali.
“We can spot it when the lightning flashes. We must look carefully on both sides!” said Sendhan Amudhan.
A lightning bolt flashed, turning sky and earth into a golden blaze, dazzling their eyes.
“There! There is a mandapam!” exclaimed Sendhan Amudhan.

Poonguzhali too saw the mandapam. In that same flash of lightning, she also noticed, a little ahead of them, a large tree lying fallen across their path. Beneath the fallen tree, it seemed as if some people were trapped.
“Amudha! Did you see the tree lying there? Underneath it…” she began.

“Yes, I saw it. It looks like the same fate is about to befall us as well. Let’s hurry and reach the mandapam!” Saying this, Amudhan seized Poonguzhali’s hand and, pulling her along, hastened in the direction of the mandapam.

The two of them reached the shelter. They wrung the water from their rain-soaked garments. After squeezing out her clothes, Poonguzhali also wrung out her long hair. The water she squeezed out fell onto the floor of the mandapam and ran in little rivulets.
“Oh dear! We’ve made the mandapam all wet,” said Poonguzhali.
“It will do the mandapam no harm. You won’t catch a chill or fever from this! But you’re completely drenched,” said Sendhan Amudhan.
“I was born and raised by the sea. My other name is ‘Samudra Kumari’—the Princess of the Ocean. Rainwater can do nothing to me,” replied Poonguzhali.

At that moment, her heart leapt from the roadside mandapam near Thanjavur’s fort to the Choodamani Vihara at Nagapattinam. Was it not at that Choodamani Vihara that she was first called ‘Samudra Kumari’?

“Poonguzhali, my garden and hut are not far from here. Once the rain stops, we can go there. My mother will take good care of you,” said Amudhan. But his words reached Poonguzhali’s ears only half-heard.
Once again, a flash of lightning split the darkness. In its sudden glare, the scene before them, which had been only dimly visible before, now appeared clearly. Both of them were startled.

Almost directly opposite the mandapam, a great banyan tree had been uprooted and lay sprawled across the road. Its wide-spreading branches and aerial roots were broken and scattered in wild disarray. Caught beneath them were two horses and five or six people. Others were trying to rescue those trapped under the fallen tree, working frantically to clear away the broken branches.
Cries such as “Oh no!” “Father!” “Here!” “There!” “Quickly!” could be heard faintly amidst the sound of the rain.

But more than all this, something else drew the attention of Sendhan Amudhan and Poonguzhali. A little distance from the fallen tree, a palanquin had been set down on the ground. Only two men stood beside it. The others—
They seemed to be intent on rescuing those trapped beneath the fallen tree.
“Amudha! Did you see the palanquin?” asked Poonguzhali.
“I saw it. It looked like the palanquin of the young queen of Pazhuvoor.”
“Couldn’t the fallen tree have landed on that palanquin?”
“Heavens! Why do you say such a thing? Didn’t you say you were going to meet the Pazhuvoor queen and accomplish something through her?”
“Yes, I did. Still, I don’t particularly like that young queen of Pazhuvoor!”
“If you don’t like her, does that mean a tree must break and fall on her? Is that what you wish?”

“Should trees fall only on the heads of common folk? Can’t they fall on the heads of queens as well? … Anyway, let that be. Shall we go near the palanquin now and see the Pazhuvoor queen? Shall we ask for her help to get into the fort?”
“Wonderful! What a fine time to meet the queen! What a splendid place! If we go near the palanquin, in this rainy darkness, they might think we are thieves and beat us to a pulp.”
“If I see the queen, everything will become easier afterwards…”
“How so?”
“I’ll mention my sister’s name, or say that the sorcerer Ravidasan sent me.”
“A good plan! But only if you can get close to the queen, right? … Look there, Poonguzhali.”

Once again, lightning flashed; in its light, two people could be seen carrying the palanquin. Ah! Had they set out already? No, no! Wasn’t the palanquin coming towards the mandapam? Yes, in a short while, the palanquin reached the entrance of the mandapam. The bearers set it down.
“Isn’t the Pazhuvoor young queen coming here in search of us?” said Poonguzhali.
Amudhan took her hand and tried to move towards the inner part of the mandapam; but Poonguzhali refused to move that way.
At that moment, a harsh voice called out, “Who’s there?”

Realizing it was the voice of one of the men carrying the palanquin, Poonguzhali replied, “Don’t be afraid, brother! We are travelers just like you. We’ve come to take shelter in the mandapam from the rain!”
“All right, all right! Don’t come near the palanquin,” said the same voice.
“Why would we want to go near the palanquin? One must have earned great merit to be blessed with the fortune of riding in a palanquin!” Poonguzhali retorted.
Senthan Amudhan began, “Even the great poet Valluvar has spoken of this. When speaking of the fruits of deeds from past births—”
“That’s enough, enough! Keep your mouth shut and stay quiet! How many of you are there?”
“There are only two of us. Even if two hundred more came, there would still be room in this mandapam to shelter from the rain!” said Amudhan.
Amudhan spoke only what he believed to be true. He did not know that, hidden behind a pillar within the mandapam, a third man was standing.

One of the palanquin bearers said to his companion, “I told you before, as soon as it started raining, we should take shelter in the mandapam; you didn’t listen. That’s why we’re in this predicament!”
“Who could have foreseen this, brother? We thought we could reach the fort before the rain grew heavy. At least that tree didn’t fall on the palanquin!” his companion replied.

At that moment, another brilliant flash of lightning lit up the sky. Senthan Amudhan and Poonguzhali’s eyes and attention were fixed on the palanquin. In that flash of light, they saw a woman part the curtain of the palanquin and peer intently in their direction. They noticed that, upon recognizing who they were, the woman smiled at them.
The next instant, darkness enveloped both the mandapam and the world outside.
In a very soft voice, Poonguzhali asked, “Amudha! Did you see?”
“Yes, I saw.”
“Who was that in the palanquin?”
“Was it not the younger queen of Pazhuvoor?”
“What did you think?”
“She looked like the queen of Pazhuvoor, but I had some doubts.”
“There is no doubt; it is certain.”
“What is certain?”
“It is not the queen of Pazhuvoor; it is my mad aunt, the queen, who is in the palanquin!”
“Hush! Don’t speak so loudly!”
“If I don’t speak out, how will anything get done?”
“What is it that needs to be done?”
“The very thing for which we have come all this way. We have found my aunt. Shouldn’t we rescue her and take her away?”
“That is not possible now, Poonguzhali! Let us see where the palanquin goes. Afterwards, we can think and find a way to set her free.”
“You want to let go of the prey and chase the tail? That will not do; my aunt must be freed now. If you are afraid, then you stay quiet!”
“Shouldn’t your aunt agree to be freed? She is sitting in the palanquin, going along without a care. Don’t we need to know where she is going, why, and who had her brought here?”
“Are they taking her to the underground prison, perhaps? If so, what can we do then?”
“Why not? I am someone who has come out of the underground prison myself. I have some influence in the palaces too. Somehow, I will free your aunt. For now, you keep quiet!”
At that moment, Poonguzhali resolved that she must indeed remain patient and silent. Just then, something entirely unexpected occurred.

The curtain of the closed palanquin seemed to part even more. From within, a figure emerged. Moving without a sound, like a cat, it walked out. In the next instant, it was right beside them. Since all this happened in the deep darkness, the guards standing at the base of the mandapam did not notice.
From the palanquin—

Poonguzhali recognized, even in that darkness, that the woman who had appeared was indeed the mute queen. The mute queen grasped both their hands and hurriedly led them to the rear part of the mandapam.

Embracing Poonguzhali tightly, she expressed her joy at seeing her. Then, for a while, a conversation took place between the aunt and the niece-in-law in the language of signs. In that pitch darkness, how did they manage to communicate with each other? How did one understand the thoughts of the other? That is something beyond our ability to comprehend or explain.
Poonguzhali said to Sendhan Amudhan, “Did you understand what aunt is saying? She wants me to get into the palanquin and go. She’s asking you to take her to your house!”
“What is your consent, Poonguzhali?” Amudhan asked.
“I am going to do as aunt says. Isn’t this the best way to find out who sent people to capture her and bring her here?”
“Think carefully before you answer, Poonguzhali! The plan is sound, but what dangers might lie in it!”
“Amudha! Do not worry! By doing as aunt says, no harm will come to me. And if any danger does arise, this knife at my waist is always here!” said Poonguzhali.
Once more, she embraced her aunt, and then, imitating her, walked silently to the palanquin, entered it, and drew the curtain closed.

chapters.title: Aniruddha’s Disappointment
paragraphs: For several days now, Prime Minister Aniruddha Brahmarayar had been staying in the capital city. To see him, government officials, minor kings, commanders of the army, foreign envoys, representatives of merchant guilds, temple administrators, and scholars of both southern and northern languages were constantly coming and going. Thus, his mansion was always bustling with crowds, a steady stream of people flowing in and out.

Aniruddhar did not keep a private guard for himself. He maintained only a very small retinue. Because of this, there was never any reason for conflict to arise between him and the Pazhuvettarayar brothers. Nevertheless, the younger Pazhuvettarayar was grumbling to himself. Ever since the Prime Minister had begun residing in Thanjavur, security had become lax. Under the pretense of wishing to see the Prime Minister, all sorts of people were continually entering the fortress. Since the Prime Minister’s mansion was situated next to the Emperor’s palace, the crowds in the palace quarter had also increased. Many came there, invoking the Prime Minister’s name or displaying his seal, and were able to see him.

Chinna Pazhuvettarayar wished to bring some order to all this. But he did not have the courage to go directly to the Prime Minister and argue with him. If the elder Pazhuvettarayar had been present, the two of them could have discussed and taken some action. But at this time, the elder had gone to Kadambur, leaving the younger one, Kaalandhaka Kandar, feeling as though he had lost the use of one arm.

It was not enough that the crowds gathering inside the fortress were hindering the security arrangements; the Prime Minister, Aniruddhar, would often send requests to the younger Pazhuvettarayar, pretending to seek his assistance, but in fact issuing commands. A few days earlier, he had asked for some soldiers to be sent to Kodikkarai. Kaalandhaka Kandar had complied and provided the men. Then, just yesterday, he had sent word that a noblewoman needed to be brought from Thiruvaiyaru, and for that, he required a closed palanquin from the Pazhuvur palace and some bearers. The younger Pazhuvettarayar fulfilled this request as well. Yet in his heart, he thought, “This Brahmarayar is up to some scheme. What noblewoman is there who needs to be brought in a closed palanquin in this manner?” Who is that woman? Why is she coming here? I must find this out at any cost. At such a critical moment, why has my brother gone away and left me alone?’—thus did his mind become agitated.

There was another man, too, who was eager to discover who had arrived at the residence of Prime Minister Aniruddhar in a closed palanquin. That man was none other than Alwarkadiyan, the beloved disciple of Aniruddha Brahmarayar.

On the morning following that day of heavy rain, Aniruddha Brahmarayar completed his ablutions, prayers, meditations, and rituals, and came to the front portico of his mansion. He summoned his attendant and asked who had come and was waiting to see him. Upon learning that Alwarkadiyan was among those waiting, he immediately ordered that he be brought in at once.
Alwarkadiyan hurried before his revered guru and stood with reverence and humility.
“Tirumalai! What happened to the task you were sent on?” Aniruddhar asked.
“Master! Forgive me, I have returned in defeat,” replied Alwarkadiyan.
“As I expected, then. You were unable to meet Aditya Karikalan?”
“I did meet him, sir! I conveyed all the messages you instructed me to deliver, but it was of no use. I could not prevent the prince from going to Kadambur Palace…”
“Is the prince at Kadambur now?”

“Yes, master! I saw him enter the palace of Sambuvaraiyar with my own eyes before I returned. Sambuvaraiyar received the prince with royal honors. The enthusiasm shown by the people gathered there is beyond description.”
“All that is to be expected. Who else has arrived at Kadambur Palace?”

“Parthibendran and Vandiyathevan have come with the prince. From here, Periya Pazhuvettarayar has arrived with the young queen. I hear that many minor kings from Nadu Nadu and Thirumunaippadi regions have also been invited…”
“Tirukkovalur Malayaman…”
“He accompanied the prince as far as the Manimudda River and then turned back…”

“That valiant old man will not remain idle. By now, he must have begun gathering his forces. I hear that the great Velan of Kodumbalur is coming from the south with a large army. Only God can save this kingdom from disaster. Thirumalai! On your way here, did you hear what the people of Chola Nadu are talking about?”
“They are mostly speaking about the sea accident that befell the younger prince. They are furious with the Pazhuvettaraiyars. Some even include us in their complaints…”
“Yes, yes; they do have reason to complain. Thirumalai! I am seriously considering relinquishing this post of Chief Minister soon…”
“Guru! If you do so, I too will gain my freedom. I will spend my days in bliss, traveling the land and singing the hymns of the Alwars. When are you planning to resign your post, sir?”
“I intend to make one last attempt to protect the kingdom from disaster; once that is done, I shall step down…”
“What is that attempt, Guru?”
“The most important first step in that endeavor has already been taken. Thirumalai! I have succeeded in a task you had abandoned as impossible…”
“There is nothing surprising in that, sir! What is that task?”

“I had asked you to find and bring here a mute woman who wanders about the island of Eezham like one possessed, hadn’t I? You returned and told me you could not accomplish it, didn’t you?” asked Aniruddha.
“Yes, sir! That mute woman…”
“Last night, she was brought to our palace.”
“Ah! Astonishing! Astonishing! How did you accomplish this?”

“I anticipated that the mute woman would come to Kodikkarai to find out whether the younger prince had survived or not. I had sent men to bring her if she arrived. Fortunately, she came without much trouble. Listen to this curious tale, Thirumalai! I had her brought from Thiruvaiyaru in a closed palanquin. For this, I even had the closed palanquin of the queen of Pazhuvur brought here…”
“Sir, yesterday evening there was a great storm and heavy rain!”
“Yes; because of that, there was a delay on the way. I too was quite anxious. Only after the palanquin arrived at midnight did I feel at ease.”
“Oh! Was it midnight already? Did you stay up all that time to welcome her?”

“I stayed awake, but I did not go to receive her myself. I had the women of the house go to welcome her. She seemed to be quite mad; I was worried about what sort of commotion she might cause. Fortunately, nothing of the sort happened. She ate well and immediately went to sleep. Thirumalai! To tell you the truth, I still feel a little afraid about meeting her. It is good that you have come at this time…”
“Guru! I too am very eager to see that lady…”

“If that is so, come! Let us go to the women’s quarters. She already knows about you, doesn’t she? She knows that you are someone trusted by the young prince. So perhaps she will feel a little more at ease with you.”
The guru and his disciple went to the rear wing of the mansion. Aniruddha Brahmarayar ordered the nursemaids to bring the lady who had arrived the previous night.
The nursemaids brought the woman and made her stand before them.
Aniruddha stared at her, struck with astonishment.
A smile played upon the lips of Azhwarkadiyan.

chapters.title: Will the Mute Speak?
paragraphs: Aniruddhar gazed intently at Poonguzhali for a while, then summoned the nursemaids who had brought her. In a soft voice, he asked them something. After they replied, he instructed them to leave the room.
Turning to Azhwarkkadiyan, he said, “Thirumalai! It seems some mistake has occurred!”
“Yes, sir! I feel the same way,” replied Azhwarkkadiyan.
“This young woman must be about twenty years old.”
“She may not even be that old.”
“The lady I was expecting should be around forty.”
“She would be older than that.”
“Yes, yes, you have seen Mandakini Devi on the island of Lanka, haven’t you?”
“Yes, sir! I saw her, and as per your orders, I tried to bring her here, but I could not.”
“This woman is not Mandakini Devi, is she?”
“No, Gurudeva! She is certainly not that lady!”
“Then who could she be? How did she end up here?”
“We can simply ask her!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
“What is the use of asking a mute?”
“Gurudeva! That she is mute…”
“That is what I asked the nursemaids. They said she has not spoken a word since she arrived here.”
“Gurudeva! Whom did you send to identify and bring her here?”
“Ah! Did that fool make some mistake, I wonder?” “What kind of fool, O Gurudeva! Would you have sent such a simpleton for these tasks?”
“He seemed clever enough; do you not recall, the day I went to Pazhaiyarai, a young man fought with Vallavaraiyan of the Vanar clan?”
“Yes! The son of the Pazhaiyarai physician, Pinagapani.”

“That’s the one! After I sent you and Vallavaraiyan to meet Karikalan, I had that physician’s son released from prison and brought before me. Seeing that he was fit for our spy network, I sent him to Kodikkarai. He was already familiar with that place, it seems.”
“Was it he who brought this woman here?”
“I gave him all the signs and instructions. He took her to Thiruvaiyaru and sent word that the task was accomplished, that all had gone well…”
“Sir! That clever spy who succeeded where I failed—where is he now? Would it not be best to ask him directly about this woman?”
“That would indeed be best! But last night, he met with an unexpected accident…”
“Alas! What accident befell him, and how did it happen?”

“He was following behind the palanquin. Since I had ordered that they must reach the fort after nightfall, they set out from Thiruvaiyaru at dusk and were nearing the fort in the early hours of the night. Surely you heard of the sudden storm that struck?”
“Yes, sir! I too, frightened by the tempest, was forced to take shelter for a while in a wayside rest pavilion.”

“When the palanquin was a short distance from the fort, a great tree was uprooted and fell across the road. By fortune, it did not fall upon the palanquin, but struck those walking behind. The physician’s son, Pinagapani, was caught beneath the fallen tree…”
As the Prime Minister spoke thus, a woman’s voice rang out, “Did that wretch have only a tree fall upon his head? Could not lightning have struck him as well?” The words were spoken with fury.
Prime Minister Aniruddha turned to look at Poonguzhali, astonishment unmeasured in his gaze. Still looking at her, he asked, “Thirumalai! Was it this woman who just spoke?”
“Yes, sir! So it seemed.”
“What is this sorcery? Can the deaf hear? Can the mute speak?” asked Aniruddhar.

“It is indeed a great wonder for the deaf to hear and the mute to speak. But as a devout follower of Lord Vishnu, who is all-powerful, is there any miracle that cannot occur if you set your mind to it? Did not the Alvar’s sacred lips declare—”

“That’s enough! Do not drag the Alvars into this and trouble them now! This did not happen by the grace of Lord Vishnu; something else has gone wrong. This woman has deceived us. Who is she? What is her intention? Why did she pretend to be deaf and mute for so long?”
“Gurudeva! Why not ask the woman herself?”
“My boy! Seeing the smile playing on your lips, I wonder if perhaps you already know the answer. Very well! I shall ask her myself. Girl! Are you not deaf? Can you hear what I am saying…?”

“Sir! There have been times when I wished I were deaf. But right now, I am glad I can hear. Did I not hear the news that the outcaste physician’s son had a tree fall on his head? Swami! Has he died and gone?”
“Ah! So you can hear; and you can speak as well; you are not mute!” exclaimed Aniruddhar.
“Certainly, this woman is not mute!” said the disciple.
“Ah! So you have discovered that I am not mute! It seems what I heard is true—that the wisest man in the Chola Empire is the Chief Minister Aniruddha Brahmarayar!” said Poonguzhali.

“Girl! Are you mocking me? Beware! If you are not mute, why have you remained silent since you arrived here last night? Why did you pretend to be mute? Speak the truth!” demanded the Chief Minister Aniruddha Brahmarayar.

“Sir! Until I arrived here last night, I was known to be quite talkative. Some even call me ‘chatterbox’. But when I saw the grandeur of the Chief Minister’s palace and the royal honors shown to me here, I was struck dumb with amazement. The women of your palace spoke to me only through signs. Since they all thought I was mute, I too replied in gestures. After hearing your conversation, my speech has returned to me…”
“There is no doubt that you are a great talker; it amazes me to think how the physician’s son managed to bring you here. Even if he is a fool, he is certainly clever.”
“Swami! That wretched fellow did not bring me here. Had he truly tried, by now he would surely be on his way to Yamaloka!” said Poonguzhali, drawing out the dagger tucked at her waist and showing it.
“Girl! May you be blessed—put that dagger back at your waist. But why are you so angry with him? Is that why you say he did not bring you here?”
“He did not bring me; but his men tied me up and threw me into the boat. They tied my sister-in-law to a tree. And for all this, that rogue of a physician’s son told me he had nothing to do with it…”
“So far, he is wise—he is behaving just as I instructed him…”
“Sir! O Prime Minister! Was it you who sent that scoundrel? Was it you who ordered him to bring my mute aunt here?”
“Your aunt? The Karaiyar maiden, Mandakini, is your aunt? Then, you…what is your relation to Thyagavidangar, the keeper of the lighthouse at Kalangarai?” asked Aniruddha.
“Sir! I am his beloved daughter!”
“Ah! I never knew that Thyagavidangar had such a sharp-tongued daughter!”
“Please do not speak of this outside, sir!”
“Why, girl?”

“It is famous throughout the land that there is nothing the Chief Minister of the Chola Empire, Brahmarayar, does not know. If there is something you do not know, will it not diminish the people’s respect for you?”

“Girl! I have no concern for my reputation. Just tell me one more thing I do not know. You said your aunt was brought here—where is she now? How did you get into the palanquin I sent? Where did you get in?” asked Aniruddha.
“Sir! Why did you send men to capture and bring my mute, voiceless aunt?”
“Daughter! That is not something I can tell you; it is a matter of great state importance.”
“Father! In that case, I too cannot answer the questions you have asked me.”
“There are ways to make you speak!”
“They will not work on me!”
“Girl! I will send you to the underground dungeon!”
“No dungeon can keep me imprisoned.”
“Those who go to the underground dungeon never return.”
“I know one who did return, sir! Only yesterday I traveled with Sendhan Amudhan, speaking with him…”
“Who is this Sendhan Amudhan?…”
“He is the son of my other aunt. He and I were coming together from Kodikkarai.”
“For what reason, daughter?”

“I have long wished to see the mansions and towering gateways of Thanjavur. I also desired to have an audience with Emperor Sundara Chola. They say the Emperor is unwell, don’t they? How is he now, sir? May I see him?”
“He is just the same, daughter! There is no improvement, so you must give up the thought of seeing the Emperor!…”
“How can I forget, sir! I must see the Emperor. I must tell him that in his righteous kingdom, such outrages as forcibly abducting women are taking place…”
“Girl! I have no time to stand here arguing with you. Nor did I order anyone to forcibly bring you here. Tell me how you got into the palanquin I sent! Did anyone force you into it?”
“No, Swami! That is not all. When the palanquin neared the Tanjore fort, it was empty. Since it was raining, I myself got into the palanquin…”

The Chief Minister, Aniruddha Brahmarayar, looked at his disciple, Azhwarkadiyan, and said, “Now, in some way, the matter becomes clear to me. On the way, when the storm and rain were raging, they must have set the palanquin down somewhere. At that time, this girl’s aunt was taken out of the palanquin, and she herself got in. The physician’s son, struck unconscious by a falling tree, could not pay attention. The other bearers did not notice. This must have happened very near the fort gates, Thirumalai! Do you think my guess is correct?”
“Swami! It happened exactly as you have surmised; I saw it with my own eyes.”
“You saw it? Why? Why have you kept your mouth shut all this time? Speak quickly!”

“Last night, in the monsoon darkness, I was approaching the fort gates. A fierce storm and rain lashed down; trees broke and fell. I thought I might stay for a while in a wayside pilgrims’ mandapam. Shortly after I took shelter there, this girl and another young man arrived. She said he was her aunt’s son; it must have been him. In the flash of lightning, I saw a rudraksha garland around his neck. Realizing he was a budding Shaivite, I thought I could speak to him of the greatness of Vaishnavism and pass the time. Just then, a palanquin was brought to the front of the mandapam. On its curtain, I saw the palmyra insignia of the Pazhuvettarayars. A woman alighted from the palanquin and came near them. In the darkness that filled the mandapam, the three of them spoke in gestures and whispers. Later, I saw this girl go and get into the palanquin. In the flash of lightning, I realized: the woman who got down from the palanquin was one person; the one who got in was another. The palanquin bearers noticed nothing; when the rain eased a little, they lifted the palanquin and left!...”
“Ah! Is that so? They have deceived me? And you kept silent all this time? What did those two do afterwards?”
“After the palanquin left, they too departed; then I also set out…”
**Chapter 23 – Will the Mute Speak?** “Thirumalai! Why did you simply stand by and watch all this unfold? Why did you not stop her aunt? Have you too become involved in their conspiracy?”

“Forgive me, Gurudeva! Forgive me! I am not one who would commit such treachery. First of all, I did not know this was all your arrangement. Since it was the palanquin from the Pazhuvoor palace, I thought it must be some business of the Younger Pazhuvettarayar. Moreover, could I have stopped Mandakini Devi? One might be able to dam a storm wind, but could anyone stop that lady? Was I not the one who tried and failed even in Lanka? Besides, that noble lady knows my face. The moment she sees me, she would flee in fear; then no one would be able to catch her…”
“Hearing that, the physician’s son seems to be quite resourceful. He managed to bring her all this way, didn’t he?”
“Gurudeva! I do not think your suspicion is correct in this matter. Mandakini Devi must have come of her own will. Perhaps, as she neared Thanjai, her mind changed…”

“That may be; that may be. Still, that Karaiyar’s daughter could not have gone very far. Wasn’t it windy and raining all night? She must be somewhere nearby. Thirumalai! Somehow, she must be found. Perhaps this girl knows where she is staying… Child! What is your name?”
“Poonguzhali, sir!”
“Aha! What a beautiful name! In naming you, Thyagavidangar’s cleverness is unmatched. Poonguzhali! You must know where your aunt is staying. If you know, tell me! No harm will come to her.”
After thinking for a moment, Poonguzhali replied, “Swami! I know where my aunt is now. If you tell me why you want to bring her here, I too will tell you where she is staying…”
“Poonguzhali! This is a great matter of the kingdom. It is a secret concerning the palace—I cannot tell you.”
“Then I cannot tell you either!”
“There is no use talking to this girl…”
“Sir! If you are willing to fulfill one condition…”
“Aha! So this girl dares to lay down conditions for me! What is this?”
“If you are willing to seat my aunt upon the throne of Thanjavur and crown her with the royal diadem, then I myself will go and bring her here.”
“Thirumalai! This girl has gone mad…!”

“Have you only just realized that, Gurudeva? There’s no point in listening to her. I know where her aunt is. Her aunt’s son, Sendhan Amudhan, is in the flower garden not far from the fort. He and his mother serve the Thalikulathar temple by offering flowers. The lady you seek is there. If you send a few men with me, I’ll bring her here!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.

Poonkuzhali shot a look at Thirumalai as if she would burn him to ashes and said, “If you do anything like that, I’ll go straight to the emperor’s palace and lodge a complaint! I’ll make sure the whole town knows of your misdeeds!”
“Thirumalai! We must have this girl sent to the underground dungeon; there’s no other way!” declared Aniruddha Brahmarayar.
“If anyone comes near me, I’ll kill them!” Poonkuzhali said, drawing the dagger she had tucked into her lap.

“Sir! There’s no need to send this girl to the underground dungeon. Instead, we can send her to the residence of the young princess, Kundavai Devi. Isn’t the young princess here now? She will cure this girl’s madness! Perhaps the princess herself has some use for this girl!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
“Why do you say that? What use could the young princess possibly have for this girl…?”
“Gurudeva! Do you not know? The storm that struck here yesterday evening has wrought havoc along the Chola country’s coastline! Messengers from all directions are waiting at your palace gates…”
“Yes, yes! I must see them at once. So much time has been wasted in conversation with this girl. If only she had been born mute, how much better it would have been…”
“Is it right to torment someone just because they cannot speak?” muttered Poonkuzhali.
“I hear that there is great danger at Nagapattinam. They say the sea has risen in fury and engulfed the entire city!”
At these words, both Prime Minister Aniruddhar and Poonguzhali started in alarm.
“It is possible that the Young Princess herself has come here to inquire about that matter,” concluded Azhwarkadiyan.
Before he could close his mouth after speaking, the sounds of victory cheers echoed at the palace entrance.
“Thirumalai, since when have you gained the eye of wisdom? It seems it is indeed the Young Princess who is arriving!” said Aniruddhar, rising and walking towards the entrance.
By then, through that very doorway, Kundavai Devi and Vanathi entered.
The moment the Young Princess saw Poonguzhali standing there, the shadow of worry that had lingered on her radiant face vanished, and a mingled expression of surprise and joy shone forth.

chapters.title: The Princess’s Urgency
paragraphs: After receiving and welcoming the princesses, seating them upon the thrones, Aniruddha too took his place.
“Devi, if you had sent word that you wished to see me, would I not have come myself? What is the reason for your coming here in such haste? The Emperor is well, is he not?” he asked.

“The Emperor’s health is as it always is, Ayya! But his mind is not at ease. The fierce storm that struck last night has deeply troubled my father’s heart. He did not sleep at all through the night. Again and again, he lamented, thinking of the hardships the poor and humble folk living in huts must have suffered. At dawn, he bade me come to you at once. He wishes that arrangements be made immediately to help all those who have suffered loss and hardship because of the storm. That is the main reason I have come to you!” said the young princess Kundavai.

“Devi! What can this humble one do? You know well that the title of Chief Minister is all I possess. Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar has left the city at this time. He must have locked the treasury tight before leaving. Even Kaalandhakandar could not open the treasury hall without his permission! What help can I give to those who have suffered loss and hardship? You must have seen the many people waiting at the entrance. Yet I am ashamed even to face them. That is why I have been hesitating to go outside,” said Aniruddha Brahmarayar, singing a song of helplessness.

“Ayya! You need not worry about that. I am ready to give all my own possessions. My mother too is willing to do the same. You may take anything you need from the Emperor’s palace. My father has sent word to that effect. Please, make some immediate arrangement—at least some temporary relief—for the suffering of the poor…”

“Your personal possessions would be like offering puffed rice to a hungry elephant. The storm raged across the whole of Chola Nadu. We have not yet received news of what has happened and where. Here stands my disciple Paramananda—he brings terrible tidings. The sea has risen and, from Kodikkarai to Nagapattinam, has submerged all the coastal towns…!”
Hearing these words, Aniruddhar noticed that the faces of the three women present there were suddenly transformed by fear.

Immediately, he continued in a soothing tone, “But I do not believe it. What he says is nothing but a rumor. The rumor has spread faster than a storm. It is still too early for any news to arrive from the coastal regions. Even if messengers come on horseback, they will only reach here after noon today. In the meantime, we can make arrangements to do whatever help is possible.”

The young princess Kundavai, having somewhat composed her troubled mind, said, “Sir! The rumor about Nagapattinam has reached my ears as well. I came here intending to speak to you about it. Only just now have we returned after offering donations to the Chudamani Vihara, have we not? If some misfortune befalls the vihara, alas, what will the monks there do?” Saying this, she turned to look at where Poonguzhali stood.
“Sir! How did this woman come here? Is she not Poonguzhali, the daughter of Thiavidangar of Kodikkarai?” she asked.

“Yes; she is indeed Thiavidangar’s daughter, but she is not as gentle as her father. She is a most troublesome girl, always meddling in matters that do not concern her and causing disturbances!” replied the Chief Minister.

A different kind of doubt arose in the young princess’s mind. Had Aniruddhar brought Poonguzhali here to gather information about Arulmozhi? He was, after all, a minister skilled in all manner of cunning and stratagems. Whatever the case, she resolved that she must stand by Poonguzhali’s side. “That is not so at all! Poonguzhali is a very good girl! Come here, dear! Why is the Chief Minister angry with you? Did you trouble him in some way?” she asked.
Poonguzhali came a little closer and said, “Devi! Ask the Chief Minister yourself! Did I trouble him, or did he trouble me? Ask him!”
“Oh ho! You too are angry! Come here, girl; sit beside me!” said the young princess, drawing Poonguzhali to sit by her side.
“Sir! For what purpose did you bring this girl here? Is it for some important matter?” she asked.
“Ammani! I did not bring this girl here. I had no knowledge that such a troublesome girl even existed—she came here entirely on her own…” hesitated Aniruddhar.
“Devi! Why does the Prime Minister hesitate? Tell us the rest as well!” said Poonguzhali.
“She herself went in search of her aunt and brought her here.”
“Who is her aunt? Oh! Is it Sendhan Amudhan’s mother? Isn’t their house outside the fort?”

“No; Amudhan’s mother is not here; she has another mute aunt. Princess! This is news you ought to know as well. In the forests of Eezham, there is a mute woman who wanders about as if possessed. I wished to bring that lady here for an important matter. I made great efforts for it; at last, just as I was about to succeed…”
Kundavai Devi, overcome by an inexpressible excitement, rose from her seat and said, “Is it true? Is that lady here now? I must see her at once.”
“Forgive me, Devi! Just as I was about to succeed, this girl intervened and ruined everything!” said the Prime Minister.
Kundavai, sitting down again with great disappointment, asked, “Poonguzhali! Is this true? What have you done?”
“Devi! Listen to the method the Prime Minister used to bring my aunt here. Then you will not blame me!” said Poonguzhali.
After that, the Prime Minister briefly recounted what had happened.
Listening intently, the young princess said, “If that is so, she must be somewhere near this fort, mustn’t she? Can’t we search for her?”
“There is no need even for that, fortunately. My disciple says he saw her this morning in Sendhan Amudhan’s hut,” said the Prime Minister.
“In that case, why waste time? All other matters can wait. Let us go and bring her ourselves; if you cannot come, I will go alone. Vanathi! Get ready, let us go!” she said.

At that moment, Azhwarkkadiyan interjected, “Devi! We must proceed with caution. If that lady sees a crowd of strangers approaching, she might be startled and take to her heels. After that, even if we chase after a whirlwind, we won’t be able to catch her!”
“Yes, what Thirumalai says is true. The moment Poonguzhali’s aunt sees us, she might panic and run away. All our efforts would be in vain! What do you suggest, Thirumalai?” asked the Prime Minister.
“Send this young woman to fetch her. In this world, there are only two people who can restrain that lady! Of those two, this girl is one.”
“Who is the other?” asked the Prime Minister. Azhwarkkadiyan hesitated slightly and replied, “The other is rumored throughout the land to have drowned in the sea!”

Kundavai Devi, as if she hadn’t noticed this, turned to Poonguzhali and said, “Daughter of the Karaiyar clan! Go at once and bring your aunt here! No harm will befall her here. I must see her immediately on a matter of great importance! Will you do me this favor?”
“Very well, Amma, I will try. But the Prime Minister need not have resorted to such a stratagem. Had I known beforehand…”

“Yes; when things are kept secret, such awkward situations are bound to arise. I myself realize this and regret it. Go quickly and bring your aunt! After that, there is another important task for you!” said the Princess.
“Thirumalai! You go along with this girl. If you face any difficulty entering through the main gate, bring her in through the secret passage to our palace!” said Aniruddha.

After Poonguzhali and Azhwarkkadiyan had left, Kundavai turned to the Prime Minister and said, “Sir! Go and tell those waiting at the entrance what needs to be said and send them away. I have some very important matters to consult with you about!”
“I shall be back at once, Mother! I too have something I must speak to you about!” said Aniruddha, and departed.
All this while, Vanathi had remained silent. Now she asked, “Akka! What other important task do you have for Poonguzhali? Are you going to send her to Nagai Pattinam again?”
“Yes, Vanathi! Do not worry needlessly! Nothing will befall Ponniyin Selvan.”
“But I am going to Nagai Pattinam with her too, Akka!”
“What will you do by going? Won’t someone else be needed to protect you?”
“That boatwoman doesn’t like me at all, Akka!”
“How did you discover what is in her mind?”
“She never spoke to me at all!”
“You didn’t speak to her; she didn’t speak to you.”
“I kept looking at her face often. Not even once did she turn to look at me; she seems angry with me for some reason!”
“Yes, Vanathi! All the unmarried maidens in this land must surely be angry with you. There is no use in being upset about that,” said the young princess, Kundavai Devi.

chapters.title: Aniruddha’s Crime
paragraphs: The Prime Minister spoke to those waiting at the entrance of his palace’s sacred hall, dismissed them, and returned swiftly.

“Lady! I have made arrangements as best as I could. I have sent men in all directions to learn of the damages caused by the storm. I have also sent word to Chinna Pazhuvettarayar, instructing that the treasury should be opened under the responsibility of both of us.”
“Sir! Isn’t there a treasury adjoining the palace of Periya Pazhuvettarayar? They say it holds untold riches. Is that true? The Periya Piratti mentioned it once.”

“If that is opened, the treasures within could build a thousand grand temples anew—that is what that lady imagines. Even I have never set foot inside that treasury, my lady! Those who enter that moonlit chamber never return alive,” said the Prime Minister.
“Let that be, sir! Will these people bring that mute woman here? I am anxious that what is within reach may slip away from us,” said Kundavai.
“Mother! What do you know of that queen? How did you come to know? Why are you so agitated about her?” asked Aniruddha.
“Sir! A few days ago, the Emperor himself spoke to me about that queen.”
“What? Did he say she is still alive?”

“No, sir! He spoke of events that happened twenty-five years ago. He believes she is dead. That is why his mind is so disturbed. Was it not you who brought word to my father that the mute woman had fallen into the sea and died? Then, how did you come to know that she is alive?”

“I intended to ask you the same question. How did you come to know, Devi?” “What of it? I will tell you. The valiant scion of the Vanar clan, when he returned from Eezham, he was the first to speak of it. Then my younger brother Arulmozhi…” Kundavai, having said thus, suddenly realized her slip and covered her mouth with her hand, as if to stifle her own words.
“Devi! If you do not wish to speak to me about Prince Arulmozhivarman, then you need not. I shall forget that you even mentioned that name.”

“No, sir! I came to you with the intention of telling you everything. I have realized that hiding and concealing matters brings only harm, never any good. Last night, this truth became clear to me. Sir! The sea did not claim my younger brother. The King of the Sea, Samudrarajan, saved Ponniyin Selvan and brought him safely to shore. He is now staying at the Buddhist Vihara in Nagapattinam. I went to Nagapattinam only to see him. Yet, I have a suspicion that you already know all this.”

“Your suspicion is justified; but, Devi, did I ever show that I knew? I have made it a rule never to interfere in your affairs, though I may meddle in the matters of others. I have given the same instruction to my men. I have faith that whatever you do will always be right. The Kodumbalur Velan and I often say to each other, ‘If only the Young Princess had been born a son, she would have brought the whole world under the white parasol of the Cholas and ruled as a sovereign!’”

“It is true that I have harbored such thoughts. Though I was born a woman, I cherished the hope that my ambition would be fulfilled through my brothers. But now, I have given up that hope, sir! I have resolved that women should not interfere in matters of the kingdom! See, I arranged for my brother to stay at the Chudamani Vihara in Nagapattinam—look at the disastrous result!”
“Nothing disastrous has happened, Mother! The Samudrarajan who saved Ponniyin Selvan in the midst of the sea—would he now bring him harm when he is safe on shore?”
“Sir! Go at once to my father and give him this reassurance.”
“Ah! Does the Emperor know, then? Does he know that the Prince is at the Chudamani Vihara?”
“I told you just last night; and it has happened exactly as I feared.”

“Ah! If only you had waited a few more days before revealing it, it would have been better. I thought what you had arranged was truly excellent! Devi, the whole of Chola Nadu is in a state of turmoil. The storm that raged yesterday has only brought to the surface an unrest that has been simmering in the hearts of the people of Chola Nadu for some time now. The people are seething with anger against both Madurantakan and the Pazhuvettaraiyars. They have learned that ships were sent to capture the prince and bring him back as a prisoner. Many believe that it was the Pazhuvettaraiyars who drowned the prince in the sea. If, at this moment, it becomes known that the prince is in this land, the people will rise up in fury. They will demand that the crown be placed upon the prince’s head at once, and a great rebellion will break out. The Pazhuvettaraiyars are waiting for the slightest pretext to start a fight. Periya Velar of Kodumbalur is gathering a great army and marching towards Thanjavur. Devi, I fear that a river of blood is about to flow in Chola Nadu. I am afraid that this vast empire may be destroyed by fraternal strife. Day and night, I pray to Sri Ranganatha that such a calamity may not come to pass.”

“That is my prayer as well, Ayya! I have given up my desire that my brothers should ascend the throne of this empire. As far as I am concerned, I have no objection now to crowning Madurantakan. I have relinquished that wish.”

“You may have no objection, but the people do! The Emperor must live long years yet in this world. But if, by fate, anything should happen to him, on that very day the whole of Chola Nadu will become a battlefield…”

“Ayya! I am greatly troubled by the fear that such a disaster may befall us soon. Last night, the Emperor’s condition became extremely worrying. That is why I had to tell him that Ponniyin Selvan was safe. Yet, even after I told him, he did not believe it! He thought I was only offering him empty words of comfort. He is possessed by the delusion that the vengeful spirit of the ‘Pazhikari’ who died many years ago is seeking revenge upon his sons…”
“Oh, Lord! What a terrible misfortune! Tell me in detail everything that happened last night!”

“That is precisely why I have come, Ayya! I came to tell you all this and to seek your counsel. The last time, when I came regarding the establishment of the Sundara Chola hospital, the Emperor himself recounted to me that old tale—the time when he was forced to take refuge on an island near Eezha Nadu, and how a Karaiyar maiden saved him from becoming prey to a bear. He spoke of how, for several months on that island, he lived with her as if in a dreamlike paradise. Later, he told me, he was summoned back to this very Thanjai city. He described how, amidst the crowd gathered at the palace gates, he saw the Karaiyar maiden, and how he asked you, his dearest friend, to go and find her and bring her to him. He told me how you went in search of her, only to return and inform him that she had fallen into the sea and perished. Since then, he said, the spirit of that Karaiyar maiden has often come to torment him, and that in recent times her visits have become more frequent…”
“Devi, did you truly believe all this?”

“The tale my father told was so extraordinary that my heart was greatly troubled. I thought perhaps it was a delusion—that the spirit of the dead woman was haunting my father. But the more I pondered, the more doubts arose. One night, Vanathi heard the Emperor’s anguished cries and went to see what was happening. She saw, standing before the King, a figure resembling the younger queen of Pazhuvoor. Struck with terror, she fainted on the spot. From then on, I began to suspect there must be some connection between the Karaiyar maiden and the Pazhuvoor Ilaiyarani. What Vallavaraiyan and Arulmozhi told me confirmed it. Ayya! Could it be that Nandini Devi is, in fact, the daughter of that Karaiyar maiden?”

“Like you, I too can only surmise, Thaaye! Judging by the resemblance, it seems likely. But can we be certain from that alone? Perhaps Nandini Devi is even the youngest sister of the Karaiyar maiden. There are only three people now who know the truth of all this…”
“Who are they, Swami?”

“The first is Periya Piratti Sembiyan Maadevi. Some secret pain gnaws at her heart. But unless she herself chooses to reveal it, we cannot learn what it is by questioning. I know that, when the great Kandaradithar was nearing his end, Periya Piratti confided it to him. Kandaradithar began to tell me, but before he could utter more than a few words, his breath ceased…”
“Who are the other two, sir?”

“The other two are mutes, unable to speak. They are none other than Sendhan Amudhan’s mother and his elder aunt. Of these, we can learn nothing from Amudhan’s mother. She possesses boundless devotion to Sembiyan Maadevi. As long as that lady lives, she will reveal nothing. That is why I have been making great efforts to bring her younger sister, Mandakini, from the land of Eezham…”
“Ah! The name of that Karaiyar maiden is Mandakini? When did you learn that she was still alive?”
“Devi! I have known this for more than twenty-five years.”
“What? What? You have known for twenty-five years and yet you did not tell my father? Sir! Do you not know how much anguish my father suffered, believing she was dead?”
“I know, Lady! I know.”
“And even knowing, you did not tell him the truth?”
Aniruddhar let out a long, heavy sigh. His face betrayed the inner turmoil raging within him. After a moment, he spoke:

“Devi! Twenty-five years ago, I committed a grave wrong. For the first time, I confess it now to you. Was it not your father who sent me to search for the Karaiyar maiden? I went, accompanied by swift riders. We reached Kodikkarai. There we learned that she had fallen from the summit of the lighthouse into the raging sea. Those who witnessed that dreadful scene recounted it. Thyaga Vidangare himself, his voice trembling, his tongue faltering, described it. That is what I too reported to my friend when I returned to Thanjavur…”
“In this, what fault is yours, sir?” asked Kundavai.

“My fault is this: Though the Karaiyar maiden fell into the sea, she did not drown and die. A fisherman who had set out in his boat upon those turbulent waters saw her, rescued her, and brought her aboard. Far beyond Kodikkarai, he landed on the shore. On my return journey, I saw that boat as it beached. I learned who the woman in the boat was. I gave the boatman a large sum of money, instructing him to take her safely to Lanka and to remain there. He agreed, and…” He went. I returned to Thanjavur and reported that the daughter of the Karaiyar had fallen into the sea and perished. I committed such a crime only with the thought that I was doing good for your father, blinded by that intention. I never imagined that this crime, after so many years, would bring about such a disastrous consequence…”

At that moment, the young princess Kundavai interrupted, “Sir! Even if what you did was a crime, you did it only with the intent to benefit my father. After that, did you ever hear anything about that Karaiyar maiden?”

“Why not? I heard about her often. After the prince’s coronation, Sundara Chola went to the Madurai war front. I went to Kashi Kshetra. I stayed there for several years, studying the Vedas and scriptures, and then returned. At that time, in Pazhayarai, I saw Eesana Battar’s father conversing intimately with that Karaiyar maiden. I was astonished. He told me a most wondrous tale. He said that the Karaiyar maiden had stayed for a few days in the garden of the Periya Piratti’s palace, and that she had given birth to twin children there and then fled, leaving them behind. He also said that, from time to time, she would secretly come to see the children. When I asked what had become of the children, he refused to tell me. He said it was a secret known only to Sembiyan Madevi. I thought it best not to probe further and left it at that. Devi! When Arulmozhi, as a child, fell into the Kaveri river, everyone used to say that Mother Kaveri herself saved him, didn’t they? At that time, it struck me that the one who truly saved him was the Karaiyar maiden…”

“What arose in your heart is the truth, sir! Arulmozhi, after seeing that queen in Eezha Nadu, came back and said the same. But listen to this strange thing! Do you know what my father believes? He thinks that the Karaiyar maiden who died falling into the sea has come in spirit form to take revenge on her children. Last night, when the storm raged outside, my father’s inner storm too gained force. He did not sleep the entire night; nor did he let me sleep. He recounted all the old tales again. ‘That vengeful woman who died falling into the sea is now taking revenge on me. She is the one who drowned my Arulmozhi in the sea and killed him! She will not spare Karikalan either!’ he cried out repeatedly. ‘Yama! Will you not take me away while at least one of my sons still lives?’ he wailed. No matter how much I tried to console him, he would not listen. Because of that, I was forced to tell him about Arulmozhivarman being safe at the Buddhist Vihara in Nagapattinam…”
“After that, did the Emperor find some comfort?”

“That was not all; after that, his delirium only grew worse! At first, he did not believe the news at all. But when I told him that I had seen it with my own eyes, he believed me. He asked why I had not brought him along. I told him that after the chills and fever, he did not yet have the strength for travel, and that I would soon make arrangements to bring him here. But I also lightly mentioned the confusion that might arise in the kingdom if he were brought here now. As soon as he heard this, his mind took another turn.

‘This kingdom itself has become a curse for my children. If it were decided that the kingdom would not be theirs, my sons would live in peace and safety. That is why I am so desperate to bring them here!’ he said.

Suddenly, another terror took hold of his mind. Last night, a fierce storm had shaken the entire palace. When the thunderclap ceased for a moment, my father was seized by a frenzy. ‘My daughter! I shall never see Arulmozhi again. I know well the storms and whirlwinds that rise from the southern seas. The storm that blows today will raise waves as tall as coconut trees on the shore. The surging sea will sweep far inland and flood everything. Just as the sea once swallowed Kaveripattinam, it may one day take Nagapattinam as well. The Buddhist vihara that stands between the shore and the canal will not escape forever. That vengeful daughter of the Karaiyar could not take my son into the sea; instead, she will come ashore and kill him! I will go now, stop her, and save my son!’ he cried, trying to rise from his bed. In that attempt, he lost his strength and fell back onto the bed. Sir! If you had heard my father’s sobbing voice at that moment, even stone and mountain would have melted!” said the Young Princess.
At that moment, tears streamed down her cheeks in torrents.

chapters.title: Confusion in the Streets
paragraphs: After witnessing Kundavai’s tears, Vanathi too began to sob uncontrollably. Even the iron heart of Aniruddha Brahmarayar, who had seen countless joys and sorrows in this world, softened at the sight.
“Mother! The one truly responsible for all the hardships the Emperor now endures is this sinner before you. I do not know what penance I must perform to atone for my sins!” he said.

“Sir! There is nothing you do not know. Yet, let me tell you what I know. That Karaiyar’s daughter is not dead. She is alive. If you inform my father of this, his suffering will end and peace will return to his heart. I came to you for this very reason—to ask you to arrange, by any means, to bring my elder sister here. But you have already taken steps towards this!” said the young princess.

“Yes, child! I too had come to the same conclusion. I have decided to inform the Emperor that Mandakini Devi is alive. But if I simply tell him, he will not believe me. How can I convince him that what I said before was a lie, and what I say now is the truth? That is why I thought to bring that lady here first, and then reveal the truth. If he sees her with his own eyes, he will have no choice but to believe. For this very reason, I traveled to the island of Lanka. But the Pazhuvettaraiyars have told the Emperor that I went to Eezha Nadu to conspire with your brother and Periya Velar. To prove that this is not the case, I am determined to bring Mandakini Devi before your father,” said Aniruddhar.
“Sir! If you suddenly bring her before him like that, it might cause harm to my father. He must be informed beforehand, and only then should he be allowed to see her!” said the young princess.

“Yes, yes, that is exactly what I intend to do. I thought I would inform him once Mandakini Devi arrived at this house. I had planned to go to the palace this morning. But before I could, the daughter of Thyagavidangar interfered and caused me disappointment. One day, I will mete out fitting punishment to that wicked woman!” declared the Chief Minister. “Ayyo! Please, do not do anything like that. I do not know whether she is a good woman or a wicked one. But wasn’t it Poonguzhali who saved Arulmozhi from drowning in the sea?”

“Say that God saved him, Mother! The Lord who reclines upon the ocean of milk protected him. Without His grace, what could this young woman have done? If astrology is true, if the effects of the planets and the movements of the stars are real, then neither sea nor fire nor storm nor earthquake can harm the prince…”

“Nothing happens without the Lord’s grace, that is true. But does not the Lord’s power work through human beings? I have decided to send Poonguzhali back to Nagapattinam, sir! Or, if you think otherwise—if you believe it is better to bring Arulmozhi here openly…”

“No, Mother! No! Until it is certain who will ascend the throne, it is best that the people do not know about Arulmozhivarman’s whereabouts. I intend to ask your father for a final decision today. If it is decided that the crown will go to Madurantaka, then it would be best to send your younger brother back to Eezha Nadu. As long as Arulmozhivarman is here, the people of Chola Nadu will never agree to crown Madurantaka. The Chola land will be filled with great battles; the rivers of Chola Nadu will run red with blood…”
“Sir! In that case, is it not best to send Poonguzhali and Sendhan Amudhan back to Nagapattinam as well?”
“That is best. If the Emperor wishes, Arulmozhivarman may come to Thanjavur in secret just once and then return!”
“Yes, yes! Only when he sees with his own eyes that Mandakini Devi and Arulmozhi are alive will the Emperor’s heart find peace.”
“Your father has no worry about the elder prince, does he?”
“None at all; the Emperor believes there is no one in this world who can bring harm to Aditya Karikalan. What do you think, sir?”

“I do not have such confidence. On the battlefield, the elder prince is a peerless hero. But in other places, it is not so difficult to deceive or betray him. The Pazhuvettaraiyars are his enemies. The younger queen of Pazhuvur—”

She is weaving some terrible secret conspiracy against him. I sent both these pieces of news to Karikalan through my disciple. Yet, it bore no fruit. No matter how many times we urged him to come to Thanjavur, he refused. But now, he has gone to the Kadambur Sambuvaraiyar’s palace…”

“Sir! I have sent word to my brother that the younger queen of Pazhuvur might be our own sister. I also sent a message to the brave warrior of the Vanar clan to protect him closely. Ah! If only Vallavaraiyar were here now, we could have sent him to Nagapattinam…”
“To ensure that boy does not fall into any trouble, I too have sent my disciple. Even now, if you send Poonguzhali, I intend to send Thirumalai along with her.”

“Those who went have not yet returned, have they? If my grandaunt arrives, three-quarters of the burden on my heart will be lifted, sir! As soon as she comes, you will meet my father and tell him everything, won’t you? I must tell my mother the whole story from the beginning…”

“Ah! How many sorrows must the daughter of Malayaman bear! And when the old lord of Thirukovalur learns of all this, what will he do? If he finds out that his grandchildren have not been crowned, perhaps Malayaman himself will rise up and threaten to destroy this very land…”

“Leave the task of pacifying my grandfather to me. It is this girl Vanathi’s elder father who worries me. He seems to desire that the woman of Kodumbalur should one day sit upon the Chola throne. Even in this girl’s heart, that desire seems to dwell…”
At this, Vanathi interrupted, her voice brimming with anger, “Akka!…”
At that moment, before Vanathi could say more, Poonguzhali entered. Seeing her come alone, all three were a little startled.
“Daughter of the Karaiyar! Where is your aunt? Where is Thirumalai?” the Prime Minister asked anxiously.
“Sir! My pride has been humbled. As I promised, I could not bring my aunt here.”
“Did you lose sight of her before you left? Or did she refuse to come? If that is so…”

“No, sir! We brought her inside the fort. Only after that did we get caught in the crowd, and then I lost sight of my aunt!” said Poonguzhali. Then she recounted the following details about the incident:

Mandakini Devi, fortunately, was at Sendhan Amudhan’s house at that time. There were reasons for her to remain there. The storm that raged the previous night had left Amudhan’s house in ruins. A tree from the garden had fallen right onto the roof. As for Sendhan Amudhan, he had caught a severe fever from being drenched in the rain that first night, and was lying down, delirious. The two sisters were engaged in clearing away the fallen trees and repairing the house. When Poonguzhali arrived, Mandakini was overjoyed to see her. She hesitated a little upon seeing Thirumalai. But once Poonguzhali assured her that he was one of their own, she gained courage.

On the way, Poonguzhali and Thirumalai discussed what they should say to the mute queen, and how they could persuade her to come with them without hesitation. As planned, Poonguzhali conveyed everything to her aunt. She explained, using sign language, that the Emperor was gravely ill and bedridden, that he could depart this world at any moment, that before his last breath he longed to see the mute queen once more, that he had never forgotten her all these years, and that perhaps, if he saw her, he might gain new strength and live a little longer. She also explained that for this very reason, Prime Minister Aniruddha Brahmarayar had sent people to bring her at any cost, and that she had spent the previous night at the Prime Minister’s palace. She told her that the Emperor’s beloved daughter, Kundavai Devi, was waiting at the Prime Minister’s house to take the mute queen to her father.

After understanding all this, Mandakini agreed to set out with Poonguzhali and Thirumalai. When they reached the fort’s entrance, the Emperor’s Velakkara guards were entering the fort. The three of them stepped aside to let them pass. Mandakini watched the Velakkara troops with unblinking curiosity. Following the Velakkara troops, a huge crowd surged into the fort. The guards’ attempts to stop them and close the gates were in vain.
“We shouldn’t go with this crowd. There is a secret tunnel that leads directly to the Prime Minister’s palace. We can take that way,” said Thirumalai.

Poonguzhali tried to explain this to her aunt. But the mute queen, paying no heed, began to follow the crowd into the fort. Thirumalai and Poonguzhali followed behind her. Even after entering the fort, when Thirumalai suggested again that they could take a different, private route—
Poonguzhali’s aunt paid her no heed. She mingled with the crowd and walked along with them.

For someone usually timid in the presence of crowds, this behavior from her was surprising to the other two. After they had gone a little distance, some people in the crowd began to take particular notice of Mandakini. “Doesn’t this lady look just like the younger queen of Pazhuvoor?” they began to whisper among themselves.

This caused anxiety for both Thirumalai and Poonguzhali. They hurried ahead to stand before Mandakini, trying to stop her. Meanwhile, some who had seen Azhwarkkadiyan said, “Who is this Vaishnavite fellow? Why is he harassing a woman?” These words reached the ears of those at the front of the Velakkara regiment, and they turned back. Encircling the mute queen, they pushed the others away. In that commotion, even Thirumalai and Poonguzhali were forced aside and separated from her.
One of the Velakkara soldiers approached Mandakini Devi and asked, “Mother! Who are you? Who has troubled you? Tell us! We’ll hang him right here!” The mute queen stood without replying.
Just then, someone said, “Doesn’t she look like the queen of Pazhuvoor?” Another replied, “She must be. That’s why she carries herself with such pride!”
“The whole Pazhuvoor clan is full of arrogance!” said another.
These events took place near the palace of the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar. Therefore, some Pazhuvoor warriors came to see what the commotion was about.
The words of the Velakkara soldier—“The whole Pazhuvoor clan is full of arrogance!”—reached their ears.
“Who dares to insult the Pazhuvoor clan? Let him come forward!” demanded one of the Pazhuvoor warriors.
“I said it! What will you do about it?” the Velakkara soldier stepped forward.
“You are the arrogant ones! The time has come for your pride to be shattered!” retorted the Pazhuvoor warrior.
“Ah! You speak so because our prince has been drowned in the sea? It is because of criminals like you that the storm has ravaged the land and brought ruin to the city!” shouted someone in the crowd.
The warrior of Pazhuvur cried, “What did you say, you rascal?” and rushed forward to attack him.
