But the Velakkara soldier intervened and restrained him. Immediately, chaos erupted in the crowd—shouts, confusion, and a flurry of movement.
“Long live the Lords of Pazhuvur!” some shouted, while others raised the cry, “Long live Sundara Chola, sovereign of the three worlds!”
“Long live the Velar of Kodumbalur!”
“Long live Malayaman of Thirukovalur!” other voices rang out.

At that moment, the younger Lord Pazhuvettaraiyar arrived, mounted on horseback, and joined the scene. The moment the crowd saw him, the fighting ceased. The people scattered in all directions, fleeing in panic. The Velakkara soldiers marched ahead, while the Pazhuvur warriors surrounded and escorted Kalandhakandar, announcing his capture. Poonguzhali and Azhwarkkadiyan slipped away to the side of the street, watching everything intently. They could not see Mandakini anywhere.

“Oh no! What is this? How could this have happened? Such is the state of governance in the capital!” Poonguzhali lamented. “How are we to find my aunt now? Could some harm have befallen her? Has someone seized her and taken her away?”
After Kalandhakandar and the Pazhuvur warriors had left, they searched everywhere, but Mandakini was nowhere to be found.

Thirumalai said, “I will search a little longer. You must go at once and inform the Prime Minister and the young Princess. It is not enough for just the two of us to search. The Prime Minister and the Princess will surely make some arrangements.”

Poonguzhali hesitated to leave. Once again, Azhwarkkadiyan urged her, “Listen to me. Nothing could have happened to your aunt. In the crowd, she saw someone she recognized. I could tell from the way she kept her eyes fixed in one direction. That’s why she came along with the crowd. Even now, I believe she has gone after that person. We will surely find her. You go and inform the Prime Minister!”
Thus, Poonguzhali made her way to the Prime Minister’s palace…
Hearing all this, Kundavai was greatly distressed. Aniruddha did not seem as troubled.

“Did you see, Princess! Have you realized now how the demon of rebellion lies in wait, ever ready for an opportunity? All that needs to be known is that Arulmozhi Varman is alive. Then, fire will blaze across the entire kingdom!” he said.

“As long as you remain the Chief Minister, nothing of that sort will come to pass. Now, tell me about my elder brother. It seems as though things are turning out just as I feared! How can we find him?” she asked.

“You need not worry about that; now that he has entered the fortress, he cannot leave without my knowledge. I will make the necessary arrangements for that. I will also arrange for a search. From now on, Mandakini Devi will not leave this place without seeing the Emperor!” he replied.

chapters.title: In the Treasury’s Moonlit Room
paragraphs: At the point where Poonguzhali parted ways with Mandakini Devi, it becomes necessary for us now to follow that lady’s path. The reason for her disappearance amidst the crowd and confusion was, as Alwarkadiyan had said, entirely true. As she entered the fort along with the Velakkara troops, Mandakini caught sight of Ravidasan, the conspirator. Is it not natural that when one sense is diminished, the others become sharper? Mandakini could not hear; she could not speak. But her eyesight was all the keener for it. While Alwarkadiyan and Poonguzhali were both intent on watching Mandakini Devi, Ravidasan, who escaped their notice, did not escape hers.

Mandakini also possessed that innate instinct which enables one to sense approaching good or evil before it arrives. Thus, she immediately understood that Ravidasan had come here with some wicked purpose. Had she not already known that Ravidasan had tried to kill Arulmozhi Varman in Eezha Nadu? Therefore, as she moved along the streets of Thanjavur with the crowd, her gaze never left Ravidasan.

At the height of the confusion, when Chinna Pazhuvettarayar rode in on horseback and the crowd scattered in a rush, Mandakini saw Ravidasan and another man hastily slip away into a side alley. At once, she too hurried in that direction and entered the same alley.

All this happened in the space of a minute, so that Thirumalai, who had been jostled and pushed by the crowd, and Poonguzhali, could not keep track of Mandakini. When they looked again, she was gone. Mandakini, after entering the alley, turned back once or twice to see if Poonguzhali and Thirumalai were following, but she did not see them. Still, she thought it more important to follow Ravidasan.
At the beginning of this tale, it was along this very path that Vandiyathevan had escaped from the men of Kaalandhakandar. Now, Ravidasan and his companion took that same way.
We have met Ravidasan’s companion before as well. He was none other than Soman Sambavan, whom we saw at the midnight conspirators’ gathering in the Thiruppurambiyam monastery.

The two of them hurried swiftly through the winding paths, darting into the thickets. They leapt over fallen trees without a care, paying no heed to the trunks strewn across their way. They crossed muddy pools formed by the rainwater, unmindful of the slippery ground. The wind still blew gently, causing the branches to sway and dance. From time to time, droplets of water fell from the leaves with a soft, splashing sound. Not for a moment did they imagine that anyone would follow them. Therefore, they did not look back, but pressed on with haste. Even if they had turned, they would not have seen Mandakini Devi.

At last, their hurried journey ended at the rear wall of Periya Pazhuvettarayar’s palace garden. A tree, uprooted by the storm, had fallen across the wall and lay broken upon it. Ravidasan and Soman Sambavan easily climbed over the tree, crossed the wall, and leapt down into the garden beyond. Watching them, Mandakini Devi too, after a short while, climbed onto the same tree and descended into the garden on the other side.

Ravidasan left Soman Sambavan at a short distance and approached Periya Pazhuvettarayar’s palace. As both Periya Pazhuvettarayar and the young queen of Pazhuvoor were absent, the palace appeared deserted. Yet, the voices of women could be heard. At one point, two nursemaids came to the rear portico of the mansion. They saw the many trees in the garden that had fallen and lay broken.
“Ah! Does it not look like the Ashoka grove destroyed by Hanuman?” said one.
“If our Sita Devi had been here at this time, she would have been greatly distressed!” said the other.

After conversing thus for a while, as they turned to go back inside, Ravidasan pursed his lips and made a sound like the hoot of an owl. Both nursemaids turned and looked back. Ravidasan was well concealed. One of the nursemaids said, “Look! An owl is hooting in broad daylight! The storm that raged yesterday has addled even the owls’ wits!” The other said nothing.

After a short while, the one who had said nothing returned. She came to the Vasantha Mandapam, which stood between the Pazhuvoor palace and the treasury chamber. Readers may recall that it was in this very mandapam that Vandiyathevan met the queen of Pazhuvoor. The maid looked intently at the garden. Again, the owl’s hoot was heard. The woman walked toward the direction from which the sound came. From behind a tree, Ravidasan stepped forward. With eyes that seemed to possess magnetic power, he gazed at her.
“Sorcerer, have you come? Even the Young Queen isn’t here! Why have you come?” she asked.
“Girl, it is the Young Queen who sent me here!” replied Ravidasan.
“Even where you went before, you didn’t leave the Queen alone? Why have you come here? If anyone finds out…”
“If they find out, what will happen? Will you drown?”

“Don’t say such things! The Younger Pazhuvettarayar already suspects us. He called me and warned me harshly one day. He has ordered that if the sorcerer comes again, I must go and inform him at once…”
“He’s a wretch, let him be! Their time is drawing to a close! You need not worry about anything! I need the key to the treasury chamber—bring it quickly!” said Ravidasan.
“Oh no! I won’t do it!”
“Look here, your mistress’s ring!” Ravidasan showed her the signet ring of the Young Queen.
“Who knows where you stole this from, or what you’ve done?”

“You wretched girl! Do you call me a thief? After seeing how the Young Queen herself trembles at my presence, do you still speak like this? Listen! Tonight, nine spirits will come and carry you alive to the cremation ground…”

“No, no! Let your spirits stay with you. What do I care? If you show me the Young Queen’s ring, I’ll bring you what you asked for. But don’t be hasty! Women often come here to see the ruined garden. I’ll bring you the key when everyone is eating—wait until then!”
“Very well; and bring me some food too! It’s been two days since I ate—bring plenty!” said Ravidasan.

After the nurse had gone, Ravidasan and Soman Sambavan sat atop a fallen tree and spoke together. Unbeknownst to them, Mandakini too had seated herself at a hidden spot some distance away. Though she could not understand what Ravidasan and the nurse had spoken, she guessed that something was about to happen.

After a long time, the old nurse returned. Ravidasan rose and went to meet her. He took from her the food bundle and the bunch of keys she had brought. Then, both of them proceeded along the path that led from the Vasantha Mandapam to the treasure vault. He inserted one key, then a second, and finally turned the third key in the lock; at last, the bolt gave way. Inside the vault, it was pitch dark.
Ravidasan turned to the old nurse and said, “Ah! I have forgotten something! How are we to go into this dark room without a lamp? Bring at least a lamp or a torch!”
“How can I bring a lamp or a torch in broad daylight? What if someone sees and grows suspicious?”
“That’s not my concern! Are you saying you lack the cleverness for such a task? I won’t believe it. Bring a lamp or a torch, somehow! Otherwise, I’ll send twelve ravenous ghouls at midnight to—”
“Oh dear, enough! I’ll manage to bring it somehow,” the old nurse replied.
“In the meantime, I’ll finish my meal,” said Ravidasan.

After the nurse set off towards the palace, Ravidasan, carrying the food bundle, entered the garden and went to Soman Sambavan. Handing him the bundle, he said, “You may have to stay in the vault for two or three days. We must wait for the right opportunity, mustn’t we? So, keep this food bundle with you. Take your tools and come with me, without making a sound! That woman has gone to fetch a lamp. You must slip into the vault before she returns.”
Both of them moved swiftly; Mandakini followed them without their knowledge.

chapters.title: The Underground Path
paragraphs: After carefully surveying all four directions, Ravidasan pointed to the open door of the moonlit chamber and instructed Soman Sambavan to go inside.
“At first, your eyes won’t see anything in the darkness, so don’t stand near the door! Go a little further in and stand there!” he said.

As soon as Soman Sambavan entered the moonlit chamber, it was as if the darkness had swallowed him whole. Then, Ravidasan turned back along the walkway and made his way to Nandini Devi’s Vasantha Mandapam. From there, he kept watch on the entrance of the Pazhuvettaraiyar palace. If anyone besides the old nurse happened to come, he might have to rush into the moonlit chamber and bolt the door from inside—wouldn’t that be necessary?

While Ravidasan stood thus in the Vasantha Mandapam, his eyes fixed on the palace entrance, Mandakini glided silently toward the open moonlit chamber and entered. For one accustomed to spending countless nights in the depths of dense forests, what fear could the darkness of that chamber hold? Within a few moments, her eyes grew accustomed to the gloom. She saw the man who had come with Ravidasan stumbling against a pillar some distance away. She moved in the opposite direction. There, she found a staircase. The path from the moonlit chamber descended below. She went down the steps and stood at the bottom.

Soman Sambavan must have heard some faint sound. “Who’s there? Who’s there?” he called out. His voice, traveling through the open doorway, reached Ravidasan’s ears faintly. At that very moment, Ravidasan saw the old nurse approaching the palace entrance, a lamp in her hand. He hurried forward, intent on warning Soman Sambavan. Entering the vestibule of the moonlit chamber, he called out, “Sambava! Where are you? Did you call me?”
“Yes, I called you!”
“Was it so urgent? What if someone outside heard your voice? Do you think I’d just leave you here and walk away?”
“No, no! I called you to ask something,” said Soman Sambavan, moving closer to Ravidasan. At that moment, a bright light appeared at the entrance of the moon chamber.
“Oh no! That woman has come with the lamp; she will see you. Go! Go! Move away and stand behind the pillar! Quickly!” whispered Ravidasan.
Soman Sambavan hurriedly retreated. The next instant, the nurse stood at the doorway of the moon chamber, holding a lamp in her hand.
“Sorcerer! Sorcerer! Where have you gone?” she called.
“I haven’t gone anywhere; I was waiting here for you,” said Ravidasan, approaching her and taking the lamp from her hand.

“Girl! Lock the door from outside. Come back in exactly one naazhikai with the key! Knock on the door; if I give the signal, open it! Make sure no one is around when you open it!” Ravidasan instructed.
“Very well, sorcerer! But I warn you—Chinna Pazhuvettarayar has grown suspicious about something. If you get caught, don’t give me away!” pleaded the nurse.
“Woman! Don’t worry needlessly! Didn’t I tell you? Even Kaalandhakakandan’s final hour has come near!”
“Why do you ask me to come back and open the door again? Isn’t there another way out of the moon chamber?”
“That way cannot be used tonight; the Vettar river is overflowing its banks. Go now! Come back in exactly one naazhikai!”

The nurse went outside and locked the door. At the very moment she locked it from outside, Ravidasan bolted it from within. Then, holding the lamp aloft, he hurried towards the place where Soman Sambavan was waiting.
“Sambava! You said you had something important to ask me? Ask now,” he said.
“Have you been here before?” Soman Sambavan asked.
“Before? I have come here many times. Where do you think all the things we have stored came from?” replied Ravidasan.
“That’s not what I meant. Just now, after you left me here, you went outside, didn’t you? Again…”
“I have only just come now, haven’t I?”
“Did you come in the middle at any point?”
“I did not come in the middle; nor at the side. Why do you ask?”
“Just a short while after you left, the light at the entrance suddenly vanished. I bumped into a pillar.”
“Perhaps the door opened and closed on its own.”
“It seemed as if some figure entered; I clearly heard footsteps.”

“It must be your imagination. This moon-chamber is just like that—in the darkness, shadows appear and vanish in an instant. Strange sounds can be heard. Some who entered here have died out of sheer terror. Their skeletons still lie scattered about. Pazhuvetarayan has deliberately left those bones untouched. He wants any intruder who enters this moon-chamber in secret to see the bones and die of fright…”
“Is it really possible to enter this moon-chamber without anyone knowing?”
“Ordinarily, no one can enter. Except for me, I do not think anyone else has come in. Even I entered only with the help of the young queen or her companion…”
“Then why did you speak of human skeletons?”

“That? If Pazhuvetarayan wishes to punish someone terribly, he leaves the door of the moon-chamber slightly open. Those who have heard of the treasure chamber, driven by greed, enter here. After that, they never leave.”
“Are you saying that, except for you, no one who has entered here has ever come out again?”
“In the past, that was true. But now, I have doubts about two people…”
“I know whom you mean—Valavarayan and Kandhamaran.”
“Yes.”
“And yet, we have let them live!”

“How many times must I tell you? The Young Queen has kept Vallavaraiyan here for an important purpose. When Sundara Chozhan’s line is destroyed, Vandiyathevan too will die. That time is fast approaching. Come! Come! I will show you all the secret passages in this underground chamber… But be careful about one thing! There is a hall here where heaps of navaratna gems are stored. For a hundred years, the Chozhas have been piling up these precious stones, mound upon mound. If your mind is ensnared by the allure of those gems, you might forget the very mission for which you have come!”
“Ravidasan! To whom are you saying these words? Did I not swear upon the headless body of Veerapandiyan, just as you did?”

“Who said you did not? Even my own mind wavered a little when I saw those heaps of gems; that is why I warned you. Let it be; come, let us go. First, I will show you the way to the Chozha palace. After I have shown you, you can take your time to explore this entire underground chamber. It may be useful to you at another time.”
Ravidasan took up the lamp and walked ahead, with Soman Sambavan close by his side.

Once, Periya Pazhuvettarayar and the Young Queen Nandini had walked this very same path. In the smoke-lit glow of the lamp, the pillars of the underground chamber and their shadows loomed like great black demons. The bats that dwelled in the darkness resembled terrifying little goblins. Here and there, gigantic spider webs could be seen, and in their midst, monstrous spiders lurked. On the ground, strange creatures of various shapes crawled—some with great speed, others very slowly. As Ravidasan had said, many unidentifiable sounds echoed through the chamber. The roar of the storm still raging outside somehow found its way into the subterranean tunnels, reverberating within.
Suddenly, Soman Sambavan stopped in alarm and said, “Ravidasan! Did you not hear something like footsteps?”

“Of course I heard! It is the sound of our own footsteps. Do not be frightened for nothing! If you are so afraid even while I am with you, how will you manage to stay here for two or three days alone?” said Ravidasan.

“I am not afraid of anything; rather than being tormented by doubts after you leave, I wish to ask and know now, while you are still here. You said that some of those who entered this underground chamber died here, didn’t you?” asked Soman Sambavan.

“Yes; their spirits still wander here. So what of it? It is the ghosts who shriek in fear when they see us! That young fellow Vandiyathevan managed to stay here without fear and somehow escaped from this chamber. You and I, who have seen so many ghosts and demons, why should we be afraid?”
“Let there be ghosts and demons; who is afraid of such things? But there might be other creatures, poisonous beasts lurking here, might there not?”
“Are you afraid of snakes and scorpions? At the mere sight of us, they’ll slither away into their holes and hide…”
“Even so, the thought of staying here for two or three days is unsettling, Ravidasan! If, before that, by chance the opportunity arises…?”

“No, no! Do not make that mistake! Today is Tuesday; you must wait through Wednesday and Thursday. Watch carefully for the time when Sundara Cholan is alone. His chief queen is always by his side. On Friday night, she will certainly go to the temple of Durga Parameswari. That night, you must accomplish your task. The day the line of Sundara Cholan is wiped out will be Friday. If anything happens before or after, the plan will be ruined!” said Ravidasan.

Speaking thus, the two of them walked swiftly. Only Soman Sambavan kept glancing all around as he went. Yet, without their knowledge, the Mute Queen, hiding behind pillars and moving without a sound, was following them closely. They reached from one side of the underground tunnel to the other. Before them stood a tall wall. Nowhere did it appear to have a doorway. But from the top of the wall, a little light filtered in through a small balcony.
Ravidasan handed the torch to Sambavan and, gripping the jutting stones and rough edges of the steep wall, climbed up. He peered out through the balcony for a while, then swiftly slid back down.
“Must we jump out through that balcony? Is that the way?” asked Sambavan.

“No, no. Through that trapdoor, only a rat could slip in. But if you look through it, you can see the Chola palace. Not just the palace—you can see the most important place within it,” said Ravidasan.
“The place where Sundara Cholan lies bedridden?” asked Sambavan.
“Yes. Through this trapdoor, you can observe the movement of people there. Now, come with me! Watch carefully what I do!”
So saying, Ravidasan bent down. He pressed his foot firmly on a round stone, then, using both hands, pushed aside a square-shaped stone. A hidden passageway opened below.
“Heavens! A subterranean path inside the moonlit chamber?” exclaimed Soman Sambavan in astonishment.
“Yes. No one knows of this passage except Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar and the younger queen. I am the third who knows! Now you know too! You have seen how to open it, haven’t you?”

Both of them descended into the passage; soon, the light from their lamp faded away. From the place where she had been hiding, the mute queen sprang forward in a single leap. She peered intently at the open passage. She placed a foot on the edge, as if to descend, but then, reconsidering, quickly withdrew her leg.

After pondering for a moment, she looked toward the spot where Ravidasan had climbed the wall earlier. In a single bound, she leapt there and, imitating his movements, climbed up the wall. Reaching the trapdoor, she sat upon it and looked beyond. Hugging the wall, she could see the garden and, beyond that, a beautiful palace with upper stories. The sight of that mansion sent a thrill through her body. Her heart told her that those dearest to her, dearer than life itself, were inside that palace. She also sensed that those who had taken the secret path intended harm to her beloved ones. She prayed silently to the deity dwelling in her soul, asking for the strength to thwart their evil intentions.

Just as she considered whether to descend, an astonishing sight appeared on the upper floor of the distant mansion. Ravidasan and Soman Sambavan, who had just been in the moonlit chamber, had climbed up and were now hiding behind the pillars. They peered intently into the inner quarters of the palace.
At that moment—

Because it was daytime, the upper storey of that palace was clearly visible. Ravidasan did not have a torch in his hand. Sambavan held only a spear. Ravidasan took that spear from him and aimed it toward the interior of the palace, as if preparing to hurl it.

At that moment, it seemed as though the heart of the mute queen had stopped beating. Fortunately, Ravidasan did not throw the spear. He only pretended as if he would, then handed it back to Soman Sambavan. The next instant, both of them disappeared from sight.

The mute queen, too, climbed down from the balcony along the wall. She kept her eyes fixed on the spot where the secret passage was visible and concealed herself there. After a short while, the light of a torch once again appeared in that passage. The two men emerged, closed the entrance to the underground path.
“You’ve learned well how to open it, haven’t you?” asked Ravidasan.

“I have learned. You need not worry anymore. The task I have agreed to—I will surely complete it! Sundara Cholan’s life will end with this coming Friday! In the same way, you too must carry out your part,” replied Sambavan.

“The young queen will take care of Karikalan; I have no worry about that. It seems that the ‘little tiger’ has escaped from the sea and is now in Nagapattinam. But this time, he cannot escape. The two ghostly women who rescued him are also here in Thanjai now. I saw the boatwoman and the mute girl among the crowd. Even that traitorous Vaishnavite is here. Therefore, the little tiger cannot escape anymore. I am going to send the signal to Nagapattinam. Sundara Cholan’s lineage will be destroyed this Friday…”
“After that, won’t there still be Madurantaka Thevan?”
“Let him be. It is better for such a fool to sit on the Chola throne for a while longer. The Pandya Emperor must also come of age, must he not?”
Speaking thus, Ravidasan and Soman Sambavan hurried away by the path they had come.

chapters.title: Royal Audience
paragraphs: After they had disappeared, the mute queen came to the spot where the entrance to the underground passage was hidden. She peered closely, examining the place, and tried to open the passage, but she could not. When Ravidasan had opened it earlier, she had been standing at a distance, so she had not been able to observe how he managed it. She was certain in her heart that at least one of the two men would surely return there. Therefore, she resolved to wait at that very spot.

Her expectation was not in vain. After sending Ravidasan outside, Soman Sambavan returned there. In his hand was a lamp, but it burned more dimly than before. He had spoken to Ravidasan with great confidence, yet it was clear from the way he glanced about nervously that fear still lingered in his heart.

He came near the place where the passage opened and sat down, trembling. After a short while, the lamp went out. Then, he kept glancing up repeatedly at the beam at the top of the wall. Through it, a faint light had entered, but now that light was slowly fading away. When he saw that the light had faded completely and realized that the sun had set, he began to open the underground passage once more. At that moment, Mandakini came and stood nearby.
The passage opened; Soman Sambavan was about to descend into it.

Just then, in that moonlit chamber, very close to him, a long, drawn-out wailing sound—“Kreech!”—echoed. Soman Sambavan was a man who had seen many terrors in his life. Yet, he had never heard such an unnatural, unearthly sound. If ghosts truly existed and if they had a voice, surely it must sound like this, he thought. At the first cry, Sambavan hesitated and stood still, waiting until the echo died away.

When the wailing cry sounded a second time, the hair on his body stood on end. After the third, even closer cry, his resolve crumbled. In that pitch-dark, moonlit chamber, he began to run blindly, heedless of the path or direction.

Once he had vanished, the mute queen descended into the passage. After a few steps, the way became level. She walked quickly, almost darting forward. Even if Soman Sambavan had seen her entering and tried to follow, he could not have caught her—so swift was her pace. Like a path leading to the very depths of hell, that dark, narrow way stretched ahead... It appeared so. Yet, even that had its end. Where the sheer wall ended, a small gap could be seen above. Some steps could be felt by hand. As she climbed up those steps, her head suddenly struck something. Between the steps of the subterranean path and the place where her head hit above, there were small gaps. Through one of those, she slipped out.

All around, massive demonic forms could be seen. Having seen grand statues on the island of Eelam, this sight did not astonish her. She carefully noted where the path she had emerged from ended. The ten-headed Ravana was lifting Mount Kailasa with his twenty arms. Upon the mountain, Shiva and Parvati were seated in majesty. Where Ravana lifted the mountain, there was a hollow below. His twenty arms held the mountain aloft. Through the gap between two of those arms, she realized she had entered the sculpted mandapam.
No ordinary onlooker would ever know that such a path existed beneath Kailasa. Nor would anyone think to descend and explore it. It was indeed a perfect hiding place in times of need.

For several hours, Mandakini gazed in wonder at the marvels of that sculpted subterranean passage. Though the light was very dim, her sharp eyes, accustomed to seeing in the night, could discern everything clearly. In one place, there was a statue depicting King Shibi, one of the Chola ancestors, cutting flesh from his own body to save the life of a dove. Was it not because they were born in the lineage of Shibi that the Cholas earned the title ‘Sembiyan’? After closely observing that sculpture, the mute queen moved on.

A grand sculpture depicted the descent of the Ganga from the head of Lord Shiva. Nearby, Bhagiratha stood with folded hands. The river Bhagirathi, falling down, entered the mouth of a great rishi and exited through his ear. The small sage collecting water in his kamandalu from the flowing Ganga must be the famed Agastya, known as the dwarf sage. He poured the water from his kamandalu onto another small mountain. The river, swelling from the kamandalu, grew larger and larger as it flowed. In these sculpted representations of the Ganga and the Kaveri, arrangements must have been made for water to flow when they were created. But now, there was no water in them.

The Kaveri wound its way through rocky hills and groves thick with trees. On either side stood many Shiva temples. At the place where the Kaveri was to merge with the sea, the wall of the sculpted mandapam stood. Something— Suspicious, the mute queen pressed her hand against the wall of the fortification at that spot. A small door opened. Through it, she emerged into the palace garden. Beyond that, the lofty terraces of the palace could be seen, not far away.

She looked all around; in the dim, wavering light of twilight, it was clear that no one was in the garden. Just as in the Pazhuvettaraiyar’s garden, here too trees had fallen and lay scattered, as if struck down. Therefore, even if someone were in the garden, they could not have seen her emerge from the sculpture pavilion. She decided to wait, pressed close to the pavilion, until it grew properly dark. Perhaps that spear-wielding Yama’s messenger might come this way. So, she kept glancing inside the sculpture pavilion from time to time.

One by one, the palace lamps began to blaze. In a short while, the entire palace shone with a dazzling brilliance. The lamps lit in the lower rooms cast their glow outside through latticed windows. The lamps burning on the upper terraces competed with the stars in the sky, shining just as brightly.
“Alas! The night seems far more dangerous than the day!” thought Mandakini.

She carefully observed the palace from all four sides. She noticed that only the part of the palace closest to the sculpture pavilion had fewer lights. It was in this section that the villain who had tried to kill her beloved prince—the very life she had saved from the Kaveri floods—and his companion had climbed to the upper terrace. It was here that Ravidasan, having received a spear from another, had taken aim as if to hurl it at someone. Fortunately, not many lamps were lit in this area. What could be the reason for that? Well, she would soon find out.

Once darkness had fully settled over the palace garden, Mandakini darted from the pavilion’s threshold with the speed of a startled deer and reached the palace. In that rear section of the palace, there were circular halls and rows of supporting pillars, and in many places, stairways leading up to the main terrace. In the lower halls, there were grand copper vessels used for cooking at great feasts, ancient ivory palanquins, broken thrones—many such objects lay scattered about.

After wandering among these for a while, Mandakini finally dared to climb one of the stairways. Just as below, on the main terrace too there were circular halls, pillars of fantastic design supporting the roof, intricately carved latticed windows, moonlit courtyards, and inlaid crystal... Terraces too could be seen. In those lofty halls, which seemed utterly devoid of human presence, Mandakini wandered in circles. She hesitated greatly to approach the inner edges of the terrace. At one spot, noticing the glow of a lamp from below, she crept forward and peered from behind a pillar. Ah! What did she see? She beheld sights from which her eyes could not turn away.

In the center of a vast hall, upon a cot adorned with intricate paintings—a sabra-manjaka bed—someone lay reclining. Around him stood four women and two men at that moment. From their demeanor, it was clear they regarded the one on the bed with awe and reverence. A little farther off, two nursemaids stood with even greater respect.

Only a single lamp burned in that hall. It too was fixed upon a stand near the bed, casting a dim and uncertain light. Mandakini first looked at those gathered around. Among them, she recognized her own beloved niece, Poonguzhali. The others she had seen before, a few times, from hidden places. Yet, she did not know exactly who each of them was.

After observing those assembled, Mandakini, with great hesitation, turned her gaze to the one lying upon the bed. For a moment, her heart stood still. Yes—it was he! The man who, long ages ago—so long it seemed like another birth—had, when she was a little girl running and playing in the forests, come to a secluded spot and stolen her heart and soul. He was the one who, for a time, had turned the haunted island where she lived into a paradise. The very man who had been taken away by those who arrived in a great ship! Ah! How changed he was now!

Even after those days that seemed like a previous birth, Mandakini had seen him many times without his knowledge. When he sailed in pleasure boats upon the Kaveri river, she had watched from the thick bushes along the shore. When he paraded through the streets of the cities in a golden chariot drawn by white horses, she had stood among the crowds and gazed upon him. But it had been some time since she last saw him. In that interval, how he had changed! A beard and mustache had grown upon his face. His cheeks had sunk and withered; wrinkles creased his brow. Ah! Where had the magnetic radiance that once shone in those eyes gone? O God! Can men truly change so much? On the island of Lanka, Mandakini had seen many stricken with poisonous fever, and at the hour of death after long illness, she had seen the mute queen.
Ah! Once, his face had shone with the radiance of the golden sun, overflowing with vigor—how greatly it has changed now! Perhaps, his final moments are drawing near!

Suddenly, Mandakini remembered the terrifying scene she had witnessed the previous evening. It was at that very spot she had seen Ravidasan, the assassin, and his companion standing. From there, they had aimed their spear. Had they, perhaps, intended to hurl it at the man now lying on the bed? This thought sent violent tremors through Mandakini’s body. Her vision blurred; she felt as if she might faint. Clutching the pillar tightly, she steadied herself, planting her feet firmly and holding on.

chapters.title: The Accusation
paragraphs: For several days, the heart and body of Emperor Sundara Chola had been greatly weakened. When the Young Princess told the Prime Minister that the Emperor had not slept at all on the stormy night, it was no exaggeration. That entire day, his mind had been restless and unsettled. In the afternoon, the Younger Pazhuvettarayar came and only increased his agitation. Most importantly, he leveled many accusations against Prime Minister Aniruddha. He claimed that ever since the Prime Minister had arrived in Thanjavur, all the strict regulations regarding who could enter the fortress had been broken. He said that many people, pretending to come to see the Prime Minister, were gaining entry into the fort, and that this could endanger the Emperor’s very safety.

Hearing these two accusations, the Emperor merely smiled to himself. He did not consider them of great importance. But he could not so easily dismiss the further allegations made by Kalandhakandar. He reported that, that day, a dispute between the people who had come from outside and the Velakkara guards had nearly erupted into a great riot in the streets, and that it was only by good fortune that he happened to be present at the time, and was able to prevent any disaster by pacifying both sides and sending them away.

He went on to say that, though the entire land knew of Aniruddha Brahmarayar’s impeccable reputation, his recent actions seemed contrary to that. He alleged that the Prime Minister had forcibly brought a woman from Kodikkarai, and had used the Pazhuvur palace’s palanquin and men for this purpose. He added that, not knowing the reason, he had sent his own men and palanquin, and that if any disgrace were to arise from this, it would fall upon the head of the Pazhuvur clan.

Finally, he spoke of yet another suspicious incident. “I had heard that some magician was frequently visiting the palace of the Elder Pazhuvettarayar, and this had caused me concern. Since I learned that he was coming to see the Young Princess, I hesitated to take any action. Nevertheless, I had appointed a spy to keep an eye on that palace. Today, the spy came and reported that someone had climbed over the back wall into the garden of the Treasurer’s mansion. I immediately sent some men to capture him. They caught a man red-handed in the garden of the mansion. When they discovered who it was, it turned out to be none other than Alwarkadiyan, the beloved disciple of the Prime Minister.”
“Why did you climb over the wall and jump down?”—when asked this question, he refused to answer. “It was the order of the Prime Minister,” he said.

Emperor! If this Aniruddha Brahmarayar continues to act in this manner, how can I be responsible for the security of the Thanjai fort? Since my elder brother is not in town, I am compelled to bring all this to your ears!”
Thus, when the Younger Pazhuvettarayar voiced his complaint, it only deepened the emperor’s inner turmoil.

“Very well, Aniruddhar is coming here this evening. I will inquire into all this. Above all, the matter of ordering a woman to be forcibly brought from Kodikkarai has wounded my heart. That is true, is it not, Commander? There is no doubt about it?” he asked.

“None at all! The palanquin bearers and the soldiers who accompanied them came to me at midnight yesterday and told me everything. When they neared the Thanjai fort, they were caught in a storm. A tree by the roadside was uprooted and fell, causing danger to some. They said it was a great blessing that the tree did not fall upon the palanquin. Fortunately, the ill omen of a woman’s misfortune was averted! Along with investigating this, Your Majesty must also conduct a thorough inquiry into the matter of Azhwarkkadiyan!” he declared, and with that, Kaalandhaka Kandar took his leave of the emperor.

The Younger Pazhuvettarayar did not wish to be present when Aniruddhar arrived. He feared that the Prime Minister might ask him some unrelated, confusing question and put him in a difficult position. Most importantly, if Aniruddhar, in his presence, managed to obtain an order from the emperor to open the treasury to aid the people afflicted by the storm, it would become a great nuisance. How would he face his elder brother the next day?

From that morning itself, the emperor had been expecting Aniruddhar’s arrival. But it was only at sunset that the Prime Minister came. Even his steadfast heart was now somewhat unsettled. The careful plan he had laid had gone awry. He had hoped to receive some news about Mandakini, and only then go to see the emperor, so he kept postponing his visit to the palace. In the afternoon, Azhwarkkadiyan came and conveyed some troubling news. He suspected that the Mute Queen might have left, that he had followed a narrow passage where she might have gone, and that he saw a woman climbing over the garden wall of the Pazhuvettarayar mansion, whom he thought could be the Mute Queen. He too had climbed the wall, and before he could begin searching the garden, the Younger Pazhuvettarayar’s men had come and apprehended him.
“I could not tell them the real reason, sir. That is why I had to use your name to secure her release!” he said.

This news caused great anxiety to the Prime Minister. “With so many palaces within this Thanjavur fort, must she enter only the residence of Periya Pazhuvettarayar? We cannot even order a public search for her. Still, let us see what can be done. In one way, it is fortunate that Periya Pazhuvettarayar is not in town. We can station guards around his palace. I also have a man inside that palace; I will send word to him as well! Even so, how much trouble this boatwoman has caused!” said the Prime Minister.
“Swami! Even if the boatwoman had not interfered, it is not certain that the mute queen would have acted as you wished. She would have tried to escape somehow!” said Azhwarkadiyan.

“I have a certain faith. A woman who has come this far will not leave without seeing the Emperor. Let us do all we can. But it is not right to delay any longer in taking her to see the Emperor. You bring that boatwoman and come with me! All news concerning the two princes must be conveyed to the Emperor. If the boatwoman who saved the younger prince from the sea tells him about it in person, perhaps the Emperor will believe?”

The Prime Minister Aniruddha, his disciple, and Poonguzhali went to the Emperor’s palace. At the entrance, the young princess and Vanathi were waiting for them. The news that the mute queen had not been captured distressed the young princess. The news that she had entered the gardens of Periya Pazhuvettarayar’s palace increased her anxiety. She feared that some terrible consequence might arise from this.
“Sir! Isn’t there a secret tunnel leading out from Periya Pazhuvettarayar’s palace? What if she escapes through that way?”

The Prime Minister remembered Vandiyathevan. “Mother! Is it so easy to find that way? Is everyone as fortunate as that youth of the Vanar clan? Still, I will arrange to station men outside the fort as well!” he said.

Afterwards, leaving Azhwarkkadiyan and Poonguzhali with the young princess, the Chief Minister alone went to the place where the Emperor lay. After paying the customary respects to the Emperor and to Vanamadevi, who was seated nearby, he explained that he could not come sooner because he had been arranging the necessary measures to address the destruction caused by the storm throughout the Chola country. The Emperor felt some satisfaction upon learning the details of these arrangements.

“At least you are here now, in the absence of the Prince! That is good. But what is this I hear? I am told you have forcibly brought a woman from Kodikkarai. The Commander of the Fort just mentioned it. Brahmarayar! I never expected such an action from you! Perhaps there was some urgent reason for it. If so, could you not have informed me? Or have you all decided that, since I am an invalid, there is no need to tell me anything, nor to consult me about anything?

Kundavai tells me that Arulmozhi Varman escaped drowning in the sea and is now staying at the Buddhist Vihara in Nagapattinam. I do not know whether I should be glad or sorrowful about this. Why has he, after reaching the shore safely, not come here? Why has no one informed me until now that he has survived and is safe? Minister! So many things are happening around me without my knowledge. In my own kingdom, many matters proceed without my awareness. In such a situation, to remain alive is more—”
As the Emperor spoke thus, his throat choked with emotion; tears brimmed in his eyes.

Aniruddha, who had remained silent all this while out of respect, now interjected, “My Lord! Please, enough. It has been forty years since our friendship began. Never once have I acted against your welfare; nor shall I ever do so. Perhaps, to spare you needless distress, I have withheld a thing or two from you. If that is a fault, forgive me. Now I shall answer all your questions. I beg you, be merciful and remain calm.”

“Chief Minister! In this life, I shall never again know peace of mind. I do not know whether I shall find it even in another birth. When my beloved children and my dearest friend, the Chief Minister himself, conspire against me…”

“My lord, soon you will come to know who are the conspirators working against you. I am not an accomplice to that treachery. I hold the post of Prime Minister now only in name. I have already told you, many times, that I am ready to hand over this position to Periya Pazhuvetarayar. Even now, I am prepared for that. If you have even the slightest dissatisfaction with me…”

“Yes, Prime Minister, yes! At any moment, all of you are ready to abandon me and walk away. The only one who will stay with me until my last breath, who will die with me, is this daughter of Malayaman. Among all the sins I have committed, perhaps I have also done some good deeds. That is why I was blessed to have her as my life’s companion!” said the Emperor.
Hearing these words, Vanamadevi, who was seated on the cot near the Emperor, was overcome with sobs. She immediately rose and went into the next room.
“O King! Every word you spoke about the daughter of Malayaman is the truth. The children born of her sacred womb, too, have unmatched devotion and loyalty towards you.”

“Yet, they do not heed my words. They do not obey my commands. They do all sorts of things without my knowledge. You too join with them! You already knew that Arulmozhi Varman escaped from the sea and is now at the Buddhist Vihara in Nagapattinam, did you not? Why did you not tell me?”

“Forgive me, my lord! Until yesterday, I did not know that for certain. I was only sure that the prince’s life was not in danger. Would all the astrologers’ predictions about the time of his birth turn out to be false?”

“Prime Minister! There is no end to the harm that astrology can cause. I am thinking of banishing all astrologers from this kingdom. It is because of what they said about Arulmozhi’s horoscope that everyone is striving to place him on the throne while I am still alive; are you not one among them?”

“By all that is true, no, my lord! On the contrary, I thought it would be better if the young prince stayed away from Chola land for a while. When I went to Lanka, I told him as much. But as soon as I returned, the Pazhuvetarayar’s men hurried to capture the prince and bring him—” They have come to Lanka. You too have given your consent for this. Since this news has spread throughout the land and cities, the people are furious with the Pazhuvettarayar brothers. Among the people, there is talk that it was they who deliberately sank the ship that brought the prince…”

“Lies, Prime Minister! Lies! All of it is utter falsehood! Parthibendran Pallavan has told me everything. The prince did not come on the ship sent by the Pazhuvettarayars. He came on Parthibendran’s ship. On the way, he jumped into the sea of his own accord. He said it was to save someone who was on another burning ship, and though Parthibendran tried to stop him, he would not listen and leapt into the raging sea. Now, when I think about it, it all seems to be a lie, a plot devised to deceive me. The pain I feel is only when I think that Kundavai too is involved in this conspiracy. Even if the whole world turned against me, I believed Kundavai would always be by my side. I have told her stories that even a father would hesitate to tell his daughter…”

“King of Kings! Even if the whole world claims that the young princess has plotted against you, I will not believe it; nor should you. If the young princess has not told you something, there must be a reason for it. There is no falsehood in the young prince jumping into the sea to save his friend. The boatwoman who rescued the prince and his friend from the sea and brought them to shore is waiting in the next room. She witnessed everything that happened in Lanka with her own eyes. Your Majesty! Shall I summon her?” said Aniruddha.
The Emperor, with great eagerness, said, “Is that so? Call her at once. Prime Minister!... Is she the same woman whom you had forcibly brought from Kodikkarai?”
“The woman who came in the Pazhuvettarayar’s palanquin is waiting in the next room. I will call her now,” said Aniruddha, and as he clapped his hands, Poonguzhali and Azhwarkadiyan entered.

chapters.title: The Dream Before Dawn
paragraphs: After closely observing Poonguzhali, the Emperor asked, “I have not seen this girl before, have I? Yet, her face seems somewhat familiar. Brahmarayar! Who is she?”
“She is the daughter of Thyaga Vidangar from Kodikkarai. Her name is Poonguzhali!”
“Ah! That explains it!” exclaimed the Emperor. Then, speaking softly to himself, he muttered, “She bears a slight resemblance to her aunt! But she is not quite like her; there is a great difference.”

These mutterings of the Emperor reached Poonguzhali’s ears faintly. Until that moment, Poonguzhali had never seen the Emperor. She had heard tales that he surpassed even Manmatha in beauty. She had always imagined that the father of the prince must indeed be such a man. But now, seeing the Emperor, whose form was worn by bodily ailments and tormented by mental anguish, she was struck with astonishment. She remembered how she had once thought to quarrel with the Emperor for abandoning her aunt, and now she felt ashamed of that thought. Fear, wonder, and shyness overwhelmed her so much that, upon beholding the Emperor, she even forgot to offer her salutations.
“Child! Is your father Thyaga Vidangar well?” the Emperor asked, turning to her.

Only then did Poonguzhali regain her senses. She realized she was standing in the presence of the Emperor, who ruled under one royal umbrella from Lanka to the Krishna River. At once, she fell to the ground in obeisance, then rose and stood with folded hands in respectful greeting.
Sundara Chozhar turned to Aniruddhar and asked, “This girl can speak, can’t she? Or is she, like her aunt, mute in one respect?”
At this, his face shrank with the pain of memory.
“Emperor! This girl can speak. She alone can speak as much as nine women put together! She must have been struck dumb with shock at beholding Your Majesty,” replied Aniruddhar.

“Yes, it seems that whenever anyone sees me, they fall silent. No one ever says a word to me!” said the Emperor. Once again, looking at Poonguzhali, Sundara Chozhar asked, “Girl! The Prime Minister says that you saved Prince Arulmozhi from the raging sea. Is that true?”
Poonguzhali hesitated, faltering, “Yes, my lord!… If that is a crime…”
The Emperor laughed; the sound of his laughter echoed with a terrible resonance.

“Brahmarayar! Listen to what this girl says! She asks, ‘If that is a crime.’ She says that saving the prince’s life is a crime. It seems as if I wished for my son to drown and die in the sea. Has someone told her that I am such a monster? Prime Minister, do all the people of the land think of me in this way?”

“Lord! She has spoken out of fear. Please do not take it to heart. Girl! For saving the prince, the entire Chozha kingdom owes you a debt of gratitude. The Emperor too has received boundless joy. For that, whatever reward you desire, you may ask and receive it. Now, narrate everything that happened in detail to the Emperor! Speak without fear!” said the Prime Minister.
“Let this girl first answer one thing. She claims to have saved the prince from the sea—how does she know that it was indeed the prince? Has she seen him before?” asked the Emperor.

“Yes, my lord! When the prince boarded the ship with his warriors to go to Eezha Nadu, I saw him several times. Once, the prince even called me ‘Samudra Kumari’—the Princess of the Sea!” replied Poonguzhali.
“Aha! Now this girl has found her tongue!” said the Chozha Emperor.

Afterwards, as the Prime Minister repeatedly prompted her with questions, Poonguzhali recounted everything from the time she took Vandiyathevan to Lanka, up to the point when she brought the prince to Nagapattinam. But, as Aniruddhar had cautioned her, she said nothing about Mandakini.

After hearing everything, the Emperor said, “Girl! You have rendered an incomparable service to the Chozha dynasty. There is nothing I can do to repay you. But I ask you one thing—tell me! After the prince reached the shore at Kodikkarai, why did you not bring him here? Why did you take him to Nagapattinam?”

“Swami! The prince had lost consciousness due to the cruel fever. We took him to the Buddhist vihara at Nagapattinam, having heard that good physicians reside there. We knew well that the bhikshus there hold deep devotion for the prince. In that condition, we could only transport him by boat; it would have been impossible to send him on horseback or by chariot…”
“At that time, the Pazhuvettaraiyar was at Kodikkarai. Why did you not inform him…?”

Poonkuzhali hesitated for a moment, then replied in a firm, resonant voice, “Emperor! The whole land knows that the Pazhuvettaraiyars are enemies of the prince. In such a situation, how could I bring myself to entrust the prince to the Pazhuvettaraiyar?”

“Yes, yes! Are the Pazhuvettaraiyars the only enemies of my sons? Even I am considered an enemy. That is how the world thinks. Let that be! Prime Minister, the storm that struck here yesterday must have been even fiercer at Nagapattinam, must it not? My heart trembles with fear that some new danger might befall the prince.”
“Lord, the Chola land is a land of fortune. Now, by the grace of fate, this land is blessed with great good fortune…”
“Yes, the Chola land is indeed blessed; but I have become unfortunate, Brahmarayar! Before I close my eyes forever, I wish to see my sons just once…”

“Sir! Do not speak so. Who is more fortunate than you, who has such sons and a daughter as well? I shall send men at once today. I will even send my disciple Thirumalai to ensure the prince is brought back safely!” said the Prime Minister.

Only then did the Emperor turn his gaze upon Azhwarkadiyan. “Aha! Has he been standing here all this while? Was it not about him that the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar spoke? Is he not the one who climbed and leapt over the walls of the Pazhuvur palace?”
“Lord, there is a fitting reason for that. Grant me permission to explain it tomorrow. You are already greatly fatigued!” said the Prime Minister.

At that moment, the daughter of Malayaman, Kundavai, and Vanathi entered the Emperor’s chamber. “Prime Minister! Let us conclude matters here for today. The physicians have strictly ordered that the Emperor must not be subjected to excessive fatigue!” declared the Maharani.
Afterwards, she said, “This girl sings sweetly, it seems. Ask her to sing a Thevaram hymn. The Emperor is very fond of music.”
“Very well, Mother! My disciple too sings Alvar pasurams beautifully. I shall ask him to sing as well!” said the Prime Minister.
Poonguzhali sang the Appar Thevaram, “Koottayinavaru Vilakkakilir.” Azhwarkkadiyan sang the pasuram, “Thirukkanden pon meni kanden.”

As soon as the singing began, Sundara Chozhar closed his eyes. After a short while, peace and tranquility appeared on his face. His breath became slow and even. It seemed he had fallen into a deep and restful sleep.

As darkness had already fallen, the nursemaid brought in a lamp and set it down. The Prime Minister and everyone else quietly left the room. Only the daughter of Malayaman remained by the Emperor’s side for a while. From the threshold of the next chamber, Kundavai signaled to her, and she too rose and departed. After that, silence settled in the room. Only the gentle sound of Sundara Chozhar’s breathing could be heard.

Because he had not slept at all the previous night and was weary and exhausted, and because of the sweetness of the Tamil hymns sung by Poonguzhali and Azhwarkkadiyan, Sundara Chozhar fell into a deep sleep that early evening. Yet, his slumber was not one of oblivious peace. Old memories and new, real events and inner imaginings, all took shape as dreams and led him through strange and wondrous experiences.
He and Poonguzhali were journeying in a boat upon the calm, blue sea. Poonguzhali was rowing the boat, singing a song in harmony with the ocean’s deep, resonant music.

“Do not grow weary, O my heart— All your longing shall one day be fulfilled! After the long night shrouded in darkness, Have you not seen the morning blossom? The sun will rise, delighting the lotus that thrills And bringing joy to all living things on earth!”

Hearing this song, Sundara Chozhar was filled with ecstasy. The weariness that had settled in his heart was swept away, and a surge of enthusiasm overflowed within him. “Sing more! Sing more!” he urged Poonguzhali on. The boat continued to drift, floating upon the deep sea.

Suddenly, darkness enveloped them; a fierce wind began to blow. Waves rose and crashed upon the once-calm sea, swelling like mountains. The boat, which had been gently rocking like a cradle only moments before, now tossed and pitched, soaring to touch the clouds and then plunging into the abyss below. The mats of woven reeds in the boat were torn to shreds and swept away by the wind. Yet, somehow, the boat itself managed not to capsize, braving the storm with remarkable endurance. At every moment, Sundara Chozha marveled at Poonguzhali’s skill in steering the boat, his heart swelling with admiration and joy.

As suddenly as the wind had come, it ceased. The turmoil of the sea gradually subsided. Once more, tranquility returned. In the southern sky, the first signs of dawn appeared. Before long, the golden sun rose, and the waters of the sea shimmered with a radiant, golden hue. Not far away, islands surrounded by lush coconut groves came into view.

From those islands, birds sang sweet, melodious songs that floated across the water. Sundara Chozhar realized that these were the islands off the coast of Eezha Nadu. A memory stirred within him—on one of those very islands, in a previous birth, he had met Mandakini.

As he gazed upon that island, he said, “Poonguzhali! In the end, you have brought me to paradise itself, have you not? How can I ever repay you?” When he saw that Poonguzhali did not reply, he turned to look at her—and was struck motionless. For the woman sitting on the other side of the boat was not Poonguzhali. It was Mandakini! She appeared exactly as she had thirty years ago.

For a few moments, he sat stunned. Then he asked, “Mandakini, is it truly you? Is it really you? Was it you, in Poonguzhali’s form, who brought me here?” He remembered then that she could not hear his words. Yet, from the movement of his lips, Mandakini seemed to understand what he was saying, and she smiled.
He tried to rise and go closer to her. But he could not stand. He remembered that his legs were useless.

“Mandakini! I have become an invalid. I am no longer able to come to you; you must come near me. Look here, Mandakini! Even if someone were to summon me once more to be crowned emperor of the three worlds, I would not leave you and go. Let us not travel to the islands near this land of Eezham. People will always come and go here. Set the boat adrift in the middle of the sea! Far away, farther still, crossing seven seas, let us go to that distant island beyond!” said Sundara Chozhar. As though she understood all he said, Mandakini smiled gently.

Upon the Kaveri river, like a royal swan, a splendidly adorned pleasure boat carried Emperor Sundara Chozhar, his queen, and their children on a joyous voyage. Masters of music sang as they went. Sundara Chozhar, lost in the bliss of the music, closed his eyes, enraptured. Suddenly, he heard a cry—“Ayyo! Ayyo!”—and opened his eyes. “Where is the child? Where is Arulmozhi?” came the anxious voices. Sundara Chozhar looked around in alarm. In the floodwaters of the Kaveri, he saw someone—a woman—grasping his precious child Arulmozhi, trying to drown him in the water. Overcome by an indescribable terror, Sundara Chozhar thought to leap into the river’s flood. At that moment, he saw the woman’s face. He recognized it—it was Mandakini’s face, contorted in anguish. At once, all strength left his body; he became as lifeless as an inanimate object. The one who had meant to leap into the water collapsed with a thud inside the boat.

Whether it was the shock of falling in the boat or something else, Sundara Chozhar awoke from both his sleep and his dream at the same moment. Because of the storm and rain, the air was colder than usual, yet his whole body was drenched in sweat. When he realized that all the visions he had seen were but dreams, a great burden seemed lifted from his heart, and he felt relief. He looked around—there was no one in the room. Only the lamp was burning steadily. Since he had fallen asleep, perhaps the others were in the adjoining chamber! He thought of clapping his hands to call them. “Let it be for a while; let the shock of the dream subside,” he thought to himself.

At that moment, a very faint sound came from the loft above. What could it be? He turned his face slightly toward the direction of the sound. It seemed as if a figure was descending from the loft, holding on to a pillar, inching along the edge.

The night’s darkness had not yet fully lifted. The eastern sky was just beginning to pale. The stars, which had shone so brightly, now seemed to fade, one by one, into the lightening heavens. The gentle breeze that blew from the river carried with it the chill of dawn, and the world lay hushed, as if awaiting some great event.

Vandiyathevan, who had spent the night in restless slumber, was caught between sleep and wakefulness. Dreams flitted before his eyes—strange, vivid dreams, woven from the threads of all he had seen and heard in these past days. He saw the mighty Chola banners fluttering in the wind, heard the clash of swords and the thunder of war drums, and glimpsed the faces of kings and queens, their eyes filled with hope and fear.

In one dream, he found himself standing on the banks of the Ponni river. The waters flowed swift and deep, gleaming silver in the dawn light. Suddenly, the river seemed to rise, its waves curling and foaming, and from its midst emerged a radiant figure—a woman, draped in shining silks, her face aglow with divine grace. She beckoned to him, her voice ringing clear above the roar of the waters.
“Son of Ponni! Heed my words. Great dangers lie ahead, but so do great deeds. The fate of the Chola dynasty rests in your hands. Be brave, be steadfast, and the river’s blessing shall be upon you.”

As Vandiyathevan reached out to her, the vision dissolved. He awoke with a start, his heart pounding, the woman’s words echoing in his mind. The sky outside had grown brighter; the first rays of the sun touched the earth, and a new day had begun.

chapters.title: “Why Do You Torment Me?”
paragraphs: Sundara Chozhar was overcome with astonishment. Who was it that descended in such a manner, along the edge of the pillars from the upper storey? For what reason should anyone come thus! Memories of the confusing dreams he had seen earlier flashed through his mind. Was this too a vision conjured by sleep? Had he not yet fully awakened from his slumber? To resolve this doubt, Sundara Chozhar closed his eyes once more. After remaining thus for a moment, he opened his eyes wide and looked towards the direction in which that figure had descended. There was nothing there now. Ah! That apparition must have been a mere illusion.

He recalled the events that had occurred before he fell asleep. The Chief Minister, his attendant, and the daughter of Thiyagavidangar, who sang so sweetly, seemed to have left after he had drifted into sleep. The daughter of Malayaman and the nursemaids, as usual, must be waiting in the adjoining chamber. The Emperor felt a pang of regret as he remembered the complaint he had voiced to the Chief Minister about Kundavai. Kundavai was a woman of unparalleled wisdom and foresight. It was she who had arranged for the prince to remain in Nagapattinam, so that no confusion would arise in the kingdom. It was his own mistake to have misunderstood her intentions. For some time now, Sundara Chozhar had been aware that his mind was not in its proper state. Then, what was the use of being angry with the princess? It was best to do everything according to her counsel. Now, the most important matter was to summon the prince from Nagapattinam. O Lord! May no harm befall him because of the storm! He must ask Kundavai about this at once. Sundara Chozhar thought to clap his hands and summon those waiting in the next room…

But what was this? It seemed as though someone was moving about near his head! Yet the footsteps were so soft—like the tread of a cat, a tiger, or some other beast. Who could it be? Could it be the daughter of Malayaman? His own daughter? The nursemaid? Were they walking so softly so as not to disturb his sleep?
“Who is it?” Sundara Chozhar asked in a gentle voice.
There was no reply. “Who is that? Come here, show yourself!” Sundara Chozhar called out in a somewhat raised voice. There was no reply.

A thought struck Sundara Chozhar, one that filled him with confusion and dread. ‘Could it be her? Or her spirit? Has the huntress who appeared in my dreams now come before me in the flesh? Has she arrived at midnight, adorned in garments and jewels, standing in the front hall? Or perhaps it is already midnight? Have I slept for so long? Is that why the Malaiyaman’s daughter and my own daughter are not here? Have the nursemaids too fallen asleep? Alas! Why have they left me alone? If that accursed daughter of the Karaiyar has come, she will not let me go so easily. Will she not torment me until my heart bursts with agony?’

‘Wretched woman! If it is truly you, come before me and finish it! Torment me as much as you wish, in every way you desire, and then leave! Why do you hover above my head, unseen, stealing my life away? Come forward! Have you come seeking a blood sacrifice? Come! Come! You always kept a dagger in your lap, didn’t you? Kill me with the same blade that slew tigers and bears! But do not harm my children! Do not take revenge on them for the crime I committed! They have done you no wrong! It was I who betrayed you! Was it I who told you to climb to the top of the lighthouse and leap into the sea to your death? Why do you torment me for that dreadful deed you yourself committed?...’

Sundara Chozhar sensed a form standing very close above his head. His body trembled with terror. It felt as if his entrails rose up from his stomach and blocked his chest! Then, as if his heart rose and choked his throat. His eyes seemed about to burst from their sockets. There was no doubt—she had come and was standing before him. Her spirit had come. She had come, just as he had feared, to exact the final blood vengeance. She would stab him in the chest and kill him. Or perhaps she would strangle him with her bare hands. Whatever her intent, let it be fulfilled! There was no more use in his living. If that ghost took her revenge and left, perhaps she would spare his children.

If he could just raise his head a little and look up, Sundara Chozhar felt he would see the ghostly form of the Mandakini spirit with his own eyes. It seemed as though that form was standing so close above his head. Even its shadow fell upon his face.

It seemed as though something had fallen. For a moment, he thought to lift his head and look, but he did not have the courage. “I will shut my eyes tightly. Let it do what it will and be gone,” he resolved, and closed his eyes.

He remained thus for a while; as he had feared, no sharp knife descended upon his chest. Nor did two ghostly hands seize his throat and strangle him. That form, the figure that had stood above his head, seemed to have moved away from there. Ah, the daughter of the Karaiyar would not let me go so easily. How long will she keep me alive and torment me as she pleases? Perhaps today she has vanished without appearing before my eyes! Well, well, I can call for someone. If anyone comes into this room, even if she is still here, she will disappear at once!
“Who is there? Where has everyone gone?” cried Sundara Chozhar in a loud voice, opening his eyes.

Ah! Who is that standing before him, at the foot of the cot? It is her, no doubt; that same dumb woman’s ghost, standing with her hair loose and wild! Blood is streaming down her forehead! It seems to say, “I have come to avenge blood!” Like a madman, Sundara Chozhar shouted at that ghostly apparition in a loud voice:

“Hey, dumb ghost! When you were alive, you tormented me by never opening your mouth to speak; now you torment me still! Why have you come here? Speak! If you have come to avenge blood, then take your revenge and be gone; why do you stand there silently? Why do you wear such a pitiful expression on your face? Have you come to ask me something? If so, say it! If you cannot speak, then tell me by sign! Do not stand there tormenting me in silence. Why are your eyes brimming with tears? Alas! Are you sobbing and weeping? I cannot bear this! If you have anything to say, say it! If not, vanish from here. Will you not go? Why will you not go? What is it you are thinking to do to me? Are you not the one who tried to drown my precious young son, that little child, in the floodwaters of the Kaveri? By God’s grace, your wish did not come to pass. It never will! You wretched woman! Why do you still look at me as though you would tear my heart asunder? Go! Go! Will you not go? Will you not go! Look, I will make you go now!…”

As he spoke thus, Sundara Chozhar looked around within arm’s reach to see what object lay nearby. All he could see within his grasp was a lamp made of the five sacred metals. Seizing it, he cried out, “Go! Begone, spirit!” and, aiming at the face of the Mandakini phantom, hurled it with all his might. Like the discus weapon flung by Lord Thirumal, the lamp blazed as it flew, its flame leaping toward that womanly apparition.
At that very moment, from the mouth of the figure Sundara Chozhar believed to be a ghost, a wailing cry erupted.

All seven of Sundara Chozhar’s vital energies seemed to shrink within him; his flesh, his bones, and the very life-force within his marrow froze. The lamp did not strike the face of that figure. Instead, it fell just short, dropping to the floor and rolling with a clattering ‘clang, clang’ sound.

Though that lamp was extinguished, by good fortune another lamp still burned on the far side of the chamber. In its dim, wavering light, Sundara Chozhar peered closely and saw that the spirit-form of Mandakini still stood there. For a moment, an indescribable anguish was visible upon its face. Then, for the last time, it looked at Sundara Chozhar with boundless sorrow, turned away, and made as if to depart.

It was at that instant that a new doubt arose for the first time in Sundara Chozhar’s heart. Was this truly the spirit-form of Mandakini? Or was it another woman, one who resembled her in every way? A twin sister, perhaps? Or could it be… could it possibly be… Mandakini herself? Had she not died after all? Was she still alive? Had all his assumptions been wrong? If it was indeed her, how cruel it was of him to hurl the lamp at her! Was that why, upon her face, the sorrow he had seen a moment ago deepened into an agony beyond words? Had she suffered at the thought of his brutality? Ah! There she was, preparing to leave, glancing about for a way to go.
“Woman! Are you Mandakini, daughter of the Karaiyar? Or are you her spirit-form? Or are you her twin sister? Wait, wait! Do not go! Speak the truth before you leave!…”

As Sundara Chozhar called out thus in a great voice, suddenly several people rushed into the chamber. The daughter of Malayaman, Kundavai, Vanathi, Poonguzhali, the Prime Minister, his disciple—all of them entered the room, and Sundara Chozhar realized this in the space of a single moment.
“Stop! Stop her from running away! Ask her who she is and why she has come!” cried Sundara Chozhar.

All those who had entered stood frozen for a moment, stunned by astonishment. The wild look on Sundara Chozhar’s face and the terror that rang in his voice filled them with dread. The sight of Mandakini Devi there left them floundering in a flood of bewilderment. For a few moments, not knowing what to do, everyone stood motionless.
Prime Minister Aniruddhar, however, managed to guess, in some measure, the nature of the situation and how it might have come to pass. He looked at Poonguzhali and asked, “Girl! Is this your aunt?”
“Yes, sir!” replied Poonguzhali.
“Tirumalai! Why do you stand there like a tree? Mandakini Devi is trying to escape! Stop her—by order of the Emperor!” he commanded.
For the first time in his life, Azhwarkkadiyan refused to obey his guru’s command.
“Sir! Rather command me to halt the storm winds! That would be easier for me!” he said.
Meanwhile, Poonguzhali did not remain idle. With a single leap, she ran and seized her aunt’s shoulder. Mandakini shook her off and darted away.

Azhwarkkadiyan acted swiftly. He hurried to the door through which the Prime Minister and the others had entered, shut it, and bolted it. Then, spreading his arms wide, he stood before it so that no one could open it.

Mandakini, like a deer surrounded by hunters, looked around in terror, her eyes darting in every direction. Realizing there was no other escape, she resolved that she must climb back the way she had descended. The others, following her gaze toward the upper floor, understood her intention.
Sundara Chozhar shouted again, “Catch her! Stop her! Ask her why she came, whom she seeks vengeance upon!”

Mandakini Devi, preparing to climb the pillar to the upper floor, was approached once more by Poonguzhali. This time, instead of trying to restrain her, Poonguzhali made a gesture with her hand, as if trying to say something. Mandakini seemed to understand her meaning, and pointed to the lamp that had fallen and lay on the floor below.
Kundavai, who had been observing all this, asked, “Father! Was it you who threw the lamp at Periyamma?”
“Yes, my dear! I could not bear the look that ghost cast upon me. That’s why I picked up the lamp and threw it!” replied Sundara Chozhar.

“Father! She is neither a ghost nor a spirit; she is a living queen. Father! Periyamma is not dead! Ask the Prime Minister! He will tell you everything!” said Kundavai, and then turned to watch Mandakini and Poonguzhali, who were engaged in a silent argument.
At once, she rushed towards them.
“My child! Do not go near her! That demoness might do something to you!” cried Sundara Chozhar, attempting in agitation to rise from his bed to stop Kundavai.
But Vanamadevi, the daughter of Malayaman, gently held his shoulders and laid him back on the bed. “My lord! Please wait a moment! No harm will come to your daughter!” she said.

chapters.title: “The Chola Clan Deity”
paragraphs: When Kundavai came near, Mandakini gazed at her intently for a moment. Then, the Young Princess did something no one expected. She knelt down, touched Mandakini’s feet, and prostrated herself in full obeisance. Tears welled up in Mandakini’s eyes. She bent down, lifted Kundavai, and embraced her. Then, the princess entwined her arm with Mandakini’s, holding her close, and together they walked toward the place where the Emperor lay.
Only now did the Empress look closely at Mandakini’s face. She saw blood trickling down from her forehead.
“Swami! Was it you who threw the lamp and injured her? Oh no! What have you done?” cried the daughter of Malayaman in distress.

“No, no! The lamp I threw did not fall on her. She was already standing there with a bleeding wound before that. But this wretch—she will surely blame me! And you will believe her. All of you are on her side. Daughter of Malayaman! Even you pity her? Do you know who she is?” asked Sundara Chozhar.
“I do, Swami! She is my clan’s guardian deity—the deity of the entire Chola lineage. Was she not the goddess who saved my beloved son from drowning in the Kaveri?”
“Ah! Even you believe such things? Did Kundavai perhaps tell you so?”

“I speak only of what I saw with my own eyes. Kundavai was a child then—what could she have known? Not only did she save Arulmozhi, but she is the deity who saved the very life of the Chola land! Was she not the one who protected you from becoming prey to the wild bear on the island of Boothath?”
“Heavens! Even that you know? Do you know that she has been alive all these years?”

“I have known for some time. From the moment I learned of it, I have been urging the Prime Minister to bring this goddess here from Eezha Nadu…” “Aniruddha! What is this the Maharani is saying? Is this woman truly the daughter of the Karaiyar? Is she really alive? Was it a lie that she had died? Was it all an illusion when I thought her spirit was haunting me? My mind is already confused. Do not all of you together drive me completely mad!” said Emperor Sundara Chozhar.

“Lord! It is true that she is the daughter of the Karaiyar. It is also true that she is not dead. Emperor! I am a great offender. There is no forgiveness for the crime I have committed, yet by your grace…”
“Prime Minister! Now I understand. The woman you forcibly brought from Kodikkarai is this very one! It was not true when you said the woman in the palanquin was that boatwoman!”
“King of kings! You must forgive this humble servant!”

“Ah! He asks for forgiveness! Since the dawn of this world, never has one called Emperor, King of kings, been deceived as I have been. Why did you have to do this without my knowledge? Why could you not have told me beforehand? Even today, you spoke with me for so long this evening—why did you not say it then? Prime Minister! Now everything is clear to me. What the Pazhuvettarayars said is true—you are all conspiring against me!”

“It is true that we have conspired, but not against you. We only wished, by any means, to bring the Karaiyar maiden to you. Through the Maharani, I learned how deeply your heart grieved over her supposed death in the sea, and so I made this decision. The Maharani also commanded it thus. But bringing her here was no simple task. Had I told you she was alive, you would have found it hard to believe. Therefore, I resolved to tell you only after I had brought her to this city. Yesterday evening, after we had almost reached the gates of the fort, Mandakini Devi disappeared. In her place, this woman came in the palanquin. All day today, we have been searching for the Devi. My disciple saw her climb and leap over the wall of the Pazhuvoor palace gardens, and so he too climbed over the wall. But the Devi was not caught. Thirumalai was captured by the men of Pazhuvoor. Emperor! I beg you to pardon my disciple for this offense.”
“Is this even an offense to be pardoned? There are far greater matters! Tell me the rest!”

“After that, even though we waited until evening today, and searched within the fortress of Pazhuvoor, we could not find her. While you were resting a short while ago, all of us were in the next room, speaking about her alone. We were wondering where she might have hidden herself, and how, or who among us, should tell you all this. But somehow, she herself has come to your presence. It is as if a ripe fruit has slipped and fallen into milk!”

The Emperor then turned his gaze to where Mandakini Devi was seated. Kundavai, Poonguzhali, and the others were gently wiping the wound on that lady’s forehead with a damp cloth, and then applying a medicinal sandal paste upon it.
“Daughter of the Vidangar! Will you ask your aunt how she came by the wound on her forehead, and tell us?” he asked.
Poonguzhali stepped forward by two paces and said, “I asked her, my lord! But the reason my aunt gives is not clear to me…”
“What does she say? Does she claim the wound was caused by me throwing the lamp?”
“No, no! She says she struck her head against a rock on the hill and was wounded. She also says she did not notice the blood flowing…”
