At that moment, Sundara Chozhar did something most unusual. He laughed aloud, a ringing, merry laugh! It had been many years since others had seen him laugh in such a manner. Again and again, he thought of it and laughed. Everyone began to look at him with concern.

“Chief Minister, why are you all staring at me so? I haven’t suddenly gone mad. Only the old madness remains! Don’t you all know why I am laughing now? She claims she was wounded by striking against a hill in the fertile land of Chozha! That is what amuses me. Who speaks of hills here? One cannot even find a stone to make a small idol! If someone wished to throw a stone at the head of the Chozha Emperor, they would not find even a black pebble! And she says she struck herself against a hill? Upon which hill did she strike herself, Poonguzhali? Listen well!” he said.
Hearing all this, a radiance appeared on Vanathi’s face. She suddenly stepped forward by two paces and offered her salutations to the Emperor.
“Sir! I have an idea—if you permit, I will speak!” she said.

“O daughter of the Velir! Are you here as well? I did not notice you all this while! Even amidst all this commotion, you have not fainted or collapsed—that itself is a wonder! What is it that you have thought of? About what? Speak!” commanded the Emperor.
“They say this lady was injured when she struck against a mountain, sir! I have an idea about that.”

“What? What? You are a clever girl! If there is any reason to be understood, you would surely grasp it! Tell me quickly! Did she come here from Eezha Nadu, having struck herself on a mountain and bearing that bloody wound?”
“No, sir; isn’t there a sculpture pavilion in the palace gardens? Inside it, there is a Kailasa mountain being lifted by Ravana. Perhaps she might have struck herself against that!”
As Vanathi spoke thus, everyone was plunged into a sea of astonishment.
“It could be! It could be!” “That must be it!” they said to one another.
Kundavai touched Vanathi’s forehead, stretched out her hand as if to ward off the evil eye, and exclaimed, “Oh my dear! What a clever girl you are! You thought of what none of us could!”

Poonkuzhali, who had been watching this with irritation, turned away and spoke in sign language to her mute aunt. Then she said, “Yes! It is indeed the mountain in the sculpture pavilion! If I had seen that pavilion, I too would have known!”

The Emperor, still gazing intently at Mandakini, said, “Yes; wandering without knowing the way, she must have struck herself against the mountain in the sculpture pavilion. I wonder where she was trying to go, searching for a path. In the end, she has come here!”
“She must have been searching for a way to come to you. There is no doubt about that. I myself was telling them—she would not leave this place without seeing you…”

“I do not believe it, Prime Minister! If she had intended to come to me, would she not have come earlier? Would she not have come twenty-five years ago? Would I have waited all these years for her to come? Would she have wandered about as a ghost around me? Yes, yes! I thought she existed in the form of a ghost. Is that not true? A ghost— It seems she has wandered through the jungles and mountains of Eezha Nadu. All this time, I have been immersed in the comforts and luxuries of the palace. What can one say about the power of fate? How many times has my heart been bewildered upon seeing a form like hers—who has witnessed it? Could it be that, just as now, she had come secretly before and seen me, then left? I do not know. I thought it was a demon and was terrified! Twenty-five years! Twenty-five ages!

Thus, speaking as if he were conversing with himself, the Emperor suddenly turned towards Aniruddhar and, with agitation, asked, “Prime Minister! You once confessed to some crime and begged forgiveness, did you not? What was that crime?”
Aniruddhar replied, “Emperor! Is it just to ask the accused about his own crime?”

“Then, whom should I ask? Indeed, there is no need to ask anyone. It is written plainly upon your face. You came and told me that she had fallen into the sea and died, did you not? That itself was a lie! For twenty-five years you have upheld that falsehood. I too believed it, Aniruddhar! Truly, your crime is a most terrible one!”

“I alone am not responsible for it, Emperor! The daughter of the Karaiyar clan is also responsible. It may be true that she fell into the sea. Afterwards, she was reborn. She made me promise not to reveal to you that she was alive; she said that if I did not give my word, she would once again give up her life. You may ask her yourself whether all this is true.”
“There is no need to ask! It must be so. Still, is it not true that all of you have conspired together against me?” said Sundara Chozhar.

“There is no forgiveness for the crime I have committed; nor do I seek forgiveness. Yet, the burden that has weighed upon my heart for so many years has today been lifted. Now, grant me leave. Permit me to go to Thiruvarangam, to serve Sri Ranganatha, and spend the rest of my days there.”

“That cannot be allowed, Brahmarayar! Because of the crime you committed long ago, countless confusions have arisen today. Should you not resolve all these matters before you go to serve Ranganatha?” said the Emperor.

Vandiyathevan, who had been watching the events unfolding in the temple with great curiosity, was startled by the sudden commotion. The crowd, which had been standing in silence, now began to murmur and shift restlessly. Some craned their necks to see what was happening at the sanctum, while others whispered anxiously among themselves.

At that moment, an elderly priest, his forehead smeared with sacred ash, stepped forward and raised his hand to command silence. The murmurs subsided. The priest’s voice, though aged, rang out clear and authoritative.

“O devotees of the Chola clan! Today, in the presence of our clan’s guardian deity, we have gathered to seek blessings for the prosperity of the land and the well-being of our king. The sacred lamp has been lit, the offerings made, and the rituals performed according to tradition. Let none harbor doubt in their hearts—the goddess has accepted our prayers!”
A wave of relief swept through the assembly. Some folded their hands in reverence; others bowed their heads, overcome with devotion.

Vandiyathevan’s eyes wandered over the ancient stone pillars, the flickering shadows cast by the oil lamps, and the faces of the people—each marked by hope, fear, and faith. He felt the weight of centuries pressing down upon him, as if the spirits of Chola ancestors watched from the darkness beyond the temple walls.
Suddenly, a sharp cry pierced the air. All eyes turned toward the sanctum. A young woman, her hair unbound, rushed forward, her face pale with terror.
“Save me! O goddess, save me!” she cried, collapsing at the priest’s feet.
The priest bent down, his voice gentle. “Child, what troubles you? Speak without fear in the presence of our mother.”
The woman sobbed, her words tumbling out in anguish. “My husband… he was taken by soldiers last night. They said he plotted against the king. But he is innocent! O goddess, have mercy!”
A murmur of sympathy rippled through the crowd. The priest closed his eyes, lips moving in silent prayer. Then he spoke, his voice trembling with conviction.
“Fear not, daughter. The goddess sees all. Justice will prevail. Let us all pray together for the truth to come to light and for the safety of our people.”

The crowd bowed their heads, united in prayer. Vandiyathevan felt a strange stirring in his heart—a sense of belonging, of being part of something greater than himself. The weight of the Chola legacy, the faith of the people, and the power of the goddess seemed to converge in that sacred space.

As the prayers rose to the heavens, Vandiyathevan resolved to do his part in protecting the honor of the Chola clan and the well-being of its people. The guardian deity of the Cholas watched over them all, and he would not let her down.

chapters.title: Danger for Ravanan!
paragraphs: Part Four – The Crown Jewel **Chapter 35 – The Emperor’s Wrath**

The Emperor Sundara Chola was seated on his golden throne, his countenance clouded with anger. The courtiers who filled the vast hall dared not raise their eyes to meet his. Even the gentle breeze that usually played through the open windows seemed to hesitate, as if fearful of disturbing the monarch’s mood.

The Emperor’s eyes, sharp and piercing, swept over the assembly. His lips, usually curved in a kind smile, were now pressed into a thin, stern line. The ministers and noblemen shifted uneasily, their hearts pounding with apprehension.
Suddenly, the Emperor’s voice rang out, echoing through the hall like a thunderclap. “Who dares to bring such disgrace upon the Chola dynasty? Who has sown these seeds of treachery within our realm?”
No one answered. The silence grew heavier, pressing down upon the gathering like a suffocating shroud.
Sundara Chola’s anger blazed forth once more. “Is there no one among you with the courage to speak the truth? Has fear so thoroughly seized your hearts?”
At last, one of the elder ministers stepped forward, his voice trembling. “My lord, we are ever loyal to the throne. If you command, we shall root out the traitors and bring them before your feet.”
The Emperor’s gaze softened, but only slightly. “Loyalty is proven by deeds, not words. Let your actions show your devotion to the Chola crown. Let none forget the might and majesty of our empire!”
The courtiers bowed low, their foreheads nearly touching the floor, as the Emperor’s wrathful gaze swept over them once more.
**Chapter 36 – In the Dead of Night**

The palace lay shrouded in darkness, the silence broken only by the distant hoot of an owl. Shadows danced along the corridors, flickering in the pale moonlight that filtered through the latticed windows.

Vandiyathevan moved silently through the passageways, his footsteps muffled by the thick carpets. Every sense was alert, every nerve taut with anticipation. He knew that danger lurked within these walls, that secrets whispered in the night could decide the fate of the empire.

A faint sound caught his ear—a soft rustle, the creak of a door. Vandiyathevan pressed himself against the wall, holding his breath. From the gloom, a figure emerged, cloaked and hooded, moving with the stealth of a shadow.

He followed at a distance, careful not to betray his presence. The figure glided through the corridors, finally pausing before a hidden door. With a practiced hand, the stranger unlocked it and slipped inside.

Vandiyathevan waited a moment, then crept forward. He pressed his ear to the door, straining to catch the voices within. What plot was unfolding in the dead of night? What secrets would be revealed before the dawn?
**Chapter 37 – Turmoil at Kadambur**

The great halls of Kadambur were filled with a restless energy. Noblemen and warriors gathered in small groups, their voices hushed, their faces troubled. Rumors swirled like storm clouds, casting a pall over the festivities.

Vandiyathevan moved among them, his keen eyes missing nothing. He sensed the tension in the air, the undercurrent of fear and suspicion. Something was amiss—something that threatened to shatter the fragile peace.

Suddenly, a shout rang out, followed by the clash of steel. The crowd surged forward, drawn by the commotion. In the center of the hall, two men faced each other, swords drawn, their eyes blazing with fury.
“Stop!” cried a commanding voice. The crowd parted, and Periya Pazhuvettarayar strode forward, his presence imposing. “There will be no bloodshed in Kadambur tonight. Lower your weapons!”
Reluctantly, the combatants obeyed, their anger still simmering. The hall buzzed with anxious whispers. What had provoked such violence? What storm was gathering over Kadambur?
**Chapter 38 – Nandini Refuses**
Nandini sat in her chamber, her beauty radiant even in the dim candlelight. Her eyes, deep and enigmatic, betrayed no emotion as she listened to the words of her visitor.
“My lady,” the man pleaded, “the time has come. You must act. The fate of the Chola dynasty hangs in the balance.”
Nandini’s lips curved in a faint, enigmatic smile. “You ask much of me. Why should I risk everything for your cause?”
“Because you alone possess the power to change the course of history. Without you, our plans will come to nothing.”
Nandini’s gaze grew cold. “I have made my decision. I will not be a pawn in your game. Go, and do not return unless you bring news worth hearing.”
The man hesitated, then bowed and withdrew. Nandini watched him go, her expression inscrutable. What thoughts stirred in her heart? What secrets did she guard behind those impenetrable eyes?
**Chapter 39 – “Danger Approaches!”**
A sense of foreboding hung over the palace like a dark cloud. Messengers hurried through the corridors, their faces pale with fear. The news they carried was dire—danger was drawing near.
Vandiyathevan intercepted one of the messengers. “What has happened? Why this alarm?”
The messenger’s voice trembled. “There are enemies at the gates. Treachery within the walls. No one is safe.”
Vandiyathevan’s heart pounded. He knew that the fate of the empire rested on a knife’s edge. Every moment was precious; every decision could mean life or death.

He hurried through the palace, seeking allies, gathering information. The warning echoed in his mind: “Danger approaches!” Would he be able to avert disaster, or would the Chola dynasty be swept away by the coming storm?
**Chapter 40 – Water Games**

The gardens of the palace were alive with laughter and merriment. The princesses and their companions frolicked by the lotus-filled pools, their laughter ringing like silver bells in the warm afternoon air.
Kundavai, ever graceful, led the games, her eyes sparkling with mischief. Arulmozhi, the beloved prince, joined in, his presence bringing joy to all.
They splashed and played, forgetting for a moment the cares of the world. Water droplets glittered in the sunlight, rainbow-hued, as the young nobles chased each other through the gardens.
But beneath the laughter, a shadow lingered. Even as they reveled in the simple pleasures of youth, the specter of danger loomed ever closer.
**Chapter 41 – Karikalan’s Bloodlust**
Karikalan paced his chamber, his face twisted with rage. His hands clenched into fists, his breath coming in ragged gasps. The fire of vengeance burned in his eyes, consuming all reason.
He remembered the insults, the betrayals, the wounds that would not heal. His heart cried out for retribution, for blood to wash away the stain on his honor.
Servants cowered as he strode through the halls, his fury a palpable force. None dared approach him, none dared speak his name.
Karikalan’s mind was filled with dark thoughts. Only one thing could quench his thirst—revenge. And he would stop at nothing to achieve it.
**Chapter 42 – “She Is Not a Woman!”**
A gasp of astonishment echoed through the chamber. All eyes turned to the speaker, disbelief etched on their faces.
“She is not a woman!” the voice repeated, trembling with emotion.
The accused stood silent, her head bowed. Whispers rippled through the assembly, shock and confusion mingling in the air.
“What do you mean?” demanded a stern voice. “Explain yourself!”
The speaker hesitated, then spoke in a low, urgent tone. “She is no ordinary woman. She is the key to our fate. Beware, for appearances can deceive.”
The words hung in the air, heavy with meaning. What secret did she conceal? What truth lay hidden beneath the surface?
**Chapter 43 – “Where Is the Tiger?”**
The question rang out, sharp and urgent. “Where is the tiger?”
The assembled warriors looked at one another, uncertainty in their eyes. The tiger—symbol of the Chola dynasty, embodiment of their strength and courage—was missing.
“Search the grounds!” commanded the leader. “Leave no stone unturned!”
Men scattered in all directions, their hearts pounding with dread. Had the tiger been stolen? Had their enemies struck at the very heart of their power?
The search continued long into the night, the question echoing in every corner: “Where is the tiger?”
**Chapter 44 – Love and Blame**
Love and blame—two forces intertwined, impossible to separate. In the palace, hearts ached with longing and regret.
Kundavai gazed out at the moonlit gardens, her thoughts troubled. Memories of laughter and tears, of promises made and broken, filled her heart.
Elsewhere, Vandiyathevan wandered the silent corridors, tormented by guilt and desire. He longed for forgiveness, for a chance to set things right.
But fate was a cruel mistress, and the path to redemption was fraught with peril.
**Chapter 45 – “You Are My Sister!”**
The words fell like a thunderbolt, stunning all who heard them.
“You are my sister!” the voice cried, trembling with emotion.
The woman stared in disbelief, her eyes wide with shock. Could it be true? Had her entire life been built upon a lie?
Tears welled in her eyes as the truth dawned. The bonds of blood, stronger than any chain, bound them together.
In that moment, love and sorrow mingled, forging a connection that could never be broken.
**Chapter 46 – The Boat Moved!**
The river flowed silently beneath the moonlit sky, its surface shimmering with silver light.
A solitary boat drifted upon the water, its occupants silent, lost in thought. The oarsman rowed with steady strokes, guiding the vessel through the gentle current.
Suddenly, the boat shuddered, as if seized by an unseen force. The passengers exchanged anxious glances, their hearts pounding with fear.
What fate awaited them on the far shore? What secrets would be revealed as the boat moved ever onward, carrying them toward an uncertain destiny?
**Part Four – The Crown Jewel**

Sundara Chozhar looked at his beloved daughter and said, “Kundavai! I must discuss matters of the kingdom with the Prime Minister for a while. You go and attend to your own affairs. Take her with you as well when you leave! Let your mother alone remain here for a little longer!”
The Emperor’s reference to “her” was clearly directed at Mandakini. In the very manner of his words, his aversion towards her became apparent.

Kundavai glanced at her father with a trace of disappointment. Noticing this, the Emperor added, “Yes, it is best to find out whether it was truly the Kailasa mountain in the sculpture hall that she became so obsessed with! Take her there and show her, and see for yourself! I cannot bear her presence here any longer.”

With a face full of disappointment, Kundavai took Mandakini by the hand and led her away. At that moment, the daughter of Malayaman approached Kundavai and, leaning in so only she could hear, whispered, “Child! You cannot bear to look at her now, can you? What is the use of being upset with your father? Why not display all your skills in the art of adornment on her and see what comes of it?”
Kundavai acknowledged her suggestion with a smile, then led Mandakini away. Vanathi and Poonguzhali followed them out.

Afterwards, Sundara Chozhar looked back and forth between the Prime Minister and Malayaman’s daughter and said, “I do not know for what reason the two of you have done this. If you thought this would bring me happiness, you are gravely mistaken! Prime Minister! Why did you go to such trouble to bring this wild creature all the way from Kodikkarai? At least now, tell me the truth! From now on, do not try to hide anything from me!”

At this, Prime Minister Aniruddhar, his voice trembling with emotion, replied, “I will not repeat the mistake I made once before. I will never again conceal anything from you. It is for the sake of bringing the truth to light that I have gone to such lengths now. Your heart has long been tormented by the thought that a woman perished, drowned in the sea. For a long time, I believed you had forgotten that incident. But as the days passed, I saw that memory had only become more deeply etched in your heart, increasing your pain…” …I learned of it. The Maharani told me that, even in sleep, you often cried out, dreaming of her. Because of this, the daughter of Malayaman suffered even more than you. Some time ago, she sought my counsel. On her request, we resolved upon this attempt. We intended to bring before you the woman whom you believed had died because of you, so that you might be freed from that sorrow. We thought you would only believe if she were brought before you in person. If this is a crime, I beg you to show mercy and forgive!”

Hearing this, the Emperor’s anger flared as he spoke: “A crime indeed! A great crime! All these days, she has haunted me like a ghost, circling around me. She came in my dreams and tormented me. And now, instead of a ghost, you have brought this mad beggar before me. Did you think this would bring me joy? Never! Had you told me the truth beforehand, I would have certainly rejected any idea of bringing her here. Let bygones be bygones; you have done what you have done. You have gone through much trouble to bring this mute lunatic here. Now, what do you intend? When and how do you propose to send her away again?”
As Sundara Chola asked thus, Aniruddha truly stood speechless.

At that moment, the Empress said, “Swami! I have no intention of sending my sister away from here. She will remain in this palace with me. I shall cherish and care for her as I would an elder sister born before me!”

“Devi! You need not strive to prove your devotion to me in this manner. In these twenty-five years, I have seen that you are a queen of chastity greater than even Kannagi. Since the day I fell ill, you have forgotten even your own precious children and devoted yourself to serving me, fasting and praying for my sake. There is no need to bring a mute beggar from the forest into the palace to demonstrate your devotion to me. Daughter of Malayaman, listen! Prime Minister, you too, listen well. Once, long ago, when I was alone on an uninhabited island, I saw this mute beggar. It is true that, at that time, I felt affection for her. I do not deny it. But if you think that I still yearn for her and pine away, you could not be more mistaken. Back then, there were many reasons for the affection I felt towards her. But over these twenty-five years, that affection has turned entirely into hatred and disgust.

Even in my dreams and waking thoughts, she has tormented me so much. I cannot bear the very thought that she is here in this palace. Send her away from here at once, and then look to other matters. Because I thought she was a ghost, I hurled the lamp at her. Had I known she was alive, a woman of flesh and blood, I do not know what I might have done!”

Hearing these cruel words, uttered in a voice trembling with wrath, both the Empress and the Chief Minister were thrown into confusion. They had never expected the Emperor to speak in such a manner. Aniruddhar had thought the Emperor would reproach him only for his past misdeeds. The Empress, for her part, had expected that even if the Emperor did not openly express it, he would inwardly rejoice and greatly praise her noble deed.

The harsh words of Sundara Chozhar not only disappointed them, but also kindled a measure of resentment and anger. As if to cap all that the Emperor had said thus far, he exclaimed, “Tch, tch! What loss would the world have suffered if this mute madwoman had not survived? How much better it would have been if she had truly perished when she fell into the sea! Which utter fool went to such trouble to rescue her?”

At this, the daughter of Malayaman could restrain herself no longer. With emotion brimming over in her voice, she cried, “Swami! Do not speak such words! It is a great sin! How many elders have declared that ingratitude is the worst of all evils? If you must, forget that this lady saved your own life. But can we forget that she saved our beloved son, Arulmozhi Varman? Even if you forget, I cannot. For sixteen lifetimes, I shall remain indebted to this divine maiden!”

“Devi, are you telling that story again?” Sundara Chozhar began, but before he could continue, the daughter of Malayaman interjected: “It is no mere story, Swami! Arulmozhi himself told me. He said that the same Devi who saved him from the Kaveri floods also saved him many times on the island of Eezham. Fortunately, he has now come to Nagapattinam and is safe. Summon him here. Ask him yourself and find out the truth!”

“Yes, yes! Arulmozhi is in Nagapattinam. But what certainty do we have that he is safe? Did he not face danger in the great storm that struck yesterday? Prime Minister! My heart is not at peace! This unknown— A danger seems to be drawing near my lineage. At this very moment, the arrival of this mute madwoman here appears to me as an ill omen…”

“Swami! The arrival of the daughter of the Karaiyar clan at this time is not an ill omen, but a good one. Her presence here is a protection for our family. The Durga Parameswari, to whom I pray without ceasing, has shown her grace upon me and sent this goddess to us…”

“No, no; Durga Parameswari did not send her—Shani, the planet of misfortune, must have sent her. Tell that madwoman to leave at once and see to other matters. If you cannot do it, then I myself must take up that task…”

“Swami! I beg you, have mercy and grant me this boon. Allow her to remain in this palace until Arulmozhi returns and joins us!” pleaded the Empress in a voice full of emotion, bowing at Sundara Chozhar’s feet.

“Prime Minister! Did you hear? Did you hear the request of the daughter of Malayaman, who believes that everything white is milk? Oh God! Can such guileless souls still exist in this world? She never asks anything of me, but now and then she asks for such a boon as this. My heart cannot refuse her. Yet, every moment that mute madwoman remains here is a torment of hell for me. Therefore, make arrangements at once to bring the prince from Nagai!”
“I shall do so at once, sire! Shall I send elephant and cavalry regiments to bring the prince openly? Or…”
“You mean, should we bring him in disguise and secrecy? You think that if the prince arrives openly, there will be great turmoil in Chozha country, do you not?”

“It is not only what I think, my lord, but what I know for certain. The people are already seething for many reasons. If any pretext arises, their suppressed fury will burst forth at once. Who can say what fate will befall the Pazhuvettaraiyars and Mathuranthaka Devar…”
“What is this talk, Prime Minister! If the citizens behave so recklessly, where have the valiant armies of Chozha gone?”

“The unrest is greatest among the armies, my lord! The common people, after all, will quiet down after some empty shouting and confusion. But the soldiers—they would tear the Thanjai fort to pieces, throw the Pazhuvettaraiyars and Madhurantaka Devar into prison, and, having crowned the valiant Arulmozhi Varman, the conqueror of Lanka, upon the throne, would then turn to other matters…”

“You too are secretly wishing for such an outcome. The people, their wits muddled, are running after the tales spun by foolish astrologers. But mark my words and engrave them in your heart. Only Madhurantakan, son of my great uncle Kandaraditha Adigal, has the rightful claim to the Chola throne. I have resolved that he alone shall be crowned. Whether the people object or the Devas and the Three come to oppose me, I shall not heed them. Even if my own sons stand in the way…”

“Swami! Such a day will never come. Your sons will never oppose your wishes. Arulmozhi has no desire for the throne. They offered him the jeweled crown of Lanka, and he refused it. Would such a man ever utter a word against your command? And what of Karikalan? You yourself performed his coronation as Crown Prince, and so he accepted it. Do I need to speak of his valor and prowess? If he wished, he could carve out a great kingdom for himself with the aid of his mighty sword. Yet he too has no desire to rule. All you need do is speak a single word to him of your wish…”
“It is precisely because I am about to speak that word, and because it may reach his ears, that he is playing this game and refusing to come here despite all my summons.”
“Emperor! The Crown Prince has built a wondrous golden palace in Kanchi and awaits your arrival…”

“I know well what he is waiting for. Like Kamsan, who imprisoned his own parents, he waits to imprison us and ascend the Chola throne. Who knows whether he has built a palace of gold or a palace of lacquer?”
“Swami! To speak thus of Karikalan is cruel!” exclaimed the daughter of Malayaman.
“They have poisoned the Emperor’s heart to such an extent!” said the Prime Minister.
“There is no one else; the one who has poisoned my mind is Karikalan himself! If he were truly my son, why has he not come, no matter how many times I have sent for him?” asked Sundara Chozhar.
“There may be other valid reasons for that, may there not?”
“You are the one who keeps guessing at reasons, are you not?”
“It is spoken all over the land that if Karikalan crosses to this side of the Kollidam, the Pazhuvettaraiyars will imprison him…”
“Someone has corrupted my son’s mind with such talk! Her father is Thirukovalur Malayaman, and the Kodumbalur Velan is another. I do not know whether you too have joined hands with them.”

“Swami! I am not one to speak behind anyone’s back. Just a moment ago, you yourself spoke of danger. You said such thoughts arose in your heart. What arises in your heart is entirely true. Danger is indeed drawing near to the Chozha dynasty. It comes from two directions. Two kinds of conspiracies are unfolding in this land now. The Pazhuvettaraiyars, the Samburayars…”

“Prime Minister Aniruddha! Enough; the Pazhuvur clan has served the Chozha dynasty for a hundred years. The elder Pazhuvettaraiyar has fought in twenty-four campaigns and bears sixty-four scars upon his body. To say that such a man now conspires against the Chozha dynasty is less believable than saying the sun has gone dark or that the sea has caught fire…”

“Emperor! Even the sun is eclipsed. In the sea, the Vadavamukha fire burns beneath the waves. But that is not what I meant to say. I never claimed that the Pazhuvettaraiyars are plotting against the Chozha dynasty. They are striving with all their might to crown Madurantakan…”
“What wrong is there in wishing to crown the son of the great Shiva devotee Kandaradithar? Is not the right to the throne justly Madurantakan’s?” said the Emperor.

“I am saying the very same thing. Moreover, you yourself, of your own will, have resolved to bestow the Chola dynasty’s jeweled crown upon Prince Madurantaka. In such a case, what fault can be found with the Pazhuvettaraiyars? They are striving only to fulfill your wishes.”
“Therefore, they are even more deserving of my gratitude.”

“But, Emperor, they are also taking certain actions without your consent. They are contemplating dividing the Chola kingdom into two—giving the lands south of the Kaveri to Prince Madurantaka, and the northern part to Karikala. That very discussion is taking place today in the Samburayar palace. Emperor! For a hundred years, your forefathers toiled to expand this realm. Vijayalaya Chola, Aditya Chola, and the great Parantaka Chakravarti established the Chola empire from Eelam to the Godavari. Is it agreeable to you that this mighty Chola empire should now be split in two?”

“Prime Minister! Never, not for a single day, would I consent to that. Before dividing the Chola kingdom, I would say, ‘Cut me in two first!’ I cannot believe that the Pazhuvettaraiyars would embark on such an endeavor. Perhaps, if I myself desired it—if I wished to grant at least half the kingdom to my son—then they might have agreed to such a plan. But if they knew I did not wish it, they would abandon the idea. Prime Minister! In this Chola empire, without reducing even a finger’s breadth of its expanse, I will crown Madurantaka as king. Whether my own children oppose it, or the Pazhuvettaraiyars themselves, I will not heed them.”

“Emperor! If the Pazhuvettaraiyars oppose, it need not be considered. Your sons will not oppose. But these are not the obstacles to crowning Madurantaka. The true obstacle comes from a far greater place. That obstacle arises from the divine lady whom you, I, and all the people of this Chola land revere and worship. Only a few days ago, I spoke with her…”

“You speak of Sembiyan Maadevi. Someone has poisoned that queen’s mind as well. She believes that I desire to crown my sons. Prime Minister! Arrange for her to be brought here at once. I shall change her mind.”

“Emperor! That is not so easily done. The great Kandaraditya, on his deathbed, gave his virtuous queen a command. I was at his side in his final moments. ‘There is a most important reason why Madurantaka must not be crowned…’”
“It exists; my wife knows about it,” said your great-grandfather…”
“Prime Minister! Does such a prohibition truly exist? Do you know what it is?”
“If I knew, would I have waited until you asked to speak of it? You must summon the elder princess and ask her about it yourself…”

“Yes; that very matter has been troubling me as well. Make arrangements to bring the elder princess here at once. Whatever the obstacle may be, I will resolve it. Whom shall we send to fetch her? Why, I shall send my own daughter. Devi! Go and bring Kundavai here immediately!” said Sundara Chozhar, turning to the daughter of Malayaman.

Though Vanamadevi had been listening with one ear to the conversation between the Emperor and the Prime Minister, her attention was fixed on the mute queen who had just passed by. Therefore, when the Emperor asked for Kundavai to be summoned, the daughter of Malayaman hurried from there to the women’s quarters.

When she reached the inner apartments, she found Kundavai, Vanathi, and Poonguzhali in great confusion. The reason for this was immediately apparent to the queen: the mute queen was nowhere to be seen. Anxiously, she asked where she was, and Kundavai replied, “Mother! Fulfilling your command was no easy task. Still, the three of us together persuaded Mandakini Devi to bathe. Afterwards, we dressed her in new clothes. Vanathi was combing and braiding her hair. Poonguzhali was adorning her with flowers. While we were fetching the ornaments, we heard a commotion from her. When we turned around, Mandakini Devi was gone. As soon as her hair was braided, she suddenly became restless and ran away. We have searched all the nearby rooms, but have not found her yet. We are still looking!”
Hearing this, the daughter of Malayaman smiled. “Was there a mirror in front of her while you were adorning her?” she asked.
“There was; it was a little distance away,” replied Vanathi.

“She must have accidentally seen her adorned reflection in the mirror. That would have made her feel shy. That’s why she must have run away and hidden somewhere. Search more thoroughly. Perhaps within the women’s quarters—”

Even if she went to the flower garden and hid herself, she would still be there. Climbing over walls, leaping down from balconies—such feats have become her usual habits, haven’t they?” said the Empress.

Then, all of them went to the pleasure garden to search. But the mute queen was nowhere to be found there; their anxiety grew. They began to wonder if they should go and inform the Prime Minister and the Emperor. Just then, from somewhere, a sound rang out—“tanar, tanar”—the clang of iron striking hard against black stone. They listened intently to discern where the sound was coming from. It became clear that it issued from the sculptors’ pavilion. At once, they sent a maid to fetch a lamp, and all of them hurried to the sculptors’ hall.

Inside the sculptors’ pavilion, they beheld a strange sight. Mandakini, adorned in some measure with garments and ornaments, stood there, holding a long-handled hammer in her hand, and was striking again and again at the arms of Ravananeswaran, who was depicted bearing the weight of Mount Kailasa. The statue, carved from the hardest stone, had not yet yielded to her assault. Yet, it seemed that soon danger might befall Ravana. If two or three of the arms supporting Mount Kailasa were to break, the mountain itself might shift and settle more firmly upon his heads! The heads might be crushed to powder! It was at such a perilous and critical moment that Kundavai and the others entered the sculptors’ pavilion.

At the sight of their arrival, Mandakini dropped the hammer from her hand, turned to face them, and stood smiling gently. Except for Poonguzhali, the hearts of all who entered the pavilion were filled with the thought, “She is nothing but a mad beggar woman! It is no wonder the Emperor feels revulsion at the sight of her!”
The daughter of Malayaman looked at the others and warned, “Women, let none of you mention this before the Emperor!”

chapters.title: The Emperor’s Wrath
paragraphs: At the very moment when Mandakini was discovered by the other palace women in the sculpted hall, a heated argument was raging between the Emperor and the Prime Minister.

No sooner had the daughter of Malayaman left than Prime Minister Aniruddha said, “Your Majesty! I have always maintained that certain matters should not be spoken of in the presence of women. Now, it has become necessary to speak of them and resolve them. The Pandya assassins are still lurking and moving about in this land. They are waiting for the right moment to fulfill their terrible vow.”

“This is nothing new, is it? Is this not news I already know? Is it not for this very reason that the Pazhuvettaraiyars have arranged such formidable protection for me?” the Emperor replied with a sardonic smile.

“It is true that you know about the assassins, but you cannot possibly know that these conspirators are receiving financial assistance from the very treasury of the Chola kingdom!” said the Prime Minister.
“Ah! What a fantastic tale this is!” exclaimed Sundara Chozhar.

“I am compelled to tell you even more astonishing tales than this. New gold coins from the treasury vault of Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar were found heaped in the midst of the Pandya assassins. Here is my disciple Thirumalai, who saw it with his own eyes. If you command, he will describe it in detail…”

“That is not necessary. The Pazhuvettaraiyars have, for generations, shed their blood and laid down their lives for the Chola dynasty. Even if Harishchandra himself were to come and tell me that they are giving gold coins from my treasury to a band plotting to kill me, I would not believe it.”
“Forgive me, I am not accusing the Pazhuvettaraiyars of such treachery. But is it not possible that, without their knowledge, gold coins from our treasury could be reaching the conspirators?”
“How could that be? Can a soul depart without Yama’s knowledge?” “If Yama, perchance, had married a young maiden in his old age, perhaps even that might have been possible, Your Majesty!”
“I too did not approve of Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar marrying at this age. I have told him so myself. But for that reason, I cannot tolerate such accusations of treachery being leveled against him.”
“Emperor! I am not accusing Pazhuvettaraiyar of treason. It is upon the young queen he has married that I lay my charge.”
“It is one thing to accuse men; that can be borne. But to cast blame upon an unfortunate, helpless woman—this, I find most distasteful.”

“No matter how distasteful it may be, there are certain truths about the young queen of Pazhuvur that I must reveal to you. Once before, I failed to tell you an important truth at the right time, and I have had to regret it ever since. Just now, you too were angry with me. Therefore, I ask you to listen with patience.”

Hearing these tactful words from the Prime Minister, the Emperor smiled. “You always manage to turn my own words against me. That is my personal affair. There is no connection between that and this. Still, speak—I am listening,” he said.

“Three years ago, the young queen Nandini Devi came to reside in the great palace of Pazhuvur. Since then, certain magicians have been coming and going frequently to the Pazhuvur palace. Even Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar is aware of this. He too dislikes the presence of these magicians. Yet, lacking the courage to oppose his elder brother, he remains silent.”
“Is this not how brothers ought to be?”
“But should brotherly loyalty be allowed to bring ruin upon the kingdom?”

“What ruin has befallen the kingdom now? Will the realm be destroyed simply because a foolish woman summons some magicians and asks them to perform their spells? Are you suggesting that it is because of the young queen’s magic that I have fallen ill?”

“Emperor! Those who come to see the young queen of Pazhuvur are not, in truth, magicians. I suspect that those who pretend to be magicians are, in fact, conspirators. I also suspect that through them, wealth from our treasury is being siphoned away…” “I am suspicious.”
“You may suspect anything or anyone you wish. But is there any proof?”
“My king! If today we were to search the palace of Periya Pazhuvettarayar and his treasury chambers, perhaps we might find some proof.”

“No one has ever suggested anything to me that I dislike more than this. Aniruddha! You are my friend alone. But Pazhuvettarayar has been a friend, dear as life itself, to three generations of Chola emperors before me. He is like an iron shield to the Chola dynasty. To the enemies of the Cholas, he is like Indra’s thunderbolt. To search such a man’s palace in his absence? Rather than believe that Pazhuvettarayar is harboring conspirators in his mansion, I would sooner believe that Malayaman’s daughter would call poison a medicine and give it to me…”

“Emperor! This is happening without Pazhuvettarayar’s knowledge. Blinded by infatuation, Pazhuvettarayar does not see what is happening before him. Without his awareness, his palace has become the headquarters for conspirators. There is reason to believe that the young queen of Pazhuvoor is allied with these plotters.”
“What further slander are you going to heap upon that foolish girl?”

“A few days ago, in the forest of Thiruppurambiyam, near the Pandya prince’s camp, a coronation ceremony was held at midnight. A five-year-old boy was seated on a throne and crowned as the Pandya king. Those who participated in this coronation swore an oath to utterly destroy the Chola dynasty…”
“Prime Minister! Do you think you can frighten me with this tale? Did you expect my hands and feet to tremble?”

“No, Emperor, no! I do not consider that farcical ceremony to be of any consequence. I only wished to inform you that the young queen of Pazhuvoor was present among those conspirators who took that oath.”
“Who is the clever person who came and told you all this after witnessing it up close? There he stands—your beloved disciple, is it not?”
“He only arrived there after everything was over. The one who saw it with his own eyes was Vandiyathevan of the Vanar clan…”

“Are you speaking of that spy who once came here and then escaped and fled?” “He is not a spy, my lord! He is the intimate friend of your royal son, Aditya Karikalan.” “Karikalan has many such intimate friends. No two of them will say the same thing. Let us suppose what he said is true. Even so, there is nothing we can do about it right now. Periya Pazhuvettarayar is not here; nor is his young queen. We can inquire into it after they return. Prime Minister! As you speak of the young queen of Pazhuvur, I myself have become curious to see such an extraordinary woman. When Pazhuvettarayar married her, I was so repulsed that I ordered she should not be brought before me. Perhaps because of that, she has developed some anger towards me—I do not know. When Periya Pazhuvettarayar returns this time, I shall have his young queen brought before me and try to dispel her anger…”

“Emperor! That is my wish as well. There are even more important reasons to calm the anger of Nandini Devi. Until Nandini arrives, you must grant permission for the queen of Eezham to remain in our palace…”
“Ah! You have already crowned her as the queen of Eezham, have you? Very well; but what connection is there between her and the queen of Pazhuvur?”
“That is what we must discover, my lord! If the two meet face to face, perhaps that connection will come to light. Perhaps the enmity that Nandini Devi harbors against the Chola dynasty may change…”
“Minister! It is surprising that you are so concerned about the enmity of a woman…”
“There is reason to be concerned about the enmity of Nandini Devi. I hesitate to say it aloud, wondering if it is appropriate…”
“Who else can tell me what you hesitate to say? Do not hold anything back—tell me everything,” said the Emperor.

The Prime Minister thought for a moment and then spoke. “Great King! What I am about to say now is a most intricate matter. It may not be pleasing to you. Yet you must listen patiently. Nandini Devi and Mandakini Devi…” All who saw them marveled at the striking resemblance in their appearance…”
“There are countless wonders in this world. One tree looks just like another. One madman resembles another madman…”
“But a tree does not disguise itself and walk about like another tree. Nor does one madman come in the guise of another’s spirit to torment the Emperor…”
“What are you saying, Prime Minister?”
“You suffered, believing that the spirit of Mandakini Devi came to torment you at night…”
“Are you saying it was not her spirit, but she herself who came?”
“No, no, Young Queen of Pazhuvoor, I am saying that someone must have acted as Mandakini’s spirit to torment you.”

Sundara Chozhar straightened up a little, his face flushed with anger. “If what you say now is the truth, then that demoness, with my own hands I will wring her neck…” But before he could finish, the Prime Minister interrupted hastily, “No, Your Majesty! Do not utter such an oath with your lips!”
“Why not? Why do you have such compassion for her? What does it matter what I do to the one who has tormented me so much?” Sundara Chozhar thundered.
“No matter how much she has troubled you, if the one who caused that pain is bound to you by a close tie… if, perchance, she is your own daughter…” the Prime Minister said, hesitating.
“Prime Minister! What nonsense is this?” exclaimed Sundara Chozhar.

“Your Majesty! I have truly tested the limits of your patience. For that, give me whatever punishment you see fit. But let us not speak of punishing Nandini Devi. Nandini Devi is not only the Young Queen of the powerful Pazhuvettaraiyar; she is also the daughter of Sundara Chozha Chakravarthi, lord of the three worlds. Who could punish her for any crime?” said Aniruddha Brahmarayar.
Hearing this, the Emperor gazed at the Prime Minister for a while, overwhelmed with astonishment. Then he laughed aloud, “Kalir!”
“Emperor! Today is a most auspicious day. I have heard you laugh twice,” said Aniruddhar.

“Brahmarayar! Until now, I thought there was only one madwoman in this palace. Now I realize you are even madder than her. She is a mute lunatic who does not speak; you, on the other hand, are a raving lunatic who speaks incessantly!” said Sundara Chozhar, and once again, he laughed heartily, recalling the thought.

chapters.title: In the Late Night
paragraphs: Even as the sound of Sundara Chozhar’s laughter still echoed, the women entered the chamber. Foremost among them was the Maharani; behind her, with Kundavai on one side and Vanathi on the other, Mandakini was gently led forward, and following them, like a procession, came Poonguzhali and an elderly nurse.

The king’s laughter had brought a spark of cheer to the women as well. Mandakini would, for a moment, lift her gaze to look at him, and the next moment, lower her eyes to the ground. Her adornment was now complete. In those days, Princess Kundavai was renowned throughout the land for her unparalleled mastery in the art of ornamentation. For this very reason, it was customary for minor kings to send their daughters to Pazhayarai to become companions to the young princess.

Kundavai had employed all her skill in adorning the mute queen. Some inexplicable emotion that had arisen deep within her heart had led her to arrange Mandakini’s hair in the same style as Nandini’s, with a regal knot. Once the adornment was finished, it became clear to all the women that Mandakini now resembled Nandini in every aspect. The twenty-five years of age that separated the two women was hardly noticeable, for Mandakini, having wandered the forests, possessed a robust health and youthful radiance. The other women brought Mandakini Devi forward with a sense of pride. Each of them had their own reason for feeling proud.

In those days when this history took place, it was common for the great emperors and minor kings of Tamilagam to marry several wives. Wars raged without end, and the royal princes were always at the forefront of battle. To ensure the survival of the royal lineage, it was customary for kings to marry many women. It was considered a noble virtue for the chief queen to embrace and support the other consorts without jealousy. In this manner, the daughter of Malayaman was filled with enthusiasm. Kundavai took pride in having displayed her skill in adornment so perfectly. Had she not transformed a woman who had appeared as a mad beggar into one of incomparable beauty and youth? As for Poonguzhali, she was delighted to see her aunt receiving such royal honors in the palace. Were not the palace women here behaving quite differently from what she had expected?

Thus, the Emperor watched the procession of women entering the chamber, their pride overflowing. In that very instant, his smile faded. Mandakini’s new appearance filled him with boundless astonishment. He blinked, half-closing his eyes with his hand and then opening them again, as if doubting whether what he saw before him was truly real. The details the Prime Minister had just been recounting were firmly imprinted in his mind. He clearly perceived the resemblance between the womanly form that had appeared before him at midnight and tormented him for some time, and the figure of Mandakini now standing before him. At the same time, he noticed certain differences as well. A desire to unravel this mystery completely and discover the truth began to dawn within him. The aversion he had first felt towards Mandakini remained unchanged. Yet, he resolved not to reveal it outwardly.

Turning to Aniruddha, he said in a gentle voice, “Prime Minister! Just now I called you mad. Now it seems that all the delusion and madness are mine. Henceforth, it will not suffice for the physician to visit me daily; I must also have a magician sent to me. Even if you catch the sorcerer who comes to see the younger queen of Pazhuvoor and send him to me, it would be no sin!”

A slight tremor stirred within Aniruddha. In his heart, he prayed, “Let none of those sorcerers come near the Emperor.” Then he said aloud, “Your Majesty! Why a magician? What need for any other spell? There is no mantra more powerful than the holy name of Sri Narayana!”
Kundavai Piratti spoke: “Father! Did you not send for me? Did you not say we must go to Pazhaiyarai? May we all go together?”

Sundara Chozhar did not reply to her, but turned to the Prime Minister and said, “Aniruddha! I have changed my mind. For some reason, these women are all in high spirits, as if a new daughter-in-law has come to the house. I do not wish to separate them at this moment. As you suggested, let them all remain here for a few days. Sembiyan Maadevi has great trust and respect for you. Therefore, you go yourself and bring her here. Send your disciple to Nagapattinam. I will instruct Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar myself to arrange for Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar and his younger queen to be brought here at once!”
“So be it, Emperor! But it may take a few days for everyone to gather. Because of the storm and rain yesterday, all the rivers are in full flood,” said the Prime Minister.

“There is no harm in that; having waited so long, there is nothing to lose by waiting a few days more. If arrangements are made to bring Karikalan here, we can settle all matters at once. If he still refuses to come, then I myself must set out to fetch him. We can discuss that later. Tomorrow itself, you must go and somehow bring the Periya Piratti here in person! As you go, pay heed also to the people who have suffered hardship due to the storm. We have become so absorbed in our family affairs that we have quite forgotten that important duty,” said the Emperor.
“No, my lord! I have not forgotten it. All matters will proceed as they should; you may rest easy,” replied the Prime Minister, taking his leave.

That night, Sundara Chozhar truly experienced a peace he had not known in many years. The news that Mandakini of the Karaiyar clan had not died had lifted a great burden that had long weighed upon his heart. The tidings that Arulmozhi Varman was safe in Nagapattinam brought him comfort as well. Knowing that the Soodamani Viharam was a strong, well-built structure, he felt assured that those within were in no danger. The suggestion by Aniruddhar that the younger queen of Pazhuvoor might be his own daughter struck him as amusing whenever he thought of it. This notion often brought a faint smile to the Emperor’s face.
For a while, he conversed cheerfully with the women, including the daughter of Malayaman. He praised Kundavai’s skill in adornment.

“You have transformed a wild jungle girl into a queen of the celestial realms! But was it this old man who fell into your hands for such a makeover? Should you not display your talents on young girls like Vanathi?” he teased.
Afterwards, he questioned Poonguzhali further about Arulmozhi Varman and learned more details from her.
At the end, Poonguzhali said, “Swami, grant me permission to return to Kodikkarai. May I depart as early as tomorrow? I no longer have any worry about my aunt!”

“You said your aunt’s son is lying sick with fever, did you not? Have you no concern for him either? There is no need for such haste to leave. Stay here a few more days before you go!” said the Emperor. Poonguzhali remained silent.

That night, Sundara Chola Chakravarthi slept peacefully. He did not dream much; and the dreams he did have were not nightmares, but pleasant ones. The women of the palace, who slept in the adjoining chamber, too slumbered in tranquility. Among them, the only one who was restless and unable to sleep well was Mandakini. The events of the day had stirred great turmoil in her mind. Most of all, her thoughts swung back and forth between the treasure chamber and the secret tunnel. Her heart was troubled, unable to find peace, as she brooded over how her attempt to block that tunnel—by breaking Ravana’s arms and sealing the way—had failed.

In the dim, flickering light of the ever-burning lamp, she kept glancing around. Most often, she fixed her gaze upon the windows of the upper storeys. Midnight had passed; the latter half of the night had begun. The third watch was nearly at its end. At that moment, she noticed a figure at one of the upper windows. A ghastly, fearsome face seemed pressed against the window, peering into the room. Somehow, she recognized whose face it was. She sprang up, startled. Again, she stared intently at the window. The face was gone. She walked softly to the doorway of the adjoining room and peered in. There, she saw the Emperor sleeping peacefully. She looked up at the windows of that room as well, but saw nothing.

She returned and, without making a sound, gently touched and shook Poonguzhali awake. Poonguzhali, who had been sleeping deeply, opened her eyes. At the sight of the mute queen’s face, she was startled. The mute queen signaled to her to follow. Poonguzhali, who held boundless devotion and trust in her aunt, rose silently and followed her.

The mute queen walked towards the sculpture hall. On the way, she took a burning lamp from the walkway and carried it with her. Upon reaching the sculpture hall, a slight anxiety arose in Poonguzhali’s heart. Is she going to break the Ravana sculpture again? If so, the noise would surely wake everyone in the palace! Wouldn’t people then become convinced that her aunt was truly mad?

If her aunt attempted such a thing, she must stop her at any cost. Even if she had to snatch the hammer away by force, she must prevent it… With such thoughts, Poonguzhali followed her aunt into the sculpture hall. Ah! What is this! The head of the Ravana sculpture seems to be moving! No, no! Ravana’s head was not moving. Between Ravana’s heads and the Kailasa mountain above— In the midst, the shape of another man's head seemed to appear! Instantly, it vanished. A useless illusion! The confusion of sleep! Perhaps it was merely the shadow cast by the sculptures in the lamplight...

Whether Mandakini too perceived that apparition, none could say; yet she walked straight towards the statue of Ravana. Fortunately, her attention did not fall upon the crowbar lying nearby. Between Ravana's heads—between the arms that held up Mount Kailasa—she lifted the lamp and shone it into the darkness. There, an opening became visible. Poonguzhali's earlier guess was proven correct. There was indeed an outer entrance to a secret tunnel there. It was so cleverly concealed that none could suspect its existence. Only the previous night, her aunt had tried to close that tunnel's entrance. Others, unaware of her intent, had prevented her.

As Poonguzhali pondered these things, the mute queen signaled to her daughter-in-law to follow, then, lamp in hand, struggled to enter the opening and began to descend. Gradually, her body disappeared, then her head, and finally the lamp she held vanished from sight. Only a faint glimmer of light remained. Then Poonguzhali, bending and twisting her body with care not to strike her head, cautiously entered the tunnel's mouth. In a few moments, she too was gone. Soon, even the lamp's glow faded, and darkness settled over the sculpted hall.

In the morning, when the daughter of Malayaman, Kundavai, and Vanathi awoke and looked about, they were startled to find neither the mute queen nor Poonguzhali in their beds. They searched throughout the palace, in the gardens, and in the sculpted hall, but could not find them. No one could fathom how they had vanished so mysteriously. When they reported this to the Emperor, he was at first somewhat troubled. Then he said, "It is for the best that those madwomen have disappeared! What does it matter how they vanished?" Yet, within his heart, an unshakable anxiety and fear took root.

chapters.title: Turmoil at Kadambur
paragraphs: From the moment Aditya Karikalan arrived at the Kadambur palace, both the permanent residents and the guests who had come to stay found themselves as if standing on thorns, as if walking over fire. No one could predict at what moment, or in what form, a weapon might spring from the prince’s tongue. Thus, everyone was in a state of constant anxiety and distress.

Karikalan would often, with sly gestures and veiled words, allude to the conspiracy to place Madurantaka on the Chola throne, causing the others to tremble with unease. Pazhuvettaraiyar could not bear this. He pressed Sambhuvaraiyar, insisting that the views of the minor chieftains must be openly conveyed to Karikalan. But Sambhuvaraiyar would reply, “Have patience; after all, he is our guest, and a mere youth. What does it matter if his intentions come to naught? Let us wait for the right moment to speak,” and thus kept postponing the matter.
Before they could resolve the dilemma of how to broach the subject, Aditya Karikalan himself, one day when all were gathered together, boldly raised the issue.

“I have come here to seek the counsel of Pazhuvur Grandfather and Kadambur Uncle on a matter of great importance. I shall ask it now. Three years ago, my father publicly crowned me as the heir-apparent to the Chola kingdom. All of you gave your consent to this. Now it seems the Emperor has changed his mind. I hear he wishes to place Madurantaka on the throne and crown him king. For this reason, he has sent me summons upon summons, urging me to come to Thanjavur. I have been refusing and putting off the journey. Why should I go to Thanjavur? Why should I stand before my father and openly defy his word? Is it not better to stay away altogether? Pazhuvur Grandfather! Kadambur Uncle! You are elders, wise in all matters of justice. Tell me yourselves: is it right for my father, after all this time, to ask me to relinquish the kingdom to Madurantaka? Would it be a crime for me to refuse?”

When Aditya Karikalan asked this so directly, everyone was struck dumb with astonishment. Pazhuvetaraiyar cleared his throat, thinking to buy some time before answering, and said, “Prince! Surely you must have consulted your grandfather of Thirukovalur about this matter? What does Malayaman say?”

“Ah! Don’t you all know that old man’s nature by now? Would he ever agree to let his grandson’s throne pass to another? He would sooner cut down both me and my mother who bore me! Even now, Malayaman has begun gathering his forces—to secure his grandson’s claim to the throne! But I am not going to act solely on his words. I will do as all of you say!” Karikalan replied, with the innocence of a most dutiful son.

Pazhuvetaraiyar, deceived by this, said, “We are not the sort to incite a son to oppose his father, as Malayaman does. Whatever command the Emperor gives, we are all bound to obey. But we do have the right to speak of what is just. It cannot be said that there is no justice in what the Emperor says on this matter. Nor can it be said that Madurantaka Devar has no claim to the Chola kingdom. Prince! Since you ask, we speak our minds. The final decision rests with your will. Allowing this debate to grow will be most dangerous for the kingdom, in our view. Therefore, it is best to come to some compromise. The Chola realm is no longer hemmed in between two rivers as before. It now stretches from Cape Comorin to the banks of the Krishna. Even if divided, each part would be a great kingdom in itself. Thus, it would be just to grant the realm south of the Kollidam river to Madurantaka Devar, and the northern part to you. This is our considered opinion. If you agree, we can proceed further. I myself will take responsibility for persuading the Emperor to consent to this arrangement!” he said.

At that, Aditya Karikalan burst into laughter, which stoked the fire in Pazhuvetaraiyar’s belly. “Grandfather! Dividing the Chola kingdom so that the Pazhuvetaraiyars rule the southern realm and the Sambuvaraiyars the northern—what a fair partition that would be! It would be a fitting reward for the service your two families have rendered my grandfather’s house since my great-grandfather’s time. But I have no desire whatsoever to split the kingdom. To divide the realm handed down through generations is one thing; to divide a wedded wife is quite another! Perhaps you elders may approve of such a thing! But for me, it is utterly unacceptable!”
“No!” declared Karikalan, and sparks seemed to fly from the eyes of Periya Pazhuvetarayar. He rose to his feet in agitation, his hand moving, ready to draw his sword from its scabbard.

At that moment, Karikalan spoke: “Grandfather! What is this? Are you trying to leave already? Listen to my proposal in its entirety before you go. I do not consent to dividing the Chola kingdom. For five generations, my ancestors and yours, and countless warriors of valor, have toiled and sacrificed their lives to bring the Chola realm to its present glory. To split it into two and reduce it to petty provinces would be a grave sin. Our forebears—Rajaditya and the rest—who now dwell in the warrior’s heaven, would curse us for such an act. Therefore, abandon that idea. I am prepared to relinquish the entire Chola empire to Madurantakan; there is justice in that. Madurantakan is the son of my elder uncle, and by rights, he should have been crowned in my father’s stead. But due to the arrangements of Emperor Parantaka, my father ascended the throne. Let that error rest with him. Even though, by the law of succession, I have full claim to this kingdom as my father’s son, I am willing to give it up. But there is one condition.

“I require an army of three hundred thousand warriors, fully equipped and provisioned for a year, to march north. I must have all the necessary arms, equipment, and supplies for the army. I need three hundred great ships capable of sailing the high seas. Let Parthibendran be appointed admiral of the fleet and sail along the coast, while I lead the land forces northward. We shall meet at the mouth of the Ganga, Parthibendran and I, and from there advance further north. The poets have sung that my ancestor, Karikala Valavan, whose name I bear, planted the tiger flag atop the Himalayas. What my forebear accomplished, I shall achieve once more. With the strength of my sword and the valor of the warriors who follow me, I shall conquer lands north of the Krishna river and become emperor of those realms. If I fall in battle, I shall attain the warrior’s heaven with the joy that we have upheld the glory of the Chola clan. Grandfather of Pazhuvur! Uncle of Kadambur! What do you say? Will you agree to fulfill these conditions?”

Thus Karikalan spoke, his voice resounding with majesty, and then fell silent. The two elders were struck dumb with astonishment. Pazhuvetarayar, faltering, replied, “Prince! Who are we to accept your conditions? What right do we have? Should we not ask the Emperor himself?”
Karikalan sprang up, boiling with rage, and thundered in a voice that echoed like a storm:

“Paata! Do you think you can deceive anyone by uttering the Emperor’s name? You cannot deceive me! You have imprisoned my father within the palace walls and made him a puppet to dance at your will! Did you think I am unaware of this? Without the permission of Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar, can anyone even see my father? Was it by my father’s own wish that he ordered my brother to be brought as a captive from Eezham? Or was it by your compulsion? What father, with his own heart, would command that his beloved son, the bravest among heroes, be brought back as a prisoner? Today, all the people of Chola Nadu are seething with fury, believing that you have brought Arulmozhi back as a captive and drowned him in the sea to his death…”
“Prince! Who uttered such a monstrous accusation? I will cut out the tongue of the one who spoke it and make him an example for all!” roared Pazhuvettaraiyar.

“If only a single person had spoken such words, you might do so. But ten thousand, a hundred thousand, a million voices are saying it. If you were to punish all of them, Chola Nadu would become a land of corpses and funeral pyres. It would be a fitting kingdom for Madurantakan, the devotee of Shiva, to rule over! But, Paata! I do not believe such talk—the people are ignorant fools. Without examining the truth, they merely repeat the tales spun by one man. You, the hereditary pillars of the Chola clan, would never have committed such a heinous crime. If Arulmozhi has perished in the sea, it must be due to his own fate. Perhaps he drowned only to put to shame the astrologers, soothsayers, and palm-leaf readers who proclaimed he was born to rule the three worlds. Paata! However great a hero you are, even you cannot summon a whirlwind in the midst of the sea, nor can you call down lightning to strike the mast of a ship. Perhaps it was the work of Pandya sorcerers; you are not responsible for that. Therefore, you are not to blame for Arulmozhi’s fate. But do not ever again tell me, ‘I must ask the Emperor and answer you.’ Next, you might even say you must ask that beloved Brahmarayan and answer me. The Emperor and the Chief Minister merely bear those titles. They cannot do anything against your wishes. If you wish, you may say, ‘I must ask the Lady Nandini Devi of Pazhuvoor and answer you’!”
At that moment, Kandhamaaran interjected, stammering in confusion, “Sir! The guests who have come to our house…”

Kaarikalan turned his gaze upon him, his eyes blazing, and laughed like Shiva who burned down the three cities. “Kandhamaaran! Is this your house? I had forgotten! I had also forgotten that you are the bravest of the brave, born in the line of the fierce archer of Kolli Hills. In your house—especially in your presence—I must speak with some caution! What wrong have I spoken? What have I done to your household guests?… Kandhamaaran! Why do your hands and feet tremble? Has the fever that spreads through Eezham reached you as well? But you have not even gone to Eezham!”
At that moment, Vandiyathevan said, “Prince! Kandhamaaran does not have a fever. He is angry because you called the young queen of Pazhuvoor ‘grandmother’!”

Kandhamaaran glared at Vandiyathevan with fury and began to reach for his dagger. Parthibendran caught his hand, pulled him down to sit, and whispered something in his ear. Kandhamaaran calmed down, though his body continued to tremble for a while.

Kaarikalan, laughing at him, turned to the Pazhuvetaraiyar and said, “Grandfather! Young men are sometimes unruly and leap about without restraint. You need not pay them any mind. Since you are my grandfather by custom, the young queen is, after all, my grandmother, is she not? My grandmother herself would not be offended if I called her so; nor are you. Why, then, do these children harbor such anger? Let it go! I have strayed far from the matter I began to discuss. Do not bear the burden in my father—the Emperor’s—name. If you agree, it is as if my father himself has agreed. The treasury is in your hands. If I declare that I am marching north to battle, not three hundred thousand, but three million warriors will come forth from Chozha land in competition. Even gathering three hundred ships would not be difficult. You must give your consent! Mathuranthaka Devar must also agree! That is all! What do you say?” Kaarikalan finished.

The Pazhuvetaraiyar, flustered and bewildered, cleared his throat and replied, “Prince! Even if I agree to your astonishing wish, the consent of Mathuranthaka Devar is essential, is it not? Can you set out for conquest without the Emperor’s permission? Therefore, let us all go to Thanjavur…”

“That alone is not possible, Paata. After going to Thanjavur, if my father commands otherwise, I will not be able to disobey him. And then, there is my mother there—the daughter of Malayaman. My younger sister, the Ilaya Piratti, is there too. They will not consent to my renouncing the world and wandering away. It will be hard for me to go against their wishes as well. Paata! This matter must be settled here, in this very Kadambur palace. You go to Thanjai and bring Madurantakan here. After we have discussed and decided among ourselves, we can inform my father. Once all preparations for the campaign are complete, I will come to Thanjai, bid farewell to my parents, and then depart. Or else, let Madurantakan be crowned at once, and let my parents come to Kanchi. I will have them stay in the golden palace I have built there, and then I shall set out.”

Pazhuvettarayar looked at Sambuvarayar. Sambuvarayar, however, was staring at the roof beams. Realizing that no help would come from him, Pazhuvettarayar said, “Prince! How can I say anything contrary to your wishes?”
“Do not call it a command, Paata! Is this mere boy to command you, whose hair has turned grey in the service of the Chola Empire? Say instead that you will fulfill my request!” said Aditya Karikalan.
“So be it,” Pazhuvettarayar replied, his voice rumbling.

“Many thanks, Paata! In that case, make arrangements to depart at once! Bring Madurantakan here openly, seated atop an elephant. Or bring him in a golden chariot. Only, let us not have the Ilaya Pattini’s closed palanquin this time!” Karikalan said, laughing.

Then, turning to Kandhamaaran and the others, he said, “Kandhamaaran! You are indeed fortunate! More guests are coming to your house. Madurantaka, who is to become emperor of the Chola land after Sundara Chola, is coming. He may even bring with him the daughter of the younger Pazhuvettarayar, who is to become his queen. The Kadambur palace will be a scene of grand festivity. Let Pazhuvoor Paata set out for Thanjai. We can set out for the hunt. Come! In archery, I was once a master. People used to say, ‘After Arjuna, it is Aditya Karikalan!’ For three years, I have not touched a bow, and I have almost forgotten the art. I must practice again. Parthibendran! Vandiyathevan! All of you, let us go! Where shall we go for the hunt? Shall we go to Kollimalai?” Karikalan asked, addressing them all.

All this while, Sambuvaraiyar had not participated in any of the conversation. Now he spoke: “Prince! Kolli Hills are far away. There is no need to go such a distance. On the western bank of the Veeranarayana Lake, there lies a dense forest. It is often called ‘Dandakaranya’. There are plenty of wild animals there, enough for any hunt. The animals displayed in our hunting pavilion were all brought from that very forest. The woods by the lake’s edge are quite close to this palace. If we set out in the morning, we can return home by nightfall!”

“Let it be so, sir! While I am a guest in this palace, your word is my law. May we invite your daughter Manimekalai to join the hunt as well? Wherever she is, laughter and merriment follow!” said Aditya Karikalan.
“I have no objection; we may ask Manimekalai herself,” replied Sambuvaraiyar.

At this, Kandanmaran interjected, “Why should women come to the hunting grounds? We would be more occupied with ensuring their safety than with the hunt itself. Besides, does not Lady Nandini need company here?”

“Yes, yes, Kandanmaran is always concerned about the matron of Pazhuvoor. There is another difficulty in taking Manimekalai along. If someone, seeing her leap and bound, mistakes her for a deer and lets fly an arrow, what then? Let the women remain in the palace; we shall go hunting. We must set out at dawn tomorrow. Tonight, let the Kuravai dance end early, and let everyone get to bed soon. Sir! Please inform the hunters at once. Vandiyathevan! Come! Let us go to our quarters!” So saying, Aditya Karikalan seized Vandiyathevan’s hand and led him away.

Kandanmaran and Parthibendran watched them go, a trace of envy in their eyes. Sambuvaraiyar went off to give orders to the hunters. Pazhuvetaraiyar went in search of Nandini, towards the women’s quarters.

chapters.title: Nandini Refuses
paragraphs: Pazhuvetarayar went to see Nandini with a measure of hopefulness. The confidence with which he had set out for Kadambur had not, until now, borne any fruit. He had believed that if the young Aditya Karikalan could be detained in the Kadambur palace, he could, through persuasion or intimidation, be made to act according to his wishes. He was certain that, at the very least, the prince would have to yield to the commands of himself and Sambuvarayar. Pazhuvetarayar was well aware of the dangers in immediately crowning Madurantakan as the sole ruler of the Chola kingdom. In the north, Malayaman would oppose it; in the south, the Kodumbalur Velan would stand against it. If Karikalan joined forces with them, civil war would be inevitable. Who could predict how such a conflict would end? The majority of the common people would side with the sons of Sundara Chola. Even Madurantakan’s own mother was opposed to him. Could one rely solely on the Kalamukha faction and plunge into a civil war? If rebellions arose in Pandya Nadu, Chera Nadu, or in the lands north of the river, they would only multiply. Therefore, if for now Madurantakan could be given half the kingdom—especially if that half were the southern Chola realm with Thanjavur as its capital—then, in the future, things could be managed as they unfolded. The influence of the Kodumbalur Velan could be dealt with in some way. Later, they could turn north and try their hand against Malayaman of Thirukovalur. Karikalan was nothing but a reckless youth; one day, he might act rashly and lose his life in some foolish adventure. If that happened, all worries would be over. For the present, it was best to arrange for half the kingdom.

It was after much consultation with the young queen Nandini that Periya Pazhuvetarayar had arrived at this decision, and only then had he come to Kadambur. He had summoned Karikalan there as well. But nothing had happened as he had expected. Instead of submitting to the elders, Karikalan had been browbeating them, making long speeches, and mocking them at every turn. Pazhuvetarayar could not tolerate the prince’s jests and double-edged words. Most hurtful of all was Karikalan’s frequent reference to him as an old man, and his habit of calling the young queen “grandmother”—each word was like a poisoned arrow to Pazhuvetarayar’s heart.

To make matters worse, Sambuvarayar’s conduct was far from satisfactory. Instead of standing by his side and helping to restrain Karikalan’s insolence, Sambuvarayar mostly kept his mouth shut and maintained a sullen silence. When he did speak, he did so hesitantly, stammering and mumbling. Karikalan’s... Since he had come as a guest to the palace, perhaps he is conducting himself with such caution so that nothing untoward or improper might occur! Whatever the reason may be, the conduct of Sambuvaraiyar was in no way satisfactory to Pazhuvetaraiyar.

How much of what Karikalan said today was genuine, how much was mockery, and how much was deceitful speech with one thing in the mind and another on the lips—it was not easy to discern. After having summoned Madurantakan there as well, who knows if he is planning to commit some great misdeed? Could he not even arrange for Malayamaan to march with a great army, besiege the Kadambur palace, and surround it?...

Thinking of all this, it seemed best to return to Thanjavur at once. The younger Pazhuvetaraiyar was a prudent man. He could consult with him as well. If Madurantakan were to be brought here, it would be wise to have Kalantakakandan assemble a large force and keep it ready on the riverbank, prepared for any situation. Whatever may happen, it would not do to let the young queen remain here any longer and be subjected to the mockery of these fools. It was absolutely necessary to take her away and leave her in Thanjavur. Now, an opportunity for that had arisen—why should he let it slip by?

Having thus come to a decision, a certain enthusiasm arose in the heart of the elder Pazhuvetaraiyar. With a brightened face, he made his way to Nandini’s private chamber. As he approached the threshold, he heard the sound of laughter ringing out from within. For some reason, that laughter irritated him. Nandini never laughed like this in the Thanjavur palace. What sudden joy had come over her now? Why was she laughing? And who was laughing along with her?...

Upon entering, he saw that the woman with her was Manimekalai. This brought some clarity to his mind. The moment Manimekalai saw him, she tried to stifle her laughter by covering her mouth with both hands. Yet, unable to contain herself, she ran out of the room, laughing still.
Nandini’s laughter ceased the instant she saw Pazhuvetaraiyar. Her face regained its usual dignity.
“Sir! Come in! Have your deliberations reached their conclusion?” she asked.
“Nandini! Why was that girl laughing so? Why did she run out, laughing all the while?” Pazhuvetaraiyar asked.

“Is that what you want me to say? Very well, I shall say it. Some of the conversation that took place in the assembly hall seems to have reached the ears of Manimekalai, who was in the adjoining chamber.
