She recounted how Prince Aditya Karikalan spoke mockingly about your grandfathers and grandmothers, and then she laughed…”
“Ugh! Wicked girl! And you—did you laugh along with her?”
“Yes, I laughed along with her. When she left, I felt like crying. But before I could, you arrived!” said Nandini, wiping away the tears that had welled up in her eyes.
“Ah! It was my mistake to bring you into the midst of such fools. At dawn tomorrow, we shall depart for Thanjavur. Bear with it just for tonight!” he said.
“Must we leave for Thanjavur? Why? Has the purpose for which we came been accomplished?” Nandini asked.
Pazhuvettarayar then recounted to Nandini the outcomes of the discussions that had taken place in the assembly hall that day.

After hearing everything, Nandini said, “Swami! You may go to Thanjavur if you wish, but I will not come. Until I have taught Aditya Karikalan a lesson, I have no intention of leaving this place. That arrogant prince must fall at your feet and beg forgiveness for his mocking words. Otherwise, he must fall prey to your sword!”
“Nandini! What are you saying? How could such a dreadful thought arise in your heart?”
“Sir! What is so dreadful about it? If someone insults the husband who took my hand in marriage, is it so wrong for me to wish for vengeance?”

“No, Nandini! Listen to me! For six generations, our clan of Pazhuvur has shared a bond of friendship with the Chola dynasty. Can I forget all that and, just because an ignorant youth uttered some nonsense, take up my sword against that clan? Can I, with my own hand, slay the son of Sundara Chola, the prince who, until today, is the heir to the throne? What kind of talk is this?” Pazhuvettarayar exclaimed in alarm.

When he had heard Karikalan’s harsh words earlier, there were moments when Pazhuvettarayar’s hand had strayed to his sword. But then, with great effort, he had restrained both his mind and his hand. Now, hearing Nandini give voice to the very thought that had fleetingly crossed his own mind, he was deeply unsettled.

“Sir! Your family has been friends with the Chola dynasty for six generations; you are bound by ties of kinship as well. Therefore, it is natural that you hesitate to draw your sword. But I have no such relationship. I am not indebted to the Chola clan in any way. If Aditya Karikalan does not come and beg your pardon at your feet, I myself shall take up the sword and kill him!” said Nandini. At that moment, her eyes reddened, her brows knit together, and her entire countenance changed.

chapters.title: “Danger Approaches!”
paragraphs: Pazhuvetarayar laughed. He laughed lightly, as though mocking Nandini’s words, but not so much as to seem openly derisive. Yet, the sound of his laughter made the chamber itself, and all the objects within it, tremble in fear. When he heard Nandini declare that she herself would take up a knife and slay those who had insulted him, a surge of pride welled up in his heart. To know that Nandini cared so deeply for the preservation of his honor filled Pazhuvetarayar with a sense of iron strength. In that same spirit, a desire arose within him to hear her speak further, to listen to her words. Yet, at the same time, another part of him wished to show that he did not approve of her speaking in such a manner.
“Why do you laugh, my lord? Do you laugh at my words out of disbelief?” she asked.
“Devi! I laughed to imagine how your hands, soft as the petals of the mandara flower, could ever wield a knife. And besides, while I am alive, with these two long arms of mine—”

“My lord! I know well the greatness and strength of your arms. Arms long as an elephant’s trunk, arms strong as Indra’s thunderbolt. Arms that have felled thousands of enemies on the battlefield, arms that have set the jeweled crown upon the heads of Chola emperors. But all that is of no consequence today. The time has come when children born just yesterday mock you as an ‘old man.’ You, who must now sit quietly, bound by your devotion to the Chola clan, like a serpent king held captive by a magician’s spell. My hands are but soft hands adorned with bangles. Yet, because I have taken the hand of a hero such as you, before the sacred fire, a little strength has come to my hands as well. If the need arises to protect my chastity or to uphold my husband’s honor, even my hands will find the strength to wield a knife. Look here…!” said Nandini.

With those words, she moved the chest that lay at the foot of the bed out into the open. She opened it and pushed aside the clothes that lay on top. From the bottom, she carelessly drew out a long sword, gleaming with a dazzling light, and held it aloft above her head with one hand.
Pazhuvetaraiyar stood for a moment, astonished by what he saw.
Then he asked, “How long has this sword been inside this chest? I thought you kept your clothes and ornaments here?”

Nandini placed the sword back into the chest and replied, “Yes; I do keep my clothes and ornaments in this chest. But among all my ornaments, this sword is the most important. It is meant to protect my chastity and my husband’s honor.”
“But there will never be a need for you to use this, as long as I am alive!”

“That is precisely why I never take this sword out. From Eezham to the land of Vengi, can you not protect your honor with the strength of your arms, which safeguard the Chola kingdom? Or is it that you cannot protect a foolish woman like me? Even so, you are often engaged in important affairs of state; you cannot always be by my side to guard me. In the times when I am separated from you, should I not be prepared to protect myself?”
“Devi! What need is there for that? Let the past be past; hereafter, I will never be separated from you…”
“Ayya! That is my wish as well; but just this once, you must leave me and go to Thanjavur…”
“What is this stubbornness? Why should I, just this time, leave you here and go?” Pazhuvetaraiyar asked, his brows knitting together.

“Swami! There are two reasons for that. If you take me with you now, these fools will mock us all the more. ‘The old lord has such faith in his young queen!’ they will say. The very thought of it makes my blood boil. The other reason is even more important. All these years, you have called and believed Sambhuvaraiyar to be your most trusted friend. But since the arrival of the prince, have you noticed the change in his words and actions? Even if you have not, I have been observing closely…”
“I too have noticed it. I am still wondering what could be the cause of that change…”

“You are a person of guileless heart; that is why you are surprised. But to me, there is nothing astonishing in this. Greed is the very nature of mankind—Sambuvaraiyar’s change of heart is only a result of that. There was once a rumor that Prince Aditya Karikalan would never even look upon women’s faces, that he would never marry. But since he arrived here, you must have noticed how he has been behaving quite the opposite. He often visits places where women are present, speaks to them in soft, affectionate tones. The reason for all this is that his heart has been captivated by Sambuvaraiyar’s daughter, Manimekalai. Did not Karikalan even ask, ‘Shall I take Manimekalai with me on a hunt?’ Sambuvaraiyar is well aware of this. That is why he has forgotten all his old arrangements. He has begun to dream that his precious daughter will soon be seated upon the golden throne of Thanjavur…”

“Yes, what you say must be the reason. Never in my wildest dreams did I imagine Sambuvaraiyar to be a man of such base character. Only two months ago, in this very palace, we all gathered and swore an oath to place Madurantaka upon the throne of Thanjai. Fie! Can a man who so easily breaks his word even be called human?” thundered Pazhuvettaraiyar.

“Swami! That is precisely why I said I would not accompany you. In your absence, I shall keep watch over what schemes these people are plotting here. If they attempt any treachery, I shall find a way to thwart it.”
“Nandini! Why should you involve yourself in all this?”
“Should not a wife share in the concerns that weigh upon her husband? Why else do they call us ‘life companions’?”
“Whatever may be, how can I leave you alone amidst these brutes and traitors? I cannot bring myself to agree to that, not even a little!”
“I will not be alone here. Manimekalai is here; for my sake, that girl will do anything…”
“That is true—I have noticed it as well. Your enchanting power has made her your slave. But how long will that last? If Aditya Karikalan ascends the throne and shows a desire to make her empress…”

“Sir! You need have no doubt about that matter. Even if I were to ask Manimekalai to accept the throne of Indra’s queen in the heavens, she would refuse if it went against my wishes. If I were to say, ‘Go and slay Karikalan with this dagger!’ she would at once—” She will do so and return. Don’t you often speak of my enchanting powers? That power has completely taken hold of Manimekalai! If you wish, I can prove it to you right now!” said Nandini.

Pazhuvettaraiyar’s body trembled. The old man’s lips quivered, his throat tightened, and his nose flared as he spoke, “Devi! I know your power. But do not attempt any such experiment with Karikalan. He is an innocent youth. He spoke out of ignorance; we must not make much of it. If Karikalan wishes to marry Manimekalai, we should not stand in the way!”

“Sir! We may not stand in the way. But fate exists! Who can stand against it? Just as Manimekalai is fond of me, so too am I attached to her. I care for her as if she were my own younger sister. How can I consent to give her in marriage to one whose life is about to be cut short?” said Nandini. At that moment, her gaze seemed fixed on something far away, as if she were watching events unfolding in the distance.

Pazhuvettaraiyar, now even more agitated, said, “Nandini! What words are these? Once, I was the commander of the Chola Emperor’s personal guard. I have sworn to protect the Emperor and his heirs, even at the cost of my own life…”
“Sir! I have never asked you to break that oath, have I?”

“If any harm should befall Karikalan because of you, the blame will fall upon me. The world will say, ‘Unable to bear a young boy’s mocking words, the old man committed a terrible crime.’ The good name our family has earned over six generations as protectors of the Cholas will be destroyed…”
“In that case, it is absolutely necessary that you leave this town at once!” said Nandini, her voice thick with mystery.
“Why do you say so?” asked Pazhuvettaraiyar.

“I was hesitant to tell you, but now it has become necessary. Durga Parameswari has granted me certain rare powers—you know this well. Through my mystical abilities, I learned that Sundara Chola, in his youth, was afflicted with the curse of harming a woman. I proved this to you. In the same way, now, with my inner vision, I see that the end of Aditya Karikalan’s life is drawing near. It will not come by your hand; nor will it come by mine.

But it is certain that Yama’s noose is drawing ever closer to him. His end may come in the very forest where he has gone hunting; or it may come while he lies in the palace. It may be at the claws of wicked beasts such as tigers or bears; or he may die from an arrow loosed in error by one of his own friends. Or, death may come to him from the dagger held in the soft hand of a woman. But, my lord, I swear to you that his death will never come by the hand you have taken in marriage—by my hand. You found me, abandoned and alone by the roadside, and made me your wife, the junior queen, for all the world to see. I will see to it that no blame ever falls upon you because of me. That is why I urge you now, you must not remain here at this time—go, leave at once.

If you are here, whatever misfortune befalls Karikalan, the world will link your name to it. Did they not blame you for the disappearance of Arulmozhi Varman in the sea? In the same way, they will accuse you in this matter too. Even if they do not say you caused the disaster, they will ask why you did not prevent it! But not even your arms, strong as Vajra’s thunderbolt, can avert the danger that is about to befall Karikalan. Therefore, you must leave immediately. If you take me with you, that too will arouse needless suspicion. They will say you took me away beforehand, knowing what was to come. Therefore, you must go alone. Whatever happens, however it happens, I will remain here to make sure no disgrace falls upon you.

My lord! Do you have such faith in me?” asked Nandini, and with her large, dark eyes, she looked at Pazhuvetarayar as though her gaze could pierce through his very heart. Poor man! The valiant old chieftain was deeply shaken by Nandini’s words. Before the arrows of her eyes, he stood bewildered and humbled.

chapters.title: Water Play
paragraphs: Six hundred years before the time in which this story takes place, apart from the three crowned kings of Tamilakam, there were seven minor chieftains who shone with fame. They were known by the title of “Vallals”—the Generous Ones. Among these seven was Ori, the lord of Kolli Hills. He was renowned as a matchless hero in the art of archery. It was said that when he bent his mighty bow, strung it, and let fly an arrow, just as Rama’s arrow pierced through seven trees, Ori’s arrow would first strike down a tiger, then a deer, then a wild boar, and finally a hare, all in one shot. Thus, poets sang of his skill in archery, and from this he came to be known as “Valvil Ori”—Ori of the Strong Bow.

In those days, the Chera king, who had grown powerful, bore enmity towards Valvil Ori of Kolli Hills. To attack him, the lord of Thirukovalur, Malayaman Thirumudikkari, sought the Chera’s alliance. Kari’s valor was in no way less than Ori’s, and in addition, Malayaman Kari commanded a larger army. Malayaman marched his forces upon Kolli Hills, slew Valvil Ori, and utterly destroyed his hill fortress.

At that same time, in the region adjoining Kolli Hills, there ruled a minor king named Athikaman Neduman Anji. He was a friend and ally of Valvil Ori. When Malayaman Kari slew Ori, Athikaman longed to avenge his friend’s death. Realizing he could not do so alone, he sought the aid of the Chola king, Killi Valavan. Killi Valavan too was angered by the growing might of Malayaman and his alliance with the Chera. Thus, Killi Valavan of the Cholas and Athikaman of Thagadoor joined forces and attacked Malayaman of Thirukovalur. Malayaman attained the hero’s heaven on the battlefield. The Chola warriors captured Malayaman’s two young sons and brought them back as prisoners.

Athikaman and Killi Valavan, determined to destroy Malayaman’s lineage entirely, ordered that the children be buried up to their necks in the earth and trampled to death beneath the feet of elephants. At that moment, a poet who had known Malayaman’s generosity and benefited from it arrived there. He pleaded with the Chola king for the lives of Malayaman’s children. “O King! Look there! Look at the faces of those children buried up to their necks! See the smiles that play upon those faces! Even as they watch the elephant approaching to trample them underfoot, even as they see its trunk swinging, those children think it is some kind of game and laugh. Are you truly going to kill such innocent children? What sin have those children committed? Is it just to punish children for the crimes of their father?” said the poet.

Hearing this, the Chola king’s heart changed. He immediately revoked his order. He had the children lifted from the ground. When the eldest among them came of age, he restored to him the kingdom of Thirukovalur.

From that time onwards, for centuries, the Malaiyaman clan of Thirukovalur maintained a grateful and friendly relationship with the Chola kings. That bond endured all the way to the time of Sundara Chola. Sundara Chola himself had married Vanamadevi, the daughter of Malaiyaman, and made her his chief queen.

The lines of Kolli Malai’s Valvil Ori and Thagadur’s Athigaman had perished and faded into history. Yet, the lords of Kadambur, the Sambuvarayars, claimed descent from their branches. The Sambuvarayars never forgot the enmity their ancestors bore towards the Malaiyaman clan of Thirukovalur. Thus, was it any wonder that they did not wish to see Malaiyaman’s grandson crowned as emperor of the Chola Empire? The arrogance of Aditya Karikalan, his utter disregard for the lesser kings, and his conduct only served to deepen the Sambuvarayars’ resentment. Therefore, the Sambuvarayars enthusiastically joined the effort to seat Kandaraditya’s son, Madurantaka, upon the throne of Tanjore.

But from the day Karikalan arrived in Kadambur, a subtle change began to take place in the heart of Periya Sambuvarayar. His beloved daughter, Manimekalai, was the reason for this change. There were many signs that Manimekalai had captivated the heart of Aditya Karikalan. Until then, it was said that Karikalan never so much as glanced at women, that he intended to remain a celibate all his life. But ever since he came to Kadambur palace, he was often seen visiting the women’s quarters and conversing with them cheerfully. Most notably, he frequently praised Manimekalai’s “chudikai” (hair ornament). From the time of Karikalan’s arrival, Manimekalai too was filled with joy and excitement. Periya Sambuvarayar believed this was because she too had developed an affection for Karikalan. Observing the happiness of both, Sambuvarayar himself was filled with hope. If Karikalan married Manimekalai, his beloved daughter would become empress of the Chola Empire! For her, the prospect was— The child to be born would also have a rightful claim to the throne of Thanjai! The pride that now fills Malayaman of Thirukovalur could then be theirs as well. Why should he himself stand as an obstacle to all this? Why should he hinder the elevation of his beloved daughter?

It was true that Sambuvaryar had once entertained the thought of marrying his daughter to Madurantakan. But Madurantakan already had two wives. He had married the daughter of the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar, and she had borne him a son. Therefore, if Madurantakan ascended the throne, it would be the descendants of the Pazhuvettaraiyars who would inherit the crown. Manimekalai would have to live as just one among the many handmaidens in the Thanjai palace.
But if Manimekalai married Aditya Karikalan, she would become the chief queen. The child born to her would be the rightful heir to the throne.

Crowning Madurantakan would be an arduous and perilous task. The people would oppose it. It would require waging a struggle against both Malayaman and the Velar of Kodumbalur. Even Madurantakan’s own mother stood as an obstacle to it. Why should he undertake such a troublesome endeavor?

Crowning Aditya Karikalan, on the other hand, was already a settled matter. There would be no difficulty in bringing it to fruition. The only major obstacle would be the stubbornness of the Pazhuvettaraiyars. Of them, the elder lord was already ensnared by the charms of the younger queen. Who could say how many more days he would even remain alive? Why risk getting involved in such a dangerous affair by relying on that old man? It was true that he had sworn an oath to support Madurantakan. But what of it? Was there no way to fulfill his aims without breaking his oath? Everyone knew Madurantakan was an innocent child. He could be persuaded to declare, “I do not desire the kingdom.” Or, it would suffice to insist that he obtain his mother’s consent!

Thus did Sambuvaryar’s mind begin to ponder. Therefore, he enthusiastically supported the Pazhuvettaraiyars’ plan to go to Thanjai. In their absence, he could speak privately with Karikalan, discern his true intentions, and act accordingly when the time was right. For this reason, he himself hastened the elder Pazhuvettaraiyar’s departure, sending him and his retinue on to Thanjai.

After the departure of Pazhuvetaraiyar, Aditya Karikalan and his companions set out for the hunt. Sambuvaraiyar was even willing to send Manimekalai and the other women of the inner palace along with them. But Kandhamaaran, who had been observing everything with a different intent, objected to this.

He had realized that all the attention Karikalan showed Manimekalai was, in truth, directed towards Nandini. Because of this, his resentment towards Karikalan had grown. He could not even explain all this to his father. Therefore, he said, “What is the use of taking women to the hunting grounds? It is better that I stay here to ensure their safety. Moreover, this is the month of Aippasi—at any moment, a heavy rain may begin. The woods along the lake’s edge will flood. The women will be stranded and struggle!” On his insistence, Sambuvaraiyar abandoned the idea. Aditya Karikalan then set out, accompanied by his friends Parthibendran, Vandiyathevan, Kandhamaaran, and the other hunters.

After everyone had left, the Sambuvaraiyar palace seemed desolate. Nandini turned to Manimekalai and said, “When the men are at home, they seem a nuisance to us. But when they go away somewhere, we feel troubled all the same. There isn’t even anything to gossip about and laugh!”

“Yes, Akka! We could have gone hunting too. I love to watch the hunt. Sometimes, I go with my father and brother. But today, for some reason, Kandhamaaran stubbornly forbade it. Perhaps he thought you do not like hunting, and so he stopped us? Or was it something else?” asked Manimekalai.

“It’s true; I do not particularly like hunting. The sight of blood makes me shudder. But Kandhamaaran did not say it for that reason, dear! He forbade it only to separate you from one of your family’s guests!” Nandini replied.

Dimples appeared on Manimekalai’s cheeks. She gazed at the floor for a moment, then said, “Let the men go off wherever they wish, Akka! We do not need their company. Let us go to the lakeside pavilion and play in the water! Will you come?” When Nandini agreed, Manimekalai spoke to her father and made the necessary arrangements.

Have we not seen the great embankment on the lower side of the Veeranarayana Lake, and the seventy-four sluices built into it? On the upper side of the lake, there is no such vast embankment. There, the depth of the lake’s water gradually decreased, and the shore sloped gently, forming a level plain. Further to the west, dense forests stretched in thick clusters.

In this region, where the lake’s water receded and the land became level, small islands appeared here and there. On these islands, trees, shrubs, and creepers grew in wild abundance. On the shore of one such island stood a bathing pavilion, half-submerged in the water. It was customary for the women of Kadambur Sambuvarayar’s household to come here to bathe and to spend their leisure hours in pleasure. To reach this spot, one had to travel around the lake for two katham in distance. For this reason, even though it was known as the bathing place of the Sambuvarayar household’s women, no outsiders ever ventured here.

Now, Nandini and Manimekalai had arrived at this island in a boat. Two of their companions, skilled in rowing, had come with them. They had brought along all the provisions needed for cooking. As soon as they reached the steps of the bathing pavilion, the companion women disembarked and began preparing the meal in the pavilion. Nandini and Manimekalai sat for a while on the steps, chatting idly. Manimekalai was a woman of natural wit and mischief; she was full of playful spirit. She mimicked the speech of the Pazhuvettaraiyar, and acted out the mannerisms of Karikalan, Kandhamaran, Parthibendran, and Vandiyathevan. Nandini laughed and laughed at her antics, her laughter ringing clear and bright. Yet, it was evident that her attention was not wholly on Manimekalai; her mind, from time to time, seemed to drift into some secret, inner contemplation.
Suddenly, Manimekalai sprang up with a leap. “Akka! We did not go hunting, but the hunt has come seeking us!” she cried, drawing the dagger tucked at her waist.
Startled, Nandini too rose and looked in the direction Manimekalai indicated. There, upon a large, slanting tree branch, a leopard was seen! It seemed to be weighing whether or not to leap upon them.
At that very moment, the sound of horses plunging into the water and galloping through it was heard from a short distance away.

chapters.title: Karikalan’s Bloodlust
paragraphs: Didn’t someone say that Aditya Karikalan had gone hunting long ago and might have even forgotten the art of archery? But those who witnessed him hunting in the forests along the banks of the Veeranarayana Lake that day did not think so. Countless wild beasts fell prey to the arrows that flew from his bow that day. Hares, deer, bears, and leopards fell dead at his feet. When no animal appeared before his eyes, his arrows soared at the birds flying in the sky. Hawks and peafowls shrieked and tumbled to the ground. Karikalan’s bloodlust only grew fiercer as time passed.

Those who accompanied him had little to do. The noise of the horses and men moving in a group startled the wild animals, causing them to scatter and flee from their hiding places. That was the extent of the others’ contribution to the hunt. Karikalan would not even allow them to shoot arrows or throw spears at the beasts that charged at him. Once, Kandanmaran shot an arrow at a bear that lunged at Karikalan. Karikalan turned to him and asked, “Kandanmara! Did you try to kill the bear? Or did you try to kill me?” Mockery and scorn flashed across Kandanmaran’s face. After that, he did not bend his bow again.

By the time the sun reached its zenith, everyone was exhausted. The thought of resting a while and then returning home arose in everyone’s mind. But Karikalan, instead, drove his weary horse deeper into the forest paths.

All morning, Kandanmaran had been riding close to Karikalan. But after Karikalan asked him, “Did you try to kill me?” Kandanmaran fell back and joined Parthibendran. He began to complain to him about the prince’s rough manner and harsh words. Parthibendran tried to pacify him.

At this moment, Vandiyathevan approached Karikalan. The two of them rode ahead together. Vandiyathevan had not brought a bow or arrows. He was not much practiced in archery. He carried only a spear in his hand. Therefore, in Karikalan’s hunt... Without interruption, Vandiyathevan proceeded cautiously. He was ever prepared to use his sword should any danger arise along the way. Yet, until midday, there was no need for such measures.

Kandamaran said to Parthibendran, “Isn’t today’s hunt enough? It seems as though he intends to wipe out every beast in this forest in a single day. To quench his hunting frenzy, we must take him to the Kolli Hills! Please, tell him, ‘Enough for today; let us return home!’”

To this, Parthibendra Pallavan replied, “Brother! There is a storm raging in the prince’s heart. Is it an easy thing to relinquish a vast empire? He is venting all that fury in the hunt. For now, that is well and good. Otherwise, he may turn that wrath upon you and me. Let him tire of it and declare, ‘Enough.’ We need not interfere.”
At that moment, a thunderous roar echoed through the forest, making the wilderness tremble. A sign of fear appeared on Kandamaran’s face.
“Alas! A wild boar! Tell the prince to stop!” he cried.
“Why such fear of a boar? Tigers and bears have already fallen to the prince’s hand—what is a boar compared to them?” Parthibendran asked.

“You speak without knowing! The boars in these woods can tear tigers and bears to shreds! They can topple elephants with a single charge! Horses are no match at all. Arrows and spears, when they strike a wild boar’s hide, simply glance off—they never pierce its flesh!… Sir! Sir! Please, stop!” Kandamaran shouted.

At that very moment, a commotion like a small whirlwind swept through the undergrowth. In the next instant, two massive, dark forms—like young elephants—emerged from the thicket: wild boars of enormous size. For a moment, they stood still, fixing their gaze upon the horses and the men who approached.
“Careful, sir! Be careful!” Kandamaran cried out.
By now, some of the hunters following behind had caught up. In frantic haste, they beat their drums and clashed their cymbals, shouting, “Ka koo!” at the top of their lungs.

What thoughts stirred in those boars’ minds, none could say. Perhaps they were thinking of their young, driven by the instinct to protect them from harm. Or perhaps the sudden clamor of drums and cymbals— Startled by the sound, the wild boars might have been frightened. Both boars, tearing through the undergrowth, began to run in opposite directions.
Watching this, Kandhamaaran said, “Prince! Let them go and vanish. Without five or six hunting hounds, it’s impossible to chase and kill a wild boar!”

Karikalan paid no heed to these words. He bent his bow and loosed an arrow. The arrow struck one of the boars squarely on its back. Seeing this, the young prince let out a cry of triumph, “Ah-ha!” In the very next moment, the boar gave its body a violent shake. The arrow was flung aside and fell to the ground; the boar ran on, unscathed.

At this, Kandhamaaran’s laughter carried a note of mockery. Karikalan turned to him and said, “Kandhamaaran! Let us make a wager! Vandiyathevan and I will pursue that boar, kill it, and bring it back. You and Parthibendran chase the other boar, kill it, and return with it! None of us shall return to the palace without having slain these two boars!” So saying, he spurred his horse forward. Vandiyathevan followed at his side.

For a while, they could track the boar’s path through the forest, for the shrubs, creepers, and thickets along its way were all disturbed and broken. But soon, a small canal crossed their path—a channel that carried the rainwater from the forest to the lake. After reaching this spot, it became impossible to tell which way the boar had gone. Had it crossed the canal and entered the woods beyond? Or had it run along the bank, either this way or that? There was no way to know.

At that moment, a scene unfolding on the broad expanse of the lake, visible along the canal’s course, caught their attention. A boat was approaching. It was clear that the passengers were women, but who they were, they could not discern. At first, Vandiyathevan and Karikalan saw that the boat was coming directly toward where they stood. Then, the boat shifted its course slightly and glided toward another island along the lake’s edge, disappearing from view.
“Vallavaraiya! Who could those women in the boat be? Did they not appear to be ladies?” asked Karikalan.
“They did look like women; beyond that, I cannot say,” replied Vandiyathevan.
“Could they perhaps be the women of the house of Sambuvaraiyar?”
“Even so, it is possible; but why should they come this far?”
“Yes, it cannot be them… Didn’t Pazhuvetarayar leave early this morning? That is certain, isn’t it?”
“It is certain, my lord! I myself saw the palace gates open and saw him ride out on his elephant.”
“Did he go alone?”
“Yes; only the elder went. The young queen did not go.”
“Where else shall we find a warrior as valiant as that elder? Even my own grandfather, Malayaman, must be named only after Pazhuvetarayar…”

“My lord! I have only heard others speak of those elders. But I have seen your valor with my own eyes on the battlefield; I saw it in the palace at Kadambur as well. How you struck terror into the hearts of elders and princes alike!”
“That is true, but for all the commotion I made, now that the moment I have long awaited draws near, my heart and body tremble. Nowhere in all Chola land will you find a coward as fearful as I…”
“Prince! When you hunted in the forest today, you did not seem afraid or trembling then. Did you not make the wild beasts, the birds, and all those who followed you quake in fear?”

“Is all this courage of the same kind? It is nothing but the courage of a hunting hound leaping upon a tiger; a wild boar fighting an elephant. Is the bravery of the hunt true bravery? Vallavaraiya, listen! My scheme has succeeded. Pazhuvetarayar has left Nandini alone and gone. Yet, the thought of meeting her in solitude fills me with dread!” said Aditya Karikalan.

“My lord! There is a reason for that; all this time you thought of the young queen of Pazhuvur in one way. Now you know she is your own sister. And she, on the other hand, has allied herself with the conspirators of Pandya Nadu who wish to destroy your dynasty. To speak of all this to her is a difficult task indeed. Even when I had the chance, I could not bring myself to say it…”

“Friend! Every piece of news you have brought is startling to hear. Still, I find it hard to believe. Yet, when I recall certain old incidents, it seems as if it could indeed be true. There has always been a veil of mystery between her and me. The great lady of Pazhayarai—Sembiyan Maadevi—once insisted that I should not keep company with Nandini. But she did not reveal the whole truth; if she had, none of this would have happened…”

“Sembiyan Maadevi herself may not have known the entire truth. She might have only known that Nandini was an orphaned, mute girl left in someone’s care. Perhaps she never realized that the daughter of Sundara Chozhar had become the young queen of Pazhuvoor.”

chapters.title: “She is Not a Woman!”
paragraphs: For a while, Prince Karikalan was lost in thought. Waves of memories from his youth crashed and surged within his heart, rising tumultuously, then subsiding to make way for other recollections before fading away. Forcibly restraining those tides of memory, Karikalan let out a long, deep sigh.

“Let us not speak of what has passed now; let us talk about what is yet to come. That is why I called you here alone. We have lost the wager. The boar is gone. Now we must think and decide what to do next, and how to do it. Vallavaraiyan! When I think of how to speak to Nandini about the relationship between her and me, fear grips my heart. I cannot even bring myself to look straight at her face. Whenever I steal a glance at her, she wears the same expression she had when she pleaded for Veera Pandiyan’s life. Her gaze feels as if it cuts through my heart like a sword. The thought that my own sister, out of love for Veera Pandiyan, pleaded with me for his life—it makes my heart feel as if it will shatter. Vallavaraiyan! What do you think? Do you still believe she does not know the truth? Do you think she does not know that she is Sundara Chozhar’s daughter, and that she is our sister?”

“Prince! If she knew all this, would she still be allied with the conspirators of Pandya Nadu? Would she have enthroned a mere child as the king of Pandya Nadu and crowned him as the emperor of the Chola empire, in opposition to the Chola dynasty? Would she have sworn an oath, sword in hand, to uphold that crown? I myself witnessed all this near the Tiruppurambiyam battlefield, in the dead of night…”
“It amazes me that, after seeing all this, Nandini let you live.”
“My lord! I am not surprised by that; perhaps it was due to the natural compassion that dwells in a woman’s heart?”

“Vallavaraiyan! You are naïve to the ways of the world. You do not know the depth of deceit and treachery that can reside in a woman’s heart. I do not know with what intent she let you live. But as for why she sent for me—” “It is known only to my innermost self that she sent for me.”
“Prince! What could be the reason for that?”
“She summoned me here to kill me, to avenge Veera Pandiyan’s death with blood for blood…”

“Sir! It was precisely because they feared some such calamity might befall you that the Young Princess and the Prime Minister sent me in such haste. But you did not heed their warning not to go to Kadambur…”

“Vallavaraiya! The Young Princess and the Prime Minister are indeed very wise. But even they cannot prevent fate, can they? Perhaps fate itself has brought me here to fulfill all that the astrologers have foretold about Arulmozhi Varman. Who can say? Vallavaraiya! Kandanmaran shot that arrow from behind me, didn’t he? Did he truly aim at the bear, or did he aim at me? Did you notice?”

“I did not notice, sir! But I can never accept that Kandanmaran would commit such treachery. Would Kandanmaran, who welcomed a guest into his home—moreover, the Emperor’s own son—shoot an arrow from behind to kill him? I do not hold such a high opinion of his intelligence, it’s true. When he lay stabbed and unconscious, I carried him away and saved him. When he opened his eyes and saw me, he believed I was the one who stabbed him. His enmity towards me has not yet faded. But though his wits may be somewhat dull, he is not one with a treacherous mind!…”
“Friend! I do not know how powerful the enchantment of a beautiful woman can be. It can drive even the best of men to acts of betrayal…”
“Sir! I too have some knowledge of women’s enchanting power. But for that very reason, I will never become a traitor…”
“Ah! Manimekalai is a good woman; she would never urge you to commit a treacherous deed…”
“I was not speaking of Manimekalai; can a firefly ever appear as dazzling as the full moon to eyes that have seen the moon?”
“Whom do you mean by ‘the full moon’?”
“Prince! Do not be angry; I am speaking only of the younger princess of Pazhayarai…”
“Ah! You impudent talker! All the kings of the world are performing penance in hopes of winning Kundavai’s hand. How could you even dare to think of my sister in your heart?”
“Sir! Even the emperors of the earth gaze upon and enjoy the beauty and cool radiance of the full moon; yet it is the poor and humble who truly revel in its light. Who can prevent them?”

“Yes, there is no use in getting angry with you. I sent you to my sister with a letter precisely because I know your nature. And you behaved yourself to her satisfaction. But do not, under any circumstance, say such things to Parthibendran! He dreams of becoming the Chola dynasty’s son-in-law and reigning as king of Thondai Nadu…”
“Sir! That may have been true some time ago. But now both Kandhamaran and Parthibendran are waiting to do whatever Nandini Devi commands, even if it means bowing their heads to her feet…”
“I have noticed that; and that is why I am afraid when it comes to them.”
“When I consider everything, it seems necessary that you meet the young queen soon and reveal all truths to her.”
“My friend! I do not think I have the courage for that. What if you meet her and tell her everything on my behalf?”
“Prince! If I tell her, the young queen will not believe me. Once, I deceived her and escaped from her presence. She may think this is yet another scheme.”
“But how can I meet Nandini alone? She is within the inner chambers!”
“Sir! It is possible through Manimekalai. I will make the necessary arrangements for that…”
“It seems you have Manimekalai wrapped around your little finger. That is good! In any case, if I can marry you to Manimekalai, my heart will find some measure of peace.”
“Sir! I consider Manimekalai as my own sister by birth. I expect that she will attain a fortune many times greater than this…”
“What are you talking about?”

“Do you not know, Prince? I suspect that the maiden Manimekalai has found a place in the heart of the crown prince of the Chola Empire. Just now, I spoke in a certain way about the daughter of Sambuvarayar. I spoke thus only to reveal my mind to you. Except for the younger princess, there is no other woman born in this world who can match Manimekalai in intellect or virtue. If only you would marry Manimekalai, all our troubles would come to an end. Sambuvarayar and Kandhamaaran would join us. The Pazhuvettarayars would be left isolated. The power of the younger queen would wane. Madurantaka Devar would never again speak of the throne. We could, in a single stroke, shatter the plots of the minor kings and the conspiracies of the Pandya country’s secret allies, and emerge victorious…”

“All that is true, brother! But I have not come to Kadambur to get married. Some great danger is drawing near. Listen to what I say! When the Pazhuvettarayar returns with Madurantakan, he is going to come with a great army…”
“Sir! If that is so, why don’t we send word to the king of Thirukovalur and have him gather his forces as well? Is it not wise to be cautious before anything happens?”

“I have been thinking about that too. Do you know what I feel at times? I feel like razing this Kadambur palace to the ground, and at the palace gates, impaling all those who have plotted here. It is only for my father’s sake that I restrain my anger. If only you had brought him to Kanchi…”
“Prince! Even delivering your letter to him has become an almost impossible task!”

“Yes; the Emperor has fallen completely into the hands of these Pazhuvettarayars. In the golden palace I built in Kanchima city for my parents, bats now fly about. I do not know whether, while I am alive, I will ever have the fortune to welcome them into that palace. I am even doubtful whether I will leave this Kadambur alive…”
“Prince! The more you speak thus, the more it seems necessary to send for Malayaman to come with his forces…”
“I am thinking of sending you for that very task…”
“Sir! Please forgive me! Your sister has commanded me not to leave your side even for a moment…”
“You have fulfilled that duty well until now.”
“Parthibendran Pallavar is simply sitting here, growing restless as the hours pass…”

“Yes; every moment he spends without seeing the young queen of Pazhuvoor feels like an age to him. I never imagined, even in my dreams, that Parthibendran could be so enslaved by a woman’s beauty. He is the one who should be sent to Malayaman.”
“That is an excellent idea, sir!”
“If anything were to happen to me in his absence, you would still be here to help…”

“Prince! Whether anyone is here or not, I do not believe there exists in this world a man bold enough to harm you. I have seen with my own eyes how those valiant elders, who spoke so much in your absence, trembled and stammered when they faced you in person.”
“Brother! I do not fear any man who dares to fight me with sword in hand. Nor do I fear men like Kandhamaaran, who shoot arrows into one’s back from behind…”
“Again you speak of Kandhamaaran in this way…”

“Listen, brother! It is only the treachery buried deep in a woman’s heart that I truly fear. Whenever I think of what she might be hiding in her mind, my heart pounds. Every mysterious glance she casts at me feels as if a spear is being thrust into my chest. The very thought of it makes my hands and feet tremble.”

“Sir! I too agree that one must fear the deceit of Nandini Devi. I have sensed how terrible a hatred dwells within her heart. Sometimes, when I think of how she let me go alive, I wonder if there is some plot behind it. But isn’t all this only because she does not know the truth? Once she learns that you are her brother, wouldn’t all these worries vanish?”

“Is that what you think? Vallavaraiyan! You are indeed a brave soul. But you are an innocent child who does not understand the ways of women. If Nandini comes to know that she is the daughter of Sundara Chozhar, her wrath towards all of us will increase a hundredfold. Even if we were to crown her as the Empress of the Tanjore Empire, her anger would not be appeased…”
“Prince! If that is your belief, then entrust that responsibility to me. I myself will tell Nandini the true story of her lineage. I will also try to calm her fury…”

“You will not succeed in that, my friend! No one can quell Nandini’s anger. Listen to me! If the Chola dynasty is to be saved, one thing must happen: either I must die, or she must die, or both of us must perish. With the same sword that killed Veera Pandiyan, I will slay her as well…”
“Prince! What dreadful words are these?”

“Vallavaraiyan! Is it a crime to kill a life for the sake of protecting an empire? What if she is a woman? What if she is my own sister by birth? In truth, she is not a woman; she is a bewitching demoness in the guise of a woman! If she is left alive, this Chola empire, which has flourished and grown since the days of Vijayalaya Chozhar, will be utterly destroyed… Ah! What is that?” exclaimed Aditya Karikalan in alarm, turning to look behind him.

At that moment, not far from where they stood, some commotion was taking place amidst the dense forest thickets. Both of them spurred their horses and rode closer to see what was happening. An extraordinary sight met their eyes. A wild boar and a leopard were locked in a fierce and savage battle.
“Ah! The one we have been seeking is here!” said Karikalan.
“Looks like the leopard will do our work for us!” said Vandiyathevan.
“Is that what you think? Just watch!” replied Karikalan.

The two of them watched, without blinking, the ferocious struggle between the leopard and the boar. The leopard leapt upon the boar, trying to attack it with its claws and teeth. But the boar’s tough hide did not yield to the leopard’s claws or fangs. The boar, in turn, charged at the leopard with great speed, butted it, and flung it to the ground and against the roots of the trees… Every time it was struck and scraped, the leopard suffered terribly. The boar’s sharp tusks tore the leopard’s hide to shreds. At last, when the boar butted the leopard down one final time, the beast lay as if dead.
“Thambi! The leopard is dead! Now the boar will turn on us! We must be ready!” said Karikalan, stringing an arrow to his bow and letting it fly.

The arrow struck the boar in the neck. The boar shook its neck violently and turned to look back. For a moment, it observed both horses and their riders. Then it glanced once at the leopard. Realizing, perhaps, that nothing more could be done there, it charged at the horses with savage fury.

Before Karikalan could notch another arrow, the boar attacked the horse he was riding. The force of the blow made the horse stumble, and its hind leg caught in the root of a tree. The horse faltered and fell to the ground. Karikalan was trapped beneath the fallen animal. The boar stepped back a little, then charged once more at the horse lying on the ground.

chapters.title: “Where is the Tiger?”
paragraphs: Vandiyathevan realized the grave danger into which Aditya Karikalan had fallen. In the blink of an eye, he spurred his horse forward and thrust the spear in his hand at the boar. The spear struck above the tough hide on the boar’s back. The animal shook its body violently and turned around. In that sudden movement, the grip on the spear slipped from Vandiyathevan’s hand. The spear, which had only lightly pierced the boar’s back, slid off and fell to the ground.

Now, the boar turned and charged toward Vandiyathevan. He understood the perilousness of his situation. His horse could not withstand the beast’s attack. He had no spear in hand. The prince was still struggling to crawl out from beneath his fallen horse. If he were to survive, he would have to leap from his horse onto the branch of a nearby tree. Shame! After escaping so many dangers, was he to be killed at last by nothing more than a wild boar?

Fortunately, there was a low-spreading tree close by. Vandiyathevan leapt from his horse and seized a branch. Using all his strength from foot to shoulder, he pulled himself up onto the branch. At that very moment, the boar butted his horse. The horse staggered, barely managing to keep its footing, and then bolted away. Karikalan still lay beneath his horse. Vandiyathevan was perched on the tree branch. The wild boar stood between them, turning this way and that, watching both.

Vandiyathevan realized that the boar was considering which of its two enemies to attack. The prince had not yet managed to free himself from beneath his horse. Even if he did, could he withstand the beast’s charge at that moment? He had no weapon ready at hand. He would have to bend his bow and shoot an arrow. He might have been injured when he fell and was trapped under his horse. In any case, it was essential to buy the prince a little time. All these thoughts flashed through Vandiyathevan’s mind in a lightning instant, and he came to a decision. Shaking the branch on which he sat with all his might, he shouted loudly, “Aaha! Oo! Koo!”
His ruse had succeeded. The wild boar, in a frenzy of rage, charged straight at the tree on which he had climbed.

“Let it come; let it come and dash itself against the trunk,” Vandiyathevan thought to himself. But even as this thought crossed his mind, the branch he had climbed and was shaking began to crack ominously. God! What danger is this? If he fell to the ground along with the branch, in the very next moment the boar’s terrible tusks would tear him to pieces. He could only survive if he managed to leap and grab hold of another branch.

He tried to leap and catch another branch. But that branch was a little farther away, and he managed to grasp it with only one hand. The branch he caught was slender and bent under his weight. His grip began to slip, his legs dangled in the air! Well, he had to fall now—death was certain! There was no doubt about it. At least, in the end, he had managed to save Aditya Karikalan, hadn’t he? When the young princess heard of this, wouldn’t she be happy? Wouldn’t she shed a tear for his death…?
Suddenly, a terrible sound rang out! At the same moment, his grip slipped completely! Vandiyathevan squeezed his eyes shut. He fell with a thud to the ground; as he fell, he lost consciousness.
When Vandiyathevan regained his senses and opened his eyes, he saw Aditya Karikalan sprinkling water on his face. He sat up with a start and asked, “Prince! Are you safe?”
“Yes; thanks to your kindness, I am still alive,” replied Aditya Karikalan.
“What happened to the wild boar?” he asked.
“There!” said the prince, pointing to where the wild boar lay dead.

Vandiyathevan looked at it closely and said, “Your Highness! What trouble this small creature has caused! What Kandhamaaran said about the wild boar was entirely true. In the end, how did you kill it?”
“I did not kill it. It was your spear and you together that killed it!” said the prince.
Vandiyathevan looked at the prince’s face as if he did not understand.
“You used my spear well! But I did nothing, did I? In the moment of danger, I could not help you at all,” he said.

“You shook the tree branch and made a noise, didn’t you? At that moment, I sprang out from beneath the horse and snatched up your spear. All the anger that had been boiling in my heart, alas, I unleashed upon that poor boar. The moment it was struck by the spear, it let out a terrible cry. I thought I would go deaf from the sound. But even the spear did not kill it. You slipped from the tree branch and fell upon its back; it was that shock that finally killed it!” said Karikalan, and laughed aloud. Vandiyathevan too, recalling the scene, burst into laughter.

Rubbing his body and examining himself, he said, “It seems I escaped without injury only because I landed on the boar. Now I can believe that Maha Vishnu took the Varaha avatar and slew Hiranyaksha. My goodness! What a ferocious creature it was!”

“Don’t judge the Varaha avatar by seeing this little wild boar, brother!” said the prince. “In the forests of the Vindhya mountains to the north, they say there is a kind of boar with a single horn on its head. It is almost as large as an elephant. If it had been such a boar, and it had butted the tree you were perched on, imagine what would have happened to the tree!”

“The tree would have snapped at the root and fallen, your spear would have broken, and our fate would have been sealed. The enemies of the Chola dynasty would have been spared the trouble of dealing with us,” said Vandiyathevan.
“Brother! Tell me the truth! When my horse stumbled and fell, you threw the spear, didn’t you? Did you aim it at the wild boar, or at me?” asked Aditya Karikalan.
With some indignation, Vandiyathevan replied, “Sir! Are you truly asking me this question? If you had such doubts, there would have been no need for you to kill the boar and save me!”

“Yes, yes! I should not doubt you. If you had not shaken the tree branch and shouted, that boar would have been my death. Yet, for a moment, when you threw the spear, I did have such a doubt. These days, I am plagued by suspicion at everything and everyone I see. I cannot rid myself of the delusion that Yama, the god of death, is following me everywhere. I even imagined that Yama had come to kill me in the form of this boar…”

“In that case, all has ended well. My lord! The Yama who was following you has now perished; what more is there to worry about? We have also won the wager we made with Kandhamaaran. All that remains is to drag the boar back. Shall we set out?”
“Isn’t it so?” asked Vallavaraiyan.
“We must indeed set out! But what is the hurry? Let us rest here for a while and leave after our fatigue has eased,” said the prince.
“This is the first time I have ever heard you admit to being tired. Ah, you must have suffered greatly, being caught beneath the horse’s hooves.”

“That is nothing; the weariness of the body is far less than the exhaustion of the mind. Should we return the way we came? Must we once again travel in the company of those fools? Would it not be better to cross this lake and be done with it?”
“Heavens! Are you suggesting we swim across this lake, as vast as the sea? After saving me from the boar, do you now intend to drown me in the lake?” exclaimed Vandiyathevan.

“I remember that you do not know how to swim. Even I could not swim across such a great lake. If only we could find a boat, our task would be much easier. Just a while ago, we saw a boat—surely it must be moored somewhere nearby along the shore? What if we search for it?”
“And what of the horses? Shall we simply abandon them to become food for the wild beasts?” asked Vandiyathevan.
Suddenly, as if struck by a memory, he sprang up and cried, “Ayya! Where is the tiger?”
“I too had forgotten about it. It must be hiding somewhere nearby. If Yama does not come for me in the form of a boar, perhaps he will pursue me in the form of a tiger,” said the prince.
Both of them began to look around carefully in all directions. After a few moments, Vandiyathevan pointed and said, “There!”

The canal that brought water into the lake grew narrower as it stretched northward. At the point where it had become quite narrow, a large tree had fallen across the canal, touching both banks. The tiger was slowly crawling along this makeshift bridge, nearing the opposite shore. Both men observed this in silence. The same thought arose in both their minds.
“Ah! The women who came in the boat!” they both exclaimed at the same instant.
Afterwards, “It must be on the shore of that island next to this canal that those women have disembarked,” said Vallavarayan.
“A wounded leopard is extremely dangerous,” said the prince.
“We must kill the tiger along with the boar and take them both away.”
“How are we to cross this canal? The horses cannot go over the wooden bridge, can they?”
“The water is shallow; we can get down and cross.”

By then, Karikalan’s horse had come up and stood near Vandiyathevan’s horse. Just as their masters had spoken in confidence, it seemed as if the horses too were discussing the danger they had just faced. Both men leapt onto their horses; they led them down into the canal. The water in the canal was not deep, but there was much mud and slush. The horses stumbled and floundered as they went.
Thinking of the muddy pits of Kodikkarai, Vandiyathevan gained courage, telling himself, “This mud is nothing to be afraid of.” He began to tell Karikalan about it.

“Friend! You have started talking about the mud outside. What do you think of the mud within men’s hearts? Do you know how hard it is for those who once step into the mire of evil thoughts to reach the shore again?” asked Karikalan. Vandiyathevan thought to himself that the prince’s heart was indeed as troubled as a pool of mud.

With great difficulty, the horses reached the other shore. The two men proceeded into the forest, looking cautiously in every direction. Karikalan’s bow and arrows were ready in his hands. Vandiyathevan held his spear, prepared to hurl it at the tiger.

Suddenly, above the usual sounds of the forest, a woman’s shrill cry rang out: “Amma! Amma! Tiger!” At the very moment when Manimekalai, perched on a tree branch, saw the leopard, another maidservant busy with kitchen work in the Vasantha Mandapam also caught sight of the tiger and screamed in terror. That cry struck the ears of both friends and sent a chill through them. Urging their horses forward, they sped towards the direction of the voice. As they turned a bend on the bank of the lake, the sight that met their eyes startled and horrified them both.

At the very moment when Nandini and Manimekalai were descending into the bathing ghat to bathe, a leopard was slowly crawling along a nearby tree branch, inching its way upward. The beast, badly wounded and battered from its fight with the wild boar, was now in a desperate state, thinking only of saving its own life. But no one except the leopard itself was aware of this.

In the next instant, both Karikalan and Vandiyathevan thought the leopard was about to leap upon the women standing in the water. Vandiyathevan hesitated to use his spear, fearing what might happen if he missed and the weapon struck the women instead. Karikalan, however, felt no such hesitation. He nocked an arrow to his curved bow, took careful aim, and let it fly.

The arrow whistled through the air and struck the leopard in its lower belly. With a terrifying roar, the beast sprang toward the women standing a little distance away. In the next moment, everything became a blur, so confused that it was impossible to see clearly what had happened. The leopard and the two women suddenly vanished from sight.
After a few moments, all three emerged from the water at different places, raising their heads above the surface. The water of the lake, mingled with blood, had turned a deep, crimson red.

chapters.title: Love and Blame
paragraphs: The two friends watched all these events unfold with astonishment and dread. They leapt down from their horses and rushed along the riverbank. By then, the leopard had already swum a little distance into the water! From the way it floated, it seemed as if its life had already departed. No one could tell how badly the two women had been wounded by the beast. Both men plunged into the water and swam towards the ladies.

Vandiyathevan reached Manimekalai first. For he was afraid to approach Nandini. Manimekalai had suffered no injury. Apart from being breathless from plunging into the water at the same moment the leopard fell, nothing else had befallen her! The moment she saw Vandiyathevan coming near, her heart surged with uncontrollable emotion and she closed her eyes tightly.

Karikalan, meanwhile, caught Vandiyathevan by the arm, stopped him, and sent him towards Nandini, then turned to Manimekalai himself. She did not realize this. With both his arms, Karikalan lifted her, held her close, climbed the steps of the bathing ghat, and gently laid her down on the ground above. Until then, she did not open her eyes. Only when Karikalan placed his finger under her nose to check if she was breathing did she slowly open her eyes. As she opened them, she looked at Vandiyathevan with a gaze overflowing with love and longing, wishing to reveal her boundless affection for him. But when she saw that it was Prince Karikalan standing before her, she sprang up and moved aside, sitting a little away.
Karikalan noticed the disappointment that flashed across her face and laughed softly.
“Manimekalai! What is this sudden leap? Why such aversion at the sight of me?” he asked.
“Sir! Shouldn’t a woman feel shy if touched by a man who is not her husband?” replied Manimekalai.

“Girl! Have you made me a stranger? Is not every effort being made to unite you and me in marriage?” said Karikalan. “Swami! Only after that effort succeeds will it become my own, isn’t it? Until then, aren’t you still a stranger to me?” asked Manimekalai.
“But you can at least say whether you wish for it or not, can’t you?”

The Kadambur princess paused to think for a moment, then said, “Ayya! You are a scion of the Chola clan; a man of great wisdom who knows all things. Is it proper for you to speak thus to a young girl like me? Should you not ask my father about this?”
“Child! If your father agrees, will you consent as well?”

“If my father agrees and asks me, I will answer him. I feel shy to speak of such things with you. You saved me from being killed by the tiger, and from drowning in the water. Out of gratitude for that, I have been patient with you all this while…”
Karikalan laughed and said, “Manimekalai! You are a clever girl. Very stubborn, too. But you have been deceived. For that, do not try to deceive me in return!”
“Ayya! What words are these! Would this ignorant girl try to deceive you? For what reason? In what way?”

“Why do you speak in circles for no reason? If, instead of me, Vandiyathevan had carried you to the shore, would you speak so harshly? Was it not thinking it was Vandiyathevan that you closed your eyes? And with the same thought, did you not open your eyes and look? Poor girl! You have been tricked!”
Manimekalai, with a blush, also felt a touch of fear. Then, mustering her courage, she said, “My lord, you already know my heart! If that is so, why do you test this foolish girl?”

“Manimekalai! I know your heart. Likewise, I know the heart of Vallavarayan as well. I think he is not worthy of your pure love. Look there, see how the young queen Nandini and Vandiyathevan converse! See the joy that sits upon Nandini’s face!”
Manimekalai looked in the direction he indicated. At that moment, the poison called jealousy rose up in her milk-pure heart.

At that very moment, Vandiyathevan and Nandini were conversing. On one of Nandini’s shoulders, the tiger’s claw had struck, and blood was oozing forth. Unlike Manimekalai, Nandini did not close her eyes. Nor did she hasten to free herself from Vandiyathevan’s grasp. Vandiyathevan, for his part, as though he were shaking off a burning ember that had scorched his hand, hurriedly set the young queen down upon the riverbank. Though she had been immersed in water, Nandini’s body still seemed to burn with heat.

A nameless fear took hold in Vandiyathevan’s heart. His body trembled. With a smile, Nandini asked, “Ayya! Why are you so agitated? Did you mistake me for the tiger? Or are you regretting that, in your eagerness to save the tiger, you have mistakenly brought me to the shore?”
“Ammani! Please do not speak such cruel words. My heart is somewhat unsettled at the thought that I was compelled to touch and lift you…”
“It is only a guilty heart that is troubled so!”
“Devi! I have committed no crime!”

“No crime? You sought my help to enter the fortress of Thanjavur. I gave you my signet ring and aided you. Then, you stealthily entered my private chambers. Even then, I protected you from harm. And how did you repay me? Without my knowledge, without a word to me, you fled like a thief. After meeting the young princess of Pazhayarai, you promised to return to me. You did not fulfill that promise. Are these not all crimes?”
“I admit to those faults. But each has its reason. I serve others. I am bound by the commands of Aditya Karikalan. If you consider this, you will not accuse me of wrongdoing…”

“Yes, indeed; even to save a woman from a tiger’s jaws, you must have Karikalan’s command. Even to bring a drowning woman to the shore, you need his permission. I was watching you closely. Ah! How agitated the prince was in saving Manimekalai! If I had drowned and died, he would have rejoiced. Unaware of his heart, you have brought me to the shore…”
“Ammani! Please do not say so! It is only because you sent the message that Karikalan has come all the way from Kanchi…”

“But you rushed here in such haste only to prevent him from coming, did you not? You came bearing the message of the Young Princess. Yet your efforts have come to nothing. Every attempt you make to interfere in my affairs will end in failure, just like this!”

Nandini’s words only deepened the confusion in Vandiyathevan’s heart. He gazed intently at her, hoping to discern the hidden meaning behind her words from her expression. But Nandini’s face betrayed no change; as always, her smile bloomed serenely.

Nandini continued, “Your face itself confesses your guilt. On the night of the new moon, near the barracks, you fell into my hands. If I had but signaled to my men, they would have killed you. Even then, I spared your life and let you go. Yet you showed no gratitude for that. Never in this world have I seen a man as ungrateful as you…”
“Devi! My heart is filled with boundless gratitude towards you. I swear it is true.”
“But all these days since we came to this town, you have made no attempt to express your gratitude. How can I trust your words?”
“I thought I would express it when I met you alone, but I never found the right opportunity…”
“You did not even try to create such an opportunity. Not a glance, not a look, not a single sign from your face or your eyes. Why? All these days, you have not once turned to look at me…”
“Devi! You are the virtuous wife of Periya Pazhuvettarayar, the great lord and sovereign of Chola Nadu…”
“So you mock me as the woman who married an old man, do you not?”
“Oh no! If I ever mocked you, may I be banished to the most wretched city…”
“No, no! Whatever else you may say, do not call me Pazhuvettarayar’s ‘virtuous wife.’ I am not his wife at all…”
“Heavens! What are you saying?”
“I speak only the truth. If a woman is seized and forced to remain in a house, does that make her a wife?”
“Devi! You are born of the noble lineage of Tamil women. You would never act against the dharma of womankind!”

“I am well aware of the dharma of women. The women of ancient Tamil Nadu, once they loved someone with all their heart, accepted only him as their husband. They would never consent to a forced marriage!”
“But you…”

“I know what you are about to say. You wonder how I agreed to the forced marriage with Pazhuvetarayar. I consented for a very important reason. The women of ancient Tamil Nadu possess another unique quality as well. They will, without fail, avenge any injustice done to them. Sir! You did not help me to fulfill my love. At least, will you help me to take revenge on my enemies?”
The last words spoken by Nandini struck Vandiyathevan’s heart as if cleaved by a thunderbolt, as though a great lightning had suddenly crashed upon his head, leaving him reeling and bewildered.
“Devi! Devi! What is this?… Love? Revenge? What connection do I have with your love? What connection is there between love and revenge?”
“There is a connection; but now is not the time to speak of it. Look, the prince and Manimekalai are approaching. If you come alone to my chamber at midnight tomorrow, I will tell you everything…”
“How is that possible, Devi! You reside in the inner quarters. How can I come there alone at midnight?”
“Did you not once escape from that very chamber without anyone’s knowledge? You can return the same way, can you not? If only you have the will…”
Vandiyathevan’s astonishment was now complete. Yet, there was no change in Nandini’s face. As ever, a gentle smile played upon her lips.

chapters.title: “You Are My Sister!”
paragraphs: Nandini and Vandiyathevan stood together as the prince and Manimekalai approached them.

The prince walked towards them, his gaze fixed on Vandiyathevan until he drew near. As he came closer, he turned his eyes to Nandini. He noticed blood oozing from wounds on her cheek and shoulder, red as if marked by crimson lines.
“Alas! Has that wretched tiger wounded you?” he exclaimed.
“Yes, my lord! But the tiger has only wounded my body; it has not wounded my heart!”
These words struck straight into Karikalan’s heart. Before he could say anything further, Manimekalai hurried to Nandini’s side in agitation.
“Oh, sister! It has scratched you badly! Luckily, I brought some ointment. Come, let me apply it! If you put it on immediately, the wound will heal quickly!” she said.
“Sister, wounds like these are quite ordinary for me. I have suffered and recovered from many such injuries. Tell me, do you have any ointment that can heal a wound to the heart?” replied Nandini.
“Oh! I have that too, sister! I have that as well!” said Manimekalai, and taking Nandini by the hand, she led her to the crystal pavilion.
The prince and Vandiyathevan followed a little behind and sat down on a stone platform beneath the shade of a large mango tree near the pavilion.
“My lord! The sooner we leave this place, the better! If we linger here too long, Kandanmaran and his father might misunderstand,” said Vandiyathevan.
“Let anyone think what they will. Will they take our heads for it? It is enough if these women do not misunderstand us. Once they return, we can take our leave,” replied the prince.

After a short while, Nandini and Manimekalai returned, dressed in fresh garments and adorned with ornaments. The wounds on Nandini’s cheek and shoulder were now hidden beneath a layer of salve, with no trace of blood to be seen. “We were waiting to bid you farewell before we left,” said Karikalan.

“That is good; but it is already past noon. You must stay with us and have your meal before you go. If I let you leave at this hour, the daughter of Sambuvaraiyar will never forgive me,” said the Lady of Pazhuvoor.

“We will stay, but only on one condition: Manimekalai has already applied ointment to my wound. But she also spoke of a balm for the wounds of the heart. If she will tell me what that balm is, we shall stay,” said Karikalan.
“Why not try to guess it ourselves without asking her?” said Nandini.
“Perhaps she meant the forgetfulness that comes with the passage of time,” said Karikalan.
“That cannot be; are there not wounds of the heart that time cannot heal?” asked Nandini.
“When it comes to women, there is indeed a fine balm for the wounds of the heart! That is—tears!” said Vandiyathevan.

“The Prince of Vallam was waiting for an opportunity to mock women; but what he says is not true. There are certain wounds of the heart that, once inflicted, rob one even of the power to weep. How then can tears serve as a balm?” said Nandini.
“If neither of us is right, then tell us your own guess,” said Vandiyathevan.

“Why not? I shall tell you. Sister! The balm you speak of—does it not reach the heart through the ear? Is it not the sweet music that flows from the yāzh, the flute, and the melodious voice that you call the balm for the wounds of the heart?” said Nandini.
“Yes, Akka! How did you know?” asked Manimekalai.
“Did I not tell you that I am a sorceress? I have the power to know what is in others’ hearts. Sir! Do you both accept the wondrous power of music?” asked Nandini.
“Yes, yes! I also admit it was our fault not to have guessed it. I remember now that Kandamaran told me Manimekalai is skilled in music and plays the yāzh beautifully,” said Karikalan.

“Is this not how a brother ought to be? If there is a single day when he does not speak of his sister’s virtues to someone, it seems as though that day has not dawned for the young lord of Kadambur. What he said about Manimekalai’s musical talent is indeed true. Manimekalai has even brought her yaazh with her. Fortunately, she is not compelled to sing today, for I alone am unworthy of knowing the glory of her musical skill. Sir! You have saved us, foolish women that we are, from becoming a tiger’s meal today. Should we not express our gratitude for that? You must dine with us, and only after partaking of Manimekalai’s nectar-like music may you depart,” insisted Nandini.
Vandiyathevan signaled to the prince that he did not wish to agree to this. But the prince took no notice of it. “The wishes of princesses are our good fortune,” said Karikalan.
“Manimekalai! Your heart’s desire is fulfilled. Go and see if the meal is ready! If not, hasten it a little,” Nandini instructed.
Manimekalai immediately rose and went towards the place where the meal was being prepared. At the same time, Vandiyathevan also stood up and looked around in all directions.

Noticing this, Nandini said, “A little while ago, I claimed to possess the magical power to discern the thoughts in others’ minds, did I not? Now I wish to put it to the test. Shall I reveal what is in the mind of the prince of Vallam at this moment?”
Karikalan laughed and said, “Let us hear it, then!”
“He is regretting that it was a great mistake to have killed the tiger and saved these women. He is thinking it would have been far better if both of them had ended up in the tiger’s belly!”
Karikalan laughed even more and asked, “My friend! Is this truly what you are thinking?”

“No, my lord! I did not think so. But it is true that my thoughts were about the tiger and about these ladies. I am merely astonished at how the tiger, once caught by them, managed to escape alive!” replied Vandiyathevan.
“What is this, brother! Are you raving? The tiger escaped alive? Again? Did not the dead tiger’s body float in the water? Where is it?” the prince asked, rising to his feet.
“There! Look!” said Vandiyathevan, pointing.

From where they stood, through the gaps between the tree branches, the riverbank could be seen within shouting distance. There, the princesses’ boat was tied up. At that very moment, a leopard, gripping the prow of the boat with its forelegs, was struggling to climb aboard.
“Aha! This tiger’s life is truly stubborn!” said Karikalan.
“My lord! Come, let us go and finish it off. It is wrong to leave a wounded tiger alive!” said Vallavarayan.

“O valiant one of the Vanar clan! Why should two warriors like you trouble yourselves over a single wounded tiger? I shall call Manimekalai. With the small dagger in her hand, she will go and kill the tiger herself!” said Nandini.
“Did you hear that, my friend? The Queen of Pazhuvoor holds our valor in such high esteem. Should I come too, or will you go alone?” asked Karikalan.
“Or shall we send Manimekalai?” Nandini suggested.
“We could send Manimekalai, but what if that girl, instead of killing the wounded tiger, applies some ointment to its wounds and brings it back alive? What then?” Vandiyathevan muttered.
“What are you thinking about?” asked the prince.

“I am wondering whether I should cut off the head of the wounded tiger and lay it at the feet of the Queen of Pazhuvoor. Let us see if she is satisfied at least then,” said Vandiyathevan, and strode off briskly.

“Did you hear what that fool said? Does it take so much bravery to cut off the head of a wounded tiger?” Karikalan asked, beginning to laugh, but when he glanced at Nandini’s face, he stopped laughing halfway.
“Shouldn’t you be the one to give your opinion on that?” asked Nandini.
A shiver ran through Karikalan’s entire body. In a trembling voice, he said, “Nandini! You sent a message to Kandamaaran. That is why I came here. Otherwise, I would not have come.”
“At least after all this time, you have honored my request! Many thanks!” said Nandini.
“I thought you had forgotten all that has passed. That is why you sent the message, I believed…”
“How can I forget all that has happened, Ayya! Have you forgotten everything…?”

“It is not possible to forget; even I cannot forget! You stood before me with tears in your eyes and asked me for a boon. I did not grant it. At that time, I was seized by some madness. I have not forgotten any of that even now. But why did you send me a message? Why did you summon me here?” asked the prince.
“Ayya! You have not come to Thanjavur for three years. You have not even come to see your ailing father…”
“He is not only my father, Nandini!…”

“Yes, he is also the father of the younger princess! He is also the father of Ponniyin Selvan! Yet, it is your absence that pains your father the most. Someone has told the Emperor that I am the reason for your not coming to Thanjai. Because of that, he refuses to even see me. Ayya! Was not the harm you have already done to me enough? Must this new blame fall upon me as well?…”
“But is it not true? It is because of you that I have not come to Thanjai…”
“If that is so, then I shall leave Thanjai. You may come to Thanjai, ascend your father’s throne, and be crowned with the jeweled diadem…”
“Nandini! That will never happen. I have no desire now for the throne. Let Madurantaka Thevan ascend the throne, wear the imperial crown, and rule the empire…”
“Ayya! You know Madurantaka well. Can he rule this vast empire even for a single day?”
“If he cannot rule, the Pazhuvettaraiyars are there to help him; you are there as well…”
“Ayya! Now I understand your wishes clearly. I shall leave Thanjai, leave the palace of Pazhuvoor… You may come to Thanjai…”
“No, no! You are mistaken! I have no such thought. The wrongs I have already done to you are enough. Let me not add to them the sin of driving you out from the palace of Pazhuvoor…”
“Sir! Can we not both remain in Thanjai? Is there not enough space in that great city for the two of us? There is not even any necessity for us to see each other, is there?”

“There may be no need to see each other, but is it possible not to think of each other? Just a moment ago, you yourself said it—you said it is impossible to forget what has passed, and spoke of the wound in your heart. There is a wound in my heart too; I cannot forget either.”
“We may not be able to forget; but can we not forgive? Even after all these years, can you not forgive the wrongs I have done?”

“Nandini! You have done nothing for me to forgive. The one who erred was I; it is I who should seek your forgiveness. Even when I set out from Kanchi, I left with the thought that perhaps I could ask your pardon and receive it. But on the way, something I learned made me unworthy even to ask your forgiveness.”
“Prince! In every way, it is unseemly for you to seek forgiveness from me. You are the son of the emperor who rules the earth; I am a poor orphan girl, abandoned by my own parents…”
“No, Nandini! You are not an orphan girl…”
“Even though the noble Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar accepted me wholeheartedly as his young queen…”
“Not only that, Nandini! I hesitate, not knowing how to tell you the truth…”
“You may tell this foolish girl anything without hesitation. All those who pass me on the road dare to say whatever they wish. They drag me into their quarrels and insult me…”

“Nandini! If anyone hereafter behaves so, I will not be able to bear it even for a moment. All you need do is tell me, and I will send him at once to the world of Yama, and then attend to other matters…”
“You have always shown me such compassion. Even as a child, you quarreled with the young princess of Pazhayarai for my sake—she who is your own sister…”
“Nandini! You too are my sister! Just as the Young Princess is my sister, so are you; I am your brother!”

“Prince! Ever since I married another, you have regarded me as your sister. That is indeed befitting the honor of your noble lineage. But how can I, who am now the wife of another, consider the son of the Emperor, one born to rule the three worlds, as my brother…?”
“Nandini, you have not understood what I mean! Truly, you are my sister; the daughter of the Emperor who shall rule the three worlds…!”
At these words, Nandini burst into ringing laughter.
“I do not know whether your mind is confused, or if I am the one who has gone mad!” she said.
“Neither delusion nor madness afflicts us.”
“If that is so, are you mocking this poor fool?”
“Look at me, Nandini! Do I truly appear to you as one who would mock you?”
