“Sir! Look at my face and tell me! When you see me, do I seem like the daughter of the Emperor? Does the mark of royal birth shine upon my face?”

“Nandini! I have seen your face since you were a girl of five. I have marveled at the matchless beauty that shone upon it. Only now do I understand the reason for it. It became clear to me only after I left Kanchi, somewhere along the way. Among all those born into the Chola clan, it is renowned throughout the world that none can rival the beauty of Princess Kalyani, the daughter of King Vaithumba. She is my grandmother; even now, she lives in Pazhayarai. Even after seventy years, the divine beauty that radiates from her face dazzles the eyes. All that beauty has now sought refuge in you. It is not in me; it is not in the Young Princess; nor in Arulmozhi. Through my father’s line, it has come to you…”
“Sir! What are you saying? Truly, it seems I am the one whose mind is deranged. Or perhaps there is some fault in my ears…”

“No, Nandini, no! There is no madness in your mind; nor is there any flaw in your hearing. You are my father’s daughter; therefore, you are my sister! Before the Emperor married my mother, he fell in love with a queen from an island in Eelam and married her in a Gandharva ceremony. You are her daughter, and thus, you are my sister!” Karikalan spoke, his voice trembling with emotion.
Nandini gazed at Aditya Karikalan for a moment, as though struck by a great shock. Then, clarity dawned upon her face.
“Sir! Was it only after you left Kanchi that you learned this news?” she asked.
“Yes, Nandini! The moment I learned it, many things that had been unclear to me before became clear.”
“Prince! Who was it that told you this news on your journey? Was it Vallavaraiyan Vandiyathevan?”
“It was he! But he did not tell me of his own accord. The younger princess, Kundavai, told him and sent him to me!”
“Ah! From the very beginning, so many schemes have been woven to keep you and me apart. Even now, their conspiracies have not ended.”

“You are mistaken, Nandini! There is no conspiracy in this. When we were children, I did not understand why the elder princess, Sembiyan Madevi, tried to keep us apart. For that, I was filled with boundless anger. Only now do I realize how she saved us from a terrible disaster. But they could have told us the truth then. By not telling, they did you a great injustice; and they have harmed me as well. Let the past be past. Let us both forget all that has gone by; even if we cannot forget, let us forgive…”
“Sir! Did Vallavaraiyan Vandiyathevan meet you on the way and tell you only this story? Did he say anything else?” Nandini asked.
“Why do you call it a story, Nandini? Do you not believe it?” asked Aditya Karikalan.

“Is the news you have told me so easy to believe? Could I, born as the Emperor’s daughter, have been fated to such a story? Could I have suffered such cruel misfortunes? Is what Vandiyathevan said truly—” “Let it be. Is that all he said? Did he not say anything else?” asked Nandini.

Kari­kalan hesitated for a moment and then replied, “Yes; he told me something else as well. He said that you are in league with the conspirators of Pandya Nadu. He claimed that you have sworn an oath to destroy the Chola dynasty at its very root. He said you keep a sword with the fish emblem in your possession and worship it for this purpose. He also said that near the banks of the Kollidam, in the forest by the encampment, you crowned a young boy with the royal diadem. Nandini! Forget all that from now on! You have as much right to the glory of the Chola clan as I do. You are the daughter of Sundara Chola Chakravarthi. Our beloved sister. From this day forth, I will make it my foremost duty to atone for all the injustices done to you…”
“Sir! Do you truly believe all this?” Nandini asked. “If so, why did you come to Kadambur and wait all these days? Why did you not try to meet me and speak to me earlier?”

“The confusion in my heart was the reason. I needed time to come to terms with our new relationship. I was waiting for the right opportunity to explain everything clearly. Is this a matter to be spoken of in front of others? By a stroke of luck, a wild boar and a leopard have today given me such an opportunity…”
Nandini interrupted, “Sir! Wild beasts are indeed ferocious! But they cannot inflict as much cruelty as humans. Only today have I truly understood this.”
“Sister! Just now, you asked if it is possible to forget all that has gone by. I agreed with you. I asked that, even if you cannot forget, you should forgive. But you did not answer me.”

“Prince! I will forgive all the betrayals and wrongs you have done to me in the past; perhaps, in time, I may even forget them. But the betrayal you have committed today—I can never forget it, nor can I ever forgive it…”
“Alas! What have I done today? I have not knowingly done you any wrong!”
“I will tell you. Look, there he comes—look at that scoundrel!”
“Are you speaking of Vallavaraiyan?”

“Yes; the one who comes empty-handed without bringing the tiger’s head, that is him. One day he saw me in Thanjai. He said that if my foot touched his body, he would consider it a ‘blessing’. I did not even wish to touch him with my foot and kick him. After I said I would call the servants, he ran away. Because I did not yield to his despicable intentions, he has spun such terrible tales and told them to you. He even swore that, if I wished, he would bring your very head to me. He is afraid that I might reveal all this to you. That is why he tried to stop you on the way and prevent you from coming to Kadambur palace. That is why he keeps circling about, never staying by your side. Such a wretch, one whom I would not even wish to touch with my foot—you made it so that he could lift my entire body in his arms and carry me to the shore. You stood by and watched it happen. Can I ever forget this? Or can I ever forgive it?”

As Nandini spoke these words, her eyes blazing with the fire of anger, Karikalan’s head truly began to spin. The crystal pavilion, the waters of the lake, the forest trees—all seemed to whirl around him. Regaining his composure a little, he said, “Sister! Nandini! Can what you say really be true? I do not know what to believe. Could Vandiyathevan truly be so base? Only a short while ago, I was even thinking of marrying this foolish girl Manimekalai to him!”
“Sir! Do not believe only what I say. You always act in haste. This time, do not do so. Wait for two days and watch his actions closely. You will see for yourself!” said Nandini.

chapters.title: The Boat Moved!
paragraphs: Vandiyathevan was hurrying in from one side. From the other side, Manimekalai approached, saying, “Akka! The food is ready!” as she drew near.

Karikalan looked from one side to the other and said, “Nandini, it was not only Vandiyathevan who tried to stop me from coming to Kadambur Palace. That Vaishnavite, Alwarkadiyan, also brought the same message! Even the chief minister Aniruddha, my father’s dearest friend and a man I revere, sent word warning me, did he not?”

“Chief Minister Aniruddha! Your father’s beloved companion! And so, he himself seeks to take your father’s very life. He is a man you revere! And so, he wishes to ensure you never inherit the throne…”
“Why? Why?”

“He thinks you are mad, that you lack divine devotion. His desire is to crown your younger brother, make him a valiant Vaishnavite, and turn this Chola land into a Vaishnavite kingdom. When your brother disappeared in the midst of the sea, a shadow fell upon his hopes!”
“For that, is it necessary to prevent me from coming to Kadambur?”
“Shall I not reveal all their secrets to you?”
“How do you know their secrets?”
“Sir! Have you forgotten that I am the sister of that Vaishnavite, Alwarkadiyan…?”
“Are you truly his own sister? Do you expect me to believe that story?”

“I myself do not believe that story. Nor do I ask you to believe it. I was raised in his father’s house. So he calls me his sister. That Vaishnavite is accustomed to calling me the incarnation of Andal. His wish is that I should travel with him from town to town, singing the hymns of the Alwars and spreading the Vaishnavite tradition!”
“Did he wish to make you a Vaishnavite ascetic, just as those Buddhist monks?” asked Aditya Karikalan.

“Nothing of the sort. His desire was to marry me, to wander from town to town as a couple, singing hymns together. He wished that I should bear him many children, to help spread the Vaishnavite faith…”
“Ugh! Where is that monkey-faced Thirumalai, and where are you? Did he truly wish to make you his wife?”
“Sir! That is my misfortune! Such was the hour of my birth! Every man who draws near to me does so with evil intent…”
“Does that old man, Pazhuvettarayar, speak of others because his own wits have gone astray?”

“Prince! Do not speak a single word against Pazhuvettarayar in my hearing. He cherished me. He married me before the whole world. I, who was an orphaned girl, he raised to the dignity of a crowned queen in his palace…”
“But what is your own wish, Nandini? Do you truly accept him as your husband and worship him? If so…”

“No, no. I am bound to him by immeasurable gratitude. But I have never lived the life of a wife with him. Sir! I was born in a poor family. I was abandoned at birth. Yet I have given my heart to only one person. I have never changed it, not for a single day…”

“Nandini! Who is that fortunate man? No, do not tell me. Who are you? Tell me the truth! If you are not my father’s daughter, if you are not my sister, if you are not even born along with Azhwarkadiyan, then who are you? Tell me that alone, Nandini! If I do not know it, I shall truly go mad!” cried Karikalan.
“I, too, wish to reveal it to you. But your friend and my companion are approaching us now. When another opportunity arises, I will surely tell you,” said Nandini.
Seeing Vallavaraiyan, who had come very close, the Queen of Pazhuvoor asked, “Sir! Why have you returned empty-handed? Where is the tiger’s head?”
“Devi! The fortune of bringing a tiger’s head and laying it at your feet has not come to me!” said Vandiyathevan.

“Ah! Is this the extent of your valor? You spoke so much about the bravery of your ancestors, didn’t you? Didn’t you say that they reaped the heads of three dynastic kings and planted them in the fields?”
“What is that song?” asked Karikalan.
“Sir! Will you say it, or shall I?” Nandini asked Vandiyathevan, turning to him.
“Rani! I have no memory of ever reciting such a song,” said Vandiyathevan.
“You do not remember, but I recall it very well. I shall recite it—listen, my lord!
With armies grown lush and rivers of crimson blood gathered, In the rare mire trampled by elephants— The king of kings, the lord of poets, reaped and planted The crowns of the three great kings!
How is that song, Prince? You have brought only the head of a single Pandya. But your ancestors, it seems, brought the heads of Chera, Chola, and Pandya kings and planted them in the fields…”
Disgust and rage danced across Karikalan’s face. “Excellent ploughing! Excellent planting!” he exclaimed, and then burst into thunderous laughter.
Vandiyathevan could not even raise his eyes to meet Karikalan’s face. He stammered, “Devi! I have never recited such a song to you!”

“What does it matter? If you did not already know, you can now learn of your lineage’s greatness! Yet, in the dynasty that once reaped and planted the heads of the three crowned kings, you could not even bring back the head of a wounded tiger?”
“Devi! That wounded tiger is dead and gone. I did not wish to sever the head of a dead beast.”
“How is that possible? I saw the tiger leap onto the boat with my own eyes!” said Karikalan.

“I was the one who showed you that scene. After it climbed into the boat and lay down, it must have died. Perhaps, overcome by remorse for having wounded the noble lady of Pazhuvoor, it gave up its life. Or who knows for what reason?” replied Vandiyathevan.

The sharpness on Karikalan’s face softened a little, and a faint smile blossomed. “But it could have died in the water itself, couldn’t it? There was no need for it to climb into the boat to die, was there?” said Karikalan.
“It seems that, like me, it too has no liking for water. Of all kinds of death, it is drowning in water that terrifies me the most!” said Vandiyathevan.
“Yet, just a while ago, you bravely jumped into the water, didn’t you? Do you have such compassion for these foolish women?” asked the prince.
“Devi! More than water, it is women who frighten me. I only jumped in at the prince’s insistence. Now I realize there was no real need for me to have done so,” said Vallavarayan.
“Yes, yes! You are only afraid of dying by drowning in water. But you have no fear of making others drown and perish!” said Nandini.
It was clear from Manimekalai’s expression that she did not like this conversation at all. “Akka, the food I cooked will get cold; come, let us go!” she said.

The four of them walked towards the crystal pavilion. Now and then, Manimekalai glanced at Vandiyathevan. With her woman’s intuition, she sensed that something troubled his mind, and that both the prince and Nandini were causing him some distress. Through the language of her eyes, she tried to comfort Vandiyathevan, as if to say, “Whoever stands against you, I will always be on your side; do not worry!” But Vandiyathevan did not even turn to look at her. He seemed as one who had sunk deep into the ocean of worry.

Nandini Devi’s deceitful words, and the terrible accusation she had cast upon Vandiyathevan, might well have filled the readers who have followed this tale with disgust. Yet, if we recall her birth and the events of her life as we know them, we may not be so greatly surprised. The traits of human nature, inherited and soaked into the blood through generations— They are shaped by nature. Circumstances, customs, and the experiences of life bring about changes in them. Mandakini, who was both mute and deaf, had spent most of her life in the forest. She had to be constantly vigilant to escape the wild beasts. At times, in order to save her own life, she was forced to kill those animals with ruthless ferocity.

For a long time, her heart remained pure as milk. Then, at a certain point, a spring of love began to flow within her. But soon, that spring dried up, turning her heart into a barren desert. The play of fate subjected her to a great disappointment. The shock of it nearly shattered her mind. Yet, in the course of time, the wounds in her heart healed. Once again, the nectar-like spring of love began to flow. All the affection she had once felt for Sundara Chozhar she transformed, as a mother’s love, towards his beloved son, Arulmozhi.

In Nandini, the daughter of Mandakini, many of the mother’s traits appeared by nature. But the world betrayed the mother; it betrayed the daughter even more cruelly. She was abandoned even by her own mother. She grew up in a stranger’s house. The torments that wild animals had inflicted upon her mother were nothing compared to the cruelties that men of the land inflicted upon the daughter. The insults and humiliations she suffered at the hands of the royal family in her youth pierced her heart like a diamond and turned into a hatred more poisonous than venom. She never received the nectar of love that could have countered such hatred. Whomever she loved, they either neglected and cast her aside, or, struck by misfortune, perished. Those who had insulted her, those whom she despised, lived on in prosperity. What more could be needed to turn a woman’s heart into something more poisonous than venom? There was no room left in her heart for anything but revenge against those who had betrayed and humiliated her. The cunning required for such vengeance had been mingled in her blood from the very day she was in her mother’s womb. The hardships, disappointments, and terrifying experiences she endured in life had swept away all compassion and tenderness from her heart, making it harder than iron or stone. In order to understand the events that are to unfold in this story, it is necessary to explain these traits here.

Even during the meal, there was no lively conversation among them. Nandini, Karikalan, and Vandiyathevan were each lost in their own worries. Of all, it was Manimekalai who felt the most distressed by this. She had come with the hope of spending a cheerful time, conversing joyfully with the Lady of Pazhuvoor, but— That day, she had arranged for water games and a picnic in the woods. When the prince and Vandiyathevan arrived unexpectedly and joined them, her excitement grew even greater. But afterwards, the words spoken by the other three and the way they conducted themselves did not give her any satisfaction. The pain she had felt upon seeing Nandini and Vandiyathevan together was quickly forgotten by her childlike heart. She consoled herself, thinking it was her own mistake to have misunderstood and given way to jealousy.
After that, the fact that the other three sat with stiff faces, without any cheerfulness, and spoke with a certain pretense—she neither understood it nor liked it.

So, after they had eaten and a little time had passed, Manimekalai asked, “Akka! Shall we begin our return journey? Shall I ask them to bring the boat? Are these two coming with us, or will they go back the way they came, on horseback?”

Only then did Karikalan return from his world of thoughts to the world around him. “Ah! Ah! Are we to leave without hearing this maiden’s music on the yazh? Not for a single day could I bear that. Nandini! Have you forgotten? Manimekalai! Do not disappoint us!” he said.

“I have not forgotten. But seeing you and your friend, you do not seem like those who would care to listen to music in the forest. You stand as if on a bed of thorns. Still, it is no matter. Manimekalai! Go, bring the yazh!” said Nandini.
“For what, Akka? Why do you ask me to play the yazh before those who do not wish to hear it?” Manimekalai retorted, a little petulantly.
“No, no! The prince himself says he wishes to hear it. If his friend does not care for the song, let him close his ears,” said Nandini.
“Heavens! It is not so—I am not an enemy of music! On the banks of the Kaveri, there was a boatwoman named Poonguzhali, who sang,
‘Though the waves of the sea are still, Why does the ocean within me surge?’
When I think of that song, even now my body thrills!” said Vandiyathevan.
“Some people like only certain songs, sung by certain people. I wonder if you will care for my song?” said Manimekalai.
“If you don’t like it, who will let you go? That’s enough from me. You, bring the yaazh!” said Karikalan.

Manimekalai brought the yaazh. She sat on the upper step of the crystal pavilion. She tightened the strings and tuned the instrument. It was a yaazh with seven tusk-strings. On each string, one note could be played up to the halfway point, and another note above that. For a while, she played only the yaazh, pouring forth a stream of sweet music. Karikalan and Vandiyathevan truly forgot all their other worries. Their hearts were swept away in rapture by the music of the yaazh.
Then, Manimekalai added her voice to the yaazh’s melody and sang. She sang the divine hymns of Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar. After a while, the prince said,
“Manimekalai! Your singing is wonderful. But you have only sung devotional songs so far. I am not so deeply immersed in devotion. I have left all that Shiva-bhakti to Madurantakan. Sing a love song!”
Manimekalai’s beautiful cheeks flushed with shyness. She hesitated a little.
“Girl! Why do you hesitate? If you sing a love song here, I will not think you are singing it for me. Nor will my friend. So sing without hesitation!” said Karikalan.
“If anyone thinks so, Manimekalai will not worry about it!” said Nandini.
“Oh, sister! Is it right to tease like this in front of two men?” said Manimekalai.

“It is your mistake to think of them as men. Can those who cannot bring back the head of a dead tiger be called men? In the old days, the brave men of Tamil Nadu would catch a tiger alive, tear open its jaws, pluck its teeth, and bring them as ornaments for their beloveds! All those days are gone! Let them go! You sing! The other day, you sang that beautiful song for me, didn’t you? Sing that one!” said Nandini.
Manimekalai played the yaazh and sang the following song. Somehow, her voice poured forth a nectarous sweetness, surpassing all she had sung so far:

“Upon the gentle stream where the waters glide…” On the slopes of the hill of delight, Beneath the shade of trees that shelter in summer, Hand in hand, all that we cherished— Was it all but a fleeting dream, my friend? Was it only a memory?
In the grove of blossoming punnai trees, In the golden glow of evening, She bade him come to me— All those honeyed words she uttered, Were they but a vision, Was that wonder a lie?
Breaking past the guards, Stealing in like a thief, With boundless love, He pressed me close and gave me kisses— Did all that truly happen? Did we truly rejoice?

Thus, again and again, Manimekalai composed and sang many such verses in different tunes. The other three were swept away in that flood of song. Even in the eyes of Nandini, who for many reasons had made her heart harder than stone or iron, tears welled up. Aditya Karikalan forgot the world entirely. Vandiyathevan, as if startled awake from time to time, kept glancing at Manimekalai. Each time, he found her looking only at him, and the warrior’s heart trembled all the more. “Alas! What wrong have I done to this girl?” his heart pounded in anxiety.

Immersed as they were in the flood of music and emotion, none of them noticed that the wind was growing stronger. They did not see the first small ripples rising on the lake, nor how those waves gradually grew larger. The wind grew fierce— It was only when a storm uprooted a wild tree and hurled it aside that the four of them awoke and looked around. They saw the fierce gale blowing, and the lake churning, with great waves rising and crashing down with a thunderous roar.

Suddenly, Nandini cried out, “Oh no! Where is the boat?” The boat was nowhere to be seen at the spot where it had been tied. Looking closely, they saw it far away, being tossed and carried off by the waves.
“Oh! What are we to do now?” Nandini wailed.
“If both of you know how to ride, mount the horses and leave. We will manage somehow,” said Vandiyathevan.
“In this storm, are you suggesting we ride out and get ourselves killed by falling trees?” Nandini retorted.

“There’s no need for that; let’s stay here until the fury of the storm subsides. What are we going to do over there? We have provisions for cooking; and for singing, we have Manimekalai. I haven’t been this happy in a long time!” said Karikalan.
“Prince! That is not right! What will Sambuvarayar and Kandanmaran think?” Vallavarayan said.
“She must have untied the boat herself when she went looking for the tiger!” Nandini accused.

“Sister! Why do you cast blame without reason? When he arrived, the boat was still by the shore. No one needs to worry; as soon as my father sees this storm, he will send large boats for us!” said Manimekalai.

What she said soon came true. Two large boats, almost like ships, approached the island. In one of them was the great Sambuvarayar himself. Seeing the four of them safe, he was overjoyed. Taking them aboard, the two boats turned back across the lake, which was still surging and boiling like a stormy sea.
Except for Sambuvarayar, in the hearts of the other four, a fierce tempest continued to rage and churn.
Part Five – The Pinnacle of Sacrifice

chapters.title: Three Voices
paragraphs: At the Chudamani Vihara in Nagapattinam, Ponniyin Selvan waited with patience. Within his heart surged a fervent longing to travel to Thanjavur and see his father and mother. He was eager to prove that the accusation laid upon him—that he sought to seize the throne of Lanka—was baseless. He also wished to quickly dispel the slander that he had acted in defiance of his father’s command.

Yet, restraining all his desires, he had firmly resolved that he would depart for Thanjavur only after receiving word from his elder sister. Time seemed to pass with great difficulty. He spent some hours participating in the daily rituals and worship conducted by the Buddhist monks. Some time was whiled away admiring the exquisite paintings that adorned the walls of the Chudamani Vihara. The hours spent conversing with the monks, especially with the chief preceptor of the Vihara, brought him a measure of solace and enthusiasm.

For the chief monk of Chudamani Vihara was a man who had journeyed for many years to lands far beyond the southern seas. He had traveled from the land of China to the island of Java, visiting many towns and cities along the way. He could vividly describe those countries, their cities, and the people who dwelled there.

To the south of China, many island nations were then united under the great Srivijaya Empire. Arumanaadu, Kamboja, Manakkavaram, Thalaithakkolam, Maapappalam, Mayirudingam, Lanka Sogam, Thamaralingam, Ilaamuri—many such lands and cities were either subject to or allied with the Srivijaya Empire. Among them all, the city of Kadaram shone as the unrivaled center, famed for its splendor and wealth.

Whenever the chief monk found respite, Ponniyin Selvan would eagerly ask him to describe those distant lands and cities. The monk, never tiring, would narrate tales of the natural riches and the flourishing trade of those countries. He spoke of their abundance of gold and gems, of red rice and sugarcane, and how, in every way, they rivaled the fertile Chola land. He recounted the ancient ties between Tamilakam and those distant realms. He spoke of the wondrous artistry of Pallava sculptors who had journeyed to those lands and erected marvels of sculpture there. He spoke of the grand temples. He described how the arts of painting, music, and dance from Tamilagam had spread through those lands. He spoke of the Ramayana, the Mahabharata, and other epics, of the deities Vinayaka, Subramanya, Shiva, Parvati, and Thirumal, and of the Buddha Dharma—all of which had mingled and taken root in the hearts of the people of those countries. The people there worshipped all these gods together, unable to separate one from the other. He mentioned that Agastya Muni, the father of the Tamil language, was accorded special reverence in those lands, and that many temples had been built in his honor.

Arulmozhi Varman listened to all this again and again, questioned the monk closely, and engraved it in his mind. The prince inquired thoroughly about the land and sea routes to each of those countries. He asked about the dangers and conveniences along the way and learned all he could.
“Swami! Might you one day journey again to those lands?” he asked.
“It will happen as the will of the Buddha dictates, Prince! Why do you ask?” replied the Bhikshu.
“Only because I wish to accompany you.”

“I am a renunciate who has forsaken the world; you are the royal son of the emperor who rules the earth. How can you and I journey together? Even the responsibility of keeping you safe in this vihara for a few days weighs heavily upon me. My heart beats anxiously, not knowing what might happen, or when…”
“Swami! I wish to relieve you of that burden at once. This very moment, from here—”

“Prince! I spoke without thinking. Though it is a burden to keep you here, I consider it a blessing. Your father, the emperor, and your sister, the young princess, have rendered great service to the Buddha Dharma. What we do now cannot repay even a thousandth part of our debt of gratitude. Is the help you have given to the Buddha Dharma so small? Can we forget your service in having the ruined stupas and viharas of Anuradhapura restored and inscribed? In return for all that, the monks came forward to offer you the very jeweled crown of Lanka as a token of gratitude. Prince! Why did you refuse it? Had you ascended the independent throne of Lanka, then on hundreds and hundreds of ships… “With such a great retinue, could you not have traveled to the southern lands? Did you never feel the desire in your heart to follow this bhikshu on his pilgrimage?” asked the Acharya Bhikshu.
“Gurudeva! Have you ever read the ‘Maha Vamsa’, the chronicle of the royal lineage of Lanka?” the prince asked.
“Sir! What kind of question is that? Could I have become the head of this Chudamani Vihara without having read the ‘Maha Vamsa’?”

“Forgive me. When I asked if you had read the ‘Maha Vamsa’, it was as if I were questioning whether you knew how to read at all. But you know well, do you not, what dreadful and terrible sins were committed by those in the royal lineage described in the ‘Maha Vamsa’? Sons imprisoned their fathers. Fathers slew their sons. Mothers poisoned their own children; sons burned their mothers alive… If such was the bond between parents and their offspring, what need is there to speak of uncles, aunts, stepmothers, elder and younger brothers…? Gurudeva! Does not the ‘Maha Vamsa’ declare that such heinous crimes were committed by the royal family of Lanka?”

“Yes, yes! It also tells of the punishments that befell them for such evil deeds. By showing those examples, the ‘Maha Vamsa’ instructs people to walk the path of dharma. Do not forget that! The ‘Maha Vamsa’ is a sacred text, a peerless scripture that teaches dharma to the world!” the Acharya Bhikshu exclaimed fervently.

“Swami, I do not blame the book called ‘Maha Vamsa’. I merely spoke of how the lust for power can turn men into demons and monsters. Is it wrong, then, that I refused the throne of Lanka, tainted by such grievous sins?”

“It was for that very reason that the wise elders of the Buddhist Sangha wished to change the royal lineage of Lanka. They desired to establish a new dynasty with you as its head. It was a mistake for you to refuse. Had you ascended the throne of Lanka, you would have had the chance to spread and protect the Buddha’s dharma throughout the world, like Ashoka the Great who ruled all of Bharata under a single umbrella…”

“Gurudeva! Where is Ashoka the Great, who ruled the whole of Bharat under one parasol? And where is this boy, now hiding in a Buddhist monastery, seeking your protection? Truly, I am not even worthy to be your disciple, let alone— “How am I to protect dharma?”
“Prince! Do not speak so. You do not yet know the great power that lies hidden within you. If only you would wholeheartedly accept the Buddha’s dharma, you would win renown like Ashoka…”

“From my childhood, Vinayaka and Murugan, Parvati and Parameswara, Nandi and Bringi, and Chandikeswara have all made temples in my heart. Would I not have to cast them all aside to make room for the Buddha’s dharma? Gurudeva! Forgive me! When I said I would accompany you on your journey, I did not mean that I would embrace the Buddha’s path. My desire to cross the seas and see distant lands is what made me wish to travel with you! Yet, when I think again…”

“Prince! It seems I misunderstood your words. Even so, there is a connection between you and the Buddha’s dharma that cannot be denied. In one of his previous births, the Buddha incarnated as King Sibi. To save the life of a dove, he cut his own flesh and gave it away. The Chola clan is descended from that very Sibi. That is why those born in your lineage bear the title ‘Sembiyan.’ Do not forget this.”

“I have not forgotten, Gurudeva! Even if I did, the blood that runs in my veins would not let me. On one side, Sibi Chakravarti and Manu Needhi Cholan mingle in my blood, my flesh, my bones, urging me always: ‘Do good to others; sacrifice your own welfare for the sake of others!’ On the other side, Karikala Valavan, Vijayalaya Cholan, and Paranthaka Chakravarti are in my blood, commanding: ‘Take up the sword! Gather the fourfold army! March in all directions! Cross the seas! Expand the Chola empire and raise it to heights the world has never seen!’ And from yet another side, Sivanadiyar Kochchenganan, Aditya Cholan who ruled over Tondaimandalam, and the great Kandaraditya dwell in my heart, instructing: ‘Restore the temples! Build grand Sivalayas! Erect towers that rise to the sky like Mount Meru!’ Caught between all these ancestors, I am torn, Gurudeva! Sometimes, unable to bear their clamoring voices, I truly feel I should embrace the Buddhist faith and become a bhikshu. Show me your compassion and tell me about the Buddha’s faith. Tell me about the Blessed One himself!” said Ponniyin Selvan.
Hearing this, the Bhikshu’s face blossomed with great delight. “Prince! What is there about the Buddhist faith or Lord Buddha that you do not already know?” he asked.

“Explain to me the scenes depicted on those walls,” said the prince. “There is a painting showing a royal prince apparently rising and preparing to leave at night. Who is he? Who is the lady lying beside him? Who is the child sleeping in the cradle? Why does the prince’s face bear such a look of sorrow?”

“Sir! Lord Buddha, in his youth, was a prince born into a royal family, just like yourself. He had married Yasodhara, a woman of incomparable beauty. A beloved son had been born to them. His father was ready to entrust the burden of the kingdom to him. At that time, Siddhartha yearned to find a way to relieve humanity from the suffering that afflicts mankind. For this, he resolved to leave behind his beloved wife, his precious child, and the kingdom itself. The scene you see is that of him departing the palace at midnight. Prince! Have you not heard this story before?”

“Yes, yes! I have heard and learned it many times. But the story, when seen in these paintings, imprints itself on my mind in a way that mere words never have. Looking at the sleeping Yasodhara, I feel compelled to wake her and warn, ‘Siddhartha is leaving you! Stop him!’ Very well; tell me about the next painting!”

The venerable Bhikshu proceeded to explain, one by one, the other paintings depicting the life of Lord Buddha. In the depths of his heart, the Bhikshu cherished the hope that Arulmozhi Varman might one day embrace the Dharma of the Buddha. Thus, with great enthusiasm, he recounted the story of Siddhartha. At last, he came to the painting of Siddhartha seated in meditation beneath the Bodhi tree, attaining the light of enlightenment. After describing this scene, Ponniyin Selvan asked, “Guru Deva! If I say something contrary to your beliefs, will you be angered?”
“Prince! I have conquered the five senses and trained my mind to be calm. You may speak your thoughts freely,” replied the Bhikshu.
“I do not believe that Siddhartha attained enlightenment while seated beneath the Bodhi tree.”
Though he had mastered his senses and mind, the Bhikshu’s face fell and grew troubled.

“Prince! A branch of the great Bodhi tree was brought to Lanka during the reign of Ashoka the Great. That branch took root, flourished, and even after more than a thousand years, it still stands, vast and radiant, in Anuradhapura, undiminished by time. You yourself must have seen that sacred tree in Anuradhapura. Then why do you say, ‘I do not believe’?” he asked.

“Revered Guru! I did not say that the Bodhi tree does not exist. Nor do I deny that Siddhartha performed penance beneath it. I do not dispute that it was there he attained the light of wisdom. What I deny is only this: the day Siddhartha abandoned his wife, his only son, and the kingdom that was rightfully his, all for the sake of finding a way to alleviate the suffering of mankind, and set forth into the night—on that very night, I say, he attained enlightenment. Nowhere in any history have I heard of a deed more wondrous than that.

Rama renounced his kingdom to uphold his father’s word. Bharata, out of devotion to his brother, refused the throne. King Harishchandra gave up his realm to fulfill a promise he had made. Emperor Sibi, to protect a dove that had sought his refuge, cut his own flesh and offered it. But Siddhartha had made no promise to anyone; he did not seek to please any individual. Of his own accord, for the sake of discovering a path to end the suffering of mankind, he renounced everything and departed. After Buddha attained enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, did he perform any deed more wondrous than this? Therefore, is it wrong to say that he attained the light of wisdom the very moment he left the palace?”

The words spoken by Ponniyin Selvan fell upon the ears of the venerable Bhikshu like drops of nectar. “Sir! There is great truth in what you say. Yet, it was only beneath the Bodhi tree that the way to end the suffering of mankind dawned upon the Blessed One. It was from there that he began to teach the people.”

“Swami! I have heard the teachings of the Buddha. But it seems to me that his act of renunciation itself contains more profound instruction than all his teachings. Forgive me. I too wish to follow in his footsteps. Just now, I told you that the three voices of my ancestors echo ceaselessly within me, tormenting my soul. I wish to be freed from that affliction. Accept me as your disciple!” said the prince.

“Prince! I must have performed countless good deeds in my past lives to be blessed with a disciple like you. Yet, I possess neither the worthiness nor the courage for such an honor. When the great Buddhist Sangha gathers in Lanka, you may submit your request there,” said the Bhikshu.
“I have no doubts about your worthiness. But you spoke of courage—what do you mean by that?”

“Yes, I lack courage indeed! For the past two days, a rumor has been spreading through this Nagai port. No one knows who started it. People are saying that you are staying in this vihara, and that we are trying to make you a Buddhist monk. Many have grown angry because of this. It is said that the people are talking of marching upon this vihara with an armed crowd to uncover the truth!”

“Ah! What madness is this? Why should the people of this town be concerned if I join the Buddhist faith? If I don the ochre robes and embrace the ascetic’s path, why should they be angered? After all, I am not even married yet! They cannot accuse me of abandoning wife and children, can they?” said the Prince.

“Sir! The people bear no anger towards you. Their anger is directed at us, for allegedly deceiving you and trying to make you a Buddhist monk. A mere rumor has caused such turmoil. If it were to truly happen, what then? The people would raze this vihara to the ground. It is only under your father’s rule that we have been able to live in peace. Every day, we pray:

‘May the sacred shadow of the Bodhi tree spread far and wide, May the illustrious Nandi’s city’s king, Sundara Chola, His valor, his glory, his steadfastness, Flourish and reign supreme in this world!’
We pray thus daily. I do not wish to see this blessed state destroyed. That is why I said I lack courage,” said the Bhikshu.
Even as he finished speaking, a great commotion of voices rose in unison from the entrance of the Buddhist vihara, the sound of many people gathering.

The Bhikshu listened for a moment, then said, “Prince! It seems the people themselves have come to prove the truth of what I said. I do not know how I shall manage this! May the Blessed Buddha show us the way!”
He said.
Around the precincts of the Soodamani Vihara, the shouts and cries of thousands of people grew louder with every passing moment.

chapters.title: Murugaiyyan Has Come!
paragraphs: Outside the Choodamani Vihara, the sound of the sea swelling and roaring was echoed by the rising murmur of the crowd. For a while, both the Acharya Bhikshu and Arulmozhi Varman listened to that tumultuous noise.
The prince was deeply troubled, thinking of how the Buddhist monastery and its monks had been drawn into this great predicament because of him.
“Swami, I am sorry that I have brought this trouble upon you,” he said.
“Prince! Even if a hundred times this trouble came upon us because of you, we would not mind. Would this ever be enough to repay the help you and your family have given us?” replied the Bhikshu.

“It is not just that. I have never liked conducting affairs in such secrecy and concealment. Why should I remain here and say ‘no’ to those who seek me? Why should I involve you in an act that goes against the truth? Thanks to your devoted care, my health has recovered well. I will leave at once, go outside, and reveal myself to the people. I will announce to them that you sheltered me, treated me, and saved my life. No disgrace must ever come to this Choodamani Vihara because of me,” said the prince.

“Sir! There is nothing here that goes against the truth. Your enemies are trying to discover your whereabouts. That is certain from the rumors they have spread in Nagapattinam these past two days. In such a situation, what is wrong in keeping your presence here a secret? It is sometimes necessary for royalty to remain hidden for a while. Did not the Pandavas spend a year in incognito exile? Can anyone say that Dharmaputra acted against righteousness then?” asked the Bhikshu.

“Gurudeva! I know well your wisdom and your skill in debate. I cannot win an argument with you. Yet, let me say this: the Pandavas were compelled to hide because of the wager they had accepted. I have no such compulsion. You speak of my enemies. Who are such enemies to me? Why should they—” “Must I become an enemy? I have not the slightest desire to rule a kingdom. I have declared this openly, and even if I do have enemies, I will win them over and make them friends. I will ensure that I cause you no trouble. If the people find some satisfaction in knowing that I am alive, let them have it. Who stands to lose anything by that?”

“Prince! All that you say is true. In your position, I too would think and act the same. But what stands in the way is the promise we have given to your noble sister, Princess Kundavai. You yourself have often declared that never has a woman of such wisdom been born in the Chola lineage as the Younger Princess of Pazhayarai. In my opinion, none such has been born in any royal family. She left strict instructions that we must keep you here and protect you until she sends word. She would not have said so without grave reason. It is being spoken all over the land that several minor kings of Chola Nadu are plotting against the family of Emperor Sundara Chola. On the other hand, there are rumors that some from the Pandya country are secretly conspiring as well. The people have gathered at our gates, suspecting that we, who dwell in this Buddhist vihara, are aiding those conspirators. In such a situation, is it wise for you to go out and reveal yourself before the people? Think on it! If, in our efforts to protect you, we must face some hardship, so be it. We shall never retreat from that duty!”
As the chief monk was speaking thus, another young ascetic hurried in, agitation written on his face.

“Swami! The situation has gotten out of hand. Thousands of people have surrounded us, shouting that they must see the Prince. No matter how much we insist that the Prince is not here, it is of no use. They are clamoring that they themselves must come inside the vihara and search. If we do not give them some answer, it seems they will force their way in!”
“What answer can we give them? Only if Lord Buddha shows us a way to change their minds is there any hope,” said the chief monk.

At that moment, the Prince spoke: “Gurudeva! I have thought of a way. I beg you to listen with compassion. Your disciples have told the people that I am not here. If I now go and stand before the people—”
“It will make liars of your disciples’ words. That is why the fury of the people may become even greater,” he said.
“It will certainly happen. And we are the ones who must bear the consequences,” said the Bikshu.
“Instead of that, I will make your disciples’ words come true…”
“Prince! Even you cannot accomplish that, I think. What has been said has been said—how can it be made true now?”
“There is a way. Before the people break into this vihara, I can leave from here, can I not?”
“Ah! To save us, must we commit such a sinful act? Must we send you away?”

“Gurudeva! There is neither sin nor blame in this. Not half a mile from here, at Anaimangalam, is the Chola palace. Just as I went to see my sister the other day, now too I can slip away along the canal and reach there. Later, when the time is right, I can return. That will suffice!” said the prince.
It seemed that the Acharya Bikshu was pleased with the prince’s suggestion.

“Yes, yes! If you do so, there will be no need to reveal yourself at once. Your sister’s wishes too will be fulfilled. But at the place where the canal leaves the vihara, might not the people be standing? They may see you leaving by boat,” he said.
“Gurudeva! There is a way around that too. Let us tell someone in the crowd to come inside and search the vihara,” said the young Bikshu.
“If one comes and searches, will that be enough? Will he not go out and tell the others?” asked the guru.

“If we keep him here a little while, it will be dark by then. The prince can leave safely. Not only that, there are signs that a great storm may break soon. Even from here, we can see the sea waves rising like mountains. The roar of the ocean is growing louder. Is it the compassion of Lord Buddha, or what? Perhaps it is the Lord’s will that a great storm should come and end our distress!” said the young Bikshu.
“Let us not speak so, Guru. Must the sea churn and a great storm arise just to resolve our troubles?” said the prince.
“Swami! I too feel we might try the way your disciple suggests. If only a single person comes inside, perhaps I can speak with him and change his mind,” said the prince.

“That thought too has crossed my mind. Two days ago, a boatman from Kodikkarai and his wife came to the entrance of the vihara and inquired about the prince. They insisted the prince must be here. The boatman’s wife made quite a commotion…!”
“Ah! Who is this boatman? Do you know his name?” asked the prince.
“Yes; he said his name was Murugaiyyan. He claimed to be the son of Thyaga Vidangar of Kodikkarai…”
“I know him well. He would never act against my wishes. Why did you not bring him to me…?”
“We thought his wife could not be trusted to keep our secret. Now, both he and his wife are among the crowd outside…”

“It is as if a ripe fruit has slipped and fallen into milk. Bring the boatman Murugaiyyan here quietly. He would never cross the fortifications I have set. After nightfall, he himself will take me in his boat and ferry me to the Chola palace at Anaimangalam!” said the prince.

The Acharya Bikshu replied, “Prince! In these times, it is not wise to trust anyone completely. I suspect that this boatman and his wife are the ones who have been spreading rumors about you in this town for the past two days.”

“Even if that is so, it does not matter. In any case, someone must be brought into the vihara, mustn’t they? He is a man who dances to his wife’s tunes a little. But still, he would never go against my wishes, not even for his wife’s sake. If possible, bring him here!” said the prince.

With the Acharya Bikshu’s consent, the junior monk departed. After a short while, the elder Bikshu said, “Prince! My mind is strangely uneasy. I too shall go outside and see. The mood of the people—” “I am going to see for myself whether it is true. Because of my foolishness, this ancient Choodamani Vihara must not come to harm; nor must any danger befall you!” Saying this, he went outside.

chapters.title: The Sea Swelled!
paragraphs: The sight that greeted the Acharya Bikshu outside the vihara filled him with turmoil. Thousands of people had gathered and were standing in a dense crowd. Their appearance, their uproar, and their agitation all revealed that they were a mob seething with passion. It would take but little to turn that passion into a frenzy of rage. Many among them held swords, spears, staffs, and other weapons in their hands.

Some even carried crowbars. It seemed they had resolved that if the monks did not yield to their demands, they would raze the vihara to the ground. Nor were they without reason for such fury. Since the reign of Paranthaka Chakaravarthi, wars had frequently broken out between the Chola kingdom and the land of Ilangai. Many Chola warriors had perished in the wars of Lanka. Is it not human nature that, if one cannot seize the true culprit, one seeks vengeance on whatever is within reach? The anger that the Chola people bore as a result of the Lankan wars had, to some extent, turned against the widespread Buddhist faith on that island. A mere spark would suffice. The common folk of Tamilagam were ready to exact vengeance upon the remaining Buddhist viharas and the monks who dwelled within them.

The Acharya Bikshu now believed that such a moment had arrived. Some malicious force had incited the fury of the common people in this manner. Only by the compassion of Lord Buddha could they hope to escape this great calamity! The moment the Acharya Bikshu appeared, the tumult of the crowd swelled even greater than before.

“Hand over Ponniyin Selvan! If not, we will tear the vihara down to its foundations!” Such cries, filled with wrath, burst forth from thousands of throats at once, sounding like the roar of the ocean.

At that very instant, the Acharya Bikshu noticed that the roar of the sea itself was growing louder. What the young monk had said was true. A storm of unimaginable force was approaching the shore. Very soon, the cyclone would strike the coast. Even if they survived the danger posed by this mob, the Acharya Bikshu now worried whether the vihara could withstand the fury of the storm.

Meanwhile, the young monk raised his hand in a gesture, and managed to quiet the crowd’s clamor, if only a little. “Great people! I have brought your leader here—please be calm for a moment. All of you cannot enter this vihara at the same time, can you? Choose one or two among you! Let them come inside the vihara and search. When they return and tell you what they have seen, you must accept their word. Is this agreeable to you? Who among you will come with me into the vihara?” he asked.
From the crowd, hundreds shouted, “I will come!” “I will come!” in a tumult of voices.

The young bhikshu raised his hand again and said, “What is the use of everyone shouting at once? Select someone among you. I have a suggestion. If any of you have seen Ponniyin Selvan within the last month, let them speak up. I will take such a person with me. It will be easier for them to recognize the prince!”
From the front of the crowd, where she had been shouting every time, Raakkammal cried out, “We have seen him!”
The young bhikshu turned to the boatman and asked, “Appane! Is what she says true?”

Murugaiyyan replied, “Swami! What she says is not entirely true. She has not seen the prince recently. But I have seen Ponniyin Selvan in Eezhanaadu within the last month. I even fell at his feet and begged forgiveness for a wrong I did him unknowingly. The way he looked at me with compassion and smiled is etched in my mind as if it happened yesterday. I can easily recognize him.”

“In that case, you are the right person for this task. There is not much wrong in what your wife says either. She must have spoken thinking that what you saw, she too saw. If you go in now, search the vihara, and return to tell us, she will accept it. Your wife must know that women are not allowed inside the Buddhist vihara where bhikshus perform their penance. So, come here!” said the young bhikshu.

Then, descending the steps at the entrance of the vihara, he took Murugaiyyan by the hand and led him up the steps again. Turning to the people, he said, “This boatman Murugaiyyan has seen the prince recently. I am taking him inside. He will search the entire vihara and return to tell you what he finds. Is this agreeable to all of you?”

The voice of assent did not rise swiftly from the crowd. Some murmured, “We agree,” in low tones. Others whispered secretly among themselves, “Could there be some mischief in this?” The hushed voices of their secret discussions mingled and competed with the roar of the sea.

The young bhikshu, noticing this, raised his voice and said, “Great people! Here is our Acharya, who has arrived. If you have anything to ask, you may question him. Meanwhile, I shall take this man—Murugaiya the boatman—and show him around the vihara, and return.” So saying, he led Murugaiya away.

The sight of the Acharya bhikshu, resplendent in his dignified bearing and serene countenance, inspired a certain awe and reverence in the hearts of the people. No one dared to ask him any bold or argumentative questions.
The Acharya bhikshu gazed at the assembled crowd for a moment. Then, he turned his eyes toward the sea, visible at a short distance behind them.

“Great people! I understand the purpose for which you have all gathered here. Today, I have come to know well how much love you all bear for the Emperor’s son, the Prince Arulmozhi Varman, the beloved of the Ponni. Like you, I too am devoted to Ponniyin Selvan. When the news came that Arulmozhi Varman had been swallowed by the sea, I stood here that very morning, and tears flowed from my eyes like a river. Anyone who follows the path of Buddha cannot help but love Arulmozhi Varman. He has rendered such great services to the Buddhist faith and to the bhikshus. It was he who arranged for the restoration and repair of the vihara and stupas at Anuradhapura, the sacred land of the Buddhas, which had fallen into ruin and decay since the time of the Buddhist kings. For such a noble prince, how could we ever be party to any harm? We have prayed unceasingly that nothing ill should befall him, that the news of his being taken by the sea should prove false. Compared to you, we have even greater reasons for our devotion to Ponniyin Selvan…”

At this moment, someone in the crowd interrupted, “That is exactly what makes us anxious. We fear that your boundless love might lead you to shave our prince’s head, clothe him in saffron, and turn him into a bhikshu!” As those around him heard this, a ripple of laughter spread through the assembly.

Somehow, at that moment, a strange fervor seized the Acharya Bikshu. His heart told him that, in this situation, there was only one sure way to dispel the people’s doubts. Without hesitation, without a second thought, he declared, as a solemn oath, what had arisen in his mind in the following words:

“I shall never ask the prince, the son of the Emperor, Ponniyin Selvan, Arulmozhi Varman, to embrace the Buddhist faith. Even if he himself were to come forward, I would not accept it. The prince, born to rule the world and beloved by you all—I shall never, not for a single day, perform the service of shaving his head and clothing him in the ochre robes. Nor shall I ever be a party to such a deed. Upon the lotus feet of Lord Buddha, I swear this as an oath! Buddham Sharanam Gacchami! Dhammam Sharanam Gacchami! Sangham Sharanam Gacchami!”

As these words, ringing with the majesty of thunder and trembling with emotion, fell upon the ears of the assembled crowd, a great transformation swept through every heart present. Tears brimmed in the eyes of many. For a moment, silence reigned.

The Acharya Bikshu continued: “It is only natural that you all hold such deep affection for the prince, the very apple of the Chola people’s eye. Perhaps now your anxieties for Ponniyin Selvan have been put to rest. Hereafter, spare a thought for your own families, your homes, your very thresholds. O great people! It seems that a terrible storm, the likes of which we have never seen or heard of in these parts, is drawing near to us. Look, turn around and see behind you!”

The people turned to look. Just as the Bikshu had said, they beheld a sight the likes of which they had never seen in their lives. It was not only a wondrous sight, but a terrifying one as well. The sea had swelled and risen, its waters reaching up to touch the black clouds gathering ever higher in the sky. That dark mountain of water did not stand still; it kept surging forward, rising higher and higher. From where the people stood, it seemed that if that watery mountain reached their place, not only they, but the entire Choodamani Vihara itself would be swallowed up without a trace.
As the people stood transfixed by this vision, the Acharya Bikshu spoke again: “Look there, all of you, at Nagai Pattinam, where you dwell!”

The city of Nagai Pattinam lay a little to the north of the Choodamani Vihara. It stretched far and wide into the distance. Along the seashore stood warehouses, customs houses, and other such buildings. Beyond them began the quarters where the people lived. The houses began to spread out, east to west and north to south, for about half a league or more.

The sea had surged past the warehouses and customs posts, and now the time had come when it began to enter the streets of the city itself. The boats and catamarans that had been in the sea now appeared, as if suspended in the sky, atop the crests of watery hills, tossing this way and that. The bamboo poles of the boats danced like possessed spirits, flying off in all directions.

“O people! We have heard that once upon a time, the sea swallowed up Kaveripattinam. May the Buddha protect our Nagapattinam from such a disaster! Even so, hurry back at once and try to save your children and your belongings as much as you can!” cried the Acharya Bhikshu in a trembling voice.

As soon as they heard this, the crowd surged forward like a wave of the sea, moving toward the city. Those at the front began to run. Those behind followed after them. At first, they moved as a mass. Then, scattering in all directions, they fled. In just a few moments, the place where a great crowd had stood was now empty.
Only Raakkammal, the wife of the boatman Murugaiyyan, remained where she stood, crying out, “My husband! My husband!”
“Mother! Nothing will happen to your husband. He will return safely. Save yourself!” said the Bhikshu.
“No, no! How can I go leaving my husband behind? I will come into the temple!” Raakkammal said.
“No, child! No! Women are not allowed inside the vihara where the Buddhist monks reside! Don’t you know that?” said the Bhikshu.

At that moment, a man who had not run away with the great crowd but lingered behind approached Raakkammal. He whispered something in her ear. Grabbing her hand, he pulled her along with him. She began to go with him, reluctantly.
“Ah, who is this man? What is his relationship to this woman?” wondered the Acharya Bhikshu as he entered the vihara. He approached the place where Ponniyin Selvan was staying.
Murugaiyyan, by now, had become one who had witnessed many wonders, and was listening to the prince’s words with devoted attention.
“Muruga! Tonight, you must return here, take me in your boat, and escort me to Anaimangalam,” said the prince.
Acharya Bhikshu said, “Prince! There is no need to wait until nightfall. The crowd has already dispersed. You may set out at once.”
Then, in a few words, he described what had happened outside. “Swami! The people have all gone away! Why should I leave now?” asked the prince.
“What certainty is there that they will not return? Moreover, did you not just now promise to fulfill the word of us bhikshus? You must grant us that boon!” said the bhikshu.
The truth was, a fear had arisen in the bhikshu’s heart that the surging sea would soon engulf the Chudamani Vihara. Therefore, he wished to send the prince away from there as quickly as possible.
Anaimangalam lay a little distance east of the seashore. Thus, the swelling sea could not reach so far. Even if it did, the great Chola palace there would not be submerged.

The prince accepted the bhikshu’s counsel. At once, he gave orders for the boat to be brought. Meanwhile, turning to the assembled Buddhist bhikshus, the Acharya Bhikshu said, “We are followers of Lord Buddha, who is the very embodiment of compassion. Now, the people of Nagapattinam are faced with a great trial. I have seen the sea surging swiftly into the city. The force of the storm has torn roofs from houses and sent them flying. Trees are crashing down with a thunderous roar. Among the people of Nagapattinam and the surrounding areas, how many elders and children must be struggling, not knowing how to escape! All of you, go in every direction and render whatever help you can to those suffering before your eyes. Give your first attention to the children and the elderly. Save as many as you can from the wrath of the Ocean King! I am old. I shall remain here and attend to the evening worship,” he said.

Hearing this, the bhikshus dispersed from there. The boat arrived at the canal. The prince saluted the Acharya Bhikshu, took his leave, and boarded the boat. Murugaiyyan too climbed in and began to push the boat away. As the boat disappeared from sight—
The mendicant stood there, gazing at the same sight. Around his face, an extraordinary radiance seemed to shine forth.

chapters.title: Nandi Was Submerged
paragraphs: As the boat continued along the canal, the prince noticed that the water level was rising higher with every passing moment. The boat was struggling against the current. Murugaiyan was exerting himself greatly to steer it. The fury of the storm was increasing by the second. On either side, trees were snapping and crashing down with a thunderous noise.
The boat drew near the Nandi Mandapam. The prince looked towards the pavilion. Water had risen above the head of the Nandi statue. From this, it was clear just how high the water level had climbed.
“Murugaiya! Stop the boat for a moment,” said the prince. Murugaiyan halted the boat, but he could not stop its rocking motion.

The prince leapt from the boat and landed in the Nandi Mandapam. Then, grasping a tree that had fallen nearby, he climbed up to the top of the pavilion’s roof. From there, he surveyed the surroundings. Downstream, the entire canal was a raging flood. In the coconut grove, half the trees had already been swallowed by the waters. Through the gaps, it seemed as if the sea itself had surged forward, reaching the very edge of the coconut grove.
To the north, Arulmozhi gazed in the direction of the Chudamani Viharam. The sea had swollen and spread up to the outer steps of the vihara.
At that moment, a thought arose in the mind of Ponniyin Selvan—a thought that sent a shiver through his entire body.
“Murugaiya! Turn the boat around! Head towards the vihara!” commanded the prince.

The son of Thyagavidangar, who was not accustomed to speaking much and who bore boundless devotion towards the prince, did not even ask why. He turned the boat and began to row towards the Chudamani Viharam.

The return journey took less time than their approach. Yet, for the prince, every second felt like an age. By the time the boat reached the vihara, the surging sea had almost encircled the entire monastery. The water level was still rising. In Eelam... At that time, the Nagai Pattinam Chudamani Viharam was not as grand or lofty as the other viharas. If the water were to rise just a little more, even the mandapa’s tower of the vihara would be submerged. The prince leapt from the boat and landed on the upper platform of a mandapa that had not yet been swallowed by the waters, without getting himself drenched. He ran here and there in haste. Instead of going to the lower levels of the vihara, he searched through every part of the upper stories. In some places on those upper floors, he had to wade through water that reached up to his chest.

With each step, his disappointment grew. At last, he reached the spot where the statue of Gautama Buddha stood. The water had risen up to the chest of the statue. There, the prince stood and looked all around. He bent down and peered into the water. From his lips burst a sound, a blend of joy and astonishment—“Aha!”—a sign that he had found what he was seeking.

Yes; beneath the Buddha statue, submerged in the water, the Acharya Bikshu was seated, clutching tightly to the lotus feet of the Blessed One. Ponniyin Selvan plunged into the water, forcefully pried the monk’s hands from the statue, and lifted him up. It was easy enough to lift the Bikshu while still in the water. Once out of the water, it was not so easy. The Bikshu, tall and well-built, was so heavy that the prince staggered under his weight.
“Murugayya! Murugayya!” he called out.
“I’m coming!” replied Murugaiyan, bringing the boat closer.
Ponniyin Selvan, carrying the Acharya Bikshu, hurried toward the boat. His steps faltered.

chapters.title: The Calf Separated from Its Mother
paragraphs: The prince, carrying the Buddhist monk, leapt into the boat that Murugaiyan had brought and steadied. At the force of his leap, the small boat rocked wildly, as if possessed by a spirit. For a moment, it seemed as though it would capsize. Murugaiyan struggled mightily to keep the boat from overturning.

“Murugaiya! Leave the vihara now! Head straight for the palace at Anaimangalam!” Ponniyin Selvan shouted in a loud voice. But the howling of the storm, now at its peak, and the roaring of the sea swelling in the tempest, drowned out his words so that they did not reach Murugaiyan’s ears. Yet, reading the prince’s intent from his expression, Murugaiyan began to row the boat away. It was a difficult task to steer the boat clear of the submerged mandapam towers and the Buddha statues of the Chudamani Vihara. But Murugaiyan, who was used to navigating boats in the open sea even during fierce storms and swirling winds, handled it with great skill and ease. The prince watched him in admiration. He thought to himself that he might lend a hand, but hesitated to release his grip on the Buddhist monk. As if sensing this, the monk suddenly tried to free himself from the prince’s hold.

At that moment, the boat was passing near the statue of Lord Buddha. Now, the floodwaters had risen to the very eyes of the statue. In a few more minutes, there was no doubt the statue would be completely submerged.

The prince held the monk tightly. The monk’s face revealed his astonishment at the strength in the prince’s hands, which, though appearing soft and gentle, possessed such power. If there is resolve in the heart, perhaps the body too gains strength! Yet, the body had grown frail from many days of fasting.

The boat passed beyond the Buddha statue. The monk kept his gaze fixed on the statue as it was being submerged. Soon, the statue disappeared from view. Tears streamed down the monk’s face in torrents.
“Prince! What have you done?” the monk asked.

From the movement of his lips, the prince understood what he was saying. Bending close to the monk’s ear, he replied, “Swami! Should not I be the one to ask that question? What were you about to do?” “Prince! This vihara has stood here for over five hundred years. It existed even during the time of the great sage Dharmapada. The mighty Pallava emperors, though fierce Shaivites, did not destroy it; they let it remain. Yet now, in my lifetime, before my very eyes, this ancient vihara has been swallowed up. This vihara, built of brick and mortar, cannot withstand the fury of this deluge! Once the floodwaters recede, only a few broken walls will remain! When the vihara is gone, what reason do I have to go on living?” said the bhikshu.

“If the vihara collapses and is destroyed, we can rebuild it anew. If the Blessed Buddha wills it, I myself will help to raise it again. But if you leave us, how could I ever bring you back?” replied Prince Arulmozhi.
The combined roar of the sea and the storm made it impossible for them to continue their conversation. Moreover, the dreadful scenes that unfolded all around them rendered them speechless.

Large boats with broken sails, as well as small fishing canoes, were being driven from the sea towards the shore. Many of these crashed upon the shore, collided with buildings, or were dashed against the dancing, uprooted trees, shattering into splinters. The roofs of houses were torn off by the mighty wind, flying through the air and falling into the floodwaters. Some roofs floated upon the waters, and upon a few of these, people clung desperately, struggling to survive, crying out in distress.

Huge trees were snapped and fell in the wind. Some of the fallen trees floated away, and people tried to save themselves by clinging to them. Cattle and goats, bleating in terror, were swept along by the flood. Witnessing such dreadful scenes, the prince and the bhikshu’s hearts were wrung with sorrow. The thought that they could do nothing to help in such a situation only deepened their anguish.

Murugaiyan, without turning his gaze left or right, rowed the boat with utmost care. The Chudamani Vihara stood on the seashore at Nagapattinam. From there, a canal ran a short distance southward, then veered southwest for half a katham, and from there turned again, running straight south. At the bend of this second turn stood the palace of Anaimangalam.

As the boat approached the Nandi Mandapam that stood midway along their route, they saw that not only was the great Nandi statue completely submerged, but the floodwaters were lapping at the very edge of the upper pavilion. Beyond the mandapam, in the coconut groves that stretched in all directions, three-quarters of the trees had been snapped and felled by the wind. On the tops of the remaining trees, the palm fronds danced wildly, resembling the disheveled hair of demons in a frenzied dance. Some of these fronds had been torn away by the wind and flung far into the distance.

At the summit of the Nandi Mandapam, a calf that had been separated from its mother had somehow found its way and was now huddled there. It looked around in terror, its eyes wide with fear. Its body shivered repeatedly, and its legs trembled uncontrollably. The pitiful cry of the calf, calling out “Amma!” reached the ears of those in the boat as a faint, plaintive sound.

“Alas! Poor thing! What will become of this calf, separated from its mother?” thought the prince at that very moment. Suddenly, a tall coconut tree snapped and crashed down behind the mandapam. Had it fallen just a little to the side, it would have struck the calf directly.

The force of the falling tree sent a great wave surging through the water, leaping up over the mandapam. The already trembling calf could not withstand the onslaught of the wave; it stumbled and fell. Swept from the summit of the mandapam by the wave, it was tossed into the floodwaters, struggling helplessly.

Until then, the prince had been holding onto the Buddhist monk with his hands. The moment he saw the calf being swept away from the top of the mandapam, he cried out, “Aha!” and released his grip on the monk. In that instant, the monk leapt into the flood.

Murugaiyan, the boatman, set his oar down in the boat and seized the prince in a firm grasp. The prince glared at him with fierce anger and shook off his hand, exclaiming, “Let go!” Meanwhile, the monk, with two swift strokes, swam to the calf and grasped its forelegs tightly. The calf, driven by the natural instinct to survive, struggled to keep its head above water. Holding onto the calf, the monk dragged it back toward the boat. The prince reached out his hand to help. Together, they first lifted the calf into the boat. Then, with the prince’s assistance, the venerable monk climbed aboard.

All this while, the calf had somehow managed to hold itself together. But now, suddenly, it gave a little leap, lost its footing, and fell with a thud. Fortunately, it fell inside the boat. The Bikshu sat down beside it. He lifted the calf’s head onto his lap and began to gently stroke it.

“Gurudeva! Just a short while ago, at the Choodamani Vihara, you tried to surrender yourself at the feet of Lord Buddha and give up your life, didn’t you? If you had done so, would you have been able to save this speechless creature now?” the prince asked.

“Ayya, I am grateful to you for stopping me from committing that sin. Yes, saving the life of this calf brings peace to my heart. Even if the Choodamani Vihara were to collapse and be destroyed, I would not grieve so much anymore,” said the Bikshu.

“Acharyare! How can saving the life of a single calf bring you such peace of mind? Today, because of this storm, how many lives are suffering? How many thousands of people—men, women, children, the elderly—are in distress? How many speechless creatures—goats, cows, horses, birds—are losing their lives? What remedy is there for all this suffering?” the prince asked.

“Ayya! We can only do what is within our power. Beyond that, there is nothing more we can do. We do not have the strength to prevent the calamities of nature. Can we restrain the storm winds? Can we stop the heavy rains? Or can we make the rains fall when we wish? When the sea rises in fury, can we hold it back? Ah! I have seen, in lands beyond the seas, volcanoes spewing fire and earthquakes splitting the earth. What can we do about such things? All we can do is help the living beings suffering before our very eyes!”

“Gurudeva! Why do natural disasters occur? Why do storms and earthquakes happen? Why do plagues come? Who is responsible for the suffering that people and other living beings endure because of these? We may not be able to prevent the calamities of nature. But can even God not prevent them? Why does God, instead of stopping such disasters, simply watch as living beings suffer?” asked the prince.

“Ponniyin Selva! From the beginning of time, great men and sages have tried to answer the question you now ask. Yet none of their answers have satisfied everyone. That is why Lord Buddha said nothing about God. He did not even embark on an inquiry about God. ‘For others— “Help others. Strive to alleviate the sufferings of your fellow beings. True bliss is found only in such efforts. From that, you will attain a state beyond pleasure and pain, a state of pure detachment!”—thus did Lord Buddha teach,” said the Bhikshu.

The boat, having left the Nandi Mandapam, now turned westward, heading towards Anaimangalam. Ponniyin Selvan’s mind was lost in deep contemplation. He compared within himself the Buddhist doctrine the Bhikshu had just expounded with the religious tenets of his own forefathers. The duty to help others is also emphasized by the Saiva and Vaishnava faiths. There is even the great maxim, “Paropakaram idham sareeram”—“This body is meant for the service of others.” Yet, at the same time, our ancestors also insisted on the duty of faith and devotion towards God. They worshipped God both as Rudra, the destroyer, and as Mahavishnu, the embodiment of compassion. To God, they gave the form of Jaganmata, the Mother of the Universe—could she not, at the same time, be the loving Uma Devi, who is the very form of affection, and also the fierce, terrifying Ranabathrakali? Why should it not be so? At one moment, a mother lovingly embraces her child; at another, she chastises it in anger. The child may not always understand why it is being punished. But can anyone say that the mother who punishes her own child does not love it?…

By now, darkness had fallen, and the boat approached the Chola palace at Anaimangalam. The surging sea had not yet reached the palace, as those in the boat could see. Murugaiyan steered the boat to the ornamental landing near the palace. Until then, nature had shown some mercy to those aboard the boat. Though a great storm raged and the sea swelled, the heavy rain had not yet begun to fall; only a light drizzle persisted.
It was only after the boat reached the palace’s edge and came to a stop that the heavy rain began to pour down in earnest.

The palace guard at Anaimangalam stood at the front entrance, holding a torch in his hand. He was conversing with the townsfolk who had come running from the surrounding areas seeking refuge for the night. When he saw a boat arrive and stop at the landing, the guard raised his torch high. The face of Ponniyin Selvan caught his eye. Instantly, forgetting everything else, he ran swiftly towards the landing.

By then, the prince and the Acharya Bhikshu had disembarked from the boat and helped the calf down gently onto the shore. The guard fell at the prince’s feet. The prince caught him and lifted him up. The torch in the guard’s hand fell into the moat, flared up for a moment, and then was extinguished.
“Prince! I myself have been worrying about the Choodamani Vihara! It is very fortunate that you have come here,” said the guard.
“Do you know that I am staying at the Choodamani Vihara?”
“I do, my lord! I found out when the young princess and the Kodumbalur princess visited. The young princess instructed me not to tell anyone… and then left.”
“You must continue to keep that promise. Who are those gathered at the entrance of the palace?”

“They are people from the villages along the seashore, who have fled here because the sea has flooded their homes. They were asking for a place to stay the night. Just as you arrived, I was about to send them away…”

“No, no! Do not send them away! Give them all a place to stay and sleep. As long as there are provisions, have food cooked and served to them. But do not speak of me to any of them. It was good that your lamp fell into the canal and was extinguished. Now, lead us by another way to the upper chambers of the palace!” said the prince.
It was just as they entered the palace that the stormy wind and heavy rain began to pour down with a deafening roar.

chapters.title: Murugaiyyan Wept!
paragraphs: Near the city of Thanjai, on the very day when a tree fell behind the palanquin in which Mandakini was carried, at the very hour when a boat was swept ashore by the wind on the banks of the heroic Narayana Lake, the events that unfolded in Nagapattinam were recounted in the previous chapters, as readers will recall.

That entire night, Nagapattinam and its surrounding regions were plunged into utter chaos and confusion. People were in such dire straits that it was impossible for them to help one another; survival itself was a blessing. Yet, the Buddhist monks wandered the streets of Nagapattinam, rendering aid to the people as much as they could.

On that same night, the Acharya Bikshu and Ponniyin Selvan remained awake for a long time within the Chola palace at Anaimangalam, conversing together. They spoke with concern about the hardships and losses that must have befallen the people living along the seashore, as the fierce storm had caused the sea to surge.

The prince summoned the palace steward and inquired about the quantity of grain stored in the royal granaries, and the amount of wealth in the treasury. It was found that the granaries were well-stocked with grain. It was also revealed that twelve copper pots filled with gold coins, sent by Sembiyan Madevi for the renovation and black stone work of the Neelayadakshi Amman temple at Thirunagai, were in safe keeping.

“Guru Deva! You have all the means necessary to perform acts of compassion befitting the will of the Buddha. Use all the grain in the palace granaries to feed the poor. Distribute all the gold coins in the copper pots to those who have lost their homes!” said the prince, Ponniyin Selvan.

“How is that just? The grain, perhaps, may be used. But can the money your great grandmother, Sembiyan Madevi, sent for the temple’s renovation be spent on something else? Will not that venerable lady be grieved?” asked the Acharya Bikshu.

“Acharya! I will appease my great grandmother myself. For now, I will spend this wealth to wipe away the suffering of the poor and destitute.
