In the future, I shall see to it that my grandmother’s heart is filled with joy and pride by making this Chola—” “I will build a hundred Shiva temples across the land. I will raise towering gopurams. Even if the sea rises in fury, I will erect stupas so tall that not even the waves can submerge them. In the great city of Thanjai, I will build a temple so vast, with a gopuram that touches the sky, that people will call it the Dakshina Meru!

Sir! Do not grieve if today the Chudamani Vihara has been swallowed and reduced to dust. Nearby, I will raise a new Chudamani Vihara of stone, so mighty that even a deluge cannot shake it!” The prince spoke, his voice trembling with fervor.
“Ponniyin Selva! It fills me with great joy to hear you speak of the future with such enthusiasm,” said the Bikshu.

“Yes, yes, it is the will of God that I should live in this world and accomplish some great deeds. That is why He has saved me from so many dangers that have threatened my life. Even today, look—this Murugaiyyan arrived at just the right moment. Otherwise, you and I would have been inside the Chudamani Vihara. Who could have imagined that the sea would rise so swiftly and engulf the vihara?”

“That is true. Who could have expected that an event which has not occurred in five hundred years would take place in a single moment this very afternoon? The ocean of compassion, Lord Buddha himself, has saved you from the wrath of the surging sea. Through you, he has also preserved my insignificant life. I fully agree with the deeds you propose to undertake. If you spend from the royal treasury, the treasurer Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar will be angered. But your noble grandmother will not be displeased if you allocate funds for temple restoration. That would be the proper course. Yet, would it not be fitting for you yourself to lead this great and meritorious work? This poor sanyasi cannot bear such a great responsibility!”

“Guru Deva! If I lead it openly, I will be forced to reveal myself. What you said about the Pandavas’ incognito exile is etched in my heart. The words of our own truthful Tamil poet also come to mind:
‘What is truth? It is to speak words That cause no harm, at any time.’
And also,

‘Even falsehood, if it brings good, is as pure as truth…’” “‘Do good, and good will come to you’—is that not what the ancient Tamil scriptures proclaim? My wise sister believes that if I reveal myself to the people at this time, it may lead to confusion and unrest in the land. By remaining in hiding, I bring no harm to anyone. Therefore, you must use the resources in the palace to help the people who are suffering from the fury of the storm,” said the prince.

“Ponniyin Selva! For some reason, my heart has changed. It seems to me that this is the right moment to reveal yourself and help the people. This thought has arisen in my mind, and I believe it is the will of Lord Buddha himself,” said the Bikshu.
At that moment, hearing someone sobbing, both of them turned around in surprise. Murugaiyan was sitting in a corner, covering his face with his hands, weeping uncontrollably.
The prince went to him, took his hand, and brought him forward.
“Murugayya! What is this? Why are you crying?” he asked.
“My wife… my wife…” Murugaiyan stammered, and his sobs grew louder.

“Yes, yes! We have completely forgotten about your wife. It is only natural that you are worried about what might have happened to her tonight in this storm and rain. But at this midnight hour, there is nothing we can do. At dawn, we will search for your wife and find her,” said the prince.
“Sir, that is not why I am grieving. Nothing bad will have happened to her. She has faced many such terrible storms and floods before!” replied Murugaiyan.
“Then why are you crying?” the prince asked.

The boatman, stammering and faltering, gave the following explanation: “I am distressed thinking about all the suspicions I have harbored about her. It was she who insisted on bringing me here from the shore. She was the one who said that you might be at the Choodamani Vihara. I came only because she insisted. I even feared that she might intend to harm you in some way. Now I see how foolish that was. Just a short while ago, you spoke kindly about this poor boatman. God, through me—”
“You said that you saved my life. But the one who urged me to do this deed was my wife. When I thought that we had suspected her, I could not help but weep!”

Hearing all this, a new doubt now arose in the heart of the prince, Ponniyin Selvan. “My friend! Your wife is truly virtuous. It was wrong of you to suspect her. But how did she know that I was here?” he asked.
“My aunt and my sister Poonguzhali set out by boat to the city of Nagai. From that, my wife somehow guessed and came to know.”
“Which aunt?” the prince asked anxiously.
“Sir, the very same mute aunt who saved you from danger many times on the island of Eezham.”
“Ah! Where are they now? What happened to your aunt and Poonguzhali? You said they set out to come here?”
“Yes, they set out. But their journey was interrupted!” said Murugaiyyan, and then he began to sob uncontrollably.

Ponniyin Selvan, deeply troubled, comforted him and gently inquired for more details. When he learned that some ruffians had forcefully seized the queen of Eezham, the prince’s anger knew no bounds. Upon hearing that Raakkammal had tried to stop them, and for that had been beaten and tied to a tree, his lingering doubts about Raakkammal vanished. Now, his respect and affection for her only grew.

“Gurudeva! Did you hear? If there is any deity I revere in this world, it is none other than Mandakini Devi, the queen of Eezham. I can never forgive anyone who harms that mute queen. I bear no anger towards the Pazhuvettaraiyars for ordering my imprisonment. But if they have done any harm to the mute queen, I will never be able to bear it. I will destroy the entire clan of the Pazhuvettaraiyars before I do anything else. Even if my own mother who bore me, or my own father, had done harm to the queen of Eezham, I could not forgive them. Gurudeva! Tomorrow itself I will set out for Thanjavur. Disguised as a merchant, and taking this boatman Murugaiyyan with me as my companion, I will depart. Until I learn the fate of the queen of Eezham, my heart will not know peace!”

“Acharyare! You must be the one to lead the relief efforts for those who have suffered because of the storm. If you do not wish to conduct it under your own name, then establish it as the ‘Eelathu Nachchiyar Charitable Institution’ and carry it out thus. Do you know that the Queen of Eelam is devoted to the Buddhist faith? It is her custom to reside, more often than not, in the monastery of Buddhist bhikkhus on the island that the people call ‘Puthatheevu’—the Isle of Buddha!” said the prince. The Buddhist monk did not contradict him, but silently agreed.

The next day, the fury of the storm abated. The surging sea retreated. But the devastation left in its wake was beyond description. In the city of Nagapattinam, half the houses had lost their roofs and stood as mere stubs of walls. Along one of those streets, Prince Arulmozhi Varman walked in the guise of a merchant, carrying a bundle on his shoulder. Behind him, Murugaiyyan followed, bearing an even larger bundle. They walked on, witnessing the chaos and destruction wrought by the storm and the flood.

From behind the crumbling wall of a ruined house, a woman watched their approach. She was none other than Murugaiyyan’s wife, Rakkammal. She waited patiently until the prince and Murugaiyyan came near the spot where she stood. Suddenly, she darted out, ran up, and fell at the prince’s feet. Murugaiyyan tried to distract her attention, signaling with his finger to his lips, gesturing for silence. “Hush, hush,” he warned. But it was of no use.

“O son of the Emperor! Bravest of the brave! Ponniyin Selva! Blessed child of the Chola land! Have you survived and returned, without being swallowed by the waves at Choodamani Vihara? What fortune have my eyes been granted, to see you again!” she cried aloud.
At that moment, the attention of all those passing by in the street turned towards the prince.

chapters.title: The People’s Exultation
paragraphs: Murugaiyyan, the boatman, was startled and bewildered by the shrill cry his wife had let out.
He turned to her again, gesturing with his hands, and said, “Woman! What nonsense are you babbling? Have you gone mad?”

“I am not mad! It is you who are mad, your father was mad, and your grandfather too! Don’t you recognize who this is? Don’t you know who this hero is, who conquered Eezham and drove King Mahindan into the hill country? Can’t you recognize the Emperor’s own son, the apple of the Chola people’s eye, the ascetic’s child whom Mother Kaveri herself saved and gave back? If you cannot recognize him, then why did you set out with him? Where are you going with him?” Raakkammal cried.

At this point, the prince interjected, “Woman! You have mistaken me for someone else. I am a merchant who has come from Eezham. I am the one who brought him along to show me the way! Take him with you! Don’t make a useless scene!” he said.
While this conversation was going on, people had begun to gather around them. The crowd grew larger with every passing minute. All those who arrived stared intently at the prince.

Then Raakkammal, in an even louder voice, cried, “Ah! O God! Has Ponniyin Selvan lost his senses? Did you lose your memory when you drowned in the sea? Or have those wretched Buddhist monks cast a spell on you and made you think you are someone else? Or—oh no! Could it be that you have died, and some sorcerer who knows the art of entering another’s body has taken possession of your form? No, that cannot be! Prince! Think carefully! You are not a merchant. You are the beloved son of Emperor Sundara Chola, born to rule the world under a single parasol. If you doubt it, look closely at your palms. You will see the lines of the conch and discus there!” she shouted.
At once, Prince Arulmozhi tightly closed both his hands.

“Woman! Will you not shut your mouth and keep quiet?” he said, then turned to Murugaiyyan and asked, “What is this nuisance? Can’t you stop her shouting?” Murugaiyyan came close to his wife and whispered in her ear, “Raakkamma! Let this be a merit to you! Be silent! The prince wishes to go to Thanjavur in the guise of a merchant, without anyone’s knowledge!”

“You wretched fellow! Couldn’t you have told me this earlier? Didn’t you say that the prince would never be at the Buddhist monastery? You still have that same foolishness! Alas! What a crime I have committed! Out of excessive eagerness, I have blurted out the truth! The hapless Pazhuvettarayars are waiting for an opportunity to imprison you and take their revenge! Even knowing that, I have exposed you like this! My prince! Still, you need not fear. The Pazhuvettarayars cannot harm even a single atom of your sacred person. There are lakhs and lakhs of people, like myself and my husband, ready to stand by your side and protect you!” she declared. Then, turning to the great crowd gathered around her, she said, “All of you agree with what I have said, don’t you? Is there anyone among you who belongs to the Pazhuvettarayar faction? If so, come forward! Kill me first, and only then think of harming the prince!” she cried out.

The people, who until then had watched and listened in astonished silence, now raised a great shout: “Long live Ponniyin Selvan! Long live the heroic conqueror of Eezham!” Hearing this, even more people gathered and joined the crowd.

Among those who came was one of the eight-member council leaders of the city of Nagapattinam. Pushing through the throng, he came forward and said, “Prince! We heard that you had come from the Chudamani Vihara of this city. We did not believe that rumor, but now we know the truth. The great storm that struck yesterday has caused much destruction in this city. Yet, the fact that you were safely brought out of the Buddhist monastery makes us forget all the storm’s cruelties. It is the fortune of our city that your feet have touched its soil!” he said.

The prince realized that there was no further use in trying to conceal himself. “Sir! My heartfelt thanks for your affection. The love of the people of this city overwhelms me. But I must go to Thanjavur urgently on a matter of great importance. It was only to avoid any hindrance to my journey that I set out in the guise of a merchant. Please grant me leave!” he said.
At that moment, a voice rose from the crowd. “No, no! The prince must stay here at least one day and accept the humble hospitality of us poor folk before he departs!” the voice rang out loudly.
Following that, a thousand voices cried out in unison, “No, he must not leave! The Prince must stay here at least for a day, rest, and only then depart!”

At that moment, the leader of the Eight-member Council said, “Prince! Have you seen the love and enthusiasm of my city’s people? You must accept our hospitality and, at least for a while, be our guest before you go. Are we any less fortunate than the Buddhist monks who cared for you? Just yesterday, the people of this city suspected that the Buddhist monks were hiding you away, and in their zeal, they nearly destroyed the entire Choodamani Vihara. At that very moment, the storm struck! What we failed to do, the storm accomplished. The vihara has collapsed and lies in ruins!”

Hearing this, the Prince replied, “Sir, it is not right to blame the Buddhist monks. It was at my own request that they sheltered me in the vihara. When I was stricken with illness and pleading for my life, they saved me from the noose of Yama himself. My heart aches to hear that the Choodamani Vihara has fallen. It is my duty to see it rebuilt!”

“Ah! All this was unknown to us before! Now that we know, we ourselves will restore and rebuild the Choodamani Vihara. Prince! You must at least be our guest for a while before you leave!” said the leader of the Eight-member Council.
“Yes, yes!” echoed the voices of tens of thousands in the crowd.

“Prince! Any delay caused by your stay here can be made up for. After all, you set out on foot. Because of the storm and rain, all the roads in Chola country are blocked. The rivers are in full flood. How long will it take you to reach your destination on foot? We will seat you upon an elephant and send you in procession. All of us will accompany you and see you safely to Thanjavur,” said the leader of the Eight-member Council. As he spoke, the crowd continued to swell.

The Prince pondered, “The matter has gone awry; the secret has been revealed. Raakkammal, in her foolishness, has blurted it out. Was it truly foolishness? Or was there some other intent behind it? Whatever it may be, it is impossible to leave immediately, disregarding the love of these townspeople. If I do so, it will only cause them distress. Moreover, if I persist in my original plan, it will surely fail. I must stay at least until noon, soothe their hearts, and only then depart. The hardships and losses caused by the storm— After offering some words of comfort to those who had come to him, it would also be easier to leave. Ah! Did not the young princess Kundavai say that if I reveal myself at this time, it will cause turmoil in the country? How true were her words! There is truly no one in this world as wise as my sister! They speak of the right to the throne of Thanjai— but in truth, should it not be Kundavai Devi who is seated upon the lion throne?...

Thus pondered Ponniyin Selvan, when he saw that the crowd was growing ever larger. He realized that their enthusiasm was increasing as well. It seemed as if the people had completely forgotten the ravages of the storm and the destruction it had wrought. From somewhere, elephants, horses, palanquins, sacred conches, banners, drums, and trumpets— all manner of instruments— had gathered together.

The prince decided that he must at least remain here until midday before departing. Turning to the leader of the Eight Commanders, he said, “Sir! I do not wish to leave, disregarding the love of so many people. I will stay here until the afternoon and depart in the evening. Will you grant me permission for that, at least?”

No sooner had the news spread that the prince had agreed to stay, than the excitement of the crowd overflowed its bounds. They began to observe every custom of expressing their joy. The instruments began to sound. Here and there in the streets, knife games, stick games, and the Kuravai dance began. It became exceedingly difficult to make their way past the people and their jubilant festivities to reach the Chola palace in Nagai town. Somehow, at last, they managed to arrive.

Inside the palace, the prince could not even rest for a short while. For the news of his appearance had spread to all the neighboring villages. People were gathering in great throngs. They expressed their longing to see the prince.

The prince, too, frequently came out and mingled with the crowds, inquiring about their well-being. He asked with sympathy about the hardships and losses caused by the storm. He assured them that as soon as he reached Thanjavur, he would make arrangements for relief for the people’s suffering. He also noticed that the people were not particularly enthused by this promise. Among themselves, they whispered, “Will the authority of the Pazhuvettaraiyars come to an end?” He overheard the conversation. In subdued voices, yet loud enough for the prince to hear, many spoke about the emperor’s health and about who might next ascend the lion throne.

Meanwhile, the officials of the Five Great Guilds of Nagapattinam and the leaders of the Eight Councils had all arrived. Grand arrangements were made to host a banquet for the prince. Provisions were also made to feed the crowds who had come to see him. Whatever grains remained in the city, after the losses caused by the storm, were gathered together. There was no worry about vegetables at all. With the bunches of plantains from the fallen banana trees, and the clusters of coconuts from the toppled palms, could they not prepare a feast for a hundred thousand people?

The banquets concluded, and the time to depart drew near. The prince came out to the upper portico of the Chola palace and stood with folded hands. In the street below, a grand and festive procession was ready to set out. An ornamented elephant stood waiting for the prince to mount. Horses and bulls stood before and behind. Bearers of sacred conches and banners, and musicians of every kind, were arrayed in order. The people, like the surging sea that had raged the previous evening, stood as far as the eye could see, clamoring and cheering.

Outwardly, the prince’s face shone with a smile. But within, a deep anxiety had taken hold of his heart. His mind beat restlessly to learn the fate of the queen of Eezham, who had captured his love many times more than even his own mother. He thought he might learn more by questioning Murugaiyan’s wife, but she had vanished into the crowd. Only Murugaiyan himself, head bowed, followed the prince to the Chola palace. He too did not know what had become of his wife, Raakkammal.

On another side, a different worry troubled the prince. The Pazhuvettaraiyars had already declared that he wished to seize the kingdom against the emperor’s wishes. Because of the uproar of these people, their claim might be accepted as truth! The prince now felt that if only he could escape from the whirlpool of affection these townsfolk showed him, it would be enough. In this situation, something entirely unexpected happened. As the prince stood with folded hands, as if taking leave of the people, the officials of the Five Great Guilds and the leaders of the Eight Councils pushed through the crowd and gathered at the palace entrance.

They came and stood. As arranged beforehand, for a few moments, the sound of the perikai drum, the murasu, the ekkalam, and a hundred other instruments thundered forth, drowning even the roar of the sea. When, with a sudden stop, all those instruments fell silent, a profound hush settled over the vast assembly.
At that moment, an elder among the city leaders ascended the moonlit platform before the palace entrance and, standing tall, spoke in a commanding voice.

“Ponniyin Selvan! A petition. On behalf of the people of Nagai city and the surrounding villages, I bring forth a request. We are all deeply concerned about the health of the Emperor. Along with this, there is another rumor we have heard that troubles us. We understand that the Pazhuvettaraiyars and several minor kings have resolved that, after the Emperor, the crown should be given to Madurantaka Devar. Madurantaka Devar has never set foot on a battlefield. If he ascends the throne, it will be the Pazhuvettaraiyars who truly rule the kingdom. The laws will be what the minor kings decree.

Prince Aditya Karikalan has not set foot in Chola country for three years. Various reasons are given for this. Some say he does not wish to accept the crown. If that is so, then who is rightfully next in line for the throne? Is it not you—the son whom the Chola land earned through penance, the treasure whom Mother Kaveri herself saved, the heroic conqueror of Lanka? People! Is not what I have said agreeable to you all?” asked the elder, turning to the crowd around him.

From that multitude arose a thunderous roar that shook the eight directions: “Yes, yes; that is our wish too!” cried ten thousand voices. The shouts continued, swelling together into a great, indistinct tumult.
As the prince’s lips began to move to reply, as if bound by some magical power, that mighty uproar subsided.

“Sirs! I am gladdened by the love you all have for me. But is the way you show that love proper? It seems to me you have forgotten that my beloved father—Sundara Chola Chakravartin—is still alive. You must join me in praying, ‘May the Emperor live long!’ While the Emperor is still alive, why should we think about who should succeed him?”

The elder, leader among the city heads, had a ready answer to the prince’s question. “Ponniyin Selvan! In Chola country, it has long been the custom to decide who is next in line for the throne while the king is still alive. The conqueror of Madurai, the lord of Thillai’s temple—” Was it not the great Parantaka Chakravarti, who thatched the temple with gold, who in his own time failed to establish the order of succession for those who were to ascend the throne after him? Was it not according to that very order that your father ascended the throne?” he asked.

“Yes, yes! Therefore, even now, is it not the Emperor who must decide who is to be the next rightful heir to the throne? It is neither proper for you nor for me to think or speak about it,” replied the prince.

“Ponniyin Selva! We agree that only the Emperor has that right. If the Emperor were in a position to make a decision of his own free will, that would be just. But now, is it not the case that the Pazhuvettaraiyars have imprisoned the Emperor within the fortress of Thanjai? Prince! To speak even more plainly, many among us are not even certain whether the Emperor is still alive. We wish to accompany you to Thanjai and resolve this doubt for ourselves. If, by fortune, the Emperor is well, we will express our wishes to him. We will petition him that, after him, it is you who must ascend the throne. Then, let the Emperor decide as he deems fit!”

The words expressing doubt as to whether the Emperor was still alive sent a great shock through the prince’s heart. A pain and fear he had never before known arose within him. It seemed as though some danger had drawn near to threaten the Emperor’s life, and as though he himself was too far away to prevent it. The memory of the Queen of Eezham being forcefully abducted by some ruffians also flashed through his mind. Now, not a moment could be wasted—he must reach Thanjai at once. In those few seconds, the prince resolved what he must do. There was no use in continuing to argue with these men; it would only delay his journey. If he pretended to agree with their words and set out now, he could devise other means as he traveled.

“Sir! I am not standing in the way of your wishes. What you have said about the Emperor has only increased my anxiety to see him. I must depart at once. If you too wish to see the Emperor, you are welcome to come with me. Let us all hear what the Emperor has to say about the right to the throne, and act accordingly!” he said.

Soon after, the prince mounted his elephant and set forth on his journey. A great procession, numbering in the thousands, began its march toward Thanjai. As they went, the procession following the prince grew ever larger.

The sun had begun its descent in the western sky. Its rays, filtered through the dense canopy of trees, cast a golden glow upon the bustling streets of Kadambur. The entire town seemed to have awakened to a new life, as if the very air was charged with excitement and anticipation.

From every direction, people thronged towards the grand palace of Sambuvarayar. Farmers, merchants, artisans, women carrying children on their hips, and even aged elders leaning on their staffs—all made their way, drawn by an irresistible curiosity. The narrow lanes overflowed with the crowd, their voices rising in a chorus of animated chatter.

At the palace gates, guards struggled to maintain order, their commands drowned out by the clamor of the multitude. The reason for this unprecedented gathering was the arrival of the Chola prince, Aditya Karikalan. News of his visit had spread like wildfire, and the people of Kadambur, eager for a glimpse of the illustrious warrior, had abandoned their daily tasks to join the throng.

Colorful banners fluttered in the breeze, and garlands of fresh flowers adorned the entrance. The fragrance of sandalwood and incense mingled with the earthy scent of the crowd. Children darted between the legs of their elders, their faces alight with excitement.

Within the palace, preparations were underway for a grand welcome. Servants hurried about, arranging seats and spreading rich carpets. Musicians tuned their instruments, ready to fill the halls with auspicious melodies.

As the sun dipped lower, casting long shadows across the land, the anticipation of the people only grew. Every eye was fixed on the road leading to the palace, awaiting the moment when the prince would appear.

chapters.title: Pazhuvettaraiyar in the Boat
paragraphs: Readers will remember that it was on the morning after the storm struck that Periya Pazhuvettarayar set out from Kadambur towards Thanjavur. He traveled along his usual path until he reached the banks of the Kollidam River, and then turned west, following the road along the river’s northern shore. He did not wish to make a long journey through the villages of Chola Nadu. Instead, he intended to cross the Kollidam directly towards Thiruvaiyaru by heading west.

Unlike his usual custom, Periya Pazhuvettarayar did not depart with hundreds of attendants on this occasion. He wished that neither his departure nor his arrival should attract anyone’s attention. Therefore, he took only ten men with him.

When Pazhuvettarayar reached the northern bank of the Kollidam, directly across from Thiruvaiyaru, the great river was in full spate, its floodwaters touching both banks and flowing swiftly. It was impossible to transport horses in the small boat available there. Signs of a coming gale were already evident. So, for convenience in returning, he left the horses on the northern bank and boarded the boat with his ten warriors.

As the boat made its way to midstream, the storm intensified. The two boatmen struggled mightily to steer the craft. The force of the river’s current pulled the boat eastward, while the storm winds tried to push it west. The boatmen attempted to steer south. Caught between these three opposing forces, the boat spun round and round in circles.

At that moment, a great storm was also raging within Pazhuvettarayar’s heart. It was his usual fate that his mind would become clouded whenever he sat before Nandini. Whatever she said would seem right to him. Even if she spoke of something he had disliked all his life, when Nandini suggested it, it would suddenly appear reasonable to him. Even if a shadow of doubt lingered in his mind, his lips would utter, “Yes, yes! We shall do as you say.” Once he had given his word, he never liked to go back on it.

Now too, when Nandini had asked him to go to Thanjavur and fetch Madurantaka, he had agreed without hesitation. But after setting out on the journey, countless doubts began to torment his heart regarding this matter. Nandini’s... He did not think that even an atom of blemish could arise in her conduct. Yet, the thought that they had left her alone amidst three young men of Nandini’s age often arose in his mind and tormented him.

There were reasons for him to harbor resentment against all three—Kandhamaaran, Vandiyathevan, and Aditya Karikalan. That night, when he and Nandini were proceeding to the treasury chamber at midnight, Kandhamaaran had confronted them and referred to Nandini as “your daughter”—that phrase had seared itself into his heart as if scorched by a red-hot iron forged in bitterness. In the fury of that moment, he had secretly ordered the guard to kill him. Later, he regretted it. Somehow, Kandhamaaran had escaped. How he survived, how the treasury guard died—he still had not been able to learn the details. After that, he could not forget that Kandhamaaran had stayed in his palace for several days, and that Nandini had tended to him with devoted care.

Then, there was Vandiyathevan, now staying at Kadambur. From the very first moment he saw that loquacious youth, he had disliked him. Later, when he learned that Vandiyathevan had tried to warn the Emperor privately in Thanjavur, and had managed to escape from the Thanjai fort without anyone’s knowledge, his aversion only grew. He also did not forget that, at that time, the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar had specifically mentioned that perhaps Nandini had helped him escape. That could never be true. For it had since become known that Vandiyathevan was an intimate messenger for Princess Kundavai and Prince Arulmozhi. Therefore, there could be no connection between him and Nandini. Yet, whenever he thought of Vandiyathevan and Nandini together, a fire blazed in the iron heart of the elder Pazhuvettaraiyar.

And then, there was Aditya Karikalan. He had heard that, once, the prince had wished to marry the daughter of a temple priest, and that this girl was none other than Nandini. Now, they had met again. For what purpose? One thing was certain: Aditya Karikalan might be a great boor, he might lack respect for his elders, but he was born of the Chola lineage. In that clan, no one had ever committed the treachery of coveting another’s spouse. Karikalan, too, was above reproach in his conduct towards women. But Nandini? Was it right that he had trusted her so far, and acted always according to her wishes? Was it certain that there was no blemish in her conduct? He still did not know her true origins. His brother, Kaalandhaka Kandan, had often warned him about her, speaking in riddles.

“Will what my younger brother said turn out to be true? Will Nandini betray me? Ah! They speak of such things in tales! Are there truly women in this world with such treacherous hearts? Is Nandini one among them?...”

As these thoughts coursed through his mind, a flame of anger blazed up within Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar; at the same moment, the fire of passion he held for Nandini too flared up fiercely. To forget the pain caused by these conflicting emotions, Pazhuvettaraiyar shook his head and cleared his throat. Only the awareness that he was amidst ten others restrained him from striking his broad forehead with his powerful hands. Unbidden, deep sighs escaped him. Gripping the edge of the boat tightly, clenching his teeth, he resolved, “Within two days, I will uncover all the truths! Never again will I repeat the mistakes I have made so far!”

chapters.title: The Shore Was Breached!
paragraphs: The others in the boat could not sense the anguish that had taken root in Pazhuvetarayar’s heart. They thought he was so troubled only because the boat had been caught in the storm. The elder Pazhuvetarayar was famed for his unparalleled courage of mind. Seeing even him so shaken, fear began to creep into the hearts of the others as well. All of them, wondering at what moment the boat might capsize, started thinking about ways to save themselves.

At last, after the boat had struggled and floundered for a long time, it drifted half a league east of the landing place where they were supposed to disembark, and drew near the shore. “Now there is nothing to worry about,” everyone breathed a sigh of relief. At that very moment, one of the trees on the riverbank, which had been dancing like a ghost in the gale, snapped with a thunderous crack and fell. The wind lifted the broken tree and hurled it into the water near the boat. The oarsmen tried valiantly to turn the boat away and steer it clear. It was no use. The tree, moving with great speed, crashed into the boat. With a resounding ‘thadaal’, the boat overturned. In the next instant, everyone in the boat was flung into the water.

Since all the others had already been thinking about how to save themselves if the boat capsized, when it actually happened, they were somewhat prepared to face the danger. As the boat had drawn close to the shore, some swam to land. Some clung to the branches of trees. Others grabbed whatever they could and floated in the water.

But Pazhuvetarayar, absorbed in other thoughts, had not anticipated the disaster that befell the boat. When it capsized, he was plunged into the water. The force of the current carried him far away. He swallowed water several times; water entered his nose and ears; he struggled and floundered, but at last, somehow managed to steady himself and rise above the current. He could see neither the boat nor any of its passengers.

At once, the old warrior’s ancient resolve sprang up in his heart. The great hero who had fought and triumphed in many battles under the most perilous circumstances now resolved to fight and conquer the flood of the Kollidam as well. He looked all around. He reached out and caught hold of a log that was floating nearby. Fixing his gaze on the shore, he began to swim. Against the force of the flood, against the fury of the storm— With great speed, and all the while fighting against the current, he swam onward. When his arms grew weary, he floated for a while, letting the water bear his weight. Several times he tried to climb up the riverbank, but the rain had turned the shore to slippery mud, and each time it pushed him back into the river. Immediately, he leapt and caught hold of the drifting log he had let go.

In this manner, battling on for more than a watch after darkness had fallen, at last his feet touched the riverbed at a spot where thick reeds grew in profusion. Then, using the help of the bending reed bushes, the old warrior staggered and stumbled, and finally climbed up the bank.

Dense darkness surrounded him on all sides. There was no sign of any village nearby. He guessed that he must have come about a league and a half east of the ferry point where he was supposed to cross the Thirumalai river. Yes, yes! He must have come ashore near Kudanthai city. Would it be possible, somehow, to reach Kudanthai tonight…?

At that moment, the storm had reached its full fury in that region. The deafening roar, as if a hundred thousand demons were howling together, made his ears ring. Trees crashed down with sharp, splintering sounds; thunderclaps, as if the very vault of the heavens were being shattered, echoed again and again. Torrential rain poured down in sheets.

“Would there not be some ruined mandapam or ancient temple somewhere? I must find shelter there and spend the night. Only after dawn can I continue my journey,” he resolved, bracing his trembling, unsteady legs and walking along the riverbank.

The floodwaters, brushing against the edge of the bank, surged onward in the river. Because of the rain, even the top of the bank was covered with a layer of water. There is no need to speak of the darkness. So, as the valiant old man walked on, he paid little attention to the place ahead where the water seemed to flow more swiftly across the bank. Suddenly, when the water reached his knees, he hesitated and thought. When it rose to his thighs, he was startled. There was no time to think further. In the next instant, he was swept headlong into the water.

The Kollidam had breached its bank at that spot, and the flood, rushing southward, rolled him over and over, battering him as it carried him away. Beyond the bank, the land sloped steeply, so it seemed as if he was being dragged deeper and deeper, down into the very netherworld. When the boat had capsized and he was swept into the river’s flood, he had managed to save himself with some ease. Now, that was not possible. He was rolled and tumbled, over and over, down and down. He could not see; he could not hear. To rise up and break the surface— He could not; his breath was strangled. Some monstrous demon seemed to be pushing him down into the water, rolling him over and over, and at the same time dragging him down toward the netherworld.

‘Ah! That demon is none other than the flood itself—the demon that broke through the banks of the Kollidam, surging through the breach with terrifying speed! Can anyone escape from its dreadful grip, from its merciless rolling? There is no ground beneath my feet! My hands find nothing to grasp! My breath is choking! It feels as if someone is wringing my neck! My ears are deafening! Durga Parameshwari! Devi! Will I survive this calamity? Wretched Nandini! See what fate has befallen me because of you! Alas! Poor woman! I left you amidst those cunning men! Fie! Fie! What happiness did I gain by being enchanted by your beauty, by pitying your plight, by marrying you? What reward did I reap except the loss of my peace of mind? In the end, here I am, caught in the breach of the Kollidam, struggling and gasping to my death! My body, which has borne sixty-four battle wounds, will not even be buried with a hero’s stone or laid to rest in the warriors’ cemetery! No one will even recover my corpse! Somewhere, in some deep pit, I will be buried in the mud! No one will ever know what became of me! Or perhaps, somewhere along the shore, this flood will toss my body aside! Dogs and jackals will tear at it to satisfy their hunger!...’
Within a few minutes, countless such thoughts arose and faded in the mind of Pazhuvetarayar. Then, at last, he lost consciousness entirely!...

A sudden blow to his head—he had struck something hard—brought him back to his senses for a moment. His hands were clutching at something—black stone, or solid ground. Some force had lifted him up and pushed him onward. He, too, summoned the last remnants of his strength, pressed his palms against the ground, and heaved himself upward. The next moment, he was lying on a hard, black stone floor. With great effort, he tried to open his eyes. The tightly shut lids parted slightly, and the light that appeared before him dazzled his eyes. In that radiance, he beheld the divine face of Durga Parameshwari! Devi! Your compassion alone is mercy! You have ended my restless life on earth and brought me to your divine presence in the heavens!...

No, no! This is not heaven. This is the goddess’s temple on earth. The image before him was the idol of the goddess. He was lying in the ardha-mandapa, the hall adjacent to the sanctum. Near the goddess, a small lamp was burning with a gentle, flickering light. It was that very light which, just now, had dazzled his eyes so much. How shameful it was! Outside, the rain still poured down in torrents, roaring with a ceaseless “sho” as the storm raged on. Yet, for all that wind and rain, the lamp burning in the sanctum of the Devi temple did not so much as flicker! Was this a good omen? Was it a sign of Durga Parameswari’s compassion towards him? Did it not seem as if, no matter how great the calamity, his life would not be extinguished? The Mother of the Universe’s mercy is the only true mercy! All his devotion, all the worship he had offered, had not been in vain.

The elder tried to rise, staggering and unsteady. His body trembled. It was only natural—after lying so long in the floodwaters, his limbs were chilled and shivering. He took the cloth that hung as a curtain before the goddess’s presence and wiped himself thoroughly. Casting aside his wet garment, he wrapped the curtain-cloth around his waist.

He saw before the goddess’s sanctum the broken coconut shells, fruits, and prasadam of pongal offered for the deity—all left there untouched. The priest who had come to perform the puja, and the devotees who had come to pray, must have abandoned everything as it was and fled. Why had they run away? Was it out of fear of the storm and rain? Or had they seen the breach on the banks of the Kollidam and fled in terror? Whatever the reason, it was his own good fortune! Durga Parameswari had not only saved him from the floodwaters of the breach, but had also left prasadam to satisfy his hunger.

Tonight, he would have to spend the night in this temple. There was no better place to be found than this. The flood from the breach would have to sweep right past this little temple. There was danger even to the temple itself. The waters would swirl and dig around the temple, perhaps even undermine its very foundations. Yet, nothing of the sort would happen tonight. Even if it did, so be it. Tonight, he would not leave this temple. His body had no strength; his heart, no will…

With reverence and awe, Pazhuvetarayar approached the presence of the goddess. He took the prasadam and ate as much as he needed, then carefully stored the rest away. In an attitude of worship before the goddess, he lay down. His eyes spun with weariness. Within moments, Pazhuvetarayar had fallen into a deep sleep.

chapters.title: Eyes Opened!
paragraphs: First swept away by the river’s flood, and then by the breach’s torrent, the great Pazhuvetarayar, exhausted beyond measure, lay for a long time unconscious, senseless, sleeping like a log. After he had slept enough, faint memories and dreams began to stir within him. At one moment, Durga Parameswari herself stepped down from the temple idol, took four steps, and came near him. Her divine mouth blossomed as she fixed him with eyes blazing like fire.

“Ah, Pazhuvetaraya! You and your clan have belonged to me for generations. Therefore, I warn you. That Nandini whom you have brought into your palace—she is a demoness in the form of a human woman! She has come to uproot and destroy your lineage and the Chola dynasty. She is waiting for the right moment. Cast her out from your palace, cast her out from your heart, and then attend to other matters! If not, an everlasting disgrace will befall you and your clan…”
Thus warning him, the goddess turned and merged back into the idol…
Pazhuvetarayar started up in alarm. His body was trembling all over. It was difficult for him to believe that what he had seen was merely a dream. Yet, he resolved that it must be so.

Dawn had broken fully. The fury of the storm had abated. The rain had ceased. Only the sound of “sho” could be heard. He walked to the edge of the temple’s outer hall and looked around. The sight that met his eyes was not encouraging.

The breach in the Kollidam had grown much larger by now. Nearly half the river’s flood seemed to be pouring through the gap with a deep, gurgling roar. To the east and south, there was nothing but a vast expanse of floodwater. Only to the west, for a short distance beside the temple, the waters whirled and leapt, rushing away. Beyond that, dense groves of small trees and thickets stretched far into the distance. He guessed that must be the forest adjoining the village of Thiruppurambiyam, and somewhere within that forest, in its midst, must stand the ancient Pallipadai temple where King Prithiveepathi of the Ganga dynasty was commemorated with a hero stone.

In that ruined mandapam, memories of the great battle that had taken place there a hundred years ago came flooding back to him. He recalled the heroic deeds performed by his ancestors in that war, acts of valor that had aided the Chola dynasty. Would it be possible that such a calamity could truly befall his ancient, illustrious lineage because of this Nandini? Was there some truth, after all, in what Durga Parameswari had revealed to him in his dream?

Whatever the case, he must henceforth be on his utmost guard. He must discover the true nature of Nandini’s intentions. Only after leaving this place could he attend to other matters. If he could reach the village of Thirupurambiyam, perhaps he could find help there. If anyone else had survived the capsized boat, they too might have made their way to that village. But how was he to cross the floodwaters and reach Thirupurambiyam?
The swirling floodwaters circled the temple, churning and eddying all around! Even if a temple elephant were to enter that current, it would be swept away in an instant. How was he to cross it?

It was certain that the floodwaters were digging a deep trench around the temple, eroding the earth beneath. No one could say when the temple itself might collapse! Only by the grace of Durga Parameswari did it stand upright still. Yet, how was he to get out? If he waited for the floodwaters to subside, who knew how many days that would take?

Fortunately, there was another way. Directly opposite the temple stood a grand neem tree, which, by some miracle, had survived the storm without falling. But the swirling floodwaters had carved a trench around that neem tree as well, so it was certain that the tree would fall before the temple did. If the tree fell, it might land like a bridge toward the forested region to the west. Even if it did not, the floodwaters might carry the tree along and deposit it somewhere along the shore. If he could scramble onto the tree as soon as it fell, he might somehow escape from there.

Until then, he would have to remain in the temple. By the goddess’s mercy, there was still enough prasadam left to stave off hunger for another day. He would have to wait there patiently, until either the tree fell or the floodwaters receded. What else could he do?

There was no use in acting hastily. Surely, the Divine Mother had spared him from death in the flood because there were yet great deeds for him to accomplish in this world. Therefore, for whatever was to come, Durga— Will not Parameswari herself show the way? That day too had passed. Another night and day slipped by. The storm, leaving devastation in its wake wherever it went, had now moved westward.

The torrential rain had ceased. Yet, for the trapped Pazhuvettarayar within the temple of Durga Devi, there was still no deliverance. The floodwaters of the Kollidam appeared to have receded. But the breach in the embankment was only growing larger. The waters swirling around the temple did not diminish; if anything, their depth seemed to be increasing. How could one measure it? Or even contemplate plunging into that breached torrent and swimming across—was that even possible to consider?

At last, as the sun was setting that day, just as Pazhuvettarayar had hoped, the great neem tree standing opposite the temple toppled. By good fortune, the fallen tree stretched across to touch the western bank of the breached flood. Pazhuvettarayar readied himself to cross over by that path. He hesitated for a moment, wondering how he would find his way through the wild forest at night. That hesitation did not last long. He resolved that he must set out at once, and, wishing to offer thanks to Durga Parameswari who had protected him from such peril, he approached the sanctum. He prostrated himself before the goddess.
At that moment, a voice rang out, making his body shiver. At first, he thought it was Durga herself speaking. But then he realized, no, the voice was coming from a little distance outside.
“Sorcerer! Sorcerer!” the voice called.
Then again, “Ravidasan! Ravidasan!” it cried. It sounded like a voice he had heard long ago.

Pazhuvettarayar rose and came to the front mandapam. Concealed behind a pillar, he looked toward the source of the voice. Across the breached flood, near the tip of the fallen neem tree, he saw a figure standing. The cry of “Sorcerer! Sorcerer!” brought to mind something his brother had once told him. A thought arose—was he about to learn some mystery hitherto unknown to him, by the grace of Durga Devi? So he stood motionless.

He saw the figure on the far bank begin to cross the breached flood, using the fallen neem tree as a bridge. At that moment, Pazhuvettarayar did something most extraordinary, something he had never done before in his life. He lay down abruptly in the front mandapam of the temple, feigning sleep.

The desire to learn about the sorcerer named Ravidasan gripped him with such intensity. Perhaps, the man who sometimes came to the palace under the guise of a magician to see Nandini was none other than Ravidasan himself. What exactly was the relationship between him and Nandini? Who was this person searching for him at this place and at this hour? And for what purpose was he seeking him? If he could uncover all this, perhaps he might also discover whether Nandini was truly deceiving him or not. If only Ravidasan himself could be caught, he resolved in his mind that he would not let him go without extracting the truth.
Pretending to be asleep, he waited as the man approached. Once more, the newcomer called out, “Ravidasaa! Ravidasaa!”

Ah! That voice—was it not the same Devaralan who, once in the Kadambur palace, had danced the Velanattam and prophesied? Should he seize this fellow by the throat and force the truth from him? No, not yet. It was more important to use this man to catch the sorcerer Ravidasan.

“Magician! Have you fallen asleep before the sun has even set? Or have you died and vanished from this world?” muttered the man as he came closer, reaching out to touch the body of the supposed Ravidasan and turning him over so that his face was visible. Yet, the body lay there, unmoving, unresponsive.

In that hour when dusk and night mingled and blurred, in the dim and uncertain light, Devaralan (yes, it was he!) peered at the face of the man before him. He wiped his eyes and looked again, more intently. With a voice trembling with fear, horror, astonishment, and disbelief, he let out a series of hoarse cries—“Ooo! Oh! Ah!”—and then, without another moment’s hesitation, he fled from that place!

Before the Paluvettaraiyar could open his eyes, sit up, and look around, Devaralan had already leapt across the open mandapam before the temple’s sacrificial altar in two bounds, and began to hurry across the neem-wood bridge. Without pausing even for a moment to look back, he ran and vaulted over the bridge, reaching the far bank. In the next instant, he disappeared into the dense thicket of bushes and trees. Paluvettaraiyar watched, blinking in astonishment, as the man leapt and fled in terror. When he vanished into the forest, Paluvettaraiyar was seized by a doubt—had he made a mistake in letting the opportunity to catch him slip by?

Immediately, he too sprang up and began to run. Unlike Devaralan, he could not cross the wooden bridge with such speed and agility. He had to go slowly, stumbling and grasping the branches here and there for support.

As soon as he reached the opposite bank, he saw that a narrow footpath led into the forested region. He examined it closely. Fresh footprints were imprinted in the mud. He decided that Devaralan must have gone that way, and hurried onward.

Though it was the early hours before dawn, the sky was still shrouded in clouds, and darkness prevailed. Strange sounds echoed through the forest. Countless creatures, battered by the storm and rain, now roamed about, expressing their exhilaration at the end of the downpour with their cries.

The narrow footpath soon came to an end. But Pazhuvettarayar did not wish to stop there. Even if he had to wander the forest the entire night, he was determined to find both Devaralan and the sorcerer Ravidasan whom Devaralan sought. Resolute, he pressed on, making his way through the undergrowth wherever he could find a passage.

After wandering in the forest for about a quarter of an hour, he noticed a light some distance away. Since the light was moving rather than stationary, he surmised that someone was carrying a torch to guide their way.

He fixed his gaze on the light and hastened toward it. He drew closer and closer. At last, the torchlight illuminated the ruins of a mandapam in the midst of the forest, and then vanished. The moment Pazhuvettarayar saw the mandapam, he recognized it as the Prithiveepathi’s Pallipadai temple in Thiruppurambiyam.

He approached the pallipadai and stood pressed against a side wall, listening intently. Yes—his expectations were not in vain. He heard two people conversing. They spoke in loud voices, and their words were clear.
“Sorcerer! Do you know how long I have been searching for you? I was afraid you might not be able to come, or that Yama himself had taken you away!” said Devaralan.

The sorcerer Ravidasan laughed harshly. “Why should Yama come for me? It is Sundara Cholan and his two children whom Yama is drawing near. Tomorrow, their lives will come to an end!” said the sorcerer.
At that moment, a lightning bolt flashed, illuminating both sky and earth.

Vandiyathevan’s eyelids fluttered. He felt as though he had been submerged in a deep, dark sea and was now slowly rising towards the surface. The world around him was shrouded in mist; his mind, too, was clouded and confused. Gradually, his senses began to return. He could hear the soft murmur of voices, the gentle rustle of silk, and the faint fragrance of sandalwood in the air.

He tried to move, but his limbs felt heavy, as if weighed down by invisible chains. With great effort, he opened his eyes. At first, everything was blurred. Slowly, the shapes around him came into focus.

He was lying on a soft bed, covered with fine white sheets. The room was spacious and adorned with exquisite carvings on the pillars. Lamps burned with a steady golden glow, casting flickering shadows on the walls. Beside him stood a woman, her face radiant with compassion and concern.
It was Kundavai Devi.
When she saw that Vandiyathevan had opened his eyes, a gentle smile blossomed on her lips. She leaned forward and spoke in a voice as sweet as honey.
“You have awakened at last! For a while, we feared you would not return to us.”
Vandiyathevan tried to sit up, but Kundavai gently restrained him.
“Do not strain yourself. You are still weak. Rest for a while longer.”
Memories came rushing back to him—the wild river, the swirling waters, the desperate struggle, and then, darkness. He looked at Kundavai with confusion.
“How did I come here? What happened to me?”
Kundavai’s eyes sparkled with mischief.
“You must have angered the goddess of the river. She tried to claim you for herself. But we would not let her have you so easily.”
Vandiyathevan managed a faint smile. “Then I must thank you, Princess, for rescuing me from her clutches.”
Kundavai’s laughter rang like the tinkling of silver bells.
“Thank me later. For now, rest. When you are stronger, we shall speak at length.”
She signaled to a maidservant, who brought a cup of cool, fragrant water. Kundavai held it to Vandiyathevan’s lips. He drank gratefully, feeling life return to his weary body.

As he drifted into a peaceful slumber, Vandiyathevan’s heart was filled with gratitude and wonder. He had escaped the jaws of death, only to find himself in the care of the Chola princess herself. What fate awaited him now? Only time would tell.

chapters.title: The Hall Collapsed
paragraphs: In the flash of lightning, Pazhuvettarayar took a moment to observe and recognize the two men who stood there conversing. One of them, Ravidasan, he had seen a couple of times before, right within his own palace. Nandini had once told him that this man was well-versed in magical arts. His own younger brother, Kaalandhaka Kandan, had harbored suspicions about this sorcerer and had warned him accordingly. The other man was Devaralan, who had performed the Velanattam ritual at the Kadambur palace. Was this truly the first time he was seeing him? What was his real name?… Could it be possible? Was he, perhaps, Parameswaran, who had been dismissed from royal service by Pazhuvettarayar himself long ago?… Let it be; let’s listen to what more they are saying.

“Ravidasan! You have been saying this for so long now. Always muttering, ‘The day is near,’ ‘Yama is approaching.’ Yama comes and takes away whomever he pleases! But for three years now, Sundara Chozhan has been lying bedridden, and yet Yama has not come for him. As for his sons, even Yama himself seems to fear approaching them. How many times have we both tried in Eezham?…”

“That is no fault of ours, father! Yama Dharmaraja is cleverer than both you and me! He has been waiting all this time to take all three of them on the same day. That day is coming tomorrow. By good fortune, you too have arrived here! You are the true messenger of Yama! Why do you tremble so? Did you get caught in the Kollidam flood? You have brought the boat and kept it ready, haven’t you?”

“I have. But it was a great struggle to keep the boat from being swept away by the flood and the wind! And searching for you everywhere all this time… Ravidasan! You asked why my body is trembling, didn’t you? Just a short while ago, I saw Yama Dharmaraja face to face. No, no; I saw Yama’s elder brother. That truly frightened me for a moment…”
“Parameswaran! What nonsense are you babbling? Yama, or his elder brother? Why should you fear them? Shouldn’t they be the ones to fear you?”

The moment Ravidasan addressed the other as ‘Parameswaran,’ Pazhuvettarayar was startled. His suspicion was confirmed! And when he referred to Yama’s elder brother, he meant Pazhuvettarayar himself—this too he understood. Instantly, he moved closer to them… His heart and hands ached to seize him by the throat and strangle him then and there. Yet, the desire to hear more of their conversation made him restrain himself with patience. They had not yet begun to speak of Nandini. What was the meaning behind the sorcerer’s words that Yama himself would come for Sundara Chozhar’s family tomorrow? Was he truly prophesying by reading the stars? Was everything Nandini had said about this man’s magical powers true? What if, as he claimed, events unfolded by divine will? Then, his own purpose would be easily fulfilled! There would be no need to divide the Chola empire! But this Parameswaran—what concern did he have in this matter? Yes, yes, was he not the very man who, twenty years ago, swore an oath that he would destroy the Chola dynasty? Ah! He is speaking about himself! Let me listen to what he has to say!

“As you instructed, I came here this morning. But you were nowhere to be found. I wandered all around, searching, thinking perhaps you had taken shelter nearby from the wind and rain. Near the breach in the Kollidam, there is a small temple. It seemed as if someone was lying inside. Thinking it might be you, fallen asleep in exhaustion, I went closer to look… Guess whom I saw? None other than Periya Pazhuvetarayar himself!”
The sorcerer let out a loud “Ha ha ha!” The birds of the forest, startled, shrieked in chorus—“Kee-reech! Kee-reech!”—while the dumb herons grunted in alarm.
“Did you see Pazhuvetarayar? Or did you see his ghost?” asked Ravidasan.

“No, not a ghost. I touched the man who was lying face down, turned him over, and looked closely at his face. Ravidasan! Can Yama have two elder brothers? Is it possible for another man to exist with the very same face, the same moustache, the same scars as Pazhuvetarayar?”

“The one you saw must have been Pazhuvetarayar himself! There is no doubt. Yesterday evening, Pazhuvetarayar crossed the Kollidam by boat. When the boat neared the shore, the wind overturned it. His attendants, who managed to escape and reach the bank, are still searching along the Kollidam’s edge for Pazhuvetarayar. They suspect he may have drowned and perished in the flood. I overheard them speaking as they returned after searching up to the breach. So, the man you saw could very well have been Pazhuvetarayar. Or perhaps you saw his corpse—who knows!”
“No, no. If he were dead, would his eyelids be visible? The eyes of the man I turned over were tightly shut. He looked as if he were simply exhausted and had fallen asleep…”
“Fool! What have you done! Did you just leave him there quietly? Couldn’t you have lifted a stone and smashed it down on his head?”
“You don’t know about the head of Pazhuvetaraiyar. If you dropped a stone on his head, it’s the stone that would shatter to dust!”
“In that case, at least you could have dragged him into the Kollidam’s floodwaters and let him be swept away?”

“Didn’t I tell you? The moment I saw him, it was as if I had seen Yama’s elder brother himself. Even at Kadambur, when he performed the spear dance before me, my heart kept pounding ‘thik, thik’ in fear. If he had recognized me…”
“Why do you tremble now, just thinking of it?”
“As long as he lives, I will always feel a little fear. I am anxious that we did not do as you said, that we left without rolling him into the floodwaters…”

“Do not worry. In one way, it is better that the great Pazhuvetaraiyar is still alive. Only then, after Sundara Cholan and his children are dead and gone, will the petty kings of Chola Nadu split into two factions and fight among themselves. The Pazhuvetaraiyars and the Sambuvaraiyars on one side, and the Kodumbalur Velar and the Thirukovalur Malayaman on the other, will wage war. That would be most advantageous to our cause. While they are busy fighting each other, we can secretly gather and strengthen our army in Pandya Nadu…”

“Ravidasan! You speak like the tale of ‘If the aunt grows a moustache, she’ll become an uncle!’ Only if Sundara Cholan and his two sons meet their end tomorrow, as you say, will the Chola chieftains turn on each other. What certainty is there that all three will meet their end tomorrow? Do you know a piece of news?”
“What are you saying?”
“Arulmozhi Varman is alive in Nagapattinam! The people are flocking around him, shouting that he must become the emperor of Chola Nadu! Have you heard of this?”

Ravidasan laughed again and said, “I did not hear of it; I already know. Do you know who revealed Arulmozhi Varman’s presence in the Buddhist vihara? It was none other than our Revathasan’s daughter, Rakkammal! She is the wife of the boatman Murugaiyan!”

“So what of it? What gain is there in Arulmozhi Varman being revealed? From now on, won’t he always be surrounded by hundreds of thousands of people? Even when he was in Eezha Nadu with only two or three companions, our efforts did not succeed,” said Devaralan.
“I told you, even that was for the best, didn’t I? When Yama can come for all three on the same day…”
“Ravidasa! How can Yama approach the prince when he is amidst a hundred thousand people? You haven’t answered that.”

“He will approach, my friend, he will approach! Yama will be seated at the tip of the mahout’s ankus! At the right moment, he will claim the prince’s life! Parameshwara! The people of Chola Nadu will place the prince upon an elephant and take him in procession towards Thanjai. If, on the way, some danger befalls the mahout driving that elephant, our Revathasan can take his place as the mahout. After that, you can imagine for yourself what will happen!”

“Ravidasa! I admit, there is no equal to your sharpness of mind. We can trust that Gramavithan will accomplish what he has set out to do. But what about Sundara Cholan? What arrangements have you made for him?” asked Devaralan.

“I have left Soman Sambavan in the treasury vault of Pazhuvetarayan. I left him there, armed with a spear. From there, a secret tunnel leads to Sundara Cholan’s palace. I have shown Soman Sambavan the very spot where Sundara Cholan lies. Even a blind man could stand at the place I indicated and hurl a weapon to kill Sundara Cholan. I warned Soman Sambavan, ‘Do not act in haste; wait until tomorrow!’ before I left…”
“Why is that? Isn’t it best to finish the task at the right moment?”

“Fool! If Sundara Cholan is killed too soon, won’t his sons become alert as soon as they hear the news? What use is there in the death of that sick old man? Leave that aside; what news have you brought? How is everyone at Kadambur Palace? Isn’t the event that is to take place there tomorrow night more important than all else?”
“Kadambur is in a state of great festivity. There are wedding talks and romantic dramas unfolding. I do not like at all the way you trust that Pazhuvur Rani…”

“Pazhuvur Rani, you say? Call her Pandimadevi! Have you forgotten that just two days before Veera Pandiyan’s death, he made her his chief queen? Have you forgotten the vow she took to avenge Veera Pandiyan’s death? Was it not right here, just a week ago, that she received the Pandya dynasty’s heroic sword from the hands of the Pandya prince…?”
“Yes, yes! But yesterday evening, you should have seen your Pandimadevi returning after a pleasure boat ride on the Veera Narayana Lake…”

“If not in pleasure, then how else should she appear? There is no one who has mastered the art of concealing what is in their heart like Nandini. Otherwise, could she have spent three years in the palace of the Pazhuvettaraiyar? Could she have helped our cause so much while staying there? Yes, you said just now that you saw Pazhuvettaraiyar at the Durga temple on the banks of the Kollidam, didn’t you? I too heard about the boat that brought him capsizing. When did Pazhuvettaraiyar leave Kadambur? Why…?”

“I am not certain why. They said he left to bring Madhurantaka Devan to Kadambur. Pazhuvettaraiyar departed yesterday morning. After he left, the princes went hunting. The princesses went to the Veera Narayana Lake for water games. If you had seen the joyous scene when the princes and princesses returned, you would not speak with such confidence…!”
“You need not worry about that at all. From the moment Pazhuvettaraiyar was sent off to Thanjai, we can discern Pandimadevi’s mind, can we not?”
“Who can ever know a woman’s mind? Sending that old man away might have been for the sake of revenge, or perhaps to stage a romantic drama…”
“What nonsense are you babbling, Parameshvara! Nandini has completely forgotten that old story. She now hates Karikalan as one would hate poison!”
“I was not speaking of Karikalan. I was speaking of his messenger, Vandiyathevan. Have you forgotten how, two or three times, Nandini let him escape?”

The sorcerer laughed aloud, his voice ringing out, and said, “Yes; soon enough, we shall know why Vandiyathevan has been spared. When that truth comes to light, do not think you alone will be astonished! Many more will be struck with wonder! Most of all, Sundara Chozhar’s beloved daughter, Kundavai, will be amazed. The very youth to whom she has surrendered her heart—if she learns that he is the one who slew her own brother, Aditya Karikalan, will she not be astounded?”
“What are you saying, Ravidasan! Is it truly Vandiyathevan who is going to kill Karikalan? Has he joined forces with us, then?”

“Do not ask all that now! What does it matter whose hand strikes down Karikalan? It is the valiant sword, engraved with the Pandya clan’s fish emblem, that will slay him. Yet the blame for his murder will fall upon Vandiyathevan’s head! Now, what do you say of our queen’s cunning?”
“Let all happen as you say; ask me later, and I shall answer.”

“Whatever else may or may not come to pass, it is certain that Karikalan’s life will end before tomorrow night is through. Nandini will fulfill the responsibility she has taken upon herself. We, too, must fulfill our own duty…”
“What is our duty?”

“Tomorrow night, we must wait, ready and watchful, at the secret tunnel that leads out from the Kadambur palace. Once the deed is done, Nandini will come that way. We must escort her safely through the night to the Kolli Hills. From there, we shall watch the chaos that will engulf Chozha country. If fortune favors us…”
“If fortune favors us, what then?”

“All the treasures stored in Pazhuvetarayar’s treasury chamber must be taken through the tunnel and gathered together. Would it not be fitting to raise an army to wage war against Chozha land, using the very wealth plundered from Chozha’s own coffers?”
Having spoken thus, Ravidasan laughed once more.

Parameswaran, who played the role of Devaralan, said, “Enough, enough! Do not build your castles in the air too high! First, let us cross the Kollidam and reach the far shore, and make our way to Kadambur. Let all happen there as you have foretold! Afterwards, Pazhuvetarayar’s—” “We can think about looting the treasure. What do you say? Shall we set out right now? Shall we cross the Kollidam tonight itself?” he asked.
“No, no! It’s enough if we board the boat at dawn. By then, the wind will have calmed down. The flood in the river will also have subsided a little.”
“In that case, shall we sleep here tonight in this ruined mandapam?”
Ravidasan thought for a moment. At that instant, the howling of jackals was heard from a little distance away. Ravidasan’s body trembled.
“Ravidasan! Why do you tremble so just hearing the cry of jackals?” asked Devaralan.

“My friend! If you had ever experienced the terror of being buried up to your neck in the muddy marshes of Kodikkarai, with a hundred jackals standing around waiting to devour you, you would not speak so lightly! The roar of a lion or the trumpeting of a wild elephant does not frighten me. But the howl of a jackal makes my very bones shudder. Come! Come! Let us not stay in this cremation ground tonight. Let us find a temple or a choultry near some village to rest. If not, you mentioned the Durga temple on the banks of the Kollidam, didn’t you? Let us go there. If that old man is still lying there, we can push him into the flood and be done with it. That would be the greatest help we could do for him. If he remains alive until the day after tomorrow, he will have to endure unbearable mental agony!”

The great Pazhuvettarayar had listened to the above conversation without missing a word. Every word they spoke felt to him as if molten lead was being poured into his ears. His heart boiled like the molten core of a mighty volcano. The woman he had loved and married had come to take revenge on the Chola dynasty for the death of Veerapandiyan, and for three years she had been deceiving him—this brought him unspeakable pain and humiliation.

At that moment, Pazhuvettarayar thought of the ties that had bound the Chola dynasty and the house of Pazhuvur for six generations. After all, who were Sundara Cholan and his children? Was not Sundara Cholan’s grandmother from the Pazhuvur lineage? Was not his anger towards Sundara Cholan’s children a recent thing? Just because Aditya Karikalan had behaved childishly, and because he did not like Malayaman, to what terrible conspiracies had he given room? The Pandya conspirators, the eternal enemies of the Chola clan, had— From within the palace, we have allowed a place for treacherous acts against the Chola dynasty, using the wealth stolen from our own treasury! Alas! As these wretches have said, are three terrible murders truly going to take place in three different places before tomorrow night? As long as there is breath in our bodies, we must strive to prevent them.

There are still sixty nazhigai left. So much can be accomplished in that time. Before night falls, I must send word from Kudanthai to Thanjai and Nagapattinam, and then set out for Kadambur. I must reach there before these villains arrive!

Should I let them go to Kadambur? Would it not be better to kill them here and leave? I have no weapons with me—but what of that? When my hands themselves are as powerful as the thunderbolt, what need have I for other arms? Yet, they might have small daggers hidden on their persons. Without giving them a chance to draw them, I must seize both by the throat and strangle them at once...

But is it wise to fight them here? I have already learned all I needed to know from them. The goddess Durga Parameswari, whom I worship as my family deity, has caused the boat to capsize and revealed these dreadful secrets to me. Is it not my foremost duty to protect the emperor and his sons from harm? Above all, it is of utmost importance to prevent any danger from befalling Karikalan at Kadambur. If something were to happen to him, an indelible stain would fall upon me and my lineage. The help rendered by the Pazhuvur clan to the Chola dynasty for six generations would be forgotten, turned to dust. If Karikalan were to be killed by the very enchantress I brought into my palace, thinking her a mere woman, there could be no greater disgrace for me.

Ah! Can such deadly poison as halahala be hidden within so beautiful a form? Can such deceit lurk behind a bewitching smile that could enchant all three worlds? Can all that these wretches said just now truly be possible?

The words of those conspirators, which had kindled a fire of rage in the heart of Pazhuvetaraiyar, also brought him a strange sense of satisfaction. Nandini may be a conspirator. She may have deceived him, pretending to love him, only to betray and cheat him. But she had no special affection for Karikalan, nor for Kandhamaaran or Vandiyathevan— He had not deceived her out of infatuation! She paid no heed to those foolish youths. She spoke kindly and mingled with them only to use them for her own secret purposes! This news, deep within the innermost chambers of the heart of the Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar, brought him a certain satisfaction, though he himself was not fully aware of it. Preventing Karikalan’s murder was not only to protect his family’s honor and to avoid everlasting disgrace falling upon himself; it was also to save Nandini from being drawn into such a dreadful, sinful deed. Perhaps, he might even change her heart. Perhaps, trapped as she was among these vile conspirators, she had no other way but to be complicit with them. If he could destroy these men here and now, might not Nandini be freed from their clutches?
Thinking thus, the valiant old warrior unconsciously cleared his throat. That sound, like the roar of a lion, startled the two conspirators.
“Who’s there?” demanded Devaralan, also known as Parameswaran.
It was no longer possible or appropriate to remain hidden. Deciding thus, the Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar stepped out into the open.

In the darkness of the rainy night, the sudden appearance of that tall, imposing figure left the conspirators frozen in shock. “It is I—the elder brother of Yama!” declared Pazhuvettaraiyar, and laughed.
The majestic sound of his laughter sent tremors through the entire grove.

The moment they realized it was Pazhuvettaraiyar, both Ravidasan and Devaralan tried to escape! But Pazhuvettaraiyar gave them no chance. Stretching out his long arms, he seized them both. His right hand gripped Ravidasan’s shoulder. The grip of those hands, stronger than the thunderbolt weapon itself, left the two men utterly bewildered.

Yet, no matter how strong his hands, it would not be possible to subdue both at once, Pazhuvettaraiyar realized. So, he pushed Devaralan headlong to the ground. Placing one foot firmly on the fallen man’s back, he began to throttle Ravidasan’s neck with both hands. But Devaralan did not remain idle. Struggling, he drew the dagger tucked at his waist and tried to stab the foot that pinned him down. Pazhuvettaraiyar sensed this. With his other foot, he delivered a powerful kick to Devaralan’s wrist. He threw it. The knife flew far away and fell. One of Devaralan’s arms became as lifeless as if it had been severed. But at that very moment, the foot that had pinned him down slipped a little. Devaralan twisted himself free in a flash, sprang up, and leapt away. With the hand that had not been struck, he began to punch at Pazhuvetarayar. Those blows were like fists striking a wall of black granite. It was Devaralan’s own hand that ached from the effort. He wondered if it too would become useless like the other.

Meanwhile, Ravidasan made a desperate attempt to loosen Pazhuvetarayar’s hands from around his neck; but nothing availed. The old man’s iron grip did not slacken in the least. Ravidasan’s eyes began to bulge and roll. Gasping and stammering, he cried, “Devarala! Quickly! Quickly! Climb up to the temple! Push down the mandapam!”

Devaralan immediately sprang up and climbed onto the upper mandapam of the temple. There, a section of the mandapam had already cracked and was poised to fall at the slightest push. They had noticed this beforehand. Devaralan understood that this was what Ravidasan meant. With all the strength left in him, he pushed at the broken part of the mandapam. As it fell, it brought down with it a tree that stood nearby.

Pazhuvetarayar realized that the mandapam above was about to collapse. He released one hand from Ravidasan’s neck and tried to hold up the falling mandapam. At that moment, Ravidasan made a great effort, broke free from his grip, and moved aside. The tree and the mandapam crashed down upon Pazhuvetarayar. Struck on the head, Pazhuvetarayar lost consciousness.

chapters.title: The Comet Disappeared!
paragraphs: After a long while, when Pazhuvetarayar regained a sliver of consciousness, he found himself in the midst of a terrifying battlefield. Swords clashed against each other, ringing out with a resounding metallic hum. On one side, victory drums thundered. Along with them, thousands of voices shouted, “Long live the Maha Rajadhiraja, the Pandya King! Down with the enemies of the Pandyas!”
On the other side, thousands of voices screamed, “The king of the Gangas has fallen! Run! Run!” Amidst these, there were also voices trying to halt the fleeing men.

Suddenly, for a moment, silence descended upon the battlefield. Pazhuvetarayar looked around. He saw the legless Vijayalaya Chozhar being carried on the shoulders of another tall, broad-shouldered man. The man who bore him on his shoulders held two enormous swords, one in each hand.
“Chozha warriors! Stand firm! Pallavas! Do not flee! Death awaits in the river, death awaits in the field! Follow me! We will scatter our enemies to the winds!” he shouted.

The Chozha and Pallava soldiers, who had begun to flee, stopped when they saw Vijayalaya Chozhar and heard his words. The exhaustion and fear vanished from their faces, replaced once more by courage and valor. Those who had retreated began to advance again. Pazhuvetarayar looked once more at Vijayalaya Chozhar, who was the cause of this miraculous transformation. He also looked at the warrior who carried him on his shoulders. Astonishing! Astonishing! He realized that the warrior bearing Vijayalaya Chozhar was none other than himself.

That Pazhuvetarayar, with one hand, held the legless Vijayalaya Chozhar on his shoulder, and with the other, brandished a long sword as he plunged into the midst of the enemy. Wherever the two of them went, the heads of Pandya warriors rolled onto the ground.
