The tide of battle had completely turned. The Pandya army scattered and fled. The Chozhas and Pallavas emerged victorious. The victory drums resounded in all eight directions. Before the Pallava emperor, Vijayalaya Chozhar was seated! Beside him stood Pazhuvetarayar. The Pallava emperor looked at the Chozha king and said, “Bravest of the brave! Today, defeat has been turned into victory because of you! From now on, the Chozha land shall be a free land! You, your valiant son Aditya, and your descendants shall forever reign as independent kings of Chozha…” “You shall rule the land!” he declared. At once, Vijayalaya Chola turned to the Pazhuvettaraiyar standing near him and said, “Elder! It is only through you that this victory has been won for us. I appoint you as the Commander-in-Chief and the hereditary chieftain of the free Chola country. As long as your descendants remain loyal to the Chola dynasty, they too shall hold these titles of chieftain and commander!”
The face of Pazhuvettaraiyar, marked by wounds, blossomed with pride.

Suddenly, a fierce anger appeared on that face. The old Pazhuvettaraiyar looked at this new Pazhuvettaraiyar. “Oh wretch! Traitor! Outcaste! You are the very axe-handle come to destroy my lineage! For six generations we have gathered this precious warrior fame, and you have brought it all to ruin! You have betrayed your friends, betrayed your lords! You have given shelter in your house to the hereditary enemies of the Chola dynasty! You have given them wealth from your own treasury! Is it not because of you that today the Chola clan faces its final hour? The blame that you have earned shall never, ever be erased as long as the world endures!” he cursed. Tears streamed in torrents from the eyes of the accursed Pazhuvettaraiyar.

Then, more Pazhuvettaraiyars arrived. Each recounted the valiant deeds he had performed. Each cursed the Pazhuvettaraiyar. Then, together, they all cursed him. “Outcaste! You have committed treachery against your clan and your king! You have destroyed all the warrior fame that we earned by risking our lives! How did your mind come to this?” they cried.

The Pazhuvettaraiyars disappeared. The Kodumbalur Velirs and the Thirukovalur Malayamans arrived. They surrounded the solitary Pazhuvettaraiyar. “Shame! Are you even a man? You used to boast that you and your lineage upheld the Chola dynasty! What do you say now? You have become the Yama of the Chola clan! Sinner! Where is your future?” they mocked, beating their drums and laughing scornfully.

Behind them, the people of Chola Nadu, gathered in a crowd, began to hurl stones and clods of earth at Pazhuvettaraiyar. At that moment, Sundara Chola Chakaravarthi pushed through the crowd and, with feeble steps, came forward. He looked at the Velirs, the Malayamans, and the others with anger.

“Shame! What are you doing? Are you throwing stones and earth at Pazhuvettaraiyar, the bravest of the brave? Are you calling him a traitor? Even if I and my dynasty are destroyed by Pazhuvettaraiyar’s betrayal, so be it. None of you should blame him! Chieftain! Come with me to the palace!” he commanded.
The crowd dispersed. Sundara Chola too disappeared. Only his younger brother, Kalanthaka Kandar, remained before Pazhuvettaraiyar.
He stood still. “Anna! The Emperor has placed such trust in us! Can we betray him? Can we keep in our palace the she-demon who has come to destroy his dynasty?” he said. At once, he too disappeared.

Vandiyathevan, Kandamaaran, and the other young men like them surrounded the great Pazhuvetaraiyar. “Old man with the graying moustache! Only your desires have not turned gray, it seems? You have been ruined by your obsession with a woman! What do the ‘sixty-four’ scars on your body say now? Are they the noble wounds earned in valor? Or are they the festering sores bought with the wages of treachery?” they taunted, and burst into mocking laughter.
Pazhuvetaraiyar tried to draw his sword to kill them. But the sword was not in its usual place.
At that moment, Princess Kundavai entered. She gestured with her hand to silence the laughter of the young men.

“Grandfather! Do not pay heed to their playful words. Drive out the venomous serpent in the guise of a woman from your palace! All will be set right!” she said. They withdrew. The women of the Pazhuvetaraiyar clan began to arrive—ten, a hundred, a thousand—women of six generations came and surrounded him.

“Alas! Must such a fate befall you? Must our heroic clan bear this great shame because of you? Did we not send our husbands, our brothers, our sons whom we bore for ten months, to the battlefield for the sake of Chola Nadu? Did they not shed their blood and give their lives, bringing unparalleled glory to the house of Pazhuvur? Have you swept all that away in a single moment?” they wailed.
“Women! Close your mouths and go to the inner chambers. No disgrace will come from me!” Pazhuvetaraiyar replied in distress.

At that moment, the women pointed in one direction. Yama, the god of death, appeared, riding his buffalo, holding a spear and the noose of death in his hands; he approached Pazhuvetaraiyar. As he passed, he said, “Pazhuvetaraiya! My deepest respects to you! Did you not help me take the lives of Sundara Chozhan and his two sons all in a single day? My thanks to you!” said Yama.

“No, no! I did not help you; I will not help you! I will stop you! Yama! Halt! Halt!” Pazhuvetaraiyar cried out. He tried to rush forward to stop Yama. But some force held him back. Some great weight pressed him down. He could not move from where he stood.

“Did you see? What we said has come true!” cried the women of the Pazhuvettarayar clan, wailing aloud. Many among them broke into lamentation and wept. The sound of their mourning grew louder with every passing minute. Pazhuvettarayar could not bear it. He tried to speak, but his words were drowned in the noise of their crying. He could not endure the weeping and lamentation. He tried to cover his ears with both hands. But his arms lay motionless; he could not lift them. With great effort, he shook his hands free and raised them. In that struggle, his eyelids opened as well. Suddenly, memory returned. He realized that all he had experienced until then were visions conjured by his fevered mind. Yet the wailing sound continued to ring in his ears. He listened more closely. It was not the wailing of women; it was the howling of jackals!
As he drifted in and out of consciousness, a snatch of conversation that had brushed his ears came back to him.
“The old man is dead!” said one voice.
“Look carefully! Pazhuvettarayar’s life is so strong that even Yama himself would fear to approach him!” said another.
“Even if Yama is afraid, the jackals are not. If there’s the slightest breath left in him, the jackals will take care of it. By dawn, only the old man’s bones will remain!”
“You pushed aside the broken mandapam at the right moment. Otherwise, I would have met the same fate. The old man would have killed me!”
“Where? Let’s see if you can move the mandapam!”
After a pause, “It doesn’t budge an inch! With one enemy’s palanquin, we’ve set up a hero’s stone for another!” said the sorcerer, and laughed raucously.
“That’s enough laughter, come! The boat is drifting away with the current. Soon, we won’t be able to cross the Kollidam!”

Recalling these words, Pazhuvettarayar examined his own condition. Yes; half of the palanquin mandapam had collapsed upon him. Its great weight was pressing him down. Yet, he was still able to breathe—how?

Fortunately, the tree that fell along with the mandapam landed upon his shoulder, and the mandapam itself crashed down upon the tree. It was that very tree, leaning against the mandapam, which saved his life. Had the mandapam fallen directly upon him, his chest and head would have been crushed to pieces. The old warrior marveled at the strength of his own body. He realized, with astonishment, that even after bearing such a tremendous weight for so long, his life had not yet left him. But could he still preserve this stubborn life of his?

Yes; by any means necessary, he must save himself. He must survive and avert the peril that threatened the Chola dynasty. If he failed to do so, an indelible disgrace would surely befall his lineage in this world. Even if he ascended to the heavens, his ancestors would curse him there as well. Therefore, no matter the hardship, he must push aside this tree and the mandapam and rise. Alas! How long had he lain here, unconscious, he could not tell. In the meantime, might the very calamities he wished to prevent have already come to pass?

Meanwhile, the howling of jackals drew nearer and nearer. He could hear the sound of their breathing close to his head! Ah! Had even these jackals lost their fear at the sight of Pazhuvetarayar? Let them come; he would show them! Not with one hand alone, but with both, Pazhuvetarayar began to test his strength. Summoning every ounce of power left in his body, he tried to lift the tree that had fallen upon him. As the tree rose little by little, the slab of the mandapam resting atop it began to shift and slide aside. The hoarse cries he uttered from time to time drove the advancing jackals back.

After what seemed an age—an endless moment of struggle—the tree and the mandapam slab that had pinned him shifted aside and released him. Exhausted by the effort, he lay there for a while, drawing deep, heavy breaths. He gazed up at the sky. Because he was close to the mandapam, and because many trees had fallen in the storm, the expanse of the heavens was clearly visible. Now, the dark clouds no longer veiled the sky. Countless stars shone, like diamonds scattered above. Wisps of cloud, at times obscuring and then revealing the stars, drifted swiftly and dissolved into nothingness.

Suddenly, a strange star appeared in the northern sky and caught his attention. Ah! Was it the very comet that, a few days ago, had possessed such a long tail? How much it had shrunk now! The tale of that star—

At one end, it stretched out to about a foot in length, pale like a wisp of smoke. What could be the reason that the tail, which just ten days ago spanned an entire corner of the sky, had now shrunk so much?...

He tore his gaze from the heavens and looked all around him. The jackals had not yet left! There must have been ten, twenty, perhaps fifty jackals. Their eyes glowed like embers in the darkness of the forest. It seemed as if they were waiting for the old man to die! Let them wait! Let them wait! Such was the respect these jackals showed to Pazhuvetarayar!...

Suddenly, the sky, the earth, and the entire forest region were flooded with light. Pazhuvetarayar’s eyes were dazzled. It was not lightning—what else could it be? He looked up at the sky. He saw a blazing fireball, shining brilliantly, traveling across a corner of the celestial sphere. Its radiance made his eyes smart. He closed his eyes for a moment, then opened them again. The fireball had grown smaller; its light was fading; suddenly, it vanished altogether. Darkness enveloped him once more.

What could this marvel mean? Pazhuvetarayar pondered, still gazing at the sky. He looked to the place where the short-tailed comet had been moments before. It was no longer there. Ah! The comet had fallen! What did this signify? What would be the consequence? It was surely an omen that some calamity was about to befall the world. It was a sign that some misfortune would strike the royal family. When the tailed star disappears, someone belonging to the royal clan will die. This is a belief that has long been widespread among the people. There are those who say it is not so. The truth or falsehood of it will be known tomorrow. Tomorrow? No! It will be known today itself…! Look, the sky in the east is turning pale! Dawn is about to break! Before this night ends, three dreadful, ominous events may occur in three different places. Only I know the details of what is about to happen. And only I possess the power to prevent them. If I succeed in stopping them, even the evil omen of the fallen comet will be overcome. If not… Pazhuvetarayar could not bear to think of it. It must be prevented! The three who belong to the Chola dynasty must be saved at all costs.

His first duty—the most important duty—was to protect Aditya Karikalan! If any harm befell him, the blame would fall squarely upon his own head. Therefore, he must cross the Kollidam and reach Kadambur at once. Before that, it would be wise to go to Kudanthai and send warnings to Thanjavur and Nagapattinam. After that, fate would take its course. That was all he could do!

Pazhuvetaraiyar tried to rise. His whole body ached with wounds. The spot where the tree had fallen on his chest caused an unbearable pain. One leg felt as if it were broken. His body was covered with various injuries. Yet, the valiant elder paid no heed to any of these. Gritting his teeth, he made a mighty effort and stood up; he looked all around. Fortunately, the jackals that had been waiting for his death had already run away. Perhaps they had been frightened by the flood of light that had burst forth when the comet fell!

He somehow determined in which direction Kudanthai city lay from there, and set out. He planted his feet firmly and began to walk. All along the way, trees felled by the storm lay strewn about. Due to the heavy rains and the breach of the Kollidam, the land was a flooded wilderness. Pazhuvetaraiyar paid no heed to these obstacles. The turmoil in his heart made him forget the hardships of his body. Even so, time kept passing. By the time two ‘jamams’ had passed after dawn, he approached the city of Kudanthai. He did not wish to go into the central part of that great city. If people saw him in this state, they would gather around him. They would ask questions—what, why, how. He would not be able to accomplish the task he wished to do swiftly and skillfully.

Therefore, he decided to remain at the outskirts of the city, in a place where there were not many people, to catch hold of someone and send a palm-leaf message to Thanjai and Nagai. Afterwards, he would procure a vehicle and set out for Kadambur. The astrologer who lived near the Durga Amman temple came to his mind; yes, that was a secluded area, with no other houses nearby. The astrologer was a suitable man, a person of gentle nature. He was needed by the royal family and the chief minister. So what? Whoever it was, they would do this task. Since he was needed by the royal family, he would do it with even more eagerness. Ah! Now, he could also test whether the astrologer truly knew astrology, and whether there was any truth in the science of astrology.

Pazhuvetaraiyar approached the Amman temple and the astrologer’s house. The tall, large tree in front of the temple had been broken and lay fallen by the storm. That caught his attention first. Next, his gaze fell on the twin-horse chariot standing beside the temple. It was a chariot of peculiar construction. The upper part of the chariot was shaped like a boat. In times of flood, when one had to travel urgently, such chariots were used. When crossing great rivers, if suddenly the river flooded—

If the water rises too much, the boat can be detached from the chariot and used separately. If the horses are unyoked, they can swim across and reach the shore. Those who came in the chariot can push the boat along and reach the bank.

Such chariots are rare in Chola country. Whose chariot could this be? It must belong to the palace; or perhaps to the Prime Minister. It seems that those who arrived in it are now inside the astrologer’s house, consulting him! Who could they be? Should I ask the charioteer? No! If he sees me, he might get frightened. It is better to go straight into the astrologer’s house and see for myself. Whoever is inside, if I can get hold of this chariot, it would be convenient for my return to Kadambur, wouldn’t it?

When Pazhuvettarayar reached the doorstep of the astrologer’s house, he heard women’s voices from within. The old man’s heart leapt. Whose voice is that? Why? Does it not sound like the voice of the young princess Kundavai? Why has she come here? Should I go in at this moment?… At first, he thought so, but immediately changed his mind. If it is indeed the young princess, then it is all for the best. Like a ripe fruit slipping into milk, fortune has favored me. If I can convey the matter into the ears of Kundavai Devi, my burden will be lifted. If I warn her specifically about the dangers that may befall her father and brother, that clever woman will take whatever precautions are needed. Then I can peacefully return to Kadambur. Is that not where my most important duty lies?

When Pazhuvettarayar entered the astrologer’s house, the same guard we have seen before—the astrologer’s disciple—stopped him. The disciple could not recognize him in his current attire. That is why he shouted “Stop!” in a harsh voice and blocked his way.

Pazhuvettarayar let out a grunt, grabbed the disciple by the neck, and shoved him aside. The disciple, performing a somersault, landed in the street. Like a raging elephant, Pazhuvettarayar strode into the astrologer’s house.

chapters.title: The Boon Kundavai Sought
paragraphs: When Pazhuvetaraiyar entered the astrologer’s house, Kundavai Piratti and Vanathi were truly there. Ever since dawn had broken and the queen of Eezham was nowhere to be seen, Kundavai’s mind had lost its peace. At the same time, the disappearance of Poonguzhali had heightened her distress. She went to see the Prime Minister Aniruddha. At that moment, news had arrived regarding Arulmozhi Chozhan. She learned that, due to the storm that struck Nagapattinam, he had been forced to reveal himself, and that a great crowd had gathered and was bringing him to Thanjai with triumphant shouts. Kundavai’s agitation knew no bounds. She felt that some calamity was about to befall them.

She wished to meet Ponniyin Selvan on the way, speak with him, and inform him of all that had transpired in Thanjai. If he tried to enter the Thanjai fort surrounded by a vast crowd, Pazhuvetaraiyar’s soldiers would surely attempt to stop him. Meanwhile, news had come that Boothi Vikrama Kesari had reached Kodumbalur with the southern forces. The two armies might clash near Thanjai. That would certainly wound her father’s heart; it might even endanger his very life. Who could say what further consequences might arise? The hearts of the people, already unsettled by the storm, were in turmoil. Surely, some misfortune was bound to occur; a great civil strife might erupt, threatening to destroy the entire Chola land. How could it be quelled afterwards? Was it not better to prevent it beforehand, rather than try to stop it once it had begun? Otherwise, all the efforts made so far would be in vain.

Therefore, Arulmozhi Chozhan must be met on the way and detained for a while at Pazhayarai. The elder Pazhuvetaraiyar must also be summoned from Kadambur. Only after informing him that Arulmozhi had no desire to rule, and obtaining his consent, should Arulmozhi be brought to Thanjai.

Having thus resolved within herself, without even telling her father, and confiding only in her mother and Aniruddha, she set out, taking with her the inseparable Vanathi. Before going to Pazhayarai, she wished to see the Kudanthai astrologer once more. Is it not human nature, when anxiety grows too great, to seek knowledge of the future through astrology? As was her custom, she left her chariot near the Amman temple and entered the astrologer’s house. She had barely begun to express her worries to the astrologer when, suddenly, a commotion arose at the entrance of the house. Above all, the unmistakable booming voice of Pazhuvetaraiyar sent a thrill of apprehension through her. There was only one man who could roar with such majesty—the great Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar himself.

It appeared that Pazhuvetaraiyar was pushing past the astrologer’s disciple, who was trying in vain to block his way, and was about to enter. How had he come here? For what reason? And at this very moment?

Ah! Perhaps he had come to consult the astrologer! If she could overhear their conversation, she might learn what was in his mind. At this time, when the kingdom and the royal family were facing such grave peril, knowing the thoughts of Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar would be of immense value. Now, a rare opportunity had presented itself. But if he saw her and Vanathi there, what would he think? Surely, he would misunderstand! There could be no doubt. Therefore, it would be best to remain out of his sight...
Kundavai, signaling her intention to the astrologer with a gesture, quickly took Vanathi by the hand and hurried into the next room.

No sooner had the door to the room they entered been closed than Pazhuvetaraiyar strode inside. The astrologer, rising in a flurry, greeted him with folded hands and gazed at him intently, then looked all around. Surprise and disappointment were evident on his face, but only for a moment. He quickly composed himself.

“Astrologer! Do you know who I am? It is I, the chief dignitary, Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar! Why do you stare at me so? Have I changed so much that you do not recognize me? I have come to you for an important matter! You must do me a great favor. But first, if you have anything to eat, bring it to me; I am very hungry. I will tell you what I need as I eat,” he said.

The astrologer, flustered, replied, “Sir! What great help could this poor wretch possibly render you? It is the good fortune earned by my ancestors that has brought you to seek out this humble hut. I cannot offer you a feast befitting your rank. Yet, whatever is in this hut is yours. Please, be seated. Why do you remain standing? I was startled the moment I saw you, and so I failed to welcome and serve you properly. Alas! There is not even a seat worthy of you in this humble dwelling. With your generous heart, you must be content to sit on that plank,” he said, pointing to the very planks upon which Kundavai and Vanathi had just been seated.

Pazhuvettaraiyar glanced at the platters and the flowers scattered beside them, then said, “Astrologer! No, I do not have time to sit. If you have anything to eat, wrap it in a leaf and hand it to me. I must send an urgent message to Thanjai, to my brother Kaalandhaka Kandan... Do you have a palm-leaf and a stylus? ...No, never mind! I do not have time to sit and write a letter. I will give you my signet ring. Can you take it and go to Thanjavur at once? Or, your disciple who was standing at the door—he looks like a sturdy fellow. Can you send him immediately?” he asked.

“Whatever your command, I shall do exactly that. Both I and my disciple can go, if needed. But, my lord! Please be gracious enough to sit for a short while in this poor man’s hut, and taste the nectar this humble one offers before you leave!”

“Astrologer! Why do you keep calling yourself a poor man, a humble one? I have heard that even kings and royal princesses often come seeking your house. I am perhaps the only one who has not come to you for astrology. I now realize that was a mistake. Had I come, perhaps such terrible calamities would not have occurred…”

“Sir! Your words cause me great distress. What disaster has befallen you? I was indeed startled when I saw you in this state. Were you caught in the storm, in the flood? I heard that the Kollidam river had breached its banks. Perhaps because of that…? My lord!…”
“The younger queen of Pazhuvur is safe, is she not?” the astrologer asked. At this, Pazhuvettaraiyar laughed with a terrible tone.

“No, no! Nothing has happened to the younger queen of Pazhuvur. She has not drowned and died in the Kollidam. She should still be safe in the Kadambur palace. But that wretch—whether she will be alive by this time tomorrow, I cannot say. Astrologer! Can you say? I have heard that you possess the horoscopes of all the royal family members. Is that true? Do you have Nandini’s horoscope—the horoscope of the enchantress I foolishly married in my old age?”

The astrologer, now even more flustered, said, “My lord! What are you saying? Are you testing me? I do not have the younger queen’s horoscope. If you can tell me her birth date and time, I can cast her horoscope.” “No, no; I do not need it. I shall divine Nandini’s horoscope myself. I have already resolved that her life shall end by my own hand. If you know about the horoscopes of others, tell me. What do the stars say about the Emperor’s fate?… Ah! You shake your head! You will not speak. You think I am testing you. Or perhaps you believe all your astrology is mere nonsense—who knows?… Astrologer! Leave aside the horoscopes for now. For some days, a comet has been appearing in the sky, and this morning it fell from the heavens and vanished—did you know of this? If so, can you tell me what it means? Does it foretell some great calamity? Does it portend danger for the Emperor or his children? If you refuse to answer even this, then your astrology is nothing but empty prattle!”

“Lord! Do not judge so harshly. It is the tradition of our profession that astrology should not be consulted in matters concerning the state. I did not witness the comet fall with my own eyes this morning. I saw a strange, dazzling light and, surprised, I immediately went outside. The comet, whose tail had been shrinking these past days, was nowhere to be seen. The appearance and fall of a comet is said to signify fortune or misfortune for royal families. But that is not part of astrological science; it is an ancient belief of the people. I do not place much faith in it. Even this morning, I have heard that the Emperor is well.”
“That is our good fortune. Nothing must befall the Emperor tonight. If he remains unharmed until tomorrow, then there is no more cause for worry. Do you know anything about Ponniyin Selvan?…”

“I heard that late last night, the prince arrived at Thiruvarur. My lord! Tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of people are said to be gathering around him. Against his own wishes, they are bringing him to Thanjavur.”

“Ah! If only they could bring the prince safely to Thanjai, how wonderful that would be. But is it possible? Even if hundreds of thousands surround him, can they hold back Yama, the god of death? Speak, astrologer, speak! Even if you will not utter a prophecy, I shall. A great danger awaits the Emperor and his two sons today. Yama is drawing ever closer to them. The Emperor’s Yama hides in the treasury vaults of the Pazhuvur palace. Arulmozhi’s Yama is concealed in the mahout’s goad. If only someone could hold them back—” It is your responsibility to protect both the Emperor and Ponniyin Selvan. Take my signet ring and let your disciple go to Thanjavur. You must go to Thiruvarur and warn the prince. Will you do it? Will you depart at once?”

The astrologer faltered. A doubt arose in his mind—had the great Pazhuvettaraiyar lost his senses? But even so, it could not be said for certain. Everything he said seemed reasonable enough. Though he spoke with agitation and urgency, he appeared to be telling the truth. The young princess would also be listening to this conversation from within. He must learn her opinion. Somehow, he must send this old man away from here at once.
“By the grace of Durga Parameswari, I will fulfill your command to the best of my ability,” said the astrologer.
At that moment, from inside, came the sound of anklets worn by women.
“Ah! Durga Parameswari herself is blessing us with the sound of her anklets. Now, I may return to Kadambur. See, I am leaving…”
“Lord! You said you were hungry? Why not take a meal at this humble man’s house before you go—?”

“No, no! My hunger and thirst have vanished. I must fly back to Kadambur. There is a chariot standing near the temple, is there not? Whose is it, astrologer? I am going to take it. Once I reach the banks of the Kollidam, I will send it back. I will take only the boat from there…”
“Sir! That chariot… that chariot… I beg you, do not take it, have mercy on me…”

“Astrologer! Do not worry needlessly. To save the life of the crowned prince of the Chola land, I am taking that chariot. Durga Devi herself will grant her consent. If she blesses us again with the sound of her anklets, I will take it as a sign of her approval. Listen, there it is.”

As the great Pazhuvettaraiyar was speaking thus, the young princess Kundavai opened the door of the adjoining room and walked in, her anklets ringing softly. Pazhuvettaraiyar was neither surprised nor startled to see her.

“Mother! My guess was correct. I thought you must be in the next room. I do not have the courage to speak to you face to face. That is why I spoke so loudly, so that my words would reach your ears. You heard everything I told the astrologer, did you not?”

“Sir! You must forgive me. Please pardon the mistake I have made. When you entered this house so suddenly, I could not be certain that it was you. That is why I was compelled to listen in on your conversation. Forgive me!” said Kundavai.

“Mother! There is no reason for me to forgive you. It is I who must seek your forgiveness. I am not even sure if I am worthy to ask for pardon. If, before this night is over, I can reach Kadambur and prevent any harm from coming to the crown prince, then I shall have earned the right to beg your forgiveness. For three years, this old man’s eyes have been clouded by delusion. You tried so hard to open my eyes. You gave me so many hints. None of them reached my ears. My brother, Kalanthaka Kandan, too, tried to open my eyes. His efforts were in vain as well. Last night, by the grace of Durga Parameswari, I happened to overhear the conversation of two Pandya conspirators. Because of that, I learned the truth. That wretch, that traitor, that venomous serpent—I kept her in my own palace, nursed her, cherished her, raised her. She made me a traitor to my own clan, a traitor to the throne. She took treasures from the Chola kingdom and handed them over to the Pandya conspirators. Unless I kill that sinner Nandini with my own hands before this night is over, the fire raging in my heart will not be quenched…”

As Pazhuvetarayar was speaking thus, Kundavai did something wholly unexpected. Suddenly, she fell at his feet and bowed to him. Startled and unsure of what to do, Pazhuvetarayar stood frozen. The young princess rose and said, “Sir! You must grant me a boon!”

“Princess, it seems you are testing me. No! I am fully aware of how terrible my sins are. I am still pondering what penance I must do for them. But before that, I must save the three members of the Chola clan from the danger that threatens them tonight. Your father and your brothers must come to no harm this night. Help me with that. Let this one day pass; tomorrow, I myself will come to you and ask, ‘What punishment do I deserve? What penance must I do?’” he said.
“Sir! I do not presume to punish you, nor to prescribe penance for you. You stand in the place of my grandfather. You are worthy of my father’s reverence. Truly, I ask you only for a boon…”
“In that case, ask at once, child! There is no time now for idle talk.”
“Promise me that you will grant it!”
“For the betrayal I have committed against you and your family, nothing I can give will ever be enough. Whatever you ask, I will grant. Ask quickly!”
“You must promise that you will do nothing to the Young Queen, Nandini Devi. That is the boon I seek!”

“Child! What is this, some kind of game? Is this the time for such play? It is true that in my old age I have lost my wits. But do you wish to make me a complete madman? If I do not mete out just punishment to that conspirator, how can I punish the other traitors? Only after I have slain her with my own hand will I attend to any other matter. I will reveal all that is in my heart, and show that this old man could not be deceived by her until the very end, and then I will cut her down with my sword. If I give her any lesser punishment, I will not be a just man. After that, I will consider what just punishment I deserve myself. Go, child! Go! Do what you must to save your father and brother from the calamity that is about to befall them today!”
“I will, Sir! But should I not also try to protect my sister? The Young Queen Nandini is my sister. Whatever harm you do to her will also be a betrayal against the Chola dynasty!”
Pazhuvettaraiyar was plunged into a shock beyond all bounds. “Am I still dreaming?” his lips murmured.

“No, no! You are not dreaming. What you see and hear is the truth. Think for a moment; recall the events of the past. Do you remember that a noble lady saved my brother Arulmozhi from drowning in the Kaveri? That lady is the mother of the Young Queen Nandini. On the day you married the Young Queen and brought her to the palace, do you remember my father fainting and collapsing? Do you remember the mother of the Young Queen—”
The Emperor fainted, thinking he was seeing a vision. For a long time, he had believed she was dead. That is why, the sudden sight of the younger queen made him lose his memory…”

Other incidents, too, came to the mind of the Pazhuvettaraiyar. He recalled how, in the dead of night, he had brought Nandini before Sundara Chozha Chakravarthi, how the Emperor had cried out on seeing her, and the reasons Nandini had given for it—all these returned to his memory now.

“Mother! I understand that what you are saying is no jest. It is fate’s play that is truly wondrous. If the younger queen is your sister, then she is also Aditya Karikalan’s sister. Does anyone else know of this relationship besides you? Does the Emperor know?”

“Until two days ago, the Emperor believed my elder sister was dead. Even when that old woman came before him the other day, he thought she was a ghost and threw away his lamp in fright—only later did he believe…”
“I did not ask about that, Mother! Does Karikalan know that the younger queen is his sister?”
“He must have come to know by now. He had sent a message through a valiant warrior of the Vanar clan. I sent word to him through that man…”
“Ah! You must be speaking of Vandiyathevan Vallavaraiyan!”
“Yes, sir!”

“I do not think he would have told Karikalan. Even if he did, Karikalan would not have believed it. Did I myself not find it hard to believe? How then would he? The younger queen cannot know this news; even if she does, it is of no use. The conspirators will try to achieve their aim by other means. Tonight, they will surely make their attempt. Mother! The news you have revealed has made my responsibility even more terrible. I must protect the younger queen, Nandini, from committing fratricide. I will go to Kadambur at once. I will take the chariot in which you arrived. It is your duty to ensure that nothing happens to the Emperor and to Ponniyin Selvan!”

“Sir! You need not worry. I am leaving for Thanjavur this very moment. I will arrange for a vehicle from Pazhayarai. There is no need to worry about Ponniyin Selvan. The day and hour of his birth will protect him!” she said.

“Girl! Do not become careless by placing your faith in astrology! Even if astrologers know the truth in their hearts, they will never speak it openly! They will always say something with double meanings. After everything has happened, they will claim, ‘Did I not say so before?’ Even if you trust astrology, never trust the astrologers themselves!” With these words, and a dismissive wave of his hand, Pazhuvettarayar strode out.

Scarcely a few seconds after he had left, Azhwarkkadiyan entered the room. “Yes, yes! I agree with what the nobleman just said. Even if one believes in astrology, one must never believe the astrologers!” he declared.

chapters.title: Vanathi’s Vow
paragraphs: Kundavai looked at Azhwarkadiyan, who had entered with a sudden, thunderous presence, and asked, “Thirumalai, how did you sprout up here? Why have you come?”

“Ammani! It’s all because of this astrologer’s deceitful words! This morning I asked him, ‘Will the task I am about to undertake succeed?’ He said, ‘It will.’ But I couldn’t even get a short distance from this place. How can my mission succeed like this? That is why I agreed with what Pazhuvettaraiyar said just now. I came to find out whether this man’s astrology itself is false, or if he has deliberately misled me. When I heard Pazhuvettaraiyar’s voice here, my suspicion about this man only grew stronger. But I never expected to see you here.”
“It is only natural that you did not expect me. Why did you come? What was the task for which you asked the astrologer if you would succeed? There is no secret here, is there?” asked the princess.

“Is it possible that there could be a secret unknown to you? By the Emperor’s command, the Prime Minister sent me last night to Nagapattinam, to bring the prince back with me. On the way, I was also instructed to see Sembiyan Maadevi and deliver a letter to her… When did you leave Thanjavur, Devi?”
“We left a little after dawn. Why do you ask, Thirumalai?”
“I asked to find out whether the Kodumbalur troops have already surrounded the Thanjai fort.”
“What? What?”

“Yes, Devi! Do you not know? Last night, after seeing the Emperor, when the Prime Minister returned to his palace, two pieces of news awaited him. The first was that the prince had set out from Nagapattinam, surrounded by a great crowd…”

“I too learned that this morning. I set out from there precisely to intercept my brother and keep him here. But you said there was another piece of news—what is it?” Azhwarkkadiyan pointed to Vanathi and asked, “Amma! Why have you brought this princess of Kodumbalur here?”
“She came as she always does; I brought her. Why do you ask?”
“I hesitate to speak of the second matter in the presence of this princess.”
“Speak, Thirumalai! Do you not know how close she is to me? Anything I know, she may know as well…”

“Even so, this matter concerns the princess herself. Last night, the Prime Minister received news that the Southern Commander, Boothi Vikrama Kesari, is marching towards Tanjore Fort with a great army. The Commander himself sent a palm-leaf letter to the Prime Minister. In it, he accused the Pazhuvettaraiyars of imprisoning the Emperor in Tanjore Fort and keeping the younger prince hidden away in some secret place. He demanded that the Pazhuvettaraiyars immediately relinquish their authority and the responsibility for Tanjore’s security, and that the prince be brought forth and handed over. Otherwise, by this evening, the siege of Tanjore Fort would begin. Ammani! Are you not aware that the Kodumbalur forces have already drawn near Tanjore from the south and the west? Did you not know?”
“I did not know. The Prime Minister has not spoken a word of this to me.”
“If he had, perhaps you would not have left Tanjore Fort. Most importantly, the Prime Minister may have wished to send the Kodumbalur Princess away at once…”
“Why is that? What harm if she were there?”
“If the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar wished, he might even imprison this princess…”
“Would he dare such a thing? Are you speaking the truth?”
“Yes, Devi! Moreover, if you hear the message sent by the Southern Commander, you will understand for yourself…”
“What? What more?”

“The royal wedding between Prince Arulmozhi Varman and Princess Vanathi Devi of Kodumbalur must be conducted at once. Since Aditya Karikalan has declared that he does not desire the throne, Arulmozhi Chozhar should be crowned as the next heir apparent, the Yuvaraja. Such are his demands. He has also sent word that if these requests are not agreed to, he will reduce the Tanjore fort to rubble within three days. He claims that the people of Chozha Nadu support him…”
Vanathi, who had been listening to all this, burst out in agitation, “Akka! Has my Periyappa suddenly gone mad?”

“Why do you say that, Vanathi?” Kundavai asked. “Your Periyappa has only now openly declared what many have long held in their hearts. Since the Pazhuvettaraiyars have begun their efforts to crown Madurantakan, the Kodumbalur king and the Thirukovalur Malayaman have started to speak out plainly in this manner…”
“Yes, mother! Even the Thirukovalur Malayaman has arrived near Kadambur fort with a great army. From what he said to me, I guessed as much. The Prime Minister has also received this information…”
“But there is news I know now that neither of those two are aware of. I must speak with both of them and prevent a civil war from breaking out. I do not know how I am going to do it…”
“Mother! The situation has reached a critical point now. It seems certain that a great Bharata war is inevitable…”

“You are right to call it a Bharata war, Thirumalai! If war breaks out now, it will be a fratricidal conflict. It will be a war of total destruction, waged among kin and kinsmen. Vanathi! Listen to this! My grandfather’s father, the renowned Parantaka Chakravarti, married a woman from the Pazhuvettaraiyar clan. Their daughter—my younger grandmother—was married to the king of Kodumbalur. My grandfather Arinjaya married a woman from Kodumbalur. My own father married the daughter of the Thirukovalur Malayaman. Thus, these three royal houses are closely bound to ours by ties of marriage. They are interwoven, one within the other. Yet now, they are girding themselves for battle against each other! What fate is this? It seems as if the Chozha kingdom itself will be destroyed by their quarrels!”

“Akka! I have no worries about all that. Let them fight and die however they wish. But why must my name be dragged into this by my great father? I feel like turning back at once and quarreling with my uncle…”

“What use is that, my dear? Your great father will not listen to what you say. Even if you and I go together and plead with him, it will be of no avail. Old men like your uncle will not heed the words of young women like us. Only through my brother Arulmozhi can this conflict be prevented. Thirumalai! Why have you returned? Where is Arulmozhi now?”

“I heard he intended to leave Thiruvarur last night. But the whole way is flooded, so he could not come. I too tried to go beyond Pazhaiyarai, but had to turn back. The Kudamurutti has overflowed and turned everything into a sea…”

“The flood will subside somehow. After that, Arulmozhi must come this way, must he not? We have no choice but to wait until then. But I am anxious that something untoward may happen in Thanjai before that. Thirumalai! Can you go back to Thanjavur at once, meet the Kodumbalur lord, and convey the message I give you? Will you tell him not to lay siege to the Thanjai fort until Arulmozhi arrives?”
“Akka! May I go to Thanjai with him as well?”
“What will you do by going with this man, my dear?”
“I will go and quarrel with my great father.”
“What will you quarrel about? Will he listen to you and stop the conflict?”
“If he stops the conflict, let him. If not, let whatever destruction must happen, happen. But I will insist that my name not be dragged into this.”
“They are dragging your name into it? For what reason?”
“Did you not hear what this Veera Vaishnavar just said, Akka?” said Vanathi, bowing her head in embarrassment.
“Who said what about you? Thirumalai! What did you say about this girl?”
“I told you, did I not, about the Commander’s insistence that she should be married to Ponniyin Selvan? It seems he is referring to that!”
“Vanathi! What objection do you have to that? Do you not wish to marry Ponniyin Selvan?”

“Whether I wish it or not, what is the point in speaking of it now? What I object to is my father discussing my marriage and coronation on my behalf. Is it not becoming clear that my elder father has started this conflict solely to seat me on the Chola throne?...”

At that moment, a woman’s voice said, “It seems the Princess of Kodumbalur has a great aversion to ascending the throne!” Hearing this, everyone turned to look in the direction of the voice. There stood Poonguzhali, the boatwoman.
Kundavai looked at her in surprise. “Girl! How did you come here? This morning, we searched everywhere for you and the Queen of Eezham, unable to find you. Where is your aunt?” she asked.

“Devi! Forgive me! My aunt forcibly dragged me through the secret passage of the Pazhuvoor palace and sent me out of the fort. She could not tolerate even a single day of my staying in the Thanjai palace! And truly, I too do not like palace life! When even the Princess of Kodumbalur has grown weary of the throne, how could someone like me enjoy living in a palace?” said Poonguzhali.
“Girl! Whatever we ask, you answer something else! It seems your mind is not in its proper state,” said Kundavai.

“Sister! Her mind is perfectly sound. She says such things deliberately to insult me. Apparently, I am eager to ascend the throne of Chola Nadu and become the Empress! That is why I wish to marry your brother—Ponniyin Selvan! I know her heart very well,” said Vanathi.
“Will the proverb ‘A snake knows the legs of another snake’ ever be proved false?” said Poonguzhali.
“Ladies! Enough! You do not know what to say at what time. Poonguzhali! Where is your aunt now?” Kundavai asked.
“She is in the treasury chamber of the Pazhuvoor palace…”
“For what reason?”

“There’s a murderer hiding there, with a spear in his hand. Ah! If only you could recall the trick we played on him together at dawn today! Thinking the two of us were ghostly women, he was so terrified—he ran here and there in panic!” With that, Poonguzhali burst into peals of laughter.
This girl is surely touched by madness, thought Kundavai to herself, and asked, “Tell me the rest! Who is he? Why is he hiding there? How did you find out?”

“I do not know all that, Devi! My aunt—though she cannot speak or hear—possesses a wondrous power to know things that none of us can perceive. Somehow, she learned that he is waiting there to kill someone in the palace. Devi! Do you know why my aunt tried to break the arms of the ten-headed Ravana statue?”
“I do not know; if you do, tell me at once!”

“When my aunt tried to shatter Ravana’s arms, you all thought she was mad—insane. But my aunt is not mad. Right between those arms of Ravana lies the secret tunnel that leads to the treasure vault of the Pazhuvettaraiyars.”
“Ah! Is that so?” Kundavai exclaimed in wonder.
“That’s how the mute queen from Eezham managed to enter the emperor’s palace!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.

“All these days, we who have lived in the palace never knew there was such a secret passage! Never mind that—why didn’t you come to the palace at once and tell us all this? Why did you leave your aunt alone and come here?” asked the young princess.
“It was my aunt’s stubbornness. She insisted on watching over the man hiding there herself and sent me out!”
“Why? Why? Is there something even more important than that? Did she send you for some urgent reason?”
“Yes, Ammani!”
“What is it, girl?”
"Ponniyin Selvan must be in some kind of danger—my aunt must have sensed it with her extraordinary powers. That is why she sent me to the place where he is!"
"Ah! So you were on your way to seek out Ponniyin Selvan’s whereabouts? If that is so, why did you stop?"

"No, Devi! I will tell you the truth. I have resolved that I will no longer involve myself in palace affairs. I was on my way to Kodikkarai; but on the way, this brave Vaishnavan met me and brought me here!… If I had known you were here, I would not have come!"
"Girl! Why have you grown so averse to the palace? Why have you come to dislike us? Who has wronged you?" asked the young princess Kundavai.

"No one has done anything to me. I have no grievance against anyone. Just as some people are not tempted by the throne, so too am I not drawn to palace life, that is all!" said Poonguzhali, and then glanced sidelong at Vanathi with a smile.
Noticing this, Vanathi, as if seized by a sudden passion, stepped forward and said:

"Akka! Once again she is mocking me. I will say it—listen, I swear it upon your sacred feet. I swear by the voice of the heavens and by Mother Earth as witness. If Ponniyin Selvan escapes safely from this land, if he willingly takes my hand in marriage, if such a great fortune is granted to me, then I vow that I shall never, not even for a single day, sit upon the throne of the Tanjai palace! This is my oath! My solemn vow!"

chapters.title: The Roof Floated!
paragraphs: At that moment, no one had expected that the Princess of Kodumbalur would make such a vow. All who heard it were struck with astonishment.

The young princess, her voice rising with a mingling of anger and pity, said, “Girl! What is this vow? Why did you take it? Is there such foolishness in the world? You speak as if you are possessed by some madness!”
“No, Akka! No! I am not mad. My mind is clear. What I have just spoken aloud for all to hear is a decision I have long pondered and resolved within myself,” replied Vanathi.

Before Kundavai could respond, Poonguzhali’s laughter caught her attention. It seemed, for a moment, as if that girl truly had been seized by madness. First, she laughed out loud, a bubbling, ringing laughter. Then, covering her face with her hands, she began to sob, her shoulders shaking. Suddenly, she stopped her weeping and, in a soft voice, began to sing:
“When the sea’s waves are stilled, Why does the ocean within surge and swell?”
Kundavai turned to Alwarkadiyan and said, “It seems these two girls together will drive me mad as well. Thirumalai! You set out to meet the prince—why have you brought her back here with you?”

“Devi! I did set out to meet Ponniyin Selvan. But the roads were flooded everywhere—I could not go further. I saw that she, too, was stranded, unable to proceed. She said that if I could arrange a boat, she would row herself to Thiruvarur. For that reason, I returned to the astrologer. When I saw your chariot-boat near the temple, I was delighted. I thought I could ask you for the boat and take her across. But the Pazhuvettaraiyar has taken both the chariot and the boat!” said Alwarkadiyan.

“What do you propose now? You heard everything the Pazhuvettaraiyar said, did you not?” asked Kundavai. “Yes, Mother! After hearing that, every minute wasted here feels like an age. From what this woman says, it seems the Emperor truly faces a terrible danger. Even the Prime Minister may not know of it. Therefore, you must take the Princess of Kodumbalur and go to Thanjavur at once. If the Kodumbalur forces have perhaps besieged the fort, none but you could get past their lines. If Vanathi Devi comes with you, it will be even easier. I will calm this boatwoman and bring her along, find a boat, and go to Ponniyin Selvan. I have already sent the astrologer’s disciple to fetch a boat!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
Vanathi, startled, sprang up and glared at him. “No! No! I will go only to Ponniyin Selvan! Even if I must die, I will die at his feet!” she declared.

Hearing this, Poonguzhali cried out in a shrill voice, “Vaishnavite! I cannot come with you! My lovers are calling me on the Kodi shore! In the dead of night, my fire-breathing lovers are calling me! The Princess sent a palm-leaf letter, and even to that valiant Vanar clan warrior I showed my lovers. I must go to them!” she shouted.

Until now, the astrologer had listened to all their conversation in astonishment, without joining in. Now he interrupted. “Mother! Mother! All of you, please be silent for a moment!” he pleaded, raising his voice.
For a minute, all conversation ceased. Then, another sound arose—a tremendous, awe-inspiring roar, like the tumult of waves in a storm-tossed sea.
“Ladies! You have come to this sinner’s hut at such a time! I am the one who foretells the future for the whole land. Yet I failed to warn you and send you away!” the astrologer lamented.
“Sir! What is this? What new danger is coming for us?” Kundavai asked.

“Mother! My disciple told me this morning that the flood in the royal canal is rising and may break the northern bank. If the canal bursts, all that water will pour into the Kaveri. If the Kaveri overflows, this poor man’s house will be completely submerged. This house stands very close to the river. Come! Come! Come outside!” cried the astrologer, running out of the house in terror.

Everyone followed him outside. With a face full of dread, the astrologer pointed and exclaimed, “Look!” In the southwest direction he indicated, an extraordinary sight appeared. A lush green wall, as tall as half a coconut tree—an expansive wall, long and slightly curved—was seen advancing towards the house with a rumbling noise. In a single instant, everyone present realized that the banks of the Kaveri had burst, and the floodwaters were surging forward like that wall.

“Amma! Come! Everyone, run this way! We can climb up onto the Amman temple mandapam and stand there! There’s no other way to escape! It was indeed wise that I sent my disciple Thirumalai to fetch a boat! Hurry, come!” cried the astrologer, leading the way.

The others followed him. All of Poonguzhali’s wildness had now vanished. “Devi! You need not fear at all. I have faced floods far greater than this!” she said as she ran. She reached the temple mandapam ahead of everyone and leapt up onto it.

By then, the flood had surrounded the temple as well. The water had risen up to the knees of those still standing below. The astrologer and Azhwarkadiyan scrambled and stumbled up onto the mandapam. Only Kundavai and Vanathi remained below. Both tried to climb up; Poonguzhali, who was already above, grasped the hands of the princess and lifted her up. Only Vanathi was left standing below. She tried twice to climb, but both times her hands slipped.

The two women above tried to pull her up into the mandapam. Poonguzhali grabbed one of her hands, and the young princess Kundavai seized the other. Vanathi suddenly looked up. She saw that Poonguzhali was holding one of her hands. Instantly, she shook it off, freeing herself from Poonguzhali’s grasp.

In that swift motion, Kundavai’s hold also slipped. Vanathi fell with a splash—she fell into the water. By then, the water had risen to her neck. She could not find her footing; Vanathi floated in the water. The flood carried her away.
All this happened in a single moment; those atop the mandapam cried out in anguish, “Ah!”
Within a few moments, the flood carried Vanathi to the roof of the astrologer’s house. She climbed up onto that roof. “What good fortune! There is no danger!” she thought.

Those on top of the mandapam also saw her. They watched as she clung to the roof of the house. They too thought, “What good fortune! There is no danger. Once a boat arrives, we can surely rescue her!”
“Don’t let go of the roof! Hold on tightly!” they shouted loudly.

Vanathi gripped the astrologer’s roof firmly. After a short while, it seemed as if even that roof was moving. ‘Oh no! Is the house collapsing?’ Yes; the walls of the astrologer’s house had collapsed. But the roof did not fall! The roof had begun to float on the floodwaters.
Vanathi clung tightly to that roof and floated along. She turned and looked towards the temple mandapam.
“Sister! I am going to see him. I am going to see Ponniyin Selvan. Mother Kaveri is taking me to him!” she shouted.
She believed in her heart that her words would have reached their ears—especially the ears of Poonguzhali.
The astrologer’s roof floated away on the flood. Vanathi drifted along with it.

chapters.title: Poonguzhali Leapt!
paragraphs: Those who have traveled through the Chola country would have noticed a peculiar feature in its natural landscape. During the floods that swell the rivers which make Chola Nadu a land of abundant rice, the water level in the rivers rises far above the level of the surrounding land on either side. It is precisely because of this that the floodwaters can be channeled through canals into the paddy fields.

In such a situation, is it not a most difficult task to keep the floodwaters within the riverbeds? Strong embankments must be built on both sides of the rivers. Otherwise, instead of the water flowing along the river, it would spill out in all directions like rainwater, turning Chola Nadu into a waterlogged marsh, rendering it utterly useless.

Bearing this in mind, from ancient times, the Chola kings paid great attention to the construction of embankments along the Kaveri and its tributaries. Readers may know the story that Karikala Valavan, after defeating the people of Eelam in war, brought them as captives and set them to work on building the embankments of the Kaveri.

To ensure that water flowed at a good height in the tributaries of the Kaveri, the Chola kings built the Grand Anicut (Kallanai) a katha’s distance east of Srirangam. Because of that dam, the water level rose further, and plenty of water could be diverted into the branch rivers.

Thus, through a combination of natural features and unceasing human effort, Chola Nadu became, even in ancient days, a land unrivaled in its water resources. Yet, just as nature bestowed these special blessings on the fertile Chola land, at times it also brought grave dangers.

To the east of the Chola country, along the coast, cyclonic storms and hurricanes frequently arise in the sea. Sometimes these winds sweep northwards along the shore, entering the deltas of the Krishna and Godavari or the land of Kalinga, bringing torrential rains and causing great destruction. At other times, they enter directly into Chola Nadu itself, rushing westward. Between Kodikkarai and the mouth of the Kollidam, it is in this region that such cyclones most often penetrate inland. This is an event that has occurred many times throughout history. Sometimes, those cyclonic winds, taking on a terrifying and dreadful form, cause the very sea to swell and rise, destroying the villages along the shore!

The tale that the sea consumed Kaveripattinam, known as Poompuhar, is not a mere legend; it is a true event that can be proven by historical evidence. When there is an excessive flood in the rivers, sometimes the banks break. Since the land around the rivers is lower than the water level of the rivers themselves, when a breach occurs, the surrounding area becomes a vast sheet of water. The villages near the rivers are submerged. In such times, the temples in the vicinity have served as a refuge for people to save their lives.

History tells us that Aditya Chola, son of Vijayalaya Chola, constructed one hundred and eight temples along the course of the great river, from its source in the Sahasya hills to the place where it merges with the sea. Just as temples are used for worshipping the gods in ordinary times, perhaps Aditya Chola’s intention was that, during times of great flood and breaches, people might climb onto the temple mandapams and use them to save their lives.

Because of breaches in the riverbanks, sometimes the very course of the rivers changes. From ancient records, we learn that rivers like Arisilaaru and Kudamurutti have changed their course and direction many times in this manner.

Now, let us return to the time in which our story takes place. When Parthibendran’s ship was coming from the island of Lanka to Chola Nadu, a cyclone arose, and after making Vandiyathevan and Prince Arulmozhi jump into the sea, it traveled along the coast, reached Kalinga, and then vanished.

But the cyclone that arose while Arulmozhi Varman was staying at the Chudamani Vihara in Nagapattinam entered Chola Nadu itself, wreaked havoc in many places, and moved westward. In a single night, it played its games on both banks of the Kaveri, and by the next day, it reached Kongu Nadu and faded away. Everywhere it traveled, it not only caused great destruction, but also brought heavy rains in its wake. The further west it went, the heavier the rain became. Thus, from the next day onwards, the Kaveri, the Kollidam, and all their tributaries were flooded beyond measure. Many rivers broke their banks. Because of the rain and the breaches, the entire Chola country became a land of floods.

But all these natural calamities did not terrify the people of Chola Nadu into helplessness or inaction. Since such events occurred often, the people knew exactly what to do in such circumstances. At such times, they would climb onto the temple mandapams or other high places to save their lives. The floods would recede as swiftly as they had come. Those who lost their homes would, with the help of their neighbors, immediately rebuild their houses. They would not sit down with their heads in their hands, lamenting, “Alas! All is lost!”
The people who lived in Chola Nadu in those days were self-reliant, tireless, and full of confidence. Otherwise, could they have achieved the marvels that astonish the world even today?

When Vanathi, instead of climbing onto the temple mandapam, slipped and fell into the water, those who had already reached the top of the mandapam were at first alarmed. But that anxiety quickly faded. Seeing Vanathi clinging to the astrologer’s rooftop gave them courage. The Young Princess even felt a certain delight. There was always a thrill for Kundavai Devi in placing Vanathi in perilous situations and watching how she would handle them. The Young Princess was determined that the bride of her valiant brother should be a courageous and resolute woman. To nurture such resolve in Vanathi’s heart, Kundavai had employed many strategies and subtle tricks. She now felt confident that those efforts had borne fruit.

Had not Vanathi, for some time now, stopped her old habit of fainting and collapsing? Now, without any of Kundavai’s schemes, fate itself had provided an opportunity to test Vanathi’s courage. Surrounded by floodwaters, Vanathi was clinging to the roof of a hut. Would she be afraid? Would she hold on bravely until the astrologer’s disciple came with a boat to rescue her? Yes, she would! There was no doubt! Would all the training given so far go to waste at this moment?
While Kundavai was thus pondering, Azhwarkkadiyan said, “My lady! What is this? It seems as though the roof is moving!”
“There’s something wrong with your eyes! The flood is flowing past; it only seems as if the roof is moving!” replied Kundavai.
Even as she said this, a doubt arose in her own heart. The sign of it was visible on her face.
“Amma! Look carefully!” cried Azhwarkkadiyan.
“Aiyyo! What disaster is this?” exclaimed the young princess.
“Jyotidar! Will your disciple arrive soon with the boat?” asked Azhwarkkadiyan.

“Enough! Enough! It is enough that we trusted the astrologer and his disciple! Thirumalai! See if you can save Vanathi; if not, I myself will have to jump into the flood! If anything happens to Vanathi, I will not keep my life for even a moment longer!” she cried.

“Mother! It is precisely in times of danger that we must not lose our composure. This is not unknown to you. I am ready to give my life to help the Kodumbalur princess; but it must be of some use, must it not? If I swim across without a boat and climb onto that roof, will it bear my weight as well as hers? Or will it sink both of us into the flood, roof and all? I must think about this a little...”

Hearing the sound of Poonkuzhali’s laughter, both of them turned to look at her. “By the time this brave Vaishnavan finishes thinking, the life of the Kodumbalur princess will be over!” said Poonkuzhali.
“If that happens, this boatwoman will be happy!” retorted Azhwarkkadiyan, and at once anger flared on Poonkuzhali’s face.

Thirumalai continued, “But, Devi! Nothing of the sort will happen! Just as Lord Thirumal, who lay upon the banyan leaf and saved the whole universe, will save Vanathi too. The very Sriman Narayana who took the Matsya, Kurma, and Varaha avatars to protect this earth will also save the Kodumbalur princess!... Look there! The astrologer’s disciple is coming with the boat!”

In the direction Azhwarkkadiyan pointed, a boat was indeed approaching. The boat was moving slowly, struggling against the current, toward the temple mandapam where they stood. The roof upon which Vanathi clung was drifting away with the floodwaters. It would take a long time for the boat to reach them and take them aboard. By then, Vanathi would have drifted far away—perhaps even out of sight.

Thinking all this, those standing atop the mandapam shouted loudly to the astrologer’s disciple in the boat; they also gestured frantically. Understanding that they were urging him to hurry, he began to row the boat faster.
He tried.
At that moment, Poonguzhali turned to Kundavai and said, “Devi! Grant me permission! I will swim across, intercept the boat, and bring back the Kodumbalur princess!”
Kundavai hesitated for a moment. She remembered that it was when Poonguzhali reached out her hand that Vanathi had fallen into the floodwaters.
“Devi, trust me. It was due to my carelessness that the princess fell into the water. Therefore, it is my duty to rescue her!” Poonguzhali declared.
“My girl, I trust you. But it is Vanathi whom I do not trust!” Kundavai replied.

“Ah! Do you think she will refuse to board the boat while I am in it? In that case, I shall put her aboard and then disembark myself!” So saying, Poonguzhali leapt into the floodwaters and swiftly made her way toward the boat.
Kundavai turned to the astrologer. “Sir! Astrologer! I had placed great faith in your science; today, I have lost that faith!”

“But it is today that I have gained complete confidence, Devi! According to the horoscope of the Kodumbalur princess, she was to face a great danger today. I thought it might come through the hands of the Pazhuvettaraiyar. When that did not happen, I was astonished. But the danger came in another form. The princess will escape this peril! Ah! Her extraordinary palm lines! Everything I have foretold about her will come true, there is no doubt!” he said.

“It all sounds very fine, but how will it come to pass? Even if Vanathi escapes this danger, your prediction will not be fulfilled. Did you not hear the vow that girl made in your own house just a while ago?” Kundavai asked.

“No matter what vow anyone makes, my prediction will be fulfilled. If it does not come to pass, I shall cast all my astrological manuscripts into the Kaveri river! That is my vow!” declared the astrologer.
At that moment, Azhwarkkadiyan said, “Astrologer! The Kaveri Mother will not wait for you to throw your manuscripts in. She has already taken them herself!”
The astrologer, realizing the truth of his words, stood stunned. “Even so, my prediction will not fail!” he muttered to himself.

The boat, which had been drifting gently upon the river’s surface, suddenly began to rock violently. Vandiyathevan, who had been lying down, was startled and sat up at once. His hand instinctively reached for the sword at his hip.

Poonguzhali, who had been rowing with measured strokes, now stood up in the boat. Her eyes, which had been calm and serene, were now blazing with a strange fire. Without a word, she threw aside the oar, gathered her garments, and leapt into the water with the agility of a fish.
Vandiyathevan, astonished, called out, “Poonguzhali! Where are you going? What is this madness?”

But Poonguzhali did not answer. Her head emerged above the water for a moment, her long braid trailing behind her like a black serpent. Then, with swift strokes, she swam towards the dense reeds that grew along the riverbank.
Vandiyathevan watched in amazement. He could not fathom what had prompted her sudden leap. Had she seen something in the water? Was there danger nearby? Or was this some trick to leave him stranded?
He looked around anxiously. The river was wide and silent, the banks shrouded in mist. The only sound was the gentle lapping of water against the boat and the distant call of a night bird.

A few moments later, Poonguzhali reappeared, dragging something heavy behind her. As she drew closer, Vandiyathevan saw that it was the body of a man, half-submerged, his clothes soaked and clinging to his limbs.
With great effort, Poonguzhali hauled the man into the boat. Water streamed from his hair and garments. His face was pale, his eyes closed.
“Who is this?” Vandiyathevan asked, bewildered.

Poonguzhali did not reply. She bent over the man, pressing her ear to his chest, listening for a heartbeat. Then, satisfied, she began to wring the water from his clothes and rub his hands and feet, trying to restore warmth to his body.
Vandiyathevan watched in silence, his curiosity mounting. Who was this stranger? How had he come to be in the river at this hour? And how had Poonguzhali known he was there?
The night deepened around them, the river flowing on in its eternal course, bearing with it the secrets of the land and the destinies of those who traveled upon its waters.

chapters.title: The Elephant Threw!
paragraphs: On the day before the events narrated in the previous chapters, we left behind Prince Arulmozhi Varman as the honored guest of the people of Nagapattinam. After the grand feast had concluded, the prince mounted a richly adorned elephant and set forth. Countless people followed him, proclaiming, “We shall come to Thanjai!” That night, the prince and the throng that accompanied him reached Thiru Aaroor.

The people of Thiru Aaroor, having learned in advance of the prince’s arrival, gave him a royal welcome, offering all honors befitting his station. From the ancient gateway of Thiru Aaroor’s Gunavasal to Kudavasal, the people gathered in great numbers. The four royal streets were so crowded that not even a sesame seed could have fallen to the ground. The facades of every house were decorated with festoons. The Chozha palace at Thiru Aaroor too was adorned by the officials. Arrangements had been made to provide a feast not only for the prince but also for the multitude that accompanied him.

The previous night, a fierce storm had swept through Thiru Aaroor. Yet, the tempest of joy and celebration that arose with the prince’s arrival made everyone forget the previous day’s storm entirely. The streets resounded with the music of drums and pipes, with singing and dancing, with the wild steps of the Kuravai dance, with puppet shows, and with displays of valor—knife games and wrestling matches accompanied by shouts of triumph.

The Chozha dynasty of Thanjavur, after the temple of the dancing Lord Nataraja at Thillai, held the temple of Lord Thyagaraja at Thiru Aaroor in special devotion, granting it many endowments. Yet, until then, Prince Arulmozhi Varman himself had never visited Thiru Aaroor. Therefore, the temple priests insisted that the prince must visit the shrine. The prince agreed and went to the temple. For many reasons, his heart was in turmoil, and he could not wholly immerse himself in the divine visions of the deity. When the worship and offerings were complete and the sacred prasadam had been received, the prince turned to the temple priests and asked, “Why is the Lord of this temple called Thyagaraja?”

The priests recounted the sacrifices made by Mahadeva, the foremost among the gods, Lord Shiva, for the redemption of all living beings in the three worlds. They spoke of the hardships undertaken by the Lord, who is capable of creating and destroying all three worlds, for the sake of granting grace to his devotees. They narrated how, for the salvation of souls, he took on the ascetic form and performed penance in the cremation ground… They spoke of this. They recounted how, forsaking even his austerities, he married Uma for the welfare of the gods. They narrated the tale of how the Lord appeared in the form of Bhikshatana, the mendicant, and begged for alms in all the worlds. They spoke of his dance in the hall at Thillai. They told how he carried earth for a bird and was struck with a cane by the Pandya king.

They reminded him that such a Lord Thyagaraja, who had now taken his abode in the temple at Thiruvarur, was worshipped there, and that in ancient times the ancestors of Arulmozhi Varman had lived in that very place. They recalled the wondrous tale of Manu Needhi Cholan, who, in order to render justice to a cow, sacrificed his own beloved son.

All these stories were deeply imprinted in Arulmozhi Varman’s heart. Until then, the prince had often marveled at the sacrifice of the Buddha; now, as he heard tales depicting Shiva, the Lord of the gods, as the very embodiment of sacrifice, he began to wonder at them as well. He had also heard the story from distant lands, of the divine son of God, who, for the sake of mankind’s welfare, was nailed to a cross and died. As he pondered all these, the thought took root in his mind that it is sacrifice alone that bestows divinity upon man.

Therefore, the boundless affection of the people surrounding him, their desire to seat him upon the throne of Thanjai and crown him king, filled his heart with immeasurable anguish. He began to think intensely about how he might escape from the prison of their love.

After the temple worship, the people of Thiruvarur offered the prince a grand feast. They arranged many entertainments for his pleasure. Though his heart was not truly engaged in any of these, he outwardly accepted them with apparent enthusiasm.

Later, around midnight, the prince returned to the Chola palace. There, some troubling news awaited him. Heavy rains had fallen to the west of Thanjai, causing great floods in the Kaveri, the Kollidam, and their tributaries, breaking the banks in many places. The land had become a vast sheet of water, making further travel difficult. They advised that it would be best to remain in Thiruvarur for two days, until the floods subsided, before setting out again. This did not please the prince. An urgent restlessness to reach Thanjai at once had taken hold of his heart. Would river breaches and floods be able to hinder such eagerness? Yes; if he were to travel surrounded by all these people and attendants, the journey would certainly be delayed. But if he went alone, riding an elephant, there was no need for any such delay. There was no river deep enough to stop an elephant— There was no road leading to Thanjai. Yet, the prince had no concern about that. He had never felt fear when it came to water. Had not the Ponni river become dearer to him than his own mother? Would not the Kaveri, who had saved him from drowning when he was but a small child, now come to his rescue again?

The real question was how to escape from this vast crowd of people. The memory of Rama slipping away from the people of Ayodhya in the dead of night came to Ponniyin Selvan’s mind. Why shouldn’t he too depart at night, when the crowds were asleep? In any case, it would be wise to instruct the mahout to be ready to leave at any moment.

As soon as this thought occurred, the prince ordered a palace attendant to summon the mahout. The attendant went out to the street, looked around, and returned immediately. He reported that only the elephant was tied at the entrance, but the mahout was nowhere to be seen.
“Perhaps he has gone to watch the singing, dancing, and festivities in the streets. Bring him to me as soon as he returns! Or else, send someone to search for him!” commanded the prince.
“So be it, my lord! There is a boatman named Murugaiyyan waiting at the palace entrance. He insists that he must see you at once!” said the attendant.
The prince felt regret for having forgotten Murugaiyyan all this while. Perhaps he could be of help in making a secret escape. He immediately ordered the attendant to send Murugaiyyan to him.

As soon as Murugaiyyan came before the prince, he fell at his feet and began to sob uncontrollably. It was a difficult task to both console this simple devotee and to glean information from him, but it had to be done. Murugaiyyan explained the cause of his sorrow: he had been separated from his wife back in Nagai Pattinam. After reaching Thiru Aaroor, he had searched through the crowds to see if she too had come there. After searching for about an hour, he saw his wife and the mahout who had driven the prince’s elephant, walking together at the corner of a street branching off from the royal road. As soon as they entered the lane, they began to walk quickly. Murugaiyyan followed them. At last, they stopped at the entrance of a house. There, it seemed, another man was waiting for them.

He joined them. Then, the three of them went together. Murugaiyyan was beset by all sorts of suspicions. He began to doubt the chastity of his own wife. Eager to uncover the truth, he followed them without revealing himself. They left the village, crossed the canal and the bunds of the fields, and finally reached a cremation ground. Murugaiyyan’s heart was seized with terror. Yet, he did not give up; he went on and hid himself behind a tree in the cremation ground.

The man who had joined Raakkammal and the mahout along the way smeared himself with ashes and began to utter all sorts of dreadful incantations. Then, turning to the mahout, he said, “Tomorrow morning, your life will be in danger! Be vigilant and escape with your life!”
The mahout, confused and alarmed, asked, “What danger? In what way will it come? Only if I know can I escape it!”

The sorcerer replied, “Suddenly, the elephant will go mad! The moment you approach it, it will throw you down and run away! The people will think that you are the reason for the elephant’s madness. They will snatch the ankus from your hand and kill you!”
“Oh no! What is the way to escape?” asked the mahout.
“Tomorrow morning, do not go near the elephant!” said the sorcerer.
“How is that possible? If I do so, I will be punished by royal decree!” cried the mahout.
“In that case, come to my house! I will give you a magical armor, enchanted for your protection; wear it and go! But do not take the ankus in your hand!” said the sorcerer.
“Let it be so, sir! But will any danger befall the prince?” asked the mahout.
“How can I say that? Only if the prince himself comes and asks can I tell him,” replied the sorcerer.

Murugaiyyan could not bear to stay there any longer and ran away. He had run mainly to warn the prince about the news that the elephant would go mad the next morning. Having narrated all this, Murugaiyyan once again broke down and wept.
“Why do you weep, my friend? You came at the right time and warned us, didn’t you? Now, I shall take care of the rest!” said Ponniyin Selvan.
“Sir! I am troubled because my wife is involved in all this. I do not know what to think of Raakkammal. Old suspicions about her are returning to my mind!” said Murugaiyyan.
“I will set her right. Do not worry! Go back at once! Somehow find the mahout and bring him here!” commanded the prince.

After the boatman Murugaiyyan left, Ponniyin Selvan sat for a while, immersed in thought. He tried to deduce, by reasoning, the meaning of what Murugaiyyan had seen and heard. The prince recalled what the Young Princess had said about the intentions of the Pazhuvettaraiyars and the schemes of the Pandya country conspirators. This incident could well be part of those conspirators’ efforts—or it might simply be a matter of foolishness. Whatever it was, he arrived at a decision about what he should do in the morning. After that, he sank into peaceful sleep.

At dawn the next day, he rose and prepared himself for the journey. He came to the entrance of the palace. The elephant tethered there, upon seeing the prince, stretched out its trunk affectionately and caressed him. The prince remembered what Murugaiyyan had said about the magician’s warning: “The elephant will go mad.” Yet, there was no sign of madness in the animal.
“Where is the mahout?” the prince called out in a loud voice. Instantly, many voices echoed, “Where is the mahout?”

Just as the prince had prepared for the journey at this early hour, crowds had gathered, ready to depart.
