Among them, the prince spotted Murugaiyyan, struggling to make his way forward, trapped in the press of people. As soon as the prince signaled to him, the crowd parted to let him through. Murugaiyyan came near and reported that after searching for a long time during the night, he had found only his wife, who flatly denied ever going to the cremation ground and insisted that Murugaiyyan had lost his wits. The mahout, he said, had not been found at all.
“Don’t worry about that, Murugaiya! Untie the chain fastened to the elephant’s leg,” the prince commanded.
As Murugaiyyan was unfastening the chain, a voice called out, “Here comes the mahout!” and several other voices echoed, “He’s coming! He’s coming!”
The mahout came running, an ankus in his hand. The people in the crowd hurriedly stepped aside to make way for him.
Ponniyin Selvan, heaving a sigh of relief, looked toward the direction from which the mahout was running.
Poor man! How much he had changed in a single night’s experience! Did he not appear like one possessed by fear and confusion?
The mahout, who held an ankus in one hand, approached the elephant and touched its trunk with his other hand.
Immediately, the elephant seized him with its trunk, swung him around, and lifted him high above its head.
With a terrifying roar that struck fear into all who heard it, the elephant hurled the mahout away!
The mahout landed far off in the distance. The ankus he had held in his hand flew even farther and fell away.
“A madness has seized the elephant!” cried a voice filled with dread from within the crowd. People began to scatter and run in all directions!

chapters.title: The Deceived Mahout
paragraphs: “Auspicious opportunity is but another name for God,” so says a modern philosopher. When God wishes not to reveal Himself as the doer of an act, He assumes the pseudonym “opportunity”! If we look into the lives of the most renowned warriors and the great men who have accomplished extraordinary deeds in the history of the world, we find that opportunity has aided them greatly. Some say that God, in His special grace, sends such opportunities to these individuals. There are those who attribute the favorable turns in life to the glory of the hour of birth, the fruits of one’s horoscope, the destiny written by Brahma, or the merit earned in previous births.
If, in our own time, the great Mahatma Gandhi had not received the opportunity to go to South Africa, would he have attained the veneration of the people as the greatest among men, as an avatar?

We know how much opportunity aided Chandragupta, Vikramaditya, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, the Duke of Wellington, and George in their lives. From this, it would be wrong to conclude that God is partial. Besides the celebrated heroes and great men of history, God continues to send opportunities to countless others as well. But it is up to man’s intelligence and his ability to make the right decision at the right moment to make use of those opportunities.
Those who let opportunities slip through their fingers live and die in obscurity, without name or fame. Those who seize and make use of opportunities etch their names into the annals of history.
What other explanation can there be for the vast differences in the fortunes of those born at the same hour, on the same day?

At this very moment, such an opportunity presented itself in the life of Prince Arulmozhi Varman. When he flung aside the mahout who had come near him, and when the cry arose, “The elephant has gone mad!” that opportunity approached him— It had arrived. Had he failed to make use of it, this history would have taken a different course. Raja Raja Chozhan could never have ascended to such an exalted place in the annals of Tamil Nadu.

Fortunately, he possessed the timely intelligence to recognize that opportunity and seize it. He recalled the tale that the boatman Murugaiyyan had told him the previous day. In an instant, he deduced that the man who had approached the elephant was not the true mahout, but someone with evil intentions—hence the elephant had tossed him aside. If he tried to discover at that moment who the man was, and for what purpose he had come, the opportunity would slip away. The confusion among the people caused by the cry, “The elephant has gone mad!” could not be exploited later. His chief aim at that moment was to escape from that crowd and reach Thanjai as swiftly as possible. There could never be a more fitting chance to fulfill that aim.

Therefore, he called Murugaiyyan to his side, whispered something in his ear, then climbed onto his shoulders and leapt onto the elephant’s back. As he did so, he struck the howdah atop the elephant. The howdah tumbled down and rolled to the ground. Then, in the elephant’s own tongue, he spoke a few words to it. Instantly, the elephant trumpeted and set off. As before, it moved swiftly, bellowing in a terrifying voice. In a few moments, it broke into a run.
At the same time, Murugaiyyan shouted loudly, “Ayyo! The elephant has gone mad! Run! Run at once!”

The people, seized by even greater panic than before, scattered in all directions. They fled through side streets and alleys nearby. Some darted into open houses and hid themselves. Even those with the bravest of hearts, who feared nothing else, would flee before a mad elephant. No matter how great a hero, none could stand against a frenzied elephant. To face it with weapons was impossible; to stand unarmed, unthinkable. What could the unarmed crowd—men, women, elders, and children—do but scatter and flee before the rampaging beast?

The Prince guided the elephant past the town of Thiru Aaroor. Instead of directing it straight along the road to Thanjavur, he turned it northwest. From the very start, he had thought to reach Pazhaiyaarai on the way, and if his noble elder sister was there, to meet and speak with her before proceeding to Thanjai. Now,

It was decided in an instant. It was only natural for a maddened elephant to break away and run across the path. If they continued along the Thanjai road, the people would surely follow them without respite. But if the elephant took an untraveled path, the crowds would not be able to keep up!

Thinking thus, and making his decision with lightning speed, he turned the elephant off the road, steering it northwest across a shortcut. Fields, bunds, canals, rivers, breaches in the embankments—without caring for any of these, the elephant thundered on, trampling everything in its way. The prince’s heart, too, was seized by a strange exhilaration, soaring like a bird freed from its cage, wheeling through the open sky. A sense of excitement and anticipation welled up within him, as if he were approaching a pivotal moment in his life.

At the very moment the elephant began its wild run, Murugaiyyan shouted, “The elephant has gone mad!” and ran after it. He made a rough guess of where the mahout, who had been tossed aside by the elephant, might have fallen, and hurried in that direction. Not far from the Chola palace where the prince had stayed, there was the famed Kamalalayam tank, celebrated throughout the land. Murugaiyyan went to the banks of that tank and looked around. Many who had been frightened by the elephant were standing on the shore; some had even waded into the water itself. One man was floundering and swimming awkwardly to the bank. Murugaiyyan looked closely at him. It was the very same sorcerer who, on the first night, had taken the elephant mahout and Raakkammal with him! What luck! His life must be truly long—he had survived being hurled by the elephant! The man who, moments ago, had rushed toward the elephant with the goad in his hand—this was he! What had happened to the goad? Had it too fallen into the tank?
Murugaiyyan went up to him and said, “Mahout! You’re lucky to have survived! Where is the goad?”
Revathasan, the village sorcerer, looked Murugaiyyan up and down and replied, “What are you asking, sir? Who are you? I’ve just come out of the tank after a swim!”
“Oh! Is that so? Aren’t you the mahout? Wasn’t it you whom the elephant tossed? If not, where is the mahout?” he asked.
The sorcerer, even more bewildered, said, “What did I see? Why are you asking me?”

“Magician! Why are you trying to deceive me? Last night, you took the mahout to the cremation ground and warned him, ‘The elephant the prince mounts will go mad.’ And yet, you yourself forgot your own warning and got caught by the elephant—” “Did you bring it? That’s your concern! Where is the mahout? Where is my wife Raakkammal?” asked Murugaiyyan. On Kramavithan’s face, the astonishment and fear grew even more than before.
“The mahout? Raakkammal? Have you gone mad?” Kramavithan muttered, glancing all around him.
“Yes, yes! Just as the elephant goes mad, so have I! Just tell me where the mahout is! Otherwise…” Murugaiyyan began to speak in a tone of authority.

Revathasan, who had been glancing about, now turned to Murugaiyyan with a smile. “You call me a ‘sorcerer’! But you are a greater sorcerer than I am! You seem to know everything! There’s no use hiding anything from you. I ran here only to warn the prince that the elephant was about to go mad, and that no one should mount it. This is the result. Your wife and the mahout are in a house over there. If you wish to see them, I’ll take you myself. The prince—nothing has happened to him, has it? He is safe, isn’t he?” he asked.
“The prince is safe. He himself ordered me to bring you and the mahout to him…”
“You must get me a good reward from the prince! After all, it was I who saved him, wasn’t it? Ah! Look there…!” the sorcerer exclaimed in surprise and broke off.

Where the sorcerer’s gaze was fixed, amidst the oleander bushes by the edge of the pond, the tip of something like a spear was just visible. “Ah! The ankus!” he cried, and dashed towards the thicket. But Murugaiyyan was quicker; he ran ahead, plunged into the bushes, and carefully seized the handle of the ankus.

Then he turned around; the sorcerer was nowhere to be seen. “Ah, have I been tricked?” he thought anxiously, and ran here and there searching, but it was no use. The sorcerer Kramavithan had vanished into thin air amidst the crowd gathered on the banks of the pond.
After the mad elephant had run away, Murugaiyyan saw that the people were once again moving towards the Chola palace. But he did not remain there.

Thinking back to which direction lay the house where he had first seen the sorcerer, he set off that way. All along the royal streets, people were gathered in little groups, talking animatedly. Among those who had witnessed the mad elephant’s rampage, some said, “It seemed as though there was someone on the elephant’s back.” Others disagreed. “How could that be? The elephant only started running after it had thrown off its mahout. Who could have climbed onto its back after that?” Thus, everyone was debating as they made their way back toward the Chola palace. All were eager to confirm that no harm had come to the prince who had captured their hearts.

Murugaiyan, however, walked in the opposite direction from the crowds, heading toward the specified marketplace. There, at that hour, there was no sign of people—everyone had gone to the royal streets. In the daylight, it was not so easy to recognize the house he had seen the previous night. Murugaiyan scrutinized each house as he walked by. Only one house was locked from the outside, and from within, he could hear faint groans. Beside that house stood a dilapidated, abandoned building. Murugaiyan slipped into the ruined house, climbed onto its roof, and leapt into the courtyard of the next house.

As he had expected, the mahout was there. He looked like a man possessed. Not only were his hands and feet bound, but he had also been tied to a post. The mahout was desperately trying to gnaw through the ropes with his teeth. Every so often, he would stop biting and shout in agony.

The moment he saw Murugaiyan, a glimmer of clarity appeared on his face. He had seen Murugaiyan before in Nagapattinam and knew that he was someone close to the prince. So now, in a flurry of excitement, he cried, “Murugaiya! Untie me! Untie me! Those wretches have tricked me! The prince—he’s safe, isn’t he?”

As Murugaiyan untied the knots, he quickly summarized the events of the morning, then asked the mahout what had happened to him. The mahout, stumbling over his words, recounted his tale: Though the elephant had gone mad, he himself had come to no harm. They had lured him to this house, promising to give him a magical charm for protection. Once he arrived, the sorcerer began chanting spells, filling the room with incense smoke. Suddenly, he had felt dizzy and lost consciousness. When he awoke, he found himself tied to the post.

Both of them left the house and hurried towards the Chola palace. When they reached the palace, they saw that a much larger crowd had gathered than before, and the people were speaking to each other with great anxiety. The reason for the people’s worry was that the prince was nowhere to be found. No one there knew exactly what had happened to him. Some said they had seen someone on the elephant’s back. They guessed that it might have been the prince. It was well known throughout Chola country that the prince was highly skilled in taming elephants, and that he even understood the language of the elephants. Therefore, some expressed their firm belief that Ponniyin Selvan must have mounted the elephant in order to subdue its rage and prevent harm from befalling anyone.
At that moment, Murugaiyyan and the mahout arrived there. When the people learned what had happened to the mahout the previous night, their astonishment and shock multiplied many times over.

The one who had tied up the mahout and run away with the goad must have been sent by the enemies of the Chola dynasty. “Perhaps it was the Pazhuvettaraiyars who sent him!” guessed some, and most of the people believed it. As a result, their anger towards the Pazhuvettaraiyars grew even greater. In a frenzy of rage, many immediately set out towards Thanjai. Some followed the path the elephant had taken, while others, with burning indignation, set off along the road leading straight to Thanjavur.

chapters.title: Thirunallam
paragraphs: Vanathi, who was clinging tightly to the thatched roof of the astrologer’s house—and with it, to her very life—was drifting along, carried by the floodwaters that had broken from the Kaveri river. The current bore her ever eastward, sometimes gently, sometimes pulling her along with great force. At other times, the roof was caught in large whirlpools, spinning and staggering as it went.

In places where the flood was not so deep, the roof floated over mounds and rises in the land. From the way the water had climbed up the trunks of trees, and from how far the mandapams along the riverbank had been submerged, Vanathi could guess the depth of the flood. Whenever she considered climbing down to higher ground, the swirling current would sweep her away into deeper waters before she could act.

Nor did Vanathi’s heart truly wish to descend. For, in her mind, a conviction had taken root: this flood of the Ponni river was carrying her towards the very place where the Prince of Ponni himself was. The ominous prophecy uttered by the Kodumbalur astrologer about the danger threatening the prince lingered in her heart. She believed that the Kaveri was taking her along so that she might protect him from that peril.

Ah! How much pride that Puṅkuzhali possesses! With what authority she claims the prince as her own! Yet, she has reason for such pride. Was it not Puṅkuzhali who saved the prince’s life today?—No, not just today! Vanathi had heard what the Kudanthai astrologer had said: the prince’s birth itself was marked by such dangers! Many more such perils might yet come his way. But nothing—neither sea nor storm nor river flood—could truly endanger the life of one born to rule the world! For such miraculous escapes, someone must always play a role. Puṅkuzhali had been granted that fortune! But does that entitle her to such pride?—Still, a longing had long dwelled in the secret depths of Vanathi’s heart: might not such a fortune come to her, just once?

At times, as the roof spun about, Vanathi saw, far behind her, a boat approaching. She could make out a woman and a man aboard, though she could not clearly see who they were. Watching the woman row the boat, Vanathi wondered if it might be Puṅkuzhali herself. Surely, she must be coming to rescue her from the flood… Is she coming? Has the Younger Princess sent her? Enough, enough! It is enough that the Prince is indebted to her. He himself need not be burdened with gratitude! She must not come along! She must not be the one to save him from this flood.

At times, it seemed as though the boat had drawn near to her; at times, the roof sped swiftly ahead, leaving the boat far behind. In this manner, when the boat had vanished from sight, the roof of the house appeared to turn and head southward. Thus, it traveled a great distance. It crossed the southern bank of the Kaveri and entered the vast floodplain that stretched southward like a boundless sea. At last, the edge of the floodwaters came into view.

Ah! Does this not look like the bank of a river? Yes, yes! This is the bank of the Arasalar! The breached floodwaters of the Kaveri, after submerging many lands along their path, have come and mingled with this river. Since its southern bank is slightly raised, the waters have been contained within it. That riverside, with its dense trees, seemed a familiar place to her. Like the scent of a previous birth, memories came flooding back. No, no! It was a place she had visited two or three times in this very life! She must be nearing the holy place called Thirunallam. There, the daughter of the Mazhavarayar, Sembiyan Madevi, is eager to build a temple of black stone in memory of her beloved husband, Kandaraditya Cholan. On the riverbank there stands a Vasantha Maligai—a Spring Palace—where the Chola clan stays when they visit. Once, when Sembiyan Madevi invited the Younger Princess there, she too had accompanied her! How much she had delighted in wandering the gardens adjoining the Vasantha Maligai, listening to the sweet songs of the birds! Ah! An incident that occurred there at that time had sunk deep into Vanathi’s heart, never to be forgotten.

chapters.title: The Fledgling Birds
paragraphs: When Vanathi first arrived in Pazhayarai from Kodumbalur, the abundance of water in Chola Nadu plunged her into a sea of wonder. There were no rivers near Kodumbalur; only tanks. During the rainy season, the tanks would brim and overflow with water. In the summer, they would dry up completely. There, one could not see rivers and canals and streams, their waters touching both banks, swirling and eddying as they flowed. Nor could one find ponds lush with blooming lotuses and red lilies. In Vanathi’s native place, such sights were unknown. She would sit, entranced, gazing at these marvels. She delighted in watching the water droplets, like pearls, rolling and dancing across the lotus leaves that shaded the fish in the ponds. She would be enraptured by the sight of bees circling and humming around the blooming lotus and lily flowers. Time would slip away unnoticed.

Once, Vanathi and Kundavai had gone to Thirunallur (in these days called Koonerirajapuram) at the invitation of Sembiyan Maadevi. They stayed in the Vasantha Maligai—the Spring Palace. Sembiyan Maadevi and Kundavai would often begin to talk about the lives of the Saiva saints and the nectar of devotion that dripped from their hymns. Vanathi had little interest in listening to such discussions. Rather than that, she was far more eager to wander through the gardens adjoining the Spring Palace, to listen to the sweet songs of the birds, and to hear the blissful drone of the deep-blue bees hovering around the trembling lotus blossoms in the pond. She was also keen to watch the river, flowing past one side of the palace, swirling in eddies, and to see the beautiful, crimson kadamba flowers spinning in those whirls. In the region of Kodumbalur, such enchanting scenes were not to be found.

One day, the daughter of the Mazhavarayar and the young princess Kundavai were conversing animatedly about something. As Vanathi approached them, the young princess said, “Vanathi! Go to the garden! I’ll come in a little while.” Vanathi, brimming with excitement, skipped and ran off. She wandered for a while in the garden, then made her way to the lotus pond. Along the bank of the pond grew many trees, their branches spreading wide and thick, shading the sky. Among them was a tall, broad, and luxuriant iluppai tree. Its fallen flowers had covered the ground completely… ...were present. Their fragrance wafted gently, spreading throughout the entire garden.

Underneath one of those trees, upon a large root, Vanathi sat. Leaning against the trunk, she gazed around—above, below, and on all sides. The sweet songs of various birds flowed into her ears like a flood of nectar. A blissful feeling, one she had never experienced before, blossomed in her heart. That inner joy often surged and overflowed, spreading through her entire being. Until that day, Vanathi had never even dreamed that life could be so filled with delight.
From beneath that tree, at a little distance, she could see the river’s flood. Now and then, through the gaps between the trees, she watched the enchanting scenes along the river’s course.

At one moment, she noticed a young man swimming in the river. In the reddish stream, his golden-hued body half-submerged and half-rising above the water made for a striking sight that captivated her heart. Fie! What foolishness was this, that her attention should be drawn to the form of some young lad? For Vanathi, who possessed modesty and maidenly reserve as her birthright, this thought brought a deep sense of shame. Yet, against her own self-control, her eyes strayed once more, twice more, towards the river.

Vanathi grew angry with herself. She wondered if she should get up and leave at once. At that very moment, another incident caught her attention. Hearing the shrill cries of baby birds from above, near where she sat, she looked up. The sight she beheld filled her at once with pity and alarm. On a branch, in the fork of the tree, there was a bird’s nest. Several chicks stretched out their heads, chirping in thin, plaintive voices. In those cries, fear, a warning of danger, and a pitiful plea for help were all mingled together—or so it sounded to Vanathi’s ears.
Near the nest, on the same branch, a wild cat was climbing, slowly and stealthily drawing closer to the nest!

Seeing this, Vanathi cried out, “Ayyo! Ayyo!” In the next instant, a voice called, “What is it? What is it?” and she heard the sound of someone running swiftly towards her. Vanathi looked in that direction. She realized it was the same young man who had been swimming in the river a moment ago, now running up from the bank.
At that same moment, two large birds appeared from somewhere and began circling the nest, shrieking harshly. They must be the mother and father of the chicks, come in haste to protect their young.

Vanathi realized that she ought to have come sooner. The birds had long, slender beaks—surely, these must be woodpeckers. One of the birds was circling the nest repeatedly, while the other drew close to the cat, pecking at it with its beak and making loud noises, as if threatening to attack! The bird could do nothing to the cat, of course. If it fell into the cat’s jaws, in the very next moment it would be inside its belly. Yet, to protect its chicks, that bird fought with such desperate courage.
For Vanathi, who had lost both her mother and father at a young age, the sight filled her with deep sorrow.

The cat, which had been sitting still for a while, suddenly stretched out one of its forelegs toward the nest. Its paw touched one end of the nest where the chicks were. Vanathi cried out again. By then, the young man had come near. Vanathi felt a great shyness at seeing him up close. She could not bring herself to speak; her tongue would not move. With a gesture, he pointed toward the birds’ nest.

Until then, he had thought that some danger threatened the girl herself. He looked intently at the spot Vanathi indicated. Then he turned to her and smiled. His gaze and his smile moved Vanathi’s heart so deeply that, for a moment, she even forgot the plight of the baby birds.

But the youth immediately hurried over and stood directly beneath the branch where the nest was. He shouted at the wildcat. The cat bent down and growled at him. “What a wicked cat!” he muttered, and quickly picked up a stone from the ground and hurled it. The stone missed the cat but struck the branch near it. The cat instantly leapt to another branch, then sprang to a dense tree nearby, and soon disappeared from sight.

But in the meantime, another disaster had occurred. Had not the cat pulled at one end of the nest with its paw? The nest, already shaken, now lost its balance even more from the force of the youth’s stone striking the branch. Slowly, the nest began to slip from the fork of the branch. Had it slipped and fallen completely, the chicks that had escaped the cat’s jaws would have fallen to the ground and perished! Fortunately, one edge of the nest still clung to the branch. The nest, with the chicks inside, now dangled below, swaying like a swing. The lives of the chicks swayed with it. The woodpeckers, more frantic than before, circled the nest, crying out in distress. If the wind blew a little stronger, the nest would fall to the ground. From such a height, the chicks’ survival would be nearly impossible.
The young man pondered for a moment. At first, it seemed he intended to leap up into the tree. But in the very next instant, he appeared to change his mind.
Turning to Vanathi, he said, “Girl! Come here for a moment! If the nest falls down, catch it with the end of your sari! I’ll be back in a second!” With these words, he dashed away.

True to his word, he returned in a very short while. But now, he was not walking back—he came riding on an elephant. Vanathi immediately guessed what he was about to do. So she left that spot and made her way to the steps leading down to the lotus pond. Descending a few steps, she sat down and watched the young man atop the elephant to see what he would do.

When the elephant reached the foot of the tree, it halted. From its back, the young man carefully took the bird’s nest in his hand and gently placed it on the same branch where it had been before. The mother and father birds now cried out even louder than before. But now, their cries seemed to ring with a note of joy.

The young man then turned and looked all around. “Girl! Where have you gone?” he called. Vanathi, overcome with shyness, remained silent. The young man climbed down from the elephant. Again, he looked all around.
Vanathi was lost in her own thoughts. Whatever she was thinking seemed to her extremely amusing. Unbidden, laughter bubbled up within her, and she burst out in a peal of ringing laughter.
Hearing this, the young man came to the steps of the pond. Looking at Vanathi, he asked, “Girl! Why are you laughing? What has happened now to make you laugh so heartily?”

As soon as his voice reached Vanathi’s ears, her heart once again swelled and overflowed as before; her shyness grew even greater. Unable to look at him, she kept glancing this way and that. “Girl! Why did you laugh? Won’t you tell me?” the young man asked again.

Vanathi gathered her courage and replied, “It’s nothing. I was just laughing at the thought of what a great hero you are. You came riding an elephant to fight a cat, didn’t you?” she asked. Hearing this, the young man too laughed.
“Girl! Was it only a cat? Hearing your scream, I was afraid it was a tiger!” he said.
By now, courage had blossomed within Vanathi; her shyness had diminished.
“Ah! Is that so? Why should anyone fear a tiger in Chola land, where the tiger banner flies high? Are you from Pandya country?” she asked.
At this, the young man’s face bloomed even more than before.

“Maiden! I am not a foreigner; I too belong to this Chola land! I have mounted elephants and gone to many other battlefields. Who are you? From which town do you hail? You seem to be quite the talkative one!” he said.
“Elephant driver! Speak with respect! What does it matter to you who I am? Why do you ask?” Vanathi retorted.
“Well then, I shall not ask. You seem to be a lady of high birth! I shall take my leave!” With these words, the youth began to climb the steps and move away.
Once again, Vanathi called out in a playful, teasing tone, “Elephant driver! Elephant driver! Will you take me on your elephant as well?”
“Very well, I will take you. But what wages will you give me?” he asked.
“Wages? I’ll speak to my uncle and get you a position in the palace at Kodumbalur. If not, I’ll have you made commander of the elephant corps!” Vanathi replied.
“Oh ho! Are you the princess of Kodumbalur?” exclaimed the young man. The face that had been blooming until now suddenly shriveled. The smile vanished; his brows furrowed.
“Why? Is being the princess of Kodumbalur such a lowly thing? Am I not allowed to ride your elephant?” Vanathi asked.

“No, no! There are so many elephants in the halls of the Kodumbalur palace; so many elephant drivers as well. Why would you need me?” he said, and with that, the young man strode away quickly. For a while, Vanathi waited, wondering if he might turn back and look at her. But he did not look back; he mounted his elephant and rode away.

This incident left a deep impression on Vanathi’s heart. It returned to her memory again and again. Whenever she recalled the appearance of that elephant driver, his blooming face, and his sweet voice, a strange joy arose within her. Whenever she remembered how he had mounted the elephant to save the fledgling birds, she could not help but smile to herself.

She blushed. Then she felt ashamed because of it. Whenever she thought of the arrogance of that mahout, and how his face had turned sour the moment he heard the word “Kodumbalur,” her anger towards him only grew. Altogether, thoughts of that mahout kept coming to her again and again. She was troubled by the doubt as to whether this was wrong.

There was talk in the palace that Ponniyin Selvan was coming to Thirunallur to see his sister. Just as all the women of the palace were eager to see the prince who shone as the apple of Chola Nadu’s eye, so too was Vanathi. But the opportunity did not come easily. Though there was talk that the prince had arrived, he never came into the women’s quarters. Naturally shy, Vanathi did not, like her other companions, seek out a chance to go and see him.

It was only on the day the prince left Thirunallur that Vanathi, standing on the upper terrace of the palace, happened to see Ponniyin Selvan. He was riding atop an elephant, setting out on his journey. If Vanathi could not believe her own eyes, it was no mere figure of speech. How could she believe that the very youth she had mocked and laughed at, daring even to command as a mere mahout, was in fact Arulmozhi Varman, the prince venerated by this realm? Only after repeatedly asking the women beside her did she finally accept it as true. The shame and heartache she felt because of this cannot be described in words.

When she remembered how she had claimed that the heir to rule the world was merely the head of the elephant stables at Kodumbalur palace, she could not help but laugh! Yet at the same time, tears welled up in her eyes. She grieved over her own foolishness. She became convinced that the reason his face had turned sour was because she had called him “mahout!” He must think her a woman lacking in all the qualities of modesty, innocence, fear, and restraint! When this thought struck her, there was no limit to Vanathi’s inner torment. Many times she wondered if she should throw herself into a river or a pond and end her life. Many times she tried to confess her mistake to Princess Kundavai. But she could not summon the courage; her tongue would not move. If the prince himself had told Kundavai Devi, she would have asked Vanathi about it. Since Kundavai Devi had not asked, Vanathi concluded that the prince had not told her. Amidst all her heartache, this thought gave her a little comfort.
She resolved that, one day, after seeking forgiveness directly from Ponniyin Selvan, she could end her life. But even for that, she could not find the courage.

After going to Pazhayarai, whenever the chance arose to meet the prince, she would run and hide herself. She felt she would rather give up her very life than appear before the prince. The young princess, unaware of what had transpired at Thirunallam, and her other companions, were only surprised, exclaiming, “How shy this girl is!” They thought it was simply a part of her timid nature.

Soon, Vanathi learned there was another, more important reason for Ponniyin Selvan to feel aversion towards her. Just as many believed that Prince Arulmozhi Varman would one day become emperor of the world, so too did her own family. For this reason, her elder father had planned to marry her to Arulmozhi Varman—a fact Vanathi had come to know in some measure. It was with this intention that her uncle, Boothi Vikrama Kesari, had sent her to Pazhayarai, as Kundavai Devi’s other companions would often remark with sly hints. Sometimes, they would tease Vanathi directly, saying, “That’s why you refuse to go before the prince! Do you think we don’t know your secret?” Such words fell harshly upon Vanathi’s ears. Perhaps this was also why the mahout’s face had fallen when he learned she was a girl from Kodumbalur.

While Vanathi’s young heart was thus agitated by these thoughts, one day Ponniyin Selvan set out for the war in Eezham. On that day, all the princess’s companions in the palace were arranged to stand with auspicious lamps in their hands, to bid him farewell and wish him victory. Even at such a time, Vanathi could not refuse to attend. A longing to see the prince once before he departed for war welled up within her. Though she could not speak, she hoped to beg his forgiveness through her expression and the language of her eyes. But what happened was entirely different from what she had imagined. As the prince approached and looked at her, Vanathi fainted, dropping her lamp and collapsing to the ground in a swoon. All that followed is already known to the readers, is it not?

As Vanathi’s boat, with its thatched roof, floated towards Thirunallam, all these events passed through her mind, one after another. She knew that Ponniyin Selvan felt sympathy for her. He had shown it both directly and through the young princess. Yet, there was always some invisible barrier that prevented his affection from becoming complete. She also knew what that was. Because of the thought that the prince might one day become emperor, she had been— The prince’s only reason for believing that they were trying to tie him down was that very misunderstanding. There was no lack of cause for him to believe so. Vanathi’s elder father had spoken about this matter many times. Why, even the young princess Kundavai Devi herself was involved in that conspiratorial discussion. Many others knew of it as well. Had not even that boatwoman, Poonguzhali, alluded to it and mocked him?
Therefore, it was no wonder that such a thought took root in the prince’s mind and became a barrier to his affection!

But when the prince comes to know of the vow Vanathi just made, will not that barrier be removed? Will he ever come to know of it? What if she herself told him? Oh, foolish Vanathi! Whenever he stands before you, your lips are sealed! When you thought he was just a mahout, you spoke so freely here in Thirunallur that he even called you a “chattering girl”! After that, you could neither look him in the face nor open your mouth to speak!

Poor orphaned Vanathi! The next time you see the prince, do not let things go so badly! Speak boldly what is in your heart! “Even if you ascend the throne, I will not! I have sworn so! If you remain only a mahout and take me with you on the elephant just once, I shall consider that greater than a life in heaven,”—say it courageously!

All that is well and good! But will there be an opportunity to say such things? Where is this flood taking me? Will I drown and die before reaching the shore? No, never shall that happen. Look, the shore is visible! The crown finial of Thirunallur’s Vasantha Maligai is in sight! Ah! Was it not only yesterday that the prince rode up on the elephant to save the fledgling birds and spoke so sweetly with me? It all feels so vivid!

What is this? Look, there is an elephant! Upon it, a mahout! How indifferently that elephant pushes through the force of the flood, moving as if it were climbing a hill! There, it has reached the bank! Now it is moving westward along the shore! Who could that be, sitting so regally atop the elephant? Could it be… No, no! What a mad thought! Why would the prince be coming here alone on an elephant?

Just because I once mistook the prince for a mahout, must I now suspect every mahout I see to be the prince? What foolishness! Still, even if he is just a mahout, might he not help me? Will he not rescue me from this thatched hut— If I could only get to the shore from this great flood, wouldn’t that be enough? If I reveal who I am, might they not lift me onto the elephant and take me straight to Ponniyin Selvan himself?

As soon as this thought struck her, Vanathi called out, “O elephant driver! Elephant driver!” Whether her voice did not reach his ears, or whether he heard but paid no heed, she could not tell. The elephant did not stop; the mahout did not turn to look back. The elephant’s pace only quickened. In a short while, both the elephant and its rider disappeared around a bend on the riverbank.

Before Vanathi could even dwell on this disappointment, a far more terrifying thought seized her mind. The thatched raft seemed to suddenly spin and whirl at a dizzying speed. Yes, yes! The river’s current had grown even swifter at that spot. The bank, and the thick roots of the grand trees that grew along its edge, were rushing toward her.

The raft was certain to crash against those roots. The moment it struck, it would shatter to pieces and sink into the water. What would become of her then? Could she somehow escape and reach the shore? Or would she be caught in the whirlpools, dashed against the roots, and meet her end?
Alas! What was that? Amidst the roots of those trees, a fearsome crocodile lay with its jaws agape! Was it a real crocodile? Or a mere log? Or was it just a trick of her terrified mind?
The shore was close now! The raft was about to collide with the roots of the trees!
Vanathi squeezed her eyes shut. “Mother! Durga Parameshwari! O Mother, I am a helpless orphan with neither father nor mother—only you are my refuge! Take me to your feet!” she prayed.

chapters.title: Life Swayed!
paragraphs: There are moments when a single second can seem like an entire age. One such moment now befell Vanathi. With her eyes tightly shut, praying fervently to Durga Parameswari, she spun along in the thatched-roof boat for what could only have been a few seconds. Yet, to her, those moments stretched into endless eons.

Then, a sudden, violent jolt shook her entire body, snapping her eyes open. She realized that the shock had come because the roofed boat had crashed against the roots of a tree on the riverbank. By a stroke of fortune, as the thatched roof splintered and broke apart, half of Vanathi’s body became entangled in the bent branches of the tree. Thus, she escaped being dashed against the roots.

Becoming aware of her situation, she clung tightly to the branches. The swirling floodwaters seized her legs and pulled at them with such force that it seemed as if they would be torn from her body. Even her sari was being tugged by the current, as if the river itself was trying to drag her away.

But at that perilous moment, a strange courage and determination welled up within Vanathi from somewhere deep inside. Gritting her teeth, she summoned all her strength, leapt, and climbed up onto the branch. She found a secure spot on a thick limb that forked into two, and sat there firmly. She twisted the ends of her sari and wrung out the water.

Just then, she heard the sudden splash of water below. The memory of the crocodile she had glimpsed before closing her eyes flashed into her mind. Leaning down, she peered all around. At first, she saw only the crocodile’s tail thrashing the water. Most of its body was still hidden beneath the broken, scattered pieces of the thatched roof she had climbed from. Slowly, using its tail and writhing its body, the crocodile freed itself from the debris. Once it emerged, it opened its jaws wide, as if to express its delight. Looking up at Vanathi, it seemed to say, “Come, come! One way or another, you must fall into my jaws!”

Vanathi, too, felt a surge of exhilaration at the thought of her narrow escape. “Oh ho! Is that what you say? You think you can swallow me whole? Crocodile! Your tricks—your tail and your teeth—will not prevail against me! You may bare your fangs, but—” “It is of no use to show you. Don’t rely on me to satisfy your hunger! Go look for someone else!” said Vanathi to the crocodile. Hearing her voice, the crocodile fixed its two terrifying eyes upon her and began to stare intently.

Vanathi said, “Oh dear! It seems your curse has not left you yet!” With that, she looked all around her. Her situation seemed rather alarming. On the water’s side, the branches of the great tree bent low, almost touching the river. But on the bank’s side, there were no such low-hanging branches to be seen. If she tried to descend by the trunk, the crocodile waited below, lurking among the tangled roots. If she leapt from the branches that hung over the river, the swirling eddies of the deep pool were ready to seize her and drag her down to the underworld. Even gazing for a moment at that great whirlpool made her head spin.
“Even if the branches on the bank’s side are high, it doesn’t matter; somehow, I can jump and manage,” she thought. Resolving to cross over by walking along the branches, she tried to rise.

But her lower body had been immersed in water for so long that her legs had gone numb with cold. When she tried to stand, her legs trembled uncontrollably. “Tch, tch! What’s wrong with you, legs?” she said, and sat down again. Who had more patience—the crocodile or herself? It seemed she would have to find out!

At that moment, the trumpeting roar of Gajendran startled Vanathi. The elephant, which had just crossed the river and gone up the bank toward the west, was now returning. At the same time, she noticed a boat approaching along the riverbank. There were two people in the boat. Yes, yes; one of them was the astrologer’s disciple, and the other was Poonguzhali! In the end, was it Poonguzhali who had to come to rescue her and take her away?

The boat came beneath the tree. Poonguzhali looked up and saw Vanathi sitting on the branch. Smiling, she called out, “Princess! You’ve found a fine place to hide. Come down quickly! Do you know who is coming on that elephant?”
A sudden realization dawned in Vanathi’s heart. Still, to confirm it, she asked, “I don’t know. Who?”
“The very person you set out in search of—him! The Prince himself!” said Poonguzhali.

Vanathi, with unrestrained astonishment, gazed for several moments at the person approaching atop the elephant. Only as he drew near did it strike her how utterly improper it was for her to be seated upon a tree branch. She realized that, as per Poonguzhali’s suggestion, she ought to descend into the boat. She glanced down. At that moment, she saw that the boat, swept by the force of the floodwaters, was drifting away from beneath the tree and could not remain in place. She also saw Poonguzhali leap into the water, unwilling to let the boat go without her.

Oh no, what is this? Did that woman not notice the fearsome crocodile lying nearby? In a single instant, nine thousand anxious thoughts surged and boiled within Vanathi’s heart. Disjointed, stammering words tumbled from her lips.

“Crocodile!”—that alone reached Poonguzhali’s ears. She turned to look. Yes; not far from her, a monstrous crocodile was opening its jaws wide. As Poonguzhali turned, the crocodile raised its tail and slapped it upon the water.

Poonguzhali was indeed courageous! She had faced countless dangers before. But what use is mere courage before a crocodile, its jaws agape, just ten feet away? One wrong move meant death! If she could not escape in a single instant, she would be lost to the crocodile’s maw! How could she save herself? She must get back into the boat!

Thinking thus, Poonguzhali plunged into the water. By then, the boat had drifted some distance away. The astrologer’s disciple, realizing he could not halt the boat at that spot, decided to steer it a little downstream and bring it to the shore. He did not notice Poonguzhali’s perilous situation.

Poonguzhali, who had dived in to catch the boat, found that the swirling eddies at the riverbank of the flooded Kaveri were more dangerous than the waves of the open sea. The current pulled her downward. She realized that the crocodile had begun to move, intent on seizing her. In this dire moment, the end of her saree got caught in the twisted branches of a submerged tree, making her predicament even more perilous.

Vanathi, seated on the upper branch, saw all this. The bitterness Poonguzhali had harbored toward her, the vow she had made in anger at Vanathi’s harsh words a short while ago, and how she had shaken off Vanathi’s restraining hand and leapt into the water—all these flashed through Vanathi’s mind and vanished in a lightning instant. Along with them, she remembered how that woman had rescued Ponniyin Selvan from the sea and brought him to the Shozhamaṇi Vihara, and how both the Chola land and she herself owed Poonguzhali a debt of gratitude for that deed.
Look—there he comes on the elephant!

He is on his way. If, before he arrives, she is swallowed by the jaws of the crocodile, what agony will torment his heart? What will he think of her? Was it not with the intention of saving her that she had followed and thus fallen into this peril?

All these thoughts arose in Vanathi’s heart in the span of a moment—barely a hundredth part of the time it takes for our dear readers to read these lines. The saying, “The speed of the wind, the speed of the mind,” is no mere phrase. Of all the forces in this world, the swiftness of thought is the greatest. In that brief instant of contemplation, Vanathi had also resolved what her duty was.

From the western branch, she let herself down onto a lower bough, stretched out her hands, and grasped Poonguzhali’s thick braid. She looked up at Poonguzhali. The latter did not try to escape from Vanathi’s grip. She reached down one arm. Vanathi caught hold of it. She began to pull Poonguzhali upward. With her other hand, Poonguzhali clutched a branch and tried to lift herself out of the flood. She managed to climb onto the branch where Vanathi sat. The branch bent under the weight of both women, unable to bear them.

Poonguzhali tried to climb higher. In that attempt, her feet slipped. In the next instant, she was dangling between the tree branch and the raging river below, suspended in midair. Only one of her hands was gripped tightly by both of Vanathi’s.

It took a few moments for the crocodile, hidden among the roots of the tree, to emerge. Now it had come out. It looked up at the figure hanging from the branch and opened its jaws wide once again. Poonguzhali’s body and soul swung between life and death.

Vanathi’s slender arms seemed about to give way under the weight of Poonguzhali’s sturdy form. Her heart thudded with the fear that, at any moment, Poonguzhali might slip from her grasp and fall into the crocodile’s gaping mouth.
If such a disaster were to occur, Vanathi could never again face the prince. If Poonguzhali fell, it would be better for her to let go and fall to her own death as well. That is what she must do.

Look—there, the elephant is drawing near. The prince is riding upon it. Will her arms have the strength to hold onto Poonguzhali until he arrives and rescues them? The elephant reached the riverbank and stood beneath the tree.
Once again—
It trumpeted. Hearing that sound, the crocodile turned in that direction. Whatever it thought, it once again slithered back to the midst of the tree roots and lay down.
Vanathi, still bent upon the tree branch, looked at the elephant. She looked at the man atop it as well. Yes; it was the prince! It was Ponniyin Selvan himself!
“Mahout! Mahout! As you once saved the fledgling birds, today save these foolish girls!” she murmured to herself in a voice so soft that only she could hear it.

Impossible; she could no longer bear the weight of this boat-girl! Even a moment’s delay, and her arms would tear away from her shoulders and fall off! Oh dear! Her name is Poonguzhali! But how heavy she is! Is her body not made of iron?
“Mahout! Mahout! Won’t you come quickly?...”
Poonguzhali screamed, “Kreech!” Hearing that, Vanathi thought the crocodile had caught her. An unspeakable terror took hold of her heart. She shut her eyes tightly.
The weight pulling her arms downward grew heavier. Still believing that the crocodile had seized Poonguzhali, she clung to her even more tightly, trying to pull her up.

“Let go! Vanathi! Let go!” came the prince’s voice, sweet as nectar, in her ear. Not knowing what else to do, she let go. The burden that had been tearing at her shoulders was suddenly gone. She opened her eyes.

She saw Gajendran, the elephant, lift Poonguzhali with its trunk, whirl her up, and set her down on the bank. Poonguzhali’s eyes were closed. It must have been when the elephant’s trunk curled around her that she had screamed like that.
Vanathi remembered how she, too, had once screamed and fainted. Now, though her danger was a hundredfold greater, she marveled at herself for not fainting or losing her wits.

If only the young princess were here to praise and admire her courage! Still, it did not matter. One day, she would know of it, no matter what. But what was to become of her now? Would the prince take only Poonguzhali with him, leaving her stranded atop this tree?

If he had done so, it would have been a fitting punishment for my own recklessness! No, no! Once again, the trunk of the elephant stretched out towards her. Vanathi closed her eyes once more. In the next moment, she felt herself lifted from the tree branch and set down upon the hard ground. When she opened her eyes, she found herself standing on the riverbank, near Poonguzhali.
Without realizing it, with a surge of affection and eagerness, she embraced the boatwoman tightly.

With tears brimming in her eyes and a trembling voice, Poonguzhali said, “Princess! Today, you have saved my life. I came to rescue you from drowning in the river flood. But instead, you saved me from the jaws of the crocodile. I will never forget this debt of gratitude.”
“Poonguzhali! Was it I who saved you? Was it not that mahout who saved both you and me? Offer your thanks to him!” said Vanathi.
“I do not care so much for my own life. But my aunt sent me with an urgent message for her beloved son. I did not wish to die before delivering it!” replied Poonguzhali.
Vanathi looked up at the man seated atop the elephant. A strange, mischievous excitement seized her at that moment.
“Mahout! Mahout! Will you take us with you on your elephant?” she asked, and then burst into laughter.

chapters.title: Joy and Sorrow
paragraphs: Hearing Vanathi’s words, mingled with the sound of her laughter, the prince too laughed as he climbed down from the elephant.

“Ah! Mounting an elephant is a most difficult task. It is much like ascending the royal throne. Climbing onto the elephant is hard; sitting atop it is harder still! But descending from it is the hardest of all. Yet, at times, one must endure such hardships!” said Ponniyin Selvan.
“Some endure that hardship even for the most trivial reasons. There are those who mount an elephant and come rushing just to save a nest of baby birds!” said Vanathi.
“Do you still remember that incident, Vanathi? Since you have never spoken of it until now, I thought you might have forgotten!” said the prince.

“Those who roam the world and engage in many brave deeds may forget. But what else is there for a foolish girl who stays within the palace to do, except to remember? I still recall the day you came riding on the elephant; I remember when I said I was a girl from Kodumbalur, and you frowned and turned away!”
“There was a reason for that then, Vanathi!”

“That reason still exists, my lord! You are the son of the emperor who rules the world; Ponniyin Selvan, the jewel of Chozha Nadu. And I—was born and raised in a remote, wild region. A princess of a minor chieftain’s clan; and even among them, the orphaned daughter of one who died in battle!…”

“Vanathi! You do me an injustice! You speak words that are unfair! Let it be, let it be! I must hurry to Thanjai! Tell me quickly—how did you come here? Why did you come alone? Did you really float here atop a thatched roof? Why did this girl come here? How did she get caught in such mortal peril?…”

“I am glad that you remembered I am standing here alone. If you give me a moment to speak with you privately, I will say what I must and leave at once!” said Poonkuzhali. At that moment, as the two women stood face to face before the prince, an extraordinary courage and boldness seemed to possess them.

“Daughter of the Ocean! Did you think I had forgotten you? How could that ever be? Was it not you who, when I called and called, silently rowed the boat forward without so much as a word in reply? How could I ever forget the sight of you, who came in such haste, swaying between the tree branch and the open jaws of the crocodile? I shall remember that as long as I live!” said the prince, and laughed.
“And I can never forget the predicament in which Vanathi clung to you, unable to lift you up or let you go. But how did the two of you come here? For what reason? One of you, tell me quickly!”

“Ponniyin Selva! Both I and your noble sister have come to prevent you from being stopped on your way to Thanjavur. The princess fears that if you come to Thanjavur now, a great war will break out there. She wishes to meet and speak with you before that happens…”
“Where is the princess now?”
“She is in Kudanthai…”
“How did you come here alone?”

“On the way, your sister and I stayed for a short while at the house of the astrologer in Kudanthai. At that time, the Kaveri river broke its banks and swept right up to the astrologer’s house. Prince! They say that Mother Kaveri saved you when you were a child. I also know how much affection you bear for this Ponni river. But today, it is terrifying even to think of the suffering this river has brought upon the towns and villages, the people and the animals. It seems as though Mother Kaveri is most cruel…”

“Vanathi! Do not speak ill of Mother Kaveri! This queen has such love for our Chola land. When that love overflows its bounds, she breaks through the banks and surges forth. Those who do not understand this speak ill of the mother! Why, some even blame the king of the seas for the tides that cross the shore. But Poonguzhali would never speak ill of the lord of the oceans!” said the prince.

“Forgive me! I shall never again blame Mother Kaveri. When your sister and I were at the astrologer’s house in Kudanthai, suddenly the river’s longing surged and overflowed. Your sister and the others ran to the temple— They climbed onto the roof of the mandapam. Because of my own carelessness, I failed to climb up onto the mandapam. I clung to the astrologer’s tiled roof and drifted along with it…”

“To save you, Poonguzhali must have boarded the boat and come after you. How beautiful it is! In the end, this Gajendran had to save both of you together. This elephant’s intelligence is truly remarkable! With its trunk, it lifted both of you as if picking up a garland of flowers—without wavering or faltering—and just a moment ago, set you safely on the shore! This very morning, the same elephant, with the mahout’s goad in hand, lifted the mahout who came running late and hurled him far away! It’s a miracle if that man is still alive!”
“Oh no! What is that? I myself wanted to ask you about it…”
“What did you want to ask me?”
“I wanted to know whether you were harmed by the mahout or the goad.”
“It’s true that I was in danger; but how did you know? Did the astrologer tell you? Has that madness not yet left the young princess?”
“The astrologer did not tell us! Even if he had, we would not have believed him. It was Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar who told us!”
“What? What? Who told you?”

“Yes, Prince! It was the commander, Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar himself who told us. While we were at the astrologer’s house, he suddenly entered. He spoke of the danger that awaited you. He even mentioned the goad smeared with poison…!”
“Aha! This is a great wonder! How did he come to know of it? Has he too become an astrologer? Or perhaps… as everyone says, was it he who arranged all this?”
“No, Prince! It was not his doing. He overheard the Pandya conspirators speaking in secret and learned of it that way…!”
“Oh! Did he say anything else?”

“It is terrifying even to think or speak of it. He said that those conspirators have plotted to send you, your father, and your elder brother Aditya Karikalan to the world of Yama on the same day. He—”
He has already hastened to Kadambur to save them. He left after telling me that I must warn both you and the Emperor…”
“Ah! Since his warning proved true in my case, it must surely be true in the case of the others as well! Samudrakumari, you said you had something to tell me?”
“Yes, Prince! The mute queen of Eezham sent me to bring you to Thanjai at once…”
“Ah! I nearly forgot to ask you about that. It was for the sake of the Eezham queen that I set out in such haste. I heard someone forcibly brought her to Thanjavur— is that true?”
“It is true, my lord! But it was the Prime Minister Aniruddha who did so, and with good intentions…”
“Oh! Was it Aniruddha’s doing? He must have brought her to present her to my father. Poonguzhali, did the Prime Minister’s intention succeed? Did they— the Emperor and the Eezham queen— meet?”
“Yes, they met!”

“My life’s dearest wish has been fulfilled. There is no news that could bring me greater joy than this. As long as my grandaunt is near my father, his life is in no danger. You know, Poonguzhali, that noble lady possesses a rare gift of foresight!”
“Yes, I know! As long as the Eezham queen is there, the Emperor is safe. But…”
“But what? Why do you hesitate, Samudrakumari?”
“It is difficult for me to say, my tongue will not utter it. The Eezham queen believes her end is near. Before she closes her eyes for the last time, she wishes to see you once more!” she said.

“Heavens! What are you saying? You give me such joyous news, and then immediately follow it with this calamity! I cannot delay even a moment longer, Vanathi! Tell the Young Princess that I beg her forgiveness!” said Prince Arulmozhi.

Vandiyathevan’s heart was overflowing with happiness. The words spoken by Kundavai Devi still echoed in his ears, sweeter than the music of the veena, more fragrant than the scent of blooming jasmine. He felt as if he were floating on air, as if the very earth beneath his feet had become light. The world seemed transformed—every tree, every flower, every bird appeared to be smiling at him.

Yet, even amidst this boundless joy, a shadow of sorrow crept into his mind. The thought of the dangers that surrounded the Chola dynasty, the conspiracies that threatened the royal family, and the uncertainty of the future weighed upon him. The faces of his friends and allies, the memory of the perils he had faced on his journey, and the responsibilities that lay ahead—all these mingled with his happiness, casting a veil of melancholy over his heart.

He walked slowly through the palace gardens, lost in thought. The gentle breeze caressed his face, carrying with it the faint sound of laughter and music from the inner courtyards. The moonlight bathed the garden in a silvery glow, illuminating the flowers and the winding paths. Vandiyathevan paused beneath a flowering tree, gazing up at the sky. The stars twinkled above, as if sharing in his joy and sorrow.

At that moment, he heard footsteps approaching. He turned to see a familiar figure—Periya Pazhuvettarayar, his face stern and unreadable, walking towards him. Vandiyathevan straightened, his mind alert. The old warrior stopped a few paces away and regarded him in silence.

“Vandiyatheva,” he said at last, his voice grave, “the time for celebration is not yet come. The shadows that threaten our kingdom grow darker by the day. Be vigilant. Do not let fleeting happiness blind you to the dangers that lie ahead.”
Vandiyathevan bowed respectfully. “I understand, Periya Pazhuvettarayar. I will not forget my duty.”
The old man nodded, his expression softening for a moment. “Good. Remember, the fate of the Chola dynasty rests in the hands of those who are loyal and brave. May you prove yourself worthy.”

With those words, he turned and walked away, disappearing into the shadows of the garden. Vandiyathevan stood alone, the weight of responsibility settling upon his shoulders. Yet, in his heart, the memory of Kundavai’s words glowed like a beacon, giving him strength to face whatever trials awaited him.
Thus, in that night of mingled joy and sorrow, Vandiyathevan resolved to fulfill his duty, no matter the cost.

chapters.title: The Armies Arrived!
paragraphs: That day, the great city of Thanjavur was in utter tumult and commotion. The people had completely forgotten the storm, the rain, and the destruction they had caused. Rumors swept through the air: “The peerless hero who conquered Eezham, the prince who has won the hearts of the Chola people, Ponniyin Selvan, emerged safely from Nagapattinam on the day the storm struck; now he is on his way to Thanjavur. Vast crowds are following him, intent on placing him upon the throne and crowning him emperor.” Such news and more spread like wildfire. Soon, those who had seen the prince in Nagapattinam with their own eyes returned and confirmed the tidings. Because of this, just as the storm had raged outside two days earlier, a tempest of excitement now swept through the hearts of Thanjavur’s citizens. The people resolved that Thanjavur must give the prince a reception the likes of which the city had never seen before. They began to decorate the streets of the outer town beyond the fort. Crowds gathered in the thoroughfares, talking eagerly. Drums, cymbals, and all manner of musical instruments were assembled. Dancers and singers, skilled in their arts, prepared themselves to display their talents on this special occasion. Men and children alike pondered how best to adorn themselves. Many, eager to be the first to welcome the prince, left Thanjavur early and waited along the roads leading in from all directions, some distance from the city. Others, seeing these early birds, mocked them for their impatience.

If the outer city was thus astir, signs soon appeared that something important was expected within the fort as well. In the morning, as usual, the gates of the fort were opened. Vegetable sellers, curd and buttermilk vendors, and those going to their duties in the palaces entered the fort as on any other day. Only a few came today to complain about the damages caused by the storm and rain. They too entered the fort. As usual, the Velakkara guards entered the fort.

Then, suddenly, all the gates of the fort were shut with a resounding clang. The noise of massive iron bars being drawn across the doors, and the clatter of bolts being fastened, echoed through the air. Those who arrived later were stopped by the guards. They were stopped. In the forenoon, when the fortress gates were locked and bolted in such a manner, the townspeople began to murmur among themselves, wondering at the reason for this unusual act. At that very moment, another strange event occurred. The bridge that spanned the moat surrounding the fort was raised. After that, no one could even approach the entrance to the fortress.

Those who were near the main gate—the northern gate—began to inquire about the western and southern gates as well. When they learned that those gates too had been locked and bolted just like the northern gate, and that their bridges had also been raised, their astonishment grew.

“What is this? There is no war going on, is there? There is no sign of enemy armies marching upon us, is there? Are there any powerful enemies in the neighboring regions to the north, south, east, or west, who might suddenly attack? Even if, by some chance, enemies from the northern double provinces were to launch a sudden assault, how could they possibly cross the Kollidam, the Kaveri, and the other rivers at this time? Aren’t those great rivers now flowing in full flood?” Thus did the people living in the outer city of Thanjai converse among themselves.

Some began to wonder if all these arrangements were being made to prevent Ponniyin Selvan from entering the fortress. “That must be it,” others replied, answering their own questions. As this rumor spread, the excitement among the townsfolk grew ever more intense. “Who are these Pazhuvettarayar chieftains to prevent a prince descended in unbroken line from Vijayalaya Chola from entering the fortress? If the Pazhuvettarayars truly attempt such a thing, then the very walls of the fort must be torn down and destroyed!” Some spoke in this spirit.

Rumor is a mysterious phantom—no one can ever discover how it arises or how it travels so swiftly. Suddenly, another dreadful rumor began to spread among the people: that the long-anticipated death of Emperor Sundara Chola had finally occurred. “Has the Emperor passed away? Is it true?” people began to ask. Some who had seen a shooting star blaze for a moment in the early dawn, shining with a radiant light before falling to earth and vanishing, pointed to this as proof that Sundara Chola had died.

“If this is true, what is going to happen next?”—was it not natural that people should discuss this with anxiety? Would disputes arise over the right to the throne? Would the minor kings split into two factions and fight each other? Such were the concerns being debated. Will the Chola Empire, which has flourished and grown strong for a hundred years, now be shattered into pieces because of internal strife? Will the armies of enemies once again penetrate the empire that has stood tall and proud for a century?

While the people were still speaking in such anxious tones, suddenly a loud cry arose: “Look, the army is coming!” Many rushed here and there to see for themselves. Some climbed atop tall buildings, others scaled lofty trees. The sight that met their eyes filled them with both wonder and astonishment.

In those days, three great roads led westward and southwestward from Thanjavur. One road passed through Kodumbalur towards Rameswaram; another led through Madurai to the southern Pandya country; the third, a long and broad road, ran through Uraiyur to Karur and the Chera land.

That afternoon, armies were marching in formation along all three of these roads. The leading ranks were visible to the eye, but where the columns ended, no one could tell. The lines of soldiers seemed endless, stretching on and on without break.

Fortunately, at the head of these armies, great banners bearing the tiger emblem fluttered in the wind, leaving no room for doubt that these were not enemy forces. They were the armies of the Chola Empire! But why were they coming? From where had they set out?

As the armies drew nearer, the smaller insignias embossed on the tiger banners became visible. From these, it was clear that the mighty army of Parantaka Chola under the command of Kodumbalur, the great force of the Kaikkolar troops from southern Pandya country, and the formidable army of Arinjaya Chola, recently engaged in the Eelam campaign, were all marching together.

Soon, it became known to the people of Thanjavur that the commander of the southern forces, Boothi Vikrama Kesari, was approaching with these combined armies. From this, it was easy to guess the purpose of their arrival. It was well known throughout Chola land that the great Velar of Kodumbalur, Boothi Vikrama Kesari, wished to wed Vanathi, the daughter of the younger Velar of Eelam, to Ponniyin Selvan, and to see him ascend the Chola throne.

The arrival of Prince Arulmozhi Varman from the east, escorted by the jubilant crowds, and the simultaneous approach of Commander Boothi Vikrama Kesari with his grand army from the west—these two events seemed to fit together perfectly.

The people already knew that the Pazhuvettaraiyars and the minor kings allied with them were striving to crown Madurantaka. Therefore, the citizens of Thanjavur surmised that Kodumbalur Boothi Vikrama Kesari was arriving with his vast southern armies to enthrone Arulmozhivarman, who was worthy of their love. This thought made their enthusiasm surge even higher, overflowing its banks. Like the swelling sea, they were ready to welcome, honor, and feast all the warriors who had come in great numbers.

At that time in Thanjavur, there were many choultries maintained by powerful merchant guilds. The Kodumbalur Manigramattar, the Thiruppurambayam Valanjiyar, the Ooraiyur Dharma Vanigar, and the Nana Desathisai Aiyirathu Aindhunoottuvar—these merchant guilds had established choultries where, from that very afternoon, arrangements were being made to feed thousands.

When the townspeople learned of this, their joy grew even greater. Everywhere, people wandered about, gathering in groups and conversing excitedly. As nearly every one of them belonged to Arulmozhivarman’s faction, they saw no need for secrecy in discussing the events to come. When the army approached Thanjavur and began pitching tents and setting up camps here and there, the townsfolk themselves went to these camps and began to converse freely with the soldiers.

Before the sun had fully set and darkness had deepened, Sena warriors had surrounded Thanjavur on three sides. On the fourth side, the Vadavaru river ran close by the Thanjavur fort, and as the river was in flood, it was neither convenient nor necessary for soldiers to approach from that direction. We have already seen the main northern gate of the Thanjavur fort, have we not? Was it not through that very gate that Vandiyathevan first entered the fort, following Nandini Devi? It was in a spot from which the fort’s main gate could be clearly seen that the commander-in-chief, Boothi Vikrama Kesari, established his headquarters.

After night had fallen and a watch had passed, the commander-in-chief circled the fort and returned to his headquarters. Nearly a hundred men had already gathered there before him. Among them were Velir chieftains, Kaikkolar commanders, leaders from the Pandya region, and chiefs from Kongu Nadu. There were also several Chola commanders who had won victories in the war against Eelam (Sri Lanka). Besides these, there were the heads of many great merchant guilds—most notably, the ‘Nana Desathisai Aiyirathu Aindhunoottuvar.’

The leaders of the world-renowned trade guild had gathered there. These were wealthy merchants who conducted vast maritime commerce with foreign lands. They possessed the means to dispatch their own warships to guard the merchant vessels that carried their goods. In addition to these, the heads of the Five Great Guilds of Thanjavur city, as well as the leaders of the Eight-member Council, had also been invited and were assembled in that pavilion.

chapters.title: The Council of Ministers
paragraphs: After the customary inquiries about each other’s well-being, the great Velar of Kodumbalur looked around at those assembled and began to speak:

“Almost everyone to whom I sent word has gathered here. Only the aged ruler of Thirukovalur, the Malaiyaman king, has not come. I believe there must be a valid reason for his absence. We have come together here to deliberate upon a matter that many would consider extremely perilous. The world knows well how devoted we all are to the Chola dynasty and to Emperor Sundara Chola. We have proved this devotion time and again, in countless affairs. Yet, our enemies may accuse us of gathering here in opposition to the Emperor’s wishes. They may even say that we have assembled an army to wage war against him. But we are unable to meet the Emperor in person. Not for a single moment are we allowed to speak with him privately and learn his true wishes. The reason for this is known to all. It is said that, for the sake of the Emperor’s health, he is kept within the fortress at Thanjavur. But in truth, it seems to me that the Pazhuvettaraiyars have imprisoned him there. I do not know what you all think…”
At this point, the Commander-in-Chief paused briefly, and from the gathering arose many voices: “Yes, yes,” “That is the truth!” “The Emperor is indeed being held captive.”

“From your agreement, it is clear that we are all united in feeling and purpose. Since the days of Vijayalaya Chola, thousands upon thousands of brave men have laid down their lives on the battlefield to raise this Chola empire to its present glorious state. It is a matter of pride for all of us to call ourselves sons of the Chola land. We have gathered here to ensure that no harm comes to the Chola dynasty or the empire. Not to conspire against the Emperor. For three years, the Emperor’s enemies have kept him imprisoned. They claim it is because his health is failing. But Vijayalaya Chola, who bore ninety-six wounds upon his body, entered the battlefield at Thirupurambiyam in his eightieth year, wielding two— Wielding his swords and spinning them like a whirling wheel, wherever he entered, he heaped the heads of his enemies into mountains! If such a valorous king as Sundara Chozhar, born of that heroic lineage, now claims bodily illness as a reason and refuses to come out—can that be believed? It seems that the traitorous schemers who have imprisoned the Emperor have, through their witchcraft, black magic, and sorcery, also brought confusion to his mind. If the Emperor’s mind were clear, would he, having two sons who are warriors greater than Bhima and Arjuna themselves, wish to crown Madurantakan, who has never even set eyes on a battlefield?…”
At that moment, many voices rose at once: “How do we know for certain that this is the Emperor’s wish?”
“It is true that we do not know directly. It may well be a tale spun by the Pazhuvettaraiyars. Yet even our Prime Minister, Aniruddha Brahmarayar, believes it…”
“Perhaps Aniruddha himself has joined with them; who can say?” said someone in the gathering.

“That too may be so. One of the main reasons we have assembled here is to uncover the truth of this matter. You must all have heard the rumor that is circulating today in this great city of Thanjai. I do not believe it. I have faith that we shall all be granted the fortune to behold the Emperor alive. When we do, let us ask him directly what his wish is regarding the succession. If, by chance, the Emperor himself declares his desire to crown Madurantakan, will all of you accept it?…”
“No! Never!” came the resounding cry.

“I too will not accept it. For if the Emperor’s mind were clear, he would never make such a declaration. The matter of succession was settled and concluded in the days of Paranthaka Chozhar himself. I myself heard, with my own ears, that king, on his deathbed, declare that only Sundara Chozhar and his descendants should ascend the throne of Thanjai. Many others who heard it are still present here. The great and departed Kandaradithar, even in raising his son, strove to ensure that he would never desire to rule the kingdom. His virtuous queen, the noble Periya Piratti—Sembiyan Maadevi, who is devoted to Lord Shiva—has always been steadfast in her opposition to crowning Madurantakan. We all know this well. There must be some important reason behind all this. In such a case, why should Sundara Chozhar wish to crown Madurantakan? I will give you yet another example to show that the Emperor’s mind is not right. After slaying Veera Pandiyan and bringing the Pandya—” After annihilating the enemy forces, my brother marched forth with an army to punish the king of Eelam, who had come forward to aid the Pandya. We failed to send him sufficient troops and equipment as support. Because of that, he was compelled to meet a heroic death on the battlefield. To wipe away that stain upon the valorous glory of the Chola land, Ponniyin Selvan and I set forth. We destroyed the armies of Eelam. We captured Anuradhapura. We forced Mahindan to flee and hide within the mountain country.

It is known to all of you that the Commander-in-Chief, Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar, did not cooperate with us. Among you, the great leaders of the merchant guilds who are present here, sent supplies and rendered immense assistance. Even so, our warriors had to endure countless hardships. Yet, bearing all those sufferings, how was it possible to utterly destroy Mahindan’s armies? It was solely due to the unparalleled courage and inspiration given by Ponniyin Selvan, the peerless hero among the great warriors of the Chola clan! And what reward did the Emperor, his own father, bestow upon such a heroic son? He heaped upon the prince the monstrous accusation of treason and ordered that he be arrested and brought in chains! Can one who is master of his own mind issue such a command…?”
“Commander! Once again, you speak of the Emperor’s order. What proof is there that the Emperor himself sent that order?” asked one among those assembled in the council.

“There is no proof for that. It is precisely to ascertain the truth of this matter directly that we have come here. If such an order could have been issued without the Emperor’s consent, consider for a moment the dreadful state in which this Chola Empire finds itself. Think also of the events that followed. The soldiers who came to arrest the prince refused to do so. The prince himself, in obedience to his father’s command, boarded Parthibendra Pallavan’s ship. That ship, it is said, was caught in a storm. Then a rumor spread that the prince had drowned and perished in the sea. I never believed this. I was certain that the Lord of the Ocean would not have claimed Ponniyin Selvan. When all the others who traveled on that ship survived, how could it be that the prince alone drowned and died? Therefore, I believed that as soon as the prince reached the shore, a plot to imprison him must have been enacted. Learning of this conspiracy, the prince must have escaped and is now safely hidden somewhere; at the right moment, he would emerge. Many of you expressed the same belief. Our faith has been fulfilled. On the day the storm struck Nagapattinam, the prince reappeared, and it is said that the people of Chola Nadu welcomed him with victorious celebrations and escorted him to Thanjai… “We also know that we have been summoned here.
