It was with the intention of standing by their side that we too have come to this place. But the scheming conspirators have once again displayed their cunning…”
“What? What is it?” several voices asked anxiously.

“I received the news only a few minutes before coming to this assembly. This morning, just as the Prince was about to depart from Thiruvarur, the elephant he was to mount went mad, seized the mahout, and flung him aside. The elephant then ran amok. Amidst the ensuing chaos, the Prince too has gone missing!”
“Alas!” “What a calamity is this?” “Has even fate joined the side of the conspirators?”—thus did many begin to lament in distress. The Commander-in-Chief raised his hand and calmed them to silence.

“When I first heard the news, I too was shaken. Somehow, I composed myself and made my way to this gathering. Prince Arulmozhi Varman, who is unmatched in valor on the battlefield, is equally peerless in intelligence; he would not so easily fall into the snare of conspirators. I am hopeful that soon we will hear some good news about him. Meanwhile, I wish to know your opinions on what we should do, and how we ought to conduct ourselves in this difficult situation.”

Having thus spoken his mind, the Commander-in-Chief fell silent, and the others began to express their views. On the main issues, their opinions were almost unanimous; only in minor details did they differ.

The representatives present agreed that they should seek an audience with the Emperor the next day, and if granted, they must clearly declare to the Emperor, “We do not wish for Madurantakan to ascend the Chola throne.” Many insisted on this. “Either the Emperor must remove the Pazhuvettaraiyars from their positions of absolute authority, or the Emperor himself must leave Thanjavur and go to Pazhayarai,” others urged.

“Since Aditya Karikalan has already been crowned as Crown Prince, he is the rightful heir to the throne; if he refuses the throne, then the next rightful claimant is Arulmozhi Varman. This must be conveyed to the Emperor without leaving room for doubt, and we must secure his agreement,” some said. Others added that if they were denied an audience with the Emperor— Some suggested that if the fortress gates were not opened, it would be necessary to lay siege to the fort. “Why a siege? It is better to order the soldiers to immediately break down the fortress gates and ramparts!” declared others. Some opined that it would be wise to wait until news arrived about the prince, and that a messenger should be sent to Aditya Karikalan to bring him here as well.

“What is the use of waiting for all that? The great Chola army under the control of the Pazhuvettaraiyars is coming from Mazha Nadu, on the far bank of the Kollidam. At this moment, due to the heavy floods in the Kollidam and other rivers, those forces cannot cross over to reach here. Therefore, this is the right time to break open the fort and rescue the Emperor from the captivity of the Pazhuvettaraiyars,” insisted several others.

While such debates were raging, a soldier who had been standing guard at the entrance of the pavilion hurried inside and whispered something into the Commander’s ear. The Commander turned to the assembly and said, “I will be back in a moment. Please continue your discussion,” and then stepped outside.

chapters.title: At the Fort Gate
paragraphs: From the place where the council of ministers had convened, Boothi Vikrama Kesari emerged and swiftly mounted the horse waiting there. He spurred it toward the northern gate of Thanjai fort. At that very moment, he noticed an elephant approaching the northern gate. Upon the elephant sat a mahout and two women. The mahout placed the horn he held to his lips and blew a long note. Then, in a high, piercing voice that rang out clear and sharp, he proclaimed:

“Parantakan of Eezhathu’s daughter, the cherished child of the young Velar of Kodumbalur, the foster daughter of Commander Boothi Vikrama Kesari of Kodumbalur, the beloved companion of Princess Kundavai Devi of Pazhaiyarai, Vanathi Devi herself is arriving! Make way! Make way!”
As the elephant reached the edge of the moat near the fort gate, the mahout once again blew the horn. Before the echo had faded, he cried out in the same shrill voice:

“Princess Vanathi of Kodumbalur brings a message from the younger princess to the Emperor! She brings important news from Periya Pazhuvettarayar to Chinna Pazhuvettarayar! Open the fort gates! Make way! Make way for Princess Vanathi of Kodumbalur and her companion Poonguzhali Amma! Open the fort gates at once!”

Hearing the mahout’s proclamation, Commander Boothi Vikrama Kesari was struck with astonishment beyond words. Where had he heard that mahout’s voice before? When, and where? Who could he be? But what did it matter who the mahout was? First, he must see whether it was indeed Vanathi upon the elephant. He must prevent her from entering the fort.

If it was Vanathi, all would be well! Until these troubles were resolved, it would be best for the child to remain with him… With these thoughts, the commander urged his horse forward and drew near the elephant. One of the soldiers following him brought a torch, and by its light he saw that the two women atop the elephant were indeed Vanathi, daughter of the young Velar, and Poonguzhali.

“Child! Vanathi!” he began to say something, but the mahout once more raised the horn to his lips and began to blow. How to stop him? Fortunately, at that moment, the women atop the elephant noticed who was approaching them on horseback… They looked closely. Immediately, Vanathi said something to the mahout, who stopped the elephant’s trumpet, and then she exclaimed, “Periyappa! Is it truly you? What I heard is indeed true!”

“Yes, child! It is I. But what is this strange affair? How is it that you have come, bearing tidings? Has no one else from the Ilaiya Piratti managed to get through? Especially in such a situation as this!” said the Commander-in-Chief.

“Yes, Periyappa! It is precisely because of this situation that she sent me with the message. News had reached us that you had arrived with your army and surrounded the Tanjore fort. If she had sent someone else, your soldiers might have stopped them. Even if you had granted permission, those inside the fort might have refused to open the gates. By sending me, she thought it would be easier to accomplish both tasks. She also sent Poonguzhali with me as my companion…”
“Yes, yes! This boat-girl is quite a clever one. I have known that for some time. But what is this message you have brought? What is so urgent that a messenger must be sent in the dead of night?”
“It is indeed an urgent message, Periyappa! I have brought news for the Emperor about Ponniyin Selvan.”
“Ah! About Ponniyin Selvan? Do you know anything about him?”

“Why not? I know a great deal. He is the bravest of the brave, the mightiest of warriors, the one who did not sink in the Kaveri, the one who would not drown even if he fell into the sea, the one who never abandons those who seek his help, the one who never forgets a favor done to him in times of danger, the one who is devoted to his mother and father, the one who never disobeys his sister, the one who has no desire for the throne…”
“That’s enough! Enough! I did not ask for all that. Is the prince safe? Do you know where he is now?”
“He is safe, Periyappa! I know where he is right now. But I cannot tell you that!”
“What? You cannot tell me? Not even to me? Is it you who speaks thus, Vanathi?”
“Yes, Periyappa! It is I who speak. I have pledged not to reveal the prince’s whereabouts to anyone.”
Commander-in-Chief Boothi Vikramakesari’s anger surged and boiled within him, though he strove to contain it.

“Girl! I sent you to the care of the younger princess, believing she would raise you well. But she has made you so stubborn! Enough, enough! Your stay in Pazhayarai is over. Come down! I will send you to Kodumbalur and then attend to other matters,” he declared.

“Periyappa! I too have no desire to set foot on the soil of Thanjavur. That is why I remain seated atop this elephant. This elephant is prone to fits of madness. Just this morning, it tossed a man into the air. So, do not come too close. Once I have delivered the messages I have brought, I will come down to you myself. If you wish to send me to Kodumbalur, do so. But for now, do not try to stop me!” Vanathi replied.
Boothi Vikramakesari pondered for a moment and then said, “Very well, child! I will not try to stop you. But what will you do if the fortress gates are not opened?”
“Periyappa! Have you not come with such a great army? For what purpose? If the gates are not opened, order your troops to break them down!” Vanathi said.

Boothi Vikramakesari was filled with pride at her words. “Daughter! You have spoken as the princess of Kodumbalur should. If the need arises, I shall do exactly that. But there will be no need. Who is this Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar to detain you, who have come from the younger princess to bring a message to the Emperor? He would never dare such a thing. But for my sake, deliver a message to Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar! Tell him that if even the slightest harm befalls you while you are within the fortress, I will utterly destroy his clan, root and branch! Tell him also that my companions and I have come to see the Emperor in person, to learn his wishes from his own lips! Make it clear that if, before tomorrow’s daylight fades, we are not allowed to have audience with the Emperor, we will begin our assault on the fortress!”
“So be it, Periyappa!” Vanathi replied.
Once more, the mahout sounded his horn. “Make way for the Kodumbalur princess! Open the fortress gates!” he shouted.

chapters.title: Vanathi’s Entry
paragraphs: Within the fortress, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar was plunged into deep distress. In matters of valor and daring, he was second to none. Yet, being one accustomed to acting only after consulting his elder brother’s counsel, he now floundered like a bird that had lost its wings in this time of crisis. From that morning onwards, one ill-omened message after another had reached his ears.

He had received word that Periya Pazhuvettarayar had departed from Kadambur Sambuvarayar’s palace for Thanjavur more than two days ago. On the day the storm struck, he had also heard that many boats crossing the Kollidam River had capsized and sunk. Not long after, a man who had been in Periya Pazhuvettarayar’s boat arrived. He reported that their boat too had gone under, and that he alone had managed to struggle to shore after much hardship.

Another spy came with news that Prince Arulmozhi Varman, who had been in hiding at the Soodamani Vihara in Nagapattinam, had now revealed himself and was approaching Thanjavur with a great crowd. He added that the prince had spent the night at Thiruvarur, and that he himself had traveled through the flood-ravaged regions by night to bring this message.

Soon after, a messenger sent by Sambuvarayar arrived. He reported that Malayaman of Thirukovalur was gathering a great army, and that Aditya Karikalan’s fury was rising unchecked. Therefore, Sambuvarayar had sent word that Periya Pazhuvettarayar must set out at once and return.

But Periya Pazhuvettarayar had yet to reach Thanjavur. How could he set out again immediately? Had the Kollidam’s floodwaters perhaps claimed that valiant elder, whom even Yama, the god of death, would hesitate to approach? Chinna Pazhuvettarayar was thrown into confusion by this thought.

Then, as if all this were not enough, spies came running from the south bearing news that struck like thunder. They reported that on all three great roads leading from the southern regions to Thanjavur, Sena soldiers were marching in columns, and that Kodumbalur Boothi Vikrama Kesari was among those advancing.
As soon as he heard this, the Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar ordered all the gates of the fortress to be locked. He strictly forbade anyone from leaving the fort or entering it from outside.

As was customary, that day too, he stationed the Velakkara soldiers around the Emperor’s palace for protection, and appointed his own loyal warriors as guards of the fortress. He thought it necessary to inform the Emperor of all these arrangements. But before that, he wished to consult with the Prime Minister Aniruddha. Though he did not have complete trust in Aniruddha, it was still better that the Prime Minister remained inside the fort rather than outside at such a time. After all, nothing could be done without his knowledge, could it? It was also wise to pretend that he was acting on Aniruddha’s counsel. If anything went wrong later, no one could lay the blame solely upon him.

It would be easier to bring Aniruddha along and speak to the Emperor together, rather than going alone. The Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar believed that Prince Arulmozhi Varman and Boothi Vikrama Kesari—who wished to ally himself by marrying his daughter to the prince—were both approaching from different directions, conspiring together to seize Thanjavur. If he reported this alone, the Emperor might not believe him easily. But if the Prime Minister Aniruddha joined him in saying it, the Emperor would have no choice but to believe.

Prime Minister Aniruddha too was somewhat disturbed. He had not liked that the young princess Kundavai had left Thanjai that morning. The disappearance of the Lankan queen and Poonguzhali that morning had also unsettled his mind. “Where could they have gone? How did they leave? For what reason?”—he pondered all these questions, but could arrive at no conclusion. The news that Boothi Vikrama Kesari was approaching with his army had greatly increased his anxiety.
Yet, he advised the Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar that there was no need to inform the Emperor of all this immediately.

“I hear that the Emperor’s mental distress is greater than ever today. The Empress’s personal maid came and reported as much. In this state, if we speak to him about Boothi Vikrama Kesari, the blood vessels in the Emperor’s brain may burst, and his very life could be endangered. Already, rumors are spreading in Thanjai that the Emperor has passed away. Just imagine what a disaster it would be if that were to actually happen.”

“If the Emperor were to die now, rumors would quickly spread that you were the one who killed him. It would be most convenient for your enemies. Therefore, let us wait and see before making any decisions. First, let us find out what exactly is the intention of Boothi Vikrama Kesari. In the meantime, we may receive definite news about Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar or about Ponniyin Selvan. Until then, be patient,” said Prime Minister Aniruddha, and his words seemed wise to Kaalandhaka Kandar as well.

“In that case, I leave to you the matter that must be conveyed to the Emperor at the right moment. I shall attend to the fort’s security arrangements,” said Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar, taking leave of the Prime Minister.

From that moment, he began to circle the ramparts of the fort, making all the necessary preparations for its defense. The fort had to be made ready for a siege that might last many days. If the Kodumbalur forces tried to break down the gates, scale the walls, and seize the fort, their efforts must be thwarted. For this, he needed to station his most trusted warriors at strategic points. If any part of the rampart was found to be weak, it must be reinforced and strengthened.
While Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar was absorbed in these arrangements, his mind also pondered how to receive news from outside.

There were only two secret underground passages leading out of the Thanjavur fort. One led from the palace of Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar through the treasury chamber to the outside. But no one could use this passage for the next few days. The reason was that, at the point where it opened outside, the Vadavaru river was in flood, its waters crashing against the banks. If the passage were opened now, the flood would rush straight into the treasury chamber.

The other secret passage began within the residence of Prime Minister Aniruddha. But no one could enter or exit through that way without Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar’s knowledge. At the point where the passage crossed the fort wall, his guards were stationed. Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar was considering sending trusted men out through that secret passage after the second watch of the night. He must send men to Kadambur and Pazhayarai to obtain definite information about Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar and Ponniyin Selvan.

At just such a moment, when the assembled chieftains had reached their decision, a soldier came running in haste to report that, at the northern gate, two women had arrived atop an elephant, and that the mahout was calling out for the gate to be opened for them.

When it became known that one of the women was Vanathi, the Younger Pazhuvettarayar was greatly astonished. While Vanathi’s uncle, the commander, was laying siege to the fort with his army, how much courage must it take for that young woman to ask to be admitted inside? At first, he resolved firmly, “The gate cannot be opened under any circumstances.” But by the time he reached the northern gate, his mind had changed.
“Would it not be a disgrace to my valor if I refused to open the gate out of fear of a mere young girl?” he thought. He was also eager to learn why that girl so earnestly wished to enter the fort.

He climbed up to the upper storey above the gate and looked out. It was clear that, apart from the mahout, only two women were upon the elephant. He also recognized that one of them was indeed Vanathi. At that moment, the elder Velar of Kodumbalur was speaking with them. A portion of their conversation drifted up to his ears. He heard the elder Velar telling Vanathi not to enter the fort, and Vanathi stubbornly insisting that she would go in. Thus, his resolve to open the gate for Vanathi was confirmed.

Once the elder Velar had moved away, he saw the elephant take a few more steps and halt at the edge of the moat. The mahout blew his horn and, as before, called out, “Open the fort gate for the princess of Kodumbalur! Make way at once for Vanathi Devi, who brings messages from the great Pazhuvettarayar to the Younger Pazhuvettarayar, and from the young princess to the Emperor!”

At the sound of this, whatever lingering doubts or hesitations the Younger Pazhuvettarayar harbored vanished. It was indeed strange that the great Pazhuvettarayar should send a message to him through Vanathi. Could there be some plot or stratagem in this? And if so, could he not uncover it? Could this young girl deceive him and escape unscathed? Let us see!

In answer to the blast of the mahout’s horn, a shout rang out from the upper storey above the fort gate, and a torch’s light became visible. In that glow, the tips of spears gleamed and sparkled. Arrows were set in the curved, strung bows.
They stood locked and ready to depart. In their midst, a human figure emerged.

“The gates of the fort shall be opened for the Princess of Kodumbalur. If anyone besides the elephant and those upon it attempts to follow, they shall at once find themselves in the realm of Yama!” thundered the figure in a voice like rolling thunder.

Hearing this, Boothivikkrama Kesari and his men withdrew a little further. The gates of the fort swung open. The bridge across the moat was lowered. As the elephant walked across the bridge, it trembled beneath its weight. Vanathi felt a flicker of fear. Yet, no harm befell them. The elephant reached the far side of the moat and entered the fort through the open gates. In the next moment, the bridge was raised again, and the gates were shut fast.
The elephant carrying Vanathi halted beside the elephant of the Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar.

“Princess! Welcome! Welcome! I am overjoyed that you have agreed to be my guest, even though your great father tried to prevent you! You need not fear any harm here!” declared the Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar in a commanding voice.
“Sir! I have no such fear. Even if, after I have delivered the messages I came to convey, you cast me into the deepest dungeon, I shall not be troubled!” replied Vanathi.

chapters.title: “Stay Here!”
paragraphs: As soon as the subject of the underground prison was mentioned, old memories flooded the mind of the Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar. Forgetting the formalities of customary speech, he said, “Yes; you have been to the underground prison once. You went with the Young Princess. Was it not to find out information about a spy who had escaped after coming to gather intelligence?”

“No, sir! What you say is not correct. We did not go to the underground prison that day to find out about the spy. We went to learn about the messenger whom Prince Aditya Karikalan had sent with a palm-leaf letter.”

“That may have been what you thought. But how do you know whether he was a spy or a messenger? You are just a young girl who knows nothing. There is no use debating this with you. The fact is, you went there! Did you find out anything about him?”
“No, the one we went to see managed to escape without even your knowledge. The command of the Young Queen of Pazhuvoor, Nandini Devi, overtook us. Alas! What could you have done?”

The Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar bit his lips. Was it not because his elder brother had given too much importance to the Young Queen, disregarding his own warnings, that even young women like this had begun to speak so boldly? Though a sense of shame arose within him at this thought, he did not show it outwardly. Instead, he said, “And for your part, you released a half-madman!”
“Sir! You mean Sendhan Amudhan, who is now performing flower service? If you knew how much good has come to the Chola land because we released him that day, you would be astonished!”

“Girl! Nothing can astonish me anymore. I am tired of being surprised at how many people this Chola kingdom is indebted to. Even you, I suppose, have come here now to do some great good for the Chola country?”
“Yes, sir! If it were not for an important matter, would your elder brother have sent me? And would he have sent me, an innocent, ignorant girl?”
“My elder brother’s cleverness seems to be ever increasing. It is evident from the fact that he sent you. Quickly tell me the message you have brought!”

“He asked me to tell you that it was a mistake to be careless about the Pandya country conspirators. Some of Veera Pandiyan’s sworn followers are indeed hatching a terrible plot; they have set a date to take revenge on the Chola dynasty. He asked me to warn you to keep the Emperor safe at all costs…”

Hearing this, Kalandhaga Kandar laughed. “Is this the grave news he sent you to deliver? For a moment, I thought perhaps you had come to inform me that your great father is marching here with his army. If he is watching the Kodumbalur forces from outside, I am watching over the Emperor inside the fort to ensure nothing befalls him. Neither he, nor you, nor even the Young Princess need worry about that!” he said.

“Sir! Knowing that you would take it so lightly, he sent another message as well. You had warned him that a certain sorcerer was frequently visiting the palace of the younger queen of Pazhuvoor. He ignored your warning and grew angry with you. ‘Brother! I have committed a great mistake. That sorcerer, Ravidasan, is none other than the Pandya conspirator. He is the leader of Veera Pandiyan’s sworn followers. He has vowed to utterly destroy the Chola dynasty. One of his men will attempt to take revenge on the Emperor today; do not be careless. Be on the utmost guard’—this is the message Periya Pazhuvettarayar has sent you! I have done my duty…”
Kalandhaga Kandar was somewhat taken aback. No one but the elder himself could have sent such a message.
“Girl! If this is true, why did he not come here at once? Why did he send you…?”
“He did not send me. He told the Young Princess. The Young Princess sent me. Danger threatens Aditya Karikalan as well today. So he has turned back to protect him.”
“From where? Where did he see you?”

“He saw me at the astrologer’s house in Kudanthai. If you still have doubts, listen to this as well. When your elder brother was crossing the Kollidam by boat, a storm struck and the boat capsized. He barely escaped and swam ashore…” While lying in the guardhouse, he had overheard and learned of the conspirators’ plans.
“Sir! Must we stand here and continue talking? Or shall we proceed to the palace?”
“Girl! Let everything you say be true. No matter what kind of conspirator one may be, it is impossible to cross the fort’s guards. It is only because you are a woman that I have allowed you inside…”
“What does it mean to insist one must come from outside? What if the conspirators are already within the fort…?”
“That is something that could never happen, not even for a single day…”
“Very well; that is your responsibility. As for my duty—”
“You have fulfilled it. Now you may return.”
“No, sir! I have only completed half my duty. Only if I see the Emperor and deliver the message from the Young Princess will my task be truly done…”
“You may tell that message to me as well.”
“That is not possible. The Young Princess has commanded that I deliver it directly to the Emperor. Here, this is the Young Princess’s signet ring!…”

“Ah! The signet ring seems to pass through many hands. What proof is there that it was the Young Princess herself who gave it to you? Your great father has besieged this very fort. How can I trust you?…”
“Are you afraid that some danger may befall you at the hands of a helpless woman?”
“Girl! The lineage of Pazhuvur knows not the meaning of fear…”
“In that case, allow me to go up to the palace. You may accompany me as well…”
“Today, the Emperor’s mind is greatly troubled…”
“I have come bearing news that will dispel that very distress, sir! When you learn what it is, you yourself will regret having delayed and hindered me…”
Chinna Pazhuvettarayar, showing a hint of surprise, said, “Girl! Have you, perchance, brought news about the Young Prince—about Ponniyin Selvan?”
“Yes, Commander!”
“Aha! Is the Younger Prince well? Where is he now? Has he—because of the conspirators, has he…”
“Yes; his life was indeed in danger from the Pandya country’s conspirators. But by the grace of God, no harm befell him—he is safe and well. Surely, this news brings you happiness, does it not?”

“What a question! Who would grieve, rather than rejoice, at the Younger Prince’s safety? Come, come! I do not wish to waste time with you. Come to the palace and say directly to the Emperor what you have to say!”

So saying, the Younger Pazhuvettarayar urged his elephant forward. He too was eager to learn more about the prince. He had never considered Arulmozhi Varman as a rival to his son-in-law, Madurantakan, for the throne of Thanjavur. He knew well that the Emperor himself harbored no such thought. Nor was Arulmozhi one to defy his father’s word. His only concern was that Kundavai should not meddle and cause any confusion. Had she already begun some intrigue? Had she, keeping Arulmozhi under her sway, sent some reckless message to her father? If this woman from Kodumbalur had truly brought news of the prince and conveyed it to the Emperor, the Emperor would not keep it from him. Once he knew Arulmozhi Varman’s intentions, he could decide what action to take. At that moment, he could also inform the Emperor about the treacherous attack led by Boothi Vikrama Kesari on the Thanjavur fortress, could he not?…

Both elephants now halted at the palace gates. The Younger Pazhuvettarayar nimbly dismounted from his elephant. The other elephant, swaying like a mountain, knelt and lay down. The two women and the mahout climbed down. Summoning the gatekeeper, the Younger Pazhuvettarayar spoke a few words. The man opened the palace’s main doors.

In the mind of Kalanthaka Kandar, the message Vanathi claimed to have been sent by his elder brother continued to trouble him. Try as he might, he could not dismiss it. Most of all, the news about the sorcerer Ravidasan disturbed his peace. He already knew of the secret aid given to Veera Pandiyan. But he had not known that such conspirators had found refuge within the very walls of Thanjavur’s fortress. The young queen of Pazhuvur summoning the sorcerer and speaking with him—he realized it was all for the purpose of further ensnaring the Elder Pazhuvettarayar under her sway.

That was what he believed. Perhaps her intention was to sow discord between the brothers. Now, the news this woman brought was somewhat alarming. Still, what could any sorcerer or conspirator possibly do? Without his permission, not even a fly could enter the emperor’s palace. The emperor never stepped outside. Nevertheless, it would be wise to strengthen the security around the palace a little more. In the name of storm and flood, and under the pretense of meeting the Prime Minister, many people had entered the fortress in the past two days. He was not sure if all of them had left. It was fortunate that the gates of the fort had been suddenly shut during the day. It would be good to thoroughly investigate whether any ill-intentioned or suspicious persons had entered the fort...

Thus, even as he rode the elephant toward the palace, these thoughts occupied his mind. At the palace entrance, he signaled to his men, who were always ready at one side. He ordered them to search the entire interior of the fort thoroughly and to bring before him anyone who appeared suspicious.

Next, he intended to instruct the Velakkara guards to keep watch over the palace and its surroundings throughout the night without sleep, and he ordered their captain to be sent to him. In this state of mind, he turned to see what had become of the women who had arrived on the elephant. By then, they had crossed the moonlit courtyard in front of the palace and were nearing the first flight of steps.

But... but... who is this? That third figure following them? Judging by the headgear, it looked like the mahout! Ah! Why is the mahout following them? What business does he have inside the palace? What affair could he possibly have with the emperor?

A terrible thought flashed through his mind like lightning, bringing with it an unspeakable agony. It kindled a flame of anger. Could there be some plot in this? Is he the conspirator? Has he deceived these women and entered in the guise of a mahout? Have we too been deceived? Is the very man who came to kill the emperor, the deadly agent of the Veera Pandiyas, now entering the palace before our eyes? Is Kalanthaka Kandar so careless? Or has he joined in the scheme of Boothi Vikrama Kesari? Whatever it may be, in another moment, all will be revealed!
Striding across the moonlit courtyard, Kalanthaka Kandar reached the mahout. “Hey! Stop right there!” he thundered.
“Why are you going inside? What business does a mahout have within the palace?” he demanded, and as he spoke, seized one of the man’s arms with a fist as hard as the thunderbolt weapon of the gods.

At the sound of his thunderous, angry voice, the two women who had gone ahead turned back to look. Their faces reflected a mixture of fear, surprise, and curiosity. At the same time, a smile blossomed upon their lips. Vanathi began, hesitantly, “Sir!... He... he...” but faltered after those few words.

Chinna Pazhuvettarayar, who had reached the peak of his wrath, neither turned to look at her nor cared to listen to what she was trying to say. The mahout’s confusion only served to confirm his suspicions further. In that instant, a wild thought flashed through his mind—could this be the same young man of the Vanar clan who had once deceived him and escaped? Had he now returned, emboldened, to trick him once more?

Tightening his grip even further, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar barked, “Aha! Speak the truth! Who are you? Are you truly the mahout? Or a conspirator? Are you the spy who once slipped away from me? This time, you will not escape!” And with these words, without loosening his hold, he turned the ‘mahout’s’ face towards him.
The light from the lamps burning in the palace’s front hall fell faintly upon the ‘mahout’s’ noble features.
“Commander! I am indeed the mahout. I have never escaped from you. I have come to surrender myself to you!” declared the mahout.

Kalanthaka Kandar gazed at that face. He listened to that voice. It was as though the seven heavens had collapsed and come crashing down upon his head. He stood there, stunned, like a figure in a painting, utterly bewildered. He did not even think to release his grip; his hand slackened of its own accord, and thus the prince Arulmozhi Varman was freed.

chapters.title: The Shout Arose!
paragraphs: What mysterious, magical power lay in the youthful golden face of Prince Arulmozhi, none could say. Even in that moment, the prince did not frown. Not the slightest sign of anger appeared on his countenance. Like Krishna caught in the act of stealing butter, he stood with an expression that seemed to confess guilt, yet without a trace of shame. There was no sign that he intended to find fault with the young Pazhuvettarayar or to rebuke him. Nor was there the least hint of defiance or intent to oppose him.

Yet, in that instant, the hands and feet of the fearless, resolute Kaalandhaka Kandar trembled uncontrollably. Sweat broke out upon his face. Not knowing what else to do, he pressed his palms together in reverence and said, his voice quivering with emotion, “Son of Ponni! Conqueror of Lanka! Blessed child of the Chola land! What is this disguise? What is this deed? What crime have I committed to deserve such punishment?… I beg you to forgive the mistake I made just now. Grant me your gracious pardon. I have become like a blind man, unable to see…”

As he was about to continue in the same manner, the prince interrupted him, “Commander! What is this? How could you, of all people, commit a crime? And how could this ignorant youth presume to forgive you?”
“Even if you were to sever the hand that held you back, it would not be punishment enough. Even if you were to cut out the tongue that called you ‘boy’—that would not suffice…”

“Your words fall harshly upon my ears. Enough, please stop! You were only fulfilling your duty, carrying out your responsibility. Where is the fault in that? The mistake is mine. I came here in this disguise, as a mahout…”

“I never expected it, truly. How could you do such a thing? For what reason? Should I have welcomed the great hero of Chola Nadu in this manner? Should I not have waited at the front entrance, observing every custom and courtesy, with the drums of victory resounding in all eight directions to greet you?”

“It was precisely because I knew you would do so that I came in this disguise. This is not the right time for such honors. Do you not know? Did not the Princess of Kodumbalur just now speak of the evil schemes of conspirators? I believe there may be truth in her words…” “Prince! Have you counted me among those Pandya conspirators as well?...”
“Heavens! I am filled with joy at heart, seeing the arrangements you have made to protect my father, the Emperor. First, let me see my father, and then…”
“Did you think I would prevent you from seeing the Emperor? If anyone has told you that I am such a sinner…”
“I would never have believed it, Commander!”
“Then why this disguise?”
“Could I have entered the fort in any other way? Think about it! Armies from the south have surrounded the fort. Periya Velar has also arrived—you know well why he has come…”
“Was it not right for me to have the gates of the fort closed? Is there any fault in that?”

“It is perfectly right. Periya Velar’s wits seem to have deserted him. I came in this disguise only because I thought he would prevent me from entering the fort. I brought his daughter along as well. Fortunately, he did not notice me. But your sharp eyes discovered me…”
“My eyes were clouded. That’s why I did not recognize you at once. Please forgive me for calling you a mahout…”
“Do not say that. I have never thought of you and my father as different. You had sent men to capture and bring me in…”
“Heavens! What are you saying? Did I send men to capture you? It was your father—the Emperor—who sent them, because he wished to see you at once…”
“Do I not know that, Commander? When I was in Lanka, they came. Those near me said, ‘It is not the Emperor’s order; it is the command of the Pazhuvettaraiyars’…”
“Our enemies must have said so…”

“I told them, ‘Just as my father’s command is binding upon me, so too is the order of the Pazhuvettaraiyars upon my head.’ I have crossed the sea and the storm, the rain and the flood, and come here. I thought that once I had crossed the threshold of the palace, I could learn your wishes. Without your command, I do not even wish to see my father…”

“Prince! Are you still testing me? What command can I give you regarding meeting your father? If you ask me to come with you, I shall come. If you ask me to remain here, I shall remain. The will of the prince is the only command that rests upon my head,” replied Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar humbly.
“Commander, it seems you must stay here. We have already spent too much time standing and talking. Look there!” said the prince.

Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar turned to look. He saw that his men, who had been standing at a distance a moment ago, were now approaching. Not only them; the palace guards had also arrived. Even among the Velakkara soldiers standing farther away, some had separated and were making their way towards them.

All those who had come near gazed at Ponniyin Selvan with unblinking, awestruck eyes. At the moment Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar turned, the lamplight fell fully upon the prince’s face, making it shine with a radiant glow.

One of the warriors cried, “Long live the prince!” Another shouted, “Long live Ponniyin Selvan!” Yet another exclaimed, “Long live the peerless hero who conquered Lanka after Mahindan was cast aside!”
Hearing these voices, all the Velakkara soldiers began to rush forward. From many throats, the cry “Long live Ponniyin Selvan!” arose.

Because of the palace entrance and the presence of Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar, the sound was at first soft and subdued. It was like the gentle rustling of a young breeze stirring the fresh leaves of a peepal tree.

As time passed, as the days went by, that gentle sound would grow and swell, becoming a mighty roar that would surpass even the tumult of a thousand waves of the great ocean—this, we shall see in the chapters to come.
“Commander! It was a mistake for us to stand here and talk. Now you see why I wished not to reveal myself until I had entered the palace?” the prince asked.
“It is clear, Your Majesty! I will go and pacify them and return. Please, I beg you, hurry inside!” said Kaalanthaka Kandar.

chapters.title: Suspicion and Misfortune
paragraphs: After Ponniyin Selvan entered the palace, Kaalandhaka Kandar approached the Velakkara soldiers who had gathered at the palace entrance.
“What is this commotion? Do you not know that the Emperor lies ill within the palace? Are you unaware that enemy forces have surrounded the fort?” he demanded in a harsh tone.
The leader of the Velakkara troops replied, “Sir! Are those who surround the fort truly enemies? How can the great Velar of Kodumbalur be our foe?”
Suppressing the surge of anger within him, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar said, “That is something you must ask him; if he is not an enemy, why has he come with an army and laid siege to the fort?”
“We have heard it is to crown the younger prince upon the throne,” replied the Velakkara captain.
“Is that agreeable to all of you?” Chinna Pazhuvettarayar asked.
The Velakkara leader turned to his soldiers and said, “You tell him yourselves!”
Immediately, the soldiers shouted, “We agree! We agree! Long live Ponniyin Selvan! Long live the prince who conquered Eezham!”
This time, their cries were louder and more forceful than before.

Chinna Pazhuvettarayar’s face flushed red; his moustache quivered. Yet, gritting his teeth, he asked, “Is the coronation to be decided by the will of the great Velar? Or by your wishes? Does the Emperor’s desire hold no value at all?”
One of the soldiers asked, “Commander! Is the Emperor well? Is it certain?”
“What kind of question is that?” Kaalandhakar snapped.

“There are all sorts of rumors spreading in the town about the Emperor. We too have not been able to see him today! Because of that, everyone is deeply worried about his well-being!” said the leader of the Velakkara soldiers.

“Did I not already tell you the reason why you could not see the Emperor? The Emperor’s mind is greatly troubled today. He does not wish to see anyone. He has even refused to come to the assembly hall…”
“What is the reason for the Emperor’s distress? Why should he refuse to grant us an audience? At least let us know that much, can’t we?”
“Very well; I shall tell you. The Emperor’s anxiety was heightened because there was no news about the prince who had gone to Eezham. Now that the prince himself has returned…”
“We wish to see the prince. We must see him clearly, in the full light!” said one of the soldiers in that force.
“Yes, we must see him! Long live the prince who conquered Eezham!” they all shouted together.
“The prince must first pay his respects to the Emperor, must he not? Afterwards, if he wishes, he will come to see you as well!”
“Is that certain? Or might he be sent to the underground dungeon?”

Had it been another day, at another time, the soldiers of Chinna Pazhuvettarayar would have attacked the Velakkara troops for speaking so boldly. It would have turned into a great commotion. But perhaps because they had just glimpsed the prince’s radiant face, or for some other reason, even the warriors of Kaalandhaka Kandar stood in silence. Chinna Pazhuvettarayar’s hand sought the hilt of his sword. For a moment, he thought to cut down the soldier who had spoken with a single stroke. But immediately, he mastered his anger and laughed aloud.

“Did you all hear the question he asked? He wants to know if the prince will be sent to the underground dungeon. Well then; it is neither in my power to crown the prince on the throne nor to send him to the dungeon. It will happen according to the Emperor’s will. Even if the prince is to be taken to the underground dungeon, it is by this very path that he must be led. At that time, you—”
"Let him be watched!" said Kaalandhaka Kandar, his eyes blazing with fire, and turned towards the palace. Ignoring the renewed shouts of the soldiers, he strode towards the palace’s main entrance.
There, near the threshold, he saw Poonguzhali standing alone.
"Girl! Why are you standing here? Did someone stop you from coming inside?" he asked.
"No one stopped me. I chose to stand here myself, sir," replied Poonguzhali.
"Why?"
"When a father and son meet after being separated for so long, what business do I have there?"
"Let it be; at least you believe the Emperor is alive, don’t you? That, at least, is some comfort!"
"I do not merely believe it; I saw with my own eyes that the Emperor is well, and only then did I return."
"Look, there they stand—go and tell those Velakkara guards what you saw! They seem to be suspicious," he said.
"Until this very moment, they have no evidence for their suspicions. Who can say that, in the next moment, it will not become true?"
"Girl! Are you also trying to disturb my mind? Has madness seized all of you?" he asked.

"Commander! Many people call me ‘mad’. Sometimes, I myself claim to be mad. But it was by following the thought of this madness that the prince was able to enter this fortress today without danger. It was possible to meet the Emperor while he was still alive..."
"Ah! What is this? Are you too wishing ill upon the Emperor’s life? Are you raving after listening to the nonsense of ignorant people and foolish astrologers? Or do you know something else?"
"Is it only the people and astrologers who wish ill? Did you not just now hear the message your own brother sent?"
"What certainty is there that it is true?" asked Kaalandhaka Kandar.
"Commander! Why would the Princess of Kodumbalur lie?"
“Who saw it? Perhaps she too harbors the desire to ascend the throne and become the chief queen…”
“Commander! That is exactly what I thought as well. But after hearing the vow the princess made this morning, I have changed my mind,” said Poonguzhali.
“Girl! Or is it you who secretly harbors such ambitions?” asked the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar, laughing lightly.
“Commander! Truly, I must be mad! Otherwise, why would I stand here talking to you?” said Poonguzhali, and turned to leave.
A sudden change came over Kalanthaka Kandar. “Girl, do not be offended! Say what you came to say, and then go,” he said.

Poonguzhali turned back again. “Yes, I must say it. Otherwise, later I too will regret it, and you may also have cause for sorrow. Sir! If any harm should befall the Emperor, the blame for it will fall upon you throughout the land and city. Even your own soldiers will say so!” she declared.

The face of the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar tightened. “If such a thing were to happen, I would not wait for others to cast blame. Before the words of reproach could reach my ears, my life would have left me! When the Velakkara soldiers swore their oath in the temple of Durga Parameswari, I was the first to take the vow and lead the others!” he said.
“What use is that? The Chola realm would lose both its Emperor and a great warrior! Would it not be better to be cautious beforehand?”

“Girl! Are you saying I am not being cautious? Look—so many soldiers stand guard around this palace, not closing their eyes for a moment! For what purpose? Even the Prime Minister Aniruddha cannot enter the palace without my knowledge! Do you understand?”
“I know, Commander! But could not danger arise even from within the palace?”

“What nonsense is this? Are you suggesting that the palace women might poison and kill the Emperor? Or perhaps, since she went inside with the prince, you suspect that woman from Kodumbalur?” he asked.
“Heavens! Those who suspect that innocent woman will come to no good end. She does not possess such cunning. Sir! Is there not a secret underground passage leading into this palace…?”

Chinna Pazhuvettarayar started in alarm. “Girl! What do you know about that? How could you know? Except for three or four people, no one knows about that path! And those who do, can never return alive!”
“Commander! It was only early this morning that I learned of it. There, I saw a Pandya country conspirator hiding, a sharp throwing spear in his hand…”
“Heavens! What terrible words you speak! That path… that path… do you know where it leads?”
“It goes by way of the treasure vault!” said Poonguzhali.

“Ah! What you say may well be true. This is the work of that magical enchantress who has taken human form! It is the doing of the sorceress who has enslaved my brother. Alas! How many times have I warned him? Girl! Is what you say the truth? Did you see it with your own eyes? How did you come to know the place where that path lies?”
“I learned of it when my aunt took me there this morning…”
“Who is your aunt?”
“She is the one who was brought from Kodikkarai in the palanquin you sent, by order of the Prime Minister, sir! While we stand here talking further about this…”
“It’s true! I must go at once to the great Pazhuvur palace and make the necessary arrangements. In the meantime, you…”
“I will stand at the corner here and keep watch…”
“Ah! How can I trust you? What certainty do I have that you are not in league with those Pandya conspirators? That you will not mislead me and betray me…”
“Commander, if so, then come with me yourself! Bring a torch with you! Let us both go and see for ourselves! As we go, I will tell you the other details I know…”

Chinna Pazhuvettarayar immediately called some of his soldiers who were standing by the entrance and spoke a few words to them. Poonguzhali guessed that they were going to the Pazhuvur palace. One of the soldiers held a torch in his hand, which the commander took from him.
“Girl! Lead the way! I will see for myself whether all you have said is true,” said Kaalanthakakandar.

Even then, his mind was not free from doubt about Poonguzhali. Was this woman trying to deceive him with lies and fabrications? Or was she seeking to learn about the secret tunnel through him? Was this some plot to let the men of Kodumbalur into the fortress by this route? If she had such intentions and tried to lead him astray, she would not find it easy to fool him. If she did, she deserved a fitting punishment. Would he, too, be deceived like Periya Pazhuvettarayar? Let her go ahead for now; first, he could find out if she truly knew the way through the tunnel. Then he could see if it was true that conspirators were hiding there. If it was true—God! What a danger! Fortunately, it would not be difficult to thwart such a plot. Like catching a fox hiding in its den, he could seize and destroy them!
With these thoughts, the Younger Pazhuvettarayar followed behind Poonguzhali. He marveled at the swiftness of her stride.
Yes; Poonguzhali’s inner agitation had reached its peak at that moment. Her steps matched the turmoil within her, quick and urgent.

For some time now, strange events had been unfolding in Poonguzhali’s life. But never before had anything happened as it did that day. At dawn, her aunt had woken her from sleep. On the upper loft of the women’s quarters where they lay, a terrifying face had appeared; at once, it vanished. Mandakini had silently risen and beckoned Poonguzhali to follow her into the closed-off sculptors’ hall. There, for a fleeting moment, the same dreadful face she had seen on the loft appeared between the heads of Ravana and the Kailash mountain held aloft by his hands, then disappeared. The two of them went to the base of that statue to investigate. Poonguzhali discovered that between Ravana’s heads, a secret passage began and led away. Mandakini descended into the tunnel first, and Poonguzhali followed her. At first, Poonguzhali could see nothing; such was the darkness that filled the tunnel. Holding her aunt’s hand, she stumbled along. After climbing a few steps from the path, they seemed to have entered a hall. Darkness reigned there as well. It was difficult to move without bumping into pillars and walls, feeling her way with her hands. After a while, a faint light began to filter in from above through small openings.

Poonkuzhali guessed that dawn must have broken by now. Along with this, she realized that they were wandering around the treasure vault. Yet, it did not seem likely that the man whom Mandakini Akka had come searching for would be caught so easily. In that moonlit chamber shrouded in darkness, there were countless places to hide. Who knew where he might be concealed? Before they could find him, he might discover them, creep up from behind, and stab them to death; in this vault, there would be no one to question or bear witness.

As Poonkuzhali was immersed in such thoughts, Mandakini let out a cry in her strange voice—a voice that could not be easily identified as human or animal. Immediately following it, a terrified human voice wailed in fear. A shadowy figure darted away with frantic speed. Poonkuzhali decided that it must be a man whose face had briefly appeared in the lamplight. Hearing Akka’s eerie cry, the man had fled in terror, perhaps thinking her a ghost or demon. The thought made Poonkuzhali smile.

From time to time, Mandakini repeated that peculiar cry, making the man run hither and thither in panic. At last, he ran and crashed into a wooden door. He began to pound on it, first pausing, then knocking four or five times. At length, the door opened. In the gap, a woman was visible. The man said something to her. The woman seemed hesitant, and it appeared the man had frightened her. After a moment, she turned and left. The man stood by the door, peering after her. After a short while, the woman returned, carrying a lamp. Together, they entered the moonlit chamber.
Mandakini took Poonkuzhali by the hand and led her to hide behind a large pillar. In the glow of the lamp, they could clearly see the man’s face.

The man and the woman with the lamp proceeded to the inner part of the vault. “A ghost? A demon? You seem truly terrified! Why would someone so frightened come here for such a deed?” the woman’s words reached Poonkuzhali’s ears clearly. But what sort of deed she referred to, Poonkuzhali could not quite understand.

As soon as the pair disappeared into the vault with the lamp, Mandakini gripped Poonkuzhali’s hand and swiftly pulled her out through the open door. They crossed the path and entered a large garden. There, in a secluded corner, Mandakini conveyed what she wished to say to Poonkuzhali through gestures.
“My final days—” It was near. “Before I close my eyes for the last time, I must see the prince once—go, convey this message and bring him here yourself,”—that was the message.

We are well aware of the love Poonguzhali bore for her aunt; at such a moment, her heart could not bear to leave her behind, nor could she bring herself to contradict her words. Yet, at the same time, the thought that this was an opportunity to see Ponniyin Selvan made her resolve at once. Taking leave of her aunt, she set out. Climbing over the garden wall, she crossed to the other side and passed through the gates of Thanjai city. There, she met Azhwarkadiyan. She learned that he too was going to see Ponniyin Selvan, by order of the Prime Minister. With the help of that valiant Vaishnavite, her journey became easier.

That day, fortune favored her at every turn. At the threshold of the Kudanthai astrologer’s house, they saw the chariot of the young princess. Thinking that Kundavai Devi might have some news about the prince, they entered the astrologer’s house to inquire. There, through the words of Periya Pazhuvettarayar, they learned about the Pandya country conspirators. Poonguzhali was certain that the one who had hidden in the treasury room was indeed one of those conspirators. At the same time, it was a relief to know that the prince too might be in danger from those conspirators. In the place where the princess Vanathi had gone to be rescued, she also met the prince.

Of all these, what gave her the greatest satisfaction was that the prince accepted her suggestion about going to Thanjavur. She knew that in Lanka, he had traveled incognito as a mahout, and she had not forgotten how he had left the commander and the soldiers behind, taken only her on the elephant, and hastened to the seashore. Therefore, she said that even now, it would be best if the prince followed the same method; if he went alone, he could not enter the Thanjai fort, but if he took her and Vanathi along, people would think he was a mahout and let them pass.
“Daughter of the Ocean! You have given a wise counsel. You are fit to be the Prime Minister of a great kingdom!”—the prince’s words echoed in her heart, filling her with joy.

But, what use was it, though everything had gone according to her plan until that very moment? Mandakini Athai was not in the Emperor’s bedchamber as she had expected! Nor had anyone there inquired about her. Each time Poonguzhali remembered how her aunt had signaled, “My end is near,” her heart thudded with dread. “What is the point of all this trouble, all this clever talk, bringing the prince here with such effort? I have not found Athai!” Her heart pounded anxiously. She wondered if her aunt was still in the moonlit chamber. Or perhaps that wicked conspirator had murdered her there—at the very thought, Poonguzhali’s heart nearly broke.

She wanted to go through the secret passage and look inside the moonlit chamber. But at that moment, the palace was in utter commotion due to the prince’s arrival. Women were hurrying to and fro in all directions. In groups, they would come, peer into the Emperor’s bedchamber, and then leave. In the midst of all this, what would people think if she alone went off toward the old sculpted mandapam? What if that conspirator was still there? It would not be wise for her to go alone and fall into his hands. Even for the brave-hearted Poonguzhali, that dark, treasure-laden moonlit chamber inspired a certain fear.

Therefore, she resolved to tell Chinna Pazhuvettarayar and take him along to search the moonlit chamber. It had taken her some time to persuade him, after arguing with Kalantaka Kandar and turning his mind to her purpose. Remembering this, she now walked very quickly. Her inner sense warned her that some disaster was about to occur. She cared little if danger befell herself, but from the depths of her heart, she wished that nothing should happen to her aunt.

As she entered the sculpted mandapam, it seemed as if a dark shadow fell from the palace terrace above. It looked as though a figure was moving along the wall. She paused for a moment to see whether it was real or just her imagination.
“Girl! Why do you stand there? Are you afraid your lies will be exposed?” Chinna Pazhuvettarayar’s voice reached her ears, and she hurried forward.
Once inside the sculpted mandapam, Poonguzhali pointed out to Chinna Pazhuvettarayar the secret door between Ravana’s heads and the Kailasa mountain.
“Very well! You go down first!” said the commander of the fort.
For some reason, Poonguzhali hesitated. Her body trembled.

At that very moment, a supernatural voice let out a piercing wail—“Kreech!” She instantly recognized it as the voice of her aunt, Mandakini. She also realized that the wailing cry was coming from within the palace, from the chamber where the Emperor lay.
Her hesitation vanished at once.
Without a thought for Chinna Pazhuvettarayar, she rushed headlong toward the women’s quarters of the palace. The dreadful, terrifying wail continued to echo through the corridors.
When she entered the chamber where the Emperor lay, the scene that met her eyes imprinted itself upon her heart like a vivid painting.

The Emperor, reclining on his bed, was clutching the hands of his beloved son, Arulmozhi, within his own. Before the two of them stood her aunt, Mandakini, crying out in anguish. To one side stood Vanathi and the daughter of Malayaman, who was to become her daughter-in-law. Everyone was staring at Mandakini, who shrieked like a woman possessed.
No one noticed the sharp spear that had come hurtling down from the upper portico.
Poonkuzhali leapt toward her aunt in a single bound.

chapters.title: She Became Divine!
paragraphs: However swift-footed Poonguzhali might be, could she ever compete with a spear hurled from above? Before she could leap to her aunt Mandakini’s side, the spear had already plunged into her aunt’s shoulder. With a dreadful cry of “Veeel!” Mandakini fell to the ground. At that very moment, cries of anguish burst forth from every throat in the room.

Just like Poonguzhali, the others too rushed toward the queen who had collapsed on the floor. At that instant, a loud commotion was heard from the upper floor. Several earthen pots were hurled down in all directions.

One of those pots fell upon the lamp burning brightly near the Emperor, dousing its flame. Darkness immediately enveloped the room. For a while, confusion reigned in that royal chamber and in the long corridors surrounding it. The hurried, frantic footsteps of people running to and fro echoed everywhere.
“Light! Bring a light!” thundered the voice of Chinna Pazhuvettarayar.

“Ah! Alas!” came a woman’s anguished cry. It sounded like the voice of the Maharani, and at that, everyone’s heart skipped a beat and their bodies trembled. Amidst all this chaos, Poonguzhali ran, guided by memory, to the spot where her aunt Mandakini had fallen. She realized that someone had already lifted her aunt and placed her on their lap.
A heart-rending sob and the sound of weeping reached Poonguzhali’s ears.
Near the threshold, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar shouted, “Who is that? Don’t run! Stop!”
Poonguzhali guessed who the fleeing person might be. At that moment, two nursemaids entered the room carrying lamps.

The scene revealed in the lamplight was one no one could have ever anticipated. For three years, the Emperor—Sundara Chola, who had lost all strength in his legs and had not been able to stand—had gotten down from his bed and walked over to sit beside Mandakini. The prince was by his side. In Mandakini’s shoulder... Blood was dripping from the tip of the spear that had pierced through and emerged on the other side. Near the bed where the Emperor lay, the daughter of Malayaman, Vanamadevi, was found. Beside her, on the pillow where the Emperor had rested his head, a sharp dagger was embedded.

When the lamp was brought, the Maharani glanced at the bed in horror, and with eyes brimming with immeasurable astonishment, she saw the Emperor sitting on the floor. At that moment, Ponniyin Selvan gently lifted Mandakini’s head and placed it on the Emperor’s lap. Tears streamed in torrents from Prince Arulmozhi Varman’s eyes. The Emperor, too, was weeping uncontrollably, sobs racking his body.

Poonkuzhali took in all this with a single glance. In the very next moment, she pieced together and understood, by intuition, all that had transpired there. The one who had thrown the spear from above had noticed that the mute queen had intercepted it. Immediately, he had thrown down the plates and vessels from above, extinguished the lamp, and plunged the room into darkness.

In that sudden darkness, he had leapt down, thinking the Emperor was lying on the bed, stabbed with the dagger, and fled. Realizing the Emperor was in danger, the Maharani had rushed to the bed, only to be pushed aside by the assailant as he escaped. It was then that the Maharani had cried out, “Ayyo!” After that, the villain must have run towards the entrance, pushed aside the little Pazhuvettaraiyar who was just entering, and escaped. Poonkuzhali deduced all this in an instant.

A desire to chase and catch the perpetrator of this heinous act began to rise in one corner of her mind. Yet, the thought that her aunt’s end was near caused a great turmoil within her heart. Therefore, without minding that Mandakini was lying with her head on the Emperor’s lap, she went near, knelt down, and cried, “Aunt! Aunt!”

“Ayyo! What you said has come true! Wretched me, I left you alone and went away!” she wailed, sobbing. But Mandakini did not turn to look at her. Her eyes were fixed with longing upon the Emperor’s noble face.
Even the Prince, who held her hand and wept, could not draw her attention. How then could she notice Poonkuzhali?

As Poonkuzhali continued to lament, the Prince mastered his own grief and said, “Samudra Kumari! What is this? Have you forgotten yourself? Have you forgotten where you are?” As he spoke, he rose to his feet.
Poonguzhali, suppressing her sorrow and blushing slightly, rose to her feet.
“My King! In this world, I have no one but my aunt!” she sobbed.

The prince wiped away the tears welling in his eyes and said, “Poonguzhali! She is your aunt, yes; but to me, she is a mother ten times greater than the one who gave me birth! It was she who sent you to bring me here! Yet, she did not even look upon my face. Do you know the reason for this? After thirty years of separation, my father and mother have finally been reunited today. Who are we to stand as obstacles between them?”
Having spoken thus, the prince cast a keen glance at everyone present, including the Maharani.

Turning again to Poonguzhali, he continued, “Child! You have helped me on several occasions before. But none of those deeds were as significant as what you have done today. Today, you have granted me the fortune of witnessing the reunion of my father and mother! I shall never forget this! Daughter of the ocean! Think of the immense merit your aunt has earned today! She saved my father from the assassin’s spear. She took that blow upon herself! She gave her life to save the Emperor’s! Not once, but twice she protected him! When the spear struck your aunt, strength returned to my father’s legs, which had been powerless for three years. He rose from his bed. Thus, his life was saved once more. The traitor, thinking he had missed his mark, extinguished the lamp and leapt down, attempting again to commit his wicked deed. But since the Emperor had risen, his plan was foiled.

Look there! See my mother, the princess of Malayaman, standing in speechless wonder! She saw the spear strike your aunt. Fearing the assassin might try again, she rushed forward, determined to make the same sacrifice as your aunt. She wished to shield my father with her own body, to bear the next weapon meant for him. That is why she cried out in anguish when she could not see my father on the bed. Had the Emperor remained there, either my father or my mother would not be alive today.

Daughter of the ocean! Do you now realize what a great service your aunt has rendered to the Chola dynasty and to the Chola land? Had the Emperor fallen to the assassin’s weapon, the Chola empire would have been plunged into chaos. An everlasting stain would have fallen upon the name of the Pazhuvettaraiyar clan. Your aunt did not save only my father’s and mother’s lives—she saved the honor of the Pazhuvettaraiyars. She saved the Chola land from disaster. She has become the guardian deity of the Chola lineage.”
“Poonguzhali! For your aunt, I shall not shed even a single tear from now on. You need not weep for her either. No one else need grieve!

What kind of divine death is granted to whom? Who is blessed with the fortune to give up their life for a husband from whom they have been separated for thirty years? Who is granted the boon of laying their head upon his lap and departing this world in peace?”
Having spoken thus, the prince once again looked all around him.
He saw that everyone standing in that chamber, and near the threshold, had listened to his words. He continued:

“Poonguzhali! Do not fear that you will become an orphan now that your aunt has passed away. I shall never forget the help you have rendered today. I shall always remain grateful to you. Even if I were to forget, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar will not. What immense help you and your aunt have given him today! If a spear or sword had been raised against the Emperor, what would the world have said? The people would have declared that even Pazhuvettarayar, the commander of the Tanjore fortress, was complicit in that heinous act. At the fortress gate, Kodumbalur Velar is waiting. He would have found the reason he sought to utterly destroy the Pazhuvur clan. Why stop there? If, with your help, I had not entered the fortress today, even I would have harbored suspicion against the commander of the fort. Therefore, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar owes you more gratitude than anyone else. Whatever reward you ask of him, he will grant. Even if you ask for half his wealth, he will give it to you!”

As the prince spoke thus, he looked at Chinna Pazhuvettarayar. He spoke these words deliberately, wishing to make him realize that he had not fulfilled his duty as he ought. The pain that appeared on Chinna Pazhuvettarayar’s face showed that he understood this well. The usual majestic expression that dwelled on his face had vanished. The signs of heroic pride, of fearing nothing and bowing to no one, were now absent from his countenance.
Now, his face bore the look of a warrior who, having fled the battlefield, is ashamed to have saved his own life only to be scorned by many. He was drowning in the shame of it.
Poonguzhali, whose heart and body had melted and softened at the prince’s earlier words, now became once again the fierce daughter of the sea when he spoke of her reward.

“Prince! I do not need anyone’s gratitude; nor do I desire any reward. The King of the Ocean is there to give me refuge. My boat is safely moored at the mouth of the canal. Now, I shall take my leave. Perhaps, if my aunt survives? …No, that is a vain hope! She told me this morning. She spoke as if she sensed what was to come. She will not survive now. I have no more business here. If, by chance, you or the Princess of Kodumbalur ever come to the seashore…” Saying this, Poonguzhali glanced towards where Vanathi was seated.
She noticed that Vanathi was watching both her and the prince with wide, anxious eyes. “Tch! What is this longing? I am leaving,” she said, and, turning away, walked swiftly towards the doorway.

Until then, Vanathi had stood as if dazed, but now a little self-awareness returned to her. She came near Poonguzhali and said, “My dear friend, where are you going? I too am an orphan, just like you!…” But before she could say more, Poonguzhali interrupted her:
“Devi, I am not your dear friend. Nor are you an orphan like me; soon the Young Princess of Pazhayarai will arrive!” she said.
Only then did Vanathi truly remember the young princess. “Oh no! My sister knows nothing of what has happened here! I must send her word!” she exclaimed.

“Is that something to worry about? Your great father is at the fortress gate, is he not? If you tell him, he will send the message,” Poonguzhali replied. Then, as if to clear her path, she gently moved Vanathi aside and proceeded further. Near the doorway, the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar once again blocked her way.

“Girl! I heard all that the Prince of Ponni said. All of it is true. You have saved the Pazhuvur clan from everlasting disgrace. I am indebted to you beyond measure. Ask for any reward you wish, and I shall grant it,” he said.

With a sorrowful smile, Poonguzhali replied, “Commander! Some here are happy that the Emperor has survived. Some are glad that he has regained the strength to walk. Others rejoice that the Pazhuvettaraiyar clan has not been shamed. But it seems no one is troubled by the cruel fate that befell my aunt. Should I alone not grieve for her? I will try to find out where the man who killed my aunt has gone. Please, let me pass!” she said.
Poonguzhali’s words struck the fortress commander, Kaalandhaka Kandara, like a thunderbolt.

“Girl! I have been defeated by you. I stand here, idle, having let the murderer escape. Merely because the Emperor survived, my dishonor is not wiped away. It was my mistake to place faith in your words! Where could the murderer have gone? He pushed me aside and fled. Yes! Yes! He must have taken the underground passage. Come! Come and help me! I do not wish to take anyone else along! Let him fall into my hands alone! Watch what I do to him!”
Speaking thus, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar seized Poonguzhali with his iron hand and, dragging her along, hurried toward the sculptors’ hall.

Everyone else in that chamber stood just as they were. Knowing the prince’s wishes, they kept their distance, not approaching the Emperor. All eyes, however, were fixed upon Sundara Chozhar and upon the queen, who lay with her head resting in his lap.

But Sundara Chozhar and Mandakini were utterly absorbed in each other. There was no room in their hearts for thoughts of anyone else. What would the experts in the science of the mind say about whether it is possible to live through thirty years of life in a few fleeting moments? Who can say? Yet there is no doubt that Sundara Chozhar and Mandakini, in those few moments, relived the long years of their lives. All that could be spoken between them in thirty years, they spoke now.

Mandakini spoke only through her own language of the eyes. Sundara Chozhar, for the most part, understood that language. In his youth, during those months of heavenly life on the island of Bootha Theevu with Mandakini, he had learned well her language of signs. He had not forgotten it, even to this day. Thus, though Mandakini now spoke only with her eyes, his heart instantly grasped the thoughts that arose in hers. In truth, Mandakini had little to say.

“I have no grievance against you. Where are you, the Emperor who rules the world? And where am I, the daughter of a Karaiyar, mute and deaf? It was I who hid myself all these years, never coming before you. From afar, I would sometimes catch a glimpse of you and content myself. And now, at the moment of death, I have been granted the fortune of laying my head upon your lap and breathing my last. What more could I wish for?”

—This alone was what Mandakini conveyed. Her heart and her eyes repeated this sentiment again and again. Upon her face, boundless bliss overflowed. Though the spear had pierced through her side and the wound had broken through to the surface, there was not the least sign of pain upon her countenance.

She did not know. It seemed as though she had lost all memory of her own body, down to her very feet. The moment when the bird would fly out of its cage had drawn near. What concern would that bird now have for the cage it was about to leave behind?
Sundara Chozhar too had forgotten all memory of his body. Was it not for that reason he had been able to forget the weakness in his legs and descend from his bed, running to Mandakini?

But unlike Mandakini, Sundara Chozhar was not content with uttering a few words. He went on speaking, pouring out countless matters. His eyes expressed what his lips could only mutter in broken words. Not a single person in that room could understand what he said. But Mandakini understood it all. Where she needed to agree, she nodded her head in assent; where she needed to deny, she shook her head in refusal. Where she ought to rejoice, she rejoiced; where she ought to offer comfort, she gave comfort.

“O dearest of my life! Today, for my sake, you are giving up your life! How many more days do you think my own life will last? Yes, I confess, I am a sinner with a heart of stone. Those born to rule a kingdom must harden their hearts in this way. Otherwise, how could the affairs of the realm be managed? Leaving you behind on that island of ghosts was the first great crime I committed. Because of that, I was forced to commit many more sins. How blissfully we lived on that island, which was like paradise itself! But it was not destined to last. The gods themselves conspired against us! All those close to me betrayed me! After the Yuvaraja’s coronation, I had resolved to come searching for you. I ran all the way to Kodikkarai in search of you. The wretched ones told me you had leapt into the sea and died. Even Aniruddha, whom I considered my dearest friend, deceived me… Yes, yes! I understand what you are saying. You say it is true that you leapt into the sea, and that someone later saved you. But though Aniruddha knew this, he did not tell me. See what calamity befell because of that! Every time I saw you, I thought I was seeing your spirit. I believed you had come to haunt me, to exact revenge. When you saved my beloved son from the floodwaters of the Kaveri, I thought it was you who had cast him into the river. Ah! If only I had known you were alive, how different my life would have been! Do you think I would have abandoned you for the sake of this vast empire? Never, not for a single day!…”
In this manner, Sundara Chozhar came, muttering aloud all the thoughts that surged and overflowed within his heart. At last, he said,

“Two days ago, when you came before me, I threw the lamp at you. Every time I saw you after that, I showed you only disgust. For all that, you must forgive me. For many years, I believed you were a spirit come to torment me. In the dead of night, you appeared before me in this very chamber and spoke strange things. I thought you were cursing my children. The hatred that arose then did not leave me even when I saw you in person. But in truth, you came as the guardian deity of our clan! You came to protect me and my children from harm! I did not realize any of this. Only after my daughter Kundavai explained it to me did I understand. Alas! What a grave mistake I have made! Forgive me for all of it. How can I now show you the love I bear in my heart? You have left me with no way! You said my sons should not be crowned. I know the reason for that. Why do you shake your head? You said it only for my good, and for the good of my lineage! There is no fault in that. But those here are saying all sorts of things, trying to make me out to be mad. They say you have borne a child. If that is true, tell me! If you have a son, tell me. I will do for him whatever I can, seeking atonement for the betrayal I have done to you…”

As Sundara Chozhar spoke thus, Mandakini looked at him for a long moment, then glanced all around. Her gaze came to rest on Ponniyin Selvar, who stood near the doorway. At once, the prince came near the place where his father and mother were seated. He sat down beside his mother.
Mandakini touched the prince with her hand and looked at the emperor’s face. From that look, the meaning “This is my son!” shone forth with utter clarity.

Thus, two or three times, Mandakini looked from the emperor to Ponniyin Selvar, and back again. Then she closed her eyes. Her head, which had been held upright for a while, gently leaned and rested upon the emperor’s lap.
Mandakini’s life departed from her body.
Never, until this day, had anyone seen or heard Sundara Chozha Chakravarthi weep aloud. But today, when he cried out “Oh!” and wept, all who witnessed and heard it were struck with astonishment.
Only Prince Arulmozhi Varman remained clear-minded.

He looked at the Emperor and said: “Father! You need not grieve for my mother’s death. She has not truly died. Has she not transformed into a deity? Forevermore, she will shine as the guardian goddess of our Chola lineage!”

Yet, Sundara Chozhar could not cease his sobbing. Was he weeping only for the death of Mandakini? Or was it because, at that very moment, the shock of another tragic event that had occurred far away struck his heart? Who can say for certain?

Only the words of consolation spoken by Prince Arulmozhi rang true. Later, when Ponniyin Selvan ascended the throne as Rajaraja Chozha, he built a temple in Thanjavur for Mandakini Devi, whom he called the “Queen of Eelam.” For some time, it was renowned as the “Singala Nachchiyar Temple.” In the course of time, the name changed to “Singachchiyar Temple.” Even today, those who visit Thanjavur may inquire and find that, in one part of the city, there still stands a small, ruined temple known as the “Singachchiyar Temple.”

chapters.title: “The Time Has Come!”
paragraphs: How wonderful it would be if we could bring this story to a close with the events narrated in the previous chapter! Perhaps some among our readers might even hope for such an ending. But that is not possible. At almost the very same hour, on that very same day, a dreadful incident was unfolding in the palace of Kadambur Sambuvaraiyar, and it is our duty now to recount it.

Nandini was pacing restlessly, alone, within her private chamber. The agitation that had seized her heart was clearly reflected in her countenance. A strange, rare gleam flashed in her eyes and vanished. She kept glancing often at the many entrances to her room, as if expecting someone. Her ears were sharply attuned, listening for the faintest sound of approaching footsteps from any of those directions. “The time is drawing near!” her lips kept murmuring again and again. At times, those murmuring lips would tremble. At other moments, her eyelids and brows would quiver. Each time, her entire body would shudder as if seized by the feverish excitement of a fanatic.

The bed prepared for Nandini’s rest was draped on all four sides with hanging curtains, concealing it entirely down to the floor. Nandini gently lifted one side of the curtain. She gazed at the murderous sword laid out lengthwise upon the bed. Like a blade forged in the fiery furnace of a blacksmith, it gleamed with a menacing light.
