“Ah? A sinful deed, is it? What is a sinful deed? Let me ask my friend.

Manimekalai! You tell me! You have given your heart to a man. When he is wounded and helpless, his enemy comes to kill him. You fall at the feet of that enemy and beg him not to slay your beloved. Yet, he pays no heed and kills him before your eyes. Would you say that avenging such a murderer is a sin, my dear?”
“Never would I say so, Akka! But, unlike you, I would not fall at his feet and plead. I would seize a knife myself and kill him right then and there!” declared Manimekalai.
Vandiyathevan turned to Manimekalai and asked, “Princess! What if that enemy happens to be your own brother?”
“Even if he were my brother, or anyone else, it would make no difference to me!” replied Manimekalai.
“Speak thus, my dear!” said Nandini.
“The princess speaks without thinking what she says. No matter what her brother Kandanmaran might have done against her, would she truly have the heart to kill him?” Vallavarayan asked.
Nandini and Manimekalai looked at each other.

Then Nandini turned to Vandiyathevan and said, “What a pointless question! I would never kill my own blood brother. When you first met me, you spoke of my brother Thirumalai. That is why I felt affection for you. It was because you were a friend of Azhwarkadiyan that I helped you escape from danger several times. Sir! If today I am forced to give up my life before fulfilling my vow, you must convey to Thirumalai that I begged his forgiveness. Tell him that even if I did not act as he wished, I never truly forgot him!”
“Lady! Why this charade any longer? Azhwarkadiyan is not your brother; you are not the sister of that valiant Vaishnavite…”
“Then who is my brother? Whose sister am I?”
“Your brother is Aditya Karikalan. Therefore, I beg you—do not let yourself be tainted by the sin of fratricide. I implore you, show mercy and hand over to me the sword that slew the Pandya king!”
“You told the prince that Karikalan and I were born of the same mother—a rare and fanciful notion, did you not?” Nandini asked with a mocking smile.
“It seemed that he believed it; but I cannot truly know what lies in his heart…”
“I know what lies in his heart. He is greatly astonished by the imaginative powers of that enchantress of Pazhayarai…”
“Lady! What I spoke was not mere fancy. Nor was it the imagination of the young princess of Pazhayarai. I saw it with my own eyes in the land of Lanka…”
“What did you see?”

“I saw a goddess—a woman who could not speak a word. She saved me, Azhwarkadiyan, and Arulmozhi Varman from mortal peril. In the streets of Anuradhapura, in the dead of night, as we passed by the edge of an old palace, she stood on the opposite side of the road and beckoned us with a sign. As Arulmozhi Varman and I moved toward her, the façade of the house where we had just stood collapsed in ruins. Ponniyin Selvan revered that woman as his family deity and worshipped her…”

“Sir! What connection does this tale have to me? You could have told all this to the young princess who wishes to seat Arulmozhi Varman upon the Chola throne; she would have listened in wonder and delight. Why do you tell it to me?…”

“There is a reason. When I saw that woman in the moonlit streets of Anuradhapura, even from a distance, I was startled and thought, ‘How has the young queen of Pazhuvur, whom we left behind in Thanjavur, come to be here?’ Lady! There is not the slightest difference in appearance between you and her. If you removed your ornaments and let your hair fall loose, you would resemble her exactly…”
“Why should I believe what you say? I know well that you possess a boundless imagination. Why should this not be one of your extraordinary inventions as well?”
“Devi! I swear to you, it is the truth.”

“No matter how much you swear, I cannot believe it!” “Queen! It is a lie when you say ‘I cannot believe it!’ You know very well that what I say is the truth. You are using that truth for your own purposes. The very first time I met you and spoke with you in the Thanjai palace, this magician came shrieking like an owl. You told me to go away. I went and hid myself in the treasury chamber, whose door happened to be open by chance. There, I witnessed some strange scenes…”
“Ah! What were those extraordinary scenes?”
“I saw Kandhamaaran walking with Madhuranthakan along the passage to the treasury…”
“So what of it?”

“A little while later, I saw you and Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar also walking along the same passage to the treasury. At that time, I did not know where you were going. Only later did I deduce and understand it. I realized you were going to torment the Emperor by pretending to be the spirit of your mother…”
All this while, Nandini had been speaking firmly, but now, suddenly, she seemed to lose her strength and sat down on a nearby seat.
“Sir! What else did you come to know?”

“When you and Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar were walking along the treasury passage, Kandhamaaran, who had earlier taken Madhuranthakan, was returning. He said something to Pazhuvettaraiyar. The elder gave a signal to the guard who was carrying a lamp…”
“What signal was that?”

“You must surely know. Pazhuvettaraiyar ordered the guard to stab Kandhamaaran in the back and kill him. I intervened and saved Kandhamaaran’s life. As a result, the blame for the knife wound on his back fell upon me…”
Nandini turned to look at Manimekalai and said, “Sir! Why do you say all these things and disturb this girl’s mind?”
“Devi! All these years, I have never spoken of these matters to anyone. If you would hand over the sword you hold in your hand to me, I promise I will never speak of it to anyone ever again…”

“I cannot give you the sword, sir! Why should I? Tell whomever you wish, say whatever you please. Add whatever fancies you like and tell them as well. Why not? Go right now to Karikalan and stop him from coming here! Why do you trouble me? Go!” said Nandini, her eyes brimming with tears.
“Ammani! I know the prince’s nature very well. I cannot stop him. If I try, his stubbornness will only grow. That is why I have come to plead with you…”

“What right do you have to plead with me? Let everything you say be true. Let it be that you saw my mother, who gave birth to me in Eezham. Why should I break my vow for that? The Emperor committed a great betrayal against my mother. Why should I show mercy to him or his children? Does this not give me even more reason to seek vengeance?”

“No, Queen, no! Think for a moment—would your mother approve of your desire for revenge? That old woman cherished the Emperor’s children as her very life. Would she wish for you to kill one of them with your own hands? She never would. If she learned of your deed, she would hate you. As long as she lives, she would be tormented by your actions. She may not be able to speak, but her gaze alone would plunge you into a hell of endless agony…”
Now, tears welled up in Nandini’s eyes. Wiping them away, she looked upward. Her face was contorted with pain, as if she beheld some sorrowful vision above.

“Mother! Mother! Is it not enough that the head and body of Veerapandiyan come separately to torment my soul? Must you too come and surround me?” she cried, and as if unable to bear the sight, she covered her eyes with her hands. For a while, only the sound of Nandini’s sobs filled the room.
Manimekalai turned to Vandiyathevan and said, “Sir! I never knew you could be so cruel!”
Hearing this, Nandini at once removed her hands, which had been covering her eyes, and said,
“There is no fault in him, sister! He speaks only for my own good. He says these things only to save me from a great sin! Even so, it torments me so!”

Then, with eyes brimming with tears, she looked at Vandiyathevan and said, “Sir! You have accomplished what no one else has managed until now. Here, as you wished, I am giving this sword back to you. Take it!”
As Vandiyathevan reached out his hand to receive it, Nandini drew it back again:

“Wait a moment! Before you take the sword, tell me if you can do me a favor. If I leave this place without fulfilling my vow, those in the hunting pavilion will not let me go so easily. They will tie me to a pyre and burn me alive. Even that does not frighten me. But before I die, I wish to see my mother once… O warrior of the Vanar clan! I said I did not believe all that you told me. That was wrong! I believe everything you said about my mother, who wanders the forests of Eelam like a madwoman. I believe every word. I have myself seen her…”
“When? How?” asked Vandiyathevan.

“When I was a child, sometimes as I lay sleeping, I would suddenly wake with a start. Then I would see the figure of a woman bent over my face, watching me without blinking. As soon as I opened my eyes, that figure would vanish. This always filled me with wonder and fear. From then on, I had a strange desire to look at my own face in the mirror. So, my own image became firmly imprinted in my mind. I used to marvel that the figure bending over me as I slept looked just like me. Our faces were the same. I had heard stories of souls that leap from nest to nest. I would wonder if my own soul had left my body and was standing above, gazing down at my face. Sometimes, I would be startled by the thought—have I died, is the body lying there my lifeless corpse? I would be troubled, wondering if all this was real, or a dream, or just my imagination, or if I had lost my mind.

But after I grew older, for many reasons, I became certain that all I had seen was real. Most of all, I was convinced by the confusion that came over Sundara Chozhar when he saw me. There were other signs too, and sometimes Azhwarkkadiyan, by mistake…” By the words that were spoken, I became certain that there must be a woman somewhere who bears a form like mine—my mother. A longing took root in my heart to see her just once, to lie in her lap and weep my sorrows away. Sir! The words you uttered today have made that longing grow a hundredfold. If you would take me to my mother, I shall abandon my quest for vengeance. I will hand over this Pandya clan sword to you right now!” Nandini said, her voice trembling with emotion.
Vandiyathevan sank into thought. “What trouble is this? The demon unleashed to dig the well has now come out!” he thought to himself.
Manimekalai pleaded, “Sir! I beg you too. Promise that you will fulfill my sister’s wish.”
With great hesitation, Vandiyathevan replied, “If it is within my power, I shall try!”
“In that case, we must leave at once. We must go before Aditya Karikalan arrives. The main entrance is dangerous; Kandhamaaran and Karikalan might come that way at any moment!” said Nandini.
“I will take you through the secret passage inside the hunting pavilion. Come!” said Vandiyathevan.
“Sister! I will come too. Please take me with you!” Manimekalai cried.
But Nandini, paying her no heed, said, “I do not wish to go into the hunting pavilion. Ravidasan and his men will not let us leave alive…”
“Lady! Just give me the sword in your hand. I will deal with all four of them myself!” said Vandiyathevan.
“No! That will only bring more trouble, Manimekalai! Is there no other way to get out of here?” Nandini Devi asked.

Manimekalai furrowed her brow and thought for a moment. “Sister! I do not know of any other way. But ask him. Once before, he vanished from this very room like a magician. Ask him how he did it!” she said.
Nandini looked at Vandiyathevan’s face.

Vandiyathevan replied, “Yes, Lady! There is another way. I discovered it by chance. But it is not an easy path. One must leap from beam to beam, from floor to floor, and then climb over the wall. Can you—”
“I suspect so. Rather than that, it would be easier to deal with the sorcerer and his men and then escape through the underground passage!” said Vandiyathevan.
At that moment, Manimekalai exclaimed in alarm, “Oh no, it seems they are coming!”
Both of them listened intently. Yes; from the front hall of the palace, the sound of footsteps approaching that room could be heard.
“Sir! Quickly, go inside the hunting pavilion!” urged Nandini.
“I have another good place to hide. Devi! Hand me that sword, please!” said Vandiyathevan.
Nandini extended the sword towards him to give it. But just then, her hand slipped, and the sword fell to the floor with a loud, ringing clang.

chapters.title: Was It All an Act?
paragraphs: When the sword slipped from his hand and fell to the ground, the sound mingled with the soft laughter of Nandini, a laughter brimming with sorrow.
In a flurry, she said, “Sir! The will of the gods is otherwise. Let the sword remain here. You must leave at once and hide yourself!”

Vandiyathevan, paying no heed to her words, bent down to pick up the sword. He tried to lift it by grasping its sharp tip. At that very moment, Nandini pressed her foot firmly on the hilt of the sword.

“No! The prince may have heard the sound of the sword falling. If the sword is missing from here, it will arouse his suspicion. Already, he harbors doubts about you. Go! Disappear from here as you did once before—vanish without a trace this time as well!” she urged.
In his attempt to pick up the sword by its tip, Vandiyathevan’s hand suffered a small cut. He let go of the sword and straightened up. Nandini noticed the thin trickle of blood oozing from his palm.
“I will fulfill the promise I made to you. By my hand, I will not kill my own brother. You will escape. But if he finds you here…”
“Go! Go at once!” Manimekalai pleaded, joining her voice to Nandini’s.
The sound of approaching footsteps grew louder.

With reluctant annoyance, Vandiyathevan hurried toward the storage chest of the veenas and other musical instruments. He opened the chest, slipped inside, and concealed himself. The footsteps now sounded very close, right by the entrance.
Nandini glanced at Manimekalai, who was staring in astonishment at the place where Vandiyathevan had hidden himself.
“Sister! You must hide as well! Conceal yourself behind the curtains of the bed! When we are speaking, slip away from here without his notice!” Nandini whispered urgently.

The very next moment, as Manimekalai hid herself behind the bed’s curtain, Aditya Karikalan and Kandanmaran entered the room. Karikalan, all the while glancing around him, drew closer to Nandini. He noticed the movement of the curtain draped over the bed, but he did not let on that he had seen it.

When he reached Nandini’s side, he looked at the sword lying on the floor, half-hidden in the shadows. Then, he fixed his gaze intently upon Nandini’s face. Unable to withstand the piercing intensity of that look, Nandini bent down, pretending as if to pick up the sword. Sensing her intention, Karikalan was quicker; he picked up the sword himself. He examined it closely, from the hilt to the sharp tip. He noticed a fresh bloodstain at the tip.

Then, turning to Nandini, he said, “Devi! The sound we heard as we entered—was it not the sound of this sword? It must have slipped from your hand and fallen to the ground! It seems you were ready to welcome us with sword in hand.”
“To receive valiant young tigers and lion-hearted youths, is that not the proper way?” replied Nandini.
“Wild tigers and lions need sharp claws and teeth. But does a leaping, playful spotted deer need such weapons? Is that why God did not grant them any?” said Aditya Karikalan.

“Even a deer may find need to use its horns, may it not? Perhaps there will come a time when the gentle deer must thank the Creator for giving it those horns. Please, in your mercy, return that sword to me!” Nandini pleaded.
“No, no! This does not suit your hands. How can the tender hands that Brahma created for plucking flowers and weaving garlands hold a sword?” said Karikalan.

“Great Prince! There was a time when these poor hands eagerly plucked flowers and lovingly wove garlands. There was a time when I waited and waited, hoping for the one worthy to wear that garland, only to be disappointed. The days of dreaming such daydreams have passed—many ages have gone by since then. Now, these helpless, orphaned hands are forced to seek solace in the sword. Sir, do not take even that solace away from me!” said Nandini.

“Devi! What is this you say? Do you call yourself a helpless orphan? How many young warriors wait, ready to fulfill with their heads the tasks you set with your feet? This is—” “Do you not know?” asked Karikalan.
“If, by some misfortune, my foot were ever to fall into the hands of such scoundrels, I would have to cut it off, my lord! For that alone, is not a sword necessary?”

“Oh! What a harsh and merciless speech is this? Are those feet, which ought to learn the graceful gait of swans and the modest walk of maidens, echoing with the tinkling of anklets in the palace halls, to be cut off? If these words were to reach the ears of Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar, how much would his heart suffer?”

“My lord! Who is there to worry about him? When that old lion lets out a single roar, did not the young tigers, trembling with fear, flee and hide? But now, how boldly those young tigers stride out in the open! Was it not only after hearing the news that he was swept away in the flood of the Kollidam that these young tigers found such courage? I kept this weapon only to ensure those tigers did not come too close to me. To protect the honor of that great man, who took me from the dust and called me to the world’s attention, granting me palace life and royal splendor, I sought the help of this sword. As you said just now, I trained these hands, meant to pluck flowers, to wield a sword…”

“Devi! Was it truly only for that? Was it only to protect Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar’s honor that you kept this sword in a casket and worshipped it, that you caressed and cherished it with cheeks softer than flowers? Or was it to keep at bay the fools who draw near, laughing foolishly as they gaze upon you? Was there no other purpose?”
“What other purpose could there be, my lord?”

“Why? There could be countless other purposes! There could be the intent of revenge. Perhaps you wished to fulfill a vow by killing the traitor who ignored your humble, pleading request and left an indelible wound in your heart!”

Nandini bowed her head and let out a long, deep sigh. Then, raising her eyes to the prince, she said, “Prince! It is true that once I did have such a thought. For that very reason, I worshipped this heroic sword. I waited for the moment when that time would come. But when the time came, in my hands—” All strength had left her; all resolve had drained from her heart. “Henceforth, I shall use this sword only to protect my chastity and my husband’s honor. Please, have mercy and give it to me thus!” she pleaded.
“Devi, may I not bear that responsibility? May I not fulfill the duty of punishing the wretch who wishes harm upon you or your husband?” asked Aditya Karikalan.
“This is not a task you can accomplish. For the sake of this helpless, forsaken woman, could you punish your dearest friend?”

“Why not? Of course I can! Nandini! That day, on the island in the lake, I did not fully believe all you said about Vandiyathevan. Later, from what Kandhamaaran told me, I realized it was all true. Even if you forgive that traitor, I am not willing to do so. Tell me where he is!... Will you not tell me?... No matter! My eyes have not gone blind... Look here!” With these words, Aditya Karikalan, his voice thundering with anger, strode toward the curtain that veiled the bed.
Nandini, falling at his feet, rose and knelt with folded hands, crying, “Prince! No! Please, no!”

“Nandini! Save your compassion for other matters! Do not show mercy to the wretch who pretends to be my friend while plotting treachery!” So saying, Aditya Karikalan brushed past Nandini and moved forward.
Nandini, bewildered and stunned, glanced all around. Then, seeing Kandhamaaran, who had stood like a statue near the doorway all this while, she cried out, “Oh! Stop him!”
Life returned to the statue that was Kandhamaaran. Yet he did not move from where he stood. He gave a slight, careless laugh, then turned to stone once more.
Karikalan, sword raised in one hand, approached the curtain by the bed and, with his other hand, drew it aside.
Inside, Manimekalai appeared, clutching a small, sharp dagger, and let out a shriek.
Aditya Karikalan stood frozen for a moment, sword poised. Then, with a sweep of his blade, he slashed the curtain to shreds.
“Ah! Is this woman a tigress, standing here? My, my! Her claws are sharper than ever!” he exclaimed, and burst into laughter—“Ha! Ha! Ha!”

Then, turning to Kandanmaran, he said, “Friend! Take your sister and escort her to her mother’s care! Who knows how many tiger cubs may be born from her womb! If she had perished just now, falling prey to this Veera Pandiyan’s sword, how many brave sons and daughters would the Chola land have lost?”

A moment ago, Manimekalai, who had truly raged like a tigress, now felt abashed upon hearing Aditya Karikalan’s words. Before Kandanmaran could approach and call her, she herself was already prepared to leave the room. Once brother and sister had departed, Karikalan turned to Nandini and said, “Devi, I staged a drama and sent those two away. Now, at least, can we open our hearts and speak the truth?”
With genuine astonishment, Nandini looked at Karikalan. “Sir! Was that an act you performed? If so, it was a marvelous performance! I too believed it to be real and was thoroughly deceived!”

“Nandini! In the art of acting, there is no equal to you in this world, in my opinion. If you were deceived, then surely you must praise my skill! Yet, when I raised my sword and went toward the place where Manimekalai was hiding, you did not try to stop me. Why was that? Did you think to add the sin of woman-slaughter to the many crimes already weighing upon me?”

“Shiva, Shiva! In this world, there is only one woman for whom I have true affection. Would I stand idly by and watch her die? I thought that once the curtain was drawn aside, you yourself would come to know the truth…”
Karikalan laughed.
“I do not understand the meaning of that laughter!” said Nandini.
“The reason you gave for not stopping me from killing Manimekalai is enough for me!” said Karikalan.
“I still do not understand!”
“If you love someone, whether man or woman, they become my mortal enemy. Do you not know this?”
“I know; I know that I am such an unfortunate soul. Still, I did not think your enmity would extend to this innocent young woman, who knows nothing of deceit or guile!”

“Or perhaps your intention is something else entirely. You might have thought that if I were to kill Manimekalai, Kandanmaran would seek vengeance against me. Or perhaps, before I could kill her, she would hurl the small dagger she carries and kill me instead…”
“Oh no! What is this? What kind of terrifying imaginings are these?”

“Imaginings, you say? The dreadful purpose you harbor in your heart is far more terrible than any of my imaginings. Tell me the truth! Do not further stoke the fire that already burns fiercely within me! Why did you summon me to this Kadambur palace? Why did you send the Pazhuvettaraiyars away to Thanjai? Do not tell me that all your efforts were to divide the Chola Empire, to bring about a compromise, or to delight in arranging a marriage between Manimekalai and myself! I will not believe such tales. If I had believed them, I would not have come here…”
“Then why did you come here, Prince? With what hope did you come to this place?”

“Hope? I have no hope left. My heart is filled only with despair and distrust. I wish to leave this land, to leave this world itself. But before I go, I wanted to see you once, to bid you farewell. Once, you asked me for a boon. You fell at my feet and pleaded for it. You raised your hands in supplication and begged. In my anger and stubbornness, I did not grant what you asked. Ever since, I have regretted it every single moment. If there is any way to atone for it, I have come to do so before I leave. Nandini! Tell me! If there is any way I can make amends, tell me!”

Hearing Karikalan’s voice, trembling with compassion, Nandini replied, “Prince! There is no atonement for that. The dead are dead! No one in this world has the power to bring the dead back to life. They speak of such things in stories and epics, but we have never seen it.”

“It is true, the dead cannot be brought back to life. But can one not atone by giving life for a life? Listen! There is no need to hide anything from me anymore. Do not think I do not know why you came here, why you summoned me, why you sent the Pazhuvettaraiyars to Thanjai! From the days when you and I were but children…” I possess the power to know the thoughts that arise in your mind. It was only to inflame my anger and drive me to commit a despicable act that you pleaded for the life of Veera Pandiyan. You married Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar and came to Thanjai only to torment me from close quarters. You could not bear to see me living peacefully in Kanchi; that is why you summoned me to this Kadambur palace. You have come here with the very intention of having me slain by Veera Pandiyan’s sword, thus fulfilling your vengeance. Go on, fulfill your purpose without hindrance! That is why I sent Kandhamaaran and his sister away. Here! Take this sword!” said Karikalan, extending the weapon.

Nandini took the sword. Her hands trembled as she grasped it. Then her whole body began to shake. Tears brimmed in her eyes. Her voice, breaking with sobs and anguish, poured forth in a tone that could shatter the heart.

“Nandini! What is this cowardice? Why this weakness of spirit? You were raised in a priest’s household; but were you not born of a valiant warrior’s lineage? Does a lion cub, raised among sheep, lose its true nature? Look here! I know your innermost thoughts. You need not send Kandhamaaran, Parthibendran, or Vandiyathevan to carry out your vengeance. Do not try to kindle my anger against them. Fulfill your vow yourself! End your vendetta with your own hands! At any moment, someone may return and interrupt us. Kandhamaaran will soon come back after leaving his sister with her mother. Parthibendran and Sambuvarayar too will return soon. My grandfather Malayaman may come with them. I do not believe Pazhuvettaraiyar has perished in the Kollidam floods; he too may appear at any moment. You will never find a better opportunity than this to fulfill your vow and complete your revenge. By killing me, you will not have done me any harm! Rather, you will have rendered me a great service!” he said.

Suppressing her rising sobs, Nandini replied, “Prince! I have nothing to hide from you. Nor do I wish to hide anything. All that you have said about my purpose in coming here is true. The reason I summoned you here is exactly as you said. But when the moment arrived, my hands had no strength; my heart, no courage. The very instant I heard your footsteps approaching, the sword slipped from my grasp and fell to the ground. Look! See how my hands tremble as I hold this sword!” she said.

“Yes, yes! I have been watching that myself. But the reason for it—I do not know. I am well aware of how steadfast your heart once was. After forging the Vajrayudha for Devendran, I have often thought that Brahma himself must have fashioned your heart from the leftover metal. For such a heart as yours to have softened in this manner—what could be the cause?”
“The news brought by your friend Vandiyathevan is the reason.”

“Ah! You mean the news he discovered, that you and I are siblings by birth? Is that what you refer to? That day, when we spoke on the island in the middle of the lake, you said you did not believe it. You claimed it was some conspiracy devised by someone to separate us once more.”
“I tried my best not to believe it. I made every effort for that purpose. But today, another piece of news he brought has shaken the very foundation of my resolve.”
“Ah! What is it? Some new fantasy? What else did he say that is new?”

“He spoke of the mother who bore me. He said he saw her on the island of Lanka. I have no reason to disbelieve that. Prince! Once, I asked you for a boon. You did not grant it. You said you have regretted that to this day. Now, I ask you for another boon. Will you grant me this, at least?”
“If you specify what the boon is, I can tell you whether I can grant it or not.”

“Prince! It is true that I swore an oath to avenge the death of Veerapandiyan. I vowed that with this sword, marked with the fish emblem of the Pandya clan, I would either kill you, or else kill myself and vanish from this world. I have neither the courage in my heart nor the strength in my arms to kill you. Even if I wished to end my own life before your very eyes, I do not have the strength for that either. I am afraid—what if, after a half-hearted attempt, my life does not leave me? Sir! Help me fulfill my oath! Take this sword from me, and with your own hand, strike me down! Then my vow will be fulfilled. Not only in this birth, but in all births to come, I shall remain ever grateful to you!”
As she spoke thus, Nandini extended the sword once more, and Aditya Karikalan took it from her hand.
“Ha ha ha!”—the terrifying laughter echoed throughout the entire palace.

chapters.title: Enveloped in Darkness!
paragraphs: The terrifying, frenzied laughter of Aditya Karikalan, echoing from the hall of the veena treasury, reached the ears of Vandiyathevan, who was hidden within. It sent a shiver down his spine. His inner sense foretold that some dreadful calamity was about to unfold. In that chamber, the shadowy form of Yama, the god of death, seemed to stand, rope of noose in hand, waiting with a grim smile for the right moment to cast it. But upon whom would he hurl it? Whose life was he about to claim? Was it Karikalan’s life? Or was it the life of Nandini Devi? Perhaps death was drawing near to both of them. Would brother slay sister, or would sister kill brother? Or would both destroy each other and perish together?

It was to prevent such a catastrophe that the Young Princess had hurriedly sent him here. He had done all he could. He had spoken to them both about the bond that existed between them. He had tried to soften their hearts. But would it bear fruit? Could the mad rage of Karikalan, or the delirium that possessed Nandini, be restrained from committing some cruel deed? Would his intervention at this moment bring about any good? Perhaps, if he were to sacrifice his own life between the two, their wrath might be appeased? Thoughts such as these churned the ocean of Vandiyathevan’s heart. Let me wait a little longer, he told himself, clenching his teeth so that his haste would not ruin everything.
After Karikalan’s wild laughter subsided, their conversation resumed.
“Sir! In all my life, I have never done anything to bring you happiness. At least at the moment of my death, I am glad to be the cause of your laughter and joy,” said Nandini.

“Yes, Nandini! Today is indeed a day of great happiness for me. All the suffering you have inflicted upon me for so many years is about to end today. When I set out from Kanchi this time, I steeled my heart in every way. I feared that, upon seeing you in person, my resolve might falter. But you yourself have placed the sword in my hand, leaving no room for hesitation!” Karikalan said, and laughed again.

“Prince! Today is an auspicious day for me as well. There will never be a sweeter death for me than to be slain by your hand. Once, I dreamed a cherished dream that you would one day place a garland of flowers around my neck. That dream could never come true. At least grant me the fortune of having your sword encircle my neck. My lord! The hour is upon us—why do you delay?” said Nandini.

“It has already been delayed for many years. What harm is there if it is delayed by a few more moments? Nandini! Look at me—look at me once, for the last time, and answer my question! With the hand that was meant to place a garland of flowers, why should I now place a garland of swords around your neck? If your cherished dream was true once, why can it not be fulfilled now? Tell me, who stands in the way of that? Instead of killing you, let me slay those who stand as obstacles, and then see to other matters!” said Karikalan.
“No, my lord! No! You are blessed with infinite virtue. Let no one else die because of me!”
“I will shatter that obstacle in a single moment. Do not lay the blame upon fate! I will rewrite what Brahma has written—watch me!…”
Nandini interrupted, “You may rewrite what Brahma has written. But can you alter a person’s birth?”

“What are you speaking of, Nandini? Are you referring to how, in our childhood, my family said you were a priest’s daughter, and that I should not befriend you because of it? Is it that? No! You and I both knew, even then, that though you were raised in that family, you were not born to it.”

“I am not speaking of that now, my lord! I speak of the message your dear friend—the valiant warrior of the Vanar clan—brought. I speak of the urgent message sent by the Younger Princess of Pazhayarai. Have you already forgotten that I am your sister?”

“Nandini! When I told you about this before, you did not believe me. You said it was yet another plot to separate us. Later, I too thought and came to the same conclusion. If you wish to be certain of it…”
“No! No! I have no doubt about it. Prince! There is no blood relation between you and me…”
“Then, what is the obstacle, Nandini?”
“I am the wife of the elder Pazhuvettaraiyar, who is your grandfather’s peer. Am I not, then, your grandmother by custom? Is that not enough for you?”

“Nandini! Do not try to deceive me again by telling that story. In the eyes of the world, you may be the young queen of Pazhuvettaraiyar. But in truth, you have not married him. For some reason or another, you have merely come to reside in his palace. Once, when I questioned you in Thanjai, you said the same. At that time, I reminded you of our cherished dreams. To fulfill them, you laid down terrible conditions! You demanded that I kill Pazhuvettaraiyar, imprison my own father and sister, and seat you upon the Chola throne. I decided then that you were a mad demoness, and I left for Kanchi. But did you leave me alone after that? No! Tirelessly, ceaselessly, you haunted me in dreams and memories. Sometimes you tormented me with your tears and laments. Sometimes, with your enchanting smile, you tormented my very soul! Sometimes, you laughed like a madwoman and drove me to madness as well!...”

“Prince! Why do you lay the blame for your delusions upon me? You have suffered the consequences for the injustice and cruelty you showed me. What can I do about that? Do you think I alone did not suffer? Do you believe I was reveling in the pleasures and luxuries of Pazhuvettaraiyar’s palace?” As Nandini spoke, her voice once again brimmed with the old anger and cruelty.
Hearing this, Vandiyathevan was seized with fear. His body trembled. Aditya Karikalan’s voice too began to rise.

“You say you suffered as well? If so, why should we waste time in idle talk now? Give me your consent to come with me, and let us leave at once. For your sake, I am ready to renounce this great Chola kingdom. I am prepared to abandon my native land, my parents, my kin and relatives. Let us board a ship and cross the seas. Beyond the seas, there are countless wondrous islands and lands. We shall find one of them. This kingdom is not greater to me than you.”
“Prince! You may renounce the kingdom, indeed you will! But would you ever consent for this low-born woman to ascend the ancient Chola throne?” said Nandini, and her laughter sparked like fire.

“Woman! Look at this from another angle! Is the Chola throne more important to you than I am? Was all the affection you showed me from that day onwards nothing but an act, performed out of your desire to ascend the throne and wear the jeweled crown?” demanded Karikalan.
“Ah! Let it be so, then. Yes, I want palace life, royal luxuries, and the king’s throne. For these alone, I married Pazhuvetaraiyar. For these alone, I tried to save Veerapandiyan…”
“You wretch! Why do you utter his name now?” roared Karikalan.

Before Nandini could reply, he continued: “Ah, now I understand. I see through all your schemes. You know that if you mention Veerapandiyan’s name, I will be enraged. I will truly come to kill you. And then, one of those young lions, waiting here to do your bidding, will rush in and kill me. That is your secret plan, isn’t it? You vile woman! Where is that Vandiyathevan? Where are you hiding him? Tell me! He must be concealed here somewhere. Now I know the real reason you refuse to come with me. Yes, he is the reason! You plan to run away with him! He is the reason you sent Pazhuvetaraiyar away from here. The two of you have plotted all this together… Ah, how I have been deceived! Where is that traitor Vandiyathevan? Where is your new lover…?”
So shouting in a frenzy, Aditya Karikalan spun his sword and began to pace back and forth across the room. At one point, he drew near the veena chest.

At that moment, Nandini sprang forward in a single bound, fell at his feet, and cried, “Prince! Listen to me! You will gain untold merit if you do. Hear me out, and then do whatever you wish. What you say about the valiant scion of the Vanar clan is a monstrous falsehood. Mother Earth herself cannot bear it. If you harm him in any way, my dear friend Manimekalai will give up her life! You will incur a terrible sin. Please, no! Here—split open my heart and see for yourself, with Veerapandiyan’s own sword. Within it, you will find nothing but your own sacred image. This is the truth! The truth! The truth!” With these words, Nandini broke down in sobs.

Aditya Karikalan’s frenzy seemed to subside a little once more. “If that is so, why do you refuse to come with me? At least tell me that! Why do you provoke me to slay you with my own hand? Speak the truth!” Karikalan cried out.

“Very well, I will tell you now. In my heart, there is no place for anyone but you. This is the truth. Yet, I cannot come with you. I cannot marry you. There is a great reason that stands in the way. Yes, Prince! In truth, it was to tell you this that I came here. I brought you here so I could confess it and beg your forgiveness. I came to plead with you to forget this wretched woman, to marry a maiden worthy of your lineage and station, and to live in happiness. Yet, I hesitated to speak. Even now, the thought of uttering it fills me with fear. I am afraid that your anger will blaze up, that some greater harm may come of it. If you promise to remain calm…”

“Speak, Nandini, speak! No matter how bitter it is, I will hear and bear it. Just now, you advised me to forget you and marry another woman and be happy! Did I grow angry at that? What else could you say that would make me angry? But do not weave any more fantasies…”

“Prince! My whole life is a fantasy. My very birth is a tale of fiction. To prolong my life a little, to fulfill the task I have taken up, I have had to spin many stories, many lies. But now, there is no more need for that. Today, I am going to end this false life of mine. Even after I learned certain truths, I did not tell you, fearing it would only increase your sorrow. I invented many stories so that you would hate me. I devised many dreadful deeds. I urged you to commit terrible acts. Within me, an unceasing battle raged. My duty, the vow I had taken, and the love I bore for you—these fought endlessly within my heart. The suffering I endured because of this cannot be described. At last, today, the moment has come for that struggle to end. I will tell you the truth about myself. After you have heard it, you may kill me with your own hand! But do not harm anyone else! Do not bring needless sin and blame upon yourself!…”

“Sin! Shame! What new sin or shame is left for me to bear? Still, tell me, Nandini! Tell me the true reason—what is it that truly stands in the way of your coming with me, of fulfilling the dreams of our youth? However terrible that truth may be, speak it! As long as I suspected that someone was hiding behind that curtain, as long as I did not know who it was, my mind was restless. Even as I spoke with you, my heart was preoccupied with that thought. But once I knew it was Manimekalai who was concealed there, my confusion vanished. Fear, anger, confusion—all these exist only as long as the truth is hidden! However bitter it may be, once the truth is known, the mind finds peace, does it not?”

“Prince! May the news I am about to tell you truly bring peace to your heart. That is my prayer. But this news will also prove that it is impossible for me to come with you, or to marry you. It will reveal that the end of my life, the deliverance from my sorrows, is nothing but death. The warrior of the Vanar clan brought news about my mother. I know it to be true. I know about the mad queen who wandered in frenzy through Eelam. I know that she is my mother. This was known to others as well. For many could see the resemblance between that queen and myself. Some even suspected that I was her daughter. But only recently did I learn the reason that drove my mother to madness. I do not know if anyone else knows it. I have never told anyone until now. Only now, for the first time, I am going to tell you. Sir! I am going to tell you who my father is. Remember the promise of mercy you gave me a little while ago. Do not give way to anger or hatred.”
With this powerful preamble, Nandini drew close to Aditya Karikalan, and in a voice so soft it trembled at his ear, she said, “The man who fathered me… is you!”
Having uttered these words, she broke down, sobbing uncontrollably.
Aditya Karikalan shuddered as if a thousand scorpions had stung him.
“No, no, no! Never! What you say is a lie, a monstrous lie!” he cried aloud.

In the very next moment, his agitation subsided. In a voice heavy with pain, he said, “Yes, Nandini, yes. What you say must surely be true. Now, I understand everything. I know the truth of the struggle that must have raged within your heart. I see how much you must have suffered. I understand the cause of your confusion, your hesitation, and your dreadful plea. That day, when you fell at my feet and begged me, how great a cruelty it was that I refused your request! Nandini! For so many evils in this world, there is atonement. But for what I have done, there is no atonement. There is no path to remove the barrier that stands between us. Alas! How did you bear this terrible burden in your heart all these days? How did you endure the existence of this sinner upon this earth? Very well! There is only one remedy for both our lives! Only one redemption. Here, Nandini! Here is my atonement!”

From within the lute chamber, Vandiyathevan listened to all these exchanges. At times, when Karikalan’s rage grew uncontrollable, he thought of intervening between them. But then, hesitating over what disaster might result, he held back. Their emotionally charged conversation rendered him powerless, as if paralyzed. Only one thing did not reach his ears clearly—what Nandini had revealed about her father. Yet, a suspicion arose in his mind as to what she might have said. Though it startled him, to put it any other way would be mere convention. Never before, in his shock-filled life, had he experienced such a jolt.

At last, when Aditya Karikalan, subdued and trembling, was uttering words in a soft voice, accepting what Nandini had said, Vandiyathevan’s curiosity overcame all caution. When Karikalan had been shouting, he had not been so afraid. But now, his fear increased. Anxious about what might happen next, he stretched his head out from the lute chamber and looked. In the place where his eyes fell, neither Nandini nor Karikalan was to be seen. But he saw another sight. Reflected in the great mirror set in the wall, he saw a terrifying face at the secret door of the hunting pavilion. It was the face of the sorcerer Ravidasan! In the very next moment, Vandiyathevan saw the secret door of the hunting pavilion slowly opening. Through the open door, first the head of a tiger, then its body, emerged. At once, life returned to his limbs. Courage sprang up in his heart. His arms and legs regained their strength. From the concealment of the lute chamber, he leapt and tried to rush out.

At that very moment, from behind, a hand as mighty as the thunderbolt of Indra wrapped itself around his neck. Vandiyathevan turned in shock; before his eyes appeared a tall, broad-shouldered figure, its face adorned in the fearsome guise of a Kalamukan. Ah! Who was this? How had he come here? What was this iron grip? His neck was being crushed! His breath was choking; his vision was blurring! If this continued for a few more moments, his very life would be snuffed out…! With a tremendous effort, Vandiyathevan twisted and broke free from that iron hand’s grasp and flung himself outside. In the force of his leap, he fell to the ground. It felt as though a great boulder had been dropped upon his head. For a moment, before his eyes, millions of suns burst forth, scattering countless rays in a blinding blaze. In the next instant, all those suns vanished. Darkness closed in from every side. In that very moment, Vandiyathevan lost consciousness.

From the music chamber, stepping over Vandiyathevan’s body that lay at its threshold, a dreadful, terrifying Kalamukan figure emerged. Hearing a heavy thud near the music chamber, Nandini turned to look. She saw the Kalamukan figure approaching her, a knife drawn in his hand. With eyes wide in astonishment, she stared at that form. It felt as if her very entrails were rising up, choking her chest and throat. Wiping her eyes, she looked ahead. She saw Karikalan lying fallen on the ground. She saw, too, that the sword of Veera Pandiyan had pierced his body.
At that moment, from her throat rose a terrible sound, a mixture of sobbing and laughter. It made even the inanimate objects in that room—the bed and all else—tremble.
“Ah, wretch! Outcaste! Have you fulfilled your vengeance?” the Kalamukan figure said, advancing upon her.

At the same time, through the secret door of the hunting pavilion, Ravidasan entered, hidden by the form of a tiger. The moment he saw the Kalamukan, he seized the tiger and hurled it aside. The dead tiger’s body struck the lamp that had been faintly lighting the room. The lamp fell and was extinguished. Before it went out, for a fleeting instant, it illuminated the terror-stricken face of Manimekalai. With a shriek, Manimekalai ran from the room.

Darkness enveloped the chamber. In that thick gloom, the sound of grief-choked sobs, the laughter of madness, the groans of those at death’s door, and the hurried footsteps of men running to and fro—all these sounds mingled together.

The sky was shrouded in thick, impenetrable darkness. The moon and stars had hidden themselves behind dense clouds. The wind, which had been blowing fiercely until then, now lay still, as if exhausted. The forest, which had echoed with the cries of wild beasts and the rustling of leaves, now seemed to hold its breath in anticipation. Not even the chirping of crickets could be heard.

Vandiyathevan, who had been walking briskly through the forest path, suddenly stopped. He looked around, trying to pierce the gloom with his eyes. The darkness was so deep that he could not even see his own hands. He could only sense the path beneath his feet by touch. The silence and the darkness together created an eerie atmosphere, making his heart beat faster.

He listened intently, straining his ears for the slightest sound. Somewhere in the distance, he thought he heard the faint gurgle of running water. He wondered if it was the Kollidam river. But he could not be sure. He took a few cautious steps forward. The branches of a tree brushed against his face. He pushed them aside and continued.

Suddenly, he felt as if someone was following him. He stopped again and listened. The silence was absolute. Yet, he could not shake off the feeling that unseen eyes were watching him from the darkness. He remembered the words of the Vaishnavite elder: “Be careful! Danger lurks in these forests at night.” Vandiyathevan smiled to himself. “Let danger come! Am I not a warrior?” he thought, and pressed on with renewed courage.

After walking for some distance, he saw a faint light flickering in the distance. His heart leaped with hope. Perhaps it was a hut or a campfire. He quickened his pace, carefully making his way towards the light. As he drew nearer, the light grew brighter. Soon, he could make out the outline of a small hut, with a lamp burning at the entrance.
Vandiyathevan approached the hut cautiously. He peered inside. An old woman was sitting near the lamp, spinning cotton. She looked up as he entered, her eyes sharp and inquisitive.
“Who are you, son? Where do you come from at this hour?” she asked.
“I am a traveler, mother. I lost my way in the forest. May I rest here for a while?” Vandiyathevan replied respectfully.
The old woman studied him for a moment, then nodded. “Come in, child. The forest is not safe at night. Sit down and rest.”

Vandiyathevan entered the hut and sat down gratefully. The warmth of the lamp and the old woman’s kindness dispelled the fear and darkness that had surrounded him outside. For a while, he forgot the dangers lurking in the night, and allowed himself to relax.

chapters.title: “I Killed!”
paragraphs: In the copper plates of Thiruvalangadu, where the lineage of the Chola dynasty is chronicled, it is written: “Desiring to behold the heavens, Adithan met his setting. The world was shrouded in the dark clouds of Kali!” Thus is inscribed the untimely death of the crown prince of the Chola Empire, the bravest of the brave, Aditya Karikalan, who fell by the hand of Veera Pandiyan.
At that moment, in the chamber of the Kadambur palace where Aditya Karikalan’s lifeless body lay, true darkness reigned.

Within the heart of Vallavarayan, who had been thrown to the floor with a thud by the man with the fearsome Kalamukha visage, a similar darkness had settled for a while. As light slowly began to dawn in his mind, as memory returned, his eyes fluttered open. Yet, because of the enveloping darkness around him, nothing came into focus. He could not discern where he was, nor in what state he lay.

The first sensation that struck him was the throbbing pain in his head. There was also pain at the spot on his neck where he had been gripped. He realized he was struggling to breathe. How had this pain in his head come about? What had caused the ache in his neck? Why was it so difficult to draw breath? Ah! That Kalamukhan! Had he truly seen him? Had the man truly tried to strangle him? Why had he tried to choke him? Was it to prevent him from making a sound? To stop him from moving further? Why? Why? Where had he been trying to go, breaking free from that iron grip? Ah! Now he remembered! To reach Aditya Karikalan! Alas! What had become of him? What had happened to Nandini? What did Ravidasan do? What could the Kalamukhan, who had thrown him to the ground to restrain him, have done next?… Where was he now? In an underground dungeon? In a secret tunnel? Vandiyathevan’s eyes darted wildly, trying to pierce the darkness all around. Nothing was visible! O God, could such utter darkness exist?… He remembered now—the place where he had fallen was Nandini’s inner chamber, near the hall of musical instruments. Was he still lying there? Or had they carried him elsewhere and left him? How was he to find out? He stretched out both hands and groped about. His fingers struck against an object. What was it? Did it not feel like a knife? Yes, it was a knife! A curved-bladed knife! Far more powerful than ordinary knives! If it were to strike anyone, that person would surely die! Where had he seen such a strange knife before? Where? In whose hand had he seen it?… One by one, all the events of that previous night returned to his memory! How had this knife come here? Oh! The blade is damp! How did it become wet? Was it water? No! Oil? That too, no! It must be blood! Alas! Whose blood? Could it be his own blood?

Vandiyathevan touched the back of his head. He felt his neck. There was pain in those places, but no sign of bleeding. Nowhere else on his body did he feel the pain of a knife wound!… Then, whose blood had this curved-bladed knife tasted before lying here beside him? He had not wounded anyone with it. He had not even held it in his hand before! Then, who could have used it?

Could it have been Idumbankari? On whom would he have used it? Was it possible that Idumbankari had come in the guise of that fearsome-looking Kalamukan? No! No! That could not be! Idumbankari was not such a tall, imposing figure…

What was that? The sound of footsteps? Was someone approaching? Should he remain silent? Should he call out? Would the newcomers not be carrying a lamp? At least then he could find out where he was. Otherwise, in the darkness, they might step on him without realizing it…
As this thought occurred, Vandiyathevan suddenly sat up. Holding the small knife ready in his hand, he called out, “Who is there?”

The sound of his own voice filled him with immense astonishment. He could not recognize it as his own. It did not sound like his voice at all. That Kalamukan’s grip on his throat must have caused this damage. Even producing a sound was difficult.
He tried once more, raising his voice, “Who is there?” But even that came out as a hoarse, growling noise, not as a clear voice.

Again, the sound of footsteps was heard, but then it stopped abruptly. Perhaps the person, hearing his strange voice, had been frightened, thinking it was a ghost or demon, and had turned back the way they came.
Thinking this, Vandiyathevan tried to laugh. But even his laughter came out as a strange, shapeless sound.

Alright; there is no use in sitting or waiting any longer. I must get up, walk, and find out where I am. He rose to his feet; his legs trembled. Yet, steadying himself, he began to walk. No matter how far he stretched out his hands, nothing met his touch. In the distance, something faintly glimmered. Ah! Was that not like a mirror? A very faint ray of light, coming from somewhere, had struck it and made it gleam. The image of Ravidasan entering with the tiger skin in his hand, reflected in that mirror, flashed across Vandiyathevan’s memory. Yes, yes! He was still inside Nandini’s private chamber. But why was it so shrouded in darkness here? Why had silence settled so heavily? What had become of all those who had been in this room just a short while ago?

Thinking thus, Vandiyathevan stumbled through the darkness. Perhaps there would be some light near the entrance—if not, he could at least step outside and ask someone what had happened, and learn the truth. With this thought, he made his way forward. Suddenly, something caught his foot and he fell once more with a thud. But this time, he landed on something soft, so he was not hurt badly. That soft object—he realized—was a tiger skin. He must have fallen upon the very tiger skin that Ravidasan had brought in and thrown down…

As he fell, the dagger in his hand slipped away. He stretched out his hand, searching for it. His fingers brushed against something soft. Vandiyathevan’s whole body shuddered. His hair stood on end. A chill of terror crept into his heart.

“Could it really be?” he wondered, and reached out again to make sure. Yes; it was a human body! What his hand had touched was the palm of a man! He hastily pushed the tiger skin aside and flung it away. Then he peered closely; the faint light reflected in the mirror fell upon the body lying below, making it just barely visible. Alas! Was it not Prince Aditya Karikalan lying there? No—it was not he, but his lifeless body! Vandiyathevan’s chest heaved, and his throat tightened. Unbidden, tears welled up in his eyes! With trembling hands, he touched various parts of Karikalan’s body. There was no room for doubt. It was a cold, lifeless corpse!

Blood, which had flowed from the prince’s side and pooled beside him, now stained Vandiyathevan’s hands. At that moment, the memory of Princess Kundavai came to him. For what purpose had that noble lady sent him here? In that task, he had not succeeded—he had utterly failed! How could he ever face her again? He had done all that was within his power. He could do no more.

Even so, it was of no use—fate had triumphed! He took the lifeless body of the prince and laid it across his lap. He did not know what to do next. He had lost even the strength to think. His throat had no power left even to cry out in anguish.

“The prince is dead; we have not succeeded in the task we undertook; I can never again look upon Kundavai’s face!”—these thoughts circled again and again in his mind. How long he sat there, lost in such thoughts, he himself did not know. Only when he saw, by the light of torches, several people approaching that chamber did a measure of self-awareness return to him.

He gently lifted Karikalan’s body from his lap and placed it on the ground, then stood up. Ten or twelve men entered from the front entrance. Two of them held torches. Others came bearing spears. At the head of them all came Kandanmaran, and next to him, Periya Sambuvarayar. The faces of all who entered were filled with terror and confusion. In the flickering torchlight, they looked like men possessed by spirits.

Only on Kandanmaran’s face did anger and fury burn fiercely. Seeing Vandiyathevan, he roared, “You wretch! Murderer! Betrayer of friendship! Traitor to the king! Did you not try to escape? Did you think you could get away?”

Then, turning to Periya Sambuvarayar, he cried, “Father! Look there—the murderer! See the traitor who acted as a friend and committed this heinous crime! See the villain who has brought an indelible stain upon our lineage! Look at his face! See how the terrible crime he has committed is written upon his very features!”

Sambuvarayar did not reply to any of this. He approached the body of Aditya Karikalan lying on the floor. Sitting at its head, he gazed intently at it for a while, then cried, “Alas, fate! Did this have to happen in my house? Must the blame of inviting a king to dinner and then murdering him fall upon my head?” He lamented thus, striking his own head again and again in grief.

Kandanmaran said, “Father! That blame will never fall upon our clan! Here, we have caught the murderer red-handed! Look, there lies the very knife he used to kill the prince! See how it is stained with blood! When I first came in, he was not here, nor was the knife—” “No. He ran towards him, but, unable to do anything, he turned back! Perhaps he came to see if the prince still clung to life! Perhaps, thinking that stabbing him with a knife was not enough, he came to twist his throat and finish him off! Father! What punishment can be given to such a great sinner—a traitor and conspirator? No punishment would suffice!” Thus Kandhamaaran spoke as he walked.

Vandiyathevan was already unable to speak, his throat choked with emotion. Kandhamaaran’s words left him bewildered and stunned. Only then did he realize that he was now in a position where others might consider him a murderer. Was not this very Kandhamaaran accusing him of killing the prince? Earlier, he had said that Vandiyathevan stabbed him in the back. Now he was declaring that Vandiyathevan had killed the prince! Such was his situation! Ah! That enchantress of Pazhuvoor—the beautiful serpent in human form—had she planned all this? Was it for this very reason that she had saved him several times before? Had she thus avenged her hatred for Princess Kundavai? Ah! Where was that woman, that demoness in the guise of beauty? How had she escaped? It seemed that, once her task was done, she had fled through the secret tunnel along with the sorcerer Ravidasan and the others!

As these thoughts raced through Vandiyathevan’s mind, suddenly his reasoning veered in another direction. He was certain that he had not killed Aditya Karikalan. But then, who else could have done it? Was it Nandini? Or Ravidasan? Or the Kalamukan? Could it have been Manimekalai, who had appeared and disappeared in that brief, forgotten moment? Or was it Idumbankari, who had brought the twisted knife? Could it be that Kandhamaaran himself, blinded by his infatuation for Nandini, had committed this heinous crime and was now trying to lay the blame on him? Or, after hearing the astonishing secret revealed by Nandini, had Aditya Karikalan, overcome by grief, taken his own life?

Kandhamaaran turned to the men standing beside him and shouted, “You fools! Why are you standing idle? Seize this murderer and bind him!” With those words, Vandiyathevan was once again reminded of the perilous situation he was in.

He looked at Kandhamaaran with eyes brimming with pity and sorrow. With great effort, he summoned life back into his throat and said, “Kandhamaaran! What is this? Do you truly believe I could commit such a terrible deed? Why would I do such a thing? What would I gain from it? My friend!…” But before he could finish, Kandhamaaran interrupted, “Shame! I am not your friend. The tongue that called me so should be cut out. For you—”
“What profit, you ask? Why wouldn’t there be profit? The desire to win a sidelong glance from Nandini, that’s the only reward! Ah! Where is that enchantress of Pazhuvoor now?” he exclaimed.

“Kandhamaaran! Truly, I do not know. I was lying here unconscious. Only a short while before you arrived did I regain my senses. I have no idea what became of Nandini. Perhaps she escaped through the underground passage. In the hunting pavilion, her people—Veera Pandiyan’s loyal followers—four of them were waiting. She may have gone with them!”

Kandhamaaran said, “Oh! So she has tricked you and left as well. But don’t pretend you know nothing. Who would believe that? Wasn’t it clear to me that you had fallen under her spell, ready to finish with your head what your feet had begun? Didn’t Aditya Karikalan himself say so? Nandini too has told him the truth about you. Whether at her instigation, or thinking it would please her, you have committed this murder! Even if I look into your face, I feel only pity!”
“Kandhamaaran! I swear to you, I did not kill the prince. I came here bearing the responsibility, entrusted to me by the Princess of Pazhayarai, to protect his life…”
“That’s how you deceived the prince! And then, with treachery, you stabbed and killed him! If not, how did you end up in this room? Why did you come here?”
“Kandhamaaran! I came to protect the prince, knowing danger was approaching him. I failed in that attempt. But it was not my fault. If you wish, ask your sister Manimekalai—she is the one who…”
“Enough! Do not speak of my sister! Do not utter her name. Beware! If you mention her again, do you know what I’ll do? I’ll seize you by the throat and strangle you here and now!”

Having said this, Kandhamaaran leapt at Vandiyathevan, grabbed the ropes binding his chest and shoulders, and gave them a violent shake. Then, turning to Sambuvarayar, who was sitting near Aditya Karikalan’s body, sunk in grief, he cried out:

“Father! Tell me what to do with him! What shall we do with this murderer who has brought undying disgrace upon our clan? If you give me permission, I’ll cut him to pieces this very instant! Father! Tell me!”

Chieftain Sambuvarayar, who had been sitting as if in a trance, running his hands over Karikalan’s body, was startled by Kandanmaran’s shout and looked up. His gaze went beyond Kandanmaran. He saw the curtain around the bed in that room stir. The next moment, he saw a figure emerge, pushing aside the curtain. Because his eyes were brimming with tears, he could not immediately discern who it was that stepped out from behind the veil. But as the figure came closer, he recognized her—it was his own daughter, the noble maiden Manimekalai. A mixture of astonishment, revulsion, and pain appeared on his face.
“Manimekalai! How did you come here?” he asked, his words making Kandanmaran turn and look as well.
“Father! I was here all along. Please tell my brother not to do anything to him. He is not at fault!” she said.
Kandanmaran, seething, cried, “Father! Did you see? How this wretch has corrupted my sister’s mind? Did you see? She claims he is not at fault at all!”
“Yes, brother! Truly, he is not at fault!” Manimekalai declared firmly. Kandanmaran was torn between anger and shame.
“Sister! Hold your tongue! Who called you here? You should not have come here. Your mind is not your own. Go at once to the women’s quarters! Go where the other women are!” Kandanmaran shouted.
“No, brother! My mind is perfectly clear. It is your mind that is clouded. Otherwise, you would not have accused him of murdering the prince!” Manimekalai replied.
Kandanmaran, enraged, said, “Foolish girl! Why do you plead for this murderer?”
“Because he is not a murderer, that’s why!” Manimekalai answered.
With a furious laugh, Kandanmaran asked, “If he is not the murderer, then who is? Who killed the prince? Was it you?”
“Yes! I killed him! I killed him with this sword!” declared Manimekalai.
Hearing these words, everyone present there was utterly stunned. They looked at each other’s faces in astonishment.
After a moment’s silence, Kandhamaaran left Vandiyathevan and rushed to Manimekalai’s side. He seized the sword from her and examined its tip closely.

“Father! Look at this! She cannot even lift this sword. Yet she claims to have killed the prince with it. If this had been plunged into the prince’s body, could she have pulled it out herself? Look at the tip! It appears as if it has been freshly wiped clean! She is saying all this only to save Vallavaraiyan! Why does she care so much for him? How deeply has this criminal ensnared her heart! He must have bewitched her with some dark magic! Look at his face! Look at how his crime is written plainly upon it!” he cried.
Indeed, Vandiyathevan’s face bore the marks of astonishment, shock, and pain. Silent until now, he finally opened his mouth and said,

“Kandhamaaran! What you say is true! I am the culprit. Your sister is only inventing this story to save me! Princess! My thanks to you! Even after my life has left my body, I will not forget the sisterly affection you have shown me. But now, listen to your brother! Go to the inner chambers at once!”
Hearing this, Kandhamaaran’s rage reached its peak. His eyes, already red, now seemed to spit fire.

“Ah! Have things come to such a pass that you dare to plead on my behalf? Will she listen to you when she will not heed my words? Does she hold such sisterly affection for you? Was she born with me, or with you? Does she respect you more than me? Why is that? What sorcery have you used to corrupt her heart so? This is reason enough for me to kill you! Here, I shall send you to the world of Yama and then attend to other matters! I shall kill you with the very sword your precious sister held in her hand. Will that not bring you joy?”
Shouting thus, Kandhamaaran raised the sword and rushed at Vandiyathevan.

chapters.title: The Fire Rages!
paragraphs: All this while, Sambuvaraiyar had been sitting motionless. Now, he sprang up and seized Kandanmaran’s hand.
“You fool! What deed were you about to commit?” he cried.
“Father! What is wrong in killing this treacherous friend?” asked Kandanmaran.

“What is wrong, you ask? By doing so, you, I, and our ancient Sambuvaraiyar clan will be utterly destroyed. If you kill him, will not the blame fall upon us for murdering both the prince and him together? Do you not understand even this?” demanded his father.
“Who has the power to accuse us thus? And even if someone dares to lay such a charge, will he live long enough to see another day?” retorted Kandanmaran.

“Alas! Rash child! Is this the time and place to display your courage and valor? It is because I listened to your counsel from the very beginning that all this calamity has befallen our house! It was you who brought the great Pazhuvettaraiyar and the other petty kings into this house. It was you who secretly brought Prince Madurantaka here. And through your precious friend, all of this has become known to everyone. Then, it was you who brought Aditya Karikalan here from Kanchi! Oh! I never imagined it would end like this! Malayaman—the ancient enemy of our clan—is now approaching with a great army. What shall I tell him?... And Pazhuvettaraiyar too has left for his town at this very moment!” Sambuvaraiyar cried, striking his forehead in despair.

Tears brimmed in Kandanmaran’s eyes. “Father! Do not torment yourself needlessly. For the disaster that has come to pass because of me, I alone shall bear the punishment. I await your command—whatever you order, I shall do!” he said.

“First, take this girl and leave her in the women’s quarters! If she utters a word, gag her mouth, bind her hands and feet, and leave her there! If not, lock her up in the secret chamber!” ordered Sambuvaraiyar.
Manimekalai, seeing the fierce wrath that had overtaken her beloved father, trembled in fear. Now she understood that there was no immediate danger to Vandiyathevan.

“Father! Forgive me, I will act according to your command. Kandhamaaran need not touch me. I myself will go at once to the women’s quarters where the mothers are!” Saying this, she walked away quickly from there.
Kandhamaaran followed her.
As soon as they left, Sambuvaraiyar turned to the men who had come with him and ordered, “Tie him to that cot, binding his legs tightly!”
The men approached Vandiyathevan. He remained calm. Even as they tied him to the cot, binding his legs, he offered no resistance. Once they had finished, he spoke:

“Sir! Think for a moment! I am a close friend, privy to the secrets of Karikalan. What benefit would I gain by killing him? In truth, the murderers escaped through the underground passage. Try to pursue and capture them. I have seen them. If you untie me, I will come with you and help catch them! I will not attempt to escape!”
“Ah! If what you say is true, what were you doing when Karikalan was murdered? Were you just watching the spectacle?” asked Sambuvaraiyar.

“Sir, when the Lady of Pazhuvoor and Karikalan were talking, suddenly the assassins entered. When I tried to stop them, a fearsome-looking Kalamukan seized me by the throat and strangled me. I lost consciousness. When I regained my senses, I saw Aditya Karikalan lying dead!” said Vandiyathevan.
At that moment, a loud commotion arose beyond the wall of the palace. It sounded like the roar of thousands of angry voices.

Sambuvaraiyar listened intently. Turning to Vandiyathevan, he said, “Very well! Even if what you say is true, stay here for a while! Be a companion to your dear friend, the prince! I will go and see what that uproar is about and return. Then I will learn your side of the story in full!” With these words, Sambuvaraiyar departed. His men followed him. As they left, by Sambuvaraiyar’s order, they locked the door of the room and fastened it from the outside.

Once again, darkness enveloped that chamber. In Vandiyathevan’s heart, an unspeakable anguish took hold! He reflected on all that had transpired since the day, some months ago, when he first arrived at this Kadambur Sambuvaraiyar palace. He recalled the comet he had seen in the sky at that time, and the talk among the people about it. Because the tailed star had appeared in the heavens, everyone believed that Sundara Chozhar’s final days were drawing near. Since Sundara Chozhar had been ailing for a long time, it was only natural for the people to expect such an end. Thus, they also began to discuss who would ascend the throne after him. Here in this very palace, the minor kings had gathered and spoken of these matters. But what everyone expected was one thing; what actually happened was quite another.

The young and valiant Aditya Karikalan had perished. His lifeless body now lay in this very chamber. Sundara Chozhar, though stricken by illness, still lived. But would he live for much longer? Would he survive even after hearing the news of his beloved son’s untimely death? Alas! How eagerly the father had longed to see his son! Was it not for his father’s sake that Karikalan had built the golden palace at Kanchi? Yet, before he could welcome and serve his father in that golden palace, the prince had departed this world. Who knows what further consequences will unfold from this? The entire Chola Empire is about to be submerged in a flood of sorrow. And is that all? Who can say what kinds of internal strife will arise? Surely, great conflict will break out among the minor kings. The commotion he had heard outside a short while ago must have been the noise made by Malayaman’s soldiers! Why had they shouted so? Were they about to attack this Kadambur palace? For what reason? Perhaps the news of Karikalan’s death had already reached them. Ah! How will Sambuvaraiyar manage this? He will try to shift the blame for Karikalan’s murder onto me and escape. But will Malayaman believe him? Even if he does, since this happened within Sambuvaraiyar’s palace, will he let him go unpunished? Malayaman must already know about the conspiracy that took place here earlier. Even if he does not, Azhwarkkadiyan must have gone and warned him. That is why he is approaching with his army. Vandiyathevan knew well how much affection Malayaman bore for his grandson. Who can say what he will do upon hearing this news? He might destroy the entire Sambuvaraiyar family and raze this palace to its very foundations.

Alas! Poor Kandamaaran! Such a good soul! How affectionately he behaved towards me! And now, has all that affection not turned into bitter hatred? It is all because of that enchantress of Pazhuvoor. Yet, if one looks closely, her own story is steeped in sorrow. How can I lay the blame solely at her feet? It is all the cruel play of fate…!

Fate! Fate! What can one say of Manimekalai’s fate? Why should she show me such boundless love? To save me, she stepped forward and confessed, “I killed him.” What love could surpass such devotion?—And what am I going to do in return for this? What recompense can I offer…?

Vandiyathevan smiled to himself. To think of repaying such love—what madness! What meaning is there in me pitying others? Is there anyone in a more wretched and perilous state than I am? They are about to accuse me of murdering Aditya Karikalan! I have no evidence to prove that I did not commit that heinous act. Nandini and Ravidasan’s band have vanished without a trace. No one has even tried to pursue and apprehend them. Even if they are caught, how can I prove that I was not involved in their conspiracy? It cannot be done!

What sort of punishment would they mete out to a traitor who murdered the crowned prince? They would not simply sentence him to death for murder! They would devise a punishment so dreadful, so torturous, that no one would ever dare even to dream of such a crime again. Let them impose whatever punishment they wish. But would not the Princess of Pazhayarai and Ponniyin Selvan themselves believe that I killed Karikalan? What torment could be worse than that? O God! Did I escape so many dangers in the past three or four months only to fall prey to this terrible disgrace…?

Thus, like waves crashing upon waves, countless thoughts rose and faded in Vandiyathevan’s heart. He had no sense of how much time had passed in this manner. Suddenly, in that darkened room, a faint wisp of smoke began to spread, breaking the thread of his thoughts. “What is that smoke? Where is it coming from?” he began to wonder. In a short while, a dim light began to spread. In that light, the body of Aditya Karikalan became visible. The doors remained tightly shut. Therefore, it could not be the light of a lamp. Then, what was this light? He began to scrutinize every corner. What could be the cause of the smoke and light coming from the adjacent hunting hall…?

Could it be that a fire has broken out? Perhaps those who had gone through the secret tunnel via the hunting pavilion had deliberately set the place ablaze before leaving? Or was it the lamp that he and Manimekalai had brought with them into the hunting pavilion that had caused this disaster…?

The smoke thickened steadily. The heat, too, grew more intense. In a short while, tongues of flame began to flicker through the cracks between the wooden plank walls that separated the hunting pavilion from this room. Soon enough, the god of fire himself stretched forth his radiant arms, probing and sweeping, and entered the very chamber!

For a few moments, Vandiyathevan watched the entry of Agni, the fire god, with unblinking fascination. At first, a strange exhilaration seized him. “The fire god is about to resolve all our troubles. Both Aditya Karikalan and I will have our cremation rites performed in the same place!” he thought. But that feeling lasted only a moment; he did not wish to leave this world under the accusation of being Karikalan’s murderer. Sambuvarayar and his son would say so outside, and some might even believe it. Whether others believed it or not, Ponniyin Selvan and Princess Kundavai must never believe such a thing. He had to prove, at least for their sake, that he had not committed that dreadful crime. Not only that—should the final rites of the valiant Karikalan be conducted in such a manner? Should his parents and kin not at least see his lifeless body? Yes, yes! Even if he could not save Karikalan’s life, he must at least save his body. He must find a way for the emperor’s son to receive the funeral honors due to him!

Until then, Vandiyathevan had not even attempted to free himself. He had not even noticed how he had been tied. Now he looked. First, both his hands had been bound together, and with the same rope, his entire body had been lashed to the leg of the cot. He could neither bend nor straighten. With all his strength, he tried to loosen the bonds at his wrists, tugging and even biting at them with his teeth; it was futile. He then tried to wriggle and loosen the ropes around his body; that too was in vain. But when he twisted his body thus, the cot shifted. Suddenly, an idea struck him. He began dragging the cot, inch by inch, toward the secret door of the hunting pavilion. It was by no means easy. He had to move it little by little, and each time he pulled, the ropes bit deeper into his flesh. The pain was excruciating. Yet, he bore it and pressed on. As he neared the doorway, tongues of flame shot through the gaps in the closed door. In those flames, he grasped the knot of rope binding his hands; the rope caught fire. At the same moment, fiery tongues licked his hands, inflicting an agony almost beyond endurance. Still, he gritted his teeth and endured. As soon as the fire burned through the bonds and his hands were freed, he hastily loosened the other ties that bound his body. Before he could finish, the curtains of the bed caught fire. Smoke filled the room. Vandiyathevan felt as if his entire body was aflame. His eyes were the first to burn; then, tears welled up and overflowed. His vision began to blur.

What is this? What is this? Am I, too, fated to die here with the prince, to be consumed by these flames? In one way, perhaps this is for the best! I could not save the prince; at least I shall have the fortune to die with him!… No, no! What kind of thought is this? I do not fear for my own death, but if the prince’s body is reduced to ashes here, will I not bear an everlasting disgrace? All who know me, whenever they think of me, will curse my name!
