Why should I die and bring such shame upon myself? Somehow, I must carry the prince’s body out. I will deliver him to his grandfather, the Malaiyaman. I will swear that I did not kill the prince, and that I will find and bring to justice those who did. Only after I have fulfilled this duty will it matter if I die. Until then, I must cling to life at any cost…

Now Vandiyathevan had freed himself from all his bonds and gained his liberty. But what is this? The bed is ablaze! The heat is unbearable! He could not even open his eyes; even if he did, the smoke swirling thickly made it impossible to see anything… Still, he must find the prince’s body. Sitting on the floor, Vandiyathevan stretched out his hands and frantically groped about, moving here and there in desperate haste. The time he spent searching was only a few minutes, but to him it felt like an eternity. At last, his hands touched the prince’s body. He lifted it, hoisted it onto his shoulder.

Only then did the thought occur to him—how was he to get out? It was impossible to go into the hunting hall! Ah! All the animals the Sambuvanar clan had collected there over the years must have perished and turned to ashes by now!… He reached the main door through which people usually exited that chamber. With one hand, he tried to force the door open; he kicked it with his foot; he hurled his body against it. “Fire! Fire! Open the door!” he shouted. Nothing worked. Nothing availed him. Tch! Tch!

What foolishness! I should have escaped through the passage of the veena treasury! Alas! But even that must remain unscathed by fire until I reach it, mustn’t it? Have I wasted all this time for nothing?

Now, that chamber was bright with light. But that brightness was useless, for smoke billowed thickly, making it impossible to open one’s eyes and see. Even straining to look, it was impossible to discern direction or path. Guessing at the location of the veena treasury, Vandiyathevan ran towards it.

Something struck his foot along the way. It made a metallic clang—“Tanar!” Ah! That must be the twisted-hilted dagger that was lying nearby, within reach, when it came to my mind. There is some mystery in that dagger. I should take it. If anyone tries to block my way, perhaps that dagger will prove useful…

Thinking thus, he bent down and picked up the dagger. At that moment, a burning ember leapt from the blazing cot and fell upon his shoulder. He brushed it off and hurried on, reaching the veena treasury. All this while, one of his hands had been gripping tightly the body of Karikalan, which he had slung over his shoulder. But it was impossible to climb the stairs to the treasury with the body still slung thus, especially since the upper door was also shut. So, he set Karikalan’s body down, climbed up, and opened the door above. Standing halfway up the treasury, he bent down to lift the body. Oh, gods! The fire had already reached the treasury! Had he delayed even a few more moments, this route too would have been lost to him…

He hoisted Karikalan’s body onto the loft of the treasury and climbed up himself, barely half alive. After being scorched so long by fire and smoke, now a cool breeze wafted over him. For a moment he wondered if he might rest there and recover his strength. No, no! Not even a moment’s delay! Who could say when that burning building would collapse? Once more, he lifted Karikalan’s body onto his shoulder and hurried along the upper loft. As before, he crossed the upper chambers. But previously, he had gone alone, and so it was possible to descend from the palace loft, cross the moonlit courtyard, climb the outer wall, and leap to freedom. Could he do that now? He was utterly exhausted, and now he had to carry the body of Aditya Karikalan as well!

At that moment, Vandiyathevan’s attention was drawn to the great tumultuous uproar rising from all four sides outside the palace. Ah! What is this? It seems as though Malayaman’s warriors have begun to attack the fortress! It sounds as if they are battering down the main entrance door! Many soldiers are climbing and leaping over the fortress walls!

Did Malayaman order the assault on Kadambur palace after hearing the news that the prince had been murdered? If so, what will those warriors do if they see me carrying Karikalan’s body? Why, they will think that I am the one who killed him! They will tear me to pieces! Therefore, I must act with the utmost caution. I must pass unseen by any eyes. I must find where Malayaman is and hand over to him the sacred body of his grandson. After that, let whatever happens, happen…

Then, Vandiyathevan moved with great care, slipping through the shadows cast by the upper halls and hiding in the darkness wherever it spread. At last, he reached the very spot where, on his first visit, he had stood and listened to the secret plotting of the petty kings below. Now he pondered how to descend. As he looked about, he noticed a ladder propped up against the wall. Not only that; beside the ladder, a human figure was visible. Who could it be? For whom was he waiting with the ladder? What would happen if he tried to descend by that way? Whatever may happen, so be it! He must use that ladder! Fortunately, he still had a knife in his hand! Whatever comes, he would face it.

At that moment, the commotion near the main entrance grew louder. Perhaps to find out what was happening, or for some other reason, the man standing by the ladder moved a little distance away. Thinking this was a stroke of luck, Vandiyathevan swiftly descended the ladder. His feet touched the ground just as the man returned.
“Swami! You took so long!” the man exclaimed, and Vandiyathevan realized it was Idumbankari. In that same instant, he guessed for whom Idumbankari had been waiting there.
When Idumbankari came closer, he asked in surprise, “Adei! Is it you? Whom are you carrying on your shoulder?”

“Yes, father! It is I! The disciple of the Kalamukha ascetic! He sent me ahead with the sacrifice for Ranabathira Kali. He is coming behind. He told me to keep you here with the ladder! Look here! He asked me to show you this dagger as a sign!” said Vandiyathevan, displaying the curved dagger.

Idumbankari, still somewhat doubtful, said, “All these days you never told me any of this! Well, let it be. But the ascetic is taking so long! How are we going to get out of here? The Thirukovalur soldiers have surrounded the palace and have even started to come inside!”

“What of that? The bigger the crowd, the easier it is for us to escape. Do I need to explain all this to the great ascetic? He will find a way somehow. You stay here and wait for him until he comes! Tell them I am in the garden!” said Vandiyathevan.
Without waiting for Idumbankari’s reply, he hurriedly walked away. Once he was out of Idumbankari’s sight, he made his way toward the main entrance tower of the palace.

chapters.title: The Sorrow of Malayaman
paragraphs: As soon as they reached the front hall, Sambuvaraiyar called Kandhamaaran aside and said, “My son! A danger that has never before befallen our clan has come upon us today. If we are to escape from it, you must do exactly as I say, without hesitation or objection.”

The death of Karikalan had shaken Kandhamaaran deeply. He now realized how grave a mistake it had been to wish for the death of Vandiyathevan. “Father! It is because of my own foolishness that this calamity has come upon our family. Please forgive me for that. Whatever command you give, I shall carry it out without fail,” he replied.

“You must, without anyone’s knowledge, leave this palace at once. You know, do you not, that there is a secret passage leading from beneath the bed in my chamber? That tunnel connects with the passage from the hunting pavilion and runs along the base of the palace wall…”
“Father! In this dire situation, do you ask me to escape through the secret way, leaving you here alone?” asked Kandhamaaran.

“My child! Have you already forgotten your promise? Yes, you must go. Now, you alone remain of the valiant line of Kollimalai’s lord, Valvil Oari. If need be, you must go to those hills and live in hiding. Only after it is certain that Madurantaka Devar is crowned and I send you word, should you return!” said Sambuvaraiyar.

“Forgive me, Father! I cannot bear to live in hiding. Must the noble house of Valvil Oari be stained by the infamy of having begotten such a coward? If you command me to give up my life this very instant, I shall do so. But I will never agree to live in concealment!” declared Kandhamaaran.

Sambuvaraiyar pondered for a moment and then said, “My son! I only spoke thus to test you. You do not wish to flee or hide. Good. Then I shall send you on a mission that may well threaten your life. Leave at once through the secret passage! But do not go to Kollimalai! Go straight to Thanjavur! Most likely, Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar will be there. If he is, tell him all that has happened here. If not, tell Chinna Pazhuvetaraiyar and Madurantaka Devar…”
“Sir! Let them tell what has happened here!”

“What sort of question is that? Speak of Karikalan’s death! Tell them, ‘The deed we intended has, by the force of fate, taken another turn; Karikalan is dead! This is the right time to crown Madurantakan!’ Let them know! Say, ‘The Malayaman and the Kodumbalur Velan will stand in the way of this. We must immediately gather all our strength and utterly destroy those two!’” said Sambuvaraiyar.
“If they ask how Karikalan died, what should I say?” asked Kandanmaran.

“What else is there to say? Say that Vandiyathevan of the Vanar clan killed him! There is another important matter. Remember this well! Vandiyathevan has gone to Eezha Nadu and returned. There, he met Arulmozhi Deva, and later, at Pazhayarai, he saw the Young Princess. News has come that Arulmozhi Deva, who was hiding in Nagapattinam, has now come out into the open. We must spread the rumor throughout Chola Nadu that Arulmozhi Deva, out of a desire for the throne, sent Vandiyathevan to kill his elder brother. We must also sow suspicion that the Young Princess of Pazhayarai is complicit in this. Tell all this to the Pazhuvettaraiyars and to Lord Madurantaka as well!...
“Father, what if what you say is actually true? Could not Vandiyathevan, the traitor to friendship, have come to this palace with such a dreadful intention?”

“It is possible, my son! But we must also find out the reason for the sudden and mysterious disappearance of the Younger Queen of Pazhuvoor, must we not? Vandiyathevan is accusing her, and the Pandya assassins who aided her, of being involved!”

“The one who commits the crime will always try to lay the blame on others. Now I understand everything. Father! The Young Princess of Pazhuvoor has never liked Kundavai Devi of Pazhayarai. After killing Karikalan, she must have arranged to abduct the Young Queen of Pazhuvoor at the same time. Chief Minister Aniruddha also seems to be complicit in this. That is why they sent this Vandiyathevan! Alas! Have we been ruined by failing to see through their conspiracy?”

“Kandamaaran! There is no use lamenting over what has already happened. We must look to what must be done next. You must set out at once! Before the news of Karikalan’s death reaches Sundara Chozhar, before anyone else in Thanjai hears of it, the Pazhuvettarayar brothers and Madurantakan must be informed. Therefore, you must hurry! You know, do you not, that there is a secret tunnel leading into the Thanjai fortress?”
“I know, I know!”
“In that case, depart at once!”
“I am leaving, Father! Only, I am a little worried about my sister, Manimekalai…”
“You need not trouble yourself with that! I will not let her babble to anyone else as she did to us. If she so much as tries to utter a word, I will kill her with my own hands…”
“Alas, that is exactly why I am anxious. It is your anger that frightens me…”

“No need! I know how to change her mind! Ah, fate is indeed strange! At first, we thought to wed her to Prince Madurandaka. Then, changing our minds, we planned to give her in marriage to Karikalan. Today, Karikalan lies a corpse. It is fortunate that Manimekalai’s heart did not incline toward him. We must now carry out our original plan…”
“But, Father! It seems now that Manimekalai’s heart has turned toward that outcaste Vandiyathevan.”
“That is nothing, my son! Manimekalai is not yet of an age to truly know her own mind. I will take care of her. You must not delay here even for a moment longer!”

At that moment, Kandamaaran heard a commotion rising very close outside the fortress walls. “Father! What is this? It seems as if Malayaman’s troops are drawing near. When you met Malayaman this evening, what did that old man say?” he asked.

“He brought good and auspicious news. On hearing that Manimekalai was to be wed to Aditya Karikalan, the old man was overjoyed. At that same wedding, he hoped to give away his own granddaughter—” “They say he has brought her here to arrange the marriage! Isn’t she beautiful? When I invited him to the palace, he replied that he would come at dawn tomorrow, at an auspicious hour. His soldiers already seem to be celebrating the wedding that is about to take place!” Saying this, Sambuvaraiyar tried to laugh, but the laughter came out only half-heartedly.

“Come! Come! I myself will take you through the underground passage and see you off. Not a moment must you delay on the way. Somewhere along the road, you must find a horse and ride swiftly!” he said.

Sambuvaraiyar took a lamp in his hand. The two of them entered the underground passage and walked quickly. After Kandanmaran had crossed the palace’s boundary wall, Sambuvaraiyar embraced him, blessed him, and turned back. “Do you need the lamp?” he asked, to which Kandanmaran replied, “No, Father! I know this way well enough. I could walk it even with my eyes closed!”

After Kandanmaran disappeared from sight in the tunnel, Sambuvaraiyar turned back. On his way, he entered the hunting pavilion. He listened carefully at the door of the next room to see if any sounds could be heard. There was nothing. He hesitated for a few moments, then, as if coming to a firm decision, he sighed deeply. He trimmed the lamp, set it down in its proper place, and hurried away.

Returning to the main hall, Sambuvaraiyar gathered all the women of the inner quarters together. They were already in a state of distress. Through the weeping and wailing of Manimekalai—whom Kandanmaran had brought and left in the women’s quarters—they had come to know, in some measure, about Karikalan’s death.

“Women! A great calamity has befallen our clan, the likes of which we have never seen. At any moment, you must be ready to leave this palace. You must have the courage to spend days, even months, in the forests and mountains. Take your clothes and ornaments and gather in the moonlit courtyard. Not a sound of weeping or lamentation must be heard—not even a whisper! Do you understand?” he warned them.

After this, Sambuvaraiyar went to the front entrance of the palace. He climbed to the top of the gateway tower, wishing to see what all the commotion outside was about. But he did not get the chance. For, as he approached the entrance, soldiers outside were already breaking down the gates and rushing in with a thunderous noise. The gatekeepers tried to stop them, but were overpowered and fell to the ground.
Apart from this, soldiers were climbing over the fortress walls and leaping inside.

A great fear and confusion arose in the heart of Sambuvaraiyar. Has the news of Karikalan’s murder somehow reached Malayaman as well? How could it have reached him so soon? — Well, let it be known if it must. Sooner or later, it is bound to come out anyway. But, for now, these men must somehow be delayed and kept here for a little while longer. If I can stall them for half a nazhikai, that will be enough. By then, the deed I have in mind will be accomplished…

Sambuvaraiyar strode with dignity to the center of the moonlit courtyard that lay between the fortress gate and the palace entrance. A sharp sword gleamed in his hand. Behind him, seven or eight warriors stood gripping long spears. Some among them held torches that cast flickering light.
Following the soldiers who had smashed and broken down the doors, Thirukovalur Malayaman and Parthibendran entered.
Parthibendran, seeing Sambuvaraiyar standing in the middle of the moonlit courtyard, pointed him out to Malayaman. Both of them advanced towards Sambuvaraiyar.

As they drew near, Malayaman called out, “Sambuvaraiyar! What is this I am hearing? Would you truly commit such a heinous deed? Oh! What is this? Why do you stand here with a sword in hand? What is your intention?”

“I should be the one asking you that question. What is your intention? Why have you broken down the doors and forced your way in? Just a short while ago, I came and invited you. You said you would come at an auspicious hour tomorrow…”

“Sambuvaraiyar! The auspicious hour has arrived now itself; that is why I have come. Where is Aditya Karikalan? Where is the heroic Pandiyan-slayer, the bravest of the brave? Where is the victorious hero of the Sevur battlefield? Where is my grandson?” demanded Malayaman.
“How should I know? The prince will be wherever he pleases. I have already told you that I have no dealings whatsoever with that unruly boy. Parthibendran knows this as well!”

“Hey, Sambuvaraiya! Do not try to deceive us with such empty excuses! Bring Aditya Karikalan here at once and hand him over to us! Otherwise, I will have your fortress, your palace, and everything you possess smashed to pieces and ground into dust!” thundered Thirukovalur Malayaman.

“Parthibendra, what is this old man raving about? Has he suddenly gone mad? Who am I to bring the prince here and hand him over to him? And who is he? Am I holding the prince captive? Or is he the one who has captured the prince and is taking him away?” retorted Sambuvaraiyar.

Parthibendran, in a calmer voice, said, “Sambuvaraiyar, do not be agitated! The elder has reason to be angry. Look at this palm-leaf letter. See for yourself!” So saying, he handed the letter to Sambuvaraiyar.
Sambuvaraiyar examined it closely in the light of a lamp burning behind him.
“Prince Aditya Karikalan’s life is in danger. Come at once with your troops and save him,” was written on the palm-leaf.
As he read it, Sambuvaraiyar’s face broke into a sweat. Earlier, when he saw Karikalan’s corpse, his body had trembled; now, he shook even more violently.
“What is this conspiracy? What is this plot? Who could have written such a message?” he stammered.
“What does it matter who wrote the message? Bring Aditya Karikalan here at once! Or take us to where he is! Otherwise, shall I order my soldiers to search for him?” demanded Malayaman.

“Very well, sir! I will take you to where Karikalan is. Parthibendra, you know the place. I just learned that he has gone to the inner quarters of the young queen of Pazhuvoor. Take him there yourself!” said Sambuvaraiyar.
Parthibendran said, “Yes, grandfather! Come, I will take you myself!”
Having said this, Parthibendran turned toward the direction of the inner quarters where the young queen of Pazhuvoor, Nandini, was staying.
“Oh no! What is this?” he cried out. For in the direction he looked, flames were leaping high, burning fiercely. Above the tongues of fire, thick black smoke was billowing.
Everyone turned to look in the direction he was gazing. “Fire! Fire!” The cry, thick with terror, rose from every throat.

Parthibendran, recovering from his momentary shock, said, “Sambuvaraiyar! At first, I did not believe this message. Now I do. Some conspiracy, some treachery has taken place. Sir! Order these traitors to be arrested at once! I will go and search for the prince and bring him here!”

Sambuvaraiyar, regaining his old commanding tone, replied, “Yes, Parthibendra! There has indeed been conspiracy and treachery. But the perpetrators are you. You broke down the doors of my palace and entered. You have ordered your soldiers to set fire to my house. If any harm has come to the prince, it must have been by your doing! Beware! The time will come when these wrongs will be repaid in kind!”

Parthibendran paid no heed to his words and ran off. At that same moment, the women of the Sambuvaraiyar household came out in a group from within the palace into the moonlit courtyard. Their faces betrayed the turmoil in their hearts, but not a single sob or wail escaped any of their lips.

Some among them turned their attention to the brightly lit spot behind the palace. They pointed out the flickering blaze to one another, embracing each other in fear; Manimekalai too saw it. At once, she cried out, “Oh no! Fire! Fire! He is there!” and began to run in that direction. Sambuvaraiyar stepped in her way and stopped her. He struck her sharply across the face.
Manimekalai, who had never been treated so in her life—Manimekalai, the beloved daughter, the apple of Sambuvaraiyar’s eye—stood frozen, staring at her father in disbelief.

In a voice tinged with regret, Sambuvaraiyar said, “Foolish girl! Did I not warn you before? Why do you provoke my anger?” Then, pointing, he added, “Look there! There is no need to scream and run about. See for yourself!”
From the direction Sambuvaraiyar indicated, Vandiyathevan was staggering forward. Draped across his shoulder, he bore the lifeless body of Aditya Karikalan.

Malaiman, who had been paying close attention to the debate between Sambuvaraiyar and his daughter, now turned his gaze toward Vandiyathevan. He watched, unblinking, as Vandiyathevan staggered forward, slowly, carrying someone slung across his shoulder. For some reason, the old man’s aged body trembled. A strange dread welled up in his heart. He wanted to ask the approaching youth something, but his tongue would not move. His throat closed up completely.
Vandiyathevan, still looking at Malaiman, came near him.

“Sir! Here is Prince Karikalan! I could not bring this heroic slayer of Veerapandiyan to you alive. I have at least brought his body, without letting it fall to the flames. Your grandson, struck down by fate and treachery, is now yours to claim!” So saying, Vandiyathevan gently lowered Prince Karikalan’s corpse to the ground and laid it down.
At once, he too collapsed to the floor with a thud and lost consciousness.

The old chieftain Malaiman sat down beside the prince’s body. For a while, he gazed intently at that valorous face. Suddenly, as if the mountain itself were shaking, his whole body trembled and swayed! From his throat, like the roar of a stormy sea, burst forth a cry of grief: “Aiyo!”
With his iron-like aged hands, he struck his head and chest again and again.
“My treasure! I came to see you in wedding finery! Instead, I see you in the garb of death!” he wailed, his lament echoing in all eight directions, making the very air shudder.

Then, that venerable elder began to recount, one by one, the events of Aditya Karikalan’s life from the day he was born, mourning as he spoke. He recalled the celebrations held on the day of his birth. He wept as he remembered how the boy, as a child, had played in his lap, in his arms, and on his shoulders. He spoke of how he had taught the prince to throw the spear, to wield the sword in battle. He sorrowed over each of the astonishing feats of valor the prince had performed on the battlefield of Sevur at the age of sixteen.

“Aiyo! Would it not have been better if you had died in those heroic battles against the Pandiyan and attained the warrior’s heaven? Instead, must you fall prey to the treachery plotted by this wretch Sambuvaraiyan and his fellow conspirators? Alas, was it not I who sent you here as his guest? I am old now. I thought you would need friends here, and so I—”

“If he had married, I believed he would be on your side, and so I sent him. I thought I was sending him to the palace of Sambuvaraiyan, but instead, I have sent him as a guest to the palace of Yama! Am I not the sinner? Am I not the one who killed you?” he cried, striking his head again and again.

Then, suddenly breaking free from his grief and consumed by wrath, he looked all around him. “Hey Sambuvaraiya! Tell the truth! How did the prince die? What treachery did you commit? Even if Devendran himself had come against him, he could not have defeated him face to face! How many men did you set upon him? Where did they hide, and how did they kill this hero among heroes? Speak the truth!” he thundered.

Sambuvaraiyan, too, replied angrily, “Old man! I am restraining myself only out of respect for your age. I know as much as you do about how the prince died! Didn’t that man bring the prince’s corpse here? If you ask him, perhaps he will tell you! What is the use of questioning me?”

“Ha! This happened while he was your guest in your palace. And you speak as though you know nothing! Who will believe this? Very well; when Sundara Chola Chakravarthi questions you, give him this same answer! Soldiers! Arrest this Sambuvaraiyan. Demolish his palace, his walls, everything—level them to the ground!” the old man commanded in a voice like thunder.
Just then, Parthibendran, who had returned, turned to Malayaman and said, “Sir! The task of destroying this palace is not ours. Agni Bhagavan has already taken up that work! Look there!”

Malayaman looked and saw that the fire, which had been seen a short while ago in one corner of the great palace, was now spreading rapidly. That mighty fire, growing grand and tall, leapt up and devoured the upper halls, the silken couches, the domed spires—reducing all to ashes, stretching out its thousand and ten thousand red tongues, rushing ever forward in search of more prey. He saw the warriors of Thirukovalur standing transfixed in awe at that terrible, fearsome sight.

“Very well! Very well! Agni Bhagavan has taken up our task. Good, Parthibendra! Let us depart at once. For three years, Sundara Chola Chakravarthi, ruler of the three worlds, has been sending word that he wishes to see his eldest son. My daughter Vanamadevi has sent recommendation after recommendation, pleading that the prince be brought to him. At the very least, let them see the lifeless body of the prince—”

“Let us see him one last time. Let us not consign the body of this bravest of warriors to the flames that have consumed the palace of that wretched Sambuvaraiyar. Let us take him to Thanjavur. Let us lay him before the Emperor himself. Let the mother and father who gave him life at least gaze upon his lifeless face and weep over him. Let the Emperor himself decree a fitting punishment for the vile murderers who slew the prince!” said Malayaman.

chapters.title: Once More to the Banks of the Kollidam
paragraphs: On the northern bank of the Kollidam, in the village of Thirunaraiyur, stood the monastery of the great Saivite elder, Nambiyandar Nambi. At the entrance of this monastery, a royal palanquin, its bearers, and palace guards stood waiting. Apart from them, the villagers had gathered a little distance away in a crowd. At the center of this gathering, it seemed as if a heated debate was taking place between two men, and the onlookers watched with eager attention.

If one were to part the crowd and peer within, it would become clear that the two men quarreling there were none other than familiar figures. One was Thirumalai, known as Azhwarkkadiyan Nambi, and the other, the valiant Saivite with whom he had argued in a boat at the very beginning of our story. This Saivite was the chief administrator of Nambiyandar Nambi’s monastery.

Learning that the great lady, Periya Piratti Sembiyan Madevi, who had come to see Nambiyandar, wished to speak with him in private, the aforementioned Saivite elder had stepped outside. The moment he saw Azhwarkkadiyan, anger welled up in him quite naturally. The memory of having once been defeated in debate by this eminent Vaishnavite only fanned the flames of his irritation.
“Hey! You masquerading Vaishnavite, deceiving the town with your holy name! Why have you come here? Are you looking for a place where you can get some pongal or tamarind rice to eat?” he demanded.

“I have already eaten all the pongal and tamarind rice I need,” replied Azhwarkkadiyan. “I came here because I heard that all of you in this Saivite monastery have grown so bloated from eating only sacred ash that you can barely move. Poor fellows! What can you do? It was only because your Lord Siva could not find any food to eat that he consumed poison. If, at that moment, our Narayana Moorthi’s sister Parvati had not grabbed his throat, what would have become of your Siva then!” retorted Azhwarkkadiyan.

“O valiant Vaishnavite! Enough of your tales! Don’t fly too high! Even your Lord, after soaring to the highest heavens, could not find the crown of our Lord Siva and had to return in defeat, did he not?” “What is this story, sir? When our Mahavishnu took the Vamana avatar and measured the earth with one stride and the heavens with another, your Shiva’s head must surely have been beneath that very foot!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
“Hasn’t your Mahavishnu’s mischief been evident ever since he incarnated ten times on this earth? And what kinds of births! Was he not born as a fish, as a tortoise?” retorted the Veera Saivar.
“That is all you know! Why did the Lord take birth as a fish? Was it not to retrieve the four Vedas that had sunk into the ocean? That is why our Azhwar sang:

‘Neither the wealth of the eternal damsels who surround me, Nor the heavenly riches, nor the earthly kingdom do I desire; In the honeyed, flower-laden groves of sacred Thiruvengadam, Let me be born as a fish—such is the boon I seek!’”
“Ah! Your Azhwars are only twelve in number! Our Nayanmars are sixty-three! Keep that in mind!”
“Oh! Is that another kind of pride? The Pandavas were only five; will you boast like Duryodhana and his hundred brothers?”
“Impertinent one! Do you compare our Nayanmars to Duryodhana’s clan? Among your Azhwars, there are Peyazhwar, Boothathazhwar, and so on!”
“Aren’t the attendants of your Shiva called the Bhoota Ganas? Have you forgotten that?”

While the ardent Vaishnavite and the staunch Saivite thus waged their war of words, supporters on both sides cheered and encouraged them with shouts and laughter. At that moment, from within the monastery, the sacred consort of Sivagnana Kandaraadittar, Sembiyan Madevi, and Nambiyandar Nambi, who had come to see her off, appeared at the entrance. At once, silence descended upon the gathering.
Mazhavariyar’s daughter took leave of Nambiyandar and, approaching Azhwarkkadiyan, said, “Thirumalai! Have you started your quarrel even here?”

“No, Devi! We did not wage a battle of arms; it was only a battle of words. This valiant Saiva Chikamani was the one who first began the fray! Our war of words brought great excitement to all those gathered here. That is why they remained outside the monastery and did not enter,” said Thirumalai.

“Appane! Even in jest, one should not debate the superiority or inferiority of the gods. Such arguments will only confuse the minds of ordinary people! My father-in-law, Paranthaka Devar, that great king, roofed the Chidambaram temple with gold. In the same way, he renovated the Anantheeswarar temple at Veera Narayanapuram and granted it lands. We must all follow the path he showed us!” said Sembiyan Madevi.
Afterwards, the Devi ascended her palanquin, and it proceeded westward. Guards walked before and behind. Azhwarkkadiyan walked close to Sembiyan Madevi’s palanquin.
After the palanquin had gone a short distance, Azhwarkkadiyan looked at the great lady and asked, “Devi! What happened to the matter for which Nambi Andar had come?”

“My mind is now clear and untroubled, Thirumalai! Nambi Andar said that if there is no other way to prevent Madurantakan from ascending the throne, then it is right to reveal the truth to the world. I have accepted this in my heart and have resolved upon it,” replied Sembiyan Madevi.

“The Prime Minister too expected that Nambi Andar would say so. Still, your journey here has been most worthwhile. Mother! There is now even greater urgency for you to decide on this matter. A terrible message has come from Kadambur. The people here do not yet know of it. If they did, not a single person would remain here. All would have gone to witness the prince’s final procession!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
“Thirumalai! What are you saying? What terrible words! Which prince? What final procession?” the Devi asked.

“Forgive me, Mother! Never before has such a dreadful event occurred in the Chola clan. In the palace at Kadambur, Aditya Karikalan has passed away. They say it was an unnatural death. By whose hand, how it happened—no one knows for certain. Many speak in many ways. After Aditya Karikalan’s untimely death, the entire palace at Kadambur was set ablaze and burned down. They are bringing the prince’s body in procession to Thanjavur. Thirukovalur Malayaman, Kadambur—” “They say that Sambhuvarayar and his family are being captured and brought here. In the procession, more than a hundred thousand people are coming before and behind! Before they reach the banks of the Kollidam, we must cross the river!”

“Thirumalai! What you say is truly a terrifying piece of news! The calamity that the people feared when the comet appeared in the sky has come to pass! Alas! Must the fate of that Asokaya Sooran end like this? Oh! What suffering Sundara Chozhar will endure when he hears of this! I am deeply worried that nothing untoward should happen to the ailing Emperor because of this news. Only Lord Shiva, the ocean of compassion, can save the Chola dynasty now,” said the daughter of Mazhavarayar.
“Mother! Let the danger that has befallen the Chola clan be one thing. I fear that this dreadful event may shatter the entire Chola empire.”
“Why do you have such a thought, Thirumalai?”

“Among the leaders of Chola Nadu—the minor kings—a great conflict may erupt. While blood flows within Chola Nadu due to internal strife, foreign enemies may gain courage and begin their invasions! Shall I speak of the consequences of that, Mother?”
“Thirumalai! Why do you say that quarrels will arise among the minor kings and leaders?”

“For a reason you already know, Mother! Some will insist that their prince, Madurantakan, should ascend the throne next. Others will demand that only Arulmozhi Varman should take the crown. Already, the armies of the Kodumbalur Velar have surrounded and laid siege to the Tanjore fort. With the prince’s body, Malayaman is heading towards Tanjore. The minor kings allied with the Pazhuvettarayars are gathering their forces. Therefore, in and around Tanjore, the warriors of Chola Nadu are about to slaughter each other and flood the land with rivers of blood. In the five rivers—Kaveri and the rest—instead of floods of water, floods of blood are about to flow! Even the wise Prime Minister Aniruddha is deeply troubled. He fears that the great Chola empire, established and ruled by Vijayalaya, Aditya, Paranthaka, and your own lord Kandaradithar, may perish in our time. Even Aniruddha himself can see no way to prevent this!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.

“Thirumalai! By the grace of God, I will prevent such a great calamity from befalling this vast empire. I know the way to do so. I have come to Nambiyandar to strengthen my resolve as to whether I should follow that path. You say that only if there is a contest for the throne between Madurantakan and Arulmozhi Varman will civil strife erupt, is that not so?”

“Yes, my lady! How else can such strife be averted? Until now, at least the fact that Aditya Karikalan was slightly older in age could be cited! Now, he too is gone. Compared to your noble son, Arulmozhi Varman is younger. But the Malaiyaman, the Velalars, and the people of Chola Nadu are all going to insist that only Arulmozhi Varman should be crowned. The Pazhuvettaraiyars will never accept that…”

“Thirumalai! Whether anyone accepts it or not, Madurantakan will not ascend the throne. I will see to that. I will fulfill the wish of my great husband. If it is decided that Madurantakan will not be crowned, then there will be no civil strife, will there?”
“Yes, mother! Only if you save the Chola empire at this time will it be spared utter destruction; there is no other way!” said Azhwarkadiyan.
“I am powerless to do anything. Lord Maheshwara, the consort of the Mother Goddess, must grant me such strength,” said the Periya Piratti.
For a while, both walked on in silence. The ferry dock on the banks of the Kollidam could be seen a little way ahead.

“Thirumalai! Just now you told me a dreadful piece of news. You said Aditya Karikalan has lost his life. It is indeed a terrible thing that that hero among heroes, who was destined to rule the three worlds, has died. You said the prince met with an unnatural death? How? Did he take his own life? Or do people say that someone murdered him?” asked the Periya Piratti.

“Devi! Many rumors are spreading about it. Since it happened in the house of Sambuvarayar, suspicion has fallen upon him, and Malaiyaman is bringing him and all his family members as prisoners. Only Sambuvarayar’s son, Kandhamaran, has managed to escape…”

“I cannot truly believe that Sambuvarayar is responsible for this. No matter how great the enmity, who would have the heart to kill the emperor’s son, who had come as a guest to their house? Sambuvarayar— “That could not have been done. What does he say about this? What does he say about how Prince Karikalan died?”
“Devi! Do you remember, once before, a young warrior from the Vanar clan came to Pazhaiyarai? Didn’t Princess Kundavai herself send him to Eezha Nadu with a letter?”
“Yes, yes; I remember. What about him?”
“They say that it was that youth who was near the lifeless body of the prince. Therefore, Sambuvaraiyar claims that he must have been the one who killed him…”
“Thirumalai! That could never have happened. I remember seeing that boy…”
“I think the same, Mother! But the circumstances and the evidence are all against Vandiyathevan!”
“Oh no! Poor thing! The younger princess had placed so much trust in that youth. If she hears this news, she will be terribly shaken!”
“Mother! I thought I should ask you about this. Once you reach Kudanthai, it would be best to meet the younger princess and bring her to Thanjai…”
“That is my intention. The younger princess is waiting there for me…”
“It is better that you tell her yourself before the news reaches her through others and causes distress…”
“In that case, are you not coming with me now, Thirumalai?”
“Devi! If you permit, I wish to take leave of you on the southern bank of the Kollidam…”
“Where are you going?”
“There is some mystery in the death of Prince Karikalan. I wish to go and uncover it.”
“How will you find it out?”
“Devi! I have already spoken to you once before about the conspirators from the Pandya land. Among those traitors, I saw one on the southern bank of the Kollidam when I was coming,” said Thirumalai.
“Why didn’t you follow him at once?” she asked.

“It was only after I reached the northern bank of the Kollidam that I heard the news of Karikalan’s death. Princess! Grant me leave! I know the place where the conspirators usually gather and converse…”
“Very well, go! What shall I tell the Young Princess Kundavai? My heart is filled with great anxiety when I think of her.”
“Tell her not to worry if accusations are made against Vandiyathevan. Assure her that I will, without fail, discover and bring back the true culprit!”
“May the grace of God ensure your mission meets with success!” said Sembiyan Madevi, that noble lady devoted to Lord Shiva.
By then, they had reached the banks of the Kollidam. Large boats were waiting for Periya Piratti Sembiyan Madevi and her retinue to board and cross.
Azhwarkadiyan quickly seized another small boat, and, urging the boatman to row fast, set off ahead of them.

chapters.title: In the Mountain Cave
paragraphs: As soon as he reached the southern bank of the Kollidam, Azhwarkkadiyan turned westward. He saw that, due to the breach in the Kollidam, the land everywhere had become a vast floodplain. Yet, it seemed that the water level in the Kollidam was receding; even in the areas where the floodwaters had spread, the water was draining away swiftly. At last, he reached Thiruppurambayam. He was astonished to see that, despite the heavy flooding, that town alone had remained unaffected. He thought to himself, “Perhaps this is why the legend arose that, when the world was submerged in the primeval deluge, only Thiruppurambayam remained above water.” With this thought, he approached the forest near the temple.

Though many trees had been uprooted and fallen due to the storm, the forest was still dense enough to offer him the concealment he needed. As he peered through the thicket, he saw three men and a woman standing and conversing at the entrance of the temple. Looking closely, he realized that all of them were people he had seen before. These three men had been among those who had first gathered in this very forest to plot their conspiracy. One was Soman Sambavan, another was Kramavithan, and the third was Idumbankari. The woman was the wife of Murugaiyan, the boatman. Among them, Idumbankari seemed to be telling the others something. The news appeared to fill them with excitement.
“All right! In that case, let us also set out at once for the foot of the Pachai Hills. It will take us two days to get there,” said Soman Sambavan, and these words reached Azhwarkkadiyan’s ears.

Thinking he should leave before they did, Azhwarkkadiyan turned to go. Suddenly, he was startled to see a small dagger pointed at his chest. The hand holding it, he realized with relief, was Poonguzhali’s. Their surprise gave way to smiles as they recognized each other.
After the conspirators had left, Azhwarkkadiyan asked, “Poonguzhali! How did you come here from Thanjavur? For what purpose?”
“I have come to avenge a wrong,” Poonguzhali replied.

“What wrong? For what reason?” “One among these men is the wretch who murdered my aunt and fled. I pursued that criminal without letting him escape, and caught up to him here. But three others had already arrived before him. Among them, when I saw my elder brother’s wife, I was struck dumb with shock! At that very moment, you came and intervened! Now, what can I do? If you are willing to help me, let us not lose sight of them. I will follow them, slay the one who killed my aunt, and return!” she said.
“Alas! Poor soul! Your aunt—do you mean that mute queen, Mandakini? Why would one of these men kill her?” asked Azhwarkkadiyan.
“She was not killed by design. The spear that was meant for the Emperor, she took upon herself!” she replied.
“Oh! Is that so? The mute queen gave her life to save the Emperor? How did all this happen? Tell me in detail, let me hear it!”
“Is this the time to go into details? They will escape if we delay!”

“Poonguzhali! I know where they are going. I have guessed for what purpose and whom they intend to meet. It is best not to hinder them on the way. Let us go to the place they are headed. Once I have learned what I wish to know there, you may exact your revenge,” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
“In that case, let us set out! I will tell you everything that happened in Thanjavur as we go!” said Poonguzhali.

The two of them crossed the Kollidam by boat and reached the opposite shore. They journeyed northwest. For three days and nights they traveled, until at last they reached the foothills of the green mountain. At the base of the mountain, the forest grew thick and wild, making it difficult to discover where those they sought might be hiding. After so much arduous travel, their spirits flagged, fearing all their efforts might be in vain.

Suddenly, the hoot of an owl rang out. In answer, another call echoed in the same manner. Azhwarkkadiyan’s face brightened. He signaled to Poonguzhali, wordlessly urging her to follow him. Where the owl calls had sounded, a clearing appeared. There, seven or eight people were gathered. Some were tending a fire, cooking their meal. Others were deep in conversation. It was clear that those who had been there before and those newly arrived were exchanging some astonishing news with one another.

Ravidasan was already among those present there. At that moment, he was pointing out a mountain cave at some distance to the newcomers and explaining something to them. Azhwarkkadiyan noticed this. In a low voice, he said, “Poonguzhali! The people I have been searching for must be inside that cave. I will quietly slip in and see. If any of these people approach the cave, give me a signal!”
“I cannot hoot like an owl. I will call out like a cuckoo,” replied Poonguzhali.

The mountain cave had several large openings to allow air and light to enter. Thus, daylight streamed inside. In that light, Azhwarkkadiyan beheld a remarkable sight. Periya Pazhuvettarayar was dressed in a tiger-skin garment, like a fearsome ascetic of the Kalamukha sect. Beside him lay a garland made of skulls. From the pallor of his face, one could guess that he must have lost a great deal of blood. He was lying on the ground, and it seemed that he had just regained consciousness and was trying to sit up. He looked as though he had just awakened from a terrifying dream world. His eyes opened wide and glittered. Nandini was by his side. Her ornaments had been removed, and her hair was loose and disheveled. Yet her enchanting beauty shone forth now with manifold brilliance, surpassing even before. With a voice overflowing with love, care, pity, and regret, she said, “Sir! Please drink this gruel!” and extended a clay vessel toward him.
Pazhuvettarayar turned to look at her. For a moment, a smile blossomed on his face, a sign of boundless joy.

“Nandini! My queen! Was it you who spoke just now? Is this your voice? Where are we now? Was it you who brought me back from the very threshold of death? Did you do for me today what Savitri once did for Satyavan? When my senses returned, I felt your soft hand upon my chest—was that real? After three years of refusing even to touch me, have you finally relented? Where is it? Give it to me! Give me the gruel! If you feed me with your own hand, it will be nectar to me!” he said.

Even as he spoke, he took the clay bowl from Nandini’s hand, but suddenly began to stare at her with a wild, terrifying gaze. In a voice utterly transformed and dreadful, he cried, “You wretch! Demoness! Was it you? To touch me, you dare— “Have you found your courage now? Did you try to stab my chest with a knife? Was it then that I awoke? Is it truly gruel that you have brought in this vessel? Or is it poison meant to kill me? Even if what you offer with your own hand is nectar from the gods, would it not be poison to me?” Saying this, he flung the earthen bowl away. It struck the cave wall with a loud crash and shattered into countless pieces, scattering across the ground.

chapters.title: “Grant Me Leave!”
paragraphs: The furious rage of Periya Pazhuvettarayar seemed to evoke no surprise whatsoever in Nandini. For three years now, she had made that great warrior, the venerable elder, dance like a puppet at the end of a string held in her hand. But today, for the first time, that string had snapped. The puppet, which had been dancing as she pleased, had now gained life and self-awareness. Nandini appeared to have anticipated this moment. From now on, she had no further use for that puppet.
Without the slightest trace of agitation, Nandini rose and bowed before Periya Pazhuvettarayar. In a voice trembling with emotion, she spoke:

“Swami, you have often told me that my words are sweeter to you than honey or divine nectar. But today, my words will taste more bitter than poison, just like the gruel I served you. Yet, I beg you, show me mercy and grant me permission to say a few words before I take my final leave from you. With the same lips that once called me ‘precious jewel’ and ‘beloved,’ today you have called me a sinner and a demoness. Yes, I am a sinner; I am a demoness! For three years, I have deceived and misled you. When I stood abandoned in the wilderness, you brought me into your palace. You made emperors and princes show me respect. You even dared to oppose your own dear younger brother, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar, for my sake. The slanderous words and mocking gossip of the townsfolk and the people of the land could not diminish the affection you had for me. Despite all this trust and the unparalleled honors you bestowed upon me, I have deceived you. That is the truth.

I have lived in your palace only to fulfill my own purpose. Without your knowledge, I have done many things. I have maintained secret dealings with conspirators. I have beguiled young men like Kandhamaaran and Parthibendran and used them for my own ends. But, Ayya, in one thing alone have I never deceived you. From the day the world knew I became your wife, I have accepted you as my husband in truth. By no fault of mine has any stain come upon your ancient and illustrious clan, which for generations has produced mighty heroes. And as long as I live, such a stain shall never befall you…”

“Nandini! What words are these that you utter? What greater disgrace could befall my lineage? Alas! By my own hand… with this very hand of mine… Oh, wretched woman! You had a sword with you, didn’t you? Where is it? Take it and sever my hand yourself! That is the only help you can do for me! No, no! Do not! This hand still has one more task to perform. A most important task remains. Do not, believing my words to be true, do anything rash!”

“Swami! I will not do any such thing. For so long, I could not use that sword even upon the one for whom I had sworn vengeance. In the moment when I feared the opportunity might slip away and my mind was clouded with confusion, you came to my aid…”

“Wretched woman! Did I come to help you? What words are these you speak? Outcaste! Demoness in the form of a woman! Had I known it would come to this, I would never have gone there! O God! When I was drowning and struggling in the floods of the Kollidam, could not that sinner Yama have taken me away then and there?”

“Swami! You did not come to help me. Nor did I ask you to aid me in my cause. You are born of a lineage that has, for generations, sworn loyalty to the Chola kings, to serve the Chola dynasty even at the cost of life itself. But I—I came with the sole purpose of avenging myself upon the Chola clan. That is why I did not reveal my true intentions to you. At times, I did wonder if I could accomplish my aim through you. Think on it! You, who today call me ‘demoness’ and ‘fiend in a woman’s form’, how many times have you lost both sight and sense, bewitched by the beauty of this madwoman’s face, as if you had drunk nectar turned to wine? In those moments, I thought, what if I were to fulfill my vengeance through you? But I did not wish to stain your lineage by making you commit such a treacherous deed. That is why I strove so hard to send you from Kadambur to Thanjavur. And you did go. Yet fate itself sought you out and brought you back at the appointed hour! You did not come of your own will to help me. But fate brought you to my aid at the most opportune moment! Yes, sir! It was fate that sowed suspicion in your heart about my virtue. If your only aim had been to prevent me from fulfilling my vengeance, you would have come openly. But it was suspicion that I had betrayed you, that I had committed some moral wrong, which made you don a disguise and come in secret. At least in that matter, your doubts must have been dispelled! If not, let them be dispelled now. Husband and wife are called partners in life by the elders—” They have said so. It is only because I have been a true and faithful wife to you that fate has brought you to me at the right moment to aid me…”

“Nandini! Enough! Stop! Your words are torturing me. Rather than this, kill me outright! I do not even have the strength in my hands to resist! My body has no vigor left. If you do not have the courage to kill me with a sword, then truly, mix poison in my gruel and give it to me!”

“My lord! Forgive me—no… you cannot forgive me. In this birth, it is impossible for you to forgive me! Let me say one thing, listen! If both of us are born again on this earth, in that next birth, we will have no memory of this life. You will not remember that I deceived you and lived in your palace, nor that I used your treasury’s wealth to accomplish my own revenge, nor the final outcome that fate brought about in Kadambur palace—none of this will remain in your memory. Nor in mine. For the treachery I have done to you in this life, I wish to atone in the next. In my next birth, I will marry you. I will be a true companion to you. This is the only prayer I shall offer to all the gods, as long as there is breath in this body.”
Hearing these words, Periya Pazhuvettarayar’s body and soul trembled with emotion.

“Nandini! Go! Leave this place at once! If you stay here and speak even a moment longer, my mind will lose all sense. I will be forced to abandon my duty! The disasters you have already brought upon me are enough! Do not shatter my mind further and drive me to madness! Go, leave now—leave at once!” he cried.

“Swami! Forgive me! If I had listened to the advice of those who came with me, by now we would have crossed the Pachai Hills and the Kolli Hills and reached the land of Kongu. But my heart would not allow me to leave without seeing you and bidding farewell. As soon as we left the Kadambur fort, you fell unconscious. They told me to leave you there and come away. I refused that as well. I made them carry you and bring you along. We have walked day and night without rest for three days. Even after coming here, they told me to leave you and go. But I insisted that I would not leave until you regained consciousness and I could speak to you. That wish has been fulfilled. You tried to kill me. There was reason for it. But fate decreed otherwise. The one whom you wished to take the life of, I have revived you. Just now, with my own hand, I gave— You called the gruel poison and threw it away. But during the three days when you lay unconscious, it was with these very hands that I poured water into your mouth and kept you alive. For three years, you placed me as the empress of your palace and bestowed upon me unparalleled honor. I can never repay that debt in this lifetime. Yet, for these three days, I was given the chance to serve you with my own hands. That memory will bring me satisfaction as long as there is breath in my body. I am leaving now, my lord! Grant me leave!”
“Nandini! Why do you ask my leave? Go without asking! The longer you linger here, the more my mind falters!”

“Yes; if you remain, you might even feel the urge to kill me again. Swami! If I must die by your hand, I would consider it a rare blessing for your servant. But was it not to kill me that you came here in disguise?”

“Why did I come in disguise? You gave some reason. You said I came to test your virtue and discover the truth. That is not so. I feared that if I appeared before you as Pazhuvetaraiyar and you spoke even two words to me, my heart would soften. That is why I donned this disguise and came secretly. I came with the intent to kill you, to hurl the dagger at you while you stood stunned, unable to utter a word. I frightened Idumbankari, the servant at Kadambur palace, and snatched the dagger from his hand. Not only that, Nandini! I came in the guise of a Kalamukan, thinking that if the rumor spread that the old Pazhuvetaraiyar, out of jealousy, killed his young wife, the world would laugh at me. But as you said just now, I thought one thing, fate thought another. Never again can I attempt such a deed. So go; just answer me this before you leave! If I had not come and interrupted at that moment, what would have happened? How did you intend to fulfill your purpose?”

“Yes, yes; I waited to tell you that as well. Your anger has clouded my mind. Swami! When you left for Thanjavur, I promised that ‘by my hand, your family’s honor would never be stained.’ I strove mightily to keep that promise. I devised many schemes, hoping to achieve my aim through one of Manimekalai, Kandanmaran, or Vandiyathevan. Chiefly, I placed my trust in Manimekalai. Karikalan, in his fury, would rush in to kill Vandiyathevan, who was hiding there for another reason; at that moment, Manimekalai would kill him. To spare Manimekalai from blame, Vandiyathevan would confess, ‘I am the one who killed him!’ ...will take it. Thus, I would have avenged myself upon Kundavai of Pazhaiyarai as well. I had planned all this. But there was no need for any of it. The prince ended his own life with his own hand…”
“No, Nandini! No! Karikalan did not end his own life. Are you trying to deceive even me?”
“Swami! If you had not thrown away Idumbankari’s dagger at that moment, in the very next instant, Karikalan would have ended himself with Veerapandiyan’s sword…”

“Yes, yes; if I had been delayed by even a moment, I would not have committed this great act of treachery. Instead, I would have suspected you. Nandini! What has happened is according to fate; it cannot be changed now. In some way, fate has done me a kindness as well. If we are born again in another life, you said you would wish to take me as your life’s companion, didn’t you? I have never heard sweeter words in my life. Not even from you. When my soul departs, it is those words I will remember as I die. Yes, Nandini! In this birth, you and I cannot live together as husband and wife. So, you must go. Before you leave, if there is any gruel left from what I spilled in anger, give it to me before you go! If there is no gruel, at least give me a little water with your own hand before you leave!” said Pazhuvettarayar.
“So be it, Ayya! For this mercy you have shown me, I will be grateful as long as I live!” said Nandini, and went to fetch the gruel from the hearth.

At that moment, Azhwarkadiyan thought to slip away from the cave. He had learned all that he wished to know. There was no use in staying there any longer. There was also danger. He thought it best to go outside and consider what needed to be done next, and so he quietly left.

chapters.title: Danger for Azhvarkadiyan!
paragraphs: Azhwarkkadiyan and Poonguzhali sat beneath a tree at the foot of the hill.
“Girl! The task for which I came is done. Shall we depart?” asked Azhwarkkadiyan.
“Vaishnavite! If your purpose is fulfilled, you may go. But the task for which I came is not yet complete!” replied Poonguzhali.
“For what purpose have you come?”
“I came seeking the murderer who killed my aunt.”
“Haven’t you found him? Isn’t he among that band of conspirators over there?”
“He is.”
“Then what?”
“Did I come merely to see him and earn some merit by his sight? I came to repay murder with murder, to avenge blood with blood.”
“Poonguzhali! Who are we to punish those who have committed crimes? There is God for that!”
“Is there a God? Even if there is, does He punish the treacherous deeds of men? I have my doubts.”
“Let us leave God aside. In this world, the responsibility of punishing wrongdoers belongs to kings. It is the duty of the officials appointed by the rulers.”
“And if the kings and their officials do not carry out their duties properly?”
“How can we decide that they have not done so?”

“Vaishnavite! Among those criminals, one threw a spear from the upper storey and killed my aunt, who was the very embodiment of love. She could not speak, she never harbored ill-will towards anyone, she was a poor, unfortunate, simple woman all her life—yet he killed her. The Emperor, his queens, and even Chinna Pazhuvettarayar, the commander of the Thanjai fort, were all watching. Yet they let him escape…”
“Poonguzhali! Did they not make any attempt to capture Soman Sambavan?”

“All his life, the Emperor who had rejected my aunt now held her upon his lap and wept. All the others stood around, struck dumb with astonishment. When I declared, ‘I will follow the murderer,’ even Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar rose and came with me. But in the underground passage, he was forced to turn back.”
“What happened?”

“As we made our way through the tunnel, he and I, a cry rang out in the darkness. Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar leapt toward the source of the voice and seized the person lurking there. ‘Here! The murderer is caught!’ came a shout. ‘No, no! I did not commit the murder!’ came another voice. The moment Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar recognized to whom that voice belonged, he was thunderstruck. ‘Alas! Why have you come here?’ he asked. ‘I came to see if the treasure is safe,’ replied the voice from the shadows. ‘Oh, heavens! If anyone sees you here, what will they think? Will they not believe you tried to kill the Emperor?’ cried Kaalandhaka Kandar. ‘Is the Emperor dead?’ asked the beloved son-in-law of Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar, Madurantaka Devar, with anxious urgency. ‘Foolish child! Come with me! Come, before anyone sees you!’ said Kaalandhaka Kandar, seizing his son-in-law by the hand and leading him away. Afterwards, I alone continued to follow the murderer. Now, after coming all this way with such effort, do you ask me to turn back without fulfilling my purpose?” said Poonguzhali.

“Girl! You should have been born a son. Had you been, you would have ruled a vast empire as its supreme authority. But let that be. Now listen, and tell me your judgment! If a man intends to kill one person, but by accident kills another, can he be accused of murder?”
“I do not understand your question. Whoever kills is guilty of murder, is he not?”

“How can you say that? You must have heard the Ramayana. Dasaratha, thinking it was an elephant drinking water, shot his arrow. It struck a rishi’s son. Was Dasaratha punished for the murder of the rishi’s son? No! Now, take this Soman Sambavan whom you have been following. He hurled the spear intending to kill the Emperor. But the Emperor is alive. Your aunt intervened, received the blow, and gave up her life. Was that not suicide? Then how can Soman Sambavan be charged with murder?”
“Vaishnavite! Your sense of justice is truly astonishing…”

“It is not only my sense of justice that is lacking. Even the justice of the Lord of all worlds, the very incarnation of Narayana Himself, seems strange indeed. In this world, those who commit sins live in prosperity, while the good—those pure of soul—struggle and die in misery. Surely, there must be some divine reason behind all this?”
“You and your Narayana can go your own way. I will see that the justice I know is fulfilled before I return.”

“Poonguzhali! I am not speaking of this for your sake alone. Look there, in that mountain cave, two people are present. One among them is the man who killed Aditya Karikalan. But he did not kill the prince with intent. The knife he threw, meant for another, struck the prince by chance and killed him. Can you call him a murderer?”
“Vaishnavite! Do not try to confuse my mind. Who are those inside the mountain cave?”

“The rightful heir of the Chola Empire, the supreme authority in the Tanjore palace, the valiant among the valiant who has fought in twenty-four battles and bears sixty-four scars upon his noble body. The god decreed by fate, the great leader of the assembly of minor kings. The husband of Nandini Devi—the great Periya Pazhuvettarayar sits enthroned in that mountain cave…!”

Thus spoke Azhwarkadiyan, his voice booming as if proclaiming a royal edict. At that very moment, Ravidasan, Revathasan, Parameswaran, Soman Sambavan, and others came running in with a clatter. Poonguzhali swiftly stepped aside. Ravidasan held a short staff in his hand, which he raised as he shouted, “Hey, you masquerading Vaishnavite! Spy of Aniruddha! At last, you have fallen into our hands? Of the three attempts we made, we succeeded in only one. We failed in the other two. We no longer care about those failures. After searching for you for three years, have we not finally caught you? This time, you will not escape us!”

Immediately, Azhwarkadiyan, in a voice louder than before, replied, “O fools! Who is the pursuer, and who is the fugitive? All are but the children of that very Narayana! Does even a single atom move in this world without Him? Ravidasan! Listen, and let those with you listen as well. Abandon all these petty deities and surrender yourselves to the great Maha Vishnu! The Lord will forgive your sins and protect you! Do not waste your lives toiling and perishing for the sake of mortals. Worship Narayana and attain the true reward of human birth; seek your place in the supreme abode! Come, join me, all of you, let us sing together and see:—
“Narayana is the Supreme God— Let us all sing His praise!”

So saying, he began to sing. Ravidasan burst into laughter and said, “Why, O Vaishnavite! Is only Narayana the true God? Is not Parameshwaran, the Great Shiva Himself, also God? If one praises Parameshwaran, will one not attain the Supreme State?”

With great enthusiasm, Azhwarkkadiyan replied, “Parameshwaran is the God who destroys! Narayana alone is the God who protects! Have you forgotten how, when the elephant king Gajaraja was caught in the jaws of the crocodile and struggled in agony, it was our Narayana Murthy who came to his rescue?”

“Ah, but my friend! Did not Vishnu Bhagavan, who saved Gajaraja, kill the crocodile? In the same way, did not your Maha Vishnu destroy Ravana, Kumbhakarna, Hiranyaksha, Hiranyakashipu, Shishupala, and Dantavakra?” asked Ravidasan.

“Those who fell by the hand of our Perumal attained none other than Sri Vaikunta itself. After slaying Hiranya, Ravana, and Shishupala, the Lord granted them the status of Vaikunta. But your Parameshwaran, when he destroyed the Tripura demons with the fire of his third eye, did he grant them liberation?”
“Enough, enough! Stop your stories! Let your Narayana come and save you now!” So saying, Ravidasan raised the short staff in his hand.

At that moment, Poonguzhali, wishing to help Azhwarkkadiyan, drew the dagger she had tucked into her waist. But just then, she saw a woman’s form come running out of the mountain cave, her hair loose and wild. For a moment, she stood astonished, thinking it was her aunt Mandakini. Then, she realized, “No, this is the Queen of Pazhuvoor, Nandini.”
By then, Nandini had reached Azhwarkkadiyan’s side. She caught Ravidasan’s upraised staff with her hands and stopped him.
“Do not! Do not harm my brother! Ravidasan! If it is true that I am your queen, lower your staff!” she commanded.
Azhwarkkadiyan said, “Sister, my thanks to you; but these men could have done me no harm. The Narayana Murthy whom I worship would have protected me!”

Ravidasan laughed and said, “How could he have saved him? Just as Narayana emerged from the pillar to save Prahlada in days of yore, do you think the Lord would split open this tree and appear before us now?”

“Sorcerer! Do you not believe my words?” retorted Azhwarkadiyan. “Very well! Look there! Do you see the Ayyanar temple a little distance away? In front of that temple, aren’t there three clay horses? By the grace of Sriman Narayana, those earthen horses will come to life! Warriors bearing spears will mount them, ride forth, capture you all, and rescue me!”

As Azhwarkadiyan spoke thus, he pointed with his hand in the direction of the temple. All eyes turned to look where he indicated. They wavered, unable to trust their own sight! For it seemed to them that the clay horses had truly come to life and were galloping towards them. Upon each horse sat a warrior, spear in hand!

chapters.title: Nandini’s Disappearance
paragraphs: Of all those astonished by the approaching horses, the first to regain his composure was Ravidasan.

“Devi! This false Vaishnavan has revealed his true colors. How many times have I warned you, ‘He is a spy, do not trust him!’ He has brought his men here to capture us. But he cannot catch us—not even his deity Narayana could do so. Come, let us leave! Before the horses arrive, we can climb up the hill!” said the sorcerer.
Azhwarkkadiyan said, “Nandini! Do not go with these criminals! Enough of the disasters that have befallen you because you joined them!”

Nandini turned to Azhwarkkadiyan and said, “Thirumalai! I have been asking you for a long time—do you remember? I begged you to take me to my mother. If you promise to take me to her now, I will come with you; otherwise, I will go with them.”
“Nandini! That is no longer possible for me…” Thirumalai began, but Ravidasan interrupted, “What can he do? I will take you! Come with me!”

“Yes, yes; he will take you to your mother—in the land of Yama! Just as he killed your mother, he will kill you and send you to the world of the dead! Nandini! You must not remain in the company of these murderers any longer. One among them is your mother’s killer! Look at the sorcerer’s face! It is written there—‘murderer’!” cried Azhwarkkadiyan.
With rage boiling on his face, Ravidasan shouted, “Lies! Lies!”
The signs of frenzy, which had just subsided, now flickered again in Nandini’s eyes.

“Thirumalai! Is this true? Has my mother truly died? Will I never see her again?” she asked. “If you have any doubts, here—ask this girl and find out. One among them, Soman Sambavan, is the very one who hurled the spear and killed your mother; she saw it with her own eyes. She followed the man who killed her aunt! Poonguzhali! Speak!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
“Yes! I saw it with my own eyes! I came here only to avenge the man who killed my aunt!” said Poonguzhali.

Nandini laughed with the frenzy of a madwoman. “You came to avenge? Revenge! Revenge! Is it not enough that I alone have taken revenge?” she cried, and then, turning to Ravidasan, said, “Traitor! Outcaste! Is this what you have done?”

“Queen! You are mistaken! I have committed no treachery. Soman Sambavan hurled the spear at the Emperor. That mute madwoman fell across his path and died! It was her fate! Now, what do you say? Are you coming with us or not? Look, the horses are drawing near!” he said.

It seemed as if Nandini did not even hear his words. Suddenly, she sat down on the ground. She covered her face with both hands, pressing her eyes shut. Her whole body shook as she sobbed uncontrollably. Amidst her weeping, a wild, crazed laughter mingled.
Ravidasan turned to his men and said, “Run! Run and climb the mountain! There is no use trusting the Queen any longer.” They all fled.
Ravidasan, turning to the Vaishnavite, said, “Vaishnavan! Here, take your reward for your mischief!” With that, he struck the Vaishnavite on the head with his staff and took to his heels.
Azhwarkkadiyan, saying, “Namo Narayana!” rubbed his head once.
All those who fled entered the mountain cave. After a short while, they stood near the summit of the hill, at the spot where the Kanari river tumbled down as a waterfall.
At the same time, the horses reached the foot of the hill. Because there was no proper path and huge rocks were scattered everywhere, it had taken the horses this long to arrive.
Azhwarkkadiyan saw that among those who came on horseback, the ones in front were Chinna Pazhuvettarayar and Kandhamaaran. Behind them, he saw Sendhan Amudhan, tied with ropes to one of the horses.

“Come! Come! You have arrived at just the right moment,” he said. Chinna Pazhuvetarayar and Kandhamaaran leapt down from their horses. Their attention first fell upon Nandini, who sat below, weeping uncontrollably.
Kandhamaaran went to Nandini’s side. He tried to say something, but no words would come from his mouth.
Chinna Pazhuvetarayar turned to Alwarkadiyan and asked, “Vaishnavan! How did you come here? For what purpose have you come?”
“Commander! I came searching for the same person you were seeking. Periya Pazhuvetarayar is inside that cave!” he replied.
“Is it true? Is he alive?” Chinna Pazhuvetarayar asked eagerly.

“Yes, he is still alive. Even Yama, the god of death, would fear to approach your elder brother! So, the attempt those murderers made did not succeed in his case!” With these words, he pointed to Ravidasan and his companions, who stood atop the Thirumalai hill.
“Who are they? Why do you call them murderers?”

“They are the sorcerer Ravidasan and his band, members of Veerapandiyan’s secret rescue force. They are the ones who tried to kill the Emperor. They are also the sinners who murdered Prince Aditya Karikalan!” said Thirumalai.
Kandhamaaran interrupted, “Lies, lies! The one who killed the Prince was Vandiyathevan! Are you trying to hide the crime your friend committed?”
“Fool! Be silent!” Chinna Pazhuvetarayar rebuked him harshly.
Then, turning to the Vaishnavan, he asked, “Did they also try to kill the steward? How did he escape?”
“It was only with the help of the young queen of Pazhuvur, who sits here weeping, that he escaped!”
“Why is the young queen weeping?”
“She heard that her mother has died. That is why she weeps! Can we not inquire about all this later?”
"Yes, yes! I must see Periya Pazhuvetarayar first; you go and tell him that I have arrived!"
Even at that moment, Chinna Pazhuvetarayar’s awe and reverence for his elder brother had not diminished in the least. Therefore, he hesitated to go and see his brother suddenly.
"Sir! Your elder brother will not go anywhere now. I will go and inform him of your arrival. But—are you not going to do anything to catch those murderers?"
Chinna Pazhuvetarayar pressed his forehead with his hand and said, "Yes, yes! Once before, my wits failed me like this! I let the one who tried to kill the Emperor escape!"
"He has not escaped yet; look, he is still up there on that hill. Quickly order your men!"

Immediately, Commander Kalanthakakandar turned to the warriors who had come with him and issued his commands. They dismounted from their horses and hurried towards the place near the waterfall on the Kanari river hill. As soon as they reached there, large round boulders began to roll down from above. The warriors scrambled this way and that to avoid being struck by the falling stones. A couple of them were hit and fell down.
Chinna Pazhuvetarayar asked, "Do you know how they climbed up there?"
"They entered through the cave. It seems there is a secret passage inside. Come, let us go and see!" said Azhwarkkadiyan, leading the way.
Kalanthakakandar and Kandhamaaran followed behind.

From within the cave, a tall and imposing figure staggered and stumbled out. Standing at the mouth of the cave, he peered intently at those approaching. It took his younger brother a moment to recognize him.
When Chinna Pazhuvetarayar realized that it was Periya Pazhuvetarayar, standing there pale and corpse-like, his whole body covered in wounds, he cried out, "Anna!" and rushed forward to embrace him.
Tears welled up in the elder brother’s eyes. In a trembling, faint voice, he muttered, "Brother! You warned me many times! I did not heed you, and now I have come to ruin!"
At that moment, Azhwarkkadiyan and Kandhamaaran prepared to enter the cave.
Periya Pazhuvettarayar stopped him and asked, “Where are you going?”
“Murderers have entered this cave…”
“Which murderers?”
“The sorcerer Ravidasan and his accomplices.”
“They are not murderers,” said Periya Pazhuvettarayar.
“See? Didn’t I say that Vandiyathevan is the real murderer?” Kandhamaran interjected.
Periya Pazhuvettarayar looked at him intently and said, “How did this foolish youth end up here!”
“Kandhamaran is the one who brought news from Kadambur.”
“What news?”
“He brought the news that Prince Karikalan has died. Sambhuvarayar has sent word through him that we must immediately gather our forces and make arrangements for Madurantakan to ascend the throne!”
“Ah! Is that so!” Periya Pazhuvettarayar said, without the slightest enthusiasm. Then he asked, “How is the situation in Thanjavur?”
“Anna! I must explain in detail. You are very weak. Shall we sit down and talk?” asked Chinna Pazhuvettarayar.
The commander sat right at the entrance of the cave.
“Ayya! If you give me a little space, I can go inside the cave and see if there is a way to climb up the hill,” said the Vaishnavan.
“For what purpose?” asked Periya Pazhuvettarayar.
“Ravidasan and his group entered this cave and climbed up the hill from inside,” said Thirumalai.

Periya Pazhuvettarayar shook his head. “There is no use going into the cave, my boy! From above, they rolled down a boulder and blocked the cave’s passage. The rock was about to fall on me. It is only by divine grace that my life was spared! Go! Both of you go! See if there is any other way to climb up the hill!” he said.
When Azhwarkkadiyan and Kandhamaaran had gone beyond, the gaze of Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar fell upon Sendhan Amudhan and Poonguzhali.
“Who are they? From where have they come?” he asked.

“That woman is Poonguzhali, daughter of the Kodikkarai Tyaga Vidangar. She brought with her the man who killed her aunt. Sendhan Amudhan came searching for her. It was through Sendhan Amudhan’s guidance that we came here and found you!” replied Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar.
“Tell me in detail all that happened in Thanjavur!” said Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar.

Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar began to narrate accordingly. He spoke of how, during the gathering of the sorcerer, one among them had hidden in the treasury chamber, waiting for the right moment to strike and kill the Emperor, and how Mandakini Devi had intervened and sacrificed her life to save the Emperor. Then he continued:

“Anna! Meanwhile, the Velan of Kodumbalur suddenly began to lay siege to the Thanjavur fort with a large army. Since you were not present, I could not decide whether to begin battle with the Velan or not. I could not even consult the Emperor. The Prime Minister Aniruddha is inside the fort. He said that we could deal with it after your return, and until then, it would suffice to defend the fort. Fortunately, at this time, Prince Arulmozhi Varman and Vanathi, daughter of the Kodumbalur Velan, also arrived within the fort. The Prince came disguised as a mahout. Vanathi claimed to have brought urgent news from the Young Princess of Pazhayarai. Thinking it would be to our advantage that the Velan’s daughter was inside the fort, I allowed the elephant on which they arrived to enter. At the entrance to the Emperor’s palace, it was discovered that the mahout was none other than Prince Arulmozhi Varman. I was somewhat taken aback. Anna! There seems to be some wondrous power about the young prince. The moment I saw his noble face, my hands and feet trembled. My heart melted. Unknowingly, my hands came together in reverence. I was compelled to welcome him with folded hands. Is it any wonder that the people of Chola Nadu dance in joy, forgetting themselves, at the very mention of Prince Arulmozhi Varman?...”

“That’s enough, enough! That much is already known! It is now clear that the tale of Arulmozhi Varman drowning in the sea and dying was mere fabrication, as I suspected. Tell me what happened after that! Why did the Prince enter the fort disguised as a mahout?” asked Pazhuvettaraiyar.

“If it had been known that he was the prince, the Velan of Kodumbalur would have stopped him and not allowed him to enter the fort. The Velan’s soldiers would have made a great commotion. Thinking thus, he came in disguise. Up to that point, we must praise the prince’s wisdom. It was while the prince was speaking with the emperor that the assassin hurled his spear from above. By divine fate, it struck that mute madwoman and she died. Had it fallen upon the emperor and killed him, an everlasting stain would have befallen our lineage…”
Periya Pazhuvettarayar muttered under his breath, “Has no stain befallen us now? Endless stains have indeed come upon us!”
