“Anna! What did you say?” asked Kaalandhakandar.
“Nothing; tell us what happened next!” said the officer.

“Then a great marvel occurred. The emperor, who had long been unable to walk, suddenly found strength in his legs. He ran, lifted the mute woman, placed her on his lap, and began to weep. For a while, we all stood astonished at the sight. This boatwoman, Poonguzhali, was the one who shouted, ‘I am going to catch the assassin!’ and ran off. She must be a remarkable woman. It is thanks to her that we have the fortune to see you in this state today…”

Tears brimmed in Periya Pazhuvettarayar’s eyes. “Brother! In the ancient epics and legends, I have heard of brothers devoted to each other. But none could be as devoted as you are. Let it be; tell us what happened next!” he said.

“Following Poonguzhali, I too went through the secret tunnel in the treasury chamber. There, in the darkness, I caught hold of someone. I thought he must be the assassin. But when I heard his voice, I realized it was Madurantaka Devan.”
“Why did he come along the passage to the treasury chamber?”
“That I do not know either; he did not give a proper answer when I asked. I was afraid that someone might begin to suspect him as the assassin.”
“Perhaps that is the truth—who knows?”

“No, elder brother, no! That Sathu boy could not have gone that far. Besides, I myself saw him with my own eyes as he threw aside his work and ran away. Before Madurantakan could return from the treasury chamber, he did not agree easily. I had to slowly persuade him, bring him into the palace, ensure he was guarded, and only then did I think of returning to the treasury. But by then, other great events had already taken place. Rumors spread outside that ‘the Emperor has passed away’ and that someone had murdered him. Immediately, the Kodumbalur Velar ordered his soldiers to attack the fort. The Velir army joined forces with the Kaikkolar troops and began to break down the gates and scale the walls to enter. Our own warriors were not prepared at that moment. I was not at the gate to command them. So the Velir and Kaikkolar troops broke through the gates, climbed over the walls, and started pouring in. By the time I heard this news and hurried to the gate, ten thousand soldiers had already entered the fort. Our own forces numbered only about two thousand. They fought fiercely against the invaders. I went and ordered them to stop the battle. I gathered all our men in one place. Deciding that there was no point in remaining inside the fort any longer, I led our men out. The Velir and Kaikkolar armies tried to stop us. We cut down and scattered all who stood in our way. I sent word to Boothi Vikrama Kesari: ‘If even the slightest harm befalls anyone of the Pazhuvur family or Madurantaka Devar, I will utterly destroy the Kodumbalur line, root and branch.’ Then, thinking you would be at Kadambur, I hurried here to join you. On the banks of the Kudamurutti river, Kandhamaaran came galloping on horseback. When he saw the Pazhuvur palmyra banner, he halted. The news he brought left me even more astonished. He said that you had left Kadambur for Thanjavur several days ago, and that Periya Sambuvaraiyar had sent word to you. When I learned that you had not yet reached Thanjavur, he too was bewildered. I then asked what message Sambuvaraiyar had sent. He said that Prince Karikalan had died, that Vandiyathevan had killed him, and that this was the right time to place Madurantaka Devar on the throne, and that all our allies should be summoned by palm-leaf letters to gather their armies at once. This seemed right to me. I believed that you too would be engaged in gathering our strength and would arrive soon. I stationed our Pazhuvur troops on the Tiruppurambiyam mound, between the rivers Manni and Kollidam. Immediately—”

I sent swift horsemen, instructing them to write letters, to Mazhapadi Thennavan, Mazhavarayar, Kundrathur Kizhar, Mummudi Pallavarayar, Thanathongi Kalingarayar, Vanangamudi Munaiyatharaiyar, Devasenadhipathi Poovarayar, Anjaadha Singa Mutharaiyar, and the Irattai Kudai Rajaniyar. I have written to all of them, commanding them to gather their forces and come to Thirumuraipadi as quickly as possible.

Brother! You need not worry in the least! We shall utterly destroy the Kodumbalur Velan and the Thirukovalur Malayaman, so that they may never again raise their heads. We will enthrone Madhuranthaka Thevar upon the lion throne!” Thus, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar thundered with martial enthusiasm.
But his words seemed to bring no encouragement to Periya Pazhuvettarayar. Suddenly, his attention turned elsewhere.
“Brother! Who is that? Who is sitting there, covering her face with her hands and weeping?” he asked.

“Brother! Do you not know? That is the Young Queen! Poor soul! It seems she has suffered greatly in her efforts to save you. Forgive me, brother, for any blame I may have spoken against her! I have learned that it was the sorcerer Ravidasan and his accomplices who captured you, and that it was the Young Queen who followed and rescued you. Is that not the truth?” asked Kaalandhakandar.

Periya Pazhuvettarayar replied, “Yes, yes! It was the Young Queen who saved my life. Had Nandini not served me, you would not have seen me alive. The truth would have remained forever hidden from the world!”
Kaalandhakandar said, “Alas! Even I did not know of the Young Queen’s incomparable virtue—how then would the world know?”
But Periya Pazhuvettarayar, paying no heed to this, asked, “Has Nandini not yet left this place? I thought she would have gone with those who ascended the cave steps?”
Chinna Pazhuvettarayar replied, “How could the Young Queen leave, abandoning you, brother!”
“Let that be. But how did you discover that we were here and come to this place?” the elder asked.

“We were staying near the Thiruppurambiyam barracks. Kandhamaaran was on guard duty along the banks of the Kollidam. There, he saw Sendhan Amudhan trying to board a boat and caught him. You may recall that, once before, I had kept Sendhan Amudhan imprisoned for a while because he had helped Vandiyathevan escape. Kandhamaaran already harbored much anger towards him. Now, suspecting that he was up to some spy work, he brought him in. When we questioned him, we learned about you. It seems his maternal uncle’s daughter, Poonguzhali, had heard that some murderer was on the loose and had set out alone to pursue him. On hearing this, he too set out in search of her. But Poonguzhali had told him not to come with her and sent him back. Nevertheless, he secretly followed her without her knowledge.

At that time, near the Thiruppurambiyam barracks, he overheard some conspirators talking among themselves while he hid nearby. Only then did he learn that Ravidasan’s group had captured you and taken you to the Pachai Malai region. On learning that Poonguzhali and the Vaishnavite Azhwarkadiyan were heading to Pachai Malai, he too tried to follow them without their knowledge. On hearing all this, Kandhamaaran and I gathered fifty soldiers and set out at once. Sendhan Amudhan insisted on coming with us. We thought it best to bring him, so we tied him to a horse and brought him along. It turned out to be a good thing. We found you! What worry is there now, brother? Set out at once. I will arrange for men to carry you so that you will not suffer any hardship. By now, a great army has gathered at Thiruppurambiyam. We can retake the Thanjavur fort within an hour!” said Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar.
“Yes, we must go to Thanjavur at once!” said Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar, rising to his feet. He slowly walked towards the spot where Nandini Devi was seated.

All this while, Nandini had been sitting on a rock, sobbing uncontrollably. At the thunderous roar of Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar’s voice, she suddenly stood up. With wild, fevered eyes, she looked all around her. Standing very close to her, Azhwarkadiyan spoke in a gentle voice, “Nandini! At least now, give your consent. Say just one word that you will come with me! Let us leave this land and go north. We will travel to Brindavan, North Madurai, Ayodhya, Kashi, Haridwar, Rishikesh, and other sacred places. Let us spend our lives in happiness, chanting the holy name of Sriman Narayana and singing the hymns of the Azhwars. I am ready to leave my government service and come with you,” he said.

Tears brimmed in Nandini’s eyes as she looked at him and said, “Thirumalai! Even after all the betrayals I have committed against you, your affection for me has not changed. The Narayana you worship will surely bless you!”
At that very moment, Poonguzhali turned to Sendhan Amudhan and said, “Look there! See the young queen of Pazhuvoor! Doesn’t she look just like my aunt?”
“Yes, if she spreads her hair out, she would look exactly like your aunt!” replied Sendhan Amudhan.
“From now on, she is my aunt; the love I have held for my aunt all these days, I will now give to the young queen of Pazhuvoor!” said Poonguzhali.
“Include me as well, Poonguzhali!” said Amudhan.

By then, Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar had come close to where Nandini was standing. Seeing him, Nandini fell to the ground before him and bowed low. She touched his feet and pressed them to her eyes. Rising from the earth, Nandini looked at Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar once, then suddenly turned away. Her gaze fell upon the horses that Chinna Pazhuvetaraiyar and the others had brought and tethered a short distance away. She ran swiftly toward where the horses stood. Leaping onto the horse that stood foremost, she seized the bridle in her hands and gave it a sharp shake. The horse sprang forward and began to gallop.

Until then, those standing by, not knowing Nandini’s intentions, had remained motionless. Now, they hastened to pursue her. Chinna Pazhuvetaraiyar, Azhwarkkadiyan, Sendhan Amudhan, and Poonguzhali all took a step forward.
“Stop!” thundered Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar. Everyone halted again, paralyzed by his command. They looked to him for guidance.

Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar stood gazing at the figure of Nandini as she rode away on the horse. The steed, flying like the wind, soon disappeared around a bend at the foot of the hill. The horse vanished from their sight.
Yes; the young queen of Pazhuvoor, Nandini Devi, too, had vanished. We shall see her no more in this tale.
Perhaps, after many years, in another place, under different circumstances, we may encounter her again—who can say?

The night was deepening. Darkness, thick as a velvet curtain, enveloped the palace and its gardens. The moon, hidden behind drifting clouds, cast only a pale, uncertain glow upon the earth. In the silent corridors of the Pazhayarai palace, shadows moved like restless spirits. The lamps had been dimmed, and the guards, weary from the day’s watch, leaned upon their spears, their eyes heavy with sleep.

In the midst of this profound stillness, a solitary figure glided silently through the inner courtyard. It was Nandini. Her face, usually radiant with pride and beauty, was now clouded with a strange, inscrutable expression. Her eyes, which could once command the hearts of kings and warriors, now darted about anxiously, as though searching for something or someone in the darkness.

She paused beneath the ancient banyan tree, its vast branches spreading like the arms of fate. For a moment, she stood motionless, listening intently. The only sound was the soft rustle of leaves and the distant call of a night bird. Nandini’s heart beat rapidly. She pressed her hand to her breast, as if to still its wild throbbing.

Suddenly, a faint footstep echoed from the far end of the courtyard. Nandini shrank back into the shadows, her breath held. A figure approached—a woman, cloaked and hooded, moving with equal stealth. As she drew near, Nandini recognized her: it was her loyal attendant, who had served her faithfully through every twist and turn of fortune.
“My lady,” the attendant whispered, “all is ready. The palanquin waits beyond the southern gate. The guards have been bribed; no one will hinder your passage.”
Nandini nodded, her face set with grim resolve. “You have done well,” she murmured. “Let us go. There is nothing left for me here.”

Together, they slipped through the shadows, moving swiftly and silently. Nandini did not look back—not at the palace where she had reigned as queen, nor at the gardens where so many secrets had been whispered beneath the moonlight. Her heart was heavy with memories—of love and betrayal, of dreams shattered and vengeance pursued.

As they reached the southern gate, the palanquin awaited, its bearers standing ready. Nandini stepped inside, drawing the curtains tightly shut. The attendant gave a final glance around, then signaled the bearers. With careful steps, they lifted the palanquin and carried it away into the night, vanishing into the darkness beyond the palace walls.

Thus, Nandini disappeared—like a shadow swallowed by the night. No one in the palace saw her go; no one knew where she had gone, or what fate awaited her beyond the confines of Pazhayarai. Only the silent moon, peering through the clouds, bore witness to her departure.
And so, the tale of Nandini, the enigmatic queen, passed into legend—her secrets buried deep within the shadows of the Chola dynasty.

chapters.title: “You Are Not My Son!”
paragraphs: When the final procession of Aditya Karikalan made its way along the banks of the Kaveri River towards Thanjavur, hundreds of thousands of people from the Chola land joined in that cortege. The custom of honoring warriors was deeply rooted in Tamil Nadu in those days. For a time, the Chola dynasty had faded, but had we not seen it rise again since the days of Vijayalaya Chola? For a hundred years, each scion born into that lineage had surpassed the other in martial glory. Vijayalaya’s son, Aditya Varma, destroyed the fame of the Pallava dynasty and seized the land of Thondai. His son, Parantaka Chakravarti, brought the entire southern country, including Madurai and Eelam, under his rule. The four sons of Parantaka Chakravarti each outshone the other in valor. One of them laid down his life in the Pandya war. The eldest, Rajaditya, waged war at Takkolam against the mighty army of the twin-mandala Kannara Devan, which surged like the ocean, and after breaking that vast force, was treacherously slain on the battlefield, earning the epithet “the god who slept upon the elephant.” Kandaraditya, though a devotee of Shiva and a man of spiritual wealth, was no less in valor. Later, during the reign of Sundara Chola, son of Arinjaya, who died at Arattur, the glory of the Chola Empire, which had waned after the battle of Takkolam, rose once more to its zenith.

Among those born in this illustrious line of warriors, none could equal or surpass Aditya Karikalan—so declared the unanimous voice of the people everywhere. At the age of twelve, the heroic and daring feats he performed on the battlefield of Sevur eclipsed even the fame of Abhimanyu, son of Arjuna. Why had such a peerless hero not returned to Thanjavur for several years, remaining instead in Kanchi? Many rumors swirled about the reason. One rumor held that the petty kings, plotting to crown Madurantakan, were scheming to keep Aditya Karikalan away from Thanjavur. Another rumor claimed that, just as the ancient Karikala Valavan had marched north and planted the tiger flag atop the Himalayas, Aditya Karikalan, bearing the same name, had sworn to do likewise, and, unwilling to return to Thanjavur until that vow was fulfilled, was being thwarted by the likes of the Pazhuvettaraiyars. Therefore, when the sudden news spread that Aditya Karikalan had died, and that he had been treacherously murdered in the palace of the Sambuvarayars, it is needless to say how the hearts of the people of Chola Nadu were stirred. Is it any wonder, then, that lakhs of people gathered to pay their last respects to that heroic prince? As the funeral procession approached Thanjavur, the crowd had swelled into a veritable sea of humanity. The citizens of Thanjavur and the soldiers of the southern army encamped around the fort joined the throng in great numbers.

On the warning of Prime Minister Aniruddha, who feared that allowing such a multitude into the fort might lead to grave consequences, the Emperor, who was already drowning in a sea of sorrow, and his family came out of the fort to meet the people.
At the sight of Sundara Chozhar, a great roar rose from the immense crowd.

“During the reign of Sundara Chozhar, not a single cry of ‘Alas!’ was ever heard in Chola Nadu,” declare the stone inscriptions. The state of the land before Aditya Karikalan’s death is inscribed in those very stones.

But today, cries of “Alas! Alas!” and “Ayyo!” rose from hundreds of thousands of voices. The memory of Arjuna, who lost his son Abhimanyu, came to the minds of many. But Abhimanyu had stood alone amidst the enemy host, performed incredible feats of valor, and died a hero’s death.

Here, however, Aditya Karikalan had fallen victim to conspiracy, slain by the land-hunger of Madurantakan and the lust for power of the petty kings. Events that confirmed this suspicion in the minds of the people began to unfold in public.

Aditya Karikalan’s body was laid outside the Thanjavur fort for all to see. People came, wept, and departed. But Madurantakan did not come; nor did the Pazhuvettarayars. Rumors began to spread that the Pazhuvettarayars were rallying their allies and mustering their forces. Thus, even after the funeral rites for Aditya Karikalan were performed with all the honors due a fallen hero, and the royal family had re-entered the Thanjavur fort, the crowd did not disperse quickly.
Cries of “Down with Madurantakan!” and “Down with the Pazhuvettarayars!” first arose softly, but as time passed, these slogans grew louder and more forceful.

Suddenly, a section of the crowd broke open the gates of the fort and surged into the city of Thanjavur. Their first destination was the palace of the Pazhuvettarayars. Standing outside, they shouted, “The Pazhuvettarayars—”
“Fall!” they shouted.
At the command of the Chief Minister Aniruddhar, the Velakkara soldiers were forced to disperse the crowds.
Amidst this, a rumor spread that Madurantaka Devan was hiding inside Aniruddhar’s house. The people surrounded Aniruddhar’s residence.
“Where is that coward Madurantakan? Tell Madurantakan to come out!” they shouted.
At that very moment, Madurantakan was indeed inside Aniruddhar’s house. Hearing the uproar of the crowd outside, he trembled with fear. Turning to Aniruddhar, he pleaded,

“Chief Minister! Somehow, send me out of the fort. Send me through the secret underground passage. I will join my supporters. If you help me in this, when I ascend the Chola throne, I will retain you as my Chief Minister,” he said.
“Prince! Why speak of ascending the throne now? Is not Emperor Sundara Chola still alive?” asked Chief Minister Aniruddhar.

“Did you not see Sundara Chola returning after performing the last rites for his son? Did you not notice how his face looked as if possessed by a ghost? I was watching from the terrace. He will not live much longer. Either Arulmozhi Varman or I must ascend the throne and rule this kingdom. Sundara Chola is reluctant to crown me. Why should you and your mother stand in the way?” said Madurantakan.

“Prince! Would your mother stand in the way without reason? Listen. Is it enough if only Emperor Sundara Chola wishes it? Should not the people of the Chola land also wish it?” said Aniruddhar, and then, “Ah! What is this?” he exclaimed, peering out into the street.
In place of the earlier shouts, now rose cries of, “Long live Arulmozhi Varman!” “Long live Ponniyin Selvan!” “Long live the heroic conqueror of Eezham!”

Majestically mounted on horseback, Arulmozhi Varman was approaching. All the people followed him. Within a few moments, the area outside Aniruddhar’s house was deserted. Madurantakan, too, slipped away from Aniruddhar’s presence.

He was watching that scene. His eyes, burning with the fire of jealousy, turned red like the ripe kovai fruit. “Ah! What sort of enchantment does this boy possess?” he muttered to himself, struggling to contain his feelings.
Aniruddhar asked, “Prince! When the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar chased after the murderer of the Queen of Eezham, why were you in the underground tunnel at that time?”

“When Ponniyin Selvan came to the palace disguised as a mahout, I was overcome with deep dejection. I felt that both he and I could not remain within this fort at the same time. The Pazhuvettaraiyars had shown me the secret passage. I was wandering around the palace gardens, wondering if I should leave by that way. Just then, I saw someone emerging from the tunnel. He approached me and said, ‘Prince! I have come to see you. Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar and Kandhamaaran have sent me to fetch you at once. Great armies are ready, standing in support of your claim to the throne.’ His appearance aroused some suspicion in me. ‘If such a great army is ready, why should I go out? Let them come here, defeat the Kodumbalur forces, and seat me on the throne themselves!’ I replied. That man said, ‘Prince! That is not all; there is a terrible secret about your birth. No one else would dare reveal it to you. I will tell you.’ ‘If that is so, come! Let us go at once,’ I said. But he replied, ‘I must first deliver a message to Prime Minister Aniruddhar. I will do so and return. You go ahead and hide in the tunnel for now.’ On his word, I went and waited in the treasury vault. Prime Minister! Did he come to see you? What could be the terrible secret about my birth?” asked Madurantakan.
“Prince! The only person who has the right to reveal that to you is your mother, Sembiyan Maadevi. Even though I know something of it, I must not speak of it,” said Aniruddhar.
At that moment, the sound of lively commotion was heard again at the entrance of the mansion. The Prime Minister peered out. “Ah! Here comes your mother herself!” he said.

In a short while, Sembiyan Maadevi, having spoken with the women of Aniruddhar’s household, ascended to the upper floor. Sorrow was writ large upon the face of that noble lady. Aniruddhar rose, greeted her, and indicated a seat. The lady sat down. For a while, she remained with her gaze lowered to the floor. Even in the upper storey, outside the palace, and along the street, silence had settled everywhere. Then, Sembiyan Madevi looked at Madurantakan and Aniruddhar once more and said, “Sir! My husband has placed this burden upon my head and departed to the western world. Whatever wrong was done, it was by me. But if he had been here at this time, I would not have had to endure such sorrow.”

At that moment, Madurantakan’s eyes flashed with anger. “Why do you grieve like this? Why do you keep invoking my father’s name? It is certain that I will ascend the throne of Thanjavur. One of those who stood in my way is now dead. Arulmozhi Varman is younger than I am. As long as I live, they will never crown him. You must show mercy and not stand in my way. Mother! Has anyone ever heard of a mother betraying her own child? You, a devout follower of Shiva—why do you seek to betray me?”

“My child! For a mother to oppose her own son is indeed a terrible betrayal. But my husband commanded me thus before he left this world. It is my duty to fulfill his command. Listen to me! The desire for land is a dangerous thing. The thirst for a kingdom is even more perilous. There is no one in this world more beset by worries than those who wear a crown upon their heads. None are as troubled and restless as those who sit upon the throne. Was it not because of the crown upon his head that Veerapandiyan lost his life? The empire of Shiva’s world is infinitely greater than any earthly kingdom. Let us leave this place. Let us go on a pilgrimage to the holy lands and journey to Mount Kailasa. There, we shall become worthy of Lord Kailasanathar’s grace.”

“Ah! You are at the right age for a Kailasa pilgrimage. But I am not yet old enough. I have not seen any of the joys or sorrows of this world. You raised me to wander about smeared in ash, chanting ‘Shiva, Shiva’ like a madman. Now, by the great grace of that Supreme Shiva, the kingdom has come near to me. Why should I give it up?” asked Madurantakan.

“Dear one! The kingdom that has come near you is accompanied by countless dangers. One obstacle to your ascent of the throne has been removed. You say that Aditya Karikalan is dead. Did you not hear the cries of the people who were gathered around this house just a while ago? Madurantaka! The people believe that you and the Pazhuvettarayars are responsible for Aditya Karikalan’s death. How will they ever accept you as emperor?”

“Mother, the people will forget all that soon enough. If I am placed upon the throne, they will accept me as emperor. Listen to me once more! Do you know who is responsible for Karikalan’s death? It is none other than Vandiyathevan, the dearest friend of Arulmozhi Varman. It was Vandiyathevan who was present at the very spot in the house of Sambuvaraiyar where Karikalan lay dead. Both Sambuvaraiyar and Vandiyathevan have been thrown into the underground dungeon. The one who plotted his own brother’s murder to gain the throne is Arulmozhi Varman himself. Let the people only learn this one truth—then we shall see what becomes of Ponni’s beloved son.”

Sembiyan Madevi’s eyes blazed with fire. “Wretch! What words are these you utter about Arulmozhi, whose heart overflows with compassion? He is ready to keep even a greedy soul like you in his temple and worship you. If you speak thus of him again, you will surely burn in the fires of hell. Neither in this life nor the next shall you find salvation.”
At these words, Madurantakan sprang up. “You fiend! You curse your own son and bless my enemy. Can you truly be my mother? Never!”
His heart seethed with pain and indignation as he spoke.
Then Sembiyan Madevi said, “My son, I had hoped never to tell you this. But your obstinacy has forced me. In truth, I am not your mother. You are not my son.”
Madurantakan, his voice trembling, said, “Ah! So my suspicions were true. If you are not my mother, then who is? If I am not your son, whose son am I?”
The Devi turned to the Prime Minister Aniruddhar and said, “Sir, please, you must tell him. Do not force me to speak of my own disgrace.”

Prime Minister Aniruddhar looked at Madurantakan and said, “Prince, you have wounded the heart of the lady who raised you from your infancy. Yet the truth is bound to come out one day. It is better you know it now.”

When Sembiyan Madevi was newly wed, she longed to bear a child of her own, to see that child crowned as emperor of the Chola Empire. While she was expecting, her husband had gone away to another land. At that very time, in that very… In those days, two mute women, sisters by birth, lived in a cottage within the palace gardens. Of the two, one was pregnant and expecting the birth of her child. When Sembiyan Maadevi had gone on a pilgrimage, she had found this pregnant woman abandoned and helpless, and brought her back with her. Upon hearing that the woman’s sister was living near Thanjavur, Sembiyan Maadevi had summoned her as well, so that she could assist her pregnant sibling.

Sembiyan Maadevi herself gave birth to a child. The chief minister, Aniruddha, came to offer his congratulations on the birth of an heir to the kingdom. But at that moment, Sembiyan Maadevi wept bitterly and cried out in anguish. The newborn child lay lifeless, unmoving as a log, and thus she was plunged into grief.

“Sir! What answer shall I give my husband when he returns and asks me?” she sobbed, her tears flowing without restraint. Unable to bear her sorrow, Aniruddha devised a plan. He knew that the mute woman living in the garden had recently given birth to twins—a boy and a girl. He went to her and, through gestures, indicated that if she left her children there, they would be raised in the palace.

But the mute woman was like one possessed, mad with grief. At first, she refused to give up her children. Yet, after a short while, she left her infants behind and ran away. Immediately, Aniruddha took her sister and sent her with the boy child to Sembiyan Maadevi. The lifeless newborn was secretly taken away by the mute sister, who was instructed to bury it where none would know. The other, the girl child, Aniruddha took to his own house and entrusted her to his disciple, Azhwarkkadiyan, who then sent her away to the Pandya country.

This exchange of children gnawed at Sembiyan Maadevi’s conscience ever after. One day, she confessed the truth to Kandaraditha Devar. That great soul replied, “There is no sin in this, dear one! What does it matter in whose womb a child is born? It is a gift from Lord Shiva. Raise this child as your own, as if he were born from your own womb. But a child born of another lineage must not ascend the Chola throne. To do so would be a betrayal of our clan. Therefore, from a young age, let us raise him as a devotee of Shiva. Let us nurture him so that he himself will one day say, ‘I do not desire the Chola empire; the empire of Shiva’s devotion is enough for me!’ But under no circumstance must we become party to placing him upon the throne of Thanjavur. Even if I am no longer alive when that moment comes, you must stand firm and protect the Chola lineage,” he pleaded.

“Madurantaka! You are not the son of Kandaraditya Devar. Nor are you the child born from the womb of Sembiyan Madevi. You are the son of that mute, destitute woman who wandered the streets, an orphan. Yet, this Devi cherished and raised you, lavishing upon you a hundred times more affection and praise than she did upon her own child. Now, do not act against her wishes! Listen to what the Devi says; only good will come to you from it,” said Aniruddhar.

chapters.title: The Unfortunate One
paragraphs: After sitting for a while as if possessed by a feverish delirium, Madurantakan suddenly sprang to his feet and, turning to Aniruddhar, exclaimed, “Prime Minister! All this is your doing! I knew it even then! You have a special fondness for the children of Sundara Chola, especially for Arulmozhivarman. It is your desire that he should be crowned king. For that purpose, you have spun such lies and deceptions to my mother, poisoning her noble heart! Oh, Brahmarayar, so full of affection! What harm have I ever done to you? Why do you seek to betray me thus? Must I, for the sake of your ambitions, leave my mother childless? Has such a dreadful, sinful plot ever been conceived in this world? You, a Brahmin born in the lineage of Vishnu’s devotees—was it for this you were born? No, no! The fault is not yours. It is the handiwork of the young princess Kundavai and Arulmozhivarman—they have somehow ensnared you and made you commit this crime!” he cried.

Aniruddhar replied in a calm, measured voice, “Prince, if I bore such hatred towards you, would I have brought you here, rescuing you from where you lay under a tree in the pouring rain? And do not speak ill of Arulmozhivarman. Do you know what that valiant conqueror of Lanka is doing at this very moment? He is going among the soldiers and people surrounding the Tanjore fort, speaking kind words, pacifying them, and bringing them to calm. He is striving to persuade them that it would not be right for him to ascend the throne while you, his uncle, are still alive, and that neither the warriors nor the people should demand such a thing. He is working to change their minds and set things right.”
“If that is so—if that is so, then the news you just told me is unknown to Arulmozhi, is it not?”
“Arulmozhi does not know; nor does anyone else!”

“Then why should it ever be revealed? Aniruddhar! If you alone agree to keep your mouth shut… The Emperor gave you a grant of ten velis of land in a village, did he not? I shall give you the whole of Pandya Nadu as a gift….”
“Sir! There is no need to grant me the Pandya kingdom just to keep my mouth shut; your mother’s command alone is enough. Tell her so!”

Madurantakan looked at the mother who had raised him, his gaze filled with sorrow. “Child! Madurantaka! What Aniruddhar says is true. He has known my secret for twenty years. On that day, he said, ‘Maharani! This is your secret. Unless you yourself reveal it to someone, no one else will ever know. It will never escape my lips—this I swear!’ He has kept that promise to this day. He swore loyalty to the Chola dynasty. He has not told even Emperor Sundara Chola. If I had agreed for you to ascend the Chola throne, he too would have remained silent…”
“Yes, Mother! I would have remained silent. But I would never have served as Prime Minister while harboring a lie in my heart. I would have gone to serve Lord Sriranganatha instead!” said Aniruddhar.

“But there will be no need for that. Madurantakan will not ascend the throne. He will fulfill my wish. He himself will refuse the kingdom! My son, agree—say ‘yes’!” said the elder princess, Periya Piratti Sembiyan Madevi.

“Mother! Then, are you the only obstacle to my ascending the throne? Now I am convinced that I am not your own son. For over twenty years, you raised me with the love reserved for a son born of your own womb. Why do you now betray me? What wrong have I done to you?”

“Child! You have done me no wrong. It is I who have wronged you. All these years I raised you as my own son, and now I say, ‘You are not my son!’ Do you think I do not know how deeply this wounds your heart? As long as I lived, I would never have revealed this. But I must fulfill the promise I made to my husband. I must not betray the Chola dynasty into which I entered. I must not place upon the Chola throne one who was not born into the Chola line. I must not become a party to such a deed. Do you think my heart does not ache over this? When I said just now, ‘You are not my son,’ my heart broke within me. Until the last moment, I hesitated to speak; my mind was in utter turmoil. To understand what my duty was, what was right, I went to Nambiyandar Nambi. That great soul…” He explained the subtlety of dharma in detail. “All the people in this world are children of Mahadeva. As a foremost devotee of Shiva, you would never make a distinction between ‘your own child’ and a ‘foster child.’ You would give all your personal possessions to the son you have raised. But the matter of the kingdom is different. To prevent another’s rightful claim through our own falsehood is a sin. To knowingly place someone not born of the Chola lineage upon the Chola throne is a betrayal of the clan. True dharma is to reveal the truth to both your son and the Emperor,” he advised me. I listened and returned.
“Kumara! Do you think I can feel joy in saying, ‘You are not my own son’? Would I ever be able to say this with pride only when I speak to the Emperor?”

At that moment, Madurantakan suddenly rose and fell at the feet of Sembiyan Madevi, crying, “Mother! I do not want the kingdom, nor the throne. If you ask me to stay here, I will stay; if you ask me to go into exile, I will go. But please, do not say that I am not your son, that I was not born of your sacred womb! Do not say it to anyone! If you do, the shame of it alone will cause my heart to burst and I will die!” he wailed.
Tears brimmed in Sembiyan Madevi’s eyes. With deep concern, she gathered Madurantakan up and seated him beside her.

“Kumara! It is only to spare you this sorrow that I tried to raise you without desire for the worldly kingdom, and with devotion to the empire of Sivaloka. In that, I have failed. Some sinners have corrupted your mind. Even now, all is not lost. If you, of your own free will, declare to the whole land and its people, ‘I do not want this kingdom. Let Arulmozhi, the son of Sundara Chola, rule,’ then there is no need for me to publicly say, ‘You are not my son!’ The pain I have now caused your heart brings me immeasurable anguish. Today, confess this before the Prime Minister Aniruddha. In three days, the great assembly of the minor kings will convene. Confess it before that assembly as well. Say, ‘I have no desire to rule the kingdom. I wish to serve Lord Shiva and devote myself to the renovation of Shiva temples. That is the command of my father and mother! Crown Arulmozhivarman!’ Swear that you will never act against the Chola kingdom, that you will not heed any evil counsel from the minor kings! If you do this, neither I nor the Prime Minister will ever have reason to reveal the secret of your birth. You will remain, as always, the precious jewel of my eye, my beloved son. Together, we two shall travel across this vast land of Bharata... “Let us go on a pilgrimage. Here and there, we shall undertake the renovation of Shiva temples. Arulmozhi Varman has boundless devotion towards me. I raised him, too, for the most part, just as I raised you. He would never refuse my word, would he?” said Sembiyan Maadevi, daughter of the Mazhavarayar clan.

Hearing this, Madurantakan clasped his forehead in both hands and sat for a while, lost in thought. “Ah! From the time I became aware of myself, vague, formless shadows of memories have often arisen and tormented me. Only now do I understand the reason for all of them. Who in this world is as unfortunate as I am? I do not even know at what hour, under what star, I was born. In a single day, in a single moment, I lost both my mother and father. I lost my clan and my lineage. I lost a vast and mighty empire. I lost the throne that had descended through a thousand years of valorous ancestors. I lost all my friends. Yes; if this truth becomes known, who will remain my friend thereafter? All those petty kings who have sworn oaths to give their lives for my coronation will, in a single instant, abandon me!… Yes, from the day this world began, there has not been one as ill-fated as I. Mother! My mind is in turmoil; I cannot think clearly. Grant me two days’ time, and I shall give you my decision!” he said.

“My child! What is there for you to ponder? I speak these words with a heart turned to stone. You must either consent to renounce the kingdom yourself, or I must declare to the whole land and all the cities that you are not the son born of my womb. In any case, you cannot ascend the throne. What is there for you to consider and decide?” said the noble lady, revered and worshipped throughout the land as the Periya Piratti.

Then Aniruddhar spoke: “Mother! There is no harm in granting two days’ time. There are still three days left before the council of ministers and the great assembly of the people convene. Until then, let the prince reflect in peace!”

“Mother! Mother! Does anyone else know this secret, apart from you and the Prime Minister?” Madurantakan suddenly asked, with a surge of eagerness. What dark thought had arisen in his heart, what kind of scheme had begun to take root, we do not know.

Madurantakan’s agitation caused a flicker of surprise in the daughter of Mazhavarayar. “Besides us, only three others knew. My son! Of them, your father, Sivanesa Selvar, who dwells ever in my thoughts, has passed away. The other two are mute women—my elder and younger sisters. Of them, one…” The woman who gave birth to you—two days ago, she met a tragic end in the palace of Sundara Chola. Even as her lifeless body lay unburied, I wondered if I should reveal the truth to you. But my heart would not allow it. I did not wish to cause you pain, so I remained silent. My son! If you wish to weep for the woman who bore you, then weep! She gave birth to you, yes, but beyond that, there is no other bond between you and her. She never even tried to come see you. She lost her mind and became a beggar, wandering mad. If you must shed tears for her, then do so!” said the Devi.

“No, no, I cannot think of anyone but you as my mother. Even if you had told me earlier, I would not have gone near her. Who is the other person who knows this secret, Mother? Who is that other mute woman?” he asked.

“She is her younger sister; she lives just outside Thanjai, tending a garden. It was she who exchanged you for the lifeless child who was born from my womb, stiff as a log. Since she was born mute and deaf, she would never tell anyone. She too has a son. Mother and son serve by offering flowers at the temple of Thalikulathar in Thanjai. I support them, granting them a stipend.”

“Ah! I know them. Mother, I know both the woman and her son. The son’s name is Sendhan Amudhan. He is the one who helped the spy named Vandiyathevan escape from here. Mother! Does the boy know anything about this?”

“He does not know, my son! He does not! His mother has sworn to me that she will never reveal this secret to anyone. You need not worry about that. Other than her, only I and the Prime Minister know.”

At that moment, in the heart of Madurantakan, many terrible, fiery thoughts arose. If these two were to depart from this world, there would be no one left to reveal the truth. I owe nothing to the Prime Minister. And this queen is not truly my mother. Why should I show them any mercy? Ah! Who was it that promised to reveal the secret of my birth in Sundara Chola’s garden? Who was it that summoned me to the treasury chamber? If only I could meet him! He tried to kill Sundara Chola and killed that mute woman. He is not at fault. They say she is my mother. If she is my mother, then who is my father? Perhaps...
Perhaps this deceitful old woman, and this master of disguises, Brahmarayan, are trying to deceive me as well? Am I truly the son of Sundara Chozhar?… Ah! How can I ever know the truth of this?

“My son! I will take my leave now; think deeply and come to a decision soon! I, who have raised you for twenty-two years with a love ten times greater than that of your own mother, would never counsel you towards harm. Renounce this unstable earthly kingdom! Seek the path to attain the eternal, indestructible empire of Sivaloka!” Thus spoke the Periya Piratti.
At that very moment, something happened that none of them had anticipated. Arulmozhi Varman entered the chamber. He walked straight to Sembiyan Maadevi and bowed before her.

“Devi! The wisdom you imparted to your beloved son, I too have accepted as advice meant for me. If this Chola empire is indeed my rightful inheritance, I am prepared to renounce it. By your blessing, may my heart find its way to the lotus feet of Lord Siva. In the empire of Sivaloka, may I be granted a small place near the great Kandaradithar, your husband! Bless me thus!” he said.
Hearing these words, Sembiyan Maadevi and Prime Minister Aniruddha Brahmarayan looked at each other, stunned.

“Devi! Just now, I happened to overhear what you were telling your precious son, though it was not my intention. I had gone out to escort the crowd gathered around this palace beyond the fort gates and had just returned. I entered the palace to speak with the Prime Minister about what must be done next. When I learned you were here as well, I felt as though a ripe fruit had slipped and fallen into milk. You were speaking louder than usual, and Mathuranthaka Devar too raised his voice. As I hesitated at the door, uncertain whether to enter or not, a portion of your conversation reached my ears. Devi! You just said that among the living, only you, the Prime Minister, and Senthan Amudhan’s mother know the secret of Mathuranthakar’s birth. That is not correct. My younger sister, the Ilaya Piratti, and I also know it. In Eezha Nadu, I often met Mandakini Devi, who gave her life to save the Emperor’s. Through the language of signs, she revealed all this to me. I told my sister, and together we pondered and reached a decision. My younger uncle, Mathuranthaka Devar, is the one who must ascend the Chola throne. He is your own son—”

He was raised with a thousand times more care than in the forest. Not only did she save me from drowning in the Kaveri flood, but Mandakini Devi, who gave birth to him, has helped me escape death on many occasions since then. Therefore, by any measure, he has the right to ascend the Chola throne. If there is any doubt regarding his claim, I shall resolve it! I will renounce whatever right I have to the Chola throne, taking your sacred lotus feet as my witness. Therefore, there is no need for you to declare that Madhurantaka Devar is not your son. Nor is there any need for Madhurantakan to renounce the Chola throne!”

Hearing these words spoken by Ponniyin Selvan, the three in that chamber were struck by astonishment and wonder such as they had never experienced in their lives. Among them, Aniruddha was the first to regain his composure.

“Prince! The words you have just spoken deserve a place in epic poetry and legend. They should be inscribed on black stone, on copper plates, and on golden scrolls. But we who are gathered here cannot decide this matter alone. We must consult the Emperor and the other feudatory kings. We must also consider what the people will say if the truth comes to light in the future. Prince! Only three days remain until the Great Assembly convenes. Until then, let each of us reflect deeply and carefully on this matter!” he said.

chapters.title: Kundavai’s Turmoil
paragraphs: Born into wealth and raised amidst luxury was the young princess, Kundavai Devi. In beauty, she rivaled Rathi; in wisdom, the goddess of arts; in fortune, the goddess of prosperity herself. From Sundara Chola Chakravarthi down to the common folk of Chola Nadu, all revered her. In the palace, many waited eagerly for the chance to fulfill even the smallest of her wishes. Lesser kings longed for the honor of having a princess from their own line serve as Kundavai Devi’s handmaiden. Across the land of Bharata, princes destined for imperial thrones undertook penance, yearning for the fortune of holding Kundavai’s hand in marriage.

Yet, this princess, blessed with every conceivable fortune, was now submerged in a boundless ocean of sorrow. All the warnings she had sent to Aditya Karikalan had been in vain. She had dispatched an urgent message, begging him not to go to the palace of Sambuvarayar. Her beloved elder brother, who always held her word in the highest regard, had brushed aside her plea and set out for Kadambur Palace. There, in mysterious circumstances, he had met an untimely death. Kundavai had always believed that Nandini was a sister to herself, to Karikalan, and to Arulmozhi. She also knew that, for some reason, Nandini harbored a deep-seated grudge against Karikalan. If it was indeed by Nandini’s hand that Karikalan met his end, there could be no greater disgrace or shame for the Chola dynasty. After Karikalan’s death, the fate of Nandini remained unknown.

The loss of her beloved brother brought Kundavai immeasurable grief. Even two days after his soul had departed, she melted in sorrow, recalling the heroic radiance that had always shone upon his noble face. Ah! What dreams that great warrior had cherished! He had spoken of conquering lands up to the Himalayas, like Karikala Peruvallathan, and planting the tiger banner atop its peaks. Such a man’s glorious body had, in the span of half a nazhigai, been reduced to ashes. He had merged with the very soil of Chola Nadu. Yet, from that mingled earth, in the days to come, thousands upon thousands of valiant heroes would arise. They would set forth from Chola Nadu in all directions, crossing seas to distant lands. They would wage mighty wars and expand the borders of the Chola Empire. Wherever they went, they would raise towering temples with sky-piercing gopurams, proclaiming the greatness of Chola Nadu. They will stand tall and majestic, as proclaimed to the world. They will spread the glory of Tamil, its arts, and the Saiva and Vaishnava faiths. The hymns of the three great Tevaram saints and the songs of the Alwars will resound in lands beyond the seas. The victorious cry of “Vetri Vel! Veera Vel!” will echo everywhere…

These are not mere dreams. They are things that can truly come to pass. If all that the elders, astrologers, and experienced mothers have said about the auspicious hour of Arulmozhi Varman’s birth is true, then all the visions Karikalan dreamed of may well be fulfilled through Arulmozhi Varman. But how many obstacles stand in the way of this? Ah! Who knows what disasters these petty kings, in their mutual quarrels, might bring about? Malayaman and Velan are stubbornly determined that Arulmozhi Varman must ascend the throne at any cost. The Pazhuvettaraiyars and their allies are gathering armies in support of Madurantakan. The Emperor, struck by two great calamities in quick succession, is sunk deep in an ocean of sorrow. He refuses to speak to anyone about anything. He is consumed by remorse, thinking again and again of the sin he committed in his youth. No one dares even to offer him words of comfort. If even his own beloved daughter fears to approach him, what can be said of others!

Arulmozhi Varman himself is ready to renounce the kingdom. He wishes to crown Madurantakan, and then, with the Chola armies, cross the seas and embark on a campaign of conquest. But even this faces an unexpected obstacle. For some reason, the venerable and much-revered elder queen, Sembiyan Madevi—whom all of Chola Nadu honors—objects to her son being crowned. She claims it is the command of her departed husband. How all these tangled knots will be unraveled, no one knows.

As if all these worries about the Chola clan and the Chola empire were not enough, another great anxiety tormented and consumed Kundavai. The valiant prince of the Vanar clan, who had captured her heart, was now imprisoned in a subterranean dungeon. They were trying to hold him responsible for the murder of Aditya Karikalan. In this, Parthibendran of the Pallava clan was being especially obstinate. Her grandfather Malayaman might perhaps listen if she spoke. But how could she, as a woman, intervene in the matter of a man who was already under suspicion? If it became known that she cared more for Vandiyathevan, a wandering adventurer, than for her own brother Aditya Karikalan, what greater disgrace could there be? Parthibendran was just the sort of man who would be eager to spread such a scandal. At the very spot where Karikalan was found murdered, Vandiyathevan was caught, red-handed… It may well be true, as Parthibendran says, that Sambhuvarayar and Kandhamaaran have been captured. But Vandiyathevan should have fulfilled the promise he made—to never leave Karikalan’s side, not even for a moment. He must have tried to save Aditya Karikalan from the assassins, and, failing in that attempt, suffered defeat.

But how can the truth of this matter be discovered? Even if I try to go and see Vandiyathevan myself, or have him brought here from prison, it will only give rise to needless suspicions and malicious gossip. No one would dare say anything about me. Even if they did, I would not be troubled. But there are some cunning people who are trying to make Arulmozhi Varman responsible for Karikalan’s death. If I act rashly and do something, it might only serve to benefit their faction—should that be allowed to happen?
O Divine Mother! O Devi! O Mother of the Universe! From the moment I was born, I have lived without a single worry—what kind of trial have you set before me now?...

Thus did Kundavai’s heart churn, wounded by thought after thought. From the moment she received the news of Karikalan’s death, and the report that Vandiyathevan was involved, the young princess had not slept a single moment at night. She pondered and pondered, seeking a way to resolve this tangled situation, considering many possible courses, only to reject each one in turn.

She even refused to confide in her dearest friend, Vanathi. Vanathi, sensing Kundavai’s state of mind, remained silent and asked no questions. Most often, she stayed by Kundavai’s side like a shadow, and like a shadow, she kept her silence.

Vanathi, who had so tactfully kept herself from intruding on Kundavai’s troubled thoughts, suddenly approached the young princess that day and said, “Akka! Akka! A woman has come to see you. She stands there in tears and distress. She looks truly pitiable!”
Kundavai was somewhat surprised by this.
“Who is she? Did you not ask her what her business is?” she asked.

“I did ask, Akka! But if I tell you, you might be annoyed, I thought… She is Manimekalai, the daughter of Sambhuvarayar! The Sambhuvarayar family is being held prisoner in the palace of the younger Pazhuvettarayar. She found her way here without anyone knowing—”
She has come running here. When I asked her what the matter was, she said she would only tell you directly. If you see her tear-stained face, even your heart will change at once!” said Vanathi.
“So, are you saying my heart is made of stone?” Kundavai asked angrily.
“For you, it truly is a heart of stone. Akka! Otherwise, would you have left Vandiyathevan in the underground dungeon and remained silent?” said Vanathi.
“All right, all right, tell that girl to come here!” said Kundavai.
Vanathi, leaping like a deer, ran out and returned the next moment, bringing Manimekalai with her.

chapters.title: The Boon Manimekalai Asked
paragraphs: Like one afflicted by hallucination, Manimekalai looked this way and that, her eyes wide and wild, as she entered. As Vanathi had described, her appearance was truly pitiable. Her face and eyelids were swollen from incessant weeping.

Yet, for some reason, Kundavai felt no compassion towards her. She could not forget that the root cause of all the recent calamities that had befallen the Chola dynasty was the conspiracy that took place in the Kadambur Sambuvaraiyar palace. Most of all, the thought that her own valiant brother, Karikalan, had been murdered in this very girl’s house only fueled her anger further.

Suddenly, another thought flashed through her mind. This girl’s brother, Kandhamaaran, and the valiant scion of the Vanar clan were old friends. It was because of that friendship that Vandiyathevan had gone to the Kadambur palace. He had returned to report the conspiracy that transpired there. Kandhamaaran had once intended to marry his sister to the Prince of Vallam. That girl must be this very Manimekalai!…

As this realization dawned, Kundavai felt a new curiosity towards Manimekalai. Ah! For what purpose had she come seeking her? Had she come to plead for her father and brother? When her brother Karikalan was invited to the Sambuvaraiyar palace, the proposal to wed this girl to him had also been raised. Perhaps this foolish girl had given her heart to Karikalan? Was her mind now unhinged because the man she wished to marry had met an untimely death? Had she come to speak of that? Or… or… could it be something else? Kandhamaaran must have spoken to her about his friend. Vandiyathevan had stayed in her house—he had stayed there once before, and now, for many days. Could it be that her heart was drawn to Vandiyathevan? If so, there could be no doubt that he had rejected her. Had she now come to heap false and terrible accusations upon him, seeking revenge for her wounded pride?… All these thoughts flashed rapidly across Kundavai’s mind and vanished. She gazed intently at Manimekalai, as though she wished to pierce through her heart and uncover what lay within. Unable to withstand that searching gaze, Manimekalai lowered her head. Two tears fell from her eyes and scattered upon the floor.

“Girl! Why are you weeping? Your brother is still alive, is he not? Was it not my brother who was murdered in your palace and lost his life? If anyone should weep, should it not be me? Yet look at me! I do not cry, nor do I shed tears. It is not the custom of women of the Chola clan to weep for those who have met a heroic death!” said Kundavai.

Manimekalai lifted her head and looked at the young princess. “Devi! If my brother had died at the tip of a sword, I too would not weep. But the one who died… the one who died…” She faltered, unable to continue, and sobbed.

Kundavai began to think that her initial suspicion might indeed be true. Perhaps this girl had given her heart to Aditya Karikalan. It seemed she was hesitant to confess it! Alas, poor girl! If that were so, she must be comforted.

“Girl! Steel your heart. Speak boldly what is in your mind! The one who died was not your brother. It was my brother. Why then should you weep? Perhaps you grieve that such a thing happened while he was a guest in your house! What can you do about it? There were many elders present in the house. The responsibility is theirs…”

“No, Devi, no! The responsibility is mine alone! That is why, however much I try, I cannot restrain my sorrow. Nor can I stop the tears from flowing from my eyes. When I think that it was by the dagger held in this hand that I killed that bravest of the brave, my heart feels as if it will shatter into a thousand pieces…”
Kundavai Devi, startled, exclaimed, “Girl! What is this nonsense you are uttering? Have you lost your senses?”

“No, no! I have not lost my senses. If I am to lose them, let it happen now. I am telling you only the truth of what happened. It was this sinner who killed Aditya Karikalan. I have come to confess the truth to you and receive whatever punishment I deserve…”
“Fie, fie! What slander is this? You expect me to believe that my brother, the bravest of the brave, was slain by the hand of a woman? Who has taught you to speak such things?”
“No one has taught me, Devi! No one believes what I say. Not even my brother or my father would accept my words.”
“Why do you spin such tales? It must have been they who instructed you to say this, or perhaps you have invented this story yourself to protect your father and brother!”

“Devi! Why should I wish to protect them? Against my will, they tried to marry me off. First, they said, ‘Wed Madhurandhaka Devar.’ Then, all of a sudden, they brought Aditya Karikalan and said, ‘You must marry him. If you do, you shall ascend the Chola throne!’ Why should I show mercy to those who sought to sacrifice me thus? Why should I confess to a crime they committed? Never! Never!” declared Manimekalai.

“Girl! Each word you speak is stranger than the last. For the fortune of marrying my brother Karikalan, how many princesses of great kings have performed penance! Yet you claim your father and brother wished to sacrifice you? Why do you consider life in the Chola clan such a terrible suffering?”
“Devi! I have no sisters, none born of my own mother. I speak to you as if you were my own sister…” said Manimekalai.
“You accuse my brother of murder, and yet you dare to claim the bond of sisterhood with me?” the young princess asked sharply.

“I have that right. Your brother Karikalan considered me his own sister. He wrote so in his own hand. It is when I remember that, that my heart aches at having been forced to slay him. I have come to you only to ask what penance I must do for this sin!” With these words, Manimekalai broke down once more in sobs.

The young princess turned to Vanathi and said in a low voice, “Poor thing! It truly seems this girl is suffering from delusion. Why did you bring her here at such a time? What if she suddenly goes mad?”
Vanathi said, “Akka! I too am filled with anxiety. Please, do not speak in anger. Let us speak kindly to her and send her back!”

Kundavai looked at Manimekalai and said, “Child! What has happened is done. All is the work of fate! Do not grieve. You may think of me as your own elder sister. You wished to say something, did you not? What is it? Or, if you prefer, you may tell me at another time if you wish.”

“No, no, I will say it now itself. Akka! Since you too were born a woman, you will understand what I say. No matter how much one tells men, they cannot comprehend it. Suppose a woman has given her heart to a man. Imagine that man stands defenseless, without any weapon in his hand, and another, armed with a great sword, comes to slay him. At that moment, if the woman truly loves him, what will she do? Will she stand by and simply watch…?”
At once, Kundavai remembered Mandakini. Tears welled in her eyes. “How could she merely stand and watch? She would rush in, even if it meant giving her own life, to try and save her beloved’s life!”

Hearing this, Manimekalai cried out, “Ah! There is no one left to advise me with such thoughts. Was it not the wicked Pazhuvoor Nandini’s counsel that led me astray? Considering me as her own sister, she planned to wed my beloved to me, and yet, by these sinful hands of mine, I have killed that noble one!” With these words, she broke down in sobs.
The young princess, Kundavai Devi, turned to Vanathi and whispered softly, “She is losing her senses!”
Then, turning to Manimekalai, she said, “Child! Do not weep! Tell us what happened! Or will you tell us another time?”

“No, no, I will say it now, Akka! My brother Kandhamaaran has long spoken to me of a certain friend of his. Some months ago, that friend came to our palace in Kadambur. The moment I saw him, my heart decided, ‘He is my lord’…”
With a slight tremor in her voice, the young princess asked, “Who is the fortunate one who has stolen your heart?”

“You call him fortunate? No, no. When my heart went to him, my misfortune too clung to him. Today, he lies imprisoned in the underground dungeon of this Thanjavur fort. Akka! The women of the Pazhuvettaraiyar household told me—the underground prison in this fort is said to be most dreadful. They say that those who are locked away in it never return alive,” she said.
“All that is just talk, girl! Even I, and Vanathi here who stands beside me, have been to the underground prison not long ago…”
“Devi! Can I go to the underground prison? Can I see him just once?”
“You still haven’t told us who he is, child!”
“He is the prince of the Vanar clan. His name is Vandiyathevan!” Kundavai and Vanathi looked at each other.
Now Vanathi interrupted, “Why are you so anxious about him? What is the relationship between you and him?”
Manimekalai turned to Vanathi and, with irritation, said, “Who are you to ask me that?”

But she immediately calmed herself. “Don’t be angry, amma! Aren’t you Vanathi, the princess of Kodumbalur? Isn’t your elder father the commander of this fort today? I fall at your feet and beg you—grant me a boon! Speak to your elder father, the Periya Velar, and have Vandiyathevan released from the underground prison! Tell them to put me in the dungeon in his place! I am the sinner who killed Prince Karikalan! When I myself confess to my crime, what justice is there in accusing another? Devi! I bow to you as well and beg you. If the Periya Velar of Kodumbalur does not grant justice, I wish to appeal directly to your father, the Emperor. You must help me in that!” pleaded Manimekalai.
Kundavai’s heart was tossed like a stormy sea by many emotions.

She herself had hesitated even to go and see Vandiyathevan in the underground prison. Yet this girl, for the sake of her love for Vandiyathevan, was ready to confess to a crime of murder! But how much of what she said was true? How much was imagination? Was she inventing such a story just to save her beloved? Or, as she had mentioned Nandini’s evil influence, could she have truly been driven mad and committed that terrible deed herself?

No, no. She could not have committed that crime. She speaks thus only to save Vandiyathevan from the accusation of murder. It is clear from her manner of speech. No one will believe her words. Nor will they release Vandiyathevan based on her testimony. Still, I must see if I can learn anything more from her. There is certainly some mystery surrounding Karikalan’s untimely death. Can it be revealed through this woman?

“Manimekalai! I praise the firmness of your heart. I commend you for coming forward to confess to a crime, for the sake of saving your beloved. Deeds such as this, we have only heard of in stories and epics. Alas, there are no poets of the Sangam age left in these days to sing of your valor. Yet, even if I believe your words, should not others also believe them? Your father and brother claim that Vandiyathevan was found beside Karikalan’s lifeless body. Will people believe their words, or yours? There is another obstacle to believing you. It was I who sent the Prince of Vallam urgently to your brother, instructing him to prevent Karikalan from going to Kadambur, and to stay by his side at all times to protect him. Moreover, the Prince of Vallam belongs to Karikalan’s personal guard. He was present when Karikalan died. Yet, he did not save him. Therefore, he has failed in his duty. He ought to have given his own life to protect Karikalan’s. Even if it is proven that he did not kill him, is there not a fitting punishment for failing in his duty?”
“Devi! He did not fail in his duty, not even in the slightest.”
“What proof do you have for that, other than your word?”
“Here is the proof! There is written testimony from your own brother!” So saying, Manimekalai took a palm-leaf manuscript from her waist and handed it over.

With boundless curiosity, Kundavai read the letter. Yes; it was indeed in Aditya Karikalan’s own handwriting. He had written it himself, so that no one else would know. He had addressed it to Kundavai herself.
To my beloved sister, the imperial princess, the younger Piratti, Kundavai Devi, written by Aditya Karikalan.

For many days now, sleep has eluded me at night. Three years ago, I committed a terrible sin. I killed an enemy who had surrendered himself to me. Both he and the woman who pleaded for his life continue to torment me. They do not let me sleep in peace.

Early this morning, unable to sleep, I stepped outside and saw a shooting star fall and vanish from the sky. I felt as though, at that very moment, something had left my body as well. Now, only an empty shell remains. Sister! Let this evil omen depart with me. May Ekambranathar protect our beloved father and Arulmozhi from all harm.

You and I, in our youth, dreamed so much about the glory of the Chola Empire. I could not fulfill those dreams. My brother will fulfill them. He was born to rule the three worlds. Vallavaraiyan Vandiyathevan will stand by his side as his companion. Devi! I am satisfied to learn that Vandiyathevan has accomplished the tasks you entrusted to him. Otherwise, you would not have sent him here on such an important mission. You would not have sent him to save me from my fate.

Sister! If anything happens to me here, let my destiny and my own stubbornness bear the blame, not Vandiyathevan. As you instructed, he tried his utmost to prevent me from coming to this Kadambur palace. Since my arrival, he has followed me like a shadow. For that very purpose, he has kept the lady of this house, Manimekalai, close to him in friendship. With her help, he has gone ahead and hidden himself in the very place I intended to go. All of it is only to protect me. But can one person save another from fate, from the consequences of karma?

You must have heard how small creatures, mesmerized by the hypnotic power of the dancing serpent, walk willingly into its jaws and perish. In the same way, I am drawn towards Nandini. You have warned me that she is our sister. I cannot believe it. Yet, there is some mystery surrounding her. I go only to uncover that secret. One way or another, today I will learn the truth.

Whatever my fate may be, there is no blame upon Vandiyathevan. He is carrying out your command faithfully. Sister! That enchantress Nandini has ensnared both Kandhamaaran and Parthibendran in her web, and they have fallen utterly. The only one who escaped without falling into her trap is Vandiyathevan. I do not know what reward to give him. There is a very beautiful woman in this house. She has become as dear to me as my own sister. If I were to arrange for Manimekalai to marry Vandiyathevan, it would be a fitting reward for him. But, sister, I do not know whether you would approve of this or not.

My beloved sister! I am going to entrust this letter to that girl. Fortunately, she cannot read. Do as you wish regarding her! You are the wisest in our family. I have always followed your word. Now I must face the consequences. May our brother Arulmozhi, at least, act according to your counsel and bring the Chola Empire to its greatest glory…”
At this point, the writing stopped. As Kundavai finished reading the letter, tears streamed from her eyes. She quickly wiped them away and looked at Manimekalai.
“Girl! How did this letter come to you? Who gave it to you?” she asked.

“Devi! The prince himself gave it to me. Nandini had spoken so ill of him that at first, I thought he had written me a love letter. I even considered throwing it into the fire and burning it. But then I thought I should see what he had written, so I kept it safe. I gave it to my friend Chandramathi and asked her to read it to me. Now, when I think that I have killed with these hands the brave man who called me his own sister, my heart trembles. Devi! Please, give me whatever punishment is due to a wretch guilty of such a heinous murder!” Manimekalai pleaded.

Her agitation, the way she spoke, and her manner all made it clear that she was imagining this, that she was saying it to save Vandiyathevan. Kundavai understood this well. Yet, the letter she had brought was no fabrication. It was in Karikalan’s own handwriting. This letter alone would be enough to rescue Vandiyathevan from prison and to prevent the terrible charge of murder from falling upon him. If only this girl would keep her mouth shut, it would be most convenient. But how to make her remain silent?
“Manimekalai! Do you still insist that it was you who killed Karikalan?” she asked.
“Yes, Devi!”
“You say you asked him to read this palm-leaf letter. In it, Karikalan refers to you as his own sister by birth. Why would you wish to kill someone who held you in such affection?”
“If I had read the letter beforehand, I would never have committed that dreadful deed. I acted without knowing his heart. That deceitful Nandini had poisoned my mind as well.”
“In what way did she poison you?”

“She kept saying that Karikalan bore hatred towards Vandiyathevan, and that he would not hesitate to kill him. And to match her words, Karikalan would often raise his sword and declare, ‘Where is that Vandiyathevan? I’ll kill him right now!’ I believed it to be true. At once, with the dagger in my hand…”
“Child! Let us leave this talk. Even if I were to believe that the mighty warrior Aditya Karikalan was slain by a helpless woman, the world would never believe it.”
“Devi! Who else could have done it? In the dark chamber where Karikalan’s body lay, only Vandiyathevan and I were present. He did not kill him. Then, must it not have been I?”

“By insisting so, you bring dishonor upon my departed brother. And think of this as well! Do you believe the prince of the Vanar clan would remain silent if you confessed to such a crime? Just as you wish to save him, would he not wish to save you? If you stubbornly declare, ‘I am the one who killed him,’ he too will say, ‘No, I am the one who did it.’ Because you are a woman, perhaps they might forgive you. But they will never forgive him. You know well what terrible punishment awaits traitors who murder royalty, do you not? They will be made to stand at the crossroads and…”
At these words, Manimekalai burst into tears with a wail. Sobbing uncontrollably, she cried, “Akka! Only you can save him!”

chapters.title: The Obstacle to Freedom
paragraphs: Kundavai Piratti pondered how she might console Manimekalai. Her heart, overwhelmed by unbearable sorrow and anxiety, was so troubled that no comforting thought would come to her. At that moment, a great commotion arose at the palace entrance. “Vanathi! Look and see what it is! These people have forgotten even the Emperor’s state of mind and health! How can they make such a clamor?” she exclaimed. Vanathi hurried to the palace front, peered out, and immediately returned in haste. With great excitement, she said, “Akka! He is coming!” “Who do you mean by ‘he’?” Kundavai asked with a smile. “It is him, Akka! Your younger brother!” At once Kundavai said, “Very well, then. Take this girl a little aside for now.” Seeing Vanathi hesitate, the young princess added, “Go quickly! He will not leave without seeing you. I will send for you myself.” Once Vanathi took Manimekalai by the hand and led her away, Ponniyin Selvan arrived at that spot. “My brother! I hear that wherever you go, crowds gather and raise a tumult. Now you have brought them right to the palace gates! If the Emperor, whose heart is wounded and sunk in sorrow, were to hear this uproar, how much pain it would cause him!” she said. “What can I do, Akka! Am I alone free from anguish? Even before Karikalan’s heroic body was reduced to ashes, these people have begun to shout, ‘Crown Arulmozhi!’ This clamor is harsh to my ears. Every moment, I feel like running away without telling anyone. But if I do so, the confusion will only grow greater…” “There is always a lingering fear—will they let me go? If Madurantakan and the petty kings plot together and kill me, the people will believe it without question. The thought of the calamities that might arise from such a belief makes my heart tremble with dread.”

“Yes, yes! Never do such a thing! Cast away even the thought! Let the people think what they may. But the Emperor’s heart would surely break. It is enough that he is already tormented by memories of Mandakini Devi and Karikalan!” said the Younger Princess.

“That is why I hesitate to flee. Somehow, I wish to speak good words to the people and the warriors, and try to win their consent to crown Madurantakan. Whenever I speak, the people listen with careful attention. But the moment I turn away, they resume their old shouts. I come away thinking I have changed their minds, but immediately, the elder of Thirukovalur and the Velar of Kodumbalur go and sway the minds of the soldiers! Akka! It is about them that I came to speak to you. You must summon Malayaman and the Velar and speak to them. No matter what I say, they do not heed me. If you speak, perhaps they will listen…”
“I too have tried to persuade them in every way, Thambi! But I have not been able to change their stubbornness. We must look for some other means…”
“Akka! There is one thing you may not have told the Velar. If you tell him this, perhaps he will not be so obstinate about crowning me.”
“What is that, Thambi?”

“You must tell him about the vow your friend Vanathi has made. Has she not sworn that she will never sit upon the throne with me? If you tell the great Velar about this, perhaps he will not be so insistent on crowning me!”

“Thambi! Did you think I had not told him that? I have already told him. Do you know what he said to that? ‘Would you ruin a great kingdom for the foolishness of a young girl? If not Vanathi, there are a hundred princesses in this land of Bharata waiting to garland Arulmozhi. They would climb the throne if asked, and would even climb a palmyra tree if told!’ Thus spoke the Commander-in-Chief, casting a fierce glance at Vanathi. The poor girl was utterly shaken!”
Arulmozhi Varman smiled and said, “It’s fortunate that I didn’t faint and fall down at that moment!” As he spoke, he glanced all around.
“I have sent Vanathi on an errand,” said the younger princess.
“Akka! If you and Vanathi stand firmly on my side, we might somehow manage this. The two of us can go to the Emperor. These two elders will obey only the Emperor’s strict command…”

“There is an obstacle to that as well, my brother! Isn’t Sembiyan Madevi standing in the way? If she stubbornly insists on the opposite of what we say, what will our father do? Even if his heart is shaken, it will be of no use. That is why I am afraid to trouble the Emperor about this matter.”

“In that case, the two of us must go together and pray to Sembiyan Madevi herself. We must try to change her mind. The reason she is adamant that the crown should not be given to Madurantaka is only what we have guessed. Just a short while ago, I met her at the house of Prime Minister Aniruddha. Today, for the first time, she told Madurantaka the truth. When she said, ‘You are not my son,’ you should have seen our uncle’s face. His beautiful face, usually shining with serenity, changed into the visage of a fierce demon. Fortunately, I arrived at that moment…”
“Is that so? What happened then?” asked Kundavai.

“In front of grandmother, I stood with folded hands and said, ‘Mother! I too know that Madurantaka is not the son born from your womb. But what of it? The beloved son you raised is your son indeed, is he not? Therefore, he should be crowned king.’”
“What did the elder princess Sembiyan Madevi reply to that?”
“Before she could reply, I turned and left.”
“Brother! Even if Madurantaka is not Sembiyan Madevi’s son, doesn’t he have a claim to the Chola throne in another way? Didn’t you say that he too is our father’s son, your brother?”
“I did not say so, Akka!”
“Why, brother! Did you fear it would bring disgrace upon our father? Or did you think you could say it later?”
“No, Akka! The faith that you and I have held onto all these days—I have now realized it was unfounded, and that is why I have not spoken of it…”
“How is that, Thambi?”

“Yes, Akka! The Prime Minister Aniruddhar knows all about it. Our father returned from the island of Eezham, and only two years after that, Madurantakan and Nandini were born as twins. Therefore, it is not possible for them to be our siblings by birth, is it?” said Arulmozhi.
Kundavai sank into thought for a while, then asked, “Arulmozhi! Even knowing this, do you still wish for Madurantakan to receive the crown?”

“Yes, Akka! After all, Madurantakan is the son born of Mandakini Devi’s womb, the child raised by Sembiyan Madevi. I have no desire whatsoever to rule the kingdom. Nor does your friend Vanathi wish to ascend the throne…”

“Thambi! In the Ramayana, Bharata refused the kingdom that came to him and went to bring Rama back. When Guha heard of this, he said, ‘A thousand Ramas would not equal you.’ The people of Chola Nadu are going to say, ‘A thousand Bharatas would not equal you.’”
“Let them say whatever they wish later. For now, all I want is to be left alone, Akka! At last, I have devised a plan and kept it in my heart. I wish to know your opinion about it…”
“What is this plan, Thambi?”
“You know that the Pazhuvettaraiyars are gathering their forces near Kudanthai, don’t you?”

“Yes; I also hear that many minor kings are joining them. But I have heard that their army is quite small. Our grandfather and the Velar say that if we march with the troops stationed here, we can destroy that army in just three-quarters of a naazhikai.”

“I have made this plan precisely to prevent such a thing from happening. Without anyone’s knowledge, I intend to mount a horse and go alone to the Pazhuvettaraiyars and surrender myself to them. They will imprison me. After that, our grandfather Malayaman and Commander-in-Chief Periya Velar will be unable to do anything, will they?”
Kundavai placed her finger on her nose in astonishment and said, “A marvelous plan, Thambi! But even in that, there is a small danger!”
“What is it, Akka?”

“As soon as you reach the army gathered by the Pazhuvettarayars, do you know what the soldiers in that army will do? They will begin to shout, ‘Long live Arulmozhi Varman! The crown belongs to Ponniyin Selvan!’ Instead of imprisoning you, they might even seize the Pazhuvettarayars themselves and throw them into prison!”

Arulmozhi Varman stood stunned for a moment. “Yes; I had not realized that such a danger might arise. It is fortunate that you warned me. Just as I entered this Thanjai fort in disguise, I shall go there too in disguise…”
