“No matter what disguise you wear, how long can the truth remain hidden, Thambi? If even one person finds out, isn’t that enough? In a single hour, everyone will know. The people nearby will gather in crowds!”
Arulmozhi’s face fell. “Akka, then what do you want me to do? Why was I born into this world? Was it only to cause trouble for others? Should I not have died when I fell and drowned in the Kaveri?”

“Thambi! Who can say? Are all the things foretold by astrologers and palm-leaf readers true, or not? Even if you refuse, it seems as if Rajya Lakshmi herself will come and find you. The moment you were born was such!”
“Akka! Have you too joined our grandfather Malayaman? Has your mind changed as well?”

“My mind is not swayed by grandfather’s preaching, Thambi! But my heart has changed a little because of the letter from our brother Karikalan. He has written that you will fulfill all the dreams he has seen. As soon as I read it…” As she spoke, tears welled up in Kundavai’s eyes and her voice trembled.
Ponniyin Selvan took the letter from Aditya Karikalan and read it. Tears fell from his eyes as well.

When he finished reading the letter, Kundavai said, “Thambi! Whatever you may think, I will tell you what is in my heart. My mind has found some peace in knowing that both Madurantakan and Nandini do not truly belong to our Chola dynasty. I have no desire to see someone not born in the Chola clan ascend the Chola throne. To Sembiyan Madevi as well—”
No matter how much devotion I have for Mandakini Devi, I cannot give in so far as to accept this. I can no longer bear, even for a moment, the thought of crowning Madurantakan.”

“Akka! Akka! What are you saying? Before Sembiyan Madevi, before Aniruddhar, before Madurantakan himself, I have declared, ‘I do not want the crown.’ I have said the same before thousands upon thousands of warriors and before the great assemblies of the people. Now, do you ask me to break my word?” asked Arulmozhi Varman.

“Thambi! For both you and me, only our family deity, Durga Parameswari, can show the way. Even I do not know clearly what advice to give you. If Aditya Karikalan had heeded my words, such a situation would never have arisen! Would such a fate have befallen that great hero?” lamented Kundavai.
“How did this palm-leaf letter come into your hands, Akka? Who brought it? When did it reach you? Why did you not tell me earlier?” asked Arulmozhi.
“It came to me only a short while ago. It was brought and given to me by Manimekalai, the daughter of Sambuvarayar.”
“Yes, yes, I have heard of Manimekalai as well. How did this palm-leaf come into her possession?”
“She is here, Thambi! Ask her yourself and find out! Even I do not know how far her words can be believed,” said the young princess.

From the moment Arulmozhi Varman entered, the young princess had resolved to bring Manimekalai before him and have her speak about Vandiyathevan. Amidst all these conversations, her mind was preoccupied with thoughts of Vandiyathevan languishing in the underground dungeon. Kundavai herself did not wish to broach the subject. She had been waiting for a suitable opportunity to summon Manimekalai. Now that the moment had arrived, she called Vanathi and instructed her to bring Manimekalai in.
Manimekalai entered with a face full of sorrow, her eyes brimming with tears. Seeing this, Ponniyin Selvan thought there must be a reason for her grief.
“Thambi! This is the maiden Manimekalai; she is the one who brought the palm-leaf. Ask her yourself how it came into her hands!”

“Sister, you safely brought and handed over the last letter written by our brother. For this, we shall be forever grateful to you!” Arulmozhi Varman had only begun to speak thus, when suddenly Manimekalai fell at his feet and bowed before him.
“Prince! Son of Ponni! Are the words you just spoke true? If you are truly grateful to me…”
She could not continue further; her voice choked, and Manimekalai broke down, sobbing uncontrollably.
“Sister! What is this? Why is this girl weeping so bitterly? Is she grieving because our brother died in her house, perhaps?”
“No, brother! There is something else weighing on her heart. Manimekalai! Tell the prince what you told me!” Princess Kundavai encouraged her gently.
“Sir! I am the sinner who killed your brother. Imprison me in the underground dungeon and set him free!” she cried, weeping all the while.
Arulmozhi Varman looked at Kundavai in astonishment. “Sister! What is she saying? Has this girl lost her mind?”
“She hasn’t lost her mind yet, brother! But if the prince of Vallam is not released from the underground dungeon soon, she might very well lose her mind!” Kundavai replied.
“What? What? Who is in the underground dungeon?” Arulmozhi asked in amazement.
“Have you already forgotten the valiant Vanar clan warrior to whom I sent a letter to Lanka, brother?”
Only then did Arulmozhi Varman appear as one who had just awakened from a long dream and returned to the memories of this world.

Since his entry into the Tanjore fort, one event after another had completely absorbed his attention. After the news of Karikalan’s death arrived, his mind had been wholly occupied with thoughts of how to place Madurantaka on the Chola throne. Concerning Vandiyathevan… Truly, he had forgotten. Now, upon hearing his name, he sprang up and exclaimed, “Who? My dear friend Vandiyathevan is in the underground prison? For what reason? Who has imprisoned him?”
Kundavai recounted to him the details that Manimekalai had shared.

Listening to everything, Ponniyin Selvan said, “Akka! There can be no one more ungrateful than I am. I have failed to inquire about the valorous scion of the Vanar clan. That is my fault! But those who dared to confine him in the underground prison are greater wrongdoers than I. I know how much devotion he has for our brother. Who are those who dared to hold him responsible for Karikalan’s death? What foolishness is this? For this woman to take the blame upon herself in order to save him is a lesson for all of us. I am ashamed even to look upon her. Let all other matters wait. I will go at once to the underground prison and bring Vandiyathevan out. Comfort the daughter of Sambuvarayar!” So saying, he turned and strode away with urgency.

As he reached the threshold, suddenly Thirukovalur Malayaman and Kodumbalur Velar appeared there. Their very presence aroused a certain suspicion in the prince’s mind. The elder Velar placed the staff he carried across the doorway, as if to bar the prince’s passage. Behind him, Malayaman stood ready, his dagger pressed to the ground, prepared to prevent the prince from advancing further.
Ponniyin Selvan, with great astonishment and a touch of anger, said, “Commander! What is this? Are you going to imprison me as well?”
“Prince! At this moment, we are preventing you from going to the underground prison. If necessary, we will even confine you!” said Boothi Vikrama Kesari.

Whether he spoke in earnest or in jest, Ponniyin Selvan could not discern. But he was in no mood to tolerate any jest at that moment. Therefore, in a voice sharper than before, he demanded, “By what authority do you seek to restrain me?”
“By what authority do you intend to release the one held in the underground prison?” retorted the elder Velar.
“Commander! Do I not possess that authority? Have you forgotten who I am? Or have you forgotten yourself?”

“I have not forgotten myself. Nor have I forgotten who you are. Today, I am the commander of the Tanjore fort. Therefore, I am the warden of the underground prison. You are the emperor’s royal son, the beloved of the River Ponni. Yet, you do not have the authority to release a man who has been accused of murdering your elder brother and imprisoned in the underground cell. That authority belongs only to the emperor. Or, to the one who is about to ascend the throne in the emperor’s place. But you yourself have declared that you do not wish to ascend the Chola throne. Therefore, without the emperor’s command, no one can be released from the underground prison!” declared the great Velalar of Kodumbalur, the commander-in-chief, Boothi Vikrama Kesari.

“My child! The Velalar speaks the truth. Since the younger Pazhuvettarayar has fled, the emperor has appointed the great Velalar as the commander of the Tanjore fort. Therefore, you have no authority to release anyone from the underground prison!” agreed Malayaman.
Ponniyin Selvan stood silent, not knowing what reply to give them. The sound of Manimekalai’s sobbing continued to echo.

chapters.title: Vanathi’s Suggestion
paragraphs: Kundavai Devi, who had been standing and listening to the debate between Arulmozhi Varman and the two minor chieftains, now stepped forward and said, “Grandfather! Uncle! Must you stand at the threshold and speak? Come inside! Ponniyin Selvan will not act against your wishes.”

Both Malayaman and the Velar entered. Looking at the young princess, the Velar said, “Lady! If only the prince would consent to ascend the throne, there would be no trouble at all. We are bound to carry out his commands. The Emperor is only waiting for the moment to relinquish the kingdom. He wishes to spend his last days in peace, in the golden palace Karikalan built at Kanchi!”

“Uncle! When you both arrived, I was telling the prince the very same thing. This girl interrupted us with her complaints. Hearing her, the prince’s heart was moved, and he wished to go to the prison and set him free…”
“Who is this girl? Why is she weeping so bitterly?” asked the Velar.
“Do you not know, uncle? She is Manimekalai, the daughter of Sambuvarayar…”

“Oh! She must be weeping, thinking of her father in prison. Do not cry, child! The Emperor has already issued orders to set your father free and bring him here. Parthibendra Pallavan has gone to the underground prison!” said Malayaman.

“Grandfather! She is not worried only about her father. She is anxious about the brave scion of the Vanar clan. Release him. She keeps lamenting, ‘It was I who killed the prince!’” said the young princess.
“Oh! If that is what she claims, then let us take her too and lock her up in the underground prison if she wishes. But we cannot release the prince of Vallam!” said the elder Velar.

Still sobbing, Manimekalai turned to Kundavai and pleaded, “That is all I ask, Princess! Please order them to lock me up wherever he is kept!” The Commander-in-Chief Velar touched his forehead with his finger, pointed it out, and in a soft voice said, “It seems this girl’s mind has become deranged!”

Until now, Vanathi had been silent, but she now interjected, “Periyappa! Manimekalai’s mind is perfectly sound. It is you and the Thirukovalur elder whose minds seem unsteady. The prince Vallavarayan, who is imprisoned, is the dearest friend of Ponniyin Selvan. He was the one who brought Ponniyin Selvan back from Lanka, carrying a letter from the young princess herself. He was the one who earned the complete trust of the brave prince who has now attained the hero’s heaven. Those who accuse him and keep him in prison are the ones whose minds must be disturbed!”

“Ah! When did this girl become so outspoken? Vanathi! Is this what you have learned from the young princess? Have you not yet learned to keep your mouth shut and remain silent before your elders? If you are asked something, you should answer. Otherwise, you must keep your mouth closed!” said Periya Velar.
Malayaman said, “Commander! Why are you angry with this child? She has only voiced what is in the hearts of those present here!”

Kundavai said, “Yes, Uncle! It is not right for you or me to think of sending Vanathi away any longer. Tomorrow, she will ascend the throne as the Empress of the Chola Empire. Then, you and I will have to obey her commands!”

“If only Arulmozhi agrees to this, there would be no trouble at all, would there? On the day of the coronation, he could order the release of all those imprisoned in the underground dungeons,” said Malayaman.
“He could also order that you, me, and all those outside be thrown into the underground dungeons!” retorted the Commander-in-Chief, Periya Velar.

“Sirs! You are both elders. I regret that I must speak against you. Yet, instead of attending to the urgent matters at hand, you are talking about all sorts of other things!” said the prince, but before he could finish, the Commander-in-Chief interrupted, “Prince! Is it not the most urgent matter to determine the rightful heir to the Chola throne and prevent any confusion?”
“You seem to have forgotten that there is already an emperor!” said Arulmozhi.

“We have not forgotten. Only a short while ago, we saw the Emperor and returned. He is the one who, having resolved the issue of the kingdom, wishes to leave everything behind and go reside in the golden palace built by Karikalan in Kanchipuram.”
“Then, I shall go to the Emperor myself. I will obtain an order for Vandiyathevan’s release and bring it back. After that, you will have no objections, will you?”

“Prince! It is not appropriate for you to mention Vandiyathevan to the Emperor now. The Emperor believes that Vandiyathevan, in collusion with the Pandya assassins and Nandini Devi, must have been the one who killed Karikalan…”
“Ah! Who planted such a thought in his mind?”
“Not us, Prince! It was Parthibendran who instilled that suspicion in the Emperor…”
“In that case, I will go see Parthibendra Pallavan myself. I shall ask him on what basis he makes such an accusation.”

“You cannot meet Parthibendra Pallavan now. With the Emperor’s orders, he has released Sambuvarayar and gone to Kudanthai. There, he is to meet the Pazhuvettarayars and the other minor kings, speak with them, and immediately bring them back, as the Emperor has commanded. He has sent word that a compromise can be reached regarding the royal succession. He has also conveyed his willingness to crown Madurantakan.”
With a brightening face, Ponniyin Selvan looked at the young princess and Vanathi, and said, “You have brought very good news.”

“There is nothing good about it at all. If Madurantakan ascends the Chola throne against the wishes of the people and the counsel of the warriors, then from that day, the era of destruction will begin for the Chola Empire, which has flourished in glory for a hundred years,” said the Commander-in-Chief.
“There is no doubt about that; from Eelam to the northern banks of the Pennai river, confusion and rebellion will erupt,” said Malayaman.
“It seems the two of you are ready to lead all that, if you so wish. In the meantime, I will go to the Emperor and try to secure Vandiyathevan’s release!” said Arulmozhi Varman, turning to leave.
“Prince! You must not go to the Emperor with this request. It will lead to great disaster, my lady! Please restrain your brother!” said the Commander-in-Chief, Periya Velar.
“Yes, child! Listen to the words of this old man!” said Miladudaiyar.
“What disaster do you think will happen because of this?” asked Kundavai.

“Some miscreants have started a false rumor. I am ashamed even to utter it. Two men came to our soldiers yesterday and claimed that Ponniyin Selvan, out of desire for the throne, sent Vandiyathevan to kill Karikalan…”
“Heavens! What a terrible slander is this?” exclaimed the young princess Kundavai.
“Do you know what our soldiers did to those two? They were beating them and dragging them towards the Vadavaru flood. I happened to go there by chance and saved them…”
Ponniyin Selvan interrupted, “No one in Chola country will ever believe such a cruel accusation. Doesn’t our soldiers’ reaction itself show that?”

“They may not believe it today, Prince! But you do not know the nature of the people. After some time, this rumor will rise again. Some who do not know you may come to believe it. In foreign lands, it is quite common for royal relatives to kill each other for the throne. You know the history of the royal family of Eelam, don’t you?”
“Commander! Are you asking me to leave my dearest friend in the underground dungeon today, simply because a false rumor might spread in the future?”

“Not in the future, Prince! If you show eagerness for Vandiyathevan’s release today, by tomorrow some will start believing that rumor. It will reach the Emperor’s ears as well. Think how much pain that will cause your father’s heart!”
Ponniyin Selvan’s face became like a full moon hidden by a dark cloud. He turned to Kundavai and asked, “Akka! What do you say?”
The young princess’s face showed deep anguish. She looked at Periya Velar and asked, “Commander! Who could be trying to spread such a cruel rumor?”

“In the Vadavaru, I took aside those among our soldiers who had been rescuing people from drowning, and questioned them both kindly and sternly. They said it was Kandhamaaran, the son of Sambuvaraiyar, who had sent them with such instructions.”

At that moment, Manimekalai stepped forward and said, “I am ashamed because of my brother’s actions. My brother, who was once a good man, has become a villain only because of the teachings of the Younger Queen of Pazhuvoor. In truth, it is I who killed Aditya Karikalan. Arrest me! Release Vallavaraiyar at once!” Her words burst forth in a torrent of anger and tears.

The Younger Princess gently touched her back and said, “Manimekalai! Be calm! No one will believe what you say. Moreover, it will only provoke further slander. We can find a way to resolve this confusion.”

Then, turning to the Commander-in-Chief, she said, “Sir! My brother and I both acknowledge your wisdom. It is true that if we try to release Vallavaraiyar now, it will give rise to needless rumors. We must first find the real culprit. I will consult with Prime Minister Aniruddha about this. His disciple, Azhwarkkadiyan, has gone in search of the Pandya assassins. He may bring back some information. We still do not know what has become of Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar and the Younger Queen of Pazhuvoor. If they are found, the truth may come to light. In the meantime, I will question this girl and learn all that happened at Kadambur! Until then, make arrangements for Vallavaraiyar to be kept comfortably in the underground prison. It is certain that he did not commit this terrible murder!” she declared.
At this moment, the Princess of Kodumbalur said, “I have an idea, Akka!”
“Speak, Vanathi!” said Kundavai.
“Do you remember, once before, you and I went to the underground prison together? Let us all go there today as well. Let us take the Kadambur Princess with us!” said Vanathi.
Kundavai turned to Periya Velar and asked, “Commander! What do you think of your daughter’s suggestion?”

“It seems my daughter can speak wisely too. On the night Karikalan died, Vallavaraiyar was the one with him in that very place. If we question him, the truth may come to light,” replied Commander Periya Velar.

Immediately, they all proceeded to the underground prison. Even before the Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar left the fortress, he had ordered the cessation of the minting of gold coins. Therefore, the mint stood deserted. Only a few guards remained. Passing beyond the place where the tigers were kept confined, they entered through the secret tunnel and reached the room where Vallavaraiyan Vandiyathevan was imprisoned.

But there, they did not find Vandiyathevan! In his room, fastened to the rings fixed on the wall with iron chains, they found the physician’s son, Pinagapani. As soon as he saw them, he cried out in pitiful tones, “Ayyo! Ayyo! Please release me, release me!”

chapters.title: Pinagapani’s Work
paragraphs: Pinagapani, the physician’s son, had resolved that he would one day rise to a high office in the government. Ever since the day he encountered Vandiyathevan, this ambition had taken root in his heart, sprouting and growing ever taller. In the past, he had not found much success in the ventures he had undertaken. It had seemed as if Nandini Devi had shown him a little kindness, but later the Queen of Pazhuvur had completely forgotten him. When he went to see Princess Kundavai, she did not even deign to speak to him properly. At the gates of the palace at Pazhayarai, when he accused Vandiyathevan of being a spy, all he got in return was a beating—there was no profit in it for him.

But when the Chief Minister Aniruddha summoned him and sent him to Kodikkarai with the task of bringing the Queen back, Pinagapani decided that his rise to high office was now certain. If only he could carry out this mission successfully, there would be nothing he could not attain through the Chief Minister’s favor. After that, his first order of business would be to deal with Vandiyathevan. Then he would humble and subdue the pride of Poonguzhali.

Building such castles in the air, Pinagapani set out for Kodikkarai. There, he slowly won over Rakkammal. She was deceived by him, believing him to be a member of the rescue group, and spoke to him about their efforts. With her help, he found the mute queen and brought her as far as the gates of Tanjore fort.

Throughout this journey, Pinagapani’s mind was constantly at work. He tried to uncover the secrets concerning the mute queen. He recalled the words of the madman he had met when he was once imprisoned in the underground dungeon. At the time, he had dismissed them as the ravings of a lunatic, but now he began to think there might be truth in what the madman had said.

When the palanquin carrying the mute queen neared the Tanjore fort, was it not then that the storm and rain struck and a tree fell upon him? After the wounds from that accident had healed, he went to see Chief Minister Aniruddha. By then, many important events had already occurred. The mute queen had given her life to save the emperor. Karikalan had been murdered. The entire land was in turmoil over who would ascend the throne next. had come under the control of the Kodumbalur Velar within the Tanjore fort. News spread that the Pazhuvettarayar and the minor kings allied with him were gathering their armies. Signs appeared that a great civil war might erupt.

In such a turbulent situation, Pinagapani, the physician’s son, went to see the Prime Minister Aniruddha Brahmarayar. Immersed in a sea of grave worries, Anbil Brahmarayar did not wish to spend much time conversing with Pinagapani. Since the task he had assigned had already been accomplished by the young man, he wanted to reward him and send him away quickly.

But when Pinagapani began to speak about the madman he had met in the underground dungeon, the minister’s interest turned toward him. When he heard that the madman knew the whereabouts of the ancient Pandya kingdom’s jeweled crown and the gem-studded necklace said to have been gifted by Devendra, Aniruddha’s curiosity was greatly piqued. Ever since the time of Emperor Parantaka, many had tried in vain to find and retrieve that crown and necklace. As long as those treasures remained unfound, there would always be someone claiming descent from the Pandya dynasty, rising up to stake a claim.

Aniruddha had already heard from Alwarkadiyan about the midnight drama at Thiruppurambiyam, where a small boy was seated on the Pandya throne and crowned in secret. From time to time, such claimants would arise. The kings of Lanka and the Chera rulers would aid them. If the Pandya country was ever to be formally merged with the Chola Empire, it was necessary that the Chola Emperor himself be crowned in Madurai. At that grand occasion, the Chola Emperor must wear the ancient Pandya crown and the gem-studded necklace.

All these were plans Aniruddha had long since resolved upon. That was why, whenever a Chola commander set out on a campaign to Lanka, Aniruddha would instruct him to search for and bring back the jeweled crown and necklace. Until now, none had succeeded in this task. Now, upon hearing that a man in the underground prison knew their whereabouts, it was only natural that Aniruddha Brahmarayar’s interest was aroused.

The physician’s son brought yet another piece of news. This increased the Prime Minister’s curiosity, but also filled him with anxiety. Pinagapani reported that the madman claimed to know a great secret about the Chola dynasty, and that one of the princes who claimed rights to the Chola throne was, in truth, not of Chola blood at all.

Hearing all this, Aniruddhar at first thought to go himself to the underground prison to see that madman. But then he changed his mind. If he went there, questions would arise—why, for what reason? Neither Malayaman nor the Velaar had complete trust in Aniruddhar. They believed that, according to the Emperor’s wishes, he supported the faction of Madurantakan. If he were to go to the underground prison, it would only give rise to new suspicions in their minds. They might even think he had gone to see Sambuvaraiyar. After carefully considering this matter, Aniruddhar decided to make use of the physician’s son instead. He gave him his signet ring and instructed him to go to the underground prison and see that madman.

Thus, Pinagapani went to see the madman. When he saw that Vandiyathevan was locked up in the adjacent cell, he was filled with delight. Standing at the doorway of that cell for a moment, he tried to converse with Vandiyathevan. But Vandiyathevan did not speak to him. Angered by this, Pinagapani scolded him thoroughly and went to the next cell. In truth, Pinagapani realized that the man was not mad at all. Then he questioned him about the Pandya country’s jeweled crown and the gem-studded necklace. The so-called madman immediately fell silent. He refused to speak about the secret of the Chola dynasty. “First, bring me an order for my release! Only then will I speak!” he declared.

Returning, Pinagapani reported his failure to the Chief Minister. He insisted that if the man were released and brought out, something useful could surely be gained. The Chief Minister too found this reasonable. In a situation where there was such confusion regarding the right to the throne, it was not wise to keep a dangerous secret-bearer like that madman in prison. He decided the man should be brought to his own palace and the truth discovered. Accordingly, he sought out the Kodumbalur Velaar and, in a certain manner, conveyed this message to him.

The great Velaar had no objection to releasing the prisoner who had been locked up years ago by Chinna Pazhuvetarayar, as per the wish of the Chief Minister. Therefore, he wrote the order for the release of the madman.

Taking this order with pride, Pinagapani went to the underground prison. First, he stood at the doorway of Vandiyathevan’s cell and declared that he had brought an order for his release. Vandiyathevan, believing it to be true, began to thank him. Immediately, Pinagapani revealed his true nature. After thoroughly insulting Vandiyathevan, he sneered, “Your release will be at the crossroads, at the foot of the gallows tree!” Then he proceeded to the next cell.
He spoke gently with the madman. He loosened the chains that had bound him to the wall. “Here, I have brought you an order for your release. Will you tell me your secrets now, at least?” he asked.

Before taking him to the Prime Minister Aniruddha, the physician’s son wished to learn those secrets himself. The madman did not appear particularly excited about his release. He did not seem eager to leave, nor did he seem to place much trust in Pinagapani’s words. “What? What is it? Who gave the order? Is it certain that I will be freed from prison? Will they let me go outside the fort?” he kept asking.

Suddenly, a few stones fell from the wall beside them. When Pinagapani turned to see what had happened, he found Vandiyathevan standing behind him. Pinagapani hastily drew the dagger tucked into his waistband. Vandiyathevan sprang upon him and seized him tightly by the neck, knocking the dagger from his hand. The two of them rolled on the ground, locked in fierce combat for a few moments. At that instant, the madman picked up one of the chains hanging from the wall and looped it around Pinagapani’s neck, pulling it tight…

chapters.title: “The Madman”
paragraphs: During the first part of the journey from Kadambur to Thanjavur, Vandiyathevan was, for the most part, in a state of unconsciousness. He had been bound and placed in a wooden cart. The smoke and fire from the night when Karikalan lost his life had tormented him greatly. Whenever he regained a little awareness during the journey, the burning in his eyes and the pain in his body caused him unbearable agony. In that half-conscious state, terrifying visions appeared before him and tormented his mind.

The head of Veera Pandiyan alone would come close to his face and say, “Hey! Is it you who stands in the way of my vengeance?”—and then glare at him in anger. Sometimes, Nandini would stand before him, adorned in jewels and finery, smiling sweetly, trying to ensnare him in her web of illusion. At other times, she would appear disheveled, weeping and lamenting. In yet another vision, she would take on a ghostly form and laugh menacingly.

A shadowy figure, following Aditya Karikalan, would approach with a dagger in hand. Whenever Vandiyathevan tried to leap forward to stop it, another monstrous shadow would come from behind and seize him by the neck, choking him. Ravidasan and his companions would then lift him and throw him into a blazing fire. As his body burned, Kandanmaran would look at him and say, “Hey, traitor to friendship! You deserve this!” Parthibendran would look at him too and ask, “Hey! Has your marriage to the young princess Kundavai been fixed? When is the auspicious day?”—and then laugh thunderously.
Sendhan Amudhan would come running from somewhere to rescue him from the fire. Pinagapani, the physician’s son, would hide behind a tree and strike Sendhan Amudhan on the head with a heavy stick.

As his entire body burned, Vandiyathevan was seized by an unbearable thirst. He wanted to cry out, “Water! Water!” but no sound emerged. His throat was parched, his tongue swollen and stuck to his palate, rendering him speechless. In this state, Manimekalai appeared, carrying divine nectar in a golden goblet, and poured it into his mouth. Before he could even think to thank her, she vanished into the darkness!… Ah, for her love, one could offer all three worlds in return! But what folly it is to think of giving Manimekalai the three worlds, when he did not even possess a span of land to call his own? Look, there is Poonguzhali! “See my lovers!” she says, pointing out the fire-mouthed demons. What a wondrous woman she is! “Why do you wander in this earthly realm? Come, I will take you to the golden world!” she calls.

“You mean the world where Ponniyin Selvan dwells?” asks Vandiyathevan. At once, the fire-mouthed demons gather from all directions and surround him. Vandiyathevan, seized by fear, closes his eyes. The demons bind him, lift him up, carry him away, climb the sandy mound of the riverbank, and roll him down…

Vandiyathevan starts and opens his eyes in alarm. He realizes that guards holding torches have placed him in a boat. He does not know which river this is—perhaps the Kollidam, or the Kaveri, or the Kudamurutti… Even as he wonders, darkness falls again, clouding his senses.

After countless such bewildering experiences, suddenly he hears a sound like the roaring of seven seas in turmoil. A great wave crashes over him, submerging him. Now, with full awareness, Vandiyathevan opens his eyes. Not far ahead, he sees the gates of Thanjavur fort. Bound and lying on a wooden cart, he sees before and behind him, and on all sides, a sea of people. The tumultuous cry of that multitude is what had seemed to him like the roaring of seven seas. He realizes that such a crowd has gathered because the final procession of Aditya Karikalan is approaching the Thanjai fort.

Soon, the entire crowd disperses from that place. Only he, Sambuvarayar, and a few guards remain, and they are led into the Thanjai fort. Ah! When the final rites of that great warrior are performed, he, who was once the prince’s closest companion, cannot even be near. Is this the extent of his misfortune? After all his efforts to protect the prince’s life till the very end, and failing, he is now accused of murdering him! It was he who ensured that the prince’s body, instead of being consumed by the fire at Kadambur palace, received the honors due to a great hero, with the homage of a vast multitude.

Yet now, he is being taken to the underground prison where murderers and traitors are confined. What does it matter if he is taken there? Soon, the young princess and Ponniyin Selvan will inquire about him. When they learn he has been imprisoned, they will be alarmed. Immediately, the prison’s… They would come running with the key and set him free. Even if he had failed to save Karikalan’s life, they would come to know of all the efforts he had made on his behalf and praise him for it...

But would they truly praise him? Would they even remember him? Those who had lost their brother—wouldn’t they, in that grief, forget everything else? Even if he declared his innocence, would they believe him? And even if they believed, would they ever again show him the same friendship and affection as before?

As he was led through the gold coin mint towards the underground prison, Vandiyathevan’s hope dwindled with every step. Chinna Pazhuvettarayar had already closed the mint not long before. Along that path, only a few guards stood here and there. They did not wear the swords engraved with the palmyra emblem. The old jailers of Kodumbalur Velar had all been dismissed, and new guards, loyal to Pazhuvettarayar, had been stationed there. The two new prisoners were eyed with suspicion and hostility. Vandiyathevan overheard them whispering to each other, “That one is Kadambur Sambuvaraiyan; this one is Vandiyathevan of the Vanar clan—the scoundrels who killed the prince.”

As they were led through the chamber where the tiger cages stood, those cages seemed to Vandiyathevan like symbols of the Chola kings’ martial mercy. Again, they were taken down a flight of steps and Vandiyathevan was locked alone in a cell. When the guards left, all hope deserted him. He felt certain he would never leave that place alive. Only his corpse, perhaps, would be carried out after his death.

Chinna Pazhuvettarayar already harbored suspicions about him. Parthibendran, for his part, felt nothing but hatred towards him. The old Malayaman trusted only Parthibendran’s word. The Pazhuvettarayars, out of regard, would soon declare Sambuvaraiyan innocent and set him free. But who would take the trouble to secure his own release? No one. They would simply accuse him of murder. Would they hold a public inquiry? If they did, perhaps he could try to tell the truth. No, no! They would not conduct any inquiry. If they did, the truth about Nandini and Ravidasan’s group might come to light. No one would want that. They would let him rot and die in that prison. Or, without any inquiry, they would declare him the murderer of Karikalan and take him to the crossroads to hang him from the gallows.

Oh God! What enthusiasm had surged within him when he first set out for Thanjai? What daydreams had he woven in his mind? Above all, ever since he had met the young princess Kundavai and Vanathi at the house of the Kudanthai astrologer, what a sea of exhilaration he had been floating in as he came to this Thanjai! At that time, he had feared that the younger Pazhuvettarayar might suspect him of being a spy and throw him into the underground dungeon. Now, that very fear had come true, though in a different manner! Like a bird that had been soaring joyously through the open sky, he was now locked inside this dark chamber! How long could he possibly endure this? Impossible! Impossible! He must quickly find some way to end his life… Thus, lost in such thoughts, overcome by anguish and helplessness, Vandiyathevan sat there, unmoving.
At that moment, he heard someone clearing their throat in the adjacent cell. After a short while, a harsh voice began to sing:
“O golden-hued one…!”

It was a line from a Thevaram hymn. At once, Vandiyathevan remembered Sendhan Amudhan. But it was not he who sang. Sendhan Amudhan’s voice possessed a divine sweetness. The voice singing now was harsh and grating. Yet, why was someone in this underground dungeon singing that very same song?
Shiva, Shiva! It was unbearable to listen to. As if being imprisoned in this dungeon was not punishment enough, must he also suffer this strange music?
“Who’s there, sir?” called out Vandiyathevan.
“It is I—the madman!” came the reply.
“Sir! Madman! Have mercy and stop your singing!”
“Why? Don’t you like my song?”
“How could I not? I like your song very, very much!”
“Will you like it even more if I stop singing?”
“You don’t seem much like a madman to me. Who taught you that song?”
“Some time ago, another young man was in the cell you’re in now. He stayed only a few days. During that time, he sang this song ceaselessly! It became a lesson to me,” he replied.

Vandiyathevan immediately concluded that the young man was indeed Sendhan Amudhan. He had heard that Chinna Pazhuvettraraiyar had imprisoned Sendhan Amudhan in the underground dungeon for a few days to aid his own escape. Surely, the one who had been in this cell must be him. Ah! What a golden-hearted youth Sendhan Amudhan was! What a remarkable friend!
“Who was the young man who stayed in this cell for a few days? Do you know?” he asked.
“How could I not know? His name is Sendhan Amudhan. They say he’s the son of a mute woman! But if the world were to learn who he truly is…?”
“What would happen if they did?”
“The whole world would be turned upside down!”
“If the world is turned upside down, will we gain our freedom from this underground prison?”
“Most certainly, we will.”
“In that case, shall I tell you who he is?”
“Would I reveal it to you so easily? I would whisper that secret only into the ears of the Chola Emperor! Is it not still Sundara Chozhar who reigns as the Emperor of the Chola land?” he asked.
“Yes; what doubt do you have about that?”

“A few days ago, some changes took place here. All the old prison guards were replaced by new ones. The gold coin mint was shut down. When it was open, the sound of the maidens working there could be heard without pause.”
“Why did they close it? Why were the guards changed?”

“They say Chinna Pazhuvettraraiyar fled from his post as the fortress guard. They say the Kodumbalur Velar has seized control of the Thanjai fort. I learned these things from the conversations among the guards…”
“Oh! Is that so?” exclaimed Vandiyathevan, genuinely astonished.

Kodumbalur Boothi Vikrama Kesari was a man who had tested and known him well. Would he, perhaps, believe his words and grant him freedom? But how could that be possible? Who would easily release one accused of murdering Prince Karikalan?
Can you set me free?
“What’s this, brother? Have you fallen silent? Shall I begin singing again?” The madman thundered, his voice echoing through the stone.
“No, no! I was just thinking about what you said. You claimed that Sendhan Amudhan is not the son of the mute woman, didn’t you? Then who could he be? That’s what I’m pondering.”
“Leave that topic aside and talk about something else.”
“Why do you call yourself a madman?”
“Because everyone who comes here calls me mad.”
“Why do they all say that?”

“I know where the Pandya dynasty’s bejeweled crown and the gem-studded necklace given by Devendran are hidden in Eezham. I tell everyone who comes here that if they set me free, I’ll reveal where those treasures are. That’s why they call me mad!”
“Those who call you mad are the real lunatics.”
“Do you believe my words?”
“I believe you completely; but what use is my belief? I can’t do anything to help you, can I?”
“Don’t say that! It’s become customary for everyone who is locked up in the room you’re in now to be freed soon,” he said.
“What custom is that? Let’s hear some examples.”

“There was a physician’s son, one called Pinagapani, who was locked up in your room. The queen of Pazhuvoor, Nandini Devi herself, came and set him free and took him away. In that very room, Sendhan Amudhan was once imprisoned. Kundavai Devi and the princess of Kodumbalur came and released him.”
Vandiyathevan let out a long, heavy sigh. “No queen or princess is going to come and set me free like that!” he said.
“In that case, I myself will set you free,” said the man in the next cell.
“Now you’re truly talking like a madman!” said Vandiyathevan.
“No, will you trust my word?”
“There is no other way; I have no choice but to trust you.”
“In that case, wait patiently until tonight, until the guards come and give us food and leave!” said the one known as the Madman.

chapters.title: “The Miracle of Faith”
paragraphs: That night, after the last watchman had come and gone, Vandiyathevan waited anxiously to find out what the madman in the next room was going to say. From one side of that room’s wall, he heard a noise, as if a rat were gnawing at it.

Vandiyathevan had no fear of tigers or lions. But he was afraid of cats and rats. He worried whether he would have to spend the whole night in that dark room with rats for company. Troubled by this thought, he called out, “Madman! Have you fallen asleep?”
There was no reply. Only the faint sound of the rat’s gnawing continued.
After a while, a few stones fell from the wall, and an opening appeared. Through it, the madman’s voice asked, “Hey there, have you fallen asleep?”
“No, I haven’t slept. I’m waiting for you. What is this work you’re doing?” Vandiyathevan replied.

“This is a task of six months. Before that, it took me six months just to break my handcuffs,” said the madman. After a short while, he made the opening in the wall even larger and entered Vandiyathevan’s room.
After helping him down, Vandiyathevan asked, “You’ve gone through so much trouble to make a hole in this wall—what’s the use? Wouldn’t it be better to make a hole in the outer wall?”

“There is no such thing as an outer wall from here. One can only get out through the tiger’s cage room. Sometimes, this room is left empty and unlocked. So, escaping from here is easier than from my own room.”
“You’ve revealed all this to me, a stranger who just arrived today, trusting me. What will you do if I betray you?”

“One can tell from a man’s voice whether to trust him or not. I would trust Sendhan Amudhan, but never Pinagapani. From your voice, I decided I could trust you. Besides, if the escape is to happen, it must happen now. This is the right moment!” “Why is that?”

“I told you, didn’t I, that the guards have been changed? I overheard two of them talking. They were discussing opening the tiger’s cage. ‘What if, when we open the cage, the tiger leaps upon us?’ one of them asked. To that, the other replied, ‘Then we must die!’ From this, it’s certain they will not dare open the tiger’s cage. Since they are new guards, I thought I might suddenly spring upon them and escape. In any case, isn’t it better to make an attempt at freedom than to lie here and die?”
“That’s true!”

“It’s easier for two to attempt this than for one alone. You’re not like me; you’re newly arrived and seem strong and sturdy. The two of us could tie up the guards, snatch the keys from them, and escape, couldn’t we?”
“That’s a good idea. When shall we set out?”
“Wait a bit; I’ll tell you when the right moment comes.”
“I’m very tired too. Even if it takes a day or two, it’s all right.”

Afterwards, that madman questioned Vandiyathevan about all the important events that had taken place in the outside world during his time in prison. When he heard that Aditya Karikalan had died, he exclaimed, “Ah! Then it is all the more important that we escape now!”
“Why do you say that?”
“Because someone must be crowned as the next heir to the throne, mustn’t they?”
“Heir to the throne? The Emperor is afflicted by illness and weighed down by sorrow. He wishes to relinquish the burdens of rule entirely!”
“Who is being discussed for the crown?”
“Some of the minor princes wish to crown Madurantaka! Others wish to place the crown upon Ponniyin Selvan!”
“What is the Emperor’s opinion?”
“To prevent unnecessary conflict in the kingdom, it seems the Emperor wishes for Madurantaka to ascend the throne.”
“In that case, it is absolutely necessary for us to leave here as soon as possible!” exclaimed that madman.

Then, he began to describe in detail how he had come to know the location of the Pandya crown and the jeweled necklace in the land of Eezham. When Vandiyathevan once again inquired about the secret of the Chola dynasty, he replied, “I will not tell you that now. If both of us manage to escape from here alive, I will reveal it. Otherwise, that secret must die with me!”

Vandiyathevan’s mind plunged into intense thought. He tried to guess what kind of secret such a madman might possess. Many shadowy memories flickered across the screen of his mind, appearing and vanishing.

Suddenly, when he caught sight of the physician’s son, Vandiyathevan was startled. He worried that the man in the next room and he, together, might have their plans thwarted by this newcomer. He did not trust Pinagapani’s deceitful words. He and the madman were of one mind in this matter. They had decided that Pinagapani had come with some evil intention. They swore that neither would leave the other behind in the prison and escape alone. They also resolved what to do if Pinagapani returned.

Therefore, when Pinagapani came a second time, both of them were on their guard. While the physician’s son was showing the signet ring to the madman and urging him to reveal his secret, Vandiyathevan silently slipped into the room through a door already made in the wall between the two chambers. As Pinagapani turned to attack him, the two engaged in a fierce struggle. At another time, Vandiyathevan would have defeated the physician’s son in an instant. But the burns on his body had not yet fully healed, and the place where the Kalamukha demon had gripped his throat was still aching, so the struggle dragged on. At that moment, the madman came with a chain in his hand and looped it around Pinagapani’s neck, tightening it. Pinagapani fell to the ground.

After that, the two of them tied him to the iron rings fixed in the walls of the room. While they were binding him thus, Vandiyathevan said, “Pinagapani! The two of us are searching for the Sanjeevani herb in order to cure the Emperor— “Do you remember when we went to the countryside? At that time, we did not succeed in bringing the Sanjeevani. But now, you yourself have come to us as a ‘religious Sanjeevani’! Many thanks for this help. As the son of a physician, it would be better for you to remain with your medical profession from now on. Why do you unnecessarily buy trouble for yourself by meddling in the work of a spy?” he said.

Pinagapani did not reply to this. Struck speechless by the suddenness of the disaster that had befallen him, he stood silent. Yet, in the light of the torch he had brought and placed on the ground, it was clear that his eyes alone blazed with the fire of anger.
Then, both of them took hold of the signet ring that the physician’s son had brought. Pinagapani removed the cloth that was wrapped around his head, and Vandiyathevan wound it around his own.

They came out of that room and locked the door behind them. Then, walking softly, they climbed the steps leading up from the underground prison. Not knowing the way well, they proceeded cautiously, glancing here and there as they went. When they heard the roar of tigers, both of them hesitated a little to go further. Perhaps, having somehow learned of their escape, someone had released the tiger from its cage!

Vandiyathevan and the madman peered carefully into the tiger-cage room. At that moment, there was only a single guard in the room. He was staring intently at the cage where the tigers were roaring. Was he perhaps thinking of opening the cage and setting the tigers upon them?

At that moment, the physician’s son had begun to shout. That shout might have aroused the guard’s suspicion, might it not? How great a mistake it was not to have gagged Pinagapani’s mouth before leaving!

chapters.title: Liberation
paragraphs: Vandiyathevan stood hesitantly for a while near the threshold, weighed down by anxiety. For a moment, he considered whether he should leap upon the guard—who stood there twirling his moustache, eyeing the tigers—and subdue him, tie him up, and make his way forward. But beyond the cages of the tigers, he could see two more guards stationed at the next entrance. One of them signaled something to this guard and then moved on. Were they, perhaps, speaking in gestures about him? Even if he managed to overpower and escape this guard, there would be many such entrances ahead, each with its own sentry. Would it be possible to overcome them all and escape? Would it not be easier, instead, to make a single bold leap, open the tiger cages, and, in the ensuing chaos, slip away unnoticed?

As these thoughts ran through his mind, the guard said, “Oh ho! Are you thinking of escaping?” Vandiyathevan started for a moment at these words. One of the tigers growled. “Hey, you dog! Lie still!” the guard shouted harshly.
When Vandiyathevan realized that the man was speaking to the tiger, he smiled. The guard turned and looked at him.
“Look here, sir! This tiger is trying to threaten me. I have seen plenty of tigers like this! This lion’s pride will not be humbled by it,” he said, twirling his moustache once more.

Vandiyathevan replied, “As long as it’s inside the cage, a tiger and a rat are one and the same! How can its pride be humbled?” With these words, he displayed the signet of the great Velar in his hand.

“Go on, sir, go on! The Prime Minister’s men are waiting for you at the entrance! Hurry up!” said the guard, and then, turning towards the direction they had come from, he shouted, “Hey, madman! Will you never keep quiet?”

At that moment, Vandiyathevan was holding the madman’s hand. Sensing the tremor in his companion’s hand, he gripped it tighter to give him courage. Then, both of them passed the guard and moved forward. As they did, they heard the guard mutter, “Everyone wants liberation, liberation! If we set everyone free, what will become of our livelihood?”

Even though Vandiyathevan was a man of great courage, at that moment his heart was pounding “pak, pak” within his chest. The words of the guard—that the Prime Minister’s men were waiting at the entrance—remained etched in his mind. It was dark inside the prison; because of this, it would be easy to deceive the guards here and slip away. But outside, there would be light, wouldn’t there? What would happen if the Prime Minister’s men discovered this exchange of identities? Still, let’s try our luck! One must be prepared for anything! Fortunately, this madman is a clever madman; he will lend a hand at the right moment!…

After passing through several gates of the underground prison, they hurried past the doors of the gold coin minting hall as well. The guards stationed here and there, upon seeing the insignia of the Velar in their possession, stepped aside and gave way. No one suspected them. No one scrutinized them closely. As they walked, Vandiyathevan, his mind racing, devised a plan for himself. As they were proceeding through a long corridor, his companion whispered in his ear, “Are you going to the Prime Minister’s house? Or will you come with me?”
“If I go to the Prime Minister’s house, it will be back to the underground prison again! I’ll come with you! But where do you intend to go?”
“If God’s grace is with us, we might even go to Eezha Nadu! In front of the Prime Minister’s men, call me ‘Pinagapani!’ What is your name?”
“Madman!”
“Your real name! The name your parents gave you?”
“Oh, that? My parents named me ‘Kariya Thirumal.’ Relatives and townsfolk called me ‘Karuthiruman!’”
“A fine name! Karuthiruma! As we walk through the streets of Thanjai, I will touch your shoulder. At once, you must be ready to run away with me. You can run well, can’t you?”
“Oh! Even Mahindan, the king of Eezham, could not compete with me in running!”
Vandiyathevan laughed. “You are truly a madman!…” he said.
They crossed the gold coin minting hall and stepped outside.

To Vandiyathevan’s relief, there were not many of the Prime Minister’s men there. Only two of them. One was a stout fellow, and Vandiyathevan felt as if he had seen him somewhere, sometime before; but he could not clearly remember. I do not remember.
“Aren’t you the men of the Prime Minister?” asked Vandiyathevan.
“What, brother? Have you forgotten already?” said one of them.
“No, no! You are the ones who are supposed to take us to the Prime Minister’s house, aren’t you?” said Vandiyathevan.
“Yes, it’s us! Even if you forget the way to the Prime Minister’s house, you’ll still get there!”
At that moment, Karuthiruman, recalling what Vandiyathevan had said, spoke up, “Ayyo, Pinagapani! I am afraid! What if the Prime Minister throws me into the underground dungeon again?”

“That won’t happen, father! It seems you don’t know our Prime Minister’s nature. But just don’t try to escape! If you do anything like that, we’ll be the ones who end up in the underground dungeon!” he said.
Saying this, the stouter of the two men walked ahead. The other followed behind Vandiyathevan and Karuthiruman, acting as their guard.

There was no bustle in the streets of Thanjavur. There was no crowd. After the disturbances caused by the funeral rites of Aditya Karikalan had subsided, those living within the fort had returned to their respective duties. Outside the fort, the Kodumbalur troops were keeping strict watch. No one was allowed to enter from outside the fort. Vandiyathevan walked on, carefully observing both sides. It would be very easy to escape from these two men. But he must not be caught again. He must also have a way to get out of the fort. With these thoughts, Vandiyathevan scrutinized both sides of the street as he walked.

Once they passed the gateway of Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar’s palace, Vandiyathevan’s excitement increased. That lane was coming up! The very same lane from which he had once escaped from the men of Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar! He had been expecting it. That winding lane had many corners and bends. On both sides were garden walls, and trees drooped over the walls, their branches hanging low. If he were to escape from these guards, this was the place. As before, he could leap into the gardens of Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar’s mansion. If he managed to jump in there—

It would be easy to hide amidst the dense trees. As before, it would also be simple to escape through the secret passage leading to the treasure chamber. There was no possibility of fleeing by any other route…
There it was—the narrow path, the very way by which he had escaped earlier, now lay before him.

Vandiyathevan thought to touch the shoulder of the man with the dark mind. But what was this? Who were those people approaching in a group? Palanquins! Horses! Guards with spears in hand! They were coming with such pomp and commotion. They must belong to the royal family or be high-ranking officials.

Realizing this, the Prime Minister’s men looked all around. The guards, too, noticed the narrow path that had caught Vandiyathevan’s attention. At once, they moved to that spot and stood aside. The two men they had brought along were placed behind them, hidden from others’ view.

The approaching group soon reached that place and passed by them. In front were several spear-bearing guards; behind them, upon three majestic white horses, rode Malayaman, the Kodumbalur Velar, and between them, another man. Vandiyathevan saw that the one in the center was none other than Ponniyin Selvan. Ah! How close he was! Yet, how far he had traveled!

For a moment, Vandiyathevan wondered if he could break through the guards and stand before him. But he immediately dismissed the thought. How could Ponniyin Selvan show mercy or embrace friendship to one accused of killing his own brother? Upon seeing him, he might even feel revulsion. Who could say what Malayaman and Velar would do?

Meanwhile, Vandiyathevan’s attention turned to the palanquins following behind them. Ah! The young princess Kundavai! The Kodumbalur princess Vanathi! The daughter of Sambuvarayar, Manimekalai! Vandiyathevan’s heart throbbed with unbearable anguish.

At any other time, he could have approached any of these three women and sought their help. They would have gladly aided him. But now? If the young princess and Princess Vanathi saw the man accused of treacherously murdering Aditya Karikalan, how much loathing would they feel?

Let it be. But look—these women had brought along that foolish girl, Manimekalai! For that, at least, he should feel glad. Had Manimekalai told them everything that happened at Kadambur, in order to save him? “Did she tell them, as she told me, ‘I am the one who killed him’? No, she wouldn’t have told them that. If she had, they wouldn’t be escorting her with such care and support.
The palanquins passed through the marketplace where they were standing. The guards following behind also went on their way.
‘Alright, let’s go! We can leave now,’ said the Prime Minister’s men, and started walking ahead.
Vandiyathevan, in a flash, decided, ‘This is the moment!’ He tapped Karuthiruman on the shoulder and darted off through the alley.
Karuthiruman ran after him.
They heard the sound of two guards running behind them. For a while, neither of them looked back; they just kept running. At last, Karuthiruman glanced over his shoulder.
‘One of them has fallen behind; only one is still coming after us,’ he said.

Vandiyathevan also looked back and saw that only one guard was pursuing them, the other lagging far behind. Even so, it would not be wise to stop and fight him. So, signaling to Karuthiruman, he ran on ahead.

He did not stop until he reached the same spot where he had once scaled the fortress wall. The broken, bent branch was still there as before. Grabbing hold of it, he swung himself up onto the wall. He then reached down and pulled Karuthiruman up after him. Together, they shook the already broken branch and snapped it off completely.

As the man chasing them came near, they pushed the branch down on top of him. Without even waiting to see if it struck him, they leapt down from the wall into the garden. They slipped into the dense trees and bushes, hiding themselves, and watched the wall to see if anyone would follow them into the garden. When they saw that no one was coming after them, they moved on.
‘Ah! We’ve escaped!’ exclaimed Vandiyathevan.
‘What now? How do we get out of the fort?’ asked Karuthiruman.
‘There’s a way. Be patient for a little while!’

As Vandiyathevan approached the palace of the Pazhuvettaraiyar, he came to a halt. The palace was not bustling with activity as it had been before. Yet, there was still some movement within. It would be most fitting to enter the secret chamber only after darkness had fully fallen.
Resolving thus, he seated himself upon a wooden log. He made Karuthiruman sit down as well.
“We must begin our journey only after night has deepened. Until then, let us pass the time—tell me your story!” he said.
“I told you already—I cannot tell that,” replied Karuthiruman.
“In that case, I cannot take you outside with me either.”
“If I do not tell you the truth, but instead make up some tale, what will you do?”
“Whether it is a true story or a fanciful one, tell it! We must while away the time somehow, mustn’t we?”
Karuthiruman began to speak. In truth, what he recounted was filled with such extraordinary incidents that it seemed more like a tale spun from imagination.

chapters.title: Karuthiruman’s Tale
paragraphs: Karuthiruman, also known as Kari Thirumal, was a native of Thopputhurai, a village situated a little north of Kodikkarai on the seashore. He made his living by ferrying boats to the island of Eezham (Sri Lanka) from there. About twenty-five years ago, as he was returning from Eezham to Thopputhurai, a storm broke out and the sea raged violently. He struggled greatly to bring his boat to shore without capsizing. As he neared the coast, close to the lighthouse at Kodikkarai, he saw a woman floating amidst the tumultuous waves. Moved by compassion, he pulled her into his boat. At that time, she was unconscious. He could not even tell whether she was alive or dead.

He tried to land the boat right there, but could not. Steering the boat in the direction of the wind, he finally managed to reach the shore near a place called Thirumaraikkaadu. Carrying the unconscious woman onto the shore, he laid her down and watched over her anxiously. Just then, several important men arrived on horseback. The woman did not speak. Karuthiruman did not even hear what the others were saying. One of them remarked, “She must have been born mute and deaf.” The man who seemed to be their leader called Karuthiruman aside and told him a strange thing: once the storm subsided, he was to take the woman back to Eezham and leave her either in that land or on a nearby island. For this, he would be paid a large sum of money.

Karuthiruman agreed and received the payment. When the sea calmed, he took the woman in his boat and set out. In the middle of the sea, he saw a man clinging to a log, floating, utterly exhausted. He took him too into the boat. At first, the woman was frightened by the new arrival, but soon she ignored him. Karuthiruman took them both and left them on an island near Eezham.

On that island lived a distinguished elder, who claimed the woman as his daughter. He said that she had always been mute, and now she did not even recognize him. Karuthiruman then recounted how he had saved her from the sea.

The man who had boarded the boat in mid-ocean handed Karuthiruman a palm-leaf letter and asked him to deliver it to the king of Lanka. From this, Karuthiruman concluded that the man must be a person of great importance. After delivering the letter to the king of Lanka, from the king’s words, he realized that… He came to know that the man who had been rescued was the king of the Pandya country. The king of Lanka sent his attendants to bring the Pandya monarch to him. Karuthiruman, being greatly exhausted, did not go with them. After a few days, the Pandya king arrived at the palace of the king of Lanka. The two monarchs together journeyed to the land of Rohana, surrounded by mountains in the southern part of Lanka. They stayed there for several days. The Pandya king, who had grown fond of Karuthiruman, took him along as well. In Rohana, the king of Lanka showed the Pandya king many places. At last, he took him to a ravine that no one could easily approach. There, in a mountain cave, were stored countless gold coins, precious gems, and priceless ornaments.

After showing him all these, the king of Lanka took a golden casket and opened it. Inside, there was a resplendent, radiant jeweled crown and a necklace of gems. From the conversation between the kings, Karuthiruman learned that the crown was the ancient crown of the Pandya dynasty, and the necklace was said to have been bestowed upon the first Pandya ruler by Indra, king of the gods. The king of Lanka urged the Pandya king to take them with him. The Pandya king refused. He said that when the day came for him to utterly vanquish the Cholas and ascend the throne in Madurai, then the king of Lanka himself should bring these treasures to Madurai and present them to him before the world.

Afterwards, the Pandya king gave Karuthiruman as many gold coins as he could carry, made arrangements for the safe care of the mute girl, and sent him back with instructions to return and join him in the Pandya country after completing these tasks.

When Karuthiruman went to Puthur Island, he could not find the girl there. Her father was also missing. Searching for them both, he went to Kodikkarai. There, he found the mute girl. But she did not recognize him. From her family, he learned some details. Her father, having fallen ill, had brought her there and left her before passing away. It was revealed that the lighthouse keeper at the headland was her brother. At first, she remembered neither her brother nor her sister. After she once again slipped and fell into the sea and was rescued, her memory of them all returned. Others discovered that she was pregnant. She herself realized this and, in great terror... She sank into herself. She often visited the Kuzhagar temple at Kodikkarai and busied herself in service there. No matter how much Karuthiruman tried, she would not even notice him now.

While he was at Kodikkarai, he met the younger sister of that mute girl. Learning that she too was mute, he felt a deep pity for her. He even thought of marrying her and living together. But before that, he wished to go to the Pandya king and deliver his message.

At that time, the Chola Empress, Kandaradithar’s queen and a devout worshipper of Shiva, Sembiyan Maadevi, came to the Kuzhagar temple at Kodikkarai for a darshan. There, she saw the mute girl, Mandakini, and took her along with her. Her younger sister Vaani also went with them.

Karuthiruman went to the Pandya country. There, he learned that the Pandya king had gone to the battlefield. When he went to the battlefield and met the king, the king asked him to go once more to Lanka and deliver a letter to the Lankan king. He also instructed him to try again to bring back the mute girl on his return.

Karuthiruman returned from Lanka and went to Pazhayarai. The memory of Vaani never left his mind. It was mainly the desire to see her that led him to Pazhayarai. But when he saw her there, he was startled, shocked, and struck with terror.

At dawn, as he was approaching Pazhayarai along the riverbank, he saw a woman bent over, digging a pit at the edge of the river. Even that did not surprise him much. Beside her lay a bundle of cloth. From within it, a very faint voice, the cry of a tiny infant, could be heard.

With a surge of anger and disgust, thinking, “What wretched sinner is preparing to bury a living child?” he hurried closer. The woman digging the pit straightened up. Karuthiruman realized that it was Vaani.
“Brother, can you imagine how I must have felt at that moment? Try to imagine it yourself!” said the dark-hued Thirumal.
“I can imagine it. Now tell me what happened next!” said Vandiyathevan.

“I cannot speak of what happened after that. Only those born to royal families can whisper such things into each other’s ears! If only I had not gone to Pazhayarai at that time, none of the troubles that befell me afterward would have happened!” said Karuthiruman.
“In that case, let us go! We can go straight to the royal family and tell them ourselves!” said Vandiyathevan, rising with a laugh.

He beckoned to Karuthiruman and made his way toward the treasury chamber. At that moment, there was no one else present. The chamber door was secured with a massive lock. Yet, the inner latch, cunningly concealed so that outsiders could never discover it, opened at Vandiyathevan’s touch. The two slipped inside and bolted the door from within.
Vandiyathevan entered the place where gold, gems, pearls, and navaratnas were heaped in abundance. He turned to Karuthiruman and asked, “Does your Rohana mountain cave hold such treasures as these?”
“There are a hundred times more than this!” Karuthiruman replied.

Vandiyathevan scooped up a few gold coins, tied them in his cloth, and they prepared to leave once more. Vandiyathevan led the way along the treasury corridor. He opened the secret door set into the fortress wall. There was no guard present at that hour. He cautiously poked his head out first.

The Vadavaru river was in flood, its waters lapping at both banks. Far in the distance, a torch’s glow could be seen. Seeing that no one was nearby, Vandiyathevan stepped outside. Karuthiruman followed, and they closed the door behind them.
As they pondered how to cross the Vadavaru, they noticed a boat caught among the roots of a tree leaning over the riverbank.

chapters.title: The Omen’s Obstruction
paragraphs: The moment Vandiyathevan saw the boat hidden beneath the tree, his spirits soared, believing that the goddess of fortune had once again favored him. Though he himself did not know how to row a boat, Karuthiruman was a man whose very livelihood depended on ferrying boats. With his help, if they could push the boat into the Vadavaru and let it drift with the current, the river’s flood would carry them halfway to Kodikkarai before dawn.

“Do you see this, Karuthiruma? This boat has floated here without sinking, waiting just for us! If you show a little of your rowing skill, we can cover half the distance before daybreak. After that, even those who come on horseback won’t be able to catch us!” said Vandiyathevan.

Karuthiruman looked around with a trace of suspicion. Amidst the thick bushes that had grown wild along the riverbank beside the wall, something seemed to move. Karuthiruman picked up a small stone and threw it into the bushes. From there, a cat leapt out, sprang onto the boat, and settled itself.
Vandiyathevan laughed and said, “Boatman! Are you braver than I am?” With that, he picked up another small stone and tossed it into the boat.
The cat, startled, jumped out of the boat again, ran towards them, and darted between the two men before disappearing.
Now Vandiyathevan, startled, took two steps back. “You don’t seem any braver than I am!” Karuthiruman said mockingly.
“I’m afraid of cats; if one so much as touches me, my whole body breaks out in goosebumps. Thank goodness it’s gone! Come, let’s go!” said Vandiyathevan.
“If a cat falls on me, I’m not afraid at all; but if it crosses my path, then I fear the omen’s obstacle!” replied Karuthiruman.
“Omen, obstacle—what does it matter?” said Vandiyathevan, grabbing Karuthiruman’s hand and pulling him toward the boat.

Karuthiruman went to one end of the boat and tried to push it away from the tangle of tree roots. Whether the boat moved or not, in a flash, four men leapt, ran, and before he could even blink, they had climbed aboard. Two of them sprang upon Vandiyathevan, shoved him into the boat, and tied him fast to the crossbeams. The other two, holding spears, stood guard on either side of Karuthiruman.

Vandiyathevan realized that the leader of the four was the stout man who had followed them from the underground prison gate. He marveled at how the man had managed to reach the boat and wait near the entrance of the tunnel before them. He must not be an ordinary guard, Vandiyathevan decided, but a highly skilled spy. Who could he be? He seemed vaguely familiar, as if he had seen him somewhere before. As these thoughts ran through his mind, the man’s voice fell upon his ears.

Looking at Karuthiruman, the guard said, “Old man! After spending so many years in prison, you have come out at last. Why did you try to run away, listening to the words of this reckless fellow? Let him go if he wishes. I have no heart to tie you up and send you back again. If you listen to what I say and do as I instruct, no harm will come to you!”

The boatman replied, “Yes, sir! The Chief Minister sent a man to grant me freedom. But I was ruined by listening to this fool’s words. From now on, I will do as you say. Only, please do not send me back to the underground prison!”

“Yes, yes! The Chief Minister wants to ask you a few questions. If you answer truthfully, he will not send you back to the dungeon. He will reward you with gold, jewels, and gifts, and set you free. Where were you planning to go?”
“We were setting out for Eezha Nadu (Sri Lanka),” replied Karuthiruman.

“How clever! Did you think you could deceive the Chief Minister, slip past the Velaar’s guards, and escape so far? But this wild youth is just the sort to hatch such a plan. Wasn’t he the one who once escaped from the guards of Chinna Pazhuvetarayar? Let it be. Now, we must row the boat against the current. Only one among those who came with me knows how to row. He learned it in haste, and since we came downstream with the current, we managed, though clumsily. Now, you must show your skill. Take the boat close to the opposite bank, and from there, row towards the northern fort gate. Let us see!”
“We could cross to the other bank and walk from there, sir! The current is flowing very swiftly. It’s difficult to row the boat upstream for such a long distance!”
“If we land on the other bank, this unruly youth will cause some new trouble. So we must go upstream along the river itself!” said the head guard.
The boatman and another man began to push the boat forward. The head guard came close to Vandiyathevan and said, “Boy! Don’t try to show your mischief again!”
“Sir! It seems you know a great deal about me!” replied Vandiyathevan.
“Why wouldn’t I? I saw you lock up the physician’s son in prison in your place and come out yourself! After that, you tried to deceive us and run away!”
Vandiyathevan, pretending to be greatly surprised, said, “Sir! You are even cleverer than I am! I thought no one noticed what happened in the underground prison!”

“Young man! There is no place in the Chola Empire where the eyes and ears of our Prime Minister do not reach. They are in Eezham too; in Kanchipuram; in the Kadambur palace; even in the underground prison. The Prime Minister knows well that the physician’s son, Pinagapani, is a complete fool. That’s why he sent me after him!”

“It seems the Prime Minister even knew I would escape by this route. His eyes and ears are truly astonishing. If that is so, he must also know that I am innocent, and that imprisoning me in the underground cell was a mistake, mustn’t he?”

“That is not the Prime Minister’s responsibility. It is the Emperor’s duty to decide whether you are guilty or not. It is the responsibility of the Periya Velar of Kodumbalur to punish you for trying to escape from the underground prison,” said the guard.
“Sir! Where are you taking me now?”
“First, I am taking you to the Velar of Kodumbalur. He is waiting at the northern fort gate.”
“Is the great Velar waiting for me?”

“Ah! Look at your arrogance! Did you think that the lord of the southern direction, the foremost among the minor kings of Chola Nadu, the pillar of the Chola dynasty, the one who uprooted the Pandya lineage, the valiant conqueror of Eelam, the Kodumbalur Velar, Commander-in-Chief Boothi Vikrama Kesari, is waiting at the fortress gate just for you?”
“Then, for whom is he waiting?”
“Parthibendran is coming, bringing with him the Pazhuvettaraiyars and the other minor kings who had assembled at Thirupurambiyam…”
“Even the Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar?”
“Yes, even him. It seems he knows the truth about Prince Karikalan’s death. Once he arrives, an inquiry will be held before the Emperor. If you are not guilty, you must prove it then.”

Hearing this, Vandiyathevan was plunged into deep distress. The Pazhuvettaraiyars and Parthibendran would surely lay the blame at his feet. Oh God! With such an accusation, how could he face the Emperor or Prince Arulmozhi? What evidence could he present to prove his innocence?

“Sir! I have done you no harm, have I? Please let me escape! Truly, I am not guilty. I was a dear friend to the late prince. By a twist of fate, this terrible accusation has fallen upon me. You are a servant of the Prime Minister. Was it not the Prime Minister himself who ordered you to bring the madman from prison? Take him with you, and let me go! You will earn great merit!” pleaded Vandiyathevan, his voice full of compassion.
“If I let you go, what will you give me?” asked the guard.
“When the time comes, I will return the favor with equal help.”
“That time will never come; even if it does, I will not need your help. Tell me what you can give me right now!”
Vandiyathevan remembered the gold coins tied in his waistcloth. “I will give you enough gold coins to fill both your hands!”
“Ah! Is that so? Gold coins? Show me where they are!” said the guard eagerly.
“Loosen my bonds a little! They are in my waistcloth; I will take them out and show you!” replied Vandiyathevan.
“Don’t go showing off your mischief again!” muttered the guard, even as he bent down and loosened Vandiyathevan’s bonds a little.
Vandiyathevan, all the while keeping his eyes fixed on the guard’s face, untied the knot of his waistcloth and drew out the gold coins, handing them over.

The guard took the coins, filling his palm, and said, “Brother! Did you take these coins from Pazhuvettaraiyar’s treasury? Or did you strike them yourself at the mint? There are now three charges against you. One, murder; two, escaping from prison; and three, stealing from the royal treasury. Three crimes in all. For each one, you could be impaled separately.”

“Sir! I have rendered many services to the Chola kingdom. I have gone on many missions. I even risked my life to save Karikalan’s. I have a right to claim these few gold coins as my reward. I took them only for my travel expenses,” replied Vandiyathevan.
“Save all that for your own defense when you are put on trial!” said the guard.
“In that case, are you not going to set me free?” asked Vandiyathevan.
“Even if the sun were to rise in the west, or if it were declared that Vishnu is greater than Parameshwaran, I will not betray the kingdom for a handful of gold coins,” said the guard.

Vandiyathevan glanced from the corner of his eye to see what Karuthiruman was doing. He noticed that Karuthiruman was watching him eagerly, as if waiting for a signal. At once, the brave youth loosened the bonds that had already been slackened a little more, and with a swift motion, grabbed the guard’s moustache and turban and yanked them off. Both came away in his hand, and there stood Alwarkadiyan in all his true form.
“Disguised Vaishnavite! Was it you?” exclaimed Vandiyathevan.

As Alwarkadiyan tried to retrieve his moustache and turban, the gold coins scattered from his hand and fell to the ground. In a flash, Vandiyathevan freed himself completely from his bonds and pushed Alwarkadiyan down. Just a moment before— He took the rope that had bound him and tied Alwarkadiyan to the cross-beam of the boat along with the oars. He drew the sword that hung at his waist from its scabbard and held it ready in his hand.

While Vandiyathevan was engaged in these actions, Karuthiruman was not idle. Suddenly, he attacked the guard standing nearby and threw him into the river’s flood. The man began to struggle in the swirling waters. Of the two remaining men, one advanced toward the boatman and the other toward Vandiyathevan. Both approached hesitantly, fear evident in their steps. As Vandiyathevan swung his sword and stepped forward, that brave soul leapt into the flood of his own accord. Meanwhile, Karuthiruman struck the other with the oar in his hand, knocking him onto the boat.
Together, they tied him up as well with the cross-beam’s rope. The boat drifted along with the river’s current. The two who had fallen into the water tried to swim toward the shore.
Vandiyathevan went to Alwarkadiyan and asked, “O valiant jewel among Vaishnavas! What do you say now?”

“What is there to say? All is the doing of Lord Narayana. The one who ties is He; the one who is tied is He. The one who pushes is He; the one who is pushed is He! He is present in the pillar, in the blade of grass, in your sword hand, and in my shoulder!”
“If that is so, then He is present in this river’s flood as well! I could tie you up and throw you into this flood, couldn’t I?”
