“Ammani! It is I, Azhwarkkadiyan, also known as Thirumalai Nambidasan. Please, be kind enough to open the door. There is an urgent matter to discuss!” said Azhwarkkadiyan. Footsteps were heard inside. Poonguzhali came to the doorway and stood there. “What urgent business do you have here at this hour? You are a staunch Vaishnavite. This is the abode of Shiva’s devotees. You know well that the master of this house is unwell. Why do you come here at night and cause disturbance?” she asked.

Azhwarkadiyan replied, “Princess of the Sea! It is true that I am a staunch Vaishnavite; that is precisely why I have come—to punish the wicked and protect the virtuous. If you do not open the door at once, it will be broken open!”

“Vaishnavite! Are you such a mighty hero? Have you come to display your valor to us?” she retorted, even as she flung the door of the hut open with a thud. In her fish-shaped eyes, sparks of anger flashed.

She had intended to vent her anger on Azhwarkadiyan, but was startled to see several soldiers standing behind him. Immediately, she subdued her anger and asked, “Sir! What is this? Who are these men? Why have they come here? Did they come with you?”
“Yes, they came with me. They are here on royal business. Anyone who obstructs their duty will be subject to royal punishment,” said Azhwarkadiyan.

“Fine royal business. Fine royal punishment. I keep wondering when I’ll be able to leave all these conversations behind, go to the shore at Kodikkarai, and listen in peace to the sound of the ocean’s waves. Never mind. Tell these men to wait some distance away and come inside alone. What royal business could possibly be conducted in this wretched hut? Wouldn’t you alone suffice to witness it? My uncle is lying on the cot, suffering in pain. If these men come in, he will be startled, and his health will worsen!” she said.
As soon as Azhwarkadiyan entered the hut, he himself closed the door and bolted it from within.

“Poonguzhali! Your words are most astonishing. When did you develop such aversion to matters of the state? What happened to your intention of marrying the crowned prince and ascending the throne? If that were to happen, wouldn’t you have to devote all your attention to affairs of the kingdom?” asked Thirumalai.

“Sir, O Vaishnavite! I have completely abandoned that intention. In these past few days, I have come to realize how burdensome it is to bear the weight of a kingdom, how much anguish it brings to the mind. Hereafter, I shall not even wish to come within ten leagues of the throne. Vaishnavite! I have joyful news to share with you. I have decided to marry my cousin, Sendhan Amudhan. Just a short while ago, I informed the noble Sembiyan Maadevi, who came here, and received her blessings as well. Once Amudhan regains his health a little more, the two of us will depart for Kodikkarai…”
Azhwarkkadiyan interrupted, “Ah! You have made a wise decision!

‘The orphaned, wealthy courtesans may rule the earth, I desire neither riches nor earthly dominion. May I be fated to be born as a fish In the honey-scented, flower-laden pools Of sacred Thiruvengadam!’

Did not the Alwar himself bless us thus? In the same way, it seems you too have resolved, ‘I want not this earthly kingdom,’ and wish to live among the fishes in the sea! But who can escape fate? If it is destined that a crown must rest upon your head and you must sit upon the throne, then so it shall be. Even if you refuse, destiny will not let you go!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
“That’s enough, sir! Enough of your mockery! Tell me, for what purpose have you come here?” asked Poonguzhali.
“Lady! Have you only abandoned your desire to rule the earth? Or have you and Sendhan Amudhan also forsaken the very wish to live in this world? I came to find this out!” said the Vaishnavite.

“What kind of question is that? Both of us still wish to live in this world for some more time. Is it not only today that we have decided to marry? Vaishnavite! Offer us your blessings! Pray that my cousin recovers soon!” said Poonguzhali.

“I am ready to offer my blessings and prayers. But my blessings and prayers must not go in vain. If you both truly wish to live in this world, why then did you help those who escaped from the underground prison?” asked Thirumalai.
A look of astonishment appeared on Poonkuzhali’s face as she said, “What is this? We know nothing about it! We have not helped anyone escape, have we?”

“Vandiyathevan, who was accused of killing Karikalan and was imprisoned in the underground dungeon, and another madman, have both escaped today. It seems they came as far as this garden. Afterwards, two people appear to have ridden away from here on two horses. In one place near this hut, there are bloodstains on the ground. There are also signs that many people have come and gone from this spot. Therefore, it is assumed that you must have helped the fugitives escape. Because of the Prime Minister Aniruddha’s affection for you, he sent me here. If the men of the Kodumbalur Velar had come, they would have arrested you immediately,” said Azhwarkkadiyan.

“Many thanks to the Prime Minister and to you, Vaishnavite! In just two more days, Aththan’s health will be restored. We will immediately depart for Kodikkarai. After that, we will never look back towards this Thanjavur side. Until then, you must help us so that none of the royal guards trouble us!” pleaded Poonkuzhali.
“I have no objection to helping you. But you must tell the truth! Apart from the three of you here, did anyone else come?” he asked.

“Why wouldn’t they? You have come now! Just a short while ago, Sembiyan Madevi and Prince Madhurantakan came and inquired lovingly about Aththan’s health before leaving. Right now, isn’t the Thanjavur fort surrounded everywhere by the movements of warriors? How can we know who came and who went? Vaishnavite! I will certainly answer only the first question you asked. We have not helped anyone escape from here…”
“Is that your honest word?”
“Yes; I say it truthfully. We have not helped anyone escape from here!”
“If that is so, then Vandiyathevan, who escaped from prison, must be here in this very hut!” declared Thirumalai.
Even as he spoke these words, a pained, pitiful groan was heard from beneath the rope cot where Sendhan Amudhan was lying.

Arulmozhi Varman stood at the edge of the riverbank, gazing at the swirling waters of the Ponni. The golden rays of dawn shimmered upon the surface, casting a thousand dancing lights. The gentle breeze carried with it the fragrance of wet earth and blossoming lotuses. Yet, the prince’s heart was heavy, burdened by thoughts that weighed more than the world itself.
From behind, the sound of approaching footsteps disturbed the tranquil silence. Vandiyathevan, ever alert, recognized the prince’s mood and approached with caution.
“My lord, the assembly awaits your word,” he said softly.

Arulmozhi turned, his eyes reflecting both the river’s brilliance and his own inner turmoil. “Vandiyatheva, what word shall I give them? They speak of crowns and thrones as if they are mere ornaments to be worn and discarded at will. They do not know the fire that burns within such a crown, the poison that seeps from the throne’s golden seat.”
Vandiyathevan smiled gently. “The people yearn for your rule, Prince. The empire’s nobles, the soldiers, the common folk—all look to you with hope. Will you not grant them their wish?”

Arulmozhi’s gaze drifted back to the river. “I have seen the world’s glory, Vandiyatheva. I have witnessed the rise and fall of kings, the fleeting nature of power. I have seen how the thirst for the throne turns brother against brother, friend against friend. I do not desire the earthly throne. My heart seeks peace, not power.”
Vandiyathevan was silent for a moment, then spoke with earnestness. “If not you, my lord, then who? The empire stands at a crossroads. Darkness gathers on the horizon. Only your light can dispel it.”

Arulmozhi smiled, a trace of sadness in his eyes. “The river flows on, unmindful of the kingdoms that rise and fall upon its banks. The sun rises and sets, indifferent to the fate of emperors. What am I, Vandiyatheva, but a drop in this endless stream? If destiny wills it, I shall accept what comes. But I shall not seek the crown for myself.”

As the sun climbed higher, its rays illuminating the prince’s noble face, Vandiyathevan bowed his head in respect. The river’s song mingled with the silent resolve in Arulmozhi’s heart—a resolve that would shape the fate of the Chola empire.

chapters.title: “A Prince for a Day!”
paragraphs: The moment Alwarkadiyan heard the groaning sound coming from beneath Sendhan Amudhan’s cot, he exclaimed, “Aha! Is that the news? O peerless devotees of Shiva! Have you begun your mischief, just like the old Paramashiva himself?” Muttering thus, he started to climb up.

Poonguzhali swiftly drew the dagger tucked at her waist and brandished it. “Vaishnavite! You, who have blasphemed Lord Shiva, shall not remain in this world for even a moment longer. If you take one more step upward, you will at once reach Vaikunta!” she threatened.

“Mother! Great Shakti! Is there any reply to your words? Attaining the abode of Vaikunta is no easy feat. If you send me there by your own hand, what greater fortune could I ever hope for?” replied Alwarkadiyan.

At this moment, Sendhan Amudhan rose from his cot and said, “Poonguzhali! Enough! Sheathe your dagger! Lord Shiva will not be diminished in any way by this Vaishnavite’s insults. No good can come from evil means. Neither lies nor wickedness will ever yield benefit. Let us tell the truth to this Vaishnavite and seek his help. Is he not also a friend of Vandiyathevan?”

“Then come, let us go! Can mere devotees of Shiva ever deceive me, a humble servant of Krishna Paramatma, the master of all cunning drama? If one surrenders to the compassionate Sriman Narayana, He will surely grant protection. Was it not our Lord Thirumal who rescued the elephant Gajendra from the jaws of the crocodile when he cried out ‘Adhimoolame’?”
“Yes, yes! But before your Thirumal descends from Vaikunta to help, your friend will have already departed this mortal world!” said Poonguzhali, and hurried toward the cot.
The others followed her. They lifted Vandiyathevan, who had been hidden beneath the cot, concealed by a pile of cloth, and laid him upon the bed.
Vandiyathevan lay unconscious. Yet, from time to time, he groaned in pain. Only by these groans could one discern that life still lingered in his body.

Vaani Amma boiled medicinal herbs, mixed them with turmeric powder, and brought them to bind upon his wounds. Azhwarkkadiyan and Sendhan Amudhan held Vandiyathevan’s arms and legs firmly. Poonguzhali and Vaani Amma pressed the hot, freshly boiled herbs onto his wounds and wrapped them with cloth.

The pain from this treatment made Vandiyathevan open his eyes. The moment he saw Azhwarkkadiyan before him, he muttered, “Vaishnavite! You have deceived me! You called me here, and then sent men behind me to kill me?” With these confused words, he slipped back into unconsciousness.

A look of distress appeared on Azhwarkkadiyan’s face. He feared that Vandiyathevan’s half-conscious words would once again arouse suspicion about him in the minds of Sendhan Amudhan and Poonguzhali, so he glanced at their faces.
The smile blooming on Poonguzhali’s lips gave him some reassurance.
“Vaishnavite! Was it you who sent Vandiyathevan here?” she asked.
“Yes, madam! But I did not send anyone after him to kill him.”
“Let that be. Why did you send him here?”
“I sent him so that he could escape. Beside this garden, I had two horses ready for him and his friend…”
“Then, how did you know he did not escape? How did you know he was in this hut?”
“I saw someone else riding away on the horse I had left for him. That’s what made me suspicious…”
“When Vishnu thinks one thing, Shiva thinks another.”
“What riddle is this, madam? How did he get wounded?”
“Vaishnavar! I do not know with what intention you sent him here. But he arrived at the right moment, and before I could become a widow before even being married, he saved me!”
As Poonguzhali was saying this, Azhwarkkadiyan and Sendhan Amudhan both exclaimed in astonishment, “What? What? What?”

Poonguzhali turned to Amudhan and said, “Yes, I did not even tell you. A man was standing outside, aiming to stab you with a spear. At that moment, he intervened, took the blow himself, and saved you!”
Tears welled up in Sendhan Amudhan’s eyes. “Alas! Did my friend face this danger for my sake?” he asked.
“What of that? How much danger have you braved to save him!” said Poonguzhali.

“Ammani! In this world, it is rare indeed for one to immediately repay a good deed with another. If only one does not harm those who have done good, that itself is a great thing. That Vandiyathevan arrived here at the right time and saved Sendhan Amudhan is truly a wondrous deed! But you spoke of marriage just now? And that he saved you from becoming a widow before marriage?”

“Yes, Vaishnavar! Only a short while ago, we decided to be wed. We even received the blessings of Sembiyan Madevi. The very moment Periya Piratti left, within a quarter of an hour, a spear was to be hurled at him. Even I could not have prevented it. If he had lost his life, what would have become of me? Would I not have become a widow before even being married?”

“By the grace of merciful Thirumal, such a thing shall never happen. Sembiyan Madevi’s blessings will not go in vain. You will marry this noble soul and live happily for a long time. But who could be the wretch who tried to kill this supremely virtuous youth with a spear? Did you see him? Did you recognize him?”

“How could I not see? How could I not know? It was that villain Pinagapani, the physician’s son! The very same who abducted my aunt Mandakini from Kodikkarai and delivered her into the hands of a murderer! Such atrocities are happening in the Chola kingdom…”

“What is this injustice you have witnessed? What you have seen is nothing compared to what is about to happen. Tonight, anarchy will erupt in Chola Nadu a thousand times over. A great conflict is about to break out among the minor kings. All across the land, people will fight one another and perish! Unless a great miracle occurs by the grace of Sriman Narayana Moorthi, there is no way to prevent the disasters that are about to befall this country!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
“Vaishnavite! Why do you speak as if you are cursing us? Can you not bless the Chola land to prosper instead?” asked Amudhan.
“Let the country go as it will! We are leaving for Kodikkarai!” said Poonguzhali.
“We can leave, but what are we to do about this noble friend who saved my life?” asked Sendhan Amudhan.

“You cannot save him, no matter what you do. There is no use in you staying here either. Even now, the king’s men are searching everywhere for those who have escaped from prison. Soon, they will come here as well. I do not know what explanation I can give to the guards standing at the entrance to bring you out safely!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.

“Sir! Vaishnavite! You are a man of great resource. You are someone who can give counsel even to the Prime Minister Aniruddha. If you can think of a way to save this valiant scion of the Vanar clan, who has been grievously wounded by a murderer, you will earn great merit. Both of us will be forever indebted to you!”
“Devi, that is not so easy!”

“Sir! With every passing moment, my respect for you increases! Until yesterday, you called me ‘boatwoman.’ Just a while ago, you called me ‘lady.’ Now you address me as ‘Devi.’ At this rate, soon you will call me ‘Princess’!”

“Yes, Princess! If you wish to save this brave young man who lies here unconscious, there is only one way. The fortunate man who is about to marry you must become a prince for a day! If he is a prince, then you too will be a princess, will you not?”
“Vaishnavite! What jest is this? How can I, or anyone, be a prince for a day? And for what purpose?” asked Amudhan.

“I am about to reveal to both of you a secret that, until now, only I have known. Listen. No—first, look at this!” So saying, Azhwarkadiyan untied the bundle he had brought with him and displayed its contents before them.
The crown that Madurantaka had worn, along with pearl necklaces and gleaming armlets, shone with dazzling brilliance.
“Ah! Are these not the very ornaments that Prince Madurantaka was wearing? Did we not see them here just a short while ago?” exclaimed Amudhan.
“Where did you find these?” asked Poonguzhali.

“I found them by the fence at the edge of this garden. And now, listen to the secret I wish to tell you. As I was coming along the banks of the Vadavaru, I saw two men riding swiftly on horseback. Those were the horses that had been left here for Vandiyathevan and for that madman who escaped from prison with him. You know of that madman, don’t you?”
“Yes, we do. He was the one who kept raving to anyone he met about the Pandya dynasty’s jeweled crown and gem-studded necklace.”
“The very same! Of the two horses racing along the Vadavaru, that madman was on one. The man on the other horse seemed to be Prince Madurantaka himself. Now, after coming here, I am certain of it.”
“What strange mystery is this? Why would Madurantaka cast aside his ornaments and flee?”
“That is what I do not know. I am about to inform the Prime Minister and send men to pursue those who have fled. But I fear that, before that can be done, great calamities may occur here.”
“What calamity do you fear?”

“The Pazhuvettarayars and the minor kings of their faction are even now approaching the gates of Thanjavur fort. Kodumbalur Velar, the Prime Minister, and Malayaman are waiting at the gates to receive them. The Emperor’s wish—his command—is that the matter of royal succession be settled peacefully through discussion. But before the Pazhuvettarayars begin any such discussion, they will demand, ‘Where is Madurantaka?’ The moment they hear he is missing, they will pounce upon Kodumbalur Velar! The Commander-in-Chief is determined to secure the crown for Ponniyin Selvan, and for that purpose, Madurantaka—”
“They will say he has been killed. Even if Periya Vellar denies it, he cannot prove otherwise. Immediately, a terrible civil war will break out. The Chola country will soon fall into ruin.”
“Before that happens, we can leave this place and escape!”
“Devi! That is not possible!”
“Then, what do you suggest?”

“Let Sendhan Amudhan wear this crown and these ornaments for a short while. I will bring the elephant that carried Ponniyin Selvan here. Let him mount it. I will instruct my men to march before and behind the elephant, shouting, ‘Long live Madhuranthakar!’ The palanquin in which Madhuranthakar arrived is nearby. We will place Vandiyathevan inside it and draw the curtains. Devi, you walk beside the palanquin. Leave everything else to me!” said Azhwarkkadiyan.
“What kind of mad idea is this?” exclaimed Sendhan Amudhan.
“If he wears the crown, will he not be recognized?” asked Poonguzhali.

“In the darkness of night, who can identify the person seated atop the elephant? Only if suspicion arises will anyone look closely! I will come with you myself. It is my responsibility to see that all of you are safely escorted into the fortress, to the Prime Minister’s house. There is no other way to save this valiant scion of the Vanar clan!”
After some more discussion, Sendhan Amudhan and Poonguzhali agreed to Azhwarkkadiyan’s plan.

chapters.title: “Sword Against Sword!”
paragraphs: When the retinue of Pazhuvettaraiyar and Sambuvaraiyar approached the gates of Thanjai Fort, it was as if the very seas themselves were clashing in turmoil.

“Here arrives the lord of Chola Nadu, the god ordained by fate, the bravest of the brave who has earned sixty-four scars in thirty-six battlefields—the great Pazhuvettaraiyar!” So thundered the heralds, roaring out such titles for each of the minor kings.
In the same manner, titles and honors were proclaimed for the Kodumbalur Velar, the Thirukovalur Malayaman, and others. Drums and conches blared in between. The fortress walls echoed with the sound.

At the fort gate stood the Commander-in-Chief, Periya Velar, Malayaman, the Prime Minister, and others, waiting below. Thus, the Pazhuvettaraiyars and their companions had to dismount from their vehicles. Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar thought that the Commander-in-Chief and the others had stationed themselves at the gate in a gesture of welcome, intending to lead them inside the fort after making them dismount from their chariots. He shared this thought with the others as well. He requested that the Commander-in-Chief himself take on the responsibility of speaking with the assembled group.

Periya Velar and the others expected that they might need to converse with the arriving dignitaries for a while. Therefore, instead of blocking the fort entrance, they stood a little apart in the open ground near the flagpole. When the minor kings approached them after dismounting, the Commander-in-Chief, Periya Velar, called out, “Welcome! Welcome, O minor kings, who are like the eight elephants supporting the eight directions of the Chola realm! Welcome! May your arrival bring prosperity to the Chola kingdom and the Chola clan!”

Immediately, Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar replied, “Yes, sir! May our arrival bring good fortune to the Chola kingdom! And likewise, may your departure also yield auspicious results!” At these words, Periya Velar’s eyes reddened.

“Sir! For the prosperity of the Chola kingdom and the glory of the Chola clan, it is the tradition of the Kodumbalur Velar lineage to journey to all directions. The whole world knows that my dear brother, Paranthakan Chinna Velar, gave his life on the battlefield of Eezham. I myself was in Eezham until just a few days ago. The art of riding a horse with a spear in hand is well known to our clan. To remain safely within fortress walls, tending to palace inner chambers and treasuries…” “We are well aware of the customs that safeguard the royal chambers and the traditions that are upheld. If it is certain that the Chola clan will benefit from your arrival and my departure, then I shall not remain here for even a moment longer!” thundered Periya Velar.

At this moment, the Prime Minister Aniruddha Brahmarayar intervened, saying, “Scions of the royal house! What doubt can there be that the coming together of all of you will bring good to the Chola kingdom? Each one of you has, for generations, toiled for the glory of the Chola realm. In every one of your lineages, there are those who have laid down their lives for the Chola clan… Now, as ever, and in times to come, your cooperation and service will be needed for the welfare of Chola Nadu. It is for this reason that Emperor Parantaka Sundara Chola grieves over the discord that has arisen among you. Even forgetting the immense sorrow of having lost his beloved son, the peerless warrior who slew Veerapandiyan—Aditya Karikalan, who met an untimely death—he has summoned you all here, seeking unity. Matters concerning the succession and all other issues can be discussed and resolved peacefully in the presence of the Emperor. Noble lords! I earnestly entreat you all—do not wound the heart of the Emperor, who is already sunk in grief at the loss of his eldest son, with your quarrels!”
These words struck deep into the hearts of all those assembled there. They realized that this was not the proper time to give vent to their own anger and grievances.

Immediately, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar said, “Prime Minister! We are prepared to act according to the wishes of the Emperor. When shall we be granted audience with him? Will it be possible to see him tonight? We wish to hear the Emperor’s will directly from his own lips!”

“Commander! Your request is just, and there is no doubt it will be fulfilled. But you all know the state of the Emperor’s body and mind. When night falls, his physical pain and mental anguish only increase. Moreover, before discussing the matter of succession with the princes, the Emperor wishes to have a final conversation with Sembiyan Madevi. He wishes to make one last attempt to change her mind. You all know for what reason. Therefore, before tomorrow’s daylight fades, the Emperor will summon you all. Tonight, he wishes that all of you come within the fort and rest peacefully in your respective palaces. For those who do not have a palace within the fort, he has instructed Periya Velar to arrange suitable accommodations…”

Once again, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar interjected, “Prime Minister! We have no need for the comforts of a palace. We are men accustomed to the open fields of the battlefield. If the Emperor is only going to see us tomorrow, what necessity is there for us to enter the fort tonight?”
The Prime Minister replied, “What necessity is there for you to stay outside, instead of coming and lodging in your own palace?”
“Commander! It seems Kaalandhakandar is afraid to come and stay inside the Thanjai fort!” said the Commander-in-Chief.

“Afraid? What does fear look like? Is it black? Is it red? Does it have horns? Does it have wings? Perhaps the great Velar, who has come running in haste from the battlefields of Eelam, might know,” said Chinna Pazhuvettarayar.

‘What is this? It seems impossible to prevent these two from clashing,’ thought Periya Pazhuvettarayar. He let out a booming “Hum!” that seemed to fill the sky, and stepped forward. Everyone turned to him with great respect.

“Brother! The Kodumbalur Velar descends from the line of the great patron Pari. The Velir clan has never broken its word. When the Periya Velar says he will grant us protection, what obstacle is there for us to enter the fort?” asked Periya Pazhuvettarayar.

“Anna! We have no need of another’s protection. Nor do we need any promises. We have our own swords, and the spears of thirty thousand warriors. I am the commander of this Thanjai fort. I will not consent to enter the fort unless it comes under my control once again!” declared Kaalandhakandar.
The Commander-in-Chief Velar looked at Periya Pazhuvettarayar and said, “Sir! If the Emperor commands it, I am prepared to obey!”
“Did he seize the fort in the name of the Emperor’s command?” asked Chinna Pazhuvettarayar.
“No; I seized this fort by the strength of my sword!” replied the Periya Velar.
“Then I too shall seize it again by the strength of my sword! Shall we test it right now?” said Chinna Pazhuvettarayar, placing his hand on the hilt of his dagger.
Periya Pazhuvettarayar restrained his younger brother with his hand and said, “Brother! This is not the time to draw swords! We have come here according to the Emperor’s wishes!”

“Anna! Once we enter the fort, what certainty do we have that he will not imprison us? How can you ask us to trust someone who seized the fort by force, without waiting for the Emperor’s command?” asked Chinna Pazhuvettarayar.
“It was by trusting him that you left our women and children within this very fort, was it not? You even left Prince Madurantaka behind and departed!” said the elder.

“I now wonder if that was a mistake. Even if some small harm should befall Madurantaka, I shall see to it later—first, I will utterly destroy the Kodumbalur clan, root and branch!” Chinna Pazhuvettarayar cried out in anguish.
Until now, Commander-in-Chief Boothi Vikrama Kesari had been speaking with indifference, but now a fierce anger seized him! In that moment, a grave and disastrous clash might well have erupted.
Fortunately, at that very instant, a commotion arose at the fort’s entrance. Everyone’s attention turned in that direction.

A short while earlier, Prime Minister Aniruddhar had summoned Azhwarkkadiyan to him with a gesture. The latter had whispered some secret message to him. Upon hearing it, the minister approached the place where the Pazhuvettarayars and Periya Velar were standing. As he came near, the words Chinna Pazhuvettarayar had spoken about Madurantaka reached his ears.

“Commander! Why worry about Prince Madurantaka? No harm will befall him from anyone. Only a short while ago, Madurantaka Devar and his mother, Sembiyan Madevi, left the fort. They had gone to visit Sendhan Amudhan, who was performing floral offerings at the temple…” the Prime Minister began, but Kalantaka Kandar interrupted him.
“Yes; mother and son came out of the fort. But only the mother returned inside!” said Chinna Pazhuvettarayar.
“Ah! How did you come to know this?” asked the Prime Minister.
“Prime Minister! Do you think only you have clever spies? Madurantaka Devar, who went out, did not return into the fort. I must know the reason for this!” declared Chinna Pazhuvettarayar.
A smile blossomed on the Prime Minister’s face. At that very moment, from the fort’s entrance, shouts arose: “Long live Prince Madurantaka Devar! Long live!”
Everyone turned eagerly toward the direction of the shouts. Within the fort’s gateway—
Upon the elephant that was entering sat ‘Madhurantaka’, adorned with the prince’s crown and other ornaments. Beside the elephant, a closed palanquin was being carried along.

“Commander! There was a slight delay in Madhurantaka Devar’s return to the fort. Vani Ammai’s son, Sendhan Amudhan, fell from his horse and has been grievously injured. Sembiyan Maadevi gave instructions that he should be placed in the palanquin and brought into the fort, and then she went ahead. The son is fulfilling his mother’s wish. He is taking Amudhan in the palanquin and is himself riding upon the elephant. Soon, when the coronation takes place, he will have to parade through the streets atop the royal elephant, will he not? He is rehearsing for that even now!” said the chief minister, Aniruddha.

chapters.title: The Fortress Guard
paragraphs: Kalantaka Kandar had been observing the elephant and the palanquin that had entered the fortress with great attention for some time.
“How astonishing this is!” he exclaimed.
“What is astonishing? What is so surprising?” asked Aniruddhar.
“That Prince Madhurantakan should enter the fortress with such pomp! The prince is known to be a man of great modesty, is he not? Does he not usually travel with the curtains of his palanquin drawn?”
“Is it not natural that one day his shyness should be cast aside? He is soon to be crowned, after all!”
“Has it been decided, then, that Madhurantakan is to be crowned? Who has made this decision?”
“Why, the Emperor himself! When all of us went and gave our consent to the Emperor—”

“What use is it if the Emperor decides and we give our consent? Is it not the armies of Kodumbalur who must give their approval? Is it not strange that Prince Madhurantakan should ride so triumphantly into the fortress guarded by them?” said Kalantaka Kandar.
He took a few steps in the direction the elephant had gone, then turned back again.

Then, looking at Periya Pazhuvetaraiyar, he said, “Brother! I do not stand in the way of all of you entering the fortress. But I alone cannot come. Until yesterday, this fortress was under my command; today, I cannot enter it subject to another’s authority. My heart will not allow it. Go and meet the Emperor, and learn what his wishes are. I will remain outside with our forces. Furthermore, Kandamaran has gone in search of Vandiyathevan. I am eager to know what news he will bring. I must find out how Vandiyathevan escaped from the underground prison, and with whose help he got out. Forgive me, and all of you proceed into the fortress!” he said. The Velar of Kodumbalur opened his mouth to say something. But before he could speak, the elder Pazhuvettarayar approached and said, “Commander! This fool’s mind has become completely muddled. Let him go to ruin if he wishes; let us leave, come!”
However, when these matters were reported to the Emperor the next day, he did not agree with the elder Pazhuvettarayar’s opinion. He insisted that Kaalandhakandar must come.

“My beloved generals! You are all worthy of my trust. But among you all, the one in whom I placed the greatest trust was the fortress-keeper, Kaalandhakandar. Why has he not come? Until he arrives, the matter for which I have summoned you all cannot be concluded!” he declared.
The elder Pazhuvettarayar said, “Emperor! Forgive me! Any decision I agree to, my brother will also accept! It is not necessary that he must come here in person!”

“It is known throughout the world that, just as Lakshmana was to the sovereign Rama, so is Kaalandhakandar to you. Even so, why has he not come today? In all the important councils I have held here before, the younger Pazhuvettarayar has always been present. We have never made a decision without consulting him. Why then should such a wise and valiant man alone be absent now?” asked the Emperor.

Prime Minister Aniruddha replied, “My lord! I shall answer that. Kaalandhakandar has now become a disciple surpassing his master. Though he was told that the Emperor was summoning him, he refused to come. The elder Pazhuvettarayar pleaded with him in many ways, but he would not listen! He has refused to enter the fortress.”
“But let us not forget one thing! He has declared that he will agree to any decision we make here in accordance with the Emperor’s wishes!” said Parthibendran.
“Even so, what is the reason for the younger Pazhuvettarayar’s refusal to come here? Has some new, grave suspicion arisen in his mind?”

“Is it not said that to a frightened man, every shadow is a ghost? Now, whatever it is, he is filled with suspicion! He doubts whether Madurantaka is safe here. He suspects that Vandiyathevan has escaped from the underground dungeon...”

“If any doubt arises in Kaalanthakakandar’s mind, there will surely be a reason for it!” declared the Emperor. At once, silence settled over the gathering for a while. In each person’s heart, different thoughts arose.

Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar cleared his throat and said, “My lord! There may be a reason for my brother’s suspicion; there may also be none. I do not wish to accuse him of any fault. But I will tell you the true reason why he refused to come to the fort. For a long time, this Thanjavur fort was under his command and protection! Now, the responsibility for the fort’s security has shifted to the Periya Velaar! Because of that, he claims he cannot enter this fort! Who can do anything about such obstinate stubbornness?”
“Why not? Justice can be done!” replied Emperor Sundara Chozha.
As soon as the Emperor spoke thus, everyone fell silent once more.

Again, Sundara Chozha continued, “Ministers! The very foundation of the Chozha clan’s glory lies in the fact that the kings of this dynasty have always stood steadfast on the path of justice. You all know the history of one of my ancestors, who sentenced his own beloved son to death for having yoked a royal chariot to a calf in place of its mother. If they dispensed justice even to cattle, what justice would they not have given to their subjects? What fairness would they not have shown to the commanders who aided their rule? Why should I alone act against that tradition and bring disgrace upon the Chozha dynasty? It was a grave mistake that the fort’s security was taken from Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar and handed over to Periya Velaar. Immersed as I was in the grief of my dear son’s untimely death, I failed to reflect on the injustice done to Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar. The Commander-in-Chief must return the fort’s security to him at once!” he said.
The face of Periya Velaar of Kodumbalur darkened.

At that moment, Malayamaan of Thirukovalur stepped forward and said, “My lord! When the security of Thanjavur fort was with Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar, was it properly fulfilled? Did not a traitor sneak into this fort, reach the inner palace, and even hurl a spear at you? Was it not only because a mute woman intervened that your life was saved? What would have happened if she had not arrived at that moment? What is the use of the countless swords, spears, and lances stacked in the armory of this Thanjavur fort? What is the point of having so many soldiers here, and the peerless warriors of the Velakkara army, for the fort’s security?” “What is the use? Can we truly say that Commander-in-Chief Chinna Pazhuvettarayar fulfilled his duty properly? How can it be wrong that our Periya Velar has now taken charge of the fortress guard from him?” he asked.

“Uncle! Against the cruelty of fate, what is the point of placing blame on anyone? Were you able to save your beloved grandson, Aditya Karikalan? Did you not all strive together and make every possible effort?” said the Emperor.

“It is indeed necessary to investigate that matter, Emperor! There has still been no inquiry into who is responsible for the terrible incident that took place in Kadambur Palace. The truth of that event has yet to come to light!” said Malayaman.
“We were waiting for the arrival of Periya Pazhuvettarayar. Now that he has come, the investigation must begin,” declared Commander-in-Chief Periya Velar.

“Before the investigation begins, we must first inquire how Vandiyathevan, accused of murder, managed to escape from the underground dungeon. Who is responsible for that? This must be thoroughly examined at once!” said Parthibendran.
“Yes, I too have heard of it, Commander-in-Chief! How did Vandiyathevan escape from the underground dungeon? Who is to be held responsible for that?” asked the Emperor.
“Emperor! The answer to that must be given by the Prime Minister, Aniruddhar!” said Periya Velar.

“My lord! I myself accept that responsibility. Vandiyathevan’s escape was due to a small mistake on my part. But I also take upon myself the duty of bringing him back and handing him over. If I fail in that, I am ready to accept whatever punishment is deemed fit,” said Aniruddhar.
“Before the Prime Minister, my friend Kandhamaaran had already taken up that responsibility! He has gone in pursuit of the one who escaped from the underground dungeon!” said Parthibendran.
While these conversations were taking place, two women sat in that chamber. They were the Empress Vanamadevi and the young princess Kundavai.
Upon hearing that Kandhamaaran had gone in pursuit of Vandiyathevan, the expression on the face of the young princess Kundavai changed—a change noticed only by the Prime Minister Aniruddhar.

Looking at Parthibendran, the Chief Minister said, “Pallava Kumara! Your friend Kandhamaran is indeed a clever fellow. But in certain matters, there is little use in relying on him. Was he able to protect the illustrious Prince Karikalan, the very apple of the Chola kingdom’s eye, when he stayed as a guest in his own Kadambur palace? Could he capture Vandiyathevan, who escaped from prison and fled? I do not think so!”
He also noticed that Princess Kundavai understood the hidden meaning in his last words.
“Moreover, I have heard that Kandhamaran and Vandiyathevan are the closest of friends!” said the Commander-in-Chief Velar.
“That is an old story, Emperor! No one who has betrayed the Chola dynasty can ever be a true friend to the house of the Sambuvarayars!” declared Periya Sambuvarayar.

“What is the use of discussing that now? The responsibility of bringing Vandiyathevan back and surrendering him has already been accepted by the Chief Minister Aniruddha. The Commander-in-Chief must now return the guardianship of the Tanjore fort to Chinna Pazhuvettarayar!” said Sundara Chola.
“If this is the Emperor’s command, I am ready to carry it out!” said the Commander-in-Chief Periya Velar.
The tone of his voice betrayed the anger that surged within him.

“Kodumbalur Uncle! You are far older and more experienced than I am. I revere you as I would my own father. How could I ever command you? I have merely expressed my opinion. In this matter, let us also hear the views of the others present, and then consider what must be done,” said the Emperor.
“I have no wish for that! Chinna Pazhuvettarayar has failed in his duty. Therefore, the guardianship of the fort should not be returned to him!” Thirukovalur Malayaman said firmly, refusing outright.
“What is the Chief Minister’s opinion?” the Emperor asked.

“What has happened, has happened. At this moment, changing the guardianship of the fort may cause some difficulties. You have summoned us all here to discuss and decide the matter of royal succession. Once that is settled, we can take up this issue,” said Aniruddha.
“We cannot come to any decision without Chinna Pazhuvettarayar! Commander, what is your opinion?” asked Sundara Chola Chakravartin.

“I agree with Malayaman’s view. My brother has failed in his duty. He did not fulfill his responsibility properly. Therefore, the command of the fort should not be returned to him!” said Periya Pazhuvettarayar.

Everyone present there was well aware of the rivalry between the brothers, so Periya Pazhuvettarayar’s reply caused great surprise among all. But what the Emperor said next created even greater astonishment and shock.

“Commander! Chinna Pazhuvettarayar did not fail in his duty. It was I and you who failed to heed his words. Both of us ignored the warnings he gave from time to time. Listen, all of you. Chinna Pazhuvettarayar often warned me about the dangers posed by Veerapandiyan of Madurai. He told me that they had established contacts even within this very fort. He insisted that stricter security be placed around my palace and the women’s quarters. He urged that the secret passages between your palace and mine be closed off, and that guards be posted between the two palaces. You all know how devoted Kaalandhakakandar is to Periya Pazhuvettarayar. Yet, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar complained to me about him. He said that his elder brother was being deceived, and that he suspected conspirators were entering his palace. He suggested that Periya Pazhuvettarayar be moved to another palace, and that the treasury be shifted elsewhere. I did not pay heed to any of those warnings!...”
At this moment, Periya Pazhuvettarayar cleared his throat once. Hearing this, Sundara Cholar paused his speech.

“Emperor! Out of your compassion for me, you have left unsaid certain things. I shall say them myself. You did not wish to reveal my disgrace. I shall reveal it myself. My brother warned me about Nandini, whom I, blinded by infatuation, married. He warned me that the leader of the Pandya assassins came and went to her, claiming to be a sorcerer. Lost in the illusion of desire, blind and foolish, I did not listen. Yet, he did not fail in his duty—” He was the one at fault! When he knew it all so certainly, he should have found out that treacherous woman and those who came to her, and killed them. If I had tried to stop him, he would not have hesitated to kill me too, brother or not, with his own sword. Was it not a dereliction of his duty that he failed to do so?” When Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar spoke thus in his deep, resounding voice, all who heard him felt a chill run through their bodies. Understanding the inexpressible anguish that overflowed in his words, each one present was moved to sorrow.

“Lord of Tanadikar! Please, restrain yourself! Your younger brother, Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar, is a man who would do his duty to the end. It was I who stood in his way. I forbade him to bring any complaint against you or your young queen, and ordered that he should not even look me in the face if he had anything to say. I also rejected the plan to move you from your palace and station a Velakkara garrison there. I asked, why should I live in fear, clinging to this life, if it must be preserved so anxiously? The sorrow that had taken root in my heart, and the illness that had seized my body, made me weary of life itself. Pazhuvur Mama! Neither you nor your brother bear any responsibility for any harm that has befallen me or my lineage. I alone have brought these calamities upon myself!”
As the Emperor spoke thus, tears streamed in torrents from the eyes of Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar.

“Yes; there is not the slightest fault with Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar. When that young man Vandiyathevan first came here, Kalandhakandar warned us. He said that Vandiyathevan had spoken secretly with the young queen of Pazhuvur outside the fort in a palanquin. He suspected that the youth might be conspiring with the enemies of the Chola clan. He pointed out that Vandiyathevan had entered the fort by showing the Pazhuvur signet ring, and that he must have escaped from here through the secret passage in the women’s quarters of the Pazhuvur palace. I paid no heed to all this and treated it with indifference. Even our chief minister, Aniruddhar, who is renowned for his wisdom, and my own daughter, the young princess, were deceived by Vandiyathevan. Through him, they sent important letters…”

At this moment, Aniruddhar spoke up: “Emperor! Perhaps I was deceived. But the young princess is not one to be so easily misled. After sending the letter with Vandiyathevan, she instructed me to keep a close watch on his actions. I sent my disciple Azhwarkadiyan to Eezham, and had him follow Vandiyathevan to Kanchi as well…”

“Let it be so. Let us assume, for argument’s sake, that neither of you was deceived by him. But it is true that he and another escaped from the underground prison, is it not? None of you can deny that, can you? Had the guard of this fortress been in the hands of Chinna Pazhuvetarayar, such a thing could never have happened. Therefore, Commander! Summon Chinna Pazhuvetarayar at once and restore to him the charge of the Tanjavur fort’s security. You may say it is my command, if you wish!”

“So be it, my lord! May we take our leave now?” asked Commander Boothi Vikrama Kesari. The anger in his voice had subsided. The affection and support that Sundara Chozhar had shown towards the Pazhuvetarayars, and the graciousness with which he praised their character while forgiving their faults, had melted the commander’s heart. For a moment, he stood there, stunned.

“Yes; now all of you may go. Once Chinna Pazhuvetarayar has arrived, we shall meet again and discuss what must be done next. I have yet to finish speaking with my elder mother, the senior queen, about the matter of the royal succession. I need some time for that as well!” said the Emperor.

As everyone was about to depart, Parthibendran spoke: “Sir! The Prime Minister has accepted the responsibility of bringing back that traitor to friendship and to the throne, Vandiyathevan, and handing him over. I wish to remind him of that. No matter who else may forget, I can never forget the cruel death of Prince Aditya Karikalan, who was dearer to me than my own life. The culprit responsible for his death must be found and punished—at any cost!”

Periya Pazhuvetarayar cleared his throat with a roar like that of an old lion. He seemed about to say something, but then appeared to change his mind. Without a word, he walked out. The others followed him.

That very evening, by the Emperor’s command, the responsibility for guarding the Tanjavur fort was once again entrusted to Chinna Pazhuvetarayar. At first, he hesitated to accept it. He voiced his objections. He expressed his suspicion that there might be some intrigue in this as well. Only after Periya Pazhuvetarayar explained that this was the Emperor’s firm order did he agree to resume charge of the fortress security.
Except for a few of the Kodumbalur warriors, all the others were expelled from the fort. At the gates and along the ramparts, the guards of Pazhuvur resumed their watch as before.
This change led to disastrous consequences. Frequent quarrels broke out between the warriors of Pazhuvur and Kodumbalur, sometimes escalating into utter confusion.
Cries of “Long live Ponniyin Selvan!” and “Long live Prince Madhurantakan!” rose in rivalry, each slogan challenging the other.

These shouts spread throughout the land. The common people too joined in. Within the next three days, the entire Chola country was thrown into utter turmoil. Verbal disputes turned into fistfights, and then into brawls with sticks. Sticks and staffs soon gave way to swords and spears.
Just as the storm and flood had recently ravaged the prosperous Chola country, now a tempest of rage and a flood of madness swept in all directions, bringing ruin to the land.

chapters.title: ‘The God Born from the Sacred Stomach’
paragraphs: After Sundara Chozhar had sent word several times expressing his wish to see Sembiyan Maadevi, the venerable queen mother finally came to visit the Emperor. Hearing of her arrival, the Emperor walked as far as the entrance to greet her, waited there, and then led her inside. He requested her to be seated beside him on the throne.

“O King of Kings! My heart, wounded by the continual tidings of sorrow, finds solace in seeing that you are in good health. By the grace of the Almighty, may you live long, rule this world for many years, and continue to protect it,” said the aged queen.

“Mother! You speak of the strength that has returned to my legs, enabling me to walk again. I too am pleased by this! I, who could not rise to welcome you—whom all of Chozha Nadu reveres and worships—am now blessed, through the power of affection from a mute and deaf divine maiden, to have regained what I had lost. I have been granted the fortune to rise, walk, and welcome you. Yet, O Devi, I find no satisfaction in the mere fact of being alive, nor do I wish to live long any further. Please do not bestow such blessings upon me. Instead, pray that I may soon attain the abode of Shiva!” replied Sundara Chozhar.

“O Emperor! All your noble ancestors have attained either the warrior’s heaven or the feet of Shiva. Surely, in the other world, they have reserved a place for you as well. When the destined hour arrives, the hosts of Shiva will come to escort you. But there is no need for you to hasten towards such a state. You still have many duties left in this world. Under your just and unwavering rule, the people live in happiness. Temple services are being conducted everywhere. Shaivites, Vaishnavites, Buddhists, Jainas, and followers of many other faiths are all praying for your long life…”

“Mother! Let none of them pray for my life any longer. Praying for the extension of my life is but a prayer to prolong my suffering. Among all the warriors Chozha Nadu has produced, the bravest of the brave, Aditya Karikalan, has been lost to us—should I continue to live in this world for long after that? Would it not have been better if my life had ended before his?...” “Emperor! The grief of losing a son is indeed most cruel. Yet, I, a simple woman, need not speak to you of the power of fate. Was not Lord Krishna the inseparable companion of Arjuna? Krishna Paramatma, the incarnation of the divine protector Thirumal himself—yet even he could not save Ghatotkacha or Abhimanyu. Did not Arjuna continue to live even after such heroic sons perished? Was Arjuna a man without love for his children? ‘For the sake of protecting the lives of others, you must preserve your own life,’ so taught Krishna Paramatma, and Arjuna accepted this and lived on. Emperor! The counsel that Lord Krishna gave to Arjuna is fitting for you as well.”
“Mother! Abhimanyu fought valiantly on the battlefield and died a hero’s death. He attained the warrior’s heaven!”

“Your son was in no way lesser than Abhimanyu in valor! At the age of twelve, in the battle at Sevur, and at eighteen, in the final war against Veerapandiyan, the heroic deeds performed by Aditya Karikalan will never be forgotten by this world! In the end, Abhimanyu was surrounded by many, rendered weaponless, and slain in an unrighteous battle. In the same way, Aditya Karikalan too was cunningly isolated, surrounded by conspirators, and suddenly attacked and killed…”
“Mother! If only I could know for certain how he died, my heart would find some measure of peace.”

“Why wound your heart over what has already passed? Karikalan’s fate was fulfilled. The sword-star has fallen. Chola Nadu has lost a great hero. What is the use of inquiring into the manner and cause of his death?”

“Because the truth is not clear, suspicion falls upon various people. Mother! Just as Adiseshan bears the weight of the earth, Periya Pazhuvettarayar, who bore the very weight of the Chola Empire, is now the subject of suspicion for some. They heap false accusations upon him.”
“Can we not ask him directly and learn the truth?”

“Who has the courage to question Periya Pazhuvettarayar? I do not, Mother! Somehow, he has become entangled in this and his heart is deeply wounded. Unless he himself speaks of what happened, who can question him? Mother! After my great father Rajaditya fell heroically atop his elephant at the battlefield of Takkolam and attained the warrior’s heaven, the Chola army was thrown into chaos and began to scatter. It was Periya Pazhuvettarayar who blocked the fleeing soldiers, rallied them once more into an army, and drove back the forces of Kannaradevan…” The great warrior, Periya Pazhuvetarayar. Had he not acted as he did that day, the Chola kingdom would not exist today. In the battle of Thakkolam, his august body suffered sixty-four wounds. Even so, without losing heart, he stood firm on the battlefield and achieved victory. After that, we forbade him from going to war and made him an administrator. Such a man—one who is equal to my own father—what could I possibly ask of him?”
“Is there no other way for the truth to come out?”

“They say that Vandiyathevan of the Vanar clan was near Karikalan’s body. I thought we could question him and learn the truth. But he too has escaped from the underground prison. In this, Chinna Pazhuvetarayar has reason to blame the Prime Minister.”
Until now, Kundavai had remained silent. Now she interjected, “Father! Has not the Prime Minister taken responsibility, promising to bring that warrior in, no matter what?”

“My child! The Prime Minister has taken such responsibility many times before. But fulfillment is never certain. I hear that Sambhuvarayar’s son, Kandhamaaran, has gone in pursuit of the fugitive. Kandhamaaran is not much of a strategist. He is a man of impulsive wit, and, moreover, he is driven by a furious desire that no disgrace should befall the Sambhuvarayar clan. The fact that he is pursuing Vandiyathevan only increases my anxiety.”
“Sir! It is best to forget what has already happened. Think instead of what must be done next!”
“Mother! That is precisely why I summoned you. I have been sending one person after another. I need your counsel and help to decide what should be done next.”

“Emperor! You have many wise ministers to advise you. What counsel could this foolish woman possibly offer? Even when that great man who sanctified my life by taking my hand lived in this world, I never involved myself in affairs of state. Since he departed for the realm of the gods, I have devoted myself only to the service of Shiva. What advice could I possibly give?”
“Devi! Please do not be angry. Not all the women born into our Chola lineage have been fools. Here stands my beloved daughter, Kundavai—I have never seen anyone to match her intelligence…”
“Forgive me, Emperor of the Cholas! Was I born into the Chola clan? Am I not a daughter of the Mazhavarayar lineage?” said the elder queen.

“Whatever clan you were born into, women can be wise. They can bring prosperity to both the family into which they were born and the family into which they are married. Yet, there are also women who, by stubbornly clinging to their own ways, become the cause of ruin for both their birth and marital families. Mother, are you about to become the cause of such a clan’s destruction?”

At these words from Sundara Chozhar, Sembiyan Maadevi trembled as if she had stepped into fire. “Emperor! What words are these? Why should the Chola clan perish because of me? Am I possessed of such power?” she asked, her eyes brimming with tears, her voice choked with emotion.

“Devi! Forgive me for speaking so harshly. The thought that my eldest son has died while I still live tears my heart apart. Yet, there is a greater sorrow that haunts me. If, in my time, this Chola kingdom—which has grown strong and flourished since the days of my ancestors—were to be shattered and destroyed, there could be no punishment more terrible for me. For three years, I have not seen my beloved son Karikalan. For my sake, he built a golden palace in Kanchi. He often invited me to come and stay there, but I did not go. I kept citing my health as the reason. But that was not the real reason. If I had set out for Kanchi, the Pazhuvettaraiyars and their allies might have thought that I had lost faith in their friendship. Other minor kings and high officials might have thought the same. I feared what disaster might befall this Chola kingdom because of such suspicions. That is why I did not go to Kanchi. Had I gone, perhaps my beloved son Karikalan would be alive today…”
“King of Kings! You are a man of great wisdom and strength. Yet, even you cannot rewrite fate…”

“Yes, Mother! I could not change fate. But the regret that I could not see my son in his final days, that I did not know the sorrow that weighed upon his heart—that regret torments me now. Why do I say all this? It is only to let you know that, for the sake of the welfare of this Chola kingdom—established by the blood and sacrifice of Vijayalaya Chola and the heroic warriors who followed him—I have uprooted all my personal desires and attachments. For whatever reason, if the Pazhuvettaraiyars and the other minor kings allied with them…” It did not please them. They strove to place your son, my brother, Madurantakan, upon the Chola throne after me. There was nothing wrong in their endeavor. The son of Kandaradithar—who was a great soul and a sage of divine wisdom—was in every way worthy to ascend the Chola throne. In truth, it was a mistake that I myself was crowned. At that time, when all the elders spoke, I could not refuse; I yielded to their wishes. Today, I am reaping the consequences of that decision. Having lost my beloved son, I yet remain alive. This suffering is enough for me. I do not wish to witness, with my own eyes, this great kingdom destroyed by civil strife. Devi! You must help to prevent such a calamity from befalling the Chola Empire!” said Sundara Cholar.

Sembiyan Maadevi wiped the tears that had gathered in her eyes and replied, “King of Kings! Nothing you have said seems right to my limited understanding. After my husband, your father, Arinjaya Devar, ascended the throne. It happened according to my husband’s wishes. That you should ascend the throne after Arinjaya was also my husband’s desire. Your grandfather, Parantaka Devar, who ruled the three worlds under one umbrella, arranged matters thus before he departed. Therefore, there was no breach of custom in your ascending the Chola throne. My lord, immersed in devotion to Shiva, became a wealthy possessor of spiritual realization. His mind was not engaged in affairs of state. Thus, during his reign, the Chola kingdom diminished. After you came to the throne, the kingdom expanded once more. The enemies who had arisen in the south and north were vanquished. The chief reason for the kingdom’s renewed glory was your beloved son, Aditya Karikalan. The world knows he was invested as Crown Prince. How could I agree to set that aside and grant the right to rule to my own son? Even if I agreed, would the world accept it? Would the people of the kingdom consent? Emperor! Just now you said you wished to prevent the kingdom’s destruction by civil strife. If, setting aside Aditya Karikalan, the crown had been given to my son, would not that very civil strife have arisen? Would not the kingdom have been destroyed?” she asked.

“Yes, Mother! That is why I too hesitated. I tried to reconcile everyone and arrange matters so that all would agree. Before that could be accomplished, fate intervened. Karikalan’s life has ended. Mother! What should I do next? You must tell me! I can no longer bear the burden of this kingdom. I wish to entrust it to someone and fulfill Karikalan’s last wish. In the golden palace that Karikalan built for me in Kanchi, I wish to spend my final days— “I wish to put an end to this. Now, tell me—upon whose head should the crown be placed? Madurantakan is older than Arulmozhi in age. Though he is younger than me, he stands in the line of the younger father. The Kodumbalur Velar and the Thirukovalur Malayaman insist that the crown must be placed upon Arulmozhi. How can I agree to this act, which is against dharma, justice, and the traditions of our lineage? Or how can you agree to it? Mother, help me! Give your consent for Madurantakan to be crowned. With your approval, I will persuade Commander-in-Chief Periya Velar and Thirukovalur Malayaman to agree as well! Earn the merit of saving this Chola Empire by granting your consent and permission!” said Sundara Chola Chakravarti.

Sembiyan Maadevi replied, “My lord! Do not ask for my consent. I cannot act contrary to the command given to me by my lord, who has attained the feet of Shiva. However, I will no longer interfere in matters of the kingdom. Summon Madurantakan, ask for his consent, and do as is appropriate!”
“Yes, yes! We must summon Madurantakan and seek his consent before deciding anything. For that too, I need your help, Devi! Where is Madurantakan?” asked the Emperor.

Sembiyan Maadevi’s throat choked, her voice trembled, “Where is Madurantakan? For the past three days, I too have been asking that question—no one has given me an answer. O King! Where is my son? Summon the commander of the fort, Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar, and ask him!”

“Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar wishes to question you. He accuses you and Prime Minister Aniruddha of conspiring and hiding Madurantakan. Mother! Now, shall I summon both Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar and the Prime Minister? Grant me permission!” said the Emperor.
“Let them be summoned as you wish. I too will question them!” said Sembiyan Maadevi. Kundavai immediately went to the entrance and instructed the guards stationed there to send for them.

In a short while, the Prime Minister and Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar arrived. The Emperor turned to Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar and said, “Commander! The venerable lady whom the Chola land reveres and worships asks the same question you did: ‘Where is Madurantakan?’ Tell us what you know about Prince Madurantakan. Speak your suspicions openly, without concealment!”
Chinna Pazhuvettarayar spoke:

“The piety and virtue of the Devi are known throughout the world. The people of Chola Nadu revere her as a living goddess, and I too hold her in the same esteem. What I am about to say now should not be considered an accusation. For reasons unknown, the Devi does not wish for her son to ascend the Chola throne; this too is known to all. Neither I nor anyone else could possess greater affection for her son than the elder princess herself. Yet, it has become necessary to clarify certain matters that remain shrouded in mystery. Especially since the Emperor himself has commanded me, ‘Bring Madhurantaka here!’ I am compelled to voice some of my doubts.

Three days ago, the elder queen and Madhurantaka Devar left the fort together. They went to the hut of Sendhan Amudhan, who tends the flower gardens, to inquire after his well-being. Later, only the Devi returned to the fort. Some time after that, my brother and I were standing a little distance from the fort’s entrance, conversing with the Kodumbalur Velar. As I was inquiring about Madhurantaka Devar, an elephant, a palanquin, and a retinue of attendants entered the fort. I heard shouts of ‘Long live Madhurantaka Devar!’ It was the Prime Minister who pointed this out to me then. He said that the one atop the elephant was Madhurantaka Devar. I felt a slight doubt about this. Afterwards, by the Emperor’s command, the fort’s security came under my control. It is customary for Madhurantaka to stay at my palace. That night, I did not inquire about it. The next day, when I did, I learned that he had not come to my palace. Then, I searched the entire fort, questioned various people, but could learn nothing about Madhurantaka Devar! How did the one who entered the fort vanish so mysteriously? Devi and the Prime Minister must forgive me for what I am about to say now. I suspect that the two of them have conspired together, told Madhurantaka some alarming news, and compelled him to flee this city—nay, even this land. If what I say is wrong, I once again beg the elder princess’s pardon.”

In a trembling voice, Sembiyan Maadevi replied, “Commander! What you have just said is entirely false. I swear by the sacred lotus feet of Lord Shiva. I have not spoken to Prime Minister Aniruddha about my son recently. Nor have I plotted anything. It is true that Madhurantaka and I went to Sendhan Amudhan’s hut that evening. When I left, Madhurantaka said he would follow after a short while. I have not seen him since. For three days, I too have been searching for him!”
“I accept what the Devi says. In that case, it is the Prime Minister who must unravel this mystery!” said Kaalanthakar.
“What mystery?” asked Prime Minister Aniruddha.
“The mystery of the disappearance of the Devi’s son!”
“Commander! Is it true that you have searched this entire fort thoroughly, as you claimed?”
“Yes, I have searched and scoured every place except your palace.”
“What was the reason for leaving out my palace alone?”
“Only out of respect for your position as the Prime Minister of the Chola Empire!”

“Ah! Then it appears you have not performed your duty properly. Let that be. Emperor! Your own elder mother, the revered Empress, cherished by the Chola land as the foremost devotee of Shiva, has told me nothing about her son. I have not conspired with her in any way. But I will say this: the god born from the Devi’s sacred womb has indeed been in my palace for the past three days. Even now, he stands at the threshold of this very chamber, waiting to behold you and his mother. If you permit, I shall bring him in!”

As the Prime Minister spoke thus, the astonishment that seized everyone present was beyond words. The Emperor exclaimed, “Prime Minister! What jest is this! Would I hesitate to grant permission to bring the Devi’s son? Summon him at once!”
Prime Minister Aniruddha went to the doorway, clapped his hands, and returned inside. In the next moment, Sendhan Amudhan entered, led by Alwarkadiyan Nambi.
With great agitation, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar demanded, “Should there not be a limit to the Prime Minister’s mockery?”
But Sembiyan Madevi, stretching out both hands, her face overflowing with love and longing, called out, “My son!” At that, the commander’s heart was thrown into confusion.

Sendhan Amudhan, his eyes brimming with tears, said, “Mother! Has your heart at last found joy in calling me to you? This is the fruit of my past deeds!” With these words, he drew near to Sembiyan Madevi.
The Devi, who bore in her sacred womb the illustrious devotee of Shiva, celebrated in history as Madurantaka Uttama Cholan, embraced him with love and, overcome with joy, shed tears of bliss.

The sun had set. Darkness enveloped the land. The great river Ponni flowed on, her waves shimmering with the last vestiges of twilight. The dense groves on the riverbank rustled in the night breeze, their shadows merging with the deepening gloom. In the midst of this darkness, a lone boat glided silently across the water, its oars dipping rhythmically, barely making a sound.

On the boat sat Vandiyathevan, his mind restless, his eyes alert. The events of the day whirled in his thoughts—the secret meetings, the whispered conspiracies, the faces masked in both loyalty and treachery. The fate of the Chola dynasty seemed to hang in the balance, and he, a mere messenger, was caught in the heart of the storm.

Suddenly, from the far bank, a faint light flickered. Vandiyathevan strained his eyes. Was it a lantern? Or the glow of a torch? He signaled to the boatman, who nodded and steered the vessel toward the source of the light. As they drew nearer, the outlines of a small shrine emerged, nestled beneath the ancient banyan trees. The light came from within, casting long, wavering shadows on the stone threshold.

Vandiyathevan stepped ashore, his hand resting on the hilt of his sword. He approached the shrine cautiously. Inside, an old priest sat cross-legged before the sanctum, his face aglow in the lamp’s golden radiance. The air was thick with the scent of incense and the murmured chants of prayer.
The priest looked up as Vandiyathevan entered. His eyes, sharp and penetrating, seemed to see through the young man’s very soul.
“Who are you, my son?” the priest asked, his voice gentle yet commanding.
Vandiyathevan bowed respectfully. “I am a traveler, seeking shelter for the night.”
The priest smiled, as if he had heard this many times before. “All are travelers in this world, my child. Some seek shelter, some seek truth. Which do you seek?”
Vandiyathevan hesitated. The weight of his mission pressed upon him. “Perhaps both, Swami. Shelter for my body, and truth for my heart.”
The priest nodded, his gaze lingering on Vandiyathevan’s face. “Sit, then. Rest awhile. The river’s song will guard your sleep, and the gods will watch over you.”

As Vandiyathevan settled beside the priest, the night deepened. The river flowed on, bearing with it the secrets of kings and the prayers of the humble. In that sacred hour, beneath the gaze of ancient gods, a weary traveler found solace—and the promise of truth yet to be revealed.

chapters.title: The Contest of Sacrifice
paragraphs: Book Five – The Pinnacle of Sacrifice

Sembiyan Maadevi, born into the Mazhavar clan and the consort of the wise and noble Kandaraditha Chozhar, is referred to in the inscriptions of her time as “the illustrious lady who bore in her sacred womb Sri Madhurandhaka Devar, the Uttama Chozha Devar.” Ordinarily, mothers bear their children in their womb for ten months before bringing them into the world. Yet, there are some mothers who raise children born of other women as their own. Because Sembiyan Maadevi had, for a long time, brought up another child as her own, it seems that someone who knew this truth made special mention in the inscription, stating that “she bore Uttama Chozhar in her sacred womb.”

When Uttama Chozhar was a boy of five, Sembiyan Maadevi happened to meet him and Vaani Ammaiyar. Many years later, when she met Vaani Ammaiyar again, Sembiyan Maadevi inquired with affection about her well-being. Naturally, the old queen’s heart overflowed with love for Sendhan Amudhan, whom she believed to be Vaani’s child. When she asked about the child, she noticed a look of shock and fear on Vaani Ammaiyar’s face. At first, she thought there might be other reasons for this. Since Vaani could not speak, it was impossible to learn anything definite from her. Nevertheless, remembering the help Vaani Ammaiyar had once rendered her, and moved by the affection she felt for the child, Sembiyan Maadevi ensured that both mother and child lived without want or worry. She arranged for them to reside near the city of Thanjavur and granted them land so that they could serve in the Thalikulathar temple by offering flowers.

Sendhan Amudhan grew up excelling in learning, virtue, and devotion to Shiva. He eagerly assisted his mother in the floral offerings to the temple. The more Sembiyan Maadevi saw this, the more her natural affection for the boy grew. One day, a strange suspicion arose in her mind. It brought her, all at once, joy, pain, and an inexplicable fear. Try as she might, she could not rid herself of this doubt. The memory of her own child, who had died a few days after birth, often came to her, disturbing her peace of mind.

At last, she resolved that one day she would ask Vaani Ammaiyar directly and learn the truth. She summoned Vaani to her in private. She told her to take her dead child and, without anyone’s knowledge, bury it somewhere… Isn’t it so? He said that a temple should be built at the place where the child was buried, as a memorial, and asked her to show the location. The very memory of these old events brought him pain. Since Vani was both deaf and mute, he had to ask all this through sign language. That caused him an even deeper, unspeakable anguish.

Vani hesitated greatly to answer his questions. At last, unable to disobey the orders of the Princess, she revealed the truth. She explained in detail that the child given to her for burial had not actually died, that Karuthiruman had shown her the child, that fearing what might happen if she returned to the palace, she had gone with Karuthiruman to Thirumuraikkaadu, and that after some time, when Karuthiruman left her and disappeared, she had returned to Pazhaiyarai.

When Sembiyan Maadevi learned that Sendhan Amudhan was indeed the child she had carried in her womb for ten months and given birth to, she was at once overwhelmed with boundless joy. Her whole body thrilled and surged with emotion. Tears streamed down her face. The urge arose within her to call out, “My son!” and embrace Sendhan Amudhan tightly. Yet, she restrained that longing. At the same time, she was filled with fear, thinking of the confusion that might arise if this truth were to come out. Because her heart had attained the lofty wisdom to consider, “Are not all children born into this world the children of God?” she was able to control the motherly affection that welled up for her own child. “What does it matter if he was raised in a palace or in a humble hut? Are not all the fleeting pleasures and luxuries of this unstable human life mere illusions? Is not the destiny that must be attained after renouncing worldly life the truly important thing? Since my husband renounced royal pleasures and lived a life of bliss in the shadow of Lord Shiva’s holy feet, it seems fitting that the child born to him should live in a hut and earn the grace of serving God!” Thus, she often strengthened her mind with such thoughts.

Nevertheless, knowing that Sendhan Amudhan was the son born from her own womb, the thought that she should not place Madurantakan, the prince she had raised, upon the Chola throne, grew stronger in her heart. She had already confessed to Kandaradithar the wrong she had done and had received his forgiveness. “What does it matter if he is the child born from your womb, or if he is the child of an orphaned woman? In the eyes of God, both are equal. Therefore, raise Madurantakan as your own son! But do not desire that he should ascend the Chola throne! Neither agree nor disagree to that! For the sake of the Chola lineage into which I was born—” It would be an act of treachery. If such a situation were ever to arise, do not hesitate to confess the truth!” Thus had Kandaradithar spoken to the queen, extracting such a promise from her. Periya Piratti Sembiyanmadevi had resolved, at all costs, to fulfill that promise.

Yet, without knowing that her own son was growing up in a humble hut as the child of Vani Ammai, that great soul had departed for the abode of Shiva. Had he known the truth, what would he have done? What orders would he have given regarding Sendhan Amudhan? Sembiyanmadevi had pondered this question countless times. “By the will of God, things have come to pass thus. That the mute woman’s son should be raised in the palace, and the emperor’s son should grow up in a hut—this too is the divine will. We must not interfere with it. If we try to change it, many confusions will arise. The heart of the foster child would be deeply wounded by such an act. Such a sin must not be committed!” Thus, she finally resolved.

It was only by the strength of her unparalleled faith in the Lord’s grace that she was able to carry out this decision in practice. Yet, she could not help but think often of Sendhan Amudhan. Whenever his memory arose, the natural motherly love within her would surge and overflow. This inner struggle had been taking place in the depths of her heart for many years.

Is it not true that a flood, long restrained by a dam, may one day suddenly break through and burst forth? Many have seen and experienced the force and swiftness with which such a flood rushes forth when the dam is breached. Likewise, the flood of motherly love that Sembiyanmadevi had long dammed up within her heart now broke through its banks and surged forth.

It was the words of the Chief Minister Aniruddha—when he referred to “the god born from the goddess’s womb”—that caused the dam within Sembiyanmadevi’s heart to break. The moment Aniruddha uttered those words, Sembiyanmadevi, in a single instant, relived the entire experience of carrying her child in her womb for ten months. Forgetting herself, forgetting the vow she had made, she called out to Sendhan Amudhan, “My son!” She embraced him and wept tears in abundance.
Even though Sembiyan Maadevi was in a state of stupefied bewilderment, overwhelmed by emotion, the words spoken by Amudhan had been deeply imprinted in her mind.

“Mother! Did your heart, even now, consent to call me ‘son’?”—had he not said so? What was the meaning behind those words? Did Amudhan already know who his birth mother was? Had he known all along, yet concealed it for so long?

For a while, she was unable to utter a word, lost in a rapture beyond speech. Then, steadying her heart, Sembiyan Maadevi spoke in a trembling voice, “My son! Did you already know that I am the sinner who bore you for ten months in my womb? Did you know, and were you angry with me? Is that why you never questioned me about it?”
At that moment, Senthan Amudhan, as if a floodgate had burst open, poured forth words brimming with emotion:

“Mother! For some time now, I have known that I am the fortunate one born from your womb. I have been performing penance, yearning for the day when you, revered by the world as a woman of virtue, would one day call me ‘son’. I have striven to make myself worthy of being called your son. Day and night, I have meditated upon the holy feet of Lord Shiva. Even if you did not call me, I had resolved to come to you myself. But I waited for the matter of the kingdom’s succession to be settled. The only right I sought was to call you ‘mother’. I wished to come to you and claim my mother’s right only after it was certain who was the rightful heir to the throne. Amma! To avoid causing you any pain, I was even prepared to renounce Poonguzhali, who had stolen my heart. Fortunately, she too changed her mind. Mother! Three days ago, a great danger befell my life—soon after Poonguzhali and I had bowed to you and received your blessings, that peril struck. A true friend saved me from that danger. At that time, I did not feel much joy about it, nor did I thank him enough. Now I realize how much I am indebted to him. You have called me ‘son’ with your own sacred lips, have you not? I have lived to see this day, have I not? That is enough! I am blessed. I want nothing more. Let what has happened here be known only to those present. Let no one else know. Let there be no further confusion in the kingdom! Please grant leave for Poonguzhali and me to depart at once for Kodikkarai!”
The storm of emotions that these words stirred within Periya Piratti Sembiyan Maadevi’s heart cannot be described in mere words.
With a voice trembling, mingled with sobs and tears, she said softly, “Child, you are my true son! You are the noble prince, born of my lord, blessed with divine grace!”

All this while, Sundara Chozhar, Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar, and the younger princess Kundavai Devi had been struck dumb with astonishment. The secret that had just been revealed, and the many consequences that might arise from it, had caused a great tumult in their hearts.
