Of them, it was Kundavai who first found the strength to speak. “Father! Now I understand why Periya Piratti was so adamant that the crown should not be placed upon Madhurantakan’s head!”

Sundara Chozhar, his amazement and bewilderment now fading, replied, “Yes, my daughter! But that reason no longer exists. Surely, my elder mother can no longer object to crowning the noble prince born of her own sacred womb?”

Sembiyan Maadevi looked at Sundara Chozhar with some agitation and said, “Emperor! Did you not hear the words my son just spoke? No one outside those present here must ever know of this matter! My son does not claim the right to the throne. He has declared this before you with his own lips!”

“Yes, my lord! The troubles that already beset this Chozha kingdom are enough! Let me not be the cause of any new strife. Grant me leave! Bless me and Poonguzhali, who has consented to be my wife, and send us on our way!... Poonguzhali! Come here!” said Amudhan.

Poonguzhali, who had been standing near the threshold, entered the room. Senthan Amudhan and Poonguzhali first bowed in reverence to Sembiyan Maadevi. Then, they paid their respects to the Emperor. Rising, Senthan Amudhan said, “My lord! Grant us leave to depart at once for Kodikkarai! Mother! Give us your blessing!”
Sembiyan Maadevi turned to the Emperor and said, “Yes, my lord! Let us grant them leave and send them on their way. Whenever I wish, I shall go to Kodikkarai and see them myself!”
Sundara Chozhar replied, “That is something that can never be! I will not grant leave!”

The Prime Minister interjected, “Emperor! Let no decisions be made at this moment. Let these people remain in my residence for a few more days. The son of the elder princess has been found, but the son-in-law of the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar has not yet been located. Until news of him arrives, let them stay here. Until then, let no one else besides those present here learn of this secret!”
“At the very least, Arulmozhi must be told!” insisted the younger princess, Kundavai Devi.
“No, no! Please, do not do that—anything but that,” pleaded Sendhan Amudhan.

At last, the Emperor said, “Devi! Let things unfold as they may. After all these days, today your son, born of your own womb, has come to you. I cannot consent to parting you from him immediately. For a few days at least, remain together here. Stay either in my palace or in the Prime Minister’s mansion. After a final decision is made regarding the right to the kingdom, we can consider sending them to Kodikkarai. Until then, let no one else besides those present here learn of this matter!”

chapters.title: Vanathi’s Theft
paragraphs: Arulmozhi Varman’s mind was greatly troubled. The main reason for this was the ever-increasing turmoil in Chola Nadu surrounding the question of royal succession. Wherever he went in an attempt to pacify the people, their fervor only grew stronger. Cries such as “Ponniyin Selvar is our king!” and “Arulmozhi Varman must be crowned!” rose up everywhere, echoing and resounding in all directions.

Competing with these were other slogans heard in certain places: “Long live the ancient clan of the Pazhuvettaraiyars!” and “Down with the tyrannical Kodumbalur Velar!” If the prince approached such gatherings, hoping to find greater support, those present would immediately begin to shout, “Long live Ponniyin Selvar!” Why was this so? Even the Pazhuvur soldiers, who had been newly assigned to guard the fort, upon seeing Ponniyin Selvar, abandoned their old slogans and joined in the chorus: “Arulmozhi Varman must be crowned!” “May the valiant conqueror of Lanka, Ponniyin Selvar, live long!”

Thus, not only did his efforts fail to win over the common people and the warriors, but Ponniyin Selvar found himself increasingly distressed by the mounting opposition to his wishes. For several days, Madurantaka Thevar had not been seen, which only deepened his anxiety. He was aware that the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar was accusing the Kodumbalur Velar of wrongdoing in this matter. There was some justification for this suspicion. Even Arulmozhi Varman himself could not entirely dismiss his doubts. The Kodumbalur Velar and the Thirukovalur Malayaman were determined to see him crowned. It seemed as if even the chief minister Aniruddha was conspiring with them. Had they all hidden Madurantaka Thevar away somewhere? Or, perhaps, had they brought harm to Madurantaka Thevar’s very life?

The Velar and Malayaman believed that the Pazhuvettaraiyars and the Sambuvaraiyars were responsible for the death of his beloved elder brother, Aditya Karikalan. Seeking vengeance, had they now done some harm to Madurantaka? Ah! What is wrong with these people? They act rashly, without thought. In the end, will not all the blame fall upon his own head? Today, the people of Chola Nadu utter his name with blessings. They urge that he must ascend the throne. But will the hearts of the people always remain thus? Is it not the nature of the masses to waver often? These very same people, tomorrow, might heap blame upon his name. They might say he is the sinner who had his uncle, Madurantakan, murdered to ascend the throne. Why, they might even accuse him of being responsible for the death of Aditya Karikalan at Kadambur Palace.

Oh, divine one! Was it for bearing such terrible accusations that the goddess Mandakini saved me from drowning in the Kaveri, instead of letting me die? Today, that very princess, now revered as a goddess, must save me from this perilous predicament. May she grant me her grace, that the worst of all infamies that can befall a man in life may not come upon me.

Stories of close kin in the royal family of Eelam killing one another to ascend the throne were etched deep in Arulmozhi Varman’s heart. The mere thought that such a disgraceful infamy might befall him too caused him unbearable anguish. If only he could confide in someone, seek counsel—yet, there seemed to be no one worthy of such trust. It seemed to him that everyone around him was plotting against him. Some truly harbored enmity towards him. Others, thinking to do him good, were in fact striving to place a dreadful blame upon his head.

In such a situation, whom could he trust? To whom could he reveal his innermost thoughts and seek advice? Even in his beloved sister, Princess Kundavai, who loved him without equal and was worthy of his devotion, his confidence had begun to waver. It seemed to him that she too was engaged in some secret endeavor without his knowledge. Why, even his dearest Vanathi—was she not, too, trying to hide something from him? Was she not slipping away somewhere in secret, returning with a mysterious expression upon her face?

He could bear anything else, but Arulmozhi Varman resolved that he could no longer tolerate Vanathi’s enigmatic behavior. He noticed Vanathi glancing around cautiously and setting off alone somewhere. At once, he began to follow her quietly, without her knowledge. Through the upper terraces and corridors of the palace, then descending to the lower floors, Vanathi proceeded further and further along a secret passage flanked by high walls on either side.
Believing that Vanathi was going to the secret place where Madurantaka was being kept prisoner, Arulmozhi Varman followed her with great eagerness and impatience.

At last, Vanathi reached another large section of the palace and tried to enter a room and close the door behind her. At that moment, Arulmozhi Varman sprang forward and managed to wedge his foot inside so that Vanathi could not shut the door.
Grasping her hand, which was trying to close the door, he said sternly, “Vanathi! Your tricks will not work with me! Who is it that you are hiding in this room?”
Vanathi, her face blossoming with a smile, replied, “Sir, in truth, my trick has already succeeded! If I had invited you, you would not have come. Now, come in and see for yourself who is here!”
Expecting to find Madurantaka Devar inside, Arulmozhi Varman was astonished and delighted to see Vallavaraiyan Vandiyathevan lying on the bed.
Vandiyathevan, seeing him, sat up and said, “My lord! Welcome! I have been waiting for you these two days. Please, somehow rescue me from the prison of these women!”

Ponniyin Selvan hurried to sit beside Vandiyathevan and asked, “My friend! What is this? How did you get here? How did one who escaped from the underground dungeon become trapped in the prison of these women? All this time, I thought you were in Eezham! I was even thinking that in a few days I would come there and join you!”

“Yes, Prince! I should indeed have been in Eezham all this time! I should have been searching for the crown of the Pandya dynasty and the gem-studded necklace given to them by Indra. I tried to prevent the physician’s son from killing the Saiva-madman Sendhan Amudhan, and thus fell into this misfortune. When Pinakapani’s spear was hurled at me, I lost consciousness and fell. I do not know how I ended up in the prison of these women. Please, have mercy and help me escape from here. Otherwise, your noble brother and my beloved lord, Aditya Karikalan, will be falsely accused of his murder, and the blame will fall upon me!” said Vandiyathevan.

Vanathi interjected, “Sir! What he says is not true. If he escapes and runs away, only then will such blame fall upon him. Until the truth is revealed, it is your noble sister’s wish that he remain hidden here in secret.”

“There is truth in what she says. Only if you attempt to escape will that accusation fall upon you. It may even fall upon me. Instead, it is better to prove to the world what truly happened. First, tell me! Tell me in detail everything that happened at Kadambur!” said Ponniyin Selvan.
Vandiyathevan then narrated everything that had happened there, as far as he knew. Even after hearing it all, the prince could not determine exactly how Aditya Karikalan’s death had occurred.

chapters.title: “I Myself Shall Wear the Crown!”
paragraphs: At last, Vandiyathevan spoke: “Prince! If only one man would speak the truth, he could clear me of all blame and reveal what truly happened. That one man is none other than Periya Pazhuvetarayar. It must have been that valiant elder who, while I was hiding in the veena treasury of Kadambur Palace, suddenly seized me by the throat, dragged me down, and left me unconscious. I can only surmise it was him—no one else could have been there at that moment. That old lord, who harbored suspicions about Nandini Devi, must have disguised himself as a Kalamukha Saiva and come in secret to see what was happening. Idumbankari, who belongs to the Kalamukha Saiva sect, must have helped him find a secret way in. But from the very first time that great warrior set eyes on me, he has harbored a deep dislike for me. That hatred only grew stronger with each passing day. He will never come forward to speak the truth and save my life. In fact, if I die bearing this terrible accusation, it might even bring him satisfaction. Therefore, Prince, grant me leave to escape! If I can, I will go to Eezha Nadu and there seek out the Pandya dynasty’s royal crown and the jeweled necklace. Or else, here and now, let your sword end my life. Do not make me a scapegoat to be paraded and executed at the crossroads, bearing the blame for killing your beloved brother, who cherished me with boundless affection! Dying by your sword would bring me far more comfort! Or, if I must, let me die by poison from the hand of this Kodumbalur princess. She and your noble sister have shown such compassion to this orphan, bringing me back from the very doorstep of Yama’s realm to this world again. For that, I shall never be able to repay them with gratitude!”

When Vandiyathevan had spoken thus, Vanathi turned to the prince and said, “Listen, my lord! Just listen! This pure-hearted warrior has no wish to die a hero’s death on the battlefield before his foes! He is ready to perform penance to die by poison at the hands of women!”

“Prince! It seems that the reproaches of your noble sister and this lady will kill me with their words alone. Would it not be better to die by their hands, drinking poison, than to endure such scorn?” said the valiant scion of the Vana clan, Vandiyathevan.

Arulmozhi Varman listened to all these conversations with only half his attention. It seemed as though his mind was intensely occupied with some other matter. Suddenly, he sprang up and stood, exclaiming, “Aha! I have made my decision. I myself shall ascend the throne as the Emperor of Chola Nadu. Throughout the land and cities, the people are clamoring, ‘Let Arulmozhi Varman be crowned!’ The wish of the warriors is the same! I shall fulfill the desire of them all. Do you know why? Only so that I may declare you innocent and set you free. If, because of that, any disgrace should come to me, let it come! It will not touch me! Some of the minor kings who bear enmity towards me may perhaps try to spread such slander. But the people will not believe it. If the petty kings dare to lay blame upon me, that blame will turn back upon themselves! I could even say that it was they who invited him to Kadambur Palace and murdered him. For such treachery of trust and for treason against the royal clan, I could punish them all. Whatever happens, I myself am going to be crowned. Even if my father, my sister, or these others oppose this, I shall act against their wishes. But I cannot stand by and watch any harm befall you!”
With excitement, Vanathi said, “Alas, the Young Princess is not here to hear these words of yours! Please say these words once again in her presence!”
“Why only once? I shall say it many times! And I shall prove it in action as well!” declared Ponniyin Selvan.

Vandiyathevan, wiping away the tears that had sprung to his eyes, said in a trembling voice, “My lord! If, for the sake of a wretch and orphan like me, you change your resolve and ascend the throne, it will be the greatest fortune that has ever befallen Chola Nadu. To speak the truth, as far as I know, Madurantaka Devar is not at all fit to be crowned. One who travels in a closed palanquin like a woman, who involves himself in conspiracies for the sake of the kingdom—how can such a man be worthy to rule an empire? Is it right that one who embodies such cowardice should ascend the Chola throne, adorned by Vijayalaya Cholan and Parantaka Cholan? It is no wonder that the people of this land do not wish for it!”
“Perhaps it is realizing this that Madurantaka Devar has vanished without a trace!” said Vanathi.
“Yes, yes! I am going to give up the effort of searching for him and finding him. I shall crown myself!” declared Arulmozhi Varman.

Even as he spoke these words, Kundavai entered the room and, hearing him, said, “Brother! Cast aside such desires at once! You have neither the throne nor the jeweled crown. Have you forgotten that my dear friend Vanathi has sworn never to ascend the throne of Tanjore? Without her, I could never bear to see you take the crown with another by your side!”
“Sister! At that moment, you need only close your eyes. If you wish, I will even help you shut them myself!” said Vanathi.

Ponniyin Selvan turned to Kundavai and said, “Sister, can the Chola kingdom go on without a king just because of your friend’s vow? Our father is stubbornly insistent on laying down the burden of the kingdom and retiring to Kanchi. Madurantaka Devar has vanished mysteriously. What other way is there? It seems I cannot escape being crowned, no matter what. Are you not aware of the turmoil spreading across the land regarding the right to the throne? How long can we leave this unrest unresolved?”

“Brother! I bring happy news. That is why I hurried here. The vanished Madurantaka Devar has reappeared. The penance performed by our Chola ancestors has not gone in vain! You need not worry about what will become of the kingdom. Even if he refuses, we must insist and perform the coronation for him!” said the young princess.

Her enthusiasm caused some surprise among the other three. It was true that for some days now, Princess Kundavai had been favorable to crowning Madurantaka. But until now, she had not shown such fervor.
Ponniyin Selvan suppressed his astonishment and asked, “Devi! Where was he hiding? Why? How did he reappear?”

“He was right near us, yet we could not recognize him. Brother! Only the one born of Chembiyan Maadevi’s sacred womb is worthy to ascend the Chola throne. This kingdom rightfully belongs to your uncle. Banish from your mind the thought of wearing the crown! Listen to this wonder, brother! Just a few days ago, our uncle faced a great danger. A murderer—”

He aimed to hurl his spear at him. Had he thrown it, Madurantaka Deva’s life would have ended then and there. Another untimely death would have struck the Chola dynasty. Do you know who was the valiant hero who prevented that from happening? Do you know who risked his own life to save our uncle?”

As she spoke, the Young Princess turned her wide, expressive eyes upon Vandiyathevan. The love, eagerness, gratitude, respect, support, and sympathy brimming in those eyes reached deep into Vandiyathevan’s heart, leaving him utterly bewildered.
Ponniyin Selvan, lost in a sea of astonishment, said, “What is this, Akka! I do not understand. My friend never told me anything about this either!”
“He would not have told you, because he himself does not realize the greatness of what he has done. He does not know how much the Chola dynasty owes him!”

“Akka! You speak as if you are giving us a riddle. Everything is shrouded in mystery! It would be better if you explained clearly, without leaving us in needless suspense. How, where, and from what danger did this Vanar clan hero save Madurantaka? And where is Madurantaka Deva now?” asked the prince.

“Ponniyin Selva! In just a few moments, he himself will be here! Knowing that you have arrived, I have sent word to bring him here. Hear the story from his own lips. Or else, ask Poonguzhali, who witnessed everything with her own eyes… Look, it seems they are arriving now.”

Indeed, at that moment, the sound of footsteps was heard outside the chamber. In a short while, four people entered. They were Prime Minister Aniruddha, Azhwarkkadiyan, Poonguzhali, and Sendhan Amudhan. Only Sendhan Amudhan was dressed unusually, unlike his usual self. Upon his head was a princely crown, he wore a silk garment, and was adorned with ornaments befitting royal lineage.
Those inside the room gazed at the group with some surprise.
“Sister! Did you not say Madurantaka would come? We do not see him,” said Arulmozhi.

“Brother! Look, before you stands one wearing the princely crown—he is the very one born of Sembiyan Madevi, the son of Sivagnana Kandaraadithar. He is our uncle by custom, the pious devotee of Shiva. All these years, he lived in obscurity under the name Sendhan Amudhan. By the fortune of the Chola dynasty, he has now come forth. Just a few days ago, a wicked man tried to kill him with a spear. It was this Vanar— The valiant scion of the Chola clan rendered incomparable service to the dynasty. Even though this brave Vaishnavite was a disciple of our Chief Minister and the other was a Saivite, he did not hesitate to bring him safely into the fortress!…”

At this moment, Thirumalai interjected, “Devi! I did not render any assistance to this Saivite. Nor did I wish to do so. I merely disguised him and brought him on an elephant so that it would be possible to bring the Prince of Vallam in a palanquin.”

Kundavai said, “Yes, yes! Thirumalai Nambi has indeed rendered great service in two ways. When he crowned Madurantaka Devar with the prince’s diadem and brought him on an elephant, perhaps he did not truly know that he was bringing the rightful heir to this kingdom’s throne. Or perhaps he did know—of that, I am not certain! Let it be as it may! Brother! The one whom we all believed to be Madurantaka Devar all these years is, in truth, not Madurantaka Devar. He is the true fruit of the Chola dynasty’s penance, born of the womb of the elder Empress. By the inscrutable play of the Lord, he was made to live all these years in humble circumstances. Yet, the noble qualities inherited from his Chola lineage have always shone forth in him, and we have all, at various times, marveled at them. Can we ever forget how, once upon a time, he and Poonguzhali brought you, the valiant son of the Vanar clan, safely from Kodikkarai to Nagapattinam? Today, through the words of Sembiyan Maadevi, we have learned that he is, in truth, our uncle. He himself has acknowledged it. Brother! On this auspicious day, I welcome him to our palace. No, no! I welcome him to his own palace. I invite him, who has lived apart from us for so long, to rejoin our family today. The reunion of one who has been separated from us for so many days should be celebrated with great festivity. But this is not the time for such celebrations. The more we keep this news within ourselves and do not let it spread outside, the better. Therefore, let us conduct this celebration among ourselves. Uncle! Please come this way! After such a long separation, we cannot express our joy at your return to the Chola clan in any other manner. Whenever my dear brothers depart for distant lands or return from their journeys, it is my custom to anoint their foreheads with sacred ash and the vermilion tilak. In the same way, today, I shall place sacred ash and vermilion on your forehead as you return and rejoin us!”
Having said this, the young princess Kundavai Devi applied sacred ash and vermilion to the forehead of Madurantakan, who had been known all these years as Sendhan Amudhan.
At that moment, Prime Minister Aniruddha raised his voice in blessing: “Long live the illustrious prince of the Chola lineage, Ilango Madurantaka! May he reign for an age!”
“Long live! Long live!” echoed Azhwarkkadiyan Nambi.

When Kundavai first began to speak, Arulmozhi Varman’s heart was filled mostly with astonishment. There was a trace of doubt mingled in it as well. He wondered if all this was merely his beloved sister’s playful jest, or if she was speaking thus for some important reason. But as she continued, his doubts melted away. He realized that the words of Princess Kundavai were overflowing with the affection that welled up from the depths of her heart. The flood of emotion that surged within his cherished sister swept him up as well.

After adorning herself with the tilakam, Princess Kundavai went to stand beside Sendhan Amudhan and said, “Uncle! I have always held you dear. There were times I wished you could have been my brother. Perhaps it is the blood that binds us which has given rise to such feelings in me!” So saying, she embraced Sendhan Amudhan and wept tears of joy.

Vandiyathevan exclaimed, “Ah! I had my suspicions before. Surely, within this devotee of Shiva, Sendhan Amudhan, the valorous royal bloodline must have lain hidden all along. Otherwise, would he have given shelter to a wanderer like me, a man with neither name nor clan, and even aided my escape from the city? O prince, once before you rendered me a great service—grant me that favor once again! It pains me that I will not be able to witness your coronation. What can I do! Yet, there is one thing that brings me immense happiness. Even more than Sendhan Amudhan ascending the Chola throne, I am delighted that Poonguzhali, who helped me cross the seas, is to become queen! The dream of the Samudra Kumari, the maiden of the waves, is about to come true far sooner than she could have imagined!”
Kundavai interjected, “Sir! It would be better if you refrained from speaking so much for a few more days. If you recover and try to run away again, at least you’ll be able to run swiftly!”

Then she turned to Arulmozhi and said, “Brother! Arulmozhi! Now we understand why our beloved grandmother opposed crowning her own son all these years. Even we could not find satisfaction in the idea of the elder Madurantaka ascending the throne. He lacked the qualities that should be found in one born to the valorous Chola clan. No matter how hard our grandmother tried, devotion to Shiva never took root in his heart. As for courage, he did not possess even a trace of it.

Even so, somehow we have managed to reconcile ourselves to crowning him. Not only are we satisfied with conferring the throne upon this new Madurantakan, but we are also filled with enthusiasm and delight. I, too, long to see Poonguzhali, who saved you and the Prince of Vallam from drowning in the midst of the sea, ascend the throne. Our Prime Minister must make the necessary arrangements for this at once!” she said.

“Devi! Periya Pazhuvetarayar must tell us what truly happened in the Kadambur palace, where he had set his heart. We must also learn what became of the old Madurantaka Thevar. How can we set a date for the coronation before these two matters are settled?” asked Aniruddha.
“I shall ask Periya Pazhuvetarayar myself. As for finding the old Madurantakan, that is your responsibility!” said Kundavai.

At that moment, the prince whom we had until then called Sendhan Amudhan—now Madurantaka Thevar—looked at Ponniyin Selvan and said, “Prince! You addressed me with the respect due to an uncle. These noble ones, too, call me ‘Prince.’ But I cannot bring myself to call you ‘son.’ Having spent twenty-two years in a humble hut, I cannot suddenly think of myself as a young scion of the imperial clan. I have a request to make of you all. Because of my part in Vandiyathevan’s escape, I was imprisoned for a few days in the underground dungeon. There, through the man in the next cell, I learned today’s news. He told me that the mute woman’s child is being raised in the palace as a royal prince, and that a child of the royal clan is being raised in the mute woman’s house. At that moment, the truth became clear to me. I guessed the reason for the affection the world-revered Sembiyan Madevi showed me. I hoped that one day she would call me ‘son.’ That wish has been fulfilled today. I desire nothing more!”
The Prime Minister interrupted, “Prince! It is not a question of whether you wish it or not! We must consider what is just, what is proper.”

“Ah! Consider well; as far as I am concerned, there is no need for deliberation. I have already thought long and hard and made my decision. Many times, Poonguzhali told me, ‘I am going to marry a royal prince and ascend the throne.’ By that, she meant to reject my secret love. Each time, my heart and tongue longed to say, ‘Girl! In truth, I am a royal prince! If I wished, this Chola Empire would be mine!’ That desire—” I controlled myself. I prayed to God that the desire to rule the land should never find a place in my heart. To fulfill that ascetic resolve, I had even decided to renounce Poonguzhali. Fortunately, this princess of the sea let go of her unworthy desire and came forward to marry this poor servant of Shiva.”

Here, Poonguzhali interrupted, “Ayya! How can you say it was an unworthy desire for me? I am worthy enough to become the empress who rules the three worlds! Even so, I agreed to marry you, to weave garlands and make a living, to push the boat and spend my days!”
“Speak thus, Poonguzhali! That alone is enough to prove your worth! How do worthiness and unworthiness arise?
‘All beings are equal by birth,’

so sings the divine poet in the Tamil Vedas! Therefore, you need not now abandon your old dream. Join us in telling this prince, who is about to take your hand! Uncle! It was just that, after knowing the truth of your birth, you developed detachment and refused the kingdom. That only shows the greatness of your birth-nature. Now, all of us are saying it— the Emperor says it, the Prime Minister says it, my brother and I say it. My friend Vanathi not only says it, but also agrees to change her great father’s mind. Why then should you refuse now?” said the young princess Kundavai Devi.

“Devi! All of you may say so, but do you know what the people of this kingdom say? Perhaps you do not. But I, who have mingled with the people, know it well. In this Thanjai, in Pazhaiyarai, in Kumbakonam, in Kodikkarai, in Nagapattinam—I know well what the people’s wishes are. In Pandya Nadu, Pallava Nadu, Kongu Nadu, and in Eelam too, I have heard the wishes of the people. The united voice of the people is: ‘Let Arulmozhivarman be crowned!’ Can I swim against such a great deluge? Even if I wished, could I rule this vast Chola empire? God! I know how much hatred the people bore towards the one you all call ‘the old Madhurantakan.’ Compared to that hatred, what would they— “Are you trying to make me the ruler? No! No! Do not do me such a great harm. I have never done any wrong to any of you!”

Before anyone else could reply, Ponniyin Selvan raised his head proudly and spoke with authority, “Let this discussion end here! When you all entered this chamber, I was telling Vandiyathevan that I am going to ascend the throne of the Chola kingdom. I will see that it is accomplished. I have also come to know the mind of this noble friend, who was born from the sacred womb of the venerable Empress. Let there be no more talk about the right to the throne!”

chapters.title: Dire Consequence
paragraphs: In the secret council chamber of the Thanjavur palace, Emperor Parantaka Sundara Chozha sat enthroned upon the Dharma Singhasana. The most prominent among the women of the palace were seated on either side of him. The ministers, commanders, and royal princes of Chozha Nadu stood before the emperor in attitudes of respectful reverence. Among the women, the senior empress Sembiyan Maadevi, the queen Vanamaadevi, the younger princess Kundavai, and the Kodumbalur princess Vanathi were present. Poonguzhali, hesitant to mingle with the others, stood a little apart.

Among the men, the elder Pazhuvettaraiyar and the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar, the chief minister Aniruddha, the commander-in-chief Periya Velar, the lord of Miladu Malaiyaman, Prince Arulmozhi Varman, the reborn Madurantaka Devar, and Parthibendran Pallavan were all present, with Parthibendran standing a little behind the chief minister.
The emperor cast his gaze over those assembled in the hall and asked, “Have all those who were summoned arrived? I do not see the lord of Kadambur.”
“The son of the Samburayar has just returned. Both father and son will be here shortly,” replied Parthibendran.
“Oh! Kandhamaaran has returned? What news does he bring? Has he captured those who fled?” inquired Sundara Chozhar.
“No, my lord! He could not capture them. But he claims to have slain Vandiyathevan. Another madman has not been caught; it seems he escaped,” said Parthibendran.
At this, the elder Pazhuvettaraiyar let out a grunt. The others expected him to speak, but he said nothing.

The emperor said, “I do not know what further consequences may arise from the mistakes I have made! Chief minister! You know well the thoughts in my heart. I have summoned here those most dear to me and to my lineage. The reason for this gathering, and my intentions, you must explain to them. You can express it more clearly than I can, can you not?”
“Yes, Your Majesty!” said the Prime Minister, and then, turning to address the assembly, he spoke:

“You are all aware of the many reasons that have wounded the Emperor’s heart. Our king was recently forced to lose his eldest son, a warrior among warriors, comparable to Abhimanyu and Aravan. The cause of the prince’s death remains shrouded in mystery. For three years, our king has not seen that valiant son. Though Karikalan sent message after message, urging his father to come and stay at the golden palace he had built in Kanchi, the Emperor did not go. You all know the reason for this. Here, in this great city of Thanjavur, the Emperor has remained under the protection of Chinna Pazhuvetarayar. Many rumors have spread throughout the land and its cities. In such circumstances, if the Emperor were to leave Thanjavur, might not some suspect that he had lost faith in the Pazhuvetarayar brothers? The Emperor did not wish to give room for such thoughts.

Now, I will openly speak of something our king hesitates to say himself. For this, I beg the forgiveness of the noble chieftains of royal blood gathered here. For some time, our king has suffered from a bodily illness that has robbed his legs of strength. This has caused him much distress of spirit. But even more than this, there is a mental anguish that has wounded his heart. You, who have long been the steadfast pillars of the Chola dynasty, who have forged bonds with this royal house through generations, who have been the diamond columns supporting this great Chola Empire—among you, divisions and enmity have arisen. This has wounded our Emperor’s heart and worsened his illness.

Under the leadership of Rajaditya, who now rests upon the elephant in the warrior’s heaven, you all fought as one on the battlefield of Takkolam. There, because Rajaditya met an unexpected heroic death, the Chola army was defeated. Yet, by your valor, determination, and unity, you turned that defeat into victory. You reclaimed the lost Thondai and Ganga territories. On the battlefield of Sevur, you repelled the Pandyas, conquered the Pandya country, and brought it under our direct rule. In Lanka, you overthrew Mahinda and raised the Tiger Banner high. All these great and noble deeds were achieved because you stood united, considering the welfare of the Chola Empire as your own.

But that harmony has changed in recent years. For some reason, divisions have arisen among you. You have split into two factions. Our Emperor has labored much to heal this rift. He knows that the root of your division is the question of who shall inherit the throne after him. None of you have spoken of this directly to the Emperor. Yet— Our incomparable Emperor, with his unmatched wisdom, divined and understood the matter. He wished to discuss the question of royal succession openly with all of you, to resolve it amicably through mutual understanding. He had intended to go to Kanchi only after settling this issue. He had decided that the Chola Empire should rightfully belong to the son of the holy Siva-gnana Kandaradithar. He believed that even Aditya Karikalan could be brought to agree to this. For that very purpose, he had sent word, asking Karikalan to come here. But in the midst of these plans, an unexpected and tragic event occurred. When the Emperor heard that Karikalan was coming to the palace of the Kadambur lord, his heart was filled with joy. He hoped that through this, the discord among you would be dissolved. He thought that if Karikalan married the daughter of Sambuvarayar, you would all once again be united in spirit, and the matter of royal succession could be resolved with ease. I too thought the same. Many among you must have thought likewise. Even our lord of Thirukovalur did not object to Aditya Karikalan going to Kadambur for this very reason. But all our hopes have been dashed. In the palace of Kadambur, Prince Karikalan met with an untimely death…”
“Are we going to find out how that happened, or not? It would be proper for you to speak further only after learning the truth of this matter,” said Malayaman of Thirukovalur.
“Yes; without knowing that, it is impossible to make any further plans!” said the Commander-in-Chief.
“Brave lords! What has happened, has happened. The Emperor believes there is no use in stirring up the past!” said the Chief Minister, Aniruddha.

“How can that be proper? The justice of the Chola dynasty is renowned throughout the world. Even if a destitute orphan dies in this kingdom, an inquiry is made into how it happened. If someone is found responsible, appropriate punishment is meted out. In that case, how can we leave uninvestigated the untimely death of the crowned prince, the heir to the throne?” said the Commander-in-Chief, Periya Velar.

Sundara Chola heaved a deep sigh and said, “Lord of Kodumbalur! Listen to me! In the untimely death of my beloved son, can anyone else feel a sorrow greater than mine? Yet, I myself say there is no need for an inquiry. Why? Because I know for certain that none here is responsible for it. It is the result of my own sins that I have lost my son. Tell me what penance I must do for that! I shall do it. There is no need to seek any other reason!” he said.

“Lord! By saying so, it will seem as though you wish to shield someone responsible for this crime. Already, the people of the land are speaking in many tongues about the cause of the prince’s death. It is best that the truth is uncovered and brought to light. Whoever the culprit may be, he must face the punishment he deserves!” said Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar.

“Not a word of that is false! That is the just and righteous way of governance. If this great crime is not investigated and punished, the people will lose faith in the very administration of justice!” declared Parthibendran.

“Elders! Why so much deliberation and debate over this matter? If this young man’s words seem too forward, forgive me. The culprit has already been punished! The wretch who slew Prince Karikalan, who ruined my sister’s life and drove her to madness—Vandiyathevan—was slain by my own spear. I have returned after killing him with my own hand. What further inquiry is needed?” said Kandanmaran.
Kandanmaran had arrived while the Chief Minister was still speaking. Only after hearing his voice did the others notice his presence.
Among them, Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar muttered in a low voice, “Fool! To think such a son was born to Kadambur Sambuvaraiyar.”
Chief Minister Aniruddha turned to him, “Kandanmara! Is it true that you killed Vandiyathevan by hurling your spear? Did you see him? Was it not at night that you pursued him?”
“Chief Minister! I know you have never trusted me. But do you think the darkness of night would make me mistake the man?”
“He too was a warrior! Did he not fight you?”

“Yes, you have no faith in my valor either. Therefore, I appeal to the Emperor himself. Two men fled. One was the madman who had been in our underground prison for years. While he tried to stop me, the other was nearing the riverbank. I hurled my spear and killed him. It must have been Vandiyathevan of the Vanar clan.”

“Did you not bring the body of the dead man with you?” “If I had known you would suspect me like this, I would have searched a little farther in the Vadavaru flood. But then, I could not have come to this council of ministers!” said Kandanmaran.
“Yes, if you had not come, it would have been a great loss!” said Commander-in-Chief Chinna Pazhuvetarayar.
“Brother! Why are you so intent on finding and capturing Vandiyathevan?” asked Periya Velar Boothi Vikrama Kesari.
“Is it necessary to ask that? That tragic incident happened in my own house. If the real culprit is not caught, would you not suspect me and my father?”
Sundara Chozhar interjected, “Child! Kandanmaran! Even if others suspect, I will not. Do I not know the devotion and loyalty your father has for me? Let it go! Where is Periya Sambuvarayar?”

“Emperor! It is my misfortune to have to recount the disgrace of our family myself. I was telling my father that I had killed Vandiyathevan and returned. My sister Manimekalai overheard me. The moment she heard it, she came at me with a knife to kill me. My father is trying to calm her and bring her madness under control. He will come soon. He sent word that whatever decision is made in this council of ministers, he will accept it!” said Kandanmaran.
“Alas! Wasn’t your sister already going about saying, ‘I am the one who killed the prince!’ as if she had lost her mind?” asked the old Malayaman.

“Yes, yes! She said so only to shield Vandiyathevan and help him escape his crime. At that time, she was not completely mad. Now, her madness has become total. Misfortune has befallen our lineage!” said Kandanmaran.

“Young Sambuvarayar! Are you so certain that Vandiyathevan himself killed Prince Karikalan? How is that? Did you see it with your own eyes? Or did someone who saw it tell you?” asked the Prime Minister.

“Minister sir! Does a wound on the hand need a mirror to see it? At the very spot where the prince lay dead, that Vanar clan warrior was present. Just by looking at his face, it was as if the word ‘culprit’ was written and pasted there. That too, the young queen of Pazhuvur—” The inner chambers. Why else would he have gone there? If he were not guilty, why would he have escaped from the subterranean prison?” asked Kandhamaaran.

“The Prime Minister took upon himself the responsibility of capturing the one who escaped from the underground prison and bringing him back. I wish to remind you of that at this moment,” said Parthibendran.

“Scion of the Pallava clan! It is true that I accepted that responsibility. But I did not expect that the young lord of the Sambuvrayar house would himself act as judge, conduct the inquiry, pass judgment, and even carry out the punishment. Vandiyathevan too hails from the ancient Vanar clan. His ancestors once ruled over a great kingdom. They established ties with the Chola dynasty by giving their daughters in marriage. When an accusation is made against one born in a royal house, it is the tradition for the Emperor himself to sit upon the throne of justice and conduct the inquiry and pronounce the verdict!” said the Prime Minister, Aniruddha Brahmarayar.
“Sir! It is also tradition that one who escapes from prison may be brought back alive or dead!” declared Parthibendran, the valiant scion of the Pallava clan.
“But the young Sambuvrayar did not bring Vandiyathevan back dead, did he? Did he not simply let him go into the floodwaters of the Vadavaru?” asked the Prime Minister, Aniruddha.
At that moment, the elder Sambuvrayar entered the council chamber. All eyes turned toward him. Everyone noticed the pain etched upon his face.
Kandhamaaran went near him and softly asked, “How is Manimekalai?”
Sambuvrayar replied in a loud, rather harsh voice, “She is the same as before. I have left your mother to watch over her!”
The Emperor looked at Sambuvrayar and said, “Sir! If it is necessary for you to be near your precious daughter, you may do so. We can postpone our deliberations until tomorrow.”

“No, my lord! There is no use in my being by her side. If the Vanar clan warrior Vandiyathevan, who lost his life to my son’s spear, were to come back to life, perhaps he might be of some use!” said Sambuvrayar.
The sorrow and bitterness that resonated in his words cast a brief silence over the assembly.

The Prime Minister Aniruddhar said, “Sir! We were discussing the tragic incident that took place in your palace. We all understand how deeply wounded your heart must be, since the prince met with an untimely death within your mansion. The Emperor in no way wishes to hold you responsible for this. However, to prevent all sorts of rumors from spreading throughout the towns and country, it would be best if we could ascertain the exact manner in which the prince met his end, would it not? Those gathered in this assembly are of the same opinion. Is there anything you can reveal to us about this? Young Sambuvaraiyar asserts that it was by the hand of Vandiyathevan of the Vanar clan that the prince was slain. What is your view on this matter?”

Sambuvaraiyar stood stunned for a moment. Then he looked around in all directions. When his gaze fell upon Kandanmaran, he said, “Yes, yes! This fool said the same thing that very day. I did not believe it then; I do not believe it now. It was upon his word that I invited Prince Karikalan to Kadambur Palace. And thus, all these disastrous consequences have come to pass. An everlasting disgrace has befallen me and my lineage!”

The elder Malayaman spoke in a voice filled with compassion, “Sambuvaraiyar! Do not be agitated! What has happened, has happened! It was with good intentions that you invited my grandson to your palace. No one here seeks to hold you responsible for Karikalan’s death. That is why we wish to know the truth. It would be well if you could help us in this!”

“How can I help? My son says one thing, and my daughter says quite the opposite. I cannot believe either of them. I myself do not know the truth. It is as though I have been blindfolded and cast into a forest. In truth, Periya Pazhuvettarayar, the lord of Thanjavur, might be able to help more than I. Ask him. He is the root cause of all this. He was the one who first secretly brought Madhurantaka Devar to Kadambur. He even suggested that my daughter be wed to him. From that moment, misfortune has clung to my family. Now I hear that Madhurantaka Devar himself has vanished without a trace. Later, Periya Pazhuvettarayar brought his young queen here. He summoned the prince from Kanchi as well. He left both of them in my palace and departed. Ask him why he left. Ask where his young queen has gone now…”
Thus, Sambuvaraiyar rambled on, speaking incoherently like a man possessed.

The Emperor interrupted, “Enough! Enough! Stop! This is why I said there is no need to investigate what has already happened, but you would not listen. Is the discord that already exists among you not enough? Do we need new quarrels? Sambuvaraiyar! You are not responsible for what happened in your palace. That is why I ordered your immediate release from the underground prison. It is my own past sins that have caused the untimely death of my brave son. No one else is to blame. You need not say anything about it. Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar, you too need not say anything!”

At that moment, Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar raised his voice like a lion’s roar and spoke in a booming tone: “O King of the Chola lineage! Have mercy and forgive me. I cannot remain silent! I must speak what is in my heart. I must tell the truth as I know it. Yes, my lord! There were times when I wondered whether I should speak the truth at all, or simply fulfill my vow in silence. I had sworn that if I could not protect the Chola lineage in times of danger, I would cut off my own head and give up my life. I could not protect Aditya Karikalan. Therefore, I must fulfill my vow. But before that, I wish to reveal the truth as I know it. If not, many unnecessary suspicions will arise, and false accusations will be laid!”
When Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar finished speaking thus, a profound silence settled over the assembly. For a moment, the hearts of all present softened and melted.

In a trembling voice, the Emperor said, “Uncle! Think for a moment! Why should you speak of what has already happened? The dead will not return to life. You would never have knowingly betrayed the Chola dynasty! Therefore, let us forget what has passed and speak of what must be done hereafter!”

“No, my lord! I must speak of what has happened. I must reveal how great a betrayal I nearly committed against the Chola dynasty. It was only our clan goddess Durga who prevented me from doing so. To that divine mother Parameswari, I must offer my sacrifice. Have mercy and listen to what I have to say!” said Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar.
Realizing that he could not stop him from speaking, the Emperor too remained silent.

Afterwards, Periya Pazhuvettarayar recounted, without concealing a single detail, everything that had happened since the day, three years ago, when he met Nandini by the roadside and became infatuated with her. He spoke of how, despite the repeated warnings of his younger brother, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar, he had paid them no heed. He confessed that, incited by Nandini, he had resolved to secure the Chola throne for Madurantaka Devar, and that for this purpose, he had conspired with other minor kings. He spoke of how Madurantaka had been taken away in Nandini’s veiled palanquin, and of the midnight meeting that took place in the Samburayar palace.

He revealed that it was only because of Vandiyathevan that the first seeds of suspicion about Nandini had been sown in his mind, and that from there, he began to suspect the Pandya conspirators. Yet, he admitted with sorrow, the enchantment and illusion of Nandini’s beauty would, time and again, cloud his judgment. At last, he described how, caught in the flood at the Kollidam dam, he learned of the Pandya conspirators’ true intentions, and how he hastened back to Kadambur. He told of how he disguised himself as a Kalamukha Saivite on the way, and, with Idumbankari’s help, reached the women’s quarters by a secret path. He explained how, out of eagerness to overhear the conversation between Nandini and the prince while hiding in the music room, he delayed for a moment—and in that instant, the prince fell dead. He described how, as he rushed forward to support the prince, the lamp was extinguished, how many people surrounded and attacked him, how he lost consciousness, how he regained his senses in the cave at Pachai Malai, and how he later returned.

“O Emperor! In this way, I have become a great traitor to the Chola clan. I gave shelter to the Pandya conspirators within my own palace. I allowed them to take what they needed for their plot from our treasury. Those conspirators planned to kill both you and your two sons at the same time. A divine woman, deaf and mute, gave her life to save you. Ponniyin Selvan was saved by nothing more than a mindless beast—an elephant. I tried to save Aditya Karikalan, but I failed. From the beginning to the end, I alone am the cause of his untimely death. My lord! In the presence of Durga Parameswari, I shall now fulfill the vow I have taken!” So saying, he raised the sword he held in his long hand.

All who understood his intent stood stunned and aghast. Only Ponniyin Selvan, who had drawn nearer little by little, sprang forward and seized Periya Pazhuvettarayar’s sword-wielding arm in a firm grip.

“Sir! Please wait! It has always been the custom, during the coronation ceremonies of the Chola kings, for the Pazhuvettaraiyars to take the crown and place it upon the ruler’s head. Even at my coronation, it must be your own hand that crowns me. After that, you may do as you wish—but until then, I beg you to wait!”
He spoke thus.
Is it necessary to say that these words plunged the Emperor and the other minor kings into a sea of astonishment?

chapters.title: The Vadavaru Turned Back!
paragraphs: Readers may have noticed that some of the characters in this long tale have, at times, spoken and acted in ways that contradict their earlier words and deeds. We must state here that we are not to be held responsible for this. Human nature is never constant. Circumstances and various events alter a person’s mind and conduct. Those who spoke and behaved in one manner yesterday may, today, speak and act in a manner entirely at odds with their former selves.

At the beginning of this story, Periya Pazhuvettarayar was the leader of a great political conspiracy. Now, having confessed to the crime that many already suspected him of, he wished to atone for his guilt by taking his own life.

Periya Sambuvarayar, upon seeing the lifeless body of Prince Karikalan, was so overcome by shock and the fear that the blame for this murder would fall upon his family, that he attempted to burn down his own ancestral palace. Driven by the desire to shift the blame onto someone else, he even incited his own son to join in this desperate act. But now, having learned that the crime did not fall upon him, and having come to realize the depth of love his precious daughter bore for Vandiyathevan, his words and behavior changed entirely.

At the outset of this tale, we led the readers to believe that the impostor Madurantakan, who traveled hidden in a closed palanquin, was the true Madurantakan, and that he would later ascend as Uttama Chola Chakravartin. This was necessary for the progression of the story. Why? Even though Prime Minister Aniruddhar knew some of the old secrets, he too believed that Madurantakan should be crowned. He did not possess a complete account of the events of those times. Therefore, even though the impostor Madurantakan was not the son of Kandaradithar, Aniruddhar thought him to be the son born to Sundara Cholar and Mandakini. Thus, he too was compelled to waver and act in contradictory ways.

Even Arulmozhi Thevar, whom we have regarded throughout this story as the epitome of honesty and truthfulness, was seen at last to speak in a manner contrary to his earlier words. All this time, he had insisted that he did not desire the throne. But now, suddenly, he changed his course and declared, “I myself shall be crowned…” He had already begun to declare to many that he would accept the crown. There is no need for us to point out that it was the circumstances themselves that caused this change in him, is there?

Yes; Arulmozhi Deva’s words filled everyone present there with astonishment and wonder. At the same time, they brought a sense of peace to their hearts. Deep within, in the innermost chambers of their souls, all of them felt that Ponniyin Selvan alone was truly worthy and entitled in every way to ascend the Chola throne. They knew that this was also the wish of the vast majority of people living in the Chola Empire. The anxiety of what consequences might arise if someone else were to be crowned against the will of the people also lingered in their minds. Yet, for various reasons, none of those present dared to declare that Ponniyin Selvan should be crowned.

Now, when Ponniyin Selvan himself stepped forward and said, “I am going to accept the crown. You must place the diadem upon my head with your own sacred hands!”—addressing Periya Pazhuvettarayar—peace and joy blossomed in everyone’s hearts. “A good resolution has been reached. And the difficult, agonizing responsibility of making that decision has passed from us!” Thus, they felt both relief and happiness.

We have already seen how that rare, radiant magnetic force that shone from Ponniyin Selvan prevented anyone from speaking against him in his presence. Why, even Chinna Pazhuvettarayar, whose heart was as hard as diamond, bowed his head and welcomed Ponniyin Selvan with a smile when he met him face to face, did he not?

Periya Pazhuvettarayar knew that Ponniyin Selvan had prevented him from taking his own life. He understood the meaning of the prince’s words. The actions and words of the young prince moved his heart deeply. Overcome with emotion, his body trembled. Tears welled up in his eyes. His throat choked.

Steeling his heart as best he could, he spoke: “Scion of the Chola lineage! Ponniyin Selva! Your words have brought me immeasurable joy. I myself wished to beg you to accept the crown. But I felt I had no right to make such a request, since I have become a traitor to the Chola clan. Your great grandfather, the illustrious Kandaraaditha Chakaravarthi, made an arrangement before he passed. That noble soul decreed that only one from his brother’s line should ascend the throne…”

He spoke with insistence. We had intended to act against the arrangements he had made. Because of the discord that had arisen among us, we thought of crowning Madurantaka Devar against the wishes of that peerless devotee of Shiva. Your father too gave his consent to this. When I think of how disastrous it would have been if our plan had succeeded, my whole being trembles.

Prince! You alone are the rightful heir to the Chola throne upon which your father sits. You alone are worthy to wear the jeweled crown of the Chola Empire! When you were but a small child, I have held you in my arms and upon my shoulders, caressing you. Even then, looking at the marks on your body and the lines adorning your palms, I would say to myself, ‘This child will one day be the king of kings, ruling over this entire earth.’ I have recounted with joy a hundred times how, when you fell from the boat into the floodwaters of the Kaveri, Mother Kaveri herself lifted you in her arms and saved you.

But in these past three years, lust, anger, and sectarian strife have corrupted my mind and turned me into a traitor. Ponniyin Selva! I have lost the right to see you ascend the Chola throne and wear the jeweled crown upon your head; my hands too have lost that privilege. The only sacred act these hands can now perform, as atonement for my crime, is to end my own life.”
“No, no! That must not be!” cried many voices in the council of ministers.

Sundara Chola spoke in a voice full of emotion, “Uncle! What words are these? What deed is this? What betrayal have you committed against the Chola clan? There is none! Instead of my own sons, you wished to seat my elder brother’s son upon the throne. How is that a betrayal of the Chola line? Does not my elder brother’s son have even more right to the Chola crown than my own children? Even now, if you allow me to speak what is in my heart…”

Prime Minister Aniruddha stepped forward and said, “My lord! Throughout the land, voices are rising, ‘Let Arulmozhi Varman be crowned!’ Even the son of Kandaraditya Devar, who has lived in obscurity all these years, is of the same resolve. Ponniyin Selvan too has come to the same decision. There is no use in considering any plan contrary to this now!”
“Even if any of you think otherwise, I cannot accept it!” declared Madurantaka Devar, also known as Sendhan Amudhan.
“My son’s words are just. There is no need to deliberate any further!” declared Sembiyan Maadevi.

“Mother! There is no one here who would dare speak against your word. Let all unfold as per the will of God. Yet, is it right for our uncle of Pazhuvoor to wish for death, believing himself a traitor to our clan? Was it truly treachery against the Chola dynasty that he strove to crown your royal son?” said the Emperor.

Periya Pazhuvetarayar cleared his throat and began to speak: “My lord! Listen! Hear what dreadful calamity would have occurred had my efforts borne fruit! I wished to end my life without ever uttering these words. Most of all, I hesitated to wound the heart of my brother, Kaalandhakakandar, who has never dreamed of anything but the glory of the Chola Empire. Yet now, I have steeled my heart and resolved to reveal the truth. Emperor! The one whom we sought to place upon the Chola throne, believing him to be the son of the great Kandaradithar, was in fact the son of Veera Pandiyan, the hereditary foe of the Chola clan!…”
“Alas!” “No!” “That cannot be!”—such cries rose up in the assembly.

“It will be hard for you to believe. Had I not heard it with my own ears, I too would not have believed it. O King of Kings! I am compelled once more to recount my shame. Three years ago, the woman whose beauty ensnared me, whose charm led me astray, whom I installed as mistress of my palace—she is the daughter of Veera Pandiyan! I heard with my own ears as she confessed this to Aditya Karikalan. She had come to the Pazhuvoor palace to avenge the death of Veera Pandiyan at the hands of Aditya Karikalan. She had been waiting for the right moment. That wicked woman and her co-conspirators plotted to murder Karikalan and to place Veera Pandiyan’s son upon the Chola throne. By the grace of our clan goddess, Durga Devi, such a terrible disaster was averted. Durga Parameshwari sent that valiant scion of the Vanar clan to open my eyes. It was through him that I learned these dreadful secrets. There were still some things I wished to learn from him. But this young Sambuvarayan slew him and cast his body into the floodwaters of the Vadavaru! Wretch!”

Hearing these words, everyone present stood stunned in shock. Only Kandamaaran spoke up, “Sir! After all, that Vandiyathevan had joined hands with the traitorous conspirators. What wrong is there in my having hurled my spear and killed him?”
Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar turned to him angrily.

At that moment, Aniruddhar interjected, “Sir! All this fellow says is that he has killed the hero of the Vanar clan. But what certainty is there that the man he killed with his spear was indeed Vandiyathevan?”
Parthibendran, in a somewhat subdued voice, said, “If the floodwaters of the Vadavaru turn back and bring the corpse of the dead man, perhaps the truth will be revealed!”
“Who has seen such a thing? Even if the Vadavaru’s flood turns back, let it do so!” said Prime Minister Aniruddhar.

As if to affirm his words, in the very next moment, Vandiyathevan entered the council chamber, water dripping from his soaked clothes, leaving a trail of droplets behind him. The terrified look on his face, his disheveled state as he entered, and his appearance—like a corpse that had drowned in the flood and, by some magical spell, risen and begun to walk—struck awe and wonder in the hearts of all who beheld him.
“Ah! The flood of the Vadavaru has indeed turned back! It has brought the dead man back to life!” exclaimed Prime Minister Aniruddhar.

At this point, it is necessary for us to inform the readers how Vandiyathevan came to be there in such a state. After Ponniyin Selvan, Princess Kundavai, and the others had left him alone, Vandiyathevan had fallen into deep dejection. For one who had always yearned to perform heroic deeds and astonish the world, it was unbearable to find himself in a situation where others looked upon him with pity. The prison of the palace’s inner quarters seemed to him even more dreadful than the dungeons below.

Thanks to the mercy of Ponniyin Selvan, perhaps they would not accuse him of the crime of killing Karikalan, nor would they punish him for it. Yet, everyone in the palace would continue to harbor suspicions about him. They would always regard him as a tainted man. Even the compassion and sympathy the young princess showed him would come to an end. To take the hand of the noble sister of Ponniyin Selvan—who was soon to be crowned emperor of the Chola Empire—and marry her was a thing that could never happen, not even in his dreams.

The women of the palace would treat him as if he were a servant who had committed some offense and been pardoned. The ministers and commanders would look upon him with revulsion. The minds of royalty are ever fickle. For how many days would Prince Arulmozhi continue to show him favor? Who could say?

Ah! If only, as he had first intended, he had mounted his horse near Sendhan Amudhan’s hut, by now he might have reached Kodikkarai. Why, he might even have reached the island of Eezham! Who were those who rode away on horseback at the time he was struck by the physician’s son? One was Karuthiruman, who had earned the name “madman.” In truth, he was not mad, but a man of cunning and intrigue. Who was the one who went with him? They say the old Madhurantaka Devar is missing—could it not be he? Yes, yes! It must be so! There must be some purpose in the two of them escaping together. If those here knew who that Madhurantakan truly was, how astonished they would be! If the two of them safely reached the land of Eezham, what would be the result? Why, the rightful heir to the Pandya country’s jeweled crown and gem-studded necklace would obtain them! With Mahindan’s help, he would begin a war to reclaim the land once more. If only that could be prevented… If only there was someone with the strength to stop it! There was only one such man! What use was there in hiding in this palace’s inner chamber, clinging to life?

With such thoughts swirling in his mind, Vandiyathevan paced restlessly around the room. Again and again, he came to stand at the edge of a balcony set into one wall, peering out anxiously. He was in an upper chamber at one corner of the palace. Beyond it, the Vadavaru flowed northward. There, the outer wall of the palace also formed the outer wall of the Thanjai fort itself. If he leapt from that balcony, he could plunge directly into the floodwaters of the Vadavaru. Or, with some effort, he could climb down the sheer wall and reach the river’s torrent below. Beneath that upper chamber, it seemed there was a door and a flight of steps leading down to the river, used by the palace women to bathe. He did not know how to descend from the upper floor and reach that door. The palace attendants and royal maidens would know. If he were to escape, he must do so without their knowledge… As he stood at the edge of the balcony, pondering thus, a sight that appeared some distance away startled him.

Next to the palace where he was staying, in the garden of the adjoining palace, a woman was running wildly, her hair loose, like one possessed by madness. Ah! Is that not the garden of Periya Pazhuvettarayar’s palace? Yes, yes! That is the very garden! And who is this woman running like one deranged? O Lord! Is it not Manimekalai? What has happened to her? Why is she running so? The memories of all the help she had rendered him on that night of Karikalan’s death in Kadambur palace came flooding back to him, making his heart ache with sorrow!

Behind her, as if in pursuit, two elderly women were also running, but they were falling further and further behind. To catch Manimekalai was an impossible task for them! Look, she has reached the outer wall. Clutching a tree that grew close to the wall, she climbed up onto the parapet! Alas! What is she doing? A small dagger glinted in her hand! What does she intend to do with it? God! She has leapt headlong from the wall into the rushing waters of the river below!

In a flash, memories surged within Vandiyathevan: the time when, at Veera Narayana Lake, both Manimekalai and Nandini were on the verge of drowning, and how he had first thought to save Manimekalai but ended up lifting Nandini to the shore instead; Manimekalai’s bitter disappointment at that moment—all these came crashing into his mind. He could not stand still any longer. From the upper floor of the palace, he hurried out through the balcony, and plunged into the floodwaters of the river.

For a few moments he struggled for breath, then steadied himself and looked around. Yes; near the spot where he had jumped, he could see the bathing pavilion and the door leading from it. It was a little distance away, on the opposite side, that Manimekalai had leapt from the wall. Fortunately, the current was flowing towards him. If Manimekalai too was floating in the flood, she would be carried in his direction.

Stumbling, Vandiyathevan reached the riverbank. Bracing himself against the current, he hurried along. Ah! There—was that Manimekalai floating towards him? Was there still life in her body? Or was it a lifeless form? Alas! Would fate once again force him to carry the lifeless body of someone who had loved him? Oh, how much affection that woman had borne for him! The melody of the song she had played and sung on her veena in the pavilion by the lake at Veera Narayanapuram drifted to him, just as her body now floated on the waters. It filled Vandiyathevan with immeasurable anguish.

Enduring that pain somehow, he plunged into the flood and, with both hands, lifted Manimekalai out of the water. O gods! Please save the life of this girl! I will go to every temple in Chola Nadu, fall prostrate in every sanctum, and offer my prayers. Shiva temple, Vishnu temple, Amman temple, Ayyanar temple—I will go to them all and give thanks to every deity. Just save the life of this innocent, blameless girl!…

Thus, praying to various gods in his heart, Vandiyathevan brought Manimekalai to the riverbank. Already, he who had escaped death’s door from the spear wound was further weakened by the shock of suddenly leaping into the river’s flood. Carrying the water-soaked, heavy Manimekalai through the river strained his breath. It seemed impossible to carry her any further. Noticing that the upper step of the landing was broad, he laid Manimekalai upon it. For a moment, he wondered what to do next. There was still a spark of life left in Manimekalai’s body. But he knew he could not revive her from her faint. He needed a woman’s help immediately. He must go into the palace and bring someone from there.

Before him, he saw the door that led from the river landing into the palace. Approaching it, he summoned all the remaining strength in his body and struck against the barred door. Fortunately, the inner bolt gave way, and the door opened. He rushed inside through the open doorway. For a short distance, the way was narrow; then came corridors and courtyards. Nowhere did he see anyone. “Is there no one here? Is there no one to save a woman’s life?” he cried, running here and there.

At last, at the entrance to a great hall, two attendants tried to block his way. He pushed past them and entered. There, he saw the Emperor seated upon a magnificent throne, surrounded by many men and women, and was struck with astonishment. The first woman his eyes fell upon was Poonguzhali, and recognizing her gave him some courage.
“Samudrakumari! Samudrakumari! Manimekalai has fallen into the river. Come at once and save her!” he cried.

chapters.title: The Tall Tree Fell!
paragraphs: Vandiyathevan entered the royal audience hall through the entrance reserved for the women of the inner palace. Because of this, he first caught sight of the ladies gathered there. Among them, Poonguzhali, who had been standing a little apart behind the others, turned around at the sound of commotion and was startled to see Vandiyathevan rushing in, drenched and disheveled. The moment he saw her, Vandiyathevan began to recount the calamity that had befallen Manimekalai. His words reached her ears, and also those of the young princess Kundavai and Vanathi, who were standing nearby. The three of them hurried out through the same entrance by which Vandiyathevan had come. Following the trail of dripping water, they quickly traced the path he had taken.

The rest of the people in the hall did not clearly hear Vandiyathevan’s words. Only the cry, “Save her!” reached the ears of a few. Kandanmaran and Parthibendran did not even catch that much; to them, it was nothing but an indistinct, anguished shout.

At first, the two of them, seeing a figure entering through the women’s quarters, wondered if it was the spirit of the departed Vandiyathevan. In those days, many believed that the souls of those who died untimely deaths would linger in this world, unable to depart. “Even if the north wind turns back, it will turn!” said Prime Minister Aniruddha, barely finishing his words when Vandiyathevan appeared before them, soaked and dripping. This uncanny sight only deepened their confusion.
But when the palace guards burst in after Vandiyathevan, agitated and breathless, and seized him, the illusion was dispelled.
“Your Majesty! Forgive us. This madman ran in through the palace gate. We tried to stop him, but he would not listen!” said the guards, attempting to drag Vandiyathevan away with them.
Oh, what a tenacious life this Vandiyathevan possesses! No matter how dire the danger, he somehow escapes and returns! This astonishment arose in Parthibendran’s heart, mingled with a burning anger.

He has run here blindly, not even knowing where he was going, and now he is caught! This time, he must not be allowed to escape again. Thus resolving in a single instant, Parthibendran, forgetting even that he was in the presence of the Emperor… He sprang forward and seized one of Vandiyathevan’s shoulders in a powerful grip.
“This man is not a madman. He is a murderer! The treacherous traitor who killed Aditya Karikalan!” he cried, and with a gesture, he dismissed the servants who had tried to drag Vandiyathevan away.

Following Parthibendran, Kandhamaaran rushed forward and seized Vandiyathevan’s other shoulder tightly. Together, they dragged him and stood him before the throne where Sundara Chola, the Emperor, was seated.

The Emperor looked intently at Vandiyathevan and said, “Are you telling me that this boy, whose face is still as innocent as milk, is the one who killed my son? I cannot believe it! Was it not he who brought me the letter from Aditya Karikalan?”

“Yes, my lord! It was he who brought the letter! He is the one who met Nandini Devi in the closed palanquin outside the Tanjore fort and spoke to her in secret. He is the one who once escaped from this very fort. Now again, he has fled from the underground prison!” declared the Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar.
“He is the one who stabbed me in the back and escaped!” said Kandhamaaran.
Prime Minister Aniruddha turned to him and asked, “Why, my son! Was it not you who just now claimed that you had killed him by throwing your spear into his back?”
“Yes, I said so! But did I ever imagine that you all would support this murderer and bring him back to life and deliver him here?” retorted Kandhamaaran.

All this while, Ponniyin Selvan had stood silent and motionless. He had thought that Vandiyathevan, in yet another attempt to escape, had jumped into the river, and, lacking enough skill in swimming, had returned to the shore in confusion and burst into the assembly in this manner. Because of this, the anger he had felt toward Vandiyathevan began to subside a little.
When he heard Kandhamaaran’s last words, Ponniyin Selvan strode forward with dignity and stood beside Vandiyathevan.

“Father! This prince of Vallam is my dearest friend, the one who saved my life in Lanka and in the midst of the sea when I faced mortal danger. I am glad that he has survived. To accuse him is to accuse me!” he declared.
The authoritative tone that resonated in his voice rendered everyone silent for a few moments.

Then, the Chief Minister Aniruddha spoke: “Ponniyin Selva! Think about this for a moment! The man who was said to have perished by the spear of the young Sambuvarayar has somehow returned alive and leapt into our midst. Already, accusations have been cast upon him. Therefore, would it not be wise to investigate and clarify the truth?”

Parthibendran said, “Yes, sir! You are about to ascend the Chola throne tomorrow. No matter how grave the crime, you have the authority to punish or pardon. But is it proper to say that there should be no inquiry at all? Would that not give rise to needless suspicions?”

“In addition to that, our prince must consider another matter. A rumor is spreading that the prince, in order to ascend the throne, sent this Vandiyathevan to conspire and murder his own elder brother. Should we allow such a rumor to gain ground?” said Kandhamaran.

Hearing this, everyone present stood frozen in terror. Only Sambuvarayar stepped forward, struck Kandhamaran sharply on the cheek, and shouted angrily, “You fool! It seems our ancient lineage will be wiped out because of you! There is no one to match you in blurting out nonsense without regard for the situation!”

Kandhamaran glared at his father. His lips quivered. Who knows what he might have done or said in the next instant! Fortunately, at that moment, Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar stepped forward, seized Sambuvarayar, and, his voice rumbling as before, said, “Sambuvarayar! Your son has already atoned for all his foolish deeds! He has rendered a great service to the Chola empire. When you come to understand it, you yourself will feel proud to have fathered him. Please, restrain yourself! Do not be angry with him!” Saying this, he pulled Sambuvarayar aside and led him a little away.

Then, turning to young Sambuvarayan, he asked, “You claimed that you hurled your spear and killed this Vandiyathevan, did you not? Can you say for certain that it was he who crossed the river on horseback at that time?”
The Chief Minister interjected, “Sir! On this matter, you must permit my disciple to say a word!”

Azhwarkkadiyan stepped forward and said, “Lords! I confess my fault. This young prince of Vallam never mounted a horse and rode away. He was wounded and fell while saving our true Madurantaka Devar from the hands of an assassin. It was I who placed him in a closed palanquin and brought him safely into the fortress. For the past four days, he has been here. Therefore, it is impossible that Ilanjambhuvarayar’s spear struck his back!”

Periya Pazhuvettarayar said, “I too suspected as much, Sambhuvarayar! Forgive all the mistakes of your son. He has rendered great service to the Chola Empire! The one who hurled the spear and killed him must be the son of Veera Pandiyan. Since that evening, the old Madurantakan has not been seen, has he? The one who tried to escape must be him. How great is the disaster from which God has saved this kingdom!”

Before the astonishment and shock caused by these words could subside, that venerable elder continued: “Emperor! Grant your ear to my final words! The comet has done its evil deed and vanished. Your valiant son, Aditya Karikalan, too, has departed. Yet, the Chola Empire, established by the blood and sacrifice of your ancestors and mine, has a bright future ahead. For a long time yet, this empire will endure. It will expand and reach a state of great glory. Thus, from a calamity unheard of even in legends, this Chola dynasty and empire have been saved. The chief reason for this escape is this valiant scion of the Vanar clan, Vandiyathevan! It was through him that my eyes, clouded by the veil of illusion, were opened. On that night when we held our midnight council in the Sambhuvarayar palace, he happened to arrive there by chance. That day, I felt the shame of having to hide something from this young man, something he should not know. Later, my brother told me that he met Nandini outside the Tanjore fort and spoke with her. He also said that it was with Nandini’s help that he escaped from the fort. From then on, a seed of suspicion took root and grew in my heart. I began to ponder all that was happening around me and their causes. Often, the darkness of illusion would cloud my mind, but again and again, rays of truth would pierce through and strive to dispel the darkness. In the end, by the grace of Durga Parameswari, I learned of the conspiracy plotted by the Madurai conspirators. Had I not hidden myself and overheard their conversations, I would not have believed it. Even after that, your noble daughter, the Young Princess, disturbed my mind in another way, confusing—”

He let go. He said that Nandini was his sister, and that I must not harm her. I wondered if perhaps he too had been deceived. Nevertheless, I wished to know the truth, so I disguised myself and went to Kadambur. The Kalamukha Saivites accepted me as their leader. Listen to my shame: it was Nandini who sowed in my heart the treacherous, wicked desire that I myself should become emperor of this Chola empire. The Kalamukha sect nurtured that ambition, fanning its flames. They wanted to crown Madurantaka, and then, after casting him aside, to make me the emperor. Among those Kalamukhas was Idumbankari, who served as a retainer in the palace of Sambuvarayar. He also acted as a spy for the Pandya brothers in Madurai. By intimidating him, I learned that at that very time, the Pandya brothers were hiding in the hunting room of the Kadambur palace. I also learned that Aditya Karikalan had gone to Nandini’s chamber, and that Manimekalai and Vandiyathevan were hiding there as well. The desire to overhear the conversation between Nandini and Karikalan, and to learn their secret, shook my resolve. I was seized by the longing to discover the truth about Nandini. I found out that there was a secret passage to Nandini’s room from the music treasury, and I went there. I arrived at just the right time. From Nandini’s own lips, I heard the truth about her. I learned that Aditya Karikalan’s conduct was without blemish. I also discovered how dreadful a plot Nandini and her associates had devised to avenge the death of Veerapandiyan. I tried to prevent that conspiracy from succeeding. But I could not overcome fate. I had the misfortune of seeing Karikalan fall lifeless before my very eyes…”

Having said this, Periya Pazhuvettarayar covered his face with his hands and sobbed. The sound of his sobbing was like the great roar of the sea during a storm.
