No one dared to open their mouth and speak at that moment. The hearts of all present melted at the sight of the mighty elder’s immense grief.
Periya Pazhuvettarayar, with the help of his iron heart forged in courage, suppressed the rising tide of his sobs. He removed his hands from his face and looked around at everyone.

“By the decree of fate, Aditya Karikalan has died. But by the grace of Durga Parameswari, at that very moment, Ponniyin Selvan, who was in mortal danger, overcame fate with his wisdom and survived. My lord! Emperor! Brahmarayar! My beloved friends, the chieftains! Place Arulmozhi Varman upon the Chola throne and crown him king! Through him, this empire shall attain its greatest glory!” he declared.

Prime Minister Aniruddhar said, “Sir! Your wish is about to be fulfilled. We feared that Ponniyin Selvan would be the obstacle to it. But by the fortune of the Chola land, he himself has consented to be crowned! Yet, you have not told us how Karikalan died?”
“Why do you ask about that? What does it matter whose hand committed the deed? In truth, his death was ordained by fate!” replied that valiant elder, his voice trembling.
“If that is not known, then the suspicion that hangs over this young man will not be cleared. Might it not come to pass that he is punished for Karikalan’s death?” asked Prime Minister Aniruddhar.
“Ah! To lay the blame on him? Who is accusing him?”
“Kandhamaaran and Parthibendran are the ones accusing him!”
“Ah! Utter fools! Kandhamaaran! Parthibendran! What reason do you have to accuse this youth? On what grounds do you claim that he killed Aditya Karikalan?”

To this, Aniruddhar himself replied. “At that time, he was hiding in Nandini Devi’s private chambers. Manimekalai was there as well. Manimekalai claims that she committed the deed. But that cannot be. There was no stain of blood on the dagger she showed. Surely, she must have said so only to save Vandiyathevan? Perhaps she saw Vandiyathevan, from his hiding place, kill Karikalan?”
“If Manimekalai did not kill him, how could Vandiyathevan have done it alone? With what weapon?”
“With this weapon! With this sharp, twisted dagger, stained and dried with blood!” said Parthibendran, displaying the twisted dagger we have seen before.

When Vandiyathevan had brought Karikalan’s body out from the burning palace and then himself fainted and fallen, Parthibendran had taken the twisted dagger from him and kept it safe. Now he produced it.
Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar looked at him and said, “Here, give me that dagger!” and took it from him.
He examined it closely and muttered, “Aha! This is Idumbankari’s dagger!”

“Kandhamaaran! Parthibendran! You and I must circle this Vandiyathevan three times in reverence and bow before him! Just as this old man fell into the snare of Nandini’s enchantment, you too would have succumbed. But he alone did not get caught in that web of illusion. He did not hurl this dagger. He did not kill Aditya Karikalan!”
“How can you say that with such certainty?” asked Prime Minister Aniruddha.
“Yes, I say it with absolute certainty. I know very well who threw this dagger and killed Karikalan!”
“Who? Who?”

“Yes, yes! I must reveal it. If I do not, your doubts will never be dispelled. Listen, all of you—this youth was hiding in the Yazh treasury. I came down that way. To prevent him from making a sound when he saw me, I seized him from behind and gripped his neck. His eyes rolled back, and he lost consciousness and fell to the ground. At that moment, he could not possibly have known who killed Aditya Karikalan.”
“Who? Who? Who was it that killed him?”

“It was I who took this twisted dagger from Idumbankari. I am the one who hurled it! This very right hand of mine—descended from the line that crowned the Chola emperors—this hand threw the dagger. But I did not throw it at Prince Karikalan. I hurled it at Nandini. I threw it, intending to slay that sorceress who plunged me into the depths of infatuation and betrayal. My aim missed, and it struck Karikalan instead!…”
“Alas!” “Ah, no!”—cries of shock and dismay rose from many in that assembly.

“For a hundred years, the house of Pazhuvoor has served the Chola dynasty with unwavering loyalty. Now I have brought disgrace upon all those services. I do not know how I will ever cleanse this stain!”
“Anna! Here and now, I shall wipe away that stain!” roared the Younger Pazhuvettaraiyar, unsheathing his dagger and rushing to his elder brother’s side.

“Whoever betrays the Chola dynasty—no matter who they are—we have both sworn to avenge them. I shall fulfill that oath now. This very moment, I will kill you and wipe away the disgrace that has befallen our clan!” cried Chinna Pazhuvettarayar, raising his dagger.
“No! No! Let not blood be shed here!” exclaimed Sundara Chola Chakravarthi.
Prince Arulmozhi and Prime Minister Aniruddha rushed forward and seized Chinna Pazhuvettarayar’s hands.

At that moment, Periya Pazhuvettarayar spoke: “Brother! I will not leave to you the task of cleansing our clan’s dishonor that I have brought upon it. Nor will I let you bear the blame of being ‘the younger brother who slew his elder.’ Here and now, I shall fulfill my vow to Durga Parameswari!” So saying, he drew a small, curved dagger from his hand and raised it toward his chest. Since he had already sheathed the great sword he had once brandished, the others believed he had abandoned his former intent. No one expected that he would use the curved dagger he had taken from Parthibendran.
“Sir! No, don’t!” cried Arulmozhi, leaping toward him, but before he could reach him, Periya Pazhuvettarayar had already carried out his resolve.
Like a mighty deodar tree, long-rooted and grown tall over many years, being uprooted and crashing to the ground with trunk and branches, he fell to the floor.
Exclamations of “Ha! Ha!” and “Alas!” echoed through the assembly.
Some rushed toward the fallen Periya Pazhuvettarayar.
At the same time, others hurried to the throne, where Sundara Chola Chakravarthi had collapsed, eyes closed. The council of ministers dissolved in confusion.

That night, as Periya Pazhuvettarayar battled with death, many came to see him one last time. The Emperor, Arulmozhi, Aniruddha, and even the young princess Kundavai were present. They spoke in praise of the great services Periya Pazhuvettarayar had rendered to the Chola dynasty and the empire. They recounted his heroic deeds in countless battlefields during his youth. They marveled at how, after the defeat at Thakkolam, he had rallied the scattered Chola forces and transformed defeat into victory. They lauded his able administration as the governor of Chola Nadu.
Without uttering a single word about the events of the past three years, they took their leave and departed.
Afterwards, the four of them concealed themselves within the very chamber where Periya Pazhuvettarayar lay, hiding in places beyond his sight.
At that moment, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar entered, bringing Alwarkadiyan with him. He led Alwarkadiyan to sit before Periya Pazhuvettarayar, and then seated himself nearby.

With eyes whose vision was swiftly fading, Periya Pazhuvettarayar looked at Alwarkadiyan and said, “Ah! Why has this Vaishnavite come here? I do not wish to go to Vaikuntha, my boy! I long to attain Siva’s abode!”
“Sir! Tomorrow at dawn is the holy day of Vaikuntha Ekadasi! Even if you desire to reach Kailasa, you must pass through Vaikuntha’s path!” replied Thirumalai.
“No! No! You may return to your Mahavishnu and…”
“Sir! I have not come now as Mahavishnu’s messenger. I bring news from my sister.”
“Who is your sister?”

“The sister who grew up with me for many years—I speak of Nandini. Sir! Nandini sent me to convey her gratitude to you. She asked me to thank you for accepting the blame, so that the guilt of killing Karikalan would not fall upon her. She bade me tell you that, no matter how many births she takes, she can never forget your kindness!” said Alwarkadiyan.

“Ah! Does she still think thus? Let her find joy in that thought. However much she has deceived me and done me harm, I cannot forget her. Is she not the daughter of that noble woman who gave her life to save the Emperor? Truly, perhaps in future births she will seek me out again—who knows?” said Pazhuvettarayar.
Upon his face, already shadowed by the approach of death, a faint smile now appeared.

“Vaishnavite! I must confess my truth to someone—let it be you. The knife I hurled did not strike the prince. He had already fallen before that. The reason I admitted to killing the prince was not only to shield Nandini from blame; there is a matter a hundred times more important than that…” There is a reason. Come closer! I will tell you! Your friend Vandiyathevan—he is a remarkable youth! The Chola dynasty owes him a great debt. He has won the heart of the Young Princess. I showed unnecessary anger towards the Young Princess. To atone for all that, if I had not confessed my guilt and offered myself as a sacrifice, people would have continued to cast aspersions upon Vandiyathevan’s name. Now, no one will dare to speak thus. Vaishnavite! Someday, please tell the Young Princess to kindly forgive me for having hated her!”

Having spoken for so long, the breath of that resolute elder began to falter. If the heart of Azhwarkadiyan, who had been listening to all this, melted within him, is it any wonder that tears streamed in torrents from the eyes of Kundavai, who had been listening from her hidden place behind?

“Vaishnavite! One more thing. Tell the Prime Minister Brahmarayar! The Pandya crown and the jeweled necklace from Lanka must somehow be brought back. The one fit for that task is the Prince of Vallam! You and he must go and retrieve them. Afterwards, you must go to Madurai and there, once, conduct the coronation of Ponni’s Beloved. Do you understand? Ask Arulmozhi, for my sake, one thing! Tell him that there is no truer companion to the Chola dynasty than he! Devi! Durga Parameshwari! I have fulfilled my vow! Here I come! Protect the Chola dynasty!”
The voice of the great Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar, which had grown weaker and weaker, now faded away completely. The life-flame of that resolute elder was extinguished.

chapters.title: Parting of Friends
paragraphs: Four horses were approaching the great river Kollidam’s ferry point.
Upon those four horses rode four warriors. They were all familiar to us: Parthibendran, Kandhamaaran, Vandiyathevan, and Ponniyin Selvan.
Of these, the first two had come prepared to board the boat and cross the Kollidam, journeying northward. The other two had come to bid them farewell.
When they reached the ferry, all four friends dismounted from their horses.
“Kandhamaaran! Has all your anger towards your old friend vanished now? Or are you still holding on to some remnants?” asked Ponniyin Selvan.

“My lord! What reason do I have to be angry with him? There is much more cause for me to feel remorse over my own foolishness. He forgot all the harm I did him and came forward to befriend me as before—such magnanimity is without equal. He saved my sister from drowning in the river’s flood; can I ever repay that debt of gratitude in this lifetime? When I think of how my mind became so clouded and corrupted, I am astonished at myself. At first, as I had intended, I failed to arrange Manimekalai’s marriage with him. Had I done so, would she have ended up in such a pitiable state today?” said Kandhamaaran.
“Why do you say that? Her memory has suffered a slight lapse due to the shock of falling into the river’s flood. Won’t she recover after a few days?” asked the prince.

“It does not seem like a simple lapse of memory. She remembers everyone else. She recalls all other matters. Only to me and Vandiyathevan does she show no recognition. When I think of the love she bore for me, my heart feels as if it will break. The cry, ‘Alas! I have killed my beloved brother with my own hands!’—that wailing voice still rings in my ears…”

“Why should she cry out like that? You are alive and well, aren’t you?” “I am still alive! How much better it would have been if I had died. Yes, sir! She is convinced that I killed Vandiyathevan, and that for that, she killed me. At times, she weeps thinking of me. At other times, she mourns for my friend, lamenting, ‘Will the river’s flood ever return? Will it bring back those who have died?’ No matter how much I tell her, she refuses to accept that I am her brother. She cannot recognize Vandiyathevan either. She even asks him, ‘Who are you? Have you ever seen the Prince of Vallam?’”
“Is that so?” asked Ponniyin Selvan, turning to look at Vandiyathevan, and saw tears brimming in his eyes.

“Ah! If only she knew that Vandiyathevan is no longer just the Prince of Vallam, but has become the King of Vallam! How much joy that would bring her! Alas, we did not get to tell her,” said Parthibendran.
Hearing this, Kandamaran looked at Ponniyin Selvan with a face full of astonishment.

“Yes, my friend! The Emperor has decided to return the land of Vanagappadi to your friend and make him the King of Vallam. Likewise, he intends to grant you, as a separate kingdom, the region near Vanagappadi that was once ruled by the Vaithumbarayars. From now on, the two of you must live as neighbors. You must always act so that nothing ever comes between your friendship,” said Ponniyin Selvan.
“It seems the Emperor’s compassion knows no bounds. In that case, I need not return to Kadambur, do I?” Kandamaran asked, a little cheer in his voice.

“There is no need. Your old palace there has most likely burned down, hasn’t it? If you go back there, old memories will only haunt you. Build a new palace on the southern bank of the River Palar. When your sister’s health improves, she too can come and live there.”

“Prince! I do not think Manimekalai will come to live with us anymore. Your grandmother, Sembiyan Maadevi, has said she will take her along on a pilgrimage. Manimekalai has become very fond of the Elder Princess. Even today, the Elder Princess has taken my sister to Thiruvaiyaru.”

“Yes; they have gone in a grand procession. Even my uncle and aunt, who have just been married, have gone along. Listen to this amusing thing: from now on, I must consider the Samudra Kumari as my aunt!”
“Never in the Chola clan has there been such a restrained wedding as this one between Madurantakan and Poonguzhali!” said Parthibendran.
“Even my own coronation will be conducted with the same restraint!” said Arulmozhi.
“That is something that will never happen!…” said Vandiyathevan.
Ponniyin Selvan, feigning surprise, asked, “What is it that will not happen? My coronation?”
Vandiyathevan, a little embarrassed, replied, “No, my lord! I meant that it is impossible for it to happen quietly. Even now, the people have begun to inquire and speak about your coronation!”

“Prince! Should we not be present for your crowning ceremony? At this very time, you are sending us northwards, while in Thanjai they are already saying that the date for the coronation will be fixed as soon as the month of Thai begins! Vandiyathevan is the lucky one; fortune’s favorite…” said Kandamaran.

“There is nothing of that sort. I am soon going to send Vandiyathevan to Eezham as well. Friends! Believe this one thing for certain! My coronation will not take place without you, my dearest friends!” Ponniyin Selvan declared firmly.
“Thank you very much, my lord! As soon as the date for the coronation is fixed, send a message through the horsemen, and we will come at once,” said Kandamaran.

“My friend! Why worry about that? I will not have my coronation without you present. Believe this without doubt. And do not forget why I am to be crowned. It is not to while away my days in pleasure beneath the palace moonlit terraces or in the palace gardens. Friends! Since my journey to Eezham, I have already shared with you the visions and dreams I have seen. Let me say it once more—listen! In our time, the Chola Empire must attain even greater glory than it did during the reign of Parantaka Chakravarthi, the father of my grandfather. The kingdom must expand in all four directions. To the north, up to the banks of the Ganga; to the east, across the seas to the kingdom of Srivijaya…” The armies of Chola Nadu must march forth and plant the tiger flag in distant lands. To the west, we must conquer the hill country and, beyond that, seize the Lakshadweep islands in the sea, establishing our forces there as a permanent presence. In the hill country, a Chera king has risen from somewhere. In Pandya Nadu too, at any moment, some Pandya prince may suddenly emerge. The kings of Lanka are the ones who lend strength to these new Cheras and Pandyas. Therefore, we must seek out Mahindan, who hides in the mountain caves of Eezham, and his armies, and utterly destroy their power at its root. The entire island of Lanka must be brought under our rule.

Is it enough if the empire merely expands? In Eezham, we must raise grand Shiva temples and Vishnu shrines on this sacred soil, so magnificent that they will eclipse the stupas of the Buddha. In this land of valor, those who come a thousand years after us must marvel at the works we have accomplished in our time.
Friends! All these dreams are destined to be fulfilled in my lifetime. I will see them accomplished. For that, each of you must lend your aid.

Parthibendran! I have bestowed upon you the highest military rank in Chola Nadu—the office of Northern Commander, which my brother Karikalan once held. You must fulfill that responsibility with utmost diligence. My brother’s untimely death will have kindled many ambitions among our enemies. The king of Vengi and the monarch of the Rashtrakutas will be hoping that internal strife and wars among the minor chieftains will erupt in Chola Nadu. Therefore, our warriors must stand guard on the northern banks of the Pennai river, like an iron fortress.

Scion of the Pallava clan! Leave Kandhamaaran as commander there, and you must return to Kanchipuram at once. There, prepare the golden palace my valiant brother built, so that the Emperor may reside there in comfort. As soon as the crown is placed upon my head, the Emperor wishes to journey to Kanchi!”

Hearing this, tears welled in Kandhamaaran’s eyes. “Prince! I have not yet had the chance to prove my valor on the battlefield. You appoint me as commander of the border guards? Am I worthy of such a post?” he asked, his voice trembling with emotion.

“My friend! The Almighty has granted me certain powers. Among them is the ability to discern easily who is worthy for which duty. Just as I have appointed you as commander of the northern border forces, I have appointed your friend Vallatharasan as commander of the Eezham expedition! I have faith that both of you will fulfill your duties well,” said Ponniyin Selvan.

“It is a wise decision to keep one of them at the northern border and the other at the southern border for some more time. If they were to be together anywhere, and if you were not present there, old memories might resurface and the two of them could end up clashing again,” said Parthibendran.
“Sir! Such a day will never come again!” Kandhamaaran declared, and as he spoke, he walked over to stand beside Vandiyathevan.
“My friend! You have forgiven all my mistakes, haven’t you?” he asked.
Vandiyathevan did not reply with words. Instead, he stretched out both his arms and embraced Kandhamaaran tightly to his chest.
For a few moments, the two friends stood in silence, tears streaming from their eyes.
Then, Parthibendran and Kandhamaaran boarded the boat that was ready and waiting for them.
Ponniyin Selvan and Vandiyathevan watched until the boat had traveled halfway down the river. Then, turning their horses toward Thanjai, they set off.

chapters.title: Meeting on the Road
paragraphs: News had spread throughout the land and cities that the coronation of Ponniyin Selvan was to take place very soon. The people, with a single-minded eagerness, looked forward to that grand event.

The untimely death of Aditya Karikalan, the self-sacrifice of Mandakini, and the fulfillment of Periya Pazhuvettarayar’s oath—these events had deeply grieved the heart of the Emperor. Yet, the disputes concerning the right to the throne had, in some measure, been resolved, and the fact that all the minor kings and the common people unanimously supported crowning Arulmozhi Varman brought some solace to his wounded heart.

As soon as the month of Thai began, the Emperor decided to choose an auspicious day, place the burden of the empire upon Ponniyin Selvan’s head, and then depart for Kanchipuram. There, he intended to spend the rest of his days in the golden palace built for him by his valiant son Karikalan. Is it any wonder that Sundara Chozhar wished to conduct the coronation without excessive pomp?

In this matter, Arulmozhi Varman too was determined to fulfill his father’s wishes to the letter. Therefore, he had resolved not to appear much among the public in the towns and cities until the coronation was over. If one were to travel directly from the ferry point on the Kollidam to Thanjavur, one would have to pass through the city of Thiruvaiyaru. If they entered that city, the people would surely gather around him in excitement. So, the two friends, avoiding that city, took a slightly western route and crossed the Kaveri river.
When they reached the Kudamurutti river, they walked along its banks toward the royal highway to Thanjavur.

In that wondrous region where five rivers flow one after another, the abundance of water and the richness of the land during the month of Margazhi presented a breathtaking sight. Compared to the season when the floods touch both banks, the scene now—with half the river a sweet stream and the other half a stretch of golden sand—was even more beautiful. On both sides of the river, coconut, areca, banana, and sugarcane flourished in abundance. In places where there were no groves, the well-irrigated fields gleamed with golden paddy, their red-tipped stalks... Their heads drooped, unable to look up. Here and there, in the ponds and streams, lotuses, kumudams, and red lilies rose above the water, presenting a scene as vivid as a painted tableau.

As Vandiyathevan gazed in wonder at all these sights, Ponniyin Selvan turned to him and said, “My friend! Is there anywhere else in this world a place endowed with such beauty and abundance? What a great fortune it is to be crowned the emperor of such a land! When I think that, until recently, I myself refused this fortune, I am amazed!”
“I see nothing surprising in that, sir! I have often heard elders speak of the fickle hearts of royal folk,” replied Vandiyathevan.
“You are a most incorrigible man. And ungrateful as well. You have yet to thank me for making you commander of the Lankan expeditionary force, and now you accuse me of having a wavering mind!”

“What is considered mockery among commoners might well be a cause for praise among royals, might it not? Today, you sentence a man to death. Tomorrow, you pardon him and make him a commander. Does not such fickleness only add to a king’s fame? ‘Ah! How compassionate is our king!’—is that not what the people will say?”
“Yes, yes! But if today I make someone a commander, and tomorrow I sentence him to death, what will the people say then?”
“They will say, ‘Here is a king who dispenses justice impartially, never swerving from righteousness; he is the very incarnation of Manu Neethi Cholan!’ and praise you all the more!”
Ponniyin Selvan laughed heartily and said, “If that is so, then if I take back from you the Vanagapadi fief and the command of the Lankan army, you will not find it at all surprising?”
“I will neither be surprised nor sorrowful. Even now, I am unsure whether you are sending me to Lanka to grant me a great command, or because you wish to exile me from this beautiful Chola land!”
“In truth, I would much prefer to have a man of such talent as you by my side as my chief minister. But I do not think Prime Minister Aniruddha will relinquish his post for your sake.”
“If that alone is the reason, I shall go and ask Prime Minister Aniruddhar myself,” said Vandiyathevan.
Ponniyin Selvan laughed and replied, “No; there is another reason as well!”
“I thought as much,” said Vandiyathevan.
“What did you think?”
“That these days, you keep one thing in your mind and speak another aloud.”
“Valaththarasar! Can you give an example to prove your accusation?”

“I certainly can. The date for your coronation ceremony has already been fixed for the beginning of the month of Thai. You know this. Yet, just a moment ago, to those who left us, you said, ‘My coronation cannot take place without you.’ What else am I to think of that?”

Ponniyin Selvan laughed again and said, “Yes, earlier I had the habit of speaking out whatever arose in my mind, just as it was. But after becoming friends with you, Vandiyathevan, I have been learning the arts of diplomacy and strategy!”

“You are praising me in vain. What strategy or secret is there in this world that you do not know? What can compare to the spell whispered into the elephant’s ear, or the trick of deceiving the world by donning the guise of a mahout?”
“Let it be so! You may learn the arts of strategy and diplomacy from me henceforth.”
“Perhaps that is why you are trying to send me off to Lanka—so that I do not learn too much from you?”
“My friend! Do you, perchance, have no desire to go to the land of Eelam?”
“Who told you so? Even if I am ordered to travel to places far beyond Lanka, I am ready to depart. The sooner you send me, the happier I shall be!”
“Is it such great joy for you to part from me and go away?”
“Yes, my lord! I have come to the conclusion that the farther one stays from emperors, the better it is. From a distance, one can preserve the friendship of kings without losing it.”
“In that case, you will be subject to disappointment…”
“Are you saying that, no matter how far I go, I cannot preserve your friendship for long?”

“No, no, what I am saying is that you cannot remain separated from me for very long. I have already decided that, after a few days, I too will come to Eezham and join you. I have planned to take you along, to cross the seas and journey to those distant islands beyond. I am only saddened that we cannot take the Princess of the Ocean with us…”
“Sir! By being with me, you have learned many magical arts and stratagems. Since becoming your friend, I have taken a vow to always speak the truth to you. May I now tell you what is in my heart?”
“Please, speak freely!”

“My friend, Sendhan Amudhan, and your uncle, Madhurantaka Thevar—you may take the Chola Empire from them. There is a kind of justice in that. You could say that it is the will of the people that you alone should wear the crown. But if you were to abduct Poonguzhali from him, there could be no greater act of betrayal. There is no justification for such a deed. Remember, the Princess of the Ocean is now the lawful wife of Madhurantaka Thevar!”
said Vandiyathevan.
Ponniyin Selvan laughed heartily and said, “It seems you are about to compare me with the ten-headed Ravana!”
Then he continued, “It is only right that you speak on behalf of your friend! But what about Poonguzhali’s feelings? Did she willingly marry my uncle?” asked Arulmozhi Varman.

“What doubt is there in that, Prince? You may become the emperor of this Chola Empire. You may conquer the whole world and rule it under one umbrella. But you cannot compel Poonguzhali Ammaiyaar to do anything against her will. I have had the fortune to witness the depth of love she bore for the son of Sembiyan Maadevi. I have seen such love in only one other place!”
“Where have you seen it? If you are willing, tell me about it!”
“I met the Kodumbalur princess, Vanathi. Where else could such love be found?”
“Lies! Lies! Have you forgotten the truth within that tale? You hide one thing in your heart and speak another aloud!”
“No, my lord! I speak only what I feel in my heart.”
“Have you not seen such love anywhere else?”
“I told you, I have not.”

“Oh, wretch! Merciless fiend! For your sake, a maiden came forward to sacrifice her life, lost her senses, and became a madwoman! Did her love not seem great to you?” Ponniyin Selvan asked, his voice filled with genuine anger.

Vandiyathevan was silent for a while. Then he replied, “My lord! You are twisting cause and effect. It is not that I felt no pity for Manimekalai. I weep when I think of her. But I am not the reason for her madness! It is her brother, Kandhamaaran! And now, both of us are as good as dead to that woman. What use is there in speaking of it further?”
“I regret having spoken so harshly just now…” Ponniyin Selvan began.
“I feel neither regret nor surprise at it. It is in anticipation of such sudden anger that I wished to leave for Lanka as soon as possible.”
“Did I not say there was another reason for sending you to Lanka?”
“Yes, my prince.”
“My sister believes that if you spend some time in a distant land and return, perhaps Manimekalai may not recognize you.”
“I understand, my lord! I see now that the Younger Princess is even more eager than you to send me away! And look—those whom we were just speaking of are coming this way!” Vandiyathevan pointed out.

The two friends who had come along the banks of the Kudamuruti river were now nearing the royal road that led from Thiruvaiyaru to Thanjavur. Upon that royal road, surrounded before and behind by attendants, a palanquin was making its way. Within that palanquin sat Princess Kundavai and the Princess of Kodumbalur.
The moment those noblewomen caught sight of the two friends approaching on horseback, their eyes widened in astonishment. Their faces blossomed with joy.

chapters.title: The Lover of the Earth Goddess
paragraphs: The palanquin in which the princesses were seated drew near to Ponniyin Selvan’s horse.
Vandiyathevan, who had reined in his horse a little behind, called out, “Careful! That dangerous palanquin of the princesses is about to collide with our gentle horse!”

At almost the same spot, he remembered, he had once driven his horse into Nandini’s closed palanquin and then shouted, “The palanquin is running into my horse!” That incident had taken place not even six months ago. Yet, in this short span, how many important events had transpired!

Kundavai, suppressing the delight that Vandiyathevan’s words brought her, said, “Brother! Looking at you both, it seems as though you are discussing some joyous matter! Your faces are positively radiant with happiness!”

“Yes, Akka! We were indeed talking about a happy subject. But it may not bring as much joy to your friend Vanathi. My wedding day is drawing near, is it not? We were rejoicing at the thought of the maiden I am to wed, the one I love. We were speaking of her beauty and grace!” said Ponniyin Selvan.

The faces of the two women, which had just moments before been bright and shining, suddenly clouded over. Vanathi bowed her head. On Kundavai’s face, anger, surprise, doubt, and irritation flickered and faded in quick succession.
“What is this shameless talk? What pleasure do you find in causing this girl pain?” she demanded.
Vanathi lifted her head and looked at Kundavai. “Akka, what are you saying? Why should I be pained?” she asked.

Ponniyin Selvan, without replying to either, stood there with a smile blooming on his face. Seeing this, the younger princess said, “Was it not to the banks of the Kollidam that you went and returned? Which maiden did you see there? What village? What name? What clan?” she asked, her questions tumbling out one after another. At that moment, Vandiyathevan interjected, “Devi! We have not seen any noble maiden whom the prince is to wed. All along this bank of the Five Rivers, we have only gazed in wonder at the resplendent Lady of the Land herself. We spoke of the natural beauty of Chola Nadu as we traveled. Is not the day drawing near when the prince will be crowned emperor of this beautiful country? It is about his love for these two maidens of the earth that he was speaking!”
“Ah! My brother never used to speak so eloquently before. It seems you have taught him this art!” she said.

Arulmozhi Varman laughed and replied, “My friend! You must take the credit! Did I not already tell you that all these clever tricks and spells have come to me only after your friendship? Now, it seems my sister thinks the same!”
“What is this baseless accusation! Both sister and brother have conspired to lay the same charge at my feet?” said Vandiyathevan.

“There are still many more accusations against you. There are even some that my brother could not bring himself to mention. All of those cannot be spoken here in the middle of the road!” said Kundavai.
Vandiyathevan said, “My suspicion has proved correct!”
“What did you suspect?”
“I suspected that sending me off as commander of the Eelam expedition was in fact a punishment for my crimes—a sentence of exile to the island!”
“Did you hear that, Akka! Now you see how much faith he has in the gratitude of the Chola clan?”
“It is true—we owe him not the least bit of gratitude!”
“What is this, even you say so?”

“We may express gratitude for the help of strangers. But how can gratitude arise between friends? Have you forgotten what Thiruvalluvar has said? ‘As the hand rushes to help when the garment slips, So friendship comes unbidden in times of trouble!’”
“Should I thank my waist and hands just because I managed to tie up my slipping garment?” asked Kundavai.
“Devi! There is no need for thanks. If you spare me from punishment, that itself will be the greatest favor!” replied Vandiyathevan.

“My brother! You and he—both of you—must remember one thing. Our elder brother, the valiant Karikalan who has attained the warrior’s heaven, sent him here to be of assistance to me. I have not yet released him from that duty!” said Kundavai.
“There is no need to release him, Akka! Even if you sentence him to a lifetime of service, I would gladly accept it!” said the prince.
“There are still some tasks I need him to accomplish for me in Lanka,” said Kundavai.
“Before I leave, I will come to bid you farewell, Devi!” said Vandiyathevan.
“In that case, you must come to Pazhayarai and take leave of me,” said Princess Kundavai.
“Akka, where are you going now?” Arulmozhi Varman asked in some surprise.

“We are going to Thiruvaiyaru. Is today not the sacred Thiruvathirai festival in the month of Margazhi? Sembiyan Maadevi, Madurantakan, and Poonguzhali all left early this morning. Will you be coming as well?” asked Kundavai.
“No, we are not coming now. We did not wish to enter the city of Thiruvaiyaru, so we walked along the riverbank to the west and have just returned.”
“Appar Peruman beheld Kailasa itself at Thiruvaiyaru and was filled with ecstasy. It seems you have no desire to go there. Have you perhaps become fervent Vaishnavites now?”
“It is nothing of the sort. If I go to Thiruvaiyaru, it is my wish to go as Appar Peruman did.”
“How did Appar go?”

“He himself has sung of it in his verses! ‘He went without leaving any trace.’ Without any pomp or display, without revealing that he was Tirunavukkarasar, he walked behind the group of devotees carrying flowers and water for the puja. That is why, in Thiruvaiyaru, he was able to behold Kailasa itself. If we go there with all these royal splendors, we too will not be able to have darshan of the Lord. The people will forget the deity and surround us instead!”

“Yes, yes! That is your special fate! The moment people see you, they will crowd around, shouting, ‘Victory to the King of Kings! Victory to the Son of Ponni!’ But we are not in so much danger. Besides, we will not go amidst the crowds. When the deity is taken out in procession for the Thiruvathirai festival, we shall behold the Lord of Aiyar from the upper terrace of our palace in Thiruvaiyaru.”

“Akka! Do you remember an old song? The Lord who created the cosmic spheres, all the worlds, and every star in the vast sky—how foolish it is for people to call Him ‘Aathirayan,’ as if He belongs only to the Thiruvathirai star, as if He is limited to that alone! Do you remember that song with such meaning?”
“I remember, Thambi! But the One who belongs to all the stars, surely belongs to Thiruvathirai as well, does He not?”
“Very well, you may go! When will you return to Thanjavur?”
“We are not returning to Thanjavur now. From Thiruvaiyaru, we are going to Pazhaiyarai.”
“What? What? You are leaving without attending my coronation?” exclaimed the prince.
“Yes, yes! What business do Vanathi and I have at your coronation festivities?”
“Aha! Without you, will my coronation even take place?”
“Everything will happen, why wouldn’t it? Who was it that fixed the date for your coronation? Are you not descended from the one who chose the auspicious day for Rama’s coronation?”
“I have no faith in auspicious days, stars, horoscopes, or omens, Akka! Every day on which we fulfill our duty is a good day! Only the days wasted in idleness are bad days!” said Ponniyin Selvan.
“May all the days of your life be as blessed as this, my brother! We shall go and pray for you at the shrine of Ayyarappan and before the Lady who nurtures virtue,” said Kundavai.
“For me? What prayers will you offer on my behalf?”

“We shall pray to the Lord of Ayyar that the love you bear for the earth goddess may be fulfilled, and that your coronation may proceed without hindrance. And before the Lady who fosters righteousness, we shall pray that your heart may never stray from the path of virtue that befits the ancient Chola lineage.”
“In that case, does it mean you will not be present at my coronation?”
“From Pazhayarai, we shall witness it with our inner eye and rejoice.”

“Akka! You are tying your support to the stubbornness of this Kodumbalur princess. She believes that if she refuses to ascend the Chola throne with me, the whole world will come to ruin! Her obstinate refusal is about to end in disaster. Instead of her, another woman is going to sit on the Chola throne! Afterwards, there will be no use blaming me for it,” said the prince, Ponniyin Selvan.
“I have never blamed him for anything, nor shall I ever do so in the future, Akka!” said the princess of Kodumbalur.
“Even if you did, it would be of no use, Vanathi! Nothing else will enter the ears of those who are consumed by love for the land!” said the young princess Kundavai.

“Let us not forget that it was you who kindled this love for the land in my heart. You, born a woman, have yourself told me many times that you could not bear to leave this beautiful Chola country, and that for that very reason you would never marry!” said Arulmozhi.

“At that time, my words never reached your ears. You kept saying there are many other beautiful lands in the world! It is the teachings of this valiant scion of the Vanar clan that have turned you into the lover of the earth goddess!” said Princess Kundavai.
“Heavens! Must even that blame fall upon me?” exclaimed Vandiyathevan.

"You have already borne so many great and terrible burdens—are you going to be frightened by these small accusations? Brother! We have spoken for a long time now! The hour for Swami’s audience is drawing near, let us go!" said Kundavai, signaling to the palanquin bearers. The palanquin moved forward.
After watching them for a while, Ponniyin Selvan too turned his horse towards Thanjai.

A short distance ahead, as Vandiyathevan drew near beside him, he said, "My friend! I do not believe these women are truly going for Swami’s darshan. I hear that the Kudanthai astrologer has now taken residence near Thiruvaiyaru! I think they are going to consult him for an astrological reading!"
"Sir! You are a greater astrologer than the Kudanthai astrologer himself!" replied Vandiyathevan.

chapters.title: The Cat and the Parrot
paragraphs: Events unfolded just as Ponniyin Selvan had surmised and foretold. As soon as Kundavai Devi and Vanathi arrived at the Chola palace in Thiruvaiyaru, their palanquin and attendants were halted there. They learned that Sembiyan Maadevi, along with her son and daughter-in-law, had gone to the temple. Informing the palace guards that they, too, would visit the temple, they took only a single brave soldier as escort and set out in search of the astrologer’s house.

Yes, after the floods had swept away his house, the Kudanthai astrologer had come to Thiruvaiyaru. On the eastern edge of the city, by the banks of the Kaveri, he had built himself a small house and begun to reside there.
Perhaps, having divined through his astrology that Thanjavur would soon eclipse Pazhaiyarai in importance, this was the reason for his move to Thiruvaiyaru.

As they stepped onto the threshold of the astrologer’s house, a sweet, childish voice from within greeted them: “Welcome, queens of dance! Welcome, queens of grace! Come in, come in!” Both the noblewomen were astonished to hear such a welcome. The astrologer who once kept a rude disciple as his doorkeeper—whom had he now set to receive guests with such courteous words? With this thought, they entered.

Their astonishment vanished when they saw, hanging from the rafters in a cage, a beautiful green parrot. The parrot cocked its head this way and that, its small eyes like tiny bells fixing them with a keen gaze, and once again it chirped, “Welcome, queens of dance! Welcome!”
Hearing both the parrot’s voice and the tinkling of the women’s anklets, the astrologer emerged from within.
Startled at the sight of the noblewomen, he exclaimed, “Welcome! Welcome, my ladies! Today, this humble hut is truly blessed!”
The green parrot, opening its coral-red beak, echoed, “Today, this hut is truly blessed!”

The astrologer turned to the bird and said, “Tch, tch! Be quiet for a while! Close your beak!” “Sir! Why are you angered by that? This hut always welcomes its visitors in the best manner. Every day, many come here and seem to make this hut their ‘lucky abode for the day’. It appears that queens and princesses themselves frequent this place without rest!” said the young princess Kundavai.
“Come! O queens of dance! Come!” cried the parrot.

The astrologer silenced the bird once more and said, “Forgive me, noble ladies! When the great saint Thirugnana Sambandar visited this sacred Thiruvaiyaru, he saw dance halls lining every street. He heard the anklets of the maidens learning dance ring out ‘kaleer, kaleer’. He even sang of it in his divine hymns. Just as in those days, even now, there are many maidens in Thiruvaiyaru who study the art of dance. They often come seeking their fortunes here at this hut! For their sake, I have trained this parrot to speak thus! Please forgive me!”
“But today, I see none of those dancing queens or maidens here,” said Kundavai.

“Devi! Today is the sacred festival of Thiruvadhirai. So, the queens and maidens of dance must have gone to serve at the shrine of Lord Aiyaru. But the true queens—you yourselves—have come here. This hut is truly blessed. I am the one who is fortunate!” the astrologer exclaimed with delight.
Then he added, “Please, be seated! Ask this poor man whatever you wish to know! I shall answer as best I can!”

The two princesses sat down. Kundavai let out a deep sigh and said, “Astrologer! What is there to ask? The first question that comes to mind is whether there is any truth at all in this science of astrology!”
“Devi! If you ask thus, what can I say? For those who have faith, astrology is true. For those who do not, it is false!” replied the astrologer.
“I used to have complete faith in astrology. But now, it is that very science which has abandoned me!”
“In what way has it abandoned you, Lady?” “Has anything happened as you foretold in your astrology? Did you ever tell me that my brother would meet with such an untimely death?”

“How could I have said so, Devi? Even if I had known, could I have opened my mouth and spoken of it? If I had spoken, would they not have counted me among the conspirators from Pandya Nadu? One can only speak in generalities about royal families and matters of state. To say, ‘Danger lies ahead, obstacles are coming, evil planets are in sight’—that itself is perilous. Moreover, I do not even possess Aditya Karikalan’s horoscope. I have never seen it!” said the astrologer.
“Even if you had seen it, you would not have spoken. And even if you had spoken, could that disaster have been averted?”
“How could that be possible, Mother! Am I Brahma himself? Can even Brahma erase what he has written?”
“If that is so, what is the use of astrology, O astrologer?”

“Mother! Why do you ask me thus? If people like you do not consult astrology, how are people like me to make a living? How else would the feet of royal princesses grace the hut of this poor man?” replied the astrologer.
At this, Kundavai burst into laughter. Even on Vanathi’s face, a smile blossomed.
“Astrologer! Do you speak like this to everyone who comes to consult you?” asked the young princess.

“Do I speak like this to everyone? The whole world sings your praises, saying that the goddess of arts and the goddess of wealth have both incarnated in you. How could I hope to match wits with such a one as you in debate? That is why I spoke so. But, Mother! Can you judge the truth of astrology by what I have not foretold? Should you not judge it by what I have said? Did I not speak of Ponniyin Selvan’s auspicious horoscope? Though many obstacles arose, in the end, the time has come for him to become the emperor of this world. Even the date for his coronation has been fixed, has it not?” said the astrologer.
“Sir! Has no one come to you to fix an auspicious date for Ponniyin Selvan’s coronation?”
“No, Devi! There are palace priests for that! And the chief minister Aniruddha himself is well-versed in the science of astrology!”
“Yes; they have fixed the date as the seventh day of the month of Thai. Is that an auspicious day, astrologer?”
“It is a very auspicious day, Amma! They have chosen it after much careful consideration.”
“It may indeed be a good day for the coronation. But tell me, will the coronation truly take place on that day?”
“What kind of question is this, Devi? Why should it not happen?”
“They chose an auspicious day for Sri Rama’s coronation as well. But did the coronation take place for him on that day?”

“Devi! On that day, Sri Rama attained a glory a hundred million times greater than a mere coronation. That is how the Ramayana was born! Let that be. But why should such doubts arise in your mind now? It seems as if you yourself do not wish for the coronation to take place on that day!”
“Your intuition is correct!”
“Is it not said that there is no one in this world who would rejoice more than you if Ponniyin Selvan ascends the throne?”
“Rightfully, I ought to experience that joy. But the stubborn, foolish vow of this woman from Kodumbalur has robbed me of that happiness. Do you remember the vow she made in your house at Kudanthai?”
“A vow? So many strange events took place that day, I do not recall anything clearly!” said the astrologer.

“She made a vow because of something that jealous boat girl, Poonguzhali, said to her. She swore that as long as she lived, she would never ascend the throne! After her death, can she ascend the throne, astrologer?”
“She cannot!”
“After hearing such a disastrous vow, it was only natural that Mother Kaveri, in her wrath, rose up in fury and tried to sweep him away in the flood!”
“Yes, I remember now. I thought that vow was merely a childish game!”

“That is the very thing that has become a matter of fate now! She will not ascend the throne, it seems. For my brother to ascend the throne and shine as the chief queen, it is said that he must marry someone else. She, it appears, will remain in his palace as a mere attendant among the nursemaids, serving him! I cannot bear even to hear such things, O astrologer! Do you remember all that you foretold about this girl?”

With a gentle smile, the astrologer replied, “I remember it well, Devi! The sacred river Kaveri has carried away all the horoscopes I had collected, those of princes and princesses from many lands. But the horoscope of this princess is imprinted on the tablet of my mind. The lines upon her palm stand before my eyes even now. Ammanni! Whatever else may or may not come to pass in my predictions, what I have spoken about her cannot fail!”
“Do you remember now what you said about this girl?”

“I remember it well. I said that the fortunate man who marries her will, in one form, wed both the goddess of fortune and the goddess of the earth. I said that emperors from distant lands would perform penance for the fortune of beholding this maiden. I foretold that the son born of her sacred womb would enter this world with the banner of victory unfurled at his birth. Wherever he goes, wherever he looks, there will be triumph.”
“Sir! The more you speak thus, the more my anxiety grows!”

The astrologer straightened up suddenly and said, “Devi! Anxiety? Why should you be anxious? The days for worry about the Chozha empire and the Chozha clan have passed. Do you remember what special day it is today?”
“Yes; today is the day of Margazhi Thiruvadhirai! An auspicious day for Shiva!”

“It is also an auspicious day for the Chozha clan. An auspicious day for divine Tamilakam, Devi! Listen! On a future Margazhi Thiruvadhirai such as this, a wondrous event is destined to occur! Without conch or discus in his hand, a child who is the very incarnation of Lord Vishnu is to be born! Through that child, this Chozha land will attain a greatness it has never known before! Ah! What marvels are yet to unfold! Perhaps I shall not live to witness them. But you shall live long to see and rejoice in them!”
As the astrologer spoke thus, seized by a sudden fervor, Kundavai too listened, utterly entranced.
Suddenly, hearing some noise, both of them turned around.
The parrot in the cage was flapping its wings frantically. Vanathi, seeing the cat attempting to leap onto it, picked up a palm-leaf manuscript and threw it at the cat!

After throwing it, she exclaimed, “Akka! The science of astrology has proven useful indeed. It was with the astrologer’s manuscript that I managed to save this beautiful, sweet-talking parrot! If not, the cat would have torn its wings to shreds by now!”

chapters.title: The Chinese Merchants
paragraphs: From ancient times, people in many lands have striven to know the events of the future. Just as the poor and unlettered common folk have sought to pierce the veil of what is to come, so too have kings and nobles, and the most learned of scholars. Astrologers, soothsayers, omen-readers, augurers, palmists, and the like have flourished in societies advanced in both knowledge and civilization. Likewise, there have always been those who doubted the truth of astrology and condemned the art itself.

Such a struggle often arose in the heart of the jewel among wise women, the young princess Kundavai. Yet, whenever anxiety for the future of the Chola Empire weighed upon her, that worry would drive Kundavai Devi to seek out the astrologer’s house.

By all rights, Kundavai’s heart should now have attained the peace that Emperor Sundara Chola himself possessed. Unexpected events had unfolded, and it was now certain that Arulmozhi Varman would ascend the Chola throne and be crowned. We know well the boundless longing Kundavai had cherished for her younger brother since their childhood. In her heart, there had always been a firm faith that Arulmozhi, born with the auspicious marks of the conch and discus upon his palms, would lead the Chola Empire to its greatest glory. The incident where he fell into the flood of the Kaveri and was saved by a woman who appeared as a goddess, and many other such events, only served to strengthen her faith. The time for that faith to be fulfilled was now drawing near. Yet, what was it that still denied peace to the heart of that royal maiden?

Just as many spoke of Arulmozhi Varman’s destiny, so too did many speak of the horoscope of Princess Vanathi of Kodumbalur. Whether they truly studied the stars and planets to divine the future, or simply wished to comfort Kundavai Devi at that time, none could say. Yet, we often see that when many voices unite in a single prediction, it sometimes comes to pass in wondrous ways. In the words of some, there is a peculiar force—their utterances come true as they are spoken.

From Kumbakonam, those who had migrated to Thiruvaiyaru... The astrologer, recalling that day as the sacred Thiruvathirai of the month of Margazhi, declared with some emphasis, “It is an auspicious day that shall bring great glory to the Chola dynasty!”

Two years later, on that very Margazhi Thiruvathirai, a male child was born into the Chola clan. When that child grew to the proper age, he shone as an emperor to be compared with Chandragupta, Ashoka, Vikramaditya, and Harshavardhana. He received the coronation name Rajendra, and from Lanka to the Ganges, from the Lakshadweep islands to the island of Sri Avijaya, he conquered and ruled with authority.

The words spoken by the astrologer thus came to pass in a most wondrous manner. But on that day, when he uttered them, Kundavai did not feel complete faith in his prediction. For Vanathi, the astrologer’s words only provoked anger.

She found an immediate way to express that anger. Lifting the palm-leaf manuscript, she flung it at the cat that belonged to the young princess, exclaiming, “Even the science of astrology has its uses!”

Hearing this, the astrologer turned and, discerning what had happened, said, “Princess! They say even a blade of grass becomes a weapon in the hands of the valiant. In the same way, by the grace of your divine hand, this palm-leaf manuscript has saved a life. In the future, will not that lotus hand grant refuge and protection to countless lives?”
Vanathi said, “Akka! This astrologer is a master at flattery—come, let us go!”
“Devi! My words may not please you today. But a time will come when all that I have said will come true. When that day arrives, do not forget this poor soul!” said the astrologer.

Kundavai intervened, “Sir! It is not that this girl dislikes your words. The more she hears them, the happier she feels in her heart. But she is angry, thinking, ‘Without a second thought, I have made some rash vow!’ She has taken out that anger on your palm-leaf manuscript! You need not take it to heart.”
“Even the anger of good people brings good results! See, the beloved parrot that I addressed with sweet words has been spared, has it not?” said the astrologer.

Afterwards, Kundavai continued to converse with the astrologer for a while longer. Chief among her questions was: when would Arulmozhi Varman’s marriage take place? There was good reason for the young princess Kundavai to be concerned about this matter. For, on the previous day, the Commander-in-Chief, Boothi Vikrama Kesari, had come to her and asked, “Mother! I am going to Kodumbalur. May I take my brother’s daughter Vanathi with me?”
Kundavai, startled, replied, “Uncle! What is this haste? Will you leave before the coronation?”

“Mother! I will return in time for the coronation. Until then, why should I remain here? I came with a great army. By divine grace, our wishes have been fulfilled without any conflict. The emperor’s son has agreed to ascend the throne. All the minor kings have accepted this. There is no longer any need to keep such a large army here. Providing food and managing so many people has become a burden for the people of Thanjavur. Therefore, it has become necessary for me to take my army, disperse them in various places, and return,” said the Commander-in-Chief.
“Do as you wish! But why do you want to take my friend Vanathi with you?” asked Kundavai.

“Devi! There is a reason for that. Yesterday, all the minor kings gathered together and came to a decision. Your grandfather, Arinjaya Devar’s father, Paranthaka Chakaravarthi, married six princesses. He took wives from my clan, from the clan of Miladudaiyar, from the clans of the Pazhuvettaraiyars, Mazhavarayars, and Sambhuvarayars—one woman from each. Thus, during his reign, there was no discord among the minor kings. Your grandfather Arinjaya too married several princesses from the minor royal clans. He married your grandmother from the victorious Vaidhumba royal line. But your father did not follow this good custom. He married only your mother, the daughter of the Malayaman clan. Because of this, jealousy and rivalry arose among the minor kings. Now, it has been unanimously decided that those who ascend the throne of this Chola Empire hereafter must, like Paranthaka Chakaravarthi and Arinjaya Devar, take wives from several of the minor royal clans. After the coronation ceremony of Ponniyin Selvan, we intend to submit this request to him. That is why I wish to take Vanathi back to our land—” “Can’t you imagine what others might think? If I leave her here, people may suspect that I am acting against our agreement,” said the Kodumbalur Velar.

Hearing this, Kundavai felt a surge of anger within her. Without revealing it outwardly, she replied, “Commander! Once, you yourself asked that I be both mother and father to your younger brother’s daughter, who lost her parents. Have you forgotten that? I cannot send Vanathi to Kodumbalur. I cannot bear to be separated from her even for a moment. If necessary, I will take Vanathi with me to Pazhaiyarai. We will remain there and not even come for the coronation ceremony. Let us not speak of marriage now. After the coronation, let the wishes of the minor kings be conveyed to Ponniyin Selvan! We can consider it later!” she said.
The Commander accepted this and left.
For Kundavai Devi, this became an even greater reason to seek out the astrologer. That is why she questioned the astrologer about Ponniyin Selvan’s marriage with such concern.
At that very moment, Vanathi’s thoughts wandered to an old memory. In that memory, a bird and a cat played their parts. Along with the cat, an elephant and its mahout were also involved.

A wild cat attacked a bird’s nest hanging from a tree branch, trying to devour the fledglings inside. The mother bird circled the nest, trying to fend off the cat. Vanathi, witnessing this, cried out helplessly. A young man swimming in the river heard her cry and rushed over. He quickly mounted an elephant and came to the scene. He rescued the nest and the tender chicks from the jaws of the wild cat.

At that time, Vanathi thought the young man was just an elephant mahout. Later, she learned that he was Ponniyin Selvan himself. Ah! Could he not have remained just an elephant mahout? Or a simple warrior? Was it not because he was the son of Emperor Sundara Chola that she had to endure such troubles? Was it not for this reason that her companions, and those like Poonguzhali, spoke ill of her, accusing her of aspiring to be the queen of the Chola kingdom…?

While Vanathi was lost in such thoughts, and Kundavai was engrossed in inquiring about her future through astrology, a loud voice suddenly rang out at the astrologer’s doorstep: “Do you want Chinese silk? Chinese silk!” Other voices could also be heard.

Kundavai and Vanathi realized that it was time for them to leave, and they rose to their feet. At that moment, the astrologer’s disciple entered and said, “Swami! Two Chinese merchants have arrived. They wish to consult you about their fortunes! Shall I ask them to come back tomorrow?”
Kundavai replied, “No need! Let them come in now; we are about to take our leave,” and, taking Vanathi by the hand, she led her away.

As the two princesses reached the entrance, they saw an elephant standing there, and upon its back sat two Chinese merchants, perched atop large bundles of cloth. It seemed that the merchants were asking the mahout, who stood below, some questions.
Without paying them much heed, the princesses called upon the warrior who had accompanied them and made their way back to the Chola palace.

chapters.title: The Vision Seen by Appar
paragraphs: That night, in anticipation of the Thiruvathirai festival, Ayyarappar and the Lady who fostered virtue made their grand procession through the broad, colonnaded streets of Thiruvaiyaru. Upon a chariot fashioned of silver to resemble the snow-clad Mount Kailasa, the Lord and His Consort were adorned and enthroned in splendor. The sight called to mind the sacred mountain shrouded in silvery mist.

At the head of the procession marched elephants, camels, and mighty bulls. Upon their backs, enormous drums and kettledrums thundered, their reverberations echoing to the eight corners of the world. Following them, in ordered ranks, came those bearing various sacred emblems. Groups of musicians played a multitude of instruments, their melodies rising in harmonious waves. Here and there, dancing courtesans paused to perform, their graceful movements enchanting the onlookers before they moved on.

Nandi Bhagavan, Chandikeswara, Vinayaka, and Muruga with his consorts Valli and Deivanai each journeyed in their own resplendent palanquins. And at the very end, Parvati and Parameswara, seated together upon the Kailasa chariot, bestowed their divine presence upon the gathering.

Further behind, the choir of Devaram singers advanced, accompanied by veena, mridangam, cymbals, and other instruments. They sang the sacred Thiruppadigams of Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, their voices blending with the music as they walked. Before and behind, thousands upon thousands of people filled the streets, moving slowly with the procession. Each was absorbed in their own way: some gazed in wonder at the elephants and camels, others listened raptly to the music, some watched the dances of the divine courtesans, but most were entranced by the sight of the deities themselves, overcome with devotion and praise.
As far as the eye could see, hundreds of blazing torches illuminated the night, transforming that extraordinary divine procession into a vision from a dream-world.

From the upper balcony of the Chola palace, Kundavai, Vanathi, and Poonguzhali watched the spectacle unfold. From the first elephant bearing the drums to the last of the Devaram choir, they observed with eager delight. They watched the devotees lost in ecstasy, the common folk entertained by the many marvels, and the divine forms—from Nandi Deva to Shiva and Parvati—parading through the streets, and their hearts were filled with joy.

Amidst that vast crowd, two Chinese merchants were seen riding atop an elephant. Now and then, they would dismount from the elephant, vanish into the throng, and then reappear to climb back onto the animal.
“Aha! Are these two Chinese truly merchants? Or are they spies sent from a foreign land to gather intelligence?” Such a suspicion arose in Kundavai’s mind.

It was only natural that news of the disputes and confusions concerning the Chola royal succession, which had arisen in recent days, would have spread throughout the world. Considering this, could not rival kings have sent these spies disguised as Chinese merchants?

As Kundavai and Vanathi discussed this, their words reached the ears of Poonguzhali. That young woman said, “Devi! Those men approached me at the temple gopura entrance and asked, ‘Do you want Chinese silk?’ I told them, ‘Come to the Chola palace; princesses from Thanjai are coming—they might buy from you!’ So, if they come here, they will surely approach us. You can clear your doubts by questioning them directly!”

At that moment, Ayyarappar, seated on the Kailayangiri mount, and the Lady who fostered virtue, had reached the entrance of the Chola palace. There, the deity was halted, and rituals such as the offering of lamps were performed. After the divine procession had passed, Sembiyan Madevi and her son entered the palace. Learning that the princesses were in the upper chambers, they went there directly.

For a while, conversation turned to the grandeur of the festival. Then, the consort of Sivagnana Kandaraadithar looked at her beloved son and said, “Child! In this very Thiruvaiyaru, Appar Peruman beheld a wondrous vision and composed a hymn about it. Sing that hymn for us once. Listening to the Devara chorus did not satisfy me fully!”
The princesses and Poonguzhali gladly agreed to this request. Then, Madurantaka Devar, also known as Sendhan Amudhan, sang that hymn in his sweet voice:

“With the maiden whose eyes are like crescent moons, And the daughter of the mountain king, they sang. With flowers and water, they worshipped and praised; I followed after those who entered, leaving no trace. When Ayyaru was reached, I beheld a wondrous sight— With his beloved, gentle peahen, A majestic elephant came forth!”
“I have seen the Lord’s sacred feet! I have seen what none have seen!”
With this line, and the ten verses that followed, Madurantakan sang, utterly forgetting himself.
Those who listened, too, lost all sense of themselves. The visions that Appar Peruman beheld long ago seemed to appear before their eyes as well.

When the song ended, a deep silence settled over the gathering for a while. Then, Kundavai turned to Sembiyan Maadevi and said, “Mother! You have told me before the story of how Appar sang this hymn. Tell it once more now! Let everyone here hear it!” At the urging of the others, the venerable princess Sembiyan Maadevi began to recount that tale.

In his old age, when Appar Swami’s body had grown weak, he desired to journey to Mount Kailasa to behold the Lord. He traveled far north, but at last, exhausted and unable to proceed, he collapsed. At that moment, a venerable figure appeared before him and said, “Appare! Why do you seek Kailasa? Go to Thiruvaiyaru, on the banks of the Ponni river! That is Kailasa on earth.” With these words, the figure vanished.

Knowing this to be the Lord’s own command, Appar turned back and came to Thiruvaiyaru. As he neared that sacred place, his heart overflowed with ecstasy. He saw many devotees carrying flower baskets and pots filled with Kaveri water, all on their way to worship Ayyarappan. They sang the Lord’s praises as they went. Appar followed behind them.

Just then, at the outskirts of Thiruvaiyaru, two elephants—one male, one female—appeared. To Appar, these elephants revealed themselves as Shiva and Shakti. Before reaching the temple, he beheld many such pairs of animals and birds: a hen frolicking with her chicks; a peacock dancing, entwined with its mate; in the nearby grove, a male and female cuckoo singing joyously together; a wild goose, trumpeting thunderously, moving along with its mate; cranes flying in pairs; green parrots chattering tenderly with their fledglings among the lush branches; bull and cow striding majestically side by side.

Thus, all these pairs of male and female creatures that appeared before Appar Swamigal seemed, to his inner vision, as manifestations of Shiva and Shakti. He saw the entire world as the play of Shakti and Shiva. He realized, “This very world is Kailasa; there is no separate Kailasa elsewhere.”

With this supreme realization, he proceeded further and beheld Ayyarappan and the Lady of Virtue, mounted on the Kailasa Vahana, making their procession through the streets. All that he saw and experienced that day, with both his outer and inner eyes, he composed and sang in sweet Tamil verse.

All these days, though she had seen with her own eyes, she had not truly understood with her mind; but today, in Thiruvaiyaru, she had seen and comprehended those very things. At the end of every song, she exclaimed again and again in wonder, “I have seen what I had never known before!”
Everyone listened, utterly absorbed, as the venerable Empress narrated this history.

When the tale was finished, the Kodumbalur Princess asked a question: “Mother! Appar Swamigal has spoken with such amazement about the love among the birds and beasts. But why has he not mentioned anything about the human race?”

Poonguzhali replied, “Because, among humans, there are no men or women who love truly, without expecting some benefit in return. That is why Appar did not mention the love between men and women of the human race!”
“That is not so, my child! If Appar Swamigal had seen you and my son, he would have sung of the love among humans as well!” said Sembiyan Maadevi.
“Yes, yes!” agreed the other two women.

At that moment, there was some commotion at the entrance of the palace. A servant came in and announced, “Two Chinese silk merchants have arrived. They say they will only leave after seeing the princesses!”
The younger princess, surprised and annoyed, said, “Who are these people to be so insistent? Tell them we do not wish to see anyone now, and send them away!”
But Poonguzhali interjected, “Devi! I had asked them to come. Please forgive me!”
“In that case, let them come and leave quickly,” said the younger princess.
In a short while, the two Chinese merchants entered, each carrying two bundles.

chapters.title: The Coronation Gift
paragraphs: The two Chinese merchants appeared with large turbans upon their heads and thick, bushy beards and mustaches covering their faces. In the auspicious lamplight burning on the upper floor of the palace at that moment, their facial features could not be clearly discerned. It was impossible even to guess their ages.

The doubts that had arisen in Kundavai’s mind only grew stronger. That wise princess commanded the servant who had brought the merchants, “This light is not enough to see the silks and fine garments. Bring a large lamp and light it!”
“I shall go and send a good lamp!” said Madurantaka Devar, and withdrew from the place. Sembiyan Madevi went with him.

After they had left, Kundavai turned to the Chinese merchants and asked, “Sirs! Why are you in such a hurry? Could you not bring your wares tomorrow during the day and show them to us? Why have you come at night itself?”

“Princesses! Forgive us! We have been in Thanjavur for many days now. Despite much effort, we could not come into the palace and meet you. The ship departs from Nagapattinam the day after tomorrow. We must leave on it as well. That is why we hurried!” replied one of the Chinese merchants.
Though his voice sounded somewhat strange, those present were astonished at how well he spoke Tamil.
“Chinese merchant! You speak Tamil very well!” said Kundavai.

“I have stayed in this Chola land for some time for business purposes. Because of that, I have learned to speak some Tamil. Both the language and the land of the Tamils are dear to me,” replied the merchant.

“Then why are you in such haste to return to your country now? Could you not stay at least until the coronation? What is the great urgency?” “If you miss the ship that departs the day after tomorrow, there’s no telling when the next one will set sail. Ships no longer leave Nagai as frequently as they once did!”
“Why is that?”

“Do you not know the reason, Devi? Sea voyages are no longer as easy as they used to be. Nor are they as safe. Pirates have multiplied. Fierce, frenzied warriors from the Arab lands now board ships and roam everywhere in the western and eastern seas. They even lurk along the shores and near the harbors. The moment they spot a merchant ship, they swoop in and attack. They fight with savage fury, slaughter everyone on board, and seize all the goods before making off with their loot. Because of this, merchant ships can no longer travel alone. Ten or twenty ships must now depart together in convoy. If you miss the ships leaving the day after tomorrow, who knows how long you’ll have to wait for the next chance? O noble ladies! Please, take a look at the silks and fine garments we have brought with us!”
As he spoke, the Chinese merchant began to untie the bundle he had brought. Another merchant, in the same manner, loosened his own bundle.

“Merchants, there is no use in displaying your wares now. In the darkness of night, we cannot properly judge the quality of your silks. And besides, we have not brought with us the goods we would need to pay for your wares!” said the young princess.

The first merchant, as if deeply astonished, immediately rose to his feet, pressed his palms together, and said, “Princess! Would we name a price and take payment from you? You speak kind words! If you would graciously accept and wear these silks, would we not consider it the reward for the penances we performed in our previous births? We did not bring these goods to sell for a price, but as coronation gifts!”

“In that case, you have come seeking the wrong people. None of us here is to be crowned. The one who will soon wear the crown is the prince, Ponniyin Selvan. Seek him out and present your gifts to him!”

“No, Devi! We have come seeking the right place. If anyone wishes to obtain the grace of Ponniyin Selvan, they say the first step is to win the favor of the young princess, Kundavai Devi!” said the Chinese merchant.
Hearing this, all the princesses present burst into laughter. “When you say ‘everyone,’ who do you mean? Where and from whom did you hear such talk?”

“Why, Lady? Even today, during the festival held in this city, many in the gathered crowd were speaking of it. They said, ‘The younger brother will never go against his sister’s word.’ If you wish, you can ask my companion here!”

The friend, who had been silent all this while, now spoke up: “Yes, princesses! It is true! People are saying, ‘If Ponniyin Selvan is to be crowned, it is as if Kundavai Piratti herself is being crowned!’ The people are saying, ‘Hereafter, the Chola kingdom will be ruled by a princess! And it will be a good reign.’”
Again, the princesses laughed merrily.
“Therefore, princesses! Kindly show mercy and accept these coronation gifts!” said one of the Chinese merchants.
“Accept them, and also present our requests to Ponniyin Selvan!” said another merchant.
“What request? What is it that you wish Ponniyin Selvan to do for you? Tell us that first!” asked Kundavai Piratti.

“Devi! There are many things we wish from him. Not just for us, but for all the merchants and common folk from the Chola land to the land of China, everyone places their trust in Arulmozhi Varman. In the days of Parantaka Chakravarti, the seas were safe. Except for the dangers posed by storms, there was no other peril in sea voyages. Attacks on ships and piracy were unheard of, even in dreams. Chola ships carrying trade goods sailed as fearlessly as royal processions along the highways. The ports of Manakkavaram, Mayirudingam, Mappappalam, Ilamuri Desam, Srivijaya, Chavakam, Kadaram, and Kambojam—Chola ships reached all these sea-girt lands, trading imports and exports, and journeyed on to our land of China. In the same way, ships departing from our Chinese land reached the Chola country without hindrance. Alas, those days are now but a distant memory, Devi! Let me tell you the truth— “Let us leave it at that. If you take these silken garments back with you, there is no certainty that they will safely reach our land. Would it not be far more significant to offer these silks as gifts to the princesses of Chola Nadu, rather than have them fall into the hands of Arab sea pirates along the way?”
As the Chinese merchant spoke thus, Kundavai Devi’s eyes, resembling the lustrous orbs of a dragonfly, widened and brimmed with boundless curiosity.

“Do you think that such a deed will be accomplished by Ponniyin Selvan? Do you imagine that, as in the days of Emperor Parantaka, sea voyages will become free from peril? Do you believe that the fame of Ponniyin Selvan will spread to lands like Manakkavaram, Mayirudingam, Kadaram, and Srivijaya?” she asked.
“What is the use of only our belief? All these great merchants of Chola Nadu believe it too. Why, just a short while ago, we visited an astrologer. Even he said the same.”
“What did he say?”

“He said that Ponniyin Selvan would gather grand fleets of ships and cross the seas; that he would vanquish the bands of pirates; that he would make sea voyages as safe as they once were; and that Chola Nadu would regain the glory it held in the days of Emperor Parantaka. But he also said that all this would come to pass only if the princesses of Chola Nadu did not stand in the way and create obstacles!”
“Is that all he said? Did he utter any further slander about the princesses?”

“Slander, you say? Oh no, nothing of the sort, Devi! In this Chola land, there is no one who would dare speak ill of the Princess of Pazhayarai or the maiden of Kodumbalur. If that is so, would the astrologer, who surely hopes for the princesses’ favor, dare to utter such words?”
“Then what else did that astrologer say about us?”

“He said that both princesses had just visited him and departed. He foretold that both would soon be wed. O noble ladies! If you do not accept these silks as gifts for the coronation, then at least accept them as wedding gifts,” said the Chinese merchant who had spoken first.
Hearing this, Vanathi exclaimed, “Akka! These Chinese merchants are nothing but mischief-makers. Tell them to leave at once!”

“Have a little patience, Vanathi! Let us see how far their quarrel goes,” said Kundavai, and then she turned to the merchants, “Merchants! Was it you who arrived at the astrologer’s house, riding atop the elephant?”

“Yes, Devi! Our search for the astrologer’s house bore fruit at once. We learned that you were here. The astrologer told us that today we would have the fortune of meeting you, and his words have come true. If only what he said about the Kodumbalur princess also comes to pass, all our worries will be over!”
Once again, Vanathi pleaded, “Akka! Please ask them to leave!”
Kundavai continued, “Merchants! Was it also you who rode the elephant into the midst of the festival crowd? Didn’t you often dismount and mingle with the people gathered there?”
“Yes, Devi! We wished to find out what the people were saying about the upcoming coronation, so we entered the crowd and wandered among them.”
“What were the people saying? Surely, they spoke with satisfaction about Ponniyin Selvan’s impending coronation?”
“No; in fact, no one spoke of the coronation ceremony at all.”
“Then what were the people discussing?”
“They were speaking only of the devotion and greatness of Madhurantaka Devar.”
“Ah, that is a good thing to hear. Poonguzhali! Did you hear that?” said Kundavai, glancing at Poonguzhali. Then she continued, “What else did they say about Madhurantaka Devar?”

“They spoke of Madhurantakan’s self-sacrificing nature. Though he had the right to celebrate his inheritance of the Chola kingdom, he declared, ‘I do not want the kingdom,’ and for this, they praised him greatly.”
“Is that so? Did they say why he refused?”

“They said that Madhurantaka Devar had fallen in love with some boatwoman and was adamant that he would make her the queen. Because of this, the minor chieftains who were in his camp have changed their minds. ‘In that case, Madhurantakan will not be crowned; the crown must go to Ponniyin Selvan,’ the chieftains said—” “They have spoken, it seems. People are talking like this. Princes! If that fortunate boat-girl were here, we would wish to present her with a silk robe as well.”
Now, Poonguzhali said, “Devi! What the Princess of Kodumbalur said is true. These merchants are nothing but mischief-makers. Please ask them to leave at once!”
“Wait a moment, Poonguzhali! Why are you angry? They haven’t spoken ill of you, have they? They are only speaking in your praise, aren’t they?” said Kundavai.
“Let them not speak of me in praise or in blame! I do not wish for any gifts either!” Poonguzhali rose as she spoke.
“Lady! Are you truly that fortunate woman? Ah! What the people are saying is absolutely right!” exclaimed one of the Chinese merchants.
“What else were they saying?” Poonguzhali asked with a smile.
