“When someone in the gathering said that Madurantaka Devar had renounced the Chola kingdom for your sake, another replied, ‘Would one renounce a kingdom merely for Poonguzhali Devi? If I had nine kingdoms, I would have given them all up for her!’ I too agree with what he said!” declared the Chinese merchant.
With feigned anger, Poonguzhali said, “Akka! You must arrange for this overly talkative merchant to be punished at once; otherwise, I will tell Ponniyin Selvan himself and have him punished!”

Just then, Madurantaka Devar came up to the upper terrace, having finished his evening worship, carrying the floral prasadam in his hand. Hearing Poonguzhali’s words, he said, “There is nothing wrong in what this merchant has said. Why should he be punished? I too agree with what he said, Poonguzhali!”

As he spoke thus, the Chinese merchant turned to look at him. Poonguzhali, meanwhile, said, “It is all well and good if a true merchant speaks so. But how can we agree when it is a merchant in disguise?” So saying, she seized the Chinese cap from the merchant’s head and pulled it off. The cap fell to the ground.
Along with the cap, the beard on his face also fell away! The very face of Vandiyathevan appeared before them.
“Sir! Save me!” cried Vandiyathevan, as he tried to seize another Chinese merchant by the neck. In that moment, his turban, beard, and moustache all came loose and fell away.
The Prince of Ponni appeared, his face radiant with a bright smile.
The three women burst into laughter, their mirth shaking their bodies for a long while.
Even after Sembiyan Maadevi ascended to the upper terrace and was told the story, they laughed again.
Poonguzhali said, “Mother! The moment I saw these men near the temple, I had my doubts. That’s why I dared to invite them to the palace!”
Madhurantakan added, “Yes; I recognized my friend at once. That’s why I left them here and went to perform my prayers!”
“Vanathi! It seems you and I alone are the fools who cannot see through men’s disguises!” said Kundavai.
“For what reason did they put on such costumes and try to deceive us? Ask them, Akka!” said the Kodumbalur Princess.
“I shall ask, Vanathi! My brother is not one to don such false disguises. It is only through bad company that he has learned to dress up and spin such lies!” said Princess Kundavai.
“Devi! Do not blame Vandiyathevan for this. The rare idea of disguising ourselves as Chinese merchants arose in my own mind!” said Arulmozhi.
“I say it is because of bad company that such ideas have taken root in your mind. Let it be, but hereafter, do not put on such false disguises again!”
“Akka! Thiruvalluvar has spoken much about the greatness of truth. Yet even he has said:
‘Even falsehood may be truth, if it brings about Unblemished good!’”
“When Thiruvalluvar composed that Kural, he could never have dreamed, even in his wildest imagination, that you would use it in this way.”

“Let’s leave Thiruvalluvar aside. When Rama set out for the forest, didn’t he use a little deception to send back the people of Ayodhya who followed him? Didn’t he tell Sumantra to drive the chariot a short distance toward Ayodhya while the people slept, and then turn it toward the banks of the Ganga?”

“Brother! If you were to follow Rama’s example in all things, it would bring me great joy! Let that be. But what good has come from you donning this false disguise? Will you tell me that?” asked Kundavai.
“By not revealing who we were, we were able to mingle among the common people, wander here and there, and learn their true thoughts and feelings!”
With a spark of interest, Kundavai asked, “What did you learn about the people’s minds, brother?”

“I learned many things, Akka! Most importantly, I discovered that everyone wishes for this Chola Empire to attain the same glory it had during the reign of Parantaka Chakravarthi. Just a while ago, my friend and I disguised ourselves as Chinese merchants, didn’t we? Even though the disguise was false, everything we said was true! We met both of you on the road and then went on to Thanjai. Near the fortress gate in Thanjai, we actually saw two Chinese merchants. We bought these bundles of silk from them for a price. Then, dressed in their garb, we returned. Everything I just told you about the Arabian sea pirates—we heard all that from those merchants. My friend and I have also personally experienced the savagery of those Arabian sea pirates. Devi! Whatever happens, after the coronation festivities are over, my friend and I are certain to set out for Eezha Nadu. Once our work there is done, we intend to journey to many lands beyond the seas. Whether we will return alive, or fall in battle and attain the warrior’s heaven in some distant place, we do not know. Therefore, until we depart, all of you must remain with us, and when the time comes, you must bless us and bid us farewell. That is why we hurried after you.”
As Ponniyin Selvan spoke thus, tears welled up in Kundavai Devi’s eyes.
With a trembling voice, Poonguzhali said, “I do not know why they have caused this war. Can’t human beings love one another and live in happiness?”

“My child! It is not so! As long as the world exists, wars will never cease. Even Parameshvara and Parameshvari themselves had to wage war! There are some who are born into this world to establish dharma. They must, indeed, wage war!”
Hearing these words from Sembiyan Maadevi—the foremost among devotees of Shiva and a supreme ascetic—everyone was plunged into a sea of astonishment.

chapters.title: The Inner Meaning of the Sculpture
paragraphs: Madurantaka, known as Sendhan Amudhan, turned to his mother, the venerable Sembiyan Maadevi, and said, “Mother! In this world, there are countless people who wander about, possessed by the madness of war. To them, any day without battle seems a day wasted. My friend Vandiyathevan and Ponniyin Selvan both belong to that group. But you—if there is a day when you do not speak of the Lord, you consider it a day not lived at all! It is truly astonishing to hear you speak in support of the profession of war!”

At this, Sembiyan Maadevi replied, “My beloved son! Let anyone else speak ill of the profession of arms, but not you. Nor should Poonguzhali. Is it not because the kings of our lineage are skilled in the art of war that you are alive today, singing hymns of praise to the Lord that melt both my heart and body?”

“Mother! Let it be that I saved your precious son’s life. But I can never forget that both he and your daughter-in-law, whom he took by the hand, saved my life as well. Is it not Poonguzhali Ammaiyar’s martial spirit that is the reason I am alive today?” said Vandiyathevan.
“Parameswaran and Durga Parameswari are the ones who protect us all! Without their grace, how could we protect one another?” said Madurantaka.

“Child! Even Lord Shiva, who is the very embodiment of compassion, has had to wage war many times. Durga Parameswari, the Mother of the Universe, who is the form of love, grace, and peace, too, has found it necessary to fight. In this sacred place, the Goddess presides in the temple as the Lady who fosters righteousness. Yet, have you not noticed that in the temple’s circumambulatory path, she also appears as Mahishasuramardhini, the Slayer of the Buffalo Demon?”
“Yes, Mother! I noticed and marveled at it. I wondered why the Mother, who gave birth to and protects all the worlds, stands upon the head of a buffalo and reveals herself thus!” said Madurantaka.

“Yes, yes! In this temple, the Goddess has already slain Mahishasura. That is why, in the face of the Goddess standing on the buffalo’s head, we see love and grace shining forth. In the cave sculptures at Mamallapuram, there is a depiction of the Goddess battling Mahishasura. There, Durga Parameswari appears as the fierce, terrifying, warlike Kali. As the Mother of all worlds—” Why, O Durga Parameswari, must there be such a commotion over a mere quarrel with a buffalo? To the onlooker, it may seem excessive to make such a spectacle of it. My dear prince, every event that dawns in the hearts of our elders holds a deeper meaning. To understand them, one needs maturity. One must also possess the earnestness to seek that understanding!”

“Devi! Whether we possess such maturity, I do not know. But earnestness, we surely have. We listen with utmost attention to every word that blossoms from your sacred lips! Why, even the ever-restless eyes of our Vallathu king seem unable to look away from you,” said Arulmozhi.

These words stirred a ripple of mirth among those present. The women, realizing that Arulmozhivarman was alluding to Vandiyathevan’s frequent glances at the young princess’s radiant face, laughed softly among themselves.

Sembiyan Madevi spoke: “If you are listening with such attention, then I shall speak—listen well. Our puranas and epics are replete with tales of wars between the devas and asuras. They tell of how Lord Vishnu incarnated in this world and battled the demons. From the very moment the Lord created this universe, the divine forces and the asura forces have been in constant conflict. If one were to ask why the Lord created the asura forces, we, with our limited understanding, cannot answer. It can only be said that it is part of His divine play. But one thing is certain: the divine and the asura forces are locked in unending battle. At times, it appears as if the asura forces are triumphant, as though they will rule the world forever. Surapadman, Hiranya, Ravana—how many thousands of years did they reign! Yet, for each of them, the end came in but a fleeting moment.”

“Yes, yes! When the ten-headed Ravana, who had made even the gods bow before him and serve him, met his end, was it not two men and a few monkeys who brought about the destruction of his entire clan?” said Madurantaka Thevar.

“Therefore, when the asura forces seem to prevail, men must not lose heart. One must hold fast to dharma and truth, believing that in the end, the divine forces will surely triumph. For those who fight thus, the gods themselves will certainly come to their aid.”
“Mother! You were about to speak of Mahishasura!” Poonguzhali reminded her.

“Yes; you have reminded me at the right moment, my daughter! There are two kinds of asura forces. One is the brute asura force; the other is the asura force endowed with cunning intelligence. Our ancestors personified the brute asura force as Mahishasura.

Have you ever seen a wild buffalo, maddened and frenzied, running amok? At that moment, the buffalo gains strength greater than even an elephant. It destroys every living creature that crosses its path. Brute force is like that wild buffalo, powerful in its madness. Sometimes, brute force even ascends the throne and begins to rule. This is what our ancestors called the reign of Mahishasura. When Mahishasura sat upon the throne of Devaloka and began his rule, chaos and turmoil spread across the three worlds. ‘No need for knowledge, no need for books of wisdom, no need for the arts of intellect, no need for music. Sculpture, painting, temples, towers—none of these are necessary. Destroy everything!’—thus commanded Mahishasura. Gods, sages, and men all trembled in fear. Many among them bowed before Mahishasura and accepted his rule. This only increased Mahishasura’s arrogance and cruelty. When arrogance and brutality join hands with brute force, need I tell you the result? Unable to bear Mahishasura’s tyranny, the people of all three worlds cried out in anguish. Even the asuras joined in their lament. At that moment, Durga Parameswari opened her eyes. She took on the form of Maha Kali and destroyed Mahishasura. Divine power triumphed over brute force. The three worlds were freed from the shackles of brute slavery. Gods, sages, and even asuras heaved a sigh of relief and praised and worshipped Durga Parameswari.

Children! Even now, brute asura forces have not vanished from this world. I hear that, beyond the northwestern borders of this sacred land of Bharata, certain brute asura forces have arisen. With savage fury, they wage war, plunder cities, slaughter innocent people, and shatter temples and idols into ruin. There are no great emperors now in the northern lands to stop them. May such a fate never befall this divine Tamil land! But if ever such a time comes, you, who are born of a heroic lineage, must be ready to fight against those asura forces, must you not?”
“We will certainly be ready, Mother! Tell us about the other kind of asura force as well!” Vandiyathevan asked.

“The other kind of asuras are those with sharp intellect. They use their intelligence for evil deeds. They perform penance and receive boons, but even those are put to wicked use. What did the Tripura asuras do?

Each person created a world of their own. They soared through the skies, descended upon towns and cities, and annihilated them. No matter how many times Surapadman’s head was severed, he possessed the power to grow a new one. Ravana, Indrajit, and other such demons had the strength to vanish into the clouds and rain down weapons upon those below. It is such cunning and powerful asura forces that our ancestors have symbolized as the demon Muyalakan. Every time the Lord performs his blissful dance, he keeps a watchful eye on Muyalakan, whom he holds subdued beneath his feet. Should he be even a little inattentive, Muyalakan would rise again. From the very beginning of creation, divine forces have been battling against asura forces—this is what Muyalakan signifies to us. Therefore, my beloved children! How can we ever say that there should be no war at all?”
“Devi! Today we have come to understand many things that were unclear to us before. What commands do you give us?” asked Ponniyin Selvan.

“My children! All I can say is that you must always stand on the side of the divine forces and fight. I cannot command you. Only your own conscience can command you. Listen to that command and act accordingly. Just a while ago, you spoke of how pirates have become rampant in the seas surrounding this ancient Tamil land. You said that because of this, Tamil merchants are suffering great losses and hardships. It is your dharma, as those born into the royal clan, to destroy those pirates and protect our merchants. If we allow these sea robbers to flourish today, will they not invade this sacred Tamil land itself tomorrow? If my husband, who now dwells on Mount Kailasa in the presence of Lord Shiva among the divine hosts, were still alive as Jivya Vandaraayar, he too would have told you the same!”
“Devi! We have understood your noble heart. We shall act accordingly!” said Prince Arulmozhi Varman.
“Ponniyin Selva! If you are willing to honor my wish, there is one more thing I wish to say now,” said that venerable elder lady.
“Devi! I do not recall ever having acted against your wishes. If I have done so, forgive me!”

“My child! All that you have done so far is one thing. What is to happen henceforth is another. Until now, you were the cherished child of the palace. We acted according to your wishes, and you fulfilled ours. Now,
“You are about to become the king who will rule this realm. After your coronation, all of us must conduct ourselves according to your wishes.”
“Mother! Please do not speak so. Even hereafter, I shall remain your beloved child and act only as you desire.”

“If that is so, then listen to me! This ancient Chola lineage must flourish, sprouting leaf after leaf, generation after generation. Those born into the royal clan must always be prepared to attain the warrior’s heaven. But for the clan to prosper, we must also make prudent arrangements in advance. Your elder brother, Aditya Karikalan, passed away without marrying. Now, you alone remain to carry forward the Chola line! Therefore, before you once again board a ship and cross the seas in search of the goddess of victory, you must make the necessary arrangements for the growth of our lineage. Along with your coronation, let us also conduct your wedding. To have a wife like Vanathi, you must have performed countless penances. The auspicious power of this princess will be like a magical shield, protecting you wherever you go!”
“Devi! I am indeed ready to wear that shield. It is Vanathi who refuses. She stubbornly insists, ‘I will not ascend the throne; I have taken a vow!’” said the prince.

Quite unexpectedly, Poonguzhali interjected, “You mustn’t believe the Kodumbalur princess’s words so easily. She wishes for all of us to plead with her even more. Ponniyin Selvan must coax her a little further!” she said, laughing.
The others, thinking this was a jest, laughed as well. But Vanathi alone began to sob uncontrollably.
“You silly girl! What is this? Why are you weeping like this?” asked Kundavai, taking Vanathi’s hand and leading her away downstairs.

chapters.title: “Is It a Dream? Or Reality?”
paragraphs: The next morning, Sembiyan Maadevi, Madurantakan, and Poonguzhali set out for Thanjavur.

Ponniyin Selvan and Vandiyathevan had planned to travel to Uraiyur and Srirangam. While departing, Arulmozhi Varman had promised to show Vandiyathevan the great dam built across the Kaveri river during the reign of Karikala Chozhan, constructed to hold back the river’s waters.
Before they set out, Ponniyin Selvan went to bid farewell to Princess Kundavai.
“Sister! Is it absolutely necessary for you to go to Pazhayarai?” he asked.
“Brother! Is it absolutely necessary for you to go to Uraiyur? Can you not come with us to Pazhayarai?” she replied.
“No, sister! I have already told Alwarkadiyan that I would meet him at Uraiyur for an important matter,” he said.
“Ah! You are not like you once were, brother! Your heart has become quite corrupted. You no longer make me your purpose. I believe the cause of this change is the friendship of that Vallam prince…”
“Do not unjustly blame him. Am I not of age now, sister? I am about to be crowned emperor of a great kingdom. Should I not, at least from now on, act according to my own wishes?”
“Very well, act as you wish! As long as you do not exercise your authority over me, it is fine! As long as you do not insist that I must act according to your wishes, it is fine.”
“Just come for the coronation. After that, you may do as you please.”
“If you wish, you may exercise your authority over me after the coronation. Until then, what right do you have to compel me?”
“In that case, are you not going to come for the coronation?” “That is Vanathi’s wish. If she wants to go, I will come too; if not, I shall not.”
“Where is that girl, Akka?”
“Your mother has gone to the Ponni river to perform her prayers. She has gone to pray that you may be blessed with good sense.”
The prince laughed and said, “Let her prayers be fulfilled. I am setting out.”

“Thambi! I have never seen anyone as cruel as you. Vanathi did not sleep all night. She kept sighing and weeping, thinking of you. Go to the Kaveri’s bathing ghat and bid her farewell!” said Kundavai.

“What if she did not sleep? It seems she has stolen my sleep as well. If two people cannot understand each other’s hearts, then they are doomed to weep and suffer. Do you wish me to marry such a girl and spend my whole life in misery?” said Ponniyin Selvan, and with that, he swiftly left towards the rear of the palace.
Once he crossed the garden, he saw Vanathi seated at the bathing ghat of the Ponni river, taking flowers from the plate beside her and offering them one by one into the flowing waters.
Had Vanathi not been engaged in her worship, she would have seemed like a golden statue of a maiden placed upon that Kaveri ghat.

Ponniyin Selvan went silently and sat on the upper step behind Vanathi. She must have sensed that someone was approaching. By her inner intuition, she seemed to know it was Ponniyin Selvan himself. So, without turning around, she ceased her worship and sat quietly.
On the petals of the flowers in the plate, a few dewdrops could be seen.
On the petals of Vanathi’s eyes, two pearl-like tears shone brightly.

As the rays of the rising sun mingled with the gentle ripples of the Ponni river, the maiden of the Chola empire appeared as if golden threads were weaving through her, her blue silk saree draped like an upper garment, gleaming in the light. On either side of that blue silk saree, the green silk borders seemed to mirror the lush groves flourishing on both banks of the river.

On either bank of the Kaveri, in harmony with the sweet music of her flowing current, myriad birds in the groves sang auspicious songs and offered their blessings. The time, the place, and the very atmosphere were most suited for wandering in the world of imagination and dreaming in broad daylight.
After a moment’s silence, the prince looked at her and said, “Vanathi! Are you daydreaming? Did I disturb your dream?”

“I am indeed dreaming in the daylight, my lord! But how could you possibly shatter my dream? Even when I dream at night, is it not you who shines as the hero in the midst of my visions? That is why, when I see you beside me, I am left to wonder, ‘Is this a dream or is it reality?’ I cannot even bring myself to call out, ‘Come!’ Yes, my lord! For so many days, I have dreamed so many kinds of dreams. When I first met you in the gardens of the palace at Thirunallam, I thought you were a mahout. Many times afterwards, I wished you could remain just a simple elephant driver. In my imagination, I have often seen myself riding behind you on an elephant, rejoicing in the vision. Yet, at those times, it never seemed to me that I was riding an ordinary dark elephant of this world. It always felt as though I was ascending the white Airavata of the celestial realms. I would imagine you as Indra himself, and myself as Indrani…”
“If that is so, then now…” Ponniyin Selvan tried to interject, but Vanathi stopped him and continued:

“Wait a moment, my king! I will at once change this fantasy of Indra and Indrani. What peace is there for Indra and Indrani? When have they ever had the chance to ride alone, joyfully, upon Airavata? Are not the gods and goddesses ever surrounded by their retinues, always in the midst of a great assembly? So I will immediately set aside that thought. Instead, I shall imagine that I was not born a princess, but into the family of a boatman living by the seashore.”
“I can see it, Vanathi! I know it! You are jealous of Poonguzhali!”

“Yes, that is true! In this whole world, it is only Poonguzhali Devi whom I envy. Her heart’s desire has been fulfilled. She and her beloved will go to Kodikkarai, sail a boat upon the surging sea, and live a blissful life serving at the temple of the prince. Why would she not laugh at me? She will surely laugh. My lord! Punish me in any other way you wish—but do not let Poonguzhali Devi laugh at me…”

Ponniyin Selvan recalled what had happened on the previous night and spoke thus: “Vanathi! Be patient for a while! Yesterday, didn’t Poonguzhali laugh at you? The time will come when you will laugh at her!”

“Swami! I do not wish to laugh at Poonguzhali Devi. Nor do I wish to laugh at anyone else. Let anyone who pleases laugh at me and go their way. My only desire is to see a smile on your golden face now and then. When you look at others, when you speak to them, your face blooms with joy. But when you look at me, your brows knit together. Even now, I am afraid to look at you…”

“Vanathi! Listen to me! There is a reason why my face tightens when I see you. No one else disturbs me. No one else unsettles my peace of mind. But you—because of you, my heart loses its tranquility. Last night, my sister told me that you did not sleep. I too did not sleep, Vanathi! For many days now, I have not slept. When I lie on the palace terrace and gaze at the stars in the sky, it is the light of your eyes that those stars remind me of. When the leaves of the grove trees rustle in the breeze, I hear only the sweet sound of your laughter. When the gentle zephyr brushes against my body, I am enraptured, imagining that you are touching me with your fingers, soft as the petals of the blue lily. Vanathi! Because your memory possesses me so, when I see you face to face, my face shrinks, my brows draw together. I fear that you may become an obstacle to all the deeds I wish to accomplish in my life…”
“Swami! You need not have that fear! I will never be a hindrance to your endeavors…”

“You will not be an obstacle. No one can be! Vanathi, have you seen the dense black clouds that the monsoon brings from the south? Those clouds are filled with rainwater. Lightning and thunder are hidden within them. The storm wind drives those rain-laden masses forward. Can anyone stop them? I am in the state of those clouds, Vanathi! There is always a restlessness in my body. There is a force in my heart. Invisible lightning flashes before my eyes. Unheard thunder rumbles in my ears. Storms, cyclones, and tempests call out to me. In all seven seas, waves rise up like mountains to welcome me. Thousands upon thousands of conch shells…” The sound of drums, the blare of trumpets, and the trumpeting of war elephants all draw me in, Vaanathi, they pull me irresistibly. No one can stop me, Vaanathi! But if someone tries to restrain me, they can certainly rob me of my peace of mind…”

“Swami! I would never do such a thing. I will not even attempt to restrain you. Even if I cannot help one born to rule the three worlds, I will never stand in your way. That is why I refuse to sit beside you on the Chola throne.”

“Vaanathi! Though the Chola throne is great in its glory, it is small in size. Only one can sit upon it. Next to the Emperor, another throne must be placed, and upon that, the Empress should be seated.”

“Swami! I do not desire a place on the throne where you sit. Nor do I wish for a separate throne beside you. Let the fortune of sitting as your crowned queen on the throne fall to the one who has earned that merit. If you grant me a small place in the throne that is your heart, I will consider it the reward of all the penance I have performed in seven lifetimes, and I will be content!”

“Vaanathi! You have asked for what I can most easily give. You have already prepared a place for yourself in the throne of my heart! There is nothing to prevent me from granting it to you! But do you truly not desire to be Empress of this vast Chola Empire? Do you not wish to wear upon your head the golden crown, studded with nine gems, that dazzles the eyes of all who behold it?”

“I have not the slightest desire for that! I have seen the ancient gem-encrusted crowns of the Chola dynasty. I have held them in my hands. If one of those were placed upon my head, I fear its weight would press down and strain my neck, making it hard for me to breathe. I do not have the strength in my body for that. Nor do I have the courage in my heart. Swami! Let those who have the strength and courage to bear the gem-studded crown wear it. Before you depart on your voyage across the seas, give me another gift. I will pluck beautiful flowers from the palace gardens and string them into a garland. Place that garland, which I can easily bear, around my neck, make me your servant, and then set forth!”
“I brought you a necklace of nine gems from the Chinese traders as a coronation gift.”
“Why do I need a gift for your coronation?”

“Very well, let it be! I shall give this to someone else, Vanathi! Let us, you and I, make a pact. Before I depart, I will place a garland upon you, as you wish. In return for that garland I place upon you, every time I return from foreign lands, you must wait for me with a fresh garland. Whenever I cross the seas and travel to distant lands, plant the tiger flag, and return in triumph, you must be waiting for me with a victory garland,” said the prince.
“A single garland? I shall wait with a hundred, a hundred garlands draped and ready! All the people of this land will wait as well!” declared Princess Vanathi.

chapters.title: The Poet’s Astonishment
paragraphs: As the coronation ceremony for Arulmozhi Varman drew nearer and nearer, the entire Chola country was swept up in a single wave of jubilation. There was not the slightest difference of opinion among the people regarding the crowning of Ponniyin Selvan with the golden diadem. The men and women of Chola Nadu, the elderly, the children, the city dwellers, the villagers, merchants, and farmers—all, with one accord, welcomed the coronation of Ponniyin Selvan with great enthusiasm. They spoke again and again, marveling at the auspicious hour of his birth and the rare virtue with which he mingled freely among his people, delighting in these tales.

The Ramayana describes in vivid detail the joy that filled Ayodhya when the people learned that Dasaratha had decided to anoint Rama as king. It is said that all the elderly women became like Kausalya, rejoicing as if their own sons were to be crowned. The young women, sharing in the bliss that Sita Devi herself had experienced, adorned themselves with fine garments and jewels, believing their own husbands would soon wear the crown. All the elderly men of Ayodhya, it is said, became like Dasaratha himself.

"Women of advanced years became as Kausalya in their hearts; The priests were as Vasishta; all other women Were as Sita; that day, the goddess of fortune herself; And all the noble men of that city became as Dasaratha."

Thus, Kamban the poet has wondrously portrayed the state of mind of the people of Ayodhya. But what great deed had Rama performed to win such affection and respect from the people? The glory of his bow was yet to be revealed in the days to come. The fame of slaying Ravana and the other demons, and freeing the three worlds from fear, was yet to be his. Had not Rama merely accompanied the sage Vishwamitra and completed his sacrifice? That alone had not greatly enhanced his stature in the eyes of the people of Ayodhya. Why? Vishwamitra himself had not even returned to Ayodhya to recount the tale!

In this world, there are some who captivate the hearts of people through rare feats of valor and acts of charity. Others earn the admiration of their peers by singing melodious songs, performing graceful dances, composing poetry, or creating wonders in painting and sculpture. Yet another few are born blessed, emerging from the womb already marked by greatness. Without any apparent reason, Mother Nature bestows upon them a power to enchant and attract all who behold them. Ah! It seems Mother Nature is most partial indeed! Yet, what do we know? Perhaps, when Mother Nature grants such captivating power, she also gives, in equal measure, certain adverse qualities—who can say for sure?

Did not Rama, who won the love and veneration of the people of Ayodhya, have to endure sufferings unknown to ordinary mortals? Was he not forced to abandon his kingdom, wander the forests, lose his beloved wife, and bear agonies beyond words?

Arulmozhi Varman was a recipient of Mother Nature’s partial favor. His very appearance captivated the hearts of all who beheld him. His sweet speech and gentle manners won the affection of everyone who had the fortune to know him. While he was in the battlefields of Eezham, opportunities for heroic deeds were few and far between. Yet, tales—often imagined—of his valor and prowess spread throughout the Chola land. When we come to love someone, are we not ready to believe any and every exaggerated praise about them?

Since the time Sundara Chola fell ill and was unable to move about, the people had been anxious that confusion regarding the succession might arise in the Chola country. Rumors spread that the minor kings—such as the Pazhuvettaraiyars and the Sambuvaraiyars—and the great officials were plotting to crown the son of Kandaradithar instead of Sundara Chola’s sons. The people knew nothing against Kandaradithar’s son, Madurantakan. However, Madurantakan had never mingled with the people. All that was known was that, like his father, he had turned away from worldly life and immersed himself in devotion to Shiva.

From the time of Vijayalaya Chola, the Chola kingdom had expanded and flourished. Trade prospered, the people’s lives improved, and treasures from conquered lands poured into Chola territory, filling the people with joy and pride. The citizens, delighted by the ever-growing glory of the Chola Empire, longed for it to flourish and spread even further. They believed it was necessary. There were doubts as to whether, if Madurantaka—who was wholly immersed in Shaivite devotion—ascended the throne, the Chola kingdom could continue its progress. Not only that, but people feared that if Madurantaka became king, the petty chieftains would have their way as law.

Although the people held Aditya Karikalan in the highest esteem as a peerless warrior, there was not much enthusiasm about his ascending the throne. Aditya Karikalan did not possess the sweet and winning nature that could captivate the hearts of the people. He did not mingle easily with everyone. Moreover, mysterious rumors circulated about Karikalan. It was whispered that he had committed some grave crime, that his conscience was tormented by it, and that he had thereby lost the affection of his father, Sundara Chola. Many other fanciful tales were woven around him. Therefore, when he met with an untimely death, though the people paid him the honors due to a great hero, they did not grieve excessively. They laid the blame upon the comet and somehow consoled themselves.

The death of Periya Pazhuvettarayar, and the manner in which it occurred, inspired a new sense of admiration and respect for him in the hearts of the people. It was rumored that the enchanting woman whom that valiant elder had married in his old age was, in truth, one of the Pandya conspirators, and that it was at her instigation that Periya Pazhuvettarayar’s mind had been corrupted; that the Pandya conspirators were the true cause of Aditya Karikalan’s untimely death; and that, upon learning the truth, Periya Pazhuvettarayar, as atonement for his crime, had taken his own life. After such rumors had spread, the people began to feel pity for Periya Pazhuvettarayar, saying, “Alas! Poor man!” Before his death, it was said, he had commanded the other minor kings, “Abandon the thought of crowning Madurantaka; let the crown be placed upon Ponniyin Selvan’s head!”—this too increased the people’s respect for him. Was it not that great and valiant elder who removed a great obstacle to the fulfillment of the people’s desire by giving up his own life? Long live his memory! Long live his lineage! Thus did the people speak of him with gratitude and praise.

The fact that a change of person had occurred in the matter of Madurantaka Devar was known to none among the common people. Except for the royal family and those closely connected with them, no one else knew of this matter. The old Madurantaka spent most of his time within the palace, rarely venturing outside. Even on those rare occasions, he did not mingle with the common people.

They did not mingle freely with others. When discussions about his coronation were underway, it was customary to bring him in a closed palanquin. The common people rarely had the opportunity to closely observe his features. Thus, the fact that the old Madurantakan had gone and a new Madurantakan had arrived was unknown to the vast majority of the populace.

Therefore, at the Thiruvathirai festival held in Thiruvaiyaru, none who saw the new Madurantakan perceived any difference in the man. Only his wife, Poonguzhali, drew the attention of a few. Some said that she was “the daughter of Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar,” while others refuted this claim. There were those who said she was the boatwoman who rowed across the sea, and that Madurantakan had recently married her.

Since it was common in those days for members of the royal family and minor kings to take multiple wives, no one found this surprising. The rumor that, despite much urging from the minor kings, Madurantaka Thevar had refused the crown had, in fact, only increased the people’s respect for him. His appearance, immersed in devotion to Shiva and in a state of spiritual ecstasy, further enhanced that respect. The talk that “Madurantakan did not desire the Chola throne because of Poonguzhali, the boatwoman,” won him the affection of many more.
Once Ponniyin Selvan’s coronation was completed, people speculated that Madurantaka Thevar would be granted some great office.

From two days before the coronation, people from all corners of Chola Nadu began to converge upon Thanjai. Outside the Thanjai fort, it was a veritable sea of humanity. The gates of the fort were thrown open. The restrictions that had once existed for entering and leaving the fort were lifted. The date for the coronation had been fixed as soon as the month of Thai began, for if it were postponed, the crowds would become unmanageable. For the convenience of the people, many other arrangements had also been made.

Of the great southern army that Kodumbalur Velar had brought with him, Ponniyin Selvan, by his command, had sent back the greater part. He kept only a thousand soldiers with him. Similarly, the minor kings of the Pazhuvettaraiyar faction, who had stationed their troops near Kudanthai, had also sent their men back to their respective places. Only the soldiers whom Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar customarily kept for the protection of the fort remained now.

The warriors of Pazhuvur, the heroes of Kodumbalur, and the valiant soldiers of the Velakkara army—forgetting all their old rivalries and enmities—embraced one another, laughing, jesting, and reveling in merriment. They did all they could to assist the throngs of people who had gathered in great numbers to witness the coronation ceremony. At times, these warriors even participated in monkey-like antics for the amusement of the crowds, but the people paid little heed to such diversions.

Both the inner fort and the outer city of Thanjavur gleamed, adorned and resplendent like Indra’s celestial city of Amaravati. Every house in the city was filled with guests who had arrived from distant lands.

At last, on the day appointed for the coronation, the sun rose. As it ascended, it dispelled the morning mist, spreading its golden rays and shining with radiant brilliance. All who beheld the sun that morning exclaimed, “Is it not today that Ponniyin Selvan is to be crowned? That is why the sun itself dazzles with golden light!” And they rejoiced.

Long before the hour set for the coronation, crowds began to gather at the entrance of the coronation pavilion. Was it possible for all the common people to find space within the pavilion? Only after the crowning ceremony, when Ponniyin Selvan would emerge from the pavilion and mount the royal elephant to begin his procession through the streets, would the people truly be able to see him and rejoice. But could they afford to come late for that? If they arrived early, they might catch a glimpse of Ponniyin Selvan as he emerged, crowned with the golden diadem!

There was a special rear pathway for the royal family to enter the coronation pavilion. Along this path came Sundara Chola and Vanamadevi, followed by Sembiyan Maadevi, Madurantaka, Poonguzhali, Princess Kundavai, and Vanathi. The chief minister Aniruddha, the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar, Samburayar, Commander-in-Chief Boothi Vikrama Kesari, Malayaman of Miladu, along with the minor kings, feudatories, leaders of the merchant guilds, fort commanders, high officials, Saiva priests, Vishnu temple priests, and the great Tamil poets—all these pressed through the throng at the entrance and made their way inside.

At last, Ponniyin Selvan himself, accompanied by Vallavaraiyan Vandiyathevan, arrived at the entrance of the coronation pavilion, seated in an open golden chariot shaped like a lotus blossom. When the crowd, vast as a surging ocean, caught sight of them, they raised a roar of jubilation like waves greeting the full moon.

All the Vedic rites required for the coronation were duly performed. The jeweled crown that Chola kings, generation after generation, placed upon their heads on the day of their coronation, the necklace of nine precious gems that adorned their chest, the royal sword girded at their waist, and the scepter held in their hand—these were all arranged on a grand, artistically decorated platter and brought before the assembly, in the presence of the elders. The elders touched the platter and bestowed their blessings.
Then, Nallan Sathanar, the court poet, rose to his feet. Behind him stood a maiden, holding a yazh in her hands; she plucked its strings, raising a sweet and melodious prelude.

Poet Nallan Sathanar began to sing, blending music and verse, of the ancient glory of the Chola dynasty and the illustrious line of warrior kings who had, through the ages, brought fame to that house. As the song was lengthy and composed in a rare style not easily understood by people of this age, we shall here relate only its essence:

“In the lineage of Manu, born of the Solar race, there was a king named Sibi. To fulfill a promise he had made to a dove, he cut the flesh from his own body to save its life. In the line of such Sibi, his descendants took the clan name ‘Sembiyan’ and attained great renown. In the Sembiyan line arose a mighty emperor named Rajakesari. His son became famed as Parakesari. The kings who followed alternately bore the titles ‘Ko Rajakesari’ and ‘Ko Parakesari’. Among them, the Chola king who rendered justice to a cow by sacrificing his own beloved son became known as Manu Needhi Cholan. In later times, in the city of Poompuhar, a king named Karikala Peruvallathan spread his fame across the three worlds. With the great Chola army, he marched north to the Himalayas and engraved the tiger emblem of the Chola clan upon the snow-capped peaks. In his line came Nalankilli, Nedungkilli, Kulamutrathu Thunjiya Killi Valavan, and Koperuncholan, a supreme devotee of Lord Shiva—these rulers brought everlasting fame and glory to this ancient house and attained the feet of Shiva.”

“Just as monsoon clouds sometimes obscure even the sun who gives light to the world, so too, for a time, the Chola dynasty, descended from the Sun, was veiled by the clouds of Pallava and Pandya enmity. To scatter those clouds, there arose Vijayalaya Cholan, equal to Indra who wields the thunderbolt. At the sight of this Chola tiger, the great rat of Pidukumulai, known for its tyranny, perished in fear. Then that mighty hero conquered the city of Thanjai and built a temple for Durga Parameswari. The Pallavas, the Pandyas, and many other kings, seeking the friendship of Vijayalaya Cholan, sent envoys at all times to that…” They waited in the courtyard of the king’s palace. To aid such rulers who came seeking help, Vijayalaya Chozhar had gone to many battlefields, fought fiercely, and upon his sacred body bore ninety-six glorious wounds. Vijayalaya Chozhar’s noble son, Aditya Chozhar, shone like another sun, scattering the clouds of enemy armies.

On the battlefield of Thirupurambiyam, when the Pallava Aparajitha was about to be crushed by the Pandya, Aditya Chozhar leapt into the fray like a tiger into a herd, and shattered the Pandya forces to pieces. Later, to teach a lesson to the Pallava who, ungrateful for the help rendered, betrayed their friendship, he marched his army into Thondai Nadu, leapt upon Aparajitha atop his elephant, and sent him to the warrior’s heaven.

Following in the footsteps of his ancestor, Kochchenganan, he built eighty-two Shiva temples from the source of the Kaveri river in the Sahya mountains to the city of Poompuhar. Aditya Chozhar’s son, Paranthaka Chozhar, was born bearing both Veeralakshmi and Vijayalakshmi upon his two shoulders. At Vellur, having routed the Pandya, that king not only conquered Madurai and Eelam, but also stood as a lion before the Chera country’s elephant army.

To the north, the Chalukyas beyond the Tungabhadra river and the rulers of the Vengi region, upon hearing Paranthaka Chozhar’s name, trembled as if in a lion’s nightmare. Unable to bear his fame, burning with envy, the Kannara Devan of the twin regions gathered a vast army as if it encompassed seven seas, and came to challenge Paranthaka Chakravarthi in war. Paranthaka’s eldest son, Rajaditya Devar, at the battlefield of Takkolam—which resembled Kurukshetra—defeated Kannara Devan and his immense, ocean-like army, and after falling upon his elephant, attained the warrior’s heaven.

After Paranthaka Chozhar built the golden hall in the temple of Lord Nataraja at Chidambaram, he reached the divine feet of that Lord! His son, Sivanjana Kandaraditha Devar, devoted himself to building Shiva temples and attained the abode of Shiva. In his time, Arinjaya Devar, who liberated the Thondai region from enemy control and established the tiger banner up to the land of Seetpuli, could not bear to be separated from his brother for long and ascended to the heavens.

His noble son, Sundara Chozha Chakravarthi, later ascended the Chozha throne. He pounced upon the Pandya fox that had emerged from its den, and drove it back to hide within once more! Under the shade of Sundara Chozha Chakravarthi’s white parasol, all three worlds now live without the slightest worry, in complete fearlessness.”

“How can we, with our mere words, ever hope to praise Ponniyin Selvan, who was born into a lineage that has shone with heroic glory for a thousand years? Perhaps if the goddess of arts herself were to take birth anew, it might be possible to recount his fame. It is not for humble poets like us to attempt such a task…”

Thus did Nallan Saaththanar conclude his song extolling the greatness of the Chola dynasty. After him, Sanskrit poets, Buddhist monks, Saiva acharyas, and Vaishnava preceptors all awaited their turn to offer their salutations. Those in charge of the coronation ceremony were greatly troubled, wondering how to bring these endless eulogies to a close. Among those so concerned was Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar. He stood ready, the ancient Chola crown in his hands, prepared to place it upon the head of Ponniyin Selvan. Yet, as he looked around, pondering how to hasten the poets and scholars to a conclusion, a new figure suddenly appeared near him. Many were astonished at how this man had managed to make his way through the dense crowds thronging the streets and enter the royal pavilion. But Vandiyathevan was not surprised. He recognized, beneath the disguise, that it was none other than Azhwarkkadiyan. Vandiyathevan glanced at Ponniyin Selvan, who too seemed to understand the signal.

What secret message did Azhwarkkadiyan whisper into Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar’s ear? No one knew. But immediately, a deep anxiety and confusion clouded the latter’s face. After hesitating for a moment, he took Azhwarkkadiyan aside to a less crowded corner of the pavilion.

Ponniyin Selvan noticed this. All the while that Nallan Saaththanar had been singing the praises of the Chola lineage, he had stood with folded hands, listening with reverence. Now, turning to the poet, he said, “Sir! Poet! All the glory you have sung of so far pertains to my ancestors, does it not? What deed have I accomplished to make myself worthy of ascending this ancient and illustrious throne, to wear the jeweled crown? For the goddess of arts to be pleased to speak of such deeds here and now is impossible. Therefore, as much as you are able, might you not curtail your song?”

Seeing the poet standing bewildered, Ponniyin Selvan continued, “Sir! It is only natural that you are taken aback; you are not at fault. I have not yet done anything to deserve having my praises sung in verse. Today is the day I am about to begin!”

The poet’s astonishment knew no bounds. He stood rooted to the spot, his eyes wide, his lips parted in disbelief. The events unfolding before him were beyond anything he had ever imagined, even in the wildest flights of his poetic fancy.

For a moment, he wondered if he was dreaming. Had he truly heard those words? Was this the same world he had known, or had he been transported to some other realm by the magic of his own verses? The air around him seemed charged with a strange energy, as if the very earth trembled in anticipation.

The poet’s mind raced. He recalled the faces he had seen, the voices he had heard, the secrets whispered in shadowed corridors. Each memory now took on a new meaning, a deeper significance. The threads of intrigue and destiny, which he had only glimpsed before, now wove themselves into a tapestry of revelation.

He glanced around, searching for someone to share his astonishment, but found himself alone. The silence pressed in on him, heavy and expectant. He felt as though the eyes of history itself were upon him, watching, waiting to see what he would do next.

With a trembling hand, the poet brushed the sweat from his brow. He drew a deep breath, steadying himself. Whatever might come, he knew he must bear witness to these events. His words would one day carry the truth to generations yet unborn.
But for now, all he could do was stand in awe, his heart pounding, his soul alight with wonder and fear.

chapters.title: The Coronation
paragraphs: Arulmozhi Varman continued, turning to the poet, “Sir! I wish to ask you one more thing. From Emperor Sibi down to the sage-king Sivagnana Kandaraadithar, you have extolled the glory of the kings of our Chola lineage. If all that praise is fitting for one such as myself, born into this ancient clan by fortune, is it not equally fitting for my younger father and for Madurantaka Devar, the noble son of the great Kandaraaditha Chola?”

The poet nodded his head in assent. All eyes in the assembly now turned toward Madurantaka Devar, who sat with humility and restraint on the other side of Sundara Chola. Only now did many begin to observe Madurantaka closely, as if seeing him for the first time. Already seated with great shyness, Madurantaka now seemed even more withdrawn, gazing fixedly at the goddess of the earth, unable to lift his bowed head.

Meanwhile, Alwarkadiyan, disguised in another garb, approached a corner of the hall where he met with Chinna Pazhuvettarayar to relay a troubling piece of news. Among the crowd gathered for the coronation festivities, he had spotted Raakkammal, a woman from the Pandya country’s secret aid society and the wife of the boatman Murugaiyyan. Curious as to why she had come here, he followed her. Near Chinna Pazhuvettarayar’s palace, she disappeared into the throng. As Alwarkadiyan stood there scanning the crowd, she reappeared—this time accompanied by another woman carrying a child at her hip. The second woman resembled Chinna Pazhuvettarayar’s daughter, and for a moment, Alwarkadiyan was at a loss, uncertain what to do. He could not say for sure if it was indeed the chieftain’s daughter. He resolved to follow them a little further to confirm his suspicion.

But following them through the crowd was no easy task, and Raakkammal must have noticed that he was trailing them. Suddenly, in the midst of the gathering, she cried out, “Oh no! This man is harassing us! He’s following women and causing trouble!” Instantly, several people in the crowd surrounded Alwarkadiyan, ready to rebuke him. He protested to them that he had done no such thing, and swore that, like everyone else, he had only come to witness the coronation festivities. After pacifying the crowd that had gathered around him, he— Before he could step outside, Raakkammaal and another woman, who had a child at her hip, had already disappeared. Azhwarkkadiyan followed after them, searching all the way to the fortress gate. Not far from the gate, he saw the woman with the child climbing into a closed palanquin. Four horsemen stood around the palanquin. As soon as the woman entered, both the palanquin and the horses sped away. Before Azhwarkkadiyan could decide whether to follow them further, a large crowd, which had come to witness the coronation, swept him up and carried him far inside the fortress, jostling him along.

Deeming it important to immediately report this incident to the commander of the fort, Azhwarkkadiyan made his way to the coronation pavilion. He explained that it was at Arulmozhi Varman’s command that he had donned this disguise, and that Ponniyin Selvan had instructed him to mingle with the crowd, listen to what the people were saying, and report back. It was while carrying out this duty that he had witnessed the aforementioned incident.

After hearing this, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar placed complete trust in Azhwarkkadiyan’s words. He had already been anxious about his daughter, the wife of the elder Madurantakan. The news brought by Thirumalai startled him and filled his mind with confusion. He resolved to go to his palace at once to learn the truth. He instructed that, through the chief minister Aniruddhar, both Sundara Chozhar and Ponniyin Selvan should be informed of his urgent departure. With that, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar left the pavilion in great haste.

There was no longer any need for Azhwarkkadiyan to speak to Ponniyin Selvan. Even as the Tamil poet Nallan Saathanaar was conversing, the prince had been watching Chinna Pazhuvettarayar closely. As soon as the commander left the pavilion, the face of Ponniyin Selvan shone with a new radiance. Turning towards the emperor, he began to speak in a majestic voice:

“Father! Our fort commander, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar, is leaving on some urgent business. That need not delay this coronation ceremony. There are still many great men present in this assembly. Chiefs of valiant clans are here. Warriors who have wielded spear and sword and earned honorable scars in many battlefields are here. Any one of them, with their heroic hands, may lift and place upon me the jeweled crown of our ancient Chola dynasty. All these noble ones have already touched this golden crown, the royal sword, and the scepter with their own hands and blessed them.”

Therefore, if I were to take this jeweled crown with my own hand and place it upon my head, there would be no wrong in it. Yet, before I do so, Father! I wish to make a humble plea to you, to the esteemed elders gathered here, and to the scions of our warrior clan.

I am descended from the line of Emperor Sibi, who cut his own flesh to save the life of a dove. That is why, like all our clan, I bear the title ‘Sembiyan’. I am of the lineage of the Manu Needhi Cholan, who, to uphold justice for a cow that lost its calf, sentenced his own son to death. Our ancestors have been praised not only as warriors who never turned their backs on the battlefield, but also as paragons who never strayed even a hair’s breadth from the path of righteousness. As one who walks in their footsteps, can I ever act against justice? Can I seize what rightfully belongs to another, whether it be wealth or position?

When our court poet sang in beautiful verse of the glory of our forebears, they all appeared before my mind’s eye. Raja Kesaris and Parakesaris stood in line, presenting themselves to me. Nalankilli, Nedunkilli, Perunkilli, and Kochchenganan gazed at me with eyes brimming with compassion, saying, “Son born to our clan! Consider well—are you truly worthy of this throne?” Vijayalaya, Aditya, Parantaka, and Rajaditya looked at me with eyes shining with valor and asked, “Prince! What deed of bravery have you performed to deserve this throne? Speak!”

I hesitated to reply to them. Then, steadying my heart, I folded my hands and bowed before them, making my humble petition: “O illustrious ancestors of the Chola clan! I have not accomplished even one in a thousand of your great deeds. But with your blessings, henceforth I shall strive to do such deeds. I shall act so that the glory of the Chola clan, which you established, will grow ever brighter and endure for ages. I shall undertake tasks that are difficult to accomplish. I shall perform deeds that will astonish the world. I shall carry out acts of valor that even you, the bravest of the brave, will behold and praise, and I shall earn the blessings of you all!”
Thus did I express myself to my ancestors. Their faces blossomed with affection, and they blessed me with love…”

As Ponniyin Selvan spoke these words, his voice trembling with fervent emotion, everyone in the assembly was overcome with awe. Among them, one cried out, “Veeravel! Vetri vel!”—“Victorious spear! Triumphant spear!” The shout rang out beyond the coronation hall, stirring the crowds gathered outside into a great tumult.
Ponniyin Selvan joined with everyone and thundered, “Victory to the spear! Valor to the spear!” When the resounding cry faded, he spoke:

“Father! Once, this battle cry of the Chola warriors was heard as far as the northern banks of the Tungabhadra and Krishna rivers, in the days of your grandfather, Emperor Parantaka. The people of Vengi, Kalinga, Kalyanapuram, and Maniyakedam, who lived beyond those rivers, trembled in fear when they heard this shout. Even further, in the western, southern, and eastern directions, thousands and tens of thousands of Chola warriors sailed in hundreds of ships to protect the trade of this land.

Father! Since the day you fell ill and took to your bed, the sound of the Chola war cry has diminished. Enemies are raising their heads on all sides. Vengi, Kalinga, Kalyanapuram, and Maniyakedam are all challenging us to a contest of strength. They do not consider the great danger posed by enemies who are coming to this ancient and vast land of Bharata from beyond the Himalayas in the north. They are consumed by envy and unrest at the prosperity of the Chola kingdom. In Lanka, Mahindan is still gathering and assembling his forces. Though Veerapandiyan is dead, there are those who, claiming descent from his line, are attempting to crown someone with the Pandya kingdom's jeweled diadem and incite rebellion. Mahindan and the Pandya kingdom’s conspirators have joined together in plotting, and have sought the life of my beloved elder brother, Aditya Karikalan, who rivals Abhimanyu and Aravan in valor.

To the west, the Chera king is assembling a mighty army of elephants and a fleet of ships. In preparing this fleet for the Chera, a new and savage band from the western lands is aiding him. This is the new, great peril that now surrounds the Chola kingdom. Father! For a long time, the Arabs have excelled in shipbuilding. They have traveled as far as China, conducting trade. They often visit our ports as well. Those ancient Arabs, who were refined in civilization, have now been subdued and suppressed by a new Arab faction that has arisen. Whether they are truly Arabs or neighboring peoples, we do not know. But nowhere have I seen any who surpass them in brutality. I myself have witnessed their deeds firsthand. To capture and bring me as a prisoner, under your orders, our fortress commander, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar, sent warriors on two ships…”

At this point, Sundara Chozhar interrupted in a trembling voice, “My son! Do you not know the reason I sent them?” “Father! I know this well. There was confusion here regarding the right to the throne. You must have heard about the dangers threatening us from the Pandya country as well. That is why, to ensure my safety and bring me securely to you, you ordered that I be taken into custody and brought here. It was only your boundless love and affection for me that made you issue such a command. I say this here so that everyone may know it well.

The soldiers who came to arrest me were in their hundreds. But the Arabs who had come ashore from the wrecked ship on the coast of Eezham numbered no more than ten. Yet, the pain I felt upon witnessing how many of our soldiers they suddenly attacked and killed has not left my heart to this day. Those new Arab settlers are helping the Chera king build ships. Not only that, they have also established contact with the people of Kalinga. The three kingdoms have joined together and resolved to utterly destroy Chola’s maritime trade. What does it matter if the pirates are Arabs or if they are Cheras who have had many dealings with us in the past? If we are to protect our maritime trade, we must strengthen our navy. We must build thousands upon thousands of new wooden ships. We must train new sailors. We must recruit warriors who can fight pirates from aboard our ships. We must plant the tiger flag on every island in the southern seas and station our soldiers everywhere.
Father! I have promised our ancestors that I will accomplish these tasks. To fulfill that promise, I need your permission. I also need the approval of the elders gathered in this assembly!”

As Ponniyin Selvan finished speaking, Sundara Chola said, “My son! Would I ever stand in the way of you bringing glory to the valor of the Chola clan? Would the elders of this great assembly oppose the protection of Chola’s maritime trade?”
At once, the assembly resounded again with the cry, “Veeravel! Vetri vel!”—“Brave spear! Victorious spear!”

“Father! Neither you nor this assembly will stand in my way. You will send me forth with your blessings, wishing that I achieve victory in all my endeavors. But if your blessings are to bear fruit, if I am to succeed in what I undertake, first there must be peace within my heart. I must have the certainty that ‘I have done nothing unjust, I have committed no act that our ancestors would disapprove of, I have not seized by greed what rightfully belongs to another.’ If I leave here having done anything that violates the code of our clan, my heart will torment me forever. If, in the face of our enemies—”
How can I achieve victory through war? How can I truly believe in my heart that we are fighting to uphold dharma? Once, a great rumor arose that I coveted the throne of Lanka…”
“My child! No one believed that! No one ever thought you capable of such a crime,” said the Emperor.

“You may not have believed it, Father! But when such words reached my ears, my heart was filled with pain. Two of my friends know that I refused the jeweled crown offered to me by the monks of Eelam. They were right beside me at that time…”
The leader of the Buddhist monks in the assembly spoke up, “Yes, yes! We too know of this.”

“A single false accusation caused me such anguish within. Even if you did not believe it, there were others who did. If, in truth, I were now to usurp a throne that rightfully belongs to another, how much disgrace would that bring upon the Chola dynasty? I would be tormented by it all my life. I would never be able to devote my mind to any great deed, nor act with enthusiasm…”

For a long while, Madurantaka Devar sat with his head bowed, not raising his eyes. Now, he looked up at Ponniyin Selvan, as if struggling to say something. Ponniyin Selvan signaled to Vandiyathevan, who immediately went and stood beside Madurantaka Devar. In a voice so soft that only he could hear, he asked, “Friend! What is the first line of the first Thevaram hymn sung by Sundaramurthi Nayanar?”
Madurantaka, surprised at such a question at this moment, replied, “Piththa! Piraisoodi!” (“O mad one! Wearer of the crescent moon!”)
Vandiyathevan, with feigned indignation, said, “What, sir, do you call me mad? Are you not the one who is mad after women? Look there! Your virtuous wife Poonguzhali is laughing at you!”

Startled by this sudden jest from his dear friend, Madurantaka glanced towards the women’s section. In truth, at that moment, Poonguzhali was not looking his way at all. Poonguzhali, Kundavai, Vanathi, Sembiyan Madevi, Vanamadevi—all the royal women—were gazing at Ponniyin Selvan, their eyes brimming with boundless interest.
When Madurantaka looked back at Ponniyin Selvan, he saw that the prince was now holding in his hands the ancient jeweled crown of the Chola dynasty.

“The Commander, Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar, has not yet returned. But what of it? If necessary, I myself shall conduct the coronation at the appointed hour! Father! From the time of Vijayalaya Chozhar, our ancestors have worn this jeweled crown. You have graciously bestowed it upon me. The vassals, commanders, fortress lords, and all the people have recognized it. Therefore, this crown is now my possession. I have the right to use my own possession as I wish, do I not?

Here stands one more worthy than I to wear this crown. He is older than I am. Though he has a greater claim to the Chozha kingdom than I, he never demanded it. He has come here, willing to rejoice at seeing me crowned and seated on the throne. Once, he saved my life. He prevented a great calamity that threatened the Chozha dynasty. I have not yet done any such noble deed for this land. Therefore, I now place this jeweled crown upon the head of the illustrious Kandaraadithar’s son, my younger father, Madhurantaka Devar!”

So saying, Ponniyin Selvan moved to the side of the Emperor, and approaching Madhurantakan, who was seated nearby, placed the crown upon his head. As he did so, Vandiyathevan, standing behind Madhurantakan, gripped both his shoulders with friendly firmness, to ensure he did not resist. But Madhurantakan made no such attempt. He seemed utterly dazed, as if he had lost all sense and reason, staring wildly in all directions.
As soon as the jeweled crown was set upon his head, Ponniyin Selvan proclaimed, “Long live Kopparakesari Madhurandhaka Uttama Chozha Devar!”
“Long live Uttama Chozha, Emperor of the Chozha Empire!” cried Vandiyathevan in a resounding voice.
All this while, the Prime Minister Aniruddha and the others stood transfixed with astonishment. Now, they too raised their voices: “Long live Kopparakesari Madhurandhaka Chozhar!”
Emperor Sundara Chozhar, overwhelmed by emotion and unable to speak, showered the many-colored flowers in his hand upon Madhurandhaka Uttama Chozhar.

The women of the palace, following the Emperor’s lead, rained flowers upon Madhurandhakan. When Madhurandhakan recovered somewhat from his shock, he rose and went straight to Sembiyan Maadevi, bowing before her. Tears streamed from the eyes of that venerable lady, flowing like a river.
“My son! Such is the divine will of the Lord! How can you or I act against it?” he said.
Ponniyin Selvan turned to the other poets, scholars, priests, and monks gathered in the hall and said, “Now, you must suitably alter your verses of praise!”
They hurriedly changed the words of their congratulatory poems and began to recite them anew.

Within moments of the golden crown being placed upon the head of Madurantaka Uttama Chozhar, the news had spread throughout the streets of Thanjavur, where crowds had gathered. Vandiyathevan and Azhwarkadiyan were largely responsible for the swift spread of this news. Following Ponniyin Selvan’s command, they had stationed men at various points along the streets. They rushed to each of them and instructed them to shout, “Long live Kopparakesari Uttama Chozhar Devar!” Word of the prince Arulmozhi Varman relinquishing the kingdom bestowed upon him and granting it to his elder uncle Madurantakan, as well as his imminent departure with a great naval fleet to subdue the sea pirates, spread rapidly among the people by word of mouth.

Some believed it immediately. They thought, “This is truly in keeping with the noble character of Ponniyin Selvan.” Others, however, were doubtful: “Who would surrender an empire already within their grasp to another?” they wondered. Tens of thousands of voices spoke in many ways at once, and the shouts of “Long live! Long live!” rose together, sounding like the mighty roar of waves whipped by a hurricane.

Soon, all doubts among the people were dispelled when Madurantaka Uttama Chozhar set out in procession, seated in a golden howdah atop a richly adorned royal elephant. When they saw Ponniyin Selvan himself seated on the mahout’s platform at the elephant’s neck, the people’s enthusiasm overflowed its bounds. The cries of “Long live Kopparakesari Madurantaka Uttama Chozhar!” resounded from the multitude. Yet, it was the noble deed of Ponniyin Selvan that truly filled their hearts. Thinking of it, their faces blossomed as their souls did. Had Ponniyin Selvan himself been crowned and paraded through the streets, the people would have rejoiced; but now, their joy was many times greater.

On the summit of the Himalayas, where Karikala Peruvazhuthan had once engraved the emblem of the tiger, Ponniyin Selvan has now surpassed him, so proclaimed the scholars with delight. They rejoiced that, upon the peak of sacrifice, he had inscribed his own insignia in a manner that would never fade. The common people, however, were not concerned with such embellishments, ornaments, or searching for apt metaphors and similes. The sight of Ponniyin Selvan riding the royal elephant after crowning Madurantaka with the jeweled diadem had utterly enchanted their hearts.

Dancing and singing, laughing and offering their blessings, embracing one another, showering flowers, and scattering handfuls of turmeric-colored rice, the people lost themselves in a single tide of celebration and joy.

Amidst this vast, ecstatic crowd, lost in the rapture of festivity, it was no easy task to guide the royal elephant forward. Ponniyin Selvan, too, did not hurry; he watched the people's exuberance with keen delight, and whenever he glimpsed a familiar face in the throng, he would exchange a jest or a merry word, steering the elephant gently onward. By the time the procession through the streets had ended and they turned back toward the palace, evening had faded into dusk, and night had arrived. The lamps lit along the streets vied with the stars above, shining in radiant competition. From the upper terraces of the palace, a rain of flowers descended.
“Mahout! Mahout!” came a sweet voice.
When Ponniyin Selvan looked up in surprise, he saw Vanathi’s smiling, blossoming face appear before him.

“Dear girl! Do not be afraid! In the righteous realm of Madurantaka Uttama Chola, the elephant and the tiger shall mingle as kin; the cat and the parrot shall play and frolic together in harmony!” declared Ponniyin Selvan.

chapters.title: Spring Has Arrived
paragraphs: It had been more than a month and a half since the coronation of Madurantaka Uttama Chozha Devar. The winter season had departed more swiftly than usual. Mounting the divine chariot of the southern breeze, the season of spring arrived. Parakeets pressed their coral-hued beaks against the saffron-tinted new shoots of the mango trees, admiring their own beauty. The golden-hued leaves of the royal trees swayed and sang in the gentle wind. From the punnai trees, pearl-like buds fell as the cuckoos called out in joyous chorus. Nature herself shivered in delight. Mother Earth overflowed with exuberance. On trees that had shed their leaves and stood bare, buds suddenly burst forth and blossomed. The bowers of madhavi vines and the jasmine and mullai bushes struggled under the weight of their abundant blooms. The rivers, their flow diminished, ran clear as crystal along their banks, murmuring softly.

The people of Chozha Nadu bloomed with joy, their faces and hearts radiant. The red paddy harvested from the fields had been gathered into the granaries. The uncertainty and anxiety that had gripped the land’s politics had now vanished. In both cities and villages, the people prepared to celebrate the festival of Kama. Arrangements were underway in the temples for the festival of spring. In every street and public square, stages for plays were being erected.

Beholding all these delightful scenes, Vallavarayan Vandiyathevan journeyed towards the city of Pazhaiyarai. This time, he did not enter that great city in disguise, nor did he hide or sneak in. He entered freely through the open main city gate and reached the palace of the young princess Kundavai Devi.

Princess Kundavai, surrounded by Vanathi and several of her companions, came to the palace entrance to greet him with a bright smile. After he had rested from the fatigue of his long journey, she asked him to meet her in the palace gardens and recount the details of his travels, then departed.

Vandiyathevan did not take long to recover. He quickly finished his bath and refreshments and went to the palace garden. There, the young princess awaited his arrival. It was impossible to say who was more eager for their meeting. Both were filled with anticipation to hear each other’s news. But was that the only reason for their excitement? Their future... Is it not possible that the desire to find certainty about life itself was the reason? The youthful spring that stirred even the inanimate objects—could it not have awakened a flutter of excitement in their emotion-filled hearts as well?
"Sir! I have come to know that you did not achieve complete success in the task you undertook. Is that true?" asked the Young Princess.
"It is true, Devi! In which of the tasks I have taken up so far have I ever achieved complete success?" replied Vallavarayan, letting out a deep sigh.
"Do not say so! Did you not bring my brother safely back from Eezha Nadu? Was it not only because Arulmozhi Varman returned at that time that the Chola country survived until now?" said Kundavai.

"I brought Arulmozhi Varman back, but only after exposing him to unnecessary dangers and bringing him as a helpless invalid suffering from a severe chill. Even that was only with the help of Poonguzhali Maharani. When I entrusted my friend to Sendhan Amudhan and Poonguzhali and asked them to take him to Nagapattinam, never in my dreams did I imagine that they would come to Thanjavur and ascend the throne of this Chola Empire, to be crowned with the jeweled diadem..."

"I have not forgotten, nor has he, that it was you who saved the life of Uttama Chola Chakravarti. Uttama Chola himself wished to appoint you as the sole authority of the Chola land in place of Periya Pazhuvetarayar..."
"Fortunately, I escaped that fate!"

"Why do you say that? Is the position of sole authority of this Chola Empire an ordinary one? It is greater than the post of Prime Minister, greater even than the office of Commander-in-Chief! Without the consent of the sole authority, even the Emperor cannot accomplish anything!"

"Devi! Once, I had to hide in the underground treasury of Periya Pazhuvetarayar. There, in the glow of the heaps of gold coins, I saw a spider's web. I also saw the skull of a dead man. I resolved then never to go near that treasury room again..."

The Young Princess smiled and said, "Even if you become the sole authority, you will not have to go to the treasury room. All the wealth stored there must be spent to build a great navy, to construct ships—" “Arulmozhi has made his decision. He has also obtained the new emperor’s permission!” she said.
“I heard in Thanjai that the new emperor and his crowned queen have gone to Kodikkarai with Arulmozhivarman.”
“Yes, when they left, they were deeply regretful that they could not take you along with them.”
“I do not regret that. Even now, I can go to Kodikkarai and join them. What I regret is that Arulmozhivarman waited for my absence to marry the Princess of Kodumbalur.”
“Why, sir! Are you displeased that your friend has married my companion?”

“Heavens, no! That is not what I meant. I only regret that I was not present at that wedding. It is Arulmozhivarman’s fortune from a previous birth that he was able to wed Vanathi. Your friend Vanathi is indeed fortunate as well, but why was there such haste?”

“They were not in haste—I was the one who hurried things. My father and mother wished to leave for Kanchi. I insisted that the wedding should take place before they departed. This also brought peace to the heart of the great Velar of Kodumbalur. On the day of the coronation, when your friend suddenly placed the Chola crown on Uttama Chola’s head, it was a great shock to the Periya Velar.”
“Many others must have been shocked at that time as well.”
“To all of us, it was a matter of astonishment. You two friends kept that secret very, very closely guarded.”
“Devi! I thought at least he would have confided in you.”
“If it had been a few months earlier, he certainly would have. Arulmozhi never did anything without asking me.”
“Why has he changed now?”
“It is the fault of his companionship! Only after joining you did my dear brother change so. One who was always transparent, inside and out, has now become adept in the arts of intrigue and cunning!”

“Devi! Do not lay false blame upon me. It was your brother alone who bore full responsibility for the deceitful drama of crowning Uttama Chozhar. I argued with him, asking whether it was right to deceive everyone in this manner. Arulmozhi cited Rama, who, after deceiving the people of Ayodhya, went into exile in the forest by night, as his example. I asked him, at the very least, whether he should not tell you. He replied that, for once in his life, he wished to do something without seeking your counsel, and only afterwards receive your praise. Devi! Was not the act performed by the prince in accordance with your own heart’s desire?”
“No one could ever do anything more pleasing to you than this. I am deeply grateful that you aided my brother in this matter!” said the young princess.
“Devi! I thought you longed to see Arulmozhivarman ascend the throne, crowned with the jeweled diadem, and rule the world.”

“It is true that I once desired it. But after my friend Vanathi took such a vow, I changed my mind. Moreover, if my brother were to ascend the throne immediately after our elder brother’s murder, what would the world think?”

“Yes, Devi! The dreadful deeds that have taken place in the royal line of Lanka have greatly disturbed Arulmozhivarman in this regard. Yet even that did not trouble him as much. When some tried to lay that heinous murder upon me, he resolved to ascend the Chola throne solely to protect me. Fortunately, Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar took that blame upon himself and saved me from that false accusation.”
“Alas! The whole Chola land seems desolate now that the old lord is gone.”
“It grieves me deeply to think that, after the elder brother, the younger too has departed.”
“Oh! Has Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar also passed away? Is it certain?” asked Kundavai.

“When I took leave of him and departed, he was still alive. But how could one survive after falling from such a steep mountain? He must surely have died. I too am, in a way, responsible for the death of Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar…” “When I think that I was the cause of it all, my heart trembles,” said Vandiyathevan.

“Sir! Please tell me all about it in detail. On the day of the coronation, you and my brother plotted together to have Chinna Pazhuvettarayar removed from the assembly hall, did you not? Tell me everything about that. I never got the chance to ask my brother for the details. I was hoping to learn it from you. Was it because of the saying ‘No secrets should be told to women’ that you did not tell me before? But now, at least, you can tell me, can you not?”
“Devi! It was not for that reason that I kept it from you. The prince wished to surprise you at least once.”
“I was not surprised at all. I guessed that the two of you were hatching some scheme together. I was only a little anxious, fearing that something might go wrong.”

“In truth, something did go wrong. Though we accomplished a very important task, we could not prevent another calamity that arose from it. If only I had sought your counsel, perhaps this would not have happened!” said Vandiyathevan.

Then, from the moment when Ponniyin Selvan decided that Sendhan Amudhan, the new Madurantaka Thevar, should be crowned, Vandiyathevan recounted in detail all the plans they made, the schemes they devised, and the actions they carried out.
