Arulmozhi Varman thought that if they announced beforehand that Madurantaka Thevar was to be crowned, there would be many objections and obstacles. The Kodumbalur Velar and the Thirukovalur Malayaman would oppose that idea as before. Periya Pazhuvettarayar, on his deathbed, had declared that the crown must go to Ponniyin Selvan. Those who were loyal to him would wish to fulfill his desire. Chinna Pazhuvettarayar had discovered that his son-in-law was not the true Madurantakan. He could not feel any enthusiasm for seating Poonguzhali, the daughter of the boatman, on the throne. Sembiyan Madevi, Sendhan Amudhan—now Madurantaka Thevar—and Poonguzhali, all would raise objections. Sundara Chola himself might not wish to disregard their protests.

Bearing all these reasons in mind, Ponniyin Selvan decided to keep his intentions secret until the very last moment. He wished to prevent any troublemakers, who might, out of love for him or jealousy towards Madurantakan, raise objections and create obstacles at the time of the coronation.

He sent each one away to distant towns, giving different reasons to each. Only to Vandiyathevan, whom he needed as an ally, did he reveal his innermost intentions. The two of them thought together, devised plans, and carried out their tasks with utmost caution.

Ilaya Sambuvaraiyan Kandhamaaran, Parthibendira Pallavan, the Kodumbalur Velar, and others had already been sent away from the city. But it was impossible to send Chinna Pazhuvettaraiyar away. There was even talk that it would be his hand that would place the jeweled crown upon Ponniyin Selvan’s head. At such a time, if someone were to suggest that the new Madurantakan, known as Sendhan Amudhan, should be crowned instead, would he remain silent? If he were to object, it would be considered a grave omen. Many other confusions could arise from that. Therefore, the two friends pondered how to devise some stratagem to remove him from the mandapam at the time of the coronation. Yet, no completely satisfactory plan presented itself. At that moment, Azhwarkkadiyan arrived with a most peculiar piece of news.

Where had Ravidasan’s band of Pandya assassins gone? Was Nandini Devi still with them? Where had the boy, crowned at midnight in the Thiruppurambiyam forest, been hidden away? To find answers to these questions, Arulmozhi Varman had, with the Prime Minister’s consent, sent Azhwarkkadiyan to investigate. Had Karuthiruman, who had escaped from the underground dungeon, joined them? Was it true, as Kandhamaaran had claimed, that the old Madurantakan was dead, or had he too escaped and joined the conspirators? Thirumalai Nambi had gone to discover the truth of these matters. They had expected it would take him a long time to return with news. Yet, Azhwarkkadiyan had come back within a few days.

He had seen members of Ravidasan’s group and Raakkammal, the wife of the boatman Murugaiyan, near Kollimalai. He thought that by following her, he might find the whereabouts of Ravidasan’s band. But to his surprise, Raakkammal had taken the road to Thanjavur. Nevertheless, believing that following her was the best way to learn about the assassins, he disguised himself and trailed her without her knowledge. As he neared Uraiyur, he saw that crowds of people were streaming toward Thanjai to witness the coronation of Ponniyin Selvan. Raakkammal too mingled with that throng. Yet, Azhwarkkadiyan did not lose sight of her and continued to follow her to Thanjai. He came as far as he could. When he saw that Raakkammaal had entered the Thanjai fort along with a large crowd and was circling around the palace of Chinna Pazhuvetarayar, he was greatly astonished. At once, he went to Arulmozhi Varman and Vandiyathevan and conveyed this news. At first, they considered capturing Raakkammaal. But then they decided against it, determining that it was more important to find out why she had come. They guessed that she must have brought some message for the daughter of Chinna Pazhuvetarayar. They resolved not to tell Chinna Pazhuvetarayar about this immediately, but to use it during the coronation ceremony to remove him from the assembly hall if necessary.

When Azhwarkkadiyan again went near the palace of Chinna Pazhuvetarayar, he could not find Raakkammaal. The crowd that had come for the coronation was growing larger and larger. Azhwarkkadiyan mingled with the crowd and kept a close watch on the palace entrance. Two women came out of the palace. One of them carried a child on her hip. The other had covered her face partially with a veil drawn over her head. Thirumalai Nambi guessed that she must be the daughter of Chinna Pazhuvetarayar. He could not decide whether to stop them or to simply watch where they were going. Meanwhile, the women disappeared into the crowd. Azhwarkkadiyan guessed that they must have gone towards the fort gate and went there. He saw them get into a palanquin that was stationed a little beyond the fort gate, surrounded by mounted guards as they departed. Now, he thought, there must be no further delay in informing Chinna Pazhuvetarayar of this news, and he hurried to the assembly hall.

At that moment, Ponniyin Selvan was speaking with the Tamil poet. When Azhwarkkadiyan conveyed the news to Chinna Pazhuvetarayar, he immediately set out with him. He returned to his palace and searched for his daughter. On learning that she was not there, he was shocked. He concluded that the news Azhwarkkadiyan had brought must indeed be true. Before he could return to the assembly hall, shouts of “Long live Madurandaka Uttama Chozha Chakravarti!” rang out. After learning what had transpired in the assembly, he realized that he had no more business there. Taking a few trusted attendants with him, he set out in search of his daughter who had run away. His daughter, the scion of the Chozha dynasty—

When he thought of joining forces with the Pandya dynasty’s sworn enemies and their loyal henchmen, his heart boiled with rage. Rather than that, he felt it would be better to kill such a daughter with his own hands, and he hurried forward, driven by this thought.

That night, after the grand and tumultuous festivities of Uttama Chola Chakravarti’s coronation procession had concluded, Azhwarkkadiyan Nambi recounted to Arulmozhi Varman all that had transpired that afternoon. Arulmozhi Varman conferred with Vandiyathevan. All three of them knew well that Ravidasan and his group were masters of cunning and sorcery. They feared that the hot-tempered Chinna Pazhuvettarayar would not be able to overcome their devious tricks, and that he might fall into their trap and be caught in grave danger. They even believed he was capable of committing the dreadful act of killing his own beloved daughter.

Therefore, they decided that it would be best for Vandiyathevan and Azhwarkkadiyan to set out together: to rescue and bring back Chinna Pazhuvettarayar, and to discover where Ravidasan’s Pandya faction was hiding and what they were plotting.

Thus, while Chinna Pazhuvettarayar pressed on, pursuing both his daughter and the conspirators who had spirited her away without her knowledge, Vandiyathevan and Azhwarkkadiyan followed his trail, making inquiries along the way. The two who followed soon realized that Chinna Pazhuvettarayar had wandered this way and that, crisscrossing the land in confusion. From this, they concluded that those who had taken his daughter must have deliberately misled him, sending him off on a false path.

After traveling a long distance westward along the banks of the Kaveri, they changed direction at the place where the Amaravati River joined the Kaveri, and journeyed southwest along the branch of that river. They reached the region of Anaimalai, which formed the border between Chera Nadu and Kongu Nadu. Once they reached the foothills of Anaimalai, the journey became exceedingly difficult. In that forested region, the trees grew thick and lush. The terrifying roars of wild beasts echoed from all directions. It was extremely hard to proceed on horseback. If they abandoned their horses and went on foot, there was the fear that the horses might fall prey to the wild animals.

At last, the two friends reached a dense forest through which it was impossible to ride any further. Somewhere nearby, the neighing of another horse was heard. When they searched for and found the spot, they saw the horse that Chinna Pazhuvettarayar had ridden, and a man standing guard over it. Chinna Pazhuvettarayar himself, along with the three who had come with him—

That man informed them that he had come that far on foot. Entrusting their horses to his care, the friends continued on their way. They traveled a great distance through dense forests, so thick with darkness that even sunlight could not penetrate. Then, they climbed up mountain paths overgrown with trees. They had to walk along trails so obscure that it was impossible to see what lay even ten feet ahead.

At last, they reached a spot where a little light shone through. Here, a waterfall plunged straight down from the mountain, creating a gap in the otherwise unbroken wilderness. Beyond this, it seemed impossible to continue their journey, for the mountain wall rose so steeply that no path upward could be found, no matter how hard they searched. The friends decided that they had no choice but to bathe in the waterfall, rest for a while, and then turn back. They thought that perhaps Chinna Pazhuvettarayar and his men, who had come with him, must have already fallen prey to the wild beasts of the forest.

At that moment, they witnessed an astonishing sight they had never expected. At the very top of the mountain, where the waterfall began its long descent, two human figures appeared. Fighting as they came, they drew closer and closer to the edge where the water fell. Looking closely, the friends realized that both were men they already knew. One was Chinna Pazhuvettarayar; the other was his son-in-law, the old Madurantakan. Ah! Was it not a wonder that Madurantakan, who used to wrinkle his face at the very mention of the word “battle,” had now learned to wield a sword with such skill? He was fighting Kalantaka Kandar as an equal! Alas! Kalantaka Kandar was retreating! Was he truly falling back out of exhaustion, or was he hesitating because his opponent was now his own son-in-law? Whatever the reason, they were both nearing the dangerous edge where the waterfall plunged down! Oh no! It seemed Madurantakan did not realize that a sheer precipice lay ahead!

Vandiyathevan and Azhwarkadiyan shouted at the top of their voices, trying to warn him. But their efforts were in vain! The roar of the waterfall as it crashed down drowned out every sound, swallowing the voices of a hundred lions and the trumpeting of two hundred elephants. How could the voices of these two men rise above such a din?

And so, as this dreadful event unfolded before their eyes, they could do nothing but watch in helpless horror. Chinna Pazhuvettarayar, fighting his adversary and slowly retreating, reached the very edge of the waterfall. His feet slipped—and he plunged headlong into the sheer chasm below!

The old Madurantakan, who had come fighting alongside him, climbed to the edge of the rock, peered down, and disappeared the next moment. The ravine below the spot where Chinna Pazhuvettarayar’s foot had slipped was about three-quarters the height of a coconut tree. It was impossible to expect that anyone who fell from such a height would survive. Yet, thinking at least they might see the body of that great warrior, the two friends ran to the edge of the waterfall’s ravine. Chinna Pazhuvettarayar’s body was nowhere to be seen. The waterfall, plunging down, had formed a deep pool there, the water swirling and crashing against the rocks all around. They surmised that Chinna Pazhuvettarayar’s body must have sunk into that deep pool. In a way, this was for the best. Had he fallen upon the rocks at the shore, the body of that great warrior would have been shattered to pieces. Because he had fallen into the deep pool, he had escaped such a fate. They waited, expecting that soon the current of the waterfall would bring his body out to the surface.

Their expectation was not in vain. After a little while, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar surfaced. The two friends quickly jumped into the pool and brought him to the shore. At first, they thought it was a lifeless body. Yet, a faint hope lingered in their hearts—perhaps there was still life left in him. Therefore, they performed all the necessary treatments to revive someone who had nearly drowned. After a long while, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar drew breath and opened his eyes. He could not speak much, but in a few words, he conveyed what needed to be said.

With great difficulty, Kaalanthakakandar reached the summit of the hill. There, amidst nearly a hundred people, stood his daughter. Ravidasan invited Kaalanthakakandar to join their cause, saying that his own son-in-law was the rightful heir to the Pandya throne, that he was about to be crowned, and that the Chera king and Mahindan, the king of Lanka, had come forward to support the new Pandya. At first, Chinna Pazhuvettarayar listened to all that Ravidasan said, seeking to learn their intentions. Then, he accused them of being conspirators and demanded that they send his daughter with him.
“If your daughter wishes to go with you, let her go!” said Ravidasan.

Chinna Pazhuvettarayar looked at his daughter. She refused to go with him, saying she would rather share her husband’s fate. “Rather than leave you with these people, I would kill you with my own hands!” declared Kaalanthakakandar, raising his sword. At that moment, Madurantakan, who had been hiding until then, suddenly appeared and cried, “Who are you to kill my wife?” and began to fight with his sword. This caused some astonishment in Kaalanthakakandar. To kill his own son-in-law with his own hands and leave his daughter a widow— A doubt arose in his mind as to whether it was just to proceed. Because of this confusion that had taken root within him, he could not fight with full intensity. Lost in thought, he began to retreat. Unaware that there was a ravine behind him, he fell into it.

After narrating all this in a faltering, stumbling manner, he said, “I am not going to survive any longer. My end is near. Leave me here and hurry on your way. Let the Chola army immediately march upon the Chera and Eezha kingdoms. Take Ponniyin Selvan to Madurai, bestow upon him the coronation name ‘Chola Pandiyan,’ and have him crowned. If these three things are not done at once, a great danger will befall the Chola empire. The Pandya kingdom will once again split off and stand apart as before! Go quickly!” Thus spoke Kaalanthakakandar.

His friends could not bring themselves to abandon him in such a state. Therefore, they decided that one of them would stay behind to care for him, while the other would go to Thanjavur. Since Vandiyathevan was the one who could ride a horse swiftly, it was he who had to set out.

chapters.title: Golden Rain Poured!
paragraphs: When Vandiyathevan finished recounting his adventures in the forests of Anaimalai, Kundavai looked at him and said, “Sir! The tale you have told is truly astonishing. At times, I even wondered if these were real events. I know well your talent for spinning stories. Especially when you frequently paused, glancing up and down before resuming your speech—my doubts only grew stronger!”

Once again, Vandiyathevan glanced up and down, then turned to Kundavai. “Devi! There are other places more suitable for telling fanciful tales. I have never displayed that particular skill before you. There is another reason for the interruptions in my speech!”
“Is that too a great secret? One that cannot be told to women?” asked Princess Kundavai.
“It is indeed a secret that should not be told to anyone. But if you grant me permission, I shall reveal it to you!” replied Vandiyathevan.
“You always have my permission to speak the truth!” said Kundavai.

“In that case, I shall tell you, and you need not be angry with me afterward. Sometimes, while I am speaking with you, my gaze inadvertently meets yours. I do not know what rare magic lies in your dark eyes, Devi, but it leaves me utterly bewildered. Only after composing myself can I resume speaking!” he said.

Kundavai’s lips parted; dimples appeared in her cheeks; her eyes sparkled with laughter. “Sir! There is no rare magic in my eyes. Not even any dark sorcery. I have even stopped applying kohl for some time now. What you saw in my eyes was only your own reflection. That alone must have startled you!”
“Devi! I have seen my own reflection in mirrors. I have seen it in clear water. Never on those occasions have I been so astonished!” said Vallavaraiyan.
“Are you comparing my eyes to mirrors and water? Mirrors can tarnish; water can become muddied!” said the princess.

“If a mirror is smudged, I can wipe it clean. I can make sure the water stays clear and unclouded. But if your eyelids close and draw a curtain over your eyes, hiding my form, is there anything I can do to stop it?” asked Vandiyathevan.

“It is only when one stands before a mirror that a reflection appears. It is only when water remains clear and undisturbed that an image can be seen. But whether my eyes are open or closed, whether you stand before me or not, your form always shines within my eyes. Can you tell me the reason for this miracle?” asked Kundavai.
A shiver ran through Vandiyathevan’s body. In a trembling voice, he replied, “I do not know, Devi!”

“If you do not know, then I shall tell you. There is some wondrous, magical power within you. Even the heart of Nandini, who came with a diamond-hard resolve to destroy the Chola dynasty, was shaken upon seeing you, was it not?”
“Just now, you spoke words sweeter than nectar and filled me with ecstasy. In the very next breath, why do you utter the name of that venomous serpent?”
“There was a time when I hated Nandini, thinking of her as a snake filled with poison. But now, when I think of her, I feel only pity for her…”
“To show pity to Nandini is like showing mercy to the deadly poison that seeks to destroy the Chola clan.”

“Ayya! She is the daughter of Mandakini Devi, who has become the guardian goddess of the Chola lineage! She is the daughter of the very woman who saved my beloved brother Arulmozhi many times! She is the daughter of the queen who gave her own life to save my father from the assassin’s spear!”

“But she is also the one who incited that assassin’s hand! She is the one who became the Yama of Aditya Karikalan! She is the one who bewitched the mind of the great and valiant Periya Pazhuvetarayar and made him dance like a puppet…”

“Was it only the mind of Periya Pazhuvetarayar that she bewitched? She turned Parthibendra Pallavan, Kandhamaran, and others too into her instruments! Even knowing all this, I cannot bring myself to hate her. She did all this to avenge the death of Veerapandiyan! She succeeded in accomplishing the task she set out to do! A woman of a heroic warrior clan! When I think that I too was a reason for her descending into such dreadful deeds, I am filled with sorrow. In her childhood, we drove her out from Pazhayarai…”

“You have done a good deed, Devi! But in the abundance of your compassion, do not forget that she is the daughter of the Chola clan’s enemy. Was it not enough that the son of Veera Pandiyan was raised in the Chola household and the calamity that resulted from it? If Veera Pandiyan’s daughter too had grown up in the Chola house and had been destined to marry Aditya Karikalan…”
“It would have ended in great good, the enmity between these two illustrious clans would have been resolved, and both houses would have become one. But is that story even true?”
“What are you asking, Devi?”
“Is it true that Nandini is the daughter of Veera Pandiyan?”

“I myself heard Nandini say so to Aditya Karikalan, with my own ears. Periya Pazhuvettarayar heard it too. That is what completely changed Periya Pazhuvettarayar’s heart and made him take on a wrathful form. That cruel word became the very Yama, the god of death, for Prince Aditya Karikalan!”

“Think a little! Perhaps she said so only to lay blame on Karikalan? When Karikalan tried to save Veera Pandiyan from his own wrath, she herself spoke differently. Would any woman ever call her own father her ‘lover’ with her own lips?”

“Devi! Karikalan was beside himself with rage at that time. Who knows what she said, what he understood, or what meaning he took from it? Was it not Karikalan himself who said it? Did he not believe it when Nandini later said, ‘My father is Veera Pandiyan’? Moreover, it is possible that she only learned of this after Veera Pandiyan’s death. You know well the efforts Nandini undertook to discover the truth of her birth. Did she not, in the dead of night, play the part of her mother’s spirit and drive Sundara Chola to madness? Did not your friend witness this and faint away?”
“When Alwarkadiyan questioned the madman who had been imprisoned in the underground dungeon for three years and was released with you, you must also know what he said…”
“How could I not know? He said that he was the father of both Nandini and her brother.”
“That could very well be the truth, could it not?”

“If that is so, then sometimes even a lie can possess immense power. If you had seen how the old Madurantaka, who once trembled at the very thought of conflict within the palace walls, transformed into a heroic warrior upon learning that he was Veerapandiyan’s son, you would have been astonished. Once, the younger Pazhuvettarayar gripped my shoulder with his diamond-hard hand. Even now, the spot where he held me aches when I recall it. Yet, that same Madurantakan—whom we all considered a coward—stood his ground in battle, matching that great hero blow for blow. It is a sight I shall never forget.”
“It is precisely that which makes me doubt your words,” I replied.

“It is indeed an event hard to believe. Who could imagine that the Madurantakan we knew—the man who traveled in Nandini’s veiled palanquin, who trembled at the mere mention of the Pazhuvettarayars—would dare to face the younger Pazhuvettarayar in single combat? Yet, it truly happened. Alwarkadiyan will return and tell you all about it.”
“Sir! Were you unable to see Nandini Devi?”
“Why should I seek out that woman, who is but a demoness in human form?”

“Do not speak of Nandini in such a manner again. One day, I myself shall meet her. I will uncover the secret of who her true father is. But know this: do not speak ill of Nandini to me. Whoever her father may be, is there any doubt about who her mother is? That alone is enough for me to love her. And there is another, even more important reason…”
“What is that reason?”

“Nandini cared for you. She gave you her signet ring. She helped you escape from the Tanjore fortress. When you were trapped in the Kollidam forest by Ravidasan’s band, she saved your life once again…”
“And finally, she placed the terrible blame for Aditya Karikalan’s murder upon me. All those intrigues were her doing!”
“Do you not know why she did so?”
“Must one seek a reason for why a snake bites? Must one explain why a leopard leaps?”
“Nandini was not born a serpent or a leopard. It was we who made her so. Circumstances conspired to shape her thus. You too were one of the causes!”
“Oh no! Why lay such blame upon me? What harm did I ever do to her?”
“You did her no harm. It was she who harbored affection for you.”
“Heavens!...”

“It seems that men, in certain matters, are blind even when they have eyes. Listen to me, sir! You never understood the depths of Nandini’s heart. But I knew her well. That unfortunate woman did not truly love Veera Pandiyan. Nor did she have any real affection for Aditya Karikalan. All her acts of love towards them were but a performance, a means to ascend the throne!”
“I know this too, Devi! In her murderous heart, there is not even a sliver of space for love!”
“That is not true. It was only upon seeing you that true love dawned in her heart. She was willing to do anything to win your affection…”
“She was even willing to lay upon me the blame for the prince’s murder.”
“And why was that? Only to ensure that you would forever remain estranged from the Chola clan, never to have friendship or kinship with them again.”
“For that, she arranged to have me paraded on a donkey at the crossroads of Thanjavur’s royal streets. She might as well have killed me outright with the dagger she held in her hand!”

“If she had truly wished to kill you, she could have done so. Or she could have had Ravidasan’s band murder you. Had Periya Pazhuvettarayar not taken the blame upon himself, had Ponniyin Selvan not intervened, had she truly ordered your execution, then Ravidasan’s group would have come and rescued you. Perhaps, by now, you would be among the company that has gathered atop Anaimalai.”
“It was only by the grace of God that I was spared such a fate.”
“He saved the Chola land, and he preserved the service of a valiant warrior like you from being lost to the Chola Empire…”
“Devi! The Chola Empire is a mighty one. The swords and spears of five hundred thousand warriors guard this realm as if it were their own eyes. It cannot be that my help alone is so essential to it!”
“You yourself said that new dangers are encircling the Chola land from all sides.”

“That is true, Devi! Ravidasan’s cunning is astonishing. He has now created two claimants to the Pandya throne. Earlier, he crowned a mere child as the Pandya king in the forests along the banks of the Kollidam. Now, along with that Parangusan Nedunchezhiyan, another has joined—Amarapujangan Nedunchezhiyan…”
“Who is this Amarapujangan Nedunchezhiyan?”

“Our old Madhurantakan now bears that name. One who claims the Pandya throne cannot continue with the name ‘Madhurantakan,’ can he? When the younger Pazhuvettarayar fell into the ravine at Aruvi Pallam, the cry ‘Long live Pandiyan Amarapujangan Nedunchezhiyan!’ rose up, drowning even the roar of the great waterfall.”
“What benefit does Ravidasan’s group gain by establishing two claimants in this way?”

“If something happens to one, the other remains. With one, they can seek the help of Mahindan, the king of Lanka; with the other, they can strive for the alliance of the Chera king. That is their plan…”

“Ayya! My brother and you together conspired to place the jeweled crown upon the head of Uttama Chozhar. I do not think you have done a great favor to Uttama Chozhar. At this moment, bearing the burden of the Chola Empire does not seem such an easy task…”

“To bear the burden of the Chola Empire at this time is indeed a most arduous task. But is Uttama Chozhar going to bear it? He will spend his days assisting his mother in the renovation of temples. The one who is going to bear and safeguard the Chola Empire is your brother, Arulmozhi Devar.”

“That is true. Arulmozhi has the strength for it. Yet, he is still young in age, inexperienced. The two great diamond pillars that upheld the Chola Empire—the Pazhuvur lords—are gone. The elder has left us! From what you say, it seems even the survival of the younger Pazhuvettaraiyar is doubtful…”
“Even if he survives, he will be of no use to the kingdom. He will only grieve for his daughter and son-in-law…”

“Sambuvarayar too has reached the same state. In just a few days, his heart and body have weakened and grown frail. Malayaman was already an old man. When one of his grandsons died and the other was denied the crown, he too lost all spirit at once. The great Velar of Kodumbalur’s mind is unsettled. He cannot forgive that Arulmozhi, after repeatedly saying he would accept the crown, deceived him at the last moment. Even Arulmozhi’s marriage to Vanathi did not bring him satisfaction. He has declared that henceforth he will not involve himself in royal affairs, and has left to devote himself to temple renovations in Kodumbalur. All the other petty kings who participated in the conspiracy at Kadambur Palace are ashamed and disheartened that their plans ended so differently from what they intended. Sir! Arulmozhi needs companions to help him. He needs loyal friends of sharp intellect, strong arms, and valorous swords by his side…”
“Fortunately, the Pallava Parthibendran is still here!” said Vandiyathevan.

“It cannot be said for certain that Arulmozhi will have his support and strength. He is angry that he was sent away from the capital and that Uttama Chola was crowned. More than that, he dislikes that Arulmozhi considers you his closest confidant…”
“His anger is justified. He has done so much for the Chola dynasty. I am a newcomer. If need be, I will ask his forgiveness.”
Kundavai thought for a moment and said, “That would be like pouring oil on a burning fire.”
“Parthibendran is a great warrior. Is there no other way to appease him?” asked Vandiyathevan.
“He himself indicated that path and expressed his wish to my father…”
“The Emperor would not have refused to fulfill Parthibendran Pallavan’s desire…”

“But it was not up to the Emperor. It was up to his daughter. His daughter refused to accept it! Yes, sir! The one who used to offer flowers at the Shiva temple suddenly ascended the throne and wore the jeweled crown—such a sight was unbearable to the scion of the Pallava clan. The girl who once set boats afloat in the sea—her mounting the throne was more than he could bear. He demanded that he be granted the right to have a stone edict inscribed, declaring himself the independent king of the old Pallava country…”
“Ah! How could that be granted? Wouldn’t that shatter the Chola kingdom to pieces?”

“My father agreed to grant that right. But even then, the Pallava prince was not satisfied. Once, it seems, a Pallava princess had married a Chola prince. In return, he demanded that Sundara Chola’s daughter be given to him in marriage!”
At these words, Vandiyathevan’s face showed deep distress. To hide it, he turned his face away.
Kundavai’s face blossomed with a faint smile. She deliberately remained silent, saying nothing more.
After a moment, Vandiyathevan asked, “What answer did the Emperor give to that?”
“How could the Emperor reply to that? Wasn’t it up to his daughter’s wish? The Emperor asked his daughter…”
“What answer did the Emperor’s daughter give?”
“She said she would not agree to take Parthibendran’s hand in marriage!”
“Why? Why?” Vandiyathevan asked, his voice brimming with uncontrollable curiosity.
“The Emperor’s daughter gave her reason. She said she had no desire to leave the sacred land watered by the divine Ponni river and go to a foreign country.”
“Is that the only reason?”
“There may be other reasons as well. Shouldn’t such things be told only to those who have true devotion? Why should I explain to those who simply ask, ‘Why so?’” said Kundavai.
“Devi! I ask with boundless devotion and eagerness.”
“Those who possess such devotion and eagerness will come to know it on their own. There is no need to explain it to them.”
At that moment, Vandiyathevan looked at Kundavai as if seeing her face for the very first time.

Lightning struck lightning. Wave crashed against wave. Heaven descended to earth. The world of mortals became the world of the gods. With a mischievous smile at the corner of her eyes, Kundavai said, “What should one think of a man who, unable to discern what lies in a woman’s heart, expects her to speak it aloud? How can one expect that such a man could unravel the cunning plots of the enemies of the Chola Empire?”

Vandiyathevan, after glancing up and down for a moment, said, “Devi! If a destitute youth, with neither a hut for shelter nor a family to call his own, were to make the same request as Parthibendran of the ancient Pallava clan, what would the Emperor think of it?”
“Whatever he thinks, he will ask what his daughter wishes. He will answer accordingly.”
“Devi! What answer would the Emperor’s noble daughter give?”
“Why do you trouble yourself circling around the question like this? Why not ask the Emperor directly? The answer will be known at once!” said Kundavai.

“How can that be asked? From Eezham to Vengi, the king who rules beneath a single royal parasol—how could a youth, with neither name nor clan, an orphan without kin or relations, dare to ask for the hand of his daughter in marriage?” asked Vallavaraiyan.

“For a warrior born of the Vanar clan, whence comes such humility? I have not forgotten what you said the first time you met me about the pride of your lineage. You said that when a male child is born in the palaces of the Chera, Chola, and Pandya kings, if the child’s chest is broad, the queens would delight that all the names of the mighty Maveli Vaanan could be inscribed upon that chest. You said that at the palace gates of the Vanar king, the three crowned monarchs would stand in waiting, and that poets, seeing the gifts received from that king, would…”
“This is my horse! This is my elephant! Wait, this is my crown! This is my royal parasol!”—you said they would boast in such ways. Then why is it that one who could take such pride is now so humble?”

“It is your brother’s friendship that is the reason for this. Arulmozhi Varman despises those who try to boast of ancient lineage and noble birth. He laughs at those who pride themselves on being born in the Solar dynasty, or as descendants of Karikala Valavan, or as heirs of Vijayalaya Chola. Do you know what he once told me? He said, ‘Whenever my ancestors had copper plates or stone inscriptions made, they would begin by tracing our lineage from the Solar dynasty, from Manu Needhi Cholan, from Emperor Sibi, and so on. If I ascend the royal throne, I will change this custom. In the inscriptions and copper plates I commission, I will have only the deeds I have accomplished engraved. Then, those inscriptions will stand as true records, leaving no room for doubt or exaggeration!’

Devi, I agreed with his view. I resolved to give up boasting of my ancient lineage. I will not go to your father and recount my ancestral glories to seek the fortune of holding your hand in marriage. Arulmozhi Varman and I have dedicated our lives to the glory of this Chola Empire. We have resolved to make the tiger flag fly from the Vindhya mountains in the north, to Trikona hills in the south, to the Lakshadweep islands in the west, and to the lands beyond the eastern seas—Java, Kadaram, Kamboja. After we have achieved at least a part of what we have set out to do, I will go to Emperor Sundara Chola and humbly request, ‘Grant me permission to adorn your divine daughter’s neck with the garlands of victory I have earned!’ I will go to Lanka, defeat Mahinda, and bring back the Pandya crown and Indra’s garland, and lay them before the princess. Then, with pride, I will say, ‘If I am worthy to hold your divine hand, grant me that fortune!’”

“Sir! I admire your resolve. I am amazed and delighted by the difference between your attitude and that of Parthibendran. But as a man, you can do all this—achieve victories, accomplish great deeds, and take pride in them. For those born as women, none of this is possible, nor is it necessary. In our land, royal women once had the custom of choosing their own husbands through a swayamvara. Now, for some reason, that custom has faded away. Sir, even if my father had arranged a swayamvara for me and invited all the princes of this vast land, I would not have placed the garland in my hand around any of their necks. Escaping from the Tanjore fort... Running swiftly, with the help of the old temple priest of Pazhaiyarai, I will board a boat, cross the stream, enter the palace gardens, and seek out the orphaned youth who met me in secret. Among all those royal princes, I will search to see if he is anywhere to be found. It is upon his neck that I will place the garland of my own choosing that I now hold in my hand!”

In Vandiyathevan’s ears, a thousand anklets rang out. From the sky, a golden rain poured down. At the treetops, where buds and blossoms trembled, insects unfurled their wings and danced. Vandiyathevan, who until then had been seated, rose to his feet.
“Did you not like what I said?” asked Kundavai.

“You ask well. I wondered if I was awake, if what fell upon my ears was real, or if I was dreaming. But I am not dreaming. I know now it is true! I have heard that the gods, after churning the ocean of milk, attained the nectar of immortality and became celestial beings by drinking it. The words you have just spoken have made me one who has tasted that nectar. They have given me new life!”

At that moment, Kundavai said, “Sir! Remember just one thing. In the places you go, you will face countless dangers. You will fight in many battles. Enemies, by treacherous schemes, will try to send you to the other world. If ever your life is truly in peril, before a princess born in this ancient and glorious Chola clan is wed, she will become a widow! Do not forget this!”

“Devi! Such a thing will never happen. I have already tasted the nectar and become immortal! Death can no longer touch me! In the deep darkness of the wild forests, when wind and rain rage and I stumble, lost and directionless, you will be waiting for me in that house amidst the woods, a lamp burning near the plank-bed, watching for my return. That thought will give me courage, and help me escape the storm and darkness. In the midst of the tossing waves, when I am adrift on a wooden boat for days and weeks and months, losing all sense of direction and time, you will shine for me as the pole star, ever steadfast beneath the constellation of the Seven Sages, guiding me with your light. I will find my way and turn my boat homeward. On nights when the sea rages and mighty waves crash against the rocks on the shore like great mountains, you will shine from the lighthouse as the life-saving beam. By that radiance, I will bring my boat safely to shore without striking the rocks. In the endless desert where not a blade of grass or flower grows, under the blazing sun that scorches like the fire of Vadavai— When I am scorched by the blazing sun and my tongue is parched with thirst, when my feet are cracked and weary, stumbling across the burning sand, you shall be the spring of life for me, surrounded by coconut palms and honeyed plantains. Devi! No matter where I go in this vast, expansive world, no matter how many hardships I may endure, one day I will surely return. I will come back, take your hand, and marry you. Until this wish of mine is fulfilled, Yama himself will not dare approach me. I shall remain immortal, as one who has tasted the nectar of the gods!”

Thus spoke Vandiyathevan, in a manner he had never before spoken in his life, and then sat down. The young princess, utterly entranced, gazed at his face. It seemed to her that these words were not being spoken to her for the first time by this warrior; rather, she felt as if, in ages long past, in countless bygone eras, she had heard this very torrent of words from him many times before.

While she was pondering the strange wonder of this mystical illusion, the voice of Vanathi rang out, “Akka! Akka!” Both of them turned to look. Vanathi hurried to their side and said, “Akka! An urgent letter has arrived for him. It is from Kandhamaaran, Manimekalai’s brother!” As she spoke, she extended the palm-leaf letter.

chapters.title: The Flower Fell!
paragraphs: Part Five – The Pinnacle of Sacrifice
Vandiyathevan took the palm-leaf letter and looked at Vanathi. “Princess! Do you remember me at all? I was beginning to think you had completely forgotten me.”
“Sir! How could I ever forget you? How could my husband and I ever forget the help you have rendered us?” replied Vanathi.
“That must be why you waited for a time when I was away to conduct your wedding!” he said.

With a mischievous smile, Vanathi replied, “Yes; if you had been present, perhaps the wedding would have taken place with all the grandeur of Ponniyin Selvan’s coronation! Who knows what schemes you might have devised? Who can say?”

“Was it I who prevented Ponniyin Selvan’s coronation? Was it not the vow you made, in rivalry with Poonguzhali, that you would never ascend the throne? The fortune fell to the boat-girl! What use is it to blame me?” said Vandiyathevan.

“Let her enjoy that fortune! I bear no grudge against her for that, nor do I bear any against you. In fact, I am happy. But when you fix the date for your own wedding, make sure you consult a good astrologer for an auspicious day!” she said.
“It will suffice if we ask the Kudanthai astrologer to choose the date! You have such faith in him!” Vandiyathevan said, looking at Vanathi.
Vanathi laughed out loud and, turning to the younger princess, said, “Akka! Now that he mentions the Kudanthai astrologer, something comes to mind!” She burst into laughter again.
“What are you laughing about, Vanathi? Are you thinking of the astrologer’s prophecy—‘The child to be born from your womb will rule all three worlds’—is that what amuses you?” asked Kundavai.
“Why do you call it mere babbling, Devi? That prophecy is bound to come true!” said Vandiyathevan.
Vanathi, embarrassed without quite knowing why, struggled to suppress her laughter. Then she said,

“Akka! Whenever I try to say something, you always turn the conversation in another direction. I asked the Kudanthai astrologer, ‘From where will a suitable husband come for the younger princess?’ The astrologer replied, ‘Even if he were to leap down from the sky this very moment, he would do so!’ The very next minute, this man came leaping in, arguing with the astrologer’s disciple as he entered! I was laughing, remembering that incident.”
Kundavai, stifling the laughter that welled up within her, spoke with feigned annoyance, “Enough of your games! Let him read the urgent letter he has brought!”
As Vandiyathevan read the letter, both women noticed the shadow of worry that crossed his face.
“What news? What has Kandhamaaran written?” the younger princess asked eagerly.
“See for yourself!” said Vandiyathevan, handing the letter to Kundavai.
The letter read as follows:

“To my dear friend, Vallavaraiyan Vandiyathevan, forgetting all the wrongs and injustices I have done to you, please come at once to see my sister Manimekalai for the last time. Ilanjambuvurayan Kandhamaaran.”
After reading it, Kundavai said, “In a way, this is good news. It seems Manimekalai has been found!”
“What is this? Where had Manimekalai gone?” Vandiyathevan asked in surprise.
“Do you know nothing about Manimekalai?”
“No! I meant to ask you about her.”
“I too wished to tell you; but I hesitated, not knowing how to bring up her name to someone who could remain so stone-hearted about her fate.”
“Devi! How could I be stone-hearted regarding Manimekalai? As far as she is concerned, am I not as good as dead?”
“No; to her, you are not dead—you have become an immortal, one who cannot die!”
“Let it be; at least now, tell me about Manimekalai.”

“It pains me even to speak of it. Sembiyan Maadevi pleaded so much that Manimekalai should remain with her. But Sambuvaraiyar did not agree. He insisted that since Kandhamaaran would be away guarding the border, his daughter at least should stay with him, and so he took her along. Since the Kadambur palace had been burnt down, he obtained the Emperor’s permission to build a new palace on the northern bank of the Paalaar river and set out for that purpose. On the way, near Veera Narayanapuram, they camped for the night. At dawn the next day, they found Manimekalai missing. Thinking she might have run back here, he sent people to check. We replied that she had not come here. From that moment, we have all been in deep worry. We feared she might have drowned herself in the Veera Narayana lake. News came that people were searching for her in all directions. From Kandhamaaran’s letter, it seems they have discovered her whereabouts and found her.”
“What is the use of me going to see her? She will not even recognize me!” said Vandiyathevan.
“Even so, you must go. ‘For the last time,’ Kandhamaaran has written. I do not know what he means by that,” said Kundavai.

“Sister! He is a man without a shred of compassion. He is not at all worthy of Manimekalai’s love. Some people sacrifice entire empires for the sake of love. But he hesitates even to undertake a journey for it!” Vanathi interjected sharply.

Vandiyathevan replied, “Princess! There are only a few kingdoms in this world. Therefore, only a few can sacrifice a kingdom for love. But what you said first is true. I am not at all worthy of Manimekalai’s love. The kind of love she has placed in me should be reserved for the divine. I am not a god, but an ordinary man full of faults and flaws. Manimekalai’s love should be offered to God alone!”
“Even so, there is no harm in you going to see her just once. Kandhamaaran too has written ‘for the last time,’ has he not?” said the young princess Kundavai.

“I did not say that I would not go, did I? I only doubt whether there is any use in going. I hesitate, thinking that I am as good as dead to her. Yet, I do not quite understand the meaning of what Kandamaaran wrote—‘for the last time’. Is he going to forbid me from seeing her again after this? Or is he planning to take her away and consign her to the Buddhist nunnery?”
“If you make the journey for just one day, everything will become clear!” said the young princess Kundavai.

Vandiyathevan traveled from Pazhaiyarai to Veera Narayanapuram for just a single day. But unlike previous journeys, this time that one day seemed to stretch into an age. So many memories and experiences churned within his heart. The first time he had traveled this way to Thanjai, he had seen countless delightful sights. He had built so many castles in the air. Not all of them remained mere castles in the air. Many things that seemed impossible had come to pass. He had gained as his dearest friend the Prince of the Chola land, the heroic young prince celebrated throughout Tamilagam, the one who had the imperial crown within his grasp, but instead crowned another and thus shone as the very peak of sacrifice, higher than Mount Meru itself—Ponniyin Selvan. He had found a place in the heart of the young princess whom Ponniyin Selvan himself revered and adored. He had attained the rank of commander of the Chola forces in Eezham. Could all this be attributed to his own cleverness? Not for a single day. It was only by chance that he had arrived at Kadambur Palace that night, discovered the conspiracy of the petty kings, and thus became entangled in all the events that followed. In these eight months, so many things had happened. Some of them were truly momentous. The comet that appeared in the sky had performed its dire deed and vanished. Aditya Karikalan had departed from this world. Could there be a connection between the comet and Aditya Karikalan? Could it be false when lakhs of people believe such things? What connection could there be between the planets and stars that wander the heavens for eons, and the lives of men who appear on this earth today and vanish tomorrow? Yet, there is no doubt that some mysterious, unfathomable power, some inexorable fate, guides the lives of men! Otherwise, how could he have fallen into so many perils in the past eight months and escaped from them all? How many, how very many people had helped him escape from those dangers! At every turn, at every crisis, those people—

Who was it that brought him help and delivered him? Was it that mysterious power which elders praise and worship as God? Is it the same power they sing of and glorify under names such as Sivan, Thirumal, and Maha Shakti? When Vandiyathevan recalled the unexpected aid he had received at the most perilous moments, he was filled with astonishment. His heart melted when he thought of those who had helped him. Though Kandhamaaran had later caused him much harm, Vandiyathevan could never forget the help he had first received from him. Azhwarkkadiyan had rendered him countless services. Even the demoness Nandini, who had assumed the form of a Mohini, had aided him! He marveled as he remembered the compassion that the younger princess still seemed to hold for him. And the help rendered by the boatwoman Poonguzhali—he could never forget that, not for seven lifetimes. She was worthy to be enthroned upon the Chola Empire’s royal seat.

What words could describe the help he had received from Sendhan Amudhan, the noble Chola he had first met? Was there any equal to it? Could he consider his debt repaid simply because he had saved him from the spear of the physician’s son? Never. Only by serving the Chola dynasty with all his life could he hope to repay the debt he owed that lineage, as long as breath remained in his body. And then there was the great nobleman, Periya Pazhuvettaraiyar! There was a time when Vandiyathevan considered it his greatest fortune just to behold that mighty warrior, who bore upon his long frame the scars of sixty-four battles. Not only had he seen him, he had also become the target of his unnecessary anger and hatred. In the end, the nobleman had atoned for all that. By confessing that the knife Vandiyathevan had thrown had missed its mark and killed Aditya Karikalan, he had saved Vandiyathevan from a terrible accusation and cruel punishment! Was he not a great soul? How could Vandiyathevan ever express his gratitude to him?

Let all these people be. That foolish girl, Manimekalai! Why should she feel such divine love for him? Why should she be so mad? Why should she step forward to take the blame for murder in order to save him? All this was the doing of that fool Kandhamaaran! At first, Kandhamaaran had praised Vandiyathevan to Manimekalai as Indra, Chandra, Arjuna, and Manmatha. It seemed that, even then, the foolish girl had lost her heart to him! But Vandiyathevan knew nothing of this.

When Kandhamaaran said, “Forget my sister! We are going to give her in marriage to a great house!” Vandiyathevan had truly tried to forget her. Meeting the younger princess had helped him in that resolve. But Manimekalai had not changed her heart; nor had she tried to. Many knew—

She did not hesitate to reveal her heart. Ah! What a woman of sweet nature! How much modesty, how much composure! How pure is her mind! A heart as innocent as a newborn child! Truly, she is but a child! A mind as white as milk; yet filled with many playful mischiefs. It is good that she thinks of me as one who is dead. She will never remain forever in this delusion! After some time, her heart will clear. She will marry another brave young man and lead a life of happiness!... But will it truly happen so? Or am I only deceiving myself? Am I the one responsible for bringing Manimekalai to this state? What is the meaning behind Kandanmaran’s letter, ‘Come to see me for the last time’? Perhaps... perhaps... Ah! Even the thought of it brings such pain!

Matching the speed of Vandiyathevan’s thoughts, the horse he rode sped swiftly onward. Fortunately, the Kollidam river was not in flood. There was no need for a boat. Nor was there any necessity to change horses. He led his horse across a small stream that ran along the riverbank, crossed the wide stretches of white sand, and reached the opposite shore. From a distance, he saw the grim sight of the Kadambur palace—some charred pillars and walls, all that remained after the fire. He passed by and continued on. Near Veera Narayanapuram, Kandanmaran’s men were waiting for him. When he asked, “Where is the young master?” they replied, “He is waiting with a boat by the lake shore!”

Wondering why he should be waiting by the lakeside, Vandiyathevan approached the Veera Narayana lake. The tall embankment of the lake rose like the wall of a great fortress, hiding the expanse of water beyond. He remembered the first time he had come to that lakeshore, when crowds had gathered there for the eighteenth flood festival, when men, women, and children had danced, sung, played, feasted, and rejoiced in merriment. Now, there were not so many people on the lakeshore. Here and there, only a few could be seen. At that time, water had gushed noisily from all the sluices of the lake, the sound roaring like the tumult of a marketplace. Now, from only a few channels, water trickled out with a gentle murmur, like the plaintive tinkle of anklets on the feet of a dancer performing a sorrowful song.

Vandiyathevan deftly led his horse up the steep embankment and reached the summit. The scene that unfolded before his eyes was altogether changed. The water, brimming and swelling, seemed as if it would burst through the embankment— The water was not surging in waves. The expanse of the lake began only from the base of the shore. The reddish hue of the water changed at the very edge, becoming as clear as crystal. Along the banks, the water lilies, lotuses, red lilies, and blue lotuses grew in thick profusion, with young leaves, mature leaves, tender buds, half-bloomed buds, and fully blossomed flowers, each in its own distinct stage. In some places, the water itself was covered by this dense growth.

On the southern shore of the lake, the current from the Vadavaru had not yet mingled with the lake’s waters, swirling and eddying as it came. Along that stream, boats with white wings spread like swans were not gliding by. Where once the river’s flood had flowed along the lake’s edge, now trees, shrubs, and thickets of reeds stood in their place. Amidst them, white storks and herons stood on one leg, as if lost in meditation.

Vandiyathevan did not spend more than a few seconds taking all this in. Soon, at a short distance along the lake’s shore, a boat came into his view. He recognized that one of the men in the boat was Kandamaran. At once, he spurred his horse toward that spot. Leaping down from his horse, he approached the boat. Kandamaran stretched out his hand, grasped Vandiyathevan’s, and helped him aboard. After signaling to the boatmen to set off, Kandamaran looked at Vandiyathevan with eyes brimming with tears, sorrow clouding his face.
“Friend! You have come so quickly! My deepest thanks! Had you come tomorrow instead of today, you might not have seen Manimekalai alive!” he said.

It was true that Vandiyathevan possessed a heart of stone! Without such resolve, could he have acted so carelessly in all his deeds over the past eight months? Could he have risked his life so recklessly, indifferent to the dangers that threatened him and others, and conducted himself with such daring in so many perilous situations?
Yet, this man of iron will was shaken by Kandamaran’s words.
Now, without a doubt, he understood the meaning of Kandamaran’s letter, which had said, “To see her for the last time.” Tears welled up in his eyes and streamed down his cheeks.

“Kandamaaran! Is Manimekalai’s very life in danger? How can that be? Was it not her mind that faltered? And that too, only because of you and me!” Vandiyathevan asked, his voice trembling with anxiety.

“My friend! Now Manimekalai’s mind has cleared. But I do not know how much longer she will remain alive. I am praying to all the gods that she stays alive at least until she can see you!” replied Kandamaaran.
Then he began to recount the events as he knew them:

In Kanchipuram, Kandamaaran had been overseeing the gilding of the golden palace in preparation for the Emperor’s stay. At that time, he heard that Sambuvarya had set out, taking Manimekalai with him. Soon after, news reached him that Manimekalai had gone missing near the banks of the Veera Narayana Lake. Immediately, he took leave of Parthibendran and hurried off to learn his sister’s fate. His father, overwhelmed by grief, was nearly driven to madness. All he could tell was, “She lay down in the tent at night. By morning, she was gone.” No other information could be gleaned from him. He said he had already sent word to Pazhayarai. He also mentioned that they had searched the burnt and ruined Kadambur palace and its surroundings.

Kandamaaran himself began to search. He did not think she would have returned to Pazhayarai. He wondered if she might have fallen into the lake and drowned, and resolved at least to find her body. Yet, in his heart, he also hoped that perhaps she was still alive, wandering somewhere in the woods surrounding the lake.

He searched all around the lake’s edge, circled its banks, and followed the canals that branched off from the lake for some distance. He took a boat and searched across the lake, both along the shore and crisscrossing its waters. He searched the forests that encircled the lake. Thus, after nearly four days of fruitless searching, a memory of the water pavilion on an island in the upper part of the lake came to Kandamaaran. He remembered how, on one occasion, Karikalan, Vandiyathevan, Nandini, and Manimekalai had all met and spent time together at that water pavilion, while Karikalan and Vandiyathevan were out hunting and Nandini and Manimekalai had come to play in the water.

It was nearly impossible for Manimekalai to have reached that place alone, without the help of a boat. Could she have made her way through the western forests, thick with bears, leopards, and other wild beasts? Even if she had crossed the forest, she would have had to traverse several small streams along the way. Still, Kandamaaran thought, “Let me check there as well,” and took a boat to the water pavilion. As he drew near the pavilion, a flood of old memories surged within him.

At first, the mandapam appeared utterly deserted. There seemed to be no one there. Descending the steps of the hall, he stood still, reflecting with a heavy sigh on how all the castles he had built in his mind had crumbled to nothing. As the echo of his sigh faded, he was startled by the sound of another sigh, as if in response. He rushed towards the source.

On the steps at the far side of the Neerazhi Mandapam lay Manimekalai. She was withered, dried, and shriveled, lying there as if lifeless. Her saree was torn in several places. Scratches and wounds could be seen at many spots on her body. At first glance, it did not seem as if there was any life left in that body. She looked like someone who had wandered the forests for days, starving and lost, finally collapsing in exhaustion and dying.

The sight pierced Kandamaaran’s heart with a thousand spears of anguish. He lifted Manimekalai and laid her in his lap, weeping bitterly. As the memory of that sigh returned to him, hope flickered—perhaps there was still a breath of life left in her. He brought fresh water and sprinkled it on her face, poured some into her mouth, and rubbed her body to restore warmth. After a while, Manimekalai’s eyelids fluttered open, and she gazed at him, her eyes slowly blooming.
“Anna! Is it really you? What I thought has come true. I believed that if I went to heaven, I would see you and him there. Where is he?” she asked in a very faint voice.
Kandamaaran struggled to suppress his sobs and replied, “He will come, Amma, he will come!”

Manimekalai believed she was in heaven, and that she was seeing Kandamaaran there. Kandamaaran realized she was inquiring about Vandiyathevan. To prevent her from suffering any mental shock, he answered in accordance with her belief, gently steering the conversation.

After this, Ilanjambuvurayan Kandamaaran recounted the efforts he had made to revive the spark of life in Manimekalai’s body, and how he had hastily written a palm-leaf letter and sent it to Vandiyathevan.

“My friend! I cannot express the gratitude I feel in my heart for your coming in response to my letter. Manimekalai will not live much longer. When a dying lamp is fanned, does it not burn a little brighter for a moment? So too, her life’s flame now glows. Most of all, it is her desire to see you that is keeping her alive! She believes we are all in heaven. You must not say anything to the contrary! It is only natural that you will feel sorrow when you see her. But you must control yourself and speak to her with a cheerful countenance!” he pleaded.
The boat had now drawn close to the Neerazhi Mandapam. The sound of the yāzh and the soft strains of song mingled in the air.

Vandiyathevan looked at Kandanmaran. “Yes, my friend! It is Manimekalai herself, singing along with the music of her yaazh!” he said. They disembarked from the boat. Vandiyathevan listened carefully, trying to discern what song Manimekalai was singing. It was the very same song she had sung before in that water pavilion, accompanied by her yaazh.

“In the gentle flow of sweet waters, at the foot of the blissful mountain, In the shade where fruit-laden trees cluster, hand in hand, all the joys we shared— Was it only a dream, O friend? Was it only a memory? In the punnai grove, beneath the golden glow of evening, He called me to him, and with honeyed words he spoke— Was it only a vision? Was that wonder a lie? Crossing the guarded gates, like a thief he crept in softly, With boundless love he embraced me and bestowed his kisses— Did it truly happen? Did we truly rejoice?”
Vandiyathevan waited on the steps until the song ended. As soon as it was over, he climbed the steps and entered the pavilion.

The moment Manimekalai saw him, she set aside her yaazh and tried to rise. But, lacking strength, she could not steady herself on her feet and nearly collapsed. Vandiyathevan rushed forward and caught her before she could fall to the ground. Gently, he seated her and sat down beside her. He drew Manimekalai onto his lap.
Manimekalai gazed at his face again and again. It seemed as if she was making sure, over and over, that it was truly Vandiyathevan, and that it was indeed his lap in which she reclined.
“My brother did not deceive me. Heaven is not just a dream. This wonder is not a lie!” her lips murmured softly.
“It is not a lie, Manimekalai, it is not a lie. This is truly heaven! My coming here is real!” said Vandiyathevan.

No matter how much he tried to restrain himself, he could not hold back the tears that brimmed in his eyes. The drops of his tears rolled down onto Manimekalai’s face like pearls. Without his knowledge, a sob escaped him.

For a brief moment, Manimekalai’s face shone with a divine radiance. From her long eyes, beams of moonlight seemed to emanate and glow. Her lips, rivaling the ripeness of a pomegranate bud, parted and poured forth words of indescribable sweetness. Vandiyathevan listened with utmost care. Yet, he could not understand what she said.

Why should he need to understand? What did it matter what words she uttered? When the golden vessel of the heart opens and the nectar of love overflows, what use are mere words? After a little while, Manimekalai’s ripe lips closed. Her eyelids fell shut. The divine radiance that had played upon her face faded. Peace settled over her features.
A gentle breeze stirred the branches of the tree that stretched above the pavilion by the water. A few crimson flowers, shaken loose, fell. Manimekalai’s soul, too, slipped away from her body.

Where did the soul that left the body go? By which path did it depart? Did it blend with the gentle breeze? Did it ascend upon the sweet music of the ripples raised by the young wind? Did it join the melodious songs of the cuckoos, who sang to soothe the heart’s burning, and fly into the sky? Where did it go? Did it reach the lotus feet of the Supreme Being, who creates, sustains, and destroys all worlds and all living beings? Or did it merge, unknowing, into the heart of Vandiyathevan, who sat there like a stone idol, his tears overflowing? No one knows. Even if one knew, it could not be told.

Only one thing is certain. The Vandiyathevan we have known—full of mirth and mischief, playfulness and exuberance, daring and restlessness, boldness and impetuosity—will be seen no more. In that moment, a ripened heart, compassion, and wisdom came to dwell in Vandiyathevan. The goddess that was Manimekalai took up residence in the temple of his heart. Wherever he went, whatever he did, that goddess would henceforth be his companion.
Vallavarayan Vandiyathevan would become a man capable of great deeds. He would be worthy of the reverence of all who knew him.
O warrior! For now, we take our leave of you. We do not wish to intrude upon the sorrowful thoughts that fill your mind.
Beloved friend of Arulmozhi Varman! May you live long and prosper! May your noble name shine forever in the lineage of valiant Tamils!

The sun had set. Darkness began to spread over the Chola country. The wind that had been blowing gently all day now grew fierce, as if it had suddenly gone mad. The trees in the palace gardens swayed and shook, their branches creaking and leaves rustling as if in mourning. The fragrance of flowers, crushed and scattered by the wind, filled the air with a bittersweet scent.

Inside the palace, the atmosphere was heavy with sorrow. The news that had spread through the corridors and courtyards was like a thunderbolt—one that shattered hearts and left the bravest souls trembling. Servants moved about silently, their faces pale, their eyes red with unshed tears. Even the guards at the gates stood with bowed heads, unable to meet each other’s gaze.

In the queen’s chamber, Kundavai sat by the side of her mother, Vanamadevi. The princess’s face, usually so radiant, was now clouded with grief. Her hands trembled as she tried to comfort her mother, who wept silently, her shoulders shaking with each sob. The sound of her sorrow seemed to echo through the palace, mingling with the howling wind outside.

Elsewhere, in a secluded room, Sundara Chola lay on his bed, his eyes closed, his breathing shallow. Physicians and attendants stood nearby, helpless. The emperor’s once-mighty frame was now frail, his face drawn and pale. Only the faint rise and fall of his chest showed that life still lingered within him.

Vandiyathevan stood at a distance, his heart heavy. He had faced many dangers, had crossed rivers and forests, had fought with sword and wit—but never had he felt so powerless. The sorrow that filled the palace seemed to seep into his very soul.

Suddenly, a loud wail rose from the women’s quarters. It was a cry of anguish, a sound that pierced the night and sent shivers down the spine of all who heard it. The flower had fallen. The great queen, Vanamadevi, had breathed her last.

The news spread swiftly. The palace was plunged into deeper mourning. Lamps were extinguished; the sound of anklets and laughter vanished. Only the sobs of the grieving remained, mingling with the wind that swept through the empty corridors.
The Chola dynasty had lost its beloved queen. The flower that had blossomed in the royal garden had withered and fallen. The fragrance lingered, but the beauty was gone forever.
